content.article_text:
Skydance shares closed down 22% Wednesday to end the session at just over $7 after the company distributed warrants to investors. Apple shares rose but tech stocks and overall markets mostly ended in the red after a worse-than-expected September inflation reading sparked fears of higher interest rates that hit debt-heavy companies particularly hard.

Apple saw its market capitalization cross the $5 billion mark again, a level it first hit last July. The stock is up 26% year to date and nearly 40% over the past 12 months. It closed up 0.5% today at $343. New CEO John Ternus took over as CEO from Tim Cook on September 1 and investors are upbeat on the tech giant, which recently unveiled the foldable iPhone Duo. Apple and Nvidia are the only two companies ever to reach the $5 trillion mark.

Related Stories

Skydance Stock Struggles In First Days Of Trading

Donald Trump Weighs In On New Skydance: "They're Terrific People, And It's Going To Be A Great Company"

Other tech companies from Meta (-3.3%), Amazon and Alphabet (both down 1.7%) to Snap (-6%) and Spotify (-0.6%) went the other direction. Netflix shares drifted lower but ended the session up a hair (+0.16%) after the company unveiled hefty job cuts earlier Wednesday.

Watch on Deadline

In the final step of its giant media merger, Skydance warrants have started trading and, as expected, its stock fell. The warrants, distributed to Skydance shareholders, allow holders to buy shares of stock at a certain price. They trade separately from the Class B common stock, which closed down 22% at $7.06. Skydance warrants, which have a 10-year maturity, can be exercised when the stock hits $12 a share. As of Wednesday, holders of Class B shares were no longer entitled to receive warrants.

The company signaled last week ahead of the October 6 close of the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger that it would let public investors access the warrants. About 90% of the investor base of the company, including Larry Ellison , the Oracle billionaire and father of Skydance CEO David Ellison, as well as RedBird Capital, Middle East sovereign wealth funds and other backers, did not receive the warrants.

Shares of Oracle fell about 9% amid a broader downturn for stocks of top AI stakeholders. Year to date, Oracle stock is down 33%.

The merged and renamed Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery had a rocky debut when it started trading under its new symbol, SKYD. The combined company has a massive debt load of nearly $80 billion. Rising interest rates can make debt harder to manage and Wall Streeters are wary of Skydance’s high leverage and ability to find a promised $6 billion in cost synergies.

Investors will be looking for strategic clarify from Skydance, Netflix and others as quarterly earnings season kicks off next week.

U.S. annual inflation accelerated to 3.7% in September, according to the Department of Labor Statistics latest Consumer Price Index. That was higher than anticipated as energy prices continued to spike, driven higher by the Trump administration’s war with Iran. Gas prices surged 34% year-over-year. Rising inflation puts pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again after a hike in September.

The Nasdaq market fell by 1.9%, the Russell 2000 by 1.9%, and the S&P 500 shed 1.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost about 50 points. All ended the day off their lows.
content.excerpt_original: Skydance shares closed down 22% Wednesday to end the session at just over $7 after the company distributed warrants to investors. Apple shares rose but tech stocks and overall markets mostly ended in the red after a worse-than-expected September inflation reading sparked fears…

"paragraph", "text": "施莱因策尔坦言，尽管人们可能会有别的看法，但他其实相当害羞和腼腆。选角工作提供了一种既能保持在某种程度上退居幕后、又能深入参与电影制作过程的方式。多年来，他一直作为迈克尔·哈内克的选角导演与其紧密合作。但哈内克也给了施莱因策尔指导背景演员并了解电影片场运作的机会。“他给予了我极大的信任，”他说。", "translated": true}, "url": "https://variety.com/2026/film/reviews/rose-review-sandra-huller-1236663868/"}, {"text": "VIFF", "url": "https://variety.com/t/viff/"}, {"text": "Sandra Hüller", "url": "https://variety.com/t/sandra-huller-2/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "施莱因策尔专门为惠勒创作了这个角色，其表演即使在无数次观看之后仍然令他动容。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“她就是女王，”他说。“无论是在后期制作中还是怎样，我已经看过一百遍了。然而，仍然有一些时刻、一些台词、一些场景，能彻底打动我，让我开始哭泣，让我再次感到愤怒，就像一个第一次看到这一切的普通观众一样。这就是她所拥有的技艺。这就是她所拥有的超能力。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当惠勒读完后，她对他说：“你疯了。这不是剧本。这是一首诗。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如果说施莱因策尔的作品中有一条贯穿始终的线索，那就是他对边缘人群的着迷。“我们作为社会处于何种境地，我们如何对待所谓的局外人，我们究竟是一个什么样的社会，这对我而言非常有趣，”他说。通过《罗丝》，他将目光转向了他所认为的世界上最大的一群局外人：女性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个想法源于与一位朋友的对话，朋友打电话祝他生日快乐，并提到刚读完一本关于大约250年前在同一天被处决的一位女性的书。她被指控的罪名是什么？穿着裤子。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个故事促使施莱因策尔去查阅档案馆，他在那里发掘了大量关于女性为了各种原因而伪装成男性的记载。有些人是为了逃避不想要的婚姻和性骚扰。另一些人这样做是为了获得接受教育、就业和服兵役的机会。他指出，其中一些人也可能是女同性恋或跨性别者。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "施莱因策尔指出，在英国，曾有一名女性晋升到高级军官军衔并为大英帝国作战。直到该军官的葬礼上，人们才发现这个被授予了无数勋章的人实际上是一位女性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些故事不仅仅是历史上的猎奇轶事，它们还揭示了精细的伪装如何在历史上和今天成为一个否定人们做自己自由的世界中赖以生存的必要手段。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“看到我们在日常生活中为了建立面具而付出的努力，这很有意思，”他说。“有时你的行为举止本身就是一种面具：你如何行动，你希望如何被解读，你如何挺起肩膀，你如何走路。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "面具可以充当盔甲，保护其佩戴者。“如果它能帮到你，我认为这没问题，”他说。“但当它变成一个笼子时，这才是诡异的地方。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他将《罗丝》形容为“写给所有那些由于各种原因不得不隐藏真实的自己、为了服务于他们真心想要服务的社区、或者为了实现若没有面具便无法达成的事情而不得不戴上面具的人的情书。他们无法过上最完整的生活，因为我们不容许。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "施莱宁泽解释说，罗斯并不是那种企图推翻周围社会的革命者。她只是想融入集体、工作并进行服务。而不公之处在于，她必须隐瞒自己的身份，才能去做其他人可以公开去做的事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我在不知不觉中生来就是一个女权主义者，”施莱宁泽说道。他在女人的环绕中长大，当他7岁开始上学时，他接触到了一套不同的规则。他记得自己意识到“世界上存在着一套不同的系统”，而这是一个他“不太喜欢”的系统。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种不适感影响了影片对性暴力的处理方式，故事中存在这种暴力，但从未进行过视觉上的具象展示。施莱宁泽刻意选择不直接描绘袭击本身，他认为图像带有责任，尤其是在一个充斥着苦难视觉呈现的文化中更是如此。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“世界上最残忍的东西是我们自己的想象力，”他说。“我越是用这样的图像去喂养想象力，我们就会变得越残忍，因为我们彻底失去了同理心。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对施莱宁泽而言，重要的是承认暴力的存在，而不把它变成奇观，同时相信观众能够理解其后果，而无需展示每一个身体细节。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "归根结底，《玫瑰》提出的核心问题不是人们是否应该被允许跨越社会的期望，而是为什么这个社会一开始会如此束缚重重——如果人们获得寻找自己位置的自由，情况又会发生怎样的改变。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“最困难的事情是找到自己的位置，”施莱宁泽指出，并提到今天觉得属于归属感的东西明天可能会变。“我们必须接受改变每天都在发生。有时我们只是应该给事物一些时间，看看这究竟会是一件好事还是坏事。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他表示，人们所戴的面具不必是固定不变的身份或永久的伪装。它们也可以是一种前进的方式。“所以，有时我们所说的这些面具，或许只是我们到达必经之地的某种载体。”", "translated": true}]

By exposing the contradictions of a society that values people for what they can contribute while restricting who is allowed to contribute, the film turns one woman’s struggle to live freely into a broader indictment of the rules governing gender and belonging.", "links": [{"text": "Rose", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/film/reviews/rose-review-sandra-huller-1236663868/"}, {"text": "VIFF", "url": "https://variety.com/t/viff/"}, {"text": "Sandra Hüller", "url": "https://variety.com/t/sandra-huller-2/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Schleinzer wrote the role specifically for Hüller, whose performance continues to move him even after countless viewings."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“She’s the queen,” he says. “I’ve seen it in post-production, whatever, I’ve seen it a hundred times. Still, there were moments, there were sentences, there were scenes, where she completely moves me, where I start to cry, where I get angry again, like an audience member who sees this for the very first time. And that’s the craft she’s owning. That’s her superpower she’s owning.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The film began as a sprawling prose work of roughly 1,000 pages, tracing Rose ’s life from early childhood. Of course, Schleinzer understood that no one was going to spend millions making a 45-hour film. “So, we just skipped the first eight hundred pages and we just concentrated on the last two hundred because the ending of the novel could stand for itself.”", "links": [{"text": "Rose", "url": "https://variety.com/t/rose/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When Hüller read it, she told him: “You are crazy. This is not a script. That’s a poem.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "If there is a through line in Schleinzer’s work, it is his fascination with people on the margins. “Where we are as a society, how we deal with our so-called outsiders, what kind of society we are is quite interesting for me,” he says. With “Rose,” he turns his attention to what he considers the largest outsider group in the world: women."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The idea grew out of a conversation with a friend who called to wish him a happy birthday and mentioned having just finished a book about a woman executed on that same date roughly 250 years earlier. Her alleged transgression? Wearing trousers."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The story sent Schleinzer researching the archives, where he unearthed numerous accounts of women who disguised themselves as men for a range of reasons. Some wanted to escape unwanted marriages and sexual harassment. Others did so to gain access to education, employment and military service. Some may have also been lesbian or transgender, he suggests."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In England, Schleinzer notes, one woman rose to a senior officer’s rank and fought for the British Empire. It was only at the officer’s funeral that it was discovered that the person they had bestowed all these medals on was, in fact, a woman."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "More than historical curiosities, such stories reveal how elaborate disguises can become necessary as a means of survival in a world that denies people the freedom to be themselves — both historically and today."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“It’s interesting to see the amount of effort that we put into our daily routine in building up our mask,” he says. “Sometimes how you behave yourself is a mask: how you move, how you want to be read, how you hold your shoulders, how you walk.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A mask can function as armor, protecting its wearer. “If it’s something that helps you, I think it’s okay,” he says. “But when it becomes a cage, that’s the weird part of it.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "He describes “Rose” as a “love letter for all those people who, for various reasons, have to hide who they are, or to serve the community they really want to serve or have to put on a mask to achieve the things they wouldn’t be able to without them. They couldn’t live the fullest life, because we wouldn’t let them.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Rose, Schleinzer explains, is not some revolutionary seeking to overthrow the society around her. She simply wants to belong, to work and to serve. The injustice is that she must conceal her identity to do what others are free to do openly."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I was born a feminist without knowing,” Schleinzer says. He grew up surrounded by women, and when he started school at seven, he encountered a different set of rules. He remembers realizing that “there is a different system that exists in the world” and it was one he “didn’t like very much.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That discomfort informs the film’s treatment of sexual violence, which is present in the story but never shown graphically. Schleinzer made a deliberate choice not to depict the assaults themselves, arguing that images carry a responsibility, particularly in a culture saturated with graphic representations of suffering."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“The cruelest thing in the world is our own imagination,” he says. “And the more I feed imagination with images like this, the crueler we can get, because we completely lose empathy.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For Schleinzer, it is important to acknowledge the violence without turning it into spectacle, trusting viewers to understand its consequences without being shown every physical detail."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ultimately, the central question that “Rose” asks isn’t whether people should be allowed to step outside society’s expectations, but rather why it’s so restrictive in the first place — and what might change if people were given the freedom to find their own place."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“The most difficult thing is to find one’s own place,” Schleinzer says, noting that what feels like belonging today may change tomorrow. “We have to accept that change is happening every day. And sometimes we just should give things time to see if this could be a good thing or not.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The masks people wear, he suggests, need not be fixed identities or permanent disguises. They can also be a way forward. “So maybe these things we sometimes call masks are just a vehicle for us to get where we have to go.”"}]
content.article_text:
As a filmmaker, Markus Schleinzer owes much to his 17-year career as a casting director.

“Directing a movie and being a casting director are quite similar jobs,” he tells Variety .

Both require making the right choices under pressure and persuading others to believe in them. For a casting director, that means convincing a filmmaker or producer. For a director, it means earning the audience’s trust.

Related Stories

'New Stanford Prison Experiment' Drops Tense First Trailer Ahead of Netflix Release

Charlie Brooker's New Netflix Series Gets Title, 'Blackmere,' as Rory Kinnear Joins Cast and First-Look Photos Revealed

Schleinzer admits that, despite what people might think, he can be rather shy and timid. Casting offered a way to remain somewhat in the background while still being deeply involved in the filmmaking process. For years, he worked closely for Michael Haneke as his casting director. But Haneke also gave Schleinzer opportunities to direct background performers and learn how a film set operates. “He put a lot of trust in me,” he says.

Popular on Variety

Haneke was also the one who urged him to step out from behind the scenes and become a filmmaker himself, giving him three months to write a script.

“I thought, yes, this was a compliment,” Schleinzer recalls. “But three months later he called me and said, ‘Where’s the script?’ And I didn’t have a single line.”

Eventually, he sat down and wrote one. Haneke liked it and refused to let it languish in a drawer, passing it along to French producer Margaret Ménégoz, who called Schleinzer to say she wanted to make it. “So I was trapped,” he says. “I couldn’t get away from it anymore. This is how I, finally, got kicked in my ass.”

His third feature, “ Rose ,” which screened at the Vancouver International Film Festival ( VIFF ), is a black-and-white historical drama starring Sandra Hüller as a woman who disguises herself as a male soldier in 17th-century Germany. By exposing the contradictions of a society that values people for what they can contribute while restricting who is allowed to contribute, the film turns one woman’s struggle to live freely into a broader indictment of the rules governing gender and belonging.

Schleinzer wrote the role specifically for Hüller, whose performance continues to move him even after countless viewings.

“She’s the queen,” he says. “I’ve seen it in post-production, whatever, I’ve seen it a hundred times. Still, there were moments, there were sentences, there were scenes, where she completely moves me, where I start to cry, where I get angry again, like an audience member who sees this for the very first time. And that’s the craft she’s owning. That’s her superpower she’s owning.”

The film began as a sprawling prose work of roughly 1,000 pages, tracing Rose ’s life from early childhood. Of course, Schleinzer understood that no one was going to spend millions making a 45-hour film. “So, we just skipped the first eight hundred pages and we just concentrated on the last two hundred because the ending of the novel could stand for itself.”

When Hüller read it, she told him: “You are crazy. This is not a script. That’s a poem.”

If there is a through line in Schleinzer’s work, it is his fascination with people on the margins. “Where we are as a society, how we deal with our so-called outsiders, what kind of society we are is quite interesting for me,” he says. With “Rose,” he turns his attention to what he considers the largest outsider group in the world: women.

The idea grew out of a conversation with a friend who called to wish him a happy birthday and mentioned having just finished a book about a woman executed on that same date roughly 250 years earlier. Her alleged transgression? Wearing trousers.

The story sent Schleinzer researching the archives, where he unearthed numerous accounts of women who disguised themselves as men for a range of reasons. Some wanted to escape unwanted marriages and sexual harassment. Others did so to gain access to education, employment and military service. Some may have also been lesbian or transgender, he suggests.

In England, Schleinzer notes, one woman rose to a senior officer’s rank and fought for the British Empire. It was only at the officer’s funeral that it was discovered that the person they had bestowed all these medals on was, in fact, a woman.

More than historical curiosities, such stories reveal how elaborate disguises can become necessary as a means of survival in a world that denies people the freedom to be themselves — both historically and today.

“It’s interesting to see the amount of effort that we put into our daily routine in building up our mask,” he says. “Sometimes how you behave yourself is a mask: how you move, how you want to be read, how you hold your shoulders, how you walk.”

A mask can function as armor, protecting its wearer. “If it’s something that helps you, I think it’s okay,” he says. “But when it becomes a cage, that’s the weird part of it.”

He describes “Rose” as a “love letter for all those people who, for various reasons, have to hide who they are, or to serve the community they really want to serve or have to put on a mask to achieve the things they wouldn’t be able to without them. They couldn’t live the fullest life, because we wouldn’t let them.”

Rose, Schleinzer explains, is not some revolutionary seeking to overthrow the society around her. She simply wants to belong, to work and to serve. The injustice is that she must conceal her identity to do what others are free to do openly.

“I was born a feminist without knowing,” Schleinzer says. He grew up surrounded by women, and when he started school at seven, he encountered a different set of rules. He remembers realizing that “there is a different system that exists in the world” and it was one he “didn’t like very much.”

That discomfort informs the film’s treatment of sexual violence, which is present in the story but never shown graphically. Schleinzer made a deliberate choice not to depict the assaults themselves, arguing that images carry a responsibility, particularly in a culture saturated with graphic representations of suffering.

“The cruelest thing in the world is our own imagination,” he says. “And the more I feed imagination with images like this, the crueler we can get, because we completely lose empathy.”

For Schleinzer, it is important to acknowledge the violence without turning it into spectacle, trusting viewers to understand its consequences without being shown every physical detail.

Ultimately, the central question that “Rose” asks isn’t whether people should be allowed to step outside society’s expectations, but rather why it’s so restrictive in the first place — and what might change if people were given the freedom to find their own place.

“The most difficult thing is to find one’s own place,” Schleinzer says, noting that what feels like belonging today may change tomorrow. “We have to accept that change is happening every day. And sometimes we just should give things time to see if this could be a good thing or not.”

The masks people wear, he suggests, need not be fixed identities or permanent disguises. They can also be a way forward. “So maybe these things we sometimes call masks are just a vehicle for us to get where we have to go.”

Festival ZUM 2026

Conheça os selecionados da Convocatória de Fotolivros do Festival ZUM 2026

A revista ZUM e a Biblioteca de Fotografia do Instituto Moreira Salles anunciam os livros selecionados pela Convocatória de Fotolivros ZUM/IMS 2026. Este ano selecionamos 45 publicações entre 265 fotolivros, zines, catálogos e livros de fotografia de todas as regiões do Brasil, além de países da América Latina e da Europa.

As publicações recebidas foram avaliadas pela seguinte equipe, composta por membros da ZUM e da Biblioteca de Fotografia do IMS: Ângelo Manjabosco, Bruna Gallo, Gabryella Roque, Daniele Queiroz, Carlos Franco e Miguel Del Castillo. Cada selecionado receberá o valor de R$ 300 como ajuda de custo.

A convocatória foi criada em 2017 para aprofundar os vínculos do Instituto Moreira Salles com a produção contemporânea de fotografia voltada ao meio editorial. Queremos conhecer, exibir e divulgar os fotolivros, bem como estreitar relações com artistas em diversos estágios de carreira, produtores, editoras, designers e o público.

Os fotolivros selecionados serão apresentados ao público no Festival ZUM 2026, no dia 7 de novembro, às 10h na Biblioteca de Fotografia do IMS Paulista. Em seguida, serão anunciados os três premiados do ano, escolhidos por um júri misto de pessoas do IMS e especialistas externos. Cada um dos três escolhidos receberá um prêmio de R$ 2 mil.

content.article_text:
Announcement

San Antonio’s Centro de Artes Celebrates 10 Years with "Mercado/Material"

Curated by Mia Lopez, 16 artists transform everyday objects into bold explorations of Latinx identity. On view in San Antonio from October 16 through March 7, 2027.

Curator Mia Lopez generates conversations around the aesthetics of Latinidad and the nuances of cultural heritage in Mercado/Material , on view at San Antonio's free Centro de Artes gallery from October 16 through March 7, 2027. The exhibition features 16 artists using vibrant imagery and popular culture to address themes of Latinx cultural identity and consumerism, playfully building on the Pop art tradition of Andy Warhol and Claes Oldenburg.

From layered screen prints of fruit cups and groceries to monumental piñata sculptures, the works engage viewers with iconic forms of Latinx visual culture — vibrant paintings, immersive installations, textile and ceramic sculptures, and works on paper inspired by markets in San Antonio, vendors in Chicago, storefronts in Mexico, and New York bodegas. Beneath the surface lie complex ideas around belonging, labor, and commerce, uniquely expressed through contemporary art.

Mercado/Material draws upon the rich cultural history of the site of Centro de Artes, from its early days as a produce annex to its current form as Historic Market Square in the heart of downtown San Antonio. For ten years, Centro de Artes has been San Antonio's premier Latinx-focused gallery, presenting the stories, histories, and creative visions of communities in South Texas and beyond.

The City of San Antonio's Department of Arts & Culture has transformed this adaptive-reuse landmark into a free, year-round platform for contemporary art—welcoming over 33,000 visitors annually and exhibiting more than 3,100 artworks by 600 artists.

Admission is always free.

Plan your visit at sa.gov .

content.article_text:
Feature

Why Pageant Is Suddenly All the Rage

In a world skewed toward artifice, the East Williamsburg performance space’s commitment to confronting, rather than escaping, one’s conditions in art feels like a renaissance.

On a Friday morning in late August, dozens packed a small auditorium at the Museum of Modern Art to watch choreographer, director, and writer Isa Spector writhe on a red-painted platform, struggling to carry out the museum’s request to make “a painting of dance” in 10 minutes. After flailing to and fro, down on all fours to the red platform floor and up to the fluorescent studio lights, and calling out to a "mom" whose name changed to “MoMA” and a "dad" to “Dada” with an alliterative tongue, Spector had an epiphany. They knew what they were to paint. Seconds later, five performers donning red gloves emerged from backstage and assembled at the center of the platform. Hand in hand, they began twirling in a circle, staging a living parody of Matisse’s modernist masterpiece displayed in the galleries just a floor above.

The five subjects of this commissioned “painting” — Sharleen Chidiac, Lili Dekker, Jade Manns, Owen Prum, and Alexa West — are the co-founders of Pageant , an artist-run Brooklyn performance space that held a month-long residency at MoMA in August. "MoMAlogue #1" inaugurated Pageant’s seven-hour MoMA performance marathon, of which Spector’s was the first, but certainly not the only, meditation on dance’s relationship to its own history and that of visual art across 25 10-minute performances.

“I think the history of dance, coming from a ballet proscenium stage into modernism, then into postmodernism, started with a pictorial form,” artist and choreographer West said in a group interview with Hyperallergic after the Pageant Presents Pageant marathon. “And it’s slowly been breaking away from that over time.”

Preceded by a different space that Manns and Chidiac ran out of their apartment, Pageant was established in 2022 in a third-story loft on Graham Avenue in East Williamsburg. According to West, there was initially “no clear marketing vision” for Pageant. It was merely a solution to the group’s shared desire “to provide context to our practices in a post-COVID landscape in which there were very few opportunities to show work at our stage of artmaking.”

“We didn’t set out with the intention for it to be like an institution,” Chidiac added during the interview. “We just needed a space to work, to show our work, and to show other people’s work.

content.article_text:
Archaeologists in Egypt have uncovered the remains of two colossal statues believed to depict Ramses II after a local landowner reported finding an inscribed stone block in the village of Behbeit El-Hagar.

The discoveries were made by an archaeological mission from Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities (SCA). According to Dr. Hisham El-Leithy, Secretary-General of the SCA, the first find was a stone head more than five-feet-high from a massive statue. It depicts a man wearing a double crown, a symbol of the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt worn by ancient Egyptian rulers.

Nearby, archaeologists found part of the statue’s back pillar. An inscription on the pillar gives one of Ramses II’s five royal titles, “Hor-Ka-Nakht-Mery-Maat” (The Strong Bull, Beloved of Ma’at), identifying him as the sculpture’s subject.

The second find consists of part of a statue of a royal personage along with its head, which was adorned with the striped cloth associated with ancient Egyptian rulers. Not including the head, the surviving section of the figure, which is missing its legs and base, measures almost eight feet high. Based on the similarity of this statue’s face to that of the first, researchers believe it may also represent Ramses II, though the identification has not been confirmed.

The archaeological mission also found a pink granite block about four feet long not far from the statues. It bears traces of hieroglyphic inscriptions that include two more titles of Ramses II: “Nesu-Bity” (King of Upper and Lower Egypt) and “Sa-Ra” (Son of Ra).

Ramses II, known to historians as Ramses the Great, was the third king of ancient Egypt ’s 19th Dynasty (1292–1191 BCE). He presided over the final peak of Egypt’s imperial power and is remembered for his 66-year rule, military campaigns, extensive building programs, and monumental temples and statues. Because of his popularity, longevity, and talent for political propaganda, inscriptions and artworks bearing his name and image can be found throughout Egypt.

Excavations and archaeological work are continuing in the area.

The starry showing for London’s offerings this week suggested that the city’s art scene still has life in it, even if some skipped it entirely for Paris, where Art Basel opens next week."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It’s not worth rehashing the well-worn—and, at this point, tedious— London-versus-Paris debate . content.article_text:
Editor’s Note: This story originally appeared in On Balance , the ARTnews newsletter about the art market and beyond. Sign up here to receive it every Wednesday.

It’s fun to celebrity watch the entrance to Frieze London in Regent’s Park before the fair begins. As the floodgates opened for the VIP preview on Wednesday, Oscar-nominated actor Andrew Garfield and his girlfriend, actress Monica Barbaro , strolled in. Also present were Tilda Swinton , Bianca Jagger , London-based designer Dilara Findikoglu , and Raf Simons , Prada’s Belgium-based co-creative director and a longtime art collector. “I like everything about London,” Simons told ARTnews , “especially its people.”

The night before, amid the horde at the opening of Thaddaeus Ropac ’s Georg Baselitz show, actor Damian Lewis was sizing up the big canvases. A couple of blocks down, you could find Serpentine Galleries artistic director Hans Ulrich Obrist casting his discerning eye at a Turner-inspired Rirkrit Tiravanija seascape at Pilar Corrias gallery. The starry showing for London’s offerings this week suggested that the city’s art scene still has life in it, even if some skipped it entirely for Paris, where Art Basel opens next week.

It’s not worth rehashing the well-worn—and, at this point, tedious— London-versus-Paris debate . But most people weren’t talking about it, either, on Wednesday at Frieze. Here’s some of what sold by the end of the fair’s first day. (While some of the mega-galleries post big ticket sales, it’s hard to gauge the overall health of the art market at art fairs because overall sales data is not made public. Plus, galleries self-report their sales, which makes them tough to verify.)

The mega-galleries have been relegated to the back of the fair’s tent, to give smaller players the spotlight near the fair’s entrance. Yet the placement did not deter Hauser & Wirth from selling most of its work by noon. Zoe Sperling , a partner at the gallery, told ARTnews she’d seen “a lot of American and Asian collectors.”

More than 20 pieces sold at Hauser & Wirth’s booths at Frieze London and Frieze Masters, totaling a sum of more than $11 million. Among the works sold were two Francis Picabia paintings, one untitled work from the 1940s sold for €1.1 million and Transparence, visage de femme (1928–29) for six-figures.

“There’s been tremendous energy here this morning,” Sperling said. “One of the things we’re really seeing is the interest from historic collectors that were maybe once more interested in traditional works and are now looking at contemporary works to complement their collections.” Avery Singer’s Solver (v.3) , 2026, sold for $800,000, George Condo’s Figure Composition (2026) for $600,000, Lee Bul’s Perdu—Silhouette VII (2026) for $290,000, and Christina Kimeze’s Game on (crane’s cut) , 2026, for $195,000.

The gallery also did well at Frieze Masters , where the offerings skew historical. Jan Brueghel the Elder’s Still Life of Flowers in a Stoneware Vase (1607–8) sold for around £5 million (about $6.58 million). “It’s one of the most important works we’ve ever been involved with,” Iwan Wirth , the gallery’s president and cofounder, told ARTnews . “The painting, made in the 17th century, stands as an exemplar of the kind of genius that contemporary artists look to in their own practice.”

At Lehmann Maupin ’s Frieze London booth, more than 10 works sold, including McArthur Binion’s dna:sketch (2024) for $150,000. Other notable works included Liza Lou’s Azure (2015) for $140,000 and Alex Prager’s Ceremony (2026) for $60,000. The gallery also said it sold several works by UK-based artists to private collections, varying from three new paintings by Billy Childish in the range of £50,000–£60,000 ($65,900 to $79,100), to two new paintings by Freya Douglas-Morris in the range of £30,000–£50,000 ($39,000–$65,900), to two new works by Rana Begum in the range of £25,000 to £40,000 ($33,000–$52,600).

The British capital has a contagious energy, according to those who made a sale on the first day. “London is buzzing. It is helped by its proximity to Art Basel Paris, as many international collectors and museums are coming first to London and then go on to Paris. Two very different birds with one stone,” Sadie Coles , who runs her eponymous London gallery, told ARTnews . “There is depth here, and so much on offer for visitors from outstanding younger galleries to major exhibitions in museums.”

Perrotin ’s solo booth of Izumi Kato’s paintings and sculptures sold for up to $250,000 each. The gallery had other notable sales from Oli Epp, whose new paintings sold for $55,000 each, and Shim Moon-Seup, who had a painting that fetched above $63,000. There was also a sculpture by Alma Allen, the artist controversially representing the United States at the Venice Biennale who will soon have a Perrotin show in Paris. It sold for $60,000.

David Zwirner moved 13 works that accounted for $4.55 million in sales. The top five pieces were paintings from Michaël Borremans for $1.5 million, a Dana Schutz for $900,000, a Lisa Yuskavage for $450,000, a Portia Zvavahera for $300,000, and a a Sasha Gordon for $400,000, the latter of which went to a European museum that the gallery did not identify. “Frieze London is still bringing people in, and it’s not just local collectors. It has been a good international morning,” James Green, associate partner and head of David Zwirner’s London gallery told ARTnews .

Rather than solely hanging its art on the wall, White Cube experimented with a metal frame for its booth featuring sketches by Ilana Savdie. The gallery recorded $1.55 million in sales, with Savdie’s painting The Great Compromise (2026) selling for $175,000 and Conspiracy of the Barons (2026) for $165,000. “The history of a place like this [London] is really hard to ignore,” Savdie told ARTnews . “I look to a lot of the artists that have been based here and the movements that have taken place, there are incredible museums to be inspired by. I haven’t spent enough time here to really be able to speak to it, but from afar I’m a big admirer.”

Edel Assanti ’s sales included the placement of two paintings by Thornton Dial, with prices ranging $160,000 to $230,000.

Collectors at the fair came from near and far. Selim Bouafsoun , the Tunisian collector based in Dubai, told ARTnews he bought Tamo Jugeli’s Swan in Lake (2026) from Bukia Vakhania for $40,000 and Jonathan Okoronkwo’s Wilderness Be the Anthem Rydee (2026) from London’s Emalin gallery for €20,000. He also snapped up Jacob Littlejohn’s Over the Rills, the Crags, and the Hills (2025) from Karma gallery for $8,000.

Alain Servais , a Belgian collector, said he bought Ella Fleck’s Training Material (2026, one of three editions) from LA’s Ehrlich Steinberg gallery for £14,000 ($18,500).

By 3 p.m., Pace Gallery had sold most of its paintings by Brazilian artist Marina Perez Simão , valued at prices up to $250,000. Pace chief executive Marc Glimcher told ARTnews stressed the wide age range of collectors. “We had a lot of older collectors buy works today, someone in their 70s and a very young collector in their 20s,” he said.

Next door, Thaddaeus Ropac also nearly sold out, with work by Italian sculptor Leoncillo Leonardi (1915–68) drawing international buyers. Long revered by Italian connoisseurs but little known elsewhere, Leoncillo is enjoying something of a revival. Ropac announced representation in June, alongside the launch of a new foundation. The gallery’s top prices included Martha Jungwirth’s 202 painting Untitled (Berggasse 19) at €560,000, Antony Gormley’s Aside (2025) at £500,000, and Adrian Ghenie’s Untitled (2026) at €380,000.

Xavier Hufkens reported selling more than 16 pieces, including a work on paper by Richard Serra for $750,000, a suite of Louise Bourgeois works on paper for $400,000, and two neon works by Tracey Emin for prices between £95,000 and £105,000.

Several young galleries in the Focus section also did well. The Amsterdam-based Diez Gallery sold Jessica Wilson’s video installation Sweet Nothing (2025–26) for more than €20,000 to the Centraal Museum in Utrecht. “Last Frieze London for me was a very bad one, and since then, the gallery has been doing its best year in terms of finances and new collections,” dealer Diego Diez told ARTnews .

Dealer Gabriella Price from Heidi gallery told ARTnews that her business relocated from Berlin to London this year to “pursue fresh opportunities.” “London feels like a really fantastic city at this time, and the Focus section of Frieze gets so much attention with all the prize giving and funds that take place,” she said.

Dealer Adam D. Miller , of the Los Angeles–based gallery The Pit , returned to Frieze with renewed energy. He sold two thirds of the paintings from his solo booth for Bella Foster. “We want to develop more, particularly with European and UK institutions,” he told ARTnews .

Over at Frieze Masters, Andrew Edlin had a booth featuring the works of Frank Walter and Beverly Buchanan, whose work is in the Venice Biennale. The gallery said that a major museum board president—one that it did not name—purchased a 1990s work by Buchanan for a price between $65,000 and $125,000.

Robilant sold a mirror work by Michelangelo Pistoletto for €45,000 ($59,300) and two ceramics by Lucio Fontana, Bullfight for €125,000 ($164,900) and Concetto Spaziale for €250,000 ($329,700). “We have all seen the renewed interest in Old Masters as the pendulum swings from speculative to secure, and as clients look to artists who have already shown they can hold their value,” gallery director Michele di Robilant told ARTnews . He expressed optimism for the top of the market: “Clients are certainly finding their feet again at the top end. There is light at the end of the tunnel.”
content.excerpt_original: Hauser & Wirth sold a Brueghel painting for $6.58 million.

Tammy Nguyen's New Opera Will Be the Coda to the Venice Biennale

The artist will present an aria from the still-unfinished opera, “Timaeus and The Teacher,” during the festival's closing program.

Timaeus and the Teacher at Wesleyan University (photo Elisabeth Bernstein, courtesy the artist and Lehmann Maupin)

Artist Tammy Nguyen will present the foreword to her debut opera Timaeus and The Teacher at the 61st Venice Biennale's closing program on November 13 and 14, capping off an eventful edition of the international contemporary art festival.

The aria is the entry point to Nguyen's still-unfinished opera, which traces the national and ideological impacts of the Vietnam War and fuses Plato’s theories of the cosmos with enduring questions of identity. Inspired by her father's experiences as a refugee aboard a vessel in the South China Sea, Nguyen centers the performance around a Vietnamese English teacher who attempts to flee Saigon (since renamed to Ho Chi Minh City) by boat, two years after North Vietnamese forces captured the capital in 1975. Grammy-nominated tenor Brian Vu will sing the libretto as the titular teacher, while a group of dancers will maneuver around him with a tapestry composed of flags.

“I was really fascinated by what happened at sea, as are many children of refugees from war-torn countries,” Nguyen told Hyperallergic in a phone interview. “The South China Sea is such a heavily trafficked area, and it created little stories where humans and the global economy collided.”

Commissioned and produced by Wesleyan University, where Nguyen teaches as an associate professor, the opera echoes themes prevalent in the artist’s other works , including a series of paintings on view at the biennale's Central Pavilion through November 22.

The tapestry of flags at the heart of the performance extends upon Nguyen's 2024 exhibition Timaeus and the Nations at the Sarasota Art Museum, where the artist rearranged 46 "flags of convenience," alluding to the practice in which ship operators change their flags for tax and regulation benefits.

Choreographed by Jamal Jackson, the opera's dancers will configure the tapestry into mountain ranges, a ship, the sea, and the cosmological diagram championed by the Pythagorean philosopher of Plato’s dialogue, Timaeus.

“Opera has a gestalt of sorts, just this massive tapestry of coming together and telling a story,” said Nguyen, adding that she's had the goal of directing an opera since learning to play and write music in San Francisco. “I took the anthems of all the countries in the flags of convenience, extracted various lyrics, and hybridized them arbitrarily for the libretto.”

As Vu’s character journeys across the sea, musical accompaniments mirror his literal and ideological movements. Nguyen assembled the libretto by breaking down traditional English language structures through a fractal sequence, while composer Neely Bruce remixed national anthems into the musical score.

Other performances slated for the final days of the biennale include a gathering around a Ouija board led by Hagar Ophir, stories of cultivation and global exchange with Lebanese artists Ziad Antar, Hatem Imam and Nayla Mabsout, and a meditation on salt as an essential mineral from Nathalie Vairac. While it’s unclear when the full production of the opera will be presented to audiences, Nguyen aims to have it completed by Bruce’s 85th birthday, in fall of 2029.

“The idea of nationhood is so flexible,” Nguyen stated. “But people die over it and fight over it, questioning whether they belong. We grapple with these questions all the time, as people who are looking to feel at home or develop a sense of agency for ourselves.”

Tammy Nguyen Plumbs Nationhood and the Sea in New Opera

The artist will present an aria from the still-unfinished opera, “Timaeus and The Teacher,” during the closing program of the 61st Venice Biennale.

Timaeus and the Teacher at Wesleyan University (photo Elisabeth Bernstein, courtesy the artist and Lehmann Maupin)

Artist Tammy Nguyen will present the foreword to her debut opera Timaeus and The Teacher at the 61st Venice Biennale's closing program on November 13 and 14, capping off an eventful edition of the international contemporary art festival.

The aria is the entry point to Nguyen's still-unfinished opera, which traces the national and ideological impacts of the Vietnam War and fuses Plato’s theories of the cosmos with enduring questions of identity. Inspired by her father's experiences as a refugee aboard a vessel in the South China Sea, Nguyen centers the performance around a Vietnamese English teacher who attempts to flee Saigon (since renamed to Ho Chi Minh City) by boat, two years after North Vietnamese forces captured the capital in 1975. Grammy-nominated tenor Brian Vu will sing the libretto as the titular teacher, while a group of dancers will maneuver around him with a tapestry composed of flags.

“I was really fascinated by what happened at sea, as are many children of refugees from war-torn countries,” Nguyen told Hyperallergic in a phone interview. “The South China Sea is such a heavily trafficked area, and it created little stories where humans and the global economy collided.”

Commissioned and produced by Wesleyan University, where Nguyen teaches as an associate professor, the opera echoes themes prevalent in the artist’s other works , including a series of paintings on view at the biennale's Central Pavilion through November 22.

The tapestry of flags at the heart of the performance extends upon Nguyen's 2024 exhibition Timaeus and the Nations at the Sarasota Art Museum, where the artist rearranged 46 "flags of convenience," alluding to the practice in which ship operators change their flags for tax and regulation benefits.

Choreographed by Jamal Jackson, the opera's dancers will configure the tapestry into mountain ranges, a ship, the sea, and the cosmological diagram championed by the Pythagorean philosopher of Plato’s dialogue, Timaeus.

“Opera has a gestalt of sorts, just this massive tapestry of coming together and telling a story,” said Nguyen, adding that she's had the goal of directing an opera since learning to play and write music in San Francisco. “I took the anthems of all the countries in the flags of convenience, extracted various lyrics, and hybridized them arbitrarily for the libretto.”

As Vu’s character journeys across the sea, musical accompaniments mirror his literal and ideological movements. Nguyen assembled the libretto by breaking down traditional English language structures through a fractal sequence, while composer Neely Bruce remixed national anthems into the musical score.

Other performances slated for the final days of the biennale include a gathering around a Ouija board led by Hagar Ophir, stories of cultivation and global exchange with Lebanese artists Ziad Antar, Hatem Imam and Nayla Mabsout, and a meditation on salt as an essential mineral from Nathalie Vairac. While it’s unclear when the full production of the opera will be presented to audiences, Nguyen aims to have it completed by Bruce’s 85th birthday, in fall of 2029.

“The idea of nationhood is so flexible,” Nguyen stated. “But people die over it and fight over it, questioning whether they belong. We grapple with these questions all the time, as people who are looking to feel at home or develop a sense of agency for ourselves.”

content.translated_excerpt_zh: 艺术家将在第61届威尼斯博览会的关闭节目中展示一场尚未完成的歌剧《蒂玛乌斯与老师》的歌剧。

content.title_original: Variety’s 2026 Artisans to Watch: ‘Obsession’ Makeup Head, ‘Project Hail Mary’ Animation Supervisor, ‘La Bola Negra’ Composer and More
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "In 2026, moviegoers came back to cinemas, packing theaters to see blockbusters like “The Odyssey,” “Project Hail Mary,” “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “Toy Story 5,” “Michael” and “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” and low-budget films like “Backrooms” and “Obsession.” But all those movies needed skilled artisans to complete the directors’ visions, including those on Variety’s 10 Artisans to Watch list. The honorees will be feted at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, which runs Oct. 24-31."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Past honorees have often gone on to earn Oscar nominations. Last year, “Sinners” DP Autumn Durald Arkapaw, “KPop Demon Hunters” songwriter EJAE and “One Battle After Another” editor Andy Jurgensen all went on to win Oscars."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Anne Jimkes Supervising sound editor, “The Mosquito Bowl” Jimkes approached the film’s World War II Pacific Theater setting with a focus on authenticity, researching the specific weapons used by the Japanese and American military forces, including the M1 Garand rifle. Its distinctive metallic “ping” served as more than just a historically accurate reference. “It adds a sense of urgency, and it’s a decision-making moment,” Jimkes says, noting the sound signals when a character must reload, switch weapons or resort to hand-to-hand combat. The sounds of the soldiers were a priority. The breaths and physical reactions recorded on set were pushed forward against the chaos of the battle to ground the characters’ humanity. Even in quieter scenes, the jungle location was alive with sound, creating a sense of pressure surrounding the soldiers. Blending these elements together is a process Jimkes refers to as a “parade of sound,” adding, “Your brain can only process so many sounds at the same time. However, it’s very good at processing rapidly successive sounds.” The sound needed to move the story forward. For Jimkes, that meant determining which sound should take priority in each moment while never losing sight of the people at the center of the film’s story. — Tanya Fedak"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Anne-Jimkes-Root.jpg?w=240", "alt": "Anne Jimkes", "caption": "", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Aulo Licinio Image Credit: Credit: Felix Guenette Animation supervisor, “Project Hail Mary” Despite having no face, eyes or traditional way to convey human emotion, Rocky became the emotional heart of “Project Hail Mary.” Licinio navigated that by developing physical language for the alien rock creature. Licinio oversaw a team of animators who studied the physical puppet used for filming, using its on-set movements as a reference while expanding Rocky’s mannerisms. “[Rocky’s puppeteer and voice] James Ortiz did a good job getting expressions out of this rock,” he says. “How can we enhance it in a way that we can use in reference? How can we tie the loose ends?” Licinio and his team looked to early puppetry and the exaggerated performances from silent film stars like Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton. Without features to convey human emotion, Rocky instead uses his elbows, body and distinctive head movements, sometimes angling himself just five degrees more to express his feelings. When he is shy, for example, he pulls an elbow in front of himself as if hiding. Some of Rocky’s mannerisms originated on set, including a tapping gesture to answer questions from Ortiz that the animators incorporated into the final character. Other movements, such as Rocky’s finger-like computing gestures, were created in CG. “It’s a collaboration at the end,” Licinio says. “That’s what I like to say about the film.” — T.F."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Aulo_Licinio_Framestore_3.jpg?w=240", "alt": "Aulo Licinio\nCredit: Felix Guenette", "caption": "Image Credit: Credit: Felix Guenette", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Landon Lott Art director, “Pluribus” SCAD alum Lott recalls “Pluribus” production designer Denise Pizzini reaching out to help develop a Norwegian ice hotel that would be built entirely on stage. Lott recalls, “The brief was to create a hotel that felt authentic and entirely sculpted from ice, while designing it around the practical limitations of a stage build.” Lott saw it as a great opportunity to bring together his background in illustration, architecture and set design. On his process, Lott says, “The initial scope of the set was actually larger than what ultimately appeared on screen and included a hotel lobby, foyer, bar and the individual hotel rooms. In 2026, moviegoers came back to cinemas, packing theaters to see blockbusters like “The Odyssey,” “Project Hail Mary,” “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “Toy Story 5,” “Michael” and “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” and low-budget films like “Backrooms” and “Obsession.” But all those movies needed skilled artisans to complete the directors’ visions, including those on Variety’s 10 Artisans to Watch list. The honorees will be feted at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, which runs Oct. 24-31.

Past honorees have often gone on to earn Oscar nominations. Last year, “Sinners” DP Autumn Durald Arkapaw, “KPop Demon Hunters” songwriter EJAE and “One Battle After Another” editor Andy Jurgensen all went on to win Oscars.

Anne Jimkes Supervising sound editor, “The Mosquito Bowl” Jimkes approached the film’s World War II Pacific Theater setting with a focus on authenticity, researching the specific weapons used by the Japanese and American military forces, including the M1 Garand rifle. Its distinctive metallic “ping” served as more than just a historically accurate reference. “It adds a sense of urgency, and it’s a decision-making moment,” Jimkes says, noting the sound signals when a character must reload, switch weapons or resort to hand-to-hand combat. The sounds of the soldiers were a priority. The breaths and physical reactions recorded on set were pushed forward against the chaos of the battle to ground the characters’ humanity. Even in quieter scenes, the jungle location was alive with sound, creating a sense of pressure surrounding the soldiers. Blending these elements together is a process Jimkes refers to as a “parade of sound,” adding, “Your brain can only process so many sounds at the same time. However, it’s very good at processing rapidly successive sounds.” The sound needed to move the story forward. For Jimkes, that meant determining which sound should take priority in each moment while never losing sight of the people at the center of the film’s story. — Tanya Fedak

Aulo Licinio Image Credit: Credit: Felix Guenette Animation supervisor, “Project Hail Mary” Despite having no face, eyes or traditional way to convey human emotion, Rocky became the emotional heart of “Project Hail Mary.” Licinio navigated that by developing physical language for the alien rock creature. Licinio oversaw a team of animators who studied the physical puppet used for filming, using its on-set movements as a reference while expanding Rocky’s mannerisms. “[Rocky’s puppeteer and voice] James Ortiz did a good job getting expressions out of this rock,” he says. “How can we enhance it in a way that we can use in reference? How can we tie the loose ends?” Licinio and his team looked to early puppetry and the exaggerated performances from silent film stars like Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton. Without features to convey human emotion, Rocky instead uses his elbows, body and distinctive head movements, sometimes angling himself just five degrees more to express his feelings. When he is shy, for example, he pulls an elbow in front of himself as if hiding. Some of Rocky’s mannerisms originated on set, including a tapping gesture to answer questions from Ortiz that the animators incorporated into the final character. Other movements, such as Rocky’s finger-like computing gestures, were created in CG. “It’s a collaboration at the end,” Licinio says. “That’s what I like to say about the film.” — T.F.

Landon Lott Art director, “Pluribus” SCAD alum Lott recalls “Pluribus” production designer Denise Pizzini reaching out to help develop a Norwegian ice hotel that would be built entirely on stage. Lott recalls, “The brief was to create a hotel that felt authentic and entirely sculpted from ice, while designing it around the practical limitations of a stage build.” Lott saw it as a great opportunity to bring together his background in illustration, architecture and set design. On his process, Lott says, “The initial scope of the set was actually larger than what ultimately appeared on screen and included a hotel lobby, foyer, bar and the individual hotel rooms. That meant thinking through the hotel as a complete environment from the beginning, establishing how the spaces connected and giving each one its own identity while making sure they all felt like part of the same place.” Lott knew that many details would be handcarved by ice sculptors. “I was essentially designing artwork that also had to function architecturally, work within the realities of a stage build and give the sculptors something tangible they could interpret and bring to life,” he says. So he turned to real ice hotels throughout Scandinavia, particularly the ICEHOTEL in Sweden and hotels in Norway and Finland for inspiration. — Jazz Tangcay

Sometimes finding this groove is deliberate and difficult, and other times, like on “Clarissa,” the experience is filled with happy accidents. “It’s like a rooster crows at exactly the right moment to keep the shot interesting and keep it going, and we were like, ‘Oh, that’s great, that guy has to stay,’” McClendon says. Raül Refree Composer, “La Bola Negra” When scoring Netflix’s “La Bola Negra,” Refree knew he wanted to pursue a timeless, orchestral and avant-garde sound. The film recounts the story of three generations of queer men whose lives are connected through love and loss. Refree tied his instrumentation to the characters rather than the eras. “Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) plays the trumpet, so his scenes rely heavily on the brass section. The film contains several songs including “La Nieve,” sung by Sebastián. “Guitarricadelafuente brought the idea for ‘La Nieve’ to Los Javis (the film’s directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo). They loved it and asked me to incorporate it into the score, so I adapted his initial concept to align with the rest of the soundtrack,” Refree says. “Having worked with Guitarricadelafuente frequently over the last few years, we have a great creative dynamic, which made it easy to co-write the song and develop the right sound.” — J.T.

Jessica Ronane Image Credit: Yellow Belly Photo Casting director, “Elsinore” Casting for “Elsinore” was a particularly nuanced feat for Ronane. She felt a responsibility to the truth. She had to cast a play within a film based on the real-life happenings of London’s National Theatre in 1989. To do so, Ronane and “Elsinore” director Simon Stone worked closely together scouring their web of actors and building a “story map of all the real people and then started to think about instinctively who has the spirit of the character, and how are we going to identify the right actors to put forward,” Ronane says. Ronane’s instincts led her to focus on performers with theater experience. Once Andrew Scott was solidified for the role of Ian Charleson, Ronane quickly thought of David Dawson to play Derek Jarman. She had seen the pair perform together in a play back in 2014 and couldn’t shake their chemistry. “Seeing the two of them on a small stage together like that in a really intimate setting, I could not stop thinking about that when we spoke about David Dawson in this role,” Ronane says. Casting Olivia Colman as Margaret was also instinctual. Her “particular brand of sensitivity and humor and wisdom and sort of spiciness” made her a natural choice to play the part, Ronane says. “What an incredible thing to be able to build on your instincts like that, to be able to really feel that your taste is appreciated by collaborators who want kind of more of that,” Ronane says. — I. F.

Allie Shehorn Make-up and hair department head/ special makeup effects department head, “Obsession” For “Obsession,” Shehorn was tasked with creating looks that could withstand the film’s practical effects while still telling the characters’ stories. For Sarah’s (Megan Lawless) face-smash sequence, Shehorn crafted multiple versions of the character’s head, including a live cast taken from the actor as she screamed and a prosthetic version that could ultimately be smashed on camera. Shehorn and the team carefully choreographed each transition, switching from the actor’s live-action performance to the prosthetic before revealing Sarah’s final smashed-in face. Working with the blood rigs presented another technical challenge, particularly because the team filmed scenes out of order. “We actually shot the end sequence of the movie before we did the blood rigs to establish the blood looks,” Shehorn says. “We had to predict where the blood was going on Bear (Michael Johnston), even on Nikki (Inde Navarrette).” One of Shehorn’s more elaborate looks was Nikki’s final appearance after murdering Sarah, which reflects her growing obsession with becoming her. Shehorn used the same lipstick and eyeliner shades on Nikki that Sarah wears, while dried blood sits beneath the fresh blood to represent the fact that Nikki never washes it from her face. She also used Sarah’s eyeliner shade to draw Nikki’s tattoos and, by the end of the film, curled Nikki’s hair as another visual connection to Sarah. “That’s why we kept Nikki’s hair straight throughout the film, because we wanted to show the difference in the characters between Sarah and Nikki, so that in the end we can really push those moments of ‘Oh, she’s really trying to be her,’” she says. — T.F.

Grace Snell Costume designer, “Sense and Sensibility” Snell is a Jane Austen fan, but she tried not to be intimidated by the fact that “Sense and Sensibility” was an Austen adaptation. “I took my role very seriously and did lots of research, but then I was reassured by our director and the producers that they wanted my version of this,” she says. “What I wanted to do was design a film that I could see myself in, see my friends in, see my family in, try and knock down the wall that often is associated with period dramas.” Georgia Oakley’s film isn’t the first “Sense and Sensibility” adaptation, and while Snell loves the 1995 version, she also knew this film was a different take. Snell was also inspired by family portraits. Danny Vermette Production designer, “Backrooms” Kane Parsons’ “Backrooms” web series became a YouTube phenomenon, amassing over 200 million views across its episodes. When Parsons began adapting the series into a feature film, Vermette had already seen the series but wasn’t fully aware of Parsons’ work. “I watched all of Kane’s stuff and came to realize how much is out there, and what a following it had,” Vermette says. Bringing the world to life as a period piece — the story is set in the 1990s — required close collaboration with the film’s cinematographer Jeremy Cox and costume designer Micah Cade to determine what would work within “the yellow universe.” One of the challenges was designing the drop ceilings. “My key thought was to keep this original to the series but bring it up to that next level of cinema and make it beautiful,” Vermette explains. content.article_text:
After 17 years of leadership, Bob Daly will step down as chair of the American Film Institute Board of Directors at the next trustee meeting on Wednesday, Oct. 21, Variety can reveal exclusively.

Daly, former Warner Bros. chair and co-CEO, joined the AFI Board in April 1981 and was named chair on Oct. 8, 2009, succeeding co-chairs Jon Avnet and John Cooke.

“In a career that brought me from running CBS to Warner Bros. to the Los Angeles Dodgers, I can honestly say that serving as Chairman of the AFI Board of Directors has been one of the greatest honors of my life,” said Daly. “This is a board that represents all aspects of the film and television communities, and to see they come together with a shared passion for the art form has been a wonder to behold. Long live the AFI!”

Related Stories

Bradley Whitford on Bringing Back ‘The West Wing’ as a ‘Limited Series’

'The Social Reckoning' First Reactions: A 'Solid Sequel,' 'Good, Just Not Great Film' and a 'Harsh Assessment of Zuckerberg'

Daly’s expansive history in Hollywood touched some of the most powerful institutions in the entertainment business, including CBS Entertainment, Warner Music Group, the Los Angeles Dodgers and, of course, Warner Bros. He began his career at CBS as a gofer in 1955. He spent 25 years at the network and eventually served as its president, overseeing all television operations. After his time at CBS, Daly joined Warner Bros. as chairman and co-CEO in 1980. During his 19 years at the studio, he and his co-CEO, Terry Semel, were credited with 16 consecutive years of record earnings. They also supervised the release of 13 Best Picture Oscar nominees, and snagged three wins with “Chariots of Fire,” “Driving Miss Daisy” and “Unforgiven.”

Popular on Variety

Following his time at WB, Daly joined the Los Angeles Dodgers as chair and CEO for four years before selling the team in 2004. Daly also served as chair of the charity Save the Children.

“Leadership is an art in itself — and in that regard, Mr. Daly is a master,” said Bob Gazzale, AFI president & CEO. “Over the past forty years, no single person has had a greater impact on AFI’s work in preservation, celebration and education than Bob Daly — and we have promised to march forward each day with a promise to prove him proud.”

The AFI, founded in 1967, is a nonprofit organization created to preserve the heritage of the motion picture, to honor the artists and their work and to educate the next generation of storytellers. Former Lucasfilm president Kathleen Kennedy serves as chair of the AFI Board of Trustees, which includes Pam Abdy, Sean Astin, Alan Bergman, Halle Berry, Jim Breyer, James L. Brooks, Ava DuVernay, Jamie Erlicht, Mike Hopkins, Alan Horn, Patty Jenkins, Michael B. Jordan, Donna Langley, Eva Longoria, Bryan Lourd, Christopher Nolan, Edward James Olmos, Shonda Rhimes, Charles Rivkin, Jay Roach, Ted Sarandos, Chris Silbermann, Octavia Spencer, Steven Spielberg, Todd Wagner and Edward Zwick.

content.article_text:
Strength in numbers? Movie theater operators are hoping the adage proves true as four new movies aim to bolster the October box office.

Paramount’s video game adaptation “ Street Fighter ” will lead over fellow newcomers, with opening weekend estimates of $25 million to $35 million from 3,500 North American theaters. Disney’s survival thriller “ Whalefall ” should secure second place with $10 million to $12 million from 3,065 venues. Meanwhile A24’s much-hyped Elizabeth Holmes documentary “ You Can See Everything ” is aiming for a strong $7 million to $8 million from just 800 locations, and the Focus Features remake of Jane Austen’s “Sense and Sensibility” is targeting $5 million to $8 million from 2,436 screens.

Related Stories

'The Social Reckoning' Soundtrack Features New Music From Composer Alexandre Desplat

Aaron Sorkin Says It ‘Never Occurred’ to Him That Jesse Eisenberg Wouldn’t Play Mark Zuckerberg in ‘The Social Reckoning,’ Claims the Paycheck Was a ‘Disincentive’

Although “Street Fighter” is projected to claim the No. 1 spot, the PG-13 action-adventure carries the biggest budget among the quartet and will need to stick around in theaters to justify its price tag. Legendary and video game developer Capcom co-financed the film for $82 million, with Paramount only on the hook for distribution. The long-gestating “Street Fighter” was originally set at Sony as part of Legendary’s pact with the studio and moved to Paramount once the initial deal expired. Overseas, “Street Fighter” is projected to earn roughly $35 million from 65 markets.

Popular on Variety

“Street Fighter” is the third movie based on the Capcom video game series. The first live-action film, released in 1994 and starred Jean-Claude Van Damme, was a commercial hit with $100 million, not adjusted for inflation. The second, 2009’s “Street Fighter: The Legend of Chun-Li,” was a major misfire for 20th Century, earning just $12.8 million against a $50 million budget. This reboot, directed by Kitao Sakurai and starring Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji, takes place in 1993 as two estranged fighters are recruited to enter a tournament that forces them to face off against each other.

“Whalefall” cost $60 million and also requires substantial staying power, since theater owners keep about half of ticket sales. Directed by Brian Duffield, “Whalefall” follows a scuba diver (Austin Abrams) who is swallowed by a sperm whale and has only one hour of oxygen left in his tank as he figures out how to escape. Reviews have been mostly positive, with one critic calling the film “ amusing genre pulp .”

“You Can See Everything” cost around $7 million to produce, and exhibitors believe the movie could become the rare breakout documentary. Earlier this year, Amazon MGM’s “Melania,” a $40-million-budgeted look at first lady Melania Trump, landed the biggest opening for a non-music or concert doc in over a decade with $7.1 million from 1,778 theaters. Most non-fiction films, however, would be lucky these days to earn that much by the end of their box office runs.

Hype for “You Can See Everything” has been high since A24 unveiled the top-secret project at Telluride Film Festival in early September. Comedian Nathan Fielder and “Primetime” filmmaker Lance Oppenheim quietly worked for more than three years on the movie, which offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder’s life a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors. The doc will benefit from stellar reviews and positive word-of-mouth; it holds a 100% on Rotten Tomatoes, with Variety’s Owen Gleiberman describing the unconventional story as a “one-of-a-kind [ …] circus.”

“Sense and Sensibility,” which carries a $25 million budget, hopes to serve as counterprogramming against the male-skewing “Street Fighter” and “Whalefall.” Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles star in the latest adaptation of the Jane Austen classic as sisters Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, who navigate love, loss and financial uncertainty as they are forced to leave their family estate in Sussex.

“Sense and Sensibility” has been reworked for the screen a number of times, most notably with director Ang Lee’s 1995 film starring Emma Thompson as Elinor Dashwood and Kate Winslet as Marianne. That film was a critical and commercial smash, earning seven Oscar nominations and generating $135 million at the box office, not adjusted for inflation. Focus Features over the years has backed two prior remakes of Austen’s work, including the 2005 version of “Pride and Prejudice” with Keira Knightley and Matthew Macfadyen as well as 2020’s “Emma,” which starred Anya-Taylor Joy. The well-reviewed “Emma” was released digitally while theaters were closed due to the pandemic.

So far, the October box office has been uneven. Tom Cruise’s dark comedy “Digger” and Aaron Sorkin’s Facebook drama “The Social Reckoning” flopped, while Colleen Hoover adaptation “Verity” and “Other Mommy” with Jessica Chastain are shaping up to be modest wins. Luckily, it won’t take much to improve upon last October, which hit a three-decade low amid a pileup of disasters including Dwayne Johnson’s MMA drama “The Smashing Machine” and Disney’s sci-fi sequel “Tron: Ares.”

content.title_original: 10 Prophetic Sci-Fi Films That Predicted Modern A.I. And Its Ethical Dilemmas
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Science fiction has long stood at the forefront of technological foresight. But what happens when the dream becomes a nightmare?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Decades before computers became household staples or smartphones dominated daily life, sci-fi cinema was light-years ahead, predicting a world where AI seamlessly integrates into our routines."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yet, what happens when that seamless convenience devolves into impending doom? These films challenge us with a crucial question: will AI inevitably surpass human control and evolve far beyond its creators?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Across these stories, filmmakers interrogate the dark ethics of artificial intelligence, exploring the danger of surrendering autonomy, the mistreatment of sentient robotics, the covert manipulation of public behavior, and the real emotional toll of replacing human connection with AI companionship."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Scroll down for 10 films that turned yesterday’s sci-fi warnings into today’s reality."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "METROPOLIS – 1927 Image Credit: Paramount Pictures Fritz Lang’s Metropolis (1927) stands as cinema’s foundational warning on the weaponization of synthetic life, introducing the archetype of the artificial human used for mass psychological control.
