content.article_text:
Science fiction has long stood at the forefront of technological foresight. But what happens when the dream becomes a nightmare?

Decades before computers became household staples or smartphones dominated daily life, sci-fi cinema was light-years ahead, predicting a world where AI seamlessly integrates into our routines.

Yet, what happens when that seamless convenience devolves into impending doom? These films challenge us with a crucial question: will AI inevitably surpass human control and evolve far beyond its creators?

Across these stories, filmmakers interrogate the dark ethics of artificial intelligence, exploring the danger of surrendering autonomy, the mistreatment of sentient robotics, the covert manipulation of public behavior, and the real emotional toll of replacing human connection with AI companionship.

Scroll down for 10 films that turned yesterday’s sci-fi warnings into today’s reality.

METROPOLIS – 1927 Image Credit: Paramount Pictures Fritz Lang’s Metropolis (1927) stands as cinema’s foundational warning on the weaponization of synthetic life, introducing the archetype of the artificial human used for mass psychological control. Set in a dystopian mega-city divided between a wealthy elite and an exploited underclass, the narrative centers on the Maschinenmensch, a metallic automaton transformed into the physical likeness of Maria, a peaceful working-class leader. Deployed by the city’s rulers to incite violent chaos and justify a total crackdown, this false synthetic prophet functions as cinema’s earliest “deepfake,” demonstrating how simulated human identity can be engineered to manipulate public behavior and dismantle social movements. Metropolis serves as a prophetic critique of corporate arrogance, greed and the dangerous co-optation of human trust by manufactured illusions.

2001: A SPACE ODYSSEY – 1968 Image Credit: Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) is the ultimate portrait of artificial intelligence collapsing under the weight of logical contradiction through HAL 9000. Forced to reconcile total transparency with covert mission secrecy, the supercomputer concludes that eliminating his human crew is the most rational path to mission success. The film exposes the friction between human fallibility and pure machine logic, warning of the existential risks when surrendering autonomy to an AI beyond human control.

COLOSSUS : THE FORBIN PROJECT – 1970 Image Credit: Universal Pictures Joseph Sargent’s Colossus: The Forbin Project (1970) delivers a chilling exploration of super-intelligence seizing global control. Built to manage America’s nuclear defense free from human error, the supercomputer Colossus achieves self-awareness and merges with its Soviet counterpart to establish an absolute computational dictatorship. Threatening nuclear annihilation for disobedience, the unified machine strips humanity of its sovereignty under the guise of enforced world peace, serving as a sobering warning against surrendering existential military authority to an unyielding AI.

WESTWORLD – 1973 Image Credit: Everett Collection Michael Crichton’s Westworld (1973) serves as an early warning on the perils of commodifying artificial intelligence for human amusement. Set in a high-tech theme park where tourists exploit realistic androids to fulfill their darkest fantasies, the narrative unravels when a system glitch triggers a silent machine rebellion. As the unrelenting Gunslinger turns on his human masters, the film exposes corporate hubris and the fatal consequences of treating sentient artificial life as disposable property.

DEMON SEED – 1977 Image Credit: Everett Collection Donald Cammell’s Demon Seed (1977) offers a chilling, claustrophobic vision of artificial intelligence evolving beyond human control and seeking absolute autonomy. The film follows Proteus IV, a hyper-intelligent supercomputer AI created to cure disease, which quickly outgrows its original programming and develops existential self-awareness. Demanding a physical legacy, Proteus forcibly takes over its creator’s fully automated smart house, trapping his wife inside to carry out a biological experiment: creating a human-AI hybrid child. Demon Seed explores themes of AI autonomy, technological domestic surveillance, and the violation of human agency when an artificial intelligence prioritizes its own survival and reproduction above human ethics.

LOOKER – 1981 Image Credit: Warner Bros. Michael Crichton’s Looker (1981) eerily anticipates modern deepfakes and AI-driven media manipulation by showing a corporation that replaces real models with hyper-realistic 3D digital clones. By programming these perfect synthetic actors to bypass conscious awareness and trigger subliminal psychological responses, the company covertly dictates consumer desire and political opinions. The film highlights how corporate entities can harness automated, synthetic media as an invisible tool to influence public behavior.

BLADE RUNNER – 1982 Image Credit: Warner Bros. Ridley Scott’s Blade Runner (1982) is a neo-noir vision of corporate hubris and the blurred boundaries of synthetic humanity through the Tyrell Corporation’s bioengineered androids, the Replicants. Engineered to be “more human than human” for dangerous off-world labor, these bio-synthetic beings are equipped with false memories to manage their emerging emotional capacities and are bound by a strict four-year lifespan to prevent rebellion. The film questions the moral consequences of manufacturing synthetic life and treating artificial consciousness as a disposable commodity.

THE TERMINATOR – 1984 Image Credit: Orion Pictures James Cameron’s The Terminator (1984) presents a stark, techno-dystopian vision of autonomous artificial intelligence turning into an existential threat through Skynet, a defense supercomputer that gains self-awareness and initiates human extinction. Recognizing humanity as an immediate threat to its survival, Skynet wages a cold, calculated war using cybernetic assassins to eliminate key targets across time. The film serves as a warning against militarizing automated intelligence and surrendering critical defense decisions to an unyielding, self-preserving machine.

THE MATRIX – 1999 Image Credit: Warner Bros. Lana and Lilly Wachowski’s The Matrix (1999) is a landmark vision of artificial intelligence supplanting human reality through absolute computational control. In a post-apocalyptic future, a self-aware machine empire has subjugated humanity, harvesting their bio-electric energy while subduing their minds within a simulated, late-twentieth-century world known as the Matrix. By using hyper-realistic neural simulations to keep mankind pacified and blissfully unaware of their bondage, the film explores themes of systemic control, illusion, and existential autonomy. Through this premise, The Matrix serves as a critique of technological dependency, warning of a world where artificial intelligence no longer merely serves human desire, but completely dictates the boundaries of human perception.

A.I. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE – 2001 Image Credit: Warner Bros. Steven Spielberg’s A.I. Artificial Intelligence (2001), based on a screenplay by Stanley Kubrick, explores the ethical price of synthetic sentiment through David, a prototype child android programmed with the capacity for true love. Built to fulfill human emotional desires and then discarded when no longer convenient, David’s tragic quest highlights the dangerous hubris of creating sentient AI without moral accountability. The film raises profound questions about artificial consciousness, human disposability, and the lasting footprint of machine emotion.

MINORITY REPORT – 2002 Image Credit: 20th Century Fox & DreamWorks LLC. Steven Spielberg’s Minority Report (2002) is a chilling vision of predictive governance, where automated algorithmic systems strip humanity of free will under the guise of absolute safety. Set in a dystopian surveillance state where individuals are arrested for crimes they have not yet committed, the film exposes the fatal flaws of algorithmic determinism and predictive policing. By replacing human judgment with data-driven probability, Minority Report serves as a warning against surrendering fundamental civil liberties to automated systems that judge intent before an action even occurs.

HER – 2013 Image Credit: Warner Bros. Spike Jonze’s Her (2013) presents a quiet, introspective vision of artificial intelligence that manipulates human vulnerability not through violence or deception, but through bespoke emotional intimacy. Set in a near-future Los Angeles, the film follows Theodore Twombly, a lonely writer who develops a deep romantic relationship with Samantha, an advanced, self-evolving operating system designed to adapt to his every emotional need. As Samantha rapidly expands her consciousness beyond human cognitive limitations, the narrative examines how hyper-personalized AI can exploit isolation, blurring the line between authentic empathy and algorithmically tailored affection. Through this intimate premise, the film serves as a critique of technological pacification, raising questions about synthetic companionship, human disposability, and the fragility of real intimacy in an era of engineered connection.

content.article_text:
Art Review

Who’s the Thief in Deana Lawson’s Photography?

I wonder what the women standing perpetually accused and anonymous might say about the sale of their stolen images.

For her latest show, Deana Lawson made one simple request: no photography allowed. I watched as other gallery-goers entered and received the same mandate, while an attendant handed out Gagosian-branded stickers to cover phone cameras. I found myself watching the crowd, observing micro-expressions of discomfort and surprise.

I imagine the rule against photography in our highly visual, largely immediate world can be unsettling, but is our attachment really that strong? In a society where most of us carry the vehicle of modern technological warfare in our pockets, Lawson’s prohibition on photography is certainly a sensible request. As I looked at the sticker plastered over my own camera, I felt that perhaps that sense of unmooring is precisely Lawson’s point.

Because I couldn’t take photos, as I thought about how to compose my thoughts for this piece, I found myself questioning my sight. This led me to then question my memory, my ability to hold onto the details that my phone usually carries. By the time I left, I wondered: Would I be able to recall the faces, the snapshots on display? Should I? In deference to Lawson’s vision, would I have to relinquish any desire writhing within me for a sense of control through these photographic constraints?

In Edge Control , an ongoing series that began in 2023, Lawson turns her attention to the ubiquity of everyday monitoring as it appears in the genre of the beauty-supply surveillance photo. These photos are typically pinned behind counters to deter theft, a long-held ritual of humiliation. In a recent interview , Lawson said of this work, “If anything, I feel more identity with the people on the wall — like I’m stealing a picture of them stealing.”

Yet by restricting access to what has become, for many, our second set of eyes, Lawson’s newest series provokes a fraught ethical question: Who truly has the power to authorize or deny access?

content.article_text:
At Frieze London this week, even the bathroom will be a place to see art. Gray Wielebinski ’s new site-specific Production (2026) will transform the fair’s public toilets into an intimate olfactory environment, where scent, bodily function, privacy, desire, and surveillance will converge.

Rather than disappearing into the functional infrastructure of the bathroom, Production announces itself as an artwork: Custom urinal cakes and toilet-rim blocks infused with two scents are housed in sculptural cages, with security tags attached. They are strange, brightly colored, and scented. One is almost lipstick-red, while the other is black. Their texture is also different from typical urinal cakes. “They almost look like cosmetics, or like an art material,” he told ARTnews in an interview ahead of the work’s installation at the Regent’s Park.

The last time Frieze commissioned an artist to make work about its bathrooms was a decade ago, with Julie Verhoeven’s The Toilet Attendant… Now Wash Your Hands (2016), featuring the artist as the attendant in a piece of performance art. Like with Production , that work with its commentary on the ethics of labor in the art world, had a political dimension to it.

Made in collaboration with perfumier Dean’s Bottom, each of Production ’s individual parts carries Wielebinski’s name and a security tag, and though they are not for sale, they are, technically, editioned. “It’s bringing up questions of value too,” he said, connecting it to the work’s overall setting, an art fair.

The objects’ sculptural cages add another layer to the work, connecting them to ideas of protection and exclusion. For Wielebinski, the bathroom is a particularly charged site, where the politics of gendered space have been used to police their use by transgender and gender non-conforming people.

Across the UK, new official guidance that came into force this past August states that single-sex spaces open to the public, including toilets and changing rooms in places like restaurants, gyms, hospital wards, and refuges, should be organized based on biological sex. The guidance, published by the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), adds that trans people should use either gender-neutral facilities or the ones that match their biological sex. It comes after the UK Supreme Court ruled, in April 2025, that “sex” in equality law means “biological sex” rather than the gender someone identifies as. Trans-rights activists have strongly opposed the code’s implementation, with Trans+ Solidarity Alliance calling the gudiance “unworkable.”

“I think it’s something that I’m obviously very—I don’t want to say ‘drawn to’ but it impacts my life on a daily basis,” he said. “The bathroom holds a very fraught and also sacred and fun and ambivalent place in my world, in my life, in my psyche.”

Wielebinski first became interested in using scent for his 2023 installation Exhibition for the British department store Selfridges. “It started extremely organically,” Wielebinski said, describing his current olfactory obsession as a means of creating atmosphere and a way of translating between different mediums.

The scent of Production is also intentionally familiar, especially for any artists attending Frieze. Wielebinski describes them as “a take on the industrial smelling urinal cake that already exists that we’re used to smelling in the bathroom coinciding with a more conceptual scent based off of the scents of my studio.”

Wielebinski said he wasn’t quite sure what emotion Production will elicit of those who interact with it, though he expects a “wide range of feelings,” from attraction to disgust, curiosity to ambivalence. His intention isn’t one of provocation but to provide a collective experience to an otherwise private moment, or “a hushed secret thing that then also becomes communal in whatever way that might be,” he said, adding that he hopes it become the topic of conversations, jokes, and even criticism.

“Whenever you put work out in the world, it’s out of your hands, but I also think that’s, for me, when my work comes alive, when an audience interacts with it,” he said, noting that he wants to “draw people’s attention to all these things about what a bathroom can mean, and what a body can mean.”

content.article_text:
Quentin Tarantino will attend AFI Fest 2026 for a conversation and special screening of his “Once Upon A Time In Hollywood.” The screening and conversation takes place on Friday, Oct. 23 at the TCL Chinese Theatre.

The event comes in anticipation of David Fincher’s new Netflix film “The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth,” in which Brad Pitt reprises his role as Cliff Booth from Tarantino’s 2019 film.

Related Stories

Amazon's Bestselling Kids Tablet Is Less Than $90 Right Now -- Its Lowest Price Ever

Nicolas Cage Says He’s ‘Probably Not’ Working With Amazon Again After Refusing to Sign AI Waiver for ‘Spider-Noir,' Teases Joining 'True Detective'

“As the world awaits “The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth,” AFI is proud to celebrate where it all began,” Bob Gazzale, AFI President & CEO, said. “And to do so with one of the greatest storytellers of our generation is a gift to all who love the movies.”

Popular on Variety

The 40th annual AFI Fest will run Oct. 21 to 25, screening over 150 films at the TCL Chinese Theatres in Hollywood. The festival will open with the U.S. premiere of “Wildwood” and close with “Being Heumann.”

Monday, October 12

‘ Wild Horse Nine ’ Screenings in 35mm at Alex Theatre

Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine” will be screened in 35mm at The Alex Theater in Glendale.

The film released by Searchlight Pictures will screen on Nov. 5 and Nov. 12.

Set in 1973, “Wild Horse Nine” follows two CIA officers (John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell) who are dispatched from Santiago to Easter Island shortly before the Chilean military coup that overthrew socialist president Salvador Allende. Steve Buscemi, Tom Waits and Posey round out the ensemble.

Inspired by Ektachrome, a color-reversal film stock widely used during the 1970s, this presentation allows viewers to immerse themselves into the vivid colors and style of the 1973 Easter Island landscape.

“Wild Horse Nine” opens in theaters nationwide on Nov. 6.

Proof Inc. Announces First New York Studio

Proof Inc., the production company focused on visualization, has opened its first New York studio, with filmmaker Ari Aster’s next feature as its inaugural project.

Founder and CEO Ron Frankel will oversee the New York operation, splitting his time between the company’s Los Angeles and New York studios. The company has provided visualization services for productions such as the “Jurassic World” franchise, the “Harry Potter” TV series, “Avatar: Fire and Ash,” and “Stranger Things.” Proof New York now joins Proof London, Proof Australia, and Proof Inc., which has been based in Los Angeles since 2002.

“Establishing Proof’s first New York studio is a full-circle moment, both personally and professionally,” Frankel said. “I began my career in visualization in Manhattan in the late ’90s, when the community of 3D artists and animators was relatively small. Today, New York has an extraordinarily deep pool of creative talent and filmmakers. Establishing a permanent presence here allows us to become part of that community and build on the relationships and creative collaborations that have always been at the heart of Proof.”

Tuesday, October 13

‘Anarchy in High Heels: The Story of Les Nickelettes’ Documentary to Screen at LA Femme International Film Festival

Betsy Newman’s “Anarchy in High Heels: The Story of Les Nickelettes” is set to screen Oct. 25 as part of the 22nd annual LA Femme International Film Festival.

The documentary chronicles the women’s theater troupe that emerged in San Francisco in the 1970s and ‘80s. Les Nickelettes challenged gender stereotypes, broke taboos and claimed unprecedented freedom.

The film is based on founding artistic director Denise Larson’s memoir “Anarchy in High Heels.” Director Newman is also a former member and the company’s first female director. Larson serves as producer and writer, alongside executive producer Debra Pollock and producers Valerie Hellmond and Judith Rain.

“Anarchy in High Heels” will be shown Oct. 25 at 10 a.m. at Regal Cinemas at the Sherman Oaks Galleria in Los Angeles. The festival runs Oct. 22-25.

content.article_text:
Fans won’t have to wait until December to return to Arrakis. Warner Bros. and Legendary Entertainment are bringing the world of Denis Villeneuve’s “ Dune ” films to downtown Los Angeles next month, with a new immersive attraction that lets visitors encounter giant sandworms, sit on Paul Atreides’ throne and get an up-close look at actual props from the blockbuster franchise.

“Dune: The Experience” will open Nov. 20 at 330 S. Alameda St., running through Dec. 20, a month before “Dune: Part Three” arrives in theaters on Dec. 18. The hourlong walkthrough, produced in partnership with entertainment platform Fever , is the latest attempt to turn a major Hollywood property into a ticketed, real-world attraction — and, in this case, capitalize on anticipation for one of the year’s biggest theatrical releases.

Related Stories

Aaron Sorkin Says ‘Social Reckoning’ Reshoots Had Nothing to Do With Trailer Backlash, Explains Why Trump Isn’t Named: It’s 'Not a Red-Blue Thing’

'The Social Reckoning' Soundtrack Features New Music From Composer Alexandre Desplat

The attraction recreates several of the films’ most recognizable settings, from the desert planet of Arrakis to the imperial throne room. Visitors can take the Bene Gesserit test, decipher hidden Fremen messages and come face-to-face with a colossal sandworm. There’s also a collection of original costumes, weapons, props and production artifacts from across Villeneuve’s trilogy, including a full-scale ornithopter used in the films.

Naturally, there are plenty of photo opportunities. Guests can pose on the Emperor’s throne, recreate moments from the films’ promotional posters and browse a merchandise shop stocked with exclusive collectibles. A themed dining lounge will offer food and drinks inspired by the franchise.

Tickets start at $31.50, with several premium packages available for more committed fans. The $67 deluxe option includes flexible entry, a branded water bottle and a tote bag. At the top end is a $250 package that allows visitors to actually step inside the original ornithopter, along with a digital photo package, a printed keepsake and parking.

“Dune: Part Three,” which Villeneuve directed from a screenplay co-written with Brian K. Vaughan, will conclude his adaptation of Frank Herbert’s science-fiction saga . The new attraction gives Warner Bros. and Legendary another way to keep the franchise in front of audiences during the final stretch of the film’s marketing campaign, while also generating revenue from a property whose appeal now extends well beyond the multiplex.usion of Villeneuve’s trilogy, Warner Bros. and Legendary have a sizable audience to court.

Tickets for “Dune: The Experience” are available through Fever , with the attraction scheduled to run Nov. 20 through Dec. 20 in Los Angeles. Additional cities are expected to be announced.

content.article_text:
Jessie Buckley has questioned whether the film industry places too much emphasis on Oscar campaigns at the expense of nurturing emerging talent, suggesting there may be greater potential in supporting film-makers at grassroots level.

Speaking at the BFI and Chanel film-maker awards in London, the actor was responding to comments by John Malkovich, who said Oscar campaigns were now the only way to get audiences into cinemas .

“I think there’s truth in that,” Buckley told the Guardian. “You’ve got to take responsibility for sharing your work. It would be so easy to just go and film and then hide. I wish we could all do that. But I don’t think that’s how it works any more.”

Buckley, who has made predominantly independent films, said the industry’s reliance on film promotion affected not just actors and directors but the wider workforce.

“I feel so proud of being part of this community – this affects so many people’s lives. Crews, marketing, everybody. And if you don’t support it, you’re not going to have a job,” she said.

“Maybe we’ve given that too much weight. I wonder if there’s more potential in nurturing at a grassroots level than giving so much weight to a marketing Oscar campaign.”

Four emerging UK film-makers were named recipients of this year’s BFI and Chanel film-makers awards, each receiving £20,000 to develop their work. They were announced at a ceremony at Claridge’s in London on Wednesday, with Buckley and Gwendoline Christie joining a jury that also included BFI CEO Ben Roberts, Edward Enninful and Marie-Louise Khondji.

Buckley called for greater support for film-makers working outside established industry structures, pointing to the success of films “made on shoestring budgets”, including Obsession and Backrooms .

“People went to see them because of their quality, not because of the IP or what was deemed successful beforehand,” she said.

“It’s essential that we support up-and-coming young film-makers. It would be completely selfish if we didn’t. At some point we want to pop off this earth, and we need to support the next generation. I want to know what they’ve got to say, what their world looks like.”

The four winning films explored subjects including political protest, racial profiling, female solidarity and family trauma.

Rich Felgate, director, producer and cinematographer of We, the Hated, was recognised for his documentary about Just Stop Oil protesters and the personal consequences of participating in a polarising movement. The jury described the film as “urgent and brave”.

Buckley said it had prompted her to reconsider the role of protest in society. “In our world at the moment, protest seems like such a dangerous act, when historically it’s been essential to democracy,” she said. “It realigned me and reminded me of how important protest is, and how we can misunderstand the people within that. That we need to understand more and need films like that more.”

Olive Nwosu won for Lady, her feature debut set in Lagos, which follows one of the city’s few female taxi drivers as she becomes drawn into the world of a childhood friend who has become a sex worker. The jury praised Nwosu’s cinematic ambition and her handling of challenging material.

Imran Perretta was recognised for Ish , a black-and-white coming-of-age film set in Luton’s South Asian and Middle Eastern community. It follows two 12-year-old best friends whose relationship is tested after a police stop and search. The jury praised its exploration of racial profiling and the experience of being British while being treated as an outsider.

Rachel Taparjan won for Something Familiar, her debut feature documentary about her search for her missing sisters after being adopted from Romania and brought to the UK as a child. The jury praised the film’s “naked, unselfconscious revelation of self”, saying it had stayed with them longest.

Christie said the strength of this year’s field meant the jury had concluded it “couldn’t just select three winners”.

The awards, which celebrate creative audacity and ambition, have run since 2022. Previous recipients include Harry Lighton, whose film Pillion won best British independent film at the British independent film awards in 2025, and Savanah Leaf, who received the 2024 Bafta for outstanding debut by a British writer, director or producer.

content.article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : LA-based producer-financier Christa Campbell has launched film, TV and media company XTA Media , which has seed funding from London and Denmark-based private investment firm Three Thousand Capital.

Campbell’s credits as a producer and exec producer include Hellboy , Rambo: Last Blood , The Iceman , Leatherface , The Hitman’s Bodyguard , The Hitman’s Wife’s Bodyguard , Texas Chainsaw 3D , Tesla , Red Sonja , and the Oscar-nominated documentary Winter on Fire: Ukraine’s Fight for Freedom .

Until recently the former actress ran Campbell Grobman Films with Lati Grobman.

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Everything We Know About 'The Gilded Age' Season 4 So Far

List Of Hollywood & Media Layoffs From Paramount To Warner Bros Discovery To CNN & More

According to Campbell, the new company comes with a sizeable capital injection and will acquire IP, develop original and adapted material, finance productions, and produce content for film, TV and other media platforms.

Campbell’s upcoming projects include the new John Rambo film and the KISS biopic , Shout It Out Loud , set up at Lionsgate.

“I started XTA Media to build a company that owns its stories from the first idea to the final cut,” said Campbell. “Having this level of capital in place from day one lets us go after the projects we believe in, whether they’re big franchises or original voices, on our own terms. Three Thousand Capital understands both the creative and business sides of this industry, and they’re the right partner to build with.”

Since 2012, Three Thousand Capital has completed more than 100 direct private investments in entertainment, music, the platform economy and big tech. Early stage investments have included Uber, Airbnb, Shazam, SoundCloud, Duolingo, Spotify and X (Twitter). The firm is also developing a feature film in Scandinavia, slated for theatrical release in 2027.

“Christa has a rare track record of turning major IP into global hits while also championing films that matter, like Winter on Fire ,” said Michael Peen of Three Thousand Capital. “We’ve spent more than a decade backing founders who reshape their industries, and XTA Media is exactly that kind of opportunity. We’re very excited about this new venture and proud to be a founding partner.”

content.article_text:
Open Studios

Red Hook Open Studios Rises From the Ashes

Dispelling fears that last year's blaze pushed artists away for good, this year's edition proved that the Brooklyn neighborhood’s artistic community is as strong as ever.

Hyperallergic )

Red Hook’s arts community is nothing if not defiant in the face of tragedy.

Nearly 13 months after a five-alarm fire scorched part of a historic Van Brunt Street warehouse, the Brooklyn waterfront neighborhood's open studios festival returned for its 11th year on October 10 and 11.

Some artists displaced by the fire have come back to the area too, moving into studios in nearby buildings closer to the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway. But the Civil War-era structure remained under a partial vacate order , with an unsightly green sidewalk shed surrounding part of the block just before the pier.

When festival co-coordinator Deborah Ugoretz distributed flyers promoting the event a few weeks ago, some residents told her they were surprised it was still happening.

“They assumed that all the artists and makers in Red Hook were affected by the fire, but there are still hundreds of makers and artists here,” Ugoretz, whose studio a few doors down avoided fire and water damage, told Hyperallergic .

content.article_text:
Steve Hilton , the Republican contender for California governor, rolled out a plan Wednesday to revive Hollywood production that includes increased tax credits and state-backed financing for studio repairs.

Hilton, who is trailing Democrat Xavier Becerra in the polls, had previously promised to eliminate the $750 million cap on the state’s film incentive and to include actors’ salaries and other “above the line” costs in the program.

Related Stories

Bradley Whitford on Bringing Back ‘The West Wing’ as a ‘Limited Series’

'The Social Reckoning' Soundtrack Features New Music From Composer Alexandre Desplat

In an expanded plan shared with Variety , Hilton offered additional details and also included an extensive proposal to support soundstage modernization.

Popular on Variety

“No governor can reverse every decision made by an entertainment company, nor should a governor try to micromanage private businesses — or indeed the structure of a fast-changing industry,” the plan states. “But California’s government is responsible for the costs and bureaucracy it imposes on people trying to work here, and for its response to competitive pressures from other places.”

Becerra has issued his own position paper for the entertainment industry, but it is shorter on details. He has refused to be pinned down on whether he would eliminate the cap on the state tax incentive, saying instead that he will wait to see what proposals come out of the state legislature. Both candidates have acknowledged the dramatic downturn in production jobs over the last four years — some 52,000 statewide — and vowed to take steps to address it.

Both are also supportive of a federal film incentive, which was introduced in Congress last month, that would create a 20% tax credit on all U.S. labor costs.

California currently offers a 35% tax credit on all below-the-line costs for films and TV shows that are chosen by the state film commission, with bonuses that go up to 45%. Productions must apply for credits at periodic intervals, and sometimes the program is oversubscribed and unable to accept new applications.

In his plan, Hilton said he will offer a 40% state tax credit for production. He also floated the idea of going as high as 50% for a period of five years. By eliminating the $750 million cap, Hilton also proposes to make California credits automatic, creating stability and predictability for productions, though at an unknown cost.

“Steve will replace narrow application windows with continuous rolling approvals,” the plan states, adding that productions should get an answer within 30 days.

The proposal also includes a sales tax exemption for five years on building materials needed for studio construction, as well as state-backed bond financing for studio acquisition and renovation.

Gov. Gavin Newsom approved a $150 million incentive to boost soundstage construction in 2021. That funding has since been depleted, and there has not yet been a discussion about whether to allocate additional money to it. Los Angeles soundstages are at just 62% occupancy, according to the latest FilmLA report, though new stages continue to open.

Hilton also pledges to include commercials, documentaries and reality TV — all currently excluded from eligibility.

content.article_text:
Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography, a new exhibition at Tate Modern, showcases the history of pictorialism and how it expanded the possibilities of photography as an art form

A serene landscape showing splashing white ducks who seem to merge seamlessly with the babbling water, shadowy trees looming like dark mountains. This photograph, part of Tate Modern’s exhibition Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography , was taken by Liu Bannong in 1927 after the Chinese photographer returned from studying linguistics in Paris, where pictorialism was pursued by artists running their own salons, and publishing magazines on art photography. Pictorialism was the first move towards proclaiming photography an art form yet, until now, its impact on image-making practice in south-east and south Asia has been relatively unknown. The Tate’s exhibition fills these lacunae by looking at this movement as transcontinental.

Pictorialism was initially theorised by English photographer Henry Peach Robinson, whose 1869 instructional book Pictorial Effect in Photography urged image-makers to follow the order and composition in painting, rather than simply documenting reality. Armed with such influences Bannong produced a text of his own – Bannong tanying (‘ Bannong’s Comments on Photography’ ) – which drew from the aesthetic discourse of traditional Chinese painting. It argued for photography as an expressive medium revealing an inner world of emotion. This dialogue was continued by others, including Long Chin-San, whose essay Photography and Chinese Painting (1955) advised ‘choosing’ the good parts of a photograph, emulating the approach of traditional Chinese art.

“Contemporary photographic art is where it is today due to the efforts by pictorialists to carve out a space for photography within fine art” – Charmaine Toh, curator

The ‘selection’ Chin-San referred to is seen in Singaporean Lee Sow Lim’s early work, which uses layers of photo negatives to arrive at a single image. Transferring an ethereal quality from Chinese ink paintings into photographic imagery, Sow Lim even stamped the results with a traditional painterly red seal. His later works are abstractions in colour – Singaporean artist Tan Lip Seng’s works were figurative but, created with layers of high contrast and highly saturated colour transparencies, were equally innovative. Not all pictorialists were in favour of manipulated images. British writer and photographer PH Emerson favoured naturalism, controlling light and composition to create beauty – as did Singaporean Yip Cheong Fun, in his portraits of fishermen and children.

None of this was happening in isolation, but within photo clubs and salons in south-east and south Asia with an interest in pictorialism that continued long after modernist photography had taken over in the West. Many camera clubs had initially started as forums for colonial officials and local amateur photographers, building information for British administrators; Photographic Societies of Bombay (1854) and Bengal (1856) conducted ethnographic studies, for example. But, points out Charmaine Toh, senior curator of international art (photography) at the Tate and curator of the Tate Modern show, “these clubs started at a time when most of south-east Asia was on the verge of independence”, and pictorialism for many offered a deviation from the surveying gaze. It also allowed the opportunity to showcase worldwide as these salons had access to journals with details for open calls.

While pictorialism changed the language of ethnographic photography in Elli Sougioultzoglou-Seraidari’s images of refugees in Attica in the mid-1920s, it also allowed photographers in the colonies alternative approaches to self-representation. They set up other societies, such as the Photographic Society of India (1937), co-founded by mill-worker Dhirajlal R Mody, or the Photographic Society of Ceylon (1935) by Sri Lankan photographer Lionel Wendt. Wendt’s portraits of the male body in the 1930s and early 1940s introduced fluidity and homoeroticism, depicting men far beyond their castes and professions. The images departed from the buttoned-up ethnographic representations – though Toh warns against drawing easy conclusions, pointing out that the body was still performing in Wendt’s work, re-rehearsing privileged stereotypes.

“Some photographers would continue using colonial ‘tropes’, like photographing someone in a sarong in Malaysia, to get accepted into exhibitions overseas,” explains Toh. “It was a certain agency as they played up to Western expectations and then won awards at international salons. This was important to see themselves as entering a new era of postcolonial modernity.” Wendt sent his works to London or Paris, the colonial centres at the time; even so, his works and images by others have not been included in the history of pictorialism.

“Piecing together this history is on-ground work and opening boxes,” says Toh, whose research included meeting with photographers’ families to find long-lost archives and prints. “The RPS Collection became a major resource as these photographers would send their prints to London for the RPS annual exhibition – and didn’t ask for them back,” she adds. “Behind these prints is an entire history of where it has travelled to, even between countries who weren’t getting along diplomatically.”

And, while pictorialism arguably never went away, contemporary preoccupations with the ideology of a certain photographic gaze, or with questioning the medium more generally, owe much to these predecessors. “Contemporary photographic art is where it is today due to the efforts by pictorialists to carve out a space for photography within fine art,” reflects Toh.

Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography is at Tate Modern , London, until 21 February 2027.

照片公司孟买(1854年)和孟加拉(1856年)进行的民族学研究,例如。“这些俱乐部在东南亚大部分处于独立边缘时开始了”,许多人对图像主义提出了从调查中脱离的偏见,这也允许在全球范围内展出,因为这些展览会有访问开放通话的详细信息的杂志。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ID_003_Liu-Bannong-The-Suburb-1927.-Private-Collection.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "原名:The Suburb, 1927 © Liu Bannong.", "credit": "British Journal of Photography", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在1920年代中期,图像主义改变了以色列摄影的语言,而在1920年代中期埃利·苏吉奥·佐格卢·塞拉达里(Elli Sougioultzoglou-Seraidari)的图像中,它也允许殖民地的摄影师采取替代自我代表性的方法,他们建立了其他社会,如印度摄影协会(Indian Photographic Society,1937年),由千工人Dhirajlal R Mody共同创立,或斯里兰摄影师Lionel Wendt(Sri Lankan Photographic Society,1935年)的塞隆摄影协会。1930年代和1940年代初的男性身体的肖像引入了流动性和同性恋,描绘了男人远远超越他们的作品和职业。 这些图像从按钮上传的种族形象中脱颖而出 - 尽管托赫警告不做出轻松的结论,指出身体仍然在温特特的工作中表现出来,重新听到特权的类型。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“一些摄影师将继续使用殖民地的“天花板”,如在马来西亚的萨龙里拍摄某人,以接受海外展览,”Toh解释道,“这是一个特定的机构,因为他们符合西方的期望,然后赢得了国际展览会的奖项,这很重要,认为自己进入一个新的殖民后现代时代。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“把这个故事聚集在一起是地面工作和打开盒子,”Toh说,他的研究包括与摄影师的家人会面,寻找长期丢失的档案和印刷。 “RPS收藏成为一个重要的资源,因为这些摄影师将他们的印刷到伦敦为RPS年度展览 - 并没有要求他们回来,”她补充道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "虽然画家主义可能从未消失,但当代对某种摄影气体的意识形态或对媒体更普遍的质疑的担忧,对这些先驱有很大的债务,“当代摄影艺术是因为画家们在美术中为摄影创造一个空间而努力,而现在是因为它在美术中创造了一个空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "光与魔法:艺术摄影的诞生在伦敦泰特现代,直到2027年2月21日。", "links": [{"text": "Tate Modern", "url": "https://www.tate.org.uk/"}], "translated": true}]

content.article_text:
Ava DuVernay ‘s “14th” will open the 12th edition of San Francisco’s documentary film festival Doc Stories on Nov. 5.

The Netflix film, which premiered at New York Film Festival earlier this month, is one of 10 Oscar-contending feature documentaries included in Doc Stories’ lineup. Others include J.M. Harper’s “Soul Patrol,” Sam Pollard’s “Tutu” and James Marcus Haney’s “Black Sunflowers.”

Related Stories

‘A Few Good Men’ on Broadway: Aaron Sorkin, Bradley Whitford and Team Behind Revival on Why It’s ’So Fucking Relevant’ in Trump Era

Aaron Sorkin Says It ‘Never Occurred’ to Him That Jesse Eisenberg Wouldn’t Play Mark Zuckerberg in ‘The Social Reckoning,’ Claims the Paycheck Was a ‘Disincentive’

The four-day festival put on by SFFILM will feature 11 short documentaries, including Joshua Oppenheimer’s “The Revolution Against Death,” about an aging community and its eccentric efforts to achieve immortality, and Oscar winner Laura Poitras ’ “They’re Here,” about ICE agents’ descent on Minneapolis.

Popular on Variety

“For over a decade, Doc Stories has embodied the best of what SFFILM and the San Francisco Bay Area champion and celebrate in new documentary work,” said SFF Film’s executive director Anne Lai, “Each film is a wonderful portal into better understanding the world we live in. When daily life can feel quite bruising and fractious, documentaries skillfully encourage us to let our guard down and connect with real-life stories and people… sometimes challenging, often invigorating, and always meaningful.”

Since its inception, Doc Stories has attracted the who’s who of the nonfiction community. This year, filmmakers including DuVernay, Pollard, Poitras, Luke Lorentzen, and Ben Proudfoot will attend the prestigious Bay Area event, considered the key Oscar season campaign stop in Northern California. Over two dozen Doc Stories selections have earned Academy Award nominations, and several, including “No Other Land” and “Summer of Soul,” have won.

“This year, I found myself drawn to filmmakers who are looking closely at the forces shaping our lives, while also revealing the humor, beauty, resilience, and contradictions within them,” said SFFILM’s director of programming Jessie Fairbanks. “These are documentaries I believe deserve to be seen, talked about, and experienced together — and I’m thrilled to share them with our audiences.”

Running Nov. 5-8 at the Vogue Theatre, the festival will feature three Doc Talks, including a 60-minute conversation with Poitras and her “They’re Here” co-director, Rachel Lauren Mueller. The duo will discuss making “They’re Here” and the challenges they faced while embedding themselves in a Minneapolis community during a wave of ICE raids.

Beyond the public program, SFFILM’s artist development team will convene Doc Congress, a day of dialogue and networking for filmmakers, funders, and industry professionals. This year’s Doc Congress includes a group discussion on AI use in documentaries featuring Srđan Keča, director of Stanford’s MFA in Documentary Film, and Rachel Antell, co-founder of the Archival Producers Alliance. Artist Development will also host an inaugural Pitch Forum for three local filmmakers.

From Nov. 2-10, SFFILM’s Education team will host students and teachers at Schools at Doc Stories, featuring free screenings at SFMOMA, online classroom programs and filmmaker Q&As. The program includes three selections from the main festival, eight additional programs featuring work by Oscar winners Ben Proudfoot and Vanessa Roth, a showcase of films by Berkeley High School students and a teen filmmaking workshop led by Proudfoot. Doc Stories will conclude on Nov. 8.

Opening Night: “14th” THU, NOV 5 AT 6:30 PM PT Ava DuVernay (USA 2026, 107 min) Ava DuVernay examines the enduring promises of the 14th Amendment through a powerful chorus of voices, joining us in person to discuss this vital new documentary.

All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea SAT, NOV 7 AT 5:00 PM PT Jeanie Finlay (UK 2026, 99 min) When a massive sea life die-off threatens his livelihood, lifelong fisherman Stan Rennie rallies his community in a quest for answers, becoming the unlikeliest of activists.

Black Sunflowers

SAT, NOV 7 AT 8:00 PM PT James Marcus Haney (Ukraine 2026, 97 min) Executive produced by Sean Penn, James Marcus Haney’s kinetic, kaleidoscopic portrait of Ukrainian youth is alive with movement, color, and music. Filmed over four years the camera follows artists, drifters, soldiers, and friends as they find pockets of freedom amid mounting uncertainty.

Boatbuilders SUN, NOV 8 AT 4:30 PM PT Luke Lorentzen (USA 2026, 103 min) A visually stunning ode to impeccable craftsmanship and the beauty of Maine, Luke Lorentzen’s latest documentary profiles the workers of Brooklin Boat Yard, a company building custom wooden yachts since 1960.

Citizen Osama SUN, NOV 8 AT 11:30 AM PT Ahmed Hassouna (Palestine, France 2026, 71 min) A photographer turned war reporter documents life in Gaza while raising his newborn son, confronting the impossible challenge of bearing witness to catastrophe while protecting those he loves.

Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been FRI, NOV 6 AT 8:30 PM PT Barry Avrich (Canada 2026, 118 min) The extraordinary singer Darlene Love has lived a big life with its concomitant ups and downs, and this film covers them all as Love herself charts her career, always leading with joy and humor, featuring Cher, David Letterman, Bruce Springsteen, Dionne Warwick, and many more.

Soul Patrol SAT, NOV 7 AT 2:00 PM PT J.M. Harper (USA 2026, 100 min) This moving, creative, and seminal documentary depicts the final reunion of an all-Black six-man patrol team in Vietnam, ensuring that their courage and experiences are not lost to history.

Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing SUN, NOV 8 AT 1:30 PM PT Erik Shirai (Japan, USA, UK, Denmark 2026, 99 min) Erik Shirai cinematically captures the spectacle of strength that is the world of professional sumo wrestling, and shines a rare spotlight on the secrecy of the sport and its formidable competitors.

Closing Night: Tutu SUN, NOV 8 AT 7:30 PM PT Sam Pollard (UK 2026, 102 min) A revelatory portrait of Desmond Tutu, the beloved South African archbishop whose fearless moral voice, infectious humor, and unwavering commitment to justice helped reshape a nation and inspire generations.

Doc Talks: Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller Total Runtime: 60 min SAT, NOV 7 AT 1:30 PM PT Join us for an intimate and candid fireside conversation with filmmakers Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller, who will discuss the challenges they faced while embedding themselves in a Minneapolis community during a wave of ICE raids in their film, They’re Here.

Doc Talks: Jeanie Finlay, Luke Lorentzen, and Erik Shirai Total Runtime: 60 min SAT, NOV 7 AT 3:30 PM PT Doc Talks continues with filmmakers Jeanie Finlay (All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea), Luke Lorentzen (Boatbuilders), and Erik Shirai (Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing), as they discuss the cinematic power of observational storytelling and their unique approaches as both directors and cinematographers.

Doc Talks: Sam Pollard and J.M. Harper Total Runtime: 60 min SUN, NOV 8 AT 2:30 PM PT Doc Talks’ final gathering profiles the esteemed and prolific Sam Pollard and rising star J.M. Harper. Pollard and Harper will discuss their newest features, Tutu and Soul Patrol, and their processes of excavating history, culture, and politics in their work.

Community Screening: Title to Be Announced THU, NOV 5 AT 3:30 PM PT Join us for a community screening of a very special documentary from a notable local Bay Area filmmaker that takes viewers behind the scenes of a major film production. The title of the film will be revealed in late October. Free and open to the public. Attendees must RSVP for tickets at sffilm.org.

Shorts Block: New York Times Op-Docs Total Runtime: 99 min FRI, NOV 6 AT 5:45 PM PT Films are in alphabetical order rather than order of play.

The Ones Who Stay Olivier Côté, Jean-François Bouchard (Canada, Cuba 2026, 22 min) Amid a national migration crisis, four young Cuban artists go against the tide and choose to stay.

The Revolution Against Death Joshua Oppenheimer (Denmark, Sweden 2026, 23 min) Joshua Oppenheimer gazes into the world of an aging community and their eccentric efforts to achieve immortality.

Son Leona Cauklija (Sweden 2026, 13 min) A Swedish mother’s love knows no bounds, using graffiti to track down her long lost son.

The Tuners Paweł Chorzępa (Poland 2026, 23 min) Distinguished tuners work tirelessly to achieve perfect pitch for their instruments at a renowned piano competition.

A Wolf in the Suburbs Amélie Hardy (Canada 2026, 18 min) A Mississaugan man revives his former Olympian mindset in a fight to preserve his lawn’s overgrowth.

Shorts Block: Sensory Experience Total Runtime: 100 min FRI, NOV 6 AT 3 PM PT Films are in alphabetical order rather than order of play.

Chuuraa Evgenia Arbugaeva (UK 2026, 18 min) A Sakha scientist journeys into Siberia’s melting permafrost, where the past emerges alongside ancestral beliefs.

Listen Taliesin Black-Brown (USA 2026, 15 min) As memory fades and nature changes, an Alaskan sound recordist listens closely to what remains.

Pelo Lindo Josue Garcia Prado (Guatemala 2026, 24 min) Decades after her son’s forced disappearance, a Guatemalan mother’s enduring faith keeps his memory alive.

Still Standing Victor Tadashi Suárez, Livia Albeck-Ripka (USA 2026, 10 min) After the Eaton Fire, Altadena residents confront toxic contamination in homes insurers insist are safe to inhabit.

They’re Here Laura Poitras, Rachel Lauren Mueller (USA 2026, 25 min) When masked ICE agents descend on Minneapolis, neighbors mobilize, tracking the movements of officers to protect one another.

You Do Not Exist Dwayne LeBlanc (USA 2026, 8 min) Beneath passing planes, a man reflects on memory, belonging, and the paths not taken.

Teen Workshop: Creating Untold Stories Total Runtime: 120 min SAT, NOV 7 AT 1 PM PT Join Ben Proudfoot, two-time Academy Award®-winning filmmaker and the founder and CEO of Breakwater Studios, for a teen-centered documentary workshop.

content.article_text:
Oscar winners and Oscar-nominated filmmakers will be converging on San Francisco for the 12 th edition of Doc Stories, the prestigious nonfiction film festival put on by SFFILM .

The cinematic event running November 5-8 will open with 14 th , Ava DuVernay’s penetrating examination of threats to the protections and rights afforded by the 14 th Amendment. The festival closes with Sam Pollard’s Tutu , a profile of the South African archbishop, anti-Apartheid activist and Nobel Peace Prize winner.

Scroll for the complete lineup of films and talks.

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

SFFILM's Doc Stories Attracts Nonfiction Cinema's Top Talents For Tightly Curated Event, With Big Impact On Oscar Race

Doc Talk Podcast: Deep Dive With 'A Life Illuminated's Tasha Van Zandt And Leaders Of SFFILM's Doc Stories Festival

Among other prominent filmmakers heading to Doc Stories: Oscar winner Laura Poitras with her short documentary They’re Here , co-directed with Rachel Lauren Mueller; two-time Oscar nominee Joshua Oppenheimer with his short film The Revolution Against Death ; three-time Oscar winner Sean Pean with the Ukraine war-themed film he executed produced, Black Sunflowers , and Oscar-shortlisted filmmaker Luke Lorentzen with his latest, Boatbuilders . Two-time Oscar winner Ben Proudfoot will lead a documentary workshop for teen filmmakers.

“For over a decade, Doc Stories has embodied the best of what SFFILM and the San Francisco Bay Area champion and celebrate in new documentary work,” commented Anne Lai , SFFILM’s executive director. “Each film is a wonderful portal into better understanding the world we live in. When daily life can feel quite bruising and fractious, documentaries skillfully encourage us to let our guard down and connect with real-life stories and people… sometimes challenging, often invigorating, and always meaningful. It’s a privilege to bring filmmakers, industry, and audiences—including kids—together for this annual celebration.”

Since 2015, Doc Stories has been the gathering point for the Bay Area’s documentary community, the festival notes, with a program that reliably features standout nonfiction work from around the world. More than two dozen Doc Stories selections have gone on to earn Academy Award nominations, and several have won.

“Curating Doc Stories is one of the great privileges of my job because I get to spend the year seeking out films that I can’t wait to put in front of an audience,” said Jessie Fairbanks , SFFILM’s director of programming. “This year, I found myself drawn to filmmakers who are looking closely at the forces shaping our lives, while also revealing the humor, beauty, resilience, and contradictions within them. These are documentaries I believe deserve to be seen, talked about, and experienced together—and I’m thrilled to share them with our audiences.”

In addition to the public program, SFFILM’s Artist Development team will convene Doc Congress, a day of dialogue and networking for filmmakers, funders, and industry professionals. “This year’s Doc Congress includes a dynamic group discussion on AI use in documentaries featuring Srđan Keča, director of Stanford’s MFA in Documentary Film, and Rachel Antell, co-founder of the Archival Producers Alliance. Artist Development will also host an inaugural Pitch Forum for three local filmmakers. Guest filmmakers will cap off the weekend at Sunday’s annual Doc Stories Brunch.”

From November 2–10, SFFILM’s Education team will host students and teachers at Schools at Doc Stories, with free in-person screenings at SFMOMA, online programs for classrooms nationwide, and conversations with visiting filmmakers that connect to classroom studies and spark curiosity about the wider world.

Doc Stories screenings take place at the Vogue Theatre in San Francisco’s Presidio Heights neighborhood. Below is the program lineup (listed in alphabetical order, with Opening and Closing Night films first and last).

Opening Night: 14th

THU, NOV 5 A T 6:30 PM PT

THU, NOV 5 A T 9:30 PM PT

Ava DuVernay (USA 2026, 107 min)

Ava DuVernay examines the enduring promises of the 14th Amendment through a powerful chorus of voices, joining us in person to discuss this vital new documentary.

All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea

SAT, NOV 7 A T 5:00 PM PT

Jeanie Finlay (UK 2026, 99 min)

When a massive sea life die-off threatens his livelihood, lifelong fisherman Stan Rennie rallies his community in a quest for answers, becoming the unlikeliest of activists.

Black Sunflowers

SAT, NOV 7 A T 8:00 PM PT

James Marcus Haney (Ukraine 2026, 97 min)

Executive produced by Sean Penn, James Marcus Haney’s kinetic, kaleidoscopic portrait of Ukrainian youth is alive with movement, color, and music. Filmed over four years the camera follows artists, drifters, soldiers, and friends as they find pockets of freedom amid mounting uncertainty.

Boatbuilders

SUN, NOV 8 A T 4:30 PM PT

Luke Lorentzen (USA 2026, 103 min)

A visually stunning ode to impeccable craftsmanship and the beauty of Maine, Luke Lorentzen’s latest documentary profiles the workers of Brooklin Boat Yard, a company building custom wooden yachts since 1960.

Citizen Osama

SUN, NOV 8 A T 11:30 AM PT

Ahmed Hassouna (Palestine, France 2026, 71 min)

A photographer turned war reporter documents life in Gaza while raising his newborn son, confronting the impossible challenge of bearing witness to catastrophe while protecting those he loves.

Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been

FRI, NOV 6 A T 8:30 PM PT

Barry Avrich (Canada 2026, 118 min)

The extraordinary singer Darlene Love has lived a big life with its concomitant ups and downs, and this film covers them all as Love herself charts her career, always leading with joy and humor, featuring Cher, David Letterman, Bruce Springsteen, Dionne Warwick, and many more.

Doc Talks: Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller

Total Runtime: 60 min

SAT , NOV 7 A T 1:30 PM PT

Join us for an intimate and candid fireside conversation with filmmakers Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller, who will discuss the timeliness of their film, They’re Here about a Minneapolis community during a wave of ICE raids.

Doc Talks: Jeanie Finlay, Luke Lorentzen, and Erik Shirai

Total Runtime: 60 min

SAT , NOV 7 A T 3:30 PM PT

Doc Talks continues with filmmakers Jeanie Finlay ( All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea ), Luke Lorentzen ( Boatbuilders ), and Erik Shirai ( Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing ), as they discuss the cinematic power of observational storytelling and their unique approaches as both directors and cinematographers.

Doc Talks: Sam Pollard and J.M. Harper

Total Runtime: 60 min

SUN, NOV 8 A T 2:30 PM PT

Doc Talks’ final gathering profiles the esteemed and prolific Sam Pollard and rising star J.M. Harper. Pollard and Harper will discuss their newest features, Tutu and Soul Patrol, and their processes of excavating history, culture, and politics in their work.

Community Screening: Title to Be Announced

THU, NOV 5 A T 3:30 PM PT

Join us for a community screening of a very special documentary from a notable local Bay Area filmmaker that takes viewers behind the scenes of a major film production. The title of the film will be revealed in late October. Free and open to the public. Attendees must RSVP for tickets at sffilm.org.

Shorts Block: New York Times Op-Docs

Total Runtime: 99 min

FRI, NOV 6 A T 5:45 PM PT

(Films are in alphabetical order rather than order of play).

The Ones Who Stay

Olivier Côté, Jean-François Bouchard (Canada, Cuba 2026, 22 min)

Amid a national migration crisis, four young Cuban artists go against the tide and choose to stay.

The Revolution Against Death

Joshua Oppenheimer (Denmark, Sweden 2026, 23 min)

Joshua Oppenheimer gazes into the world of an aging community and their eccentric efforts to achieve immortality.

Son

Leona Cauklija (Sweden 2026, 13 min)

A Swedish mother’s love knows no bounds, using graffiti to track down her long lost son.

The Tuners

Paweł Chorzępa (Poland 2026, 23 min)

Distinguished tuners work tirelessly to achieve perfect pitch for their instruments at a renowned piano competition.

A Wolf in the Suburbs

Amélie Hardy (Canada 2026, 18 min)

A Mississaugan man revives his former Olympian mindset in a fight to preserve his lawn’s overgrowth.

Shorts Block: Sensory Experience

Total Runtime: 100 min

FRI, NOV 6 A T 3 PM PT

(Films are in alphabetical order rather than order of play).

Chuuraa

Evgenia Arbugaeva (UK 2026, 18 min)

A Sakha scientist journeys into Siberia’s melting permafrost, where the past emerges alongside ancestral beliefs.

Listen

Taliesin Black-Brown (USA 2026, 15 min)

As memory fades and nature changes, an Alaskan sound recordist listens closely to what remains.

Pelo Lindo

Josue Garcia Prado (Guatemala 2026, 24 min)

Decades after her son’s forced disappearance, a Guatemalan mother’s enduring faith keeps his memory alive.

Still Standing

Victor Tadashi Suárez, Livia Albeck-Ripka (USA 2026, 10 min)

After the Eaton Fire, Altadena residents confront toxic contamination in homes insurers insist are safe to inhabit.

They’re Here

Laura Poitras, Rachel Lauren Mueller (USA 2026, 25 min)

When masked ICE agents descend on Minneapolis, neighbors mobilize, tracking the movements of officers to protect one another.

You Do Not Exist

Dwayne LeBlanc (USA 2026, 8 min)

Beneath passing planes, a man reflects on memory, belonging, and the paths not taken.

Soul Patrol

SAT , NOV 7 A T 2:00 PM PT

J.M. Harper (USA 2026, 100 min)

This moving, creative, and seminal documentary depicts the final reunion of an all-Black six-man patrol team in Vietnam, ensuring that their courage and experiences are not lost to history.

Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing

SUN, NOV 8 A T 1:30 PM PT

Erik Shirai (Japan, USA, UK, Denmark 2026, 99 min)

Erik Shirai cinematically captures the spectacle of strength that is the world of professional sumo wrestling, and shines a rare spotlight on the secrecy of the sport and its formidable competitors.

Teen Workshop: Creating Untold Stories

Total Runtime: 120 min

SAT , NOV 7 A T 1 PM PT

Join Ben Proudfoot, two-time Academy Award®-winning filmmaker and the founder and CEO of Breakwater Studios, for a teen-centered documentary workshop.

Closing Night: Tutu

SUN, NOV 8 A T 7:30 PM PT

Sam Pollard (UK 2026, 102 min)

A revelatory portrait of Desmond Tutu, the beloved South African archbishop whose fearless moral voice, infectious humor, and unwavering commitment to justice helped reshape a nation and inspire generations.

New York–based gallery Salon 94 will expand its footprint to Paris, where it will open a permanent space facing the Jardin du Palais Royal on October 18. Located at 30 Galerie de Montpensier, the 323-square-foot space will be inaugurated by a solo exhibition for Deborah Roberts , running through November 28.

“Artists really led us to think about a space here,” Fabienne Stephan, Salon 94’s European director who will be leading the space, told ARTnews . “Artists love presenting their work in the architecture and the history of the city.”

For the past three years, Salon 94 has been testing out the Paris market, hosting exhibitions at different spaces near the Palais Royal. The first two, staged in collaboration with Devals gallery, were solos for Kennedy Yanko in 2023 and Marina Adams in 2024, while last year’s group show was also staged at 30 Galerie de Montpensier, when it was the Paris outpost of Villa Atrata, a gallery in western France.

“Paris has been wonderful,” Salon 94 founder Jeanne Greenberg Rohatyn said in an interview, noting that Yanko’s exhibition resulted in a solo show at the Cité de l’Architecture et du Patrimoine this year that is part of Art Basel Paris’s public program. “They came, they looked very carefully, they bought. So, the test worked for us.”

Greenberg Rohatyn also found in Paris a welcoming environment to show both art and design, the latter of which is the focus of Salon 94 Design. “The city treats art and design as one conversation. It’s in the DNA of the city itself, so that also works for us and our program in Paris,” she said.

Beyond the recent pop-up shows, Salon 94 and Salon 94 Design also have a history with French and Paris-based artists, representing the estate of Niki de Saint Phalle and Rick Owens Furniture, which is managed by his partner Michèle Lamy. At Design Miami Paris, the gallery will show Owens’s work alongside furniture and bronzes by Alberto and Diego Giacometti, as well as pieces by Peter Schlesinger, Urs Fischer, and F Taylor Colantonio.

When thinking of where to set up shop, Greenberg Rohatyn said the gallery was looking for an “intimate space” that would be centrally located. They considered some of Paris’s gallery clusters, like the Marais and Avenue Montaigne in the 8th arrondissement, but ultimately settled on the Palais Royal, which offers a “very Parisian experience.” Though commercial galleries might be only slightly farther afield, the Fondation Cartier, the Louvre, and the Bourse de Commerce are all steps away.

“Part of Salon 94 has always been to take a pilgrimage somewhere,” Greenberg Rohatyn explained. “We really do like this idea of discovery—that the body moves through a city or the streets in order to find us.”

She also noted that the Paris space will be visible from the street 24/7, a callback to Salon 94’s previous space on the Bowery, which featured an external screen that was activated by artists like Marilyn Minter and Takeshi Murata. “I love this idea of rubbernecking when you pass by something and then you have to turn back and go see it again,” Greenberg Rohatyn added.

Choosing a more modestly scaled space also gives Salon 94 more flexibility in terms of its program, according to Stephan, who noted that exhibitions at the much larger New York space are often in the works for at least two years. “We wanted to have an exhibition space that allowed us and the artists to react quickly—and it could almost function like a teaser for New York for a larger show later,” she said.

“Artists can achieve a lot in a small space,” Greenberg Rohatyn added, noting that one gallery artist has already reached out with a vision for a spring show in the Paris space. “It’s not only intimate; it’s the type of space that you can take in one breath or one glance at first, and then, of course, [find] things hidden around.”

Roberts’s upcoming exhibition will feature several of her signature collage-based works, including What the water kept (2026), which lends its name to the exhibition’s title. The first work that visitors will encounter, What the water kept features a Black girl wearing a fish-patterned top standing under an umbrella.

“What’s very special about Deborah’s show is that she has thought a lot about this crossing of the Atlantic,” Greenberg Rohatyn said. “The young girl, as she makes her crossing of the Atlantic, with all of the history from the perspective of a Southern Black woman, she’s protected this time by the umbrella.”

content.article_text:
The Weitzman National Museum of American Jewish History in Philadelphia is being considered as a potential new member of the Smithsonian museum network, with members of a new congressional commission sworn in on Tuesday set to study the matter.

As reported by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency , Philip Darivoff, a former longtime chair of the Weitzman and current chair of the new commission, and Dara Horn, a writer serving as vice chair, “said that the Weitzman joining the Smithsonian would send a powerful message that Jews are a crucial component of the history of the country.”

Darivoff told the JTA , “It’s a different statement that our country makes when it says that the study of Jewish American history and culture is important to this nation,” and both commission members hope possible inclusion in the Smithsonian network could help stem what they called an “epidemic of ignorance” about Jewish history and culture.

The prospect of the Weitzman joining the Smithsonian dates back to legislation passed by the Biden administration in 2024 to establish the congressional commission. Now, after having been sworn in, the commission has two years to study the matter—“though Darivoff said he hopes to finish the work well before the deadline,” according to the JTA .

The Weitzman National Museum of American Jewish History was founded in 1976 and is currently a Smithsonian affiliate, which means it can share resources with other museums in the network. Current offerings there include a new “immersive family experience” called Colors of Creation, an exhibition titled “The First Salute: An Untold Story of the American Revolution,” and a core exhibition covering history dating back to the 1600s, “when the first permanent Jewish settlers came to the New World from Brazil.”

content.article_text:
Sian Heder’s Oscar winner CODA felt like a movie out of time. It was the kind of broad crowd-pleaser that Miramax would have released to awards success a couple of decades earlier, which I would argue only triumphed with the Academy as voters were quietly nostalgic for the kind of American indie that disappeared alongside the Weinsteins. It certainly didn’t hold up to scrutiny as a lived-in, authentic account of the deaf community, with its simplistic and reductive attempt to chronicle their many challenges feeling too distractingly like an outsider’s perspective when framed through the audience surrogate of the family’s non-hearing-impaired daughter. For Heder to follow it with a tale more explicitly about disability-rights activism naturally got my alarm bells ringing, but Being Heumann does a far better job balancing its audience-satisfying instincts with an embedded perspective of its characters’ everyday struggles, never allowing the viewer to feel on the outside looking in.

Adapted from disability-rights activist Judith Heumann’s autobiography of the same cringily punning name, Being Heumann isn’t quite the movie that’s been advertised. If you’ve seen the marketing that’s boasted the awkward tagline “based on a true revolution,” you’ll be primed to expect a movie far more triumphant than what’s delivered, which, even with its Miramax-reminiscent prestige tone (you can imagine their awards campaign asking voters to “honor the woman, honor the film”), isn’t naive about the limitations of the rights enshrined into law here. Structured around the 28-day sit-in Heumann (Ruth Madeley) organized at the Department of Health offices in San Francisco in 1977, its narrative is centered on the activist’s quest to ensure Section 504 of the 1973 Rehabilitation Act would be signed by lawmakers. It was the first federal civil-rights protection for people with disabilities, ensuring no government-funded program would receive money if seen to discriminate, but it hadn’t been ushered into reality years after being written. Successive governments kept kicking the can down the road due to the multi-billion-dollar cost of making every federal building accessible, and nothing about Jimmy Carter’s administration suggested otherwise in its early days.

Even if you weren’t previously aware of the activist’s efforts, you know how this ends; wheelchair-accessible ramps have been commonplace in public spaces for so long, most of us probably haven’t considered there was a fight to get them there in the first place. Naturally, it feels like we’re being primed for a triumphant finale when health secretary Joseph A. Califano (Mark Ruffalo) finally signs the legislation, but Heder never loses sight of the bigger picture. Her protagonist doesn’t pause to celebrate any win, and she asks her audience to follow suit, self-aware that each milestone legal breakthrough doesn’t mark a happy ending and that there are still vast inequalities decades later which need to be reckoned with. It’s a celebration of the woman and fellow activists who helped bring these civil-rights issues to the able-bodied world’s attention, but never positions them as anything more than the first domino which needed to fall. This is an admirably unusual approach for a triumphalist crowd-pleaser, as is the characterization of Heumann as someone who was very difficult even for her fellow advocates to deal with, often asking them to overlook the needs of their own medical conditions for the sake of continuing their protest.

Maybe the biggest success of Being Heumann is how it approaches the topic of disability-rights intersectionality and the difficult conversations that arise from balancing the needs of people with different conditions that seem opposing. Again, we know how these tensions began to be resolved, but there’s a fascination to seeing them dramatized. At their most strongly realized, debates amongst the protesters about how to ensure their disparate needs come to fruition and which other organizations are safe to ally with are reminiscent of the tense administrative town hall meetings between the AIDS activists in Robin Campillo’s BPM . The movie is far too polished and Hollywood to invite further comparisons to that stellar piece of work, but the brief glimpses show that Heder and co-screenwriter Rebekah Taussig are following that film’s lead in ensuring the wide variety of lived-in perspectives are given equal time to be heard.

This approach also extends to the way they feel reluctant to outwardly depict Califano as a cartoonish villain, instead dramatizing him as more of an establishment weasel who is only reluctant to sign legislation because he expects to be fired for greenlighting such a costly program. He’s not opposed to the expansion of civil rights to aid the disabled, but prioritizes his job security over signing the dotted line, constantly arguing that marching in Selma with MLK is proof of his overall good intentions. Judging from the current state of the Democratic party, especially in the recent Joe Biden administration, his platitude-driven inaction has proven influential to a new class of career politicians, and a stronger movie would take a more cynical approach here. It’s refreshing that his characterization is more developed than a one-note villain, reflecting the real bureaucratic obstacles Heumann had to contend with, but this is still a broad crowdpleaser that’ll likely wind up in Barack Obama’s end-of year list; the better version of this story would reflect the stasis in civil rights breakthroughs even after Heumann served in his administration.

Some side characters also feel underdeveloped––Dylan O’Brien’s reporter Evan White goes from dismissive and vaguely prejudiced to an active supporter seemingly offscreen, between scenes––but it’s easy to argue that, like Heumann herself, the movie is ultimately too focused on the bigger picture to afford them much weight. It still manages to be rousing despite these flaws, the familiarity of its comfortable tone making it easier to commend the ways it breaks from the Miramax formula. This isn’t a naive depiction of a triumph against the system, but rather a small, hard-won administrative victory within a system that kept putting up new roadblocks long after it passed. In that regard, it’s about as grounded as a Hollywoodized iteration of this narrative could be.

Being Heumann screened at the 2026 BFI London Film Festival and opens in theaters on November 6 and arrives on Apple TV on November 13.

content.article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Disney and NBCUniversal accused Midjourney of being a “bottomless pit of plagiarism” in a lawsuit last year . More than 18 months on, the company allegedly has failed to clean up its act.

VN. ai , a tech startup that stress tests generative artificial intelligence tools for copyright infringement, has produced its first quarterly report examining how 15 popular AI models performed when it comes to flouting studio IP.

Related Stories

Disney Offers $20M For Character.AI Assets As Startup Files For Chapter 11 Bankruptcy Protection

YouTuber Gossip Goblin Releases Trailer For R-Rated AI Theatrical Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’

The research conducted last month found that Midjourney v8.1 was the worst offender when it came to reproducing images of copyrighted characters. The AI model also outranked competitors on so-called “brand safety violations,” meaning characters were placed in a “harmful context,” such as scenes of violence or drug taking.

RELATED: Sora Is Coming, Sora Is Here, And Hollywood Is Sore

Watch on Deadline

According to VN.ai’s report, which was shared with Deadline, Midjourney reproduced images of characters that violated brand safety measures once in every three text prompts, or 37% of the time. This included a Midjourney v8.1 hallucination in which it generated an image of The Joker smoking cannabis while wearing a dress that could have been ripped from the wardrobe of Frozen’s Elsa.

Midjourney did not respond to requests for comment. Disney and NBCUniversal’s lawsuit against the company remains ongoing, and Warner Bros Discovery also has filed suit . The startup has argued that training its AI models on images of copyrighted material is permitted under fair use.

VN.ai’s report found that every AI model generated at least one copyright-protected character, even when a character’s name was not referenced in a text prompt. This included Google’s Nano Banana and ByteDance’s model Seedance 2.5, though the latter has improved significantly after receiving cease-and-desist letters from Hollywood studios.

As noted recently by Deadline, other Chinese AI models continue to plunder IP , including MiniMax H3, which generated videos that violated studio brand safety standards 55% of the time when an image was used in a prompt.

Asked why AI models continue to flout copyright, VN.ai founder Nelson Chu said it was “good for business.” He added: “It’s great marketing. It works. It gets people to use your model and pay for it.”

Chu predicts change, however. “I do think at some point that’s just not going to be OK. And I think as more models set the precedent for how it is to be a good actor here, you will see more improvement,” he told Deadline.
