content.article_text:
On his campaign website, Xavier Becerra has a page devoted to Hollywood. The 1,600-word policy statement is long on platitudes — “California Is the Home of Film and TV and We Intend to Keep It That Way” — but short on concrete promises.

It may also have been written with artificial intelligence. According to Pangram, a widely used AI detector, “100% of this text is AI,” though the campaign denies it.

Related Stories

Lego's 'Heartlake the Musical' Heads to Peacock in the U.S., Tencent in China Amid Global Sales (EXCLUSIVE)

'Hatchet' Movie: Netflix and Derek Cianfrance to Adapt Gary Paulsen's Survival Book (EXCLUSIVE)

“These AI assessors are notoriously inaccurate,” said Jonathan Underland, Becerra’s spokesman.

Popular on Variety

Becerra is cruising toward the California gubernatorial election with a 20-point lead in the polls and a 96% chance of victory in the prediction markets. He has denied most requests for interviews and has avoided making firm commitments on a range of issues from AI to housing to electric vehicles.

On the campaign trail, he has turned his lack of promises into part of his pitch.

“It’s easy when you’re a candidate to make all sorts of promises. It’s harder to prove you can deliver,” he said at a stop in Glendale on Monday. “Vote for someone who knows how to deliver, because the promises go away after Election Day.”

Introducing Becerra to the crowd, Assemblyman John Harabedian offered a similar line: “He is someone who will underpromise and overdeliver.”

Assuming he is elected, Becerra will face immediate calls to expand the state’s incentive for film and TV production, now capped at $750 million a year. Even if Congress passes a federal film incentive, state lawmakers argue that California must do more to compete for film jobs. Attorney General Rob Bonta has said he will sponsor a bill to eliminate the cap entirely.

“We do need to, early next year, take steps to strengthen it,” said Rick Chavez Zbur, the Burbank Assemblyman who is one of Hollywood’s best allies in Sacramento. “A number of us have wanted to uncap the program for some time.”

Another proposal is to include “above the line” salaries — actors, directors, etc. — in the program. Such ideas would cost money — maybe a lot of money — and would have to be reconciled with the state’s other fiscal priorities.

How would Becerra do that? At the event on Monday, the candidate was not much more definitive than his website.

“I will support anything that will help us keep Hollywood in Hollywood,” he said. “We have to fight for this industry.”

Asked whether he supports eliminating the $750 million cap or including “above the line” costs, he was noncommittal.

“I’ll sit down with all the legislators to see what kind of proposals are put before us,” he said. “But we’re going to fight.”

Becerra’s Republican opponent, Steve Hilton , has vowed to eliminate the cap and to include above-the-line costs. According to Pangram, Hilton’s film policy was also written by AI, though because it is shorter and mostly made up of bulleted lists, rather than complete sentences, it is harder for Pangram to analyze. (The Hilton campaign declined to comment.)

Becerra’s film platform includes some of the tells of AI writing, such as the “it’s not this, it’s that” construction: “California did not just produce the film industry. It built it.”

Ironically, it also endorses a state mandate for AI disclosure by productions.

Underland said that AI was not used to brainstorm or develop the platform in any way.

“We don’t do that,” he said. “We don’t talk to AI about policy. We talk to people about policy.”

Pangram claims a false positive rate of 1 in 10,000, and claims the tool is especially accurate when reviewing political speeches, with human writing flagged as AI 0.0% of the time. Independent research has also backed up Pangram’s accuracy.

Last month, the Economist used Pangram to analyze parliamentary speeches, finding that 10% of the words spoken in the British Parliament were drafted with AI. AI use was also prevalent in Australia, Canada and the U.S. When the speakers were asked about it, the most common response was “surprise and denial,” the publication reported.

The Hilton campaign has used AI to create campaign ads , and has disclosed that usage in accordance with state law . In one such ad, an AI-generated Becerra endorses the idea of sending out a “vague policy tweet” — “Great idea, but keep it vague like all the other ones. Not too much detail.”

Becerra’s campaign has said it does not use AI in its videos, and has criticized Hilton’s “AI slop.” The state AI disclosure requirement covers audio, video and images, but does not extend to text.

At the campaign event, Becerra denied that his policy statement was AI-generated.

“No,” he said, “that’s absolutely incorrect.”

content.article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Ron Perlman is still man of action. The indefatigable Hellboy and Sons Of Anarchy star, now 76, has half a dozen films in production, and next year is aiming to play Hemingway in a new biopic set in Cuba and will co-star in the anticipated Sons Of Anarchy spinoff Legends .

A year on from Deadline announcing the launch of Perlman’s Asylm Studios banner, we caught up with the veteran actor (who made his screen debut almost 50 years ago) and the company’s co-founder Willie Morris about their indie slate and Perlman’s anticipated studio projects.

DEADLINE : Ron, we almost met at the Venice Film Festival last month. I gather you were at the festival with a new project of yours called Sedona, but it wasn’t in the official lineup…

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

'Grey's Anatomy' EP On How Harry Shum Jr. Juggles Medical Drama & 'Dancing With The Stars' & If It Affects His Presence On ABC Show

'Line Of Fire' Gets Backup Script Order As Lisa Katz Talks NBC Fall Rollout, 'Newlyweds' Exit, 2027 Pilot Season, Peacock Strategy & 'Dungeon Crawler Carl'

RON PERLMAN : Yeah, that’s right. Willie can touch on that project specifically…

WILLIE MORRIS : We just kicked off a partnership with Google and 100 Zeros [Google’s JV with Range]. We recently launched a teaser for Sedona on our new YouTube channel and we used some of their tech to give it depth, so that you could view it with VR glasses or spatial glasses if you wanted to as an additive feature.

PERLMAN : Last year I got to know Google VP Jon Zepp [VP Partnerships, formerly Managing Director of Entertainment Content] after I did the Doug Liman immersive film Asteroid . So he invited us along to the festival where they were doing some work in the immersive section. To me, Venice symbolizes a connection that’s temporarily lost, because it symbolizes the glamor and scope and pageantry of the way we used to enjoy our cinema.

DEADLINE : It’s a great festival for sure…So Google put money into Sedona?

MORRIS : Google put some money into our indie project, which is in post, and then in return we used their technology to create spatial videos that’ll appear on some of their launch campaigns with the glasses. So they they wanted some spatial content and to support the arts, and we needed some funds to help get this little indie movie up and going.

PERLMAN : Sedona won’t be ready for close to a year. But Google has been helpful in the launch of our YouTube channel. I’ve been evolving with regards to the intersection of tech and Asylm Studios. Tech isn’t something you can run away from, but it is something you can use as an enhancement to exploring the human experience.

DEADLINE : A.I. has been one of the hot-button topics of late. You recently acted in a short called The Ride that used A.I. I take it you’re not against working on projects that use A.I.?

PERLMAN : My barometer will always be whether the AI. is the tail that’s wagging the dog. If it is, I’m not interested. I’m not interested in any technology that replaces the unique contribution of the human heart and the human soul, but I am fully bracing myself for a way to use these new technologies to our advantage. Asylm is a celebration of conventional filmmaking, and and an extension of the shoulders upon which we stand. But everything that we’ve done here at Asylm just came out of the blue. It was like a punch in the nose. It was like that with our first movie, Kodak Super XX and with Sedona , which are both in post-production.

We wanted to create an environment where artists, particularly filmmakers, could flourish and have an opportunity to spread their wings with very original contributions to what has always been an edgy, dangerous and original art form, which has lost its way because streaming has diminished the pageantry and the scope of the space that cinema once occupied. Ours is basically a mandate to go back and and create an environment where that can happen as a norm rather than as as an aberration. At Asylm, we will try to be as much of an old legacy studio where we not only produce, but we also want to market and distribute our own films. Theatrical is the engine upon which everything else is based and it’s an incredibly potent revenue stream.

We don’t have the infrastructure or the war chest yet to to do all of the things I’m describing, but the dream is to become a full strength studio where we we make the movie and we put the movie out and we control all facets of its life all the way down to its last stop, which happens to be home entertainment.

DEADLINE : Do you have backers or is the company funded by yourself?

PERLMAN : We are in the process of building the war chest, but we’re a way off accomplishing that. It takes time. We have two movies in post and two or three others in development, and a TV series and a documentary.

DEADLINE : We’ve previously covered Kodak Super XX with David Dastmalchian and Kelly Marie Tran. Tell us about Sedona. There’s not so much online about that one. Lili Simmons stars, right?

MORRIS : Lili Simmons, Israel Broussard, Nicholas Cirillo from Outer Banks , and Toby Sandman from Running Point . I joke that it’s The White Lotus on acid, but it’s about an actress who meets a very average guy, convinces him to come to Sedona for the weekend, and then her and her friends pretty much gaslight him for the entire weekend. It’s a bit of a fever dream psychological horror, and it’s very fun. Meanwhile, Kodal Super XX — which is likely to be called Super XX ultimately — is being submitted to festivals at the moment.

DEADLINE : What’s going into production next?

PERLMAN : I was recently filming in Ireland on Amazon MGM and Blumhouse-Atomic Monster’s horror movie Seasons . But for Asylm, it’s a foot race between two projects that we came to the party with. One is a Hemingway project, which has a look at Hemingway in his last couple of years, everything leading up to his suicide. It’s when he’s beginning to lose everything. That’s a project that’s very close to starting production. And then there’s a comedy called Auxiliary Man , which is a Tarantino-esque comedy, essentially because it’s a lot of white guys speaking ebonics, thinking they’re gangsters when they’re nothing but losers and bodies are dropping left and right, but you’re always realizing that you’re watching a comedy. It’s a crazy ass script, and that’s close to getting into production as well.

DEADLINE : It’s the centenary year of The Sun Also Rises’ publication, so there have been various Hemingway events globally. And I have covered other projects about Hemingway towards the end of his life. Would you play Hemingway and what sets this one apart?

PERLMAN : Asylm will produce. I’m playing Hemingway. I’m also co-directing the film with the celebrated Mexican DoP Gabriel Beristain, who is the guy who originally brought me to Cuba, and this is where I became infected with with this story and unable to get it out of my my psyche. After a decade, we’re finally going to make it very soon.

DEADLINE : I’ve always been a big fan of his work and like many, have been fascinated by his life. Even if he’s been more out of fashion in recent years for some of the ways he lived and thought …

PERLMAN : I don’t know a writer that doesn’t blurt that out. But we’re leaning into all of that. Look, he had a profound influence on the last century as an artist. And yet all of that was eclipsed by the man and how colorful and interesting he was. He caused a lot of debate and discussion, and he was polarizing. That’s what began to fascinate me. That and the fact that during his last years he he was at the vortex of the fall of Batista, the rise of Castro, and the wrath of J. Edgar Hoover.

DEADLINE : And he used to write standing up at an easel, right?

PERLMAN : He did, because he had back problems…

DEADLINE : Is this an original screenplay or based on a book?

PERLMAN : It was a story told to me by Cuban writer Enrique Cirules, who passed away a decade ago. He was obsessed with Hemingway and was his major biographer in Cuba, and had great access to parts of Hemingway’s life and psyche. The logline for the movie is ‘of all Hemingway’s mistresses, Cuba is the one that killed him’. So, when Enrique he told me the story about this perfect storm of Hemingway circling the drain, and then adding all of these political elements, all these psychological elements, all this paranoia where he thought J. Edgar Hoover was following him, which everybody thought was crazy at the time, but turned out to be true. It just was a story that I couldn’t get out of my mind.

DEADLINE : Is the Hemingway estate involved?

PERLMAN : The Hemingway estate is completely behind us. In fact, they’ve offered us his former home, the Finca Vigía, which is now a musem, for us to shoot in. We have the complete cooperation of many cultural players in Cuba. We have access to the La Bodeguita del Medio bar where he drank mojitos. We have access to the El Floridita bar, which he drank daiquiris in. We have access to the hotel Ambos Mundos where he wrote standing up, and he had two other rooms in the hotel that he had dalliances in. We have access to his famous boat Pilar. We have access to all of that.

DEADLINE : So what needs to happen next on the project?

PERLMAN : The dream was always to shoot it in Cuba. We’re figuring out if that’s possible. We have a backup plan to shoot in Spain if need be, but we’re hoping to make use of all these great places in Cuba.

DEADLINE : How does this fit with your schedule on Legends, the upcoming Sons of Anarchy spinoff?

PERLMAN : I’m trying to get Hemingway finished before we start filming Legends , which is slated to be sometime in March. I always wanted to film the Hemingway movie in January or February because it’s a little bit cooler in Havana, and after that it gets brutally hot and hard to wear prosthetics, which I obviously will do.

DEADLINE : How excited are you about Legends?

PERLMAN : I was blown away by what Charlie [Hunnam] was able to do there. I know how long he’s been floating this, and I know how hard it was to to get this boulder up the mountain, and the fact that he succeeded, and then the reaction on the internet was pretty singular. I don’t remember seeing anything that had more enthusiasm in terms of the way the world reacted to the news. We can’t wait to get back to work with with FX. John Landgraf, for me, was the greatest executive I’ve ever worked for because he has the the genius of an administrator, but the soul of an artist. The stories he has greenlit and made happen on his network I’ve never seen from an executive before.

DEADLINE : And you’ll be playing versions of yourself, right?

PERLMAN : Yeah. Believe me, having to audition for that was was humbling [laughs].

DEADLINE : Do you think Taylor Sheridan will be back for it? Your characters famously clashed in the first two seasons…

PERLMAN : Not over my dead body, motherfucker [laughs].

DEADLINE : You’ve read scripts?

PERLMAN : The only thing that’s been written so far is the pilot. Charlie is just assembling the writing room right now. When I get back, I’ll sit in and listen to things that are being bandied back and forth. But I’ve read a version of the pilot. I’m pretty sure it’ll evolve before we shoot in March in New Mexico.

DEADLINE : So it’s the same world and tone of Sons Of Anarchy or is it a departure?

PERLMAN : It’s both. It’s incredibly divergent initially, but it morphs into something that has the kind of outlaw danger aspect that Sons had.

DEADLINE : Sounds fun…And as for Asylm, will you be looking for investors in the company as you look to ramp up?

MORRIS : We haven’t officially gone our for a raise, but I think over the next couple months Ron and I will probably go down that path. We’ve been trying to figure out a way to bring industry figures in so that it’s not just traditional VCs and investors, but it’s more open to the people that we love.

DEADLINE : Finally, there’s always interest in your potential return to the Hellboy universe. Is that in any way possible? There have been non-studio/Guillermo Del Toro Hellboy movies since your last outing in the franchise 20 years ago…

PERLMAN : I’ve said so much about this and pissed off enough people, but I’ll say it again for you: the original movies were meant to be a trilogy. In Hellboy II , we left off at a very awkward moment where the Liz Sherman character is pregnant with twins, and none of the promises of Hellboy being summoned into existence to destroy the world has been addressed. That would all have been in the third film, and I’ll always advocate for the making of the third film. I’m not interested in doing any other version of Hellboy other than finishing the trilogy with Guillermo [Del Toro]. It would be so epic. Like a Greek epic. Hubris, hamartia, destiny, nature vs nurture, it would be such an adventure. I’m 76 now, and if he comes to me and I’m 86, we’ll still do the motherfucker.

DEADLINE : Do you still speak to Guillermo about doing it?

PERLMAN : No comment.

DEADLINE : Well, lot of fun things going on at Asylm and beyond.

PERLMAN : To borrow [and adapt] a phrase from Al Jolson, ‘you ain’t seen nothing yet’. We’re building a great thing at Asylm.

content.article_text:
After buying Brad Pitt’s Plan B Entertainment in 2022 and Peter Chernin’s North Road earlier this year, Mediawan has enlisted another major Hollywood player, Reese Witherspoon ‘s Hello Sunshine .

As with its previous acquisitions which were financed partly through stock, Mediawan is bringing Witherspoon into its shareholder base, joining a stellar roster of talent and producers who have invested in the Paris-based group, including Pitt, Chernin and Plan B partners Dede Gardner and Jeremy Kleiner, as well as See-Saw’s Iain Canning and Emilie Sherman. The company also launched LuckyChap International, the London-based arm of Margot Robbie’s company, last November.

Related Stories

'East of Eden' Hits 6.5 Million Views in Four Days on Netflix

David Fincher Ending Netflix Deal After Six Years and Three Movies, Including 'Cliff Booth'

“For our 10th anniversary today, we’re working with Brad Pitt, Margot Robbie and Reese Witherspoon — all three of whom are extremely creative and recognized as such — it defines the company’s DNA in terms of its independence, its commitment to talent and its creativity,” said Mediawan co-founder and chairman Pierre-Antoine Capton in an exclusive interview with Variety less than a day after unveiling the deal.

Popular on Variety

Mediawan also managed to pick up Hello Sunshine at a fraction of the $900 million valuation the company had when Blackstone-backed Candle Media acquired a majority stake in 2021.

Variety understands that Mediawan paid on the lower end of tens of millions of dollars, although Capton declined to disclose the exact figure or financial terms.

“I won’t confirm. The bottom line is that we acquired 100% of Hello Sunshine along with Reese and Mediawan, from Candle Media, and the money we’re investing is going toward development and content creation. It’s truly being invested in the company,” said Capton, who credited Chernin and Jesse Jacobs, former shareholders in Hello Sunshine, for bringing the opportunity to Mediawan.

The momentum has shifted in favor of European companies, as traditional Hollywood power players are under pressure to cut costs, streaming platforms are becoming pickier and U.S. indie producers are eager to work in Europe, where they can produce at lower costs and own IP. While Mediawan has made a name for itself in Hollywood in the last five years, another European giant with French roots, Banijay, which just merged with British powerhouse All3Media, is also looking to invest in the U.S. scripted market where it hasn’t yet broken through.

The acquisition of Hello Sunshine by Mediawan also illustrates how much the business has changed since the streaming boom that fueled Hello Sunshine’s previous valuation. Candle Media, founded by former Disney executives Kevin Mayer and Tom Staggs, had bet heavily on Witherspoon’s star power, social media presence and book club, but that model became more difficult to monetize in recent years.

On whether Hello Sunshine will fare better under Mediawan than it did under Candle, Capton pointed to the prestigious track record of Witherspoon’s company, notably “Big Little Lies,” “The Morning Show” and the Apple TV series “Lucky,” adapted from a Reese’s Book Club selection.

“They’ve really excelled creatively. That said, unfortunately, from time to time, there are investment deals with companies that may be perceived as financial strategies. That’s not the case for us,” said Capton, who worked on the deal alongside Mediawan CCO Elisabeth D’Arvieu and Guillaume Izabel, head of strategy and M&A. “With Reese, we’re really looking for creativity, independence and vision. That’s what interests us, so we don’t put financial pressure on it. It’s truly an editorial, artistic and creative addition that we’re seeking.”

Capton also said Mediawan intends to bring Reese’s Book Club internationally, including through potential productions in France and elsewhere in Europe.

“For all Mediawan producers — whether they’re Italian, German, British or Australian — access to all the IP that Reese can leverage through her book club is something very rare,” Capton said. “Yesterday, when we announced Reese and Hello Sunshine’s arrival at Mediawan, all our producers called us asking: ‘How can we work with them? How can we access the IP? How can we co-produce with them?’ There was a very strong desire from all our producers.”

“The goal isn’t for Reese to produce more herself, because she’s already produced a lot, but for this to also to fuel and create co-productions with our various producers. That’s what we’re hoping for,” he added.

Asked about the skepticism surrounding the Hello Sunshine deal, similar to the doubts raised when Mediawan acquired Plan B, Capton pointed to the latter’s recent hits.

“Plan B has produced ‘F1’ and ‘Adolescence’ last year. They’ve announced a pretty incredible lineup of series and films, so we’re very happy,” Capton said. “We had to trust each other, and it also took time to show what Mediawan was all about.”

Capton also sees further avenues for Mediawan to expand its footprint in the U.S. “We’re going to continue. Peter Chernin ’s arrival at the group has helped us become more ambitious, and with KKR’s support and the help of our local teams, we’re going to do something quite unique.”

While he declined to address rumors that Mediawan was one of the companies circling Lionsgate, he said, “In our model, the more we can distribute worldwide, the better off we’ll be. So, we’re looking at all possible opportunities.”

The French executive, who splits his time between Los Angeles and Paris, is also optimistic about the prospects for groups like Mediawan following the recent Paramount-Warner Bros. merger, even as Skydance prepares to make massive cuts.

“Skydance has committed to producing a certain number of films each year. I believe we have a company built on the creativity of our talent, and so, together, we’ll continue to develop and produce even more,” he said, pointing out that “Backrooms” (North Road), “Adolescence” (Plan B) and Florian Zeller’s “Bunker” (Blue Morning Pictures), starring Javier Bardem and Penelope Cruz, were made by producers who are part of Mediawan. He also revealed that the company will soon announce a major deal on vertical formats. “I’m convinced that these successes will only grow with our global consolidation,” Capton concluded.

content.article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Actress Eva Longoria has signed on to executive produce La Tierra del Valor (Home of the Brave) , the new film from L.A. Times Short Docs directed by award-winning filmmaker Cristina Costantini .

The documentary, which debuts Thursday on latimes.com/shortdocs, centers on Nezza, the Latina American pop star who bravely sang a Spanish-language version of the U.S. National Anthem at Dodgers Stadium last year even as ICE agents were causing an uproar in the city with immigration raids.

Watch the trailer for the documentary above.

Related Stories

Eva Longoria & Eugenio Derbez To Star In 'Marcelo In The Real World'

All The Songs In Prime Video's 'The Last Sunrise': Bad Bunny, Sabrina Carpenter, Sombr & More

“On June 14, 2025, as No Kings Day protesters filled the streets of Los Angeles, Nezza stepped onto the field at Dodger Stadium to sing the national anthem,” notes a release. “But instead of the traditional English version, she boldly performed ‘El Pendón Estrellado,’ a Spanish-language rendition commissioned in 1945 by President Franklin D. Roosevelt. It was a small but mighty act that gave a community hope when it needed it most; a declaration of belonging not just for the city’s Spanish-speaking communities, but for generations of immigrants who left behind the lives they knew in pursuit of something better for their children.”

Watch on Deadline

Costantini’s credits include Science Fair , co-directed with Darren Foster; Mucho Mucho Amor: The Legend of Walter Mercado (co-directed with Kareem Tabsch ), and Sally , her documentary about astronaut Sally Ride. La Tierra del Valor is produced by Costantini and Alfie Koetter, Costantini’s husband; together, they directed the award-winning 2022 short film The Originals .

“I was raised on a vision of America that families like mine could belong, could build, could live without fear,” Costantini stated. “Watching the promise of our country collapse as ICE agents continue to terrorize innocent people has been gutting. When so many have chosen the comfort of silence, though, Nezza chose courage. And in that moment, she made me proud to be an American again. I hope that Nezza’s story is a reminder to all of us that bravery isn’t reserved for politicians and those in power, but that it is the stuff of everyday people.”

Along with actress-filmmaker Eva Longoria, the film is executive produced by Cris Abrego and Rachelle Mendez of Hyphenate Media Group, the production company co-founded by Longoria and Abrego. They join are joined as EPs by the Muck Media team of Emmy Award winners Mariana van Zeller, Darren Foster, Jeff Plunkett, Alex Simmons and more.

“At a moment when ICE raids were tearing through Latino communities, Nezza stood on a national stage and reminded the world that being American has never been defined by asingle language or heritage,” Longoria observed. “By singing our national anthem in Spanish, she reclaimed a symbol of our shared identity and turned a moment of fear into a powerful declaration of belonging. I’m proud to join Cristina and the filmmaking team, especially as the violence and injustice Nezza stood against continue to terrorize communities across the country.”

L.A. Times Short Docs, now in its fourth season, is an Academy Award-winning series that “celebrates documentary filmmaking with a West Coast perspective… [showcasing] the work of established and emerging voices who break with convention and present undiscovered stories that challenge, move and inspire audiences.”

La Tierra del Valor (Home of the Brave) is presented by LA Times Studios and produced by Muck Media in association with DoctoraStories and Hyphenate Media. The film is directed and produced by Cristina Costantini, produced by Alfie Koetter, and edited by Mohammed El Manasterly. Music is by Jeff Morrow; the director of photography is Daniel Hollis Diamond, with additional photography by Keean Johnson.

Executive producers include Eva Longoria, Yuna Ma, Jihan Robinson, Mariana van Zeller, Jeff Plunkett, Alex Simmons, Darren Foster, Juan Arenas, Myrna Perez, Josh Albillo, Sarah Schoellkopf, Terry Tang, Anna Magzanyan, and Jason Spingarn-Koff.

Watch the trailer for La Tierra del Valor (Home of the Brave) above. It begins with Nezza at Dodgers Stadium being told she should sing the national anthem in English.

content.article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: It’s been called “beautifully crafted and meticulously composed,” praised by Werner Herzog, awarded at Sundance and honored with five Critics Choice Documentary Awards nominations.

On Wednesday, MUBI released the trailer for Nuisance Bear and announced the theatrical release plan for the documentary directed and filmed by Jack Weisman and Gabriela Osio Vanden : It will open in Los Angeles on November 6 and in New York, Canada and the UK on December 4. Watch the exclusive trailer above.

“For thousands of years, polar bears have migrated along the shores of Hudson Bay in northern Canada,” notes a synopsis. “Today, that ancient rhythm collides with a human world of tourism, surveillance, and control. Nuisance Bear immerses viewers in the experience of a polar bear forced to navigate tourists, wildlife officers, and hunters as climate change delays the freeze and pushes bears closer to human settlements. When a sacred predator is branded a ‘nuisance,’ it becomes unclear who truly belongs in this shared landscape.”

Related Stories

'A Long Winter': Watch First Trailer For Andrew Haigh Drama Starring Fred Hechinger, Ebon Moss-Bachrach, Caitríona Balfe & Kit Connor

New York Times Op-Docs Acquires 'The Revolution Against Death,' Oscar Nominee Joshua Oppenheimer's Film On Quest For Immortality

The filmmakers shot Nuisance Bear in Churchill, Manitoba, which calls itself the “Polar Bear Capital of the World.” “[W]ith striking intimacy and scale, the film observes bears that are constantly monitored, photographed, and redirected,” the synopsis continues. “In tracing this uneasy coexistence, Nuisance Bear becomes a meditation on how humans manage, commodify, and redefine wildlife—overturning the conventions of the nature documentary and reframing animals not as spectacle, but as active agents in a rapidly changing world.”

Watch on Deadline

The film is produced by Jack Weisman, Gabriela Osio Vanden, Will N. Miller, Teddy Leifer, and Michael Code.

“Ultimately, our aim is to collapse the distance between audience and subject,” Weisman and Vanden said in a statement. “By immersing viewers in the bear’s perspective while exposing the human forces shaping every step of its path, we challenge them to see this landscape, both natural and political, as a shared and increasingly contested space. Nuisance Bear invites us to reconsider who truly belongs here and what coexistence demands of all of us.”

Among the many awards for the film are the Grand Jury Prize for U.S. Documentary at the Sundance Film Festival, the 2026 Werner Herzog Film Award, the top prize from the Silk Road International Film Festival in China, and the James Balog Creative Vision Award at Mountainfilm in Telluride, CO. On Tuesday, it was nominated for Best First Documentary Feature, Best Science/Nature Documentary, Best Cinematography and two other awards for the upcoming Critics Choice Documentary Awards.

“From the time we saw the film, we were mesmerized by not only the incredible story of the nuisance bear, but what it says about humanity,” commented Arianna Bocco, Global SVP of Distribution and Acquisitions, MUBI. “The film is beautiful and profound – and we are thrilled to be working with Jack and Gabriela on their stunning feature debut.”

Nuisance Bear is edited by Andres Landau; Cristóbal Tapia De Veer composed the music. Mike Tunalaaq Gibbons narrates the film. Jack Weisman and Gabriela Osio Vanden serve as directors of photography, with additional cinematography by Sam Holling, Michael Code, Ian Kerr, and Jack Gawthrop. Executive producers include Nicole Stott, Emily Osborne, Harry Go, Nicole Quintero Ochoa, Eric Anoee, Joe Karetak, Alex Pritz, Moudhy Al-Rashid, Sam Frohman, Christine D’Souza, Julia Nelson, Adriana Banta, Emily Goldner, ZZ, and Mike Anders.

Watch the Nuisance Bear trailer above.

content.article_text:
DOC NYC announced its influential short lists Wednesday, often a reliable gauge of which documentaries are connecting with awards voters as Oscar season heats up.

Among the films making the festival’s short list of features: Ava DuVernay’s 14 th ; You Can See Everything , the Elizabeth Holmes-focused documentary directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim; Sundance winner To Hold a Mountain , directed by Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić, and Once Upon a Time in Harlem , directed by David Greaves. Two films centered on Gaza also made the short list: American Doctor , directed by Poh Si Teng, and NAZA , directed by Oscar winners Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.

Related Stories

DOC NYC Set To Honor Documentary Visionaries Alex Gibney, JT Takagi, Stephen Maing, And Raney Aronson-Rath

DOC NYC: Top Awards Go To 'Imago,' 'Traces Of Home,' 'The Pink Pill'

Scroll for the complete list of films to make the DOC NYC short lists for features and shorts. DOC NYC also announced films its Winner’s Circle and Selects Encore sections, completing the 2026 program. The festival runs in person from November 11-19 at IFC Center, SVA Theatre, and Village East by Angelika in New York City; it continues online through November 29 (with films available to viewers across the U.S.).

Watch on Deadline

DOC NYC’s Short List: Features selection committee is overseen by Artistic Director Jaie Laplante and Director of Special Projects Thom Powers.

“The Short Lists sections showcase a selection of nonfiction features and shorts that the festival’s programming team considers to be among the year’s strongest contenders for Oscars and other prizes,” notes a release, “while Winner’s Circle is a celebration of films already awarded at major international and U.S. film events that are worthy of additional consideration. Selects Encore showcases significant titles from DOC NYC’s year-round Selects screening series—films that continue to be part of our awards season conversations.”

Winner’s Circle screenings include the NYC premiere of Pegah Ahangarani’s Rehearsals for a Revolution — winner of the L’Œeil d’Or prize for Best Documentary at Cannes and the UK submission for Best International Feature Film at the Oscars – and Closure , Michał Marczak’s documentary that won the Golden Alexander at the Thessaloniki International Documentary Festival in Greece.

Among short documentaries making DOC NYC’s short list: The Baddest Speech Writer of All , directed by two-time Oscar winner Ben Proudfoot and NBA great Stephen Curry; The Boys and the Bees , directed by Arielle Knight; La Tierra del Valor (Home of the Brave) , directed by Cristina Costantini; They’re Here , directed by Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller; The Revolution Against Death , directed by Joshua Oppenheimer; The Tuners , directed by Pawel Piotr Chorzepa, and Water Cooler , directed by Emma V.F.

This year’s selections for Short List: Features are:

14TH

Director: Ava DuVernay; Producers: Ava DuVernay, Spencer Averick, Tammy Garnes, Paul Garnes

A powerful film essay exploring the legacy of the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

AMERICAN DOCTOR

Director: Poh Si Teng; Producers: Poh Si Teng, Kirstine Barfod, Reem Haddad

A visceral, unflinching film following three notable U.S. physicians as they provide in-person support at a Gaza hospital treating victims of mass-casualty events from the Israeli war campaign.

THE BEND IN THE RIVER

Director: Robb Moss; Producers: Lisa Remington, Kristin Feeley

A masterful meditation on the eternal, the temporal and the inevitable, from veteran filmmaker Robb Moss.

EVERYBODY TO KENMURE STREET

Director: Felipe Bustos Sierra; Producer: Ciara Barry

An uplifting portrayal of resistance focuses on an incident in 2021 when immigration officers conducted a raid on Glasgow’s Kenmure Street.

A FOX UNDER A PINK MOON (NYC Premiere)

Directors: Mehrdad Oskouei, Soraya Akhlaghi; Producer: Mehrdad Oskouei

A young, talented Afghan woman living under the thumb of the patriarchy in Iran channels her emotions into unforgettable expressions of art.

THE GREAT EXPERIMENT

Directors: Stephen Maing, Eric Daniel Metzgar; Producers: Stephen Maing, Eric Daniel Metzgar, Farihah Zaman

Traversing the U.S. from 2016 to 2020, patient observational filmmaking becomes a temperature check on American democracy—what George Washington described as the last great experiment in promoting human happiness in civil society. Co-director Stephen Maing will receive the Robert and Anne Drew Award for Documentary Excellence at this year’s DOC NYC Visionaries Tribute.

MUSK

Director: Alex Gibney; Producers: Alex Gibney, Jessie Deeter, Erin Edeiken, Zhang Xin, Joey Marra, Nick Shumaker, Jessica Grimshaw, Dana O’Keefe

An epic work profiling the world’s first trillionaire, Elon Musk. Director Alex Gibney will receive the Lifetime Achievement Award at this year’s DOC NYC Visionaries Tribute.

NAZA

Directors: Yuval Abraham, Rachel Szor; Producers: Harry Davies, Lindsay Poulton, James Wilson

Anonymous members of the Israel Defense Force candidly reflect on their attitudes toward civilian casualties, known as NAZA, and how they process the meaning of genocide.

ONCE UPON A TIME IN HARLEM

Director: David Greaves; Producers: Liani Greaves, Anne de Mare

A glorious night, capturing a vital period of American culture, when luminaries who had been active in the Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s recount their memories.

ONE IN A MILLION

Directors: Itab Azzam, Jack MacInnes; Producers: Will Anderson, James Bluemel, Andrew Palmer, Raney Aronson-Rath

A chronicle of one Syrian daughter’s journey in fleeing war and seeking refuge in Germany, and how over ten years, new pressures and opportunities present themselves.

SOUL PATROL

Director: J.M. Harper; Producers: Sam Bisbee, Danielle Massie, J.M. Harper, Nasir Jones, Peter Bittenbender

A hidden chapter of American military history—the Vietnam War’s first Black special ops team, an elite unit operating deep behind enemy lines.

TIME AND WATER

Director: Sara Dosa; Producers: Shane Boris, Elijah Stevens, Jameka Autry, Sara Dosa

A letter to the next generation by an Icelandic poet, reflecting on the melting glaciers that are a harbinger of climate change.

TO HOLD A MOUNTAIN (NYC Premiere)

Directors: Biljana Tutorov, Petar Glomazić; Producers: Biljana Tutorov, Petar Glomazić, Quentin Laurent, Rok Biček

In the remote highlands of Montenegro, the spirit of motherhood, the violence of men, and the sacredness of the mountain collide and reconcile.

WILD INSIDE

Director: Penny Lane; Producers: Gabriel Sedgwick, Nickolas Hasse

In 2023, Flaco the Eurasian Eagle Owl became an international folk hero and a mythological figure for a world in which so many find themselves living in circumstances far away from their roots.

YOU CAN SEE EVERYTHING

Directors: Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim; Producers: Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, Tatiana Bears, Maggie Ambrose, Jack Davis

As she prepares to begin serving her federal prison sentence, disgraced Silicon Valley tycoon Elizabeth Holmes continues to claim she has never lied, as America’s premiere absurdist documentarians record her every word.

SHORT LIST: SHORTS

The Short List: Shorts showcase of 15 titles is now in its ninth year at DOC NYC. The selection process is overseen by Artistic Director Jaie Laplante, Director of Special Projects Thom Powers, and consultant Samah Ali. In 2025, the showcase included All The Empty Rooms, which went on to win the Oscar.

This year’s selections for Short List: Shorts are:

THE BADDEST SPEECHWRITER OF ALL

Directors: Ben Proudfoot, Stephen Curry; Producers: Stephen Curry, Erick Peyton, Ben Proudfoot

At 93, Martin Luther King Jr. ‘s lawyer and speechwriter offers a living testament to history, and reminds us that silence is still our most urgent problem.

THE BOYS AND THE BEES

Director: Arielle Knight; Producer: Sean Weiner

On an idyllic farm in rural Georgia, beekeeping parents tenderly share their knowledge of life, love, and nature with their young sons while restoring their homestead.

BUCKSKIN

Director/Producer: Mars Verrone

A ground-breaking African-American and indigenous forester reflects on his life’s work of conservation and ancestral knowledge, while he approaches the twilight of his days.

A DERAILMENT

Director: Nathan Truesdell; Producers: Kat Nguyen, Will Lennon

A 2023 freight train derailment in rural Ohio corporate gives rise to a shocking new low in corporate maleficence.

THE GRANDFATHER PUZZLE

Director: Ora DeKornfeld; Producers: Zsofia Paczolay, Noémi Veronika Szakonyi, Máté Artur Vincze

Ora wants to better understand her aging grandfather before it’s too late. When she travels to Hungary to see if she can unlock the mysteries of his defense mechanisms, she finds a world left behind that illuminates a deep appreciation for life as it is now.

LA TIERRA DEL VALOR (THE HOME OF THE BRAVE)

Director: Cristina Costantini; Producers: Cristina Costantini, Alfie Koetter

In the face of growing antipathy towards immigrants, Latina pop star NEZZA makes the bold choice to perform the National Anthem at Dodger Stadium in Spanish, sparking an outpouring of outrage, support, and discussion about freedom of speech and who decides what ‘American’ means.

LISTEN

Director: Taliesin Black-Brown; Producers: Taliesin Black-Brown, Sam Davis, Greg Moga

An Alaskan sound specialist works for preservation within two levels of loss – the fading songs of wildlife disappearing from the wilderness, as climate change threatens natural populations; and his mother’s disappearing memory, as she slowly succumbs to dementia.

THE OATH

Directors: Liane Aviram, Louis Hollis; Producer: Liane Aviram

Dr Lina Qasem-Hassan, a Palestinian living and working in Israel, teaches medical ethics as well as practising as a physician – walking a tightrope of activism and professionalism while working through the trauma of her people.

ONE LAST ORDER

Directors: Lauren Defilippo, Sam Soko; Producers: Lauren Defilippo, Sam Soko, Amanda Pollak

After 37 years at Mac’s Drive-Thru in Gainesville, Florida, sunny and beloved Sighle is retiring. As customers travel from near and far to say goodbye, this heartwarming portrait celebrates an everyday worker who always went above and beyond, and the joy and community one person can inspire.

AN OPEN FIELD

Director: Teboho Edkins; Producers: Don Edkins, Carine Chichkowsky

One hundred and fifty seven people died when a new Boeing 737 MAX crashed in Ethiopia in 2019. While Boeing callously deflects blame for their negligence, a family of one victim finds strength in gathering collective mourning.

OUTPOSTS – NOTHING HERE IS YOURS

Director: Hilla Medalia; Producers: Hilla Medalia, Sheila Nevins, Yael Melamed

In the West Bank, Palestinian shepherd communities face escalating settler violence and displacement, while a group of Israeli activists stand in solidarity with shepherd communities as they struggle to remain on their land.

THE REVOLUTION AGAINST DEATH

Director: Joshua Oppenheimer; Producer: Signe Byrge Sørensen

A sharp, provocative look at the anti-aging industry and our increasingly elaborate efforts to resist mortality.

THEY’RE HERE

Directors: Laura Poitras, Rachel Lauren Mueller; Producers: Rachel Lauren Mueller, Laura Poitras, Yoni Golijov

A view of the evils of ICE through an organized resistance group of citizens in Minneapolis during the 2025-26 winter, using a unique cinematic language.

THE TUNERS

Director: Pawel Piotr Chorzepa; Producer: Joanna Chorzepa

Behind the scenes of Warsaw’s Chopin Festival, a group of expert tuners vie to achieve the perfect pitch so that the champion pianist will win on their instrument.

WATER COOLER

Director/Producer: Emma V.F.

In the halls of NYC’s immigration court, the casual chitchat of ICE agents waiting to arrest their unsuspecting targets stands in stark contrast to the horrors these detainees are likely to face.

WINNER’S CIRCLE

The DOC NYC Winner’s Circle for documentary features, introduced in 2019, highlights films that arrive at DOC NYC with significant awards pedigrees already in place. Past films shown in Winner’s Circle that all went on to further acclaim include Writing with Fire, The Mole Agent, A House Made of Splinters, Hollywoodgate, In the Rearview, Bad Axe, Midnight Family, and Advocate. To qualify for inclusion in this category, films must have won a major award at a significant international or US film festival.

This year’s selections for Winner’s Circle are:

AMERICAN PACHUCO: THE LEGEND OF LUIS VALDEZ

Director: David Alvarado; Producers: David Alvarado, Lauren DeFilippo, Everett Katigbak, Amanda Pollak

Against political resistance and industry skepticism, Luis Valdez pushes Chicano storytelling forward, creating iconic works that challenge, celebrate, and expand America’s story. Winner, Audience Award: U.S. Documentary and Festival Favorite Award, 2026 Sundance Film Festival

BUCKS HARBOR

Director: Pete Muller; Producers: Pete Muller, Nathan Golon, Noel Paul

Striking cinematography marks this observant, verite film about men in East Maine, the traditions of their elders, and their complex inner lives. Winner, Golden Eye Award for Best Documentary Film, 2026 Zurich Film Festival

CLOSURE

Director: Michał Marczak; Producers: Monika Braid, Rémi Grellety, Michał Marczak, Katarzyna Szczerba, Karolina Marczak

A haunting portrait of what it means to seek closure that’s a testament to parental love. Winner, Golden Alexander International Competition Award, 2026 Thessaloniki International Documentary Festival

AN EYE FOR AN EYE

Directors: Tanaz Eshaghian, Farzad Jafari; Producers: Christoph Jorg, Katayoon Arsanjani, Gelareh Kiazand, Joey Marra

A tense examination of Iran’s justice system and one family torn asunder by a legacy of abuse and mariticide, unfolding like a Shakespearean tragedy. Winner, Grand Prize Impact Documentary, 2026 Fipadoc

GIVE ME THE BALL!

Directors: Liz Garbus, Elizabeth Wolff; Producers: Liz Garbus, Elizabeth Wolff, Chris James, Dan Cogan, Dominic Crossley-Holland, Gentry Kirby

Billie Jean King, the iconic athlete who changed both the worlds of tennis and of women’s athletics, offers new perspectives on her legacy and the state of the sports world. Winner, Audience Award / Best Documentary Feature, 2026 Provincetown International Film Festival

NUISANCE BEAR

Directors: Gabriela Osio Vanden, Jack Weisman; Producers: Will N. Miller, Michael Code, Teddy Leifer, Jack Weisman, Gabriela Osio Vanden

The modern clash between human beings and polar bears takes on an ironic meaning when an Inuit elder shares his perspectives on the ancient belief and customs of his people. Winner, U.S. Documentary: Grand Jury Prize, 2026 Sundance Film Festival

REHEARSALS FOR A REVOLUTION (NYC Premiere)

Director: Pegah Ahangarani; Producers: Parnian Farnam, Pegah Ahangarani, Arash Ashtiani

Celebrated Iranian actor Pegah Ahangarani creates an essayistic documentary, weaving together home movies and news broadcasts to construct a vivid portrait of Iran’s modern history in the four decades since the revolution. Winner, L’Œil d’or Documentary Award, 2026 Cannes Film Festival

STEAL THIS STORY, PLEASE!

Directors: Carl Deal, Tia Lessin; Producers: Carl Deal, Tia Lessin, Karen Ranucci, Diana Cohn, Caren Spruch

Amy Goodman of Democracy Now! pursues the news with integrity and dauntlessness, seeing independent journalism as a major force for good. Winner, Greg Gund Memorial Standing Up Competition, Cleveland International Film Festival

SELECTS ENCORE

Selects Encore showcases a selection of films that screened at DOC NYC Selects, the festival’s ongoing screening series extension that runs annually from late winter through summer. The films chosen for Selects Encore represent works that continue to be present in the season’s awards conversations.

This year’s selections for Selects Encore are:

DAYLIGHT

Director: Jon Kasbe; Producers: Jon Kasbe, Zoe Rogovin

Serving a life sentence for murder, Joe Garcia finds unexpected refuge in Taylor Swift’s lyrics. When an essay he writes about love and music goes viral, it cracks open the past and rekindles a connection, opening the door to a life and love he thought were lost forever.

A LIFE ILLUMINATED

Director: Tasha Van Zandt; Producers: Tasha Van Zandt, Sebastian Zeck, Jessica Harrop, Kathryn Everett

A daring quest to document a bioluminescent phenomenon that could forever change how we understand life on Earth.

MANHOOD

Director: Daniel Lombroso; Producers: Kerry Mack, Rebecca Shaid

Manhood explores shame, sex, and the fragile myths of American masculinity, with dark humor and unexpected empathy.

MARY OLIVER: SAVED BY THE BEAUTY OF THE WORLD

Director/Producer: Sasha Waters

If poetry had a pop icon, Mary Oliver would be it, and Sasha Waters’ beguiling portrait is as poetic as its protagonist.

SCENES FROM THE DIVIDE

Director: Alison Klayman; Producers: Alison Klayman, Courtney Powell

A fierce battle among American Jews over identity, history, and responsibility is revealed in the homes of New Yorkers on both sides of Zohran Mamdani’s 2025 mayoral campaign.

THEYDREAM

Director: William D. Caballero; Producers: William D. Caballero, Brad Jones, Erin Ploss-Campoamor, Elaine Del Valle

A deeply personal documentary that examines the transformative nature of grief for a close-knit Puerto Rican family.

WHO MOVES AMERICA

Director: Yael Bridge; Producers: Yael Bridge, Jeremy Flood, Yoni Golijov, Mars Verrone

Examines the tense 2023 contract negotiations between UPS and its 340,000 unionized workers, as a microcosm for the larger struggles of labor justice in the U.S.A.

content.article_text:
“ Whalefall ” is an undersea thriller that would like to do for whales what “Jaws” did for sharks. But it doesn’t work out that way. The movie comes closer to doing for whales what “Howard the Duck” did for barnyard superheroes — it makes you never want to see one of them again. Whales, of course, are beautiful creatures, and the one in “Whalefall” is a sperm whale with the boxy shape of a submarine, long and angular, a sleekly gliding beast that rules the ocean. Yet for most of the movie, we’re inside that whale. Literally inside it. The central character, Jay Gardiner ( Austin Abrams ), has gone scuba diving off the coast of Monastery Beach near Monterey, Ca., in search of the body of his father, a gruff seaman who committed suicide. (He had mesothelioma, a form of cancer that meant he couldn’t dive anymore; for him, that meant life was no longer worth living.)

Related Stories

Disney Licenses Slew of Titles to Netflix, Including All Five 'Ice Age' Movies, 'Percy Jackson and the Olympians,' 'Felicity,' 'Will Trent,' 'Elio' and More (EXCLUSIVE)

After submerging himself, Jay gets entangled in the tentacles of a giant squid, and that’s when the whale, who feeds on squid, pulls both Jay and the squid into his oversize gaping mouth. Moments later, Jay is trapped inside, surrounded by gooey protrusions of undulating flesh. For the rest of the movie, he’ll attempt to survive inside that whale, which means keeping himself from getting sucked out of the creature’s digestive antechamber (which glows phosphorescent blue) and into its inner stomach cavity (which glows a hellish red), where the stomach acid will start to dissolve him.

Popular on Variety

For a moment, it occurred to me that Jay might run into his father, à la Jonah or Geppetto. But no, he’s on his own, doing all he can to escape this tight squeeze of whale flesh. Is it gross? At times. Claustrophobic? A bit. Scary? Not even a little. The place Jay finds himself looks like a colonoscopy designed by H.R. Giger. The visual effects are…okay. At times, it’s as if we were locked in some pop-up theme-park ride called Full Cavity Search. At one point, Jay uses a jellyfish the whale has eaten to light his way, and that’s as close as he comes to finding a companion. “Whalefall” is a fearless tale of human perseverance and mammalian stomach lining. It should have been called “Project Hail Fish Guts.”

Watching “Whalefall,” I kept thinking, “Why would anyone want to see this movie?” But the answer is obvious. “Whalefall” was adapted from Daniel Kraus’s 2023 novel, which in addition to being a bestseller was greeted with a great deal of acclaim. But something got lost in the translation. The thuddingly literal-minded movie that director Brian Duffield has made of it is a piece of thriller kitsch, full of unintentional laughs. With a hero who spends the heart of the film sucking on his oxygen mouthpiece, not so much talking as making frantic grunts of fear, “Whalefall” shuts us off from the most basic rooting interest. Sure, we want to see Jay get the hell out of there, but only because the whole ordeal is so stultifying and unpleasant.

It’s saying something that this is the second movie in a month where Austin Abrams has to fight his way out of the grip of fleshy tentacles, and only one of those movies isn’t terminally preposterous, and that’s “Resident Evil.” Abrams had an indie-hipster-on-the-run appeal in Zach Cregger’s horror hit, but in “Whalefall” he’s too wimpy by half, a simpering college kid who never proves to the audience that he has the right stuff. The film, like the book, takes off from the troubled relationship between Jay and his father, Mitt, played by Josh Brolin with a mean glare and body tattoos, in one of those brusquely overstated performances as an abusive macho dad — a Not So Great Santini who thinks the best way to prepare his son for what a tough world it is out there is to make the kid hate and respect him, in that order. As Brolin plays him, Mitt is like Robert Shaw’s Quint in “Jaws,” only ratcheted up several notches of boozy psycho masochism.

The film keeps jumping to flashbacks of Jay and Mitt at different points in their relationship, which is basically one long downhill slide. By the second half, though, Jay starts to realize that Mitt has actually taught him everything he needs to know to free himself from his predicament. The message? The young man who bonds with the ghost of his a–hole father while trapped in a gooey cushion of whale intestines stays with the ghost of his a–hole father. “Whalefall” even has an “ecological” side: The title refers to what happens when a whale’s carcass sinks to the ocean floor, an event that can give rise to a rich marine ecosystem. But “Whalefall,” the movie, is a carcass of a thriller that never rises.

Kim joins Netflix VP Film Doug Belgrad who also is departing as part of the layoffs.

content.article_text:
Art Review

Richard Dadd’s Strange and Delicate Worlds

Known primarily for his work of fantastical landscapes and mystical woodland creatures, a new retrospective tells the full story.

LONDON — Most British viewers know Richard Dadd from “The Fairy Feller’s Master-Stroke,” replete with its controlled chaos of subject matter and unavoidable depiction of a man suffering from mental illness. The diminutively scaled work, now in Tate Britain’s permanent collection and on view at the Royal Academy of Art’s retrospective exhibition, Richard Dadd: Beyond Bedlam , was painted between 1855 and 1864 and worked over repeatedly for nearly a decade while Dadd was incarcerated at Bethlem Royal Hospital. The work is filled with minutely detailed fantastical figures and fairies, overlaid ad infinitum under a web of flowers and grass blades that bisect its surface.

Dadd was born in 1817 in Chatham, England, worked during the Victorian era, and studied at the Royal Academy art schools. He was recognized as a leading talent among a group called The Clique , alongside other English artists such as Augustus Egg and William Powell Frith. But his biography is overshadowed by mental illness, which first became acutely evident on an expedition through Europe to Greece, Turkey, and Syria as a draftsman and culminated in a delusional episode in 1843 when he killed his own father and fled to France . After his arrest and return to England, authorities committed him to Bethlem Hospital's criminal department.

Though his meticulously realized, highly individualized output sits largely outside the historical canon, the Royal Academy wisely avoids treating their new comprehensive survey of Dadd’s career as outsider art. The exhibition also avoids psychological interpretation and refers visitors to the Bethlem Museum of the Mind, from which many pieces have been loaned, for further medical and historical detail about Dadd’s stay there.

content.article_text:
World sales outfit Filmotor has acquired the global sales rights to “Hazara Town,” the debut feature documentary by Khadim Dai. The film will have its world premiere in the International Competition at the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam, known as IDFA .

Filmed over six years, “Hazara Town” is a “chronicle of survival, exile and the bond of family,” Filmotor said. Forced from Central Afghanistan by the Taliban in 1998, Dai’s family sought refuge in a walled enclave in Quetta, Pakistan, where the Hazara community continues to face targeted violence. Following a 2013 school bombing that killed 126 people—including Dai’s classmates—his family urged him to flee.

Related Stories

'The Monster of Florence' Director Stefano Sollima on 'Completely Different' Second Chapter of Netflix's Hit Serial Killer Series: 'A Very Complex Story to Tell' (EXCLUSIVE)

Original ‘Willy Wonka’ Oompa-Loompa Rusty Goffe ‘Shed a Tear’ at Gene Wilder’s Voice Recreated by AI: ‘It Was Lovely Hearing It Again’

After four failed attempts to reach Australia by boat and years spent stranded in Indonesia, Dai returned to Quetta in 2019 to film his community before their stories faded.

Popular on Variety

The documentary captures the family’s daily life alongside their gradual, painful dispersal across the globe: his parents relocating to Canada, Dai and his niece taking refuge in the United States, and remaining relatives settling in Australia.

“Restrictions on filming kept my camera largely within the home, school and cemetery. I wanted to bear witness to the slow disappearance of my community,” Dai said. “Years from now, someone might find this film and come to know them. I cannot bring my classmates back or restore the years of family separation, but I can pass on something of their lives through cinema. That possibility kept me filming.”

The producing team said in a statement, “It is Khadim’s first feature film, but also the first film of its kind made in Quetta, a city in Pakistan far removed from the world’s gaze. We believe the film offers a rare opportunity to encounter the lives, experiences and perspectives of the Hazara people, who remain largely absent from cinema.”

“Having tracked ‘Hazara Town’ since its pitch at Sunny Side of the Doc in 2023, we knew immediately that this was a story the world needed to see,” said Petar Mitric from Filmotor. “Khadim Dai’s deeply personal lens captures raw, human emotion in a way that is both heartbreaking and essential.”

“Hazara Town” is produced by Ilyas Yourish for Congoo (Belgium), and co-produced by Khadim Dai, Graeme Isaac for Mayfan Films (Australia), and Anke Petersen and Lilian Tietjen for Jyoti Film (Germany).

The film will compete for the IDFA Best Film and IDFA Best First Film Award.

The project was developed with support from the Sundance Institute Documentary Film Program (with Open Society Foundations), the IDFA Bertha Fund Classic, Asian Cinema Fund, DMZ Industry (Special Jury Award), Docs Up Fund, Close Up Initiative, InMaat Foundation, Flanders Audiovisual Fund (VAF), MOIN Filmförderung Hamburg and Documentary Australia, among others.

content.article_text:
After starring in the blockbuster biopic “Michael,” Nia Long has joined the cast of Teyana Taylor ‘s directorial debut “Get Lite.”

The Paramount movie stars Emmy winner Storm Reid and NFL rookie-turned-actor Ceyair Wright. Wright (“Space Jam: A New Legacy”) plays a talented, but sheltered, dance student who finds inspiration, love and family in the last place he expected: the subways of New York City. Reid (“The Last of Us,” “Euphoria”) is the girl who opens his life to new possibilities.

Related Stories

'Sesame Street' Movie Set at Netflix, Plus 'Gabby's Dollhouse' Spinoff and 'KPop Demon Hunters' Game

Netflix’s Ted Sarandos on If He Sees Paramount-Warner Bros. As Competition, and If He Courted Casey Bloys: ‘We Had a Very Well-Publicized Lunch’

The role reunites Long and Reid after they co-starred in the hit 2023 thriller “Missing”; Long has also appeared in multiple projects for producer Kenya Barris, including his 2023 Netflix comedy “You People” and his 2020 series “#BlackAF.” She joins an acclaimed ensemble cast that features Leslie Odom, Jr., Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor, Jodie Turner-Smith, Asante Blackk, Woody McClain, Tylil James and Khayr Bullock.

Popular on Variety

Production on “Get Lite” is underway in New York City, with Taylor directing from a screenplay by Maurice Williams, based on a spec script by Eric Gross that appeared on the Black List in 2020. Paramount has slated the film for a wide theatrical release on Aug. 20, 2027.

In addition to starring in the film, Reid will produce alongside Barris and Anni Weisband for Khalabo Ink Society; Robyn Simpson for A Seed & Wings Productions, Reid’s banner; and Bill Karesh for Offbrnd. Taylor is also producing the film with Courtney “Coco” Gilbert, under their production banner, The Aunties.

Last month, Long, a four-time NAACP Image Award winner, received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame , literally cementing her status as a film and TV icon. She most recently starred in “Michael,” the blockbuster biopic about late pop star Michael Jackson, directed by Antoine Fuqua and produced by Oscar winner Graham King. The Lionsgate film grossed more than $1 billion worldwide, surpassing “Oppenheimer” as the highest-grossing biopic of all time. In the film, Long portrays Katherine Jackson, matriarch of the Jackson family, alongside Oscar nominee Colman Domingo as Joe Jackson and Jaafar Jackson, Michael Jackson’s nephew, as the king of pop.

Up next, Long executive produces and stars in the Netflix film “Don’t Ever Wonder,” reuniting with her “Love Jones” co-star Lorenz Tate. She is also set to star with Ice Cube in “Are We Done Yet?“, the third film in their “Are We There Yet?” family comedy franchise, and reprise her role in the next “Friday movie.”

Long’s memoir — which chronicles her life and career, including iconic roles in “Boyz n the Hood,” “The Best Man” franchise, “Soul Food,” “The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air,” “Third Watch,” “Tyler Perry’s The Single Mom’s Club,” “Dear White People,” “Fatal Affair,” The Banker,” “Roxanne, Roxanne” and more — will be published in 2027.

Long is represented by Untitled Entertainment and Brecheen Feldman Breimer Silver & Thompson, LLP.

content.article_text:
Jamie Foxx has joined the indie crime thriller “East of the River” as a producer. He boards through his Foxxhole Productions alongside Alex Marks.

The film, directed by Dennis Latos, follows two estranged brothers reuniting to face the underground poker ring that destroyed their family. The film stars Ben Barnes (“The Chronicles of Narnia” franchise, “The Punisher”), Ben Ahlers (“The Gilded Age,” “Little Brother”), Callie Hernandez (“The Flight Attendant,” “Alien: Covenant”) and Maria Sten in here first film role since starring in television’s “Neagley.”

Related Stories

Michelle Dockery, Genevieve O’Reilly, Quintessa Swindell Join Jessica Gunning in Netflix Jungle Drama ‘Feral’

Shawn Levy Enters Disney Overall Deal After Nearly a Decade at Netflix

The cast also includes David Zayas (“Dexter,” “Dexter: Resurrection”), John Bedford Lloyd (“Ozark”, “The Bourne Supremacy”), Catherine Curtin (“Stranger Things,” “Orange Is the New Black”), Nathan Wallace (“Daredevil: Born Again,” “NCIS: Origins”), and Steven Gregory (“Gravesend”). The film also features former WWE wrestler James Storm and former NFL running back Dalvin Cook.

Popular on Variety

Post-production of the film recently wrapped. Global distribution rights are available through CAA Media Finance.

“East of the River” was and written by Elise Finnerty with story by Jim Tamburino. Ben Grant served as director of photography on the film.

In addition to Foxx and Marks, the film is produced by Nicolas Alvo at Ruta 5 Films, and Benjamin Wiessner at Vanishing Angle, alongside Latos and Finnerty. Executive producers include David Schuster of Gloves Up Entertainment Steven Gregory, John Harms, Gerry Ambrose and Foxx’s daughter Corinne Foxx. The film is presented by Gloves Up Entertainment in association with Echo Bend Productions.

“We’ve been fans of Dennis since first discovering his short film, ‘Leylak’, where his command of character and storytelling immediately stood out. This film is a powerful continuation of that voice, and we’re proud to support this exceptional project,” Jamie and Corrine Foxx and Marks said in a joint statement.

Latos said, “I wanted to capture the kinetic, dangerous energy of a world most people never see. This isn’t just a story about poker, it’s a high-octane look at what happens when you’re backed into a corner and forced to gamble with your life. We’ve fused a gritty family drama with the pulse-pounding stakes of the criminal underworld to give the audience a cinematic experience that is both deeply felt and truly thrilling.”

Schuster added, “When Dennis Latos and I set out to make our first independent feature film, I never imagined that we’d have such a talented cast and amazing crew. With Dennis and I originally being from Queens, this project is close to our hearts. I am grateful to our amazing producing partners, Jamie, Alex, Nicolas, Benjamin, and Elise.”

Barnes is represented by Gersh, Luber Roklin Entertainment and ID Public Relations. Ahlers is represented by Gersh, Artists First and Felker Toczek Suddleson McGinnis Ryan LLP. Hernandez is represented by Independent Artist Group, Entertainment 360 and Paul Hastings. Sten is represented by CAA, Brillstein Entertainment Partners, The Initiative Group and Granderson Des Rochers. Zayas is represented by Buchwald, ATA Management, Jill Fritzo Public Relations and Schreck Rose Dapello Adams Berlin & Dunham. Bedford Lloyd is represented by CESD Talent Agency. Curtin is represented by Artists & Representatives, Fusion Entertainment and Sullivan Talent Group. Wallace is represented by UIA Talent & Brian Twohig of Roger Paul Talent. Gregory is represented by Bright Artists Management.

content.article_text:
Community

Art Problems: Do I Need an Agent?

Artist agents are not the panacea we imagine them to be, but AI agents won’t solve all your problems, either. Paddy Johnson breaks it down.

Hyperallergic )

My career has stalled, and I spend more time on studio admin than actually working in it. I keep hearing about artist agents. I also keep hearing about AI agents that can do a lot of the administration for you. Do I need an agent or an agent? —Double Agent

I don’t know how much time you spend in the studio versus doing studio administration, but it sounds like the balance is off. The average artist should spend about 30 to 50% of their time on studio administration, depending on how they participate in the industry. And by studio administration, I mean the nuts-and-bolts stuff: inventory management, grant and residency applications, website maintenance. There are exceptions, and most artists will have stretches where admin takes over and vice versa. That’s normal. But the majority of your time shouldn’t be spent on administration. So, let’s get to fixing that.

First order of business: Artist agents are not the panacea we imagine them to be, assuming we can even agree on what they do. The term covers everything from estate planning to brand deals to career strategy. Few of them will write your applications or keep your inventory up to date. Fewer still place artists with galleries. Those agents are a bit like the narwhal, whose tusks were sold as unicorn horns in medieval Europe; the real thing exists, but it rarely lives up to the legend. It may be a spouse who runs the studio, or in one case I know of, a former gallerist placing artists who didn’t speak English at blue-chip galleries. The gallerist took 20% of sales, half from the artist and half from the gallery. It’s an expensive arrangement and it depended on the artists already having a market.

You keep hearing about these roles, though, because the market has had a few rough years. Sales by contemporary art dealers were stagnant in 2025, according to the Art Basel UBS Art Market Report . “Galleries are having to make thoughtful decisions about how they allocate their resources, and many can't carry the staff they once did,” consultant Kristen Becker of KB Art Strategies told me in a recent conversation. Becker offers strategic advice to galleries, nonprofits, artists, and art sponsors. “That means they can't always offer artists the level of support they used to, so we're seeing a range of services, including artist agents, step in to fill that gap.”

content.article_text:
Shares of Skydance Corp., formed through the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, fell as much as 25% in trading Wednesday. The drop came as the Skydance, led by chairman and CEO David Ellison, distributed about 471 million warrants giving holders of Paramount Skydance’s PSKY Class B shares the option to purchase stock in the new company.

As of 11 a.m. ET, the stock price of Skydance — which began trading Oct. 6 on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol “SKYD” — was down 25.4%, to $6.78/share. The company’s current market capitalization is estimated at about $34 billion.

Related Stories

Netflix Lays Off 6% of Employees, Elimination About 1,000 Jobs in Biggest Cutbacks to Date

'Man on the Inside' to End With Season 3 at Netflix

Each warrant issued to PSKY holders initially allows them to buy one share of Skydance for $12. If all of those warrants were exercised, that would raise about $5.65 billion for the company, while it would also increase the share count and dilute ownership of current shareholders. It’s not known how many warrants have been exercised so far.

Popular on Variety

In connection with Skydance’s distribution of stock warrants to PSKY holders, the NYSE announced after market close Tuesday that it will adjust the official closing price of Skydance’s Class B common stock downward by $0.19368 per share (from approximately $9.27 to approximately $9.07) based on the official closing price of the warrants of $2.20 (trading on NYSE under “SKYD WS”).

The warrants issued to PSKY shareholders are intended to provide them the opportunity to purchase shares of Skydance’s Class B common stock “on similar terms” to those offered to the parties in the $47 billion equity syndicate backing the Warner Bros. Discovery deal, including David Ellison; his father, Larry Ellison; Gerry Cardinale, head of RedBird Capital Partners; LionTree; and the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi. Those equity investments in SKYD were priced at $12 per share.

While the movement of Skydance’s stock price Wednesday has more to do with the issuing of the stock warrants, Wall Street has not been bullish on the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. The company will have pro-forma annual revenue of nearly $70 billion — but it also will have to deal with almost $80 billion in net debt .

The distribution of the warrants “marks the final step in the WBD transaction closing process,” Wells Fargo analysts led by Steven Cahall said in a research note published Wednesday morning. They noted that “media mergers have a less than ideal history in terms delivering on pro-forma EBITDA expectations,” citing CBS and Viacom, Disney and 21st Century Fox and Discovery and WarnerMedia.

That said, the Wells Fargo analysts wrote, “We think SKYD will successfully deliver its ~$6bn in planned cost synergies. The main risk is whether the integration and disruption causes some leakage in core ops, and/or whether Media fundamentals change or are disrupted by tech. This history means investors may discount pro forma EBITDA to account for the leverage & risk.” The firm has an “underweight” rating on Skydance’s stock with a 12-month price target of $7.00/share.

The Paramount-WBD deal, valued at $111 billion including the assumption of WBD debt, brings together two major studios, TV networks including CBS, CNN, Comedy Central, MTV and TBS, and streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max.

Last week, after the deal closed, Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz (former chief of Mattel) announced their senior executive leadership team for the new Skydance.
