content.title_original: Sex, Love and War: How the Racy Gay Epic ‘La Bola Negra’ Could Win Netflix’s First Best Picture Oscar
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "For Guitarricadelafuente and Miguel Bernardeau , the romance that fuels “ La Bola Negra ” wasn’t the challenge.", "links": [{"text": "Guitarricadelafuente", "url": "https://variety.com/t/guitarricadelafuente/"}, {"text": "Miguel Bernardeau", "url": "https://variety.com/t/miguel-bernardeau/"}, {"text": "La Bola Negra", "url": "https://variety.com/t/la-bola-negra/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“It wasn’t hard to fall in love with him,” Bernardeau says, looking at his co-star. The two men, both 29-year-old Spaniards, haven’t tired of one another yet, despite a global tour that began in Cannes this spring and has now brought them to New York. “It was hard to create war.”"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Related Stories"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/The_New_Stanford_Prison_Experiment_n_S1_E2_00_21_32_12_R.jpg?w=250&h=167&crop=1", "alt": "THE NEW STANFORD PRISON EXPERIMENT. Episode 102 of THE NEW STANFORD PRISON EXPERIMENT. Cr. Courtesy of Netflix. © 2026", "caption": "", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "'New Stanford Prison Experiment' Drops Tense First Trailer Ahead of Netflix Release", "links": [{"text": "'New Stanford Prison Experiment' Drops Tense First Trailer Ahead of Netflix Release", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/tv/news/new-stanford-prison-experiment-trailer-netflix-1236878294/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Feral-Netflix.jpg?w=250&h=167&crop=1", "alt": "Jessica Gunning, Michelle Dockery, Genevieve O'Reilly, Quintessa Swindell", "caption": "", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Michelle Dockery, Genevieve O’Reilly, Quintessa Swindell Join Jessica Gunning in Netflix Jungle Drama ‘Feral’", "links": [{"text": "Michelle Dockery, Genevieve O’Reilly, Quintessa Swindell Join Jessica Gunning in Netflix Jungle Drama ‘Feral’", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/tv/global/jessica-gunning-michelle-dockery-netflix-feral-1236900016/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/La-bola-negra-Variety-cover-FORWEB.jpg?w=792", "alt": "", "caption": "Davis Bates for Variety", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Those two forces, love and war, coexist painfully in what may be the most ambitious film of this year’s Oscar season. Directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, the two-man team known as Los Javis , “La Bola Negra” depicts the lives of multiple gay men in Spain over three separate timelines: In 1932, young Carlos (Milo Quifes) is blackballed — hence the film’s title — from a social club over his sexuality. In 1937, at the height of the Spanish Civil War, Guitarricadelafuente and Bernardeau play, respectively, a soldier and the prisoner of war he must guard, as their affections blossom inexplicably across political lines. And in 2017, historian Alberto (Carlos González) struggles to figure out how the two preceding tales intersect, stumped until an academic (Glenn Close in a brief, striking cameo) steps in to help.", "links": [{"text": "Los Javis", "url": "https://variety.com/t/los-javis/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The story of Spain’s rupture and its fall into repressive dictatorship wasn’t news to the actors. “It’s something that has touched everybody — our great-grandparents were all involved,” Guitarricadelafuente says. “It’s common in our DNA in Spanish society.” But to make the history feel real and immediate, they had to learn how to behave like soldiers. “We received military preparation — how to hold a rifle,” says Guitarricadelafuente, who has a gentle, soft-spoken bearing both in person and onscreen. His Sebastián would rather be playing his trumpet — he fights only reluctantly; he’s more at home in his feelings than in combat. “There’s a naiveness to him,” he continues, “but he’s not stupid. Playing the trumpet is what makes him have hope in the future — one day, he’ll be able to go to Madrid and be a musician.” Indeed, an encounter with a vivacious lounge singer, played by Penélope Cruz, convinces Sebastián that the world is broader than he ever suspected, in a dazzling scene at the heart of the movie."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At least one stakeholder in “La Bola Negra” wanted to be sure Guitarricadelafuente could be credible as a fighter as well as a lover: Meeting him for the first time, Pedro Almodóvar, one of the movie’s producers, asked whether the singer had any edge at all."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Guitarricadelafuente relates Almodóvar’s question first in Spanish before translating it: “Is he gonna avoid just being, like … nice ?”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "He’s going to need some armor as he gears up for awards season. After it blew up a sleepy Cannes earlier this year, earning a 20-minute standing ovation, winning a shared best director prize and selling to Netflix , “La Bola Negra” has been an object of fascination across the film world. And since it became the first non-English-language film since 2011 to win the People’s Choice Award at the Toronto International Film Festival, it’s been perceived as the only Oscar contender that might topple “The Odyssey” come March. (“The Odyssey” is a technically dazzling, timeline-toggling examination of the power of love set against the madness of war, while “La Bola Negra” is … also all of those things, just made on a much smaller budget. And for those who consider Los Javis too out of nowhere to get past Nolan — well, who’d heard of the Daniels before they beat Steven Spielberg?)", "links": [{"text": "Netflix", "url": "https://variety.com/t/netflix/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/La-bola-negra-Variety-7.jpg?w=819", "alt": "", "caption": "Davis Bates for Variety", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Which means that these two actors, not yet well-known in the U.S., are about to be everywhere. And that niceness that Almodóvar identified might take Guitarricadelafuente a long way. The singer has a sweetly earnest disposition, with a floaty tendency to remember the emotional truth of working with Los Javis, while Bernardeau is more plainspoken, analytical and forthright, and never once slips into speaking Spanish, even as his co-star lets off soft “Sí”s like punctuation. Together, though, they are comfortable enough to pick up sentences where the other leaves off, and to chuckle — sometimes ruefully, sometimes giddily — while remembering the film shoot that made Guitarricadelafuente an actor, and that changed both their lives."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "If the film does score at the Academy Awards, it’ll be a milestone for global cinema, for Netflix and for queer artists: Although Bernardeau doesn’t identify as queer, Guitarricadelafuente is among several out gay actors playing gay characters in the Oscar race, including Andrew Scott of “Elsinore” and Jordan Firstman of “Club Kid.” That makes this year, perhaps, an even gayer Oscar race than the one where “Moonlight” beat a musical, befuddling Faye Dunaway."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But more than 20 years after 2005’s “Brokeback Mountain” won nearly every precursor but lost on Oscar night, are audiences ready for a movie this steamy and provocative? What’s onscreen is potent, so much so that the actors say they had to take care to keep the romance from becoming so overwhelming that it strained credulity. “We had to work against it and try to manage the volume of that love,” Bernardeau says, “because it’s an impossible love.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Through their efforts, something universal emerges — assuming a post-“Brokeback,” post-“Moonlight” audience is open to it. “Older generations that would have been scandalized by this 20 years ago are gonna understand it right now,” Guitarricadelafuente says. “And this transcends: It’s a story about love that everybody can feel linked to.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“La Bola Negra” links itself to the audience’s sentiments through deep specificity. It refuses to hold our hand, trusting us to keep up as the work and life story of Spanish poet and playwright Federico García Lorca grow increasingly woven into the text, or when a notification sound from gay sex app Grindr is the cue that first shunts us into modern times. “I don’t like movies that treat me like I’m dumb,” says Calvo, 35, via Zoom during a joint interview with Ambrossi. “The audience is smart enough. When I see ‘Chernobyl,’ I maybe don’t get some nuclear stuff, but I’m in it. In the gay world — no difference.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In an unprecedented show of confidence, Netflix is giving the film a 47-day theatrical release, starting Oct. 16."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/La-bola-negra-Variety-3.jpg?w=819", "alt": "", "caption": "Davis Bates for Variety", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“We made this movie for the screen,” says Ambrossi, 42. “We shot it in 35mm. So that was good news, that people can experience the movie as we thought they would. But Netflix, you can rewatch — you can see all of Penélope Cruz’s numbers again and again.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“And over and over and over again!” Calvo jumps in."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Netflix’s acquisition deal was announced on the festival’s last day. For a streamer that has earned Oscars — but, frustratingly for its ambitious leadership, never best picture — for films by global cinema stalwarts like Jane Campion, Alfonso Cuarón and Guillermo del Toro, the relative upstarts Los Javis may, surprisingly, represent its best chance yet at Oscar’s top prize. Two years ago, the company bet on a different Cannes prize winner about queerness told in the Spanish language, and the fate “Emilia Pérez” met after lead actress Karla Sofía Gascón’s incendiary old tweets emerged may help account for why team “La Bola Negra” speaks, to a one, thoughtfully and deliberately. The directors are eager to make the leap into being globally known auteurs: Los Javis previously created the biographical TV series “Veneno,” about trans Spanish singer Cristina Ortiz Rodríguez, which aired stateside on HBO Max in 2020. In their home country, they’re famous as judges on “Drag Race España,” and became the subject of speculation over their romantic relationship — they broke up during the making of “La Bola Negra,” but remain creative partners."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Calvo mentions that while both “Brokeback Mountain” and “Moonlight” boosted acceptance of queer love, he hopes that “La Bola Negra,” which is more direct in its depiction of gay sensuality and the male body, can push still further. “There’s no better way to get people to understand things than art and movies,” he says. “They’re a really good vehicle for creating empathy — because when you cry with someone, you’re always bonded to that story, to that person, to that community.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "He sees the change films have made, though, as incremental rather than revolutionary. “Thanks to the work of activists, artists, step by step, it’s a better place. But hate is a shadow that still haunts us.” The success of “La Bola Negra” may indicate something hopeful in our dark historical moment — that a love story, especially a seemingly impossible one, can stop us in our tracks and make us feel."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But to get there, the directors needed to find their perfect leading men. What Almodóvar may have deemed simply nice, Calvo calls “this sad-eyes, little-gay-soldier look” — an easily wounded, fragile quality that had shown through in Guitarricadelafuente’s music. As a singer, he’s collaborated with the Australian pop star Troye Sivan, and, sylphlike and dreamy, he cuts a similar figure, just in the Spanish language; though he hasn’t crossed over stateside, Guitarricadelafuente sells out arenas in Spain."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The singer’s casting also felt political: As a young actor, Calvo played a gay character in the issue-driven teen drama “Física o Química.” “And then nobody hired me anymore,” he says. “People tend to hire straight stars because they don’t want to risk money, which I think is homophobic. We wanted to make this statement.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/La-bola-negra-Variety-5.jpg?w=819", "alt": "", "caption": "Davis Bates for Variety", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The directors approached Guitarricadelafuente at Primavera Sound, a music festival held in Barcelona, where he lives. “You’re saying this because everybody’s drinking right now,” the singer recalls telling them. “You’ve had too many drinks!” The next day, though, Calvo messaged Guitarricadelafuente and asked him to come to Madrid, where Los Javis live. They explained the character they had in mind, one they hadn’t yet started writing but knew was right for him. It was a “Star Is Born” moment — which Guitarricadelafuente has now heard a thousand times."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Gaga is the exact example that everybody talks to me about!” he laughs. “You’re Lady Gaga! You’re Lady Gaga!” (He relates more to Rosario Flores, a Latin Grammy-winning songstress who appeared in Almodóvar’s “Talk to Her.”) While he was uncertain about acting, his character’s sweetness and connection to music, felt legible to the newly minted actor. “If I was born in that village, in those circumstances,” Guitarricadelafuente says, “that would exactly be me.” Among the points “La Bola Negra” makes is that our contemporary understanding of queerness isn’t a historical constant — that it was learned, and fought for, by people following their hearts despite colossal opposition. A young man in a small town in 1937 might never have realized what lay beyond."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Guitarricadelafuente’s background as a musician only helped make his case to his prospective directors. “All the decisions you take when you’re singing to make things one line louder, one line softer — everything is an acting decision,” Calvo remembers telling him. “So we’ll guide you. We’ve been acting teachers — we know how to work with newcomers.” But Guitarricadelafuente’s scene partner needed to be someone less green. “We couldn’t have two nonactors,” Calvo says. “There’s something interesting in having a wildness in a newcomer that is ready to give all of himself, reminding actors with long careers that they have to let themselves go, and the technique of the professional actors teaching the newcomers.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Enter Bernardeau, who studied acting in Los Angeles but returned to Spain to find fame on the Netflix teen soap “Elite.” In it, he played the popular stud at an exclusive prep school. The show ran eight seasons, but Bernardeau departed after the fourth. “I learned a lot doing ‘Elite’ about what I wanted and what I didn’t want,” he says. The practice of being on camera on a major production was helpful, he says, but global popularity on a Netflix hit brought tabloid fame. Not every actor wants their Wikipedia to have a “Personal life” section, as Bernardeau’s does."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“What happened later was something that we didn’t expect, and changed our lives and made us reconsider everything,” he says. “I had to protect myself from not getting too busy in what people were saying. It helped me to know what I want — the kind of actor I want to be.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/La-bola-negra-Variety-6v2.jpg?w=803", "alt": "", "caption": "Davis Bates for Variety", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Bernardeau met Los Javis at the Goya Awards, and they told him that they wanted him to read for them. A week later, he did, and felt he’d botched it. “I woke up every morning and I was like, ‘Please give me another chance.’ Then the casting directors called me again.” At their next meeting, the directors offered Bernardeau the role."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I hate auditions!” Ambrossi says — he doesn’t even recall that first audition. Los Javis knew they wanted Bernardeau, and the rest was a formality. “We trust ourselves a lot as actors’ directors. It’s what I told Álvaro.” (Guitarricadelafuente’s real name is Álvaro Lafuente Calvo; his grandmother gave him his nickname, which combines “guitarrica,” a diminutive that means “small guitar,” with his surname.) “It’s not your song, but you will have to find a middle point between our text and your voice.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It had been important to the directors to give an out gay performer a chance to lead their movie. But Bernardeau’s straightness didn’t stand in the way of his being cast. “I totally get why straight actors want to play gay roles,” says Ambrossi. “It’s their craft to portray people that are different from them. I’m not against that. The political statement is still there with the LGBTQ+ people on camera and behind the camera. I guess Miguel is in such a good moment in his career that he wanted a challenge.” Bernardeau’s character, Rafael Rodríguez Rapún, was a real person — an activist and actor who’d been Lorca’s romantic partner before the poet’s 1936 assassination by Franco’s forces, spurring Rodríguez Rapún to fight the fascists. Ambrossi notes that his sexuality was a source of confusion. “Rafael was not an open gay man. He was confused — someone that was not able to say what he wanted.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For his part, Bernardeau says he felt no doubt whatsoever about playing a gay role, even though, until the last decade or so, many actors shied away from onscreen intimacy with other men. “I never thought about it like that, or cared what people would think about my sexuality,” he says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Once shooting was underway, Los Javis leaned on the trust they’d built with their leading men during the casting process. Though there are credited intimacy coordinators, “we just worked it out with the Javis,” Bernardeau says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“ Sí ,” adds Guitarricadelafuente. “I remember Ambrossi saying, Just kiss. Just a little bit more. ” The cast and crew were living in the northern town of Comillas, where they were shooting in an old hospital. They gathered one night in Ambrossi’s kitchen to “go, How are we gonna do this? ” Guitarricadelafuente says. “We wrote the script of what’s going to happen the next day between us — meeting ourselves, thanks to the direction of the Javis.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“We learned how to be directors doing our thing and learning by ourselves,” Ambrossi says, “so we are super aware how much you need the space to make mistakes, to try new things, to get mistaken. We always wanted to give them that space of freedom.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/La-bola-negra-Variety-2v2.jpg?w=786", "alt": "", "caption": "Davis Bates for Variety", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Bernardeau had a teen TV-hunk image that he was subverting not just by playing gay but by allowing himself to be objectified by Sebastián. And yet he didn’t feel conflicted about it when shooting a nude scene where his character is recovering from his injuries on an army cot. “I was very comfortable doing everything,” he says, “because I understood exactly what they needed. And they were not like these directors that are on the monitors and have this tent where they’re away. They’re holding your hand, crying with you many times and telling you, Thank you for this .”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It wasn’t just during the love scenes that the directors shed tears. “They cry with you,” Guitarricadelafuente agrees. “When we were preparing the character, I went to Madrid to meet them and to do some acting exercises to reach the emotion — places of your inner self that you didn’t reach before.” He offers an example: Because the innocent Sebastián is deeply connected to his mother, Calvo and Ambrossi asked Guitarricadelafuente to imagine being held in his mother’s arms. On shooting days, they would pull him aside, put on music and discuss what the singer calls “the traumas” — they’d weep, then get ready to shoot."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“There was a very therapeutic thing about it,” Guitarricadelafuente says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“We cried so many times together.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Los Javis speak with me the day of the movie’s Toronto debut, and they present a study in contrasts. For Guitarricadelafuente and Miguel Bernardeau , the romance that fuels “ La Bola Negra ” wasn’t the challenge.

“It wasn’t hard to fall in love with him,” Bernardeau says, looking at his co-star. The two men, both 29-year-old Spaniards, haven’t tired of one another yet, despite a global tour that began in Cannes this spring and has now brought them to New York. “It was hard to create war.”

Related Stories

'New Stanford Prison Experiment' Drops Tense First Trailer Ahead of Netflix Release

Michelle Dockery, Genevieve O’Reilly, Quintessa Swindell Join Jessica Gunning in Netflix Jungle Drama ‘Feral’

Those two forces, love and war, coexist painfully in what may be the most ambitious film of this year’s Oscar season. Directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, the two-man team known as Los Javis , “La Bola Negra” depicts the lives of multiple gay men in Spain over three separate timelines: In 1932, young Carlos (Milo Quifes) is blackballed — hence the film’s title — from a social club over his sexuality. In 1937, at the height of the Spanish Civil War, Guitarricadelafuente and Bernardeau play, respectively, a soldier and the prisoner of war he must guard, as their affections blossom inexplicably across political lines. And in 2017, historian Alberto (Carlos González) struggles to figure out how the two preceding tales intersect, stumped until an academic (Glenn Close in a brief, striking cameo) steps in to help.

The story of Spain’s rupture and its fall into repressive dictatorship wasn’t news to the actors. “It’s something that has touched everybody — our great-grandparents were all involved,” Guitarricadelafuente says. “It’s common in our DNA in Spanish society.” But to make the history feel real and immediate, they had to learn how to behave like soldiers. “We received military preparation — how to hold a rifle,” says Guitarricadelafuente, who has a gentle, soft-spoken bearing both in person and onscreen. His Sebastián would rather be playing his trumpet — he fights only reluctantly; he’s more at home in his feelings than in combat. “There’s a naiveness to him,” he continues, “but he’s not stupid. Playing the trumpet is what makes him have hope in the future — one day, he’ll be able to go to Madrid and be a musician.” Indeed, an encounter with a vivacious lounge singer, played by Penélope Cruz, convinces Sebastián that the world is broader than he ever suspected, in a dazzling scene at the heart of the movie.

At least one stakeholder in “La Bola Negra” wanted to be sure Guitarricadelafuente could be credible as a fighter as well as a lover: Meeting him for the first time, Pedro Almodóvar, one of the movie’s producers, asked whether the singer had any edge at all.

Guitarricadelafuente relates Almodóvar’s question first in Spanish before translating it: “Is he gonna avoid just being, like … nice ?”

He’s going to need some armor as he gears up for awards season. After it blew up a sleepy Cannes earlier this year, earning a 20-minute standing ovation, winning a shared best director prize and selling to Netflix , “La Bola Negra” has been an object of fascination across the film world. And since it became the first non-English-language film since 2011 to win the People’s Choice Award at the Toronto International Film Festival, it’s been perceived as the only Oscar contender that might topple “The Odyssey” come March. (“The Odyssey” is a technically dazzling, timeline-toggling examination of the power of love set against the madness of war, while “La Bola Negra” is … also all of those things, just made on a much smaller budget. And for those who consider Los Javis too out of nowhere to get past Nolan — well, who’d heard of the Daniels before they beat Steven Spielberg?)

Which means that these two actors, not yet well-known in the U.S., are about to be everywhere. And that niceness that Almodóvar identified might take Guitarricadelafuente a long way. The singer has a sweetly earnest disposition, with a floaty tendency to remember the emotional truth of working with Los Javis, while Bernardeau is more plainspoken, analytical and forthright, and never once slips into speaking Spanish, even as his co-star lets off soft “Sí”s like punctuation. Together, though, they are comfortable enough to pick up sentences where the other leaves off, and to chuckle — sometimes ruefully, sometimes giddily — while remembering the film shoot that made Guitarricadelafuente an actor, and that changed both their lives.

If the film does score at the Academy Awards, it’ll be a milestone for global cinema, for Netflix and for queer artists: Although Bernardeau doesn’t identify as queer, Guitarricadelafuente is among several out gay actors playing gay characters in the Oscar race, including Andrew Scott of “Elsinore” and Jordan Firstman of “Club Kid.” That makes this year, perhaps, an even gayer Oscar race than the one where “Moonlight” beat a musical, befuddling Faye Dunaway.

But more than 20 years after 2005’s “Brokeback Mountain” won nearly every precursor but lost on Oscar night, are audiences ready for a movie this steamy and provocative? What’s onscreen is potent, so much so that the actors say they had to take care to keep the romance from becoming so overwhelming that it strained credulity. “We had to work against it and try to manage the volume of that love,” Bernardeau says, “because it’s an impossible love.”

Through their efforts, something universal emerges — assuming a post-“Brokeback,” post-“Moonlight” audience is open to it. “Older generations that would have been scandalized by this 20 years ago are gonna understand it right now,” Guitarricadelafuente says. “And this transcends: It’s a story about love that everybody can feel linked to.”

“La Bola Negra” links itself to the audience’s sentiments through deep specificity. It refuses to hold our hand, trusting us to keep up as the work and life story of Spanish poet and playwright Federico García Lorca grow increasingly woven into the text, or when a notification sound from gay sex app Grindr is the cue that first shunts us into modern times. “I don’t like movies that treat me like I’m dumb,” says Calvo, 35, via Zoom during a joint interview with Ambrossi. “The audience is smart enough. When I see ‘Chernobyl,’ I maybe don’t get some nuclear stuff, but I’m in it. In the gay world — no difference.”

In an unprecedented show of confidence, Netflix is giving the film a 47-day theatrical release, starting Oct. 16.

“We made this movie for the screen,” says Ambrossi, 42. “We shot it in 35mm. So that was good news, that people can experience the movie as we thought they would. But Netflix, you can rewatch — you can see all of Penélope Cruz’s numbers again and again.”

“And over and over and over again!” Calvo jumps in.

Netflix’s acquisition deal was announced on the festival’s last day. For a streamer that has earned Oscars — but, frustratingly for its ambitious leadership, never best picture — for films by global cinema stalwarts like Jane Campion, Alfonso Cuarón and Guillermo del Toro, the relative upstarts Los Javis may, surprisingly, represent its best chance yet at Oscar’s top prize. Two years ago, the company bet on a different Cannes prize winner about queerness told in the Spanish language, and the fate “Emilia Pérez” met after lead actress Karla Sofía Gascón’s incendiary old tweets emerged may help account for why team “La Bola Negra” speaks, to a one, thoughtfully and deliberately. The directors are eager to make the leap into being globally known auteurs: Los Javis previously created the biographical TV series “Veneno,” about trans Spanish singer Cristina Ortiz Rodríguez, which aired stateside on HBO Max in 2020. In their home country, they’re famous as judges on “Drag Race España,” and became the subject of speculation over their romantic relationship — they broke up during the making of “La Bola Negra,” but remain creative partners.

Calvo mentions that while both “Brokeback Mountain” and “Moonlight” boosted acceptance of queer love, he hopes that “La Bola Negra,” which is more direct in its depiction of gay sensuality and the male body, can push still further. “There’s no better way to get people to understand things than art and movies,” he says. “They’re a really good vehicle for creating empathy — because when you cry with someone, you’re always bonded to that story, to that person, to that community.”

He sees the change films have made, though, as incremental rather than revolutionary. “Thanks to the work of activists, artists, step by step, it’s a better place. But hate is a shadow that still haunts us.” The success of “La Bola Negra” may indicate something hopeful in our dark historical moment — that a love story, especially a seemingly impossible one, can stop us in our tracks and make us feel.

But to get there, the directors needed to find their perfect leading men. What Almodóvar may have deemed simply nice, Calvo calls “this sad-eyes, little-gay-soldier look” — an easily wounded, fragile quality that had shown through in Guitarricadelafuente’s music. As a singer, he’s collaborated with the Australian pop star Troye Sivan, and, sylphlike and dreamy, he cuts a similar figure, just in the Spanish language; though he hasn’t crossed over stateside, Guitarricadelafuente sells out arenas in Spain.

The singer’s casting also felt political: As a young actor, Calvo played a gay character in the issue-driven teen drama “Física o Química.” “And then nobody hired me anymore,” he says. “People tend to hire straight stars because they don’t want to risk money, which I think is homophobic. We wanted to make this statement.”

The directors approached Guitarricadelafuente at Primavera Sound, a music festival held in Barcelona, where he lives. “You’re saying this because everybody’s drinking right now,” the singer recalls telling them. “You’ve had too many drinks!” The next day, though, Calvo messaged Guitarricadelafuente and asked him to come to Madrid, where Los Javis live. They explained the character they had in mind, one they hadn’t yet started writing but knew was right for him. It was a “Star Is Born” moment — which Guitarricadelafuente has now heard a thousand times.

“Gaga is the exact example that everybody talks to me about!” he laughs. “You’re Lady Gaga! You’re Lady Gaga!” (He relates more to Rosario Flores, a Latin Grammy-winning songstress who appeared in Almodóvar’s “Talk to Her.”) While he was uncertain about acting, his character’s sweetness and connection to music, felt legible to the newly minted actor. “If I was born in that village, in those circumstances,” Guitarricadelafuente says, “that would exactly be me.” Among the points “La Bola Negra” makes is that our contemporary understanding of queerness isn’t a historical constant — that it was learned, and fought for, by people following their hearts despite colossal opposition. A young man in a small town in 1937 might never have realized what lay beyond.

Guitarricadelafuente’s background as a musician only helped make his case to his prospective directors. “All the decisions you take when you’re singing to make things one line louder, one line softer — everything is an acting decision,” Calvo remembers telling him. “So we’ll guide you. We’ve been acting teachers — we know how to work with newcomers.” But Guitarricadelafuente’s scene partner needed to be someone less green. “We couldn’t have two nonactors,” Calvo says. “There’s something interesting in having a wildness in a newcomer that is ready to give all of himself, reminding actors with long careers that they have to let themselves go, and the technique of the professional actors teaching the newcomers.”

Enter Bernardeau, who studied acting in Los Angeles but returned to Spain to find fame on the Netflix teen soap “Elite.” In it, he played the popular stud at an exclusive prep school. The show ran eight seasons, but Bernardeau departed after the fourth. “I learned a lot doing ‘Elite’ about what I wanted and what I didn’t want,” he says. The practice of being on camera on a major production was helpful, he says, but global popularity on a Netflix hit brought tabloid fame. Not every actor wants their Wikipedia to have a “Personal life” section, as Bernardeau’s does.

“What happened later was something that we didn’t expect, and changed our lives and made us reconsider everything,” he says. “I had to protect myself from not getting too busy in what people were saying. It helped me to know what I want — the kind of actor I want to be.”

Bernardeau met Los Javis at the Goya Awards, and they told him that they wanted him to read for them. A week later, he did, and felt he’d botched it. “I woke up every morning and I was like, ‘Please give me another chance.’ Then the casting directors called me again.” At their next meeting, the directors offered Bernardeau the role.

“I hate auditions!” Ambrossi says — he doesn’t even recall that first audition. Los Javis knew they wanted Bernardeau, and the rest was a formality. “We trust ourselves a lot as actors’ directors. It’s what I told Álvaro.” (Guitarricadelafuente’s real name is Álvaro Lafuente Calvo; his grandmother gave him his nickname, which combines “guitarrica,” a diminutive that means “small guitar,” with his surname.) “It’s not your song, but you will have to find a middle point between our text and your voice.”

It had been important to the directors to give an out gay performer a chance to lead their movie. But Bernardeau’s straightness didn’t stand in the way of his being cast. “I totally get why straight actors want to play gay roles,” says Ambrossi. “It’s their craft to portray people that are different from them. I’m not against that. The political statement is still there with the LGBTQ+ people on camera and behind the camera. I guess Miguel is in such a good moment in his career that he wanted a challenge.” Bernardeau’s character, Rafael Rodríguez Rapún, was a real person — an activist and actor who’d been Lorca’s romantic partner before the poet’s 1936 assassination by Franco’s forces, spurring Rodríguez Rapún to fight the fascists. Ambrossi notes that his sexuality was a source of confusion. “Rafael was not an open gay man. He was confused — someone that was not able to say what he wanted.”

For his part, Bernardeau says he felt no doubt whatsoever about playing a gay role, even though, until the last decade or so, many actors shied away from onscreen intimacy with other men. “I never thought about it like that, or cared what people would think about my sexuality,” he says.

Once shooting was underway, Los Javis leaned on the trust they’d built with their leading men during the casting process. Though there are credited intimacy coordinators, “we just worked it out with the Javis,” Bernardeau says.

“ Sí ,” adds Guitarricadelafuente. “I remember Ambrossi saying, Just kiss. Just a little bit more. ” The cast and crew were living in the northern town of Comillas, where they were shooting in an old hospital. They gathered one night in Ambrossi’s kitchen to “go, How are we gonna do this? ” Guitarricadelafuente says. “We wrote the script of what’s going to happen the next day between us — meeting ourselves, thanks to the direction of the Javis.”

“We learned how to be directors doing our thing and learning by ourselves,” Ambrossi says, “so we are super aware how much you need the space to make mistakes, to try new things, to get mistaken. We always wanted to give them that space of freedom.”

Bernardeau had a teen TV-hunk image that he was subverting not just by playing gay but by allowing himself to be objectified by Sebastián. And yet he didn’t feel conflicted about it when shooting a nude scene where his character is recovering from his injuries on an army cot. “I was very comfortable doing everything,” he says, “because I understood exactly what they needed. And they were not like these directors that are on the monitors and have this tent where they’re away. They’re holding your hand, crying with you many times and telling you, Thank you for this .”

It wasn’t just during the love scenes that the directors shed tears. “They cry with you,” Guitarricadelafuente agrees. “When we were preparing the character, I went to Madrid to meet them and to do some acting exercises to reach the emotion — places of your inner self that you didn’t reach before.” He offers an example: Because the innocent Sebastián is deeply connected to his mother, Calvo and Ambrossi asked Guitarricadelafuente to imagine being held in his mother’s arms. On shooting days, they would pull him aside, put on music and discuss what the singer calls “the traumas” — they’d weep, then get ready to shoot.

“There was a very therapeutic thing about it,” Guitarricadelafuente says.

“We cried so many times together.”

Los Javis speak with me the day of the movie’s Toronto debut, and they present a study in contrasts. Ambrossi can’t sit still, and has left his hotel to speed-walk through the city, speaking rapidly and barely glancing at his phone screen. Calvo, meanwhile, sits at a desk in his hotel room, gazing into the camera lens placidly while idly sketching on a sheet of paper.

As we speak, the film’s success at TIFF lies ahead. And waiting doesn’t suit them. Indeed, at Cannes, Calvo sat through the screening in a state of torment. He’d shown up at the theater at 3 a.m. the night before to set the volume. “I was so tired, and I was like, Play it really loud . And then when we were there, I was like, I think I put it too loud . Javi was like, Shut up! Let me enjoy it! ” It was only after the movie ended that Calvo dialed back into the experience, and began to cry.

Ambrossi is accustomed to micromanaging — because he’s always had to. “The posters, the merchandising, calling networks — Please, I need more money — I’m very used to that. So this movie — everything was very hard. It was the biggest effort I ever made.” So Cannes provided a moment of serenity. “I felt peaceful, and it was a new feeling for me to feel peaceful. I saw Tilda Swinton’s face in the next row — Oh my God, what’s happening? ”

Diva worship is a thread that connects the ex-lovers: Calvo gravely corrects my statement that, between Cannes and “Drag Race España,” the pair toggle between high and low culture. “For me,” he intones, “drag is high art.” For their part, the stars of “La Bola Negra” marvel at their directors’ varied interests. “I think it would be cool to have Christopher Nolan as a ‘Drag Race’ juror,” Bernardeau says. “Woody Allen!” Guitarricadelafuente fires back drily.

Calvo uses drag-club slang to describe Cruz’s character, Nené Romero — “She is mothering!” he says. Nené is a cupletista , a Spanish singer whose bawdy, openly sexual acts were inspired by the goings-on at the Moulin Rouge. “They talked about sex, drugs, all the experiences in the street, and they were friends with gay and lesbian writers. They were the first pop stars you get in Spain,” Calvo says. Cruz’s performance — which has, despite its brevity, sparked Oscar chatter, and which might, along with her work in Olivia Wilde’s “The Invite,” make her the first performer to get two nominations in one category under the Academy’s new rules — recalls Liza Minnelli’s in “Cabaret.” Minnelli’s Sally Bowles lived loud and hard in the last days before Weimar Berlin fell to Adolf Hitler. On the precipice of Franco’s dictatorship, Cruz’s character is doing the same.

Nené — outrageous and drag-inflected — opens Sebastián up to the power of queerness, and Cruz played a similar role for Guitarricadelafuente. “She was a godmother in every single aspect,” Ambrossi says. “Guitarricadelafuente, she took such care of him. But she was so generous — she wanted to support the message of this movie and the importance of the political statement behind it.”

“She was so generous and gentle and trying to encourage you,” Guitarricadelafuente says. “This poor guy in the middle of the civil war, this beautiful show is the first time you see him smiling. And her role in this is very important, because she’s going to be a mother for a lot of queer people that are going to see this.” Guitarricadelafuente notes that Nené seems to intuit that about his sexuality that Sebastián cannot yet put into words. “She’s like the English teacher who encourages you to see beautiful things — she already knows. She knows before you know.”

In the midst of telling a story about self-discovery and new love, Los Javis transitioned from romantic and creative partners to solely creative partners. Endlessly protective of their actors, they kept their breakup under wraps during the shoot.

“I didn’t even notice,” Guitarricadelafuente says. “I noticed after we ended filming.”

“They told me on my last day,” says Bernardeau.

Guitarricadelafuente didn’t want to believe the news, despite gossip swirling around the production. “There was like a fuss, because they are very known in Spain,” he says. “I was like, I’m having dinner with them every day, and they’re so close.”

Today the directors are philosophical about their split. “When we get into a project, it’s a road to the unknown,” says Calvo, “and we always trust that by the end of the road, we are going to be different people.”

“Yeah!” interjects Ambrossi.

“And that’s the good thing about doing what we do,” Calvo says. “The way I see creation is: You can’t make a project that is not going to change your life forever, and I was grateful for this project to make us evolve and make us explore new ways of living.”

This evolution happened at the moment the pair’s stature on the film scene was about to shift, first with Cannes and possibly again next March. But they’re not allowing themselves to think as far ahead as the Oscars, even as Netflix, with “La Bola Negra” as the crown jewel in its 2026 slate, clearly is.

“Javi Ambrossi — I think he’s a witch. Not a witch, but he has a spiritual thing. He knows things about the future, and he’s not telling us,” Guitarricadelafuente says.

“And his phrase is always ‘Step by step, step by step,’” Bernardeau adds. “And you’re like, ‘Step by step’?! These are big leaps!”

Ambrossi learned this incrementalism from moviemaking. He used to be an actor, too, and becoming a director — with so many tasks competing for his attention all at once — was terrifying until he simplified the process for himself. “You have to go frame by frame — it’s the only way to do things,” he says. “Day by day, frame by frame. You do your best every single second, and it will be OK. Today is the Toronto premiere. Hopefully, people will connect. We’ll see tomorrow.”

For his part, Calvo emphasizes the film’s potential impact — illuminating a story of queer hope during a dark stretch of history, then as now. His ambitions reach beyond the Oscar race. Academy attention, he says, “would be a dream come true, but you should remember why you made the movie. Making the movie was a dream. Everything is a dream. So we just keep dreaming.”

content.article_text:
Netflix ‘s film VP Doug Belgrad has been let go amid a massive restructuring at the streamer.

Netflix is laying off around 1,000 employees , around 6% of its workforce, in what marks the company’s largest axing to date. Most of the cuts will effect employees on the product, technology, legal and HR teams, co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters told the staff on Wednesday morning.

Sheroum Kim, who served as Netflix’s director of film and worked on lower-budgeted releases like Sunny Sandler’s “Don’t Say Good Luck,” has also been let go, Variety has confirmed.

Popular on Variety

Related Stories

John Steinbeck's 'East of Eden' Returns to Top of Book Charts Following Netflix Adaptation's Release

‘Under Siege,’ Netflix’s Second Most Ambitious Colombian Series – a 'Huge Undertaking Even by Our Standards' – Bows Nov. 6

Netflix declined to comment.

“Decisions like these are never easy, and we don’t take them lightly. Our top priority today is to support those who are leaving Netflix,” the co-CEOs said in the memo, which didn’t name any of the departing employees. “The process will vary somewhat by country, but leaders will be connecting with impacted employees soon. If you are leaving, please know that we will support you throughout this transition and make sure you have as much clarity and context as possible. We also want to say thank you. What you’ve built, and the care you brought to Netflix, have made a lasting difference and we will always be grateful.”

Belgrad was hired in May 2024 and marked the first major executive appointment by film chairman Dan Lin after he succeeded Scott Stuber. Belgrad was responsible for managing Netflix’s slate of originals and just launched Ben Affleck’s crime thriller “Animals.” Before joining the streamer, Belgrad was an executive at Sony for over 25 years and most recently held the title of president of the Sony Pictures Entertainment Motion Picture Group.

Netflix’s last major layoffs were in 2022, when about 450 staffers were let go after a rough quarter at the streamer. Earlier this year, the company pink slipped several dozen members of its global product team .

content.article_text:
Book Review

John Berger in His Own Bruised Time

The late novelist and art critic asked Tom Overton to wait to write his biography until after his death. The result is deeply informative, deferential, and perceptive, sometimes lyrically so.

These days, we tend to take his ideas for granted: that art — making it or contemplating it — creates knowledge. That by foregrounding the processes by which we see, we can discover the mechanisms and deceptions through which we make meaning. And, of course, that it’s important to know who is footing the bill. John Berger, who died in 2017 , was famous not for challenging the Western canon but for making its revelations feel so evidently connected to everything else about life. His essays often read like personal letters, offering to us the gift of our own passions and imaginations.

Berger was an electric presence in the 1972 BBC series Ways of Seeing , in which he appears to be standing in a museum, a kind of anarchist-angel with his unruly curls and groovy white shirt, slicing a detail out of a Botticelli with a box-cutter. This is revealed to be an illusion: The “museum” is in fact a television studio set, and the Botticelli is a reproduction. Berger was making a point about how technology changed the way we interact with images, but the subtext is clear: that he was there to cut through exclusionary and pedantic framings that, even a half-century later, persist in giving art a cordoned-off quality.

A new biography, Tom Overton’s John Berger: From Life (2026), is less interested in applying the critic and Booker Prize-winning novelist’s ideas to our cultural moment, in which human creativity is vampirically extracted and homogenized by artificial intelligence, than it is in fixing him within his own bruised 20th century, shaped by modernization and imperialism. Overton and Berger met in 2009, when he donated his archive to the British Library; Overton edited two collections of Berger’s writing on art ( Portraits: John Berger on Artists and Landscapes: John Berger on Art ) and co-edited a collection of his essays on miners, The Underground Sea . Berger, whom Overton refers to as “John” throughout, granted the author permission to write his biography after his death.

The result is deeply informative, deferential, and perceptive, sometimes lyrically so. In laying his thematic groundwork, Overton tells two stories. One is about Berger’s father, who, in the aftermath of World War I, remained in France to supervise the identification and transfer of fallen soldiers’ remains, “trying to give order and meaning to death.” The other draws from Berger’s memories as a teenager during the Blitz. Each month, he and his girlfriend would walk through bombed-out London to the National Gallery, where a single masterpiece at a time was shown — a lesson in survival “by our wits and with the Old Masters,” as Berger put it.

content.article_text:
Christophe Leribault , who recently took the reins at the Louvre in Paris, said that the museum could close altogether if it does not receive renovations that would improve the institution’s security and aging infrastructure.

“Whoever forms the next government must keep in mind that if the Louvre is not repaired, updated and transformed, it will very quickly fall behind and will eventually have to close its doors to the public,” Leribault told Le Figaro on Wednesday. “That would be a disaster.” Related Articles Dalí-Designed Bronze 'Livre de l'Apocalypse' Book Cover Stolen from French Museum As Right-Leaning Politicians Attack Cultural Institutions, a Basque Country Museum Director Believes in a Different 'Vision of the Museum Worth Fighting For'

The Louvre, which received 9 million visitors in 2025, is typically known for its masterpiece-laden collection, which is rich in great artworks by Leonardo da Vinci, Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres, and Eugène Delacroix, along with a range of famed ancient artifacts. But more recently, the museum has made headlines for perceived weaknesses in its management and security systems.

During a daytime heist that took place almost exactly one year ago, in October 2025, thieves stole million in French crown jewels collectively valued at $102 million, some of which have still not been recovered. The ensuing controversy surrounding the heist spurred the museum’s last director, Laurence des Cars, to resign, leaving the post open for Leribault, who started earlier this year.

Plans to update the Louvre, accounting for crowd flow and security issues, have themselves become the matter of debate. In February, the Louvre postponed a competition to select an architect in charge of expanding the museum that had been announced less than a year prior. Previously, the plan had been given a $788 million price tag; it had faced protests from Louvre workers, who claimed that it focused too much on moving the Mona Lisa to its own gallery at the expense of systemic issues in need of fixing.

Then, in May, with Leribault now at the helm, the museum resumed the project, naming Selldorf Architects and Studios Architecture Paris as the winners of the competition.

In prior interviews, Leribault pegged the cost of the renovations project at $1.24 billion. He has said the project, begun by des Cars prior to her departure, would prioritize security, telling the Financial Times , “Security must be integrated from the outset into all our choices.

Leribault appeared to suggest that any plan to alter the Louvre would be costly and difficult in his Le Figaro interview published on Wednesday. “There is no easy, miracle ‘surface’ solution,” he said. “Everything is interconnected, everything is linked.”

content.article_text:
LYON, France — French distributor Malavida has picked up Wang Chao ’s “A Woman,” the Chinese filmmaker’s 2022 drama that won the screenplay prize at San Sebastián but has never received a theatrical release in France. Malavida is also preparing a wider retrospective of his work for spring 2027.

The acquisitions, announced during Lyon’s International Classic Film Market ( MIFC ), also include three earlier Wang titles — “The Orphan of Anyang” (2001), “Day and Night” (2004) and “Luxury Car” (2006) — with plans to restore “The Orphan of Anyang” and bring the filmmaker to France for the retrospective, scheduled to launch March 24.

Related Stories

A24 British Shows ‘It Gets Worse,’ ‘Major Players’ and ‘The Ministry of Time’ to Stream on Paramount+ in U.S.

A separate theatrical release is being considered for “A Woman.”

Popular on Variety

For Malavida co-founder Anne-Laure Brénéol, the acquisitions are a chance to bring back into view a filmmaker whose work has become harder to see.

“It’s a discovery, an incursion, into China with an extraordinary dissident filmmaker who has somewhat fallen into oblivion because the movies he made during the 2010s weren’t released internationally,” she told Variety. “His last film, even though it won prizes, was never released [outside of China]. It really felt like the right moment to rediscover Wang Chao’s work.”

The company is also adding three Dino Risi titles to its theatrical slate: “The Easy Life” (1962), screened at this year’s Lumière Film Festival , “The Monsters” (1963) and “Tolgo il disturbo” (1990), known in France as “Valse d’amour.” The latter, starring Vittorio Gassman and Elliott Gould, has never been re-released theatrically in France. The three films will form part of a Risi retrospective scheduled for summer 2027.

Malavida is also screening a newly restored 4K digital version of Michael Radford’s “1984” in Lyon as part of the festival’s Lumière Classics program —– its first French theatrical showing since its original 1984 release. The restoration was supervised by Oscar-winning cinematographer Roger Deakins , who shot the original film.

The distributor is also preparing a new French-language version of Soviet animator Fyodor Khitruk’s 1969 “Winnie and His Friends,” narrated and sung by French musician and actor Philippe Katerine . Set for release on Feb. 25, 2027, the program will also be available in a French-subtitled version and has received the backing of French arthouse cinema association AFCAE’s young audiences group.

The collaboration continues a long relationship between Katerine and Malavida, which is celebrating its 20th anniversary. His directorial debut “Peau de cochon” was the first film the company ever released, in 2005, and is now being brought back to theaters.

“At the time, it was very complicated. Philippe wasn’t as known as today. He was just making music and wasn’t the superstar he later became,” Brénéol recalled. “The press was excited about the film, but its theatrical release was not a success. We’re very happy to bring it back for Malavida’s 20th anniversary.”

The film, an unconventional and deeply personal work mixing humor and fantasy, will receive its first DCP release, having originally been distributed on video. Malavida has also previously worked with Katerine on the French-language version of Soviet animated shorts by Eduard Nazarov.

The distributor’s 2027 slate also includes Konrad Wolf’s “I Was Nineteen,” scheduled for April 21. Malavida discovered the East German filmmaker’s 1968 feature during a retrospective at last year’s Lumière Festival, an encounter Brénéol described as an extraordinarily powerful emotional experience, and subsequently acquired it for French distribution.

Another rediscovery is Jean-Henri Meunier’s 1979 “La Bande du Rex,” a rock-infused film starring French singer Jacques Higelin as Franckie Mégalo, a rebellious film projectionist. Featuring an original soundtrack composed by Higelin, the film is scheduled for re-release in May.

The MIFC runs alongside Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival until Oct. 16.

Nárnia: O Sobrinho do Mago | A aventura começa no trailer do novo filme de Greta Gerwig — assista

Filme chega aos cinemas em 11 de fevereiro.

(Imagens: divulgação/Netflix)

A Netflix divulgou o trailer de “ Nárnia: O Sobrinho do Mago “, novo filme de Greta Gerwig e um dos mais aguardados do ano. Assista acima (dublado).

Foi divulgado também o primeiro cartaz oficial do filme, abaixo.

O filme é uma releitura moderna do primeiro livro da série “As Crônicas de Nárnia”, de C.S. Lewis. A história acompanha os novos amigos Polly Plummer (Beatrice Campbell) e Digory Kirke (David McKenna), que descobrem que o tio de Digory, Andrew Ketterley (Daniel Craig), pode ser louco o suficiente para ter arquitetado uma maneira de transitar entre mundos infinitos.

Além de Campbell, McKenna e Craig, o elenco conta ainda com Carey Mulligan, Kobna Holdbrook-Smith, Denise Gough, Susan Wokoma e Meryl Streep. Direção e roteiro são de Greta Gerwig.

content.article_text:
Doug Belgrad is departing Netflix where he has been Vice President of Film for more than two years. His exit, which was confirmed by the streamer, is part of the major layoffs at Netflix today .

Ironically, Belgrad was Head of Film Dan Lin‘s first hire after a round of layoffs when Lin replaced Scott Stuber and restructured Netflix’s film department.

Before joining Netflix in May 2024, Belgrad spent 25 years at Sony Pictures, and was ultimately co-president under Amy Pascal. He joined the Culver City lot in 1989 and was promoted to become co-president of production at Columbia in 2003 and president in 2008. He shepherded the Men in Black franchise, the Adam Sandler canon at Sony, and Oscar-nominated American Hustle and Captain Phillips , to name a few.

Upon exiting, he formed 2.0 Entertainment, and produced Gran Turismo and Bad Boys: Ride Or Die .

Watch on Deadline

More to come.

content.article_text:
Paul McCartney has a bone to pick with Sam Mendes , the director of the upcoming four Beatles movies starring Paul Mescal as McCartney, Harris Dickinson as John Lennon, Joseph Quinn as George Harrison and Barry Keoghan as Ringo Starr. What’s the issue? It all comes down to how tall Mescal is compared to his co-stars.

“We were all the same height!” McCartney declared on the “Good Hang” podcast, noting how movies based on the Beatles wrongly depict him as shorter than his bandmates. “We were all the same height, and Ringo was a bit smaller. And if you look at photos, we’re all the same height.”

Related Stories

'Cyberpunk 2077' Movie in the Works at Paramount

Skydance to Fully Reorganize International; Kevin MacLellan Will Not Lead Key Group

“Guess what?” McCartney added about Mescal. “He is smaller than the guy who plays John. Sam Mendes is making the film. I said, ‘Sam, I’ve got just one thing that I need to say to you. You know, Paul [Mescal is] a bit smaller.’ I don’t know how Sam’s gonna deal with it. He sent me a picture, a still from the filming they were doing, and they’re crossing the Abbey Road crossing, and the Paul character is markedly smaller. I texted him: ‘Sam! Smaller? Don’t do this! You said you wouldn’t do it.’”

Popular on Variety

McCartney also once expressed his frustration to Sam Taylor-Johnson, director of 2009’s “Nowhere Boy,” which starred Aaron Taylor-Johnson as a teenage John Lennon. Thomas Brodie-Sangster had a supporting role as McCartney in the biographical drama but is shorter than Taylor-Johnson.

“The John character, who she later married, Aaron — he’s bigger than me in the film,” McCartney said. “My character is kind of wimpy. Smaller than John. John knocks me to the floor. And it’s like, ‘Sam, this is not true!’ Her only explanation, bless her, because she’s still a good friend, she said, ‘This is a movie, it’s not a documentary.’ And I thought, ‘Well, I don’t like that explanation.’ But I couldn’t do anything, because by now she’d made the film. There was I, little Paul. John, the great big hero, and it’s like: No! It’s not true.”

Mendes is directing four Beatles movies, one centered on each of the band members. The project, officially titled “The Beatles – A Four-Film Cinematic Event,” has the backing of Sony Pictures and is currently in the middle of its year-long production. All four movies will be released theatrically in April 2028.

“We want people to be able to experience them in the cinema at the same during the same period,” producer Pippa Harris recently said at the BFI London Film Festival , noting she does not expect audiences to “see all four films on the same day.”

“Within the same month — you might see one a week, or you might see one weekend and two the next and one the next. However you see it, I think our hope is that people will see all four films,” she added.

Watch McCartney’s full interview on “Good Hang” in the video below.

content.article_text:
Sakhya Byamba’s “ Zogsool ” was the biggest winner at the Busan International Film Festival ’s Vision Awards on Wednesday, taking home four prizes.

The film won both the Netpac Award and the Fipresci Award, along with the Vision of Jiseok Award. It also shared the Hylife Vision Award with Sailesh Rathnakumar’s “ Selvi ,” which separately picked up the Taipei Film Commission Award.

Related Stories

Josh Goldstine to Oversee Marketing and Distribution at Warner Bros., Paramount and All Skydance Film Labels (EXCLUSIVE)

Among Korean titles, Jeong Jihye’s “ Full Moon ” won three prizes: the CGV Award, the K-Movie Award and the Songwon Vision Audience Award – Korea. Park Songyeol’s “Beyond Love’s Horizon” won the KBS Independent Film Award and the Critic b Award, and Won Hyangra received one of two Actor of the Year honors for her work in the film. Kang Seung-ho took the other for “Cosmic Trace.”

Oh Sehyeon’s “Baler” won twice, with the Jeong-in Award and the Citizen Critics’ Award. Kim Si-jin’s “The Flower” received the DGK Plus M Award.

Popular on Variety

The BIFF Mecenat Award in the Asian category went to Yang Bo’s “Agaar,” and Yi Seungjun’s “Can I Talk to You?” won the Korean award. Choi Se-dam’s “A Woman Dancing on the Waves” got a special mention.

Soroush Shahpouri’s “Fatima” won the Asian Sonje Award, and Yun Taerang’s “Toe’s” won the Korean one. Jung Jaeseo’s “The Boy Who Fell to Earth” was singled out with a special mention.

Kumamoto Ryohei’s “After the Song” won the Face of the Future Award, and Arvin Belarmino’s “Ria” won The Heart of Eurasia Award. “There Will Be Snow,” from Chen Jianying, received the Bishkek International Film Festival-Central Asia Cinema Award. Darkhan Tulegenov’s “The Cord” took the International Film Festival of India – Vision Asia Award.

Audiences picked Shashank Walia’s “Birds in the Dark” for the Songwon Vision Audience Award – Asia. Im Yeonjeong’s “Recovery” won the Documentary Audience Award, and “La Bola Negra,” directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, won the Flash Forward Audience Award. Janay Boulos and Abd Alkader Habak’s “Birds of War” won the Busan Cinephile Award.

The 31st edition of the festival opened Oct. 6 and will close Oct. 15. Its industry arm, the Asian Contents & Film Market, ran from Oct. 10 to Oct. 13.

content.title_original: Iris Lebedeva  : « En Russie, la souffrance est omniprésente »
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://www.troiscouleurs.fr/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MINOTAURE-photo-inedite-copyright-MK-Productions-CG-Cinema-1024x429.png", "alt": "MINOTAURE photo inedite copyright MK Productions CG Cinema", "caption": "", "credit": "Trois Couleurs"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Vous avez étudié à la prestigieuse école de cinéma VGIK de Moscou. Quel souvenir en gardez-vous ?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Oui, j’y ai étudié le cinéma et le théâtre avec Sergueï Soloviov. Je ne sais pas s’il est connu aujourd’hui, mais c’était un grand maître du cinéma russe. Il était ami avec des gens comme Fellini et Antonioni. En Russie, dans les écoles de théâtre, c’est du non-stop : on vit presque sur place ! Quand j’ai rencontré Soloviov, je l’ai tout de suite adoré car c’était un vrai punk. Il nous disait : « Je vous aime tels que vous êtes, alors restez vous-mêmes, ne jouez pas les bons élèves ! » Cela m’a libérée d’un poids. Je me suis sentie autorisée à ressentir les choses, à ressentir mon corps. J’ai changé ma manière de voir les films, j’ai fréquenté de nouvelles personnes, je me suis habillée différemment… tout a changé ! Il voyait quelque chose en moi dont je n’avais pas conscience. Je ne sais pas où je serais si je ne l’avais pas rencontré."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Vous avez découvert les films d’Andreï Zviaguintsev lors de vos années étudiantes. Que vous inspirait son œuvre avant de travailler avec lui ?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "J’ai vu un de ses films quand j’étais encore jeune, c’était peut-être Le Retour [son premier long-métrage, Lion d’or à la Mostra de Venise 2003, qui voit deux frères confrontés au retour mystérieux d’un père qu’ils n’ont jamais connu. Le cinéaste s’est exilé en Europe depuis plusieurs années, dans le sillage de l’invasion russe en Ukraine, ndlr] mais je me souviens en tout cas d’avoir été hypnotisée. Je n’avais jamais vu ce qu’on pourrait appeler un film d’art, un film d’atmosphère. Je rêvais de travailler avec Andreï, mais une voix dans ma tête me disait que c’était impossible, que l’écart entre lui et moi était trop grand. Cette voix s’est évanouie à la seconde où je suis entrée dans la salle de casting, où il se tenait avec son coscénariste Simon Liachenko. Il s’est toujours adressé à moi d’égal à égal."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "En quoi votre préparation pour le rôle a-t-elle consisté ?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Andreï n’aime pas les acteurs qui psychologisent trop, qui veulent tout savoir. J’ai cherché de mon côté à embrasser l’état émotionnel de Galina, par exemple à travers la musique. Pour exprimer son désespoir, Andreï m’a donné l’image d’une ligne de vibration qui soudain s’étiole ou disparaît. C’est très similaire. Je n’avais pas envie de trop réfléchir pour rester proche de mon corps. Andreï nous a d’ailleurs laissé improviser. Lorsqu’on tournait, une fois les dialogues prononcés, il ne coupait pas : il nous demandait de prolonger la scène, de vivre à l’intérieur. Celle où Galina implose au balcon, la nuit, durait moins d’une minute dans le script. Tout le reste a été improvisé."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Dans un entretien pour Flanelle Magazine, on peut lire que vous et Dmitri Mazourov, qui joue Gleb, vous disputiez sur le tournage car vous n’étiez pas d’accord quant aux motivations de votre personnage. C’est assez amusant…"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Lors des auditions, j’essayais d’expliquer à Dmitri ce qui, selon moi, n’allait pas dans leur couple. Il m’a dit : « Elle a tout, une belle maison, de l’argent… qu’est-ce qu’elle veut de plus ? » Cela m’a rendue folle ! Nous nous sommes disputés en salle de casting et, quand je me suis tournée vers Andreï et Simon, ils faisaient un grand sourire. C’est arrivé une seconde fois sur le tournage, mais Andreï refusait de donner raison à l’un d’entre nous. En lisant les interviews de Dmitri, j’ai compris qu’on avait juste deux points de vue opposés sur la situation. Beaucoup d’hommes penseront sans doute comme lui, mais moi, je comprends ce vide que ressent Galina. Et je comprends surtout qu’Andreï a bien choisi son casting. (Rires.)"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Andreï Zviaguintsev nous a déclaré qu’il avait voulu tirer un film « profondément russe » de l’œuvre originale de Chabrol. Hormis le contexte de la guerre en Ukraine, selon vous, qu’est-ce qui fait de Minotaure un film russe ?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "C’est une question difficile. content.article_text:
Vous avez étudié à la prestigieuse école de cinéma VGIK de Moscou. Quel souvenir en gardez-vous ?

Oui, j’y ai étudié le cinéma et le théâtre avec Sergueï Soloviov. Je ne sais pas s’il est connu aujourd’hui, mais c’était un grand maître du cinéma russe. Il était ami avec des gens comme Fellini et Antonioni. En Russie, dans les écoles de théâtre, c’est du non-stop : on vit presque sur place ! Quand j’ai rencontré Soloviov, je l’ai tout de suite adoré car c’était un vrai punk. Il nous disait : « Je vous aime tels que vous êtes, alors restez vous-mêmes, ne jouez pas les bons élèves ! » Cela m’a libérée d’un poids. Je me suis sentie autorisée à ressentir les choses, à ressentir mon corps. J’ai changé ma manière de voir les films, j’ai fréquenté de nouvelles personnes, je me suis habillée différemment… tout a changé ! Il voyait quelque chose en moi dont je n’avais pas conscience. Je ne sais pas où je serais si je ne l’avais pas rencontré.

Vous avez découvert les films d’Andreï Zviaguintsev lors de vos années étudiantes. Que vous inspirait son œuvre avant de travailler avec lui ?

J’ai vu un de ses films quand j’étais encore jeune, c’était peut-être Le Retour [son premier long-métrage, Lion d’or à la Mostra de Venise 2003, qui voit deux frères confrontés au retour mystérieux d’un père qu’ils n’ont jamais connu. Le cinéaste s’est exilé en Europe depuis plusieurs années, dans le sillage de l’invasion russe en Ukraine, ndlr] mais je me souviens en tout cas d’avoir été hypnotisée. Je n’avais jamais vu ce qu’on pourrait appeler un film d’art, un film d’atmosphère. Je rêvais de travailler avec Andreï, mais une voix dans ma tête me disait que c’était impossible, que l’écart entre lui et moi était trop grand. Cette voix s’est évanouie à la seconde où je suis entrée dans la salle de casting, où il se tenait avec son coscénariste Simon Liachenko. Il s’est toujours adressé à moi d’égal à égal.

En quoi votre préparation pour le rôle a-t-elle consisté ?

Andreï n’aime pas les acteurs qui psychologisent trop, qui veulent tout savoir. J’ai cherché de mon côté à embrasser l’état émotionnel de Galina, par exemple à travers la musique. Pour exprimer son désespoir, Andreï m’a donné l’image d’une ligne de vibration qui soudain s’étiole ou disparaît. C’est très similaire. Je n’avais pas envie de trop réfléchir pour rester proche de mon corps. Andreï nous a d’ailleurs laissé improviser. Lorsqu’on tournait, une fois les dialogues prononcés, il ne coupait pas : il nous demandait de prolonger la scène, de vivre à l’intérieur. Celle où Galina implose au balcon, la nuit, durait moins d’une minute dans le script. Tout le reste a été improvisé.

Dans un entretien pour Flanelle Magazine, on peut lire que vous et Dmitri Mazourov, qui joue Gleb, vous disputiez sur le tournage car vous n’étiez pas d’accord quant aux motivations de votre personnage. C’est assez amusant…

Lors des auditions, j’essayais d’expliquer à Dmitri ce qui, selon moi, n’allait pas dans leur couple. Il m’a dit : « Elle a tout, une belle maison, de l’argent… qu’est-ce qu’elle veut de plus ? » Cela m’a rendue folle ! Nous nous sommes disputés en salle de casting et, quand je me suis tournée vers Andreï et Simon, ils faisaient un grand sourire. C’est arrivé une seconde fois sur le tournage, mais Andreï refusait de donner raison à l’un d’entre nous. En lisant les interviews de Dmitri, j’ai compris qu’on avait juste deux points de vue opposés sur la situation. Beaucoup d’hommes penseront sans doute comme lui, mais moi, je comprends ce vide que ressent Galina. Et je comprends surtout qu’Andreï a bien choisi son casting. (Rires.)

Andreï Zviaguintsev nous a déclaré qu’il avait voulu tirer un film « profondément russe » de l’œuvre originale de Chabrol. Hormis le contexte de la guerre en Ukraine, selon vous, qu’est-ce qui fait de Minotaure un film russe ?

C’est une question difficile. Quelqu’un m’a dit que le peuple russe a beaucoup souffert et qu’on le retrouve dans sa littérature, où la souffrance est omniprésente. Mais je me rends compte que les spectateurs s’approprient le film partout dans le monde. Peut-être que les enjeux patriarcaux sont plus forts, car en Russie c’est tout à fait normal qu’une femme abandonne son métier une fois qu’elle s’est mariée. Je me suis toujours dit que Galina se sentait piégée par cette situation. À l’intérieur, c’est une femme morte. Elle ne vit plus pour elle-même.

Avez-vous eu des échos sur la réception du film et de son prix à Cannes en Russie ?

Je ne vis plus en Russie, mais les gens m’écrivent pour me dire leur excitation à l’idée de voir le film… ou de trouver un moyen de le voir. D’autres sont très remontés contre Andreï, alors même qu’ils ne verront sans doute jamais Minotaure . À ceux-là, je leur conseille de le voir et de se forger leur propre opinion. C’est le pouvoir d’un grand film que d’inviter à la conversation, de poser davantage de questions qu’il ne donne de réponses toutes faites.

Pour finir, quels sont vos trois films russes préférés ?

Je vous cite les trois qui me viennent instantanément : J’ai vingt ans de Marlen Khoutsiev (1965), Assa de Sergueï Soloviov (1987) et Léviathan d’Andreï Zviaguintsev (2014).

content.translated_excerpt_zh: 几个月前,38岁的女演员从她的出席中播放了被驱逐的俄罗斯电影演员安德烈·齐维亚金塞夫的新电影“Minotaure”,在最后一次戛纳电影节的陪审团奖和法国代表在奥斯卡上,在广场上周三。

content.article_text:
T he great Australian actor Gary Waddell – known for his gooseflesh-raising ability to portray rough-as-guts characters so real you swear you’ve met them before – has died aged 74. Waddell was a fixture of the Australian film and TV industry for decades, bursting on to the scene, bleary-eyed and angsty in Bert Deling’s cult classic drug drama Pure Shit , a production so notorious that its first public screening, in 1976, was raided by the vice squad.

This legitimately great film – the best ever made about heroin addiction and subculture in Australia – was famously described as “the most evil film I’ve ever seen” by Melbourne Herald critic Andrew McKay (an example of hysterical overreach if ever there was one, although, as they say, those were different times). It remains a thrilling piece of social realist cinema, full of drug-taking, petty crime and tomfoolery, with the story revolving around Waddell’s character Lou, who arrives five minutes in, grousing about how he “hasn’t had a hit for 10 hours”.

Since then, Waddell went on to appear in countless productions, usually in small albeit often high-impact roles, in TV shows such as A Country Practice, E Street, Stingers, Blue Heelers , Water Rats, Bad Cop Bad Cop, Home and Away, City Homicide, Upright and Rake. His films included The FJ Holden, Chopper , Dirty Deeds, Gettin’ Square , Black and White, Charlie’s Country , The Stranger and 2022’s The Survival of Kindness , which featured his final screen performance.

There were many more. Waddell was hired again and again because he was rock-solid reliable, bringing weight to even the smallest roles, though he was sadly rarely given the screen time he deserved. Waddell told me in a 2012 interview for Crikey that in the early days this was partly because he “sabotaged” his career, including with substance abuse. Then came self-doubt: “I actually thought for a long, long time – until around ’86, ’87 – that my career was one of the greatest con jobs I’d ever pulled off. I never thought I could act … I had no idea until an actor said to me – and he was a trained actor – that what I did on film was what most people go to school to learn.”

Another great actor – the inimitable David Gulpilil – had lots of small roles and just one true leading performance: in Rolf de Heer’s 2013 film Charlie’s Country. Just as De Heer righted that wrong with Charlie’s Country, he did something similar in his very fine, very wily 2012 black comedy The King Is Dead!, casting Waddell as the titular character – a drugged-up layabout with a weird gleam in his eyes.

Dan Wyllie and Bojana Novakovic play a sensible, fairly strait-laced married couple who buy a suburban house, only to discover that the residence over the fence is a haven for ne’er-do-wells – including Waddell’s King, an astonishingly well-played fiend. He’s charming, but also dangerous and weird; the kind of person you cross the street to avoid. I was so smitten by his performance that, as the film critic at Crikey at the time, I described Waddell as “out of this world good” and wrote an open letter to Aacta , imploring voters to give him the gong for best supporting actor.

I was far from the only critic to heap praise on this majestically odd and darkly comedic performance. Margaret Pomeranz called it “hilarious”, while The Australian’s Evan Williams wrote it was “wonderfully touching and humorous”. Variety’s Richard Kuipers wrote that “Waddell’s spot-on performance keeps the character human, and even evokes a strange sympathy”, while Fairfax’s Jake Wilson saw a “perfect role for Waddell, who well and truly earns his place in the ratbag hall of fame”.

After I wrote that open letter, Waddell contacted me and was extremely grateful. We hung out in person, and went for beers at Melbourne’s Young and Jackson hotel. We spoke on the phone several times and, in our last communication a few years ago, exchanged photos on Facebook of our jack russells. Waddell was humble, friendly, smart and down-to-earth – and as a screen presence, he was electrifying. He will be missed.

content.title_original: ‘I must continue until I die’: inside the fight to bring Iran’s thriving art scene to the world
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "W hen the call came early one morning, Tehran resident Elham Issari knew it must be urgent. The voice on the line was offering something precious. “Miss Elham,” he said excitedly, “I have a single tube of white paint!
