content.article_text:
W hen the call came early one morning, Tehran resident Elham Issari knew it must be urgent. The voice on the line was offering something precious. “Miss Elham,” he said excitedly, “I have a single tube of white paint! It’s overpriced and I know it’s overpriced but, if you want it, you have to buy it right now because there’s this other guy in this other city who wants it and you have to tell me within the next five minutes.”

The tube of white paint would have cost Issari 5m tomans (about $36), she recalls. “I was like, I don’t think so, because that’s overpriced, and the next thing you know is it’s 4am and I’m on YouTube watching how to make lead white in your backyard without getting lead poisoning.”

It is a revealing slice of life in Iran these days. Since the US and Israel launched joint airstrikes and combat operations on 28 February, and turned the screws on Iran’s economy, thousands of visual artists have been plunged into economic and professional limbo.

The sudden onset of war shuttered commercial galleries in central Tehran, cancelled scheduled solo exhibitions, severed shipping channels and destroyed the fragile domestic market that allows creators to pay rent and sustain studio practices.

But it was out of this systemic breakdown that Continuum: Artist Relief for Iran was born. The initiative connects contemporary artists living and working inside Iran with international audiences, collectors and institutions through a dedicated platform at iranartistrelief.org .

The project owes its existence to Dario Duran , a Canadian-Iranian curator and founder of Duran Art Projects. Born in Shiraz, but raised in Canada, Duran holds degrees in photography, art history and curatorial studies. Six years ago, driven by nostalgia and a desire to connect with his heritage, he moved to Iran, where he fell in love with the dynamism of the domestic art scene.

When war broke out, Duran found himself caught directly in its crosshairs. “I was displaced,” the 38-year-old explains from Shiraz in Iran . “My mom and dad were visiting from Canada and we had to flee Shiraz because Shiraz was being hit pretty hard every day. It was becoming unbearable. We went by ground to the north of the country, where it was relatively quiet.”

In the north, Duran encountered dozens of other displaced cultural workers who had fled bombed urban centers such as Tehran and Isfahan. He linked up there with Mariam Rasti , co-founder of Duran Art Projects, who had also fled the capital.

“We were in constant communication with the artists,” Duran recalls. “One thing we saw over and over again was that, like never before, the artists were losing hope. Cancelled exhibitions, galleries closing, not being able to find materials, artists being displaced – every single person was going through the exact same uncertainty of what happens tomorrow.”

I ran’s contemporary art world operates inside a structural bubble, isolated from international banking networks. Typically, an artist works for one or two years to prepare a body of work, relying on a single gallery showcase to generate enough sales to survive for the next two years. When conflict brought that domestic cycle to a dead halt, creators faced immediate ruin.

Duran says: “We realised that at this moment, exhibition making, curation, archiving – these things do not matter. What matters, more than anything else, is simply sales. These artists were not able to pay their rent.

“One artist put up his paintbrushes and paint tubes for sale on Divar [a classifieds site] just to carry on. Another artist told me: ‘I’m going to go work in a coffee shop for the time being because I have no idea if this art thing is going to work out for me’.”

Determined to make a difference, Duran bought a couple of gigabytes of internet access so he could get on WhatsApp. From his laptop in the north, he drafted an open letter to international collectors, museum directors and gallerists across the diaspora, laying bare the plight of creators inside Iran.

The response was immediate and overwhelming. Gallerists and curators in London, New York, Paris, Dubai, Toronto and Mumbai wrote back, eager to assist. What had originally been planned as a modest PDF catalogue featuring a dozen imperilled acquaintances rapidly transformed into a nationwide initiative.

Over five months of feverish development, Duran, Rasti and a coalition of domestic galleries built Continuum. The digital platform brings together more than 500 original artworks by over 200 contemporary artists living and working inside Iran.

Eleven commercial galleries across Iran agreed to voluntarily waive 100% of their sales commissions. Duran Art Projects charges no platform fees. As a result, 100% of every completed artwork sale goes directly to the artist. To make acquisitions realistic for global buyers during an economic downturn, prices were capped across three accessible tiers: up to $500; $500–$2,500; $2,500–$5,000.

While the online front end of Continuum offers a catalogue of striking abstract canvases, delicate line drawings and minimalist photography, the back-end operation is a masterclass in guerrilla logistics. Delivering physical artworks out of a country under heavy military bombardment and stringent international sanctions requires ingenuity bordering on subversion.

“The logistics of it – we thought about this ad nauseam,” Duran says with a weary laugh. “Currently, this matter is changing on an hourly basis. The sanctions obviously have been very disruptive.”

Initially, Continuum relied on two domestic courier services capable of flying artwork packages from Tehran to shipment hubs in Dubai and Istanbul, where international carriers could take over. But as geopolitical tensions soared, regional airspace closed and commercial flight paths dissolved.

Duran explains: “The flight connections through the UAE were cancelled so the couriers told us that UAE is off the table. But the second UAE comes off the table, they figure out another way. There is a man who had a courier company that was forced to shut down. In order to keep his business going, he is now using the ground borders, moving overland from Iran into Armenia. He goes by the land border, carries the artworks into Armenia and ships them out from there with full insurance.”

To manage expectations, Continuum informs international buyers that delivery may take three to six months. Yet collectors worldwide, ranging from private patrons in North America to major European institutions, have shown extraordinary patience.

For Duran, the real tragedy of the current crisis lies in the indiscriminate cruelty of international economic sanctions, which target ordinary citizens while doing nothing to alter political outcomes. “These sanctions are not putting much pressure on the government,” he observes. “It’s mostly punishing everybody that’s trying to live a life here. Everyone’s complaining but we’re trying to find solutions.”

A mong the artists trying to make a way out of no way is Mehrdad Jafari , 43, who grew up in the northern province of Mazandaran, where his relatives worked as sculptors and painters. Speaking from Tehran through a Farsi interpreter, he says: “Growing up, I always had the dream that one day I would be in Tehran and have an art studio in this city, to create work and fully realise my potential.

“My entire life has been dedicated, and continues to be dedicated, to my work. In fact, my existence is connected to my work. I have no other way of being. I must continue until I die.”

As the father of a three-year-old child, Jafari’s experience of the war is filtered through the anxieties of parenthood. His artwork, which centres on the complex emotional tapestry of human relationships and community interactions, has had to adapt to severe material deprivations.

“Because of the effect of sanctions, we’ve had to be a lot more imaginative in order to decide what materials we use,” Jafari explains. “Materials are quite difficult to find right now. But what I’ve had to do, and what others are doing, is replace this lack of materials with imagination. We use alternative materials to carry on.”

Jafari views this enforced improvisation as a double-edged sword. “In one way we use our imaginations more, creating a more creative space and ways of thinking. But on the other hand, of course, we would love to be part of the global system and have access to the things everybody else has access to. That’s just not available to us right now.”

For Jafari, Continuum’s launch during a time of active military conflict carries symbolic resonance. “It’s an extraordinary moment. It’s a bridge for us to connect with an international audience. For me personally, it brings a sense of calm – that we are not forgotten. Because of Continuum, I am more invigorated than ever to work. It gives us hope that life can carry on.”

From the outset, Duran and Rasti insisted that the initiative would not function as an exhibition about war, nor would it force artists to turn their pain into visual entertainment for foreign viewers.

Duran argues: “Iranian contemporary art doesn’t look like any one thing. Iran is not a style, and the Iranian identity is not a medium. An artist living in Shiraz shouldn’t have to make work that visually announces ‘Iran’ before an international audience is willing to take it seriously. We wanted the work to be encountered first as art, not as evidence about a country.”

While some participating artists choose to directly address conflict, Continuum refused to make political commentary or suffering a requirement for inclusion.

“There is a difference between giving artists visibility during a crisis and asking artists to make the crisis visible,” Duran adds. “I definitely didn’t want crisis to become the reason their work deserves attention. Context should deepen our understanding of an artwork; it shouldn’t imprison the artwork.”

The breadth of work included on the platform bears out this philosophy. Across 500 pieces, viewers encounter delicate geometric abstraction, haunting figurative portraiture, avant-garde photography, experimental printmaking and sculpture.

T he financial relief generated by Continuum is already providing vital support to Iran’s artistic ecosystem. In a country where currency devaluation has eroded savings, a single $500 artwork sale can provide significant income towards studio rent or much-needed pigments.

Issari, 38, reflects: “It creates a chain. If an artist is not so worried about their income, maybe they can continue teaching. If they can continue to teach, kids can continue to learn. The whole chain does not stop and we don’t fall into this pit of absolute hopelessness.”

Issari could not bring herself to work during the first weeks of heavy bombardment in Tehran. “I was here for the whole show. Hearing explosions five times, six times per day, every day – having to gather the cats and run to your safe place and count to 10. Then, as soon as it’s over, pick up the phone, check if your father is alive, if your mother’s alive, if your loved ones are OK. On repeat. It does a number on you.”

The trauma was physical as much as psychological. “I didn’t touch a brush,” she recalls. “Actually, I did once, and my hands were shaking so badly that I literally just put it down. I was like, ‘I am not going to do this right now.’ And that’s OK, because I’m just not there.”

While Issari, who studied art in London, is hopeful her paintings on Continuum will find homes in international collections, the initiative’s primary gift is emotional validation. “Even if you don’t sell, it’s that feeling of being seen,” she says with quiet determination. “For me, it’s tremendous. It’s easy to feel like you’re a pariah and you’re invisible. Just the fact that you’re being seen means a lot.”

She adds: “I always have faith in the fact that art will survive, regardless of everything and anything. Artists are the best. If problem-solving were an Olympic sport, we would win a gold medal every time. We will find a way.”

伊朗的库拉特和创始人杜兰艺术项目. 出生在希拉兹,但在加拿大长大,杜兰在摄影,艺术史和库拉托研究学位。 六年前,由诺斯塔利亚和与他的遗产联系的愿望驱动,他搬到伊朗,在那里他爱上了国内艺术场景的动态。", "links": [{"text": "Dario Duran", "url": "https://www.instagram.com/darioduran/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d330d73fe38521adc2b1ffd932fb0e4bda4579bc/0_0_5000_4000/master/5000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "白色和黑色肖像 玛丽亚姆·拉斯蒂和达里奥·杜兰", "caption": "玛丽亚姆·拉斯蒂和达里奥·杜兰(Mariam Rasti and Dario Duran) 作曲:《继续的勇气:伊朗的艺术援助》", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当战争爆发时,杜兰发现自己直接被困在他的十字架上,“我被驱逐出境,”38岁的伊朗西拉兹解释道,“我妈妈和爸爸从加拿大访问,我们不得不逃离西拉兹,因为西拉兹每天都被打得很硬。", "links": [{"text": "Iran", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/world/iran"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在北方,杜兰遇到了数十名其他流离失所的文化工人,他们逃离了炸弹袭击的城市中心,如德黑兰和伊斯法汉,他与杜兰艺术项目的共同创始人玛丽亚姆·拉斯蒂联系在一起,他也逃离了首都。", "links": [{"text": "Mariam Rasti", "url": "https://www.instagram.com/mariamrasti/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我们一直在与艺术家沟通,”杜兰回忆道,“我们一次又一次看到的一件事是,像从未见过一样,艺术家失去了希望,展览被取消,画廊关闭,无法找到材料,艺术家被驱逐出境,每个人都经历了明天发生的事情的同样的不确定性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我跑的当代艺术世界在一个结构泡沫内运行,隔离国际银行网络,通常,一个艺术家工作一年或两年,以准备一个工作体,依靠一个单一的画廊展览室,产生足够的销售,以生存下两年。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "杜兰说:“我们意识到,在这个时候,展览制作,治疗,档案 - 这些事情并不重要,重要的是,比其他任何东西,只是销售,这些艺术家无法支付租金。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“一位艺术家把他的绘画刷子和绘画管放在迪瓦尔(一个分类网站)上,只是为了继续下去,另一位艺术家告诉我:“我要去咖啡店工作,因为我不知道这件艺术事物是否会为我工作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "决定做出差异,杜兰购买了一些吉加比特的互联网访问,以便他可以通过WhatsApp。从他的笔记本电脑在北方,他制定了一个开放的信给国际收藏家,博物馆导演和画家在整个隔离,放松了创作者在伊朗内部的麻烦。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "答案是即时的,令人惊叹的,伦敦,纽约,巴黎,迪拜,多伦多和孟买的画家和校长写了回来,渴望帮助。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "五个月的热情发展,杜兰,拉斯蒂和一联盟的国内画廊建造了Continuum. 数字平台聚集了超过500个原创艺术作品的200多名当代艺术家生活和工作在伊朗。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "伊朗11家商业画廊同意自愿辞职100其销售佣金的百分比. Duran Art Projects 不收取平台费。100为了在经济衰退期间全球买家实现收购的现实,价格在三分之三的可用范围内收购:$500;$500- -$2,500;$2,500- -$5,000是的", "links": [{"text": "Duran Art Projects", "url": "https://www.instagram.com/duranartprojects/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "虽然Continuum的在线前端提供了一份令人震惊的抽象字符串、微妙的线路绘图和最小化的摄影目录,但后端操作是战斗机物流的硕士课程。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“它的物流 – 我们想到了这个广告的恶心,”杜兰笑着说,“目前,这个问题正在按时变化,制裁显然是非常干扰性的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/002f0dc03a8ddd62fa9a3c65305932234255ff7e/0_0_1000_1000/master/1000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "无衣男子争斗", "caption": "无标题,Shayan Sajadian,2024. 数字摄影. 80cm x 80cm. 摄影:Shayan Sajadian/艺术家的短信和Continuum:艺术家帮助伊朗,由Duran Art Projects介绍。", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "起初,Continuum依靠两家国内航班服务,能够从德黑兰飞往迪拜和伊斯坦布尔的运输中心,但随着地缘政治紧张局势爆发,区域空域关闭,商业航班路线解散。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "杜兰解释说:“通过阿联酋的航班连接被取消,所以库尔人告诉我们,阿联酋在桌子上,但第二个阿联酋在桌子上,他们发现了另一种方式,有一位有一个库尔公司被迫关闭,为了保持他的业务,他现在使用地面边界,从伊朗转移到亚美尼亚,他走过地面边界,将艺术品带到亚美尼亚,并从那里发送他们全保险。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为了管理期望,Continuum向国际买家报告,交付可能需要三到六个月,但全球收藏家,从北美的私人经纪人到主要的欧洲机构,表现出极大的耐心。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于杜兰来说,当前危机的真正悲剧在于国际经济制裁的无歧视残酷性,针对普通公民,而不是为了改变政治结果而做任何事情,“这些制裁不会对政府施加太多的压力,”他指出,“这主要是惩罚所有试图在这里生活的人,每个人都在抱怨,但我们正在寻找解决方案。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "艺术家们试图从未走过路的一个小伙子是Mehrdad Jafari,43岁,在马桑达兰省北部长大,在那里他的亲戚作为雕塑家和画家工作。 通过一个法尔西翻译,他说:“长大,我总是梦想有一天我会在德黑兰,在这个城市有一个艺术工作室,创造工作,并充分实现我的潜力。", "links": [{"text": "Mehrdad Jafari", "url": "https://iranartistrelief.org/product/mehrdad-jafari2/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我的一生都被献给了我的工作,而且仍然被献给了我的工作,事实上,我的存在与我的工作有关,我没有别的存在方式,我必须继续,直到我死去。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/37e096c8b4c279c24c115a0468d46d9fda64324a/0_0_3024_4032/master/3024.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "抽象绘画", "caption": "未标题,Mehrdad Jafari,2026年 油在纸板上 40 x 30 厘米 照片:艺术家的礼貌和Continuum:艺术家帮助伊朗,由Duran Art Projects介绍。", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为一个三岁的孩子的父亲,贾法里的战争经验通过父母的焦虑被过滤,他的艺术作品,专注于人际关系和社区互动的复杂情感背景,不得不适应严重的物质剥夺。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“由于制裁的影响,我们不得不更具想象力来决定我们使用哪些材料,”Jafari解释道,“材料现在很难找到,但我不得不做的事情和其他人正在做的事情就是用想象力取代这种缺乏材料,我们使用替代材料来进行。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贾法里认为这种强迫的 improvisation 是一种双重的剑:“一方面,我们使用我们的想象力更多,创造更多的创造空间和思维方式,但另一方面,当然,我们会喜欢成为全球体系的一部分,并获得其他每个人都可以访问的东西,这只是现在不适合我们。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于Jafari来说,在积极的军事冲突时期,Continuum的启动具有象征性的响应:“这是一个非凡的时刻,这是我们与国际观众联系的桥梁,对我个人来说,它带来了平静的感觉,我们不会被遗忘,因为Continuum,我比以往任何时候都更有兴奋,希望生活能继续下去。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从一开始,杜兰和拉斯蒂坚持,该举措不会作为关于战争的展览,也不会强迫艺术家将他们的痛苦转化为外国观众的视觉娱乐。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "杜兰说:“伊朗当代艺术看起来不像任何东西,伊朗不是风格,伊朗的身份不是媒体,居住在希拉兹的艺术家不应该做一个视觉宣布“伊朗”的工作,而国际观众愿意认真对待它,我们希望这项工作首先作为艺术,而不是作为一个国家的证据。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "虽然一些参与的艺术家选择直接解决冲突,但Continuum拒绝发表政治评论或遭受参与的要求。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“在危机期间给予艺术家可见性和要求艺术家让危机可见之间存在差异,”杜兰补充道,“我绝对不想危机成为他们的作品值得关注的原因。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该平台上包含的作品的宽度引发了这个哲学,大约有500件作品,观众会遇到微妙的地质抽象,寻找形象肖像,前卫摄影,实验印刷和雕塑。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "由Continuum产生的财务援助已经为伊朗艺术生态系统提供了重要支持,在货币贬值破坏了储蓄的国家,单一500美元的艺术作品销售可以为工作室租赁或非常需要的色素提供显著的收入。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "38岁的伊萨里说:“它创造了一个链条,如果一个艺术家对他们的收入不那么担心,也许他们可以继续教学,如果他们可以继续教学,孩子们可以继续学习,整个链条不会停止,我们不会陷入绝对绝望的陷阱。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/bb28e4082983b41d2d3154db8bbe61cf26e79a03/0_0_1000_802/master/1000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "馬的抽象畫", "caption": "Azargun, Elham Issari, 2020 石油在容器上. 24cm x 30cm. 照片: 艺术家的慈善和Continuum: 伊朗艺术家帮助,由 Duran Art Projects 提出。", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "伊萨里不能在德黑兰重型轰炸的第一周内把自己带到工作中,“我在这里参加了整个节目,每天听到爆炸5次,6次,每天 - 必须收集猫,跑到你的安全地点,计算到10次,然后,一旦结束,拿起电话,检查你的父亲是否活着,你的母亲是否活着,你的亲人是否好。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我没有触摸刷子,”她回忆道,“事实上,我做了一次,我的手打得那么糟糕,我字面上只是把它放下来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在伦敦学习艺术的伊萨里希望在Continuum上看到她的绘画在国际收藏中找到家园,该倡议的主要礼物是情感验证,“即使你不出售,那就是被看到的感觉,”她静静决心说,“对我来说,这是令人惊叹的,很容易感觉像你是一个偶像,你是看不见的,只是你被看到的意味着很多。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她补充说:“我总是相信艺术会生存,无论什么,艺术家是最好的,如果解决问题是奥运会,我们每次都会赢得一枚金牌,我们会找到一种方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "艺术", "links": [{"text": "Art", "url": content.article_text:
Cameras have started rolling in the French Alps on “Pumping Black” a high-adrenaline thriller being led by Jonathan Bailey (“Wicked,” “Jurassic World: Rebirth”) and Oscar winner Natalie Portman (“May December,” “Good Sex”).

First announced by Variety earlier this year ahead of its market launch in Cannes by Anton Studios, the film also stars Lukas Gage (The White Lotus), Alex Akpobome (Industry), with new additions Daniel Quinn-Toye (“Sterling Point”), Lucas Lynggaard Tønnesen (“The Weight”), César winner Arieh Worthalter (“The Goldman Case”) and Emmy winner Tony Hale (“Veep”) now having joined the ensemble cast. The shoot will runs until early December.

Related Stories

David Ellison's 'Day One’ Skydance Press Conference: Studio Lot Dibs, Trump Ties and Everything Else We Learned

Josh Goldstine to Oversee Marketing and Distribution at Warner Bros., Paramount and All Skydance Film Labels (EXCLUSIVE)

Set in the cut-throat world of elite professional cycling, “Pumping Black” follows Taylor Mace, 35 years old and aging out of the sport. He is taken under the wing of Andrea Lathe, a doctor driven by her own thirst for victory and power. As the race progresses, Taylor must take increasingly dark measures to protect both his secret and his lead.

Popular on Variety

Mimi Cave (“Holland,” “Fresh”) directs from a screenplay by Haley Hope Bartels. Producers include Stacey Sher for Shiny Penny (“The Hateful Eight,” “Heretic”), Portman and Sophie Mas for MountainA (“May December,” “Arco”), Cave and Sébastien Raybaud for Anton Studios (“Victorian Psycho,” “My Darling California”).Katie Aquino from Shiny Penny and Kai Raka from Catchlight Studios serve as executive producers.

Anton Studios is fully financing the film and handling worldwide sales with CAA co-repping the US.

Cave’s creative team includes cinematographer Justin Brown (“I Am Not Okay with This”), production designer JC Molina (“Honey Boy”) and casting director Kharmel Cochrane (“Saltburn”). Martin Pensa, who edited Cave’s “Fresh,” returns as editor. Pierre-Yves Gayraud (“Cloud Atlas”) serves as costume designer, with Géraldine Lemaire (“The French Dispatch”) and Fabienne Robineau (“Robin Hood”) as hair and make-up.

Bailey is repped by CAA, Conway Van Gelder Grant and Anonymous Content; and law firm Hansen, Jacobson, Teller, Hoberman, Newman, Warren, Richman, Rush, Kaller, Gellman, Meigs & Fox LLP. Portman is repped by CAA, George Sheanshang and Agence Adéquat. Cave is repped by CAA and Jackoway Austen. Sher is repped by CAA and Gang, Tyre, Ramer. Bartels is repped by CAA, Untitled, and Yorn Levine. Gage is repped by WME, Luber Roklin Entertainment and Goodman Genow Schenkman. Akpobome is repped by Gersh and Range Media Partners. Quinn-Toye is repped by Independent Talent Group, CAA, Public Eye Communications and Gang, Tyre, Ramer, Brown & Passman. Tønnesen is repped by Accelerate and Lindberg Management. Worthalter is repped by Agence Adéquat. Hale is repped by UTA and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller, Hoberman, Newman, Warren, Richman, Rush, Kaller, Gellman, Meigs & Fox LLP.

Pakistan’s Karachi Biennale has cancelled its fifth edition, themed “ Kal ” (Tomorrow), due to “war conditions prevailing in the region,” according to an Instagram announcement, Hyperallergic reports . The art exhibition was due to run January 16 to 31, guided by curator Noor Ahmed, who reportedly was not consulted on the decision to cancel. “Artists and partners have been contacting me, and they are all quite disappointed about how communications and commitments with them are being handled,” Ahmed told Hyperallergic . She added that the event’s closure was “detrimental for Pakistan’s international art ecosystem,” and that “during a time of stated war and unrest, art becomes all the more powerful.” Over 100 artists and three co-curators were engaged with the project. The Karachi Biennale Trust , which organizes the event, did not respond to a request for comment. To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter .

Good Morning!

Pakistan’s Karachi Biennale has cancelled its fifth edition due to “war conditions prevailing in the region.”

A 300-year-old Jingdezhen porcelain bowl and box mysteriously shattered inside a British Museum display case, sparking a debate on Chinese social media.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has warned of nationalist threats to “freedom of art.”

The Headlines

KAL CANCELED . Pakistan’s Karachi Biennale has cancelled its fifth edition, themed “ Kal ” (Tomorrow), due to “war conditions prevailing in the region,” according to an Instagram announcement, Hyperallergic reports . The art exhibition was due to run January 16 to 31, guided by curator Noor Ahmed, who reportedly was not consulted on the decision to cancel. “Artists and partners have been contacting me, and they are all quite disappointed about how communications and commitments with them are being handled,” Ahmed told Hyperallergic . She added that the event’s closure was “detrimental for Pakistan’s international art ecosystem,” and that “during a time of stated war and unrest, art becomes all the more powerful.” Over 100 artists and three co-curators were engaged with the project. The Karachi Biennale Trust , which organizes the event, did not respond to a request for comment. Related Articles DNA Cracked Renoir Theft Case, Johnny Depp's Art Representation and Exhibition, and More: Morning Links for October 13, 2026 Cindy Sherman Collaborates with Chanel on Arts & Culture Magazine, Austrian Presidential Candidate Promises Return of Aztec Headdress to Mexico, and More: Morning Links for October 12, 2026

GONE TO PIECES . A Jingdezhen porcelain bowl and box mysteriously shattered inside a display case at the British Museum , and when photos spread on social media, so did questions about their preservation and a perceived lack of attention around the incident, reports Artforum and the South China Morning Post . The museum confirmed the incident occurred on October 4 but found no signs to explain how a three-hundred-year-old bowl could have fallen onto a box below, breaking both objects, which are now being repaired. Chinese visitors posted photographs of the broken pieces in the display, which “has sparked debate on Chinese social media over how museums should protect fragile works,” reported SCMP .

The Digest

In a speech at the opening ceremony celebrating the newly expanded Kunsthalle Würth in the German town of Schwäbisch Hall, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier warned of nationalist threats to the “freedom of art,” referencing institutions such as the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation museum and design center, which “fears for its survival.” [ dpa ] Art Cologne, an art fair founded in 1967, is moving to a new, more spacious venue in Hall 1 of the Confex Conference and Exhibition Center , starting with the October 2027 edition. [ Monopol ]

Donald Insall , an architect and “pioneering conservationist,” who notably worked on renovating and preserving Windsor Castle after it was damaged in a 1992 fire, has died at age 100, his studio announced. [ Dezeen ]

Meet Invictibellatrix amberina , a newly discovered cousin of the Tyrannosaurus rex whose fossil was uncovered on the Isle of Wight. Better yet, the new name partly means “unconquered female warrior.” [ Times of London ]

In a first, Israel returned 22 antiquities to Greece amid the latter government’s campaign to restitute missing parts of the Acropolis that were removed and placed in museums around the world, including the Parthenon Marbles . [ The Associated Press ]

A 15th-century mosque in Thessaloniki, which at one point was used as a cinema called Alacazar, has just reopened as an arts and cultural exhibition space run by the Metropolitan Organization of Museums of Visual Arts of Thessaloniki (MOMus) following years of restoration work. [ The Art Newspaper ]

The Kicker

MAKING A SPLASH . Archaeologists have just uncovered the oldest-known shipwreck off the Turkish coast, dating to between 4,400 and 4,700 years ago, or around the time that Egypt’s Great Pyramid of Giza was built, reports Independent and the Journal of Maritime Archaeology . Researchers found double-handled ceramic containers and stone anchors that would have been carried in what was likely a wooden trade ship, the remains of which have long vanished. “The three-holed stone anchors found in the wreck area resemble those seen in Bronze Age Minoan, Cypriot, Anatolian, Levantine contexts,” stated researchers, who noted these details could reveal new information about Bronze Age shipping techniques.

content.article_text:
T en years ago, my dad called to say he had found these amazing images hidden under piles of maps and stuff in an attic in our family home in Piemonte, northern Italy. He had come across a leather-bound album of 53 black and white photographs: portraits of Japanese “native types”, reflecting the 19th-century colonial way of representing people, cultures and views of Japan .

It turned out we had a treasure in our hands: it was an album of photographs by Felice Beato , the first foreign photographer to arrive in Japan in 1863 at the end of the Edo period and on the eve of the Meiji era.

When Beato arrived, Japan was still largely closed to foreigners. He started accompanying British diplomatic and military delegations and later set up a portrait studio where he photographed geishas, fishers, samurai, teachers, government officials – creating a kind of visual encyclopedia of people, professions and ways of life. These were the first images of Japan that the western world saw.

I have always worked with historical archives. Finding this album was amazing, but I couldn’t understand why it had ended up in our house. I needed to know and decided to look for clues. A year later, I found a 19th-century manuscript written by one of our ancestors, Mathilde Ruinart , an intellectual and a painter. She had married the first Italian ambassador to Japan, who was sent there in 1867 partly to help secure Japanese silkworms, as a disease was devastating the European silk industry. She had accompanied her husband – the journey took four months – and they stayed for four years. The manuscript was her diary, as well as letters, detailing her time there.

I was so fascinated that I read it all in one night. While Beato is well known, no one had heard of this remarkable woman, who knew she was witnessing a major transition in Japan and wanted to leave a trace of her years there. She rode her horse through parts of the country forbidden to foreigners with a gun in her dress and reportedly once shot a group of bandits dead.

I found as many of Mathilde’s descendants as I could and uncovered more of her archive, including her netsuke collection, brought back from her time in Japan. I photographed her objects and belongings – I dedicated an entire year to her. She was the same age as Beato and in Japan at the same time, so it was obvious to me that they must have met there, and that she must have selected and bought the photographs from him, which is how they came to be in my house.

From that came The Yokohama Project , a dialogue between the three of us – Beato, Ruinart and me – across 150 years. Three ways of seeing Japan, past and present, trying to understand and build a bridge. In the first chapter of the project I followed their footsteps, going to places they went, shooting on large-format film, echoing the slow process of observation. For the second chapter, I photographed about 40 Japanese professions, some still linked to those photographed by Beato, such as the geisha and the shamisen player , but also going beyond them to contemporary Japan. I invited people to a studio in Tokyo to present themselves in the ways they wanted to be seen. I photographed Lolita girls, and a fishmonger who was like a movie star. In Tokyo fishmongers are superstars – he came with €1,000-worth of red snapper in a basket and told me we had 10 minutes or the fish would go bad, which is a problem shooting on large-format as it’s a very slow process.

Karen, who appears in this portrait, describes herself as a BDSM dominatrix and a rope artist. She practises shibari with cross-dressing, tying and binding – a broader term than bondage. It is a visual and technical practice of tying the body with rope that can be erotic or not. It originates from the way samurai would bind their prisoners. Karen also practises kinbaku , a specific term for tight binding. She uses it in an intimate way with her clients, who are mostly men with high social and professional pressures.

Her practice allows them to step outside their day to day identities and express a side they can’t show elsewhere. She is a therapeutic person for them, and they talk to her – it’s not just a physical relationship but a cathartic experience. It allows her clients to transcend daily life. The man in this image is actually an assistant who worked on the project with me and agreed to be part of the picture. The two of them talked, and she decided how to tie him. He had never experienced it before – and he admitted afterwards that he enjoyed it.

The Yokohama Project by Giada Ripa is published by Gost Books

Giada Ripa’s CV

Born: London, 1974 High point: My first museum solo exhibition, Displacement, at the Moscow Museum of Modern Art in 2011 T op tip: Follow what genuinely makes you curious. Research can give you the starting point, but it’s through looking, questioning and having a personal encounter with the subject that the work begins to come alive

content.article_text:
It seems as if nobody can decide who should shoulder most of the blame for the recent box office flop of Digger .

Was it the ousted Warner Bros film executives Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, whose love of big-budget auteur cinema usually came with a hefty price tag? Or was it the marketing team, who were responsible for hiding the movie’s biggest swing from all trailers, ensuring many viewers would be left alienated from its early meta-reveal onwards?

The truthful answer is that the film’s fate was sealed long before anybody could point fingers over its failure. In the past year it’s become clear that audiences have grown tired of the worn-out cinematic trend Digger is a part of: the eat-the-rich satire.

There was a brief moment when audiences couldn’t get enough movie takedowns of the uber-wealthy, with the breakout success of Parasite inspiring Hollywood to seize upon its class-conscious themes and drag them into the west. The sustained fallout from the Covid pandemic brought issues of wealth inequality further into the spotlight, and titles as varied as Glass Onion , Saltburn , Triangle of Sadness and The Menu all spoke to the zeitgeist with their distinct, controversial takedowns of the 1%.

On the small screen, Succession and The White Lotus rapidly increased their audiences after acclaimed first seasons, thanks to the promise of darkly comic social commentary skewering those at the top of the food chain. Audiences were more than ready to eat the rich, but their appetites were satiated long before Hollywood had even considered switching up the menu.

Digger is the most high-profile casualty of this trend running its course, with some reports predicting it could lose a staggering $250m (£190m) during its cinema run. The divisive reviews and audience reactions are easy to blame, but perhaps it would have been better received had audiences not grown exhausted by constant cinematic reminders about how much they’ve been screwed over by the rich and powerful.

The theme hasn’t grown any less urgent, but interest in movies that hold a cracked mirror up to this reality has waned. Already this year, two action-revenge movies pitting lower-class protagonists against the super-rich in fights to the death – Ready or Not 2 and They Will Kill You – belly-flopped at the box office, and even arthouse audiences seem to be exhausted by this brand of topical satire, if receipts for Rosebush Pruning and I Love Boosters are anything to go by.

On the small screen, the return of anthology series Beef, an awards sensation and streaming hit in its first run, failed to register as it pivoted to this familiar class satire, barely cracking Netflix’s daily top 10 before disappearing entirely.

Later this week, Romain Gavras’s Sacrifice will debut on Netflix with no fanfare, more than a year after its hotly anticipated festival premiere landed with a thud . It’s a tale of shallow but self-righteous celebrities at a fundraising gala infiltrated by violent activists, boasting an A-list cast including Chris Evans, Anya Taylor-Joy and John Malkovich. It echoes many of the previously mentioned titles’ themes about the tension between the wealthy and their commitment to political causes. And even with its starry ensemble and clear cultural relevance, it took several months to find a distributor, and this paragraph may be the first you’re hearing of it.

The strangest thing about the death of this trend in movies is that many of its ideas are finding more ground in the mainstream. Even the most vanilla tax on higher earners is supported by 75% of Britons, according to YouGov , and a clear majority of 60% in the US . People are becoming more openly critical of the super-wealthy, so it is strange that pop culture taking aim at their unsustainable lifestyles is being met with fatigue.

We’re living through a time when the world’s richest man is also one of the most widely disliked, and the real-estate mogul US president keeps hitting new lows in approval ratings. Despite the not-so-secret allegiances of some studio heads – Skydance CEO David Ellison is an enthusiastic Trump backer – Hollywood creatives are aware of how detested among the public these figures are beyond their bases, and studios haven’t been shy in greenlighting movies with a satirical disdain for everything they represent, politically and culturally. Why has it stopped striking a chord?

The most obvious explanation is pure exhaustion. Doomscrolling has become a daily activity for millions, so why would anybody need to part with their money to see a movie satirising the people responsible for the state of the world when they could get sharper, more topical gags on their timeline for free?

In trying to speak to the times without the responsibility of reacting to more specific headlines, the eat-the-rich movie often winds up preaching the obvious, late to the joke even if the sentiment remains relevant. It’s the Stewart Lee routine about political satire – “Was it funny? No, but I agreed the fuck out of it” – blown up to blockbuster scale, and nobody is spending their hard-earned cash to politely nod along to a movie they should be laughing at.

The irony of Digger being the final movie released by Warner Bros as an independent studio hasn’t been lost, with its theme of billionaires trying to control the narrative foreshadowing the arrival of a new studio owner with an interest in appeasing the president.

We might become nostalgic for this brand of movie very quickly if the worst assumptions about Ellison’s studio takeover come true, as well as being thankful that a movie of this kind could have ever been greenlit at this level. Unfortunately, no passage of time will make this and every other late-stage capitalism satire become laugh-out-loud funny.

content.article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Production has wrapped in Los Angeles on the indie drama 1 Am Pacific Time , with Peter Facinelli ( Twilight ) among the leading cast.

The film also stars Alex Vaughan ( Monster: The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story ), Billiards U.S. Open Champion Jeanette Lee, and Erica Muñoz ( Grey’s Anatomy ). Filmmaker Brandon DeLany ( Broadway Sandwich ) has written and directed the film.

The film follows a struggling pool hustler, played by Vaughan, who sees a shot at redemption when he wins a large sum of money from the wrong person. He is thrust into a world of dangerous criminals, impossible odds, and life-altering choices, ultimately forced to decide what his own life is worth.

Muñoz and DeLany, who previously served as producers on the six-time Emmy-nominated PBS series Broadway Sandwich , are producing under their production company, Alexandria Films. Other producers include Meg Saricks, Aaron Champion, and Facinelli.

Watch on Deadline

Facinelli recently starred in and produced The Unbreakable Boy , and co-directed, produced, and starred in On Fire . Muñoz is a Broadway performer known for her breakout role as Mimi in Rent , as well as her leading role in HBO’s Long Gone By . DeLany is known for producing the OWN series Deep Shift .

content.article_text:
Netflix is swinging the axe — laying off around 1,000 employees, representing 6% of its workforce, in what is its biggest layoff to date.

Most of the layoffs will affect workers in Netflix’s product, technology, legal and HR teams, co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters wrote in an email to employees Wednesday morning about the layoffs.

“Our mission — to entertain the world — is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources,” the co-CEOs said in the memo, a copy of which was obtained by Variety (read it in full below).

Related Stories

Skydance to Fully Reorganize International; Kevin MacLellan Will Not Lead Key Group

Bradley Cooper to Star as Duke in 'G.I. Joe' Reboot From Danny McBride

A Netflix spokesperson said the company did not have any comment beyond the memo from Sarandos and Peters.

Popular on Variety

Netflix, the industry’s biggest premium streaming provider with more than 325 million customers globally, has posted double-digit growth in both revenue and profits in recent years. In 2025, the company had $45.2 billion in revenue (up 16%) and net income of $11 billion (up 26%). But investors have been concerned that Netflix’s engagement on a per-user basis slowed in the first half of 2026.

“Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full-year forecast,” Sarandos and Peters said in the memo. For 2026, Netflix projects revenue of $51.0 billion-$51.4 billion (up 13%-14%) and operating margin of 31.5% (versus 29.5% in 2024).

The co-CEOs continued, “We’ll continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation.” However, they said, “Doing that means making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees, and investors.”

As of the end of 2025, Netflix had about 16,000 full-time employees.

The last major Netflix layoffs came in 2022, when it axed about 450 staffers following the streamer’s net decline of 200,000 subscribers in the first quarter of that year, its first such drop in more than a decade. The company has made additional smaller cutbacks since then, including letting go several dozen members of its global product team earlier in 2026.

Netflix is scheduled to report third quarter 2026 earnings on Tuesday, Oct. 20, after market close. For the second quarter, the streamer posted earnings in line with Wall Street forecasts , with revenue up 13.4% year-over-year to $12.6 billion and operating margin of 33.4% (down from 34.1% in the year-earlier period). But Netflix issued Q3 revenue guidance below analyst expectations, driving the stock price down.

Shares of Netflix were down 0.3% in trading as of 10:10 a.m. ET Wednesday, to $70.26/share, amid a decline in the broader market.

Read the memo from Sarandos and Peters to Netflix staffers:

Team — We wanted to share that we are making a number of organizational changes and, as a result, we’ll be letting go of roughly 6% of our colleagues, with the greatest impact to our product, tech, legal, and HR teams.

Decisions like these are never easy, and we don’t take them lightly. Our top priority today is to support those who are leaving Netflix. The process will vary somewhat by country, but leaders will be connecting with impacted employees soon. If you are leaving, please know that we will support you throughout this transition and make sure you have as much clarity and context as possible. We also want to say thank you. What you’ve built, and the care you brought to Netflix, have made a lasting difference and we will always be grateful.

For the rest of the team, we know you have questions, too. Our mission — to entertain the world — is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources. Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full year forecast. We’ll continue to invest aggressively in high impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation. Doing that means making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees, and investors.

We know changes like this are tough, but let’s stay focused. This is one of the most dynamic times in the history of entertainment — and it’s a moment perfectly suited to a company like ours that’s built at the intersection of technology and entertainment. Now it’s on us to step up and meet the moment, together, like we always do.

Ted and Greg

content.article_text:
Qatar Museums has announced the programme for the inaugural Rubaiya Qatar Quadrennial, bringing together more than 120 artists from over 45 countries across Doha from 21 November 2026 to 30 April 2027.

Led by Her Excellency Sheikha Al Mayassa bint Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, chairperson of Qatar Museums, the initiative is presented by the institution and developed and organised under ALRIWAQ Arts + Architecture, which will serve as the quadrennial’s principal venue and institutional base. The programme will present exhibitions, commissions and public art to venues across Doha, addressing global ecology, water’s place in human history and the maritime connections that have shaped Qatar and the Gulf.

Sheikha Reem Al Thani, Deputy CEO of ALRIWAQ Arts + Architecture, Public Art and Rubaiya Qatar noted: “Rubaiya Qatar reflects our commitment to creating platforms that support artistic research, experimentation and production over the long term. As the institutional home of the quadrennial, ALRIWAQ Arts + Architecture brings together artists, curators, researchers and communities from Qatar and around the world to generate new knowledge, foster creative exchange and shape meaningful cultural dialogue.”

Sheikha Alanood Al Thani, director of Rubaiya Qatar, also emphasised the importance of the Quadrennial: “Cultural institutions in the SWANA region are no longer merely participating in the global discourse about contemporary art. They are setting its tone and shaping its future. The inauguration of Rubaiya Qatar marks a defining moment in this change, with Doha as the stage on which contemporary art from our region and beyond is presented to the world. Foregrounding non-Western perspectives, fostering ambitious new commissions and embedding deep ecological and historical research into its curatorial core, Rubaiya Qatar offers a fresh paradigm for international exhibitions of contemporary art.”

The inaugural edition takes shape around Unruly Waters , a headline exhibition curated by Tom Eccles, Ruba Katrib , Shabbir Hussain Mustafa and Mark Rappolt. Featuring more than 30 new commissions, including Bani Abidi, Lawrence Abu Hamdan, Yousef Ahmad, Sophia Al-Maria, Farah Al Qasimi , Majid Al-Remaihi, Simone Fattal, Dala Nasser, Lydia Ourahmane, Wael Shawky and Ahlam Shibli, whose practices contribute to the quadrennial’s wider engagement with ecology, water and maritime histories. The works span multiple media and historical periods, from tenth-century ceramics to contemporary digital installations.

The wider exhibition programme will include Our Common Currents , curated by Lina Patmali, which explores shared relationships with water through artistic and ecological perspectives, and Seething Sea , curated by Wadha Al-Aqeedi with assistant curator Loulwah Kutbi, which traces the sea’s influence on artistic practices across the Arab region and beyond. Public art commissions will also extend across sites throughout the country.

Taking place across cultural institutions and public spaces in Qatar, the quadrennial includes presentations at the Museum of Islamic Art, Katara QM Gallery and Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art.

Beyond the exhibitions, Rubaiya Qatar will host five months of public programming, with more than 130 artists, curators, thinkers, educators and cultural practitioners contributing to talks, lectures, workshops, screenings, performances and tours.

content.article_text:
Andrew Haigh returned this fall with another tender drama, this time adapting a Colm Tóibín story with a cast including Fred Hechinger, Ebon Moss-Bachrach, Caitríona Balfe, Kit Connor and D’Pharaoh Woon-A-Tai. A Long Winter , which recently played at New York Film Festival, will be coming to U.S. theaters on January 22, 2027 with select screenings in New York starting December 4.

Here’s the synopsis: “In 1951, high in Colorado’s Rocky Mountains, Mike’s (Hechinger) world is thrown into uncertainty when his mother vanishes into the wilderness. Alongside his complicated father, and with their small mountain community rallying together against the unforgiving winter, Mike embarks on a search that leads him toward an unexpected journey of self-discovery, belonging and the quiet strength required to carry on.”

Kent M. Wilhelm said in his NYFF review , “In his second decade of feature filmmaking, Andrew Haigh has stealthily become one of cinema’s most emotionally perceptive voices. His characters never anticipate what’s coming their way, and he uses that element of surprise to test their mettle. Through internal struggle, he interrogates both our frailty and resilience through richly textured characters. Along with his thematic preoccupations (queerness, solitude, vulnerability), Haigh’s studies are reliable in their approach and quality. He has yet to make a bad movie; A Long Winter maintains the streak. While his adaptation of Colm Tóibín’s short story is sketched more broadly than previous work, it’s still a reflection of Haigh’s empathy, intelligence, and keen narrative instincts.”

Watch the trailer below, along with a NYFF Q&A and talk between Andrew Haigh and Ira Sachs.

Packed to its entirety by first and second-time directors, the 12 projects at this year’s Ventana Sur Proyecta co-production forum delivers a new generation snapshot backed by some of Latin America’s finest producers which delivers a searing portrait of the contemporary realities.

In key casting Brazil’s Maeve Jinkings, renowned for her pivotal role in Walter Salles’ Oscar-winning “I’m Still Here,” is set to star in “Cabildo 71.” Natalia Oreiro (“Yosi, the Regretful Spy”) in “The Other Mountain.”

Related Stories

A24 British Shows ‘It Gets Worse,’ ‘Major Players’ and ‘The Ministry of Time’ to Stream on Paramount+ in U.S.

Josh Goldstine to Oversee Marketing and Distribution at Warner Bros., Paramount and All Skydance Film Labels (EXCLUSIVE)

Of project confirmed Tuesday by the San Sebastián Oil. Festival, which partners on Proyecta with Cannes Festival’s Marché du Film and Ventana Sur, “Give Me Shelter” marks one of the latest projects from Rei Pictures . Based in Argentina, Mexico and Spain, it is behind Lucrecia Martel’s Venice Selected “Our Land,” Argentine Oscar submission “Kill the Jockey” and Cannes Un Certain Regard winner “The Settlers” of just recent films.

Popular on Variety

“Give Me Shelter” will mark Nicolás Pérez Veiga’s feature debut after an prize-laden adversing career, including seven Cannes Lions, an International Emmy nomination for “Out There” and directing “Ringo, Glory and Death.”

Set up at Cannes Critics’ Week Next Step workshop, “The Absence” is produced by Julio Chavezmontes’ famed Piano, a Mexico City-based producer and co-producer on movies from Apichatpong Weerasethakul, Ruben Östlund, Lucrecia Martel and Leos Carax.

“Rabbits” marks the first new Colombian director title from Colombia-based Ocúltimo, co-founded by Simón Mesa Soto , director of acclaimed “A Poet,” a Cannes Un Certain Regard Jury Prize. Ocúltimo aims “to become a platform for new generations of Colombian filmmakers with bold, director-driven films,” Mesa Soto told Variety .

“Los Mejores Días” is set up at Juan Pablo Miller’s Tarea Fina , a bastion of Argentine arthouse cinema, behind such standouts as Cannes Camera d’Or winner Las acacias,” “Incident Light” and “Sleepwalkers.”

Boarded by France’s Luxbox Spain’s Amore Cine, Ventana Sur Proyecta Co-Production Forum Title “Portrait Huaco” weighs as the second feature from Melina León, whose “Song Without a Name” (“Canción sin nombre”) world premiered at the 2019 Cannes Directors’ Fortnight.

A closer look at the 12 film projects at this year’s Proyecta lineup:

“ The Absence,” (“La Ausencia,” Jorge Sistos Moreno, Mexico)

The feature debut of Sistos Moreno, whose “The Darkness was selected for Cannes Critics’ Week in 2022. In 18th century Morelia, a mestizo woman, the lady of an estate, invokes an ancestral deity in search for a for her husband’s syphilis, passed on to her. “This film speaks to a wound that remains open even today: racism, and the inability to accept ourselves and our heritage because of the forces and paradigms imposed upon us,” says Sistos Moreno.

“ Cabildo 71,” (Victoria “Pitoka” Pena, Uruguay, Brazil, Argentina, Spain)

A sophomore outing for Victoria “Pitoka” Pena, whose debut feature, “Delia”, won the Silver Biznaga for Best Director at the Málaga Film Festival, “Cabildo 71” is based on real-life events about the women imprisoned in Cabildo — a prison-convent run by the nuns of the Good Shepherd. An intimate take on the biggest women’s jail break in history. Boarded by Una Presencia (Argentina) and Vitrine Filmes (Brazil/Spain), lead produced by Monarca Films of Uruguay and co-producer Boulevard Filmes, Brazil.

“ Dirty Face” (“Cara sucia,” Ignacio Acconcia, Spain)

Acconcia draws on a decade working with people with intellectual disabilities for his fiction feature debut. Led by Ayhe Productions alongside Kabiria Films and Barcelona-based Contraria Media, the drama follows a Black teenager with vitiligo who finds acceptance while performing community service at a disability care home. The producers are also behind the upcoming “March 14th,” winner of the Berlinale Co-Production Market’s VFF Talent Highlight Award. Ayhe’s David Aymerich says the film aims to bring underrepresented communities to the screen.

“ Give Me Shelter,” (“Un Lugar Seguro,” Nicolás Pérez Veiga, Argentina, Mexico)

“A true facts-based thriller, set just days before Argentina’s 1976 military coup, “a story of resilience and courage that almost nobody knows,” says Pérez Veiga. When his father is kidnapped by a paramilitary task force days before the coup, doctor Gustavo Vaca Narvaja returns to his family and decides to risk everything on a desperate escape. “There’s only one problem: they are twenty six, and none can be left behind.”

“ Isabel Hernández” (Giorgio Giampà, Italy-Mexico)

Italy’s Zoe Films, behind Venice competition entry “A Bit of Light,” leads Giampà’s feature debut alongside LaDoc and Mexico’s Fiasco and Madrefoca. Set in Guatemala, the drama follows a young agronomist investigating her long-absent father amid the migration crisis. With established Italian arthouse distributor Teodora Film on board, the project participated in TorinoFilmLab’s FeatureLab 2026. “I was immediately drawn to the depth and complexity of its characters and its careful exploration of how trauma translates across generations,” says Fiasco’s Elena Fortes.

“ Los Mejores Días,” (Maria Zanetti, Argentina)

The second feature from María Zanetti, a 2025 Argentina AMPAS best first feature for debut “Alemania.” Set over three timelines and straddling Argentina and Spain, a potentially powerful portrait of young love and an enduring passion, despite a darker side, an “exploration of love with no adornment nor emphases,” says Zanetti.

“ The Other Mountain” (“La otra montaña,” Horacio Reyes Páez, Uruguay-Argentina)

Natalia Oreiro (“Wakolda”) is attached to star in a new take on the 1972 Andes plane crash, told from the perspective of a mother awaiting news of her missing son. Reyes Páez, her real-life grandson, calls it “the intimate, invisible battle of a mother, far from the snow and the wreckage.” Uruguay’s U Films and Sueño Cine produce alongside Argentina’s FAM Contenidos.

“ The Place and the Hope,” (“El lugar y la esperanza,” Ariagna Fajardo Nuviola, Cuba-France)

Nuviola revisits the impact of a community filmmaking initiative launched 30 years ago in her native Sierra Maestra. Produced by Julio Raúl Vega Garcés’ Torrente Films, the feature documentary draws on family archives to explore cinema’s power to preserve collective memory. Backed by Cuba’s Film Promotion Fund, it won a Eurodoc special mention at Montreal’s RIDM Forum.

“ Portrait Huaco,” (“Huaco Retrato,” Melina León, Peru, France, Spain)

An awaited adaptation of Peruvian author Gabriela Wiener’s autobiographical novel “Portrait Huaco.” Gabriela returns to Lima after her father dies. Back home, she discovers a book by her great-great-grandfather, Austrian explorer Charles Wiener. Her search into the family past becomes a reckoning with the lingering legacies of colonialism, internalized racism and abandonment. Produced by Peru’s Mano de Obra Cine, led by Melissa Cordero, and La Vida Misma Films, both behind “Song Without a Name.”

“ Rabbits,” (“Conejos,” Sara Nanclares, Colombia, Chile, Germany, France)

A powerful high-caliber Latin-America-Europe co-production that revisits a social experiment in birth control carried out in Colombia for over 30 years. “With a sharp script and a witty, outspoken protagonist who refuses to be defined by her circumstances, the film challenges conventional views of teenage pregnancy, bringing to light the desires and contradictions that lie beneath it,” says Nanclares.

“ Salamanca,” (Juan Sebastian Torales, Argentina, France)

The second feature from Torales whose “Almamula,” a coming-of-age drama , rooted in the legends and folklore of the Argentine countryside, played Berlín’s 2023 Generation 14Plus. Set up at Lorena Quevedo Argentina’s Twin Latin Films (“Venezia”), who co-produced Torales’ debut.

“ Unfit Mother,” (“Mala madre,” Manuela Espiñeira, Chile)

Chilean outfit Pinda Producciones, behind Berlinale players “Skin in Spring” and “The Nature of Invisible Things,” teams with Espiñeira’s MoveShot on her feature debut. Actress and co-scribe Nicole Rubio stars as a progressive politician whose baby dies after she accidentally leaves him in her car, triggering a devastating personal and public reckoning. “The Movie Teller” actress Sara Becker co-stars. It explores how a woman is judged “not only for what happened, but for the way she has worked, loved and mothered,” Espiñeira says.

content.article_text:
The first reactions are in for DC Comics ‘ body horror thriller “ Clayface ,” with journalists and fans calling it “freakishly awesome” and “everything you want from a villain-led movie.”

Directed by “Speak No Evil” filmmaker James Watkins from a screenplay co-written by “The Haunting of Hill House” creator Mike Flanagan , “Clayface” stars Tom Rhys Harries as the DC Universe character and Batman adversary. Clayface is Matt Hagen, an actor whose face is disfigured by a local mob boss. Desperate, he volunteers as a test subject for scientist Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie), who transforms his body into clay and causes him to lose his sanity.

Related Stories

After Kelly Clarkson Slams Brooklyn Novelty Store, Shop Says the ‘One-of-a-Kind’ Singing Bird She Wanted Wasn’t Actually For Sale

Kelly Clarkson Joins Brandi Carlile's Girls Just Wanna Weekend Festival as Co-Headliner

“‘Clayface’ was fantastic,” Collider editor-in-chief Steven Weintraub wrote on X. “An awesome addition to the DCU that doesn’t require any knowledge of DC to enjoy. It’s hard R and loaded with brutal scenes that really surprised me. Audience freaked out a few times during my screening to what was being depicted on screen.”

Popular on Variety

Film critic Peter Gray added that it “has that comic book flair” but that doesn’t “diminish how BRUTAL it is! Dark, violent, with little levity to offset the nastiness, this is an exciting addition to Gunn’s DCU.” He added that Harries “brings equal boyish charm and quiet menace to the role.”

YouTuber Brandon Davis called the film “freakishly awesome” and praised Watkins for getting “creative with Clayface’s abilities.” He added that Harries “is a star” and “kills it.”

With a story by Flanagan and screenplay co-written by Flanagan and Hossein Amini, “Clayface” also stars David Dencik, Max Minghella and Eddie Marsan and is produced by “The Batman” director Matt Reeves alongside James Gunn and Peter Safran. It’s set to hit U.S. theaters via Warner Bros . on Oct. 23.

See all the first reactions below.

content.article_text:
One of the most spiritually transporting experiences I had at the New York Film Festival this year was the world premiere of Paul Thomas Anderson’s Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall on 35mm. Shot with a vision at once affectionately timeless and fittingly playful, it’s truly something to behold how the One Battle After Another director frames Winter’s passionate performance. Ahead of Janus Films and Criterion’s theatrical roll-out beginning on November 20, the first trailer has now arrived.

Here’s the NYFF synopsis: “Even for those who already admired the talents of Brooklyn’s own Cameron Winter, both as a solo artist and as the front man of the band Geese, his performance at Carnegie Hall on December 11, 2025, was a revelation. A stripped-down set in which he accompanied himself on a Steinway grand, the show cemented Winter’s status as a one-of-a-kind cabaret art-pop balladeer, his soaring vibrato resonating throughout a theater known for its legendary acoustics. Oscar-winning filmmaker Paul Thomas Anderson was there with a crew, including his Licorice Pizza collaborator Benny Safdie, to capture this major star-is-born moment, and the result is a smashing cinematic concert, shot on 16mm and 35mm with a perfect mix of intimate images of Winter and of the cavernous space, keyed into the singer-songwriter’s effortless combination of bravado and sensitivity, darkness and light. A Janus Films and Criterion release.”

content.article_text:
France’s Luxbox and Spain’s Amore Cine have boarded the Peruvian drama “Portrait Huaco” (“Huaco retrato”) by Melina León, best known for her debut feature “Song Without a Name” (“Canción sin nombre”), which world premiered at the 2019 Cannes Directors’ Fortnight.

“ After the incredible journey we shared with ‘Song Without a Name,’ I’m thrilled to continue collaborating with Melina, now as both international sales agent and co-producer,” said Luxbox’s Fiorella Moretti.

Related Stories

Cynthia Erivo Called Sunny Hostin to Explain Why 'The View' Host's Comments on Cornell 7 Case Sparked Backlash: 'Lead With Empathy' and Not the Law

Cynthia Erivo Says ‘Not Enough Credit Is Given to Intimacy Coordinators’: ‘They’re Often Given a Hard Time’ but ‘What They Do Is Important’

She added: “As a Peruvian, it is especially meaningful to help bring Gabriela Wiener’s bold and contemporary work to the screen through Melina’s singular vision. ‘Portrait Huaco’ explores questions at the heart of today’s conversations in a truly original way, and I have no doubt it will resonate with audiences around the world.”

Popular on Variety

For Paz Lázaro, who co-founded Amore Cine alongside Edson Sidonie (“Karnawal”) and Juan Pablo Felix (“Mil pedazos”), “Adapting Gabriela Wiener’s ‘Portrait Huaco’ means bringing to the screen a work that bridges Latin America and Spain, weaving colonialism, racism, identity and desire with a voice both ancient and radically contemporary.”

“For Amore Cine, alongside our fellow producing partners, this is an opportunity to champion a film with international reach that challenges perspectives and reexamines our shared history.”

Based on the autobiographical novel of the Peruvian author, the project participates in the 8th Proyecta Co-Production Forum at Ventana Sur , which takes place in Montevideo, Uruguay this year from Nov. 30 – Dec. 4.

Amore Cine and Luxbox join Peru’s Mano de Obra Cine, led by Melissa Cordero, and La Vida Misma Films, which produced “Song Without a Name.”

The story follows Gabriela who returns to Lima after her father dies. Back home, she discovers a book by her great-great-grandfather, Austrian explorer Charles Wiener. Her search into the family past becomes a reckoning with the lingering legacies of colonialism, internalized racism and abandonment.

“’Portrait Huaco’ combines a distinctly Peruvian perspective with universal themes of identity, memory and colonial heritage. Under the direction of Melina León, the film seeks to preserve its cultural roots and Peruvian creative leadership while embracing an international scope through strategic co-production partnerships,” said Cordero.

This is the second time for Mano de Obra to co-produce with Amore Cine. Late coming-of-age drama, “Ofelia,” currently in post,’ is a European-Latin American co-production that includes Amore, Argentina’s Bikini Films, Quijote Films of Chile, Brazil’s África Filmes and CUP Filmes, Spain’s Potenza Producciones and France’s Reality Films.

Said Cordero: “I’m interested in producing auteur-driven films with a distinctive cinematic voice and strong cultural identity, as well as genre films that can connect with wider audiences. I’m particularly drawn to stories rooted in Peru and Latin America that explore universal themes, bringing local perspectives to an international audience.”

“My near-term strategy is to strengthen Mano de Obra Cine’s position as a production company focused on feature films, building strategic co-production partnerships across Latin America and Europe. I aim to combine public and private financing with international partnerships and distribution opportunities to develop a sustainable slate of films with strong creative identities and international reach.”

content.article_text:
Brazil’s Maeve Jinkings, renowned for her pivotal role in Walter Salles’ Oscar-winning “I’m Still Here, ” leads the cast in the upcoming prison convent escape drama “Cabildo 71,” which is selected to participate in Ventana Sur ’s Proyecta Co-Production Forum.

Jinkings is also best known for her roles in “ The Secret Agent” director Kleber Mendonça Filho’ s lauded dramas “Neighboring Sounds” and “Aquarius.”

Related Stories

Cynthia Erivo Says ‘Not Enough Credit Is Given to Intimacy Coordinators’: ‘They’re Often Given a Hard Time’ but ‘What They Do Is Important’

Cynthia Erivo Called Sunny Hostin to Explain Why 'The View' Host's Comments on Cornell 7 Case Sparked Backlash: 'Lead With Empathy' and Not the Law

Una Presencia (Argentina) and Vitrine Filmes (Brazil/Spain) have come on board as co-producers of the project, which is backed by Argentina’s INCAA minority fund and the Ancine–ACAU bilateral minority fund. They join lead producer Monarca Films of Uruguay and co-producer Boulevard Filmes, Brazil.

Popular on Variety

Written and directed by Victoria “Pitoka” Pena, whose debut feature, “Delia”, won the Silver Biznaga for Best Director at the Málaga Film Festival, “Cabildo 71” is based on real-life events about the women imprisoned in Cabildo — a prison-convent run by the nuns of the Good Shepherd, which included Lucía Topolansky, who later became the VP of Uruguay and wife of former President José “Pepe” Mujica, her twin sister Elia Topolansky and other women who became prominent figures in Uruguay’s political and social life.

Story follows La Parda who joins forces with 12 political prisoners to form a women’s choir, using it as a cover to escape from the Cabildo prison-convent. During Mass on March 8, 1970, they rush down the chapel aisle and escape right under the noses of the nuns guarding them.

A year later, La Parda is captured again. This time, there are no nuns—only police and a growing number of prisoners, including her sister, Lucía. The two barely speak, but La Parda senses that Lucía is hiding something.

Behind the prison walls, a daring plan is taking shape: the biggest women’s prison escape in history.

“I am interested in telling this story from an intimate and personal point of view, giving this dimension precedence over the heroic narrative of the feat. Without diminishing what was achieved — quite the opposite — I want to delve into the issues that shaped the prisoners’ lives within the intimacy of the prison: the differences among them that give substance to their experience, in order to explore identity, betrayal and the need to find one’s own sense of justice,” said Pena.

Said Monarca Film’s Eugenia Olascuaga: “We want to portray the female characters within their variety of social class and the kind of life they led, not under the “guerrilla women” stereotype that the popular imagination tends to default to.” “The eight Uruguayan actresses who will play the Tupamaras are confirmed — it was very important for us that they all be Uruguayan, as a political and artistic choice.”

She added that the actresses playing the Topolansky sisters are Graciela Ingold and Carolina Genoni while the rest of the cast are Camila Parard, Renata Denevi, Luche Bolten and Matilde Colacce. Jinkings plays one of the nuns in the convent-prison.

Principal photography is slated for Sept. to Nov. next year.

Ventana Sur takes place in Montevideo, Uruguay over Nov. 30 – Dec. 4.

content.article_text:
Stephen Chow ’s “ Kung Fu Soccer ” will hit cinemas in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and Ireland on Oct. 23, with Singapore-based distributor Encore Films releasing the action-comedy in its original language as well as in a newly produced English-dubbed version.

Jimmy O. Yang, MC Jin and Chow all voice their own characters in English for the dub. A Cantonese-language dub has also been finished, with its voice cast yet to be revealed.

Related Stories

Cynthia Erivo Says ‘Not Enough Credit Is Given to Intimacy Coordinators’: ‘They’re Often Given a Hard Time’ but ‘What They Do Is Important’

Cynthia Erivo Called Sunny Hostin to Explain Why 'The View' Host's Comments on Cornell 7 Case Sparked Backlash: 'Lead With Empathy' and Not the Law

The North American and U.K. rollout comes after the film’s cinema run in Asia and Oceania. Released in mainland China on July 11, “Kung Fu Soccer” was the country’s top-grossing title of the summer season, earning some $349 million. It then opened across Southeast Asia in August, starting in Singapore and Cambodia on Aug. 6, then Indonesia, Hong Kong, Macao, Malaysia, Brunei and Thailand.

Popular on Variety

Zhang Xiaofei, Dilraba Dilmurat and Lay Zhang Yixing head the cast, which also includes Carina Lau, Satoh Takeru, Sisley Choi, Angel Woo, Xue Ye, Louis Cheung, Yang and MC Jin. The story centers on the Emei Women’s Football Team, written off as underdogs, as it competes for the Supreme Invincible Cup. Led by captain Shuangshuang, striker Yulong and mentor Xu Feng, the players fuse martial arts technique with ball skills in their push for the title.

The film sees Chow return, 25 years on, to the sports-meets-kung-fu territory he staked out in 2001 with “ Shaolin Soccer ,” which built a global fanbase. He followed it in 2004 with “Kung Fu Hustle,” known for its intricate fight choreography and visual inventiveness. This time, a team of women takes the field.

“Following the tremendous response to ‘Kung Fu Soccer’ across Asia and Oceania, we’re excited to bring the film to cinema audiences in the U.K., Canada, U.K. and Ireland,” said Joyce Lee, managing director of Encore Films.

Lee said Chow’s films had always crossed language and cultural lines, uniting audiences through his mix of action, comedy and heart. “At Encore Films, we believe that great films and the filmmakers behind them deserve more than just a theatrical release. Their creative vision and legacy should be respected, carefully nurtured and developed for generations to come,” she said.

Founded in 2003, Encore has released titles including “Ne Zha 2,” “John Wick: Chapter 4,” “Suzume,” “The Boy and the Heron,” “The New King of Comedy” and “La La Land.” The company is also active in production, with “Young & Fabulous,” a box office success in Singapore, among its credits. Its second feature, “Fat Hope,” is in post-production.

content.title_original: Winter of the Crow review – Lesley Manville magnificently on edge in intriguing cold war thriller
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "P art cold war thriller, part Kafkaesque reverie, this movie takes us back to the sinister drear of Poland in 1981, when General Jaruzelski has just introduced martial law in reaction to the dangerous new mood of freedom occasioned by the Solidarity trade unions. The director is Kasia Adamik, daughter of The Green Border’s Agnieszka Holland; the film is adapted from a story by Olga Tokarczuk , called Professor Andrews Goes to Warsaw.", "links": [{"text": "Olga Tokarczuk", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/books/olga-tokarczuk"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Lesley Manville plays Professor Andrews, an academic clinical psychologist (like Tokarczuk) from Britain with testy, peremptory mannerisms; her indulgence is a fondness for taking Polaroid photos. She has attained a certain level of celebrity for a book on dreams, despite claiming that she never dreams herself. Andrews has been invited to give a lecture in Warsaw, during which she begins to outline views on mental illness not unlike those of Laing or Foucault; but her speech is chaotically disrupted by students shouting that Poland itself is an oppressive asylum."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The chief protester’s sister Alina (Zofia Wichlacz) happens to be the postgrad student tasked with showing Professor Andrews around, but from the very first, there is confusion. Andrews loses her bag, then has to give her passport to Alina so she can go back to the airport and look for it; she can’t go to a hotel and must stay at a flat in a sketchy area, belonging to relatives of Alina. content.article_text:
P art cold war thriller, part Kafkaesque reverie, this movie takes us back to the sinister drear of Poland in 1981, when General Jaruzelski has just introduced martial law in reaction to the dangerous new mood of freedom occasioned by the Solidarity trade unions. The director is Kasia Adamik, daughter of The Green Border’s Agnieszka Holland; the film is adapted from a story by Olga Tokarczuk , called Professor Andrews Goes to Warsaw.

Lesley Manville plays Professor Andrews, an academic clinical psychologist (like Tokarczuk) from Britain with testy, peremptory mannerisms; her indulgence is a fondness for taking Polaroid photos. She has attained a certain level of celebrity for a book on dreams, despite claiming that she never dreams herself. Andrews has been invited to give a lecture in Warsaw, during which she begins to outline views on mental illness not unlike those of Laing or Foucault; but her speech is chaotically disrupted by students shouting that Poland itself is an oppressive asylum.

The chief protester’s sister Alina (Zofia Wichlacz) happens to be the postgrad student tasked with showing Professor Andrews around, but from the very first, there is confusion. Andrews loses her bag, then has to give her passport to Alina so she can go back to the airport and look for it; she can’t go to a hotel and must stay at a flat in a sketchy area, belonging to relatives of Alina. And when she awakens the next morning, Andrews sees a tank in the wretched and surreally deserted tower block wasteland. The clampdown has begun, murderous secret police are everywhere and she has no passport. Perhaps Andrews had better get used to staying in Poland for the foreseeable future – or maybe for ever.

It is an intriguing and disquieting movie, though one whose storytelling impulse slows a little, and perhaps the film could have benefited from closer editing – although this might have meant losing some of the bizarre and surreal details, like the live carp that people queue up to buy for food and keep in the bath.

content.article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Beverly Hills-based film finance specialist Launch Financing is poised to scale up its short-term gap loan services for indie productions in the U.S., Canada and the UK having secured its first ever institutional $15M senior credit facility.

The film-lending arm of producer-financier Chris K. Daniels’ The Launch Company , has previously funded more than 60 media loans against tax credits, pre-sales and other committed production receivables.

Past recipient productions include thriller The Dutchman , black comedy Thumb and coming-of-age comedy The Marshmallow Experiment .

Related Stories

Eric McCormack Set For Nimisha Mukerji's Psychological Thriller 'You're Safe Now'

'A Long Winter': Watch First Trailer For Andrew Haigh Drama Starring Fred Hechinger, Ebon Moss-Bachrach, Caitríona Balfe & Kit Connor

The new $15 million senior credit facility has been provided by specialty lender Pier Asset Management and is Launch Financing’s first institutional warehouse facility.

Watch on Deadline

The line, extendable to $25 million over time, will enable Launch Financing to scale its short-term production lending to independent films in the U.S., Canada and the UK.

“A production’s money always comes slower than the production wants it to. Tax credits, bank closings, equity cashflow and distributor payments arrive on their own schedule, and the schedule is not the shoot’s,” said Daniels.

“We built a standardized loan structure that clears diligence in two to five business days and wires within forty-eight hours of signing, because that is the only thing a producer in prep actually needs from a lender. This facility allows us to expand beyond our current pipeline and work more closely with high-quality producers, production companies, agencies and studios, improving the process one film at a time.”

Launch Financing advances senior secured capital against money a production is set to receive and is repaid when that money arrives. Loans run eight to twenty-six weeks and are secured in first position against government production incentives, distributor minimum guarantees, pre-sales, committed equity, institutional capital and library-backed corporate guarantees.

The money typically covers production cashflow while a bank or institutional lender closes, as well as cast escrow and union deposits, production payroll and finishing funds.

Launch Financing sits inside The Launch Company alongside Launch Development, which develops and packages film projects; Cinelaunch, the company’s business-affairs and back-office platform; and Launch North, its physical production operation in Toronto.

The lending team has sat on both sides of the table, as producers who have borrowed against tax credits and pre-sales and as the institutional capital that structures those loans.

Daniels, who is also a strategic partner at Esme Grace, the boutique firm behind Michael Mann’s Ferrari , serves as chief executive officer of The Launch Company and its lending arm. Wyatt Cavalier is Launch Financing JV’s chief investment officer , and Jess Mastro is head of development for The Launch Company.

content.article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Here’s your first trailer for Andrew Haigh ‘s Telluride, Toronto and New York Film Festival drama A Long Winter , starring Fred Hechinger, Ebon Moss-Bachrach, Caitriona Balfe, Kit Connor and D’Pharaoh Woon-A-Tai.

Based on Haigh’s adaptation of Colm Tóibín’s short story of the same name, the film is set during the early 1950s in a remote part of the Colorado mountains “as fall comes to an end and a family prepares for the long winter ahead”.

Pic is produced by Tristan Goligher for The Bureau, Chad Oakes and Mike Frislev for Calgary-based Nomadic Pictures, and Michael Elliott. The film, which plays the London Film Festival this evening, was developed by Mubi and is co-financed by Mubi and Film4. Mubi is handling most of the release with the film in cinemas January 15 in the UK and Ireland, January 22 in the U.S. and Canada, and February 18 in Germany, Austria, Italy, Spain and Latin America.

Haigh’s All of Us Strangers received six BAFTA nominations, including best director and best adapted screenplay for Haigh. It was also the recipient of four Gotham and three Independent Spirit Awards nominations. Haigh’s previous features include Film4-backed Lean on Pete and 45 Years , for which Charlotte Rampling earned an Oscar nomination, and breakout indie hit Weekend .
