content.article_text:
W here pornography once trod, horror has now become the genre that infiltrates and apes all others. With a host of out-of-copyright cartoon characters recently grave-robbed for not-so-fresh IP, now classic literature is apparently fair game for a gruesome glow-up, in this case, Emily Brontë’s regular GCSE-botherer. But Becca Hirani’s laboured reworking makes the book’s gothic subtext crashingly, jugular-spurtingly textual.

As in the novel, wide-eyed Mr Lockwood (Ross Townsend-Green) pays a courtesy call to his brooding landlord Heathcliff (Sky Cheema) at Wuthering Heights. But this time, his sojourn is more like Jonathan Harker’s at Dracula’s castle; everywhere he turns, the shrouded phantom of Heathcliff’s beloved Catherine Earnshaw (Elle O’Hara) is lurking, and she leaves an extra dollop of gore on the windowsill in her famous nocturnal apparition. The tetchy host doesn’t do much to put Lockwood at ease – even before he’s trapped in the house by a bubo-inflicting malady. Between the hallucinations, the surly servants, and the weird absence of Heathcliff’s rumoured son Linton, he begins freaking out that it’s a different kind of moors story he’s stumbled into.

Hirani puts undeniable effort in getting her plot points to line up with Brontë’s – even if most of the characters, including poor old Lockwood’s horse, meet a much grislier fate. Rationed out in snippets of Catherine’s diary, the confidences of housekeeper Nelly (Nicola Wright) and more random supernatural flashbacks involving Lockwood, the manor’s backstory is rather garbled, though with the OTT hook of Heathcliff as an 18th-century Yorkshire Ripper. Rather than amping up the camp, as the likes of Kate Bush and Emerald Fennell did in their takes on the novel, Hirani plays it straight and dour, mystifyingly so, given the extra stranglings, slashings and pitchfork-impalings she’s chucked in.

At the same time, diffident acting undermines the film’s claim as pure slasher fare: Townsend-Green’s jumpy turn feels as if he has strayed out of Jeeves and Wooster, while, despite the Rasputin looks, windy-voiced Cheema is too loose to convince as Byronic bad boy. For much of the runtime, we’re left with too little that makes his conversion to homicidal mania credible, until the last-minute lowdown on his Hellraiser-like scheme for his ward, Cathy (Anna Coupé). Reanimating the corpse of Brontë in this rickety way, this update not only feels pointless, but short on self-awareness or fun.

content.article_text:
チケットは160万円から！ BLACKPINKのロゼ、LAの美術館ガラで初パフォーマンスへ

BLACKPINKのロゼが、11月7日に ロサンゼルス・カウンティ美術館（LACMA） で開催される「アート＋フィルム・ガラ」に出演する。今年は、画家のヴィヤ・セルミンスと、 映画 『デューン』などを手がけた監督の映画監督のドゥニ・ヴィルヌーヴが表彰される。

K-POPグループ、BLACKPINKのロゼが、11月7日に ロサンゼルス・カウンティ美術館（LACMA） で開催される「アート＋フィルム・ガラ」でパフォーマンスを披露する。

今年で15回目を迎える同イベントでは、自然界を緻密に描写した作品で知られるラトビア系アメリカ人アーティストのヴィヤ・セルミンスと、 映画 『デューン』や『メッセージ』などの SF作品 で知られる映画監督のドゥニ・ヴィルヌーヴを表彰する。今年も グッチ がプレゼンティング・スポンサーを務め、俳優の レオナルド・ディカプリオ とLACMAの理事 エヴァ・チョウ が共同議長を務める。

チョウは声明で、「LACMAのアート＋フィルム・ガラは、創造性を体現する人々と、世界中のあらゆる表現分野のつながりを称える場です。世界的なポップスターであるロゼは、比類ない才能とスタイルで、この夜の祝祭をさらに盛り上げてくれるでしょう」と期待を込めた。

タイトルの通り、同ガラは毎年、文化の発展に貢献したアーティストと映画監督の2名を表彰している。初開催となった2011年版でジョン・バルデッサリとクリント・イーストウッドが称えられて以来、 ロサンゼルス のアートシーンにおける恒例行事の1つとなっている。2025年の開催では650万ドル（約10億2800万円）を調達し、前年の640万ドル（約10億1200万円）をわずかに上回った。

これまでにも、同ガラには数々の著名ミュージシャンが出演してきた。2025年は ドージャ・キャット 、2017年はアニー・レノックスがパフォーマンスを披露し、2024年にはチャーリーXCXに加えてトロイ・シヴァンがサプライズ出演を果たした。ロゼも2022年と2023年に同ガラに出席しているが、パフォーマーとして参加するのは今回が初めてとなる。

BLACKPINKのメンバーとして世界的な成功を収めるロゼは、ソロアーティストとしても活躍している。初のソロアルバム『rosie』は、累計ストリーミング再生回数が100億回を超えた。ブルーノ・マーズとのコラボレーション曲「APT.」は世界的なヒットとなり、グラミー賞で3部門にノミネートされている。

「アート＋フィルム・ガラ」のチケットは、1万ドル（約160万円）から。（翻訳：編集部）

content.article_text:
Artists, collectives, researchers and curators worldwide are invited to apply for the Art Explora and Cité internationale des arts Residency Programme in Paris, France, offering funded opportunities to explore the intersections of art, science, technology and contemporary social and ecological challenges.

Open Call:

Art Explora has announced its 2027 residency programme in partnership with Cité internationale des arts, inviting international artists, collectives, researchers and curators to develop projects that investigate relationships between artistic practice, scientific enquiry and technological innovation.

The programme encourages interdisciplinary approaches to contemporary social and ecological questions, giving participants time, space, and resources to advance their creative and research practices.

Two residency formats are available:

SOLO Programme: Designed exclusively for individual artists.

COLLECTIVE Programme: Open to artist collectives or collaborations between artists and researchers or curators.

Residencies run for three or six months, with two sessions scheduled between March 2027 and February 2028.

Institutional Context:

Established in 2021, the Art Explora residency programme in Paris supports artistic research and experimentation while fostering connections between artists, cultural professionals and audiences.

Since its inception, the programme has welcomed more than 145 residents from 58 countries, representing diverse artistic disciplines, generations and cultural backgrounds.

The initiative forms part of Art Explora’s broader commitment to developing encounters between art and audiences at local, national and international levels.

Through its partnership with Cité internationale des arts, the programme provides access to dedicated creative spaces in Paris alongside curatorial guidance, production support, mentorship and professional networking opportunities.

Eligibility and Criteria:

Applications are open to artists, artist collectives, researchers and curators from around the world, subject to the requirements of the selected residency format.

Eligible artistic disciplines include:

Visual arts

Performing arts

Digital arts

Eligible research fields include:

Humanities

Social sciences

Sciences

Technological innovation

Ecology

Proposed projects should explore connections between art, science and technology while engaging with contemporary social or ecological issues.

The SOLO Programme is reserved for individual artists, while the COLLECTIVE Programme accommodates collaborative artistic practices and partnerships involving artists, researchers and curators.

Evaluation Process:

The programme seeks proposals that engage with its interdisciplinary focus and address contemporary questions through artistic or research-based approaches.

The On the Move announcement does not detail specific assessment criteria, jury composition, or selection procedures. Applicants should consult the official Art Explora application guidelines for further information about the selection process.

Practical Information:

Application deadline: 30 October 2026

Location: Cité internationale des arts, Montmartre, Paris, France

Residency duration: Three or six months

Residency sessions:

Session 1: March to August 2027

Session 2: September 2027 to February 2028

Each resident receives:

A fully furnished and equipped live-work studio of approximately 50 m².

A monthly living allowance of €1,000.

A production grant of €3,000.

Round-trip travel to Paris.

Curatorial and production support throughout the residency.

Access to mentorship and professional networking opportunities.

The programme offers participants the opportunity to develop their practices in an international creative environment while building connections across artistic and research disciplines.

Applications and Queries:

Submit applications by 30 October 2026 through the official Art Explora application platform.

Applicants should consult the programme’s official guidelines for submission requirements, supporting documentation and any additional conditions applicable to their chosen residency format.

Programme information and applications: Art Explora Residency Programme

Additional information: On the Move, Residency Programme 2027

Wildlife photographer of the year 2026 winners – in pictures

A selection of the winning images from this year’s competition across topics ranging from underwater to urban wildlife, and photojournalism to mammal behaviour. The overall winner is Federico Veronesi of Italy for his powerful image of an elephant carrying a dead calf

The winning photographs will be showcased at the Natural History Museum in London from 16 October 2026 until July 2027

Wed 14 Oct 2026 08.41 BST

Wildlife photographer of the year 2026 | The Aftermath by Federico Veronesi, Italy | Winner, Behaviour: Mammals

Escape Artistry by Michał Michalski, Poland | Winner, Natural Artistry

The Great Divide by Alex Visbal, Colombia | Winner, Wetlands: The Bigger Picture

Shedding Light by Agorastos Papatsanis, Greece | Winner, Plants and Fungi

Night-Time Catch by Alex Lindbloom, US | Winner, Oceans: The Bigger Picture

bagan , or mobile net-fishing platform, in the inky waters off Papua. He started searching for sharks around dawn when the nets were still in the water. Initially lacking natural light for his drone’s camera, he found these sharks illuminated by the

bagan ’s bright lightsPhotograph: Alex Lindbloom/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026

A Watchful Eye by Aaron Sanders, UK | Winner, Animal Portraits

Shifting Sand by Sitaram Raul, India | Winner, Behaviour: Invertebrates

The Meeting Place by James Lewin, UK | Winner, Animals in their Environment

Afternoon Snack by Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas, Germany | Winner, Rising Star Award

Secret Worlds by Kutub Uddin, Bangladesh/UK | Winner, Portfolio Award

Cribraria aurantiaca is at a tiny and often overlooked stage in its life. Uddin became interested in slime moulds in 2024, and devotes much of his time to revealing this hidden world – exploring his local woodlands in West Sussex, where fallen logs and damp forest floors provide opportunities for discovering these fascinating organismsPhotograph: Kutub Uddin/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026

Warning Sign by Francisco Negroni, Chile | Winner, Photojournalism

Birdsong Painted in Light by Konrad Gräeter, Germany | Winner, 15-17 Years

Protective Pose by Anton Sorokin, US | Winner, Behaviour: Amphibians and Reptiles

Young wildlife photographer of the year 2026 | Labour of Love by Oscar Whitfield, Zimbabwe/UK | Winner, 11-14 Years

Making Morays by Tony Wu, USA/Japan | Winner, Under Water

Scenes from the Swamp by Isak Pretorius, South Africa Winner | Behaviour: Birds

Wily Coyotes of San Francisco by Loren Elliott, US | Winner, Photojournalist Story Award

Urban Jungle by Seth Forestson | UK Winner, Urban Wildlife

Flight of the Bumblebee by Amelie Davis, UK | Winner, 10 Years and Under

content.title_original: Todd Haynes on Pedro Pascal-Led ‘De Noche,’ What You Can’t See on Screen and the Radical Power of Love
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "LYON, France — When Mexican costume designer Anna Terrazas told Todd Haynes that the most important thing about a costume was what it smelled like, the filmmaker had just one response: “You’re hired.”", "links": [{"text": "Todd Haynes", "url": "https://variety.com/t/todd-haynes/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Oscar-nominated director shared the anecdote about his upcoming Pedro Pascal-starring romantic noir drama “De Noche” at the Lumière Film Festival on Tuesday, offering a glimpse into his approach to filmmaking, from the music and sounds that shape his movies to the senses that cannot always be expressed on screen.", "links": [{"text": "Lumière Film Festival", "url": "https://variety.com/t/lumiere-film-festival-2/"}]}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Related Stories"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Peacock-Your-Bravoverse-Playback-Experience.png?w=250&h=167&crop=1", "alt": "Peacock - Your Bravoverse Playback Experience", "caption": "", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Peacock App Launches 'Your Bravoverse,' Featuring a Personalized TikTok-Style Video Feed Hosted by AI-Generated Andy Cohen", "links": [{"text": "Peacock App Launches 'Your Bravoverse,' Featuring a Personalized TikTok-Style Video Feed Hosted by AI-Generated Andy Cohen", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/tv/news/peacock-app-launches-your-bravoverse-ai-andy-cohen-1236909580/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/bfa79580-47a8-4fe7-ad92-1fd4c30a057f-e1791924228990.jpg?w=250&h=167&crop=1", "alt": " Jesse Jo Stark ", "caption": "", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Music Industry Moves: Jesse Jo Stark Signs With WME, Rebecca Allen Steps Down at Universal Music U.K.", "links": [{"text": "Music Industry Moves: Jesse Jo Stark Signs With WME, Rebecca Allen Steps Down at Universal Music U.K.", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/music/news/jesse-jo-stark-wme-1236910696/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“We see movies with our ears and our eyes,” Haynes explained. “But movies that evoke smell and touch and other kinds of senses are the ones that keep allowing us to fill in.”"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Popular on Variety"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Haynes is in Lyon with longtime producer Christine Vachon for a retrospective featuring four of his films: “Poison,” “Safe,” “Far From Heaven” and “I’m Not There,” including newly restored versions of the first two.", "links": [{"text": "Christine Vachon", "url": "https://variety.com/t/christine-vachon/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The director – whose latest film follows the story of a detective (Pascal) and a younger schoolteacher (Danny Ramirez) who flee the corruption of 1930s Los Angeles for Mexico – described the homework he sets himself before each production. He said he immerses himself in films that share its genre or cinematic style, rather than necessarily its historical setting."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“It’s as if I give myself an assignment each time,” he said, explaining how that research feeds into what he calls his “image books,” which he shares with his collaborators."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While putting together the image book for his Oscar-nominated “May December,” starring frequent collaborator Julianne Moore alongside Natalie Portman, Haynes began listening to Michel Legrand ‘s score for Joseph Losey’s “The Go-Between.”", "links": [{"text": "Michel Legrand", "url": "https://variety.com/t/michel-legrand/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The music soon became central to the project. He played it on set from the very first day, using it to choreograph camera movements. By the editing stage, the music had become so integral to the film that Haynes asked composer Marcelo Zarvos to rearrange and adapt it. “We couldn’t let it go,” he recalled. “It became a definitive part of the structure, the language, and the energy of the film.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Having watched the restored version of “Safe” the previous evening in Lyon, Haynes praised sound designer Leslie Shatz for the unsettling soundscape of the 1995 drama, in which Moore plays a woman suffering from a mysterious illness."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "He described “all of the strange, lurking, unconscious sounds” in the film, that created what he called “a kind of magnetic field in which the contamination she senses from her surroundings becomes literally audible.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Turning to his six-time Oscar-nominated 2015 romance “Carol,” Haynes recalled how journalists kept congratulating him and stars Cate Blanchett and Cannes Best Actress winner Rooney Mara for portraying strong women. Blanchett, he said, would object: Carol wasn’t some invincible heroine but a woman constrained by her time, struggling to understand herself and how she wanted to live.", "links": [{"text": "Cate Blanchett", "url": "https://variety.com/t/cate-blanchett/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“There is something radical and anti-social about love,” Haynes said, citing great French writer Roland Barthes’ “A Lover’s Discourse,” passages of which he shared with the actors."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Haynes also paid tribute to Vachon, who helped rescue “Safe” when he was struggling to raise its $1 million budget. content.article_text:
LYON, France — When Mexican costume designer Anna Terrazas told Todd Haynes that the most important thing about a costume was what it smelled like, the filmmaker had just one response: “You’re hired.”

The Oscar-nominated director shared the anecdote about his upcoming Pedro Pascal-starring romantic noir drama “De Noche” at the Lumière Film Festival on Tuesday, offering a glimpse into his approach to filmmaking, from the music and sounds that shape his movies to the senses that cannot always be expressed on screen.

Related Stories

Peacock App Launches 'Your Bravoverse,' Featuring a Personalized TikTok-Style Video Feed Hosted by AI-Generated Andy Cohen

Music Industry Moves: Jesse Jo Stark Signs With WME, Rebecca Allen Steps Down at Universal Music U.K.

“We see movies with our ears and our eyes,” Haynes explained. “But movies that evoke smell and touch and other kinds of senses are the ones that keep allowing us to fill in.”

Popular on Variety

Haynes is in Lyon with longtime producer Christine Vachon for a retrospective featuring four of his films: “Poison,” “Safe,” “Far From Heaven” and “I’m Not There,” including newly restored versions of the first two.

The director – whose latest film follows the story of a detective (Pascal) and a younger schoolteacher (Danny Ramirez) who flee the corruption of 1930s Los Angeles for Mexico – described the homework he sets himself before each production. He said he immerses himself in films that share its genre or cinematic style, rather than necessarily its historical setting.

“It’s as if I give myself an assignment each time,” he said, explaining how that research feeds into what he calls his “image books,” which he shares with his collaborators.

While putting together the image book for his Oscar-nominated “May December,” starring frequent collaborator Julianne Moore alongside Natalie Portman, Haynes began listening to Michel Legrand ‘s score for Joseph Losey’s “The Go-Between.”

The music soon became central to the project. He played it on set from the very first day, using it to choreograph camera movements. By the editing stage, the music had become so integral to the film that Haynes asked composer Marcelo Zarvos to rearrange and adapt it. “We couldn’t let it go,” he recalled. “It became a definitive part of the structure, the language, and the energy of the film.”

Having watched the restored version of “Safe” the previous evening in Lyon, Haynes praised sound designer Leslie Shatz for the unsettling soundscape of the 1995 drama, in which Moore plays a woman suffering from a mysterious illness.

He described “all of the strange, lurking, unconscious sounds” in the film, that created what he called “a kind of magnetic field in which the contamination she senses from her surroundings becomes literally audible.”

Turning to his six-time Oscar-nominated 2015 romance “Carol,” Haynes recalled how journalists kept congratulating him and stars Cate Blanchett and Cannes Best Actress winner Rooney Mara for portraying strong women. Blanchett, he said, would object: Carol wasn’t some invincible heroine but a woman constrained by her time, struggling to understand herself and how she wanted to live.

“There is something radical and anti-social about love,” Haynes said, citing great French writer Roland Barthes’ “A Lover’s Discourse,” passages of which he shared with the actors.

Haynes also paid tribute to Vachon, who helped rescue “Safe” when he was struggling to raise its $1 million budget. The film, he said, wouldn’t exist without her.

Vachon, who already had a grasp of the industry’s commercial realities, recalled the practical advice she gave him years earlier when he proposed making his first feature, “Poison” as three interconnected 20-minute stories.

“I said, you know what, Todd? Make it 90 minutes,” she recalled.

The producer made some pointed observations about the state of independent cinema. She sees younger Americans flocking to repertory theaters, including her own 26-year-old daughter, but worries about what the industry is offering them.

“I feel like we are creating a new generation of cinemagoers, but we’re just not giving them enough movies to see,” she said.

Haynes also revisited his childhood obsession with Lucille Ball, which inspired his autobiographical short “Dottie Gets Spanked.” He went on to tease a possible screening of the film alongside “Superstar: The Karen Carpenter Story,” his cult short made with Barbie dolls that has rarely been shown publicly since legal disputes over its music rights. The filmmaker was hinting heavily at what might be in store for the festival’s surprise screening Wednesday evening at the Institut Lumière.

The Lumière Film Festival runs in Lyon through Oct. 18.

content.title_original: The Negative Melted, the Legend Didn’t: Inside the Resurrection of Kamal Amrohi and Meena Kumari’s Storied Indian Epic ‘Pakeezah’
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "On the night of Feb. 3, 1972, the prints of “ Pakeezah ” arrived at Bombay’s Maratha Mandir cinema in a palanquin pulled by four horses. Military bands played outside, police held back the thousands crowding the gates, and inside, the film’s star, Meena Kumari , sat beside her husband, director Kamal Amrohi, and gripped his wrist so hard through the screening that her nails drew blood.", "links": [{"text": "Pakeezah", "url": "https://variety.com/t/pakeezah/"}, {"text": "Meena Kumari", "url": "https://variety.com/t/meena-kumari/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Amrohi’s son Tajdar was in the theater that night. His father never pulled his arm away."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Related Stories"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SL-Updated-Headshot_Credit-Anderson_Sam05-1000.jpg?w=250&h=167&crop=1", "alt": "sam levinson", "caption": "", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "'Euphoria' Creator Sam Levinson Enters Overall TV Deal at Amazon MGM Studios", "links": [{"text": "'Euphoria' Creator Sam Levinson Enters Overall TV Deal at Amazon MGM Studios", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/tv/news/sam-levinson-amazon-mgm-studios-overall-deal-1236910082/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2292781425.jpg?w=250&h=167&crop=1", "alt": "THE KELLY CLARKSON SHOW -- Episode A5174 -- Pictured: Kelly Clarkson -- (Photo by: Weiss Eubanks/NBCUniversal via Getty Images)", "caption": "", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Kelly Clarkson vs. Art of Play: Footage Revealed of Singer’s Visit to Brooklyn Novelty Store She Slammed for 'Pretty Woman' Treatment", "links": [{"text": "Kelly Clarkson vs. Art of Play: Footage Revealed of Singer’s Visit to Brooklyn Novelty Store She Slammed for 'Pretty Woman' Treatment", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/music/news/kelly-clarkson-art-of-play-molly-bird-footage-revealed-1236910838/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“He just gave a smile, and she also smiled in an embarrassment, you can say,” Tajdar Amrohi says. “And it seems that even after 54 years, I feel as if that incident took place yesterday.”"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Popular on Variety"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Kumari died on March 31, 1972, weeks after the film opened. Now, Film Heritage Foundation’s (FHF) 4K restoration of “Pakeezah,” carried out with the Amrohi family, is back in front of audiences. Thierry Frémaux presents its world premiere at Festival Lumière in Lyon on Wednesday. It then plays a gala at the BFI London Film Festival ’s BFI Imax on Oct. 18 that Shivendra Singh Dungarpur, the foundation’s director, will introduce with Tajdar Amrohi, his sister Rukhsar Amrohi and Kamal Amrohi’s grandson Bilal Amrohi. Dungarpur says he heard the Imax screening sold out “in no time.”", "links": [{"text": "BFI London Film Festival", "url": "https://variety.com/t/bfi-london-film-festival/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The film is set in Lucknow as the age of the nawabs (Muslim nobles) fades. Kumari plays Sahibjaan, born in a graveyard to a courtesan who was spurned by her husband’s aristocratic family. Raised in a brothel, Sahibjaan grows up to be the most celebrated courtesan of her day, though she longs for love and respectability. Then Salim, a forest officer played by Raaj Kumar, wanders into her train compartment by mistake while she is asleep. Taken with her feet, he leaves her a note in verse and slips away. When they meet again, they fall in love, but the stigma attached to her profession stands between them."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Few Indian films carry a backstory as heavy as this one. Amrohi was already married, with three children, when he married Kumari. Rukhsar grew up with her mother in the family’s hometown of Amroha, in Uttar Pradesh, until she was 13, while her father lived in Bombay (now Mumbai) with Kumari, whom the children called Chhoti Ammi (little mother). Amrohi conceived “Pakeezah” in the mid-1950s around Kumari, his wife and muse, and shooting began in 1956, in black-and-white, before moving to Eastmancolor and then CinemaScope. The production stalled in 1964 when the couple separated, and Kumari’s health declined sharply over the following years. The film’s German cinematographer, Josef Wirsching, who had come with Himansu Rai and Devika Rani from Bombay Talkies, died partway through. Composer Ghulam Mohammed died in 1968 after writing the songs, leaving Naushad to complete the background score."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Through all of it, Amrohi refused to let the film go."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“His relations, his health, his wealth – he put everything into ‘Pakeezah,’” his daughter Rukhsar Amrohi says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "She remembers that every household request, from new decor to things for himself, got the same answer: after “Pakeezah.” His kurtas (tunics), which usually arrived from Lucknow a dozen at a time every six months, wore thin during the shoot. When she pressed him to reorder, he told her that people came to see him, not his clothes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I’ll order all of this after ‘Pakeezah’ – not 12, I’ll get 24 – but let my ‘Pakeezah’ get into theaters,” she recalls him saying."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tajdar Amrohi says that by the time the film was ready for release, his father didn’t have a penny to keep for himself and was deep in debt. Financiers, Rukhsar says, pushed him to drop Ghulam Mohammed’s music as old-fashioned and credit Laxmikant-Pyarelal or Shankar-Jaikishan instead. He refused, whether or not that meant the film got made."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The family’s own life bent around the production. When Kumari left and the shoot stopped, Amrohi sent Rukhsar and her mother back to Amroha. He didn’t want anyone to say that his first wife and daughter had arrived and driven Kumari out. He later wrote to Rukhsar asking her to raise her small hands in prayer that he would finish the picture. He had expected to complete it in a year, and it now felt like a noose around his neck."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Isn’t that a sacrifice?” she says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When shooting resumed, the haveli (mansion) set on Stage 3 at Filmistan Studio in Goregaon was modeled on the Amrohis’ ancestral home in Amroha. Rukhsar went to the set every day because her father wanted her there. She also traveled with the unit to Mysore for the outdoor shoot of the song “Mausam Hai Aashiqana” and the elephant attack sequence. Her mother’s paandaan (a box for paan, or betel leaf), part of her wedding trousseau, was lent at Amrohi’s request. It appears in the Gulabi Mahal (Pink Palace) scenes beside the actor Nadira. It now sits in the drawing room of the Amroha house, which Rukhsar restored and filled with her father’s furniture, photographs and belongings. Locals, she says, began calling it Kamal Amrohi’s museum."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The siblings are protective of how their father’s marriage is remembered. Tajdar Amrohi is adamant that the couple never divorced, and says that Kumari had asked Amrohi to promise he never would, calling him Chandan, her pet name for him. He also pushes back on the widely told account that actors Sunil Dutt and Nargis and composer Khayyam persuaded Kumari to return to the film in 1969. Dutt deserves credit for going to her, he says, but many others in the industry, Ashok Kumar among them, had urged the same."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Frankly speaking, if Meena ji herself hadn’t wanted to complete this film, she wouldn’t have,” he says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nor, he says, did “Pakeezah” become a hit because its star died weeks after release, a reading his sister also rejects. If that were how it worked, he argues, “Every producer-director would pray that once the film is complete, one of their main artists leaves the world, and the film will be a hit. That’s not how it is. A good thing is good, and a bad thing is bad and won’t run.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tajdar Amrohi was at St. Elizabeth Nursing Home on Malabar Hill when Kumari died, and says it was the first time he had ever seen tears in his father’s eyes. Amrohi died in 1993 and is buried beside her. His son sees that as a kind of divine verdict on decades of gossip about the pair."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Just as Shah Jahan immortalized Mumtaz Mahal by building the Taj Mahal, Kamal sahab [sir] immortalized Chhoti Ammi, Meena ji, across the whole world by making ‘Pakeezah,’” he says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For Rukhsar Amrohi, who also calls Kumari Chhoti Ammi, the film is a token of the couple’s love, made by her father out of his love for Kumari. “‘Pakeezah’ is the love child of our Baba [father] and Chhoti Ammi,” she says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For Dungarpur, the film goes back to his own childhood. He was 3 when it was released, and his grandmother, Usha Rani, the Maharani (queen) of Dumraon in Bihar, was obsessed with it. She played its LP and later took him to see it on rerelease. He founded FHF in her memory in 2014 and had wanted to restore “Pakeezah” ever since."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“It’s one of my most beautiful memories of restoration, and the most important film in my life,” he says. “She was the driving force on seeing this restoration.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The job turned out to be among the hardest the foundation has taken on. When the FHF team examined the film’s original camera negative at a Mumbai lab, it had melted, with no images left on the celluloid."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Meena ji went into a coma two days before her death, and the negative of ‘Pakeezah’ had also gone into a coma,” Tajdar Amrohi says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The team rebuilt the film from an interpositive, a CinemaScope print and a color reversal internegative held at the National Film Archive of India, which Dungarpur credits to archivist P.K. Nair. The sound negative had also survived. The two-year restoration was carried out at L’Immagine Ritrovata in Bologna, with the soundtrack remixed in 5.1."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The on-and-off shoot left its own scars. Day-for-night sequences didn’t match from one stretch of the film to the next. The opticals, meaning the fades and shot changes, drifted in and out of focus. Padma Khanna and other doubles performed some of the dances instead of Kumari, which made the continuity puzzle harder."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Color was the biggest test. The available versions had faded badly, and accounts differed on whether Kumari’s costume in “Inhi Logon Ne” was pink or red. Original color photographs were scarce, since continuity stills were usually shot in black-and-white to save money. FHF found a few, and Rukhsar Amrohi, who had been on set, came to Dungarpur’s studio to check them. She told him the lyric itself mentions a dupatta (scarf) dyed pink, so red couldn’t be right, and pushed for a deep magenta. That is what made it to the screen."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“You have to make sure that you don’t do something which he had not done, or you enhance it to that level, but keep it exactly his vision, the way he had conceived the film,” Dungarpur says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "He points viewers to the tracking shot at the end of the “Chalte Chalte” song where the camera glides over a fountain. For him it shows what the film’s camera team pulled off before zoom lenses were in common use. The film also has an anniversary this month: Dungarpur notes that Oct. 8 marked the 100th birthday of its male lead, Raaj Kumar, who replaced an aging Ashok Kumar as Salim."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "FHF has run into missing negatives before. content.article_text:
On the night of Feb. 3, 1972, the prints of “ Pakeezah ” arrived at Bombay’s Maratha Mandir cinema in a palanquin pulled by four horses. Military bands played outside, police held back the thousands crowding the gates, and inside, the film’s star, Meena Kumari , sat beside her husband, director Kamal Amrohi, and gripped his wrist so hard through the screening that her nails drew blood.

Amrohi’s son Tajdar was in the theater that night. His father never pulled his arm away.

Related Stories

'Euphoria' Creator Sam Levinson Enters Overall TV Deal at Amazon MGM Studios

Kelly Clarkson vs. Art of Play: Footage Revealed of Singer’s Visit to Brooklyn Novelty Store She Slammed for 'Pretty Woman' Treatment

“He just gave a smile, and she also smiled in an embarrassment, you can say,” Tajdar Amrohi says. “And it seems that even after 54 years, I feel as if that incident took place yesterday.”

Popular on Variety

Kumari died on March 31, 1972, weeks after the film opened. Now, Film Heritage Foundation’s (FHF) 4K restoration of “Pakeezah,” carried out with the Amrohi family, is back in front of audiences. Thierry Frémaux presents its world premiere at Festival Lumière in Lyon on Wednesday. It then plays a gala at the BFI London Film Festival ’s BFI Imax on Oct. 18 that Shivendra Singh Dungarpur, the foundation’s director, will introduce with Tajdar Amrohi, his sister Rukhsar Amrohi and Kamal Amrohi’s grandson Bilal Amrohi. Dungarpur says he heard the Imax screening sold out “in no time.”

The film is set in Lucknow as the age of the nawabs (Muslim nobles) fades. Kumari plays Sahibjaan, born in a graveyard to a courtesan who was spurned by her husband’s aristocratic family. Raised in a brothel, Sahibjaan grows up to be the most celebrated courtesan of her day, though she longs for love and respectability. Then Salim, a forest officer played by Raaj Kumar, wanders into her train compartment by mistake while she is asleep. Taken with her feet, he leaves her a note in verse and slips away. When they meet again, they fall in love, but the stigma attached to her profession stands between them.

Few Indian films carry a backstory as heavy as this one. Amrohi was already married, with three children, when he married Kumari. Rukhsar grew up with her mother in the family’s hometown of Amroha, in Uttar Pradesh, until she was 13, while her father lived in Bombay (now Mumbai) with Kumari, whom the children called Chhoti Ammi (little mother). Amrohi conceived “Pakeezah” in the mid-1950s around Kumari, his wife and muse, and shooting began in 1956, in black-and-white, before moving to Eastmancolor and then CinemaScope. The production stalled in 1964 when the couple separated, and Kumari’s health declined sharply over the following years. The film’s German cinematographer, Josef Wirsching, who had come with Himansu Rai and Devika Rani from Bombay Talkies, died partway through. Composer Ghulam Mohammed died in 1968 after writing the songs, leaving Naushad to complete the background score.

Through all of it, Amrohi refused to let the film go.

“His relations, his health, his wealth – he put everything into ‘Pakeezah,’” his daughter Rukhsar Amrohi says.

She remembers that every household request, from new decor to things for himself, got the same answer: after “Pakeezah.” His kurtas (tunics), which usually arrived from Lucknow a dozen at a time every six months, wore thin during the shoot. When she pressed him to reorder, he told her that people came to see him, not his clothes.

“I’ll order all of this after ‘Pakeezah’ – not 12, I’ll get 24 – but let my ‘Pakeezah’ get into theaters,” she recalls him saying.

Tajdar Amrohi says that by the time the film was ready for release, his father didn’t have a penny to keep for himself and was deep in debt. Financiers, Rukhsar says, pushed him to drop Ghulam Mohammed’s music as old-fashioned and credit Laxmikant-Pyarelal or Shankar-Jaikishan instead. He refused, whether or not that meant the film got made.

The family’s own life bent around the production. When Kumari left and the shoot stopped, Amrohi sent Rukhsar and her mother back to Amroha. He didn’t want anyone to say that his first wife and daughter had arrived and driven Kumari out. He later wrote to Rukhsar asking her to raise her small hands in prayer that he would finish the picture. He had expected to complete it in a year, and it now felt like a noose around his neck.

“Isn’t that a sacrifice?” she says.

When shooting resumed, the haveli (mansion) set on Stage 3 at Filmistan Studio in Goregaon was modeled on the Amrohis’ ancestral home in Amroha. Rukhsar went to the set every day because her father wanted her there. She also traveled with the unit to Mysore for the outdoor shoot of the song “Mausam Hai Aashiqana” and the elephant attack sequence. Her mother’s paandaan (a box for paan, or betel leaf), part of her wedding trousseau, was lent at Amrohi’s request. It appears in the Gulabi Mahal (Pink Palace) scenes beside the actor Nadira. It now sits in the drawing room of the Amroha house, which Rukhsar restored and filled with her father’s furniture, photographs and belongings. Locals, she says, began calling it Kamal Amrohi’s museum.

The siblings are protective of how their father’s marriage is remembered. Tajdar Amrohi is adamant that the couple never divorced, and says that Kumari had asked Amrohi to promise he never would, calling him Chandan, her pet name for him. He also pushes back on the widely told account that actors Sunil Dutt and Nargis and composer Khayyam persuaded Kumari to return to the film in 1969. Dutt deserves credit for going to her, he says, but many others in the industry, Ashok Kumar among them, had urged the same.

“Frankly speaking, if Meena ji herself hadn’t wanted to complete this film, she wouldn’t have,” he says.

Nor, he says, did “Pakeezah” become a hit because its star died weeks after release, a reading his sister also rejects. If that were how it worked, he argues, “Every producer-director would pray that once the film is complete, one of their main artists leaves the world, and the film will be a hit. That’s not how it is. A good thing is good, and a bad thing is bad and won’t run.”

Tajdar Amrohi was at St. Elizabeth Nursing Home on Malabar Hill when Kumari died, and says it was the first time he had ever seen tears in his father’s eyes. Amrohi died in 1993 and is buried beside her. His son sees that as a kind of divine verdict on decades of gossip about the pair.

“Just as Shah Jahan immortalized Mumtaz Mahal by building the Taj Mahal, Kamal sahab [sir] immortalized Chhoti Ammi, Meena ji, across the whole world by making ‘Pakeezah,’” he says.

For Rukhsar Amrohi, who also calls Kumari Chhoti Ammi, the film is a token of the couple’s love, made by her father out of his love for Kumari. “‘Pakeezah’ is the love child of our Baba [father] and Chhoti Ammi,” she says.

For Dungarpur, the film goes back to his own childhood. He was 3 when it was released, and his grandmother, Usha Rani, the Maharani (queen) of Dumraon in Bihar, was obsessed with it. She played its LP and later took him to see it on rerelease. He founded FHF in her memory in 2014 and had wanted to restore “Pakeezah” ever since.

“It’s one of my most beautiful memories of restoration, and the most important film in my life,” he says. “She was the driving force on seeing this restoration.”

The job turned out to be among the hardest the foundation has taken on. When the FHF team examined the film’s original camera negative at a Mumbai lab, it had melted, with no images left on the celluloid.

“Meena ji went into a coma two days before her death, and the negative of ‘Pakeezah’ had also gone into a coma,” Tajdar Amrohi says.

The team rebuilt the film from an interpositive, a CinemaScope print and a color reversal internegative held at the National Film Archive of India, which Dungarpur credits to archivist P.K. Nair. The sound negative had also survived. The two-year restoration was carried out at L’Immagine Ritrovata in Bologna, with the soundtrack remixed in 5.1.

The on-and-off shoot left its own scars. Day-for-night sequences didn’t match from one stretch of the film to the next. The opticals, meaning the fades and shot changes, drifted in and out of focus. Padma Khanna and other doubles performed some of the dances instead of Kumari, which made the continuity puzzle harder.

Color was the biggest test. The available versions had faded badly, and accounts differed on whether Kumari’s costume in “Inhi Logon Ne” was pink or red. Original color photographs were scarce, since continuity stills were usually shot in black-and-white to save money. FHF found a few, and Rukhsar Amrohi, who had been on set, came to Dungarpur’s studio to check them. She told him the lyric itself mentions a dupatta (scarf) dyed pink, so red couldn’t be right, and pushed for a deep magenta. That is what made it to the screen.

“You have to make sure that you don’t do something which he had not done, or you enhance it to that level, but keep it exactly his vision, the way he had conceived the film,” Dungarpur says.

He points viewers to the tracking shot at the end of the “Chalte Chalte” song where the camera glides over a fountain. For him it shows what the film’s camera team pulled off before zoom lenses were in common use. The film also has an anniversary this month: Dungarpur notes that Oct. 8 marked the 100th birthday of its male lead, Raaj Kumar, who replaced an aging Ashok Kumar as Salim.

FHF has run into missing negatives before. Dungarpur says the restored “Sholay” had the same problem. So did the foundation’s work on “English, August,” which was rebuilt from a single print, and Shaji N. Karun’s Cannes winner “Piravi,” for which only subtitled prints survive.

“So much money is spent on the production, so much money is spent, but there’s very little money spent on preserving these elements,” he says. “And that’s been quite a tragic story of India’s cinematic history.”

The foundation has had a busy 12 months on the festival circuit. It took “In Which Annie Gives It Those Ones” to Berlin, “Amma Ariyan” to Cannes and “English, August” to Venice, with stops including New York, Toronto, Shanghai, Singapore and the Festival of Three Continents. Dungarpur says FHF deliberately programs Indian commercial landmarks such as “Sholay,” “Pakeezah” and “Amar Akbar Anthony” next to independent titles. That way, Western audiences who would otherwise never see them get the chance. “Pakeezah” is set to travel to the Smithsonian and the Academy Museum, and its producers plan a wide release in India.

FHF’s next restorations are Shyam Benegal’s “Bhoomika” and “Mandi,” John Abraham’s “Agraharathil Kazhuthai” (“Donkey in a Brahmin Village”) and Aribam Syam Sharma’s “Imagi Ningthem” (“My Son, My Precious”). The Abraham film will be the foundation’s first Tamil-language restoration. With Criterion, FHF is restoring Bimal Roy’s “Bandini,” “Devdas” and “Madhumati” as well as Satyajit Ray’s “Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne,” and it plans to take on “Piravi.”

Tajdar Amrohi still regrets that “Pakeezah” won no awards. When he once complained about it to his father, the director just smiled.

“You haven’t noticed one thing,” he told his son. “All these people who are coming to watch the picture – that is my award.”

content.article_text:
The New Museum has unveiled the artists and collectives participating in the sixth edition of its Triennial, set to take place from 4 February until 16 May 2027.

The New Museum Triennial was established in 2009 as a recurring international exhibition dedicated to early-career artists. Entitled The Outside Expands , the 2027 exhibition will bring together 36 artists and collectives from 34 countries, including Mandy El-Sayegh, Nour Jaouda and Fehras Publishing Practices, with the most expansive international representation so far. It will also be the first edition to take place in the museum’s newly opened, OMA-designed expansion.

Co-curated by Vivian Crockett and Isabella Rjeille, The Outside Expands takes part of its inspiration from a 1979 intervention by Brazilian collective 3NÓS3 and X Galería, which placed duct-taped Xs over the entrances of multiple São Paulo galleries. Accompanied by a message, “What is inside remains, what is outside expands,” which questioned the boundaries of cultural institutions during Brazil’s civil-military dictatorship. It also references artist and writer Jota Mombaça’s 2018 intervention in Rio de Janeiro, in which the phrase “What has no space is everywhere” was cut from a temporary museum wall, leaving its absence visible. The “X” also refers more generally to a crossroads and a space for reflection and decisions.

These references inform the triennial’s consideration of how artistic practices can challenge established boundaries around territory, gender and identity, while opening up possibilities for alternative forms of collaboration.

Participating artists:

Jean Barth Luz Broto Virginia Chihota Omyo Cho Paloma Contreras Lomas Biraaj Dodiya Mandy El-Sayegh Hamishi Farah Fehras Publishing Practices Levi van Gelder Jacqueline Kiyomi Gork Léann Herlihy Jesús Hilario-Reyes Nour Jaouda Josi Li Yong Xiang Maria Louizou Dakota Mace Rui Magalhães Rene Matić Jota Mombaça Cem Örgen Linda Pongutá Agnes Questionmark Liesl Raff Sofía Salazar Rosales Florencia Sadir Akane Saijo Sin Wai Kin Tiempo de Zafra Thato Toeba Paz Ulloa T. Vinoja Sun Woo Inês Zenha Kukay Bautista Zinampan

‘At war with the obvious’: the everyday genius of William Eggleston – in pictures

As a new exhibition looks at how the pioneering photographer sparked a colour revolution, his son, William Eggleston III, explains his father’s unique approach

content.article_text:
K iri is a lively yellow dinosaur, Lou is an amiable purple palorchecie (a fictional beast, vaguely resembling a palorchestes , which in turn vaguely resembles a giant tapir) – and if you’ve been watching their CBeebies show, which hails from New Zealand and consists of 5-minute episodes, you’ll know they’re the best of friends despite their ingrained temperamental differences. But how did they become friends in the first place? For the uninitiated, Kiri and Lou Go Raaa! functions as an introduction to the characters and their world, while for fans it’s a delightful origin story.

At only one hour long, the runtime is toddler-friendly – and to be honest, there are plenty of films marketed at adults that could learn a lesson from writer-director Harry Sinclair’s economical storytelling. (Sinclair is also the writer of the TV series, alongside Buffy the Vampire Slayer writing alum Rebecca Kirshner.) With the voice acting talents of Olivia Tennet (Freda in Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers) and Jemaine Clement (Flight of the Conchords), plus dreamy songs from Don McGlashan (Blam Blam Blam, The Front Lawn), Kiri and Lou Go Raaa! would arguably work superbly as an audiobook or radio show – except the visuals are a treat too.

It’s a cliche to bang on about the fingerprints in the modelling clay, as if effort and a handmade aesthetic automatically equate to great storytelling, but in this case, the tactile quality of the animation does help underscore the gentle perils of the duo’s various adventures. There’s the sense that they aren’t just computer sprites existing in some nebulous cloud, ergo they actually could be washed away in the sea, or melted by a “smoky mountain”. And there’s a wholesomeness to stop-motion that’s hard to beat; it’s a tangible reminder of the physical world, outside screens and digital ephemera. Co-director Anthony Elworthy’s long list of credits, including The Boxtrolls, My Life as a Courgette and Kubo and the Two Strings, also functions as a whistle-stop tour of some of the best children’s animation of the last decade-plus, so perhaps it shouldn’t be a surprise that this big-screen adventure has turned out so beautifully.

content.article_text:
ゲッティイメージズ、米破産法11条の適用申請へ。競合との大規模統合を断念、再建目指す

アメリカ の画像・動画ライセンスビジネス大手で、世界各国でサービスを提供する ゲッティイメージズ が、米連邦破産法第11条の適用を申請することを10月12日に発表した。背景には、競合企業との大型事業統合計画の中止がある。

3億点を超える画像・動画などの素材を保有する大手ライセンスビジネス企業、 ゲッティイメージズ が、日本の民事再生法にあたる米連邦破産法第11条（チャプター11）適用を申請すると発表した。同社は、著名実業家チャールズ・コッホ（コーク）が率いるコングロマリットの投資部門による支援を受け、非公開企業として再建を目指すとザ・ハリウッド・リポーター誌（THR）が 伝えている （*1）。

*1 US版ARTnewsとザ・ハリウッド・リポーターはいずれも、2022年秋からゲッティイメージズと世界的な独占メディアパートナーシップを結んでいるペンスキー・メディア・コーポレーションの傘下に属している。

10月12日の発表の背景には、ゲッティイメージズの競合である画像・動画ライセンスビジネス大手、シャッターストックとの37億ドル（約5800億円）規模の事業統合が不調に終わったことがある。2025年1月に公表された統合の目的は、「対等な立場での統合を通じて業界屈指のビジュアルコンテンツ企業を創出すること」とされていた。新会社の社名はゲッティ・イメージズ・ホールディングスで、ゲッティイメージズの最高経営責任者（CEO）であるクレイグ・ピーターズが、そのまま新会社のCEOとなる予定だった。

統合が取りやめになった大きな理由は、 イギリス の競争・市場庁の出した規制条件だった。当局はシャッターストックのエディトリアル部門の売却を求めたが、ゲッティ側はこれを「受け入れ不可能」と判断。THRの報道によると、ピーターズCEOは8月の業績発表で、不成立に終わったシャッターストックとの統合に1億ドル（約158億円）以上が費やされたことを明かしている。

ゲッティイメージズは、2018年から同社を支援してきたコッホ・エクイティ・デベロップメント（Koch Equity Development）から約5億ドル（約790億円）の資金提供を受け、今後数カ月のうちに公開企業から非公開企業へ移行する。ゲッティイメージズの広報担当者はTHRの取材に対し、破産手続きに伴う人員削減は行われず、同社の事業、コンテンツパートナー、および取引先にも影響はないと回答した。（翻訳：石井佳子）

content.title_original: A Long-Awaited Art Museum in a Former Renault Factory Finally Arrives on Paris’s Idyllic Île Seguin
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "To get to France’s newest contemporary art center, the journey is part of the experience. To reach Île Seguin in Boulogne-Billancourt, in the western suburbs of Paris, you must first go to Pont de Sèvres, the final stop of Métro Line 9, and then either take a 15-minute walk or a five-minute bus ride. It is worth the trek: Crossing onto the island means leaving the dense urban fabric behind for a site surrounded by water, with views toward the banks of the Seine and the hills of Meudon."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This is where Le Large has found its place. The art center is part of Pointe des Arts, a €450 ($504.5 million) cultural development that also includes a cinema, a hotel, and other amenities. Its construction marks another chapter in the transformation of an island whose identity has long been tied to industrial production. For much of the 20th century, Renault’s factory occupied the site, employing thousands of workers and sending cars out by road and river.", "links": [{"text": "Le Large", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/le-large/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The center’s name intentionally evokes both scale and possibility. Designed by Pritzker Prize–winning RCR Arquitectes, the building has a distinctive geometry, its footprint increasing from 5,382 square feet at the base to 16,146 square feet on the fifth floor. Its warm, copper-colored anodized-aluminum façade is composed of diamond-shaped elements arranged like overlapping scales, a nod to the double entendre embedded in the institution’s name. In French, prendre le large means to head out to sea."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“The expression resonates with the island setting and its relationship to the water. It conveys the possibility of escape, departure, and discovery,” director Paula Aisemberg told ARTnews in an on-site interview ahead of its opening."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "With an annual operating budget estimated at €5 million ($5.6 million), Le Large will vary how it uses its 26,910 square feet in exhibition space, oscillating between a single exhibition that takes over the entire museum, as its opening show does, or having “several shows running simultaneously, one on the fifth floor, another across the sixth and seventh floors. That will be the case for our second season,” Aisemberg said."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/1.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "View of Le Large’s copper-colored anodized-aluminum façade with diamond-shaped overlay. Nicolas Trouillard", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Le Large’s ambition is to attract the broadest possible audience, imagining what lies beyond art itself. The center was designed to be a gathering space as much as an exhibition venue, and around 40 percent of its public-facing spaces are free to enter. The first floor encourages visitors to spend time in the building, where they can take in a few works from the temporary exhibitions but mostly luxuriate in the sundrenched lobby’s ample seating areas for extended conversations. Nearby, a bookshop and concept store sit alongside a flight of stairs that doubles as an amphitheater-like seating area."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This multipurpose staircase leads to a mezzanine, from which escalators lead directly to the fifth floor. There, before visitors can reach the exhibition galleries, they will find two spaces by designer Constance Guisset: Extra Large, an 80-seat coffee shop serving seasonal food and panoramic views, and Le Petit Atelier, a dedicated section for kids aged six to ten who can participate in free workshops."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "To support its ambitions, Le Large operates on a hybrid model, combining a nonprofit association that has an endowment fund and a commercial entity responsible for venue rentals and private events. The association, chaired by collector Laurent Dumas, manages all of Pointe des Arts on Île Seguin, with a mission to promote French artistic creation. Its main patron is the Emerige Endowment Fund, the philanthropic arm of Dumas’s company, Emerige. Le Large is the latest in its contemporary art–focused initiatives, which include a grant for emerging artists and a commissioning program called 1 immeuble, 1 oeuvre (1 Building, 1 Artwork)."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/FEL-2026-Moteur-Imaginaire-010.jpg?w=400", "alt": "View of a museum exhibition showing a sculpture of a wooden car that has been cut up into pieces and encased in various plexiglass containers. ", "caption": "Installation view of “Imaginary Engine,” 2026, at Le Large, Île Seguin, showing Arman’s Renault Wooden Pieces – Accumulation Renault n o 151 (1968) at center. Photo Aurélien Mole; Art ©2026 Arman, ADAGP, Paris", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Dumas’s Pointe des Arts will almost certainly draw comparisons to Paris’s two other collector-founded private museums: the Fondation Louis Vuitton (by Bernard Arnault) and the Bourse de Commerce (by François Pinault). Architecturally, the Fondation Louis Vuitton and Le Large are similar, both being purpose-built cultural projects, while the Bourse de Commerce transforms a historic building through contemporary interventions by Tadao Ando and heritage specialists. Curatorially, the Fondation Louis Vuitton presents major retrospectives and international exhibitions, positioning itself as an important venue for new scholarship on well-known artists. The Bourse de Commerce is more directly anchored in Pinault’s collection, which informs its thematic exhibitions and artist-focused presentations. While its opening exhibition presents a dialogue between the Renault art collection and contemporary artists, Le Large’s longer-term curatorial direction remains to be established."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Rather than building a permanent collection or being a permanent home to Dumas’s own holdings, Le Large will focus on presenting on a changing program of temporary exhibitions. The inaugural show, titled “Moteur Imaginaire” (Imaginary Engine), pulls out all the stops, with one of today’s most closely watched curators attached: Cecilia Alemani , director and chief curator of High Line Art in New York and the curator of the 2022 Venice Biennale. “[The display] follows the car on an imaginary journey, from the factory floor to the assembly line, out into the world as an object of desire, and finally into the algorithm,” she told ARTnews . “That metamorphosis, from mechanism to living organism, is what drives the whole exhibition.”", "links": [{"text": "Cecilia Alemani", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/cecilia-alemani/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/FEL-2026-Moteur-Imaginaire-003.jpg?w=400", "alt": "A large-scale sculpture by Jean Dubuffet consisting of various abstract forms against a wall. ", "caption": "Jean Dubuffet, Le Mur bleu , 1967–69, installation view, in “Imaginary Engine”, 2026, at Le Large.", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Drawing on Renault’s industrial history, “Moteur Imaginaire” brings together more than 100 works by 55 artists from 23 countries, dating from the 1930s to the present. Renault has a history of commissioning artists via its Art, Research and Industry program, which invited artists into the car maker’s factories. Jean Dubuffet, Arman, Jean Tinguely, and Victor Vasarely were among those who participated. Their works are some of the 50 pieces from the Renault collection, which are complemented by historical photographs and archival material documenting the factory and its workers to connect the exhibition to the island’s former life. “We felt it was essential to acknowledge that history,” said Aisemberg."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The exhibition layout, conceived by French designer Pascal Rodriguez, unfolds across four successive spaces, separated by partition walls pierced by large circular openings at their centers. Aligned along a single axis, these apertures create a perspective that evokes the assembly-line logic of the automotive industry. “You feel as though you’re inside a machine, a car park, a tunnel, or perhaps inside an engine cylinder,” Aisemberg explained."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Added Alemani, “For almost a century, the Île Seguin was home to the Renault factory, a fortress of production that turned out some 30 million cars: a machine for making machines. I wanted the exhibition to work the same way, as an assembly line for machines and for ideas.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/FEL-2026-Moteur-Imaginaire-017.jpg?w=400", "alt": "View of a green car that is overload inside and has more stuff on top in a museum between two circular openings. ", "caption": "Installation view of “Imaginary Engine,” 2026, at Le Large, Île Seguin, showing Mohamed El Khatib’s commissioned work R12 cathédrale (2026) at center. Photo Aurélien Mole/©2026 Mohamed El Khatib & Louise Sari, ADAGP, Paris/Collection of the Fonds de dotation Emerige, Paris", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At each opening, Alemani has positioned a car. The first installation is an 1898 Renault automobile transformed by Ghanaian artist Paa Joe Junior into a painted wooden palanquin. (It is part of Laurent Dumas’s collection.) Next comes Arman’s intervention on a life-size wooden model of a Renault 10, originally made by Renault engineers. Invited into the factory, the French artist cut it into fragments, which he arranged in Plexiglas boxes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Also included in Dumas’s collection is Mohamed El Khatib’s Renault 12. Loaded with suitcases, documents, and cassette tapes, it recounts the experiences of immigrant families who drove from France to the Maghreb for summer holidays from the 1970s to the ’90s. Bertrand Lavier’s contribution is a Formula One Renault, repainted with the thick, dynamic brushstrokes that have been characteristic of his work since the 1980s."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/FEL-2026-Moteur-Imaginaire-018.jpg?w=400", "alt": "A wall-hung sculpture of various photos affixed to multiple pieces of metal assembled to look like a scrunched-up car. ", "caption": "Mohamed Bourouissa, Untitled , 2018. Photo: Aurélien Mole; Art: ©2026 Mohamed Bourouissa and ADAGP, Paris/Courtesy the artist and Mennour, Paris/Private collection, Paris", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For her first exhibition in France, Alemani explained that it was important to focus on French artists; nearly half of those included live in France. “Curating it was a wonderful opportunity to get to know the French art scene more closely,” she said, noting that she was able to work with artists whose careers she had followed for years, like Sara Sadik, Randa Maroufi, and Mohamed Bourouissa, as well as ones who were new to her, such as Valentin Ranger, Romuald Jandolo, and Bertille Bak."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Along the way, several artists also found a personal tie to Renault. “Johanna Benaïnous learned that her grandfather had worked on the island,” Alemani said. “I met a generation that treats history as living matter. They went into the archives, sat with former workers, and came back with pieces that are urgent, tender, and very much their own.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Moteur Imaginaire” also features 17 newly commissioned pieces, like Clément Cogitore’s film, Untitled (2026), which revisits the 1947 Renault factory strike through a nearly motionless scene of a woman knitting beside a stationary assembly line. Inspired by documentary footage, the work draws attention to a quieter, often overlooked dimension of labor activism. As the light gradually fades, the scene conveys both the workers’ determination and the suspension of industrial activity."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/6.-Clement-COGITORE-.jpg?w=400", "alt": "A video still of women knitting in a car factory. ", "caption": "Clément Cogitore, Untitled (still), 2026. ©2026 Clément Cogitore, ADAGP", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Cogitore’s film finds a parallel in a tapestry by Zhenya Machneva depicting the engine of her grandfather’s Renault Kangoo. “Woven on a manual loom, the work brings personal memory into dialogue with industrial history,” Aisemberg said. “Its painstaking technique offers a deliberate contrast to the speed and efficiency of mechanized production.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Works like these are just one of the many surprises Alemani hopes visitors will find when they visit Île Seguin. “Opening a new institution is always rare, and doing it on an island so charged with memory is a real privilege,” she said. :The Renault factory was dismantled long ago, and today a brand-new building rises in its place, open to everyone. Le Large gives this extraordinary site back to the public, and ‘Moteur Imaginaire’ brings its stories back to life.”"}]

To reach Île Seguin in Boulogne-Billancourt, in the western suburbs of Paris, you must first go to Pont de Sèvres, the final stop of Métro Line 9, and then either take a 15-minute walk or a five-minute bus ride. It is worth the trek: Crossing onto the island means leaving the dense urban fabric behind for a site surrounded by water, with views toward the banks of the Seine and the hills of Meudon.

This is where Le Large has found its place. The art center is part of Pointe des Arts, a €450 ($504.5 million) cultural development that also includes a cinema, a hotel, and other amenities. Its construction marks another chapter in the transformation of an island whose identity has long been tied to industrial production. For much of the 20th century, Renault’s factory occupied the site, employing thousands of workers and sending cars out by road and river.

The center’s name intentionally evokes both scale and possibility. Designed by Pritzker Prize–winning RCR Arquitectes, the building has a distinctive geometry, its footprint increasing from 5,382 square feet at the base to 16,146 square feet on the fifth floor. Its warm, copper-colored anodized-aluminum façade is composed of diamond-shaped elements arranged like overlapping scales, a nod to the double entendre embedded in the institution’s name. In French, prendre le large means to head out to sea.

“The expression resonates with the island setting and its relationship to the water. It conveys the possibility of escape, departure, and discovery,” director Paula Aisemberg told ARTnews in an on-site interview ahead of its opening.

With an annual operating budget estimated at €5 million ($5.6 million), Le Large will vary how it uses its 26,910 square feet in exhibition space, oscillating between a single exhibition that takes over the entire museum, as its opening show does, or having “several shows running simultaneously, one on the fifth floor, another across the sixth and seventh floors. That will be the case for our second season,” Aisemberg said.

Le Large’s ambition is to attract the broadest possible audience, imagining what lies beyond art itself. The center was designed to be a gathering space as much as an exhibition venue, and around 40 percent of its public-facing spaces are free to enter. The first floor encourages visitors to spend time in the building, where they can take in a few works from the temporary exhibitions but mostly luxuriate in the sundrenched lobby’s ample seating areas for extended conversations. Nearby, a bookshop and concept store sit alongside a flight of stairs that doubles as an amphitheater-like seating area.

This multipurpose staircase leads to a mezzanine, from which escalators lead directly to the fifth floor. There, before visitors can reach the exhibition galleries, they will find two spaces by designer Constance Guisset: Extra Large, an 80-seat coffee shop serving seasonal food and panoramic views, and Le Petit Atelier, a dedicated section for kids aged six to ten who can participate in free workshops.

To support its ambitions, Le Large operates on a hybrid model, combining a nonprofit association that has an endowment fund and a commercial entity responsible for venue rentals and private events. The association, chaired by collector Laurent Dumas, manages all of Pointe des Arts on Île Seguin, with a mission to promote French artistic creation. Its main patron is the Emerige Endowment Fund, the philanthropic arm of Dumas’s company, Emerige. Le Large is the latest in its contemporary art–focused initiatives, which include a grant for emerging artists and a commissioning program called 1 immeuble, 1 oeuvre (1 Building, 1 Artwork).

Dumas’s Pointe des Arts will almost certainly draw comparisons to Paris’s two other collector-founded private museums: the Fondation Louis Vuitton (by Bernard Arnault) and the Bourse de Commerce (by François Pinault). Architecturally, the Fondation Louis Vuitton and Le Large are similar, both being purpose-built cultural projects, while the Bourse de Commerce transforms a historic building through contemporary interventions by Tadao Ando and heritage specialists. Curatorially, the Fondation Louis Vuitton presents major retrospectives and international exhibitions, positioning itself as an important venue for new scholarship on well-known artists. The Bourse de Commerce is more directly anchored in Pinault’s collection, which informs its thematic exhibitions and artist-focused presentations. While its opening exhibition presents a dialogue between the Renault art collection and contemporary artists, Le Large’s longer-term curatorial direction remains to be established.

Rather than building a permanent collection or being a permanent home to Dumas’s own holdings, Le Large will focus on presenting on a changing program of temporary exhibitions. The inaugural show, titled “Moteur Imaginaire” (Imaginary Engine), pulls out all the stops, with one of today’s most closely watched curators attached: Cecilia Alemani , director and chief curator of High Line Art in New York and the curator of the 2022 Venice Biennale. “[The display] follows the car on an imaginary journey, from the factory floor to the assembly line, out into the world as an object of desire, and finally into the algorithm,” she told ARTnews . “That metamorphosis, from mechanism to living organism, is what drives the whole exhibition.”

Drawing on Renault’s industrial history, “Moteur Imaginaire” brings together more than 100 works by 55 artists from 23 countries, dating from the 1930s to the present. Renault has a history of commissioning artists via its Art, Research and Industry program, which invited artists into the car maker’s factories. Jean Dubuffet, Arman, Jean Tinguely, and Victor Vasarely were among those who participated. Their works are some of the 50 pieces from the Renault collection, which are complemented by historical photographs and archival material documenting the factory and its workers to connect the exhibition to the island’s former life. “We felt it was essential to acknowledge that history,” said Aisemberg.

The exhibition layout, conceived by French designer Pascal Rodriguez, unfolds across four successive spaces, separated by partition walls pierced by large circular openings at their centers. Aligned along a single axis, these apertures create a perspective that evokes the assembly-line logic of the automotive industry. “You feel as though you’re inside a machine, a car park, a tunnel, or perhaps inside an engine cylinder,” Aisemberg explained.

Added Alemani, “For almost a century, the Île Seguin was home to the Renault factory, a fortress of production that turned out some 30 million cars: a machine for making machines. I wanted the exhibition to work the same way, as an assembly line for machines and for ideas.”

At each opening, Alemani has positioned a car. The first installation is an 1898 Renault automobile transformed by Ghanaian artist Paa Joe Junior into a painted wooden palanquin. (It is part of Laurent Dumas’s collection.) Next comes Arman’s intervention on a life-size wooden model of a Renault 10, originally made by Renault engineers. Invited into the factory, the French artist cut it into fragments, which he arranged in Plexiglas boxes.

Also included in Dumas’s collection is Mohamed El Khatib’s Renault 12. Loaded with suitcases, documents, and cassette tapes, it recounts the experiences of immigrant families who drove from France to the Maghreb for summer holidays from the 1970s to the ’90s. Bertrand Lavier’s contribution is a Formula One Renault, repainted with the thick, dynamic brushstrokes that have been characteristic of his work since the 1980s.

For her first exhibition in France, Alemani explained that it was important to focus on French artists; nearly half of those included live in France. “Curating it was a wonderful opportunity to get to know the French art scene more closely,” she said, noting that she was able to work with artists whose careers she had followed for years, like Sara Sadik, Randa Maroufi, and Mohamed Bourouissa, as well as ones who were new to her, such as Valentin Ranger, Romuald Jandolo, and Bertille Bak.

Along the way, several artists also found a personal tie to Renault. “Johanna Benaïnous learned that her grandfather had worked on the island,” Alemani said. “I met a generation that treats history as living matter. They went into the archives, sat with former workers, and came back with pieces that are urgent, tender, and very much their own.”

“Moteur Imaginaire” also features 17 newly commissioned pieces, like Clément Cogitore’s film, Untitled (2026), which revisits the 1947 Renault factory strike through a nearly motionless scene of a woman knitting beside a stationary assembly line. Inspired by documentary footage, the work draws attention to a quieter, often overlooked dimension of labor activism. As the light gradually fades, the scene conveys both the workers’ determination and the suspension of industrial activity.

Cogitore’s film finds a parallel in a tapestry by Zhenya Machneva depicting the engine of her grandfather’s Renault Kangoo. “Woven on a manual loom, the work brings personal memory into dialogue with industrial history,” Aisemberg said. “Its painstaking technique offers a deliberate contrast to the speed and efficiency of mechanized production.”

Works like these are just one of the many surprises Alemani hopes visitors will find when they visit Île Seguin. “Opening a new institution is always rare, and doing it on an island so charged with memory is a real privilege,” she said. :The Renault factory was dismantled long ago, and today a brand-new building rises in its place, open to everyone. Le Large gives this extraordinary site back to the public, and ‘Moteur Imaginaire’ brings its stories back to life.”

content.excerpt_original: Le Large’s opening exhibition, “Moteur Imaginaire” (Imaginary Engine), reframes the legacy of its former occupant, Renault, through contemporary art.

content.title_original: Dealer Adam Shopkorn’s Alternative Route to Frieze London With Haitian Artist Myrlande Constant

content.article_text:
Dealer Adam Shopkorn of New York–based gallery Fort Gansevoort has always taken an unorthodox route when it comes to the business he cofounded in 2015 with his wife, Carolyn Tate Angel. After participating at Frieze Los Angeles this past February, he will show at the fair’s London edition this week with a solo booth dedicated to the textile flags of Haitian artist Myrlande Constant , who is living in a state of emergency in her home country.

Frieze London will mark his third fair this year after last showing at one in January 2020. “It’s important for us to be in these places now,” Shopkorn told ARTnews on a Zoom call before heading to London, noting that demand for Constant’s work has soared in the past few years after appearances in the 2022 Venice Biennale, Prospect.6 in 2024, and the 2025 São Paulo Bienal.

At Frieze London, he will show five of Constant’s monumental textiles, priced between $90,000 and $450,000. Each work takes its cues from Vodou spiritual practices in Haiti that are grounded in their African roots. Measuring more than 10 feet by 9 feet, Amwan Agwe… (2026), for example, depicts green hills and blue waves alongside the skulls, candles, and fish that nod to Fèt Gede, Haiti’s annual festival honoring the spirits of the dead.

These latest works also reflect a change in Constant’s own way of working, as she is no longer able to maintain an atelier as she once did in Port-au-Prince. For she used to worked with a team of women to produce the beautiful detailed work she has become known for. Now, she crafts her elaborately decorated flags on the go. Because of the ongoing violence in Haiti, she has to move between different cities for safety.

Since late 2023, Shopkorn might go months without hearing from Constant, whether it is to know if she is okay or how her next body of work is coming along. But then, out of the blue one day, he will receive one of her larger-than-life-size pieces in New York, arriving from Haiti via the Dominican Republic. “There’s no white-glove fine-art service truck that’s going into Port-au-Prince to collect artwork for an art fair in London,” Shopkorn said, noting that her works did arrive in time in order to go on view in London.

To support Constant’s production, Shopkorn approaches their relationship in a more old-school model, sending her money as a stipend instead of waiting for a sale to go through and split it 50-50 as is now the norm. “If we did that, she would be waiting forever,” he said, adding that the proceeds are often “sliced and diced in many different ways” to accommodate this structure.

Though Constant may not have reliable access to internet and phone services to communicate with Shopkorn, the best place to find what she has to say is in her textiles. Lasirène Diamant (2025), depicting the feminine Vodou spirit Lasirène who rules the sea, shows the mermaid spirit wearing a diamond necklace that symbolizes prosperity on one side, while on the other, she is shown in a raft filled with fruit, cake, and sweets surrounded by creatures from the sea such as mermaids, dolphins, a seahorse, and an octopus.

“Myrlande is [trying to] survive in Haiti and take care of her family,” said Shopkorn. “The moment an artwork leaves her hands, she’s not terribly interested in what happens after that. When one of her pieces enters a permanent collection, it’s not relevant to her because she’s worried about the safety of her family.”

content.article_text:
Clayface premiered at the Hollywood Legion Theater in Los Angeles, where its stars reunited for the big event.

Tom Rhys Harries plays the title role in the DC Comics film, which also stars Naomi Ackie and Max Minghella.

The film also includes Eddie Marsan, David Dencik, Nancy Carroll, Joshua James, Francesca Corney, Ruby Sear, and Wil Coban.

RELATED: ‘Matchbox: The Movie’ Red Carpet Premiere Photos: John Cena, Jessica Biel, Teyonah Parris & More

Per DC, the film “unravels one man’s horrifying descent from rising Hollywood star to revenge-filled monster in a story that explores the loss of one’s identity and humanity, corrosive love, and the dark underbelly of scientific ambition.”

Mike Flanagan and Hossein Amini penned the script for the pic, produced by Reeves, Lynn Harris, and DC Studios’ James Gunn and Safran. Executive producers are Michael E. Uslan, Chantal Nong Vo, Lars P. Winther, Rafi Crohn, and Paul Richie.

RELATED: Luca Guadagnino’s ‘Artificial’ Red Carpet Premiere Photos: Andrew Garfield, Jason Schwartzman, Billie Lourd, Ike Barinholtz & More

At Comic-Con , director James Watkins teased that Clayface was going to give people a lot of ick and a lot of gore,” adding, “But there’s also an emotional core that gives it a dimension. When you sit and watch this, and you feel the anima of an audience responding to the film, there’s some comfort in that, I suppose.”

“RELATED: ‘Verity’ Red Carpet Premiere Photos: Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson, Josh Hartnett & More
