content.article_text:
For its fourth edition, the Ronan Guillou Grant is launching a call for proposals for a creative grant open to professional photographers from Europe and the southern shores of the Mediterranean.

The Ronan Guillou Grant, created by the non-profit organisation Eyes Wide Open (a label of The Eyes), explores the relationship between human and the sea, with the aim of restoring a shared sense of purpose to our cultures and examining the key challenges facing the sea today.

The project must examine the challenges facing our future in relation to the marine world and/or present a progressive, committed or activist vision capable of contributing to collective awareness. In particular, it may address issues relating to ecology, human activities, the transmission of knowledge and the concept of heritage, economic and geopolitical challenges, or the relationships between the Occitan region and other areas of the Mediterranean basin.

The photographer awarded the grant will receive €4,000 (comprising €3,000 in remuneration and €1,000 expenses) to carry out their project, which may take place over a period of five months, including two months on location. An exhibition is planned for September 2027 at the Musée de l’Étang de Thau in Bouzigues, as part of the 2nd edition of the FLOW Biennial (18 September – 31 October 2027).

The 4th edition of the Ronan Guillou Fellowship is supported by Sète Agglopôle Méditerranée, M28-Terres de culture, the Musée de l’Étang de Thau, Hahnemühle and the Tomoé laboratory.

Call for applications: October 1st to November 15th 2026 (6.00 pm) Jury: late November 2026 Announcement of the winner: during December (the winner will be notified in advance) Residency in Sète: between February and June 2027 (2 months on site) Exhibition: September 2027 at the Musée de l’Étang de Thau as part of the FLOW Biennial

content.article_text:
As one of the select few French actresses who has earned definite-article status in her homeland — referred to routinely as La Huppert, alongside the likes of La Binoche and La Deneuve — it’s immediately, amusingly jarring to see Isabelle Huppert cast as a thoroughly indefinite article: a jobbing movie extra whose name nobody recalls, no matter how many headshots and résumés she desperately forces into the hands of higher-ups on set. Casting Huppert as an industry nobody is the chief gag of “ All About Corinne ,” Marc Fitoussi ‘s winningly droll film-biz comedy, but there turns out to be a lot of mileage in it, particularly with co-star Sandrine Kiberlain — cast not just as an industry somebody, but as Sandrine Kiberlain herself — as her imperious foil.

Related Stories

Quentin Tarantino to Attend AFI Fest for ‘Once Upon A Time In Hollywood’ Screening and Conversation - Film News in Brief

Khalil Cherti's 'Our Way to You,' Selected by Cairo Film Festival, Boarded by Salaud Morisset (EXCLUSIVE)

Both sending themselves up in contrasting ways, the stars’ perceptive, vanity-free performances lend some weight and feeling to what is otherwise a frothy exercise — as is to be expected from Fitoussi, a specialist in female-driven French divertissements , including the uncharacteristically chipper Huppert vehicle “Copacabana” and the recent Laure Calamy hit “Two Tickets to Greece.” Given its starry, easy-breezy charms and accessibly inside-baseball humor, “All About Corinne” should have little trouble securing global arthouse distribution following a festival run that began as Locarno’s closing night selection, continuing through a gala slot in Toronto; audiences au fait with “Call Your Agent!” and its good-humored brand of industry satire will feel right at home.

Popular on Variety

“You might want to ask yourself why you’re still in the same place at your age,” says a colleague, with casual cruelty, to Corinne Maclou (Huppert), an actress who, for decades, has been steadily and invisibly working at the least glamorous end of the business — and who, in her sixties, hasn’t yet given up hope of stardom. In fringe theater, at least, she’s had the odd inspired moment in the spotlight; in film, she’s lumped with countless other, younger extras and bit players, fighting for the rare gift of a single line.

Not for lack of ability — Huppert may dim her light a bit, but doesn’t stretch so far as to play a bad actor — she’s simply never had the break, and while Corinne’s efforts to ingratiate herself with A-listers are played for squirm-inducing comedy, there’s also gentle pathos to her desperation, underlined by the ironic star casting. She knows, and we know, that she’s a Huppert-level talent. Why can no one else see it?

Corinne’s standard line to try curry favor with bigger-name actresses is to cheerfully remark on their physical resemblance to each other, noting that they could play sisters — an approach that doesn’t get the diminutive redhead far with the tall, beachy-haired Kiberlain when they share a scene (or at least occupy the same frame) together. But Corinne’s persistence coincides with a sudden phase of insecurity for the soignée leading lady, who’s trying to cultivate a more down-to-earth image after her agent pithily tells her that “even Cotillard is less detached from reality.” And so she pityingly takes Corinne’s CV, as well as the proferred recording of an obscure Chilean play which Corinne believes to be her finest hour.

Nothing comes of it, of course, until months later, when Corinne sees the news that Kiberlain is taking to the Paris stage in a production of the very same play, and bitterly confronts her outside the theater. Out of resentment and shamefaced guilt, a highly conditional friendship is forged, as each actress uses the other to very different ends: In Kiberlain, Corinne sees her long-awaited connection to the top; through Corinne, Kiberlain believes she can keep it real. Fitoussi’s writing is fizzy and lightly bitchy throughout, but it’s the stars, playing freely with their respective screen personae, who make it genuinely funny. In a more obvious iteration of this story, their roles might be swapped: There’s as much inherent comedy in Huppert playing a spiraling, faintly tragic rube as in Kiberlain, best known for her neurotic comic work, revealing the brittle hauteur of her “real” self.

Other good sports turning up as themselves, to wickedly unflattering effect, include Emmanuelle Bercot, tetchily directing a big-budget period drama that could turn things around for Corinne, and Diane Kruger — hilariously glamazonian as she competes with Kiberlain for maximum miscasting in a new Dardenne Brothers film about a tiler in Liège. If that raises a chuckle from you, as it certainly did from this critic, then consider yourself squarely in the film’s target audience. You can cut precisely without cutting too deep: More sweet than scathing, “All About Corinne” loves its stars too much to really draw blood. We love them too, so that’s just fine.

content.article_text:
‘Water: Our Shared Story’ invites photographers worldwide to document how water shapes our world and the people who depend on it with a US$23,000 prize pool

HIPA has launched ‘Water: Our Shared Story’, a global photography competition inviting photographers to explore one of the world’s most vital resources through compelling visual storytelling.

Held in cooperation with the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the 2026 United Nations Water Conference, the competition comes ahead of the UN conference, which will take place in Abu Dhabi from 8-10 December 2026. Photographers worldwide are invited to submit a photo story of 5-10 photographs with a total prize pool of US$23,000.

Commenting on the competition, Ali Bin Thalith, Secretary General of HIPA, said: “We are proud to collaborate with the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the 2026 UN Water Conference by using the cultural and awareness-raising power of photography to encourage a global conversation about water. We invite photographers and photography communities worldwide to participate and share visual stories that are compelling, accessible and impactful, supporting the objectives of the conference.”

Entries close on 15 October 2026. Full competition rules, eligibility requirements and submission details are available on the official HIPA website: www.hipa.ae .

content.article_text:
In this episode, we look back at the story of Aina, an organisation set up to train a new generation of Afghan journalists, photographers and documentary-makers, so that Afghanistan can tell its own story through its own media. These initiatives are carried out with a particular focus on the Afghan women being trained.

Reza, co-founder of Aina, shares his experiences on the ground in Afghanistan.

He recounts meeting a young boy proudly holding a small plant in his hands, which for him has become a symbol of a possible future.

Rachel Deghati, co-founder of Aina, reflects on the organisation’s work, the efforts to pass on knowledge and the challenges encountered. She also pays tribute to those humanitarian workers from around the world who, within Aina, worked collaboratively with Afghan women and men to create spaces for freedom and reconstruction.

content.article_text:
Leica Camera AG honours the Mexican photographer Graciela Iturbide by presenting her with the 2026 Leica Hall of Fame Award.

She is the world’s most famous contemporary Mexican photographer: this year, Graciela Iturbide was awarded the ‘Leica Hall of Fame’ prize in recognition of her life’s work. The award ceremony took place as part of the ‘Celebration of Photography’ on 8 October 2026 at Leica World in Wetzlar. The accompanying exhibition, featuring more than 50 photographs, will be on display at the Leica Gallery in Wetzlar until January 2027. Iturbide’s photograph ‘Na’ Lupe Pan’, from the series ‘Juchitán’, Oaxaca, Mexico, 1986, was voted ‘Leica Photo of the Year 2026’. The exhibition offers an in-depth insight into the artist’s work, which is primarily devoted to Latin American cultural history. Exploring universal themes such as life and death, rituals and everyday experiences, Iturbide’s visual world is characterised by its moving poetry and magic. The photographer highlights the tensions between culture and nature, tradition and modernity, identity and representation, ensuring that her images retain an enigmatic ambiguity. Deeply rooted in indigenous Mexican culture and blending surrealist elements with religion and mysticism, Graciela Iturbide has, over many decades, developed an inimitable visual language – predominantly in black and white. Birds and masks appear time and again as symbolic companions. The photographer’s most famous work, the astonishing ‘Nuestra Señora de las iguanas’ (Our Lady of the Iguanas), was taken in 1979 at a market in Juchitán. It is a mysterious portrait of a market vendor wearing a crown of live iguanas: a Mexican hydra, but also, according to Christian interpretation, a female figure of Christ wearing a crown of thorns with an animalistic character. Graciela Iturbide’s photographic work is part of a humanist tradition that incorporates psychological and spiritual elements, transforming the documentary image into a form of subjective photography that is extraordinarily rich in nuance. In addition to her still lifes and landscapes, it is her social reportage on the living conditions of Mexico’s indigenous communities and on the importance of matriarchal social structures that has caused a sensation and established her as one of Latin America’s most important photographic voices. The exhibition, organised to coincide with the presentation of the Leica Hall of Fame Award, brings together more than 50 photographs from five series: ‘Juchitán’, featuring images of this Mexican city in the state of Oaxaca (1979–1988); ‘México Clásicas’ (1974–2008); ‘Pájaros ’ (Birds, 1987–1998), ‘Desierto de Sonora’ (1979) and ‘Viajes’ (Travels), taken in Ecuador, Panama, Argentina and Cuba (1972–1994).

Graciela Iturbide was born in Mexico City on 16 May 1942. Even as a child, she was fascinated by photography: her father was a keen amateur photographer. She married the architect Manuel Rocha Díaz (1936–1996) at the age of 19 and went on to have three children. In 1969, she began studying film at the Colegio Nacional de México, at the Centro Universitario de Estudios Cinematográficos (CUEC). In 1970, she spent a year as an assistant to the photographer Manuel Álvarez Bravo, accompanying him on numerous trips and thereby discovering rural Mexico and the diversity of its indigenous communities. A twist of fate – the death of her six-year-old daughter Cláudia – radically changed Graciela Iturbide’s life, leading her to decide to become a professional photographer. In 1975, she held her first exhibition in Mexico City, followed by her first in New York in 1976. From the 1980s onwards, she began to gain international recognition. She has received numerous awards, including the W. Eugene Smith Prize (1987), the Hugo Erfurth Prize (1989), the Rencontres Internationales de la Photographie d’Arles Prize (1991), the Hasselblad Award (2008), the Gold Medal from the Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes y Literatura (INBAL) in Mexico City (2024) and the Princess of Asturias Award for the Arts (2025). Iturbide lives in Mexico City.

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "A booksellers’ prize for photography books, awarded by booksellers France PhotoBook, an association of leading French publishers of photography books, is delighted to announce the fourth edition of the Booksellers’ Prize for Photography Books!"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For its fourth edition, the Booksellers’ Prize brings together a jury of fifteen booksellers from across France. Their task is to select a winning book from among 24 titles published during the 2025–2026 academic year by France PhotoBook’s member publishers. The prize, worth €3,000, is awarded to the photographer. The publisher of the winning book also receives support to promote the work, by organising bookshop events. A booksellers’ prize for photography books, awarded by booksellers France PhotoBook, an association of leading French publishers of photography books, is delighted to announce the fourth edition of the Booksellers’ Prize for Photography Books!

For its fourth edition, the Booksellers’ Prize brings together a jury of fifteen booksellers from across France. Their task is to select a winning book from among 24 titles published during the 2025–2026 academic year by France PhotoBook’s member publishers. The prize, worth €3,000, is awarded to the photographer. The publisher of the winning book also receives support to promote the work, by organising bookshop events. The prize is awarded thanks to the support of the Académie des Beaux-Arts, Pollen Diffusion and the MEP – Maison européenne de la photographie. The jury for this fourth edition is chaired by the writer Maylis de Kerangal. A shortlist of ten titles will be presented in September. A list of five finalists will be announced in early October, ahead of the announcement of the winner on 19 October 2026.

渋谷・SAIで10月17日より、坂本龍一が1980年代に撮影した写真を紹介する展覧会「PHOTO RYUICHI SAKAMOTO」が始まる。

1980年代の坂本龍一は、音楽家として世界を舞台に活動しながら、カメラを手に、日々の風景や人々の姿を記録していた。そこに写っているのは、特別な出来事ばかりではなく、何気なく目にしたものや旅先で見た風景、ふと差し込む光、その瞬間に感じた空気だ。

一枚一枚の写真には、坂本がその時代を過ごした時間と、彼が見ていた世界が静かに残されている。親密な視線の先にあるものの、小さな声を聞くように。彼の目に映った残像を見るように。写真は、わたしたちに静かに語りかける。美しく、詩的で、どこか私的な写真。その一瞬一瞬から、坂本龍一が見つめていた世界に触れたい。また写真集『 PHOTO RYUICHI SAKAMOTO』が先行発売されるというので、合わせてチェックしたい。

content.article_text:
Rurality(ies): the departmental photographic collection

This project has been awarded the ‘Bicentenary of Photography’ label by the Ministry of Culture and forms part of the official programme for the Bicentenary, running from September 1st 2026 to September 30th 2027.

Two hundred years ago, in Burgundy, a new image was born, regarded as the first photograph: ‘View from Le Gras’ by Nicéphore Niepce (1765–1833). We must appreciate the impact that Nicéphore Niepce’s persistent ingenuity has had on our lives, at a time when we are constantly capturing images with our mobile phones. The first photograph was, therefore, a landscape, viewed from a window, fixed onto a tin plate.

In the Gers, the rural landscape lies at the heart of our daily lives. In this department, where agriculture still predominates – a subject that has become a major social issue in recent years the Departmental Heritage Centre in Flaran has sought to place rural life at the centre of its focus through the medium of photography. Stemming from a meeting with the photographer Daniel Maigné, an annual series of exhibitions entitled *La profondeur des champs* ( the depth of field) has been running for over 15 years. Each guest photographer charts his/her own ‘course’ and offers his/hers perspective on this subject. The first edition was, of course, dedicated to Gascony; the scope then broadened to rural life in France, then Europe and the wider world.

A departmental photographic collection has been assembled, and it is this photographic journey exploring the theme of rural life here and elsewhere that we wish to present to the public as part of the large national celebration of the Bicentenary of Photography. Seventeen photographers, both men and women, are represented, each with their own unique perspective, allowing visitors to explore a wide variety of expressions linked by a common thread ranging from documentary, artistic or intimate approaches, and using different techniques (from film to digital, from vintage cameras to smartphones, from black and white to colour), …

The retrospective, with its unique worlds, nevertheless highlights the common thread linking each exhibition such as the depiction of the gestures and settings of peasant labour and the impact of human activity on the landscape.

As a prelude to this exhibition, recalling the early days of photography, prints by Pierre MENDOUSSE (1870–1933) will be on display. A teacher and ‘amateur’ photographer, he documented life in the Gers region particularly in Simorre at the turn of the twentieth century, whilst maintaining an open outlook on the world.

From October 20th 2026 to March 21st 2027

content.title_original: Maha Harada Talks “In My Father’s Room”, Mark Rothko, The Book of Tea and Communicating Without Words
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Maha Harada Talks “In My Father’s Room”, Mark Rothko, The Book of Tea and Communicating Without Words"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Maha Harada discusses “In My Father’s Room”, Mark Rothko, Japanese museums and how poems and objects can communicate without words."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "After establishing herself as one of Japan’s most successful novelists, Maha Harada moved behind the camera for “In My Father’s Room”, adapting her own short story “An Unnecessary Man” into her first feature as a director. The film brings together many of the interests that have shaped her career outside cinema as well, particularly museums, visual art, Japanese aesthetics and the ways people communicate through objects rather than direct conversation. Speaking with Asian Movie Pulse, Harada discussed the transition from literature to filmmaking, the influence of Kakuzo Okakura and Mark Rothko, her own experience as a curator, the casting of Issey Ogata and Eri Watanabe, and why silence can sometimes carry more weight than words."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "In My Father’s Room is screening at Busan International Film Festival", "links": [{"text": "Busan International Film Festival", "url": "https://www.biff.kr/eng/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://asianmoviepulse.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Busan-2026.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Asian Movie Pulse"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Moving from writing to directing did not feel as unnatural as might be expected. Harada explains that when she writes fiction, she already visualizes scenes very clearly, almost as though there were a camera operating inside her mind. Landscapes, rooms and movements appear to her while she works on the page, meaning that directing became another way of realizing something she had already been doing imaginatively for years."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The decision to adapt “An Unnecessary Man” also has a history stretching back around 15 years. content.article_text:
Maha Harada Talks “In My Father’s Room”, Mark Rothko, The Book of Tea and Communicating Without Words

Maha Harada discusses “In My Father’s Room”, Mark Rothko, Japanese museums and how poems and objects can communicate without words.

After establishing herself as one of Japan’s most successful novelists, Maha Harada moved behind the camera for “In My Father’s Room”, adapting her own short story “An Unnecessary Man” into her first feature as a director. The film brings together many of the interests that have shaped her career outside cinema as well, particularly museums, visual art, Japanese aesthetics and the ways people communicate through objects rather than direct conversation. Speaking with Asian Movie Pulse, Harada discussed the transition from literature to filmmaking, the influence of Kakuzo Okakura and Mark Rothko, her own experience as a curator, the casting of Issey Ogata and Eri Watanabe, and why silence can sometimes carry more weight than words.

In My Father’s Room is screening at Busan International Film Festival

Moving from writing to directing did not feel as unnatural as might be expected. Harada explains that when she writes fiction, she already visualizes scenes very clearly, almost as though there were a camera operating inside her mind. Landscapes, rooms and movements appear to her while she works on the page, meaning that directing became another way of realizing something she had already been doing imaginatively for years.

The decision to adapt “An Unnecessary Man” also has a history stretching back around 15 years. After the story was included in Japanese high-school textbooks, Harada received a letter from a student who told her that the final scene had felt as though she were watching a movie. That response stayed with the author. It was the moment when she began seriously imagining the story as cinema, while also feeling that if it ever became a film, she wanted not simply to hand it over to someone else but to become involved herself, potentially as director. museum interview

Kakuzo Okakura’s “The Book of Tea” became one of the major philosophical foundations of both the original story and the film. Harada is particularly interested in Okakura as someone who belonged to the Meiji period yet spent substantial time outside Japan, eventually working in the United States. What matters to her is the perspective this gave him: the ability to look back at Japanese culture from outside rather than simply experiencing it from within.

That perspective also connects with Harada’s hopes for the film itself. From the beginning, she wanted “In My Father’s Room” to reach audiences outside Japan. After screenings in San Sebastian and Busan, she was encouraged by the way viewers from very different cultural backgrounds responded to the film’s attention to small things. Whether the object is a person, an artwork or something seemingly insignificant, Harada believes concentrating deeply on a small detail reflects a particular sensibility that international audiences were nevertheless able to recognize and appreciate.

Check review of the film

Mark Rothko became the other major artistic presence in the film. Harada’s interest in his paintings predates the project considerably, going back to her years working as a curator. She points out that Japanese collections acquired significant Rothko works decades ago, before the enormous prices currently associated with the artist became standard. For Harada, the fact that Japanese curators recognized the importance of his work at that point remains a source of pride. museum interview

What interests her most, however, is not the market value of Rothko’s paintings but their spirituality. She feels there is something in his work that connects naturally with the spirit of the Japanese way of tea. These two apparently distant cultural traditions therefore became parallel motifs within “In My Father’s Room”: Rothko’s abstract painting on one side and chanoyu on the other, both creating spaces where contemplation and emotion can exist without requiring conventional explanation. museum interview

Harada’s own curatorial background also informs the protagonist considerably. She acknowledges that there are many similarities between her experiences and those of the central character, particularly in relation to museum work. This naturally led the conversation toward the current position of cultural institutions in Japan, which Harada views with concern. She points to financial difficulties surrounding museum acquisitions and feels governmental cultural policy in Japan remains behind that of a number of other countries in the level of support it provides to art and cultural activity.

Casting, meanwhile, was a collaborative process between Harada and her producers. Although she had performers in mind, the final decisions emerged through discussion rather than from a completely predetermined list. Her enthusiasm for the resulting cast is particularly evident, describing the lead performance in exceptionally strong terms and emphasizing how completely the actors came to embody people she had originally created on the page.

Issey Ogata’s casting ultimately affected the screenplay itself. Once he had been confirmed as Yuichi, Harada rewrote parts of the script specifically while imagining him performing them, including the tea-related gestures and scenes. His interpretation went beyond what she had initially imagined for the character to such an extent that she now finds it difficult to imagine anyone else inhabiting the role.

Eri Watanabe, by contrast, had been one of Harada’s principal choices from much earlier in the process. The contrast between her character and Ogata’s was particularly important. Harada describes the two as fundamentally different personalities, almost opposites in temperament and in the way they approach life, yet ultimately capable of being connected through something they both recognize as beautiful.

That point of connection is poetry. A poem Yuichi writes becomes something capable of surviving beyond their failed marriage and even beyond his death. For Harada, this is one of the film’s central ideas: communication does not necessarily depend on constant conversation. Japanese culture, as she describes it, often places importance on what remains unsaid, with feelings conveyed through gestures, objects or something created and given to another person.

The poem therefore matters precisely because it lasts. Even after the relationship has ended and years have passed, the words remain in Shuko’s memory. Harada connects this again with the way of tea, where meaning can be transmitted without extensive explanation. A single object or gesture can preserve an emotional connection far longer than a conversation that disappears the moment it ends. museum interview

This philosophy ultimately explains much of “In My Father’s Room”. The movie is built around the things people leave behind: paintings, poems, memories, rooms and objects that gradually communicate what characters were unable or unwilling to say directly. Harada’s literary and curatorial backgrounds consequently do not function merely as decoration around the narrative. They provide the way in which the film itself understands human relationships.

Harada has not yet decided what her next directing project will be, although the international response to “In My Father’s Room” has made her increasingly aware of expectations surrounding another film. She is clear that she would like to direct again and hopes to bring that future work back to festivals such as Busan before presenting it to audiences elsewhere. One thing, however, already seems certain: her next film would once again be based on one of her own literary works.

For a first-time director, “In My Father’s Room” therefore represents less a sudden departure from Maha Harada’s previous career than the continuation of ideas she has been exploring through literature and museums for years. Cinema simply gives her another space in which to consider beauty, memory and the connections between people—and another way to demonstrate that sometimes the most important things are communicated precisely when nobody is speaking.

content.article_text:
When a filmmaker tells a story based on real events, especially ones that are inspiring or heroic, there’s always a risk of hagiography. “ Clean Hands ” is a movie where the storytellers either take a lot of license with an actual person’s life to add drama, or don’t seem aware just how unflattering their subject’s behavior actually is. Written, produced and directed by Jake Allyn (“Ride”), the film chronicles the relationship between real-life Hagerstown, MD narcotics officer Kevin Simmers ( Zach Braff ) and his efforts to rescue his daughter Brooke ( Esther McGregor ) from the grip of drug abuse. But while the “happening right under his nose” details lend a heartbreaking edge to a sadly familiar story, the script’s argument against criminalizing addiction reconciles uneasily with its portrayal of Simmers’ determination to save Brooke by any means necessary.

Related Stories

Nicolas Cage Says He’s ‘Probably Not’ Working With Amazon Again After Refusing to Sign AI Waiver for ‘Spider-Noir,' Teases Joining 'True Detective'

'WandaVision' Creator Jac Schaeffer to Develop 'Stargate' Series at Amazon (EXCLUSIVE)

Simmers is a hero cop, looked up to by his colleagues and liked better than one might expect by the local townspeople, given his by-the-book approach. Though he maintains a close relationship with 19-year-old Brooke, he’s blindsided when he learns that she’s addicted to Percocet and has been consorting with abusive dealer Brick (Kraig Dane). After unsuccessfully trying to enroll her in a private rehab facility, Simmers learns that she’s moved on to heroin; he takes a tough-love approach to let her get arrested, hoping to scare her straight. But when even that fails, he becomes determined to cut off her supply at the source, pursuing local addicts in the hopes of apprehending anyone who might deal her drugs.

Popular on Variety

Despite the support of his religious wife Dana (Abigail Spencer) and colleagues on the police force, including an ambitious deputy (Lucas Till) eager to succeed him as the precinct’s role model, Simmers’ efforts to help get Brooke clean fail over and over again. As he faces the prospect of losing her to addiction, he begins to conceive an alternative path for struggling drug abusers, even while witnessing members of the Hagerstown community — including some of his fellow officers — exploiting addicts instead of helping them.

Given the infomercial pasted at the top of the closing credits for Brooke’s House, the rehab facility Simmers created in response to his daughter’s addiction, it feels safe to assume that the former police officer fully endorsed this portrait of him and his family’s struggles. Yet the typical disclaimer absolving the filmmakers of responsibility for dramatizing these real people’s lives is oddly posted at the beginning of the closing credits rather than at the very end, suggesting that some of the narrative leaps taken here by the filmmakers are bigger than usual. To that end, one can understand why Allyn wouldn’t want to risk misrepresenting Hagerstown law enforcement. But should audiences accept at face value every action taken by Simmers in his crusade to save his daughter?

By all accounts, he was a dedicated cop with honed instincts as an investigator, and a loving father to Brooke — so much so that, in the film, Dana accuses the two of them of being addicted to each other. But the character’s compassion towards perpetrators and his cool detachment under pressure seem only to apply when he doesn’t have an active stake in a crime. When he does, he seems willing to abuse his power and take any measures that he thinks will result in whatever he’s already decided the outcome should be — whether that’s lying to a healthcare provider to get his daughter treatment, or arresting an individual he deems complicit in Brooke’s condition.

As the film tells it, Simmers eventually learns that waging war against dealers and community enablers makes less of an impact on people who are addicted than providing them consistent, patient, loving support. But the character is so relentless for so long with his methods that it’s hard not to pin a portion of the blame for Brooke’s addiction on him.

Again, that seems distantly like the point (or at least one point) of “Clean Hands.” But Allyn is entirely too interested in Simmers’ police work, meaning high-pitched chases and strong-arm interrogations, to strike the right balance between his day job and his earnest efforts to help his daughter. As a viewer, it’s possible to forgive a character who’s so determined to protect his daughter that he takes overbearing or inappropriate measures, but when the film wants the crime stuff to be tense and exciting — amplified with music by instrumental rock act Those Who Ride With Giants — it undercuts the humanity of what that character is facing.

Simmers marks a departure from the kinds of roles for which Braff is best known, and the actor commits to the character’s tenacity and determination in a way that suggests he’s either prioritizing authenticity regardless of how the character is perceived, or he misunderstands how sympathetic Allyn’s version of Simmers can be. The problem is the contrast between his well-meaning actions and their impact on others: Brooke faces beatings in jail because her father antagonizes the guards and other inmates, God-fearing Dana flinches every time he drops an f-bomb or angrily dresses down a rehab administrator, and until the very last scene in the film, he ignores or dismisses the addiction, poverty or desperation of anyone he encounters who’s struggling.

McGregor offers a welcome counterbalance as Brooke, whose general disposition emanates from her relationship with her father, even as it’s hobbled by troubles the script pinpoints with delicacy. Though the film doesn’t quite know what to do with Dana as Simmers bulldozes his way to a cure for Brooke, Spencer similarly offers grace — or at least a less rigid form of support — that hints at how his initial way of helping may not be the most effective one.

To whatever extent this story is told accurately, Simmers was of course doing the best that he could to reckon with a challenge he’d dealt with in the line of duty, but never with a person so close to him — and years of repetition reinforced a one-size-fits-all reaction to an affliction that must be addressed individually. But the film builds to the founding of Brooke’s House and its immediate, overwhelming success, indicating that all Simmers needed to do was change his tactics, instead of the more meaningful, moving change in his perception of addiction as something to be mechanically repaired. A handful of appealing performances aside, “Clean Hands” ignores too many messy realities in favor of quick solutions; the stuff that gives a true story like this power is the hard work and struggle that happens between an epiphany about oneself and the reality of implementing its lessons in the world.

‘Clean Hands’ Review: Zach Braff Is a Cop on a Crusade to Save His Addict Daughter in an Uneasy Fact-Based Crime Drama

content.article_text:
Once Upon a Time in Harlem is continuing its strong push for Oscar recognition, earning five nominations Tuesday for the Critics Choice Documentary Awards. That’s added to the distinction of premiering at Sundance, and being honored with berths at the Cannes, Telluride, Toronto and New York film festivals – the only documentary to do so this year.

Related Stories

Critics Choice Documentary Awards Nominations: ‘14th’ Nabs 6; Elizabeth Holmes Doc, ‘Once Upon A Time In Harlem’, ‘Nuisance Bear’ Land 5 Each

Neon Acquires U.S. On Documentary ‘Once Upon A Time In Harlem’ Following Sundance Premiere

The film directed by David Greaves and produced by Liani Greaves (David’s daughter) is based on extraordinary footage from an event in 1972 – a reunion for one afternoon only of the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance. They gathered at the home of Duke Ellington for what would be a final opportunity to renew friendships, share stories and engage in vigorous debate about the Harlem Renaissance, its artists and scholars, and Black cultural and political life in America.

Watch on Deadline

The documentary, based on material shot by William Greaves – David’s father and Liani’s grandfather – opens theatrically in New York this Friday and in Los Angeles on October 23. David and Liani join the latest edition of Deadline’s Doc Talk podcast to discuss their remarkable nonfiction feature and how they crafted it from almost 30 hours of raw footage.

David was one of the original cameramen on the 1972 shoot. He recalls working with his father to capture the once-in-a-lifetime gathering and how William wanted the finished film “to be a theatrical experience that moves at a snappy pace.” Liani reflects on her grandfather who was a true Renaissance man himself: actor, sculptor, poet, dancer, songwriter and filmmaker.

RELATED: ‘Once Upon A Time In Harlem’ Trailer: Oscar Contender Reveals Extraordinary Reunion Of Harlem Renaissance Leaders

The Greaves also explore the interpersonal dynamics at play in the reunion of so many artists and thinkers who gathered that day in Harlem. Disagreements emerged among the group on how to define the Harlem Renaissance and whether its legacy would continue or be lost. The Greaves speak to the importance of women to the Harlem Renaissance and how their integral role is sometimes overlooked.

Certain frictions or frustrations became apparent during the reunion as some of those women tried to make their voices heard in the din of lively conversation.

Liani Greaves reveals why the presence of George Schuyler at the gathering triggered strong emotions among some of the attendees (having to do with his contrarian politics). She also relates one unflattering remark aimed at Schuyler — a moment not included in the documentary. Doc Talk co-host John Ridley explains why he particularly identified with comments made in the film by Richard Bruce Nugent, one of those fascinating living luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance featured in the documentary.

That’s on the new episode of Doc Talk hosted by Oscar winner Ridley ( 12 Years a Slave , Shirley ) and Matt Carey, Deadline’s senior documentary editor. The pod is a production of Deadline and Ridley’s Nō Studios.

Listen to the episode above or on major podcast platforms including Spotify , iHeart and Apple .

content.article_text:
Going on two years after the wildfires that devastated Pacific Palisades and other Los Angeles-area neighborhoods, a popular moviehouse is ready for its closeup. Paramount Pictures and real estate developer Rick Caruso said Tuesday that the Bay Theater in Palisades Village will reopen before year’s end.

Related Stories

Celebrities Who Lost Their Homes In The Los Angeles Wildfires

Discovery+ Raises Prices In One Of Skydance’s First Streaming Moves After Merger Close

The high-end five-screen venue at 1035 N. Swarthmore Ave., shuttered since the Palisades Fire in early January 2025, is being restored, and luxury cinema operator The Lot will manage it. Along with first-run movies and classics, the Bay will host special screenings and immersive theatrical experiences, said Paramount, which is taking over the theater formerly operated by Netflix and Cinepolis before that.

“Together with Caruso, we are proud to help bring the Bay back to life as a place for the Pacific Palisades community to gather around the shared experience of cinema,” said David Ellison, chairman and CEO of Skydance. “This theater has always meant more than movies alone — it’s woven into the fabric of this neighborhood, and helping restore it is a privilege. We’re inspired by the resilience of Pacific Palisades residents, and we’re honored to help support this community’s comeback.”

Watch on Deadline

The surrounding Caruso-owned Palisades Village reopened during the summer, and now the Bay Theater is set open its doors by the end of 2026, though no date is set.

The original Bay Theater opened down the road on Sunset Boulevard in 1949 before closing in 1978. The venue’s current iteration debuted in 2018.

“The Bay has always been at the heart of the Palisades,” said Caruso, who was runner-up in the race for Los Angeles mayor in 2022, “and its return is one of the most meaningful signs yet that this community … is coming back stronger than ever.”

The Lot, which will oversee operations for the Bay, runs luxury dine-in theaters in La Jolla, Newport Beach and other California cities.

content.article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: The New York Times’ prestigious Op-Docs platform has acquired The Revolution Against Death , the new short film directed by two-time Oscar nominee Joshua Oppenheimer .

The documentary set at an annual longevity conference known as the Revolution Against Aging and Death Festival will be co-released globally in early December by New York Op-Docs and MUBI . It premiered at the Tampere Film Festival in Finland and recently screened at the Telluride Film Festival.

At sessions as part of the Revolution Against Aging and Death Festival, “fear is in the air — of illness, of invisibility, of dying alone,” notes a release. “Directed by Oppenheimer, the film offers a visceral portrait of aging, death and the quest for immortality.”

Related Stories

'JAŸ-Z In 8' To Stream Internationally On Mubi

'Teenage Sex & Death at Camp Miasma' Production Designers Brandon Tonner-Connolly & Matt Hyland Talk Building Its Surreal Landscape

Oppenheimer ( The Look of Silence , The Act of Killing ) is no mere impartial observer of the festival proceedings.

Watch on Deadline

“Haunted by a fear of death since I was a child, I traveled to a gathering of would-be immortals,” he writes of the film project. “I recognized myself, clinging white-knuckled to the hope that I might defeat death. In the years that followed, I discovered that because nothing lasts, everything matters — and eternity lies in change itself. This film is my poem about that journey.”

In a statement, Op-Docs Executive Producer Alexandra Garcia commented, “We are honored to bring Joshua Oppenheimer’s work to the Op-Docs audience with this unique film that is a haunting, observational look at the fundamental human conflict between the reality of death and the relentless drive for immortality.”

The Revolution Against Death joins seven other films on Op-Docs’s 2026 slate of awards contenders, including Living With a Visionary , winner of the Short Film Jury Award for Animation at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival; The Tuners , winner of a Silver Dragon at the 2026 Krakow Film Festival, and A Wolf in the Suburbs , which premiered at SXSW this year. Op-Docs won an Academy Award for its 2021 short The Queen of Basketball , directed by Ben Proudfoot. The series has claimed seven Oscar nominations, including in 2025 for Instruments of a Beating Heart , directed by Ema Ryan Yamazaki, and in 2024 for Island In Between , directed by S. Leo Chaing.

The Revolution Against Death screens Saturday at the Chicago International Film Festival and next month at IDFA in Amsterdam, the world’s biggest documentary film festival.

Oppenheimer is the recipient of a MacArthur Fellowship, widely known as the “genius grant,” that is awarded to “extraordinarily talented and creative individuals as an investment in their potential.” The filmmaker made his fiction debut in 2024 with The End , a post-apocalyptic musical thriller starring Tilda Swinton, Michael Shannon, and George MacKay.

The New York Times Op-Docs is a collection of more than 450 short films that “have sparked global conversations, influenced national policies and garnered an array of industry distinctions, including Emmy Awards, Peabody Awards and an Oscar.” Alexandra Garcia is executive producer of the series and Yvonne Ashley Kouadjo is the producer.

content.article_text:
Not since Zhang Yimou’s 2002 wuxia spectacle “Hero” has China landed an Oscar nomination for Best International Feature — and this dry spell surely won’t be broken with this year’s bombastic submission “ Once Upon a Time in the Middle East .” Like most of the country’s entries over the past decade, this blockbuster epic — a summer box office hit at home — makes for an extravagant display of the strength of the nation’s commercial film industry. Strength, in the sense that no modest operation could conceivably pull off the technical wizardry and large-scale worldbuilding showcased here, where an entire city is at one point turned into an inferno of crumbling buildings, and a massive military base is, in a later scene, ambushed in a rain of blazing pyrotechnics.

Related Stories

Amazon's Bestselling Kids Tablet Is Less Than $90 Right Now -- Its Lowest Price Ever

Nicolas Cage Says He’s ‘Probably Not’ Working With Amazon Again After Refusing to Sign AI Waiver for ‘Spider-Noir,' Teases Joining 'True Detective'

The film is also, as expected from this state-backed production, blatantly propagandistic — but in a way that is particularly baffling, and shockingly tasteless. If those sound like the elements for a good time, in the B-movie sense, then you are also correct. Against the odds, “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” is also, both regrettably and miraculously, extremely watchable. The Jekyll part of your brain will tell you to leave but the Hyde-side will keep you seated in morbid, twitchy-eyed fascination over the film’s two-and-a-half hour runtime.

Popular on Variety

To cut straight to the point, this is a film in which China symbolically emerges from the rubble of the Iraq War as a pacifistic patriarch and guardian of all the world’s children. Director Wen Muyue delivers this subtext through the story of Xu Fu (Shen Teng), a debt-ridden chef who agrees to temporarily take over a Chinese restaurant in the fictional Gulf-region city of Bahata, intending to return to his daughter and mother in China in two years time.

Flash-forwards to an elder Xu Fu with liver spots and a conspicuous scar on his cheek tell us that he will indeed make it back to his family, but it’ll take much longer than a few years — the frankly absurd reasons for his delay a consequence of his, let’s say, geopolitical misfortunes. He’s a man in the wrong place at the wrong time, though, cleverly, the film makes the point that a good Chinese meal is never unwelcome. In fact it’s globally in demand — a lifeline that ensures Xu Fu’s survival through the film’s whirlwind of events.

Before we get to the grisly images of dead children covered in ash, the film starts out as a feel-good dramedy in which Xu Fu adapts to his new surroundings. Frazzled softie Ma Junsheng (Jiang Qiming), the restaurant manager, is our hero’s bridge between China and his new home, translating for Xu Fu between Arabic and Chinese during tense but diplomatic discussions with the restaurant owner Zaid (Sherif Sabby). Glossy, mouthwatering closeups of grilled meats and bubbling stone-pot stews testify to the success of Xu Fu’s kitchen takeover. Nurturing local talent is also on the agenda when he takes on a mentee, Seif (Omar Sharif — no, not that one), an angsty orphan who learns to sublimate his rage into the art of Chinese cooking. Though as the film goes on, this anger grows into a furious, war-hardened desire for retribution. Does a delicious roasted duck stand a chance? It does, in this film’s mind, with the help of the preternaturally compassionate Xu Fu.

“Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” is something of a both-sides film in that both the Americans and the not-so-thinly-veiled Iraqis are gross caricatures of themselves, and there’s particular ire reserved for that most treacherous of abominations: Chinese-American … food. In epic-handshake-meme solidarity, Xu Fu and Zaid agree that their restaurant will never serve U.S.-style Chinese dishes like General Tso’s chicken; and when the US troops bomb Bahata to smithereens and occupy the city, a crass Chinese-American private (Aarif Lee Zhi-ting) bullies his way into free meals at Xu Fu’s restaurant. Not a pushover but a practical-minded realist, the chef takes the punches, striking up a booze-smuggling deal with the Americans to keep the orphans living in his restaurant safe.

The maddening implausibility that sustains the film’s relentless, weirdly hypnotizing forward momentum means we’re never in one place — or one mood — for too long. Zaid’s home is bombed in one intensely melodramatic sequence that culminates in a slow zoom over Zaid cradling his dead wife and child. Next thing we know, he’s radicalized and joins a terrorist group. Xu Fu, Ma Junsheng and Seif — the cooking trio — are promptly captured by the U.S. Army and forced to preside over the kitchen on base. This allows for more sumptuous shots of delicious food while Xu Fu is, for whatever reason, targeted by an aggro, block-jawed American soldier. Xu Fu and Ma Junsheng also play surrogate dads to Seif, whose increasingly violent eruptions threaten to change the course of his life more than once.

For all its dewy-eyed sentimentality, the film is also startlingly brutal and bloody, making for a deranged whiplash effect that’s felt most powerfully in the film’s final act, which is set in a terrorist stronghold where pipsqueaks are brainwashed into becoming suicide bombers. Cozy, brotherly scenes (as when Ma Junsheng slips Seif a smuggled can of soda) are directly followed by executions and montages of plush-bear-wielding kiddies invoking jihad. There’s a slickness to the carnage that rubs uncomfortably against the film’s humanist ethos, rendering artificial (for all Shen Teng’s trembling and mouth-contorting labors) the horrific tragedies that befall its characters. It’s a vision of wartime brutality that’s both blithely matter-of-fact and desperate to pull at our heartstrings; utterly delusional, in other words, and hard to look away from.

Sin la carga de ningún recuerdo se elevan sin problemas sobre los hechos. ¡De qué van a ser testigos!, en un segundo se disipan en todas direcciones. Que exista la gente si quiere, y después que se muera uno tras otro, poco les importa a las nubes esas cosas tan extrañas. content.article_text:
Con la descripción de las nubes debería darme mucha prisa, en una milésima de segundo dejan de ser ésas y empiezan a ser otras. Es propio de ellas no repetirse nunca en formas, matices, posturas y orden. Sin la carga de ningún recuerdo se elevan sin problemas sobre los hechos. ¡De qué van a ser testigos!, en un segundo se disipan en todas direcciones. Comparada con las nubes la vida parece tener los pies sobre la tierra, se diría que es inmutable y prácticamente eterna. Frente a las nubes hasta una piedra parece un hermano en el que se puede confiar y las nubes, nada, primas lejanas y frívolas. Que exista la gente si quiere, y después que se muera uno tras otro, poco les importa a las nubes esas cosas tan extrañas. Sobre toda Tu vida y también la mía, aún incompleta, desfilan pomposas igual que desfilaban. No tienen la obligación de morir con nosotros. No necesitan ser vistas para poder pasar.

Wisława Szymborska , Las nubes (Chmury) , en Instante (2002)

Todos los seres somos vulnerables y efímeros. En la tierra como en el cielo, algunos seres viven desde partículas muy pequeñas, nadie y nada es inerte, todo fluye y se transforma. Pasando de un estado a otro, las nubes son vapor que dejó de ser invisible: agua condensada, reunida en bruma, que atrapa partículas de smog, la radiación; son atravesadas por rayos UV, guardan agua, tormentas y son capaces de acumular carga y soltarla en forma de rayos.

Aquí, otros cielos , exposición curada por Fernanda Ramos Mena en el Museo de Arte Carrillo Gil trata de un proyecto de sitio específico de Valentina Guerrero Marín . La artista chilena propone recuperar la observación del cielo como una práctica sensible, a través de dos dispositivos ópticos hechos de cristales y espejos que incluyen una audioguía. Estos aparatos, con diseños y formas geométricas de cristal y elementos de acero, fueron concebidos para la terraza del museo, rodeados de árboles justo a un costado de la Avenida Revolución. La intemperie es un espacio propicio en el que Valentina invita a detenernos, a interactuar, mirar y escuchar las nubes, no como un fenómeno distante, sino como una relación abierta, capaz de atravesar nuestros cuerpos y, así, modificar nuestra experiencia de lo cotidiano.

Este trabajo de largo aliento, una investigación cuasi científica sobre nubes, pone de manifiesto la observación como método, pero también como una forma de estar presente y de reflexionar sobre los elementos que conforman el cielo. En medio de la ciudad, sobre una de sus avenidas más importantes y, al mismo tiempo, más ruidosas, la obra propone una pausa, un momento para detenernos y mirar hacia el cielo, pero también para acortar, aunque sea por un instante, la distancia frente a una inmensidad de la que apenas somos una minúscula parte.

Según la Organización Meteorológica Mundial , una nube es un conjunto de partículas diminutas de agua líquida, hielo o ambas, suspendidas en el aire son materia atmosférica en suspensión. Se forman cuando el vapor de agua se condensa alrededor de partículas presentes en la atmósfera. En ellas convergen agua, aerosoles, temperatura, luz y movimiento; son, por tanto, formas transitorias de una atmósfera en constante transformación.

Las nubes ocultan el sol y la luna —a la vista desde la tierra—, y sobre ellas se posan los colores que la atmósfera dispersa en atardeceres y amaneceres: desde los azules celestes, los blancos y grises, hacia un vanilla sky, con ocres y lilas. Luego se esfuman. Sin dejar rastro, se abren para dejar ver paisajes de azules vibrantes, ahí cuando el sol brilla con toda su intensidad. Más radiación ultravioleta llega hasta nuestras células por el adelgazamiento de la capa de ozono. ¿Cómo ha cambiado nuestra experiencia de detenernos a mirar hacia arriba y qué hay detrás del fenómeno atmosférico?

Bajando un cerro en un poblado mexicano de gran altura, vi las nubes. Estaba entrando en un espacio intermedio entre la tierra y el cielo y, por un instante, lo sentí celestial. Era como contemplar las nubes desde la ventana de un avión: esa experiencia suspendida, contemplativa y hermosa, pero también atravesada por el terror que puede producir una tormenta, cuando la turbulencia hace surgir la pregunta: ¿y si esto se cae?

No sé exactamente dónde estoy; lo único que sé es que estamos a unos treinta mil pies de altura. Quizá esa sea una de las particularidades de volar en la atmósfera, el habitar un espacio intermedio, estar entre un lugar y otro a la vez. También el pensamiento se desplaza así, de un lugar a otro, de sentir a pensar, de la percepción a la imaginación. Algo nos atraviesa mientras transitamos entre los cuerpos materiales y atmosféricos, entre el más acá y el más allá.

La obra de Valentina Guerrero me ha seducido visualmente desde que tengo memoria de conocerla. Hay en ella algo misterioso y, al mismo tiempo, delicado y sutil. Su aproximación al uso y corte de cristales de múltiples colores retoma una práctica que me hace pensar en los vitrales de las catedrales medievales europeas, donde el vidrio funcionaba como un dispositivo para capturar la luz y transformarla al atravesar el espacio arquitectónico. La luz, asociada entonces con lo divino, ingresaba al interior de las iglesias para bañar de color aquello que tocaba y producir una experiencia sensible que también se asociaba con lo espiritual.

Robert Grosseteste , un pensador y científico medieval inglés del siglo XIII, propuso en su tratado Sobre la Luz ( De Luce , en latín) una innovadora visión filosófica-científica que fusionó la metafísica con la experimentación natural. En su teoría central postuló que la luz actúa como la primera forma corpórea, la cual, mediante una multiplicación infinita y uniforme en todas las direcciones, extiende la materia primordial para originar el universo físico.

Su teoría señala que este cosmos geocéntrico está compuesto por trece esferas, abarcando desde las inmutables regiones celestes hasta los elementos corruptibles de la Tierra. También integró conceptos matemáticos y astronómicos que sugieren que la luz no solo es el principio de extensión y continuidad, sino también la causa fundamental de los movimientos celestes y de la armonía del universo.

Pero, para la física actual, una nube no tiene “ausencia de luz”. Una nube es, entre otras cosas, un medio óptico; la luz entra en ella, interactúa con sus gotas de agua o cristales de hielo y puede ser reflejada, dispersada, transmitida y parcialmente absorbida. En el Atlas Internacional de Nubes de la OMM (1975) se describe precisamente la luminosidad de una nube en función de la luz que sus partículas reflejan, dispersan y transmiten. [1]

En la obra de Valentina Guerrero, sin embargo, la luz parece desprenderse de ese lugar trascendente para volver a la materia y al entorno. El vidrio ya no es únicamente un soporte que recibe la luz: la refracta, la fragmenta, la colorea y modifica nuestra manera de percibir aquello que tenemos frente a los ojos. Es aquí donde su investigación sobre las nubes encuentra una resonancia particular. Si el vidrio transforma la luz al atravesarlo, las nubes también funcionan como una suerte de materia atmosférica que filtra, dispersa y modifica la luz solar. Ambas producen, desde lugares radicalmente distintos, una alteración de nuestra percepción del cielo.

Los dispositivos que Valentina construye para Aquí, otros cielos van más allá de definir qué es una nube o un cristal: trabajan directamente con la luz —cómo se refleja, se dispersa, se transmite y se absorbe— para crear las condiciones de volver a mirar las nubes, y ese proceso de observación produce un efecto estético.

El cristal, el espejo, la luz y el cielo entran en relación para producir una experiencia en la que aquello que parecía distante se vuelve próximo y corporal. La nube y su luz dejan de ser únicamente una forma que observamos desde la tierra para convertirse en una presencia atmosférica que interviene sobre la luz, sobre el paisaje y sobre nuestros propios cuerpos.

En este desplazamiento, la investigación de Valentina parece ir de la luz celestial a la luz atmosférica: de aquella que alguna vez fue entendida como signo de lo divino a una luz material, cambiante y terrestre, atravesada por el clima, las partículas, la humedad y el movimiento. Mirar las nubes implica entonces también mirar cómo la atmósfera transforma la luz y, con ella, nuestra percepción del mundo.

Helène Cixous apunta:

Y alIá arriba se pulveriza el concepto de rapidez en sí.

Ya no se les ve —Los sentidos se eclipsan. Los amantes se hurtan a la vista ordinaria. Nubes. Metáfora también de Ia mística. Aquello en lo que se convierten no se puede ver únicamente con los ojos del cuerpo, hay que abrir también los ojos de Ia pasión, cuyas miradas avanzan a más velocidad que Ia luz. [2]

Las nubes y el reflejo de su luz son un paisaje, un adorno del cielo en la tierra, una manera de acumular agua y regar los bosques, selvas y entrar en contacto con el mar. Chocan con montañas, se enredan en sus rocas y a veces, cuando se cargan, se escucha el trueno. Son tan fugaces como la luz que las golpea, que está y de pronto se va. Son impredecibles, y de cómo se comporten depende en parte lo que podamos anticipar del clima que viene. ¿Cuándo es que el mundo se va a acabar? ¿Acaso pasar de un cielo azul a un cielo gris en la atmósfera no despierta una forma de terror?

Hoy el cielo y la luz no pertenecen por igual a todos. Pensemos en el cielo de Gaza, en Palestina: ¿de qué color son sus nubes?, ¿qué sobrevuela sus alturas?, ¿quién puede alzar la mirada después del genocidio que vemos desplegarse, minuto a minuto, en pantallas y redes? Quizá la única certeza es que, como nos decía Wisława, las nubes no van a morir con nosotrxs.

[1] World Meteorological Organization, International Cloud Atlas. Volume I: Manual on the Observation of Clouds and Other Meteors , rev. ed., WMO-No. 407 (Geneva: Secretariat of the World Meteorological Organization, 1975).

[2] Hélène Cixous, “Aquiles es Pentiselea es Aquiles” en La risa de la Medusa: ensayos sobre escritura . (Pensamiento crítico, Pensamiento utópico: 88; Teoría feminista y cultura contemporánea). Barcelona: Anthropos; Madrid: Comunidad de Madrid. Consejería de Educación. Direeción General de la Mujer; San Juan: Universidad de Puerto Rico.1995.

content.article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Milo Manheim , the 25-year-old L.A. native recently tapped to co-lead Disney’s live-action Tangled , has landed a lead role in Michael Showalter’s redo of rom-com Serendipity for Amazon MGM Studios and Miramax .

No word yet on the role Manheim will play. We announced the project in August; Showalter described this as not a straight remake or reboot of Serendipity , but rather a contemporary “rebuttal” of the original film centered on new characters.

Written by the original’s Marc Klein, the new Serendipity will be produced by Showalter and Jordana Mollick for Semi-Formal Productions, alongside Simon Fields, who produced the original. Jonathan Glickman, Alexandra Loewy, and Thom Zadra are exec producing for Miramax, alongside Klein.

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Steve Stark's Toluca Pictures Extends MGM TV Overall Deal, Expands Amazon MGM Studios First-Look Pact & Taps Max Kisbye As President

'Project Hail Mary' DoP Greig Fraser Says The Film Was The "Most Complicated" He's Ever Shot - Contenders London

Emily Crook is overseeing the project for Semi-Formal, which is under a multi-year, first-look film deal with Amazon MGM, while Arianna D’Andrea will oversee for Miramax.

Directed by Peter Chelsom and starring John Cusack and Kate Beckinsale, 2001’s Serendipity centers on a couple of strangers who fall for each other one Christmas night in New York, despite being engaged to other people. Separating, their potential future together is left unresolved — until, seven years later, each begins searching for the other.

Miramax released the film to major success — a worldwide gross exceeding $77 million — at a much different moment for the rom-com. Peter Abrams, Robert L. Levy and Simon Fields produced.

No word yet on whether the new take will be for theaters or streaming. But the original just celebrated its 25th anniversary with a screening at Wollman Rink, the Central Park ice skating venue that played a memorable supporting role.

Recently seen starring in the Paramount+ series School Spirits and Eli Roth’s horror flick Thanksgiving , Manheim is among the latest crop of young talents emerging from the world of Disney Channel to lead major studio projects. He’s best known for starring in their Zombies franchise, having also taken on roles in the likes of Prom Pact , Doogie Kameāloha, M.D. , and Camp Rock 3 .

Manheim remains in the Disney family today, as he’s currently set to star opposite Teagan Croft, in the lead role of charming thief Flynn Rider, in the studio’s live-action Tangled , heading to theaters on March 31, 2028. He is repped by Framework Entertainment, CAA, and Goodman, Genow, Schenkman.

content.title_original: Blackpink Superstar Rosé Tapped for LACMA’s Art+Film Gala
content.editorial_title_zh: BLACKPINK成员Rosé将在LACMA艺术与电影晚宴献唱
content.editorial_excerpt_zh: 这位韩国流行歌手将参加美术馆第15届年度筹款晚宴，活动将表彰拉脱维亚裔美国艺术家维娅·塞尔明斯与丹尼斯·维伦纽瓦。
content.editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "韩国流行歌手Rosé将于11月7日在LACMA即将举办的艺术与电影晚宴上表演。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这位BLACKPINK主唱将参加美术馆第15届年度筹款晚宴。本届晚宴将表彰拉脱维亚裔美国艺术家维娅·塞尔明斯（Vija Celmins），以及导演丹尼斯·维伦纽瓦。塞尔明斯长期以对自然世界精细入微的描绘著称；维伦纽瓦则执导了《沙丘》《降临》等富于思辨的科幻热门作品。活动再次由Gucci呈献，演员莱昂纳多·迪卡普里奥和LACMA董事Eva Chow继续担任共同主席。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Eva Chow在声明中说：“LACMA艺术与电影晚宴庆祝来自世界各地的创意标志性人物，以及各种创作形式之间的联系。作为全球流行巨星，Rosé将以无可比拟的才华与风格，让当晚的精神更加鲜明。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如活动名称所示，艺术与电影晚宴每年分别表彰一名视觉艺术家和一名电影人。首届于2011年举办，致敬约翰·巴尔代萨里与克林特·伊斯特伍德；此后，它已成为洛杉矶艺术日历中的固定活动。2025年晚宴筹得650万美元，略高于前一年的640万美元。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "此前受邀表演的知名音乐人包括2025年的Doja Cat、2017年的安妮·伦诺克斯，以及2024年的Charli XCX；后者还邀请特洛耶·希文作为惊喜嘉宾同台。Rosé并非首次参加艺术与电影晚宴，她在2022年和2023年都曾出席。除了BLACKPINK取得的巨大成功，她的首张个人录音室专辑《rosie》也在《APT.》带动下，累计流媒体播放量突破100亿次。这首与布鲁诺·马尔斯合作的热门歌曲，为她赢得了三项格莱美提名。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "若你负担得起最低10000美元的入场券，就去向这位“number one girl”打个招呼吧。", "translated": true}]

content.article_text:
K-pop star Rosé will perform at LACMA’s upcoming Art+Film Gala on November 7.

The Blackpink vocalist joins the museum’s 15th annual fundraiser, which will honor Latvian American artist Vija Celmins, long celebrated for her meticulous renderings of the natural world, and Denis Villeneuve, the director behind cerebral sci-fi hits Dune and Arrival . The event is presented again by Gucci, with actor Leonardo DiCaprio and LACMA trustee Eva Chow returning as co-chairs.

“The LACMA Art+Film Gala celebrates creative icons and the connections between all forms of creativity, all around the world,” said Chow in a statement. “As a global pop superstar, Rosé will amplify the spirit of the evening with her incomparable talent and style.”

As its name suggests, the Art+Film Gala each year honors a visual artist and a filmmaker, and has become a fixture of Los Angeles’s art calendar since its first edition in 2011, which was dedicated to John Baldessari and Clint Eastwood. The 2025 gala raised $6.5 million, a figure slightly higher than the $6.4 million it brought in the previous year.

Rosé follows a roster of high-profile musical guests that includes Doja Cat in 2025, Annie Lennox in 2017, and Charli XCX, who brought out Troye Sivan as a surprise guest for her 2024 performance. Rosé’s appearance at the Art+Film Gala is hardly a first: she attended in both 2022 and 2023. Beyond Blackpink’s stratospheric success, her debut solo studio album, rosie , has surpassed 10 billion streams, buoyed by “APT.” That hit collaboration with Bruno Mars earned her three Grammy nominations.

For those who can afford a ticket, which start at $10,000, say hello to the number one girl .

content.article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Sony Pictures has rounded out the cast for its coming-of-age comedy Narcs , with three additions: Callan Farris ( Grimcutty ) has landed the third lead opposite Mason Thames and Ella Bright, with Lexi Minetree ( Elle ), and Josh Macqueen (upcoming Thunder Road ) also coming aboard.

Character details are being kept under wraps; the film’s plot also remains a mystery.

Slated for release in theaters on August 20, 2027, Narcs marks the directorial debut of John Phillips, whose writing credits include the R-rated comedies No Hard Feelings , Good Boys and Dirty Grandpa . Phillips is working from a script by Jordan & Justin Shipley, creators of the TBS comedy Wrecked , with a rewrite by Phillips & frequent collaborator Gene Stupnitsky, who’s producing through his Big Name Entertainment banner. Robert Lamonaca is exec producing via Big Name, alongside Phillips and Joseph Micucci.

Related Stories

Sony's Screen Gems Sets YouTube Exec Fede Goldenberg To Top Genre Label; Ashley Brucks Segues To Producer Role

Sony Pictures Acquires Casey Giltner Thriller Spec 'This Land Is Our Land'

Farris comes to Narcs with credits including the films Kings and Grimcutty , as well as Disney Channel’s Gabby Duran & The Unsittables and Disney Jr.’s cartoon The Rocketeer . He is repped by Coast to Coast Talent Group, Protégé Entertainment, and Myman Greenspan Fox.

Watch on Deadline

Best known for playing the title role in Prime Video’s Legally Blonde prequel series Elle , Minetree will next be seen in Neon’s horror film The Young People from Longlegs ‘ Osgood Perkins. She is repped by CAA, Framework Entertainment, and Jackoway Austen Tyerman.

An Australian actor with credits like Motorheads and Black Snow , Macqueen’s next to be seen in The Sticks , a hockey drama series from Netflix and 21 Laps, and the AMC NASCAR drama Thunder Road . He is repped by Innovative Artists, Anonymous Content, and Goodman, Genow, Schenkman.

New York Newsletter

NYC Artists Open Their Doors

Open studios and houses, plus reviews of Betty Parsons, Riddikuluz, and the L train burlesque.

I was way too productive throughout the three-day weekend. A grueling closet overhaul (five-drawer wooden tallboy vs. fourth-floor walk-up), an overdue bathroom bleachout, a close friend’s 30th birthday party, a drop-in cat-sitting visit that turned into a rare accidental nap, and an arduous round-trip trek to the distant land of Nassau County were accomplished, and yet I still feel haplessly behind on my never-ending to-do list.

Looking at the upcoming roster for the rest of the month, I’m positive that I’m not the only one who’ll be letting that to-do list pile up again in favor of ✨ immersing myself in the culture ✨. Much like my closet door for the better part of the last eight months, the doors to New York City are going to be wide open this weekend. Sunset Park and Gowanus are hosting their annual open studios, which happen to coincide with the broader Open House New York (OHNY) weekend programming. We’ve highlighted a selection of intriguing OHNY happenings at the bottom of this newsletter! :)

In observance of Indigenous Peoples’ Day, we highlighted a wealth of Native American art happenings across the city and state. Take a look at our round-up of seven exhibitions embodying Indigenous survivance and Associate Editor Phillip Pyle’s rich Q&A with Diné artist and composer Raven Chacon, who recently led an hour-long improvisational sound performance at the Park Avenue Armory last week. In the same vein, Staff Writer Anna Lee reported that the Gochman Family Collection is set to open its Katonah site for exhibiting contemporary Indigenous art next month!

Remember last week’s newsletter, when I mentioned that the Department of Cultural Affairs announced that city-funded artists' grants jumped from $5,000 to $10,000? Well, an additional perk has been revealed: starting October 19, those who are afforded grants will also gain access to the city’s beloved Materials for the Arts warehouse on the second Monday of each month. Congratulations in advance to those who will deservedly reap these benefits!

Happy reading, and I’ll see you at the Tompkins Square Dog Halloween Parade!

7 New York Exhibitions That Embody Indigenous Survivance

To commemorate Indigenous Peoples’ Day here in New York, we highlighted seven ongoing exhibitions of Native art and history in Manhattan, the Hessel Museum of Art at Bard College, and the Long Island Museum in Stony Brook. Across solo and group presentations, the featured artists, who represent a diverse tapestry of Indigenous populations across Turtle Island, embody survivance by tracing and rejecting narratives of dispossession and irrelevance, upending and satirizing stereotypes, preserving and reinventing traditional art forms, and bringing underrepresented histories out from the margins. | Rhea Nayyar

Read More

Raven Chacon Sounds the History of the Land

The Pulitzer Prize-winning Diné artist talks about his recent performances at the Park Avenue Armory, the freedom of improvisation, and the privilege of “deep listening.” | Phillip Pyle

Read More

Quilt Along: Sit and Sew at the National Museum of the American Indian

Meet artist Margaret Wood (Diné/Seminole), one of five contemporary Indigenous artists featured in the museum’s first-ever Quilt Along program. The artists designed patterns inspired by different eras of United States history, as seen through a Native lens.

Learn more and join us Saturday, October 17, 1–3 PM.

Register Now

From Our Critics

Hrag Vartanian

Pleasure Dome: Continuum at SoMad

"The gathering became a fête of therapeutic sound, queer political rally, vaudeville tribute, and a vibe manifesto for a city that is constantly shattering the old to make way for the new."

Daniel Larkin

KLAB at Salma Sarriedine gallery

"In Ridikkuluz’s work, the irascible dog emerges as a symbol for the ongoing genocide and its unrestrained perpetrators."

Julia Curl

settle for a good fantasy at Luhring Augustine

"In one set of eight prints, the artist rubs dark makeup from her eyes, a gesture reminiscent of crying. As her eyeshadow smears, it leaves what look like bruises, creating a dissonant, double feeling of pain and pleasure — and the acknowledgment that it’s all just an act."

Seph Rodney

Betty Parsons: An Expanded World at the Hessel Museum of Art at Bard College

"Regardless of the aesthetic merit or caliber of the work, this artist, like any other, deserves to have her own space free of another artist’s intervention because she is well able to stand on her own two feet."

A Hyperallergic Halloween

Join us on October 28 in Brooklyn, NY, for an evening of spooky cocktails, devilish delights, an art-themed costume contest, and more.

Learn more and Get Tickets

News

After a five-year pause, the New Museum in Manhattan will open its sixth triennial for emerging artists in early 2027.

Materials for the Arts is launching a new free shopping program for artists who receive city-funded grants.

The Gochman Collection of Indigenous Art is opening a space in Katonah this November.

Over two dozen people assembled down the street from the Museum of Modern Art calling for the removal of disgraced billionaire Leon Black from the museum board.

What Else Is Happening?

Sunset Park Open Studios is this weekend! (Fri Oct 16 through Sun Oct 18) [ sunsetparkopenstudios.org ]

Print Center New York is hosting a rubber stamp workshop. (Sat Oct 17) [ printcenternewyork.org ]

The Tompkins Square Dog Halloween Parade returns this Saturday for its 36th edition. (Sat Oct 17) [ nydogparade.org ]

Pioneers in Hand Papermaking commemorates 50 years of NYC’s fine arts papermill, Dieu Donné, with a display of over 100 artworks and material innovations. (Sat Oct 17) [ OHNY.org ]

Tom's Sons, a diasporic Armenian family-owned textile pleating business in the Garment District, explains their generationally perfected craft. (Sat Oct 17) [ OHNY.org ]

The New York Sign Museum invites visitors to check out its collection of preserved hand-painted and craft signage embodying different eras of design thinking throughout the 20th century. (Sat Oct 17 and and Sun Oct 18) [ OHNY.org ]

Gowanus Open Studios is this weekend! (Sat Oct 17 through Sun Oct 18) [ artsgowanus.org ]

Palestine Will Be Free: The Story of Hanzala is a concert built around 100 of Palestinian cartoonist Naji al-Ali's drawings, animated and projected above a nine-piece ensemble playing twelve songs of childhood, freedom, and return. (Sun Oct 18) [ thebrooklynnomads.com ]

Slo Slo Studio is hosting a handmade ceramic bookends workshop. (Sun Oct 18) [ sloslostudio.kilnfire.com ]

The Center for Book Arts is hosting live demonstrations of historic and contemporary bookmaking steps and techniques, including letterpress printing to sewing frames. (Sun., Oct 18) [ OHNY.org ]

Rizzoli Bookstore celebrates the new monograph, Brilliant: Unexpected Art from Everywhere , with a conversation between Roxane Gay and her wife, Debbie Millman. (Mon Oct 19) [ Rizzoli Bookstore ]

AI Now Institute and More Perfect Union are leading the People's AI Assembly, an evening bringing together leading organizers, cultural figures, and policy leaders shaping the frontlines of AI. (Mon Oct 19) [ actionnetwork.org ]

content.article_text:
On Monday, before the eyes of Washington, D.C., water once again filled the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool .

A sign, posted by National Park Service on the premises, reads : “The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is being refilled as the National Park Service and contractors put the final touches on a historic effort to clean, repair, and beautify this iconic national landmark. As part of the normal refilling process, the water may temporarily appear cloudy before clearing.”

Earlier this year, after a restoration that involved painting the bottom of the reflecting pool—a color described by President Donald Trump as “American Flag Blue”—the new coating began to peel, prompting a second round of repairs even as Trump declared the work “totally complete.”

Atlantic Industrial Coatings, which was awarded a no-bid contract to renovate the pool, announced on its website that warranty repairs had been completed on October 2, adding, “It has been an honor to serve our great nation!”

The fenced-off, slate-blue basin had sat exposed through the summer, a stark reminder of the project’s other protracted troubles: a major algae bloom, controversial contract awards, and most recently, flaking paint. The Trump administration initially attributed the pool’s peeling coating to vandalism, leading to criminal charges against several people, including former Olympic canoeist David Hearn. The Justice Department dropped the case against Hearn in July, after a determination that the coating’s installation was “botched.”

Despite evidence contradicting the vandalism claims and a ruling barring Hearn from being prosecuted again, President Donald Trump reiterated at a Tuesday press conference that vandals had cut pieces out of the basin.

“We had vandalism there, and we have it about as vandal-proof as you can get,” he said. “But only sick people do that, and we have their pictures.”

The project has also faced a legal challenge. In May, the Cultural Landscape Foundation (TCLF), a nonprofit education and advocacy organization, sued the NPS; its acting director, Jessica Bowron; the Department of the Interior; and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, alleging that they bypassed required historic-preservation review in pursuit of a poorly planned renovation.

Of the basin’s new color, “American Flag Blue,” the suit noted that the pool’s original gray coloring helped preserve the visual cohesion between the Lincoln Memorial and the Washington Monument.

“A blue-tinted basin is more appropriate to a resort or theme park,” Charles A. Birnbaum, TCLF’s president and chief executive, said in a statement.
