content.article_text:
Black Bear has acquired the rights to a comedy spec script from up-and-coming writing duo Cassidy Alla and Read Masino, Variety can reveal exclusively

According to an official logline, the untitled film “tells the story of when a mother and daughter inadvertently start dating the same man; the whole family – each at their own crossroad in life and love – must deal with the chaotic fallout.”

Related Stories

Emmys Move to Prime Video in Six-Year, Global Deal Worth Around $15 Million a Year

Amazon Launches Faster Fire TV Stick 4K and Redesigned Remote, Adds Alexa+ Hub to Fire TV Interface

Alla and Masino, both working toward their feature breakouts, have a movie in development at Netflix with Berlanti/Schechter producing and Nahnatchka Khan (“Totally Killer”) directing. The duo met while working as assistants at Apatow Productions. Masino worked as a writers’ assistant on Amazon’s “Spider-Noir” and Apple’s “Brothers” and “The Muppet Show,” while Alla worked for showrunner Justin Noble, co-creator of “The Sex Lives of College Girls.”

Popular on Variety

“This script is one of the funniest and most poignant scripts we have seen in years about romance, family and the dysfunction so often associated with both,” said Michael Heimler, Partner, President of Production & Operations at Black Bear. “Cassidy and Read are two of the most exciting voices we’ve read in some time, and we can’t wait to bring this story to life.”

Alla and Masino added in a joint statement, “We had so much fun writing this chaotic comedy about a family (not to be confused with a family comedy) and couldn’t ask for a better partner on this project than Black Bear.”

Black Bear, which launched its distribution arm in 2025, is the studio behind recent films like “Train Dreams,” “Sing Sing” and “The Imitation Game.” The upcoming Black Bear slate includes “Honeymoon / Funeral,” starring Rebecca Ferguson, Greta Lee and Carrie Coon; “Wicker,” starring Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård and Peter Dinklage; and Guy Ritchie’s “Wife and Dog” with Benedict Cumberbatch and Rosamund Pike.

Alla is represented by UTA and Mosaic. Masino is represented by UTA and Artists First.

content.editorial_excerpt_zh: 利奥教宗向Bizot小组成员讲话。该小组汇聚了世界上一些最大博物馆的负责人。

content.article_text:
Pope Leo XIV addressed a group of directors of globally renowned museums on Saturday at the Apostolic Palace at the Vatican, underlining the Catholic Church’s “special affinity with the arts.”

The pontiff spoke to members of the Bizot group, also known as the International Group of Organizers of Major Exhibitions, whose member institutions include the Louvre in Paris, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, the National Gallery of Singapore, the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg, the Art Gallery of Ontario, the British Museum in London, and the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, among other world-class institutions.

Founded in 1992, the group takes its name from Irène Bizot, former director of France’s Réunion des Musées Nationaux, who was instrumental in its establishment. Rijksmuseum director Taco Dibbits is its current president. The organization’s members met in Rome and Vatican City, including at the Vatican Museums, for a meeting devoted to the theme of materiality.

“Art is the means by which persons, through their ingenuity, enhance and transfigure matter—that is, the creation in which they dwell as made in the image and likeness of God,” Pope Leo said in his address on Saturday. “The theme of your meeting, ‘Materiality,’ is therefore of particular interest, not only for exploring the relationship between an object and the interpretation of a work of art, but also for reflecting on the distinctive quality of matter as the place in which God chose to reveal himself.”

Quoting a 2015 letter from Pope Francis, the current head of the Catholic Church compared artists with Jesus, saying that Christ “worked with his hands, in daily contact with the matter created by God, to which he gave form by his craftsmanship.” Matter is also memory, said Leo, adding, “The works preserved in museums bear witness to a history that speaks to every person, from one generation to the next. Museum objects thus offer to the present the wisdom of the past.”

“I therefore congratulate all of you for your efforts in directing and administering the museums to which you devote yourselves, safeguarding a heritage that belongs to all humanity,” he concluded his remarks.

The address to museum directors came just days after the pope spoke to artists and curators , saying that the Church needs them, adding, “This is especially true in this age of artificial intelligence, in which we urgently need to distinguish human art from what is produced by machines.”

content.article_text:
Long Long Night (2026) by Youm Kyu-bock, film review

From Ru Ri’s bestseller, an animated coming-of-age journey through fatherhood and grief, with the voices of Park Ki-wook and Suzy

The only animated film in the competition section of the 31st Busan International Film Festival, Youm Kyu-bock’s “Long Long Night” is based on the book of the same name by Ru Ri, a celebrated tale with over 800,000 copies sold. Director Youm approached the story together with his daughter. The book had already inspired a musical and a pansori version, so bringing it to the big screen was, as the director himself rightly pointed out, a truly long night .

Long Long Night is screening at Busan International Film Festival

The film arrives after some very famous productions, and it won’t be hard to feel transported to the landscapes of “Flow”, the Latvian hit of 2024, or to recall the humor of the penguins in “Madagascar”, the DreamWorks franchise with fans all over the world. Here too, the penguins are hilarious.

The film features the voices of Kim Kyu-na and Suzy, who bring the little penguin to life, while Park Ki-wook, with his dense timbre, voices Norden.

The story is very simple and moving but never loses its cheerfulness, and follows the unusual life of Norden, a white rhino rescued from poachers and taken to an elephant reserve, where he learns, first of all, how to be an elephant. Just as he nestles into what he believes is his world, he is offered the freedom and the identity that are rightfully his. Running “faster than the wind,” he meets another white rhino and, with her, a family. The last of their kind.

Once again, just when he thinks he has found happiness, a tragedy forces him back into solitude and confinement. Norden is transported to a zoo and manages to escape only because war breaks out among his own jailers, who are, of course, human beings. Having survived, he sets off once more, this time with Chiku, a grumpy penguin who walks carrying a precious bucket in his beak, in which he keeps his egg, still waiting to hatch. When the egg hatches, the second part of the film begins: the second, greater voyage of Norden and the newborn, toward the sea.

“Long Long Night” is an animation made with contemporary techniques, namely Unreal Engine, a video game graphics engine, much lighter and cheaper than better-known animation software such as Maya. If technically it is an experimental undertaking, from a narrative standpoint, the film follows a classic arc. The hero’s journey, as Campbell would have it.

And yet Norden is not a traditional hero. He is a survivor, who processes multiple traumas and who channels his mission into fatherhood. It is touching to consider how closely the “Long Long Night” project itself aligns with the film’s theme, since it was born from a father (the director himself) reading a story to his daughter. That bond and the theme of parenthood find an echo in the characters who, animated though they are, show an emotional depth that leaves no one indifferent.

The film is neatly divided into sequences, or perhaps it is better to say into stages of life: youth, adulthood and old age. Norden matures through his experiences, which, once acquired, are ready to be passed on. Even to a penguin. This blend of species nods to unconventional families, and the solutions the film proposes are plainly, lovingly successful.

There is nothing this rhino won’t come up with to make the penguin appreciate his “penguinness” and to nurture in him the desire to reach an ocean he has never seen, but toward which he must head all the same. Norden wields the magic of storytelling, which educates, reassures, comforts and energizes. It is a poetic dynamic that points back to cinema itself: a film about the power of stories, folding back on itself. We are both outside and inside the screen without even knowing it.

Drawing on the freedom the digital environment has given him, Youm Kyu-bock plays festively with the action scenes. He doesn’t necessarily make the film adrenaline-fueled; he offers them as fitting entertainment for the viewer. A herd of wildebeest migrates, enraged and out of control, and not even a rhino can withstand its force. From this pitiless surge comes a thrilling scene in the waters of a raging river, where a rhino father’s desperation becomes the will to survive. It is also the scene where the software’s technical limits, especially in the rendering of water, are most visible, though in the emotional whirlwind they vanish.

The director deliberately chooses not to describe certain moments precisely: the protagonist’s thoughts, most of the time reserved and taciturn, are told by the starry sky. Likewise, some memories and emotions return and are reworked as bedtime stories. “Long Long Night” is truly rich in ideas that are not handed over gratuitously but revealed gradually. It allows us to embrace the natural course of loss and to accept the impermanence of existence, though not without a few tears. Vulnerabilities evolve into acceptance and perseverance, thus revealing themselves as strength.

Confident in his background in advertising, Youm Kyu-bock cuts the film at a frenetic rhythm where needed and slows it down when we need rest, a gathered, introspective moment. This wise alternation fosters the fullest immersion in, and involvement with, the challenges Norden and his extended family face.

It is a family film, and one that draws viewers toward the environmental cause without growing rigid on the theme. Above all, it breathes infinite landscapes, saturated colors and long shots, daring point-of-view shots and carefully worked details, not so common in traditional animation. Purists will notice a certain “robotic” stiffness in the movements and video-game pacing. But in front of a rhino teaching a penguin to believe in an ocean he has never seen, that detail can be overlooked.

content.article_text:
Feature

“Cornell 7” Case Sparks Fury and Protests in Solidarity With Jane Doe

A Nationwide Day of Action on October 8 gathered artists, activists, and survivors in a collective call for institutions to hold abusers accountable.

Washington, DC — Approximately 250 protesters gathered beside the Washington Monument on the National Mall on October 8 as part of a National Day of Action event calling for accountability and justice for sexual assault survivors. The protest was just one of more than a dozen “I Am Jane Doe” demonstrations held across the country last week, “from the frat house to the White House,” as described by the Women’s March.

The National Day of Action was largely organized in response to allegations that seven Cornell University men, now known as the “Cornell 7,” gang raped a female student and advertised it in a fraternity Snapchat group. When the woman, known as Jane Doe, reported the incident two years ago, two of the men she accused were expelled, while the rest were required to write essays . Two years after the university’s response, Jane Doe’s lawyer filed another suit .

“We are in a moment of reckoning,” Dani Bensky, a vocal Jeffrey Epstein survivor and victims’ advocate, thundered into the microphone. She was one of six speakers who called for the passage of legislation to hold abusers accountable, including Alva Johnson, a 2016 campaign staffer who publicly accused Trump of sexual assault, and Claire Barnett, a JD candidate and president of Advocates Against Sexual Violence at Georgetown Law.

Protestors cheered them on and lifted signs reading “History Has Its Eyes on Us” and “Give Me Back My Girlhood, I Had It First.”

Hyperallergic )

Among them was activist and curator Nadine Seiler, known for her work on the preservation of artworks in the Black Lives Matter memorial fence. She held a poster that with the words “I Am Jane Doe” spray-painted on one side and “rapists are not victims” on the other, a response to criticism from the Cornell 7 and their supporters that these men’s lives were disrupted when their photos and names were shared online as part of calls for justice. Seiler told Hyperallergic that she was deeply offended by these arguments.

“I am a victim of sexual assault, and so are many people. Our experiences are important and life-changing,” Seiler said, adding that the argument that “boys will be boys is old.”

In New York's Foley Square, protesters dressed up as characters from The Handmaid's Tale and carried signs calling out systemic violence. (photo Bonnie Biess/Getty Images for Women's March)

Days earlier, on October 5, hundreds of Cornell students staged a campus rally against the Ivy League school’s administration , expressing solidarity with Jane Doe and calling out what many view as a toxic and openly sexist fraternity culture.

When asked about the choice of location for the action, protest organizer Riley Reed told Hyperallergic that they wanted to situate survivors and advocates against the backdrop of recognizable DC emblems, with the Washington Monument obelisk behind them and the White House in sight.

“It’s a big statement [that] we will not accept sexual abusers in the White House, and we have one currently in the White House,” Reed said, referring to the multiple sexual assault allegations against President Trump.

“We want to hold the leaders at the top accountable for their actions, and this is a pretty poetic and powerful spot between the Monument and the White House, which are symbols of power,” Reed continued.

Hyperallergic )

The protest lasted two hours with speeches, chants, and eventually music performed by two singers with guitars that called on Americans, in Johnson’s words, to “vote the rape regime out of office.”

As the group marched towards the White House and dispersed, Johnson’s words still hung in the air: “I am not afraid. They feed off fear, so we starve them with courage.”

content.article_text:
E XCLUSIVE : The Black List has named the six writers and projects chosen for its 2026 Writers Lab. They are Elton de Almeida ( A Mark of Kin ), Yasmin DeWinter ( Guillaume ), Scott Leddy (Nightwatch) , Marcelle Pallais ( One Last Summer ), Alexander Seltzer and Kyle Jutkiewicz ( Depths ) and Emma Taylor Stock ( Denial ).

The program, now in its 13th year, provides creative mentorship and professional support to promising feature writers as they further develop their selected project during a weeklong workshop in Ojai, CA.

The Black List’s Annual Lab program supports two distinct cohorts: writers and ﬁlmmakers. The Writers Lab focuses on developing feature scripts to be sold in the studio system and/or used as voice samples. The Projects Lab, which will be announced in November, offers writer-directors the chance to develop a screenplay that they intend to direct.

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Spiegel & Grau's Full Catalog Available On The Black List Online Platform

Deadline's L.A. Law Summit: Nina Shaw & Patricia Glaser Honored On Day Of Big Ideas, Big Insights; Watch The Video Presentations

During the Lab, each writer will develop their screenplay through peer workshops and one-on-one sessions with working professional screenwriters, including returning mentors Travis Braun ( One Night Only ), Stephany Folsom ( Toy Story 4, The Lord of the Rings: Rings of Power ), Katie Silberman ( Set It Up, Don’t Worry Darling ), Victoria Strouse ( Seekers of Infinite Love, Finding Dory ) and Christina Hodson ( Birds of Prey, Bumblebee ).

Black List Annual Lab alumna Savion Einstein ( A Cuban Girl’s Guide To Tea and Tomorrow ) will also join as a session mentor. After the lab concludes, the writers cohort will participate in a yearlong support program involving monthly meetings with screenwriters, agents, managers, producers, and executives. Pitching and peer workshop sessions will be led by Scott Myers ( The Protagonist’s Journey , Spec Script Deals: 1991-2025) who has been a part of every single annual Black List Lab so far.

“We’re excited to welcome the latest cohort of screenwriters to the Black List Lab fold. At a time when the industry can seem particularly challenging and harder than ever to break into, we’re thrilled to be able to support projects that make us excited to go to the movies. These writers are bringing distinctive voices, bold points of view, and stories that deserve to be heard to the Lab and we’re privileged to be able to give them space to take risks, challenge themselves, and build community with other writers, in Ojai and beyond,” said Megan Halpern, Black List SVP.

Submissions for the 2027 Labs are now open on the Black List website .

Previous Black List Lab alumni include Claire Ayoub ( Empire Waist ), Minhal Baig ( We Grown Now ), Tom Dean ( Carolina, Caroline ), Gia Gordon ( Law and Order ), Danny Hogan ( The Pitt ), Jimmy Keyrouz ( Broken Keys ), Dagny Looper ( The Resort) , Alexandra Qin ( ThirstyGirl) , Michelle Steffes ( For When You Get Lost ), and Jason Young ( The Magic Flute) .

Learn more about the 2026 Writers Lab projects, and the creatives behind them, below.

2026 Writers Lab Projects:

Elton de Almeida – A MARK OF KIN

Haunted by her family’s tragic past, a cunning scammer seeks revenge on the uncle who abandoned her decades ago — only to be trapped by a demonic curse that feeds off her bloodline.

Yasmin DeWinter – GUILLAUME

Paris, 1898. Two American brothers walk into a brothel. One vomits on a girl. The other pulls a knife. Within the hour, they owe a madam five thousand francs they don’t have. Their ship sails at dawn. The elder just had a seizure in a piss-soaked alley – and if anyone finds out, he loses his wife, his childen, and his name.

Scott Leddy – NIGHTWATCH

In the midst of an apparent nuclear attack on NATO and the US, a communications blackout with the President places the Defense Secretary in the hot seat on America’s Doomsday Plane, but with the minutes ticking down, a comms expert discovers an anomaly that could change everything.

Marcelle Pallais – ONE LAST SUMMER

A restless, sharp-witted teen aching for meaning and adventure escapes to a wealthy beach town, only to be pulled toward a charming boy and his family’s deadly secret. Adapted from NORTHANGER ABBEY by Jane Austen.

Alexander Seltzer and Kyle Jutkiewicz – DEPTHS

Trapped aboard a US nuclear submarine, a former priest turned navy engineer must stop a demon-possessed Soviet defector before she turns the Cold War hot.

Emma Taylor Stock – DENIAL

When a health insurance giant denies their bestie’s cancer treatment, three friends attempt to approve the claim themselves. But their plan spirals when they accidentally kidnap the CEO and must expose his fraud to save themselves.

content.article_text:
Preview

Art Films We Look Forward to Watching at DOC NYC

Documentaries on a giant pencil that became a local watering hole, the afterlife of Frida Kahlo through her image, and collagist Romare Bearden are among the festival’s most enticing offerings.

Frida: The Girl Just Doesn't Go Away (2026), directed by Trisha Ziff (all images courtesy DOC NYC)

I’ve never put much thought into how I want to be portrayed after I die. Perhaps I’d opt to be plastered on Etsy mugs, tea sets, and journal covers, à la Frida Kahlo (though I doubt I’d have many buyers, or that Kahlo would’ve enjoyed how her self-image is often nowadays detached from the politics and life behind it), or I would begin things early by enlisting an artist to paint their best guess at my posthumous body. Maybe I'd like to be dipped in ink and stamped onto rice paper, as Molly Tenzer does with the roadkill she finds on New York City streets.

The lineup at this year’s DOC NYC, which returns to venues throughout the city from November 11 through November 29, offers many reflections on this question — and more regarding documentary's capacity to sensitively portray communities currently under threat, examine artists' legacies, and narrate some of art's most idiosyncratic stories. We’ve selected 13 films we’re looking forward to seeing in-person or online at the festival's 17th edition.

Frida: The Girl Just Doesn't Go Away

Village East by Angelika , 181-189 2nd Ave, East Village Nov. 14 & 16

Go to any gift shop in an art museum, and there’s a decent chance you’ll find Frida Kahlo’s image draped over mugs, t-shirts, or decorative tapestries. Simultaneously a political icon, feminist celebrity, and a global household brand, Kahlo presents an interesting case study about how artists’ images define their legacy long after their deaths. Director Trisha Ziff taps into the commercial fascination with Kahlo and how her image has taken on a distinct life from her motivations and work.

The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs

SVA Theatre , 333 W 23rd St, Chelsea Nov. 11

The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs (2026), directed by Èlia Gasull Balada and Matteo Norzi

Èlia Gasull Balada’s and Matteo Norzi’s documentary on Indigenous artist Sara Flores (Shipibo-Konibo) was born out of a decade-long collaboration during which the painter began to receive international recognition. Using natural dyes sourced from her home in the Peruvian Amazon, Flores paints intricate geometric patterns with striking symmetry. Equally channeling the visual and matrilineal language of the Shipibo-Konibo practice of Kené, Flores creates works as a form of resistance against environmental, political, and social ills.

content.article_text:
Preview

13 Art Films to See at DOC NYC

Documentaries on a giant pencil that became a local watering hole, the afterlife of Frida Kahlo through her image, and collagist Romare Bearden are among the festival’s most enticing offerings.

Frida: The Girl Just Doesn't Go Away (2026), directed by Trisha Ziff (all images courtesy DOC NYC)

I’ve never put much thought into how I want to be portrayed after I die. Perhaps I’d opt to be plastered on Etsy mugs, tea sets, and journal covers, à la Frida Kahlo (though I doubt I’d have many buyers, or that Kahlo would’ve enjoyed how her self-image is often nowadays detached from the politics and life behind it), or I would begin things early by enlisting an artist to paint their best guess at my posthumous body. Maybe I'd like to be dipped in ink and stamped onto rice paper, as Molly Tenzer does with the roadkill she finds on New York City streets.

The lineup at this year’s DOC NYC, which returns to venues throughout the city from November 11 through November 29, offers many reflections on this question — and more regarding documentary's capacity to sensitively portray communities currently under threat, examine artists' legacies, and narrate some of art's most idiosyncratic stories. We’ve selected 13 films we’re looking forward to seeing in-person or online at the festival's 17th edition.

Frida: The Girl Just Doesn't Go Away

Village East by Angelika , 181-189 2nd Ave, East Village Nov. 14 & 16

Go to any gift shop in an art museum, and there’s a decent chance you’ll find Frida Kahlo’s image draped over mugs, t-shirts, or decorative tapestries. Simultaneously a political icon, feminist celebrity, and a global household brand, Kahlo presents an interesting case study about how artists’ images define their legacy long after their deaths. Director Trisha Ziff taps into the commercial fascination with Kahlo and how her image has taken on a distinct life from her motivations and work.

The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs

SVA Theatre , 333 W 23rd St, Chelsea Nov. 11

The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs (2026), directed by Èlia Gasull Balada and Matteo Norzi

Èlia Gasull Balada’s and Matteo Norzi’s documentary on Indigenous artist Sara Flores (Shipibo-Konibo) was born out of a decade-long collaboration during which the painter began to receive international recognition. Using natural dyes sourced from her home in the Peruvian Amazon, Flores paints intricate geometric patterns with striking symmetry. Equally channeling the visual and matrilineal language of the Shipibo-Konibo practice of Kené, Flores creates works as a form of resistance against environmental, political, and social ills.

content.article_text:
Feature

Sara Flores Paints What the World Stands to Lose

“Every opportunity to show my work is a platform to raise attention on the struggle for self-determination and cultural resistance of the Shipibo people,” the artist told Hyperallergic.

The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs (2026) (all images courtesy Shipibo Conibo Center)

A long canoe floats onscreen to the throbbing hum of insects; a frail woman expertly strips bark from a tree. She boils it slowly, a small tamarin monkey curled on her head like a crown. Dipping a blade into a bowl of tree juice, the woman free-hands a series of geometric shapes. Her nails are stained with age and ink, her grip remarkably steady.

Directed by Èlia Gasull Balada and Matteo Norzi, The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs (2026) follows artist Sara Flores throughout her rapid ascendance to art world fame as the representing artist of the Peruvian pavilion at the current Venice Biennale . The film will screen at the 50th annual São Paulo International Film Festival starting on October 19, and will make its United States premiere as the opening night selection at DOC NYC on Wednesday, November 11, streaming online as part of the festival from November 12–29.

After an opening sequence set deep in the Amazon rainforest, we encounter Flores smiling at a flute of champagne on a first-class flight to New York. At her exhibition at the now-defunct Clearing gallery on the Bowery, she stands proud in a crimson blouse, admiring the admirers. In Central Park, she feeds the pigeons after watching a man extend acorns to the squirrels.

content.article_text:
T here is a tender sweetness to this silver-years romance of new experiences and new ideas – and also some sugary sentimentality, an autumnal woodwind score telling us how to feel, and a bit of sitcom-cartoony characterisation in the all-star gallery of supporting turns. Sometimes that works and sometimes it doesn’t. But the movie’s easy-going good nature wins out – and there’s a terrific contribution from Joanna Lumley, playing Belinda, an elegant woman poignantly suffering from early onset dementia. Screenwriter Martin Sherman adapts the two-hander stage-play by Ben Weatherill in which Roger Allam and Ian McKellen originally starred. They return here for the expanded movie version and Sean Mathias once again directs.

Allam plays Frank, a retired history teacher whose wife died of cancer a few short years ago (Belinda is his sister-in-law) and who now likes to walk his dog Toffee on Hampstead Heath. McKellen is Percy, an academic sociologist and climate scientist who can be found there too, with his dog Bruno. Percy is rather acrimoniously separated from his now ex-partner, a waspish and querulously self-pitying figure gamely played by Stephen Fry .

In their differing ways, the men are lonely; Frank has nothing to do but mope around the garden centre, brooding over memories from his marriage, and volunteering at a charity shop where he has to stand, and Derek Jacobi , as a salaried employee, is allowed to sit. Percy goes in for age-gap dates from a niche website called Papa Search – some broad comedy cameos here for Ncuti Gatwa and Hugh Skinner – but he’s not satisfied. His friendship with Frank grows, his mischievous donnish sense of fun vibing unexpectedly with Frank’s stolid northern common sense. Then one day over a drink, Percy asks if it might be quite all right if he kissed Frank. Wonderingly, Frank agrees – and it is the start of something new; he says: “I felt like I did when I had a cataract removed.”

This leads Frank to ponder if he is bisexual – but perhaps it is more that he is simply sexual, and sexual in a way that he never expected to be at this time of life, or any time of life, and could only have been with this individual person. We get some bittersweet comedy as Frank and Percy realise that their social life consists of funerals, and Percy has a startling Yorick moment looking at the churchyard’s headstones. “Oh my God! I’ve had him!”

Naturally, the course of true love, or any sort of love, does not run smooth and at one stage Belinda, in a moment of lucidity, tells Frank: “How lucky you are to have a broken heart at 77!” True enough. It’s a love story as comforting as the cups of tea and slices of cake to which the characters are partial.

content.title_original: Lunch With Adam: Met Curator Alisa LaGamma on Repatriation, the Revitalized Rockefeller Wing, the Benin Bronzes, and More
content.editorial_title_zh: 与 Adam 共进午餐：专访策展人 Alisa LaGamma，谈文物归还、焕新的 Rockefeller 展翼、贝宁青铜器等议题
content.editorial_excerpt_zh: “今后我们都需要想出富有创意的解决方案。”
content.editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa LaGamma 是大都会艺术博物馆非洲、大洋洲与美洲艺术部 Ceil and Michael E. Pulitzer 策展人。我毕生收藏非洲艺术，多年来看过她策划的许多展览，也曾多年担任该部门委员会成员，近年还任过主席。这些物件的历史引人入胜：从痛苦的殖民时代，到人们努力让艺术界广泛接纳这些艺术。很少有人意识到，大都会直到 20 世纪 80 年代才展出这些作品；在那之前，许多人眼里它们不过是文物。如今，围绕归还政治及遣返复杂现实的讨论仍在持续。上个月我们从巴黎的经典非洲与大洋洲艺术博览会 Parcours du Monde 归来；此前不久，博物馆整座展翼耗资 7000 万美元翻修一周年。此时探讨当下热议的几个议题，正合时宜。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Artnet News 精选内容，直达你的收件箱。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "订阅我们的每日简报。", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Artnet News 精选内容，直达你的收件箱。订阅我们的每日简报。请输入有效的电子邮件地址。订阅失败，请稍后重试。谢谢！你已成功订阅 Artnet News。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：Michael C. Rockefeller 展翼是什么？能否介绍大都会与经典非洲、大洋洲和古代美洲艺术之间的关系？", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Artnet News 精选内容，直达你的收件箱。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "订阅我们的每日简报。", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Artnet News 精选内容，直达你的收件箱。订阅我们的每日简报。请输入有效的电子邮件地址。订阅失败，请稍后重试。谢谢！你已成功订阅 Artnet News。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：当然，这是个引人入胜的故事。1969 年，纽约州州长 Nelson Aldrich Rockefeller 与大都会艺术博物馆宣布将兴建一座新展翼，以接收他捐赠的撒哈拉以南非洲、大洋洲和古代美洲藏品。在此之前，这批藏品一直陈列于他创办的原始艺术博物馆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这一发展从根本上重塑了大都会的使命。当时的大都会——如今亦然——是美国的顶尖博物馆之一。此举让占世界艺术传统约四分之三的艺术，突然得以与西欧艺术史巅峰——西方古典大师作品——并列受到认可；此前，这些传统常被归入自然历史博物馆。几乎一夜之间，大都会成为一家全球性机构，立志呈现所有文化。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：这在当时是相当激进的一步——一次重大转变，改变了西方人看待世界广大地区艺术的方式，也对收藏家、画廊和博物馆产生了深远影响，拓宽了人们对何为美术的理解。但人们或许不知道，大都会起初并不支持这件事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：确实如此。Rockefeller 推动的这场转型来之不易。他对非西方艺术的热情起初并未得到大都会认同，因此他在 1954 年于现代艺术博物馆对面创办了自己的私人机构。当时艺术史中这些领域尚十分新兴，他在相关顶尖专家的建议下，着手梳理大都会尚未涵盖的主要艺术传统。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/TWO-PANEL-SPLIT-WITH-BACKGROUND-2-1024x819.png", "alt": "Alisa LaGamma 与 Adam Lindemann 的双人照片。", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa LaGamma 与 Adam Lindemann。照片：大都会艺术博物馆及作者提供。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：这位政治家出身于美国最富有的家族之一，可以说是美国最接近王室的人物；他却希望把那些被视为来自世界边远地区的民族志材料的物件，当作美术来认可。他为何如此热衷？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：Nelson 于 1930 年从达特茅斯学院毕业，那一年便成为大都会的受托人。作为 John D. Rockefeller 与 Abby Rockefeller 之子，他从母亲那里受到影响，认识到非洲和古代美洲艺术在 20 世纪艺术转型中发挥的重要作用。此后，他以国际主义者和政治家的身份，通过艺术传统学习较少为人熟悉的地区，并由此坚信“所有人都有艺术”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nelson 的儿子 Michael 也怀有父亲那份使命感，并在哈佛主修人类学。他深受太平洋地区的文化与艺术启发，旅居当地期间也以新的方式探究艺术实践。展翼中展出的 Asmat 雕塑极为醒目，是他在新几内亚西南部研究并收藏的。1961 年，他第二次前往巴布亚新几内亚，研究、收藏并记录当地艺术家的作品；途中，他乘坐的小船在 Betsj 河口燃料耗尽，漂向阿拉弗拉海。他试图游向岸边时不幸溺亡。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：这一切发生在 20 世纪 60 至 70 年代，当时包括美国在内的许多地区都经历着文化与社会的重大变革。这些变化如何影响了相关藏品进入大都会？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：20 世纪 60 年代（1960 年代），美国国内外的重大变化——民权运动以及非洲新兴民族国家步入成熟——使 Rockefeller 纳入非西方艺术的计划终于在 1969 年得以实现。除了时机的重要性之外，将一家已有的先驱机构并入大都会，也是一个复杂的过程。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从后勤角度看，这或许类似于近期公布的 Ronald Lauder 的 Neue Galerie 合并案。然而，Rockefeller 当年的计划不只是增添一家重要私人机构、引入大量艺术品；它从根本上重新界定了一家美国顶尖博物馆的使命。新展翼决定以 Michael Rockefeller 命名，以纪念他深入了解 Asmat 艺术的追求。在此后的 10 年里，原称原始艺术博物馆的员工、藏品、档案和图书馆陆续迁入如今的 MCR 展翼所在区域。", "links": [{"text": "merger", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/art-world/met-museum-neue-galerie-merger-2773237"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Installation-view-of-the-Arts-of-Africa-Galleries_Bruce-Schwarz-33-1024x621.jpg", "alt": "非洲艺术展厅的展陈一景。", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "非洲艺术展厅一景。摄影：Bruce Schwarz。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：你们刚在去年完成展翼全面翻修和重新构想后重新开放。过去几十年里，相关地区艺术研究当然已有巨大进展。但为何要全面翻修？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：展翼施工的大部分时间里，Nelson Rockefeller 正担任副总统。他在展翼于 1982 年完工前去世。展翼拥有 4 万平方英尺展厅，位于当时大都会园区最南端；最初那套先进展陈几乎没有涉及展出作品原本的文化语境。展翼大获成功，相关研究因此在学术界蓬勃发展，博物馆藏品也拓展至新的方向。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种变化日益明显：常设藏品展厅与我们策展团队为临时展览开展的开创性研究之间，差距不断扩大。对我而言，当务之急是让那些深化藏品所代表的主要传统认知、并与作品来源地区的机构及同行建立有意义合作的特别项目，也体现在常设展厅中。十多年前，我因此提议启动 Rockefeller 展翼更新工程。我的策展团队希望重新构想博物馆的这一部分，并以三组独立的世界艺术概览重新呈现常设藏品：既以历史为基础，也纳入多层次内容，并通过与来源国专家交流而丰富起来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这也体现在我们增添的数字内容中，目的是提供更丰富的背景信息。其中包括一组三部音频导览，呈现一批来自巴马科至波哥大等地、在艺术与人文学科领域颇具影响力的国际公共知识分子的观点。我们还邀请电影人 Sosena "Adam：美国博物馆与欧洲博物馆很不一样。艺术界的每种情况都各有特殊之处。例如，一些欧洲收藏是殖民势力搜集的作品构成的；美国博物馆则是由在公开市场上购买物件的收藏家建立。我想多数人不知道，欧洲第一次非洲艺术展是什么时候举办的。1920 年是非洲艺术首次在卢浮宫办展吗？当我得知这件事时，我觉得博物馆承认非洲抽象艺术和非洲艺术对当时当代艺术的影响，真是太好了。后来我才知道，那不过是一次殖民炫耀，目的是显示法国有多强大，拥有多少异国珍宝。大英博物馆也是如此。“大英帝国的太阳永不落下”，他们收集其他地方的文化象征、纪念物和珍宝，就是为了彰显自己的强大。一方面，这些行为是错误的；另一方面，若非如此，或许这些东西都无法保存下来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：我认为我们常常把这些机构的性质过度简化。一方面，它们是某些历史时期的遗产，那时人们挪用、盗窃和掠夺他人财物；另一方面，它们也属于人们拓展交流网络、努力认识自身之外世界的历史时期。那是欧洲以外传统的学术好奇心和研究的开端。今天我们之所以如此了解过去，很大程度上是因为 18、19 世纪的收藏。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们不想过度美化启蒙运动时期，但世界的确因此变得更小。这一点也体现在各种不断丰富和扩大的博物馆收藏上。博物馆是鲜活的机构，反映着社会的热情。1870 年，纽约人决定创建一所可以通过汇集藏品了解广阔世界的机构，并由此建立了今天的大都会；这令人惊叹。它体现了人们对熟悉范围之外世界的好奇，以及亲身体验的愿望。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种初衷非常值得尊重，不该被轻易搁置。真正重要的是让人们意识到，世界比他们眼前所见复杂得多。在我们生活的这个时代，这一点尤其重要：我们身处多元文化社会，也生活在全球相互依存的世界中。理解多样性以及构成我们身份的众多传统，既重要又不可替代。博物馆有责任启发我们去了解并尊重那些看似陌生、相对难以接近的文化。理想情况下，它们也能成为起点，鼓励我们走出馆舍，亲自前往文化源头。", "translated": true}]

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa LaGamma is the Ceil and Michael E. Pulitzer Curator of the Department of the Arts of Africa, Oceania, and the Americas at the Metropolitan Museum of Art . As a lifelong collector of African art myself, I have seen many of her shows and also served on her committee for years, more recently as chairman. The history of these objects is a fascinating one, from the painful colonial era to the struggle to have this art broadly accepted in the art world. Few people realize that it wasn’t until the ’80s that the Met exhibited these artworks, and before that, many saw them as little more than artifacts. This field is currently the subject of ongoing debate regarding the politics of restitution and the complex realities of repatriation. On our return from Parcours du Monde , the classic African and Oceanic art fair in Paris, last month, and not long after the one-year anniversary of the $70 million rebuild of the entire wing, it felt timely to explore a few topics in the zeitgeist."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "The best of Artnet News in your inbox."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sign up for our daily newsletter."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "The best of Artnet News in your inbox. Sign up for our daily newsletter. Please enter a valid email address Signup failed. Please try again later. Thank you! You have successfully subscribed to Artnet News."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: What is the Michael C. Rockefeller Wing? Can you explain the Met’s relationship to classic African, Oceanic, and Ancient American art?"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "The best of Artnet News in your inbox."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sign up for our daily newsletter."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "The best of Artnet News in your inbox. Sign up for our daily newsletter. Please enter a valid email address Signup failed. Please try again later. Thank you! You have successfully subscribed to Artnet News."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: Sure—it’s a fascinating story. In 1969 New York’s Governor Nelson Aldrich Rockefeller and the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced that a new wing of the museum would be built in order to accept the gift of his collection of sub-Saharan Africa, Oceania, and the Ancient Americas. The collection had until then been housed at his Museum for Primitive Art."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This development fundamentally redefined the mission of the Met, which was then, as it is today, one of America’s leading museums. The move established that suddenly artistic traditions of three-quarters of the world, previously relegated to natural history museums, were to be recognized shoulder to shoulder with the then pinnacle of art history—the Old Masters of Western European art. Overnight the Met’s identity became that of a global institution whose aspiration was to represent all cultures."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: It was a pretty radical move at the time—a major shift that changed the way we in the West see art from these huge regions of the world, and had a big impact on collectors, galleries, and museums by expanding notions of what is considered fine art. But people might not realize that the Met wasn’t on board with it at first."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: That’s right—that transformation led by Rockefeller was a hard-fought one. His enthusiasm for non-Western art was not originally shared by the Metropolitan, so actually in 1954 he established his own private institution across from the Museum of Modern Art. He was being advised by the leading specialists in what were then very young branches of art history, as he sought to assemble a survey of the major traditions absent from the Met."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/TWO-PANEL-SPLIT-WITH-BACKGROUND-2-1024x819.png", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa LaGamma and Adam Lindemann. Photos: The Met and the author"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: Here’s this politician from one of the wealthiest families in the U.S., as close to American royalty as we get, and he’s asking for these objects, which were considered ethnographic material from what was then the farthest reaches of the world, to be recognized as fine art. What drove this passion of his?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: In 1930, the year Nelson graduated from Dartmouth he was made a Met trustee. The son of John D. and Abby Rockefeller, his mother had instilled in him an awareness of the important role that African and Ancient American art had played in the transformation of 20th-century art. As an internationalist and a statesman, in the years that followed he embraced learning about less familiar parts of the world through their artistic traditions. This led to his conviction that “all people have art.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nelson’s son, Michael, shared his father’s passion for that mission and majored in anthropology at Harvard. He was deeply and personally inspired by the cultures and art of the Pacific and pursued new avenues of inquiry into artistic practice during his travels there. We have incredibly striking Asmat sculptures he researched and collected in southwest New Guinea on view in the wing. In 1961, during his second trip to research, collect, and document the works of artists in Papua New Guinea he was in a small craft at the mouth of the Betsj River that ran out of gas and was drifting into the Arafura Sea. In attempt to swim to shore he tragically drowned."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: And this is all happening in the ’60s and ’70s, when so much of the world, including the U.S., was undergoing major shifts in culture and society. How did that play into these collections coming to the Met?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: Major developments at home and abroad over the course of the 1960s relating to Civil Rights and the coming of age of new nation states across Africa were such that by 1969, Rockefeller’s campaign to incorporate non-Western art within the Met finally succeeded. In addition to the significance of the timing, the process of absorbing an existing pioneering institution into the Met was a complex one."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "On a logistical level it might be considered comparable to the recent announcement of Ronald Lauder’s Neue Galerie merger . The prior Rockefeller development, however, was not simply the addition of a major private institution and epic infusion of art but one that fundamentally redefined the mission of one of America’s leading museums. It was decided that the new Met Wing would be named for Michael Rockefeller’s quest to deepen his understanding of Asmat art and over the next decade, the staff, collection, archives, and library of what had been known as the Museum of Primitive Art was transferred into the footprint of what is today the MCR Wing.", "links": [{"text": "merger", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/art-world/met-museum-neue-galerie-merger-2773237"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Installation-view-of-the-Arts-of-Africa-Galleries_Bruce-Schwarz-33-1024x621.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Installation view of the Arts of Africa Galleries. Photo: Bruce Schwarz"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: And now you’ve just last year reopened the wing after a complete renovation and rethinking of it. Of course, scholarship on art from these regions has evolved dramatically over the last few decades. But why the full renovation?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: For much of the time that the wing was under construction, Nelson Rockefeller was vice president. He died before its completion in 1982. Encompassing 40,000 square feet of galleries at what was then the southernmost frontier of the Met campus, its inaugural state-of-the-art display made minimal reference to the original cultural contexts of the works featured. Its success was such that their study blossomed in the academy and the museum’s collection expanded in new directions."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This was increasingly evident in a growing contrast between the permanent collection galleries and the groundbreaking research that we directed toward temporary exhibitions organized by the Met’s curators. It was a priority for me that those special projects that advanced deeper understanding of major traditions represented in our collection and that developed meaningful partnerships with institutions and colleagues in the regions of the world from which the works originated be reflected in the permanent collection galleries. This led me to propose a capital project to renew the Rockefeller Wing over a decade ago. A priority for my curatorial team was to reenvision our section of the museum and reintroduce the permanent collection within three independent surveys of world art that were at once grounded in history and many layers of content enriched by engagement with experts in source countries."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This is reflected in an infusion of digital content we developed to afford greater context that includes a series of three audio guides highlighting the perspectives of an international cohort of leading public intellectuals in the arts and humanities based in centers ranging from Bamako to Bogota. We also hired filmmaker Sosena Solomon to document interviews and landmarks at a dozen sites across sub-Saharan Africa featured in a series of critically acclaimed short documentaries that widen the lens on major cultural centers relevant to deeper engagement with the decontextualized works on display. That project has created all kinds of new bridges between the Met and regional partners some of which have led to signing of new memoranda of understanding, and we have followed up with a series of workshops held at museums from Gaborone to Zanzibar in which we screen the films with regional audiences.", "links": [{"text": "series", "url": "https://www.metmuseum.org/perspectives/series/africa-cultural-landmarks"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Another important dimension of this reset is that we have leveraged the adjacencies of neighboring sections of the museum to be more meaningful. For example, the interface of the Africa galleries and those devoted to European Renaissance sculpture and decorative arts highlights works created along the coast of West Africa from the 15th century for the earliest European traders. Completed at the end of May 2025, the reinvigorated MCR Wing has shifted from its original design as a museum within a museum to a major crossroads of the museum that is at once physically and intellectually illuminated and in dialogue with adjacent galleries of Greek and Roman, European sculpture and decorative arts, and modern and contemporary art."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Horse-head_Yoruba-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A horse head by a Yoruba artist from the 12th century–15th century on loan to the Met from the Nigerian National Commission for Museums. Photo: Met"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: Alisa, how long have you worked at the Metropolitan Museum?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: I have been at the museum since I was a graduate student some 31 years ago. For the last 12 of those I’ve overseen the Michael C. Rockefeller Wing and its team of specialists that I recruited to care for the three areas of the world covered by its collections. Prior to that I was simply a senior African art specialist."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: You were born in Africa. Tell me how that shaped your interest in studying African art?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: My father was an American diplomat who spent his career in both Africa and Europe. He had a deep love for the many places he worked in across sub-Saharan Africa and I was born in Lubumbashi in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and spent formative years in Zambia, Côte d’Ivoire, and Togo. My family was living in Senegal, Nigeria, and South Africa when I was in college and graduate school, the period I was myself increasingly turning my focus to art history and African art."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: We recently attended the annual African and Oceanic Art Fair in Paris called Parcours du Monde (“Trip Around the World”) along with a group of friends of the Met. While there we saw all the dealers and went to both the Louvre’s Cinq Continents wing and the Quai Branly Museum for world art. I thought the most interesting and provocative part of the trip was when we went to Brussels to the Royal Museum for Central Africa at Tervuren. I’ve been enjoying African art since my late 20s, and I’ve read about Belgium’s violent colonial history in King Leopold’s Ghost by Adam Hochschild. Still, only then did it strike me that we’re in 2026, and they’re still sitting on thousands of objects, things taken or stolen by King Leopold II’s privateers when it was the “Congo Free State.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: Tervuren is a unique vestige of the European colonial presence in Africa and one of its darkest chapters. It is an institution that was essentially created as a showcase for the wealth and rich natural resources of the vast territory of Central Africa to which King Leopold of the Belgians had laid claim."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: In what year was this?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: This was in the late 1800s, 1898 following the temporary colonial exhibition featured at the 1897 Brussels International Exposition. It was a branch of Leopold’s propaganda. It’s not, and was never conceived of, as an art museum. It was really an institution that showcased the minerals, the woods, the wildlife, the sheer wealth of its resources. The artifacts at Tervuren reflect decades and decades of Belgian presence in that region. Many of them were things that Belgians brought back with them, after their tours of duty and then either sold to Tervuren or transferred as gifts. There were all kinds of people coming back from the Congo. You had missionaries as well as individuals who had been part of military campaigns. Some were just pure administrators, so it’s an assemblage of artifacts that reflect the Belgian presence there over an extended period of time and the result of different interactions between Belgians and residents of this region of Central Africa. Many were very violent and brutal, some of them were more benign, but it’s an especially traumatic past. Joseph Conrad was witness to the early years of the Congo Free State and he channeled his observations in the powerful critique of European colonialism that is Heart of Darkness ."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Commemorative-portrait_Edo-812x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ùhúnmwèlaò (commemorative portrait) by Ìgùn Ẹ́rọ̀nwwọ̀n (brass-casting guild), Edo peoples, ca. 16th century on loan to the Met from the Nigerian National Commission for Museums. Photo: The Met"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: We were looking at that amazing Kongo power figure with all those ribbons on it and that gripping face. It’s an incredible masterpiece, with a story. The military privateer Alexandre Delcommune attacked chief Ne Kuko over tariffs owed when goods were coming through their regions. The dispute was about the amount charged for passage. The people’s magical fetish was confiscated. Ne Kuko wanted it back. Delcommune refused to give it back, and eventually it ends up at Tervuren. He had seized their idol, but why did he give it to Tervuren? Why didn’t he just keep it?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: He was an unregulated tradesman taking the law into his own hands in response to tariffs that were going to be introduced and levied against him. He was outraged by that and he wanted to throw his weight around. Having spent time in the region, understanding the efficacy of that object and that it had a very important psychological role in the arbitration and adjudication of cases, his seizure of it was the ultimate way of diminishing the authority of local officials. I can’t imagine that somebody like that cared about holding on to the work. It was the removal that counted as far as he was concerned."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One of the ironies of an institution like Tervuren is that we have these stories, very detailed histories of the role specific works performed in their original communities. We know a lot about the identity of this sculpture before it was removed and that in and of itself is an incredibly important piece of historical documentation. This work which is such an incredible tour de force visually is also the materialization of a conflict. The Tervuren collection can teach us so many lessons as a result of this. These are very, very precious records that shouldn’t sit in obscurity. It really should be material that is more widely accessible, and that gives us a deeper understanding of what unfolded historically."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: And that raises the obvious question: What happens now? What should museums do with these collections?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: That is precisely where provenance research and sustained dialogue with colleagues and communities connected to these works become so important. At the Met, that research has long been embedded in our curatorial practice, with specialist expertise in the field developed over more than 25 years. There isn’t necessarily a single answer that applies to every object or every collection. Belgium has passed legislation concerning existing state collections and is in active discussions with the Democratic Republic of the Congo around cultural heritage and restitution that raise larger questions about access, conservation, scholarship and where works can be most meaningfully encountered. What is essential is that these histories are researched and made transparent, and that the institutions and communities most closely connected to the material are part of determining what comes next."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Queen-Mother_Edo-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Iyọ́bà (queen mother) figure by Ìgùn Ẹ́rọ̀nwwọ̀n (brass-casting guild), Edo peoples, ca. 18th century, on loan to the Met from the Nigerian National Commission for Museums. Photo: The Met"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: Simply saying “send everything back” doesn’t capture the complexity nor the realities. You’re talking about an enormous country, different communities, different histories and thousands of individual objects."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: Those questions need to be worked through collaboratively rather than answered abstractly. In doing so we should not lose sight of the importance of the works themselves as cultural achievements to be respected and honored as cultural achievements."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And in a way, that brings us back to what we were talking about with the Rockefeller Wing. Museums inherited ways of collecting, categorizing and presenting works that were products of particular moments in history. Our responsibility now is to examine those histories openly, to deepen the scholarship, to deepen the presentation of the significance of specific works, and to strengthen relationships with colleagues and communities in the places where these works originated. The museum shouldn’t obscure complexity. It should help people understand it."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: There’s a real effort now to reckon with the histories of these objects and, where appropriate, to return them. My view on all these things and more is that we can’t wind back the clock—we have to find a way forward. Where do we go from here?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: We all need to come up with imaginative solutions moving forward. This month we announced a three-way agreement in which an American philanthropist who has been a longtime supporter of African art at the Met is transferring her legal title to three historical masterpieces created in what is today Nigeria to its National Commission of Museums and Monuments, which is in turn loaning the works to the Met for at least 25 years so they may be studied and experienced here in New York City. These are now on view in the Rockefeller Wing, and this fall we’re looking forward to hopefully welcoming back the director general of the NCMM, Olugbile Holloway, who joined us for the opening of the wing last year and has been a steadfast partner in this work together.", "links": [{"text": "three-way agreement", "url": "https://www.metmuseum.org/press-releases/ncmm-landmark-agreement"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Objects have circulated, and people have circulated to define the world that we live in today. Since the end of the 19th century when these objects were traded or removed from their places of origin, the world has fundamentally changed by diasporas. Our communities are highly cosmopolitan and comprised of people from all over. And so, our institutions also reflect that. There are many historically tragic events that may be a part of the path of works of art. We shouldn’t shy away from those stories. We’re not going to reverse what happened, but we can help people understand what unfolded. In my experience, communities we have had the opportunity to represent are enormously proud of their participation. Telling those stories should heighten our sensitivity to wrongs that were done and should equip us to be more compassionate and committed to not perpetuating further damage. Museums can be places where you just go to look at beautiful things, but they should also be places where you learn about dimensions of human history that you might not be exposed to in the classroom as part of your traditional education. They’re a portal to other dimensions of how interconnected we all are, both in the past and in the present."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Asmat-artists_Body-Mask.-Mid-20th-century-661x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Body mask by Asmat artist(s), mid-20th century. Photo: The Met"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: How about the famous Benin bronzes. Andrea Emelife is the curator of the new Museum of West African Art in Nigeria. Many of the Benin bronzes were taken by the British army in 1897 in what is called the “Punitive Expedition.” The museum sought to get many of them back to Nigeria and built a museum for them as well as other Art. When international museums started sending back certain works, the Oba (king) of Benin appeared and sought ownership of the works. Given his family’s ancestral ownership of the objects, it becomes even more complicated to unwind the situation. What’s the fallout of that Benin story and what happens now?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: Benin art is one of the world’s great art traditions. Those works were produced in parallel to works that were created in Europe during the Renaissance. They were created by artists who had a mastery of the same technology as Donatello, Brunelleschi, Ghiberti, and Cellini. They tell a story that you cannot tell with other traditions from sub-Saharan Africa because, given that they were composed of durable materials of cast metal and carved ivory, we have exemplars of creations from this tradition going back to the 14th century, which is not the case for much of the rest of the sub-continent. For African American cultural historians like Alain Locke and W.E.B. Du Bois, an awakening to the existence of Benin art was critical to their understanding of what defined their identity, and to their writing about an African heritage."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We have very important holdings of that material because, during the late 1950s through 1960s, Nelson Rockefeller wanted to put together a collection of masterpieces. He bought the works that are now icons of the Met’s African art collection on the art market—from art dealers and at auctions. These were works that had circulated over the past generations."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: Yes, but the Met gave back a few, I recall."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: In 2021, the Met voluntarily returned two Benin works from the collection to Nigeria and helped facilitate the return of a third work from an outside collector, after our collaborative research determined that the Met did not (or could not) have proper title. And that effort led to a real blossoming of partnership between the Met and Nigeria’s National Commission for Museums and Monuments. We have since entered into an ongoing collaboration outlined in a memorandum of understanding that now includes the long-term project to facilitate the digitization and cataloguing of the NCMM’s collections together with a Nigerian team. And the new loan agreement I mentioned earlier builds on this foundation in a really powerful way."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: Klaus Perls, Calder’s dealer, gave a lot of these works to the Met. Where did he get them from?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: Yes, the majority of the works in our collection from the Court of Benin were given by Klaus Perls. He was a major dealer of modern art who had immigrated to New York from Germany and his private passion was collecting art from the Kingdom of Benin. He gave his collection to the Metropolitan in 1991. At that time, the Metropolitan did provenance research, which is an area of research that has continued to advance significantly over the past few decades; exhibited the collection; toured it internationally; and published the works and their histories online."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The works in our collection are now displayed in our new wing, contextualized within our survey of major artistic movements and living traditions from across the subcontinent. The new presentation is grounded in contemporary research and exchanges with a network of experts at the Met and around the world, including, importantly, the voices and input of experts from Nigeria, which can all be read and heard by visitors right in the galleries alongside these works."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The day we opened the wing was the museum’s highest single-day attendance since before the pandemic. And the works are widely available not just to our more than six million yearly visitors, but also to an even larger number of people on our website and ultimately, they’re accessible to a global audience. When we reopened, we welcomed General Director Holloway and many partners and scholars from across the regions who we worked with on the display, and it was an incredibly powerful moment to celebrate culture, community, and collaboration. And we’ve also heard from many, many New Yorkers whose heritage this is who deeply appreciated seeing their culture celebrated here in New York City."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Chief-Omas_Drum-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Chief Omas, Drum, mid-20th century. Photo: The Met"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: There’s a built-in injustice because all these things are in museums, but if you go back to the country that actually created them, you can’t find them."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: Nigeria has had among the largest holdings of Benin art even before all this transfer of works in the last couple of years. It has enormous national collections. They have not been visible because of issues with the museum’s infrastructure."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A huge part of our work together with Nigeria has been around supporting their capacity needs. Five years ago, we had a heart to heart with our counterparts in Nigeria and we asked them what is it that they felt we could be most helpful with. They responded that they didn’t have a digital collection database. So, we’ve been investing in creating a pilot for one with them and beginning the process of photographic documentation accompanied with accession records—the goal will be for the tens of thousands of works of incomparable importance in their collection to become part of that database over time."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We have the responsibility to help by being true partners, supporting the training of museum professionals and engaging in meaningful exchanges. content.article_text:
Alisa LaGamma is the Ceil and Michael E. Pulitzer Curator of the Department of the Arts of Africa, Oceania, and the Americas at the Metropolitan Museum of Art . As a lifelong collector of African art myself, I have seen many of her shows and also served on her committee for years, more recently as chairman. The history of these objects is a fascinating one, from the painful colonial era to the struggle to have this art broadly accepted in the art world. Few people realize that it wasn’t until the ’80s that the Met exhibited these artworks, and before that, many saw them as little more than artifacts. This field is currently the subject of ongoing debate regarding the politics of restitution and the complex realities of repatriation. On our return from Parcours du Monde , the classic African and Oceanic art fair in Paris, last month, and not long after the one-year anniversary of the $70 million rebuild of the entire wing, it felt timely to explore a few topics in the zeitgeist.

Adam: What is the Michael C. Rockefeller Wing? Can you explain the Met’s relationship to classic African, Oceanic, and Ancient American art?

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.
