Alisa: Sure—it’s a fascinating story. In 1969 New York’s Governor Nelson Aldrich Rockefeller and the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced that a new wing of the museum would be built in order to accept the gift of his collection of sub-Saharan Africa, Oceania, and the Ancient Americas. The collection had until then been housed at his Museum for Primitive Art.

This development fundamentally redefined the mission of the Met, which was then, as it is today, one of America’s leading museums. The move established that suddenly artistic traditions of three-quarters of the world, previously relegated to natural history museums, were to be recognized shoulder to shoulder with the then pinnacle of art history—the Old Masters of Western European art. Overnight the Met’s identity became that of a global institution whose aspiration was to represent all cultures.

Adam: It was a pretty radical move at the time—a major shift that changed the way we in the West see art from these huge regions of the world, and had a big impact on collectors, galleries, and museums by expanding notions of what is considered fine art. But people might not realize that the Met wasn’t on board with it at first.

Alisa: That’s right—that transformation led by Rockefeller was a hard-fought one. His enthusiasm for non-Western art was not originally shared by the Metropolitan, so actually in 1954 he established his own private institution across from the Museum of Modern Art. He was being advised by the leading specialists in what were then very young branches of art history, as he sought to assemble a survey of the major traditions absent from the Met.

Alisa LaGamma and Adam Lindemann. Photos: The Met and the author

Adam: Here’s this politician from one of the wealthiest families in the U.S., as close to American royalty as we get, and he’s asking for these objects, which were considered ethnographic material from what was then the farthest reaches of the world, to be recognized as fine art. What drove this passion of his?

Alisa: In 1930, the year Nelson graduated from Dartmouth he was made a Met trustee. The son of John D. and Abby Rockefeller, his mother had instilled in him an awareness of the important role that African and Ancient American art had played in the transformation of 20th-century art. As an internationalist and a statesman, in the years that followed he embraced learning about less familiar parts of the world through their artistic traditions. This led to his conviction that “all people have art.”

Nelson’s son, Michael, shared his father’s passion for that mission and majored in anthropology at Harvard. He was deeply and personally inspired by the cultures and art of the Pacific and pursued new avenues of inquiry into artistic practice during his travels there. We have incredibly striking Asmat sculptures he researched and collected in southwest New Guinea on view in the wing. In 1961, during his second trip to research, collect, and document the works of artists in Papua New Guinea he was in a small craft at the mouth of the Betsj River that ran out of gas and was drifting into the Arafura Sea. In attempt to swim to shore he tragically drowned.

Adam: And this is all happening in the ’60s and ’70s, when so much of the world, including the U.S., was undergoing major shifts in culture and society. How did that play into these collections coming to the Met?

Alisa: Major developments at home and abroad over the course of the 1960s relating to Civil Rights and the coming of age of new nation states across Africa were such that by 1969, Rockefeller’s campaign to incorporate non-Western art within the Met finally succeeded. In addition to the significance of the timing, the process of absorbing an existing pioneering institution into the Met was a complex one.

On a logistical level it might be considered comparable to the recent announcement of Ronald Lauder’s Neue Galerie merger . The prior Rockefeller development, however, was not simply the addition of a major private institution and epic infusion of art but one that fundamentally redefined the mission of one of America’s leading museums. It was decided that the new Met Wing would be named for Michael Rockefeller’s quest to deepen his understanding of Asmat art and over the next decade, the staff, collection, archives, and library of what had been known as the Museum of Primitive Art was transferred into the footprint of what is today the MCR Wing.

Installation view of the Arts of Africa Galleries. Photo: Bruce Schwarz

Adam: And now you’ve just last year reopened the wing after a complete renovation and rethinking of it. Of course, scholarship on art from these regions has evolved dramatically over the last few decades. But why the full renovation?

Alisa: For much of the time that the wing was under construction, Nelson Rockefeller was vice president. He died before its completion in 1982. Encompassing 40,000 square feet of galleries at what was then the southernmost frontier of the Met campus, its inaugural state-of-the-art display made minimal reference to the original cultural contexts of the works featured. Its success was such that their study blossomed in the academy and the museum’s collection expanded in new directions.

This was increasingly evident in a growing contrast between the permanent collection galleries and the groundbreaking research that we directed toward temporary exhibitions organized by the Met’s curators. It was a priority for me that those special projects that advanced deeper understanding of major traditions represented in our collection and that developed meaningful partnerships with institutions and colleagues in the regions of the world from which the works originated be reflected in the permanent collection galleries. This led me to propose a capital project to renew the Rockefeller Wing over a decade ago. A priority for my curatorial team was to reenvision our section of the museum and reintroduce the permanent collection within three independent surveys of world art that were at once grounded in history and many layers of content enriched by engagement with experts in source countries.

This is reflected in an infusion of digital content we developed to afford greater context that includes a series of three audio guides highlighting the perspectives of an international cohort of leading public intellectuals in the arts and humanities based in centers ranging from Bamako to Bogota. We also hired filmmaker Sosena Solomon to document interviews and landmarks at a dozen sites across sub-Saharan Africa featured in a series of critically acclaimed short documentaries that widen the lens on major cultural centers relevant to deeper engagement with the decontextualized works on display. That project has created all kinds of new bridges between the Met and regional partners some of which have led to signing of new memoranda of understanding, and we have followed up with a series of workshops held at museums from Gaborone to Zanzibar in which we screen the films with regional audiences.

Another important dimension of this reset is that we have leveraged the adjacencies of neighboring sections of the museum to be more meaningful. For example, the interface of the Africa galleries and those devoted to European Renaissance sculpture and decorative arts highlights works created along the coast of West Africa from the 15th century for the earliest European traders. Completed at the end of May 2025, the reinvigorated MCR Wing has shifted from its original design as a museum within a museum to a major crossroads of the museum that is at once physically and intellectually illuminated and in dialogue with adjacent galleries of Greek and Roman, European sculpture and decorative arts, and modern and contemporary art.

A horse head by a Yoruba artist from the 12th century–15th century on loan to the Met from the Nigerian National Commission for Museums. Photo: Met

Adam: Alisa, how long have you worked at the Metropolitan Museum?

Alisa: I have been at the museum since I was a graduate student some 31 years ago. For the last 12 of those I’ve overseen the Michael C. Rockefeller Wing and its team of specialists that I recruited to care for the three areas of the world covered by its collections. Prior to that I was simply a senior African art specialist.

Adam: You were born in Africa. Tell me how that shaped your interest in studying African art?

Alisa: My father was an American diplomat who spent his career in both Africa and Europe. He had a deep love for the many places he worked in across sub-Saharan Africa and I was born in Lubumbashi in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and spent formative years in Zambia, Côte d’Ivoire, and Togo. My family was living in Senegal, Nigeria, and South Africa when I was in college and graduate school, the period I was myself increasingly turning my focus to art history and African art.

Adam: We recently attended the annual African and Oceanic Art Fair in Paris called Parcours du Monde (“Trip Around the World”) along with a group of friends of the Met. While there we saw all the dealers and went to both the Louvre’s Cinq Continents wing and the Quai Branly Museum for world art. I thought the most interesting and provocative part of the trip was when we went to Brussels to the Royal Museum for Central Africa at Tervuren. I’ve been enjoying African art since my late 20s, and I’ve read about Belgium’s violent colonial history in King Leopold’s Ghost by Adam Hochschild. Still, only then did it strike me that we’re in 2026, and they’re still sitting on thousands of objects, things taken or stolen by King Leopold II’s privateers when it was the “Congo Free State.”

Alisa: Tervuren is a unique vestige of the European colonial presence in Africa and one of its darkest chapters. It is an institution that was essentially created as a showcase for the wealth and rich natural resources of the vast territory of Central Africa to which King Leopold of the Belgians had laid claim.

Adam: In what year was this?

Alisa: This was in the late 1800s, 1898 following the temporary colonial exhibition featured at the 1897 Brussels International Exposition. It was a branch of Leopold’s propaganda. It’s not, and was never conceived of, as an art museum. It was really an institution that showcased the minerals, the woods, the wildlife, the sheer wealth of its resources. The artifacts at Tervuren reflect decades and decades of Belgian presence in that region. Many of them were things that Belgians brought back with them, after their tours of duty and then either sold to Tervuren or transferred as gifts. There were all kinds of people coming back from the Congo. You had missionaries as well as individuals who had been part of military campaigns. Some were just pure administrators, so it’s an assemblage of artifacts that reflect the Belgian presence there over an extended period of time and the result of different interactions between Belgians and residents of this region of Central Africa. Many were very violent and brutal, some of them were more benign, but it’s an especially traumatic past. Joseph Conrad was witness to the early years of the Congo Free State and he channeled his observations in the powerful critique of European colonialism that is Heart of Darkness .

Ùhúnmwèlaò (commemorative portrait) by Ìgùn Ẹ́rọ̀nwwọ̀n (brass-casting guild), Edo peoples, ca. 16th century on loan to the Met from the Nigerian National Commission for Museums. Photo: The Met

Adam: We were looking at that amazing Kongo power figure with all those ribbons on it and that gripping face. It’s an incredible masterpiece, with a story. The military privateer Alexandre Delcommune attacked chief Ne Kuko over tariffs owed when goods were coming through their regions. The dispute was about the amount charged for passage. The people’s magical fetish was confiscated. Ne Kuko wanted it back. Delcommune refused to give it back, and eventually it ends up at Tervuren. He had seized their idol, but why did he give it to Tervuren? Why didn’t he just keep it?

Alisa: He was an unregulated tradesman taking the law into his own hands in response to tariffs that were going to be introduced and levied against him. He was outraged by that and he wanted to throw his weight around. Having spent time in the region, understanding the efficacy of that object and that it had a very important psychological role in the arbitration and adjudication of cases, his seizure of it was the ultimate way of diminishing the authority of local officials. I can’t imagine that somebody like that cared about holding on to the work. It was the removal that counted as far as he was concerned.

One of the ironies of an institution like Tervuren is that we have these stories, very detailed histories of the role specific works performed in their original communities. We know a lot about the identity of this sculpture before it was removed and that in and of itself is an incredibly important piece of historical documentation. This work which is such an incredible tour de force visually is also the materialization of a conflict. The Tervuren collection can teach us so many lessons as a result of this. These are very, very precious records that shouldn’t sit in obscurity. It really should be material that is more widely accessible, and that gives us a deeper understanding of what unfolded historically.

Adam: And that raises the obvious question: What happens now? What should museums do with these collections?

Alisa: That is precisely where provenance research and sustained dialogue with colleagues and communities connected to these works become so important. At the Met, that research has long been embedded in our curatorial practice, with specialist expertise in the field developed over more than 25 years. There isn’t necessarily a single answer that applies to every object or every collection. Belgium has passed legislation concerning existing state collections and is in active discussions with the Democratic Republic of the Congo around cultural heritage and restitution that raise larger questions about access, conservation, scholarship and where works can be most meaningfully encountered. What is essential is that these histories are researched and made transparent, and that the institutions and communities most closely connected to the material are part of determining what comes next.

Iyọ́bà (queen mother) figure by Ìgùn Ẹ́rọ̀nwwọ̀n (brass-casting guild), Edo peoples, ca. 18th century, on loan to the Met from the Nigerian National Commission for Museums. Photo: The Met

Adam: Simply saying “send everything back” doesn’t capture the complexity nor the realities. You’re talking about an enormous country, different communities, different histories and thousands of individual objects.

Alisa: Those questions need to be worked through collaboratively rather than answered abstractly. In doing so we should not lose sight of the importance of the works themselves as cultural achievements to be respected and honored as cultural achievements.

And in a way, that brings us back to what we were talking about with the Rockefeller Wing. Museums inherited ways of collecting, categorizing and presenting works that were products of particular moments in history. Our responsibility now is to examine those histories openly, to deepen the scholarship, to deepen the presentation of the significance of specific works, and to strengthen relationships with colleagues and communities in the places where these works originated. The museum shouldn’t obscure complexity. It should help people understand it.

Adam: There’s a real effort now to reckon with the histories of these objects and, where appropriate, to return them. My view on all these things and more is that we can’t wind back the clock—we have to find a way forward. Where do we go from here?

Alisa: We all need to come up with imaginative solutions moving forward. This month we announced a three-way agreement in which an American philanthropist who has been a longtime supporter of African art at the Met is transferring her legal title to three historical masterpieces created in what is today Nigeria to its National Commission of Museums and Monuments, which is in turn loaning the works to the Met for at least 25 years so they may be studied and experienced here in New York City. These are now on view in the Rockefeller Wing, and this fall we’re looking forward to hopefully welcoming back the director general of the NCMM, Olugbile Holloway, who joined us for the opening of the wing last year and has been a steadfast partner in this work together.

Objects have circulated, and people have circulated to define the world that we live in today. Since the end of the 19th century when these objects were traded or removed from their places of origin, the world has fundamentally changed by diasporas. Our communities are highly cosmopolitan and comprised of people from all over. And so, our institutions also reflect that. There are many historically tragic events that may be a part of the path of works of art. We shouldn’t shy away from those stories. We’re not going to reverse what happened, but we can help people understand what unfolded. In my experience, communities we have had the opportunity to represent are enormously proud of their participation. Telling those stories should heighten our sensitivity to wrongs that were done and should equip us to be more compassionate and committed to not perpetuating further damage. Museums can be places where you just go to look at beautiful things, but they should also be places where you learn about dimensions of human history that you might not be exposed to in the classroom as part of your traditional education. They’re a portal to other dimensions of how interconnected we all are, both in the past and in the present.

Body mask by Asmat artist(s), mid-20th century. Photo: The Met

Adam: How about the famous Benin bronzes. Andrea Emelife is the curator of the new Museum of West African Art in Nigeria. Many of the Benin bronzes were taken by the British army in 1897 in what is called the “Punitive Expedition.” The museum sought to get many of them back to Nigeria and built a museum for them as well as other Art. When international museums started sending back certain works, the Oba (king) of Benin appeared and sought ownership of the works. Given his family’s ancestral ownership of the objects, it becomes even more complicated to unwind the situation. What’s the fallout of that Benin story and what happens now?

Alisa: Benin art is one of the world’s great art traditions. Those works were produced in parallel to works that were created in Europe during the Renaissance. They were created by artists who had a mastery of the same technology as Donatello, Brunelleschi, Ghiberti, and Cellini. They tell a story that you cannot tell with other traditions from sub-Saharan Africa because, given that they were composed of durable materials of cast metal and carved ivory, we have exemplars of creations from this tradition going back to the 14th century, which is not the case for much of the rest of the sub-continent. For African American cultural historians like Alain Locke and W.E.B. Du Bois, an awakening to the existence of Benin art was critical to their understanding of what defined their identity, and to their writing about an African heritage.

We have very important holdings of that material because, during the late 1950s through 1960s, Nelson Rockefeller wanted to put together a collection of masterpieces. He bought the works that are now icons of the Met’s African art collection on the art market—from art dealers and at auctions. These were works that had circulated over the past generations.

Adam: Yes, but the Met gave back a few, I recall.

Alisa: In 2021, the Met voluntarily returned two Benin works from the collection to Nigeria and helped facilitate the return of a third work from an outside collector, after our collaborative research determined that the Met did not (or could not) have proper title. And that effort led to a real blossoming of partnership between the Met and Nigeria’s National Commission for Museums and Monuments. We have since entered into an ongoing collaboration outlined in a memorandum of understanding that now includes the long-term project to facilitate the digitization and cataloguing of the NCMM’s collections together with a Nigerian team. And the new loan agreement I mentioned earlier builds on this foundation in a really powerful way.

Adam: Klaus Perls, Calder’s dealer, gave a lot of these works to the Met. Where did he get them from?

Alisa: Yes, the majority of the works in our collection from the Court of Benin were given by Klaus Perls. He was a major dealer of modern art who had immigrated to New York from Germany and his private passion was collecting art from the Kingdom of Benin. He gave his collection to the Metropolitan in 1991. At that time, the Metropolitan did provenance research, which is an area of research that has continued to advance significantly over the past few decades; exhibited the collection; toured it internationally; and published the works and their histories online.

The works in our collection are now displayed in our new wing, contextualized within our survey of major artistic movements and living traditions from across the subcontinent. The new presentation is grounded in contemporary research and exchanges with a network of experts at the Met and around the world, including, importantly, the voices and input of experts from Nigeria, which can all be read and heard by visitors right in the galleries alongside these works.

The day we opened the wing was the museum’s highest single-day attendance since before the pandemic. And the works are widely available not just to our more than six million yearly visitors, but also to an even larger number of people on our website and ultimately, they’re accessible to a global audience. When we reopened, we welcomed General Director Holloway and many partners and scholars from across the regions who we worked with on the display, and it was an incredibly powerful moment to celebrate culture, community, and collaboration. And we’ve also heard from many, many New Yorkers whose heritage this is who deeply appreciated seeing their culture celebrated here in New York City.

Chief Omas, Drum, mid-20th century. Photo: The Met

Adam: There’s a built-in injustice because all these things are in museums, but if you go back to the country that actually created them, you can’t find them.

Alisa: Nigeria has had among the largest holdings of Benin art even before all this transfer of works in the last couple of years. It has enormous national collections. They have not been visible because of issues with the museum’s infrastructure.

A huge part of our work together with Nigeria has been around supporting their capacity needs. Five years ago, we had a heart to heart with our counterparts in Nigeria and we asked them what is it that they felt we could be most helpful with. They responded that they didn’t have a digital collection database. So, we’ve been investing in creating a pilot for one with them and beginning the process of photographic documentation accompanied with accession records—the goal will be for the tens of thousands of works of incomparable importance in their collection to become part of that database over time.

We have the responsibility to help by being true partners, supporting the training of museum professionals and engaging in meaningful exchanges. For example, we host residencies in my department and periodically co-organize workshops with colleagues in institutions from Lagos to Gaborone and Dar es Salaam.

Adam: American museums are very different from European museums. Every situation in the art world is kind of a unique situation. For example, some of these European collections were built with works collected by the colonizing forces—unlike U.S. museums, which were built by collectors buying objects on the open market. I don’t think most people are aware when the first African show in Europe happened. Was 1920 the first time that African art had a show in the Louvre? When I learned this, I thought it was wonderful that the museum was acknowledging the influence of African abstraction and African art in the contemporary art of that time. I later found out this was just a colonial flex. This was to show how powerful France was, and that they possess all these exotic trophies. That’s the same with the British Museum. The sun never sets on the British Empire, and so for them to collect these cultural talismans, and monuments, and treasures from other places just showed how powerful they were. On the one hand, those actions are wrong, but on the other hand, perhaps if not for them, none of these things would have been preserved.

Alisa: I think we tend to oversimplify the nature of those institutions. On the one hand they are a legacy of periods in history when things were being appropriated, stolen, and looted. They’re also a part of the period in history when people are engaged in expanded networks of exchanges and trying to understand the world outside themselves. It’s the start of intellectual curiosity and scholarship concerning traditions outside of Europe, and we know so much today about what came before because of what was collected in the 18th and 19th centuries.

We don’t want to over glorify the Enlightenment period, but it is a fact that the world became a smaller place as a result. This is true with all kinds of museum collections that are diversifying and expanding. Museums are living institutions that reflect the passions of their societies. It’s incredible that in 1870 people in New York City decided to create an institution where they could learn about the world at large by assembling what is today the Metropolitan. It’s a reflection of people’s curiosity about the world outside of what they’re immediately familiar with, and their desire to experience it.

This is a very honorable intention that we shouldn’t just put to the side. It really is about sensitizing people to a more complicated world than the one that they’re immediately aware of. That’s an important thing, especially in the moment that we are living in, where we are a multicultural society in a globally interdependent world. It’s important and invaluable for us to understand diversity and the many traditions that define us. Museums have a responsibility to inspire us to learn about and respect cultures that appear to be foreign and relatively inaccessible to us. Ideally they are a springboard to venture beyond their walls and go to the source ourselves.

content.article_text:
In New York real estate , a good amenity can add serious dollars to the asking price: a private gym is nice, a rooftop pool even better. An original Keith Haring mural? That’ll tick the price up to $25 million.

A seven-bedroom loft containing a work the artist painted in 1979 has hit the market for $25 million, according to the New York Times . The catch? The mural is painted directly onto the building’s walls, ceiling, and structural supports, so the art literally comes with the listing (or vice versa). Related Articles Art Collector Beth Rudin DeWoody Lists Upper East Side Co-Op for $12 M. Jackson Pollock's Former West Village Loft Hits the Market for $1.99 M.

The 8,000-square-foot triplex occupies part of the American Thread Building at 260 West Broadway, a Renaissance Revival building completed in 1896. In addition to Haring’s black-and-white artwork, it has 28-foot ceilings, nine bathrooms, a screening room, a gym, and a sauna.

Haring painted the work in 1979, shortly after arriving in New York to study at the School of Visual Arts, which, at the time, used part of the building as a student exhibition space. Executed in a mixture of shoe polish and alcohol, the mural features the swirling, graphic forms and figures that would soon become hallmarks of his work.

The mural could easily have disappeared. After the school vacated the premises, the space was converted into a restaurant, and the mural was concealed behind wallboard. It remained hidden for decades before being uncovered in 2007 during renovations by previous owners.

As Tribeca Citizen reported, the discovery was first reported by New York magazine in 2008 . Architect Todd Ernst, who helped uncover the mural, compared the experience to discovering an Egyptian tomb. Remarkably, the water-soluble artwork had survived despite its proximity to a sprinkler pipe.

The apartment’s current owner, Adam Zoia, an executive in the recruiting industry, bought the apartment in 2021 and later undertook a two-year renovation. He told the Times that he recognized the unsigned mural immediately as a Haring. (The Keith Haring Foundation later authenticated the work, according to Zoia.)

During the renovation, Zoia installed a bar in front of the mural, partly to protect it from accidental damage. The artwork extends across an iron column, a beam, the ceiling, and the surrounding walls.

That presents an unusual problem for anyone hoping to put a price on it.

New York dealer Jenn Singer told the Times that the mural’s site-specific nature makes it nearly impossible to value separately from the property. Unlike a painting that can be removed, sold, and installed elsewhere, this Haring is effectively inseparable from the apartment. Zoia was less cautious about its potential value. Were it possible to remove the work, he said, it might be worth more than the apartment itself.

For now, the mural and the loft are being offered together through Ian Slater, Michael Koeneke, and Eduardo Martinez of Trove Partners at Compass.

content.article_text:
Peter Nagy , an artist who became a star of the East Village in 1980s New York before ascending as one of India’s leading art dealers in the 1990s, has died at 67. Nature Morte , the New Delhi–based gallery that he ran, said that he had battled a long illness in a statement posted to social media.

“He lived exactly as he chose: fearlessly, irreverently and wildly free,” the gallery wrote . “He had no patience for convention for its own sake, and endless patience for ideas, for artists and for the people he loved. He made the art world more daring, more generous and far more interesting.”

The arc of Nagy’s career was an unusual one. He fostered a generation of appropriation-minded artists based in New York and helped stake a claim for India’s importance to the international art world. And in his art, he found his own take on commodification and reproducibility, two notions frequently addressed by artists of his generation.

In his own practice, Nagy pondered heady subject matter related to the corporatization of art and transmission of ideas and images across the globe. His works of the 1980s borrowed corporate logos and pictures from art history textbooks, showing that everything and anything could be endlessly copied until it signified nothing much at all. These early pieces synced with the bitter mindset of the Pictures Generation of the late 1970s and early ’80s, whose artists took up appropriation as a means of testing authorship and ownership.

“People don’t have anything to express, except the trademark,” Nagy said in one interview from the early ’80s. “We’re being fed information all the time.”

Relying on his education in design, Nagy would often clip out images and collage them together, using a similar method enlisted to create paste-ups used in the creation of print media in the pre-Photoshop age. He excised elements of floor plans, art books, and advertisements, then mashed together. Often, he would then Xerox the collages, blowing them up in the process.

The works looked machine-made, even when they were not. “The irony is that they’re handmade paintings that look like they might be computer-derived,” he told ARTnews in 2020 amid a revival of interest in his art. “I was interested in the degradation of the image and the information the image contained. I also thought there was additional information to be gleaned from that degradation. I was really into this idea: making copies of copies and noticing how long the original information maintained its integrity the longer I continued.”

Nagy went on to exhibit his spare art during the mid-’80s with International with Monument Gallery, a New York space that brought early attention to Jeff Koons, Ashley Bickerton, and Peter Halley. Later, he showed with dealers Jay Gorney and Nicole Klagsbrun.

At the same time, Nagy was running Nature Morte, which he founded with Alan Belcher in the East Village in 1982. He initially ran the gallery out of an East 10th Street storefront that he and Belcher rented for $500 a month. “We had no fucking clue what we were doing, but it was small and it was easy,” Nagy said the 2020 ARTnews interview. And yet, the space would go on to make a substantive mark on 1980s New York.

Steven Parrino, an artist whose punkish paintings defiled the aesthetic purity of the modernist monochrome, had his first solo exhibition with Nature Morte in 1983, the same that Gretchen Bender, a video artist known for stealing televisual material from the airwaves, also made her debut there. Cady Noland, Louise Lawler, Sherrie Levine, Robert Gober, Richard Pettibone, and others of note also showed at Nature Morte early on before its closure in New York in 1988.

Nagy continued working as an artist in the years afterward, eventually shedding his austere black-and-white collage aesthetic to make colorful paintings and installations in the ’90s. And then, for a while, he stopped doing solo exhibitions altogether. There was a 23-year interval between his 1997 Nicole Klagsbrun show and his next New York solo show, which got considerably more notice: a 2020 Jeffrey Deitch exhibition staged in collaboration with Magenta Plains, which now represents Nagy.

At the same time, Nagy was putting down roots in India. In 1992, he relocated to New Delhi; he spent the next five years moving between that city and New York. In 1997, he formally opened Nature Morte in New Delhi.

As Nagy recalled, being an artist with any stake in the market was confusing for many observers. “I am conscious of being penalized for being a dealer: Artists aren’t supposed to be interested in the market (ha ha), and my choice is, apparently, seen by some as opportunistic and manipulative,” he wrote in Artforum in 1999 . He also added, “I prefer the combination of market, media, creativity, and personality that comes together in a gallery.”

Peter Nagy was born in 1959 in Bridgeport, Connecticut. He attended New York’s Parsons School of Design, studying communication design, art history, and theory; he graduated in 1981. During his time at Parsons, he began making works that he described as “large-scale, black-and-white drawings influenced by Futurism.”

He quickly ascended in the New York scene, exhibiting in the 1985 Whitney Biennial via the collective Group Material, whose installations often combined objects produced by others. That same group brought Nagy’s art to the 1987 edition of Documenta in Kassel, Germany.

Today, Nagy is best known as a dealer, with Nature Morte continuing to maintain operations in New Delhi and Mumbai. Its roster today includes giants of Indian art such as Vibha Galhotra, Subodh Gupta, Jitish Kallat, Bharti Kher, Mrinalini Mukherjee, Pushpamala N, and the Raqs Media Collective. Dayanita Singh and Vivan Sundaram also previously showed with Nature Morte. The gallery, a mainstay at fairs ranging from the Armory Show to Frieze, has previously made attempts to broaden its reach, formerly operating branches in Berlin and Calcutta.

Nagy viewed Nature Morte’s Indian iteration as a project born from the impulse toward globalism in the art world. But he also cautioned that such globalism had its downside.

Western curators, he said in a 2010 Art in America interview , “often approach Indian contemporary art with very little knowledge of India itself, so they tend to misinterpret or even ignore artists that may have great relevance to the Indian context but seemingly little to the international context. But, hey, cultural translation is one of the obvious pitfalls of the globalization of the contemporary art world.”

More recently, interest in Nagy’s art of the 1980s has grown, thanks in part to the 2020 Jeffrey Deitch show. “How amazing to discover that Nagy’s early output, which shows the artist’s penchant for mapping transformations wrought by expanded media, increased corporate power, and concentrated flows of capital, felt downright prescient today,” wrote critic Jan Avgikos in his Artforum review of that show. “Like Warhol, Nagy was practically clairvoyant in his observations about art and its commodification, the ballooning culture of the copy, and our ongoing anxieties about authenticity.”

content.article_text:
BondIt Media Capital , Buffalo 8 Distribution and Sandaled Kid Productions have partnered on a new slate of horror films.

The partnership will develop three commercial, high-concept horror films. BondIt will finance the slate, while Buffalo 8 will release the titles. Sandaled Kid Productions will focus on development and production of the projects.

“This partnership brings together companies with complementary strengths and a shared belief in bold, commercial genre filmmaking,” James Cullen Bressack, Sandaled Kid Productions founder, said in a statement. “We wanted to build a slate that feels fresh, marketable and genuinely scary, while giving each film the opportunity to stand out in a crowded marketplace.”

Related Stories

Prime 'Big Deal Days' 2026: What to Know About Amazon's October Prime Day Sale

Nicolas Cage Says He’s ‘Probably Not’ Working With Amazon Again After Refusing to Sign AI Waiver for ‘Spider-Noir,' Teases Joining 'True Detective'

The deal was negotiated by Bressack and Matthew Helderman, CEO and co-founder of BondIt and Buffalo 8. Bressack and Helderman will both serve as executive producers for the three films.

Popular on Variety

“James is a longtime collaborator with our teams at both BondIt and Buffalo 8 — and we’re excited for another adventure with him as we target the release of these films for 2027,” Helderman said in a statement. “This genre slate of original films reflects our continued expansion and focus on greenlighting new commercial projects for VOD audiences.”

Additional details, including titles, filmmakers and production schedules, have yet to be announced.

Helderman founded Buffalo 8 in 2010 as an independent media studio focused on production, post-production and distribution. BondIt launched in 2013 with a focus on the eliminating the strain in capital from deposits productions leave with guilds to ensure their members are paid in a timely manner.

Sandaled Kid launched in 2020 with a focus on micro- and mid-budget genre films, particularly action and horror. Bressack’s credits include “Darkness of Man,” “Hot Seat” and “Fortress.”

content.article_text:
Getty Images , a massive image licensing company with hundreds of millions of assets in its library, is filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy . According to The Hollywood Reporter , the company plans to undergo a restructuring process and emerge as a private company, with support from billionaire Charles Koch’s investment firm, by the end of the year. ( ARTnews and THR are both owned by Penske Media Corporation, which has had an exclusive global media partnership with Getty Images since the fall of 2022.)

The bankruptcy announcement on Monday follows a failed $3.7 billion merger between Getty Images and Shutterstock, a rival photo and video licensing marketplace, announced in January 2025. The goal at the time was to “combine in a merger of equals transaction, creating a premier visual content company.” The new company would be called Getty Images Holdings, Inc.; Getty Images’s chief executive Craig Peters would stay on as CEO of the new entity.

Instead, a year and half later, the deal was off , due to a regulatory roadblock in the UK that would force Getty Images Holdings, Inc., to sell off the editorial side of Shutterstock, which the board of Getty Images viewed as a nonstarter. At its earnings call in August, THR reported, Peters said that Getty Images had spent more than $100 million on the failed Shutterstock merger.

In the coming months, Getty Images plans to transition from a publicly traded company to a private one, with the help of some $500 million from Koch Equity Development, which has backed Getty since 2018. A Getty Images spokesperson told THR that the bankruptcy process would not involve layoffs, nor would the company’s operations, content partners, or vendors be impacted.
content.excerpt_original: In the coming months, Getty Images plans to transition from a publicly traded company to a private one.

content.article_text:
Art Review

Roy Lichtenstein Has Lost His Luster

He went from being a satirist of America’s ideals to a parody of himself, an artist content with other artists’ masterpieces.

Hyperallergic )

Roy Lichtenstein’s paintings stick in your mind. They are memorable and congenial. When I went to Roy Lichtenstein: Like New , the first major survey of his work in more than 30 years, at the Whitney Museum, I expected to be surprised by something new the curators dug up in their research into the sources of many of the more than 130 paintings, sculptures, drawings, and prints on view. I was not initially disappointed.

Throughout his life, Lichtenstein credited Hoyt Sherman, his teacher at Ohio State University, with teaching him how to see. Lichtenstein gave his first son the middle name “Hoyt” and, after becoming successful, endowed the Hoyt L. Sherman Studio Art Center at the university in the 1990s. Sherman developed an experimental program where students were shown objects briefly in a darkened room and asked to draw them, an experience that is the opposite of traditional life drawing classes. Near the beginning of the exhibition, there is a darkened room with a 15-minute video reenacting one of Sherman’s “Flash Labs.” Artist Alex Da Corte, also one of the curators of the show, acts as Sherman; he wears prosthetics, and playfully teaches the class. Hung on the wall, at different heights, are some of Lichtenstein’s works from the ‘60s.

Da Corte and his team also recreated four murals, including “Greene Street Mural” (1983), which is nearly 100 feet (~30.5 m) in length, and “Super Sunset Billboard” (1967) in the museum’s west-facing window, so museum visitors can time their visit and see two sunsets at once. I think these and other jokes muddied the waters of a famous artist widely celebrated for his charming, emotionally empty (or should I say repressed?) paintings drawn from comic strips, advertising, and paintings by other famous artists, including Pablo Picasso, Claude Monet, and Chinese classical masters such as Mi Youren. Perhaps they didn’t want us to think too long about what happens when charm loses its allure.

content.article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Narges Rashidi , who recently won the BAFTA for Leading Actress for her portrayal of Nazanin Zaghari Ratcliffe in BBC’s Prisoner 951 , has signed with TFC Management .

The series, directed by Phillipa Lowthorpe and also starring Joseph Fiennes, told the true story of Zaghari Ratfcliffe’s wrongful seven-year imprisonment in Iran and her husband’s subsequent fight for her release. In addition to the BAFTA, Narges also received two Royal Television Society Awards along with several other award nominations for her portrayal of Nazanin.

Narges is perhaps best known in the U.S. and the UK for her role as fearless mobster Lale in Gangs of London for Sky/AMC, which is heading into its fourth and final season in 2027. Narges also performs the majority of her own stunts across the series.

Related Stories

TFC Management Signs 'Going Dutch' Creator Joel Church-Cooper

Lucius Cary Joins TFC Management

Her breakthrough role was leading Babak Anvari’s 2016 acclaimed and award-winning Persian-language film Under the Shadow , which premiered at the Sundance Film Festival. For her performance, Narges received a nomination for Best Actress at the BIFAs, a well as the Breakthrough Actress award at the New York International Film Festival.

Watch on Deadline

Narges’ other credits include Netflix feature Havoc opposite Tom Hardy and indie feature Last Swim , which won at Berlinale 2025. Narges has a long list of German credits including series The Allegation , which won the Dior Grand Prize at Canneseries in 2021.

Founded in 2020 by David Stone and Ben Jacobson, TFC Management reps on-camera talents such as Dakota and Elle Fanning, Shira Haas, Lashana Lynch, JD Pardo, Dan Ings and Josh Hutcherson, as well as such creators, filmmakers, novelists and producers as Warren Littlefield, Brian Yorkey, Megan Park, Adam Reed, Akiva Goldsman, Courtney Lilly, Josh & Jonas Pate and Rebecca Serle.

TFC’s sister company, TFC Productions, most recently produced the Apple series Margo’s Got Money Troubles , created by David E. Kelley and starring Elle Fanning, which recently received eight Emmy nominations , including Outstanding Comedy Series.

Rashidi will continue to be repped by The Artists Partnership in all areas.

content.article_text:
Melissa Auf der Maur: A Bass and a Nikon

Bassist for Hole and later the Smashing Pumpkins, the Montreal-born musician brings more than two hundred photographs from the heart of the grunge years to Toronto. An intimate, searing archive of the last analogue decade.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Melissa Auf der Maur .

When she joined Hole in the summer of 1994, the bassist and photographer Melissa Auf der Maur had one unusual clause written into her contract. A roll of 35mm film was to be waiting for her backstage at every show. Billy Corgan, of the Smashing Pumpkins, had recommended her to Courtney Love. Their album Live Through This had hit stores four days after Kurt Cobain, Love’s husband and Nirvana’s founder, was found dead. Kristen Pfaff, whose place on bass she took, had died of an overdose. She was stepping into a band in mourning.

Born in Montreal in 1972, she had been taking photographs since the age of thirteen, and found behind the lens, and in the darkroom, a shelter for her shyness. At Concordia University, in her home city, her professor Raymonde April, a celebrated Quebec photographer, introduced her to Francesca Woodman, the American who made herself her own subject, her body dissolved by the long exposure, in rooms left to ruin.

Melissa Auf der Maur turned Hole down at first, meaning to begin a master’s in photography. Then she changed her mind. “I remember being on Canal Street and asking for the most durable point-and-shoot Nikon,” she told The New Yorker. “I knew I was on assignment.” Press photographers are allowed the first three songs from the pit and nothing more. Nobody was timing her. With a self-timer and a cable release, she caught herself mid-song. With the Smashing Pumpkins, she would go on to mount the camera on her amplifier.

The photographs in “My ’90s Rock Photographs” breathe the camaraderie of the road. The band poses at a dressing-room mirror, above a catering table strewn with paper cups and coffee pots. The flash bursts in the glass, and Courtney Love, in an ivory slip, stares the lens down. Elsewhere she pedals barefoot on a bicycle down an empty concrete corridor. Against the barriers, teenage girls with damp hair press together, all smiles. Thirty years have passed. And with them, a whole generation is looking back over Melissa Auf der Maur’s shoulder. generation is looking back over her shoulder.

“My ’90s Rock Photographs” runs through June 6, 2027, at the Art Gallery of Ontario , Toronto.

The book My ’90s Rock Photographs is published by DelMonico Books with the museum, 240 pages, $49.95.

content.article_text:
Peter Farrelly’s “ I Play Rocky ” has won the Audience Award in the Galas & Special Presentations category at the 2026 Vancouver International Film Festival ( VIFF ).

The film, which tells the underdog story behind Sylvester Stallone’s journey to make and star in “Rocky,” was among 10 titles selected by audiences as favorites across the festival’s programming sections — including international cinema, emerging filmmakers and Canadian features.

Related Stories

Prime 'Big Deal Days' 2026: What to Know About Amazon's October Prime Day Sale

Amazon's Bestselling Kids Tablet Is Less Than $90 Right Now -- Its Lowest Price Ever

Banchi Hanuse’s documentary “Ceremony, ” which hadpreviously took home the the juried Tides Award, won in the Showcase category. It follows the disappearance of the ooligan, a culturally significant fish in Bella Coola, and the Nuxalk Nation’s efforts to understand its decline.

Popular on Variety

Former Pixar animator Louis Clichy’s “ Iron Boy , ” which explores themes of disability and agricultural modernization, took the Panorama prize. The Vanguard award went to Fernanda Salgado’s “ Ana, En Passant ,” an animated drama about a young Black woman returning to her late grandmother’s native town in Brazil.

Cody Lightning’s hockey drama “Smudge the Blades,” following a team of Indigenous youth in Northern Alberta, earned the Northern Lights award.

Other category winners include Faraz Shariat’s “Prosecution” (Focus on New German Cinema: Extreme Tension), Asmahan Bkerat’s “Concrete Land” (Insights), Otilia Portillo Padua’s “Daughters of the Forest” (Spectrum), Rebecca Tansley’s “Tenor: My Name Is Parti” (Portraits), and Marco Nguyen and Nicolas Athané’s “ Jim Queen” (Altered States).

The 45 th Vancouver International Film Festival ran Oct. 1-11 and included 162 features and 91 short films, representing 76 countries.

content.article_text:
The first look at Greta Gerwig ’s vision for Narnia has been revealed.

Today, Netflix is giving a first look at her vision for CS Lewis ’s magical world in the trailer for The Magician’s Nephew, the first chronological book in the beloved series.

With the soundtrack of Led Zeppelin’s Stairway to Heaven, the trailer opens with magician Andrew Ketterley ( Daniel Craig ) intoning that “sometimes one story is the beginning to all the others”, as he gives a group of kids a magic ring that will transport them to strange and wonderful lands.

Elsewhere, the trailer gives a first look at many locations and characters familiar to fans, including Jadis (Emma Mackey, the future White Witch) and Aslan, the mythical lion voiced by Meryl Streep .

The Magician’s Nephew tells the story of two children in Edwardian England named Digory and Polly (newcomers David McKenna and Beatrice Campbell) who chance upon the Wood Between Worlds, a realm with many portals to different dimensions. There, they witness the birth of Narnia.

In a trailer premiere event in New York this morning, Gerwig spoke of her longtime passion for CS Lewis’s series. “I don’t remember a time I didn’t know the books,” she said, per Variety . “I wouldn’t be who I am without these books.”

The film, which is Gerwig’s first since her $1bn-grossing megahit Barbie , will open for an eight-week theatrical window on 12 February before it streams on Netflix starting 2 April, in the studio’s first global theatrical release.

“I told Ted [Sarandos, CEO of Netflix] I only know how to make movies for the big screen,” Gerwig said. “He said: ‘Make the movie for the biggest screen and trust the process.’”

The director added that she petitioned Led Zeppelin’s Robert Plant and Jimmy Page for permission to use Stairway to Heaven in the trailer.

“I talked to them about a lot of the themes of the film,” Gerwig said, as reported by Rolling Stone . “They saw the heart and the story and the drama in it.”

“It’s an epic song,” she added. “It’s about the two paths of good and evil … It is a spiritual quest and a spiritual journey. So to me, this was a song that made sense to introduce the film to the world.”

content.article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Elsinore and La Bola Negra collected key awards for the audience favorite and jury pick for top narrative feature, respectively at the just-concluded 34th edition of the Hamptons Film Festival .

Audiences who attended 205 screenings of the fest’s 140-plus features and shorts from October 2-12 selected La Bola Negra as Best Narrative Feature. The film, directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, is Spain’s official submission for the Best International Feature Film category at the upcoming Oscars. It emerged from the Toronto Film Festival with heat after winning the TIFF People’s Choice award , often an Oscar bellwether.

Related Stories

‘La Bola Negra’ Review: Spain’s Javier Calvo And Javier Ambrossi Capture Hearts With Their Unashamedly Romantic Decades-Spanning Drama – Cannes Film Festival

‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Heartbreakingly Great As AIDS-Stricken Star Determined To Play ‘Hamlet’ – Telluride Film Festival

Another hopeful with a presence at the Hamptons is Elsinore , which made its East Coast premiere at the event. Directed by Simon Stone, the film starring Andrew Scott won the international people’s choice award at Toronto, along with prizes at other festivals in recent weeks.

Watch on Deadline

Because of its timing in between larger fall festivals and the surge of campaign season later in the year, the Hamptons has built a reputation as a fest of note. It doesn’t hurt that it takes place near the beaches of Long Island’s East End about 90 miles from New York City, long a vacation destination and a place to see and be seen.

NAZA , which has drawn packed screenings and ovations but also protests and controversy for its documentary portrait of Israeli military attacks on Palestinian communities, also collected an award. The film, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, received the Victor Rabinowitz & Joanne Grant Award for Social Justice. The film recognizes a film that exemplifies the values of peace, equality, global justice and civil liberties.

Burgundy , directed by Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw, captured HIFF’s documentary audience award.

La Bola Negra was described in a statement by HIFF Narrative Competition jury members Cara Cusumano, Jeremy O. Harris and David Rooney as a “triptych of queer desire, queer memory and queer resistance weaves together an epic story using revisionist history and builds to an emotional climax that rips to the core.”

The narrative jury also gave a Special Mention to The Guest , which is directed by Mads Mengel.

Best Documentary Feature honors went to If Pigeons Turned to Gold . Documentary Competition Jury members Carlos A. Gutiérrez, Mark Obenhaus and Sky Sitney called it “a bold, deeply personal story of the filmmaker’s own family struggles with addiction. It is told with provocative rawness and inventiveness.”

Other HIFF honors included the Junior Jury Award, from a panel of East Hampton High School students, given to Mouse ; the Artemis Rising Foundation Raise the Vibration Award for Social Impact, to The Drug in Our Pocket and A Song for the Snow Lion ; the Peter Macgregor-Scott Memorial Award, to Laser-Gato ; the Sherzum Award, for films tackling LGBTQ+ people, issues and concerns, to What Will I Become? and Welcome to Paris ; the Brizzolara Family Foundation Award for Films of Conflict & Resolution to The Choice ; the Suffolk County Next Exposure Grant to Barbizon ; and the Zelda Penzel “Giving Voice to the Voiceless” Award, to Wild Inside .

Ben’Imana and The Drug in Our Pocket won the documentary and narrative categories, respectively, of the New York Women in Film & Television’s awards for excellence.

content.article_text:
The only individual ever actually charged in the fatal 1996 shooting of Tupac Shakur was sentenced Tuesday to 40 years to life in prison.

Convicted of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon on August 31, Duane “Keff D” Davis was in court in Las Vegas today to learn his fate from Judge Carli Kierny.

Related Stories

Sky, Propagate & Passion Going Inside Tupac Shakur Trial

All Eyez On Guilty: Tupac Trial Jury Reaches Verdict In ‘Poetic Justice’ Star’s 1996 Drive-By Shooting Death

“You don’t get to take a man from his family,” the judge told Davis in announcing his sentence. Acknowledging how long it has taken for justice to be served in the death of the hip hop icon, she added: “You don’t get to take his very life, his whole future, from him… especially when that man is Tupac Shakur.”

Even with his bragging of involvement in Shakur’s murder in his memoir Compton Street Legend , to the cops, on TV and elsewhere over the years, Davis has insisted since his 2023 arrest that he was not guilty. In fact, the ex-gang leader has said he wasn’t even in Sin City that September night more than 30 years ago. Prosecutors claimed Davis acted out of revenge for Shakur and his crew previously beating on Orlando Anderson, Davis’ nephew.

Watch on Deadline

As he did when found guilty earlier this year, Davis today said, “I’m appealing this case for sure.”

In the aftermath of a September 7, 1996 Mike Tyson fight at Vegas’ MGM Grand, and at the height of the West Coast/East Coast rap beef, Shakur was shot by two rounds in the chest, one in the arm and one in the thigh, while in a car. Death Row Records boss Suge Knight was in a black BMW with Shakur when a mysterious a white Cadillac appeared and gunfire began. Knight lived, but the son of Black Panther activist Afeni Shakur died at the hospital six days later.

Like the subsequent death of Christopher “ Notorious B.I.G. ” Wallace in March 1997, what happened to Shakur and who was responsible for his demise remained an open case. Over the decades, as Shakur’s stature grew and evolved, there were flare-ups of media interest and theories but no conclusions or arrests.

The arrest and trial this year of Davis seemed to have ended a lot of that speculation.

Although Davis earlier in the hearing disputed not being allowed time served due to an incident with another inmate, he was silent today when Kierny delivered his sentence.

Before that, Tupac’s sister Sekyiwa Shakur addressed the court Tuesday on the personal and cultural loss resulting from the ‘California Love’ rapper’s death. Through Shakur’s remarks, Davis was seen rolling his eyes and making other reactions to her words. The Shakur sister asked Judge Kierny to give Davis the maximum time possible behind bars. It was a request reiterated in the Nevada courtroom by Shakur’s stepbrother Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur too.

Already a legend by the time of his death and a movie star to boot, Shakur has been the posthumous subject of the likes of USA Network’s 2018 series Unsolved: The Murders of Tupac and Biggie Smalls , the 2017 doc Who Shot Biggie and Tupac? , the 2017 biopic All Eyez on Me from Summit, Morgan Creek, Program Pictures and Codeblack Films over the years.

Like the endless stream of remixes and unreleased tracks, there was also Nick Broomfield ’s 2002 feature-length documentary Biggie & Tupac ; FX’s Emmy-nominated series Dear Mama: The Saga of Afeni and Tupac Shakur , which premiered in 2023; and the Oscar-nominated 2003 film Tupac: Resurrection .

Dead at 25, Tupac would have been 55 if he were alive today.

content.article_text:
Trump Administration

Utah Groups Sue Trump Administration Over Nine Mile Canyon Construction Project

The environmental organizations filed a suit against the Bureau of Land Management for approving the project that endangers centuries-old Indigenous petroglyphs.

Hyperallergic )

Months after the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) approved a road expansion proposal to expedite oil tanker truck transit through Utah's Nine Mile Canyon, three environmentalist groups have joined forces on a lawsuit to stop the project from progressing. The filing parties claim that the Duchesne County proposal will inevitably damage various Indigenous petroglyphs , historic structures, and the habitats of threatened wildlife species.

The Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance (SUWA), the Nine Mile Canyon Coalition (NMCC), and the Center for Biological Diversity (CBD) jointly filed the complaint on October 6, alleging that the Trump administration deliberately obscured and sidestepped the approval process and rejected the public's requested involvement in the decision.

The three organizations accused the BLM of failing to analyze and disclose the potential impacts of revising the existing roadway and the projected traffic increase on a cultural, environmental, and historic level. The complaint notes that the federal agency did not consult the United States Fish and Wildlife Service regarding foreseeable impacts on endangered and threatened wildlife species — including the Mexican spotted owl — and was in violation of multiple preservation and land use acts through its procedural omissions.

The BLM declined to comment on the matter, citing pending litigation.

content.article_text:
Don’t worry, Tom Cruise, you’re in great company among iconic films that bombed at the box office, only to eventually find their audience as cult classics.

Cruise’s latest film, Digger , written and directed by Alejandro G. Iñárritu, hasn’t quite drawn the theater crowds expected for an epic about the world’s most powerful man embarking on a frantic mission to prove he’s humanity’s savior before his own disaster destroys everything.

Despite a stacked cast featuring Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg, and Jesse Plemons, the reported $125 million epic opened to just $8 million domestically and $20 million worldwide. At a current worldwide total of $35 million, it’s fair to say the box office wasn’t quite saved.

Still, box office bumps are hardly unprecedented for eventual classics. While many high-profile stumbles never recover, history shows that some go on to recoup and vastly exceed their original investments. The 1975 midnight phenomenon, The Rocky Horror Picture Show , starring Tim Curry, famously overcame an initial theatrical flop to gross over $120 million since it’s release, against a $1.2 million budget.

Similarly, the Coen brothers’ The Big Lebowski struggled to find its footing during its initial run before turning its $15 million budget into a profitable $48.3 million worldwide victory.

Take a look back at a few other major theatrical misfires that went on to become timeless cult classics.

content.article_text:
Mia Goth did not post a selfie of herself to Instagram wearing a shirt that read “MY EX IS MY BIGGEST FAN” just days after news broke about her filing for divorce from Shia LaBeouf — and she has slammed Meta for allowing the AI-altered image to circulate.

The image posted on Thursday by “miagoth_,” complete with a blue verified checkmark on the account, circulated throughout multiple news outlets as though it were a genuine post from Goth two days after her divorce filing. But a spokesperson for Goth, Christine Tripicchio, said in a statement to The Verge it could not have been genuine because, well, Goth does not have any social media accounts. Instead, Goth’s team has filed multiple complaints with Instagram over the account’s repeated posting of “counterfeit, AI images” of the actress.

Related Stories

'The Housewife' Review: Naomi Watts Anchors a Watchable but Underpowered True Story of Hidden Nazism in Suburban Queens

'Ancestors' Review: An Exquisite Éanna Hardwicke Carries a Queer Elegy for a Lost Generation

“The fact that this fan account meets Instagram’s criteria to qualify for a ‘blue check’ is disconcerting on a fundamental level,” Tripicchio said in the statement. “Beyond that, it is incomprehensible that Instagram evidently prioritizes the dissemination of forged and manipulated images over the protection and integrity of a public figure’s likeness.”

Popular on Variety

A Meta spokesperson said in a statement the account was “removed for impersonating a public figure.” Tripicchio did not respond to an immediate request for comment.

The “miagoth_” account was labeled as a fan account, but its inclusion of a blue checkmark and its roughly 1 million follower count run the risk of confusing fans about the account’s veracity. While Meta does not ban AI-generated depictions of real people — instead, it labels content modified using AI as such, while also noting if a profile is an “AI-generated profile” — the account appears to have been taken down as of Tuesday afternoon.

It comes as several Hollywood figures, including Scarlett Johansson, Cate Blanchett and Steven Soderbergh, have condemned deepfakes brought on by the age of AI. Blanchett cofounded the nonprofit Human Consent Foundation to help people register how AI models can — or cannot — scrape their likenesses in an effort to combat such spoofs.

content.title_original: Chanel Culture Fund and Cindy Sherman Collaborate on Arts & Culture Magazine Ahead of Hauser & Wirth Exhibition
content.editorial_title_zh: 香奈儿文化基金与辛迪·舍曼合作推出艺术与文化杂志，配合豪瑟沃斯展览
content.editorial_excerpt_zh: 这位艺术家身披并裹着香奈儿未经缝制的面料和档案藏布料。
content.editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "香奈儿文化基金推出《艺术与文化杂志》第二卷。该杂志首卷于 2025 年夏季发行。新一卷将于 10 月 23 日上架，恰逢巴黎巴塞尔艺术展举行；艺术家辛迪·舍曼身着全套香奈儿粗花呢服饰登上封面。", "links": [{"text": "Chanel Culture Fund", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/chanel-culture-fund/"}, {"text": "Cindy Sherman", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/cindy-sherman/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这本 300 页的杂志将在 22 个国家的 33 家精选独立书店和杂志店免费发放，地点从香港的 ACO Books、墨西哥城的 Casa Bosques，到伦敦的 Rococo News & Magazines 和巴黎的 7L。杂志收录了 Patti Smith 亲笔书写的原创歌词；普利策奖得主、剧作家 Lynn Nottage 与伦敦国家剧院院长 Indhu Rubasingham 将探讨故事如何转化为舞台作品；作家 Andrew Durbin 则撰文回望 Peggy Guggenheim 的生平与遗产。她也是英国皇家艺术研究院一场展览的主题人物，该展览将于 11 月 21 日开幕。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/chanel-cindy-sherman-magazine.jpg?w=400", "alt": "辛迪·舍曼香奈儿艺术与文化杂志", "caption": "辛迪·舍曼登上香奈儿《艺术与文化杂志》封面。香奈儿文化基金惠允。", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“香奈儿文化基金工作的核心，是悉心呵护思想、艺术家，以及创造新事物这一不可替代的行动。《艺术与文化杂志》留下了这种实践的印记。第 2 卷封面人物没有谁比辛迪·舍曼更合适；五十年来，她一直探究身份的建构，以及女性掌握自我角色的力量。”香奈儿艺术、文化与遗产事务总裁 Yana Peel 说。“在她的摄影作品中，她以赋权和关怀的方式呈现现代女性，以及她不断成为自己的自由。因此，舍曼从 Gabrielle Chanel 和我们创始人的珍贵档案中为她的最新系列汲取灵感，也就不足为奇了。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这本杂志也将在豪瑟沃斯位于伦敦的展览空间发放；辛迪·舍曼的“Fabric Matrons”系列摄影作品正在那里展出。", "translated": true}]

content.article_text:
Chanel Culture Fund is back with the second volume of its Arts & Culture Magazine, the inaugural edition of which launched in the summer of 2025. Its new edition, which hits shelves on October 23, coinciding with Art Basel Paris, artist Cindy Sherman graces the cover in full Chanel tweed.

The 300-page magazine will be available free of charge at 33 select independent bookstores and magazine shops in 22 countries, from ACO Books in Hong Kong and Casa Bosques in Mexico City to Rococo News & Magazines in London and 7L in Paris. Inside the pages, there are original, handwritten lyrics by Patti Smith; Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright Lynn Nottage and London’s National Theatre director Indhu Rubasingham discuss how storytelling translates to the stage and writer Andrew Durbin muses on the life and legacy of Peggy Guggenheim, who is the subject of a Royal Academy exhibition opening on November 21.

“At the heart of the work of the Chanel Culture Fund is cultivating care for ideas, for artists, and for the irreplaceable act of making something new. Our Arts & Culture magazine is where that practice leaves its trace. There could be no one better to grace the cover of Vol. 2 than Cindy Sherman, who for five decades has examined the construction of identity and the power over personae that women hold,” said Yana Peel, president of arts, culture and heritage at Chanel. “In her photographs, she renders the modern woman – and her freedom of becoming – with empowerment and care. It’s no surprise then that Sherman found inspiration for her latest series in Gabrielle Chanel, and in the magical archives of our founder.”

The magazine will also be available at Hauser & Wirth’s London site, where photographs from Cindy Sherman’s “Fabric Matrons” series are on view.

content.title_original: Where the New York Art World Eats: A Guide by Artnet News and Caper
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "The art industry is loyal to its restaurants and watering holes. There is no real reason for dealers and collectors to return to the same hokey fondue spot in Basel every year, or the same mildewed dive bar on Miami Beach, but they do, driven perhaps by the promise of friendly faces and easy familiarity. There are memories in these places."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "The best of Artnet News in your inbox."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sign up for our daily newsletter."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "The best of Artnet News in your inbox.
