content.article_text:
La película de Christopher Nolan desembarcará en formato digital en noviembre, tras su exitoso paso por los cines. Su estreno en un servicio de streaming por suscripción todavía es una incógnita.

Después de conquistar al público en las salas, La Odisea se prepara para dar sus primeros pasos fuera de la pantalla grande. La nueva película de Christopher Nolan ya tiene fecha de lanzamiento para su alquiler y compra digital, aunque quienes esperen encontrarla en el catálogo de una plataforma de streaming deberán tener un poco más de paciencia.

La producción, protagonizada por Matt Damon , adapta el célebre poema épico de Homero y sigue las aventuras de Odiseo durante su largo regreso a Ítaca después de la Guerra de Troya. En el camino, el héroe deberá superar peligros, enfrentarse a criaturas mitológicas y sortear distintos obstáculos para volver a reunirse con su esposa Penélope, interpretada por Anne Hathaway, y su hijo Telémaco, a quien da vida Tom Holland.

El reparto se completa con figuras como Robert Pattinson , Zendaya , Charlize Theron , Lupita Nyong’o , Samantha Morton , Jon Bernthal y John Leguizamo , entre otros nombres destacados.

La película tendrá su lanzamiento digital el próximo 17 de noviembre de 2026 , una fecha que permitirá a los espectadores disfrutarla desde sus hogares. Además, la edición incluirá materiales especiales que revelarán detalles sobre el ambicioso proceso de producción encabezado por Nolan.

Los detalles detrás de la producción de La Odisea

Uno de los atractivos del lanzamiento será el contenido adicional, que ofrecerá más de 90 minutos de material sobre la realización de la película. La propuesta contempla 12 piezas especiales con imágenes del rodaje, entrevistas y detalles sobre las decisiones artísticas y técnicas que dieron forma a esta adaptación de la mitología griega.

Te puede interesar

¿Dónde fue filmada La Odisea de Christopher Nolan?

Christopher Nolan prohibió que usarán ésta prenda en el rodaje de ‘La Odisea’

Los espectadores podrán conocer cómo se construyeron los escenarios, cómo se diseñaron los vestuarios y de qué manera el equipo trasladó al cine algunos de los episodios más emblemáticos del relato de Homero. También habrá material dedicado a la recreación de Troya y a las locaciones utilizadas para representar Ítaca.

La producción combinó rodajes en diferentes lugares del mundo con escenarios construidos especialmente para la película. Entre ellos se encuentra un castillo del siglo XV situado en la isla italiana de Favignana, utilizado para representar el hogar al que intenta regresar el protagonista.

El apartado técnico también tendrá su espacio, con detalles sobre las secuencias de acción, los efectos visuales y especiales y el rodaje de las escenas marítimas. Además, Ludwig Göransson explicará el trabajo realizado para crear la banda sonora, en la que recurrió a instrumentos antiguos, voces y distintas técnicas musicales.

La edición física incorporará algunos extras exclusivos, como una entrevista del creador de contenido Reece Feldman a Nolan, un prólogo especial para IMAX y el videoclip de When I’m Home , interpretado por James Blake, Travis Scott y Göransson.

¿Cuándo se estrena La Odisea en HBO Max?

El primer paso para ver La Odisea en casa será el 17 de noviembre de 2026 , cuando estará disponible para alquiler y compra digital en plataformas como Apple TV y Prime Video . Ese mismo día también está previsto el lanzamiento de las ediciones físicas en 4K UHD, Blu-ray y DVD.

Sin embargo, esta fecha no corresponde a su estreno en streaming por suscripción . Por el momento, no se anunció cuándo podrá verse sin costo adicional dentro del catálogo de un servicio.

Una posibilidad es que la película siga una estrategia de distribución similar a la de Oppenheimer , otro de los grandes éxitos de Nolan, que tardó varios meses en incorporarse a una plataforma de streaming. La repercusión comercial de la nueva producción y su posible presencia en la temporada de premios podrían influir en los tiempos de lanzamiento.

En Latinoamérica, HBO Max aparece como una posible candidata para recibir la película, teniendo en cuenta los antecedentes de distribución de Universal Pictures en la región . De todos modos, todavía no se confirmó qué plataforma tendrá los derechos de exhibición por suscripción.

Mientras tanto, los fanáticos de Nolan podrán acceder a la película a través de las opciones de alquiler y compra digital desde noviembre. Para su llegada al streaming tradicional, habrá que esperar novedades oficiales.

Frieze Week is a long week, with some 309 exhibitors at Frieze London and Frieze Masters in Regent’s Park alone. But if you want an atmosphere reset and are still craving art without the sound of champagne popping or air kisses, London has much to offer this season with shows such as “Renoir and Love” at the National Gallery, Tate Britain’s divisive show “ The 90s: Art and Fashion ,” “Salman Toor: Someone Like You” at the Courtauld Gallery, and “ Tim Walker’s Fairyland: Love and Legends ” at the National Portrait Gallery.

London’s cultural scene, despite the country facing an upswing in right-wing politics, is still very much alive and kicking. Here are seven exhibitions that display its energy.

“Salman Toor: Someone Like You” at Courtauld Gallery Image Credit: Courtesy Courtauld Gallery Édouard Manet’s A Bar at the Folies-Bergère (1882) hangs in the Courtauld Gallery, where, next door, Pakistani American artist Salman Toor has his first European solo exhibition, “Salman Toor: Someone Like You.” In it is a work depicting a different kind of bar in The Bar on East 13th (2019), in which a man with pigtails and painted nails holds a lemon and raises it above a margarita glass. It’s one of the 19 paintings by Toor on display. There are also Phone Watcher (2022), in which a figure is dead behind the eyes with a smartphone in hand, and Fag Puddle with Carriers (2026), in which limp bodies lie on top of each other as others roam around. Until January 10, 2027.

“Renoir and Love” at National Gallery Image Credit: ©Musée d’Orsay, Dist. RMN-Grand Palais/Patrice Schmidt The works of Pierre-Auguste Renoir have made headlines recently, with several of the Impressionist artist’s paintings stolen from his home-turned-museum in southern France. (The thieves left behind two of the four paintings they tried to take; the remaining two have been recovered .) That suspenseful news story unfolded only a few weeks before the more joyous “Renoir and Love” opened at the National Gallery. The exhibition focuses on how the artist represented friendship, love, and everyday gestures across 40 paintings, from the crowded scenes in Bal au Moulin de la Galette (1876) to Danse à la campagne (1883), depicting his friend Paul-Auguste Lothe dancing with his future wife, Aline Charigot. Until January 31, 2027.

“Tim Walker’s Fairyland: Love and Legends” at National Portrait Gallery Image Credit: Courtesy the artist “Tim Walker’s Fairyland: Love and Legend,” at the National Portrait Gallery, is a who’s who of contemporary icons. The exhibition captures portraits of the Gay Liberation Front; there are also musicians such as Björk, Lady Gaga, Frank Ocean, and Chappell Roan, as well as a nude Harry Styles hugging himself. “The running theme throughout the exhibition is love—at its core this exhibition is about everyone’s right to love. It celebrates love in all its forms—the power of connection between friends, chosen families, couples and communities,” Susanna Brown, curator of the exhibition, told ARTnews recently. Walker began the project in 2020, after inspiration struck out on a walk in Highbury Fields, where he noticed a plaque tucked away on the side of a public building marking the spot where 50 earlier 150 people had gathered to protest for gay liberation. The date of the demonstration was November 27, 1970, the very same day he was born. This exhibition relays both queer history and Walker’s personal history. Until February 7, 2027.

“Robert Ryman: The Real Thing” at Barbican Art Gallery Image Credit: Courtesy Barbican Centre Before Robert Ryman turned to painting, he wanted to become a professional jazz saxophonist, and to make ends meet, he took up shifts as a security guard at New York’s Museum of Modern Art, which at the time was rapidly acquiring works by Mark Rothko, Willem de Kooning, and Jackson Pollock. The Barbican Art Gallery’s survey of Ryman’s work traces his beginnings to The Painting of the Mysterious Shadow (1966), which he created after leaving his day job at MoMA, and also includes such works as Surface Veil II (1971). The latter piece is situated in front of a bench for visitors to gather their thoughts as they gaze at Ryman’s white paint. Until February 28, 2027.

“Still Life, Then and Now” at Robilant Image Credit: Courtesy Robilant A bouquet of fresh and colorful flowers by Osias Beert the Elder, a basket of fruit by Bartolomeo Cavarozzi, a ram with its legs tied by Francisco de Zurbarán (another version was recently part of the artist’s show at the National Gallery), and a resting skull by Andy Warhol: These are among the works on show at Robilant, which is surveying the still life genre as it shifted between the 16th century and today. The gallery is also participating in Frieze Masters with a booth that holds John Singer Sargent’s Constantinople and Warhol’s portrait of Erich Marx, the German art collector and real estate developer. “We have all seen the renewed interest in Old Masters as the pendulum swings from speculative to secure, and as clients look to artists who have already shown they can hold their value,” gallery director Michele di Robilant told ARTnews . Until December 18.

“Es Devlin: Other Worlds” at Design Museum Image Credit: David Parry for the Design Museum The artist and set designer Es Delvin is a creator of worlds. (After all, she has three Emmy Awards, three Olivier Awards, and a Tony Award for production design, and has helped building sets for musicians such as Beyoncé, The Weeknd, and Adele.) In her exhibition at the Design Museum, she opens her library of work, from installations to films. She recreated her London studio and is now displaying a wall installation, titled Archive Unboxed , that combines the work she produced in her formative years in school, university and art college. The artist also partnered with Penguin Random House UK on a book installation titled Infinite Library . Exhibited at the end of the show, it includes books that will be donated to local charities. Until April 4, 2027.

“The 90s: Art and Fashion” at Tate Britain Image Credit: Courtesy Tate/Juergen Teller “ The 90s: Art and Fashion ” at Tate Britain has left art critics “dissatisfied” and “buzzing,” making it the type of exhibition you need to see for yourself. It’s a fresh and different perspective on the 1990s, and sure enough, there are works by Tracey Emin and Damien Hirst there. But the show also spotlights names not typically associated with the Young British Artists (also known as the YBAs), including Hamad Butt, Eileen Perrier, Yinka Shonibare, and Barbara Walker. Whether you walk away from the exhibition feeling empty or elated, you can let everyone know you went to the exhibition by getting one of the T-shirts that Sam Taylor-Johnson wears in her photograph Fuck, Suck, Spank, Wank (1993). You can guess what the T-shirt says. Until February 17, 2027.

content.article_text:
The Baltic Event Co-Production Market has revealed its 15 projects to be pitched Nov. 18-20 at Tallinn’s Black Nights Film Festival industry sidebar Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event.

Picked out of 110 submissions from 34 countries, the slate of pics in development looking for co-financing, distribution and sales spans 10 territories – Finland, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Ukraine, Poland, Slovakia and Spain.

Related Stories

Telly Awards Adds Microseries Competition Track, With Dozens of New Categories (EXCLUSIVE)

Raindance to Launch U.K.'s First Major Vertical Festival and Market (EXCLUSIVE)

Leading the charge are “La Korena” by Basque helmer Joana Moya, produced by Sirimiri Films, founded by Estibaliz Urresola , director of the Berlinale winner “ 20,000 Species of Bees ,” and the horror satire “Wild Love” helmed by Lithuanian Jonas Trukanas (“Pensive”) for high profile prodco Afterschool , behind the 2021 Venice Horizons winner “Pilgrims” and 2024 Locarno winner “ Drowning Dry .”

Popular on Variety

Other buzzy projects taking in the Ukrainian-German-Czech “ Family Squad ” from Ukraine’s largest animation studio Animagrad , credited for the hit “Mavka: The Forest Song”, and the Latvia-French-Polish coming-of age “In the Truth by Tomas Harjo, produced by pedigreed Latvian outfit VFS Films (“The Rossellinis,” “Immortal”).

“ La Koreana ” forms part of a spotlight on the Basque region from the Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF), while a dominating Baltic crop (6 out of 15 titles) is aimed at boost the region’s top talent and co-production opportunities of other attendees with one of Spain’s most vibrant production hubs over the last five years.

For the Baltic Event Co-Production Market’s co-managers Helen Räim and Kärt Väinola, focusing on the Baltics was “very natural” as PÖFF turns 30, the Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event is 25, and after the Oscar for “Flow,” the momentum on Baltic films shows no sign of waning. Not only was the Latvian doc “Ulya” selected at this year’s Cannes Film Festival (at Un Certain Regard), but so was “Vesna,” a co-production between Lithuania, France, Ukraine and Estonia, which was pitched at last year’s Baltic Event Co-Production Market and landed at Cannes’ Special Screenings.

Quizzed about common threads at this year’s lineup, Räin and Väinola cited belonging, love and growing up as “the strongest collective themes. “Heavier themes such violence, war and death also appear,” they said, “although often as secondary threads, approached through humor, satire and the search for oneself.”

“This year’s lineup shows filmmakers who are not afraid to face their own questions, doubts and worries about the world they live in and to dream of the world they hope for,” they added. The co-honchos also highlighted the substantial number of feature debuts (eight), often backed by “producers with strong track records at Venice, Berlin and Locarno,” and the strong slate of “imaginative stories for children and families, bringing fantasy and animation to the market.”

The 15 projects vying for the €20,000 ($22,300) Eurimages Co-Production Development Award will be judged by a panel of industry professionals including Eurimages’ Stefan Prohorov, Holly Daniel, director of the Red Sea Souk, and heavyweight Estonian producer Ivo Felt of Allfilm (“Tangerines,” “The Fencer”). A closer look at the Baltic Event Co-Production Market lineup:

“At Your Service” (Til þjónustu reiðubúinn,” Magnús Jónsson, Iceland, Estonia)

A dark comedy about a terminally ill artist who starts a euthanasia business after Iceland closes its nursing homes. From Icelandic producers Guðný Guðjónsdóttir and Sara Djeddou Baldursdóttir, also selected at Tallinn’s TV Beats showcase with the series “Kalmann.” The co-production with Estonia’s Munchhausen Films is backed by the Icelandic Film Centre, RÚV and Sambíóin.

“The Boy Who Loves the World” (“De jongen die van de wereld hield,” Steven Wouterlood , The Netherlands)

From the multi-awarded Dutch helmer of “ My Extraordinary Summer with Tess ,” and Int’l Emmy Kids winner “Anything Goes.” “Adapted from one of the most celebrated Dutch children’s books of recent years, [‘De jongen die van de wereld hield’], it’s an adventurous family film that dares to reflect on a polarized world, while leaving audiences with a deep sense of wonder and zest for life,” says Maiike Neve who produces with Joram Willink for Bind.

“Clusterfuck” (Läppä oli,” Juho-Pekka Tanskanen, Finland)

It’s a portrait of “youth and violence and how easily things can go sideways,” says producer Paria Eskandari of Danish Bear Productions. “At a time when young people are portrayed as dangerous or lost, the film explores how the lines between belonging, having fun and bullying can become blurred.” Co-produced with Finland’s Mohzi Films.

“Family Squad” (“Наша Файта,” Kostiantyn Fedorov, Ukraine, Germany, Czech Republic)

Pitched earlier at Cartoon Movie and Stuttgart’s Animation Production Days. Next feature from Animagrad and producer Anna Eliseeva, the team behind the animated hit “Mavka: The Forest Song,” which was released in 149 countries and grossed more than $25 million worldwide. Comedy drama in which a loser who dies by accident, is given a second chance in life, and sets off on a journey of self-discovery. Co-produced by Germany’s Telescope Animation and PFX, Czech Republic.

“Hide and Seek” (“Paslēpes,” Dace Puce, Latvia, Estonia, Sweden)

From the helmer of “The Pit,” Lübeck-Nordic Film Days top winner 2020, produced by Munchhausen Films, one of the Baltics leading servicing outlets. Thriller in which a Latvian mother’s life in Sweden unravels after she is accused of abusing her young daughter. “The project addresses themes that extend beyond Latvia: migration, belonging, adaptation, parental responsibility, children’s rights, and the challenges of navigating unfamiliar legal and social systems,” say producer Elīna Jozauska.

“In the Truth” (“Patiesībā,” Toms Harjo, Latvia)

Deeply personal pic from photographer, actor-turned filmmaker Toms Harjo, about his experience of growing up in a Jehovah Witness community. Produced by Latvia’s prominent doc and fiction outlet VFS Films, credited for “The Rossellinis,” Venice Critics Week closing film in 2020 and “Immortal,” best doc at Karlovy Vary 2019. “The Informatics Olympiad” (“Informatikos olimpiada,” Adas Burksaitis, Lithuania)

Estranged for years from his family, Domas has to take over his father’s job at school and prepare his niece for the informatics Olympiad. “Rooted in the specific world of provincial Lithuania and post-Soviet education, the film speaks universally about loneliness, addiction, burnout and the struggle to move beyond the identity imposed on us by others,” says Greta Akcijonaite from Magic Films.

“Lady Thatcher’s Feast” (“Uczta Pani Thatcher,” Marcin Kluczykowski, Poland)

From Polish prodco Telemark and producer Piotr Śmiechowski who won the Midpoint Series Award at last year’s TV Beats Forum in Tallinn for the comedy “We Are Still Here.” Set in 1996, we follow Maria, owner of a modest canteen, who is chosen to prepare a banquet for Margaret Thatcher. In this drama based on true events, “food is not simply part of the setting,” explains Śmiechowsk. “It becomes a way of expressing emotions, class differences, care, ambition and identity. The canteen itself becomes a microcosm of a society in transition.”

“La Koreana” (Joana Moya, Spain)

Feature debut from Basque director Joana Moya, produced by Sirimiri Films’ Estibaliz Urresola, director of the Berlinale winner “20,000 Species of Bees.” Set against a landscape shaped by iron mining, the film explores the relationship between nature, memory and human exploitation. Won the Ikusmira Berriak Prize at San Sebastian 2025.

“My 19-Year Old Granny” (“Moya 19-richna Babtsya,” Victoria Zadorska, Ukraine, Lithuania, Czech Republic)

Produced by Olena Yershova for Tato Film, in co-production with Lithuania’s Magic Films and the Czech Republic’s Breatless Films. Debut feature by fantasy author Victoria Zadorska, in which a retro dress teleports a schoolgirl to 1975 Soviet Ukraine, where she meets her hippie grandparents. “We want to connect three generations of women across two timelines and reveal what it truly costs to finally trust yourself,” says Yershova.

“My World Upside Down” (“Nikomu to nepoviem,” Daniel Rihák, Slovakia)

Feature debut by Rihák, whose short film “The Trip” was shortlisted for the BAFTA Student Film Awards. When Miško, a 12-year-old boy from a Slovakian village, discovers his brother is gay, he decides to save him “from hell.” But his plan backfires and Miško’s world turns upside down. Produced by What If Films.

“Shadows of Summer” (“Suve varjud,” Helen Takkin, Estonia)

“Shadows of Summer” tackles sensitive and deeply relevant issues of power dynamics, bullying, and co-dependency,” says producer Elisabeth Madisson of Nafta Films. “By intertwining a present-day participatory theater performance with events from 16 years earlier, the film gradually blurs the boundaries between past and present, reality and performance, bringing a fresh and distinctive cinematic approach to themes that are both universal and pressing today.”

“Summer of the Moth” (“Yöperhosen kesä,” Veera Lamminpää, Finland)

Produced by Petri Kemppinen of Good Hand Production. Story of a grumpy old elderly gardener and a magical time-traveling moth whose unexpected journey into the past helps them rediscover imagination, trust and hope. “Told through a rare mix of stop motion animation and live action, the film combines an appealing sense of humor with layered storytelling,” says Kemppinen.

“Wild Love” (“Laukine Meile,” Jonas Trukanas, Lithuania, Estonia)

From rising genre talent Trukanas whose breakthrough pic “Pensive” was bought by Cinedigm for their specialized platform Screambox. Produced by Afterschool, behind Lithuania’s Oscar hopefuls “Pilgrims,” and “Drowning Dry.” Co-produced by Estonia’s Tallifornia. “’Wild Love’ is a rare Baltic horror satire,” say producers Klementina Remeikaitė and Rūta Kiaupaitė. “Set on Saaremaa Island, it plays on the nostalgia for Robinsons, the 2000s reality hit that whole Baltic families watched, and sends it spiraling into a zombie outbreak, in which the reality show at the heart of the film reflects a world where our sense of what is real keeps shifting and truth slips into lies.” “Zona” (“Samosioły,” Bartosz Brzeziński, Poland, Lithuania, Estonia)

Directorial debut produced by Zizu Films. Intimate drama set in the Chernobyl exclusion zone, where a young Ukrainian deserter finds refuge with an elderly woman and forms an unlikely bond. “War trauma is explored through a fresh lens, combining an intimate character study with the haunting backdrop of the Chernobyl wilderness,” says Klaudia Pachuta who produces with Konrad Zagórski, and Karol Zagórski.

content.article_text:
Jonathan Davies’ article ( Abide with me: English choral music is a living part of our cultural heritage – we should cherish it, 7 October ) speaks beautifully to the contribution of English choral music to our living cultural heritage, highlighting the importance of cathedral choirs in particular, in giving children access to “world-class musical training, extraordinary cultural experiences and educational opportunities that might otherwise be beyond their reach”.

What he misses however, is just how under threat these bastions of England’s religious, cultural and spiritual heritage actually are.

Despite recent research from the Theos thinktank suggesting 74% of adults in England have visited a cathedral over the last three years, 80% of cathedrals in England are now in structural deficit. Several have recently reached crisis point, including those in Peterborough and St Davids . One in four cathedrals in England is now charging for entry, and even after significantly diversifying their income portfolios (including through controversial silent discos ), they continue to struggle.

More than 90% of visitors surveyed by Theos (including 94% of non-religious visitors) thought of cathedrals as a hub for community life, and the same number see them as a symbol of local identity and a way to connect with history and tradition. Despite their significant social and cultural contributions to communities, and being some of our oldest and most historically significant buildings (two are Unesco world heritage sites and many are almost 1,000 years old), cathedrals receive no secure state funding and limited contributions from central church authorities. Unlike museums and galleries offering free admission, cathedrals are also not subject to the same VAT exemptions on repairs or maintenance.

This has left many cathedrals crumbling, and their finances with them. Without cathedrals, English choral music would cease to exist. If more is not done to protect them, that reality could be closer than we think. Dr Coco Parkinson-Huggins Researcher , Theos

Such an inspiring tale of the transformative power of cinema ( The one change that worked: numb with grief, I sat in the dark, surrounded by strangers – and began to heal, 12 October ). Having lost my only sister, my father and my wife within a relatively short period, I can attest to the ability of this precious activity to distract, uplift and, well, simply rescue one from the deepest pit of despair. Cinema saves lives – that is absolutely clear to me. Geoffrey Meenan London

I was there at the other Battle of Hastings on 5 March 1966 ( Letters, 12 October ). I was 16 and went with my then boyfriend, who was at Leicester art college. I recall the sack costume and wildly rushing down a hill. That evening I ate spaghetti bolognese (English version) for the first time. My taste for Italian food lasted longer than the boyfriend. Elaine Fear Horsted Keynes, West Sussex

Emma Beddington is looking for autumnal glimmers ( 12 October ). She should join me in our morning bathroom at this time of year, when we have a rainbow on our toilet roll, as the low sun refracts through then reflects from the edge of the mirror opposite. Julia Leach Norwich

My library always sends me a “pre-overdue” notice a few days before the return date for books I’ve borrowed ( Letters, 12 October ). Surely my books are simply due? Lynne Scrimshaw London

Now I feel discriminated against. No one asked me which school I attended when I was at Teesside Polytechnic ( Letters, 11 October ). Keith Langton Kirkcudbright, Dumfries & Galloway

Warner Bros. isn’t the only Los Angeles institution getting absorbed into Skydance this month. The Bay Theatre in Pacific Palisades, which was formerly operated by Netflix and before that by Cinepolis, will be taken over by Paramount Pictures with San Diego’s The Lot handling operations. The opening is planned for later this year.

The Bay Theatre has been closed since the wildfires damaged much of the upscale Los Angeles community in January 2025. The five-screen multiplex is located in Rick Caruso’s Palisades Village shopping area, which reopened in August after extensive remediation and repairs due to the fires. The theater’s vintage-looking sign is a nod to the community’s historic Bay Theatre, which stood nearby on Sunset Boulevard until closing in 1978.

Caruso made the deal with Paramount to showcase first-run theatrical releases, classic films, events and special programming. The theater offers luxurious seating, state-of-the-art sound and projection, in-theater dining and signature cocktails.

Popular on Variety

“The theater will also serve as a dynamic entertainment destination that extends the theatrical experience beyond the screen, through experiential activations and immersive theatrical moments,” the companies said in a statement.

David Ellison , Chairman & CEO of Skydance, said in a statement, “Together with Caruso, we are proud to help bring the Bay back to life as a place for the Pacific Palisades community to gather around the shared experience of cinema. This theater has always meant more than movies alone – it’s woven into the fabric of this neighborhood, and helping restore it is a privilege. We’re inspired by the resilience of Pacific Palisades residents, and we’re honored to help support this community’s comeback.”

Caruso said, “Paramount is one of the world’s leading entertainment studios, with an extraordinary legacy of cinematic storytelling and, importantly, a deep commitment to the City of Los Angeles and to the future of the theatrical experience. Together, we see an opportunity to bring that to the Bay with the care, design and hospitality we’re known for, so that every visit feels special. The Bay has always been at the heart of the Palisades, and its return is one of the most meaningful signs yet that this community, following the reopening of the Palisades Village this summer, is coming back stronger than ever. David Ellison and I have a shared ambition to make it one of Los Angeles’ premier moviegoing destinations. I am grateful for David’s leadership and commitment to Los Angeles and the entertainment industry.”

content.article_text:
Salaud Morisset has boarded worldwide sales rights to “Our Way to You” (Ce qui nous mène à toi), the first feature from French-Moroccan filmmaker Khalil Cherti , and produced by Amaury Ovise of Kazak Productions.

While the film already won two awards after its world premiere at this year’s Angoulême Film Festival, it will begin its international tour with the Cairo Intl. Film Festival in November.

Related Stories

Raindance to Launch U.K.'s First Major Vertical Festival and Market (EXCLUSIVE)

Telly Awards Adds Microseries Competition Track, With Dozens of New Categories (EXCLUSIVE)

The film is distributed in France by Condor Distribution, hitting French theaters on Nov. 11.

Popular on Variety

The plot delves into Charlie and Hicham’s love story and desire to start a family, as they navigate through the struggle of infertility and assisted reproductive treatment. Over the course of three years, through hope and heartbreak, they will put their love and their bodies to the test.

The cast is led by César award-winning actress Nina Meurisse (“Souleymane’s Story,” 2024; “The Rapture,” 2023) as Charlie, Sofian Khammes (“My Brothers and I,” 2021; “The Big Hit,” 2019) as Hicham, and Jeanne Balibar, who won the Cesar for best actress in 2018 for “Barbara.”

Connection and relationships are recurring themes in Cherti’s work, whether he chooses to relate complicated family bonds (“Wherever Comes the Pain From,” 2013 – selected at Locarno and awarded at Clermont-Ferrand) or the deepness of love in the face of life challenges (“Je, d’un accident ou d’amour,” 2025 – selected at Tribeca and Clermont-Ferrand; “T’embrasser sur le miel,” 2021).

For his first feature film, the director says he wanted to capture one of the most important relationships in a person’s life, as in his opinion, simply being a couple is “an odyssey.”

Cherti added: “I made this film because there is something quietly moving about two people trying, together, through years of hardship, to reinvent themselves.”

Paul Jullien, head of sales at Salaud Morisset, said: “With ‘Our Way to You,’ Khalil Cherti explores the universal themes of parenthood, love and family with remarkable depth and sensitivity, turning an intimate story into something that resonates with us all.”

Amaury Ovise, producer, said the film “sensitively captures the joy and pain of a couple navigating the challenges of assisted reproduction. Charlie and Hicham embody that fragile part of ourselves whose story deserves to be told.”

content.article_text:
French giant Gaumont is launching a new 4K restoration of Louis Malle ‘s 1958 classic crime thriller “Elevator to the Gallows,” starring Jeanne Moreau .

The special edition is being released in celebration of this year’s 70th anniversary of the French New Wave, the upcoming 70th anniversary of the film in 2028 and, in the same year, the centenary of Moreau’s birth.

Released 1958, “Elevator to the Gallows” marked the directorial debut for the young Malle, who was 25 years old at the time.

Related Stories

Set in Paris over the course of a night, the film stars Moreau and Maurice Ronet as lovers who set out to murder her husband and his boss (played by Jean Wall), only for the plan to go awry. Distinguished by Miles Davis’ award-winning jazz score, the film established both Malle and Moreau as verifiable talents.

Popular on Variety

Another Gaumont classic, “Betty Blue,” Jean-Jacques Beineix’s iconic tale of amour fou run rampant, is making its long-awaited return to the big screen at this year’s Lumière Film Festival .

Originally released in 1986 as “37°2 le matin,” the award-winning erotic drama chronicles the doomed romance between Zorg (Jean-Hugues Anglade), a handyman and aspiring writer in his 30s, and the volatile, impulsive and fragile 19-year-old Betty (Béatrice Dalle).

The film is also one of this year’s highlights for Gaumont, which is presenting the new 4K master of the full 185-minute version — “a film that has been invisible in theaters in this version since 1991,” noted Jérôme Soulet, head of catalogue at Gaumont.

The 4K restoration of “Betty Blue” was carried out by Gaumont at the GP Archives laboratory.

The film screens this year as part of the Lumière Festival’s Big Films on the Big Screen sidebar that offers the opportunity to rediscover cinematic masterpieces in their intended format.

Soulet will also be on hand at the Lumière Festival’s International Classic Film Market in Lyon to present the company’s lineup of new releases at the annual Catalogue Holders’ Premiere Presentation on Wednesday.

content.article_text:
Taiwan is getting a dedicated national focus at the International Classic Film Market ( MIFC ), the industry arm of Lyon’s Lumière Festival, the first for a non-European country, according to the Taiwan Film and Audiovisual Institute (TFAI).

A new 4K restoration of Chen Kun-hou’s “ Osmanthus Alley ” leads the Taiwan in Focus program, which runs alongside this year’s guest country, Greece.

Related Stories

‘Sin Filtro’ Producer JK Media Producing First Original Microdramas Shot in the U.S. for TelevisaUnivision’s ViXMicrO (EXCLUSIVE)

Telly Awards Adds Microseries Competition Track, With Dozens of New Categories (EXCLUSIVE)

TFAI is using the showcase to seek international distribution and programming partners for the island’s restored classics. “Osmanthus Alley” made its world premiere at the festival on Oct. 12, with Chen and star Lu Hsiao-fen in attendance. TFAI says distributors it has previously worked with have expressed interest, with release terms and timing still under negotiation.

Adapted from Hsiao Li-hung’s novel, the film follows Thik-hông (Lu), an orphan who marries into a wealthy family, is widowed young and sees her son sent away to Japan, leaving her isolated behind the walls of the family estate. Simon Yam and Tuo Tsung-hua appear in guest roles. Lu won best actress at the 1987 Asia Pacific Film Festival, and the theme song, with lyrics by Wu Nien-jen, took the Golden Horse for best original film song.

Popular on Variety

The restoration also brings back the film’s original Taiwanese soundtrack. Chen insisted on shooting in Taiwanese, but state-run Central Motion Picture Corporation (CMPC) chose to release the film in Mandarin, in line with the government’s policy of promoting the language at the time. Chen eventually persuaded the studio to produce a Taiwanese version, but it played in only a limited number of theaters and gradually faded from view.

Its selection coincides with the 70th anniversary of Taiwanese-language cinema, which TFAI traces to 1956’s “Xue Pinggui yu Wang Baochuan.” An estimated 1,200 Taiwanese-language films were made between the 1960s and 1981, but only about 200 survive in TFAI’s collection. The restoration also anticipates TFAI’s 2027 focus on literary adaptations, while Chen’s lifetime achievement award at the 2023 Golden Horse Awards prompted renewed interest in his work.

Chen began as a cinematographer, winning a Golden Horse for “He Never Gives Up” (1978), and from 1979 worked closely with Hou Hsiao-hsien, the pair often trading roles behind the camera. Chen’s “Growing Up” won him the Golden Horse for best director in 1983.

TFAI restored “Osmanthus Alley” from its original 35mm negative, filling missing frames from an interpositive, with audio drawn from the 35mm Taiwanese sound negative. The source was generally in good condition, but mold spots and dense clusters of small white specks required careful treatment. Aggressive cleaning settings risked erasing image detail, so technicians used masks and adjusted processing settings before completing frame-by-frame manual repairs.

In line with FIAF’s code of ethics, Chen was repeatedly consulted. An intermediate version had more saturated, vibrant colors, but discussions with the director led to a more subdued final grade, closer to the original photography.

Tu Duu-chih, who handled the film’s original sound mix, returned to help restore the Taiwanese soundtrack from six primary audio reels. The team synchronized the material, repaired damaged sections and reduced noise through multiple passes using light processing settings.

The soundtrack holds another connection to Taiwanese cinema history. Cast members who did not speak Taiwanese were dubbed in post-production: co-star Lin Hsiu-ling voiced Lu’s dialogue, while Hou provided the voice for Tuo.

TFAI, which holds about 20,000 film titles, restores 10 to 12 films a year and has restored more than 100 since 2013. Physical deterioration prompts climate control and emergency digitization, but a full restoration depends on whether a film has “a clear purpose and an audience ready to experience it right now,” the institute says. Recent restorations include Tsai Ming-liang’s “Vive L’Amour,” which screened in Venice Classics in 2025, and “The Dull Ice Flower,” chosen by Taiwanese audiences in a public poll and selected for Cannes Classics this year. Taiwanese-language titles “Love Never Ceases” and “Zhang Di Seeks A-Zu” were restored for the anniversary.

Overseas, TFAI prioritizes in-person screenings to introduce lesser-known titles before pursuing distribution and streaming partnerships.

“We want audiences to discover Taiwan cinema beyond Taiwan New Cinema and see the many different facets of Taiwan,” TFAI tells Variety .

TFAI will also pitch its ongoing restoration of Yao Feng-pan’s “All in the Dim Cold Night” (1974) at MIFC’s Re>birth program on Oct. 15, seeking distributors and festival slots for the horror film. Often called Taiwan’s “King of Horror,” Yao built the film’s eerie atmosphere without modern visual effects, relying on practical techniques such as low-angle green lighting and burning straw on location.

Taiwan in Focus also includes a round table with TFAI chair Arthur Chu and programmer Howard Yang, a networking event and an exhibition of original Taiwanese film posters.

The institute hopes to build longer-term programming partnerships with international archives, giving restored Taiwanese films a life beyond their festival premieres. For “Osmanthus Alley,” the next step is securing overseas releases following its return to the screen.

content.article_text:
French police investigating the theft of two paintings by Pierre-Auguste Renoir from a museum on the French Riviera believe the suspects were preparing to rob another institution, the Fondation Maeght in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, prosecutors said Monday.

The investigation led to the recovery of the two paintings, valued together at around $4.6 million, and the arrest of six people last week. Four men have since been charged, including two who remain in pretrial detention, according to Le Figaro , citing Agence France -Presse. Related Articles Rare Cache of Ancient Roman Sculptures Discovered at Chartres Codex Azcatitlan Goes on View in Mexico City, as Culture Ministry Continues Centuries-Long Quest for Repatriation

The paintings, Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and Femme au puits ( Woman at the Well ), were stolen from the Musée Renoir in Cagnes-sur-Mer on September 8. At around 5:50 a.m., two men cut through a fence and broke a window to enter the museum, housed in the artist’s former home. Using a saber saw, they removed four paintings from the walls in approximately two minutes before an alarm sounded. They abandoned two of the works and fled with the other two.

A cover left behind by the thieves provided investigators with DNA evidence that led them to a 29-year-old man from the Var department who was already known to police. Investigators subsequently identified a second suspect, a 41-year-old man living in Corsica.

“We were very clearly dealing with the repetition of a criminal project,” Eric Antonetti, director of the Alpes-Maritimes judicial police, said at a press conference, according to Le Figaro . Fearing another burglary was imminent, investigators moved to arrest the suspects on October 7.

Police first planned to wait until they could recover the paintings before making arrests. But the investigation took an unexpected turn on October 3, when officers observed the younger suspect visiting the Fondation Maeght, a major modern art institution whose collection includes works by Joan Miró, Alberto Giacometti, and Marc Chagall.

Police also observed a meeting between the principal suspect and an art dealer described by investigators as having a history of working with known forgers. Nevertheless, authorities believe the original theft was opportunistic rather than commissioned.

“The preferred hypothesis is that there was no sponsor, a priori, of the theft,” Antonetti said.

The following day, investigators recovered the two Renoirs from a house in Clermont-l’Hérault, where they had been concealed behind a false wall constructed from bricks and plasterboard. The hiding place was disclosed by a third suspect during questioning.

Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said the paintings were in relatively good condition, although both sustained damage during the burglary. They have since been transferred to the Interdisciplinary Center for Heritage Conservation and Restoration in Marseille for examination under the supervision of the Musée d’Orsay. France’s Culture Ministry said the works would eventually return to the Musée Renoir.

The case comes as French museums face renewed scrutiny over security following a series of high-profile thefts, most notably the October 2025 robbery of the Louvre, in which thieves escaped with crown jewels valued at more than $100 million . Those jewels have yet to be recovered.

content.article_text:
Ava DuVernay’s timely and viscerally moving “ 14th ” leads this year’s Critics Choice Documentary Awards nominations with six, including best documentary feature. Close behind with five nominations apiece are Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s examination of Elizabeth Holmes, “ You Can See Everything ”; Gabriela Osio Vanden and Jack Weisman’s polar bear migration story, “Nuisance Bear”; David Greaves’ archival portrait of Black cultural history, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” and Pegah Ahangarani’s Iranian historical documentary, “Rehearsals for a Revolution.”

Related Stories

Telly Awards Adds Microseries Competition Track, With Dozens of New Categories (EXCLUSIVE)

‘Sin Filtro’ Producer JK Media Producing First Original Microdramas Shot in the U.S. for TelevisaUnivision’s ViXMicrO (EXCLUSIVE)

Netflix led all distributors with 17 nominations, nearly double the nine earned by runner-up Neon.

Popular on Variety

DuVernay, Fielder and Oppenheim are among the directing nominees, alongside Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor for “NAZA,” Felipe Bustos Sierra for “Everybody to Kenmure Street,” Ross McElwee for “Remake” and Orlando von Einsiedel for “The Cycle of Love,” the only directing nominee whose film did not land a documentary feature nom.

Now in its 11th year, the Critics Choice Documentary Awards will take place Nov. 8 at the Edison Ballroom in New York City, with television host and producer Ross Matthews serving as host. The awards celebrate excellence in nonfiction filmmaking.

The organization’s track record of predicting Oscar success has been mixed over the years. Its inaugural top prize winner, “O.J.: Made in America” (2016), went on to win the Academy Award for documentary feature. Since then, only three other top prize winners or nominees have crossed over to the Oscars: winner “Summer of Soul (…Or, When the Revolution Could Not Be Televised)” (2021) and nominees “Will & Harper” (2024) and last year’s “The Perfect Neighbor” (2025). All others failed to be nominated, or in some cases, not even make the preliminary shortlist (i.e., 2022’s “Good Night Oppy”).

As previously announced, Ron Howard will receive the Critics Choice Impact Award. Visionary filmmaker Jehane Noujaim will receive the CCA’s Pennebaker Award, presented by Chris Hegedus, Pennebaker’s widow and longtime collaborator. Named in honor of trailblazing documentarian D.A. Pennebaker, the award, formerly known as the Critics Choice Lifetime Achievement Award, recognizes filmmakers whose careers have made a profound and lasting contribution to documentary storytelling.

Feature-length documentaries, two-part documentaries and short-form documentaries are eligible for nomination if they were first released commercially in the U.S. between Jan. 1 and Dec. 31, 2026.

The full list of nominees are below.

Interview

Jonathan Nez on Indigenous Perseverance

The former Navajo Nation president running for Congress in Arizona speaks to Hyperallergic about his upbringing, how Diné culture shapes his political thinking, and the importance of historical memory.

This November, Jonathan Nez could become the first Native American to represent Arizona in Congress. Nez, who served as president of the Navajo Nation from 2019 to 2023, is running to flip the state's largest congressional district by area, a seat currently held by Republican Eli Crane. His “ Warrior Up ” platform is structured into four pillars, a tribute to the number's significance to Diné people, for whom the world is bound by four sacred mountains , one in each cardinal direction.

Nez has campaigned on lowering healthcare and housing costs, building sustainable rural infrastructure, tackling corruption in Washington, and the belief that “water is life and food is medicine.” In Arizona, where long-term drought and water supplies strain the Colorado River, one in three Diné households lack access to clean water.

As the Trump administration continues to roll back protections for Native land and sacred sites, Nez’s perspective feels especially urgent. A few days before Indigenous Peoples’ Day, we spoke about his upbringing, how Diné culture shapes his political thinking, and the importance of historical memory in fostering perseverance and resistance.

On the day of our interview, a Trump-aligned Political Action Committee (PAC) ran ad against Nez that mistakenly used a photograph of a different Navajo leader (ironically, a Republican supporter). The PAC acknowledged the mistake and corrected the ad, but the egregious error illustrates the political climate in which Nez is campaigning, as well as the continued discrimination against Indigenous people in the United States. The interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.

Hyperallergic: You were born on the Navajo Reservation and raised in Shonto, a small Navajo community in northeastern Arizona. Can you tell me a little bit about what your upbringing was like?

Jonathan Nez: I grew up in a very small community, Shonto, where we lived without running water or electricity. There's a lot of folks, including my wife, who grew up that way. But we had livestock, we had our farms, and so it was an upbringing of hard work: tending to our animals, herding sheep, herding cattle, riding horses, going to the farms, getting our food — getting the corn from the farm, starting a fire, and roasting the corn on an open flame while we're tending to our livestock. Those were fun days. We didn't know that was a hard upbringing, right? We were just growing up, and that's what was expected of us. I say that because it has shaped who I am today. And I think over my 20-plus years in public service, I have worked hard and gotten things done because of my upbringing.

I grew up in a very conservative home. Both parents Republican, sitting in a Baptist church early on, but at the same time knowing who I am as a Navajo. I'm a Democrat today, but my parents instilled in us, my brothers and sisters, a bootstrap mentality to do things for yourself. There was always that challenge from our elders, my parents and the elders in the community, to go get an education and get a job outside the Nation, to get that experience. And to come home with that experience to help your community, your people, your Nation.

My wife and I did that. We went home, and I got elected at an early age, in my mid-20s, to the local community government, then became a lawmaker, a council member of the Navajo Nation. I also got elected twice to the county Board of Supervisors, the equivalent of a county commissioner, which gave me a better understanding of county and state relations. I became the vice president and the president of the largest Indian tribe in the country, which gave me a better understanding of working with the federal government one-on-one.

Cartelera de Cinépolis – Estrenos del 15 de octubre, 2026

Staff Cine PREMIERE

¿Qué verás esta semana?

Esta semana la cartelera Cinépolis se renueva con una selección de estrenos que van desde grandes producciones comerciales hasta propuestas más arriesgadas para quienes buscan algo distinto en la sala de cine. Ya sea que tengas ganas de una historia emotiva, un thriller intenso o puro entretenimiento para desconectarte, los nuevos lanzamientos ofrecen opciones para todos los gustos. ¿Qué películas nuevas llegan a la cartelera de Cinépolis? Entérate aquí.

Aquí te contamos cuáles son las películas que llegan a la cartelera Cinépolis esta semana y la siguiente. Una guía rápida para decidir qué ver, cuándo ir y no perderte los títulos más comentados del momento.

Cartelera Cinépolis: estrenos del jueves 15 de octubre de 2026

Sacrificio los elegidos (Sacrifice) / Dir. Romain Gavras / Reino Unido, Grecia, Chipre, Estados Unidos, Francia, Italia, Australia / 2026

La caída de la ballena (Whalefall) / Dir. Brian Duffield / EE. UU. / 2026 Tras la muerte de su padre, Jay Gardiner se lanza a bucear frente a las costas de California en busca de sus restos. Pronto se ve envuelto en una desesperada lucha por la supervivencia cuando una enorme ballena lo engulle por completo. Atrapado en su vientre, debe encontrar la manera de escapar mientras su suministro de oxígeno comienza a agotarse.

El cadáver de la novia (Corpse Bride) – reestreno / Dir. Tim Burton / EE. UU. / 2005 Cuando un novio tímido practica sus votos matrimoniales en presencia involuntaria de una joven fallecida, ella se levanta de la tumba creyendo que se ha casado con ella.

La isla de las muñecas / Dir. Homero McDonald Chávez / México / 2026 Cuenta la leyenda de este lugar, que cerca de las chinampas de Don Julián una joven se ahogó entre los lirios y ahi su cuerpo fue encontrado.

Sacrificio los elegidos (Sacrifice) / Dir. Romain Gavras / Reino Unido, Grecia, Chipre, Estados Unidos, Francia, Italia, Australia / 2026 En una gala benéfica de la élite, celebridades y miembros de la alta sociedad se ven en peligro cuando activistas armados irrumpen en el lugar en busca de una reliquia legendaria que podría desbloquear poderes sobrenaturales. Protagonizan Chris Evans, Anya Taylor-Joy y Vincent Cassel.

Street Fighter / Dir. Kitao Sakurai / EE. UU., Japón / 2026 Ambientada en 1993, los distanciados peleadores Ryu (Andrew Koji) y Ken Masters (Noah Centineo) vuelven a entrar en combate cuando la misteriosa Chun-Li (Callina Liang) los recluta para el próximo World Warrior Tournament: un brutal enfrentamiento de puños, destino y furia. Pero detrás de esta batalla campal se esconde una conspiración mortal que los obligará a enfrentarse entre sí y a los demonios de su pasado. Y si no lo hacen… ¡GAME OVER! Dirigida por Kitao Sakurai, Street Fighter llevará la batalla de las máquinas arcade a la pantalla grande, con Hadokens, patadas giratorias y todos tus personajes favoritos.

Súper canino (Charlie the Wonderdog) / Dir. Shea Wageman / EE. UU. / 2026 Danny es un niño tímido cuya vida cambia cuando su querido perro, Charlie, es abducido por extraterrestres y regresa con superpoderes, convertido en el famoso Súper Canino. Pero Puddy, un gato con poderes extraordinarios, está decidido a conquistar a la humanidad junto con su pandilla felina. Ahora, Danny y Charlie deberán superar sus diferencias y unir fuerzas para detener sus diabólicos planes.

También te podría interesar: Cartelera de Cinépolis – Estrenos de esta semana .

Amarte / Dir. Roberto Girault / México / 2026 Cuando una famosa estrella de telenovelas en peligro se cruza inesperadamente en su camino, un excéntrico creador de cómics recurre a su propio superhéroe ficticio para protegerla, dando inicio a un romance improbable que pone a prueba su peculiar sentido de la realidad.

Tierra de mi padre (Fatherland) / Dir. Paweł Pawlikowski / Polonia, Alemania, Italia y Francia / 2026 En plena Guerra Fría, Fatherland se centra en la relación entre el escritor Thomas Mann y su hija Erika —actriz, escritora y piloto de rally— mientras emprenden un viaje por carretera en un Buick negro a través de una Alemania en ruinas.

Kraken, terror en lo profundo (Kraken) / Dir. Pål Øie / Noruega / 2026 Cuenta la leyenda de este lugar, que cerca de las chinampas de Don Julián una joven se ahogó entre los lirios y ahi su cuerpo fue encontrado.

El poder de la red (The Social Reckoning) / Dir. Aaron Sorkin / EE. UU. / 2026 La historia sigue a Frances Haugen, una joven ingeniera de Facebook, que solicitó la ayuda de Jeff Horwitz, un reportero del Wall Street Journal, para sacar a la luz los secretos mejor guardados de la red social.

Klara y el sol (Klara and the Sun) / Dir. Taika Waititi / Reino Unido, India, EE. UU. / 2026 Una niña robot diseñada para prevenir la soledad intenta salvar a una familia de humanos desconsolada.

La leyenda del Charro Negro / Dir. Alberto Rodriguez / México / 2026 Leo debe rescatar a Xochitl del inframundo, donde Charro Negro la recluyó. Mientras tanto, Xochitl, Evaristo, Finado y Moribunda han escapado de la prisión de Charro Negro para salvar a Don Andrés y Alebrije de una casa donde aún viven.

Ali G: Kién Ez Yo? (Ali G: Who Iz I?) / Dir. Sacha Baron Cohen / Reino Unido, EE. UU. / 2026 El periodista de hip-hop Ali G regresa después de 20 años para realizar un documental con personas reales. Las cámaras lo siguen durante más de un año mientras toma clases, camina por las calles y aparece en programas, a menudo con su novia embarazada.

Clayface / Dir. James Watkins / EE. UU. / 2026 La estrella emergente de Hollywood, Matt Hagen, se transforma en un monstruo terrorífico y sediento de venganza cuando su ambición científica le arrebata su identidad y su humanidad.

El desconocido del gran arco (L’inconnu de la Grande Arche) / Dir. Stéphane Demoustier / Francia, Dinamarca / 2026 La historia de Otto von Spreckelsen, un profesor de arquitectura de la vida real originario de Copenhague, que sorprendió al mundo al ganar un concurso abierto convocado por el presidente francés François Mitterrand.

Cacería mortal (The Bitter Taste) / Dir. Guido Tölke / Alemania / 2026 Una ex pentatleta es capturada por una condesa no muerta y sus seguidores malditos. Para sobrevivir a una cacería mortal, deberá recuperar sus habilidades atléticas y forjar una alianza incómoda con un encantador pescador y un policía gruñón.

content.article_text:
At the Swiss Church in Covent Garden, London, artist Maria Kreyn has crafted an immersive world that echoes the spiritual and psychological themes of the historic 18th-century Palladian-style venue itself.

Timed to Frieze Week and organized by the M.O.N. Art Foundation , “ Dream Logic ,” which runs through Monday, October 19, brings together a new body of paintings that capture swirling, light-filled storms, where sharp geometric forms cut through soft, atmospheric clouds. At the church—originally built in 1855 and later updated with a mirrored screen by architects Emanuel Christ and Christoph Gantenbein —Kreyn’s work plays off the layering of old and new, approaching the site’s architecture as an active collaborator rather than a neutral backdrop.

Installation view of “Maria Kreyn: Dream Logic” (2026). Courtesy ofCourtesy of Ministry of Nomads.

Kreyn operates in the tradition of such Romantic painters as J.M.W. Turner , and, like her forebears, the American shows a reverence for nature and its power, while layering in something more mathematical and otherworldly—a sense that beneath the chaos of the atmosphere, a hidden structure is at work. Her new show, in particular, takes further inspiration from surrealists like Leonora Carrington and David Lynch , artists who understood how to communicate the unbounded, idiosyncratic logic of dreams through their work. Kreyn’s paintings, likewise, express an alternate form of order, one built on intuition and association, rather than cause and effect.

Maria Kreyn, A Palm Reader’s Manual (2026). Courtesy of Ministry of Nomads.

Anchoring the exhibition is the monumental 2026 canvas The Alchemist’s Coil , which is installed at the altar in place of an expected religious centerpiece. Here, Kreyn renders a golden spiral staircase that doubles as a DNA helix, winding its way upward through a glowing landscape that evokes a type of alien inferno. The composition draws loosely on assembly theory, a scientific framework linking the origins of life to ideas about complexity and memory embedded in matter itself—fitting territory for an artist who studied mathematics and philosophy at the University of Chicago before teaching herself to paint.

Installation view of “Maria Kreyn: Dream Logic” (2026). Courtesy of

“Dream Logic” marks Kreyn’s third major presentation inside of a sacred space, following a pair of shows abroad. In 2024, her exhibition for the 60th Venice Biennale , “ Chronos ,” filled St. George’s Anglican Church with a suite of tempestuous seascapes that also built on the tradition of artists like Turner and Caspar David Friedrich , reflecting a shift in her practice away from the figure and toward pure atmosphere. And, last autumn, “ Hyperobject ” brought a new set of storm paintings to London’s Fitzrovia Chapel , anchored by an altarpiece built around the show’s titular concept of hyperobjects, phenomena too vast in scale for humans to comprehend or grasp fully.

All three shows were produced by the M.O.N. Art Foundation, helmed by curator and gallerist Maria Vega , who founded the organization’s parent gallery, Ministry of Nomads , in 2008. Vega has described her mission as pushing contemporary art outside of the conventional gallery model, pairing artists with culturally rich, unconventional spaces where dialogue between art, science, and belief can unfold. Her ongoing collaboration with Kreyn has become a true through line and exemplary of this mission.

Maria Kreyn, The Second Concerto (2026). Courtesy of Ministry of Nomads.

“ Maria Kreyn: Dream Logic ” is on view at the Swiss Church, Covent Garden, London, through October 19, 2026.

content.title_original: Reimagining Liberation: Brandon Gercara Between Maloya and Voguing
content.editorial_title_zh: 重新想象解放：Brandon Gercara 如何让 Maloya 与 Voguing 相遇
content.editorial_excerpt_zh: 留尼汪艺术家 Brandon Gercara 在法国诺瓦谢尔的 La Ferme du Buisson 展出《Destin Vogoya》。展览将当地的 Maloya 音乐传统与 Voguing 舞结合，通过表演、摄影等媒介探讨酷儿身份、文化记忆与解放的可能。
content.editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "在法国诺瓦谢尔的 La Ferme du Buisson 艺术中心，留尼汪艺术家 Brandon Gercara 的展览《Destin Vogoya》通过表演、视觉艺术和想象性叙事，让酷儿表达、去殖民思想与文化传统展开对话。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/still-2026-03-17-173703_1-107-2-1030x579.webp", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "传承下来的传统，如何成为争取解放的工具？在《Destin Vogoya》中，留尼汪艺术家 Brandon Gercara 探索酷儿身份、文化记忆与抵抗之间的交汇，以艺术实验挑战既有的权力结构。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是 Gercara 首次在当代艺术中心举办个展。展览呈现虚构世界 Majik Kwir 的新篇章，故事围绕来自留尼汪的七位 LGBTQIA+ 主角展开。展览的核心是 vogoya：一种将 Maloya 与 Voguing 融合的形式。前者是一种根植于留尼汪抵抗历史的音乐传统，后者则是与黑人及拉美裔酷儿舞厅文化密切相关的舞蹈。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Gercara 的创作横跨表演、摄影、录像、装置、素描与绘画，探究文化实践如何通过重新诠释，为不同的身份认同和集体表达开辟空间。这种跨媒介的创作方式借鉴去殖民女性主义、交叉性和克里奥尔化思想，把艺术实践视为质疑主流社会叙事的途径。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览之外，Gercara 也通过支持留尼汪 LGBTQIA+ 社群的 Requeer 项目开展社会行动，推动社群获得更多公共可见性，并促进文化交流。《Destin Vogoya》邀请观众思考：传统、想象力与集体创造，如何为归属感和解放带来新的可能。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览在法国诺瓦谢尔的 La Ferme du Buisson 举行，展期至2027年1月24日。", "links": [{"text": "La Ferme du Buisson", "url": "https://www.lafermedubuisson.com/fr/brandon-gercara"}], "translated": true}]

content.article_text:
At La Ferme du Buisson in Noisiel, France, Réunionese artist Brandon Gercara’s ‘Destin Vogoya’ brings queer expression, decolonial thought and cultural traditions into dialogue through performance, visual art and speculative storytelling.

How can inherited traditions become instruments of liberation? In ‘Destin Vogoya’, Réunionese artist Brandon Gercara explores the intersections of queer identity, cultural memory and resistance, challenging established structures of power through artistic experimentation.

Marking Gercara’s first solo exhibition at a contemporary art centre, the presentation introduces a new chapter of Majik Kwir , a fictional universe following seven LGBTQIA+ protagonists from Réunion. Central to the exhibition is vogoya, a hybrid form bringing together maloya, a musical tradition rooted in Réunion’s history of resistance, and voguing, a dance form associated with Black and Latin American queer ballroom culture.

Working across performance, photography, video, installation, drawing and painting, Gercara examines how cultural practices can be reinterpreted to create spaces for alternative identities and collective expression. Their multidisciplinary approach draws on decolonial feminism, intersectionality and creolisation, positioning artistic practice as a means of questioning dominant social narratives.

Beyond the exhibition, Gercara’s activism through Requeer, an initiative supporting LGBTQIA+ communities in Réunion, reflects their commitment to visibility and cultural exchange. ‘Destin Vogoya’ invites audiences to consider how tradition, imagination and collective creativity can generate new possibilities for belonging and emancipation.

This exhibition is on view at La Ferme du Buisson , Noisiel, France, until 24 January 2027.

content.title_original: Beyond the Image: Steve McQueen Explores the Power of the Human Voice
content.editorial_title_zh: 影像之外：史蒂夫·麦奎因探索人声的力量
content.editorial_excerpt_zh: 史蒂夫·麦奎因在毕尔巴鄂古根海姆美术馆展出的《66–76–26》，让妮娜·西蒙与大卫·鲍伊演唱的 Wild Is the Wind 以纯粹的人声相遇。作品将聆听置于中心，探究记忆、渴望与情感的共鸣。
content.editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "在西班牙毕尔巴鄂古根海姆美术馆，英国艺术家、电影导演史蒂夫·麦奎因（Steve McQueen）的《66–76–26》让妮娜·西蒙与大卫·鲍伊展开一场出人意料的对话，探究渴望、记忆，以及声音触动情感的力量。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/013GalerIa-Steve-McQueen-1030x773.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当艺术家把影像彻底移除，还会剩下什么？在《66–76–26》中，英国艺术家、电影导演史蒂夫·麦奎因邀请观众感受人声所蕴含的表达可能。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这件在毕尔巴鄂古根海姆美术馆呈现的装置，把两版 Wild Is the Wind 的录音放在一起：妮娜·西蒙于1966年演唱的版本，以及大卫·鲍伊于1976年演唱的版本。两者相隔十年，背后有着不同的历史与个人境遇；如今，剥去器乐伴奏与视觉影像，这两道声音在昏暗的展厅中相遇。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "麦奎因的创作一贯关注历史、暴力、身份与人的经历。这一次，他转向声音，将其作为承载记忆与表达情感的媒介。两段录音分别位于展览空间的两端，构成一场想象中的对唱，邀请观众思考：个体的经历如何跨越时间，彼此产生共鸣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "由 Lekha Hileman 策展的《66–76–26》挑战了人们对视觉艺术的惯常期待，把聆听置于观众与作品相遇的中心。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "通过缺席、重复，以及人声自身的脆弱，麦奎因让观众重新思考渴望、在场，以及艺术如何传达可见之物以外的体验。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览在西班牙毕尔巴鄂古根海姆美术馆举行，展期至2027年2月21日。", "links": [{"text": "Guggenheim Museum Bilbao", "url": "https://www.guggenheim-bilbao.eus/en/exhibitions/steve-mcqueen"}], "translated": true}]

content.article_text:
At the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao in Spain, British artist and filmmaker Steve McQueen’s ’66–76–26′ brings Nina Simone and David Bowie into an unexpected dialogue, exploring longing, memory and the emotional power of sound.

What remains when an artist removes the image entirely? In ’66–76–26′, acclaimed British artist and filmmaker Steve McQueen invites audiences to encounter the expressive possibilities of the human voice.

Presented at the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao, the installation brings together two recordings of Wild Is the Wind , performed by Nina Simone in 1966 and David Bowie in 1976. Separated by a decade and shaped by distinct historical and personal circumstances, their voices meet within a darkened gallery, stripped of instrumentation and visual imagery.

Known for his investigations into history, violence, identity, and human experience, McQueen turns to sound as a vehicle for memory and emotional expression. Positioned at opposite ends of the exhibition space, the recordings create an imagined duet, inviting visitors to consider how individual experiences resonate across time.

Curated by Lekha Hileman, ’66–76–26′ challenges conventional expectations of visual art, placing listening at the centre of the encounter.

Through absence, repetition and the vulnerability of the human voice, McQueen offers a meditation on longing, presence and the ways art can communicate beyond what is visible.

The exhibition is on view at the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao in Spain until 21 February 2027.

content.article_text:
At the Chau Chak Wing Museum in Sydney, Nigerian artist Victor Ehikhamenor’s first Australian solo exhibition, ‘Undoing the City: Making Home’, examines how communities preserve their histories and identities amid urban transformation.

At the Chau Chak Wing Museum in Sydney, Australia, Nigerian artist Victor Ehikhamenor’s first Australian solo exhibition, Undoing the City: Making Home, examines how communities preserve their histories and identities amid urban transformation.

What happens to a community’s identity when the places that hold its memories disappear? In ‘Undoing the City: Making Home’, Nigerian artist Victor Ehikhamenor explores the human consequences of urban redevelopment, displacement and the struggle to preserve cultural belonging. The exhibition brings together new and recent works connecting the experiences of communities in Sydney, Cairo and Port Harcourt. Drawing on research into neighbourhoods threatened by redevelopment, Ehikhamenor examines how architecture, collective memory and cultural practices shape our understanding of home.

Informed by the visual and spiritual traditions of the historic Benin Kingdom, his multidisciplinary practice engages with colonial histories, identity and the relationship between people and place.

Presented in partnership with Blacktown Arts, the exhibition also extends beyond the museum through a mentorship programme supporting emerging African and African-descended creatives in Western Sydney. By placing geographically distinct communities in conversation, Undoing the City: Making Home asks whose histories survive urban transformation and how artistic practice can resist erasure.

The exhibition invites audiences to reconsider home not simply as a physical location, but as a repository of relationships, histories and cultural continuity.

This exhibition will be on view at the Penelope Gallery, the Chau Chak Wing Museum , University of Sydney, from 15 October 2026 to 26 April 2027.

content.article_text:
Tarung: Unforgiven (2026) by Razaisyam Rashid Film Review

"Welcome to Tarung! Tonight, a new leader will rise!"

Malaysian filmmaker Razaisyam Rashid is best known for “Kahar: Kapla High Council” (2024), the school action drama that earned him the Best Director award from the Kuala Lumpur Film Critics Council. He made his feature directorial debut with “CEO” in 2014 and has since worked extensively across cinema, television movies and drama series.

“Tarung: Unforgiven”, Rashid’s latest martial arts feature, continues his interest in action while moving into the violent world of underground fighting. Released theatrically in Malaysia in 2026, the production brings together a large local cast and once again reunites the director with cinematographer Stephen Chua, who also worked on “Kahar: Kapla High Council”.

The story follows Hatta, a former silat champion haunted by his past. Ten years earlier, he accidentally killed an opponent during a tournament after losing control of his anger. Since then, he has vowed never to fight again. He now works as a delivery man and lives with his sister Aisha, although the tragedy continues to weigh heavily on him.

When Aisha becomes gravely ill and requires an expensive operation, Hatta finds himself without the money needed for her treatment. Left with few options, he enters Tarung, an underground fighting tournament connected to the Marga gang. His return to combat forces him to confront his past once again, particularly when he discovers that one of the opponents waiting for him has a direct connection to the fighter he killed years earlier.

Regarding the story, “Tarung: Unforgiven” is hardly original. Here we get the standard angry protagonist, a sick family member, underworld fights providing brutal action, and a setup that becomes fairly predictable and formulaic. Fortunately, the movie’s greatest strengths lie in the heartfelt performances of the Malaysian cast and, above all, its engaging emotional content. Deep down, “Tarung: Unforgiven” deals with human relationships, guilt, forgiveness and redemption.

Most of the outdoor scenes take place around the backstreets of Kuala Lumpur, but the city is hardly presented as a glossy cosmopolitan environment bathed in neon lights. Instead, Rashid and cinematographer Stephen Chua focus on its rougher spaces. The gangster headquarters and underground arena are particularly atmospheric, with creative, moody lighting adding considerably to their impact. Interestingly, even the Petronas Twin Towers are not constantly forced into the compositions simply to establish the location, allowing Kuala Lumpur to emerge in a more organic way.

Apart from the acting, the silat sequences are equally impressive. Action director Ubai Amir delivers set pieces that are hard hitting, full of energy and extremely well designed, while becoming quite brutal at times. More importantly, the fights are closely connected to the emotional aspects of the narrative rather than existing simply as spectacle, which keeps them engaging throughout.

Mierul Aiman portrays Hatta as a believable, three dimensional character. He effortlessly displays a range of emotions, while his grounded performance remains heartfelt without becoming excessive. His piercing eyes, particularly inside the ring, make the shifts in his mood and the anger he struggles to control even more convincing.

Equally memorable is Aedy Ashraf as Isa, the bitter fighter who eventually faces Hatta. Although initially appearing almost entirely aggressive, he gradually emerges as a much more tragic and vulnerable character, and Ashraf is particularly effective at presenting both sides of his personality. The dynamic between Hatta and Isa consequently provides the emotional core behind much of the violence.

Although some of the supporting characters could have benefited from further development, they generally add depth to the narrative. Bront Palarae plays Khalid, the supreme leader of the Marga gang, while Zul Ariffin portrays Badrul, who is eager to take over as an election approaches. Hatta’s loyal friend Ucop, wonderfully played by Amir Ahnaf, is another standout. Even though her screen time is relatively brief, Sharifah Sakinah also makes an impression as Aisha, whose illness ultimately pushes Hatta back into fighting.

The performances work particularly well because the emotional aspects of the story are treated almost as seriously as the physical confrontations. Hatta is fighting not simply to win matches, but because guilt, financial desperation and loyalty have left him with very few choices. Isa is similarly driven by feelings that have accumulated for years. This gives their eventual confrontation significantly more weight than it would have had as a simple tournament finale.

The fight sequences themselves are amazingly intense, with virtually every punch feeling physical and carefully put together. For that reason, it would be unfair to label Rashid’s silat production as merely another action movie. The emotional storyline, dealing with honor, loyalty, redemption and the personal struggles of the characters, gives the violence additional substance. The two central characters in particular are engaging and adequately developed.

At the same time, “Tarung: Unforgiven” is hardly perfect. The plot involving deadly combat, betrayal and revenge is predictable, and a number of developments can be anticipated well before they occur. The familiar structure prevents the narrative itself from becoming as memorable as the performances and action.

Nonetheless, “Tarung: Unforgiven” is an engaging and entertaining action movie with heart, presenting a human story whose emotional themes actually work alongside the martial arts spectacle. The familiarity of the narrative remains its most evident weakness, but Rashid compensates through strong performances, atmospheric imagery and particularly effective silat choreography. The hinted continuation, “Tarung: The Rise of Marga”, should provide another opportunity to expand the world introduced here.

content.article_text:
At Bag Factory Artists’ Studios in Johannesburg, ‘Site Forming: Where Encounter Takes Form’ brings together the practices of two emerging artists to examine memory, identity and the transformative possibilities of space.

How do the places we inhabit shape who we become? In ‘Site Forming: Where Encounter Takes Form’, artists Swaline Mkhonto and Zovuyo Pendu investigate the shifting relationships between bodies, memories, environments and inner worlds.

Presented at Bag Factory Artists’ Studios, the exhibition marks the culmination of their participation in the 2025/2026 Young Womxn Studio Bursary Award. Mkhonto’s interdisciplinary practice draws on printmaking, installation, writing and mark-making to explore fragmentation, memory and the body’s relationship with space. Pendu’s figurative paintings investigate the psychological tensions between faith, ego and the unconscious, questioning how identity is shaped through personal experience. Together, their practices approach the idea of a site as something continually transformed through encounter rather than a fixed location.

The exhibition includes curatorial contributions from Penina Chalumbira and collaboration with Letsema collective members Ntabiseng Mofokeng, Mbako Moemise and Eva Rose London. Supported by Sam Nhlengethwa, Bag Factory Artists’ Studios and the National Arts Council, the exhibition reflects the bursary’s commitment to nurturing emerging womxn artists and encouraging experimentation within Johannesburg’s contemporary art landscape.

This exhibition is on view at Bag Factory Artists’ Studios in Newtown, Johannesburg, until 6 November 2026.
