content.article_text:
Quel a été votre parcours avant de devenir producteur de films ?

Pendant mes études d’ingénieur, quelqu’un qui travaillait à l’INA [ Institut national de l’audiovisuel, ndlr ] m’a parlé d’une petite unité d’une quarantaine de personnes qui s’appelait le Département des programmes de création et de recherche et avait pour mission de découvrir de nouveaux auteurs et de nouvelles formes d’écriture. J’y ai travaillé cinq ans et j’y ai rencontré les frères Dardenne et plein de cinéastes avec qui j’allais travailler plus tard comme Nicolas Philibert, Chantal Akerman, Jean-Louis Comolli. C’était un lieu de très grande liberté qui a généré les essais vidéo de Jean-Luc Godard, les films de Raoul Ruiz et de Jean Eustache. Même si je n’étais pas directement producteur et m’occupais plutôt d’organisation générale, cette aventure créative a formé mon goût.

Jean-Pierre et Luc Dardenne : « On a toujours le désir de filmer comme si c’était la première fois que ce que nous filmons apparaît. »

C’est suite à cette expérience que vous avez créé les sociétés de production Archipel 33 et Archipel 35 ?

Après l’INA, je rejoins un ami qui venait de créer sa société, Initial Groupe. On a produit Le Miraculé de Jean-Pierre Mocky ou Les Jeux de société d’Éric Rohmer. Et en 1988, je crée une première structure pour la télévision, Archipel 33, où je produis des documentaires puis des fictions, comme Les Derniers jours d’Emmanuel Kant de Philippe Collin. En 1997, je crée Archipel 35, pour des longs métrages de cinéma, et je commence avec Saint-Cyr ( sorti en 2000, ndlr ) de Patricia Mazuy , avec Isabelle Huppert. Une de mes collaboratrices avait lu La Maison d’Esther , livre d’Yves Dangerfield qui raconte la création de l’école de Saint-Cyr par Madame de Maintenon, et j’ai cherché pour l’adaptation quelqu’un qui puisse apporter un regard personnel et dynamiter le genre du film en costumes. J’avais été impressionné par Peaux de vaches [ premier long métrage de Patricia Mazuy, sorti en 1989, ndlr ] et j’ai donc approché Patricia Mazuy. On s’est lancés dans la production du film, qui m’a bien secoué !

L’idée d’Archipel 35 était donc d’emblée de produire des films ambitieux artistiquement ?

C’était mon héritage de l’INA. J’étais dans un cinéma quand même atypique, avec l’envie d’avoir un regard d’auteur affirmé sur la façon de traiter la narration, la forme. Le Fils, des frères Dardenne, est le film qui a suivi Saint-Cyr et qui m’a un peu sauvé car j’étais mal financièrement. Quand j’avais connu les Dardenne à l’INA à la fin des années 1970, je n’étais pas encore vraiment producteur et Jean-Pierre et Luc n’étaient pas encore vraiment cinéastes – l’un était assistant opérateur et l’autre assistant réalisateur. Nos chemins s’étaient croisés durant les vingt années suivantes car ils avaient réalisé beaucoup de documentaires avant de passer à la fiction et on avait ça en commun. En 2000, alors que les Dardenne venaient d’avoir la Palme d’or pour Rosetta , Luc me dit que ce serait bien qu’on travaille ensemble et il m’envoie le scénario du Fils. Cela a été le début d’une longue et heureuse aventure puisqu’on a fait neuf films ensemble et que tous ont été en compétition à Cannes. Et même si je n’aurai plus de société de production, car Archipel 35 appartient désormais à mk2, je serai à nouveau coproducteur pour la France du prochain film des Dardenne [ prévu pour être tourné l’année prochaine, ndlr] par l’intermédiaire de Diaphana.

Vous avez aussi produit Bamako d’Abderrahmane Sissako, qui avait la particularité d’être une production franco-américano-malienne. Avec Danny Glover, acteur américain vu notamment dans L’Arme fatale , comme producteur associé.

Au départ, le film était pour Arte et la télévision. Danny Glover a lui été amené dans le financement par Abderrahmane Sissako, qui le connaissait et lui a aussi confié dans le film un rôle de cow-boy. L’aventure a été extraordinaire : se retrouver au Mali dans cette cour avec tous ces avocats était très joyeux [Bamako imagine un procès intenté au FMI et à la Banque mondiale par la société civile africaine et fait jouer de vrais avocats, ndlr] . Quand on a vu le film, on s’est dit qu’on pouvait peut-être sortir du seul circuit de télévision. Il a été sélectionné hors compétition à Cannes en 2006, avec un accueil formidable, et j’ai discuté avec Arte de la possibilité de le sortir en salles. On l’a retransformé en film de cinéma et il a fait plus de 200 000 entrées en France.

Parmi vos productions mémorables, il y a L’Exercice de l’État de Pierre Schoeller, sorti en 2011. L’idée était là encore de bousculer les codes ?

En fait, je choisis les cinéastes avant de choisir les projets. Pierre Schoeller avait réalisé Zéro défaut | présenté en 2003 à l’ACID à Cannes, ndlr] et je lui ai dit que je voulais travailler avec lui. Il m’a parlé de son désir de faire un film politique sur la notion de service de l’État. Mais il est ensuite passé à autre chose et a écrit le scénario de Versailles. Je lui ai avoué que je ne serais peut-être pas le bon producteur pour ce film, qu’il a donc fait sans moi. Mais après Versailles, il me rappelle car il avait enfin trouvé la forme de son film politique. Ce sont parfois de longs processus. Et L’Exercice de l’État a clairement marqué le genre du cinéma politique. Olivier Gourmet [ qui joue dans L’Exercice de l’État un ministre français des Transports confrontés à diverses crises, ndlr] est d’ailleurs l’acteur avec lequel j’ai le plus travaillé, entre les films des frères Dardenne, Home d’Ursula Meier ou le cinéma de Pierre Schoeller.

Oui car vous avez aussi produit le film suivant de Pierre Schoeller, Un peuple et son roi …

Pierre voulait depuis longtemps réaliser un film sur la Révolution française. Et cela a pris huit ans. Le projet était de faire un film en deux parties : Pierre a écrit le premier volet [ qui va de la prise de la Bastille du 14 juillet 1789 à l’exécution de Louis XVI en janvier 1793, ndlr ] et le deuxième volet commençait après l’exécution du roi et allait jusqu’à la fin de Thermidor en juillet 1794. On a chiffré le scénario de la première partie à 21 millions d’euros, mais on s’est vite aperçus qu’avec toutes les coproductions possibles mises bout à bout on réunissait seulement 15 millions. Pierre a dû couper dans le scénario et ce n’était pas simple car il y a trois niveaux de récit : l’atelier du verrier avec Olivier Gourmet, la cour de Louis XVI joué par Laurent Lafitte et l’Assemblée nationale [ avec Louis Garrel en Robespierre, ndlr]. Et il y a en plus des histoires intimes comme la relation entre Gaspard Ulliel et Adèle Haenel. Le film avait un côté visionnaire mais le premier coup sur la tête fut de ne pas être sélectionné en compétition à Cannes, alors que tout le monde s’y attendait. Un peuple et son roi a finalement été montré à Venise hors compétition et a fait 320 000 entrées en France, ce qui n’était pas suffisant pour faire une suite. Cela a été douloureux, mais c’est un film que j’aime beaucoup. Je pense qu’il va durer et il est souvent demandé pour des projections à l’étranger.

Entretemps, vous aviez produit Bird People, sorti en 2014, qui reste le dernier film en date de Pascale Ferran…

J’avais très envie de travailler avec Pascale Ferran, dont j’adore Petits arrangements avec les morts et Lady Chatterley . Elle m’a parlé de Bird People et c’était un vrai pari [ le film suit une femme de chambre, jouée par Anaïs Demoustier, qui se transforme en moineau, ndlr ]. On est parfois devenus fous avec ces moineaux… Pascale est passionnée par les questions de rapport avec le vivant et de communication entre le monde humain et le monde animal et elle avait trouvé une manière de travailler avec les moineaux : elle leur avait donné des prénoms et savait exactement quel moineau elle souhaitait pour telle ou telle prise. On était bluffés de voir les oiseaux faire ce qu’elle voulait ! Pascale n’a malheureusement plus refait de film depuis Bird People, oui. Elle a été très investie dans La Cinetek et les César, mais j’espère qu’elle reviendra un jour au cinéma.

De votre côté, vous arrêtez donc vos activités au sein d’ Archipel 35 et avez choisi de transmettre votre catalogue de films à mk2. Qu’est-ce qui a guidé ce choix ?

J’ai vu les différents types de transmission de films qui peuvent exister et j’ai vu qu’il y avait parfois des films dont les droits se retrouvent bloqués, comme ce fut le cas pour La Maman et la Putain . Selon moi, la détention individuelle des droits d’un film n’est pas forcément la solution, donc je me suis dit qu’il ne fallait pas m’y prendre trop tard pour transmettre et qu’il fallait anticiper. Et mk2 est extrêmement bien organisé pour la gestion des catalogues et réfléchit à la façon dont on peut aujourd’hui faire vivre des œuvres de patrimoine, trouver des nouveaux modes d’exploitation, toucher de jeunes publics.

Ils ont ainsi créé mk2 alt , une alternative pour la distribution dans des circuits particuliers et ont mis au point une plateforme permettant de gérer les demandes de festivals, de salles indépendantes ou d’associations qui voudraient faire une projection unique. C’est important pour les cinéastes car il s’agit de la qualité des regards plus que de rentabilité. Vingt ans après avoir fait un film, vous pouvez avoir une projection avec un public intéressé et un débat.

De façon plus globale, comment voyez-vous l’avenir du cinéma et les menaces qui pèsent parfois sur lui ?

Ma conviction est que pour continuer à faire vivre les œuvres, il faut continuer à faire vivre les salles de cinéma. Le jour où il n’y aura plus de salles, mêmes si les œuvres sont conservées et accessibles sur des plateformes, quelque chose sera perdu dans le rapport au cinéma et dans ce sentiment d’émotions collectives partagées. On a en France la chance exceptionnelle d’avoir un parc de salles formidable. La base c’est que les films soient conservés. Je suis d’accord avec ce que disait Henri Langlois ( pionnier de la conservation des films et cofondateur de la Cinémathèque française en 1936, ndlr ) : « Il faut tout garder ».

Parce qu’on ne sait pas ce qu’il peut se passer autour d’une œuvre. On a parfois l’impression que certains films vieillissent et meurent puis tout d’un coup ils ressuscitent. Il faut garder cette possibilité ouverte de redécouvrir un film. Je pense qu’il y a aussi une appétence des jeunes générations pour le cinéma de patrimoine et pour la circulation et la continuité de l’histoire du cinéma. Quand je me suis construit une cinéphilie dans les années 1970, il y avait quand même moins de films qu’aujourd’hui, où l’on peut se perdre dans une masse incroyable. Il faut éditorialiser et guider, comme j’ai moi pu être guidé dans ma jeunesse par des ciné-clubs ou des émissions de cinéma à la télévision qui aujourd’hui existent moins.

content.article_text:
Tanzanian filmmaker Neema Ngelime’s “The Ones With the Tempered Flowers,” Palestinian director Fitnat Waked’s “On the Sea Road” and “Where Do I Belong?,” from Sudanese director Ibrahim “Snoopy” Ahmad, were among the big winners at this year’s Durban FilmMart , which wrapped with an award ceremony on Monday night.

Ngelime’s directorial debut took home five awards, including the prize for best non-fiction film from South Africa’s National Film and Video Foundation and awards from DOK Leipzig, Sheffield Doc Fest and Visions du Réel. The film tells the story of a woman studying her body’s relationship to self and society, and the political weight placed on women’s bodies in Tanzania, and challenging duty masked as love.

Related Stories

Telly Awards Adds Microseries Competition Track, With Dozens of New Categories (EXCLUSIVE)

‘Sin Filtro’ Producer JK Media Producing First Original Microdramas Shot in the U.S. for TelevisaUnivision’s ViXMicrO (EXCLUSIVE)

“Where Do I Belong?” is the latest from Ahmad, who co-directed last year’s Sundance-premiering documentary “Khartoum.” The winner of four prizes at the DFM forum, it follows the director as he decides to leave Nairobi and return to his family in the Sudanese capital, combining documentary footage and hand-drawn pencil animation to tell an intimate and unconventional road movie. Also taking four awards was “On the Sea Road,” the debut feature from Waked, a documentary about the friendship forged between two Palestinian women separated by borders.

Popular on Variety

Among other standout projects was “The Boy Who Spoke Static,” from Nigeria’s Agbajowo Collective, the filmmaking group behind the 2024 Toronto premiere “The Legend of the Vagabond Queen of Lagos,” which won three prizes, including the prize for best fiction film from South Africa’s NFVF.

The ceremony capped a rousing edition of the pitch and finance forum at the DFM, which kicked off its 17th edition with a celebration of DFM alumnus “Ben’Imana,” from first-time Rwandan filmmaker Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo, which won the Cámera d’Or in Cannes and became that country’s first ever submission in the Oscar category for best international feature film.

Durban FilmMart Institute director Magdalene Reddy praised the “dynamic array of filmmakers and industry leaders” taking part in this year’s event and stressed how “the talent showcased in this year’s program and film projects exemplifies the strength of African cinema.

“The Durban FilmMart Institute…remains committed to building the industry,” she said. “Thank you for participating with such passion and professionalism in all the programs presented over the last four days. Thank you for connecting, for telling your stories. And thank you for shifting the world with us.”

Thirty-nine awards were handed out on Monday night, with a value totaling north of $120,000. Here’s a rundown of all the winners:

content.article_text:
At the Gibbes Museum of Art in Charleston, South Carolina, USA, ‘Fighting for Freedom: Black Craftspeople and the Pursuit of Independence’ explores how African American artisans used creativity, skill and craftsmanship to assert agency and pursue liberation.

How can an everyday object become an expression of resistance? ‘Fighting for Freedom: Black Craftspeople and the Pursuit of Independence’ examines Black artisans’ contributions to American history, challenging narratives that have long overlooked their creative and cultural legacies.

Spanning the American Revolution to the present, the exhibition brings together more than 30 objects, including furniture, ceramics, metalwork, textiles, tools and personal accessories. Created by both free and enslaved craftspeople, these works reveal how artistic skill became a means of asserting identity, independence and agency within systems of oppression.

Through objects dating from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the exhibition foregrounds the experiences of recognised makers alongside those whose names have been lost to history. Their craftsmanship offers insight into the relationship between labour, creativity and the pursuit of freedom.

Organised by the Daughters of the American Revolution Museum in partnership with the Black Craftspeople Digital Archive, the exhibition invites visitors to reconsider Black artisans’ role in shaping America’s material and cultural heritage.

This exhibition will be on view at the Gibbes Museum of Art , Charleston, South Carolina, from 16 October 2026 to 9 May 2027.

content.article_text:
At Kunsthalle Münster in Germany, Mozambican artist Euridice Zaituna Kala explores colonial memory, historical erasure and the voices that persist beyond official narratives.

What happens to the histories that archives fail to preserve? In ‘Daylighting: aber es ist Wasser, das spricht’, Mozambican artist Euridice Zaituna Kala examines the relationship between memory, colonialism and the enduring consequences of historical erasure.

Presented at Kunsthalle Münster, the exhibition marks Kala’s first institutional solo presentation in Germany, bringing together installations, performances, paintings, objects and books that challenge established historical narratives.

Drawing on personal memories and archival research, Kala investigates how histories are constructed, whose experiences are documented and which voices remain unheard. Her practice engages with the representation of Black bodies in colonial archives, questioning the power systems that determine visibility and remembrance.

Bringing together ecological, feminist and Indigenous perspectives, the exhibition considers the connections between historical injustice, collective memory and contemporary struggles.

Previously presented in Rennes and Brussels, the exhibition has evolved through its engagement with each location. For Münster, Kala introduces new works that extend her investigation into the relationship between place, history and belonging.

Curated by Merle Radtke, ‘Daylighting’ invites audiences to reconsider the archive not as a fixed record of the past, but as a contested space where forgotten histories can be recovered and re-examined.

This exhibition is on view at Kunsthalle Münster , in Germany, until 24 January 2027.

content.article_text:
The Art of Light brings South African light installations to the gardens of Norval Foundation in Cape Town, from 20 to 29 November 2026.

As daylight fades over Cape Town, the gardens of Norval Foundation will become a setting for artistic encounters with light, space and the natural environment. ‘The Art of Light’ brings a selection of installations from LUMENOCITY to Tokai, giving visitors the chance to experience works by South African artists in a new setting.

Moving beyond their original urban context, the installations will be presented among trees, lawns and winding pathways, inviting audiences to consider how light transforms familiar landscapes and alters our perception of space.

Rather than a conventional gallery exhibition, ‘The Art of Light’ unfolds as an outdoor journey. Visitors can explore the illuminated installations at their own pace, with the experience taking approximately 60 to 90 minutes.

The presentation offers an opportunity to encounter contemporary artistic practices beyond the museum’s interior, where the relationship between artwork, environment and audience becomes central to the experience.

Suitable for all ages, the event will also feature food trucks and refreshments, creating an accessible evening of art and exploration.

This event will take place at the Norval Foundation in Tokai, from 20 to 29 November 2026, excluding 23 and 24 November.

content.article_text:
Lubov , a closely watched gallery in New York’s Chinatown neighborhood, will remain open after the death of its founder Francisco Correa Cordero earlier this year.

Cordero, who died at 37 in August , founded Lubov in 2016 and exhibited artists such as Eunnam Hong, My Barbarian, Andres Serrano, Mimi Park, Shannon Cartier Lucy, and Covey Gong. The gallery was named after Luba Drozd, to whom Cordero was married when he first opened the space.

On Tuesday, the gallery announced that it would continue under the leadership of Mode Bonafilia and Kristen Wasik . Bonafilia had already been with the gallery, serving as its director of community programming and education since 2025. Wasik had been a director at the gallery between 2023 and 2024, and returned to Lubov earlier this year, having previously worked at Chart and the now-defunct Lyles & King .

“Following Cordero’s sudden passing in August, Bonafilia and Wasik committed without hesitation to carrying the gallery forward,” the gallery wrote in a statement posted to Instagram . “At a time in which alternative spaces in New York are becoming increasingly scarce, they regard Lubov’s continuation as essential. Whether or not to continue the gallery was never a question. Under their direction, the gallery will honor Cordero’s legacy while building upon it, supporting artists who make work out of necessity rather than for market value.”

Lubov’s first exhibition under the gallery’s new ownership will be a solo show for Michael Hafftka, a New York–based painter. His exhibition opens there on October 24.

content.article_text:
Composer Hildur Guðnadóttir , who won an Oscar with “Joker,” is already deep into “ The Bell Jar .”

Sarah Polley ’s Sylvia Plath adaptation, which recently wrapped, will give pop icon Billie Eilish her first starring role, while offering the composer a new kind of creative partnership.

“[Working with a fellow Oscar-winning musician like Eilish] makes a huge difference,” Guðnadóttir tells Variety . “You know she understands the process that goes into writing music, so what you write can really resonate with her.”

Related Stories

Raindance to Launch U.K.'s First Major Vertical Festival and Market (EXCLUSIVE)

WWE Enters Microdrama Space With 'Agent of Shadows,' Drew McIntyre Takes Central Role

Building on a relationship forged on 2022’s Oscar-winning “Women Talking,” Guðnadóttir joined Polley’s latest project early, writing themes the filmmaker could play on set. She was equally keen to connect with Eilish before the singer stepped in front of the camera.

Popular on Variety

“We talked about what we envisioned for the music, and how we could translate what Sylvia experiences into it,” Guðnadóttir says. “For me, the core of Plath’s writing is that she’s searching for identity. She keeps asking, ‘Who am I?’ and then uses her writing to understand that. Billie, Sarah and I have been exploring how we hear that, how to translate it into music, and what music Sylvia herself might have been listening to.”

Guðnadóttir calls the film a career highlight.

“It’s one of the most exciting projects I’ve ever done,” she says. “Sarah and I are good friends, so getting to tell this story with her is amazing. I think it’s one of the most amazing books ever written.”

“You can feel it in every word Sylvia Plath writes,” she continues. “This burning need and yearning to find herself through her writing. I’ve been reading a lot of her work, including her books, essays and poems, and it’s vast. People tend to remember the drama of her story, that she had mental health struggles and a sad end. But her writing is so full of life, creativity and energy, and that’s what people tend to forget. I really hope this film can bring that back to center and celebrate her magnificent way of living.”

Variety caught up with the composer at this year’s World Soundtrack Awards in Ghent, where she was guest of honor. Hours before her trip to Belgium, Guðnadóttir was still mixing “Enemies,” the Ari Aster-produced A24 thriller. Directed by Henry Dunham and starring Jeremy Allen White and Austin Butler, the Chicago-shot cop drama let her play with urban ambient sounds.

“I find it really interesting how the sounds of the city work with the film,” she says. “I’m working a lot with environmental textures and city sounds, and how they can relate to the film’s music. Listening is always at the heart, along with my curiosity.”

Guðnadóttir would also love to return to the “28 Years Later” franchise, whenever the next installment arrives . At the World Soundtrack Awards, she described the “nerve-wracking” experience of watching the first in the new series, scored by Young Fathers, after finishing her work on Nia DaCosta’s “ 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple .”

“I never got to hear a single note or see a single frame of [Danny Boyle’s ‘28 Years Later’] while I was working [on ‘The Bone Temple’],” she says.

“I kept asking whether we should have some connective tissue between the scores, but it was a deliberate decision to keep the two completely separate. So when part one came out, I went to the cinema with everyone else. I was sitting there thinking, ‘Please work together, please work together,’ because I had already delivered my part and couldn’t change a thing. It was funny, but nerve-wracking!”

The description could apply to the series as a whole.

“The amazing thing about these stories, and about [‘The Bone Temple’] in particular, is that they look very gory, aggressive and violent, but at the same time, they’re very human, soft and funny,” she says. “I think part two is hilarious. So the question was how could the music amplify that.”

DaCosta wanted strings, while Guðnadóttir sought to counter their ethereal quality with something more grounded. Taking the film’s title literally, she turned to an unlikely source for percussion.

“I have a friend who runs a hamburger place just outside of Berlin,” she explains. “She has a good relationship with her butcher, so I got a deal to take the leftover bones. All the percussion in the film is made from bones. The shoulder bones made interesting clapping percussion, and the bigger ones suited deeper beating percussion. The smaller ones were better suited to flutes.”

Bur first, she had to prepare her instruments.

“I do everything myself, and that includes boiling the bones,” Guðnadóttir says with a smile. “I’m very hands-on.”

content.article_text:
An ancient mummy portrait has received a new restoration in Egypt ahead of a rare voyage abroad.

The work, known as the Tondo of the Two Brothers , dates back to the 2nd century and belongs to a group of paintings known as the Fayum portraits. Discovered in the titular city, they were attached to mummies of elite individuals who lived in Egypt during the Roman Period. They were painted on wooden board using the encaustic technique, in which hot wax is mixed with pigment.

The Egyptian Museum in Cairo spent three weeks restoring the tondo, working on the project with Italian conservators from the Museo dell’Ara Pacis in Rome. During that time, the restorers managed to recreate some of the features of one of the figures, whose definition had been lost to time because termites had eaten away at the painting.

The restoration also accounted for previous errors made by past experts who had touched up the painting, fixing, for example, pieces of the painting depicting the figure’s mouth and chin, which had been set in the wrong place. A video released by Egypt’s Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities details the restoration process .

The tondo will set sail for a show at the Museo dell’Ara Pacis called “ The Power of Portraiture: Egypt and Rome: Faces of Fayum ,” opening on November 5 and featuring nearly 60 works. The painting, which has never before left Egypt, is headed there alongside loans from institutions such as the Louvre in Paris.

“The restoration of the Tondo of the Two Brothers is an important example of what can be achieved through international cooperation in the preservation and study of cultural heritage,” Sherif Fathy, Egypt’s minister of tourism and antiquities, told the Associated Press . “Egypt and Italy share deep historical and cultural ties, and this project brings together Egyptian and Italian expertise to preserve an exceptional work of art for future generations.”

content.article_text:
Manhattan Beach Studios in Southern California is a pinnacle of revolutionary technology, home to both the “volume” screens where Jon Favreau filmed the “Mandalorian” franchise and Lightstorm Entertainment, where James Cameron has spent years bringing the Na’vi to life.

Tucked away at Stage 21 lies Innovative Dreams, an AI offshoot of director Jon Erwin’s Entertainment company Wonder Project. Here, chief operating officer Bryan Yee sips from a Diet Coke can as he showcases the soundstage housing Innovative Dreams’ crown jewel: a collection of LED screens where a team of AI artists weaves generative AI into productions. It’s not the first time the space has been shown to a journalist. But that it’s happened multiple times this year shows that three-quarters of the way into 2026, AI is no longer Hollywood’s ultimate bad word.

Related Stories

WWE Enters Microdrama Space With 'Agent of Shadows,' Drew McIntyre Takes Central Role

‘Sin Filtro’ Producer JK Media Producing First Original Microdramas Shot in the U.S. for TelevisaUnivision’s ViXMicrO (EXCLUSIVE)

The term “AI” has emerged as an addendum to the Hays Code, the 20th-century guidelines dictating what studios should and shouldn’t include in their films. It’s spooked the worlds of corporate and art alike, especially after months of headlines over the potentially world-ending nature of AI models and warnings that progress needs to be paced . Americans are also increasingly believing the tech is doing more harm than good, according to a recent Gallup poll .

Popular on Variety

But much like the way studios and directors of the 1960s and ’70s embraced the once-taboo profanity and nudity, this year AI has found a new wave of advocates eager to go public. The technology turned up at marquee film festivals, including Tribeca, which premiered the AI-generated docudrama “Dreams of Violets.” Oscar winner Reese Witherspoon declared that “the AI revolution has begun,” and Martin Scorsese said filmmakers had to be “open to how [film] can evolve.” George Lucas was perhaps the most blunt in a July interview: “There’s nothing you can do about it.”

Part of what’s spurred this breakthrough involves creatives getting to know the technology. Some have found it additive to their projects: Veteran producer Ryan Kavanaugh says his firm, Acme Studios, lowered the cost of Doug Liman’s film “Bitcoin” from $200 million to $70 million with the use of AI. Below-the-line costs on “Bitcoin” were brought down from $130 million to $35 million. Others have experimented with AI features or used AI tools to help with things like audio syncing. Kathleen Kennedy, who served as the president of Lucasfilm from 2012 to 2026, helped organize a group of industry dignitaries to put together a framework for how Hollywood should talk about it.

“When you have a set of tools that all of a sudden, ‘I can dream it, and I can create it, and I can show it to somebody,’ what you realize is that it heightens your creativity and did not diminish it at all,” Erwin says.

But even with such attitudinal strides, Pew Research shows that people’s fears about AI’s societal impact are high, and digital choirs hurl insults at any project featuring the tech. It’s led creatives to walk a tricky line between the wish to experiment with AI and the havoc disclosing its use can wreak.

“If the creative is great and it engages the audience on a different level than just ‘Hey, look at this thing that’s AI,’ the audience is going to understand it,” says Kathleen Grace, Lionsgate’s chief AI officer. “But it’s challenging when you lead with AI as the only hook.”

Some directors have gone all in. Oscar-winning director Steven Soderbergh sparked discourse earlier this year when he revealed how he used roughly 10 minutes of AI in his upcoming documentary “John Lennon: The Lost Interview.” He also disclosed his plans to use AI in his Wagner Moura-starring film about the Spanish-American War.

While Soderbergh recognizes AI remains a “very emotional subject,” he says the loudest voices raging against its use are those that haven’t bothered to engage with it at all. “I’ve seen the version of the John Lennon doc without that material, and I’ve seen the version with the material that we generated, and the version with that material is a better version of the movie,” Soderbergh says. “Here’s what’s really funny to me: If I told people that nine minutes and 40 seconds was VFX that took two and a half million dollars in two years, there would have been no debate at all. So what are we talking about?”

It’s a mindset that “Bourne Identity” director Liman brought to “Bitcoin,” an upcoming Casey Affleck and Gal Gadot-led picture tracing a man’s quest to prove he invented the controversial currency. The project recruited Acme, which specializes in “gray box” soundstages that host real humans while a team of 150 AI artists generates the location imagery and lighting.

Liman, according to Jed Weintrob, the CEO of Liman’s content studio 30 Ninjas, “likes to push the envelope” and thinks AI tools can be “real superchargers for storytellers.” “We’re creating a world that would be almost financially impossible to make without this technology,” he says.

Kavanaugh claims the industry shift toward embracing AI was caused by Liman’s decision to go public with his use of it. After the initial disclosure, Acme took several meetings with a mix of studios and filmmakers eager to understand how a project managed to dramatically lower costs. (Kavanaugh wouldn’t disclose the names of the group.)

After those meetings, Kavanaugh says, the creatives realized that “we’re not killing the art; we’re enhancing the art.“ He adds, “It’s making it more efficient. It’s creating better tool sets. And all of a sudden, we really saw a big shift … from people that we thought were going to be like, ‘No, we can’t do that,’ to ‘Well, can we use it in this show?’”

Still, such curiosity doesn’t mean all-encompassing acceptance — either by the industry or the audiences that sustain it. This summer alone saw the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences disqualify synthetic performers and AI-written scripts from awards consideration, while the Cannes Film Festival issued a blanket ban on AI-generated productions. When the Urbanworld Film Festival said in June it would accept AI-generated productions for its 30th edition, the Writers Guild of America ended its long-standing sponsorship. The move was consistent with the union’s concerns about the improper use of AI, but it was a choice Urbanworld CEO Stacy Spikes says risks creating a “very slippery slope” — after all, should anyone dictate what tools aspiring filmmakers can experiment with?

Actors have taken action against the harmful effects of AI. Soderbergh endorsed the Human Consent Foundation, a nonprofit cofounded by Cate Blanchett in June, that created a database where people are encouraged to register how their likenesses can or can’t be pulled by AI models. Blanchett told Variety at the time that while the registry may not revolutionize how people engage with AI, “the more people adopt it, the more chance it has of making a real impact.” She added, “We do have to start somewhere, because thoughtlessness is the enemy of creativity.”

Audiences have also revolted against AI’s intersection with Hollywood, criticizing the initially undisclosed use of the technology for a sequence in Eli Roth’s horror film “Ice Cream Man” and a marketing campaign featuring podcasting dogs for Warner Bros. Discovery’s “The End of Oak Street.”

Jeffrey Katzenberg, the veteran Hollywood executive who wrote a 2,377-word essay on X last month urging the film industry to work with Silicon Valley and responsibly adopt the technology, says he’s noticed a pervasive sense of “concern and fear” surrounding AI’s presence in Hollywood. The resistance mimics what he calls a pattern of averting “innovation and change.” But, he warns, “to resist technology is to risk irrelevance.”

Katzenberg is entering the fray himself, developing an AI animation studio that will serve as a vehicle for tools he thinks the industry can adopt. But he hopes to also create a project that could spur a true sentiment shift in the way “Toy Story,” created by his former studio Pixar, did for CGI in the ’90s. “We’ll all know when we see it,” Katzenberg says. “Tools are never the point. What matters is taste, creativity and imagination.”

For Hollywood to progress, Katzenberg says, it has to accept the wave of change — and progress — AI can bring. It’s part of the ethos of his AI animation studio, capitalizing on what he sees as “a true renaissance for Hollywood storytelling” and “a complete transformation of all forms of video creation.”

Walking the tightrope between acceptance and resistance puts studios, eager to save money with AI, in a bind. How do you greenlight original stories that may use AI when faced with audiences and creatives wary of the technology? “I don’t really know,” one AI-adopting studio executive admits.

But a lot of people’s consternation, the executive says, comes from how U.S. political leaders and tech executives are handling the messaging surrounding AI and fears around its impact on jobs, a factor those in Hollywood have little control over. “Right now, the political context of it would be “Well, gee, if you used AI, you displace people’s jobs. You would have hired 1,000 people rather than 100,’” the executive says. “Yeah, that’s probably true.” But, he claims, studios can now make 10 times as many projects due to the efficiency of AI. And more projects will ultimately amount to the same number of people working. No one can argue with the fact that the industry will benefit from having more stories to tell.

Hollywood’s next battle? Getting the AI-powered work produced by industry professionals to resonate with audiences, as opposed to the online video slop made by people without industry experience.

“The reality is the excellence that you see in cinematic storytelling is because there are creators, directors, filmmakers, costume designers, production designers,” the executive says. “They think very deeply [about] what that experience is going to be. The people creating the slop have not thought deeply about it.”

content.article_text:
Oscilloscope Laboratories has acquired U.S. rights to the psychosexual thriller “ Act One ” from writer-director Sophia Takal (“Always Shine,” “Black Christmas”), and will release it in theaters in 2027.

“Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story” star Ella Beatty will play the leading role of Hannah, a sheltered seventeen-year-old aspiring actress. “Act One” follows Hannah as she joins an elite acting studio led by its magnetic founder, Melanie (Ari Graynor). Per the press release, “Drawn to Melanie’s intensity and increasingly extreme methods, Hannah throws herself into the work. But as dedication turns to obsession and the lines between performance, desire and manipulation blur, she is pulled into a dangerous game that tests how far she’ll go to become the artist she wants to be.”

Related Stories

Open to AI: Hollywood Is Embracing Artificial Intelligence Tools Despite Doomsday Fears

The film also stars Sinclair Daniel (“Insidious: The Red Door”), Tavi Gevinson (“Gossip Girl”), Elizabeth Reaser (“Twilight”) and Robert Sean Leonard (“House”).

Popular on Variety

“I’m thrilled Oscilloscope is releasing ‘Act One,’” Takal said. “Getting to work with them again after ‘Always Shine’ feels like a homecoming. It’s heartening to know there are people out there with the taste, nerve and good sense to champion movies like ours. I can’t wait for audiences to see the incredible work of all the talented people who made this film!”

The film debuted at Tribeca Festival on June 10. “Act One” is produced by Takal, Allison Rose Carter (Savage Rose Films), Julie Christeas (Tandem Pictures), Jon Read (Savage Rose Films), Stephanie Roush (Foxglove Films), and Julie Waters (Watermark Media). Executive producers are Evan Dyal of Watermark Media, Ryan Kampe of Visit Films, Lawrence Michael Levine, Allison and Jon Stockel and Marilyn White.

content.article_text:
E xactly 13 years ago this month, Tom Rhys Harries was hanging by his ankles from a meat hook every night. Playing a teenage rock’n’roll idol abducted by gangsters in a revival of Jez Butterworth’s Mojo, Harries was fresh out of drama school and the only unknown in a cast led by Ben Whishaw and Rupert Grint. The Guardian’s Michael Billington likened him to “an embryonic Elvis”.

Now the 36-year-old Cardiff-born actor has the title role in Clayface, a violent DC Comics supervillain blockbuster set in Batman’s stomping ground, Gotham City. This puts him in the company of fellow Brits in the comic-book universe, such as Tom Holland (Spider-Man), Robert Pattinson (Batman) and David Jonsson, recently announced as the new Black Panther. “I felt ready to do this,” says Harries. “Had I been younger, I’d have been suffocated by the insecurity of wanting to do a good job but not having that quiet trust in getting there.”

Harries is speaking over video call from the beach-adjacent Los Angeles home he shares with his girlfriend, Amy Allen. She is the professional musician of the two: songwriter of the year at the Grammys two years running, no less, for her work with Sabrina Carpenter and others. It is Harries, though, who is giving rock star this morning, even all this time after Mojo, in his grey denim shirt with a silver chain against tanned skin and assorted silver rings on his fingers. Stadium-rocker pomposity, however, is in short supply. Standing up to shut the door, he draws attention to his fashion faux pas. “I’ve got a smart shirt on but then these ,” he laughs, gesturing to his navy-blue shorts. “Party on the bottom, business on top. Classic Zoom.”

Harries has earned the right to relax. He spent three months auditioning to play the severely mutilated protagonist of Clayface for producers James Gunn (Guardians of the Galaxy) and Matt Reeves (The Batman). How did he stay sane all that time? “I didn’t.”

His character is rising star Matt Hagen, who has just received his first Oscar nomination when he sleeps with the girlfriend of a razor-wielding mob boss and pays the price. His face slashed to ribbons and his career in tatters, Matt’s only hope lies with scientist Dr Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie) and her miracle serum. This restores his good looks and gives him the power to change his appearance at will but comes with unstable side effects. In one scene, his eyelids melt, forcing him to snip away at the resulting sticky mess with a pair of nail scissors. Described by Harries as “the film’s tipping point of ickiness”, it is a moment that will be triggering for any conjunctivitis sufferers and plain disgusting for everyone else.

Closer to horror than anything in the superhero canon, Clayface is a cross between Darkman , in which Liam Neeson is a disfigured scientist who creates synthetic faces, and The Substance , the Demi Moore gross-out satire on ageing, vanity and celebrity. Despite being a pretty-boy actor playing a pretty-boy actor, Harries shrugs off any personal resonance in his own film about losing face. “I’m not interested in the vanity of it.” His looks, he says, “just happen to be an aspect of my work”.

A perceptive actor he may be but it is his otherworldly appearance which grabs you: penetrating eyes, a square, sinewy face, defiant chin and floppy vanilla hair. What does he see when he looks in the mirror? “I don’t know, man,” he says, squirming at the thought of analysing his own appearance. It has been integral, though, to films such as the 2016 folk horror Crow , where he exuded a Bowie-esque alien quality as a woodland-dwelling teenage mystic. “A Bowie-esque alien quality,” he muses. “You’re not the first person to say that. It’s not for me to comment on. I would hit a creative roadblock very quickly if I got too mired in aesthetics.”

Bowie was also a reference point in Harries’s first film role in 2011. Not only was Hunky Dory, starring Minnie Driver as an inspirational teacher, named after one of the singer’s albums, it also boasted a scene in which Harries leads his classmates in a mandolin-and-brass-tinged rendition of The Man Who Sold the World. Screen International singled out Harries as the cast member who “may ultimately become the star here”.

He was oblivious to the buzz. “And yet I’ve got negative reviews seared into my mind.” Proving his point, he quotes one from his early days. “It said, ‘Newcomer Tom Rhys Harries is out of his depth’. I read that and thought, ‘I don’t know if I’m going to get out of bed today’.”

The son of two teachers at Welsh-language schools, Harries has his parents to thank for being “ahead of the curve” in getting him tested for ADHD at the age of seven. “I don’t think I would be doing this job if I didn’t have ADHD. I notice traits within myself that I think are fairly commonplace with [the condition]. If I’m interested in something, I will hyper-fixate on it. That’s born out of a kind of peacefulness in being able to zero in on one thing because it gives your brain a rest.”

School was a struggle. “I was very naughty. I can really see a fork in the road where, had I not been supported by teachers and mentors, my life could have gone in a different direction.” That realisation instilled in him the need to prove himself. “It’s about repaying those people,” he says.

He “fell into” drama school, aced the audition for Hunky Dory in his first year, went from Bowie to Elvis with Mojo and has been building his career ever since: he took posh-boy roles in the horror-comedy Slaughterhouse Rulez , where he was a boarding-school bully, and the TV kidnapping whodunit Suspicion , opposite Uma Thurman. He went wild as an Ibiza DJ who meets a nasty end in the Netflix murder mystery White Lines , then joined Ralph Fiennes and Juliette Binoche in The Return , a Homer adaptation which pipped The Odyssey to the post.

Still, he has never had a showcase like Clayface. The gooey, grisly special effects may be the main attraction but the movie would count for little without his notes of rage, torment and vulnerability.

There is no escaping the fact, though, that Clayface arrives at a precarious time for any comic book movie not featuring Batman, Spider-Man or the Avengers. Box office disasters such as The Marvels , Joker: Folie à Deux and Supergirl , Clayface’s recent DC Comics stablemate which is predicted to lose more than $100m , indicate that fatigue has set in.

On this matter, Harries’s glass is half full. “That’s what excites me about Clayface,” he says. “It is trying to do something different in a space that is asking for that. The medium needs a shake-up and I hope that people feel they can support the film purely on the basis that it will allow studios the confidence to experiment.”

It seems unlikely, in the wake of the costly Tom Cruise catastrophe Digger and the recent Warner Bros-Paramount merger, that studios will be in the mood to do anything but play it safe, irrespective of whether Clayface triumphs or tanks. “Who’s to say? No one would have expected Backrooms or Obsession to come out of nowhere and do what they did. It’s such an unknown quantity.”

Time will tell if Harries is any kind of industry prognosticator but a star he undoubtedly is. Face it.

content.article_text:
La representante de RJ Mitte confirmó este martes que el actor, reconocido mundialmente por interpretar a Walter “Flynn” White Jr. en Breaking Bad , murió por suicidio el lunes 12 de octubre en su residencia de Brownsville, Texas. El artista tenía 34 años.

Según informó el Departamento de Policía de Brownsville (BPD), los agentes recibieron una llamada alrededor de las 12:50 del mediodía, hora local, y encontraron al intérprete sin vida en su domicilio. En un primer comunicado, las autoridades habían señalado que la causa y la manera de la muerte permanecían pendientes mientras avanzaba la investigación.

“Es con profunda tristeza que compartimos el trágico fallecimiento del querido actor, filántropo y apasionado defensor de los derechos de las personas con discapacidad RJ Mitte”, expresó su representante en un comunicado sobre el actor de Breaking Bad . Luego, se conoció que el intérprete decidió quitarse la vida .

RJ Mitte, el actor que interpretó al hijo de Walter White en Breaking Bad

Mitte alcanzó reconocimiento internacional gracias a su participación en Breaking Bad , la aclamada producción creada por Vince Gilligan que se emitió por AMC entre 2008 y 2013. A lo largo de sus cinco temporadas, el actor apareció en 56 de los 62 episodios de la serie, en los que interpretó al hijo adolescente de Walter White, el personaje de Bryan Cranston.

El intérprete había sido diagnosticado con parálisis cerebral durante su infancia, una condición que compartía con su personaje . Esa experiencia personal le permitió aportar autenticidad a su actuación y, con el tiempo, convertirse en una voz reconocida en la defensa de los derechos de las personas con discapacidad.

“Partiendo de su propia experiencia viviendo con parálisis cerebral, Mitte aportó autenticidad al papel y construyó una plataforma en torno a la concienciación sobre la discapacidad y la inclusión”, agregó su representante.

Todo sobre “Pluribus”, la nueva serie del creador de Breaking Bad que es furor

Fuera de la pantalla, el actor también desarrolló una importante labor solidaria. Se desempeñó como embajador de United Cerebral Palsy y de Shriners Children’s, además de presidir The Mitte Foundation, una organización dedicada a respaldar iniciativas filantrópicas y comunitarias.

The Mitte Cultural District también le dedicó unas palabras de despedida y lo recordó como un “querido amigo y dedicado defensor de las artes”. La institución destacó su compromiso con Brownsville y el aporte que realizó a la comunidad a través de la cultura.

“Fue un amigo, un socio y alguien que genuinamente creyó en el poder de las artes y la cultura para unir a las personas”, expresó la organización.

Bryan Cranston despidió a RJ Mitte

La noticia generó numerosas muestras de cariño por parte de sus compañeros de Breaking Bad . Bryan Cranston, quien interpretó a su padre en la ficción, compartió un extenso mensaje en redes sociales para recordar al actor y expresar su dolor por la pérdida.

Cranston contó que conoció a Mitte cuando tenía apenas 14 años, luego de que fuera elegido para interpretar a Walter White Jr. En su publicación, destacó la determinación con la que afrontó los desafíos de su condición y el compromiso que mantuvo durante el rodaje.

“Nunca —jamás— permitió que ese desafío fuera una excusa para nada. Afrontó el exigente calendario de rodaje con gran determinación”, escribió el actor.

Sin embargo, uno de los aspectos más dolorosos del mensaje estuvo relacionado con el vínculo que ambos habían mantenido a lo largo de los años, incluso después de que terminara la serie.

“Es especialmente devastador saber que se quitó la vida”, expresó Cranston. “¿Por qué? Nos estábamos enviando mensajes de texto hace apenas unas semanas, buscando cuándo podríamos almorzar juntos”.

El intérprete también reflexionó sobre ese último encuentro que habían intentado organizar y sobre el cariño que sentía por su compañero.

“No sé si ese almuerzo habría cambiado su futuro… Pero sé que lo amé y disfruté plenamente estar con él durante todos esos años en la serie, y después de que el foco de Breaking Bad se apagara… Te voy a extrañar, hijo”, concluyó.

View this post on Instagram

Al final de su publicación, Cranston compartió información sobre la línea 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, destinada a brindar asistencia a personas que atraviesan una crisis en Estados Unidos, y dejó un mensaje de esperanza.

También hicieron lo propio Paul y Norris

Dean Norris , quien interpretó a Hank Schrader en la ficción, también expresó su tristeza por la muerte de Mitte. El actor recordó el vínculo que había construido con él durante las grabaciones y el cariño con el que lo acompañó desde sus primeros años en el set.

“Estoy destrozado. Aunque RJ no interpretaba a mi hijo en la ficción, siempre lo cuidé como a un chico joven en el set. Era un joven de buen corazón y se lo va a extrañar mucho. Esto es tan desgarrador, no puedo creerlo. Pienso en él y en su familia”, escribió.

View this post on Instagram

Por su parte, Aaron Paul, quien dio vida a Jesse Pinkman, manifestó estar “sin palabras” tras conocer la noticia y le dedicó un mensaje a su compañero.

“Estoy destrozado por esta noticia. RJ, te quiero, amigo mío. Te vamos a extrañar. Y a quien esté leyendo esto: sepan que son amados y que no están solos. Recuérdenlo siempre”, expresó.

La muerte de RJ Mitte deja un profundo dolor entre sus compañeros y seguidores de Breaking Bad , una serie que marcó su carrera y lo convirtió en una figura reconocida por su trabajo artístico y su compromiso con la inclusión.

content.article_text:
Communiqué – collaboration commerciale avec l’Institut français.

Les Princes noirs de Saint-Germain-des-Prés (1975)

Fraichement débarqués dans la capitale, des jeunes hommes originaires d’Afrique de l’Ouest, chiquement sapés mais fauchés, séduisent les Parisiennes en se faisant passer pour les riches héritiers de royaumes légendaires. Derrière sa mélodie afro-jazz légère et nonchalante, le film du Sénégalais Ben Diogaye Beye se joue de la persistance des stéréotypes et fantasmes coloniaux.

Bal poussière (1988)

Surnommé Demi-Dieu, un riche agriculteur règne en maître sur ses cinq épouses, et décide d’en épouser une sixième. Mais Binta, jeune femme indépendante revenue de la ville, compte bien imposer ses propres règles. Succès à l’international, cette comédie de mœurs féministe et jouissive de l’Ivoirien Henri Duparc dénonce avec humour la polygamie, interdite en Côte d’Ivoire depuis 1964.

Le retour d’un aventurier (1966)

De retour de chez l’Oncle Sam, Jimmy offre des costumes de cow-boys à ses amis, qui commencent à semer le chaos dans leur village. Drôlatique, cette parodie de western du Nigérien Moustapha Alassane, cinéaste pionnier du continent africain, tourne en dérision la fascination pour les mythes venus d’Amérique, tout en moquant les conflits de générations qui traversent une société en pleine mutation.

Mouna ou le rêve d’un artiste (1969)

Dès ses débuts, Henri Duparc s’est distingué par sa manière inédite, et un peu folle, de raconter ses histoires, à la fois décalées et pleinement ancrées dans le quotidien de la société ivoirienne. Dans son premier moyen-métrage, il mêle ainsi humour, satire et fantastique en mettant en scène un sculpteur de masques à la dérive, dont le délire grandissant finit par donner vie à ses créations.

La Chapelle (1979)

Demeuré invisible pendant près de cinquante ans avant sa restauration en 2023, ce film du Congolais Jean-Michel Tchissoukou, l’un des premiers tournés après l’indépendance du pays, croque avec humour la confrontation, dans la première moitié du XXe siècle, entre les religions africaines traditionnelles et l’Église catholique, autour de la laborieuse construction d’une chapelle.

The DNA of a 29-year-old left on a protective painting cover helped investigators identify a prime suspect in the September 8 theft of two Pierre-Auguste Renoir paintings from the artist’s former home-turned-museum in southern France, reports Le Figaro . That person eventually led investigators to a second suspect and to the admission that the paintings were hidden behind a wall in another accomplice’s home. Three out of four suspects were already known to police for other crimes. The two stolen paintings were recovered in record time, but one, “Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano,” was torn and needs restoration, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone told reporters. He estimated both recovered works are worth about $4.7 million. Investigators also discovered that one of the first suspects, age 29, recently visited the Maeght Foundation in Saint-Paul-de-Vence with the alleged intention of planning another burglary at the modern and contemporary art institution. The giveaway? As detectives followed his trail, the suspect met with a fourth person known to authorities for art theft and forgery. Police soon swooped in, given the “very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent,” said Bessone. The two men suspected of nabbing the Renoir paintings have been charged with “theft committed by an organized gang,” but insist they are innocent. The third suspect admitted to receiving and hiding the two Renoirs. To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

Good morning!

DNA of thief left on a protective painting cover helped investigators identify a prime suspect in the theft of two Auguste Renoir paintings.

Johnny Depp ‘s London exhibition opens at the Halcyon Gallery, who now also represents him.

Morocco has opened the first publicly funded museum dedicated to over 2,500 years of local Jewish history in the town of Fes.

The Headlines

CRACKED CASE. The DNA of a 29-year-old left on a protective painting cover helped investigators identify a prime suspect in the September 8 theft of two Pierre-Auguste Renoir paintings from the artist’s former home-turned-museum in southern France, reports Le Figaro . That person eventually led investigators to a second suspect and to the admission that the paintings were hidden behind a wall in another accomplice’s home. Three out of four suspects were already known to police for other crimes. The two stolen paintings were recovered in record time, but one, “Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano,” was torn and needs restoration, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone told reporters. He estimated both recovered works are worth about $4.7 million. Investigators also discovered that one of the first suspects, age 29, recently visited the Maeght Foundation in Saint-Paul-de-Vence with the alleged intention of planning another burglary at the modern and contemporary art institution. The giveaway? As detectives followed his trail, the suspect met with a fourth person known to authorities for art theft and forgery. Police soon swooped in, given the “very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent,” said Bessone. The two men suspected of nabbing the Renoir paintings have been charged with “theft committed by an organized gang,” but insist they are innocent. The third suspect admitted to receiving and hiding the two Renoirs. REPRESENTING DEPP. Johnny Depp is taking his art career seriously and it seems so is the London-based Halcyon Gallery, who now represent the actor alongside names such as Bob Dylan, Dominic Haris and Ernesto Cánovas, reported Arts & Collection . On Sunday, the gallery teased New Bond Street with a larger-than-life facade featuring Depp’s art, which is on display from today through to November 15. “Johnny Depp is a defining cultural icon with a unique artistic vision. Known for his unparalleled ability to connect with audiences through the authenticity of his characters, an encounter with Depp, the artist, is equally compelling,” said Paul Green, president and founder of Halcyon. “Depp has drawn and painted his whole life and we’re very proud at Halcyon to be hosting his first major exhibition in the UK.”

The Digest

Morocco has opened a publicly funded museum dedicated to over 2,500 years of local Jewish history in the town of Fes, marking the first of its kind in an Arab-Muslim country. [ Le Figaro ]

The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pools are finally being refilled with water, after President Trump ’s rushed renovation left the newly painted pool floor peeling off in large chunks, which the administration continues to allege was caused by vandals. [ The Washington Post ]

The University of Amsterdam ’s museum has returned a third-century BC vase to Sicily, nine years after Italy requested its restitution, and due to its “problematic” provenance. [ The Art Newspaper ]

Influential Berlin art dealer Matthias Arndt has opened an “art salon” in Athens, and says the city reminds him of Berlin in the 1990s for its “spirit of optimism” and creative output. [ Die Welt ]

As his sound installation titled 66 76 26 opens at the Guggenheim Bilbao, Steve McQueen tells reporters, “We live in an era where we talk about AI, we talk about the fear factor—because there is a lot of fear around us right now, with the rise of fascism in the West—and for me, what’s interesting at this moment is the idea of love… it becomes fundamental.” [ El Pais ]

The Kicker

WHERE WERE THE WOMEN? Artist Prune Nourry is bringing back forgotten women sculptors in art history, through her forthcoming show, Visionaries , at the Petit Palais museum in Paris, on view October 20 to January 24, she told the Financial Times . “I was invited to the Petit Palais museum in Paris about two years ago, and walking through its galleries I realized that most of the sculptures represented women—often as muses or models—but only 4 percent of the artworks were created by women,” Nourry said. This led her to research little-known women sculptors from the 19th and early 20th centuries, who worked at a time when French art schools were barred to women. Then, Nourry sculpted their portraits using her free interpretations. In over a year and a half, she made 18 busts of women. This is then put in dialogue with Nourry’s other artworks around the theme of women as mythological beings. The show “is about learning to look in a direction where art history hasn’t looked enough, and also to see through the eyes of those women at that time—to reflect on today, and realize how much we owe them,” she said.

“I was lucky to be alive when things were happening,” says James Barnor. Accra on the eve of independence, London in the days of the Beatles: reason enough to call himself Lucky Jim. A lucky man, in short ( Lucky Jim is also a Kingsley Amis novel, published in 1954, different era, same vein). At 97, he headlines an opening that doubles as a housewarming.

At 51, rue Saint-Louis-en-l’Île, Galerie Clémentine de la Féronnière reopens after several weeks of work. More than 250 m² (about 2,700 square feet) of exhibition space extending from the street-front bookshop, a showroom, an office dedicated to digitizing and consulting photographic collections: the back room has taken on the air of an archive reading room. The choice of guest was obvious. Since 2015, the team has worked on James Barnor’s archive, sorted and catalogued with him on site between 2017 and 2021. A long-haul loyalty.

There is a certain delight in finding James Barnor in his own pictures, the man who spent his life composing other people’s. Accra, 1952: a young father dressed all in white, straight as a rod against a whitewashed wall, he holds his son Daniel in his christening gown. That same year, on assignment for the Daily Graphic , he leans over a staircase banister, twin-lens camera in hand and saucer flash at the ready, a friend with a cigarette on his lips playing prompter. Dressed to the nines, already.

Then England. James Barnor landed in Liverpool on December 1, 1959, and worked night shifts in a factory alongside a Ghanaian boxer, Attuquaye Clottey, who thought he was mad to have left his studio. In 1960 came Dennis Kemp, a lecturer for Kodak: “Look I can offer you board and lodging but no pay,” he told him (Barnor recalled it in 2019). His friend photographed him draped in his kente, leaning on an “England” road sign in Shropshire, motorbike parked in the hedge, or seated beneath a giant “CAFÉ” sign. The ease of a prince on tour.

Back in Accra in the late 1960s, James Barnor was hired by Agfa-Gevaert to set up the country’s first color lab. There he posed an assistant among bottles of developing chemicals, pink, green, white, coral, in place of a color chart. A makeshift swatch book, mischief intact. Elsewhere, a grid of 12 frames shot at the Agfa-Gevaert laboratory in Mortsel, Belgium: he slips in beside a model in a striped top, then takes the colored backdrop alone. Self-portrait as a diligent student.

On October 22, the Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain opens “Le temps des récoltes” (The Time of Harvests) by Ibrahim Mahama, which includes the “Agip” series, made for the brand’s 1974 calendar. The occasion for James Barnor’s return to Paris. “I’m lucky to be alive and to be telling the story about my work,” he says. Lucky Jim, still.

James Barnor, “Lucky Jim” is on view through November 21, 2026 at Galerie Clémentine de la Féronnière , Paris.

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "quote", "text": "“What requires attention in cinema are the traces of these palpable things ingrained on the cinematic surface.” — Shiguéhiko Hasumi, Directed by Yasujirō Ozu “That everyone in the world, including myself, is totally nuts.” — Nathan Fielder in a 2014 Reddit AMA responding to the question “Nathan, what has your show taught you about human nature?”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/tfs-criticspick-star-orange.png", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Let’s agree Lev Kuleshov was wise to stress a performer’s expression. If Samuel Fuller was also correct for stating, vis-à-vis Jean-Luc Godard, that the love, hate, violence, action, and death strewn across cinema’s battleground all lead towards emotion, we can Frankenstein these two notions into the concept, monstrous or otherwise, that great directors winnow both intellectual and instinctual fascinations to the human face. Ozu found much of human experience within the pained half-smile; Kubrick externalized id through the head-down, eyes-up glare; “Lynchian,” seemingly indefinable, is often defined by fear in the eyes; Spielberg asks that the eyes (and mouth) go wide to convey awe; Buster Keaton wore a stone face that only the scariest stunts a filmmaker has ever put themselves through would break, and just into a sort of bafflement."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nathan Fielder has the uncomprehending stare. The very real people encountered throughout Nathan for You and The Rehearsal tend to look at him—or “Nathan Fielder,” a composite between auteur and selfsame character—half-blank, half-concerned. Sometimes it’s contempt only quelled for the sake of a camera; at other turns it’s an uneasy facsimile of politeness towards this strange man who’s placing an impossible scenario before them; and often their sole recourse is a low-power autopilot. You can find this a hilarious, incisive vision of human behavior or wholly unpleasant showcase for its creator’s misanthropy—these are such questions prodded by artists of serious intent."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nathan Fielder now wears the uncomprehending stare. He’s directing it at Elizabeth Holmes in the days before her 11-year imprisonment over a nine-figure defrauding for her blood-testing project Theranos, a scam orchestrated at such uncommon size that it must be made into the harshest example. Why she and her husband have trusted Fielder, a constant chronicler of errant human behavior, to craft a sympathetic portrayal of her ostensible plight is never quite clear. Holmes, resembling a Chuck Jones cartoon and sounding like she’s just overcome airway constriction, returns a stare that’s not so much uncomprehending as it is incomprehensible . Her vague visage creates an organizing principle: not just for the basic film-grammar question of when to cut between hers and Fielder’s, but how this face, even once cut from, seems to echo and radiate across the scene."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I was thinking about the ping-ponging point-counterpoint between people’s faces—Fielder and Holmes and her husband and some others who show up—through many of the 174 minutes comprising You Can See Everything , his often-extraordinary feature-filmmaking debut during which nearly every expression that can be made with a person’s eyes will occur and recur to our amusement, if not knowledge. A camera has seldom fixated so hard on expressions to crack what is (or might be) resting beneath the surface. It stares and stares and stares : at faces, their musculature, at eyes, their shifts through smiles or frowns, the device like an interrogator forcing a confession or a psychic trying to explode a head. You Can See Everything is vertiginous in its staticity, a concentric circle that expands or contracts by the smallest brush of discomfort; it operates through an inability to manage its own tasks, entering a cocktail-napkin-sized pantheon of films that succeed so brilliantly on the basis of failure."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Though co-directed by Lance Oppenheim—whose involvement Fielder obviously did nothing to discount during a post-screening Q&A, and which one can connect to nothing less than a film du jour —it’s nigh impossible envisioning You Can See Everything as (co-)made by anyone else (or, pending availability, the ghost of Abbas Kiarostami). It is also, by all counts, Fielder’s inaugural time playing straight. This is evident quickly, if not quite instantly: the first laugh earned at a beyond-sold-out New York Film Festival premiere was not from Holmes’ several appearances throughout the opening minute, but from Fielder, and just part of him—an obscured face making what any neophyte would naturally read as a resting expression. It’s a fair-enough response when taken hand-in-hand with the serious-documentary form (slightly overbearing music, greyscale color-grading) this movie wears like an odd suit, and one from which we see the paradox in being a major artist: the deeper one goes to establish their own style, the less a devotee’s willing to let them turn elsewhere.", "links": [{"text": "a film du jour", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/venice-review-lance-oppenheims-primetime-is-a-thrilling-indictment/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But it can be hard, once an admirer, to discuss Nathan Fielder without lapsing into overly fawning, even obsequious tones. Yet Nathan for You is replete with Fielder seeming to possess some frightening, Dr. Mabuse-esque capacity for bending reality to his will; it’s no exaggeration to say turning these powers for persuasion and problem-solving towards evil could engender global catastrophe. The authorities exhibited therein haven’t burned quite as bright in the nine years since: The Rehearsal , for whatever honest greatness it has achieved, can suffer in comparison—a tad too strong the sense of controlled experiment, a tad too many seams visible in its editorial practice. You Can See Everything left me considering Fielder’s genius as choosing when or when not to engineer. Acknowledging that this film simply couldn’t have been made in real time or without certain stretches built on careful organization, it’s also his first project since Nathan for You that has the quality and danger of open-air experiment. The camera is not just turned on, we know full well; but once it is and allowed to rest on a subject facing direct, difficult questions, Fielder’s skills for social manipulation thrives on a Rick Rubin-like let-them-be-them philosophy. In a world where everyone, including himself, is totally nuts, Elizabeth Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, just happen to be so on another level. Who inches the other out is a question you may be asking while reading this, then will continue asking after You Can See Everything ."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I’ve been less fascinated with Elizabeth Holmes, whom I only knew to identify circa The Dropout , a 2022 miniseries that starred Amanda Seyfried as the turtleneck-wearing, mottle-throated scammer. I say this to establish a personal bias—likely less than many will bring—that shapes my sense You Can See Everything ’s first stretch lacks much of its own. What these scenes (some built on candid conversation, some a tad more structured) instead exemplify is Fielder’s genius for the open-air investigation—often through his own failure to explain why he’s in Holmes’ seaside house to begin with, and from the contradiction borne of respecting those who have opened their doors but, in so doing, expose habits for which respect is an uneasy match."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Holmes, facing an incredibly harsh future on the basis of her mendacity, stands by the remarkable insistence that she’s never lied. Evans, amidst postures as a nice and caring husband, quickly steps in when his wife can’t whisk eggs fast enough, forcing Fielder to break his interrogation mid-sentence. Holmes claims ignorance towards the notion that words might have more than one direct meaning, leaving her equal parts helpless to explain Theranos’ failure or understand “Who’s on First?” while nevertheless—or for this?—grasping the depth of her situation. Evans downplays the extent of his family’s wealth when Fielder suggests it’s attractive to an erstwhile-billionaire wife. Holmes sends Fielder a text that is both the source for this film’s title and, despite my best efforts to parse, completely incoherent to the conversation they’ve just had or anything I might tether to greater happenings. Evans insists he’s prioritizing spousal care, a performance that spurs disturbing questions amidst his resistance to cooperate during the film’s second half. Or a second half that blooms exclusively through his cooperation and willingness to share (for his sake, for the film’s, for nothing’s) revelation after revelation.", "links": [{"text": "the extent of his family’s wealth", "url": "https://growjo.com/company/Evans_Hotels_San_Diego"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These and many such perplexities abound until we witness Holmes enter prison from behind and afar, vanishing at You Can See Everything near-exact halftime. Whether Fielder and Oppenheim knew where to go next isn’t so obvious. A “Two Years Later” title card launches us from the spring 2023 to late 2025, and subjects now viewing the material we’ve sat through certainly implies thorough editing in that interim. What then ensues deserves discussion and, I’m sorry to say, is highly discouraged from such. The NYFF Q&A began with a notice that it a) should not be recorded by us and b) would not be made public until after the film’s release, a two-factor security system that still found Fielder and Oppenheim cautious to name any person or thing relevant to their movie’s second half."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Suffice to say, Fielder’s career-long investigation-through-recreation method is a more-than-suitable tool for You Can See Everything ’s well-established perspective on duplicity and sycophancy. Nor is it some deep spoiler to note that other figures will, almost by necessity of length, enter the frame. How that front-and-centering alters alchemy is a deeper quandary.
