content.article_text:
T his small-town police thriller sets its stall out intriguingly, with a murder that seems actively begging to be solved. The perp chose to dump his victim – the 14-year-old daughter of a local political bigwig – into a part of the Mississippi River where she was likely to resurface, and from a highly visible bridge. When veteran detective Alan Kramer (Devon Sawa) and rookie forensic psychologist Amelia Pembrock (Maggie Grace) show up to investigate, they are immediately alerted to a gun in the bushes just yards away. As a colleague observes: “This isn’t a clean-up. It’s a message.”

But Brando Benetton’s debut film sadly fails to capitalise on the misdirection at play in this open-goal crime scene. Instead of using it to pry open community secrets, he gives us a ropey and implausible manhunt. As Kramer and Pembrock race to locate the girl’s twin, who is presumably still in the killer’s clutches, they zero in on local butcher Boris (Darron Dunbar). He has a sex-pest rap sheet and lives with his mother – which apparently ticks all the boxes for a profiling genius such as Pembrock. Kramer pulls her up for being unbothered by the lack of actual prosecutable evidence. But carping is about the only investigative contribution this seasoned criminologist makes here (and what’s a criminologist – a crime sociologist – doing out in the field anyway?).

If the killer leaves behind a parody of a crime scene, The Girl in the River offers up its own parody noir, though in a cliche-strewn and far less careful fashion. We have the obsessive desk jockey, the boozy, trauma-harbouring vet halfway out the retirement door, Tiffany Haddish’s angry black captain (as satirised in the Jump Street franchise), and the affable town coroner (The Karate Kid’s Ralph Macchio). Whenever the detectives are floundering, the over-directed script is always on hand to put them back on the rails. The local media seem strangely willing to share their voluminous stash of damning evidence; a transparently staged mutiny among the townsfolk fires up Kramer and Pembrock just as they’re out of leads.

Grace, with her twitchy defensiveness, and the frazzled Sawa manage to half-ballast this dubious sleuthing, and Benetton keeps the film moving fast enough so the many infelicities don’t register too horrifically. But with no time to accumulate any proper gravitas, Kramer’s capstone speech about universal corruption is, like the victim, dead in the water.

content.article_text:
I n the 1990s, the late Chicana artist Laura Aguilar was living with depression. A friend took her on a road trip to New Mexico, where Aguilar made some nude self-portraits in the mystical landscapes. Those photographs evolved into a pivotal series shot in desert environments across the American south-west, Aguilar’s notable 1996 Nature Self-Portrait – considered an early work of intersectional feminist art, before the word had entered academic discourse.

London gallery Autograph first worked on an exhibition of Aguilar’s in 1997, the year after she made Nature Self-Portrait, so this is something of a homecoming, a generation on. Aguilar’s contours, folds, and crevices sometimes disappear into the barren desert landscapes, assimilating the shapes of boulders or trees; at other times, her body is incongruous, soft flesh that can’t be held by the harsh, barren conditions. These images capture the paradox of a body that is both hypervisible and ignored.

Several works from Nature Self-Portrait appear at the beginning of Our Bodies Have Been Bridges, Autograph’s new three-person headline show. They’re so quiet and minimal, shot in black and white, they’d be easy to coast past – which is partly Aguilar’s point. Bodies like hers – large, queer, Chicana – had no visibility in culture at the time Aguilar made these works, while in real life her experiences were of an uncomfortable, scrutinised presence. Out here in the terrain of nowhere, Aguilar returns her body to the earth – a body wanting to just be a body, to not ache to fit in. A body with the same cracks, dents and curves as the land; hardy, wild and free. They’re photographs about rejection, but also embrace.

This is the beginning of three concurrent exhibitions at Autograph about rebellious bodies. In the first and largest, Our Bodies Have Been Bridges, Aguilar’s story continues through two younger artists who also use their bodies as anchors, in pursuit of healing, truth and connection to ancestral female knowledge. In a diaristic, family album-style account of matriarchy and ritual, Other Stories/Historias Bravas, the artist Koyoltzintli re-enacts remembered scenes from her childhood in the Andean mountains of Ecuador.

Her bare breasts are blessed by her aunt, for protection. In another picture, her mother braids her hair tenderly, the same way, the caption tells us, her grandmother had once done for her. Her mum takes her to sit among the iguanas at the local park, to cure her of her phobia of the reptiles. Routines of care passed down generations of women, through their bodies. Tangible, physical, felt knowledge and history is reflected in Koyoltzintli’s very direct, intimate approach to photography. In a group of works from the series Meda – indebted to Aguilar’s self-portraits – Koyoltzintli asked women to interact with the land as their ancestors might have, to trace a collective, imagined, silent story of the first woman on Earth. An alternative origin story.

These works appear with Peruvian Tarrah Krajnak’s grainy, photocopied, archival images that focus on 1979 – the year the military regime ended in Peru, and also the year of the artist’s birth. The works explore the dissonance between women’s bodies portrayed in the country’s media and the private, personal experiences of living as a woman through that time and the years of armed conflict that followed. She takes images cribbed from newspapers and magazines published that year, and to query their veracity, photocopies, rephotographs, and interrupts them with her own image. The bodies here are agitated, unstable and unresolved.

Upstairs, this dovetails seamlessly into Charan Singh’s Your Tongue in My Mouth. As the unforgettable title promises, Singh’s work is a joyful provocation, but also a serious meditation on desirability, sexuality and reciprocity – when certain bodies are seen by some as a burden, a threat.

Singh’s lucid colour portraits of Hijra, Kothi and trans people combine a realist sensibility and theatricality – the subjects’ authenticity contrasts with choreographed poses; beautiful hand-painted backdrops behind them evoke a world of fantasy and escape. Riveting, regal portraits such as Umrao and Sonu have a timeless elegance: the subjects’ decision to wear traditional salwar kameez or anarkali-style dress, ornate brocade fabrics, their bodies adorned with henna and bindi, are intentional gestures that they also belong to a longer history in south Asia. These portraits are statements of dignity that claim their right to that place without words or apology.

after newsletter promotion

The subtle tension between realism and artifice takes on a particular urgency against the backdrop of India’s deteriorating trans rights. In March 2026, legislative amendments to the country’s Transgender Persons Act 2019 rolled back protections for gender self-identification, raising profound questions about bodily autonomy, recognition and the right to define oneself. A timeline of transgender history and rights, displayed on a table at the centre of Singh’s exhibition, situates these intimate portraits within a longer struggle for visibility and legal recognition, grounding their gestures of self-fashioning and self-expression in a shifting and often hostile political reality.

content.title_original: Devil in the detail: 100 years on, FW Murnau’s Faust scrapbook reveals the secrets of his silent masterpiece
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "F W Murnau was one of the greatest of all silent film-makers, with a rare genius for making beautiful images on screen. His peers liked to say he “had a camera instead of a head”. The director of such stunning films as vampire tale Nosferatu (1922) and marital romance Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans (1927) died at the age of 42 in 1931, meaning that his career barely scraped into the talkie era. Still, Murnau’s tremendous run of silent pictures included some beautiful, often disturbing classics, in which he sent his camera roaming through changing vistas of shadows and light, and plumbed the depths of the human soul. Nowhere more so than in his tour-de-force Faust, released 100 years ago this month, based on Goethe’s play about a deal with the devil. And the making of Faust is depicted in a stunning new book, which is both a document of, and in a sense an artefact from, the production of this classic film."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Murnau was also one of the most mysterious of directors: secretive about his methods, with an intense devotion to his work. Early collaborator Edgar G Ulmer called him “a great purist who worked under a sort of hypnosis”. Murnau banned producers from his sets, and executives from watching his rushes. Bar a few exceptions, he did not allow on-set photography to reveal the secrets of his camerawork and special effects. This mystique created room for speculation as to whether Murnau, or his talented crew, were responsible for the success of his films. The Faust Bible: The Making of FW Murnau’s Masterpiece publishes unseen images from the shoot of one of his best films, and gives a rare insight into the collaborative way it was made."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5fc337135f6fc9e46a53cec1cf295016fe1e740b/0_0_1684_1250/master/1684.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "FW Murnau photograped on the set of Faust by Hans Natge .", "caption": "FW Murnau photographed on the set of Faust by Hans Natge. Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, Paris", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Faust was Murnau’s final German film before he went to Hollywood, and at the time it was the most expensive, complex film that the Ufa studio had ever produced. It is an adaptation of Goethe’s tragedy about the scholar Faust (played by Swedish actor Gösta Ekman) who sells his soul to the devil, represented by the grinning, black-clad demon Mephistopheles (German star Emil Jannings). A commercial flop on its release, Faust is now acclaimed as one of the greats. French New Wave director Éric Rohmer, a Murnau devotee, wrote his doctoral dissertation on the film. The Faust Bible reveals how Murnau and his crew achieved some of the incredible shots and special effects in this film, but it is also an enhanced facsimile of an artefact from the film’s production, which has survived against all odds to spill its secrets. In the film, Faust owns a hefty, leather-bound Bible, which he throws on the fire in a moment of despair. But the prop was to become something more. Art directors Robert Herlth and Walter Röhrig pulled the book from the ashes and pasted designs, stills and behind-the-scenes photographs on to its blank pages so they could present the souvenir as a gift to the director at the end of the shoot. Murnau left it behind in his flat in Berlin when he went to Hollywood, not knowing he would never return to retrieve it. After his death, Murnau’s brother stashed his belongings in various city-centre basements, which were susceptible to flooding, and worse, once the bombs began falling on Berlin during the second world war."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/f52a21ce08b0f58f4629635791b22230f8ec4f57/152_32_979_783/master/979.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Emil Jannings and Gösta Ekman in costume as Mephisto and Faust.", "caption": "Emil Jannings and Gösta Ekman in costume as Mephisto and Faust. Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, Paris", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Film scholar and archivist Lotte Eisner came to Berlin looking for Murnau’s archives in the 1950s, but found no sign of the Bible. It was not until the 1960s that a German curator from the city’s Akademie der Künste, Engelbert von Mallinckrodt, told Henri Langlois at the Cinématheque Française that he had bought some of Murnau’s photo albums for a small sum from a restaurateur called Rolf Conscienze, who had film industry connections. It turned out that these albums included the Bible – though no one knows how they ended up with Conscienze. Then, to deepen the mystery, Mallinckrodt vanished, and his flatmate became the book’s custodian for several decades: it was wrapped in brown paper sitting on top of a cupboard. Eisner searched for the Faust Bible her whole life but she was never to see it. She died in 1983."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/f72555a7f09459053031b00ee939a45876eb7736/0_0_1777_1246/master/1777.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "The film-makers creating special effect clouds above a model mountaintop.", "caption": "The film-makers creating special effect clouds above a model mountaintop. Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, Paris", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Now the book is in the safekeeping of the Cinémathèque Française, which bought it in 2017, and there it remains, a memento of the once-contested collaborative nature of Murnau’s methods. I went to see it this summer, and it is appropriately grand in scale, an unusually majestic scrapbook. Restored by the cinema’s director of heritage Laurent Mannoni and his team, the book looks good for an abandoned, 100-year-old prop. The water-damage has been smoothed out, leaving only a few scuffs, and the shadows where some enterprising thief has prised the metal crucifix and corner pieces from the leather."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Inside, sketches for individual scenes are arranged opposite matching stills from the film. Turning these hallowed pages, you can see how the compositions of figures and objects by the designers known as “film architects” – the forced perspectives, contrasting arrangements of light and dark, sweeping shadows, steam and flames – were re-created on film by Murnau and his talented cinematographer Carl Hoffmann. The director encouraged his designer to draw not just the spaces, but the actors too, creating something closer to a storyboard image than a set design."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/35dc76735699fb2f8e28af77bd205464367b7c8a/0_0_2381_1826/master/2381.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Mephisto appears in a still from the film.", "caption": "Mephisto appears in a still from the film. Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, Paris", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“The sketch became the equivalent of a contract,” Herlth later wrote. “[Murnau] insisted that every stroke of the pen should be faithfully rendered in the execution.” This meant not only building sets according to the designs but Murnau and Hoffmann making extensive adjustments to the lighting to produce the velvety shadows that the director demanded. Hoffmann then navigated these settings with bold, fluid camera movements in a technique called entfesselte Kamera (unchained camera), originated by cinematographer Karl Freund when working with Murnau on The Last Laugh (1924). Murnau was not short of visual references. He had a strong interest in the occult, and his background was in art history. Albrecht Dürer’s Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse woodcut was a direct influence on the film’s opening scene."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/919e99cb6411efb8763116e38f7ede707822d371/0_0_1777_1121/master/1777.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "A behind the scenes photograph by Hans Natge. content.article_text:
F W Murnau was one of the greatest of all silent film-makers, with a rare genius for making beautiful images on screen. His peers liked to say he “had a camera instead of a head”. The director of such stunning films as vampire tale Nosferatu (1922) and marital romance Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans (1927) died at the age of 42 in 1931, meaning that his career barely scraped into the talkie era. Still, Murnau’s tremendous run of silent pictures included some beautiful, often disturbing classics, in which he sent his camera roaming through changing vistas of shadows and light, and plumbed the depths of the human soul. Nowhere more so than in his tour-de-force Faust, released 100 years ago this month, based on Goethe’s play about a deal with the devil. And the making of Faust is depicted in a stunning new book, which is both a document of, and in a sense an artefact from, the production of this classic film.

Murnau was also one of the most mysterious of directors: secretive about his methods, with an intense devotion to his work. Early collaborator Edgar G Ulmer called him “a great purist who worked under a sort of hypnosis”. Murnau banned producers from his sets, and executives from watching his rushes. Bar a few exceptions, he did not allow on-set photography to reveal the secrets of his camerawork and special effects. This mystique created room for speculation as to whether Murnau, or his talented crew, were responsible for the success of his films. The Faust Bible: The Making of FW Murnau’s Masterpiece publishes unseen images from the shoot of one of his best films, and gives a rare insight into the collaborative way it was made.

Faust was Murnau’s final German film before he went to Hollywood, and at the time it was the most expensive, complex film that the Ufa studio had ever produced. It is an adaptation of Goethe’s tragedy about the scholar Faust (played by Swedish actor Gösta Ekman) who sells his soul to the devil, represented by the grinning, black-clad demon Mephistopheles (German star Emil Jannings). A commercial flop on its release, Faust is now acclaimed as one of the greats. French New Wave director Éric Rohmer, a Murnau devotee, wrote his doctoral dissertation on the film. The Faust Bible reveals how Murnau and his crew achieved some of the incredible shots and special effects in this film, but it is also an enhanced facsimile of an artefact from the film’s production, which has survived against all odds to spill its secrets. In the film, Faust owns a hefty, leather-bound Bible, which he throws on the fire in a moment of despair. But the prop was to become something more. Art directors Robert Herlth and Walter Röhrig pulled the book from the ashes and pasted designs, stills and behind-the-scenes photographs on to its blank pages so they could present the souvenir as a gift to the director at the end of the shoot. Murnau left it behind in his flat in Berlin when he went to Hollywood, not knowing he would never return to retrieve it. After his death, Murnau’s brother stashed his belongings in various city-centre basements, which were susceptible to flooding, and worse, once the bombs began falling on Berlin during the second world war.

Film scholar and archivist Lotte Eisner came to Berlin looking for Murnau’s archives in the 1950s, but found no sign of the Bible. It was not until the 1960s that a German curator from the city’s Akademie der Künste, Engelbert von Mallinckrodt, told Henri Langlois at the Cinématheque Française that he had bought some of Murnau’s photo albums for a small sum from a restaurateur called Rolf Conscienze, who had film industry connections. It turned out that these albums included the Bible – though no one knows how they ended up with Conscienze. Then, to deepen the mystery, Mallinckrodt vanished, and his flatmate became the book’s custodian for several decades: it was wrapped in brown paper sitting on top of a cupboard. Eisner searched for the Faust Bible her whole life but she was never to see it. She died in 1983.

Now the book is in the safekeeping of the Cinémathèque Française, which bought it in 2017, and there it remains, a memento of the once-contested collaborative nature of Murnau’s methods. I went to see it this summer, and it is appropriately grand in scale, an unusually majestic scrapbook. Restored by the cinema’s director of heritage Laurent Mannoni and his team, the book looks good for an abandoned, 100-year-old prop. The water-damage has been smoothed out, leaving only a few scuffs, and the shadows where some enterprising thief has prised the metal crucifix and corner pieces from the leather.

Inside, sketches for individual scenes are arranged opposite matching stills from the film. Turning these hallowed pages, you can see how the compositions of figures and objects by the designers known as “film architects” – the forced perspectives, contrasting arrangements of light and dark, sweeping shadows, steam and flames – were re-created on film by Murnau and his talented cinematographer Carl Hoffmann. The director encouraged his designer to draw not just the spaces, but the actors too, creating something closer to a storyboard image than a set design.

“The sketch became the equivalent of a contract,” Herlth later wrote. “[Murnau] insisted that every stroke of the pen should be faithfully rendered in the execution.” This meant not only building sets according to the designs but Murnau and Hoffmann making extensive adjustments to the lighting to produce the velvety shadows that the director demanded. Hoffmann then navigated these settings with bold, fluid camera movements in a technique called entfesselte Kamera (unchained camera), originated by cinematographer Karl Freund when working with Murnau on The Last Laugh (1924). Murnau was not short of visual references. He had a strong interest in the occult, and his background was in art history. Albrecht Dürer’s Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse woodcut was a direct influence on the film’s opening scene.

Herlth recalled the experience of working with Murnau as good-humoured, if challenging, as the director was cheerful but always ambitious to create shots and camera effects that had not been achieved before. The crew spent long days and nights discussing and experimenting with new ideas. “Each day on the set was a fresh opportunity to surpass ourselves in inventiveness and ingenuity,” he said.

Leafing further through the Bible, the chiaroscuro sketches and stills give way to playful collages, images of the cast and crew having fun on set, the legendarily tall Murnau hunched over as he instructs Jannings how to leer malevolently. And there are pages that speak to that boundless technical ingenuity. One of the most celebrated moments in the film is the Weltflug (“flight around the world”) sequence, in which Mephistopheles flies Faust through the sky on his cloak, the world lurching below them. The Bible retains the diagrams that explain just how they achieved this uncanny flight simulation. The secret was a low wooden trolley moving along a plaster ramp, an idea that came to Herlth and Röhrig when they saw a truck being unloaded in the street.

The facsimile edition reprints the Weltflug diagrams on gatefold pages so you can study century-old secrets of film technique at your leisure. It also comprehensively reprints all the Bible’s images, with explanatory captions, enlargements, and quotations from the screenplay, which was written in epigrammatic, almost poetic prose. There are also essays and additional drawings from the Cinémathèque’s archives.

We may never fully understand the workings of Murnau’s mysterious “camera-head” and his collaborations with his team. But this fascinating souvenir takes us close.

The Faust Bible (Mubi Editions, £75). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.

Faust streams on Mubi from 14 October, with live-scored centenary screenings in Paris on 17 October, Munich on 25 October, and Los Angeles on 1 November

FW Murnau

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

content.article_text:
At the Iziko South African National Gallery, ‘Matereality V2’ explores how contemporary artists across Africa transform everyday materials into powerful expressions of memory, identity, labour and belonging.

What happens when the materials we overlook become the very substance of artistic meaning? In ‘Materiality V2’, curator Andrea Lewis brings together emerging and established artists whose practices challenge conventional distinctions between art, craft and everyday life. From textiles and found objects to industrial waste and organic matter, the exhibition reveals how materials carry histories of extraction, cultural knowledge, human experience and transformation.

In conversation with ART AFRICA, Lewis reflects on the evolving relationship between material and meaning, the importance of physical making in an increasingly digital world, and museums’ role in reconsidering what we preserve, value, and remember. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

Suzette Bell-Roberts: The title ‘Matereality V2’ brings together material and reality. In this exhibition, what does “matereality” mean, and how has that idea evolved in this second iteration?

Andrea Lewis: For me, matereality is the point at which material and lived reality become inseparable. Materials are never neutral: they arrive with histories, associations, labour, politics, memory and social realities already attached to them. A blanket means something before it becomes an artwork. Hair means something. Soil means something. A cement bag, clothing, plastic, beads, soap or electronic waste all carry social and cultural associations. Artists activate those histories. These materials are not simply unusual substitutes for paint, bronze or marble; their meanings are inseparable from the meanings of the works themselves. The material is not decoration around the idea. It is part of the idea.

The first ‘Matereality’ developed out of something I had been noticing at ISANG: artists were increasingly moving beyond traditional media in ways that challenged the categories museums rely upon. Paintings incorporated rubber, hair, engine oil, textiles and found objects. Sculpture drew from craft, industry, clothing and performance. The distinctions between painting, sculpture, textiles, installation and works on paper were becoming increasingly difficult to maintain. That exhibition included artists who were already very well known, including Igshaan Adams and Usha Seejarim, alongside many others experimenting deliberately with unconventional materials. And then COVID happened. The exhibition opened in 2020 and almost immediately entered this strange period in which museums and galleries were closing. But the idea stayed with me.

Six years later, the context has shifted again. We are living through extraordinary digital acceleration and the rapid rise of artificial intelligence, while many artists are investing enormous amounts of time in intensely physical processes: stitching, weaving, cutting, binding, layering, assembling and repeating. I do not necessarily see this as a rejection of technology, but physical making feels more significant in an increasingly dematerialised world. Materials have weight, texture, resistance and physical presence. So ‘Matereality V2’ gives us insight into the realities of individual artists, but also into the state of the world around us. Through material, it opens onto questions of land and belonging, labour and the body, memory and family, indigenous knowledge, colonial histories, consumption and waste, environmental concerns, and value. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

How were the artists and works for ‘Matereality V2’ selected , and what conversations emerged among their different practices?

The selection process began while the first ‘Matereality’ was still on exhibition. I started writing down the names of artists I wished I had known about, or had been able to include, the first time around – artists such as Sepideh Mehraban, Gaelen Pinnock and Promise Mapondera. That list stayed pinned to my wall for the next six years. Whenever I encountered a work that made me think differently about material, I would add the artist’s name. Sometimes that happened in an exhibition, during a studio visit, at an art fair, in the news, or even on Instagram. I would then do a deeper dive into the artist’s practice and, wherever possible, visit their studio and speak to them. Sometimes an artist also made something specifically with this exhibition in mind.

Eventually the list grew to around 150 artists, so the difficulty was not finding enough work. It was deciding what to leave out. There are many artists I would dearly have loved to include. For that reason, I do not see ‘Matereality V2’ as a definitive survey. It is more a bird’s-eye view of what I have been noticing over the past few years – a snapshot of emerging and established artists finding inventive ways to make material inseparable from meaning. The process also became very visual. I had images of the works with me and, over time, I found myself linking particular works together. Sometimes those connections were material, but often they were conceptual, emotional or contradictory.

For example, I began thinking about Warren Maroon’s work in relation to Senzeni Marasela’s because both opened up complicated ideas around home – home as a place of comfort, intimacy and belonging, but also of pain, absence or difficulty. I also realised that placing Sepideh Mehraban’s work alongside Ben Stanwix and Xhanti Zwelendaba’s BAWA work created an interesting conversation around place and printing. In different ways, both use imprinting and reproduction to think about how place is recorded, remembered and mediated. From there, Mehraban’s work connected very strongly to Tamlin Blake’s. Mehraban’s carpet carries newspaper imprints, while Blake works directly with newspaper and references book burning. Both bring to mind the ways authoritarian societies can limit access to knowledge and, in doing so, restrict individual autonomy. The newspaper becomes more than a material or source image; it carries questions of information, censorship, power and who is allowed access to knowledge. Gaelen Pinnock’s work began speaking to Lungisa Qwanta’s in ways that became clearer the longer I lived with the images.

Other pairings came almost instinctively. I could not resist placing Yonela Makoba’s teabag work in conversation with Zaneaca Singh’s sugar works. Tea and sugar are so intimately linked to comfort, hospitality and everyday ritual, yet both are deeply entangled with colonial trade, extraction and systems whose consequences continue to be felt today. Atang Tshikare and Lyndi Sales were another pairing that became exciting to me. Their works open onto connections between cosmology, science, plants, natural systems and forms of knowledge that move between the earthly and the speculative. I placed the work of Chris Soal in conversation with Hanien Conradie’s work. Soal found the bottle caps he uses in the streets of Johannesburg, while Conradie gathered her materials from riverbanks and plants. I was interested in that contrast between the inorganic and the organic – two artists collecting from their immediate environments but encountering very different traces of place. One gathers the discarded remnants of an urban and consumer landscape; the other works with materials embedded in natural systems. I also put Sahlah Davids and Jeanne Gaigher in the same room. Both had been working abstractly and, for works made specifically for this exhibition, began experimenting with figuration. I loved that parallel: two artists independently shifting their visual languages and then finding themselves in conversation within the exhibition.

There are many more connections, and they became central to the curatorial process. One work would lead me to another, sometimes through material, sometimes through process, and sometimes through a shared political or emotional concern. The exhibition gradually became a web of relationships rather than a series of isolated objects. At one stage I considered making the exhibition entirely South African. There was certainly enough work to do that. But ultimately, it felt too restrictive, partly because of the political moment we are living through, when xenophobia and increasingly narrow ideas about nationality and belonging remain so present, but also because this kind of material experimentation is something I have noticed strongly across the African continent.

The final selection was never simply about finding unusual materials. I was interested in artists for whom material is fundamental to the meaning of the work – where you could not simply substitute one material for another without changing what the artwork is saying. That is also why I am drawn to thematic exhibitions. They allow artists across race, gender, age, generation, geography, medium and levels of recognition to enter into a shared conversation. Their differences are not erased, but neither are they confined to fixed categories. Instead, the question becomes: what might very different artists contribute to the same conversation? I am always interested in creating encounters between works that might otherwise never occupy the same room. At the same time, I do not want to explain every connection. Some relationships are quite deliberate, and others emerged unexpectedly, and I hope audiences discover many of them for themselves. A viewer may make a connection that I did not anticipate at all, and that is part of what makes an exhibition alive. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

Material can carry histories of place, labour, culture and exchange. How does the exhibition explore meaning gathered through use, movement and transformation?

Many of the materials in ‘Matereality V2’ have already had lives before they enter the museum. They have circulated through homes, industries, communities, ceremonies, economies or systems of trade and consumption. Through cutting, stitching, weaving, assembling, burning, layering, binding or repetition, those meanings can shift again. Something disposable can become precious. An ordinary domestic material can become political. An industrial product can suddenly speak about the body, land, memory or belonging. As the exhibition developed, I found myself returning to Jane Bennett’s idea of “vibrant matter”. Bennett asks us to reconsider the assumption that matter is passive – that human beings act upon materials and materials obediently receive that action. Instead, she encourages us to think of materials as having their own properties, behaviours and capacities. That became very useful to me while thinking through ‘Matereality’, because artists do not always completely control their materials. Materials sag, crack, stretch, absorb, rust, decay, reflect and resist. Sometimes the artist is working with the material rather than simply imposing something upon it. So you cannot really separate material, process and meaning in many of these works. Very often, the material itself helps to produce that meaning. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

What role does experimentation play in the exhibition, especially in how artists encounter, manipulate or reconsider their materials?

Experimentation is everything. I am constantly fascinated by the ability of artists to look at a material that most of us might overlook and imagine an entirely different function, language or aesthetic for it. There is often an enormous amount of testing, intuition and problem-solving involved: discovering how far something will stretch, what happens when it is heated, cut, stitched, compressed, layered, woven or combined with another material. Sometimes the material refuses to behave as the artist imagined. That resistance is important. There can be a negotiation between artist and material. Materials have characteristics and limitations of their own. They can buckle, unravel, stain, rust, fade, harden, break down or change over time. I think that curiosity is one of the great pleasures of ‘Materiality ’. The exhibition repeatedly asks a very simple question: what else can this thing become? And very often the answer is something completely unexpected. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

How does ‘Matereality V2’ invite audiences to think about the relationship between an artwork’s physical qualities and the ideas or experiences it communicates?

I hope people first encounter the works physically. Before reading a wall text or knowing the story, there is texture, scale, weight, fragility, repetition, colour, density and surface. You might immediately wonder what something is made from, how it was constructed, or even what it might feel like to touch. Then, when you understand why that particular material has been used, the artwork can shift completely. A material that initially appears seductive might carry a difficult history. Something apparently cheap or disposable might involve extraordinary labour. Something visually delicate may come from an industrial or violent process. That relationship between the sensory and the conceptual is central to the exhibition. Sometimes the conversation between two works only becomes apparent when you stand between them. A material used in one work might change the way you understand another. A shared concern with home, violence, memory, science, comfort or colonial history may surface even where the artists are working in completely different ways. For me, that is one of the pleasures of a thematic exhibition. Meaning does not only exist within individual works; it can also happen in the space between them. And I hope viewers find links that I have missed entirely. I also think this physical encounter has particular resonance now. So much of our experience of art – and of the world generally – happens through screens. We scroll past images incredibly quickly. These works ask for another kind of attention. The exhibition asks us not only to look at what an artwork represents, but to consider what it is physically made from, what that material has already experienced, and what the artist has asked it to become. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

The exhibition brings different artistic approaches into conversation within a museum context. How did Iziko’s spaces and collections shape your curatorial thinking?

Working within Iziko inevitably means thinking about history, because the museum contains layers of collecting, classification and ideas about what kinds of artworks and materials have historically been considered worthy of entering a national collection. That becomes particularly interesting with an exhibition such as ‘Matereality’, because many of the artists work with practices or materials historically associated with craft, domestic labour, informal economies or everyday life rather than so-called “fine art”. This second iteration places a stronger emphasis on textile practices, Afro-centric perspectives and indigenous knowledge systems. I am particularly interested in the way practices such as weaving, stitching, beadwork and other forms of hand-making hold knowledge. Historically, many of these practices were separated from “fine art” and placed into categories such as craft, decoration or domestic production. But they contain sophisticated systems of knowledge, memory and transmission. Many contemporary artists are actively drawing upon, disrupting or transforming those traditions. This connects to why thematic exhibitions are so useful within a museum context. I can only speak from my own position as a curator, and I would never claim that an individual exhibition can resolve the much larger structural contradictions within museums or art history. But exhibitions remain one of the most immediate and practical tools available to me. They allow me to work across some of the divisions through which art history and museum collections have traditionally been organised.

There is also a practical institutional reality behind this. When budgets and procedures for growing collections are very limited, exhibitions become another way of bringing artistic voices into the museum, even when we are not yet in a position to acquire those works. They allow us to broaden the conversation, introduce artists who may be absent from the permanent collection and test new relationships between historical holdings and contemporary practice. There is another contradiction that ‘Matereality’ brings into focus too. Museums are designed to preserve things. We try to prevent objects from changing. But many contemporary artists deliberately work with materials that change. They fade. Rust. Break down. Become brittle. Decay. So these works raise fascinating questions about what a museum actually preserves. Is it the original material? The artist’s intention? The process? Can components eventually be replaced? At what point does replacing something fundamentally alter the artwork? That tension is increasingly important for contemporary collections: the museum seeks permanence, while matter itself is often impermanent.

How do questions of place and contemporary life in South Africa enter the exhibition through the artists’ materials, processes and perspectives?

They enter organically because materials are deeply connected to place. Artists work with what surrounds them – culturally, economically, environmentally and politically. Within South Africa, materials can carry extraordinarily complicated histories. They can speak about mining and extraction, land and displacement, migrant labour, clothing and identity, domestic work, inequality, environmental degradation, spirituality, indigenous knowledge systems and histories of making. But I did not want those themes to become neat categories. I did not want textiles in one room, plastic in another and found objects somewhere else. The interesting part is precisely how these histories and materials become entangled. At the same time, I did not want the exhibition to imply that South African artists are somehow only responding to South African concerns. These practices are connected to much larger questions around climate change, consumption, migration, technology, sustainability and belonging. That is one reason the exhibition extends beyond South Africa to selected artists elsewhere on the continent. There is extraordinary material experimentation happening across Africa, often using objects or substances that are locally specific while simultaneously speaking to global systems and concerns. What interests me is precisely that movement between the local and the universal. A material might have a highly specific social history in Cape Town, Johannesburg, Accra, or Harare, but the artwork can simultaneously open onto a much broader conversation about contemporary life. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

What questions do you hope ‘Matereality V2’ leaves open about the materials around us and how we understand their histories, possibilities and value?

I hope people leave the exhibition looking at ordinary materials differently. We live surrounded by objects and substances whose histories we rarely think about: where they came from, who made them, what labour was involved, what systems of trade or extraction produced them, what environmental cost they carry, and where they will eventually end up. Artists are particularly good at disrupting that familiarity. They can take something we think we understand and make it strange again. Questions of value are crucial here. Why is one material considered precious and another disposable? Why are certain forms of making described as art while others have historically been classified as craft, domestic labour or decoration? Who decides what is worthy of preservation? I also hope people leave thinking about the relationships between the works. I have spent years carrying these images around, mentally and quite literally, and gradually seeing connections between artists who may never have imagined themselves alongside one another. But once the exhibition opens, those relationships no longer belong only to me. A visitor may see an entirely different connection between two works – through a material, a memory, a colour, a history or an experience. I like the idea that the exhibition can keep generating conversations beyond the ones I consciously constructed. So perhaps it leaves visitors with fairly simple questions: what histories are contained within the objects we encounter every day? Whose labour is embedded within them? Why do we value some things and discard others? What happens when the same material can signify comfort and violence, familiarity and exploitation, intimacy and enormous global systems at the same time? And what possibilities might exist in a material once we stop seeing it only in terms of its intended function? Of course, exhibitions centred on materiality are incredibly common, and artists have been investigating material for centuries. I am certainly not suggesting that ‘Matereality’ introduces something entirely new. My hope is rather to pull together some of the many threads running through contemporary practice – labour, ecology, indigenous knowledge, craft, memory, technology, consumption and value – and see what becomes visible when they are considered together.

In that sense, ‘Matereality V2’ is perhaps an opportunity to take stock: a kind of summary of what I have been noticing over the past several years, and of the extraordinarily inventive ways in which emerging and established artists are making material inseparable from meaning. What I hope it offers is another chapter in that much longer conversation. And perhaps it encourages us to pay closer attention to the things around us – to what materials already contain, to the labour and histories embedded within them, and to what happens when an artist takes something familiar and allows us to see it completely differently.

This exhibition is on view at the Iziko South African National Gallery in Cape Town until 30th June 2027.

"六年后，环境再次发生了变化。我们正经历着数字化的飞速发展和人工智能的迅速崛起，而许多艺术家则投入大量时间进行密集的物理过程：缝合、编织、切割、装订、分层、组装和重复。我并不一定认为这是对技术的拒绝，但在日益非物质化的世界中，物理制造感觉更重要。材料具有重量、质地、阻力和物理存在。因此，《Matereality V2》让我们深入了解个别艺术家的现实，同时也让我们了解我们周围世界的状况。通过材料，它探讨了土地和归属、劳动和身体、记忆和家庭、土著知识、殖民历史、消费和浪费、环境问题和价值等问题。展览安装图“物质现实 V2”，2026 年，Iziko 南非国家美术馆。图片由画廊提供。", "source_hash": "还有更多的联系，它们成为策展过程的核心。一项工作会将我引向另一项工作，有时是通过材料，有时是通过过程，有时是通过共同的政治或情感关注。展览逐渐成为一个关系网，而不是一系列孤立的物体。我曾一度考虑过让展览完全是南非风格的。当然有足够的工作来做到这一点。但归根结底，它感觉过于限制性，部分原因是我们正在经历的政治时刻，仇外心理和关于国籍和归属感的日益狭隘的观念仍然存在，但也因为这种材料实验是我在整个非洲大陆强烈注意到的。", "最终的选择绝不只是为了寻找不寻常的材料。我对艺术家感兴趣，对他们来说，材料对于作品的意义至关重要——你不能简单地用一种材料替换另一种材料而不改变艺术品所表达的内容。这也是我被主题展览所吸引的原因。它们允许跨越种族、性别、年龄、世代、地域、媒介和认知水平的艺术家进行共同对话。它们的差异并没有被消除，但也没有局限于固定的类别。相反，问题变成了：不同的艺术家可能会对同一个对话做出什么贡献？我总是对在作品之间创造相遇感兴趣，否则这些作品可能永远不会占据同一个房间。同时，我也不想解释每一个联系。有些关系是经过深思熟虑的，有些关系是出乎意料的，而我希望观众能够亲自发现其中的许多内容。观众可能会产生一种我完全没有预料到的联系，而这正是使展览充满活力的部分原因。 Image Courtesy of Gallery.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "材料可以承载地方、劳动、文化和交流的历史。展览如何探索通过使用、移动和转变所收集的意义？", "source_hash": "224405b5d7765050bda05eb4a7212963888e5e68287775fc25a18c88d88f59ab", "translated_parts": ["材料可以承载地方、劳动、文化和交流的历史。展览如何探索通过使用、移动和转变所收集的意义？"], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《物质现实V2》中的许多材料在进入博物馆之前就已经有了生命。它们通过家庭、工业、社区、仪式、经济或贸易和消费体系进行流通。通过切割、缝合、编织、组装、燃烧、分层、装订或重复，这些意义可以再次转变。一次性的东西可能会变得珍贵。普通的家庭材料可以变得政治化。工业产品突然可以谈论身体、土地、记忆或归属感。随着展览的展开，我发现自己又回到了简·贝内特的“充满活力的物质”的想法。贝内特要求我们重新考虑物质是被动的假设——人类对材料采取行动，而材料会顺从地接受这种行动。相反，她鼓励我们将材料视为具有自己的属性、行为和能力。这变得非常有用对我来说，在思考“物质现实”时，因为艺术家并不总是完全控制他们的材料。材料会下垂、破裂、拉伸、吸收、生锈、腐烂、反射和抵抗。有时，艺术家是在材料上进行创作，而不是简单地在材料上强加一些东西。因此，在许多这样的作品中，你无法真正将材料、过程和意义分开。很多时候，材料本身有助于产生这种意义。 2026 年 Iziko 南非国家美术馆展览“Matereality V2”展览现场。图片由画廊提供。", "source_hash": "6c99caa55603d6b2ebe37578a0cd061b6189458c0d1f238496ce691942ead94e", "translated_parts": ["《物质现实V2》中的许多材料在进入博物馆之前就已经有了生命。它们通过家庭、工业、社区、仪式、经济或贸易和消费体系进行流通。通过切割、缝合、编织、组装、燃烧、分层、装订或重复，这些意义可以再次转变。一次性的东西可能会变得珍贵。普通的家庭材料可以变得政治化。工业产品突然可以谈论身体、土地、记忆或归属感。随着展览的展开，我发现自己又回到了简·贝内特的“充满活力的物质”的想法。贝内特要求我们重新考虑物质是被动的假设——人类对材料采取行动，而材料会顺从地接受这种行动。相反，她鼓励我们将材料视为具有自己的属性、行为和能力。这变得非常有用", "对我来说，在思考“物质现实”时，因为艺术家并不总是完全控制他们的材料。材料会下垂、破裂、拉伸、吸收、生锈、腐烂、反射和抵抗。有时，艺术家是在材料上进行创作，而不是简单地在材料上强加一些东西。因此，在许多这样的作品中，你无法真正将材料、过程和意义分开。很多时候，材料本身有助于产生这种意义。 2026 年 Iziko 南非国家美术馆展览“Matereality V2”展览现场。图片由画廊提供。"], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MaterealityV2_Opening20Aug26_51-1030x686.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "实验在展览中发挥什么作用，特别是在艺术家如何接触、操纵或重新考虑他们的材料方面？", "source_hash": "1fe7eba5c58fb9658278df0063feb39adeffac91354ff1624a7baeb850fc681b", "translated_parts": ["实验在展览中发挥什么作用，特别是在艺术家如何接触、操纵或重新考虑他们的材料方面？"], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "实验就是一切。我一直对艺术家的能力着迷，他们能够观察我们大多数人可能忽视的材料，并为其想象出完全不同的功能、语言或美学。通常涉及大量的测试、直觉和解决问题：发现某物会拉伸多远，当它被加热、切割、缝合、压缩、分层、编织或与另一种材料结合时会发生什么。有时，材料拒绝表现出艺术家想象的那样。这种抵抗很重要。艺术家和材料之间可以进行协商。材料有其自身的特性和局限性。随着时间的推移，它们可能会弯曲、散开、染色、生锈、褪色、硬化、分解或变化。我认为好奇心是“物质性”的最大乐趣之一。展览反复问一个很简单的问题：这个东西还能做什么？变得？而答案往往是完全出乎意料的。 2026 年 Iziko 南非国家美术馆展览“Matereality V2”展览现场。图片由画廊提供。", "source_hash": "ca561838b37635c59f2c8af59a615cd40f50cc35711533b2f7276fe1872db31b", "translated_parts": ["实验就是一切。我一直对艺术家的能力着迷，他们能够观察我们大多数人可能忽视的材料，并为其想象出完全不同的功能、语言或美学。通常涉及大量的测试、直觉和解决问题：发现某物会拉伸多远，当它被加热、切割、缝合、压缩、分层、编织或与另一种材料结合时会发生什么。有时，材料拒绝表现出艺术家想象的那样。这种抵抗很重要。艺术家和材料之间可以进行协商。材料有其自身的特性和局限性。随着时间的推移，它们可能会弯曲、散开、染色、生锈、褪色、硬化、分解或变化。我认为好奇心是“物质性”的最大乐趣之一。展览反复问一个很简单的问题：这个东西还能做什么？", "变得？而答案往往是完全出乎意料的。 2026 年 Iziko 南非国家美术馆展览“Matereality V2”展览现场。图片由画廊提供。"], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Matereality_V2_Installation-Views2Aug26_29-1030x686.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“物质现实V2”如何邀请观众思考艺术品的物理品质与其所传达的想法或体验之间的关系？", "source_hash": "a73673be1bde4f5b1e50a8887233c7f4547a12808940afa02757ed0deb5eb594", "translated_parts": ["“物质现实V2”如何邀请观众思考艺术品的物理品质与其所传达的想法或体验之间的关系？"], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我希望人们首先亲身接触这些作品。在阅读墙上的文字或了解故事之前，先有纹理、规模、重量、脆弱性、重复、颜色、密度和表面。您可能会立即想知道某物是由什么制成的，它是如何构造的，甚至触摸起来感觉如何。然后，当您了解为什么使用该特定材料时，艺术品就可以完全改变。一种最初看​​起来很诱人的材料可能承载着一段艰难的历史。看似便宜或一次性的东西可能需要大量的劳动力。视觉上精致的东西可能来自工业或暴力过程。感官与概念之间的关系是展览的核心。有时，只有当你站在两件作品之间时，它们之间的对话才会变得明显。一件作品中使用的材料可能会改变你理解另一件作品的方式。即使艺术家以完全不同的方式工作，对家庭、暴力、记忆、科学、舒适或殖民历史的共同关注也可能会浮现出来。对我来说，这就是专题展览的乐趣之一。意义不仅仅存在于个人作品中；它也可能发生在它们之间的空间中。我希望观众能找到我完全错过的链接。我还认为这种身体接触现在引起了特别的共鸣。我们对艺术以及整个世界的大部分体验都是通过屏幕发生的。我们以惊人的速度滚动浏览图像。这些作品需要另一种关注。展览要求我们不仅要看一件艺术品代表什么，还要考虑它的物理构成、材料已经经历过什么，以及艺术家要求它成为什么。 2026 年 Iziko 展览‘Matereality V2’展览现场南非国家美术馆。图片由画廊提供。", "source_hash": "9f2bb312ad5bab0943000f9f8a4c675f5ca45cfcb91532d1af606ead0b9aeda2", "translated_parts": ["我希望人们首先亲身接触这些作品。在阅读墙上的文字或了解故事之前，先有纹理、规模、重量、脆弱性、重复、颜色、密度和表面。您可能会立即想知道某物是由什么制成的，它是如何构造的，甚至触摸起来感觉如何。然后，当您了解为什么使用该特定材料时，艺术品就可以完全改变。一种最初看​​起来很诱人的材料可能承载着一段艰难的历史。看似便宜或一次性的东西可能需要大量的劳动力。视觉上精致的东西可能来自工业或暴力过程。感官与概念之间的关系是展览的核心。有时，只有当你站在两件作品之间时，它们之间的对话才会变得明显。一件作品中使用的材料可能会改变你理解另一件作品的方式。", "即使艺术家以完全不同的方式工作，对家庭、暴力、记忆、科学、舒适或殖民历史的共同关注也可能会浮现出来。对我来说，这就是专题展览的乐趣之一。意义不仅仅存在于个人作品中；它也可能发生在它们之间的空间中。我希望观众能找到我完全错过的链接。我还认为这种身体接触现在引起了特别的共鸣。我们对艺术以及整个世界的大部分体验都是通过屏幕发生的。我们以惊人的速度滚动浏览图像。这些作品需要另一种关注。展览要求我们不仅要看一件艺术品代表什么，还要考虑它的物理构成、材料已经经历过什么，以及艺术家要求它成为什么。 2026 年 Iziko 展览‘Matereality V2’展览现场", "南非国家美术馆。图片由画廊提供。"], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MaterealityV2_Opening20Aug26_40-1030x686.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Iziko 工作不可避免地意味着要思考历史，因为博物馆包含多层收藏、分类和关于历史上哪些类型的艺术品和材料被认为值得进入国家收藏的想法。对于像“物质现实”这样的展览来说，这一点变得特别有趣，因为许多艺术家使用历史上与手工艺、家务劳动、非正规经济或日常生活相关的实践或材料，而不是所谓的“美术”。第二次迭代更加强调纺织实践、以非洲为中心的观点和本土知识体系。我对编织、缝纫、珠饰和其他形式的手工制作等实践掌握知识的方式特别感兴趣。从历史上看，许多这些实践都与“美术”分离，并被归为工艺、装饰或国内生产。但它们包含复杂的知识、记忆和传输系统。许多当代艺术家正在积极借鉴、破坏或改造这些传统。这与为什么主题展览在博物馆环境中如此有用有关。我只能从我自己作为策展人的角度来说，我绝不会说一个个展就能解决博物馆或艺术史中更大的结构性矛盾。但展览仍然是我可以利用的最直接、最实用的工具之一。它们使我能够跨过传统上组织艺术史和博物馆收藏的一些部门。", {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这背后还有一个现实的制度现实。当增加藏品的预算和程序非常有限时，展览就成为将艺术声音带入博物馆的另一种方式，即使我们还没有能力获得这些作品。它们使我们能够扩大对话范围，介绍永久收藏中可能缺席的艺术家，并测试历史藏品与当代实践之间的新关系。 “物质现实”还引起人们关注的另一个矛盾。博物馆的目的是保存事物。我们试图阻止对象发生变化。但许多当代艺术家刻意使用会变化的材料进行创作。它们会褪色。锈。分解。变脆。衰变。因此，这些作品提出了关于博物馆实际保存什么的有趣问题。是原始材料吗？艺术家的意图？过程？能组件最终会被替换吗？在什么时候更换某些东西会从根本上改变艺术品？这种张力对于当代藏品来说越来越重要：博物馆寻求永恒，而物质本身往往是无常的。", "它们有机地进入，因为材料与地点紧密相连。艺术家与周围的事物合作——文化、经济、环境和政治。在南非，材料可能承载着极其复杂的历史。他们可以谈论采矿和开采、土地和流离失所、移民劳工、服装和身份、家政工作、不平等、环境退化、灵性、土著知识体系和制造历史。但我不希望这些主题成为整齐的类别。我不希望一个房间里有纺织品，另一个房间里有塑料，并在其他地方找到物体。有趣的部分正是这些历史和材料如何纠缠在一起。同时，我也不希望这次展览暗示南非艺术家在某种程度上只是在回应南非的担忧。这些做法与更大的有关气候变化、消费、移民、技术、可持续性和归属感的问题。这就是该展览扩展到南非以外的非洲大陆其他地方的选定艺术家的原因之一。非洲各地正在进行非凡的材料实验，通常使用当地特定的物体或物质，同时与全球系统和关注点进行交流。我感兴趣的正是局部与普遍之间的运动。一种材料可能在开普敦、约翰内斯堡、阿克拉或哈拉雷具有高度具体的社会历史，但艺术品可以同时开启关于当代生活的更广泛的对话。 content.article_text:
W hen the German painter Georg Baselitz died this year a chunk of Europe’s rapidly diminishing historical memory went with him. Baselitz was born in 1938, experienced Hitler’s Germany and the second world war as a young child, then found himself growing up in communist East Germany before escaping to the west and becoming an artist. His acidic, honest perceptions of the history he’d lived through will no longer be those of the living person I was lucky enough to encounter. But he has left us a gift: an exhibition in London he helped plan of his most astonishing history paintings, The Heroes.

It’s a savage, merciless vision of modern history with feelings of horror, disgust and irreparable guilt hanging heavy in the poisoned air. But there’s a terrible joy too, the thrill of speaking the truth. You sense the liberation Baselitz must have felt when he set brush to canvas to start these paintings in 1965. Comparing the explosive rage and nihilism of his art to punk may be inadequate but the title of this series of colossal imaginary portraits is so scathingly ironic it’s like being spat at.

Mit Rote Fahne – or With the Red Banner – depicts a massive, square-shouldered yet exhausted soldier holding a half-lowered flag that is a smear of red and black. A banner of blood, the redness congeals to form black scabs that suggest the shadow of the swastika. All around the soldier is a wasteland. Do we owe him compassion? No, he had none. The devastated world at his feet was destroyed by Germany’s heroes who fought in the second world war. When Baselitz painted these furious homages in the mid-1960s, these men were running West Germany’s banks and car companies.

Another long-haired Hero, in a uniform with shorts, stands in a trashed, blood-stained landscape. This bland-faced character balances two crimson mittens, preparing apparently to let them go and to live on without these gory encumbrances, with clean hands.

It’s as if Baselitz was walking around the increasingly affluent streets of West Germany, seeing healthy, optimistic faces and retching at how easily the crimes of the second world war could be shoved into the past. The Holocaust only ended 20 years ago, these paintings scream, when the armies advancing on Hitler’s Reich discovered the places where six million Jews were systematically murdered – how can we Germans hold our heads high and strut on?

But if Germany is mired in shame, what about German art? Baselitz and his artistic peers Joseph Beuys and Anselm Kiefer, all of whom face German history head on, were sometimes accused by critics of glorifying it, or feasting on it, but there’s no hint of Teutonic grandeur here. In Ein Moderner Maler – A modern painter – Baselitz depicts an artist who can’t work because both hands are caught in man-traps. He sits defeated on the ground in military-looking clothes with armbands, as guilty and mad as all the other Heroes. He literally spills his guts in a parody of inner angst: a curl of intestines lies between his legs, while another section of bowel emerges from his side and becomes a spiralling pig’s tail. This is what the German artist’s romantic inner life has become. It’s OK to laugh. His hair is flattened on his head and he has a hint of a square moustache to remind you that Hitler, too, fancied himself an artist.

Baselitz reserves his deepest disgust for his own artistic mastery: painting has been smashed, it is no longer possible, say these brilliant paintings. Their uncoordinated, lumpen figures look like Frankensteinian monsters, made from bits and pieces of mud and flesh pathetically sewn together. One soldier, sitting under the trees, has a square head on top of a slumped, square body as blood drips on his head from two branches. He is a ghost inside his garments, there and not there.

This way of depicting the human figure makes Baselitz unique. He has little in common with British postwar figurative artists such as Bacon and Freud for whom there is always a real, pulsing body they’re trying to record. Baselitz’s bodies are abstract, designed with irony and black humour, their sufferings absurd. Another Hero stands with his flies undone, grey spurts of semen emerging from his black trousers as he towers over a shattered landscape. His ecstatic expression tells us he’s turned on by it all while at his feet is a Disneyish duck, an emblem perhaps of the innocence he will feign in postwar life.

What has happened to the art of memory? After all the artistic reckonings, the history books and Holocaust memorials, the far-right AfD is winning one election after another in Germany. For extremists of all hues it isn’t even necessary to deny the Holocaust – nowadays you can shrug it off, trivialise it, dismiss it as belonging to the distant past. And the Heroes walk again. Baselitz paints one of them waving, or is it saluting, in blood-soaked trousers with a ghostly shadow of a face. Around him in the European night white flecks fall slowly, like snow or ashes.

content.article_text:
“ Other Mommy ” may have dominated “ The Social Reckoning ” at the box office this past weekend, but there’s no hard feelings between longtime friends Jessica Chastain and Jeremy Strong .

Chastain, who stars as a demonic mother in horror movie “Other Mommy,” shared on her Instagram Story Monday night a playful string of text messages with Strong, who plays Mark Zuckerberg in Aaron Sorkin’s “Social Network” follow-up.

Related Stories

Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound

Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart

Strong texted Chastain a Vulture headline about “Other Mommy’s” box office success which read, “‘Other Mommy’ Spanks ‘The Social Reckoning’ at the Box Office.” Indeed, it did — “Other Mommy” scored the No. 1 spot with $27.5 million , while “The Social Reckoning” flopped with just $5.5 million.

Popular on Variety

“Omg,” Chastain replied, to which Strong fired back with a middle finger emoji and kiss emoji.

“These pics are hysterical,” Chastain commented of Vulture’s photo choice, featuring them side-by-side in character. “Its so funny,” Strong said, to which Chastain responded: “You look SO SAD!”

“Other Mommy” debuted well above box office expectations, considering the fact that it received poor reviews and a D+ grade on CinemaScore. With a budget of just $18 million, Blumhouse and Universal’s campy thriller is well positioned financially.

“The Social Reckoning,” on the other hand, failed to live up to its projected debut of $7 million to $8 million. Critics were mixed on the film, which follows a Facebook engineer (Mikey Madison) who leaks thousands of internal documents to a reporter (Jeremy Allen White) to blow the whistle on the company’s dark practices. Strong once again went Method to portray Zuckerberg, with Sorkin telling The New York Times that the actor treated his co-stars “the way he imagines” Zuckerberg would.

“I told all the other actors in his scenes: ‘Guys, he’s not going to be hanging out with you at craft service. He’s not going to be yucking it up with you between takes. He’s probably not going to speak to you at all. He is going to treat you the way he imagines Mark treats the people around him,'” Sorkin said. “And that’s what happened. You cannot argue with the results.”

Alternativa Distribution Unveils New Acquisitions, Including Cannes Prize-Winner “Elephants in the Fog” and Berlinale Opener “No Good Men”

The latest slate includes award-winning films from Cannes, Venice, Berlin and Busan, as well as titles connected to the 2027 Academy Awards.

Alternativa Distribution, a non-profit distribution label of the global film initiative Alternativa , supported by mobility platform inDrive , has announced its latest acquisitions ahead of MIPCOM 2026 . The new slate includes Cannes Un Certain Regard Jury Prize winner and Nepal’s official submission for the 99th Academy Awards, “ Elephants in the Fog ” (2026), directed by Abinash Bikram Shah , Berlinale 2026 opening film “ No Good Men ” (2026), directed by Shahrbanoo Sadat , “Lost Land” (2025), directed by Akio Fujimoto , and the Academy Award-nominated documentary “ Four Daughters ” (2023), directed by Kaouther Ben Hania .

Launched in July 2026, Alternativa Distribution aims to create a fairer distribution model for filmmakers from the Global South while expanding the international reach of films with strong social and cultural themes. The latest acquisitions bring the distributor’s catalogue to 14 titles during its first year of operation.

Four Acquisitions with International Recognition

The new slate brings together films that have received recognition at major international festivals and awards ceremonies.

“Elephants in the Fog”, directed by Abinash Bikram Shah, won the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. It is also Nepal’s official submission in the Best International Feature Film category for the 99th Academy Awards. Alternativa Distribution will represent the film in multiple territories across Asia and Latin America.

“No Good Men”, directed by Shahrbanoo Sadat, was selected as the opening film of the 2026 Berlin International Film Festival. The film is also among the titles submitted to German Films for consideration in the Best International Feature Film category at the 99th Academy Awards. Alternativa Distribution will handle multiple territories across Asia, the Middle East and North Africa, and Sub-Saharan Africa.

“Lost Land”, directed by Akio Fujimoto, received the Orizzonti Special Jury Prize at the 2025 Venice Film Festival, the Golden Yusr Award for Best Feature Film at the Red Sea International Film Festival, and the Nativa Award at the 2026 Alternativa Film Festival. Alternativa Distribution will represent the film across Southeast Asia, excluding Malaysia, as well as the Nordic countries, Poland and Portugal.

“Four Daughters”, directed by Kaouther Ben Hania, won the L’Oeil d’or for Best Documentary at the Cannes Film Festival and was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature. The distributor will represent the film in multiple territories across Latin America and Asia.

A Fairer Distribution Model for Filmmakers

Alternativa Distribution focuses on exclusive, first-window regional and international non-theatrical distribution rights for scripted, documentary and animated feature films with strong social and cultural themes. Its model is designed to help filmmakers reach broadcasters, streaming platforms and educational institutions beyond the traditional festival circuit.

Under its fair-terms approach, the distributor offers filmmakers an upfront minimum guarantee alongside a share of revenues once distribution deals are signed. It also provides localization support and seeks to make acclaimed international titles available to buyers at accessible licensing fees. Income is reinvested to expand the distributor’s reach and support filmmakers and regional film industries across the Global South.

One of the four newly announced titles was previously recognized at the Alternativa Film Festival, a travelling event and industry initiative dedicated to supporting impact-driven cinema. The festival’s most recent edition took place in Medellín, Colombia, in April 2026, with the next edition planned for Africa in 2027.

Supporting Stories from the Global South

Avital Lavi, Head of Alternativa Distribution, said the new slate would expand the distributor’s international reach and bring more acclaimed films to buyers and audiences who might otherwise have limited access to them: “With our second film slate, we are expanding our global reach to give buyers and audiences access to even more exceptional, high-impact storytelling,” Lavi said. “Our latest acquisitions have already proven themselves on the world stage, from a Cannes prize-winner to acclaimed titles featured at Venice and Berlinale. We’re incredibly proud to represent them and look forward to getting them in front of broadcasters and streaming platforms, and by extension audiences, that might not have had the chance to see them otherwise.”

Arsen Tomsky, CEO and Founder of inDrive, highlighted the challenges filmmakers from the Global South face in reaching international audiences: “Exceptional filmmaking can come from anywhere, but access to international audiences remains hindered by a deeply unequal system,” Tomsky said. “Alternativa Distribution was created to challenge that imbalance. This slate has been carefully curated and showcases the high quality and transformative power of filmmaking from the Global South, and the positive impact these films can have when they reach wider audiences.” Tomsky added that building a portfolio of 14 titles in the distributor’s first year represents an important milestone in its mission to connect these stories with audiences worldwide.

content.editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "本次比赛的评审团由摄影师Louis Lepron担任主席，成员包括《Fisheye》主编Fabrice Laroche、Arc’teryx品牌大使兼攀岩者Coraline Ribeil，以及《Fisheye》创意制作人Diane "黑白照片、荧光般的色彩、令人头晕目眩的透视——这是三位获奖者带来的视觉经验。在Arcadi De Miguel Sanz的作品中，我们来到虚空边缘，影像将我们悬在两条绳索之间，邀我们攀登。人物消隐于风景，与环境融为一体。岩石仿佛将我们吸入，人逐渐消失在自然中，也让我们想随他一同跃入。Emilien Guyard则采用了不同的视角：他的作品构成一个色彩绚丽、却并不让人安心的世界。蓝色岩石与红色天空形成对照，整个世界如梦一般，几乎带着惊悚感，让人仿佛置身一部真正的惊悚片。这个人能成功攀上去吗？岩石似乎融入熔岩色的天空，随后又渐渐变成冰。冬天带着蓝调而来，人物不再是绿色的外星来客，而变成了黄色——难道他也在燃烧？最后，Amandine Joset营造了奇幻的场景，人物轮廓格外鲜明。但在这里，天空吸引了我们的全部注意：那是星星吗，还是闪粉？重返黑白的画面，让我们为那个坠落的人影感到战栗与不安。摄影师仍把我们带进她的梦中，让这个身影置于世界的中心。攀岩者如此渺小，仿佛与石块的海洋融为一体；她独自处于画面中心，令这幅照片升华。三个世界大不相同，却都让我们屏息，将我们带向高高的天空。", "translated": true}, content.article_text:
Avec pour président le photographe Louis Lepron, le jury du concours était composé de Fabrice Laroche, rédacteur en chef de Fisheye , de l’ambassadrice Arc’teryx et grimpeuse Coraline Ribeil, ainsi que de Diane Mathé-Dumaine, productrice créative à Fisheye : ce jury s’est réuni en ce début de septembre afin de désigner leurs trois lauréats. Les images abordent le thème de l’ascension, du corps et de la grimpe.

Une ascension vertigineuse et visuelle

Amateurs de la grimpe, grimpeurs passionnés ou simples observateurs de la roche, tous ont pu participer au concours organisé par Arc’teryx et Fisheye . L’objectif était de réussir à raconter l’escalade sous des prismes inédits. Le plus important était de faire cohabiter l’image avec la hauteur pour pouvoir passer de l’intimité du bloc à la grandeur de la voie. Par ce concours, la paroi devient le terrain de jeu des regards où la gravité est défiée grâce à l’image. La thématique, « Ascension visuelle », amène le spectateur à renouveler l’iconographie traditionnelle de la discipline. Les lauréats désignés ne sont autres que : Arcadi De Miguel Sanz, Emilien Guyard et Amandine Joset.

Un jeu de perspective, entre onirisme et fantastique

Des photos en noir et blanc, des couleurs fluorescentes, des perspectives qui nous retournent la tête, c’est ce que nous proposent les trois lauréats de ce concours. Avec Arcadi De Miguel Sanz, nous sommes au bord du vide, ses images nous tiennent entre deux cordes et nous invitent à grimper. Les personnages se perdent dans le paysage pour ne faire qu’un avec l’environnement. La roche nous aspire, l’homme disparaît dans la nature et nous donne envie, nous aussi, de plonger avec lui. Pour Emilien Guyard, les perspectives sont différentes. Il fait de son travail un univers coloré, pour autant il n’est pas rassurant. La roche bleue contraste avec le ciel rouge, l’univers semble onirique, presque effrayant, nous donnant l’impression de vivre un vrai thriller. L’homme va-t-il réussir à grimper ? La roche semble se fondre dans le ciel couleur lave, puis peu à peu elle se transforme en glace. L’hiver arrive avec ses tons bleutés et l’homme n’est plus un extraterrestre vert, il devient jaune, peut-être brûle-t-il lui aussi ? Pour finir, Amandine Joset amène un décor fantastique, chez elle, les silhouettes se remarquent. Mais ici, c’est le ciel qui attire toute notre attention. S’agit-il d’étoiles ? Ou peut-être de paillettes ? Le retour du noir et blanc nous fait ressentir des frissons et de l’angoisse pour cette figure tombante. La photographe réussit tout de même à nous plonger dans son rêve, là où cette silhouette se trouve au centre du monde. La grimpeuse est si petite qu’elle ne fait qu’un avec l’océan de cailloux, elle est seule au centre de l’image et elle sublime le cliché. Des univers bien différents mais qui pour autant nous laissent sans voix et nous transportent très haut dans le ciel.

Curiosité

content.article_text:
T his fly-on-the-wall documentary about the former Irish Green party leader and cabinet minister Eamon Ryan reminded me of the political satire The Thick of It – but without the cynical gags and hapless self-serving politicians. Even after you factor in the skewing effect of it being a favourable portrait, showing him in the best possible light, Ryan comes across as one of the good guys: principled, likable and extremely hard working. The film follows his final 18 months serving in Ireland’s coalition government as minister for the environment and transport before stepping down in 2025.

The title is something that Ryan’s 25-year-old son Tommy repeats over and over. “Forever … forever … forever.” Tommy is autistic and requires full-time care. When Ryan resigns from government, one of his reasons is to spend more time with Tommy. We see the pair of them at the allotment picking raspberries and walking the dog. But other than a quick glimpse of his wife, Victoria, the rest of Ryan’s family life is kept firmly behind closed doors.

Instead, the cameras trail him on the road, talking to angry residents of an Irish town submerged by flood waters (again), and hustling at the UN general assembly in New York and two Cop conferences. At his side is formidable media adviser Edel Hackett (Malcolm Tucker with morals), who sifts through the daily torrent of online abuse, harassment and intimidation slung Ryan’s way.

The film is lacking a little context: perhaps an interview or two with Ryan might have been helpful, giving some background to the Cop conferences and – for those unfamiliar with Irish politics – the ambitious climate laws he pushed through in office. Something on the general election wipeout of Greens in November 2024 would have been useful too. But no explanation is necessary watching Ryan’s crumpled crestfallen face in January 2025 as he packs up his ministerial office, watching Donald Trump’s inauguration on TV.

Daily Newsletter

Vermeer the Immortal

Tracing the Dutch painter’s enduring influence, free back-to-school art supplies for NYC teachers, and a glitch at a Pioneer Works exhibition is unexpectedly illuminating.

Vermeer is everywhere. Not only in the hallowed halls of museums, but also in the gentle light that streams through the window just so, or in the crisp pages of a love letter set down gently at one’s writing desk. Historian Ruth Bernard Yeazell seems to agree in Vermeer’s Afterlives , her new title tracing the Dutch painter’s enduring presence across the arts, from film to verse. Lauren Moya Ford brings us into its exquisitely illustrated pages.

In another must-read today, a glitch at Finnegan Shannon’s Pioneer Works exhibition yields insights on institutions and accessibility. “The installation’s deviation from what I expected, like disability itself, offered me a new perspective on the world,” Bryan Martin writes, “a reminder of our collective responsibility to those who live in it.”Hyperallergic Halloween is around the corner. RSVP for our art costume party with snacks and an open bar in Brooklyn on Wednesday, October 28 — members get discounted tickets!

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

Finding Vermeer in Unexpected Places

As strange as it may sound, Johannes Vermeer’s fame is a relatively recent phenomenon. The Dutch painter known for his exquisite, enigmatic interior scenes fell into obscurity shortly after he died deeply in debt at only 43 years old in 1675. Vermeer was barely a footnote in the annals of art history until the mid-19th century, when the Parisian critic Théophile Thoré rediscovered his work. “Here’s someone we don’t know in France, and who very much deserves to be known!” the writer proclaimed in 1866. | Lauren Moya Ford

content.article_text:
盗まれたルノワールの絵画を「住宅の壁の裏」で発見。6人が逮捕、カンバスには裂け目も

南 フランス の ルノワール 美術館から盗まれた絵画2点が、約1カ月ぶりに回収された。作品は住宅のコンクリートブロック壁の裏に隠されていた。事件に関連して6人が逮捕され、地元市長は作品の発見に安堵を示している。

南 フランス のカーニュ＝シュル＝メール市にあるルノワール美術館から盗まれた絵画2点が、フランスの捜査当局によって回収された。

同館は、 オーギュスト・ルノワール （1841-1919）が晩年を過ごした住居を美術館にした施設で、絵画や彫刻、家具などを公開している。事件前には、ルノワールの絵画12点が展示されていたと報じられている。

事件が起きたのは9月8日早朝。窃盗犯はルノワールの絵画4点を持ち出し、このうち《コロンナ・ロマーノ夫人の肖像（Portrait de Madame Colonna Romano）》（1913頃）と《井戸端の若い女性（Jeune femme au puits）》（1886頃）を持ち去った。一方、《スティーヴン・ピション夫人の肖像（Portrait de Madame Stephen Pichon）》（1895頃）と《読書するココ（Coco lisant）》（1905頃）の2点は、逃走時に置き去りにされた。4点の評価額は、計900万ユーロ（約16億円）とされていた。

同市の市長、ブライアン・マソンは事件当時、「ルノワール美術館への攻撃は、カーニュ＝シュル＝メールの歴史と文化遺産の一部に対する攻撃です」と述べた。また、窃盗犯は「電動ナイフ」か「金属用のこぎり」を使い、絵画を壁に固定していたボルトを切断したという。

アイルランドの公共放送 RTÉ によると、その後10月7日に6人が逮捕された。マルセイユの検事ニコラ・ベッソンはパリで記者団に対し、8日に南フランスのクレルモン＝レローにある住宅を捜索した結果、絵画を回収したと説明した。

ベッソンは、発見時の状況と捜査の経緯を次のように語った。

「絵画は頑丈なコンクリートブロックの壁の裏に隠されており、外からは全く見つけられない状態でした。捜査員による取り調べの結果、容疑者が実際に絵画を受け取っていたことを認めたのです」

回収された2点は「比較的良好な状態」だったものの、いずれにも損傷が見られた。《井戸端の若い女性》は額縁に軽微な傷があり、《コロンナ・ロマーノ夫人の肖像》は、ドレスが描かれた部分のカンバスに裂け目があった。ベッソンによれば、2点とも修復が必要だという。

作品の回収を受け、マソン市長は声明で次のように述べた。

「この2点の絵画は、単なる美術作品ではありません。私たちの街の歴史と文化遺産の一部であり、オーギュスト・ルノワールがカーニュ＝シュル＝メールに残した遺産なのです。作品が見つかったことは、市民の皆さん、そして美術館を大切に思う全ての人にとって、大きな安堵をもたらしました」

一方、ロンドンの ナショナル・ギャラリー では現在、ルノワールの絵画40点を集めた大規模展「 Renoir and Love 」が開催されている。会期は2027年1月31日まで。（翻訳：編集部）

content.article_text:
The U.K. may have been slower than other markets to jump onto the boom in short-form vertical media, projected to generate $150 billion in revenue in markets outside China this year, but it is now getting its own dedicated festival.

British indie film stalwart Raindance is launching Raindance Vertical, a one-day festival and financing market in London for vertical film and series.

Popular on Variety

Related Stories

Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart

Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound

The event will take place on Dec. 4 — conveniently timed between Content London and the British Independent Film Awards — at Soho’s Karma Sanctum Hotel and is set to encompass two competitive categories, Vertical Short Film and Vertical Series. Submissions open today via FilmFreeway and are open to UK and international filmmakers until Nov.

“The British film industry needs to stop sneering at the shape of the screen and start watching what’s on it,” said Raindance founder Elliot Grove. “We started Raindance to give filmmakers a chance when the industry wouldn’t. Raindance Vertical carries that forward: discover the talent, take the work seriously and put filmmakers in the room with people who can finance their next project.”

Alongside the competitions, which will see awards juried by filmmakers working in the format, the festival will include panels and workshops, and what it’s describing as a “vertical mini-market” run with Charlotte Knowles’ Creative HQ, which will match pre-vetted producers with financiers, platforms, commissioners and brands.

According to Raindance, U.K. filmmakers are already producing vertical work to a professional standard but have “few routes to the financiers, studios, streamers and brands who could back it,” with the festival and market designed to address that.

The festival’s advisory group includes director Dan Löwenstein, founder of House of Create, vertical drama critic and consultant Jen Cooper of Vertical Drama Love, and Christine Hartland, co-founder and chief operating officer of My Smash Media.

“Vertical takes the same directing discipline, the same crews and the same storytelling rigour, just with a different structure and pace,” said Löwenstein, who has directed 36 vertical dramas for broadcasters, streamers and dedicated microdrama platforms. “It’s fast, data-informed and, yes, low budget, but within those constraints you find real invention. This festival is a chance to show the best U.K. and international vertical drama alongside outstanding features and shorts, and I’m excited to see what the U.K. brings to the format.”

The Raindance Vertical programme will run across one day, with all work screened in 9:16.
