content.article_text:
Oscar-winning French actor Marion Cotillard will preside over the competition jury at the 23rd Marrakech Film Festival in November.

Alongside her to be announced jury members, the “Inception” and “Dark Knight Rises” star will lead the decision of which film is awarded the Étoile d’Or out of Marrakech’s international competition, which consists of first and second features.

“I have been fortunate enough to attend the Marrakech International Film Festival since its very beginnings; I’ve had wonderful experiences there and met some truly remarkable people,” Cotillard said in a statement. “Supporting filmmakers as they take their first steps is a vital part of what this festival is all about — it’s in its DNA — and it is a great joy for me to chair the jury this year.”

Related Stories

'Other Mommy' Nips 'Verity' in Photo Finish for U.K., Ireland Box Office Summit

'Breaking Bad' Star RJ Mitte's Cause of Death Confirmed as Suicide

Cotillard first broke out in the 1998 French action comedy “Taxi,” before making her Hollywood debut in Tim Burton’s “Big Fish” in 2003. In 2007, she portrayed French singer Édith Piaf in “La Vie en Rose” and won the Oscar for best actress, becoming the first actor to win an Academy Award for a French-language performance. She earned her second best actress Oscar nomination in 2015 for the Dardenne Brothers’ drama “Two Days, One Night.”

Popular on Variety

Most recently, she starred in Guillaume Canet’s Cannes-premiering “Karma,” “Lee” alongside Kate Winslet and on the TV series “The Morning Show” opposite Jennifer Aniston and Reese Witherspoon. She is currently filming “The Enraged,” a historical drama from Emmanuelle Bercot.

This year’s Marrakech Film Festival takes place from Nov. 20-28.

They are continually moving between jobs, places and problems, reacting to whatever circumstances impose upon them. Handheld camerawork, restless movement and the editing rhythm were all designed around this lack of stability, giving the sense that the characters are heading somewhere without ever knowing exactly where."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Check the review of the film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The film’s female character is approached very differently. Singh repeatedly films her from behind or avoids presenting her fully because the movie experiences her largely through the young man’s perspective. To him, she is almost a ghost from his past: the person who drew him toward the city but who never completely belongs to him. Singh was also conscious of stereotypes surrounding Nepali women in Delhi, particularly assumptions connecting them with salons, massage parlors and nighttime work. Rather than explaining exactly what she does, he deliberately preserves uncertainty around her life and keeps part of her identity beyond both the protagonist and the audience."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The resulting film is undeniably bleak, although Singh does not consider that a general statement about all Nepali migrants. He knows people who have overcome extremely difficult circumstances and built successful lives through their work. The bleakness instead reflects what he sees in the particular social environment occupied by these characters. As outsiders living within the urban underbelly, they remain especially vulnerable when something goes wrong: they can be blamed first, dismissed first and reminded immediately that they are considered not to belong."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alcohol consequently appears less as casual recreation than as a way of temporarily escaping a reality over which the characters have little control. Singh clarified that another substance appearing in the story is not a recreational drug but steroids used in an attempt to pass army recruitment requirements. Alcoholism, however, is something he sees as a genuine social problem, particularly among people whose hopes remain alive while their surroundings continually undermine them. For such characters, drinking can become a way of briefly “checking out” from a claustrophobic existence."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One of the film’s most striking sequences, in which the young man’s head is forcibly shaved during army training, comes directly from Singh’s own experience. Coming from an army family and once expected to join the Indian Army himself, he remembers having his long hair shaved before recruitment. He also witnessed hair cutting being used to discipline and humiliate recruits who appeared insufficiently serious. In “Khoriya”, the humiliation acquires another layer because the other recruits laugh specifically when the Nepali character is subjected to it."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Remarkably, the scene itself was largely documentary. Singh filmed at a functioning training center using real army hopefuls and a real coach, without controlling their routine. The production had to arrive during their early-morning training and simply place the actors within the existing environment. Singh told the coach that the protagonist was a new recruit who had not been attending properly and asked what he would normally do. The coach replied that he would shave his head. Singh handed him a clipper and allowed the situation to unfold, even without discussing the decision with the actor beforehand. Four months of street casting followed, particularly in Delhi neighborhoods with significant Nepali populations, but Singh initially encountered understandable suspicion from people who did not know him and had never considered themselves actors. Eventually, he travelled to Sikkim and contacted the National School of Drama’s local repertory. At around 4:30 one morning, Singh was scrolling through Instagram when he encountered an absurd reel that made him laugh. He immediately messaged the young man about meeting for the film, received a response within a minute and quickly became convinced that he had found not simply an actor but the character himself. The performer playing the elder brother brought an even more direct connection to the material, having grown up around a family business involving a momo shop and poultry farm."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That authenticity meant Singh had to surrender some control. Since he was not from the community and did not fully speak the language, he refused to dictate dialogue and linguistic details he could not genuinely understand. Casting director Vinita Chamling Rai and the actors helped shape the language, tone and cultural specificity of individual scenes. A month and a half of workshops allowed them to repeatedly rewrite and perform dialogue until Singh could recognize its emotional rhythm almost musically, even when he could not understand every word literally."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Post-production proved almost as lengthy as the production itself. Because “Khoriya” was shot across separate periods, Singh initially edited the material himself after the first schedule. Following the second shoot, another editor reconstructed and expanded that version over approximately eight months. Selection for an NFDC film lab subsequently brought post-production funding and mentorship from experienced editors, while executive producer Ashim Ahluwalia helped further refine the film’s voice and structure. Altogether, Singh estimates that the editing process lasted roughly a year and a half."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Singh has already begun writing his next project, which moves into very different territory. The film will concern Indian soldiers during World War II, and he is currently taking meetings while preparing to pitch it. He also revealed that he discussed the project with Wim Wenders the previous year, although he is not yet ready to disclose further details."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Khoriya”, however, remains closely connected to the filmmaker’s original documentary impulse. Rather than attempting to speak completely on behalf of a community outside his own, Singh built the production around collaboration, observation and occasionally relinquishing authority. The resulting film reflects characters who rarely control what happens to them, while the filmmaking itself repeatedly allowed an unpredictable reality to enter the frame."}]
content.article_text:
Vishwendra Singh Talks “Khoriya”, Nepali Migrants, Documentary Realism and Life on the Margins of Delhi

Vishwendra Singh discusses “Khoriya”, Nepali migrants, documentary realism and finding authenticity through actors and real locations.

Vishwendra Singh’s “ Khoriya ” emerged from an attempt to document a community that, despite being highly visible within Indian cities, remains largely absent from mainstream representation. Centered on Nepali migrants living and working in Delhi, the film combines fiction with an intensely observational approach, following characters whose financial insecurity, precarious employment and outsider status leave them almost permanently in motion. Speaking with Asian Movie Pulse, Singh discussed the documentary origins of the project, the connection between the film’s bird-flu outbreak and COVID, its relentless tension, working with Nepali actors, and a production process that frequently allowed reality to determine what happened next.

Khoriya is screening at Busan International Film Festival

The origins of “Khoriya” go back to 2019, when Singh began making an informal documentary about Nepali migrants working in Indian cities. The subject had personal significance for him: he had grown up around Nepali people, had Nepali classmates, and his brother-in-law is Nepali. Yet he felt this substantial migrant community was rarely discussed within India. When COVID arrived in 2020, the documentary collapsed as Singh lost contact with several of his subjects. The stories, however, remained with him, eventually pushing him toward fiction as another way of exploring the same world.

COVID also entered the film indirectly. The avian-flu outbreak depicted in the story functions partly as a metaphor for the pandemic and for the experience of seeing livelihoods suddenly disappear. Singh points particularly toward Nepali workers occupying some of the least secure positions within poultry businesses, handling animals while facing the greatest physical risks and enjoying little protection. One of his protagonists has actually risen to become a poultry-farm manager, putting a Nepali character unusually in a position of authority, only to watch that status disappear when the outbreak destroys the business.

The constant tension running through “Khoriya” reflects this instability. Singh did not want the characters to appear as people with enough security to stop, evaluate their circumstances and calmly decide what to do next. Their lives simply do not provide that luxury. They are continually moving between jobs, places and problems, reacting to whatever circumstances impose upon them. Handheld camerawork, restless movement and the editing rhythm were all designed around this lack of stability, giving the sense that the characters are heading somewhere without ever knowing exactly where.

Check the review of the film

The film’s female character is approached very differently. Singh repeatedly films her from behind or avoids presenting her fully because the movie experiences her largely through the young man’s perspective. To him, she is almost a ghost from his past: the person who drew him toward the city but who never completely belongs to him. Singh was also conscious of stereotypes surrounding Nepali women in Delhi, particularly assumptions connecting them with salons, massage parlors and nighttime work. Rather than explaining exactly what she does, he deliberately preserves uncertainty around her life and keeps part of her identity beyond both the protagonist and the audience.

The resulting film is undeniably bleak, although Singh does not consider that a general statement about all Nepali migrants. He knows people who have overcome extremely difficult circumstances and built successful lives through their work. The bleakness instead reflects what he sees in the particular social environment occupied by these characters. As outsiders living within the urban underbelly, they remain especially vulnerable when something goes wrong: they can be blamed first, dismissed first and reminded immediately that they are considered not to belong.

Alcohol consequently appears less as casual recreation than as a way of temporarily escaping a reality over which the characters have little control. Singh clarified that another substance appearing in the story is not a recreational drug but steroids used in an attempt to pass army recruitment requirements. Alcoholism, however, is something he sees as a genuine social problem, particularly among people whose hopes remain alive while their surroundings continually undermine them. For such characters, drinking can become a way of briefly “checking out” from a claustrophobic existence.

One of the film’s most striking sequences, in which the young man’s head is forcibly shaved during army training, comes directly from Singh’s own experience. Coming from an army family and once expected to join the Indian Army himself, he remembers having his long hair shaved before recruitment. He also witnessed hair cutting being used to discipline and humiliate recruits who appeared insufficiently serious. In “Khoriya”, the humiliation acquires another layer because the other recruits laugh specifically when the Nepali character is subjected to it.

Remarkably, the scene itself was largely documentary. Singh filmed at a functioning training center using real army hopefuls and a real coach, without controlling their routine. The production had to arrive during their early-morning training and simply place the actors within the existing environment. Singh told the coach that the protagonist was a new recruit who had not been attending properly and asked what he would normally do. The coach replied that he would shave his head. Singh handed him a clipper and allowed the situation to unfold, even without discussing the decision with the actor beforehand. Afterward, the production took a day off to recalibrate, while the character’s newly shaved appearance ended up changing the rest of the film visually.

Casting presented one of the production’s greatest difficulties. Singh found that established casting networks in Mumbai and Delhi offered very limited access to Nepali and northeastern performers. Four months of street casting followed, particularly in Delhi neighborhoods with significant Nepali populations, but Singh initially encountered understandable suspicion from people who did not know him and had never considered themselves actors. Eventually, he travelled to Sikkim and contacted the National School of Drama’s local repertory. Two performers ultimately resigned from the repertory in order to join the film.

The younger brother was discovered in a considerably less conventional manner. At around 4:30 one morning, Singh was scrolling through Instagram when he encountered an absurd reel that made him laugh. He immediately messaged the young man about meeting for the film, received a response within a minute and quickly became convinced that he had found not simply an actor but the character himself. The performer playing the elder brother brought an even more direct connection to the material, having grown up around a family business involving a momo shop and poultry farm.

That authenticity meant Singh had to surrender some control. Since he was not from the community and did not fully speak the language, he refused to dictate dialogue and linguistic details he could not genuinely understand. Casting director Vinita Chamling Rai and the actors helped shape the language, tone and cultural specificity of individual scenes. A month and a half of workshops allowed them to repeatedly rewrite and perform dialogue until Singh could recognize its emotional rhythm almost musically, even when he could not understand every word literally.

Post-production proved almost as lengthy as the production itself. Because “Khoriya” was shot across separate periods, Singh initially edited the material himself after the first schedule. Following the second shoot, another editor reconstructed and expanded that version over approximately eight months. Selection for an NFDC film lab subsequently brought post-production funding and mentorship from experienced editors, while executive producer Ashim Ahluwalia helped further refine the film’s voice and structure. Altogether, Singh estimates that the editing process lasted roughly a year and a half.

Singh has already begun writing his next project, which moves into very different territory. The film will concern Indian soldiers during World War II, and he is currently taking meetings while preparing to pitch it. He also revealed that he discussed the project with Wim Wenders the previous year, although he is not yet ready to disclose further details.

“Khoriya”, however, remains closely connected to the filmmaker’s original documentary impulse. Its fiction repeatedly opens itself to real locations, real routines and people whose experiences are close to those of the characters. Rather than attempting to speak completely on behalf of a community outside his own, Singh built the production around collaboration, observation and occasionally relinquishing authority. The resulting film reflects characters who rarely control what happens to them, while the filmmaking itself repeatedly allowed an unpredictable reality to enter the frame.

content.article_text:
I n retrospect, David Fincher’s 2010 film The Social Network was a landmark for a quiet, even counterintuitive reason. Before the film was released, some questioned whether Aaron Sorkin, a writer not exactly known for his mastery of, nevermind obsession with, the technical sphere, was the right man to tell the origin story of Facebook. And while Sorkin may well have converted Mark Zuckerberg into terms he could better understand – namely, a motormouthed wiseass who deep down wants to impress a smart, serious-minded girl – he and Fincher also made one of the first internet-centric movies to treat online life as a natural extension of IRL dynamics, rather than the otherworldly tech portal seen in so many 90s internet movies.

Granted, that’s the whole deal with Facebook: its viral spread of social networking, something so simple and addictive that aunts, grandpas and co-workers everywhere could understand it. Yet understanding its simultaneous extension and distortion of the real world wasn’t a given; four years later, for example, 2014’s Men, Women and Children was widely derided for taking an alarmist approach to the internet as a haven for adults seeking an affair, teenagers nursing porn addictions and fame-hungry strivers of all ages. The Social Network, on the other hand, is remarkably nonjudgmental about the basic mechanics of Facebook , rooting its nascent flaws in the human weaknesses that birthed it. In retrospect, the movie only feels outdated to the extent that it underestimates Zuckerberg’s grasping for power and the potential for grim carelessness that his online kingdom was built on.

The Social Reckoning, a sorta-sequel written and directed by Sorkin without Fincher’s involvement, aims to correct the record while still giving voice to a character who believes that the site has real utility. Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), who works for the site’s civics team, is socially awkward and anxious, and when she notes that some people are better at a keyboard than they are in person, it’s clear she’s thinking of herself, even though she never says so. Frances is distraught to learn that Facebook is contributing to radicalization of some of its users, funneling them into extremist groups as a function of its give-the-people-what-they-want approach to free speech. She turns to a luddite-adjacent journalist (Jeremy Allen White) doing some digging on the company, and together they challenge the orthodoxy of Zuckerberg, last seen in The Social Network fruitlessly refreshing a Facebook page hoping for a reciprocated friend request.

Appropriate for a movie set largely in the early 2020s, The Social Reckoning’s Zuckerberg is a completely different person, literally: famously intense Jeremy Strong steps in for the comparably charming Jesse Eisenberg. But Zuck isn’t the main focus here anyway; though he is depicted as a sort of mutation of the aggrieved nerd from the first film, still issuing cutting sarcastic remarks, but in the voice of an empty-suit automaton, the movie wants to be about the ways that social networking has metastasized beyond Zuckerberg’s control. He can’t do anything about ill effects on real life – he laments the both-sides attacks he’ll face no matter what he does – so he might as well keep the profits churning in.

It’s here where Sorkin both oversteps and falls short in his analysis of how online reality has bled into the real world. On one hand, he connects the radicalization of some Facebook users to the January 6 insurrection riots in Washington, jumping into the Facebook control room for a chilling look at their inaction in the face of fomenting violence in our own country. Connecting that particular dot requires some timeline fudging of the dual whistleblower-and-Zuckerberg story threads, but you understand why Sorkin went to the trouble. It’s an event representing the kind of behavior that Facebook probably enabled, both ideologically and logistically.

Yet Sorkin also insists on containing that behavior in stodgy, old-fashioned terms. The January 6 riots are framed as particularly far beyond the pale in large part because they bring harm to police officers – which connects back to the movie’s opening sequence, where a drunk and racist woman livestreams her horrible comments to non-white police officers on Facebook. Won’t someone please think of the cops?! (It’s as if Sorkin can’t conceive of racism so blatant unless it’s been officially documented by the police.) This is how Sorkin knows the proper order has been threatened.

When Frances quits her Facebook post and testifies in front of Congress, the movie implies with her moment of triumph that the reckoning is at hand, and that Zuckerberg has been, on some level, chastened and/or humiliated. The world has been pulled back from the brink. Meanwhile, the existence of even more damning cases against Facebook, like the idea that the company enabled genocide in Myanmar , doesn’t get so much as a mention. One movie can’t be expected to cover the whole of the global internet, but that doesn’t stop The Social Reckoning from feeling awfully small.

A more subtle sign that Sorkin hasn’t oriented himself in the actual 2020s, and instead prefers a world that no longer exists: every cultural reference point he summons throughout the movie dates from around the middle of the 20h century. The reporter loves Show Boat. Later, he expresses his surprise and gratification that Frances makes reference to Frank Capra – then proceeds to recommend more of the director’s films, because she’s only seen two of them. A Zuckerberg handler makes reference to Gilligan’s Island to illustrate a point about the public’s gullibility. The most contemporary he gets, apart from the unavoidable current events, is name-checking Woodward and Bernstein. Has there ever been a movie that has somehow both depicted the Covid-19 pandemic and refused to acknowledge popular culture less than a half-century old?

Doubtless he’d consider this a personal quirk; Sorkin loves musical theater and remembers classic-era television, and so shall his characters. What he’s unintentionally done is create a world nearly as insular and fantastical as the ones in early internet fantasies such as Hackers or Virtuosity, one where a Capra-esque triumph remains within arm’s reach of his plucky protagonist. Sorkin gets that the internet is a part of real life, not a mystical fad or a wholly internet world. He’s not raging against the machine, the way some of his detractors feared he might back in 2010. But his conception of real life itself feels stuck in a time that is, if not pre-internet, at very least pre-Trump. January 6 may have been a sobering event in that Facebook control room, but in this world, everyone was pardoned and the president who used social media to egg it was re-elected and further emboldened. Maybe, all these years later, those more alarmist takes on the internet via cinema weren’t so off-base after all. Compared with the rabbit holes of Eddington, the psychosis of Red Rooms, or even the mediated worlds of David Cronenberg’s The Shrouds, The Social Reckoning’s take on the internet movie doesn’t seem nearly paranoid, angry or scared enough. Sorkin may think he’s looking at the internet with clear eyes, but he’s wearing blinders.

content.title_original: Can Daniel Weiss Fix the Philadelphia Museum of Art?
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Daniel Weiss had a part-time job as a stock clerk in the gift shop at the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C., while in school at George Washington University studying psychology and art history. When his boss was fired for substantial revenue losses, Weiss told the people in charge at the Kennedy Center: “I think I can fix this.” He was offered a six-month tryout the week he graduated in 1979, and over the next four years continued to run the retail business and supervise a staff of 175."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It wouldn’t be the last time he stepped in to fix things."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Along the way, I realized I was interested in pursuing graduate training in art history, but I also had an interest in how organizations function,” Weiss said this summer at the Philadelphia Museum of Art , where he started as director and CEO last December, a month after the board of trustees fired his predecessor, Sasha Suda. While at the Kennedy Center and throughout “the rest of my career,” he explained, “it became clear to me that if one cares about culture and the arts and higher education, one has an obligation to care also about how these institutions are run.”", "links": [{"text": "Philadelphia Museum of Art", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/philadelphia-museum-of-art/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Weiss, now 69, is widely viewed as a smart and thoughtful straight shooter, skilled at solving organizational problems. With an MBA from Yale and a PhD in Western medieval and Byzantine art from Johns Hopkins, he had a long career in academia, working in tandem as president and professor at Lafayette and then Haverford colleges, before being hired as president and chief operating officer of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2015. In his eight years at the Met, he helped steer the institution out of a $40 million financial deficit and through a change in directors and internal culture. Now at the PMA, which is also facing a major budget deficit after years of high staff turnover and low morale, Weiss is being looked to as a steady hand to right the ship.", "links": [{"text": "Metropolitan Museum of Art", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/metropolitan-museum-of-art/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Dan brings a combination of qualities that’s uncommon,” said PMA board chair Ellen Caplan. “He obviously understands art and scholarship, but also how to lead large, complex organizations. Things are never that black and white.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Asked if the PMA board had considered conducting a search for a new director, vice chair Osagie Imasogie said the trustees had unanimously agreed to appoint Weiss to the position. “If you look at the market for top-notch leaders in museums of the caliber of the PMA, it’s just a handful of people who would fit that profile,” he said. “There was no point in going through a performative process when we already had the best person we could think about.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/HLY_8934.jpg?w=400", "alt": "A man standing on a grand staircase.", "caption": "Daniel Weiss. content.article_text:
Daniel Weiss had a part-time job as a stock clerk in the gift shop at the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C., while in school at George Washington University studying psychology and art history. When his boss was fired for substantial revenue losses, Weiss told the people in charge at the Kennedy Center: “I think I can fix this.” He was offered a six-month tryout the week he graduated in 1979, and over the next four years continued to run the retail business and supervise a staff of 175.

It wouldn’t be the last time he stepped in to fix things.

“Along the way, I realized I was interested in pursuing graduate training in art history, but I also had an interest in how organizations function,” Weiss said this summer at the Philadelphia Museum of Art , where he started as director and CEO last December, a month after the board of trustees fired his predecessor, Sasha Suda. While at the Kennedy Center and throughout “the rest of my career,” he explained, “it became clear to me that if one cares about culture and the arts and higher education, one has an obligation to care also about how these institutions are run.”

Weiss, now 69, is widely viewed as a smart and thoughtful straight shooter, skilled at solving organizational problems. With an MBA from Yale and a PhD in Western medieval and Byzantine art from Johns Hopkins, he had a long career in academia, working in tandem as president and professor at Lafayette and then Haverford colleges, before being hired as president and chief operating officer of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2015. In his eight years at the Met, he helped steer the institution out of a $40 million financial deficit and through a change in directors and internal culture. Now at the PMA, which is also facing a major budget deficit after years of high staff turnover and low morale, Weiss is being looked to as a steady hand to right the ship.

“Dan brings a combination of qualities that’s uncommon,” said PMA board chair Ellen Caplan. “He obviously understands art and scholarship, but also how to lead large, complex organizations. He has a proven track record and a compelling vision for the role that museums play in society right now.”

When Weiss stepped down from the Met in 2023, his plan was to teach, write books, spend time on his boat, and, he said, “just live the life of somebody who wakes up not in charge of anything.” He took a faculty position at Johns Hopkins, where he had begun his teaching career in 1993, and was asked by several institutions, including the PMA—on Suda’s introduction—to advise on governance practices. “I’m something of a voice in that area,” said Weiss, who articulated his views on the importance of shared governance at mission-driven institutions in his 2022 book Why the Museum Matters .

Working with the PMA’s board on a governance review over the next two years, Weiss “got to watch, from a fairly close point of view, the dissolution of Sasha’s relationship with the institution and the board,” he said. After Suda’s termination in November 2025, according to the public record, she filed a lawsuit contending that she was fired “without a valid basis,” and pushed to have a jury trial; the board responded that “Suda misappropriated funds from the museum and lied to cover up her theft.” A court ruled early this year that the matter would be settled privately in arbitration, as per a clause in Suda’s contract.

The board’s decision to terminate Suda was made “completely independent of anyone that we were going to bring in to follow up,” Caplan said. “One had nothing to do with the other.”

Weiss said that at first, when the board approached him to step in, he was hesitant to take the helm. “My initial reaction was: ‘I’m not your guy,’” he recalled. “On the other hand, I thought, I know how to do this. I understand the issues. Maybe we can get this place back on track, where it’s doing what it should in the world.”

According to a veteran of the New York museum world, speaking on background, Weiss’s replacement of Suda could have at least the appearance of opportunism. “Dan, who is a consultant to the board, slip[ped] into that job really quickly. He has a way of being like a board whisperer,” said the person, adding, “I’m not saying that there weren’t reasons for both Dan to accept it and the board to do what they were doing. Things are never that black and white.”

Asked if the PMA board had considered conducting a search for a new director, vice chair Osagie Imasogie said the trustees had unanimously agreed to appoint Weiss to the position. “If you look at the market for top-notch leaders in museums of the caliber of the PMA, it’s just a handful of people who would fit that profile,” he said. “There was no point in going through a performative process when we already had the best person we could think about.”

If the board had brought Weiss in on only an interim basis, that would have diminished “the full authority to get on with the work that needs to be done,” Imasogie added. “It was also important that we ensure stability be brought back to the institution after the challenges we have had.”

In his work with the governance committee, Weiss had presented to the full board. “There was an immediate comfort level, both because we knew Dan,” said Jennifer Rice, chair of the governance committee at the time, and “he also came with such a stellar reputation for the work he did at the Met.”

DURING AN INTERVIEW OVER LUNCH in his office, Weiss came across as direct and efficient, at once businesslike, candid, and personable. Before addressing the first question he was posed, he paused to point out that, like his interviewer, he, too, wore a coin on a chain, pulling from underneath his shirt and tie a third-century Hellenistic coin with the image of Alexander the Great, given to him by his family. “I’ve worn it around my neck for 25 years,” he said. “It feels like a connection to the ancient world and the continuity of human existence.”

Born in Newark, New Jersey, and raised on New York’s Long Island, Weiss described himself as “a completely lackluster student” early on. Wandering into an art history survey class at GW, he fell under the spell of a charismatic young professor who was a medievalist. “He changed my life,” said Weiss, who is friends with him to this day. “That was where it began for me.” With his dual graduate training in art history and business, Weiss began teaching at Johns Hopkins as well as writing books; by the time he was tenured, he’d also become involved in administrative work. “I knew how to run a meeting and had experience in things that most faculty don’t,” he said. He rose to the position of dean in 2001, before moving in 2005 to lead Lafayette College for eight years, then Haverford College for two. He described being very surprised when the Met approached him.

“I’d never worked in a museum before, and they were asking me if I wanted to run it,” Weiss said. “They were looking for someone who could bring management and fiscal knowledge and experience into a role that was also completely sympathetic and sensitive to the mission. It opened up a world for me that I didn’t really plan on.”

In his first weeks on the job, he dug into the museum’s financial statements and discovered that what had been presented to him as a modest $4 million deficit on a budget of more than $300 million was, in fact, a $40 million deficit.

“The museum was drawing down reserves in ways that weren’t really kosher to meet operating deficits,” he said. “We had been overspending and, as it were, undermanaging the institution, and it had resulted in various patterns of accommodation to these problems that were not fully transparent to the board.”

Under Tom Campbell, a former tapestries curator promoted in 2009 to director and CEO after the retirement of Philippe de Montebello, who had led the Met for more than 30 years, the museum had been investing heavily in its digital operations as well as its modern and contemporary satellite, Met Breuer (which operated in the former Whitney building from 2016 to 2020).

“To Tom Campbell’s credit, I made him aware right away of a very substantial deficit, and he was perfectly willing … to do whatever it took to figure it out,” Weiss said.

Campbell would ultimately resign under pressure in 2017. The Met’s board voted unanimously that Weiss would assume the title of president and CEO, and that a new director would report to him. Max Hollein was appointed to that role in 2018, and by 2020, working together, the two leaders had balanced the budget. When Weiss stepped down in 2023, Hollein assumed the additional title of CEO.

“Dan is a leader who doesn’t shy away from complex issues,” said Candace Beinecke, cochair of the Met’s board. “His tenure at the Met was defined by his tremendous commitment to the museum’s mission. Working in partnership with the museum’s director, he steadily and effectively helped lead the Met through crucial moments. He brings deep analytical skills, expertise, and a strong sense of purpose to his work.”

Central to Weiss’s management at the Met was his reinforcement of the principles of shared governance. “It starts with the relationship between the CEO and the board,” he said, “but all the constituencies that have a vested interest in the well-being of the institution—the curators, the professional staff, the mayor’s office, the unions—also need to have a voice.”

Weiss enlisted the staff as partners in helping to fix the deficit, creating a task force of some 15 representatives to advise on budgetary decisions. They were part of tough conversations about how to cut the program, cut salaries, make layoffs. Weiss’s proposed changes to the museum’s longtime admissions policy of “pay what you wish”—after a decline of 67 percent in the average fee people paid during the previous decade—was controversial internally. The task force gave presentations to every department to involve the staff of 2,000 in the logic of Weiss’s proposition.

“We went through a long, difficult process to find the right approach based on principles, economic interest, and what’s best for the institution,” Weiss said. The new policy, instituted in 2018, maintained “pay what you wish” for New York State residents, who already support the Met through their taxes, but charged $25 (since raised to $30) for out-of-town adults. “In the end, it generated the revenue we needed, and it had no negative effect on visitation,” he said. “It was one step of 40 that we had to do to bring the budget into balance.”

A longtime Met employee, speaking on background, described Weiss as popular overall with the staff. “He was accessible, somebody you could talk to,” the employee said. “He’s a very rational, reasonable, and reasoned man.”

Weiss also instituted a review process at the Met, requiring the board to evaluate his own performance annually and perform a “360”—including feedback from employees—every other year. He later required the same for all department heads at the Met. “You must be accountable to the people you lead,” he said, noting that nobody would ever have given de Montebello a review. “I think it was a great disservice to Tom Campbell, who was a brand-new leader with no experience, not to have a performance evaluation of any kind.”

What Met trustee and former board chair Daniel Brodsky appreciated most in working with Weiss was “his willingness to listen,” he said. “He made time for staff at every level of the museum, and he genuinely cared about creating an environment where they could do their best work. During a period that included leadership transitions and the pandemic, that steady approach served the museum well.”

The PMA—RANKING IN THE TOP FIVE largest encyclopedic art museums in the US by both physical and collection size—now stands to gain from Weiss’s brand of leadership.

In late July, The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that the museum had a deficit of $10 million on an operating budget of $76.5 million and that its leadership expected the deficit could grow to as much as $15.9 million in the next year. Weiss said his goals for his first year are to fully assess the museum’s finances, rebuild the senior leadership team, and move forward on an action plan with open lines of communication across the board and staff.

In 2020, during the tenure of Timothy Rub, who led the PMA from 2009 to 2022, more than 400 staff members signed a petition calling for accountability changes in the wake of complaints about the behavior of former managers. Later that year, the staff voted to unionize. Museum workers went out on strike in 2022, on Suda’s first day on the job as new director (she chose to cross the picket line).

“Over the last several years, staff levels have decreased very dramatically,” Weiss said, from some 500 employees five years ago to about 385 now, through a combination of attrition, firings, and layoffs to reduce operating costs. “At the same time, the programmatic ambition during Sasha’s years here was very high, so there was more to do and fewer staff to do it. That led to a really strong sense of disappointment and frustration.”

Weiss has recently recruited Mitchell Wein, from the Brookings Institution, as executive vice president, chief financial officer, and chief operating officer; Lavita McMath Turner, from the Met, as chief people officer; and Neil Batiancila, from the Philadelphia Zoo, as chief advancement officer. He’s also promoted longtime curator Jennifer Thompson to deputy director of collections and exhibitions, to work alongside Jessica Smith, chief curator.

“I didn’t want a hiring freeze when I arrived, because the institution couldn’t survive that way—you have to have people in the right jobs,” Weiss said, acknowledging that he had added to the expense base. “We’ll balance the budget—it’s just a matter of exactly how. I know what the levers are.”

Caplan said that Weiss’s consistent internal communication on his action plan—addressing nine areas, including facilities, visitor experience, technology, and security—has already helped with morale. “He’s continuing to provide updates on progress being made or challenges he’s facing, and that transparency is appreciated by both the staff and the trustees,” she said.

Weiss appointed an internal task force to reevaluate a controversial rebranding campaign rolled out last fall under Suda, which included the institution’s name change to the Philadelphia Art Museum (mocked by critics as “the PhArt Museum”). A collaborative decision was made early this year to reinstate the original name but keep the new logo, featuring a griffin—a decorative architectural element repeated across the museum’s 1928 Beaux-Arts building.

The plan for a second phase of an ambitious expansion—originally approved by the board in 2004, during the tenure of Rub’s predecessor, Anne d’Harnoncourt, then designed by the late Frank Gehry—is now on hold. (The first phase of the plan was completed under Rub in 2021, for $233 million.) “We have a series of deferred building maintenance issues that have to be addressed before we return to the question of the Gehry project,” Weiss said.

He believes the museum’s current annual attendance of about 675,000 is “way too low,” he said, given the size and quality of the institution’s world-renowned collection of more than 240,000 objects and its stature in the city. But he has yet to set a specific target number for visitation, or dig into the question of admissions cost. “We feel very strongly that admissions pricing is a necessary evil, but whatever we do has to work for Philadelphia, so people come,” he said. The museum’s endowment—now almost $600 million—could always be better, Weiss said, but “it’s totally respectable.”

Weiss, who has committed to staying through 2028, told The Philadelphia Inquirer that he expects to have the budget balanced in three years. He and the board will then decide whether he will continue on for longer, he said, stating firmly, “I’m not going to stay 10 years.” He and his wife, a corporate healthcare lawyer whom he met at GW, live near the museum in a high-rise building. In Easton, Maryland, where he serves on the board of the Academy Art Museum, among several other institutions, they have a second home, with an extensive book collection that reflects Weiss’s diverse interests. His boat remains docked in the marina there.

While the skills of museum leadership may be transferable, Weiss recognizes that he is “not operating on the same patient,” he said. “The PMA is not the Met. They have different issues, different cultures, different communities. You need to listen very carefully and take what you know and apply it respectfully to this place in this ecosystem. I don’t have it all figured out.”
content.excerpt_original: One of America’s oldest and largest institutions is in trouble. Can its recently installed director right the ship?

This seemingly straightforward question can actually be quite loaded."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A faked artwork is generally considered to be a copy of an existing work. This seems clear enough, but what about when an artist copies his or her own work? A forgery, on the other hand, imitates an artist’s style to create a new work. But what if the forged artist was someone who challenged concepts of artistic originality and appropriated images from others?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Art trickery can get tricky. And yet it persists. Some experts estimate that around half of the secondary art market consists of forgeries and misattributions. Certain inauthentic works—made by infamous forgers such as Han van Meegeren (who made bogus Vermeers) and Wolfgang Beltracchi (responsible for hundreds of phony works)—are prized for their novelty and tales of exposure. Other times, artworks can initially be written off as forgeries but later identified as genuine through scientific analysis."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Museums are not impervious to these phenomena. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, for example, has a 1624 portrait of Spain’s King Philip IV that it deemed in the 1970s to have been created by an assistant to Diego Velázquez, only to reauthenticate it fully to the Spanish Baroque painter in 2010."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When in doubt, experts lean on the three-legged stool of art authentication: stylistic scrutiny, provenance, and scientific analysis. (The Velázquez reattribution was thanks to the latter, after varnish removal.)"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In a comprehensive 1963 book titled Forgeries, Fakes, and Reproductions , author George Savage writes at the close of the preface that “the collector may take heart from the fact that at no time during the history of the art-market has forgery been so difficult as it is now, or more likely to be detected, and the forger’s task is becoming continually more difficult.” Be that as it may, it doesn’t appear that forgers have stopped in the decades since."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Below are nine of the most faked and forged artists."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot (1796–1875) Image Credit: Collection of the University of Delaware. https://exhibitions.lib.udel.edu/things-arent-what-they-seem/home/art-forgery/ There’s a famous quip about French painter Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot from art historian René Huyghe, who claimed that “Corot painted three thousand canvases, ten thousand of which have been sold in America.” Corot was one of the most copied 19th-century painters, with fakes produced abundantly between 1870 and 1939. A single Belgian studio manufactured 235 fake Corot landscapes in 1888 alone. Even so, Huyghe’s number is exaggerated, and there are as many fake Corots in Europe as there are in the United States (entering museum collections in the early 20th century, including the Louvre’s). Corot’s success, especially in his later years, inspired other artists to forge his work. The artist also had a lax attitude toward forgeries. sometimes adding finishing touches to fakes and passing them off as his own. According to one anecdote, a man showed the artist some small Corot canvases that he had just bought, to which Corot replied, “How the devil can you think I painted such horrors? And you actually paid money for these?” The man then told him how much he’d paid; taking pity on him, Corot offered to fix it and touched up the painting by the next day, turning it into an “authentic” Corot."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/landscape-sketch-e1579642742679.jpg?w=400", "alt": "Undated landscape, probable forgery of Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot.", "caption": "Image Credit: Collection of the University of Delaware. https://exhibitions.lib.udel.edu/things-arent-what-they-seem/home/art-forgery/", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Honoré Daumier (1808–79) Image Credit: Collection of the Oklahoma City Museum of Art. Photo: Shannon Kolvitz. https://www.intenttodeceive.org/ When a curator was preparing a 1937 exhibition of HonoréDaumier works at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, he struggled to find pieces that were absolutely authentic. content.article_text:
What makes an artwork real? This seemingly straightforward question can actually be quite loaded.

A faked artwork is generally considered to be a copy of an existing work. This seems clear enough, but what about when an artist copies his or her own work? A forgery, on the other hand, imitates an artist’s style to create a new work. But what if the forged artist was someone who challenged concepts of artistic originality and appropriated images from others?

Art trickery can get tricky. And yet it persists. Some experts estimate that around half of the secondary art market consists of forgeries and misattributions. Certain inauthentic works—made by infamous forgers such as Han van Meegeren (who made bogus Vermeers) and Wolfgang Beltracchi (responsible for hundreds of phony works)—are prized for their novelty and tales of exposure. Other times, artworks can initially be written off as forgeries but later identified as genuine through scientific analysis.

Museums are not impervious to these phenomena. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, for example, has a 1624 portrait of Spain’s King Philip IV that it deemed in the 1970s to have been created by an assistant to Diego Velázquez, only to reauthenticate it fully to the Spanish Baroque painter in 2010.

When in doubt, experts lean on the three-legged stool of art authentication: stylistic scrutiny, provenance, and scientific analysis. (The Velázquez reattribution was thanks to the latter, after varnish removal.)

In a comprehensive 1963 book titled Forgeries, Fakes, and Reproductions , author George Savage writes at the close of the preface that “the collector may take heart from the fact that at no time during the history of the art-market has forgery been so difficult as it is now, or more likely to be detected, and the forger’s task is becoming continually more difficult.” Be that as it may, it doesn’t appear that forgers have stopped in the decades since.

Below are nine of the most faked and forged artists.

Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot (1796–1875) Image Credit: Collection of the University of Delaware. https://exhibitions.lib.udel.edu/things-arent-what-they-seem/home/art-forgery/ There’s a famous quip about French painter Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot from art historian René Huyghe, who claimed that “Corot painted three thousand canvases, ten thousand of which have been sold in America.” Corot was one of the most copied 19th-century painters, with fakes produced abundantly between 1870 and 1939. A single Belgian studio manufactured 235 fake Corot landscapes in 1888 alone. Even so, Huyghe’s number is exaggerated, and there are as many fake Corots in Europe as there are in the United States (entering museum collections in the early 20th century, including the Louvre’s). Corot’s success, especially in his later years, inspired other artists to forge his work. The artist also had a lax attitude toward forgeries. sometimes adding finishing touches to fakes and passing them off as his own. According to one anecdote, a man showed the artist some small Corot canvases that he had just bought, to which Corot replied, “How the devil can you think I painted such horrors? And you actually paid money for these?” The man then told him how much he’d paid; taking pity on him, Corot offered to fix it and touched up the painting by the next day, turning it into an “authentic” Corot.

Honoré Daumier (1808–79) Image Credit: Collection of the Oklahoma City Museum of Art. Photo: Shannon Kolvitz. https://www.intenttodeceive.org/ When a curator was preparing a 1937 exhibition of HonoréDaumier works at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, he struggled to find pieces that were absolutely authentic. An article published in Time magazine around the time of the exhibition opening lamented that “more than any other great 19th century French artist, Daumier has been imitated, forged and mistreated.” Dedicated to presenting only real deal Daumiers, the exhibition catalogue included technical notes describing the X-ray and infrared photo studies done for certain works. In the case of the prolific French artist and caricaturist, only prints produced in his lifetime and by his authorized publisher are considered originals; all others are fakes. According to the Daumier Register, a digital catalogue raisonné for the artist, Daumier created 1,340 drawings in total, but there are another 1,562 drawings designated as “after Daumier” and “unconfirmed.” His oil paintings are even more off balance, with the Register claiming that he created 283 paintings but that 609 additional works are purported to be by the artist. “It is not even possible to calculate the number of forged lithographs or reprints,” notes the Register. “This is a great compliment to the artist Daumier, who already complained during his lifetime that many of his works were forged.”

Auguste Rodin (1840–1917) Image Credit: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/339725 French sculptor Auguste Rodin has been forged so often that some of his forgers are known by name. Among these is Odilon Roche, who collected drawings by the artist. Another prolific forger was Ernest Durig, who claimed to be Rodin’s last student and sold his forged drawings under the pretense that they were gifts from the master (including one that made it into the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art). Nine fakes by Durig were included in a traveling 1971-72 exhibition titled “Roding Drawings: True and False,” which showed at Washington’s National Gallery of Art and then moved to the Solomon R. Guggenheim Mseum in New York. It included 132 Rodin drawings alongside 28 forgeries of his work, and a “true and false” section where viewers were challenged to look at 30 unlabeled pieces and see if they could determine what was what. Rodin’s bronze sculptures are also catnip for forgers. Posthumous bronze “originals” have repeatedly been cast from the artist’s plaster models, often lacking clear markings that they are reproductions. In 2019, for example, the Musée Rodin (which holds the rights to the artist’s works) pressed charges against Parisian art dealer Robert Crouzet and American art dealer Gary Snell; Crouzet sold 16 Rodin models to Snell, who proceeded to cast around 1,700 works that weren’t marked as reproductions. Some of Snell’s casts even bore Rodin’s signature and the Fonderie Rudier foundry mark (instead of the mark of the foundry where they were actually made).

Frederic Remington (1861–1909) Image Credit: Frederic Remington catalogue raisonné, Buffalo Bill Center of the West, Cody, Wyoming. https://centerofthewest.org/2018/12/21/points-west-finding-real-frederic-remington/ Hailed in his lifetime as the “pictorial historian of the Great West,” Frederic Remington is among the most copied, faked, and forged American artists. His paintings and illustrations were featured often in popular magazines, which boosted their popularity and rendered them copyable. A large-scale Remington exhibition at the Buffalo Bill Historical Center in Cody, Wyoming, was the catalyst for a catalogue raisonné, and between 1985 and 1996 the museum formalized an authentication process for Remington works. The artworks had to be inspected at the museum, and so 248 works were reviewed for the eventual two-volume catalogue. Of those 248, only 53 were deemed authentic (roughly 20 percent, a proportion that has remained consistent in ongoing authentication reviews since). The review committee categorized four types of inauthentic works: pastiches, copies, fakes, and forgeries. Pastiches (the smallest category) are intended to deceive; they copy parts of multiple Remington artworks with the addition of a faux signature. Copies could be unsigned, are the most prevalent, and presumably could have been painted as an artistic exercise. Fakes account for almost a quarter of the inauthentic works submitted for certification and consist of fraudulently signed paintings or drawings unrelated to known Remingtons but of a subject that interested the artist. A forgery is a work by another artist whose name has been removed or covered and replaced with an inauthentic Remington signature.

Amedeo Modigliani (1884–1920) Image Credit: Scott and Pamela Richter. https://www.intenttodeceive.org/ The former global director of Art Basel, Marc Spiegler, once quoted a Parisian dealer as saying: “The drama here is that I could find a Modigliani in an attic tomorrow, with a letter from Modigliani attached to it, and people would still hesitate.” The hesitation is warranted—given the drama surrounding the modernist painter’s forgery market and the unsettled state of Modigliani scholarship and his catalogue raisonné. Modigliani gave away many drawings, making provenance hard to track. His lack of a firm paper archive makes it easier to try to slip new works into his oeuvre. Some believe that fellow artist and close friend Moïse Kisling completed some of Modigliani’s unfinished works after the latter’s death. Whether or not that is true, fakes started emerging right after the artist’s premature death at age 35 in 1920 and have persisted ever since. The situation is so extreme that in 2017 a Modigliani exhibition at Genoa’s Palazzo Ducale ended abruptly when one-third of the works were seized by the Italian police on suspicion of being phony. So what’s an auction house or gallery to do? Many require that a Modigliani be included in art critic Ambrogio Ceroni’s catalogue raisonné, first published in 1958 and updated in 1970, which lists 337 works but does not include pieces Ceroni didn’t see in person (such as those in the United States). Modigliani scholarship, however, is changing all the time. Just this past year, a long-anticipated catalogue raisonné by Marc Restellini was published (following lawsuits) and a public online catalogue was released by the nonprofit Modigliani Initiative.

Giorgio de Chirico (1888–1978) Image Credit: Christie’s. It’s one thing when artists are forged by others, and another thing entirely when artists forge themselves. Such is the surreal case of Giorgio de Chirico. His early works of dreamlike, eerie vistas, his “metaphysical style,” remained highly popular even after he moved on to painting in a neoclassical technique that collectors found less desirable (including subjects such as horses and knights in armor). Ever the pragmatist, de Chirico retreated to duplicating his earlier (and more his commercially successful) works himself, which wouldn’t be entirely problematic in and of itself—except he also backdated them. He dubbed them verifalsi , meaning “true-fakes,” and didn’t see an issue since the originals were his intellectual property. In one instance, in 1919, de Chirico imitated one of his own paintings after Surrealist collector Simone Collinet asked if she could buy a work that he had already sold; he painted the same thing to please her. A few years later, in 1924, de Chirico copied his painting Le muse inquietanti (1918), which was owned by art historian Giorgio Castelfranco, for Paul Éluard and his wife, Gala. He would go on to paint many more . Complicating matters, de Chirico wasn’t the only one forging himself. Some Surrealists, such as Óscar Domínguez, Max Ernst, and Remedios Varo, allegedly created de Chirico replicas. So did others. The artist took to policing his own market, publicly calling out forgeries. According to a 1961 article in Time , a Milanese art critic said that “sixty percent of the paintings he sequesters are really fakes. Thirty percent he painted himself, and ten percent he painted himself but has forgotten about it.”

Salvador Dalí (1904–89) Image Credit: Yves Gellie/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images. The artist who famously melted clocks and bent reality also played with authenticity, signing thousands of blank sheets of paper for publishers to use later for limited-edition prints. Unsurprisingly, many of these sheets were misused. (According to Dalí’s secretary, John Peter Moore, the artist signed around 350,000 blank sheets of paper over the course of his career.) Provenance standards are looser with prints since they exist in multiples, making them easier to forge, but there have been instances where even Dalí’s pre-signed papers were forged. As a result, the artist’s print market is riddled with fakes. Forgeries are often exposed when they go on display at prominent museums. In 2025, Italian art police seized 21 Dalí artworks from the exhibition “Dali: Between Art and Myth,” at Palazzo Tarasconi in Parma, claiming that they were forged. According to art fraud investigator Colette Loll, the incident was the third major seizure by the carabinieri of Dalí works.

Andy Warhol (1928–87) Image Credit: MSCHF. https://moforgeries.org/ The subject gets trickier with artists such as the frequently forged Andy Warhol, who intentionally played with issues of originality. A master of the mass-produced look, Warhol used a popular photo-silkscreen technique that is relatively easy to duplicate. According to Warhol expert Richard Polsky, there are a few telltale clues that a work might be a fake Warhol. For one thing, the ink on Warhol’s silkscreens wasn’t perfectly uniform—in some places too heavy on the ink, in others too light—so prints lacking this variation might be off. Also be wary of anything in mint condition, a possible indication that a work was re-screened by a print shop. Warhol’s Marilyn Monroe works are among his most commonly faked, a telling giveaway being the hand-drawn slash used to differentiate between the print number and the edition size (which forgers usually get wrong). Besides the Marilyns, other commonly counterfeited Warhols are the Flowers, Maos, and Electric Chairs. Of his pre-Pop works, Warhol’s drawings of shoes and cats are popular among forgers. In 2021, the Brooklyn-based art collective MSCHF bought a $20K Warhol drawing, Fairies (1954), and created 999 identical copies. Destroying the record that identified the original, the perpetrators mixed in the real Warhol with the shuffled lot and the drawings were sold for $250 each . “The capital-A Art World is far more concerned with authenticity than aesthetics,” the collective wrote. “By forging Fairies en masse, we obliterate the trail of provenance for the artwork. Though physically undamaged, we destroy any future confidence in the veracity of the work. By burying a needle in a needlestack, we render the original as much a forgery as any of our replications.”

Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960–88) Image Credit: TNS/Getty Images. Works by American artist Jean-Michel Basquiat have been sought after since his heyday in the 1980s, but a steady stream of fakes cropped up after one of his paintings sold for $110.5 million at a 2017 sale at Sotheby’s New York. Just five years after that, a 2022 Basquiat exhibition at the Orlando Museum of Art was shuttered prematurely when FBI agents seized all 25 artworks on view, on the grounds that they were part of a fraud and conspiracy. ( The museum’s director was fired , and the FBI later announced that someone had confessed to forging most of the pieces.) According to Richard Polsky, who authenticates Basquiats, there are a few hints that a Basquiat may be a fake. Forgers tend to include gold crowns and prominently sign works on the front or the verso (even though Basquiat never signed his works on the front, and many are unsigned). Paintings on found objects, or works that have an incredible backstory (one that conveniently explains the lack of a paper trail for the work) are also frequent offenders. Unlike earlier artists, whose forgeries can be identified through scientific testing of materials, this part of the three-legged authentication stool isn’t helpful in weeding out fake Basquiats since the materials he used are still widely available.

content.article_text:
ヨーロッパ貴族所有、ブルガリの24カラット・ピンクダイヤモンドリングが初競売へ。最高28億円予想

不純元素をほとんど含まない非常に希少な24カラット・ビンクダイヤモンドの指輪が、 クリスティーズ の オークション に出品される。1950年代に ブルガリ で製作され、由緒ある貴族が所有していたもので、オークションに登場するのは初めて。

11月10日、ジュネーブで行われる クリスティーズ の「マグニフィセント・ジュエルズ（絢爛たる宝石）」 オークション に、 ブルガリ が1950年代に製作した伝説の「ファンシー・インテンス・ピンク（彩度が非常に高いピンク）」ダイヤモンドの指輪が出品される。同オークションはオータム・ラグジュアリー・ウィークの一環として開催されるもので、指輪の予想落札価格は1200万から1800万ドル（約19億〜28億円）。

プレスリリースによると、24カラットのピンクダイヤモンドは現在の所有者の曽祖父がインドで入手したもので、1950年代に ローマ を本拠地とするブルガリに指輪の製作が依頼された。70年以上にわたりこの指輪を所有していたのは、「由緒あるヨーロッパの貴族の家系」とされ、オークションへの出品は初となる。

世界的な高級宝飾品ブランドのブルガリは、19世紀の創業以来ローマを本拠地としている。ローマは、第2次世界大戦の敗戦後に新生イタリア共和国の中心として復興し、指輪が製作された1950年代には賑わいを取り戻していた。その華やかさについて、プレスリリースでは次のように述べられている。

「ハリウッドの大作映画の数々がチネチッタ・スタジオで撮影され、世界的なスターたちが集まったローマは、『テヴェレ川のほとりのハリウッド』と呼ばれるようになった。コンドッティ通りにあるブルガリのブティックは社交や文化交流の場となり、 エリザベス・テイラー とリチャード・バートン夫妻、オードリー・ヘプバーンとメル・ファーラー夫妻といった大物カップルや、各国の著名なセレブを数多く顧客として抱えていた」

今回出品されるダイヤモンドは、窒素やホウ素などの不純元素をほとんど含まない「IIaタイプ」に分類されている。これは全世界の天然ダイヤモンドのうち2％未満しか存在しない非常に希少なもので、その色合いは「coveted fancy pink（垂涎の的のファンシーピンク）」と形容される。

米フォーブス誌の 報道 によると、独特のピンク色は「地球内部での形成過程で非常に強い圧力が加わることによってダイヤモンドの結晶格子に希有な歪みが生じ、この構造的変形がダイヤモンドを透過する光の進み方を変える」ことによって生み出されるという。（翻訳：石井佳子）

content.article_text:
Skincrawl Studios has debuted a first glimpse at Chilean filmmaker Patricio Valladares ’ supernatural horror feature “The Divine Comedy,” a modern re-telling of Dante’s “Inferno.”

The Irish production and distribution shingle, which specializes in horror and adjacent genre movies, is handling worldwide sales on the film, which recently wrapped principal photography.

“The Divine Comedy” is a co-production between Italy’s Anxur Films and Skincrawl Limited. Alessandro Gatto produces for Anxur, with Corrado Camilla and screenwriter Loris Curci producing on behalf of Skincrawl.

Related Stories

‘God of War’s’ Bruno Velazquez, ‘Mandalorian & Grogu’s’ Hal Hickel Detail Cinema-Gaming Crossover at View Conference

Raindance to Launch U.K.'s First Major Vertical Festival and Market (EXCLUSIVE)

Starring Christopher Rygh (“Vikings: Valhalla”), Matthew Metcalfe, Tilda Metsola and Fadhillah Othman, the film is a contemporary reimagining of Dante Alighieri’s 14th-century narrative poem describing a journey into Hell.

Popular on Variety

Valladares directs from a screenplay by Curci (“The Ghosts of Monday,” “Havana Darkness”) that follows Dante, a grieving writer who descends into the realm of the dead in an attempt to bring back his deceased wife, Beatrice. Guided by Virgil, a former priest, he journeys through increasingly nightmarish circles of Hell, confronting supernatural entities and manifestations of guilt, desire and suffering.

“The challenge here was to turn Dante’s ‘Inferno’ into a visual experience,” Curci tells Variety . “We took into account only the Hell segment of ‘The Divine Comedy.’ Of course, given the context and the complexity of the epic poem, we tried to focus mainly on the relationship between Dante and Virgil, and their voyage to the very bowels of the Inferno. We also took the liberty of giving Beatrice a different, more dramatic role.”

Taking a cue from Dante himself, Curci also borrowed motifs from popular mythology.

“When writing the screenplay, I thought I’d use elements of the Greek tragedy. Dante populated his realms of Hell and Purgatory with figures, monsters and moral frameworks borrowed directly from classical Greek and Roman myths. He borrowed extensively from them, and then so did I. But our ‘Divine Comedy’ is after all a modern fantasy-horror film. It’s definitely the most ambitious film we’ve worked on at Skincrawl, albeit it’s small budget.”

Curci co-penned Skincrawl Studios’ recent thriller “The Sarajevo Murders” with Barry Keating ( Valladares’ regular collaborator ) and also directed the company’s upcoming “Island of the Minotaur.” He previously worked with Valladares on the director’s 2017 horror pic “Nightworld.”

“The Divine Comedy” marks Valladares’ latest international genre production following his recent works, “Invoking Yell” and “Invoking Scream,” both written with Keating. Earlier works include “Hidden in the Woods,” starring Michael Biehn (“Terminator,” “Tombstone”).

The 2023 found-footage horror feature “Invoking Yell” is currently available on AMC Networks’ horror streaming service Shudder in multiple territories. His latest film, “Invoking Scream,” recently bowed at FrightFest in London and is set to hit theaters in Chile next year.

Dublin-based Skincrawl Studios will present “The Divine Comedy” to international buyers at next month’s American Film Market and early next year at the Berlinale’s European Film Market .

“We’ll have a teaser-trailer ready for AFM and plan to have the film screened at the Berlin film market in February,” says Skincrawl’s Camilla. “From then on it’s doing as many festivals as possible. We’re fully aware that this is not your average horror movie, so we plan to reach out to all sorts of different markets, and see how they react.”

Among Skincrawl Studios’ other recent titles, “The Sarajevo Murders,” directed by Giorgio Bruno, about the disappearance of a documentary film crew in Bosnia, is distributed in the U.S. by Cleopatra Entertainment. “Island of the Minotaur,” currently in post-production, follows an archaeologist and his team who discover more than they bargained for after awakening an ancient and monstrous bull-headed creature in the subterranean depths of a forbidden island.

content.title_original: When Photography Turns to Painting to Reinvent Itself, with Zoë Zimmerman
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Rivalry, imitation, mutual influence: since its beginnings in the 19th century, photography has maintained an ambiguous relationship with painting. The Impressionists, for instance, refused to compete with the camera’s mechanical precision and staked everything on sensation, light and the fleeting moment. They sought to invent their own language and move away from the mere reproduction of reality. In an irony of history, a few decades later the Pictorialist photographers attempted the opposite, producing soft-focus images with almost painterly atmospheres that flirted with the texture and gesture of the brush."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As Walter Benjamin observed in The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction (1936), the advent of photography upended the perception of art. Images, now reproducible ad infinitum, shook the aura of the unique work, forcing painting to rethink its means and reinvent itself in the face of this new mechanical eye. Where the camera captured the moment with a precision the brush could not match, painting had to find other paths, other intensities, other ways of holding on to time."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Today, history seems to have come full circle, and it is photography that looks to painting to reinvent itself. The pictorial reference is no longer imitation; it has become a way of thinking about the image. In a world where images follow one another faster than they can be looked at, where infinite scrolling and algorithms shape our attention, some photographers are choosing to slow down, anchoring each image in time and space."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/7.zoe--coral-snake-jpg-1024x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/2.zoe--pandemic17--1024x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/1.zoe--quarantine57-1-819x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/4.zoe--pandemic-89--866x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Landmarks emerge in this dialogue between painting and photography. In her series “Xteriors,” Dutch photographer Desiree Dolron explores territory on the border between portraiture and landscape. Her images, often bathed in diffuse light against dramatic backgrounds, evoke Baroque paintings. Bodies stand out against neutral or dark grounds, as if suspended in time, and the sculpted light recalls Caravaggio or the Flemish masters. Laetitia Molenaar, for her part, took Edward Hopper’s paintings as the starting point for her artistic project. In her series Here Comes The Sun , landscapes and figures become paintings in motion, where every frame tells a story."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Conversely, contemporary painters such as Peter Doig and Gerhard Richter let photographic traces float through their canvases. Through shifts, overlays and hybridizations, the two mediums feed off each other in an endless creative back-and-forth."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Time regained"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For the American photographer Zoë Zimmerman, the relationship with painting is even more direct. Her recent work draws explicitly on the still lifes of the 16th and 17th centuries. Her compositions, often made in natural light against a dark background, immediately evoke the legacy of Caravaggio. It is a sense of composition she owes to years spent contemplating paintings: “What satisfies my eye? The painter’s point of view: giving up the clever angles and complicated lighting that dominate so much of photography. Natural light has always been my simplest solution. A dark background and raking light coming from one clear direction, falling across the subject (whatever it may be)… and there you have it: Caravaggio!”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But the pictorial reference is not merely aesthetic. It also concerns the way the image is conceived. Zoë Zimmerman speaks of a “pre-photographic vision”: a composition in which every plane of the image carries equal visual weight. Unlike modern photography, accustomed to blurred backgrounds and shallow depth of field, she aims for overall sharpness, recalling the structure of Vermeer’s paintings. “This is how artists built their compositions before lens-based art taught us to accept blurred backgrounds and soft objects as signs of their lesser importance within the frame.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Until 2020, her work was strictly black and white, shot on film with a large-format view camera. When she ventured into color, she did so cautiously. “I found that I could only handle one or two dominant colors at a time. I was overwhelmed by choices that simply did not exist in my earlier work. My palette has broadened over time, but I still lean toward something limited and dark.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/8.zoe--odalisque--1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/11.zoe--peregrine--1024x819.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In her series “Covid Vanitas,” these compositions even become a discreet commentary on the pandemic.
