content.article_text:
Kehrer Verlag releases José Antonio Rosas : Somewhere We Feel Free .

For a decade, José Antonio Rosas has photographed from deep inside the crowds at some of the world’s great gatherings. From music festivals and religious pilgrimages to cultural rites, he found a common impulse: the desire to step outside everyday life and experience a sense of connection and release.

In 2015, standing in a crowd at Glastonbury Festival, José Antonio Rosas experienced a sense of collective euphoria that stayed with him. Over the next ten years, he followed this feeling across four continents, photographing seven of the world’s great gatherings—from the explosion of colour at India’s Holi, the candlelit devotion of Christmas in Lalibela, the vibrant dances of Peru’s Candelaria, the icy pilgrimage to Qoyllur Rit’i in the Andes, the vast human tide of Kumbh Mela and the unrestrained joy of Brazil’s Carnaval.

Though separated by culture, geography and purpose, these gatherings share a powerful common thread: the suspension of ordinary life and the collective release of uninhibited emotion. Within the press of bodies and the roar of music or prayer, individuality does not disappear, it transforms. Closed eyes, open mouths and gestures of serenity or ecstasy become expressions of freedom, connection and transcendence.

Somewhere We Feel Free moves across cultures, faiths and continents, revealing the shared human impulse to gather, to surrender and, somewhere within the crowd, to feel free.

With an essay by art critic Jean Dykstra and an interview with José Antonio Rosas by artist Janelle Lynch, the publication brings together this powerful decade-long body of work in the photographer’s second monograph.

José Antonio Rosas is a documentary photographer based in Lima, Peru. He has built his work through repeated visits and sustained attention to mass celebrations, religious pilgrimages, remote wildlife, and communities far from home. His award-winning work has been exhibited and published internationally.

Jean Dykstra is an arts writer and editor. The former editor of photograph magazine, she writes The Photosphere , a Substack publication about contemporary photography. She’s contributed to numerous publications, including The New York Review of Books , The Brooklyn Rail , and Dear Dave .

Janelle Lynch is an artist, writer, and educator, based in New York City. She is represented by Flowers Gallery and has three monographs published by Radius Books. Lynch teaches at the International Center of Photography and writes for LensCulture and The Brooklyn Rail .

content.article_text:
Galerie Frank Elbaz announces Ubiquitous Conjunction , the first solo exhibition of Kunié Sugiura in Paris, presented at the gallery from October 19 to December 31, 2026, and curated by Ryo Sawayama. The exhibition is part of the celebrations of the Bicentennial of Photography, which in 2026 mark 200 years since the invention of photography.

The exhibition is accompanied by this essay by Ryo Sawayama on the artist’s work.

In 1963, at the age of twenty, Kunié Sugiura moved from Japan to the United States and enrolled at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago—an institution which descends from the New Bauhaus lineage. It was in Chicago that Sugiura first encountered photography as a medium and began her career as an artist. From that point on, Sugiura has consistently worked with photography as her primary medium.

At the time, photography was still regarded within the art world as a secondary field, subordinate to painting and sculpture. It was only later that a number of women artists—such as Cindy Sherman, Francesca Woodman, Ana Mendieta, Laurie Simmons, Barbara Kruger, among others—would take up photography as an important medium. Sugiura’s work anticipated this shift (a contemporary parallel can be found in Betty Hahn).

Photography came to be actively taken up by women artists precisely because it had long been dismissed as a secondary mode of expression. Unlike painting and sculpture, traditional fields largely occupied by male artists, photography was seen as a democratic field open to those on the margins. Therefore, Sugiura—a foreigner and a woman—turning to photography as her medium was a conscious and theoretical choice bound up in these very issues.

Although Sugiura embraced photography as her primary medium, she has distanced herself from presenting so-called “photographic works” associated with straight photography, and likewise from being regarded as a “photographer.” Instead, Sugiura has continued to pursue and expand the latent plasticity inherent in photography, experimenting with how photography might become a means of expression equal to painting and sculpture. Sugiura’s work does not treat photography as a privileged medium in itself; it engages photography through hybridization and its conjunction with other media.

The use of hybridization can be seen in Sugiura’s Photocanvas Island 2 (1971), where photography conjoins with painting. Here, acrylic paint is layered over a photograph of the surface of the Coney Island breakwater, where the rough “ground” of the photographed breakwater is superimposed onto the “ground” of the painting, and the brushstrokes are combined with the pre-existing pattern of the rock surface. The three-dimensional object of the breakwater and the two-dimensional picture plane, the figurative and the abstract, are brought into conjunction. Here, rather than placing the brushstrokes freely, Sugiura arranges them along the textures and patterns already formed by the rocks.

For Sugiura, the conjunction of photography and painting meant collaborating with an already-existing nature: creating a superposition of nature and artifice.

This kind of conjunction can be found throughout Sugiura’s work: the conjunction of photography and painting in Island 2 (1971), Christmas Lights (1979) and Hossawa (2022); the conjunction of multiple frames in Arita and Miyazaki (both 2023); the connection of different sequences in Story of Catfish (1993); the linking of skeletal structure and joints through X-ray photography in Vertebra (2021) and Racks (1994), in which a photo rack holding postcard-sized X-ray photographs recalls the connective structure of bones, or the structure of DNA. This conjunction can also be seen where Sugiura binds flowers together with thread, or in the large photocanvas of a couple having sex. In Sugiura’s work, photography is a plastic material that carries out endless operations of severance and conjunction with everything it touches. Through these conjunctions, new forms are produced. By staging these encounters, conjunctions, and hybridizations, Sugiura turned photography into a site of experimentation, revealing its open, transversal, and mediating nature.

Sugiura was also known in Japan as a writer, with a regular column in Bijutsu Techō . Before the widespread use of the internet, the information she sent from New York, from the 1980s onward, was extremely valuable. Sugiura introduced the New York art scene to Japan, welcomed and looked after many Japanese visitors in her studio, and connected them with people on the ground in the local art community—she was herself a mediator in every sense. Sugiura understood, better than anyone, that the encounter between two things generates a new form, and that chance encounters give rise to new events. In a sense, Sugiura’s stance as a mediator resembles the very attitude she takes toward photography as a medium.

Sugiura’s work carries forward a New Bauhaus mode of thinking that crosses and conjoins photography with a variety of other media, in parallel with her treatment of photography as a site of formal experimentation. What characterizes her practice is its continuity with early experimental and avant-garde photography—through the use of photograms, X-ray photographs and the material and fluid use of photographic emulsion. Sugiura treats photography not simply as a means of reproducing an existing scene, but as an experimental field for formal invention.

Experimental and avant-garde photography explored precisely this plastic potential inherent in photography, and such experiments were themselves preceded by occult photography, including early spirit photography. Notably, the birth of photography and the rise of spiritualism were historically contemporaneous. Multiple exposures on wet and dry plates, stains, chemical unevenness, and irregular reduction reactions during development often produced unexpected double images or hazy forms. This made it possible for different moments in time to coexist within the same pictorial space, as in Futurist painting (although, more precisely, Futurist painting was influenced by experimental photography, rather than the reverse). These photographic processes and their unpredictable effects all served to expand photography’s plastic potential.

At the time, photography was believed to reveal the presence of spirits automatically and objectively, without human intervention. Avant-garde and experimental photography consciously and aesthetically repurposed techniques first seen in early spirit photography: multiple exposure, solarization and the photogram. Therefore, it could be said that spirit photography had already realized photography’s chemical plasticity, preceding experimental photography and the avant-garde.

One could say that photography announces the existence of another “nature”—a parallel world. Photography reveals that the perceivable world runs parallel to a supernatural world, and to a world beyond human perception, that includes electromagnetic waves such as ultraviolet light and X-rays. X-ray photography visualizes precisely that behind the visible lies a reality beyond human perception. By chemically combining multiple substances, photography demonstrates that the world is a superimposition and conjunction of multiple universes, exceeding what human beings can coherently grasp. Through developments in contemporary science and early photography, it became clear that the way human beings had grasped the world was no more than a contingently generated pattern—a subjective convenience.

Early photography served as evidence in police records and as a form of historical documentation. At the same time, however, its chemical process of mixing volatile substances and its capacity to reveal what would otherwise be invisible gave early photography a magical, even suspect quality. Photography and spirit photography were bound together by this same unpredictable process of development. The word “occult” carries the meaning of “hidden knowledge.” In this sense, occult photography sought to make visible an invisible, hidden world—the latent plasticity of the world and its hidden creativity.

It was this expectation—that photography possessed an automatism capable of revealing a hidden, surreal world, an automatic productive force independent of human agency—that drew the Surrealists, who placed automatism at the center of their methodology, so intensely to photography. The emergence of an image through chemical reactions in photography shares the same structure as a spirit medium, who similarly makes the invisible visible. Photography is thus the perfect medium, in both senses of the word. Through its chemical plasticity, photography binds together different worlds and reveals another, invisible nature.

In this way, photography transmits a hidden world into the here and now. For example, Sugiura’s The Kitten Papers (1992) was made by leaving two kittens alone in a darkroom for a week and turning the traces they left—their footprints and movements—into the work itself. The traces are made not by the artist but by cats moving of their own will; they record the cats’ unpredictable movements, which are beyond human intention. This device—a cat in a darkroom—recalls the thought experiment in quantum mechanics known as “Schrödinger’s cat”, in which a cat sealed inside a box is described as simultaneously alive and dead—an object in quantum superposition. Here the contents of the box constitute a literal “black box”, and whether the cat is alive or dead cannot be known until the box is opened.

Although Schrödinger’s cat is a thought experiment modeling the indeterminacy of measurement in quantum mechanics, Sugiura’s The Kitten Papers is an experiment actually carried out in a darkroom. Among the works exhibited in this exhibition, Story of Catfish , made by Sugiura during the same period, belongs to the same artistic trajectory. In both The Kitten Papers and Story of Catfish , the accumulation of uncontrollable, probabilistic deviations produced by the behavior of animals in the darkroom appears as material traces fixed onto photographic paper.

An important point to note is that the word “Papers” in The Kitten Papers evokes the documentary practice of reconstructing an event after the fact from its material traces—a movement of nature that no one observed. Here, Sugiura functions simultaneously as the maker and observer.

Sugiura’s photograms, in dealing with the physical movement of living creatures in the darkroom, reveal the countless deviations possible within nature—the superposition of multiple worlds. The unrestrained movement and energy of these creatures arise not because the world is fixed and static, but because countless possibilities remain latent and open within it. It is because these innumerable worlds are superimposed simultaneously, that the world possesses creativity. Here, the living creature is not merely an object being photographed, but it is itself the subject that produces the image.

The fact that Sugiura has repeatedly chosen living things—such as humans, animals, and flowers—as her subjects is congruous with her interest in the formation of natural forms. A living creature, which produces its own form through its own agency, is structurally similar to photography, which also produces an image automatically (for example, a flower grows by its own power and forms its own shape as a flower, entirely by its own power). As Sugiura herself has said, a flower is a reproductive organ: the stamen produces pollen, and the pistil receives that pollen to create a new life that ultimately becomes the seed.

Sugiura’s works that bind flowers together with thread appear to show, quite literally, the conjunction of male and female—pollination and fertilization—within a process of biological reproduction. Here, photography’s automatism responds to nature’s process of self-formation.

The photographic emulsion itself is, materially, a forced homogeneous dispersion and suspension of substances that do not naturally dissolve into one another—a mixture of water-based gelatin and fine particles of silver salts. The very support of a photograph embodies, at the material level, the conjunction between heterogeneous elements, as photography arises through an operation—emulsification—that binds together things that are chemically unmixable by nature. This operation recalls the Hindu creation myth of the Churning of the Ocean of Milk, in which every manner of plant and seed is placed into the ocean of milk and churned, and from that churning, the sun, the moon, the gods, and all animals are born.

This conjunction in reproduction and photography can also be linked to the alchemical term coniunctio . In the alchemical process, the chymical wedding—the chemical marriage of opposites, sulfur (the male principle) and mercury (the female principle)—was said to produce a new substance: the philosopher’s stone. Coniunctio meant a chemical conjunction, while at the same time serving as a metaphor for the conjunction of the sexes.

The mixing and blending of heterogeneous elements—emulsification—could be thought of as the emergence of life itself. The human body, living creatures, flowers, and the earth itself—subjects that Sugiura has persistently captured—belong precisely to this realm of nature and living things, onto which she superimposes the chemical process of photography’s own formation, together with her own acts of painting and image-making. Photography, rather than serving as a means of reproduction, can be understood as a self-generating movement that, through acts of conjunction, generates new forms—releasing a creative productive force inherent in the world itself. Sugiura’s work reveals the ubiquity of an automatic creative power that permeates the world.

Born in Japan and based in New York since 1967, Kunié Sugiura has spent more than six decades developing a body of work at the crossroads of photography, painting, and sculpture. Through a selection of works made over the past sixty years, Ubiquitous Conjunction looks back at a practice that has never ceased to push the boundaries of the photographic medium and to explore the possibilities of its dialogue with other art forms.

Ryo Sawayama

Curated by Ryo Sawayama

content.article_text:
Photographer and filmmaker Neal Slavin returns to his alma mater for a conversation with artist and author M. Leona Godin . Their conversation will explore perception and what it truly means to see.

Neal Slavin met M. Leona Godin at the New York Public Library, where Godin was the 2025–26 Jean Strouse Fellow in the Cullman Center for Scholars and Writers. As a fellow, Godin was working on a book about blindness, photography, and image description. Their first encounter sparked many long conversations on the ways perception shapes how we experience the world through photography.

This evening’s conversation will explore the phenomenon of synesthesia, where the boundaries among the senses dissolve and the languages of music, poetry, painting, and photography intermingle. Together, they will discuss how perception moves beyond eyesight alone, and how photography continues to expand our understanding of what it means to see.

Slavin’s portraits have been published in several books, including Portugal , Britons , and When Two or More Are Gathered Together , recently republished and expanded with new photographs that bring together portraits taken over a span of 50 years (1974–2023). He was the recipient of a Fulbright Fellowship in Photography and of Cooper Union’s highest honor, the President’s Citation. Slavin’s photographs are in numerous permanent collections, including The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Centre Pompidou, and the New York Public Library, where Godin first encountered his work.

M. Leona Godin is a blind writer, artist, and the author of There Plant Eyes: A Personal and Cultural History of Blindness . She is currently working on a project about photography, blindness, and what it means to see, which received recent support from an NYPL Cullman Center Fellowship.

THURSDAY, OCTOBER 15, 2026, 6 – 8PM The Cooper Union Located at 7 East 7th Street, between Third and Fourth Avenues

content.article_text:
Archives – October 13, 2011

The second portfolio, which Jean-François Jonvelle began for Photo in the 1980s, is devoted to French actresses. The book features a lovely preface by Frédéric Beigbeder, followed by a short biography:

Jean-François Jonvelle was snatched by the hand of death with a suddenness to match the photographs that were his life. Just as that life was dedicated to capturing these stolen moments, so death followed suit, carrying him off in the midst of life. A tumour discovered in early January, a final farewell just a fortnight later. He was gone in a flash. As I turn the pages of my friend’s last book my eyes mist over. My tears dissolve Jonvelle’s photographs into the soft focus of a David Hamilton.

Jonvelle’s work is often described as being – in the time-honoured formula – ‘sexy but not vulgar’. I prefer his own description of what he sought out: ‘la poésie du quotidien’, ‘the poetry of the everyday’. Photographs freeze moments of truth, all you have to do is choose the ones that do it best. ‘I tell myself that the present and the future don’t exist,’ he also used to say. ‘Everyone, every day, creates their own past.’

The quality that makes his images more moving than the rest is their vulnerability. Jonvelle taught me one crucial lesson: in photography, as in literature, what counts is feeling. Eroticism and tenderness are not sworn enemies. A downy arm, the frail nape of a neck, an uptilted breast, the curve of a back beneath the sheets, damp hair, closed eyelids, the trace of a kiss on the neck all these can be arousing.

Jonvelle’s women are fresh and natural because they are unaware of our gaze. Jonvelle makes adoring voyeurs of us all. He shows us why heterosexuality can be so painful: everywhere, in every house and every bathroom, paradise lurks. Paradise delicately removes her T-shirt, brushes her teeth, buttocks pert, the curve of her breasts taut, timeless. Suddenly paradise parts her legs in silence, biting her fin- gernails as she looks you straight in the eye, teasing you as she waits for you on the sheets. Jonvelle is in paradise now, but for him nothing has changed: he was already there in his lifetime.

As I gaze in wonder, the way I always do, at these images, so far removed from the familiar clichés, my thoughts turn to the beautiful women he immortalized. Photographs fix the fleeting, immortalize the ephemeral. Many of the women Jonvelle photographed are now old or dead, but – thanks to this photographer who is now also dead – their perfection will never fade.

Every one of Jonvelle’s photographs is a declaration of love. One day, at my request, he photographed Delphine Vallette, the mother of my daughter. I wanted to give this brunette whom I loved a portrait. Never have I felt such a cuckold – though in the most erotic of ways.

Beauty is an evanescent mystery that some artists have the ability to capture. As I look again at these wonderful images, I’m reminded of the title of that American comedy Drop Dead Gorgeous. Jonvelle’s work as a whole is not an ode to femininity; the story it tells is of the battle to vanquish death by means of the celebration of desire. All these shoulders caught by surprise, these half-seen breasts, these finely- arched insteps, these flawless backs, this sensual solitude, this calm between two storms, all these beautiful women who don’t give a damn are simply doors softly opened, through which we may catch a glimpse of eternal life.

Frédéric Beigbeder

Jean-François Jonvelle was born in 1943 in Cavaillon, south of France. Soon he will sell famous melons to buy Hasselblad. Its inspirations will come from the painting of Balthus, Bacon, of Schiele, but the true influence comes from films from Mankiewicz, Lubitsch, Fritz Lang, Orson Welles, Arthur PEN, Minnelli and more recently of Terry Gillian of which it acknowledges to have seen eleven times the film Brazil ; Finally its preferred film: Jules and Jim of François Truffaut.

In 1959, it is the photographer George Glasberg who initiates him with photography while making him make the turn of France of the cathedrals. It is a photographic revelation which will leave it never again.

At the age of 20 he becomes the assistant of the American photographer Richard Avedon. After this enriching experiment he becomes his own “Master” whose favorite subject will be the woman. Her mom and her small sister of whom he always was very near will be her “first agreeing victims”. Then come the first “muse” and accomplice, Tina Sportolaro whom he meets in 1982 and with which he carries out some of his more beautiful images. Will be then Béatrice, Myriam and many others …

He is in particular the author of the photographs of the pub campaign which had revolutionized the advertising display in the Eighties “Tomorrow I remove bottom”.

He published many books; some of which are: in 1983: Those which I Like ; 1989 Jonvelle (s) 1994: April, May, June ; 1996: Mad of them ; 1998: Balconies . An important monograph will be published in 2011.

Jonvelle said readily that its preferred subject was the woman that it liked. “When I photograph a woman said he, I want that she knows that she is most beautiful on earth, because a woman who feel beautiful becomes really the most beautiful woman. My happiness, it is also never not to have puted in chains my freedom, nor lost my freshness, my perfect moment”.

Jean François left us on January 16, 2002

content.article_text:
Archives – October 13, 2020

Opening on November, Tate Modern hosts the the first major exhibition in the United Kingdom of Zanele Muholi . The show gathers about 260 photographs presenting the full breadth of their career to date. Muholi often describes their* work not as a photographer or a videast but as a “visual activist”. From the early 2000s, the artist documented and celebrated the lives of South Africa’s black lesbian, gay, trans, queer and intersex communities. The following videos, produced by Tate Modern, explores Muholis various aspects of her arts and describer their series.

“In the early series Only Half the Picture , Muholi captures moments of love and intimacy as well as intense images alluding to traumatic events – despite the equality promised by South Africa’s 1996 constitution, its LGBTQIA+ community remains a target for violence and prejudice.

In Faces and Phases each participant looks directly at the camera, challenging the viewer to hold their gaze. These images and the accompanying testimonies form a growing archive of a community of people who are risking their lives by living authentically in the face of oppression and discrimination.

Other key series of works, include Brave Beauties , which celebrates empowered non-binary people and trans women, many of whom have won Miss Gay Beauty pageants, and Being, a series of tender images of couples which challenge stereotypes and taboos.

Muholi turns the camera on themself in the ongoing series Somnyama Ngonyama – translated as ‘Hail the Dark Lioness’. These powerful and reflective images explore themes including labour, racism, Eurocentrism and sexual politics.​”

Zanele Muholi – In My World, Every Human Is Beautiful 5 November 2020 – 7 March 2021 Tate Modern Bankside, London SE1 9TG, United Kingdom

The exhibition is organised by Tate Modern in collaboration with the Maison Européenne de la Photographie, Paris, Gropius Bau, Berlin and Bildmuseet at Umeå Universit

*Zanele Muholi sees theirself as a non-binary person, and therefore uses the pronoum “their”. The Eye of Photography wishes to respect this use.a

content.article_text:
Toni Collette will make her feature directing debut with “The Best Of,” her screen version of Graeme Simsion’s bestselling novel, which is one of 75 projects sharing more than AUD16.9 million ($11.7 million) in production and development money from Screen Australia .

Collette, an Emmy and Golden Globe winner, produces alongside Christopher Simon. The story centers on two ex-lovers who come back into each other’s lives after spending decades apart, only to find old feelings stirring with messy and mixed results. Screen Australia made a major production investment in association with Screen NSW. Kismet handles local distribution and Cornerstone holds international sales.

Related Stories

ABC Alleges FCC's Attempts to Curb Its Free Speech Were Designed to Evade Judicial Review

'30 Rock' 20th Anniversary Reunion: Tina Fey and Tracy Morgan Try to Remember Their Lines, Alec Baldwin Riffs as Jack Donaghy and More Best Moments

The round, announced Tuesday, covers features, series and shorts.

Popular on Variety

“Australian storytellers continue to captivate audiences with their creativity, originality and distinctive perspectives. This latest round of funding supports an exciting range of projects from emerging creatives forging new paths to established voices exploring new creative territory. Screen Currency 2026 found that local stories matter deeply to Australians, and these projects will deliver on the authenticity and ambition that audiences have come to expect,” said Louise Gough, Screen Australia’s director of narrative content.

Brouhaha Entertainment, the company behind “Boy Swallows Universe,” is making “The Dark Lake,” a series based on Sarah Bailey’s award-winning novel. Tonkin plays a detective in a rural town whose investigation into the killing of a former high school classmate forces her to face buried secrets of her own. Troy Lum and Andrew Mason produce, with Becca Johnstone writing and executive producing. Giorgia Stawaruk, Tonkin and Katarina Mandic are also executive producers. Screenwest partners on the major production investment, with additional financing from Screen NSW.

Jeffrey Walker (“The Artful Dodger,” “Fing!”) directs “Bull” (working title), a feature from Infin8 Studios and Total Fiction Films. Drawn from a true story, it follows a smooth-talking prisoner who signs up for a debating team inside Tasmania’s harshest jail, hoping to change course and finally give his mother a reason to be proud. George Pullar stars, co-writes with Taylor Danworth and produces with Michael Lawrence, John Molloy and Suzanne Walker. Richard Roxburgh, Robyn Malcolm, Teresa Palmer, Thomas M Wright and Harrison Gilbertson round out the cast. Screen Queensland is on board, with Kismet distributing locally and Cornerstone handling international sales.

Sooshi Mango’s untitled feature debut follows three obstinate Italian immigrants who mobilize their multicultural neighborhood when a mysterious wellness club puts their cherished social club at risk. Nick Kozakis (“Kick On”) directs from a script by the group’s Joe Salanitri, Carlo Salanitri and Andrew Manfre with Declan Fay. Paul Dainty and Cathy Rodda produce, with Timothy Whiting as co-producer. VicScreen partners, and Roadshow has local distribution.

Rodd Rathjen directs “No Friend But the Mountains,” adapted from Behrouz Boochani’s acclaimed memoir, from a screenplay he co-wrote with Boochani. The Kurdish journalist, fleeing persecution, is intercepted at sea and sent to Manus Island, where he documents the gradual breakdown of the men held there. Gal Greenspan, Sharlene George, Amy Parry, Arkos Armont, Katy Roberts, Boochani and Antony Waddington produce. The New Zealand Film Commission, Screen Queensland and VicScreen are partners, with Madman distributing in Australia.

On the development side, Mithila Gupta’s “Desi Down Under” will turn her coming-of-age Indian-Australian audio series into a romantic comedy feature about three misfits who head from Kerala to the beach at Coogee, where they hope to pick up surf-lifesaving skills they can use to help their compatriots. Gupta writes and produces with Nina Aujla, Smriti Mundhra and Maya Gnyp.

Goalpost Pictures’ series “The Caretaker,” adapted from Gabriel Bergmoser’s bestselling novel by Alexei Mizin and Ryan van Dijk, both members of Screen Australia’s 2026 Talent Gateway cohort, also landed development backing. The thriller centers on a woman hiding out as caretaker of a ski resort out of season, who goes to ever more extreme lengths to hold on to the life she has built.

Among the shorts, BAFTA-nominated Rosie Westhoff (“The Main Part”) writes and directs “Solastalgia,” in which a young girl tries to reassemble scattered memories of the bushfire that destroyed her home while looking for connection in a transformed place. Chloe Brennan (“We Used to Own Houses”), Amanda Browne and Ashlee Russell (both “Mothmama”) produce, with Kitty Green (“The Royal Hotel”) as mentor.

Green also mentors the team behind a family short from Pasifika-led Mana Film Productions that mixes live action and animation, “My Life as a 12-Year-Old Demon Hunter… With Great Hair!” It tracks 12-year-old Tala over a single day as she fends off demons out to steal her powers – a bigger headache than her homework. AWGIE winner and bestselling author Maria Lewis writes, directs and co-produces, with Shonee Samia co-producing and Herbert Leota animating. Animator Jake Duczynski (“Magic Beach”) joins Green as mentor. Both shorts received principal production funding.

Full lists of production, development and short film approvals are on Screen Australia’s website. The agency will reveal more recently funded projects alongside the ABC Media Showcase on Oct. 21.

content.article_text:
The full list of MCU characters who will appear in “Avengers: Doomsday” may still be a mystery, but Jeremy Renner has made it clear he didn’t return as Hawkeye — and says The Avengers “will probably lose” as a result.

“No, no, no, no. Not in that one,” said Renner when asked if he was returning for “Doomsday” in a recent interview . “’Doomsday’ I’m not in, so the Avengers will probably lose, just so you know… they didn’t call me, so it’s their fault. They’re going to lose.”

Related Stories

'Breaking Bad' Star RJ Mitte's Cause of Death Confirmed as Suicide

Ben Affleck Calls 'Justice League' Reshoots the 'Low Point of My Career': 'It Was So Gross' How the Studio Replaced Zack Snyder With Joss Whedon

Though he isn’t reprising the role of Hawkeye for “Doomsday,” the actor did note that he was excited about the re-release of “Avengers: Endgame,” which brought the 2019 film back to theaters ahead of “Doomsday’s” Dec. 18 release. Renner has played the superhero previously in “The Avengers,” “Avengers: Age of Ultron” and “Endgame,” in addition to other films like “Thor” and “Captain America: Civil War,” in which he made brief appearances.

Popular on Variety

In 2025, Renner said that he was open to returning to the MCU, whether it was for Season 2 of “Hawkeye” or something else. “I’m always happy to be in that world, man. I love all those guys, I love the character,” Renner told Empire. “I’m sure we’ll end up doing Season 2 [of ‘Hawkeye’], and do other things. And I’m happy to do it. My body’s getting ready for something like that. I don’t know if anybody wants to see me in tights, but my body will look good in the tights.”

At the time, he’d also noted that he’d recovered “more than 150%” from his 2023 snowmobile accident, meaning he was ready to do his own stunts for the Marvel films. Renner had been hospitalized after his Sno-Cat, a large snow plow that weighs at least 14,330 pounds, ran him over, resulting in eight of his ribs being broken in 14 places, his right knee and ankle broken, left leg tibia broken, left ankle broken, right clavicle broken, right shoulder broken and more.

content.article_text:
Universal’s horror entry “ Other Mommy ,” directed by Rob Savage and starring Jessica Chastain and Jay Duplass, squeaked to the top of the U.K. and Ireland box office in a dead heat, debuting at No. 1 with £1.97 million ($2.66 million).

The horror debut narrowly edged Sony’s psychological thriller “ Verity ,” which moved to second place in its sophomore session by a razor-thin margin of just £33,263 ($43,970), collecting £1.94 million ($2.62 million). The Colleen Hoover adaptation lifted its running cume to £7.3 million ($9.8 million).

Related Stories

How South Africa Rescued Its Rebate and Pulled the Industry Back From the Brink: We're ‘Back in Business’

Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart

Paramount’s action thriller “Heart of the Beast,” starring Brad Pitt and J.K. Simmons, held third position in its third frame with $1.1 million, elevating its gross to $7.3 million. Sony’s franchise reboot “Resident Evil” took fourth spot in its fourth session, generating $1 million to advance its total to $17.1 million. Sony also claimed fifth position with the debut of Aaron Sorkin’s political drama “The Social Reckoning,” which collected $840,538.

Popular on Variety

Universal’s “Sense and Sensibility” followed in sixth place during its third weekend, adding $797,038 for a running total of $6.8 million. Entertainment Film Distributors’ historical drama “The Uprising,” directed by Paul Greengrass and starring Andrew Garfield, opened in seventh position with $732,547.

Studiocanal’s animated feature “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom” landed in eighth place in its fourth session, collecting $665,849 to raise its total to $5.1 million. content.article_text:
Amid the hustle and bustle of Frieze London , where champagne bottles pop and deals are orchestrated, Brazilian abstract artist Marina Perez Simão wants to invite guests to contemplate inside a spaceship in Pace Gallery ’s booth. She’s painted 11 canvases in three main colors: three in blue, three in gray, and five in magenta.

The booth is arranged in the shape of the letter X, with two blue paintings on either side, a gray painting in the middle, and two others on the other side. Guests can either enter through the middle or on the sides.

“The structure is super open and closed at the same time, but there’s also a sense of discovery depending on which side you walk through,” Simão told ARTnews , speaking from São Paulo.

She wants viewers to take the paintings in and to get real close to her work. She describes the paintings as “more or less vague descriptions of strange worlds” and says that each artwork has its own “nature and behaviors.” “It’s abstract yet it has so many elements of landscape. Nature is a big, complex and vast organism that we don’t fully understand how it works, art is a way to approach these things that are difficult to explain,” Simão said.

Simão added that she wanted to remind her viewers that looking at art is a physical experience. “We see so many images through Instagram and digital platforms, which is fine, but we can’t forget that when you get close to a painting, there are different layers and textures,” she said, noting that she hopes people see the imperfections in her art—which is one of the reasons she doesn’t varnish her paintings.

When she started these paintings at the beginning of the year, she felt a natural development in her practice was taking place, but she found that it was still inexplicable.

Her paintings are often rich and bright in colors, with sky blues sitting atop grass green or bright reds paired with orange. These new works are cooler; they draw their inspiration from Pablo Picasso’s Blue and Rose Periods and Fra Angelico’s usage of the color pink.

“Pink is a difficult color because when you look at mass culture, there’s Barbie pink, bubblegum pink, and cotton candy pink. I didn’t want all these industrial pinks and their associations,” Simão said. She instead settled on magenta, given that it can be manipulated to mimic colors found in nature.

Simão found blue more challenging. She worked with the color straight from the tube because the pigment is already super strong, only occasionally relying on a dash of white for tinting. Yet she also combined different blues, mixing cobalt and cerulean, for example, to transform them into a greenish tone. The blue paintings “are almost impossible to photograph,” Simão explained. “We had to do three sessions of photographing as the pigments change so much.”

The gray paintings combine magenta and blue. In the first layers of the paintings, she hides hints of yellow and ocher, creating an effect similar to the hazy glow created when fog passes in front of the sun. According to Simão, the blue paintings are warm like summer, and the pink paintings are cold like winter. Together, they represent an abstract season.

Simão began experimenting with darker hues in 2024 with her exhibition “Solanaceae” at Pace in Los Angeles. The show’s name was inspired by the scientific name for the nightshades family of plants and the paintings had fragments of darkness. The same silhouette appeared in a show at Mendes Wood DM’s Paris gallery later that year. “I’ve been thinking about working with a limited color range [for a while] because color in my work is super important, and I wanted to study tonalities and limit myself, I’m always evolving,” said Simão.

Simão’s paintings at Frieze London changed her artistic routine. She hid everything in her studio that featured an ounce of color and resumed her usual position of painting away from the door and by a little terrace with a window.

“I paint standing up and in my socks. I don’t use chairs and sometimes I sit on the ground. These paintings required my body to be engaged,” said Simão.
content.excerpt_original: Across 11 paintings in blue, gray, and magenta, she envisions an abstract season.

content.title_original: ‘I knew I was being followed’: Keira Knightley on her hacking nightmare – and new Stasi spy play The Lives of Others
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "U npacking assorted tubs of carrot sticks and salad, Keira Knightley winces apologetically. “I just realised I’ve got very crunchy food,” she says. How apropos that she should consider the impact that her lunch might have on my audio recording when we are here to discuss The Lives of Others , a new play in which the characters are divided between the spies and the spied-upon.", "links": [{"text": "The Lives of Others", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/apr/29/keira-knightley-returns-to-west-end-the-lives-of-others-stephen-dillane-luke-thompson-adelphi-theatre-robert-icke"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Based on the Oscar-winning 2006 film and set in East Berlin in 1984, the play stars Knightley as Christa-Maria, a theatre actor in a relationship with a playwright, Georg, played by Luke Thompson. Photograph: Sony Picture Classics/Sportsphoto/Allstar", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck’s original movie opens with an interrogation scene in which a persecuted citizen is grilled relentlessly for 40 hours – the length of time it takes, according to Wiesler, for a suspect to crack under questioning. I have only been allotted one-fortieth of that time with Knightley and Thompson, who has brought along his own leafy lunch to the north London town hall where rehearsals are under way. But I am still hopeful of extracting a few details about what the play’s visionary writer-director Robert Icke has up his sleeve. This is the man who introduced Sliding Doors-style alternate-reality scenes into Romeo and Juliet , put a countdown clock on stage in Oedipus (and others), and added the Beach Boys to Oresteia .", "links": [{"text": "Romeo and Juliet", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/mar/12/it-feels-like-flying-sadie-sink-and-noah-jupe-on-child-stardom-passion-and-the-heady-rush-of-romeo-and-juliet"}, {"text": "Oedipus", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2019/aug/16/oedipus-review-kings-theatre-edinburgh-festival-2019-robert-icke-sophocles"}, {"text": "added the Beach Boys to Oresteia", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2015/jun/07/oresteia-review-icke-brings-us-aeschylus-for-the-modern-age"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d3639d0a13b90bfb53e4542fbee1a55f929fada9/0_0_4748_3159/master/4748.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Oresteia by Aeschylus at the Almeida, directed by Robert Icke, in 2015.", "caption": "Oresteia by Aeschylus at the Almeida, directed by Robert Icke, in 2015. Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Interrogation techniques turn out not to be necessary today. “It’s quite a technical show,” volunteers Thompson, the 38-year-old Bridgerton star who worked with Icke previously on Hamlet ( with Andrew Scott as the Prince ) and Oresteia. “Rather than different scenes, it’s like one big set-piece with people coming in and passing batons. It’s almost musical.” Which is odd, laughs the 41-year-old Knightley, “because Rob hates dancing. He is not a man who dances.”", "links": [{"text": "with Andrew Scott as the Prince", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2017/mar/05/hamlet-almeida-review-andrew-scott-robert-icke"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "She has some beans of her own to spill. “We’re on a revolving stage,” she says, “so we’re always on the move.” This will enable the audience to see Christa-Maria and Georg at the same time as their Stasi eavesdropper. Thompson believes this lends the stage version an advantage over the movie: “Bringing a story about watching into the theatre is maybe even better, because the audience is literally peering in on what’s happening. Whereas in a film, there’s the barrier of the screen.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/3c073bce63b1c6b45f9cdb3a1567cc3afb2e241c/0_0_3072_1291/master/3072.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Compromised … Ulrich Mühe as a Stasi operative in the 2006 film.", "caption": "Compromised … Ulrich Mühe as a Stasi operative in the 2006 film. Photograph: Buena Vista", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Only when I ask whether they are using the play’s new Max Richter score during rehearsals does Thompson become remotely tight-lipped: “I don’t know if I’m allowed to say that.” Knightley throws caution to the wind: “We are using it in rehearsal, yeah. Icke used screens in the penetrating version of Orwell’s 1984 which he co-adapted with Duncan Macmillan; in his Hamlet, the Ghost turned up on CCTV. Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The nature of surveillance in society has changed markedly, even in the two decades since the movie opened. “You want there to be a camera at the bus stop when your bag’s been nicked,” reflects Knightley, displaying a touching faith in police priorities. “You feel safer because of that surveillance. But then you ask: ‘Who is surveying me?’”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In the same year that The Lives of Others was released, she became part of the first wave of public figures to discover that their phone messages had been hacked by tabloids. How far has that helped her understand the sort of paranoia that dominates the play? “I do have a personal experience of what that is. Then again, I knew that my phone was being hacked because I had something tangible to show for it. There were stories. Or for me, it was mostly pictures. I knew I was being followed and then I could see that I was being followed. I didn’t feel like I was going mad. The Lives of Others, she wrote in 2007, “doesn’t accurately portray the way totalitarian systems work, because it needs to leave room for its hero to act humanely (something such systems are designed to prevent).” Another of her charges is that the movie inadvertently legitimised the ongoing campaign by former Stasi agents to launder their reputation."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/3165614b19403bb11c336d7c2a406d3fb2654426/0_0_4882_3648/master/4882.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Robert Icke, director of The Lives of Others.", "caption": "Visionary director … Robert Icke, who once added the Beach Boys to Oresteia. One Israeli whistleblower singled out The Lives of Others as the catalyst for his own awakening. U npacking assorted tubs of carrot sticks and salad, Keira Knightley winces apologetically. “I just realised I’ve got very crunchy food,” she says. How apropos that she should consider the impact that her lunch might have on my audio recording when we are here to discuss The Lives of Others , a new play in which the characters are divided between the spies and the spied-upon.

Based on the Oscar-winning 2006 film and set in East Berlin in 1984, the play stars Knightley as Christa-Maria, a theatre actor in a relationship with a playwright, Georg, played by Luke Thompson. Earwigging on them is Wiesler (Stephen Dillane), the Stasi officer whose principles are gradually challenged and weakened by his round-the-clock exposure to this cultured couple.

Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck’s original movie opens with an interrogation scene in which a persecuted citizen is grilled relentlessly for 40 hours – the length of time it takes, according to Wiesler, for a suspect to crack under questioning. I have only been allotted one-fortieth of that time with Knightley and Thompson, who has brought along his own leafy lunch to the north London town hall where rehearsals are under way. But I am still hopeful of extracting a few details about what the play’s visionary writer-director Robert Icke has up his sleeve. This is the man who introduced Sliding Doors-style alternate-reality scenes into Romeo and Juliet , put a countdown clock on stage in Oedipus (and others), and added the Beach Boys to Oresteia .

Interrogation techniques turn out not to be necessary today. “It’s quite a technical show,” volunteers Thompson, the 38-year-old Bridgerton star who worked with Icke previously on Hamlet ( with Andrew Scott as the Prince ) and Oresteia. “Rather than different scenes, it’s like one big set-piece with people coming in and passing batons. It’s almost musical.” Which is odd, laughs the 41-year-old Knightley, “because Rob hates dancing. He is not a man who dances.”

She has some beans of her own to spill. “We’re on a revolving stage,” she says, “so we’re always on the move.” This will enable the audience to see Christa-Maria and Georg at the same time as their Stasi eavesdropper. Thompson believes this lends the stage version an advantage over the movie: “Bringing a story about watching into the theatre is maybe even better, because the audience is literally peering in on what’s happening. Whereas in a film, there’s the barrier of the screen.”

Only when I ask whether they are using the play’s new Max Richter score during rehearsals does Thompson become remotely tight-lipped: “I don’t know if I’m allowed to say that.” Knightley throws caution to the wind: “We are using it in rehearsal, yeah. It’s very beautiful. Everyone’s in the room: we’ve got the sound designer, the costume designer, the video designer …” Video, eh? Another hint. Icke used screens in the penetrating version of Orwell’s 1984 which he co-adapted with Duncan Macmillan; in his Hamlet, the Ghost turned up on CCTV. It’s a convention that risks seeming passe now. “Video can feel gimmicky,” Thompson concedes. “But it’s relevant here because it’s all about surveillance.”

The nature of surveillance in society has changed markedly, even in the two decades since the movie opened. “You want there to be a camera at the bus stop when your bag’s been nicked,” reflects Knightley, displaying a touching faith in police priorities. “You feel safer because of that surveillance. But then you ask: ‘Who is surveying me?’”

In the same year that The Lives of Others was released, she became part of the first wave of public figures to discover that their phone messages had been hacked by tabloids. How far has that helped her understand the sort of paranoia that dominates the play? “I do have a personal experience of what that is. Then again, I knew that my phone was being hacked because I had something tangible to show for it. There were stories. Or for me, it was mostly pictures. I knew I was being followed and then I could see that I was being followed. I didn’t feel like I was going mad. Whereas the characters are in a funny world where they don’t know when or if they’re being monitored.”

Modern parallels have been part of the rehearsal room discussions. I mention the likelihood that visitors to the US now have their social media accounts probed at immigration, and Knightley’s eyes light up. “Ah, but did that ever happen?” she asks. “Or is it enough that you say it’s going to happen for people to self-censor? You don’t even have to follow through on the threat. You just have to put it out there.” Thompson agrees: “It’s what’s so clever and efficient about the Stasi. The best way to create surveillance is for people to do it themselves.” And not only through self-censorship: estimates are that there was one informant for every 6.5 citizens in East Germany.

Top of the cast’s reading list for the play is Stasiland, Anna Funder’s 2003 account of life in the GDR. Funder has called Von Donnersmarck’s film “superb” but also “a fantasy narrative that could not have taken place (and never did) under the GDR dictatorship”. The Lives of Others, she wrote in 2007, “doesn’t accurately portray the way totalitarian systems work, because it needs to leave room for its hero to act humanely (something such systems are designed to prevent).” Another of her charges is that the movie inadvertently legitimised the ongoing campaign by former Stasi agents to launder their reputation.

In at least one documented instance, however, the movie has had a real-world benefit. In 2014 , 43 veterans of an elite, clandestine Israeli military intelligence unit withdrew from participating in “the state’s actions against Palestinians”, protesting that their government was guilty of “political persecution” in refusing to distinguish “between Palestinians who are and are not involved in violence”. One Israeli whistleblower singled out The Lives of Others as the catalyst for his own awakening. He and his colleagues, he realised, “were similar to the kind of oppressive intelligence in oppressive regimes”.

Not everyone regards von Donnersmarck’s picture as a force for good. When a journalist recommended it to the actor Julie Christie in 2007, she replied: “I’m not sure I can bear to see a film they gave the Oscar to, that tells you what awful people communists are.” Thompson mulls this over. “There are characters who are mouthpieces for something along those lines,” he says. “But it’s not just a politics play. Part of the fun, I think, is that the characters are mysterious and you never know quite which way they’re going to go. If what audiences take from the play is ‘Communists are awful’, then I’d feel like we’d failed.”

Audiences can take what they like from it – as long as they don’t take photographs. It was the sight of phone cameras being whipped out for the curtain call at Icke’s Oedipus that sent its star, Lesley Manville, into a huff. (“Clap or don’t clap,” she later said, “but don’t just stick your phone in our face.”) Despite starring on stage in Ivo van Hove’s four-hour adaptation of Hanya Yanagihara’s A Little Life , where a phone ban failed to prevent the leaking of nude snaps of his co-star James Norton , Thompson trusts the audience. “I think people broadly follow the no-phone rule,” he says. Knightley may not have set foot on stage for 11 years (“Small children, no sleep” is her pithy explanation for the hiatus) but, as a punter, she notes approvingly the “absolute fucking fury from everyone if somebody’s phone goes off in the theatre”.

I wonder how they both feel about the standing ovations which have become ubiquitous to the point of meaningless at West End productions. Knightley thinks ticket prices might explain it. “I took my kids to see a musical recently and we really did enjoy it, but it cost so much that I was, like, ‘We are going to love this!’” With tickets for The Lives of Others peaking at £225, she and Thompson can expect to see audiences springing to their feet every night.

“In a strange way, though, the exchange that happens between actors and an audience during the clapping is the least important or interesting moment of it,” says Thompson. “If people see something good, it stays with them. Perhaps we’ve been missing that – and that’s why people get so excited.”

“I like your optimism,” says Knightley, clearing away the lunchtime detritus. “There’s me going, ‘Maybe it’s because the tickets are expensive.’ And you’re like, ‘It’s because the play transports you!’”

The Lives of Others is at the Adelphi theatre, London , from 14 October until 9 January

content.article_text:
「美」を「見る」とはどういうことか。ポーラ「B.A」がTokyo Gendaiでひらいた新たな視点

江戸時代の浮世絵と鏡台、東信のアートワーク、そして現代アートの見方をひらくガイドツアー。 Tokyo Gendai 2026にオフィシャル・ビューティー・パートナーとして参加した ポーラ B.Aが、アートフェアという場を通じて提示した「美」と「見ること」の可能性をレポートする。

2026年9月に横浜で開催された国際アートフェア「 Tokyo Gendai 」で、会期を通じてひときわ賑わっている一角があった。同イベントにオフィシャル・ビューティー・パートナーとして参加した、 ポーラ の最高峰ブランド「B.A」のブースだ。

太古の自然から植物、そして人間の気配へ──異なる時間軸に属するものを作品の中に重ねることで「時間とは何か」を考えさせる、フラワーアーティストの東信による象徴的なアートワークが、ブースの入り口で来場者を迎え入れる。長年コラボレーションを続けるB.Aと東に共通するのは、固定された「美」ではなく、変化し続ける生命そのものに美を見出そうとする視点だ。

ブランドが「Inclusion Black」と呼ぶ黒を基調としたその空間に足を踏み入れると、まず、江戸時代後期の浮世絵に目が奪われる。展示されたのは、化粧文化を学術的に研究するポーラ文化研究所が所蔵する《江戸名所百人美女》から選ばれた4点のレプリカ。同研究所では、国内外の化粧道具や装身具、文献、浮世絵などの歴史資料を収集し、時代によって移り変わる美容や化粧の文化を研究してきた。

《江戸名所百人美女》には、江戸の名所とともに、その土地にゆかりのある女性たちの日常が描かれている。今回紹介された作品にも、櫛で髪をとかす、湯で顔をぬぐう、眉を整える、鏡で首元を確かめるといった仕草が登場する。その傍らには、作品の中にも描かれている江戸時代後期の鏡台が置かれ、紅や白粉、刷毛といった当時の化粧道具も展示された。

鏡を見る。肌を整える。髪を整える。そしてもう一度、自分の姿を確かめる。江戸時代に鏡の普及が進み、鏡台が一部の特権階級だけではなく裕福な町人にも広がっていったことを考えれば、鏡の前で自分自身を見つめる時間そのものが、人々の日常へと入り込んでいった時代だったことが窺える。

人の身体から生まれたB.Aのかたち

その数百年後に位置するものとして展示されていたのが、1985年に誕生し、41年目を迎えたB.Aだ。昨秋、第7世代へとリニューアルしたB.Aのボトルには直線がなく、人間の身体を思わせる曲線によって構成されている。そのため、見る角度によって輪郭や表情が変化する。社内デザイナーが人体のスケッチを繰り返し、人の造形美と向き合うことから生まれたデザインには、B.Aが掲げる「人の可能性は広がる」という考え方の通り、その人の中に存在する可能性をどう引き出すかというブランドの思想が反映されている。そして、「美」とは完成された一つの理想像に近づくことではないというメッセージも受け取ることができる。

ブースにはさらに、プリツカー賞建築家であり、世界各地の美術館建築でも知られるSANAAの妹島和世が空間設計を手がけたポーラのグローバルフラッグシップストア、ポーラ ギンザの模型も展示された。

アートフェアの「舞台裏」

そして今回、ブース展示と並んでもう一つの重要な取り組みとなったのが、Tokyo Gendaiの会場を巡るスペシャルガイドツアーだ。

会期を通じてTokyo GendaiのVIP、ポーラの顧客、ARTnews JAPANの読者など、約73人が参加した。Tokyo Gendaiを含むアートフェアそのものを訪れるのが初めてという人が半数以上を占めた一方、海外の美術館を訪ねたり、国内の展覧会に足を運んだり、美大で制作を学んでいたりと、それぞれに異なるかたちでアートと接点を持つ人が多かった。

ツアーが目指したのは、注目作品を順番に紹介する、いわゆる「見どころツアー」とは少し異なるものだった。ガイドは参加者の関心や当日の会場の状況に応じてルートを変えながら、個々の作品や作家だけでなく、そもそもアートフェアとはどのような場所なのか、ギャラリーはどんな役割を果たし、作品の評価や流通はどのように形づくられていくのか、といった背景にも話を広げた。

ガイドの一人、キュレーターの三宅敦大は、作品の解説以上に「フェアという場所の特性や意義、多様性」を伝えることを意識したという。フェアの構造を俯瞰することは、ギャラリーの立場やアーティストの社会的評価を理解し、自分自身で作品の背景や文脈を探っていく手がかりになるからだ。実際、作品についてあえて説明しすぎないことで、参加者同士が自分の気になった作品を紹介し合う場面も生まれたという。

教える人と教えられる人に分かれるのではなく、それぞれの「見る」が交換されていく。それは、アートフェアを別の角度から体験する方法でもあった。

見る人自身の「視点」をひらく

参加者の反応が大きかったのも、必ずしも有名作家の作品解説だけではなかった。たとえばHaruka Ito by Islandのブースでは、谷口正造の作品を目当てにVIPプレビューの入場列に並んだコレクターが複数いたことや、作品が早々に売約となったエピソードを紹介。参加者は、作品そのものだけでなく、作家を支えるギャラリーとコレクター、そして市場の関係にも強い関心を示した。別の回では、参加者が会場に居合わせたライアン・ガンダーと10分ほど言葉を交わす場面もあった。

現代美術を理解するためには、必ずしも美術史の知識から入る必要はない。自分がすでに持っている経験や知識を足場にして、目の前の作品や、それを取り巻く世界へ入っていくこともできる。ガイドを務めた半田颯哉がツアーで意識したのも、参加者が後日、別の展覧会で知らない作家の作品に出会ったときにも楽しめるような「視点」を持ち帰ってもらうことだった。

普段なら「わからない」と通り過ぎてしまうかもしれない作品の前で立ち止まり、見る。疑問があれば質問し、自分なりに考え、誰かと感想を交わしてみる。こうした体験もまた、多くの作品と、それをつくり、売り、買い、見る人々が一つの場所に集まるアートフェアならではの醍醐味であり、そこでのコミュニケーションを通じて、ひいては作品を所有するという選択肢を考える最初の一歩にもなり得る。

こうして振り返ると、Tokyo Gendaiで展開された、江戸時代の浮世絵や鏡台、B.A、東信のアートワーク、そしてガイドツアーという一見異なる試みに、一つの共通項が見えてくる。

それは、何を美しいとするかを一方的に提示するのではなく、見る人自身の視点をひらくことだ。江戸時代の女性が鏡台の前で自分の姿を見つめる。現代の私たちが鏡の前で自分の肌に触れる。そしてアートフェアで、これまで知らなかった作品の前に立ち止まる。そこで行われているのは、すでに知っている「美」を確認することだけではない。これまで見えていなかった何かを見つけること。そして、自分自身の見方が変わる可能性に出会うことなのかもしれない。

content.article_text:
Cannes animated comedy “ Jim Queen ” has picked up a new batch of international sales after screening at the Busan International Film Festival , its first outing in Asia.

Global Constellation , the sales arm of pan-European studio Vuelta, has closed deals with Prorom for the Czech and Slovak Republics, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria. HBO has secured first-window pay-TV and SVOD rights in Eastern Europe. Elsewhere, Folkets Bio has taken Sweden, AS Fidalgo has Norway and Films4You has Portugal, while CDI/LAT-E has acquired Argentina, Chile, Uruguay and Paraguay. A South Korean deal is now in negotiation.

Related Stories

Documentary Festival IDFA to Open With 'White Tiger Column,' Following Rookie Resistance Fighters in Myanmar

Disney Bids on Character.ai Assets as Chatbot Provider Files for Chapter 11 Bankruptcy

The new territories add to earlier sales to I Wonder Pictures (Italy), O’Brother (Benelux), Capelight Pictures (Germany), Praesens (Switzerland), Polyfilm (Austria), Elastica/Filmin (Spain), Lev Cinema (Israel), Madman (Australia and New Zealand), Photon Films (Canada), Pandora Filmes/Belas Artes Grupo (Brazil), Pimienta Films (Mexico) and Creative Century (Taiwan). Creative Century Distribution will open the film in Taiwanese cinemas on Oct. 23.

Popular on Variety

For the U.S., Global Constellation is weighing several offers, with a release set for 2027. Jordan Firstman and Matteo Lane were recently unveiled as the English-language voices of Jim and Lucien.

Set in Paris, the story centers on Jim, a gym-obsessed influencer and the most desired man on the city’s gay scene. His status collapses overnight when a strange virus called Heterosis begins converting gay men to heterosexuality. Dropped by his followers and shunned by his circle, Jim has only Lucien on his side, a skinny and fiercely loyal admirer. The pair head into the Marais in search of a renegade doctor who may hold a cure.

The film world premiered at Cannes, where festival chief Thierry Frémaux called the screening “one of the most beautiful in the festival’s history in terms of atmosphere.” The Jokers Films opened it in France on June 17, and it entered the box office chart at No. 3 behind “Toy Story 5” and “Backrooms.” It has since passed 385,000 admissions there and taken more than $3 million.

Reviewing the film for Variety , Guy Lodge wrote : “The humor and storytelling can be likened to ‘South Park’ in their senseless, fast-moving escalation toward absurdity, and the broadly cartoonish animation style – clean lines, popping eyes, flat expanses of color in ’80s mall-decor shades of pink, lilac and spearmint – is a running reminder of just how seriously to take the whole enterprise.”

Nguyen and Athané, both Gobelins graduates, co-wrote the screenplay with Simon Balteaux and Brice Chevillard. Between them they have worked on series, games and features including “The Summit of the Gods,” “Ernest & Celestine,” “The Big Bad Fox and Other Tales,” “The Swallows of Kabul,” “The Rabbi’s Cat” and “The Red Turtle.”

David Alric and Arthur Delabays produced for Paris-based adult animation outfit Bobbypills. The studio’s credits include James Gunn’s DC Studios series “Creature Commandos,” “Captain Laserhawk: A Blood Dragon Remix,” a Netflix series made in partnership with Ubisoft Film & Television, and the Netflix titles “Crisis Jung” and “Vermin.” Umedia (“The Count of Monte Cristo,” “The Night of the Zoocalypse”) co-produced, with backing from Eurimages, the CNC’s Avance sur recettes, the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region, the Charente department and the Réunion region.

Global Constellation was formed in 2025 by combining London’s Film Constellation with Munich-based Global Screen.

content.article_text:
Danny Trejo , who sparked backlash after it was revealed he’d be starring in the pro-ICE movie “ Pawn Shop ” from Ben Shapiro ’s production company, Daily Wire, had “never heard” of the conservative political commentator and is contractually unable to say anything negative about Shapiro — or the project — his son, Gilbert Trejo, said.

Gilbert shared a post to his Instagram story responding to the outcry from fans of the actor over the weekend, addressing claims that Danny is pro-ICE or supports Shapiro’s politics. He began by saying that only two weeks into shooting the project did any of the cast learn that Shapiro was involved, and that this father “has never heard of Ben Shapiro.” “I had to explain to him who that is, and what kind of guy he is,” wrote Gilbert.

Related Stories

Linda Duncombe, Beloved Banking Executive and Movie Producer, Dies at 55

Grace Helbig Reveals Upcoming Surgery for Brain Tumors Three Years After Beating Breast Cancer

He went on to write that Danny is unable to “badmouth” Shapiro or the film contractually. He also can’t “walk away without being sued for breach of contract. He couldn’t even release the statement he wanted to.” (Danny had previously told TMZ that he is a “proud Mexican who has always been and will always be a supporter of my community. I am also obviously pro-immigrant. I am not pro-ICE.. I know where I come from and I know our struggles. I am an actor. My job is to tell a story.”)

Popular on Variety

“It’s fucked up,” he continued. “He’s handcuffed to this stupid project, and swaths of people have instantly turned their back on him without knowing any of the facts.”

He said his father’s agent described the film as a “complicated story about a complicated time, where everyone looks bad except you, the hardworking Mexican shop owner who just wants peace,” to which Danny “jumped” at the idea of playing “a good guy.”

The logline for the film reads: “When a Minneapolis riot forces a young ICE officer to complete a high-stakes arrest alone after his partner is killed, he is hunted through the streets by a furious mob intent on freeing the prisoner and punishing anyone who still upholds the law. Barricaded inside a neighborhood pawn shop with a hard-edged Hispanic veteran and the man’s progressive college-age grandson, ordinary men must choose between the rule of law and the chaos that wants to burn it all down in a modern siege of honor and defiance.”

Read Gilbert’s full statement here.

For anyone seeing this shit with my dad…

He was booked on a film, it’s not pro-ice, its not overtly pro anything. His agent described it as ‘a complicated story about a complicated time, where everyone looks bad except you, the hardworking Mexican shop owner who just wants peace.”

He jumped at the idea of playing a good guy.

About 2 weeks into shooting everyone, including us, found out Ben Shapiro was involved.

My 82 year old dad has never heard of Ben Shapiro, I had to explain to him who that is, and what kind of guy he is.

My dad contractually can’t badmouth him, the film, or walk away without being sued for breach of contract. He couldn’t even release the statement he wanted to.

It’s fucked up. He’s handcuffed to this stupid project, and swaths of people have instantly turned their back on him without knowing any of the facts.

Ben Shapiro got Mexicans to abandon one of their heroes, got his own name to the top of google searches, and made us look like angry fools lacking any nuance. He wins.

Gu You Talks “The First Taste of Loneliness”, Shanshui Painting, Family, the Moon and Finding New Possibilities in Cinema

Gu You discusses family, loneliness, shanshui painting, moon symbolism and the formal rules behind “The First Taste of Loneliness”.

Gu You, the filmmaker previously known professionally as Gu Xiaogang, continues his exploration of the relationship between traditional Chinese art and contemporary cinema with “ The First Taste of Loneliness ”. Built around three women from different generations, the film approaches family without the constant conflict that frequently defines the genre, while using the moon, long takes and carefully controlled camera movement to connect intimate emotions with broader philosophical questions about loneliness, happiness and the meaning of life.

The First Taste of Loneliness is screening at Busan International Film Festival

Speaking with Asian Movie Pulse, Gu first explained the decision to adopt the name Gu You. His legal identity remains Gu Xiaogang; the change is closer to the traditional Chinese practice in which historical figures could be known by more than one name, or to the modern idea of an artistic name. The choice emerged from his increasingly deep engagement with shanshui painting , an ancient Chinese art form that has become central to his filmmaking and his thinking about cinema. Chinese director

That interest is visible not only aesthetically but also in the emotional structure of “The First Taste of Loneliness”. While many contemporary Chinese family dramas focus on resentment, arguments and damage passed between relatives, Gu deliberately wanted something different. He acknowledges that conflict-heavy family narratives often resemble real life, particularly within a culture where people may struggle to express affection directly. But precisely because of that reality, he wanted his three female characters to care for one another openly, share their fears and eventually communicate their love.

For Gu, this choice was also personal. He wanted to make something that his own family—or other Chinese families—might watch and take some warmth from. Cinema, in that sense, could become a small encouragement toward expressing feelings that are often left unspoken. The absence of major domestic confrontation is therefore not an attempt to idealize family life, but a conscious decision to imagine another possibility for how people might relate to each other.

The names and identities of the three women are closely connected with the moon, one of the film’s central philosophical images. Gu explains that the film could almost have been called “The First Taste of Happiness” or even “The First Taste of the Meaning of Life”. Within the Chinese Zen tradition as he understands it, the full moon can represent an ultimate form of meaning or happiness: something complete, constant and always present even when human experience changes beneath it.

Check the review of the film

The three women consequently represent different stages and experiences of life, including love, family, relationships, separation and death. Gu compares their experiences to reflections of the same moon appearing on different bodies of water. The reflection may change depending on whether it falls on a river, lake or sea, but the moon itself remains whole. Pain, loneliness and happiness therefore become different experiences through which a person can move closer to understanding what actually matters.

This philosophical approach also shaped the film’s distinctive visual grammar. Before shooting began, Gu and his team established six rules governing how the movie could be filmed, somewhat in the spirit of filmmakers imposing formal restrictions on themselves. One of the most important was that camera movement should proceed from right to left, inspired by the directional movement found in ancient Chinese visual documents and paintings.

Another principle involved creating transitions between different spaces and even different moments of time within a single shot. Gu connects this to traditional Chinese painting, where one image can contain multiple spaces and temporal experiences rather than following a single fixed perspective. The long take therefore becomes more than a stylistic signature. It allows geography, time and emotion to shift inside the same composition.

The restrictions were also a response to contemporary technological freedom. In an era when digital tools and artificial intelligence make almost any visual effect possible, Gu became interested in the opposite approach: restricting what he could do in order to discover possibilities that might otherwise remain invisible. Rather than treating technological freedom as inherently creative, he believes clearly defined limitations can force filmmakers to reconsider the basic language of cinema.

The final scene demonstrates how visual form and the film’s emotional ideas come together. Gu clarified that a sound heard after the protagonist leaves is not something breaking, but the closing of a door. Her departure leaves the apartment empty, but the absence is important because there is another form of loneliness present throughout the film that audiences may not immediately recognize: that of the dead grandfather.

Gu explains that the camera can be understood as carrying the perspective of the grandfather’s soul. The film becomes, in part, the story of his final hundred days of saying goodbye to the three women. When Jiang Yue finally leaves and the door closes, the empty frame represents not only her departure but the loneliness of the person who has already died and remains connected to those who continue living. The long takes thus have an emotional function beyond their connection to shanshui aesthetics.

Preparing the actresses required an equally unusual process. Gu rented the apartment used in the film well before principal photography and asked the three women to live there together. There were no crew members, assistants or managers present—only the actresses and Gu himself observing. They cooked, slept, used the bathroom, learned where objects were kept and gradually became accustomed to sharing the space as though they were genuinely a family. Only after establishing that familiarity did shooting begin.

Casting itself was connected partly to geography and temperament. Gu was interested in performers who had some relationship to Zhejiang and who could feel naturally connected to the place. In choosing Zhou Xun, he also considered the public impression surrounding her: someone thoughtful and interested in larger questions about life. That quality matched Jiang Yue, whose father’s death sends her toward her own search for meaning. Gu felt Chinese audiences could therefore intuitively believe in her journey.

Despite the film’s apparently simple construction, editing became unexpectedly difficult. “The First Taste of Loneliness” consists of only around 50 shots, with more than 20 of them extended takes. Gu initially assumed such a limited amount of footage would make post-production comparatively straightforward. Instead, the editing process stretched across approximately a year, with periods of two or three months between different versions. Chinese director

The difficulty was philosophical rather than technical. Gu compares it to a Chinese saying suggesting that characters made with very few brushstrokes can be among the hardest to write correctly. With so few cuts available, every decision carried additional weight. More importantly, he was still asking himself throughout writing, production and editing what loneliness actually means. The movie could not be completed simply by finding the right technical rhythm; he first had to continue confronting the question at its center. Chinese director

His next work will continue investigating the relationship between shanshui painting and cinema , although Gu is now considering moving the experiment in another direction. While the rules of “The First Taste of Loneliness” primarily governed cinematography and visual language, the next project may apply a similar principle to genre itself. He is considering whether romance, the road movie, crime or another established form can be rethought through the principles he has been developing from traditional painting.

The goal, however, remains consistent. Gu is less interested in reproducing traditional Chinese art on screen than in asking what its ideas can offer contemporary cinema. “The First Taste of Loneliness” uses family, the moon, empty rooms and moving images to bring emotional experience into contact with something more philosophical. In doing so, Gu continues searching for a cinematic language in which ancient forms can generate genuinely new possibilities.

content.article_text:
The actor Selma Blair was arrested on Sunday at John F Kennedy airport in New York after she allegedly attacked two flight attendants on a Delta Air Lines flight, and separately charged with two counts of assault for allegedly kicking a police officer and a nurse after landing.

Blair’s arrest happened at about 11pm, after Port Authority of New York and New Jersey officials said they responded to a call “about a physically abusive passenger aboard Delta Air Lines flight 938 which was parked at the gate” at JFK after arriving from Los Angeles.

The 54-year-old “was taken into custody and transported to the hospital for evaluation”, the port authority said on Monday. “Two flight attendants also reported injuries, and one was transported to the hospital for further evaluation.”

Several news outlets on Monday reported that Blair allegedly punched a flight attendant, bit another and tried to open the airplane door.

The Guardian has reached out to Blair’s representatives for additional comment. Her publicist told the Hollywood Reporter: “Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is [now] in stable condition.”

The FBI, which handles reports of crimes on airplanes, has issued Blair a notice charging her with assault related to her actions aboard the aircraft, according to a federal law enforcement official who spoke to the Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly about the matter.

Those charges will be handled through the petty violations court in federal court in Brooklyn. No date has been set for Blair’s appearance.

Separately, Blair was charged on Monday night at a court in Queens with two counts of second-degree assault, for allegedly assaulting a police officer who was taking her to hospital after the flight, as well as a nurse after she arrived there.

In charging documents, a police officer taking her to Jamaica Hospital Medical Center alleged that while she was securing Blair to a stretcher, Blair pulled a leg from the straps and kicked her repeatedly around the face, neck and chest, causing serious pain and substantial swelling. A nurse who was moving Blair in hospital alleged the actor then kicked her in the chest, causing substantial pain.

On Monday night, a judge set Blair’s bail at $20,000 cash or $60,000 bond and set the next hearing for January. Blair then left court with her lawyers.

Details of what happened aboard the aircraft weren’t immediately disclosed by the airline, police or the FBI, which was investigating, but a Delta spokesperson said the airline “has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first”.

An air traffic control audio recording from the flight Blair was on captured the pilot saying “one flight attendant and one passenger … sustained some minor injuries – a bloody nose as well as some bite marks”.

“I don’t think we need an ambulance or anything like that – but we just want to get some medical personnel at the gate to look at their injuries,” the pilot said, according to the recording, a copy of which was published by NBC Los Angeles.

The flight controller replied that paramedics were approaching the gate – and that law enforcement was already there.

Sunday marked at least the second time Blair was reported to be involved in an incident on a plane. In 2016, she reportedly began screaming uncontrollably before being removed on a stretcher while on a Los Angeles-bound flight from Cancún, Mexico.

Blair apologized after the earlier episode, saying that she “mixed alcohol with medication”.

“That caused me to black out and led me to say and do things that I deeply regret,” Blair said at the time.

The actor has also made news headlines for a 2018 multiple sclerosis diagnosis . And in February 2024, she apologized for an Islamophobic comment on social media.

Blair’s starring film credits include Cruel Intentions, Legally Blonde and Hellboy. She earned a best spoken world album for children nomination at the 2011 Grammy awards for her work on Anne Frank: The Diary of a Young Girl – The Definitive Edition.
