content.article_text:
Vietnamese female-led franchise entry “ Sister Sister 3 ” has been picked up by U.S.-based specialty distributor 3388 Films for the Americas, Europe, Australia, Taiwan and Japan.

The deal was closed at the Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) in Busan.

Directed by Nguyen Huu Hoang and produced by Will Vu for Muse Films, the film is the third chapter in one of Vietnam’s most recognized franchises built around women. Ninh Duong Lan Ngoc, Chi Pu and Ky Duyen head the cast, with Steven Nguyen and Quoc Anh also starring. The original Vietnamese title is “Chị Chị Em Em 3.”

Related Stories

Selma Blair Charged with Second-Degree Assault Following Plane Incident, Released on $20,000 Bail

Raindance to Launch U.K.'s First Major Vertical Festival and Market (EXCLUSIVE)

Set in northern Vietnam of a bygone era, the period piece draws its look from traditional Vietnamese culture. It reworks Thị Mầu, the free-spirited, flirtatious heroine of a classic Chèo play who defies Confucian norms and rebels against feudal prejudice. Chèo is a traditional Vietnamese form of popular musical theater.

Popular on Variety

In the film, Thị Mầu is a gifted young beauty hemmed in by rigid custom and the demands of her family. Following her own heart pulls her into a tangle of romance, jealousy, hidden truths and forbidden relationships. As private longing collides with honor and social codes, each character has to reckon with what their choices cost.

“We’re constantly seeking daring, character-driven stories that resonate with the global audience and 3388 Films is ecstatic to have acquired such a bold and brazen female-led film,” said Thien A. Pham, founder of 3388 Films.

The film will open in Vietnamese cinemas at the end of October, with 3388 Films’ theatrical rollout across several continents set to follow later this year.

“I’m very excited ‘Sister Sister 3’ will soon be seen by international audiences and proud to be able to share our film which showcases the beauty of traditional Vietnamese culture while telling a seductive and emotionally gripping story of love, desire, and secrets,” said Vu.

3388 Films is a production and distribution company that prioritizes theatrical releases and has worked with Asian content for more than two decades, with experience across five continents. Its recent distribution slate includes “Mai,” which became the first Vietnamese film to gross more than $2 million at the combined North America and Europe box office. The company also produced the independent thriller-horror “Actress Wanted.”

content.article_text:
10月14日から、和歌山県立近代美術館にて鈴木崇の個展が開催される。写真というメディアを介して、視覚と知覚の関係性や認識の変化に注目し、作品を展開する鈴木崇。鈴木の眼差しを手がかりに不確かなこの世界のあり方を探る。普段の生活のなかで出会う数々のものやイメージ。私たちは視覚を通してさまざまなことを把握している。しかし、それらは実際どのように理解されているのか？「All is not as it seems」（すべてが見かけ通りとは限らない）と、鈴木は問いかける。

本展では、鈴木の新旧作品とともに、作家が選んだ当館コレクションもあわせて展示される。「もののをかし」をテーマに構成した会場によって、視覚と知覚をめぐる思索に誘われてみてはいかが。

content.article_text:
Selma Blair has been charged with second-degree assault after being arrested following a violent incident on a Delta flight on Sunday, according to Queens Criminal Court. The actress posted $20,000 in bail, paid by credit card, and was released on Monday.

Following her removal from the Delta plane on Sunday, the “Cruel Intentions” actress was arrested on Monday by a Port Authority police officer after allegedly attacking an officer and a nurse, per TMZ. She then appeared in Queens Criminal Court Monday evening, where she appeared before Judge Indira D. Khan, per court documents viewed by Variety.

Related Stories

Peruvian Filmmaker Sami Hawka Explores Polyamory, Indigenous Rights and Resistance in ‘While Everything Falls’: ’Power Can Oppress People in Different Ways’

Cannes Queer Animated Comedy ‘Jim Queen’ Scores New Sales at Busan (EXCLUSIVE)

On the plane, she allegedly punched one flight attendant and bit another while heading from Los Angeles to New York. Blair also attempted to open the plane door while in the air. Law enforcement was waiting for the 54-year-old “Legally Blonde” actress at John F. Kennedy airport, where police took her into custody and transported her to a hospital for evaluation. Two flight attendants reported injuries, with one receiving treatment at a hospital.

Popular on Variety

After the incident, a representative for Blair told Variety : “Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition.”

In 2016, Blair experienced a previous outburst while on a plane, during which she was removed from a flight on a stretcher while traveling with her then 4-year-old son after she “had a total psychotic blackout,” as she described it. Blair attributed the incident to drinking a glass of wine and taking a pill. “It was horrible and frightening, and I had empathy for myself actually afterward because it was actually so out of character for me, especially because I’m a mother,” she said at the time.

content.article_text:
Tokyo Docs Looks Beyond Japan as “Call & Response” and “Mission100” Seek International Paths in Busan

Tokyo Docs’ Kenichi Imamura discusses taking Japanese documentaries global, as “Call & Response” and “Mission100” present their projects in Busan.

Japanese documentary cinema has never lacked filmmakers willing to devote years of their lives to a subject. What it has often lacked, according to Tokyo Docs co-founder Kenichi Imamura, is a structure capable of taking those films beyond Japan. That is increasingly the focus not only of Tokyo Docs, the international pitching platform launched in 2011, but also of the newer J-Docs Hub, which is designed to give Japanese documentary filmmakers the skills, contacts and development support necessary to work internationally. Imamura currently serves as managing director of J-Docs Hub.

Speaking with Asian Movie Pulse in Busan, Imamura described a Japanese documentary scene that is healthier domestically than outsiders might assume. He cited close to 100 Japanese documentaries receiving theatrical releases in a recent year, but stressed that the way many of those films are made and distributed remains remarkably self-contained. Directors frequently finance projects themselves, shoot and edit alone, open in one or two small Tokyo cinemas and then spend considerable effort expanding gradually to another ten or twenty venues. The films exist, and many are strong, but their creators often conceive them almost exclusively for Japanese audiences.

For Imamura, that is the missed opportunity Tokyo Docs has spent years trying to address. “I want to push them to go to the world,” he explains. The arrival of support through the Japan Creator Support Fund offered a chance to develop that ambition much further. J-Docs Hub was established as a multi-year initiative under Tokyo Docs, with international development rather than simply individual pitching sessions at its center. The official program describes its three stages as Learning, Networking and Creating, covering everything from project development and fundraising to overseas markets and support for actual production development.

The first part is education. The Project Lab selects a small number of projects for a year-long process led by producer Eric Nyari, during which filmmakers learn how to construct pitch decks and trailers and how to present their projects at international industry events. Other initiatives concentrate specifically on producers, while Asako Fujioka’s Documentary Destinations seminars examine what filmmakers should do once a film is completed: which festivals, markets, educational platforms and distribution routes may actually suit a particular documentary.

The second stage is practical international exposure. Imamura mentioned supporting teams attending Docs by the Sea in Indonesia, as well as filmmakers and producers traveling to Berlin, Cannes, Ji.hlava’s Emerging Producers program and IDFA Academy. The purpose is not simply to finance a trip, but to allow Japanese documentary professionals to experience the environments in which international co-production, sales and festival relationships are actually formed.

The third stage concerns development itself. While the support cannot simply be used as production financing, it can cover development-related shooting, editing, travel and mentorship. Imamura is particularly interested in creating a system in which the knowledge gained does not remain with the original participants. Filmmakers who acquire international experience can return as tutors for the next generation, allowing information to circulate rather than repeatedly disappearing when a single funding cycle ends.

Choosing which projects can travel internationally is not necessarily straightforward. Imamura initially tended to look for subjects that obviously seemed to have relevance outside Japan. Yet the success of deeply local documentaries has complicated that assumption. A story may concern a single Japanese family and still connect powerfully with audiences elsewhere. For him, the more important quality is increasingly whether the filmmaker genuinely wants to enter that international conversation: to seek foreign producers, collaborate across borders and rethink how the project might reach different audiences. English helps, but motivation matters more.

The two projects presented in Busan illustrate exactly how broad that definition of internationally relevant Japanese documentary can become. One looks inside institutions that Japanese society rarely sees; the other follows an obsessive spearfisher across oceans in pursuit of an almost impossible goal.

“Call & Response”: Kaori Sakagami Turns the Camera Toward Japan’s Closed Correctional System

Kaori Sakagami is already familiar with the difficulty of getting a camera inside Japan’s correctional institutions. Her earlier “Prison Circle” was filmed at the Shimane Asahi Social Reintegration Center, a public-private partnership prison, and examined an institution where private-sector organizations participate in areas including security and vocational training while the prison itself remains part of the public correctional system.

During our conversation in Busan, Sakagami was careful to distinguish this arrangement from the privately owned prison model associated with the United States. Japanese prisons remain public institutions; certain operations are contracted to private companies. What interests her is whether even that limited presence can introduce different thinking into an extraordinarily rigid system. In her view, private-sector involvement has made certain practices somewhat less closed, while the broader prison bureaucracy remains resistant to change.

Sakagami points to the remarkable longevity of rules and customs governing the treatment of prisoners. Legal reform has occurred, but institutional habits can survive far longer than legislation. Part of the problem, she argues, is the distance between prisons and ordinary Japanese society. With a comparatively small incarcerated population and correctional facilities largely closed to public observation, prison conditions are easily framed as something concerning “them” rather than “us”. A combination of social apathy and lack of information allows extreme discipline and outdated protocols to continue without sustained public discussion.

Her new documentary, “Call & Response”, shifts the focus toward juvenile training schools and uses rap workshops as a means through which young people can articulate experiences that are frequently difficult to express directly. The completed Japanese version runs 229 minutes, divided into two parts, continuing Sakagami’s preference for giving institutions and the people inside them enough time to become more than abstractions.

The film’s nearly four-hour running time is first and foremost connected to the unprecedented nature of the experiment Sakagami was documenting. The workshops inside Japan’s juvenile correctional facilities created a degree of freedom for the young participants that would previously have been almost unimaginable within such an environment. Rather than compressing the process into a series of highlights, Sakagami wanted to record carefully how that freedom developed over time: how the participants responded to it, how relationships changed and what happened when young people who were normally subjected to strict institutional control were given greater space to express themselves.

This was particularly important because, as Sakagami explains, Japanese correctional institutions have long operated according to a deeply ingrained assumption that giving young people greater freedom would cause them to become uncontrollable. The film attempts to test that assumption through the concrete process of the workshops rather than simply arguing against it. At the same time, the extended running time also allows Sakagami to expose the broader institutional structures surrounding the participants, including forms of discipline and deeply established practices that rarely receive public scrutiny. The Japanese theatrical version will retain its approximately four-hour duration, with more than twenty cinemas already committed to screening it at the time of our conversation.

What makes the project particularly suited to the broader mission Imamura describes is that the film begins with a very specific Japanese system but reaches questions far beyond it: what society expects punishment to accomplish, why people outside an institution remain indifferent to those trapped within it, and whether rehabilitation is possible without communication between the two sides.

“Mission100”: One Breath, One Spear and Five Years Following an Obsession

If “Call & Response” deals with an almost completely closed environment, “Mission100” heads in the opposite direction: into an enormous, unpredictable natural space.

Producer Kentaro Osaki is himself a recreational spearfisher, and the project began through coincidence. In 2020, while camping on a Japanese island, he stayed at the same guesthouse as spearfisher Kunpei Kosaka. The future director and another photographer were also there for unrelated reasons. Conversation eventually turned toward Kosaka’s extraordinary ambition: hunting increasingly enormous fish through freediving and eventually attempting to take a 100-kilogram dogtooth tuna with a single hand spear.

Osaki immediately recognized that this was larger than material suitable for a YouTube video. He was already impressed by the scale of Kosaka’s catches—while Osaki might consider an eight-kilogram fish substantial, Kosaka was pursuing animals weighing 30, 40 or 50 kilograms and ultimately aiming beyond 100. More important, however, was the philosophy behind it. Kosaka imposed his own rules on himself and approached the sea with an intensity that seemed almost irrational in its purity. That obsession became the reason to make a feature documentary.

It also makes Kosaka an occasionally infuriating documentary protagonist. Osaki describes him as someone who is almost completely faithful to whatever he personally wants to do and remarkably unreliable when asked to deal with anything else. Meetings can be forgotten, promises broken and phone calls ignored. Even something as basic as sending a photograph required for a sponsor can become a struggle. Osaki jokingly describes him as a “social misfit”, but the same quality that makes production difficult also makes the character compelling: his selfishness and purity come from the same place.

Kosaka eventually achieved the 100-kilogram goal, but Osaki does not see that as the natural ending of the story. Catching the fish was never primarily about establishing a record or winning a competition. His deeper desire is to encounter aspects of nature he does not yet know. Once one apparently impossible target has been reached, another unknown remains. He continues traveling and spearfishing and is considering settling somewhere where he can make the practice part of his life as a fisherman.

Taken together, “Call & Response” and “Mission100” make a useful argument for Imamura’s insistence that Japanese documentaries should not be divided too easily into subjects that can travel and subjects that cannot. One is an institutional film about punishment, communication and the social distance surrounding incarcerated young people; the other is an adventure documentary about a man who organizes his entire existence around descending into the ocean on a single breath.

What connects them is not subject matter but commitment, along with a willingness to let that commitment enter an international context. This is ultimately what Tokyo Docs and J-Docs Hub are trying to change. Japanese filmmakers have long demonstrated that they are prepared to spend years shooting, editing and financing stories on their own. Imamura’s concern is what happens next: whether those stories remain inside a small domestic circuit, or whether the infrastructure finally exists for them to move outward.

content.article_text:
Kim Jung-hoon, Roh Jeong-eui and Show Kasamatsu on genre and cross-cultural collaboration in “Shaving”

Presenting in the competition section at the 31st Busan International Film Festival

Kim Jung-hoon gained recognition with his debut feature “Tinker Ticker” (2013), which competed in the Asian Future section of the Tokyo International Film Festival. More than a decade later, he returns with “Shaving”, a horror-thriller based on a screenplay by Hong Seong-yoon and Roh Dohyeon, presented in the competition section of the Busan International Film Festival.

On the occasion of his film “Shaving”, director Kim Jung-hoon and his two leads, Roh Jeong-eui and Show Kasamatsu, talked about how the project began, the blend of genres, the physical and emotional demands of the roles, and the interplay of Korean and Japanese on set.

Shaving is screening at Busan International Film Festival

The act of shaving becomes the catalyst for the film’s central events. How did the project begin, and what role does shaving play in the film?

I received the script around June last year. It was written by two screenwriters, Hong Seong-yoon and Roh Dohyeon, who are close friends from schooldays. As I understand it, they were working together, and one day the male writer went to the female writer’s home for a meeting. Since they have known each other for so long, Hong hadn’t shaved that day because he’d been busy working. She teased him about his stubble and told him to go and shave. They found a razor that had belonged to Roh’s ex-boyfriend, and he actually ended up using it. About halfway through, an idea struck them, and that is how the project began, or so I was told.

From the moment I received the script to the day the film was finished, I kept thinking about what shaving means. For men it is an everyday routine, something done daily. But if you stop and think about it, a razor can also be dangerous, even chilling. Our film begins with what looks like the ordinary life of a couple and grows steadily more dangerous, and I felt that fit the concept perfectly.

What did you enjoy most while working on the film, and what did you most want to try?

Roh Jeong-eui: Action was a new genre for me, and the first time I had tried it, so everything about it was exciting and fun, and I enjoyed every day of shooting. We rehearsed the choreography together, looked after one another, and talked a lot about how to bring out each character and each situation as well as we could. It was a fresh challenge and a really happy experience, and I think it will remain a good memory.

Show Kasamatsu: I had never done anything quite like this. When I first received the project, I was told it was a romance. I’m not an actor who does much romance. I’ve mostly played villains and dark, menacing characters, so people teased me, saying, “So it’s a romance now!” But after we shot the film, I felt it was a much deeper kind of romance. The simpler, surface-level romance matters in the film too, and I hope audiences enjoy it. But to me, honestly, it is a romance rooted in the pain and struggles of one young woman.

Was the genre mix already there in the screenplay, or did you deliberately bring in elements of the many genres you love? Why did you choose such a hybrid approach?

Kim Jung-hoon : Most of the genre framework you describe was already in the screenplay. Some elements, such as the creature, changed during the adaptation. When I first read the script, those were exactly the things that attracted me most. The challenge was how to present them in a rich and fresh way without losing the coherence of the whole film, and above all how to follow the protagonist’s emotional journey so that everything comes together at the end. That was the most important thing for me.

This film depends heavily on the strength of its actors, and working in tandem within such a confined setting can’t have been easy. What did you talk about on set and in rehearsals to find your rhythm together?

Show Kasamatsu: Before shooting began, I talked at length with the director. What mattered most to me was this: can the audience be sure that the person they are watching is who he appears to be? Can they ever really know who this man is? I discussed that a great deal with the director and with my co-star. In my scenes, she responded and reacted to what I was doing, and we built the performance up bit by bit. I hope viewers will enjoy asking themselves, “Who is this man?” as they watch.

Roh Jeong-eui: As Show said, the person the protagonist loves and trusts most becomes the person she can trust least, and she goes from happiness to nightmare. We needed to talk a great deal during filming to portray that journey.

During the action scenes, thanks to our wonderful director and the fellow actors around us, we felt secure, and we exchanged many ideas about how to express the emotions more fully. And my character, So-yeon, like anyone, carries trauma. Confronting that trauma and rebuilding her life is at the heart of her story. In rehearsals with my co-stars we tried many different approaches, including a lot of improvisation, in an effort to enrich the details of the film.

Director Kim, please share the motivation behind choosing Roh Jeong-eui and Show Kasamatsu

Let me start with Roh Jeong-eui. I first came across her a long time ago, when she was cast as a young actress in a film from the same production company. She came in to audition, she was cast, and I followed her through the making of the film and its release, and I thought she was a very appealing actress. I kept seeing her in different projects after that and felt she was growing well. While reading this script, I felt that she could bring out sides that audiences hadn’t seen from her. She has always been cute, bright and lovable, but I believed she could also express a more reactive, more vulnerable side, and that she would be a wonderful fit.

As for Show Kasamatsu, I first saw him in Michael Mann’s “Tokyo Vice”, whom I deeply respect. I was captivated. Then our production company, Star Platinum, cast him in “Good News” (2025), and his name came up again around the time we were casting. In the original screenplay the couple is in a long-distance relationship, and since they are meeting again after a long time, I thought it might work to make him foreign altogether. That would make the difference between the ex-boyfriend and the current boyfriend much clearer, and the unease and sense of alienation when an everyday boyfriend suddenly transforms could be heightened by shifting between Korean and Japanese. It seemed like a good idea, so I proposed the role to him.

How did the two actors feel about working together?

Roh Jeong-eui: To me, Show is a senior I look up to, someone ahead of me in life, and I truly feel he is remarkable. I often wondered whether I could go abroad and show my abilities as he has done. Seeing him made me realize how young I still am and how much room I have to grow. I hope he will keep making many films in Korea.

Show Kasamatsu: I keep saying that too, and I’ll be bringing more projects to Korea. What surprised me was how cold it was during the shoot. Korea is so cold!

The back-and-forth between Korean and Japanese gives this film an important nuance. In the script, all of my lines were in Korean. I studied hard and performed them, but pronunciation was a real struggle. The director and the team helped me a great deal, and we worked together to decide naturally, “Here Japanese is better, here Korean is better.”

Roh Jeong-eui: When Show improvised in Japanese, even if I didn’t fully understand the words, I could feel exactly what the nuance was. That made it very frightening and even more chilling. As I performed, I kept being confused: is this the boyfriend who truly loves me speaking, or is my nightmare starting all over again? Korean and Japanese sound so different, with such a subtle effect, and I think Show chose his ad-libs with great care. I hope audiences will look out for that as well.

Mr. Kasamatsu, as an actor who has now worked in both countries, how do you see the differences between filming in Korea and in Japan, and how do you feel about Korean films?

There is a difference in the shooting systems. I believe Korea is stricter about protecting actors’ working conditions. Japan is working hard on this, but it isn’t perfect yet. There is also a difference in creative approach. The impression I have is that Korea sets out to make a miracle happen in front of the camera. To do that, everything is carefully built, from the atmosphere to the costumes, the makeup and the direction. But if every image is constructed too tightly, there can be moments when the actors’ energy drops.

In Japan, good films, good dramas, good actors and directors wait for a miracle and make it happen on set. So the temperature is different, but I wouldn’t say one is better or worse. I enjoy both, and I want to keep learning in Korea and in Japan from wonderful actors in each.

Con sede en Ambika P3, la feria contará con 22 galerías y proyectos internacionales, junto a una selección de artistas independientes, un programa de videoarte centroamericano y una sección de publicaciones y ediciones independientes."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Paraíso busca poner en diálogo a artistas contemporáneos de la región con referentes del arte moderno y posmoderno latinoamericano. Para Weiss, la cámara de video era una extensión de su propio cuerpo y una vía alternativa para cuestionar los lenguajes audiovisuales dominantes y las convenciones sobre la representación de la experiencia femenina. content.article_text:
Del 15 al 18 de octubre de 2026, Londres acogerá la primera edición de Paraíso Latin American Art Fair, una nueva plataforma centrada en el arte moderno y contemporáneo latinoamericano. Con sede en Ambika P3, la feria contará con 22 galerías y proyectos internacionales, junto a una selección de artistas independientes, un programa de videoarte centroamericano y una sección de publicaciones y ediciones independientes.

Paraíso busca poner en diálogo a artistas contemporáneos de la región con referentes del arte moderno y posmoderno latinoamericano. La programación se complementa con conversaciones públicas, presentaciones en vivo y actividades especiales, con el propósito de ofrecer al público londinense una perspectiva amplia y diversa de la producción artística de América Latina.

Cada edición de la feria pondrá el foco en un país de la región, y México inaugura el formato.

México en el centro: Felipe Ehrenberg, Pola Weiss y Carlos Amorales

Las propuestas convocadas para esta primera edición conectan varias generaciones y lenguajes artísticos, desde la experimentación conceptual y el arte postal hasta los primeros ensayos con el video y las intervenciones in situ.

Destaca la presentación especial de Felipe Ehrenberg (Ciudad de México, 1943-2017), figura clave del arte experimental mexicano, cuya práctica abarcó el dibujo, la performance, la edición independiente y el arte postal. Bajo el título Felipe Ehrenberg: 26 Maculate Letters from Mexico | An Unfinished Conversation , la muestra incluye 26 obras concebidas originalmente para una exposición en Londres prevista para 2016, que finalmente no llegó a realizarse.

El proyecto recupera una faceta significativa de la obra de Ehrenberg: el uso de la correspondencia como medio artístico y vía de circulación. Mostradas diez años después de la exposición inicialmente proyectada, las cartas abren una conversación que quedó interrumpida y que ahora encuentra una nueva oportunidad de continuar.

La programación también rinde homenaje a Pola Weiss (Ciudad de México, 1947-1990), pionera del videoarte y la videodanza en México y América Latina. Su trabajo ensayó las posibilidades expresivas de la imagen en movimiento a través del cuerpo, la música y la experimentación con efectos visuales analógicos. Para Weiss, la cámara de video era una extensión de su propio cuerpo y una vía alternativa para cuestionar los lenguajes audiovisuales dominantes y las convenciones sobre la representación de la experiencia femenina. La feria presentará dos piezas de la artista que reivindican la vigencia de una obra que desafió los límites entre tecnología y subjetividad.

El enfoque mexicano llega al presente con Carlos Amorales (Ciudad de México, 1970), quien realiza una instalación site-specific en el área VIP de esta primera edición de la feria. Amorales también ha diseñado el bolso de Paraíso, una pieza con identidad autoral que lleva la presencia de la feria fuera de su sede.

Somers & Paraíso: las grandes apuestas de Javier Calderón

Paraíso busca crear un espacio de visibilidad y reflexión para el arte latinoamericano desde sus propias especificidades culturales, políticas y estéticas, frente a los relatos históricos que han simplificado e incluso exotizado sus escenas artísticas y culturales. Su director, Javier Calderón , apuesta por el papel estratégico de Londres como nodo del mercado internacional y por la necesidad de generar nuevas maneras de coleccionar comprometidas con América Latina.

“Durante la semana de Frieze, la capital británica se convierte en el epicentro del mercado global del arte […]. Nuestra apuesta es clara: Londres ofrece las condiciones únicas para que el arte latinoamericano dialogue, en igualdad de condiciones, con los grandes actores del mercado internacional”, explicaba Calderón en una entrevista reciente.

Paraíso tiene sus raíces en una serie de proyectos centrados en el arte mexicano iniciados en 2009 y, de manera más formal, en Somers Gallery , fundada en 2015 por Calderón bajo el nombre de Chalton Gallery . Nacida como un espacio de proyectos pensado sobre todo para apoyar a artistas de México y el Reino Unido, en 2022 adoptó su nombre actual y amplió su enfoque hacia el arte contemporáneo de América Latina y el Reino Unido.

En el marco de la feria, Somers acogió el prelanzamiento de Paraíso con dos exposiciones que cruzan distintas maneras de trabajar la memoria, la escritura y los objetos cotidianos. Please Read Carefully , curada por Fortunata Calabro , muestra una faceta más íntima de Felipe Ehrenberg a través de obras procedentes de su colección personal, varias de ellas exhibidas por primera vez. Recuerdos, experimentos y referencias privadas nos acercan a una práctica en la que vida y obra se mantienen estrechamente ligadas. Londres es también la ciudad donde Ehrenberg residió desde 1968 y donde desarrolló algunas de las ideas que marcarían su manera de entender la producción artística.

Por su parte, A Hotel With My Name , de la escritora y artista argentina Cecilia Pavón , con curaduría de Sandra Sánchez , traslada su universo poético al espacio expositivo. A partir de objetos ordinarios, textos y elementos recogidos en la vida urbana, Pavón construye una suerte de hotel imaginario en el que la escritura sale de la página y propone otro trato con los materiales y las cosas. Lejos de las jerarquías tradicionales del valor artístico, su propuesta encuentra en los objetos cotidianos y en los encuentros fortuitos con la ciudad una fuente de historias, afectos y posibilidades poéticas. El resultado es una invitación a habitar temporalmente ese universo, en sintonía con una obra que entiende la poesía como una práctica cercana, cotidiana y abierta a todos.

Galerías y proyectos

La primera edición de Paraíso reúne galerías y proyectos de varios países de América Latina, con presentaciones tanto individuales como colectivas que reflexionan acerca de la memoria, la migración y los modos de producción. Además, una sección está dedicada a 13 artistas independientes: Débora Delmar, Jorge Rosano e Yvonne Venegas (México); Alessandra Risi y Aquiles Paredes (Perú); Emilia González (Ecuador); Felipe Pineda (Chile); Constanza Pullit, Laura Kazaroff y Sofía Clausse (Argentina); Gusty Ferro y Malu Laet (Brasil); y Ernesto Crespo (Cuba).

La galería londinense Cecilia Brunson Projects lleva a Francisco Valdés con un nuevo conjunto de pinturas que toma el ping-pong como metáfora lúdica de las dinámicas de poder y control, y a Mónica Pérez , pintora uruguaya que elabora sus propios pigmentos a partir de materiales recogidos en su país, entre ellos arcilla de Garzón, negro de hueso, ocre rojo y residuos industriales de lana. Estas materias enlazan su trabajo con la historia de las praderas uruguayas y la economía ganadera que conectó la riqueza agrícola del país con la industria británica.

Desde Chile, Aninat Galería trae una selección de obras de Paula Ceroni, Catalina Swinburn, Estefanía Tarud, Alicia Rinsche, María Ossandón y Jaime Gil . La propuesta reúne distintas aproximaciones a la pintura, el textil, el dibujo y la escultura, para dar cuenta de la diversidad de lenguajes y búsquedas que conviven en la escena contemporánea chilena.

Isabel Croxatto Galería participa con una individual del artista chileno Nelson Hernández , nacido en la Patagonia y actualmente radicado en Londres. Bajo el título Errantes , expone una nueva serie de pinturas en las que imágenes, referencias culturales y fragmentos de distintos orígenes conviven en escenas de construcción minuciosa e inestable.

La galería Victoria Law Projects exhibe What the Ground Holds , una propuesta curatorial en la que conviven obras de Lucía Pizzani y José García Oliva , artistas de origen venezolano radicados en Londres. Pizzani concibe la tierra como un cuerpo capaz de conservar registros, mientras García Oliva dirige su atención al trabajo externalizado, las economías migrantes y las jerarquías sociales que sostienen la vida urbana. Ambos ponen la mirada en aquello que los sistemas de extracción mantienen fuera de campo y cuestionan el valor atribuido a la tierra y al trabajo cuando se los considera únicamente en función de su rendimiento.

La galería Piloto Pardo agrupa obras de los artistas chilenos Juan Martínez Macari , quien trabaja a partir de la observación cercana y la tradición del bodegón; Alejandra Prieto , que investiga qué une a materiales como el carbón y la piedra con el trabajo, la extracción y el capitalismo global; y Cosima zu Knyphausen , establecida en Berlín, quien revisita referencias de la historia del arte y la literatura y se detiene en el deseo y las experiencias queer. A ellos se suma la artista argentina Martina Quesada , que vive entre Buenos Aires y París, cuya obra combina sistemas geométricos, simbolismos sagrados y referencias a la naturaleza para indagar en la percepción y los límites entre lo visible y lo invisible.

La galería boliviana NUBE llega con Velos de silencio , una exposición curada por Douglas Rodrigo Rada con obras de Carolina Aranibar-Fernández, José Ballivián , Cecilia Lampo, Óscar Abraham Pabón y Alex Zapata . Con miradas diversas, los artistas trabajan en torno a la identidad, la memoria y sus transformaciones.

La participación marca el regreso de NUBE a las ferias internacionales y se complementa con charlas de la artista de video boliviana Claudia Joskowicz y de Raquel Schwartz , directora de NUBE y KIOSKO Galería , junto a la académica Giuliana Borea y el curador Diego Chocano .

Carlos Caamaño participa con obras de algunos de los artistas peruanos que representa su galería, mientras que The LAACC propone Elsewhere and Here , una exposición colectiva que reúne a seis artistas de México, Colombia, Guatemala y Brasil: Sofía Alrich Veytia, Daniel Arteaga, Aline Bittar Künzel, Joe Gómez, Mena Guerrero y Cayetano Sanz .

Videoarte centroamericano: imaginar desde el istmo

Para el ciclo Desde el estrecho dudoso (From the Doubtful Isthmus) , el curador Juan Canela ha seleccionado cinco piezas de videoarte contemporáneo de Centroamérica que plantean el istmo como un lugar geográfico y como una forma de mirar y pensar desde la incertidumbre.

A partir de la noción que reivindicó la curadora Virginia Pérez-Ratton , el programa propone recorridos por la memoria, los cuerpos, los paisajes y los archivos, sin pretender definir una identidad centroamericana única. Las obras transitan entre el documento y la ficción, la observación y la imaginación, y entienden la imagen en movimiento como un espacio abierto a los cruces y las transformaciones.

La selección incluye Ruta a la inmortalidad (2024), del artista guatemalteco Gabriel Rodríguez Pellecer ( Extra Galería , Guatemala), que revisita los discursos de progreso y desarrollo asociados al Canal de Panamá y a las intervenciones políticas de Estados Unidos en América Latina; Paisaje Simpoiético (2026), de la costarricense Mimian Hsu ( SatisFactory , Costa Rica), que explora la pertenencia y la experiencia diaspórica a través del deseo de integrarse en el bosque nuboso costarricense; y The Irazú Sweets Recipe, (Disarming) a Body with Sweetness (2025), de la salvadoreña Gabriela Novoa ( Matia Borgonovo , El Salvador), una pieza que recupera la memoria familiar para examinar los afectos y las estructuras patriarcales.

Completan el programa Life Is Sweeter than It Seems (2024), del artista hondureño Leonardo González ( LL proyectos , Honduras), sobre la explotación y la migración infantil centroamericana, y Danza de la lluvia con sol (Melancolía tropical) (2026), de la panameña Andrea Santos ( Arteconsult , Panamá), que indaga en lo que une al paisaje, la identidad y la memoria colectiva a partir de una expresión popular compartida en el Caribe y América Latina.

Programa público y publicaciones

Paraíso complementa las exposiciones con un programa público de conversaciones y actividades en vivo, con la participación de profesionales del arte y la cultura internacional.

Consulta el programa público completo .

La feria cuenta también con una sección dedicada a ediciones y publicaciones independientes, que agrupa propuestas editoriales vinculadas a la producción y circulación del arte.

Conoce la selección de ediciones limitadas y publicaciones .

Paraíso Latin American Art Fair

Ambika P3, 35 Marylebone Road, Londres NW1 5LS.

Del 15 al 18 de octubre de 2026.

Horario de apertura al público

Viernes 16 y sábado 17 de octubre: de 11:00 a 19:00 h.

Domingo 18 de octubre: de 11:00 a 18:00 h.

VIP: jueves 15 de octubre (solo por invitación).

content.article_text:
Linda Duncombe , a longtime banking executive who spent the last past years as an independent film producer, died on Sunday of complications from a stroke. She was 55.

An infectiously friendly face at industry events, Duncombe — who was diagnosed with Stage 2 lung cancer days before she died — served for five years as chief marketing officer at City National Bank. She helped direct more than $12 million in investments tied to organizations such as Habitat for Humanity, Broadway Cares, SAG-AFTRA and the Grammy Museum.

Related Stories

Jeremy Strong Texted Jessica Chastain After 'Other Mommy' Dominated Box Office Over 'Social Reckoning' Flop

BBC, ZDF Cold War Thriller ‘Honey’ Offers Sex, Lies – and Prosthetic Testicles: ‘There’s an Innate Comedy and Absurdity to Spying’

Duncombe’s last public appearance was at the Motion Picture & Television Fund’s “The Evening Before” the Primetime Emmy Awards on Sept. 13, where she reunited with friends and rubbed shoulders with some of Hollywood’s biggest stars.

Popular on Variety

Born on Feb. 10, 1971 in Australia, where she spent the early years of her life, Duncombe enrolled in Harvard Business School in 2008. She officially moved to the United States in 2015, first living in New York and then in an apartment near the beach in Santa Monica. She produced two movies: the family adventure “The Queen’s Jewels” and suspense thriller “Killing Time.” Both films are planning a global release in 2027, and Duncombe was intricately involved in all elements of production from financing to publicity.

“Linda was a source of light, always smiling, laughing, gossiping — which, she’d say to her friends, ‘is never gossip between us, love’ — and someone who adored Hollywood with all her heart,” says Variety’s co-president and co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh, a close friend. “Growing up as a young girl in Australia, she dreamed of finding her way in the film industry. In the last few years, she finally realized her calling as a producer, which made her beam even more. This is a devastating loss, and I will miss Linda so much.”

Duncombe began her decades-long banking career at Citibank in Australia in 2010 as marketing director of digital and customer experience and rose to managing director, head of growth and chief marketing officer. Five years later, she transferred to New York as a founding member of the company’s subsidiary, Citi Fintech.

She joined City National Bank in Los Angeles in early 2019, establishing business, sponsorship and community relations with organizations like SAG-AFTRA Foundation, the Recording Academy, the Motion Picture Television Fund and Tribeca Festival. During the pandemic, she led efforts at City National Bank to deliver more than $1.8 billion in Paycheck Protection Program loans to support the entertainment industry.

At City National Bank, she quickly became friends with Variety staffers while working to keep the magazine’s annual “Business of Broadway Breakfast” afloat during COVID. Over the years, the event has attracted theater mainstays from Lin-Manuel Miranda to Rachel Zegler.

“Linda was initially my client but quickly became my very good friend, always including me in her gatherings,” says Variety publisher and co-president Dea Lawrence. “A true warrior woman who understood the importance of shared experiences and letting go with that unforgettable, infectious laugh. She was fiercely loyal, endlessly generous, and embraced life with so much passion and heart. It is hard to fathom that her brilliant light has gone out.”

Duncombe’s friends remember her sunny spirit, boisterous laughter, unbridled optimism and passion for new experiences. She took pride in mentoring younger generations and was deeply loyal to those in her orbit. Duncombe’s inner circle included her producing partner and best friend Josh Friedman, who was always by her side at industry events.

“Losing Linda is going to change the lives of so many people,” says Friedman, whom Duncombe affectionately called her little brother. “She made life look really easy in managing many things but remaining the most humble, kind and generous person. The emojis next to her name in my phone were a princess, heart and unicorn. She was a unicorn in this life for a lot of people.”

Added Bob Beitcher, MPTF’s president and CEO, “Linda was a gift to everyone who knew her. She was vital, fun, whip-smart, caring and compassionate, and always, always there to lend a hand and lift you up. As a friend and advisor, she is irreplaceable, and her passing dims the light for me and for MPTF.”

Duncombe was recognized on Variety’s “Most Powerful Women in Hollywood” list and was honored by the Australian Governor General with the Order of Australia Medal. She sat on the boards of several groups including the SAG-AFTRA Foundation, Grammy Museum, Habitat for Humanity Greater L.A. and the Australian Wildlife Conservancy.

After leaving Australia, Duncombe was proud of the success she’d achieved in the decade in which she lived in the United States.

“As a 9-year-old, I told my parents I wanted to live in New York when I grew up. My parents did not hesitate in their support of a shy, young girl’s big dreams,” she told the magazine Beauty Is in 2025 . “We lived in government housing and while we had no money, our family and home was rich in love, support and laughter.”

As a child, she was inspired by the “Wonder Woman” television series starring Lynda Carter, and her parents taught her that treating people with kindness and respect would make her unstoppable. “Now I am a woman who has worked hard,” she said. “I try my very best to share my learnings, experiences, and networks to help people go after their dreams and live their best life.”

She is survived by her mother, Doreen Thompson, and nieces and nephews Shannen, Damien and Jarred.

content.article_text:
Book Review

The Trafficker Who Furnished the Museums of LA

A team of researchers excavates the story of Earl Stendahl, a mid-century gallerist who shamelessly stole ancient Mesoamerican objects and marketed them to the institutional art world.

In a 1940 photograph by Man Ray, Academy Award-winning actor Teresa Wright poses misty-eyed alongside an ancient Chacmool sculpture. The reclining figure, with its head contorted toward viewers, offered a refreshed vision of modernity to both Hollywood stars and a growing clientele of collectors and museums interested in pre-colonial art from ancient Mesoamerica. In 1947, for instance, the Minneapolis Institute of Art purchased a “King Chak Mool” for $10,000. That sculpture toured Europe as part of an exhibition from 1958 to 1960 and quickly became a cornerstone of the museum’s collection. Just a decade later, one specialist made a dreaded discovery: The sculpture was a forgery.

This story, and that of the gallerist at its center, is chronicled in Artifacts to Art: Collecting Ancient America in Midcentury L.A. (2026) by Andrew D. Turner, Mary E. Miller, and Khristaan D. Villela. The book elaborates on the various conditions that shifted the classification of “pre-Hispanic” artifacts from anthropological items of study to art objects that could be collected by museums and patrons alike. It also helped answer a question I’ve always had about Los Angeles museums as a curator myself: Why is so much cultural heritage of ancient Central and South America preserved in our city’s collections?

As Artifacts to Art discusses, the Stendahl Art Galleries were a key driver in the illegal looting, smuggling, and sale of these objects to its Los Angeles clientele. The Galleries’ archive is now housed at the Getty Research Institute (which published this book), allowing for a deep investigation into the shady dealings of an art dealer who had little regard for the cultural histories he exploited. Turner, Miller, and Villela present five years of groundbreaking research into that archive here. Over its non-chronological chapters, the book describes the various forces that collided to create a market for these objects, including revered international museums, Hollywood actors, and looters across Mexico.

content.article_text:
Because of Coraline , LAIKA’s first effort as a studio and still its best-known, there’s an expectation that each subsequent project will fit comfortably within the horror realm, each new release a rite of passage for thousands of kids previously unaware that movies could give them nightmares. This will inevitably be the same case with Wildwood , director Travis Knight’s lavish and ambitious adaptation of the 2011 YA novel by Decemberists lead singer Colin Meloy, not least because it cold-opens with a young boy committing suicide, ripping out his insides to reveal he was an automaton operated by cogs. The gothic imagery hardly subsides from there, with Knight soon recreating the haunting image from Hitchcock’s The Birds , a murder of crows swarming over a playground ready to feast on unsuspecting children.

Labelling a LAIKA production a straightforward riff on horror hasn’t been accurate since 2012’s Paranorman ––their weakest, most surface-level referential effort––with the studio’s work since then better appreciated as part of an ongoing attempt to revive other genres unfashionable with today’s kids. It’s won them as much acclaim as it has come at a cost; Missing Link , their 2019 globe-trotting adventure that’s partway between Jules Verne and The Lost City of Z , holds the title for most expensive stop-motion film of all-time, and made the smallest fraction of that cost back.

Wildwood might be an easier sell as a modern-day fairytale, but it doesn’t make any concessions to what children might want or expect from such a proposition—more Brothers Grimm by way of Tolkien than Disney. If it does have a contemporary parallel, it’s with the equally dark, unsanitized female empowerment tales of Hayao Miyazaki, where wonder and grimness co-exist as they did in the oldest bedtime stories. Characters are shaped forever by the darkness they encounter as much as they are thrilled by any fantastical, otherworldly creatures who cross their path, all of whom are crafted with an attention to detail unrivaled within their respective forms of animation.

After the prologue, we head to modern-day Portland, where Prue McKeel (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) has been tasked with babysitting her baby brother Mac, advised by her hippie parents (Jake Johnson and Maya Erskine) not to take him outside. It’s a rule she breaks often, but their carefree trip into the city that morning ends in disaster when crows swarm over her brother in the playground and whisk him off to the vast woods surrounding the city. Along with nerdy classmate Curtis (Jacob Tremblay), they venture into the unknown, even though they’ve long been warned that the overgrown forests are impossible to enter.

Mysteriously, a path opens for the pair, who are soon separated after encountering an anthropomorphic coyote army; Prue makes it to a nearby town, where she’s held captive as an outsider. Jacob is taken to meet the former governess Alexandra (Carey Mulligan) who, instead of treating him as a captive, sees him as a replacement for the long-dead son of whom she’s repeatedly tried to build a replica. Alexandra is holding baby Mac for sinister reasons just as tensions among the different clans in the woods have grown worse due to the actions of her army; saving her brother means having to save the realm from her.

There’s an eeriness to Wildwood that never becomes fully fleshed horror, toeing the line when it comes to the limits of darkness in a fairytale; it earns its PG-13 rating before we’re even a minute into the runtime, and that’s just Knight testing the waters of acceptability. It’s easy to write this off as the director and his screenwriter Chris Butler targeting a slightly older audience who are weaned on campfire ghost stories and on the cusp of seeing their first scary movie at a sleepover, but as with Miyazaki’s coming-of-age tales, I see this as the distinct work of creatives who trust their young viewers’ intelligence, knowing that they can handle something darker than what’s offered by rival animation studios. It’s only because it’s in stop-motion that this darkness is presented as novel.

Adaptations of Tolkien, C.S. Lewis, and other widely read fantasy authors from most people’s childhoods have been embraced by young viewers, after all, and in its character designs and staging of sweeping action sequences, Wildwood frequently invites the lofty comparisons to Peter Jackson’s original Lord of the Rings trilogy that it manages to live up to. Yes, it’s on a smaller scale because of the limits of a team of stop-motion animators, but that a battle scene can feel positively reminiscent of Jackson’s Helm’s Deep––even when it pauses to breathe amidst the chaos to show how the violence may scar its characters forever––is one of several technical achievements that don’t call themselves out as such. The soaring aerial sequences, gag-a-minute slapstick chase scenes, and transformation of the sets as reeds quickly grow on every surface represent some of the most ambitious moments the studio has ever put to life. In the moment, it’s easy to look past how the enormous scale of this ambition is paying off; the movie satisfies the heart so much that the head stops seeking to work out how they did it.

The majority of LAIKA efforts close with a mid-credits, behind-the-scenes look at the painstaking work that went into creating their character models and expansive sets. As much as they want you to be transported into their lovingly crafted worlds, they’re magicians who have no issues revealing their secrets, and part of the charm of Wildwood is seeing just how the sausage gets made before heading to the exit. We’re in a period where studio animation is becoming increasingly risk-averse, and there’s something oddly moving about seeing a member of Knight’s team walk us through the process of designing characters.

The movie may not resonate with younger audiences or even attract many of them into the theater to begin with, but just like the famous line about how the few who first heard The Velvet Underground & Nico formed their own bands, it offers the hope that the kids who do see it will be inspired to make art of their own. For anybody older, it’s a reminder of the magic and terror of the classic fantasy stories we grew up with recaptured on a breathtaking scale. It’s among the best animated films in recent memory.

Wildwood premiered at the 2026 BFI London Film Festival and opens on October 23.

content.article_text:
Dora (2026) by July Jung Film Review

Women’s bodies, scars and sisterhood in the new film from the director of “Next Sohee”, with Kim Do-yeon and Ando Sakura

The much-loved Korean director July Jung , the mind behind “A Girl at My Door” (2014) and, more recently, “Next Sohee” (2022), returns to directing a female lead in “Dora”, which premiered at the Cannes Film Festival and arrives on home soil in the Gala section of the Busan International Film Festival.

Dora is screening at Busan International Film Festival

The film tells the story of Dora (Kim Do-yeon), a teenager whose distress and trauma manifest in a troublesome skin condition. Her skin seems to rot in the face of life’s stresses, and Dora becomes keenly aware that this outbreak is driven by an inner turmoil. Her mother and father, in the midst of a crisis, decide to retreat to a small house by the sea to bring some comfort to their marriage and to their daughter. The neighbors are old friends of the father’s, with two lively twins who immediately treat Dora as their big sister.

Dora exerts a magnetic pull on everyone who crosses her path, to the point that the positive energies of this extended family help her heal. The couple of friends in particular benefit: Yeon-su (Song Sae-byeok) takes up painting again and wants her as a model, while Mina (Sakura Ando) goes out of her way to make her feel less out of place, well aware of how hard it can be to fit in. Just when Dora seems to have finally found a balance, the crystal castle begins to crack, and those who had rejoiced in her presence no longer seem to consider her welcome.

July Jung has a wealth of experience in telling stories of women and complex female portraits, where shadows and light alternate. In her previous, acclaimed work, “Next Sohee” (2022), she portrayed adolescence as a gradual passage, giving voice to young people misunderstood by adults. Dora at first seems to show us a different world, one of affable, welcoming adults. But that welcome suddenly turns into selfishness. And not only that: truth and lies wear the same face and warp themselves to suit personal convenience.

The director’s intention is plain: not to offer a complete resolution to the crisis of the two gracious female figures she focuses on, namely Kim Do-yeon’s Dora on one side and Sakura Ando’s Mina on the other. Both are misfits, misunderstood victims of different forms of exile. Dora, masterfully drawn, is a teenager who has had to withdraw from the system, suspended as if she were a ghost; when she arrives at the summer house, she drags herself along, surviving, hidden and shy of the sun and the sea. Few words, eyes lowered; every inch of her exposed skin is experienced as a risk and a weakness.

Mina, Japanese by birth, has had to give up her profession and her life because of an illness that, like Dora, has left her scarred. In Korea, she withdraws into the greenery because nature soothes her pain. Outside her vegetable garden, she does not belong: not to the family, not to the place, and this sense of suspension binds her to the newly arrived girl. Ando gives us first a woman who shows her scar with resignation, marked by physical and mental alienation; and then, when she discovers she can reclaim the body she had forgotten, she does so with joy and avidity.

Yet society does not seem to grant full rehabilitation to those who have lost their beauty: they are “empty shells,” as her husband calls her, a stranger by now, with whom she is forced to live with. It is in sisterhood, then, that sincere comfort is found.

The husbands in the film, though perfectly integrated, are incapable of understanding, processing, accepting and fighting for their bonds. When a relationship ages, they look for something else. Dora watches in astonishment as they seek to renew themselves at the expense of those who stand beside them. Dora is accused of being the destructive, destabilising element, but hers is a revealing force. She unmasks the lie and bombards the foundations of falsehood. And yet it is almost painful to watch how she takes pity and feels responsible even in the face of abuse, making plain the psychological pressure she is under.

Cinematographer Irina Lubtchansky condenses the protagonist’s emotional life through sharp chiaroscuro that opens up to saturated colors as her slow, gradual healing progresses. The viewer feels the closure and introspection of the moments of crisis, and the openness and connection with the environment and the outside world when Dora lives more joyful moments. The editing too tends to disappear, making the passing of time felt less in step with the protagonist’s happiness, which thus becomes the spark of the whole work.

Alongside the main drama, July Jung sets small interludes of childlike tenderness, youthful jealousy and sunny summer liberation. The film thus approaches the darkest and hardest-to-process part without too much heaviness, leaving the audience the right breath to return to suffering over the wounds of young Dora’s emaciated body, covered in sores. The setting is also a fundamental component, underlining the division between these worlds that at first do not belong together, and then end up blending.

Dora’s family home is designer architecture, but cold and unwelcoming; Mina’s home, by contrast, is lively, lit by warm lights, colored by her husband’s paintings and by the lush vegetable garden that yields fruit despite the torrential rain. It goes without saying that the two women’s clothing becomes their human icon, and that young Dora’s transformation as she blossoms into adulthood corresponds to a shift in her wardrobe toward lightness and carefree ease. And so her skin, once concealed, becomes a new garment to wear and display with pride and pleasure.

Despite some narrative slowdowns that pull us away from a thrilling protagonist we never wish to leave, “Dora” manages to offer a stimulating dialogue between two complex femininities, thanks to truly successful casting choices. Kim Do-yeon and Sakura Ando are two opposite poles that attract at first and explode in collision: once we focus on the uniqueness of these two portraits, the partial fog lying at the edges of the story tends to lift.

content.article_text:
Pocket Review

A Little Fantasy Goes a Long Way

In this photography exhibition, works vacillate between intimacy and unknowability, like a fractured peep show.

Hyperallergic )

“Abandon the search for Truth; settle for a good fantasy.” These words, taken from Fran Lebowitz and written on the wall to warn all ye who enter Luhring Augustine’s Chelsea gallery, set up the premise for its current group show: settle for a good fantasy .

It’s an admittedly juicy quotation. So juicy, indeed, that the gallery has hung Shaun Pierson’s photograph of a very voluptuous strawberry — seriously, it’s like the Venus of Willendorf of strawberries — right next to it, as if to underscore the point: Photography is always chasing a fantasy.

The exhibition’s main room leans into this, showing portraiture's fragmentary, erotic side. Works by Pierson, David Seider, and Janice Guy vacillate between intimacy and unknowability, like a fractured peep show. Curved, freckled backs touch. Beautiful shards of women’s faces are pieced together, seemingly pulled from the dark. Guy’s grids of self-portraits from the 1970s are particularly arresting, and not just because she also happens to be beautiful.
content.excerpt_original: In this photography exhibition, works vacillate between intimacy and unknowability, like a fractured peep show.

content.article_text:
News

NYC to Provide Free Art Supplies to Grantees

Winners of the city's recently doubled grant for artists can also enjoy unlimited supplies from Materials for the Arts.

Hyperallergic )

Materials for the Arts (MFTA) is launching a new free shopping program for artists who receive city-funded grants on October 19, nearly three weeks after Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Department for Cultural Affairs (DCLA) announced that they are doubling grants for individual artists and small nonprofits in New York City.

The new MFTA program functions as a free supply base for the selected artists, who can now receive up to $10,000 in city-funded grants, which had remained at a $5,000 cap for the last 20 years. The organization will open its 35,000-square-foot warehouse to artist grantees on the second Monday of every month (apart from federal holidays) from 3 pm to 6 pm, offering materials such as leather spools originally used to make airplane seats, tomes dedicated to the visual arts, and dinosaur masks. The first iteration of the program will take place on Monday, October 19.

“By broadening our operations to offer shopping days directly targeting these art grantees, we can ensure that more artists, more changemakers, and more New Yorkers have access to our city program,” Tara Sansone, the executive director of MFTA, told Hyperallergi c.
content.excerpt_original: Winners of the city's recently doubled grant for artists can also enjoy unlimited supplies from Materials for the Arts.

content.article_text:
Book Review

Finding Vermeer in Unexpected Places

Artists, filmmakers, poets, and the art market itself still bear traces of the Dutch painter’s influence, writes historian Ruth Bernard Yeazell in “Vermeer’s Afterlives.”

As strange as it may sound, Johannes Vermeer’s fame is a relatively recent phenomenon. The Dutch painter known for his exquisite, enigmatic interior scenes fell into obscurity shortly after he died deeply in debt at only 43 years old in 1675. Vermeer was barely a footnote in the annals of art history until the mid-19th century, when the Parisian critic Théophile Thoré rediscovered his work. “Here’s someone we don’t know in France, and who very much deserves to be known!” the writer proclaimed in 1866.

Thoré was drawn to Vermeer for the same reason he still fascinates museumgoers today: His small selection of attributed paintings — some 35 to date — and still-hazy biography spark more questions than answers. But in the three and a half centuries since his death, Vermeer’s mysterious works have also inspired a wealth of visual art, cinema, poetry, and literature.

These artistic echoes are the focus of scholar Ruth Bernard Yeazell’s Vermeer’s Afterlives (2026), a richly illustrated exploration of the artist’s enduring and remarkably widespread impact through a careful survey of works made in his mythologized shadow. From Danish painter Vilhelm Hammershøi’s hushed canvases to experimental 20th-century film and sensual contemporary verse, Yeazell meticulously catalogs and analyzes the Delft painter’s iconography — especially his recurring solitary female figures gently illuminated by daylight filtered through nearby windows — and persistent commitment to open-ended interpretation over a singular narrative.
content.excerpt_original: Artists, filmmakers, poets, and the art market itself still bear traces of the Dutch painter’s influence, writes historian Ruth Bernard Yeazell in “Vermeer’s Afterlives.”

content.article_text:
Pocket Review

When the Accessibility Conveyor Belt Jams

A malfunction in Finnegan Shannon’s installation at Pioneer Works led to new insights.

There's no me without you at Pioneer Works (photo Bryan Martin/

Hyperallergic )

Finnegan Shannon’s There's no me without you at Pioneer Works considers the fragility of systems and the consequences of their breakdown for disabled bodies.

The installation is a 12-foot-long square conveyor belt — think conveyor-belt sushi — in a maroon-carpeted room that carries and displays objects for visitors to interact with, from plush chairs to open spaces for individuals who can’t access the seating. Masks, accessible text, hand sanitizer, DIY air purifiers, and descriptive audio are also available, defining Shannon’s vision for an equitable, gentle engagement with art.

Three artists will be presented during the show’s run. For the first month, Ariana Martinez places small objects in dishes atop the moving presentation for visitors to pick up and touch. These small, tactile, fidget-like objects range from ceramic strips to masses of rope, all of which delight.

Installation views of There's no me without you at Pioneer Works (photo Bryan Martin/ Hyperallergic )

Unfortunately, during my visit, the conveyor belt wasn't turned on, which undermined the apparatus's accessibility intent. Staff eventually came up to switch it on, but when the machine proved stuck, they left without resolving the issue. The inert belt became a frustrating metaphor for institutions and a larger social apathy toward accessibility needs.

Spurred by fellow visitors’ confusion, I gently rocked a jammed plate side to side to see if it would help, and the belt started moving. Although accidental, Shannon's intent crystallized. We are all interdependent. Creative solutions are inexorably linked to disability, making the subject ripe for artmaking. The installation’s deviation from what I expected, like disability itself, offered me a new perspective on the world — a reminder of our collective responsibility to those who live in it.

There’s no me without you continues at Pioneer Works (159 Pioneer Street, Red Hook, Brooklyn) through December 20. The exhibition was organized by Pioneer Works.
content.excerpt_original: A malfunction in Finnegan Shannon’s installation at Pioneer Works led to new insights.

content.article_text:
Community

A View From the Easel: Flor Khan

“Here, I am allowed to play, to not know the answers, to let the message evolve on its own timing.”

Welcome to the 358th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Flor Khan collapses time and tenderly revives the memories of her ancestors.

Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form ! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.

Flor Khan , Bronx, New York City

How long have you been working in this space?

I have been working out of this particular space since March; before then, I worked in a number of artist studios and my own apartment.

Describe an average day in your studio.

The average day at the studio starts around 4pm, following my daytime job. Typically, I work on two to three pieces at once: Something is usually developing color in my photo processing work station, another piece is drying on the work line, and the other piece is steeping in tannins. If I'm lucky, I get to work with my sewing machine when the fabrics have dried. Before beginning my work, I turn on my salt lamp and light a candle for the ancestors; I ask for their permission to bring their memories back to life. With each stitch, and each photo transfer, I am brought closer to their memory, whether that's working with Victorian-era postcards featuring my Indo-Caribbean aunties or tapping into the photo albums of my late father. For background music, NPR 's Tiny Desk plays whichever artist is being featured for the week.

How does the space affect your work?

My studio is a sacred space. It is a blessing to be surrounded by works in progress, keeping me in the flow: The pieces and I are in continuous conversation with one another. If the rain comes, I nest myself in the dim light of the candle and find myself in another world, one where the colors of grief are allowed to float around me, where catharsis is not shied away from, where I am allowed to be slow, intentional, soft with myself and the imperfections of the creation process. Here, I am allowed to play, to not know the answers, to let the message evolve on its own timing.

How do you interact with the environment outside your studio?

Being apart of the Kreate Hub community has been a beautiful experience. The Bronx community has been so welcoming. The hallways are covered in art from my neighboring studios and it inspires us all to be in conversation with one another. Down the hall you can find small business: studios for makeup design, costume, and film production. My studiomate and partner is a muralist and painter. We often find ourselves spending late nights creating, dreaming of world where we get to co-create workshops for our community. In fact, in the next coming weeks, we will be hosting a mashup of our artistries: a cyanotype-painting workshop on New York City landscapes.

What do you love about your studio?

I love the silence in the late night. Because I'm away from the main road, there are less ambulances whirring in the background; instead, I hear the train in the distance, I hear the raindrops, the candle flickering. When I am here, I am able to lose myself in the creation process because I am away from the distractions of home and house responsibilities. I love that I can leave my pieces unfinished, unbothered, no need to pick up the mess because the space allows for the process to bloom on its own time.

What do you wish were different?

If I could have more space for my tannins, this would be excellent! Right now, my water basin is down the hall and the slop sink is necessary for washing out my photo processors. Because I work primarily with photo processing liquids, running water near my workspace would be a dream! But, for now, I am grateful for my humble beginnings.

What is your favorite local museum?

El Museo del Barrio is one of my favorite museums uptown, one because it is accessible for the artist communities I live near and two because it centers on the contributions of Latin American and Caribbean culture and history. Their recent exhibition Sophie Rivera: Double Exposures spoke to the many layers of identity women hold in the art world. I was particularly blown away by her gelatin prints of children portraits shot in the 1980s, showcasing the class systems and lives lives in New York City streets. Being able to go to museums near me that represent my own culture is a powerful, affirming experience. As a Xicana-Latina, I felt seen in her art.

What is your favorite art material to work with?

I am deeply moved by photography and alternative photographic processes. Working with images allows me to revisit memories of family and loved ones who have passed; image-making also allows me to reinterpret the image itself: I overlay meaning by working with cartography, sewing news images atop, or mending parts that feel untrue or not whole. In the case of working with 19th-century postcard images, I disrupt the colonial gaze and bring historical context and agency back to the women that were often eroticized through the camera, staged in front of backdrops that removed them from their truer lived lives. Alternative photographic process reveal layers of colors and shadows that all exist with a single image, bringing truth to the saying "a picture is worth more than a thousand words"; the difference here is that I, as the artist, get to rewrite them.
content.excerpt_original: “Here, I am allowed to play, to not know the answers, to let the message evolve on its own timing.”

content.title_original: Christie’s to Sell Barbara Hepworth Sculpture Featured in Vogue Portrait by Lee Miller
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Christie’s modern British and Irish art evening sale, taking place in London on October 21, will feature a mid-career sculpture by Barbara Hepworth with an estimate of £5 million–£8 million ($6.6 million–$10.5 million).", "links": [{"text": "Barbara Hepworth", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/barbara-hepworth/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Hepworth, one of the most well-known British modernist sculptors, carved Sculpture with Colour (Eos) in 1946 from a single piece of Hopton Wood stone, a type of limestone. The approximately two-foot-tall egg-shaped sculpture sits on a short platform and has three hollowed-out areas that are painted pale gray, off-white, and deep blue, colors that reference “the depths of the ocean, the boundless sky and the infinite reaches of the cosmos,” according to a statement from Christie’s."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In addition to being an early work Hepworth’s to incorporate color, Sculpture with Colour (Eos) was also featured in a 1948 photograph taken by Lee Miller for the October 15, 1949, issue of American Vogue . Miller, who was a friend of Hepworth’s, visited the artist at her studio at Carbis Bay, on the coast of Cornwall, where she had moved with her family in 1939, before the start of World War II. content.article_text:
Christie’s modern British and Irish art evening sale, taking place in London on October 21, will feature a mid-career sculpture by Barbara Hepworth with an estimate of £5 million–£8 million ($6.6 million–$10.5 million).

Hepworth, one of the most well-known British modernist sculptors, carved Sculpture with Colour (Eos) in 1946 from a single piece of Hopton Wood stone, a type of limestone. The approximately two-foot-tall egg-shaped sculpture sits on a short platform and has three hollowed-out areas that are painted pale gray, off-white, and deep blue, colors that reference “the depths of the ocean, the boundless sky and the infinite reaches of the cosmos,” according to a statement from Christie’s.

In addition to being an early work Hepworth’s to incorporate color, Sculpture with Colour (Eos) was also featured in a 1948 photograph taken by Lee Miller for the October 15, 1949, issue of American Vogue . Miller, who was a friend of Hepworth’s, visited the artist at her studio at Carbis Bay, on the coast of Cornwall, where she had moved with her family in 1939, before the start of World War II. (Soon after the photo was taken, Hepworth moved to St. Ives; her home and studio there is now the site of the Barbara Hepworth Museum and Sculpture Garden.) The black-and-white photograph shows Hepworth seated with her arms and legs crossed, a tea set in the foreground and a cat curled up on a couch. Sculpture with Colour (Eos) is resting on a table to right.

The consignor of the sculpture purchased the piece at Christie’s in 2016 for $5.4 million (est. $1.2 million–$1.8 million) from the estate of American philanthropists David and Geraldine Pincus, who had themselves purchased it from Martha Jackson Gallery in 1962. (The Pincus estate also sold Orange, red, yellow , 1961, the second most expensive Mark Rothko painting to be sold at auction, for $86.9 million in 2012.)

Sculpture with Colour (Eos) has been at the heart of Hepworth’s story for 80 years, said Alice Murray, head of modern British and Irish art at Christie’s London, noting its inclusion in Hepworth’s first postwar solo gallery show in 1946 and “Hepworth in Colour,” which was on view at the Courtauld in London this summer.
