content.article_text:
As much as the word “fascism” has been bandied about for the past decade to describe all manner of ominous political and cultural sins, our era of perpetual crises has bred surprisingly few compelling cinematic examinations of authoritarianism, either as a historical or personal force. For every Zone of Interest there are a half-dozen Jojo Rabbit or Mickey 17 s, live-action cartoons that marry the iconography of totalitarianism with the most obvious tropes of contemporary political discourse to smugly pander to the audience’s presumably liberal leanings from the word go. Genuine visions of what it might feel like to actually live under a state of authoritarianism remain few and far between. Whether that be from a pervasive lack of ambition, some fear around genuinely challenging audiences, or the simple, lazy tendency to fit into easy, popular, effortless modes of resistance is not for me to say. Cinema is, however, weaker for it, often left feeling of its moment yet rarely capable of meeting its moment in the form of meaningful, impactful critique.

Emmanuel Marre’s A Man of His Time is, in this context, a worthwhile attempt at political analysis whose interest is not in appeasing us, but making us actively think through how we engage with our social environment. Based on the life of Marre’s own great-grandfather, it follows an exceptionally unexceptional bureaucrat in the Vichy regime, Henri Marre (Swann Arlaud), as he weasels his way into a position of minor importance. The film is less interested in any sort of dramatic arc around Henri’s rise and fall than capturing his banal existence as just one more gear in that great tapestry of evil called Nazism. While early scenes find him trying to convince ministers that he’s a visionary through his treatise on the importance of Vichy Marshal Philippe Pétain, Henri is really nothing more than a stooge, adept at sanding away all moral compromises while clinging to a semblance of integrity. In Henri’s most flagrantly repellent moment, he penalizes a subservient for buying toiletries for a train full of Jews getting sent to the camps. His icy stare and serpentine smile are the benevolent mannerisms of any halfway-decent middle-manager, making clear that he doesn’t disagree with the gesture, that he sympathizes with Jews and does not want to punish his colleague, but it’s just the way things are. The system must push forward; there is nothing one can do to stop or change it.

Emmanuel Marre shoots all of this with a constantly roving, documentary-like handheld camera as if history were actually proceeding in front of us. In A Man of His Time ‘s opening moments, we’re immediately thrust into a party where Henri is nothing more than an unimportant background player amidst a sea of socialites. The camera pans around the group, catching snippets of one conversation after another with no clear focus besides a general sense of ambience. Henri is revealed to us in bits, as if he were some pesky, persistent extra who can’t stop unknowingly flopping into the foreground. He hovers over people’s shoulders, lingering as they pontificate about the future of the country, but goes largely unnoticed, seemingly unimportant. Sometimes upon trying to involve himself, he gets dressed down for voicing opinions that are too trite and sycophantic. After the party, it takes a good stretch before any major narrative events occur; the film follows Henri as he tries getting a job, but seemingly less from a sense of dramatic expectation than simple curiosity. As he wanders the city, lazes about in bed, and tries pushing his book on whoever might give him an audience, the questions for us, as viewers, are over who he is, what made him this way, and what motivates him.

A Man of His Time ‘s documentary-like aesthetic offers a sense of both immediacy and distance, reminiscent of Peter Watkins’ experiments with docu-fiction simulations. It carries a sharp semblance of realism while simultaneously reminding us of the levels of artifice behind such a project. The latter is further underscored by the director’s jarring use of ’80s synthpop at key points—during a dance, during a montage of the character’s career moving along—which adds another layer of temporal juxtaposition into the aesthetic, placing Henri’s life against not just the present, but the recent past as well. Like the film’s title, which both places Henri as a historical subject and asks us to consider what it means to belong to a time and place, it’s one more fascinating wrinkle in the subtle probing of how we might find a sense of the present in the past.

These small musical moments also puncture A Man of His Time ‘s regular rhythm, which flows at a considerably even pace—the banality of evil may be an invitation to monotony as well. This, if anything, is Marre’s main weakness. There’s little variation in tone or rhythm across a nearly three-hour runtime, and initial concepts made in the opening acts rarely get deeper or more nuanced. While this flatness might work well as a synecdoche for the experience of fascism as a numbing, petty, wholly ordinary experience, it also feels limited both politically and dramatically. It’s great at illustrating a feeling and state of being, less adept at offering much to critically consider besides the now-somewhat-cliché didea of the banality of evil. Like Henri, A Man of His Time does its job well enough, but fails to make a lasting impression before simply disappearing into the maw of historical memory.

A Man of His Time screened at the 64th New York Film Festival and will be released by 1-2 Special.

content.article_text:
Nobody makes clumsier social allegories than Guy Nattiv. His first American effort, the 2018 short Skin , followed a violent white supremacist who was kidnapped, drugged, and held hostage while his entire skin was tattooed jet-black as revenge for a hate crime; it was the most-embarrassing Oscar winner in a year when Green Book and Bohemian Rhapsody dominated the ceremony. That is arguably more tasteful than how he frames the true story at the heart of his most personal effort to date, The Liberation . Inspired by his grandmother’s indoctrination into a cult in the early 1980s, Nattiv keeps attempting to draw heavy-handed parallels between her youth in a concentration camp and recruitment into an organization that asked her to shun family, healthcare, and any other unwelcome intrusions from the outside world.

Rita Cooper’s (Carrie Coon) time being brainwashed by younger cult leader Ricki King (Lily James) is harrowing on its own, but looks deeply insignificant when framed as a continuation of her trauma as a Holocaust survivor. The Liberation trivializes some of the gravest crimes against humanity for how it frames the all-female cult’s secluded Harmonia commune, lingering on the fences that separate its crimes from the outside world and introducing its members doing unpaid manual labor in near-matching outfits. If such visual parallels weren’t clear enough, Rita’s youngest daughter Ella (Bella Ramsey) stresses that her distant mom looks like “she’s just got out of the camps.” The context of Rita’s childhood is important in establishing why she’d be coerced by a group leader adamant she can rid her of the horrors she’s carried her entire life, but that unimaginably horrifying past is invoked so clumsily it becomes distasteful.

These are flaws with Nativ and Noa Berman-Herzberg’s screenplay, not Coon’s characteristically terrific performance. Told across two separate storylines––in 1982, when the depressed office drone Rita first meets Ricki, and 1984, when Ella and her older daughter Jo (Odessa Young) track down the cult’s new commune––the actress effectively articulates how unprocessed emotions could lead her into a cult’s warm embrace, and why she would be so reluctant to any calls to deprogram once caught in its web. Her ease in such a demanding role is likely because we saw her tackle a more challenging variant on this grief-avoidance storyline during three seasons of The Leftovers , where each surreal detour was a result of trying to regain some sense of order after losing her family. The Liberation , where it’s much easier to get an emotional handle on this material, is less demanding by default. She makes the relationship between her past and present seem messier, more human than the neatly drawn continuation of past trauma the screenplay suggests. It’s based on true horrors, but comes across like a too-polished Martha Marcy May Marlene .

The Liberation is most effective in its 1984 stretches––although the absence of a delightfully crotchety Tracy Letts, stunt cast as Coon’s husband in the 1982 sequences, is felt––as the younger daughter tries saving her mother while the older becomes hypnotized by Ricki’s way of life. It increasingly resembles a thriller about walls closing in on the family, especially when Ella realizes how disastrous the anti-healthcare policy could be if her diabetic sister is left to fend for herself, and Ramsey has one of her best theatrical showcases as the emotional center of this stretch.

In fact, the only weak link of this ensemble is James as the cult leader; she fails to convince as an emotionally manipulative figure who could bring women her senior under her spell. The brief suggestion that it’s because she awakens suppressed sapphic desires is more tangible, though the screenplay discards that idea almost as soon as it’s introduced. James is a particularly strange casting decision considering she replaced Vicky Krieps, whose offbeat energy can have an undercurrent of menace if applied correctly. It’s admirable that James wanted to be cast against type so boldly, but she doesn’t have the built-in intensity required to make me suspend disbelief that she could manipulate her way under someone’s skin. Through her leadership, it becomes a cult of no personality.

The Liberation is Nattiv’s strongest effort to date, but that’s not saying much, and it’s thanks entirely to an almost uniformly excellent ensemble elevating his material. He remains as clumsy as ever in transforming his stories into incisive social commentary.

The Liberation screened at the BFI London Film Festival and opens on January 8, 2027.

If you were asked to identify Johannes Vermeer , you might answer that he is one of the world’s most famous Old Masters, that his Girl with the Pearl Earring (ca. 1665) is perhaps the pinnacle of the Dutch Golden Age, or that he was one of the Netherlands’s greatest-ever artists.

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

But if you were to ask the same question to someone in 1800, the answer would likely be “who?”

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

While his mammoth reputation today would suggest otherwise, for the 200 years following his death, Vermeer was largely forgotten. His unlikely return to the spotlight was thanks to a single French art critic. But why did he disappear?

When Vermeer died aged just 43 in 1675, he was in debt and had mostly fallen into obscurity outside of his hometown of Delft in the Dutch Republic. Only 34 paintings are firmly accepted to have been painted by Vermeer, as he worked slowly and fastidiously. He didn’t work in a large studio, leaving no pupils behind who were dedicated to the continuation of his style after his death. He rarely travelled, and so had not built a reputation in major cities. His widow was forced to sell most of his works to pay off their debts, spreading his work across the country. All of these factors stunted the development of Vermeer’s legacy.

By the mid-19th century, Vermeer was of such little repute that works by him were sometimes forged with a signature by Pieter de Hooch —an artist whose name carried significantly more weight at the time—to increase their prices. So how did he re-enter the spotlight?

Johannes Vermeer, View of Delft (ca. 1660–61). Photo: Buyenlarge/Getty Images.

Etienne-Joseph-Théophile Thoré was a French art critic and collector living in exile across Western Europe from 1849–1859 due to his support of French Revolutionary radicals. During that time, he wrote under the pseudonym W. Bürger . He had first seen Vermeer’s work, View of Delft (ca. 1660–61) in 1842 and was bowled over, but found locating more work by Vermeer so impossible that he referred to the artist as his “sphinx,” the riddle-providing creature of Greek mythology. As he travelled through Europe he began to collect paintings he believed could have been by the enigmatic artist.

In 1866, an exhibition of Old Master paintings was held at the Palais des Champs-Élysées and Thoré-Bürger contributed six Vermeer works to the show. Five additional paintings attributed to Vermeer were also displayed, although several were later reattributed to Vermeer’s contemporaries. Nonetheless, thanks to the exhibition and two articles Thoré-Bürger published about the artist, in addition to a catalogue of his works, Vermeer was back in the art world.

Johannes Vermeer, Girl with a Pearl Earring (ca. 1665). Photo: Sepia Times/ Universal Images Group via Getty Images.

The market took its time to catch up with Vermeer’s mounting legacy, however, and when Girl with a Pearl Earring came to auction in 1881 it sold for just two guilders and 30 cents—the equivalent of $35 . Today, estimates for the painting’s value reach $600 million.

After his death, a number of Thoré-Bürger’s Vermeer paintings were sold. Three of them are now held in public collections: A Young Woman Standing at a Virginal (ca. 1670–72) and A Young Woman Seated at the Virginal (ca. 1670–72) are at London’s National Gallery ; and Young Woman with a Pearl Necklace (ca. 1664) is held at Berlin’s Gemäldegalerie . Meanwhile, The Concert (1664), one of 13 works stolen from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in 1990, is considered the most valuable missing piece of art in the world, valued at $200 million.

Another painting— A Young Woman Seated at the Virginals , long in a private Belgian collection—resurfaced at Sotheby’s London in 2004, selling for $30.1 million to casino magnate Steve Wynn . It was the first Vermeer to appear at public auction in over 80 years and remains his auction record.

Despite there being fewer than 40 known paintings attributed to him, thanks to Thoré-Bürger’s dogged pursuit of his sphinx, Vermeer isn’t going anywhere.

Sotheby’s Institute has been at the forefront of educating arts professionals for fifty years. The Institute now has more than 8,000 alumni around the globe who hold top positions in all facets of the international art world. To learn more about our programs in London, New York, and Online, visit www.sothebysinstitute.com .

Text by Verity Babbs

content.article_text:
Editor’s Note: This story is part of Newsmakers , a new ARTnews series where we interview the movers and shakers who are making change in the art world.

In the last decade, the UK has been hit with Brexit and its aftermath, a global pandemic, and seven new prime ministers, but the country has retained its number two ranking in terms of global trade by value behind the US, according to the 2026 Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report . When Frieze London and Frieze Masters take over the grounds of Regent’s Park starting on Wednesday, spirits could remain high; the positive mindset may also be found at fairs like Minor Attractions and the London Invitational, which will also take place during Frieze Week.

As in the past, there remains a wrinkle: Art Basel Paris is taking place next week, and many are skipping London for that fair. However, this edition of Frieze London is bigger than the last’s years, with 176 galleries from 43 countries. In 2025, there were 160 galleries operating from 44 countries.

Kristell Chadé, Frieze’s executive director of fairs, has been with the organization for 15 years and now oversees eight fairs across the Frieze portfolio. “Global does not by any means mean uniform and we don’t export a fixed concept to the other fairs. Each fair has its own identity and as we become more global, we are more interconnected, which is a real strength for us,” she said. This year’s fair has an increased presence from South Asia; Frieze London has its first Sri Lankan participant in Saskia Fernando, for one. There’s also going to be a notable South Asian presence at Frieze Abu Dhabi next month, too.

ARTnews spoke with Chadé about London’s position in the art market, competing with Art Basel Paris, the health of the fair, and how it’s navigating Abu Dhabi amid political turmoil.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and concision.

ARTnews: What is the big theme at this year’s Frieze London and Masters?

Kristell Chadé: Frieze London and Frieze Masters are our most global fairs across the board, and that’s something we’ve definitely continued year on year. The thread between the two fairs is a sense of discovery. History is being told, reexamined, expanded, and rewritten. This year, as with previous editions, there’s experimentation and ambition, putting emerging artists in conversation with established practices, and that’s always been a fundamental element of the fair. Frieze’s broader role is supporting artists through their careers, and what we did with the 2024 redesign of the fair was push initiatives around putting young voices at the forefront and make sure that all segments of the market are represented

With Frieze Masters, the focus is very different: It is rooted in scholarship and expertise. But what makes it so unique is that it doesn’t present art history as a single and linear story. The idea is really to open new connections and narratives between periods, cultures and geographies.

Frieze London prides itself on its global energy. What geographic areas are the focus this year?

We’re very pleased to see year-on-year applications from new geographies, and that’s really something we’re trying to continue to promote year after year. Frankly, for us, it’s a real indicator of success: The breadth of geographies and perspectives that you can encounter at the fair is something that we closely track and that we continue to work to expand.

The main trend this year across both fairs is an increased presence from South Asia, which is really exciting for us, especially considering our presence in the region for the last five years. Having a foot in South Asia has really allowed us to strengthen those connections. We have our very first gallery participating from Sri Lanka this year. We’re seeing a strong contingent from Brazil, which has stemmed from past curated initiatives such as the Breeze Curator Travel Grant, an initiative with the Instituto Guimarães Rosa and the Embassy of Brazil in London. The grant offers five Brazil-based curators the opportunity to participate in the fair. Another region that remains strong is South Korea, as well as the Gulf and North Africa. From the numbers we’re looking at and from the trends we’ve seen so far, we are excited to welcome more collectors from India, Pakistan, Singapore, Indonesia, Turkey, and Canada. We’re also expecting an increased number of American collectors to visit the fair this year.

It goes without saying that London is an incredible global city. We know that it remains one of the world’s most important cultural centers—it’s the second largest art market globally, and it has real appeal in that sense for galleries and collectors. London allows creative talent to thrive. We have highly regarded art schools, world-class museums, and a thriving gallery scene, probably more than most cities can claim.

London is being called the city where artists work and live taking over from Berlin. What still connects artists to this city? And what is Frieze as an organization doing to keep artists, international dealers, and collectors coming back?

We are a commercial platform, there’s no denying that and ultimately, we want galleries to be able to make sales at the fair, that’s a big part of why they participate. Our responsibility goes way beyond just the commercial aspect of the fair. Frieze London and Frieze Masters have acquisition funds that support museums purchasing works from the fair, from the Tate Fund to the new Dasha Shenkman Focus Fund.

We also have great opportunities for major commissions and exhibitions for artists who are showing at the fair such as the Frieze Artist Award and the Camden Art Centre Emerging Artist Award, those are incredible opportunities for artists and it’s a very pivotal moment in their careers. At the same time, we collaborate with a number of organizations and embassies that allow travel from different countries to the fair for curators that are based in their countries. We’ve worked with Brazil and Italy. Frieze’s mission is to turn visibility at the fair, which is something very easy to experience, into long-term support. The idea is to have a long-term legacy for the art world and the art community.

Even though people say London has lost to Paris, it’s still a city that’s dominated by all types of art fairs, from the London Invitational and Minor Attractions to Frieze. What’s your feeling about London’s art scene? Has it really lost to Paris?

The autumn season clearly revolves around two well-established centers of gravity, London and Paris. But I do think they’re different and complementary offers. Galleries and collectors choose to do both, and there’s a clear rationale for them to do so. Our best argument in favor of London is that the city has so much to offer and London remains unmatched in the richness and diversity of its ecosystem. Frieze is about discovery and London is that place for it with new artists, studios, gallery openings, and new nonprofit or artist-run spaces opening.

When it comes to business, what is the health of Frieze London and Masters right now? And are you making any adjustments?

Both Frieze London and Frieze Masters galleries are full with really strong and diverse galleries, that speaks for itself. For the actual numbers, we do have slightly higher numbers of galleries and countries this year, which is always an interesting data point. However, beyond just the numbers, what’s helpful for us is to look more specifically at the quality of the content and breadth of what’s being represented at the fair.

To your question around adjustments, we’re not a fixed model and we’re conscious of our responsibilities—we talk to galleries all the time, also collectors, advisers, museums and those conversations really inform our decisions. We know it’s a demanding time for galleries who are under a lot of pressure. We know costs have gone up across the board and that galleries, especially mid-sized and younger ones, have to make decisions and are thinking very carefully about where they show, why, and what. And I think that’s actually healthy. We don’t want to have a fixed model when the world around us is evolving so quickly. We represent all segments of the market, from international blue-chip to established mid-market galleries to younger, more emerging galleries. They’re all equally important constituents for us to consider.

What are the challenges that Frieze as an organization is facing right now?

The pressure that galleries are under and how it forces us to think on our feet probably is the biggest challenge that we’re facing right now. Over the last few years, we have shown how we’ve been able to make changes and respond to those shifting requirements. If you think about gallery pricing, we always aim to keep annual increases minimal, if not keep the prices flat year-on-year where possible because we are conscious of the financial impact on our participating galleries. In 2024, we introduced a sliding-scale pricing model to help galleries make the move from Focus into the main section of the fair—it’s something that’s very dear to our heart in terms of supporting that next generation of galleries. We also have a number of curated sections that have lower entry points and what we’re trying to do is have different ways for galleries to participate, depending on where they are in their careers and what their priorities are at certain point in time, which artists they’re working with, and what part of their program they’re keen to show at the fair.

The fair’s first curated thread is devoted to a hot topic—queer visual history. How did you decide on “Queering Modernism” during such a shaky political climate?

It shows that Frieze acts as a platform for what is happening in the world and gives opportunities to encounter themes and ideas that are sometimes radical and sometimes new to provoke reactions and discourse. For us to be part of that discourse and conversation is ultimately what we thrive to do. The section is an example of how closely we work with curators and we find our legitimacy in our collaborators. We shine a spotlight on curators, artists, and galleries.

Frieze started in 2003 and has grown to include eight art fairs. How has this growth been possible? How are you partnering up with other countries, but still having a point of difference?

When I started at Frieze, we only had one fair. The growth over a decade has never been about adding points on a map. We wanted to see what Frieze could bring to each city’s existing ecosystem or a gap in the market. London is all about that trailblazing energy, whereas New York is a snapshot of what’s being made today: It’s the epicenter of the global art market. In LA, there’s a strong civic engagement that runs through everything we do from gallery presentations to artist projects. Seoul is the balance between tradition and cutting-edge practices, and Chicago is rooted in the midwestern community. When Abu Dhabi happens next month, it really takes its roots in the growing ambition of the cultural offer that the Emirate has been building. For us, global does not by any means mean uniform, and we don’t export a fixed concept.

You’ve been at Frieze for almost 15 years. How has your role changed, but also the business of running an art fair?

I came to the role from the gallery perspective. I was initially working very closely with all the galleries that participated in the fair, and that’s been quite instrumental for the growth of the business and how we’ve strategically expanded. We feel very strongly that what we do is for galleries—they remain our core constituents. A part of my role is to try and make sure that the Frieze voice is maintained and carried through all that we do.

As Frieze Abu Dhabi gets ready for its opening in November, it’s been an unsettling time for the Middle East. How are you navigating that?

We’re approaching the situation with open communication with all our galleries and collectors, both in the region and around the world, because it is another international fair. There’s a strong appetite for the upcoming fair and it’s an important milestone for us and the region. We’re cognizant of the context, and we’re in close contact with our local partners to ensure that everything runs very smoothly. Frieze Abu Dhabi follows the same logic as every other fair that we’ve started. It is a combination of a very specific cultural moment for that city as well as an opportunity for galleries. Abu Dhabi as a city offers an existing infrastructure and credibility—it has built a very ambitious ecosystem on Saadiyat Island, where the fair will take place, and it includes world class museums such as Louvre Abu Dhabi, the Zayed National Museum, the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi opening in December.

The fair has existed for 17 years, but with our takeover, we’re bringing the Frieze expertise and scaling it internationally by building on solid foundations in the region, which already has an engaged community. Abu Dhabi is rapidly growing with artists, galleries and collectors—the ingredients are all there.

Have any galleries dropped out of the fair because of what’s happening politically?

We have had transparent conversations with everyone involved. With every fair, there’s a level of flexibility with the gallery list. We have a full fair; everyone who’s participating is bringing very high-quality work, and part of that is shaped by the fact that we’re always working with talented curators and partners. We will have our usual Focus section for younger galleries and Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi is curated by Marika Sardar with the idea of exploring the history of cultural exchanges across the Indian Ocean. Global Futures, curated by Tarini Malik, will focus on cultural histories from the region.

It’s been 10 years since Brexit was announced. How has this affected Frieze London and Masters?

The facts speak for themselves. The UK remains the second-largest art market globally, after the US, where we’re also heavily present. By nature, we operate across different continents and cities, meaning that we have to constantly adjust to the changing landscapes of different regions. London is where it all started, and there’s such a good understanding of the opportunities that are possible here. We’ve been able to capitalize on the rich ecosystem that supports the fair.
content.excerpt_original: ARTnews spoke with Chadé about London’s position in the art market, competing with Art Basel Paris, the health of the fair, and how it’s navigating Abu Dhabi amid political turmoil.

content.article_text:
Lehmann Maupin and Gallery Wendi Norris will collaborate on a two-part exhibition pairing the work of Surrealist artist Leonora Carrington and artist and poet Cecilia Vicuña for the first time.

The first part of the exhibition, titled “Leonora Carrington & Cecilia Vicuña,” will open at Lehmann Maupin in New York on November 19, while the second part will open at Gallery Wendi Norris in San Francisco in January. The two parts have distinct checklists, to accommodate for the different scale of each location, though the parts share some overlap.

Dealer Wendi Norris proposed the show to Rachel Lehmann, one of Lehmann Maupin’s cofounders, a few years ago. Lehmann was reminded of the conversation after visiting Vicuña’s solo show at the Irish Museum of Modern Art (IMMA) last November. (That exhibition was co-organized with Whitechapel Gallery in London, where a version of it opened last week.)

“Things sometimes take time until they sit in the right place,” said Lehmann, who reached out to Norris to see if she would still like to work on the exhibition. “One of the things we do is try to position our artists in different ways, and [it] became suddenly so obvious to me that I had missed out actually on something with Wendi.”

Norris began representing Carrington in 2004, seven years before the artist’s death in 2011 at 94. Over the years, she has placed Carrington’s work in intergenerational group exhibitions and staged reenactments of her plays, but this is Norris’s first show featuring both the Surrealist’s art and the work of a living contemporary artist.

“I love putting Leonora Carrington’s work in new context,” Norris told ARTnews . “I’m constantly trying to imagine how she would respond to things that we do, like this exhibition. One thing I feel I can say very certainly is that she would be overwhelmingly excited about an exhibition like this.”

The connection between Vicuña and Carrington extends back much further. In 1969, Vicuña, then in her early 20s, met Carrington in Mexico City while she was en route back to Chile after a trip to New York. In New York, Vicuña had “a vision [of] the painting that I needed to do,” she recalled. During that fateful meeting, which was explored in the IMMA exhibition, Carrington gave Vicuña advice that helped the young artist “transfer” what she saw to canvas, for a process she would call Calcomanías. “Carrington enables this transfer from the poetry of the very unusual or uncategorized forms into something which was very tangible, like a painting,” Lehmann said.

Norris added, “The exhibition, I think, will enable viewers to delve deeper into Carrington’s iconography and language, and the way it feels to read it, alongside Cecilia’s. I, for one, am excited to see what it will uncover. I don’t want to predict it because I’m excited about what I’m going to discover myself.”

The exhibition will feature new works by Vicuña alongside important historical ones by Carrington. In selecting which pieces to feature, the two galleries were guided by “the relationship that both artists had,” Lehmann said. “What has struck me most in speaking to Cecilia over the years was the influence that Carrington brought to her practice.”

One of Vicuña’s new paintings is Polvo del Sahara/ Saharan Desert Dust (2026), an underwater scene showing the light reflecting into the depths of the ocean, where a stone staircase leads to somewhere beyond the horizon. Lehmann hopes the exhibition will shed light not only on how Carrington’s influence will help us “to understand where Cecilia’s paintings are coming from,” but also on how “Cecilia continues Carrington’s legacy.”

Norris described the building of the checklists for each show as “an iterative process” that involved sharing images of potential works and their contexts over several months. “We were trying to think of Leonora’s love of the environment, her sense of humor, and her hybrid creatures and how that might speak to some of the similarities we see in Cecilia’s work,” Norris said, noting that after each proposal, she would ask: “How does that land with you and your audience?”

Norris has also thought about which of Carrington’s works to show in which venue, including showing two works that were included in her 1990 show at the Brewster Gallery and have not been shown in New York since. One is Eye Witness (1987), a wintry landscape of two figures who seem to look away from an apparition of sorts; a skyscraper in the distance bears a resemblance to the Empire State Building.

The two artists’ work has been featured in one recent exhibition, the 2022 Venice Biennale, whose title of “The Milk of Dreams” came from one of Carrington’s books. Vicuña was awarded the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement ahead of the Biennale’s opening. However, the two artists were featured in separate sections of the Biennale, so they were not positioned together, as they will be in this show.

Since the 2022 Biennale, Carrington’s work has also been seeing a revival lately, as it has been the subject of two traveling surveys, one that opened at the Palazzo Reale di Milano in 2025 and another that is currently on view at the Faro Santander in Spain. Beyond Carrington and Vicuña’s stylistic affinities, Lehmann and Norris pointed out how the reception of the artists’ work has changed over the decades and that both have only been canonized relatively recently.

“This has been a long time coming for artists like Leonora and Cecilia,” Norris said. “I think Leonora probably knew it was coming but was nonplussed about it. She knew she was planting seeds, and they were going to bear fruit one day.”

content.article_text:
When Frieze Week arrives in London, there is always one exhibition that you’d be embarrassed to admit you missed. This year, that honor goes to Gagosian for its immaculately produced ode to René Magritte and his sprawling influence. The smash-hit show has received some 10,000 visitors since opening September 24, with lines often stretching around the block.

René Magritte, The Empire of Light (1961). Photo: Prudence Cuming Associates Ltd, Heidi Horten Collection, © 2026 ADAGP, Paris and DACS, London.

Featuring a whopping 120 works by the Surrealist master and 45 of contemporary art’s biggest names—including Jeff Koons , Glenn Ligon , Jordan Wolfson , and Issy Wood —” This Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte ,” through December 12, was always going to be big deal. Less predictable is how the show captures a prevailing mood. It stuck in my head, its themes and motifs reverberating throughout a recent gallery hop in Mayfair and East London. Again and again, I was reminded of what seems to be the Gagosian show’s central thesis: that a once-novel strain of Surrealism is now the dominant artistic lens on our world.

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

Here are just a few of the surprising parallels I encountered.

Impossibility

Nicole Eisenman, The Waiter (2026). Image: Katie Morrison, © Nicole Eisenman, courtesy the artist and Sadie Coles HQ, London.

Just a few streets from Gagosian, an exhibition of 10 new works by Nicole Eisenman at Sadie Coles (through November 21) offered the same incongruity that characterizes many Magritte masterpieces. The Waiter (2026) is an epic, 11-by-21-foot spectacle in which high-definition planets and swirling galaxies float above the lichen-covered slabs of Stonehenge . The kicker is the lone figure of a waiter, his shirt collar open and bowtie limp as though at the end of his shift. What is he doing there? The man gazes up, as confused by the cosmos as we are by his impossibly mundane presence within it.

From left to right: René Magritte, Pictorial Content (1947). Photo: Margaret Carrigan. Nicole Eisenman, Parking Lot of Violent Forces and Depressive Positions (2026). Image: Katie Morrison, © Nicole Eisenman, courtesy the Artist and Sadie Coles HQ, London..

The empty, flat expanse of Magritte paintings like The Flowers of the Journey (1926) and The Leader of the Band (1955) takes on new meaning in Eisenman’s Parking Lot of Violent Forces and Depressive Positions (2026). The effect is ominous, yes, but also absurd, infusing irony into the Philip Guston -style satire, in which ICE agents pile into a clown car to patrol the desolate, gray surrounds of a strip mall. A monstrous, dripping figure, apparently composed of exhaust fumes, brings to mind the same oozing forms found in Magritte’s Pictorial Content (1947), one of the cruder images he made during his short-lived vache period.

Ambiguity

From left to right: René Magritte, The Commonplace (1964) Image: © 2026 ADAGP, Paris and DACS, London. Louis Fratino, Summer in the city (2026). Image: Kerry McFate, © Louis Fratino, courtesy David Zwirner.

Distorted spatial logic gives a claustrophobic feel to the canvases of Louis Fratino , who has prepared 12 new paintings for “ Prose ” at David Zwirner , through October 31. Summer in the City (2026) uses an unusual vantage point to divide the picture plane, layering the disparate lives of urban strangers and leaving its central figure as dislocated as the one in Magritte’s The Commonplace (1964).

From left to right: Louis Fratino, The green bath (2026). Photo: Kerry McFate, © Louis Fratino, courtesy David Zwirner. Victor Man, Titiriteros (2023). Image: def image, © Victor Man, courtesy Gagosian.

Fratino’s running interest in everyday domesticity turns a little sickly in The green bath (2026), where two languid nudes sit entwined. It is impossible not to think of the similarly emerald-tinged palette preferred by Salman Toor , who is having his solo European museum debut at the Courtauld , until January 10. His paintings seduce us into a dreamy otherworld, filled with queer intimacies that have too often been pushed into the shadows. A more sinister comparison is Titiriteros (2023) by the ever-mysterious Victor Man , included in the Gagosian survey. Glowing lime green and with all the moody atmosphere of an El Greco , it closes in on three women burning a piece of paper that bears the artist’s initials. As in Fratino’s painting, expressionless faces and averted eyes leave the viewer guessing as to the composition’s true meaning.

Reinvention

From left to right: René Magritte, The Triumphant March (1948). Image: © 2026 ADAGP, Paris and DACS, London, courtesy Brachot Gallery. M: Alex Da Corte, Slow Graffiti (2017). Image: Joseph Hu, © Alex Da Corte, courtesy the Artist and Sadie Coles HQ, London. R: Installation view of Adam Lewis Jacob’s “Short Vamps for Long Wear” at Neven, 2026. Image: Dominique Croshaw, courtesy of the artist and Neven, London.

Vast, central podiums filling the main rooms of the Gagosian show are not to be overlooked. Many of the smaller objects assembled call for close examination, as is the case with Alex da Corte ‘s Slow Graffiti (2017). Sexualized objects like the high-heeled shoe have long held a fetishistic appeal for the Surrealists, and Da Corte’s mini, winged stiletto installation flattens the distinction between real life and fantasy.

In Magritte’s The Triumphal March (1948), meanwhile, a disembodied calf in a high-heeled shoe gains a life of its own while donning pieces of fancy dress. At Neven gallery in Bethnal Green, Adam Lewis Jacob has broken apart used stilettos to build wacky new constructions that still contain telling signifiers of their former life for his show “ Short Vamps for Long Wear ,” until October 24.

Doubling

From left to right: Charlotte Kingsnorth, Marshmallow Bench (2026). Image: Jack Elliot Edwards, courtesy the artist and Rose Easton, London. R: Sarah Lucas, SLAG (2022). Image: Steve Russell Studios, © Sarah Lucas, courtesy Sadie Coles HQ, London.

A short walk away, at Rose Easton , the group show “ Lumps and Bumps ” was inspired by the Comme des Garçons Spring/Summer 1997 collection “Body Meets Dress, Dress Meets Body,” but has plenty of incidental callbacks to the Magritte survey. Through December 12, it features the newly commissioned Marshmallow Bench by Charlotte Kingsnorth , a plump, pink leather sofa with an uncomfortably corporeal quality.

For Magritte, too, the body can double as an object, as in works from the Gagosian show like The Music Lesson (1965), in which an ear is attached to a bell, and The Red Model (1935), in which shoes become feet. In his The Art of Living (1967), a head balloons, becoming ridiculously oversized. A similar lack of constraint governs the slumped, stuffed figure, its bulging seams all awry, in Sarah Lucas ‘s SLAG (2022), also included in the show.

The Gagosian survey’s oldest work dates to 1926, exactly one century ago, but many of the later pieces were made in the past five years. If Magritte’s influence has undoubtedly endured through the decades, my recent gallery hop left me with the sense that his eye for the enigmatic and absurd is more relevant now than ever.
content.excerpt_original: Surrealism abounds, from Nicole Eisenman at Sadie Coles to Louis Fratino at David Zwirner.

content.article_text:
Artnet’s Source Material column asks artists to share their creative journeys beyond the studio.

On September 26, Santa Fe-based artist Cannupa Hanska Luger unveiled his latest site-specific installation, in Curaçao’s five million year-old cave known as Kueba di Indjan . Tour guides also call this expansive earthen alcove, rife with awe-inspiring stalagmites and stalactites, Kueba di Brua (“Voodoo Cave”). Rumor has it that indigenous folks did witchcraft here.

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

Inside, Luger found a spot where sunlight sneaks through the surface. There, he supplemented existing vines with hand-woven ropes cradling clay whistles created at three workshops he’d hosted over the previous week. Luger—a member of America’s Three Affiliated Tribes of Fort Berthold himself—left the whistles unfired, so they return to the earth. His son, meanwhile, activated the installation with an ambient site-specific composition the day the artist presented the piece to the public. Bats zipped past attendees as if they were dancing, conjuring the cave’s mystic history.

The artist helming the ship, All Seaing, with first mate Santo. Photo: courtesy of Cannupa Hanska Luger artist studio.

Luger created this work for the second edition of Novo Collective ‘s experimental public art program Uncommissioned , which brought six new public artworks to Curaçao. These include stained glass by local artist and organizer Avantia Damberg , plus a performance, an environmentally integrated sculpture, and another such desert installation by her cohorts Nash Caldera , Giovanni Abath , and Ailsa Anastatia , respectively.

Luger’s practice encompasses multiple modalities, too. His latest endeavor, however, may be his wildest, most fast-paced yet, turning social practice into sculpture within the span of a week. His family, of course, helped make it happen—a throughline within his work. “We did a project last year for Desert X , where we transformed our family van into a fog drip system to gather moisture out of the air,” Luger told me on the remote, uninhabited island of Klein Curaçao, where he, along with his family, Damberg and I, had arrived to install Damberg’s final work for Uncommissioned. Luger’s latest endeavor, however, eschews extraction—employing whistles, instead, as a symbol for generosity.

Here, Luger recounts how he made it happen.

Photo: courtesy of Cannupa Hanska Luger artist studio.

My work is place-based. I consider the land my primary audience. I had done workshops before making whistles, so we started with that idea as an opportunity to meet people from Curaçao and hear from them—not necessarily around the whistle or around the project, but just around being people around a table doing something. I’ve found that when people build with their hands, all the defense mechanisms fall off.

Photo: courtesy of Cannupa Hanska Luger artist studio.

The first time we met Jerry [Guo] and Chuman [Zhang, founders of Novo Collective], they picked us up in a dinghy right on the beach by our accommodation, and we boated over to a floating dock, in mangroves. The landscape here was so bizarre to me. I’ve been to a couple of islands in the Caribbean, and they have been incredibly tropical. The density of the thorny trees and cacti and mangroves, all in the same location—just trying to get a sense of that was fascinating. The very next morning, we visited with an archaeologist. She came with us to some sites that have cave paintings, pictographs, a bit further up from the Kueba di Indjan.

Photo: courtesy of Cannupa Hanska Luger artist studio.

She also provided a soil map of Curaçao. When we went and visited the cave painting sites, we harvested clay. All of the clay that we harvested was full of salt, so we didn’t use it in any of the workshops. That was store-bought. For the installation, though, I ended up using some of the clay that we processed.

Photo: courtesy of Cannupa Hanska Luger artist studio.

One of the workshops we had was at Farm to Crafts . They have a machine there that processes banana stalks from the island. Using those in the work was a way to reuse materials—sometimes the farmers will use it for fertilizer, but the amount of material produced would overwhelm any compost. That’s what was available, so that’s what we used. Waste materials are always an interesting material for me to work with. I like things that are part of a secondary industry, a byproduct.

I was expecting to get cordage, but it was literally just fibers. My wife Ginger [Dunnill] grew up making Ti Leaf Leis. She’s from Maui, and she was like, “I’ll just twist them up. It’s no problem.” The net, the suspension, all of that stuff was not part of the original plan. We were just responding to the materials we had, the landscape we were in, the environment. There was no time to second guess.

Photo: courtesy of Cannupa Hanska Luger artist studio.

I’ve been building flutes for 15 years now, off and on. Doing a workshop with folks, it’s nice to have some sort of reward. The reward of transforming a small handful of clay into a whistle, there’s a dopamine rush. Something happens in that form and its simplicity that excites any maker at any age, at any ability level.

Photo: courtesy of Cannupa Hanska Luger artist studio.

It took me years to make something I was really proud of. But through my experience, I found this simple whistle. It’s not about aesthetics, it’s about function. Once we got here, I was surprised to learn of the gogorobi , which is a similar-looking instrument made from the calabash fruit. It was really cool to hear the shape that I was making in clay predated my being here, predated the Dutch being here.

There are so many things in the world that take more than they give. Creating a little tiny clay whistle and making sound that can fill an entire space feels like the opposite.

Photo: courtesy of Cannupa Hanska Luger artist studio.

While I was learning, Ginger and the boys would go record things. When we would do workshops, we brought the recorders and asked people to play the whistles all at the same time. It was just always having the recorder there to gather sounds because we knew we wanted to build a sound bank for my son to compose with. The first day that I went down to the site to install, he built one composition. We recorded that and then played it on a Bluetooth speaker. And then the day of the reception, he composed a new one. The two played across the cavern. But all of it was literally just making in the moment—if something turns out exactly like I plan it, I feel like I’ve failed somehow.

Photo: courtesy of Cannupa Hanska Luger artist studio.

I had this red clay slip that I was going to decorate the pieces with, but I started to think about the history of that red iron painting on the caves. I started to question, ‘who am I to do that here?’ I don’t know what these symbols mean. I don’t know what their purpose is. Instead, I used the slip to inform the gravity of the stalactite and the stalagmite, to stain the banana leaf and bind the clay vessels together. All of those whistles that people had made, no matter where they came from, whether they knew each other or not, they’re a part of this place. Pouring the slip over those vessels was a way to acknowledge and recognize that the land binds us.
content.excerpt_original: The artist's new site-specific installation in Curaçao engages with a five million-year-old limestone cavern.

content.title_original: Sohn Hyun-lok Talks “The Birds”, Korean Education, Invisible Misfortune and Finding Freedom in Flight
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Sohn Hyun-lok Talks “The Birds”, Korean Education, Invisible Misfortune and Finding Freedom in Flight"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sohn Hyun-lok discusses “The Birds”, Korean schools, generational conflict, the meaning of birds and his challenging 18-month edit."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Returning to the Busan International Film Festival has particular significance for Sohn Hyun-lok. Born and raised in the city, the filmmaker premiered his debut feature “That Summer’s Lie” in BIFF’s New Currents section in 2023, where it received the FIPRESCI Prize. Three years later, he returns with his second feature, “The Birds”, a considerably larger and more ambitious production that combines family drama, criticism of the Korean educational system and increasingly strange genre elements."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Speaking with Asian Movie Pulse in Busan, Sohn discussed the progression from his first feature, shifting the perspective from daughter to mother, his thoughts on Korean schools and parenting, the origins of the bird metaphor, working with professional actors, the lengthy editing process and the radically smaller project he has already shot as his third feature."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "My Mother is screening at Busan International Film Festival", "links": [{"text": "Busan International Film Festival", "url": "https://www.biff.kr/eng/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://asianmoviepulse.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Busan-International-Film-Festival-scaled.jpg", "alt": "31st Busan International Film Festival", "caption": "", "credit": "Asian Movie Pulse"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For Sohn, premiering two consecutive features at BIFF inevitably carries an emotional dimension beyond professional recognition. He was born and spent his adolescence in Busan, making the festival closely connected to his own personal history. Having both his debut and sophomore film introduced there consequently feels particularly meaningful, although the circumstances under which the two productions were made could hardly have been more different."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“That Summer’s Lie” was produced without significant financial support and with a crew of only around seven people. The limitations meant that Sohn had relatively few options regarding how the movie could be made. “The Birds”, by contrast, received funding and allowed him to work with a substantially larger group of technicians and actors. It remained a low-budget production, but the increase in resources gave him the opportunity to experiment with ideas that would simply have been impossible on his debut."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "He hopes that difference is visible in the finished film. Rather than attempting to reproduce the intimacy and limitations of “That Summer’s Lie”, Sohn treated the second feature as an opportunity to discover what else his cinema could become. The larger ensemble, genre elements, visual effects and considerably broader narrative all emerged partly from that desire to try things he had not previously been able to attempt."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Check the review of the film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "https://asianmoviepulse.com/ the-birds-2026-by-sohn-hyun-lok-film-review", "links": [{"text": "https://asianmoviepulse.com/", "url": "https://asianmoviepulse.com/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the same time, the central character of “The Birds” developed directly from questions raised by his first film. “That Summer’s Lie” followed a teenage girl whose actions create increasing complications, but while making it Sohn began wondering about the mother on the opposite side of those conflicts. Why did the mother fail to understand what her daughter wanted? Why could two members of the same family look at the same situation and arrive at completely different interpretations?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“The Birds” reverses the viewpoint. Instead of remaining with the troubled daughter, Sohn wanted to follow a mother attempting to comprehend a child whose behavior increasingly escapes her understanding. Ye-ok’s position becomes even more complicated because she is simultaneously a parent and a teacher. At home she struggles with her own daughter, while at school she is professionally responsible for other people’s children."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This dual role also allowed Sohn to examine the way Korean adults look at young people. Although the behavior of some students in the movie can appear exceptionally harsh, he does not regard the film as an accusation against contemporary teenagers. Instead, he is more interested in the structures through which adults attempt to understand and control them."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In his view, the Korean school system has traditionally required teachers to manage students very strictly. One consequence is the temptation to classify children according to simple categories: those who study hard, those who do not, and those whose behavior adults find difficult to comprehend. Sohn wanted “The Birds” to push against precisely that way of thinking."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The students in the movie cannot be reduced to good and bad children. They possess different personalities, desires and ways of understanding their surroundings, while the adults frequently fail because they attempt to impose straightforward categories upon something far more complicated. Although Sohn believes Korean schools are gradually changing and teachers are increasingly trying to understand students rather than merely control them, that older mentality remains visible."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Parents participate in the same system from another direction. Sohn does not believe the adults presented in “The Birds” simply do not care about their children, even when their behavior can appear apathetic. Sohn Hyun-lok Talks “The Birds”, Korean Education, Invisible Misfortune and Finding Freedom in Flight

Sohn Hyun-lok discusses “The Birds”, Korean schools, generational conflict, the meaning of birds and his challenging 18-month edit.

Returning to the Busan International Film Festival has particular significance for Sohn Hyun-lok. Born and raised in the city, the filmmaker premiered his debut feature “That Summer’s Lie” in BIFF’s New Currents section in 2023, where it received the FIPRESCI Prize. Three years later, he returns with his second feature, “The Birds”, a considerably larger and more ambitious production that combines family drama, criticism of the Korean educational system and increasingly strange genre elements.

Speaking with Asian Movie Pulse in Busan, Sohn discussed the progression from his first feature, shifting the perspective from daughter to mother, his thoughts on Korean schools and parenting, the origins of the bird metaphor, working with professional actors, the lengthy editing process and the radically smaller project he has already shot as his third feature.

My Mother is screening at Busan International Film Festival

For Sohn, premiering two consecutive features at BIFF inevitably carries an emotional dimension beyond professional recognition. He was born and spent his adolescence in Busan, making the festival closely connected to his own personal history. Having both his debut and sophomore film introduced there consequently feels particularly meaningful, although the circumstances under which the two productions were made could hardly have been more different.

“That Summer’s Lie” was produced without significant financial support and with a crew of only around seven people. The limitations meant that Sohn had relatively few options regarding how the movie could be made. “The Birds”, by contrast, received funding and allowed him to work with a substantially larger group of technicians and actors. It remained a low-budget production, but the increase in resources gave him the opportunity to experiment with ideas that would simply have been impossible on his debut.

He hopes that difference is visible in the finished film. Rather than attempting to reproduce the intimacy and limitations of “That Summer’s Lie”, Sohn treated the second feature as an opportunity to discover what else his cinema could become. The larger ensemble, genre elements, visual effects and considerably broader narrative all emerged partly from that desire to try things he had not previously been able to attempt.

Check the review of the film

https://asianmoviepulse.com/ the-birds-2026-by-sohn-hyun-lok-film-review

At the same time, the central character of “The Birds” developed directly from questions raised by his first film. “That Summer’s Lie” followed a teenage girl whose actions create increasing complications, but while making it Sohn began wondering about the mother on the opposite side of those conflicts. Why did the mother fail to understand what her daughter wanted? Why could two members of the same family look at the same situation and arrive at completely different interpretations?

“The Birds” reverses the viewpoint. Instead of remaining with the troubled daughter, Sohn wanted to follow a mother attempting to comprehend a child whose behavior increasingly escapes her understanding. Ye-ok’s position becomes even more complicated because she is simultaneously a parent and a teacher. At home she struggles with her own daughter, while at school she is professionally responsible for other people’s children.

This dual role also allowed Sohn to examine the way Korean adults look at young people. Although the behavior of some students in the movie can appear exceptionally harsh, he does not regard the film as an accusation against contemporary teenagers. Instead, he is more interested in the structures through which adults attempt to understand and control them.

In his view, the Korean school system has traditionally required teachers to manage students very strictly. One consequence is the temptation to classify children according to simple categories: those who study hard, those who do not, and those whose behavior adults find difficult to comprehend. Sohn wanted “The Birds” to push against precisely that way of thinking.

The students in the movie cannot be reduced to good and bad children. They possess different personalities, desires and ways of understanding their surroundings, while the adults frequently fail because they attempt to impose straightforward categories upon something far more complicated. Although Sohn believes Korean schools are gradually changing and teachers are increasingly trying to understand students rather than merely control them, that older mentality remains visible.

Parents participate in the same system from another direction. Sohn does not believe the adults presented in “The Birds” simply do not care about their children, even when their behavior can appear apathetic. Instead, he points towards a tendency among Korean parents to entrust a very large part of their children’s education and daily development to schools.

The result can be a peculiar transfer of responsibility. Parents expect teachers and institutions to educate, supervise and solve problems, while teachers themselves are already overwhelmed by the demand to control large numbers of very different students. The apparent indifference visible in the film therefore emerges less from a complete absence of concern than from a system in which responsibility is continually being delegated.

The image of birds, however, predates almost every other aspect of the finished film. Sohn first conceived the basic idea approximately thirteen years ago while completing his mandatory military service. Frustrated by the restrictions of military life and facing a long period before his service would end, he watched birds simply fly across the boundary surrounding him.

He remembers envying them. They could pass freely over the fences that contained him, producing the uncomplicated thought that he wanted to become a bird himself. That image eventually generated the earliest version of what would much later become “The Birds”.

The story at that stage was very different, but one central idea was already present: students would jump from a building after seeing birds. As Sohn continued thinking about the project over the following years, however, the symbolism gradually changed. Freedom and escape remained part of it, but birds increasingly came to represent something less reassuring.

He began thinking about the unexpected misfortunes that enter people’s lives without warning. These events often seem impossible to identify beforehand, yet once they arrive they can completely alter everything around them. Sohn eventually transformed the birds into a metaphor for precisely that kind of invisible, unpredictable disaster.

This idea is closely connected with Ye-ok’s personality. She attempts to understand the world through distinctions and classifications, much as the educational system categorizes students. If she can name something, separate it and place it within the right conceptual box, perhaps she can control it. The tragedy confronting her refuses to operate according to those rules.

The birds become the physical representation of something that may already be surrounding a person without being visible. Misfortune exists nearby, but it cannot necessarily be identified until the moment it suddenly arrives. “The Birds” thus turns a childhood-like fantasy of freedom into something far more unsettling: an image simultaneously associated with escaping confinement and confronting forces that cannot be understood.

Sohn also deliberately changed his approach to casting. On “That Summer’s Lie”, he had primarily searched for unknown performers and auditioned actors for practically every part. With his second feature, he wanted another kind of filmmaking experience and decided to work more extensively with established professional actors represented by agencies.

His first meeting with Kang Kyung-heon, who plays Ye-ok, immediately reassured him about that decision. They spent a long time discussing the screenplay, and Sohn discovered that she had already been thinking deeply about its philosophical implications, including ideas connected with the “Butterfly Dream”. Their interpretations of the material connected quickly, making the first conversation unusually productive.

Other cast members were similarly attracted to the peculiar nature of the screenplay. Their professional experience allowed the production to progress differently from Sohn’s debut, where much of the process had involved finding performers without established screen personas. With “The Birds”, he was able to concentrate more directly on exploring the material with actors accustomed to the demands of a film set.

Post-production proved considerably more difficult. Sohn edited the movie himself and spent approximately a year and a half attempting to find its final form. The process involved repeatedly changing the structure and duration, making versions longer and shorter, abandoning particular approaches and occasionally stepping away from the edit entirely when exhaustion made it impossible to see the material clearly.

The visual effects made the process particularly challenging. Several sequences had to be assembled before the completed effects existed, forcing Sohn to imagine what elements would eventually appear within shots while simultaneously judging their rhythm. For a filmmaker coming from the comparatively stripped-down production of “That Summer’s Lie”, editing this type of material required learning an entirely different process.

An even greater challenge was determining exactly what kind of film “The Birds” should become. Sohn knew that it needed to operate as a genre movie, and therefore required a certain rhythm and ability to sustain mystery. At the same time, he did not want the demands of genre to overwhelm his own filmmaking sensibility.

Much of the lengthy editing period was devoted to finding that middle ground. Too much emphasis on conventional genre mechanics risked producing a film that no longer felt like his own, while leaning completely into his previous style could undermine the increasingly strange narrative. The finished 139-minute version represents his attempt to retain both impulses.

After such an exhausting post-production period, Sohn responded by doing something almost completely opposite. Rather than immediately trying to make another film on the expanded scale of “The Birds”, he has already shot his third feature with only a handful of actors.

This time, he wanted to experience making a movie almost entirely alone. He operated the camera and recorded the sound himself, deliberately stripping away the larger crew that had enabled the ambitions of “The Birds”. The new project centers on actors and the question of creativity, although Sohn is not yet revealing many additional details.

The decision seems particularly fitting after a second feature defined by expansion. “The Birds” allowed Sohn to work with more people, experiment with genre, incorporate visual effects and spend a year and a half shaping a complicated narrative in the editing room. His next film appears to be an attempt to discover what happens when practically all of that infrastructure disappears.

In that sense, Sohn’s early career already shows a filmmaker deliberately testing opposite methods rather than settling into one. “That Summer’s Lie” emerged from severe limitations, “The Birds” used increased resources to explore a much larger world, and the third feature now returns voluntarily to an almost solitary mode of production. What connects them is an interest in people who cannot quite understand one another, particularly adults and young people attempting to communicate across an increasingly difficult divide.

content.article_text:
Editor’s note: This story is an edition of Link Rot , a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet. The column will appear every other Monday.

The development of generative AI text-to-video models has been charted over the past few years through a simple prompt: “Will Smith eating pasta.”

The first videos, posted in 2023 using newly released Stable Diffusion models, feature a ravenous, monstrous rendering of the actor shoveling a pasta-shaped blob into his mouth with his hands, only for it to slide, morph, stretch, merge with surrounding artifacts, or simply disappear. Within three years, the test has nearly reached its endpoint, with the pasta responding naturally to gravity and interacting correctly with the other objects in the scene: the fork, the plate, and Smith’s mouth. But as each new model arrives in relentless succession, what happens to those that came before it, or to the videos produced during their training?

That question drives “Post Generation,” a new exhibition at tiat gallery in San Francisco. Three artists reflect on a video archive generated by Veo 1, a now-defunct model developed by Google in 2024. Released only for internal use, though eventually leaked, the model seemed barely functional. It could produce only six-second videos, with long waits between generations and predictably surreal results: a six-legged horse galloping across a wet field, a staticky smudge that might be children playing in a pile of leaves, and a three-limbed hominid swimming in a pool. Researchers generated hundreds of thousands of videos before the model was shut down and superseded by successive generations, Veo 2 and Veo 3, both of which were released to the public.

“Because these models are so resource intensive and because each new model is faster and more efficient, it’s hard to justify keeping old models around. No one can generate using Veo1, and the outputs it produced aren’t publicly available,” said Tina Tarighian, a senior creative technologist at Google’s Creative Lab and the show’s organizer. “So I thought, what can we do with these leftover scraps of a model? Can we gift this archive to artists?”

Tarighian shared a portion of the archive with choreographer Zelia ZZ Tan, creative engineer Karyn Nakamura, and fiber artist Haley Mortin, asking each to respond with new work. The resulting exhibition is a multimedia meditation on the nature of this technology and an archive of a particular moment in its development.

For Mortin, working with this training data was a natural extension of her practice, which incorporates AI-generated images, images sourced from research papers, and other AI artifacts into knit works. Her fascination with these artifacts stems in part from a former job as a data annotator, a form of often-invisible human labor in which workers around the world categorize and tag images to teach AI models to “see” and correctly identify objects.

“It was 2018, I had just graduated college, I didn’t know what AI was, and I needed money,” said Mortin. “I thought it was just a data entry job.”

Over the next two years, Mortin found herself solving CAPTCHA tests and labeling images not only by the objects and subjects they contained but also by more subjective categories, such as the emotion she thought a person in a photo was expressing. The Veo 1 outputs are, albeit indirectly, a product of this kind of labor. In examining them, Mortin decided to focus on the strange forms of text the model generated.

“It produced two flavors of nonsense, these glyph-like shapes or empty phrases,” said Mortin. “These [visual] models don’t learn text like an LLM [large language model] does, rather, they learn text as a texture.”

This led Mortin to consider the embroidery samplers made by women in the 18th century. Many young women first encountered writing not through ink and paper but through embroidery. As they practiced stitching text, they often used these samplers to record family histories. Mortin’s resulting work, Soup Is Made of Water (10 Samplers) (2026), comprises ten knitted pieces that capture the different forms of garbled text generated by Veo 1, reflecting on the histories of text production and the practices through which it is preserved and archived.

Rendered in black and white yarn, the pieces depict a looping scribble, a calligraphic font attempting to spell, perhaps, “beauty” [b eurt], and what can only be described as a sigil tattoo of the kind commonly inked on thighs in Ridgewood, Brooklyn. The work deftly brings into conversation, and inverts, different practices of language learning and history-making: those of 18th-century women, contemporary machines, and artists attempting to process and document a machine’s training.

Karyn Nakamura also took up Tarighian’s invitation to explore the research histories behind Veo 1 and other generative models, combining several video technologies in a single work. In Labor of Light (2016), an assemblage of technologies comes together as a kind of altar to the history of video production. Suspended from a pair of cables, a white device emits a beam of light that appears stable to the viewer but contains, in its flicker, the analog signal of Quicker ’n a Wink (1940), a film explaining how MIT’s Harold Edgerton developed the high-speed photography technology used to produce slow-motion footage.

The beam of light leads down to a projector that casts a collage of Veo 1-generated videos onto a white cloth, each clip emerging from a static-like field of vivid colors. Nakamura uses RGB noise, a key component of generative AI, in which images and videos are generated from an initial field of noise. Beneath the cloth, small toothpicks held in place with putty support printouts of landmark research papers that advanced the techniques behind modern AI generation, including diffusion.

“I find the process of image making and the process of video and video systems incredibly beautiful, there’s a lot of craft in there,” said Nakamura.

Even as someone who sees beauty in these technologies, Nakamura worries that the pace of development makes their inner workings increasingly difficult to understand, limiting people’s ability to intervene creatively and exercise agency in contemporary image-making processes. For this reason, her work often dwells in the glitches and gaps of earlier models, such as Stable Diffusion 1.5.

“Because I like Stable Diffusion 1.5, sometimes I think, ‘Oh, am I being a Luddite?’” Nakamura mused. “Like, what is even progress right now?”

Against a backdrop of increasingly morbid present and future outcomes, these artists reckon with a technology advancing at breakneck speed despite being barely a few years old. Yet in a culture that equates progress with perpetual acceleration, to pause is to risk obsolescence. Choreographer Zelia ZZ Tan explores this tension in a ten-minute dance performed at the exhibition’s opening on October 8. Combining choreography with animated avatars, the performance captures the ways bodies move and gesture in Veo 1 videos.

“I searched the archive through movement rather than only through words when I started to realize that between generated bodies, physical bodies, and the computational body, there are a lot of similarities and also a lot of rules based on how they can perform,” said Tan. But dancing with the limitation of movement of the generated body required vulnerability.

Tan continued: “It’s such an honor to have a body, to be able to be present there, and maybe I’m not showing the most trained technique, but to listen, to be hesitant on stage, to wait for something to happen – that’s part of the power of being there as a performer.”

content.title_original: Tarek Atoui’s Turbine Hall review – hallelujah, it’s raining musical instruments!
