content.article_text:
O n the floor of the Turbine Hall , there are wide water basins and huge flattish rough-hewn rocks you might see on moorland or in a desert. You can sit or stand or climb on them. But if you look up, you won’t be able to stop looking up – because it’s raining musical instruments. Immense elongated brass trumpets and giant glowing drums seem to float in the air, suspended from the girders of the former power station’s roof.

If Lebanese artist Tarek Atoui had just left it at that, it would be an impressive, intriguing installation, but this is Tate Modern , honey, and Atoui hasn’t been asked to occupy its grandest space with mere physical objects. Instead, his sculptural creations and found stuff resonate and echo with an ever-changing, invisible art of noises. An earth-shaking bass note throbs from a hanging trumpet – or is it from that translucent cone rising out of the ground like an ethereal minaret? Then a drumbeat booms through the space and a woman’s plangent, achingly lovely voice sings notes of infinite nostalgia and melancholy.

It’s entrancing. The music has you hooked. It is music, I think, though abstract, non-melodic, a rising and falling of sounds that lead you around and through the installation’s forest of solid things. But then – is music ever not sculptural? Listening to the scything percussive notes of Stravinsky certainly is; and the desire to crystallise sound waves into something visible has haunted everyone from the inventors of opera to designers of psychedelic lightshows.

Yet Tarek Atoui still manages to do something new and beautiful with sound and vision. He teases you and boggles your mind with how his musical instruments relate to the sounds you hear, how the stones and water basins, pipes and strings have produced this sonic outpouring. The entire installation is an interconnected musical machine.

It’s funny too. There’s a warm, generous if absurdist humour to it all. In the past, a crazy mechanical contraption like this would be called “Heath Robinsonish”, after the early 20th-century British cartoonist who came up with such things. A better comparison is Leonardo da Vinci, who invented wild musical instruments among his other real and impossible machines: organs worked by water, a string instrument shaped like a fantastic beast.

Atoui, like Leonardo, seems to be looking for a lost harmony in the world, a secret note that pleased the Lord. Sadness hovers in the sounds that fill this vast grey space, as the bass notes pound harder, building up to an apocalyptic blast. What is being mourned and where is he taking us? You start to feel you are in a city of sounds and sights. The crowd of towering, floating pinnacles, the mysterious voice and crescendo of percussion, suggest an ancient, tumultuous labyrinth of a city. I thought of Lahore and Marrakesh, of a street-singer heard once in an Istanbul market. Yet this city is purer, less tangible. Its towers fly in the air.

Ultimately, you can’t reduce this magical, elusive work of art to a fixed meaning. You have to surrender to it. The sound gathers you up in its ecstasy like a spiralling mystical dance. There is a strong similarity with Sufi drummers and dervishes who use music and motion to inculcate a liberating, trancelike calm. I certainly didn’t want to leave. The vibrations and complex visual composition keep your brain busy but you are also soothed and at peace.

It also suggests the urban life all around this site, the exotic sounds of Bankside: the music of the city, gathered into Atoui’s collage of random noise. But reality slips and fades as you are shown a world beyond the physical. All these objects, from the cones to the stones to the electric guitar played live at the press view, are but as air. They fascinate the eye but the sound eventually dissolves the material world. The solid stuff Atoui begins with becomes as unreal as a reflection in a courtyard pool.

Atoui has grabbed the opportunity to work in this vast space with both hands, creating something rich, ingenious, funny, sad, mystical. This is a Turbine Hall installation to lose yourself in for hours, dreaming and wondering. It’s the sonic answer to a sun indoors – and Atoui is a modern magus.

content.article_text:
Queer Gaze est la rubrique de notre journaliste Timé Zoppé sur le cinéma LGBTQ+.

Mon éducation à la queerness au travers des images de cinéma s’est beaucoup faite par des figures féminines. Parce que mon père aime une seule chose dans la vie : Almodovar ! Et la culture hispanique, parce qu’on est espagnol dans la famille. Il y avait aussi ces grandes figures féminines : Rossy de Palma, Carmen Maura et Victoria Abril, qui avait déjà quelque chose de Loli, son personnage dans Gazon maudit de Josiane Balasko (1996). J’ai compris plus tard qu’elles étaient des figures queer et ça m’a pas mal nourri.

Après, mon imaginaire queer s’est beaucoup développé sur la « non-image » dans le cinéma, je pense notamment au film Sexe Intentions (1999) de Roger Kumble que j’adorais quand j’étais jeune, où il y a un personnage gay qui est payé pour avoir une relation avec un mec hétéro. Rien n’est montré, mais la suggestion de cette homosexualité ou de cette bisexualité, ça me rendait fou ! Je pense aussi à Elephant (2003) de Gus Van Sant, quand les deux gamins qui s’apprêtent à faire la tuerie s’embrassent, comme deux ados complètement perdus qui s’apprêtent à faire quelque chose de fou et qui du coup se disent “Y a plus de tabou, y’a plus rien qui tient”.

A l’adolescence, avec les premiers réseaux sociaux, MySpace et tout, j’ai eu la chance de me retrouver dans les groupes de personnes qui allaient voir les films de Bruce LaBruce , John Waters , Gregg Araki … J’ai grandi à Toulouse, où il y avait pas mal de cinéma arty et indépendants, donc on avait quand même la possibilité de voir ces films-là. J’étais dans des petites communautés qui organisaient des espèces de mini-festivals où ces films passaient. Donc j’ai été beaucoup marqué par cette imagerie très pop, très queer, au-delà de gay, très colorée, très saturée, très engagée. Épileptique, quoi !

J’ai appris ce qu’était le cabaret en le faisant. Je suis directement arrivée chez Madame Arthur [le premier cabaret travesti de Paris, ouvert en 1946, ndlr] qui reste un lieu d’histoire queer primordial, un des premiers à avoir accueilli des personnes travesties sur scène et aussi et surtout des personnes trans. Pour moi, il y a cette idée qu’une fois qu’on s’est débarrassé de tous les tabous, et notamment du tabou ultime qui est celui du genre, ça ouvre un champ d’exploration artistique infini.

Parmi les films de cabaret qui m’ont marqué au cinéma, je pense à Moulin Rouge (2001) et Roméo + Juliette (1996) de Baz Luhrmann, tous ces films qui ont quelque chose de camp , de débonnaire. Tous les films que j’ai cités avant ont justement cet élément du cabaret qui est celui du camp, du kitsch, de l’outrance, des mondes un peu épileptiques dans lesquels il n’y a que du trop et pas de ridicule. J’aime beaucoup les films musicaux en général et j’ai beaucoup aimé Phantom of the Paradise (1974) de Brian de Palma, qui était vraiment mon film favori dans ma fin d’adolescence et que j’ai poncé. Le Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975) de Jim Sharman, évidemment ! C’est typiquement un film qu’on s’est passé sous le manteau avec les copains au lycée.

Je trouve qu’aujourd’hui les conditions de création du cinéma indépendant sont de plus en plus compliquées, et que c’est ahurissant et regrettable de voir que tous les films queer qui ont de la visibilité sont majoritairement signés par des mecs blancs cis. J’ai suivi de près avec un peu de tristesse ce qui s’est passé autour de Jim Queen (2026) [des spectateur-ices ont reproché au film un manque de diversité et des clichés homophobes, ndlr] de Nicolas Athané et Marco Nguyen, et pour moi c’est représentatif d’un monde où ces histoires ont du mal à se raconter. Quand un film queer important pour la communauté sort, je me bouge pour aller le voir. Et si j’y vais pas souvent, c’est peut-être aussi qu’il n’y en a pas assez !

Je suis en couple avec une femme trans et je n’ai rien à me mettre sous la dent en termes de représentation. À 37 ans, il y a plein de choses que j’aimerais comprendre grâce à des représentations au cinéma, et la dernière fois que j’ai vu un film qui montrait une histoire comme celle-là, c’était Laurence Anyways (2012) de Xavier Dolan – on parle d’un film qui a de l’âge. On ne voit pas assez de films réalisés par des personnes trans, par des femmes, notamment des films sur la queerness réalisés par des femmes.

Ce que j’aimerais aujourd’hui, c’est qu’il y ait un queer gaze au cinéma sur tout un tas de choses. J’adorerais voir un film sur l’architecture fait par une personne queer, avec ce regard-là, sans que ce soit le thème central. Je trouve que dans les archives de John Waters, Gregg Araki, on retrouve un queer gaze posé sur des choses qui ne parlent pas de ça.

content.article_text:
Alex Gibney, director of the new four-hour documentary about Elon Musk, said that Universal, owners of the film’s international distribution rights “wavered” over releasing the film outside North America.

Gibney was speaking to the New York Times as the film opened in the US (where it is being released by the independent distributor Bleecker Street), and appeared to confirm a story in the Hollywood Reporter that Universal, which had acquired the international rights to the film in 2023 , had got cold feet. Asked by the New York Times, “Did Universal Pictures waver in setting up its international release plans?” Gibney replied: “Yes.”

A subsequent story in Variety suggested that Universal had been concerned about “legal threats from Musk”, but that the studio had “always been enthusiastic about releasing the film internationally”. Gibney was asked: “So it wasn’t about legal clearances?” The film-maker replied: “You can walk and chew gum at the same time.”

However, it appears plans are back on track, as Gibney added: “We just had a meeting with [Universal], and we’re talking very concretely about a release plan.”

Gibney also said his producer Jessie Deeter, who knew Musk from two previous films, had attempted on several occasions to ask Musk to be interviewed for the film. Musk’s response was to post “Gibney is a douche” on X, the social media platform owned by Musk-founded company SpaceXAI.

In the wake of the film’s premiere at the Venice film festival, Musk posted a string of criticisms of the film and insults aimed at Gibney , including calling the film a “hit piece that misses” and threatening legal action.

Universal declined to comment further, pointing to its previous statement: “We’ve always been committed to releasing this film, and our plans haven’t changed.”

Cartelera Cinemex – Estrenos de películas 15 de octubre, 2026

Por: Staff Cine PREMIERE

¿Qué verás esta semana?

Ya sea que tengas ganas de una historia emotiva, un thriller intenso o puro entretenimiento para desconectarte, los nuevos lanzamientos de películas en la cartelera Cinemex ofrecen opciones para todos los gustos.

Aquí te contamos cuáles son las películas que llegan a la cartelera Cinemex esta semana y la siguiente. Una guía rápida para decidir qué ver, cuándo ir y no perderte los títulos más comentados del momento.

Estrenos Apple TV – Películas y series nuevas del 12 al 18 de octubre 2026

Staff Cine PREMIERE

¿Qué verás este mes?

Conoce aquí todos los estrenos de películas y series nuevas que llegan a Apple TV en octubre 2026. Es cierto que la plataforma de streaming de la manzanita no estrena tantas series y películas como otros sistemas, pero la calidad de cada uno de sus títulos justifican esta aparente austeridad de novedades. Aún así, una de las grandes ventajas de Apple TV es la facilidad que provee para rentar y comprar títulos de manera independiente aunque no sean parte de su catálogo.

Los estrenos de series y películas nuevas en Apple TV de esta semana están destacados en amarillo .

content.article_text:
Artículos

Estrenos Disney Plus – 12 al 18 de octubre 2026 y todo el mes

Staff Cine PREMIERE

¿Qué verás este mes?

Conoce todas las películas y series nuevas que llegan al catálogo de Disney Plus. Cada mes, la plataforma de Disney Plus ofrece estrenos de series, películas y especiales de todas sus marcas. Conoce aquí todos los títulos nuevos. Recuerda que la plataforma también contiene un extenso catálogo. Títulos de Disney, Pixar, Marvel, Star Wars, National Geographic, Star (Searchlight Pictures, 20th Century Studios y FX) y deportes en vivo con ESPN. Los estrenos de esta semana están destacados en amarillo.

¿Cuánto vale el Disney Plus al mes?

La suscripción a Disney Plus tiene dos paquetes. Estándar por $219 pesos mensuales o $1,839 pesos anuales y Premium por $299 pesos mensuales o $2,509 pesos anuales . En ambos casos, la membresía permite crear hasta 7 perfiles, así como descargar contenido para ver sin conexión a internet. Pero hay variantes entre la calidad de video/audio y el número de dispositivos para transmitir en simultáneo.

También te podría interesar los estrenos de:

Estrenos de películas en Disney Plus (octubre 2026)

Katseye: Wild Hearts (KATSEYE: Wild Hearts, Dir.a Nadia Hallgren, 2026) (16/10/2026) Documental sobre el ascenso meteórico de Katseye, el grupo femenino de pop global nominado dos veces al Grammy en 2026. A través de imágenes inéditas, videos de sus fans (los Eyekons) y entrevistas íntimas con sus seis integrantes —Sophia, Manon, Daniela, Lara, Megan y Yoonchae—, la película recorre el camino desde el exigente proyecto Dream Academy hasta convertirse en uno de los actos emergentes más importantes del pop mundial. El estreno en Disney+ llega tras su paso por cines y el debut en el número 1 del Billboard 200 de su tercer EP, Wild. Producida por Interscope Films y Boardwalk Pictures, en colaboración con HYBE x Geffen.

Estrenos de series en Disney Plus (octubre 2026)

África: El hogar de la vida salvaje (Africa: Earth’s Wild Home) (03/10/2026)

Coven Academy: El secreto de las brujas (Coven Academy) (02/10/2026) Serie sobrenatural para jóvenes adultos ambientada en Nueva Orleans. Tres jóvenes brujas en formación están unidas por el destino para proteger su ciudad de fuerzas antiguas y peligrosas. Entre desentrañar oscuros secretos, dominar una magia volátil y enfrentarse a rivales irresistibles, también deberán navegar los primeros amores y las amistades profundas que forja la adolescencia. Creada por Tim Federle ( High School Musical: The Musical: The Series ), con Malina Pauli Weissman, Malachi Barton y Tiffani Thiessen.

África: El hogar de la vida salvaje (Africa: Earth’s Wild Home) (03/10/2026) Serie documental de siete episodios producida por BBC Studios Natural History Unit para National Geographic. Filmada durante casi cuatro años en cerca de 30 países, captura comportamientos y especies nunca antes documentados en televisión, e incluye la primera filmación de la rara pantera negra africana salvaje. Narrada y producida ejecutivamente por la actriz Wunmi Mosaku ( Sinners, Loki) . Lanzamiento de una ambiciosa franquicia multianual que documentará el planeta continente por continente.

Grey’s Anatomy – Temporada 22 (07/10/2026) Nueva temporada de la longeva serie médica creada por Shonda Rhimes, ambientada en el hospital Grey Sloan Memorial.

Temporada de amor (07/10/2026) Ambientada en una idílica isla japonesa, Temporada de amor sigue a la trabajadora agricultora Karin Shirahama mientras entrega su corazón y alma a cultivar las mejores fresas posibles. Un día, Lee Yubin, un chico de ciudad con mala suerte llega a la isla y, tras un primer encuentro hilarantemente incómodo, ambos terminan pasando mucho más tiempo juntos debido a un malentendido inesperado. Nuevo episodio por semana .

Vampirina: Una vampirina adolescente – Temporada 2 (Vampirina: Teenage Vampire) (07/10/2026) Segunda temporada de la serie live-action basada en los personajes de la serie animada original. Vampirina navega los retos de la adolescencia mientras equilibra su vida como joven vampiresa.

The Kardashians – Temporada 8 (08/10/2026) Nueva temporada del reality que sigue la vida de la familia Kardashian-Jenner.

Entre pasos: En busca de un sueño (05/10/2026)

VisionQuest (13/10/2026) ESTRENO EN DISNEY PLUS ESTA SEMANA Entrega final de la trilogía iniciada con WandaVision (2021) y Agatha All Along (2024). Tras ser reiniciado y escapar de quienes querían convertirlo en un arma, Visión vive escondido del mundo mientras consulta las inteligencias artificiales integradas en su programación —J.A.R.V.I.S., F.R.I.D.A.Y., E.D.I.T.H. y la siniestra presencia de Ultrón— en busca de un nuevo propósito. Su vida encubierta se interrumpe cuando se ve obligado a huir junto a Thomas Shepard, un misterioso joven que podría ser la reencarnación de su hijo. Creada por Terry Matalas (Star Trek: Picard), con Paul Bettany, James Spader y Ruaridh Mollica. Nuevo episodio por semana .

Toda la verdad – Temporada 2 (14/10/2026) ESTRENO EN DISNEY PLUS ESTA SEMANA

Phony: La otra madre (Phony) (20/10/2026) Misterio adolescente con tintes de comedia negra. Sonny despierta en el hospital tras un accidente automovilístico y descubre que su madre —su único padre y su mejor amigo— parece haber sido reemplazada por una impostora. Para encontrar a su verdadera madre, contrata a Sharla, una detective privada que cree en el «conocimiento alternativo». Creada y dirigida por Nick Paley ( Marcel the Shell With Shoes On ). Con Connie Britton y Sam Nivola.

Coppola, el representante – Temporada 2 (01/10/2026) Segunda temporada de la aclamada comedia argentina sobre Guillermo Coppola, el legendario representante de Diego Armando Maradona. Creación de Mariano Cohn y Gastón Duprat, con dirección de Ariel Winograd. Con Juan Minujín en el papel protagónico.

La casa de Mickey Mouse – Temporada 2 (Mickey Mouse Clubhouse+) (01/10/2026)

The Drop: Una saga de Snowfall (The Drop: A Snowfall Saga) (28/10/2026) Spin-off de Snowfall , la aclamada serie sobre el narcotráfico en Los Ángeles. Ambición, lealtad y supervivencia colisionan mientras todos arriesgan todo para construir algo duradero. Creada por Malcolm Spellman. Con Gail Bean e Isaiah John.

Estrenos MUBI – 12 al 18 de octubre de 2026 y todo el mes

Staff Cine PREMIERE

¿Qué verás este mes?

Para cinéfilos que busquen ampliar sus horizontes y descubrir ambiciosas películas de autores visionarios, desde realizadores emergentes hasta directores consagrados, existe MUBI. Con títulos exclusivos y una colección en constante rotación que son cuidadosamente seleccionadas por sus curadores. Conoce aquí todos los estrenos de películas y series que llegan este mes al catálogo de MUBI.

¿Cuánto cuesta la mensualidad de MUBI?

En México, la suscripción mensual cuesta $179 pesos , después del período de prueba de 7 días. O si lo prefieres, puedes ahorrar un 34% con la suscripción anual que asciende a $1,500 pesos.

Para estudiantes universitarios existe una opción especial para contratar y acceder a las películas de MUBI por solo $89 pesos al mes, tras una prueba gratuita de 30 días.

Aunque te puedes suscribir directamente en su plataforma, también lo puedes obtener de manera fácil a través de Prime Video .

También te podrían interesar los estrenos de:

NOTA: Los estrenos de esta semana están destacados en amarillo.

Estrenos de películas en MUBI (octubre 2026)

Toro salvaje (Raging Bull, Dir. Martin Scorsese, 1980) (23/10/2026)

Videodrome (Videodrome, Dir. David Cronenberg, 1983) (01/10/2026) El presidente de un canal de televisión de cable descubre una señal que transmite escenas de tortura y asesinato, y empieza a obsesionarse hasta el punto de no poder distinguir entre la realidad y las alucinaciones. Obra maestra del body horror que explora la violencia mediática, la tecnología y la carne como superficies intercambiables. Uno de los títulos fundamentales de Cronenberg y del cine canadiense.

Day of the Dead (Day of the Dead, Dir. George A. Romero, 1985) (01/10/2026) Tercera entrega de la saga de muertos vivientes de Romero. En un bunker subterráneo, un pequeño grupo de científicos y militares intenta sobrevivir mientras el mundo exterior ha sido ya devorado por los zombis. Un retrato de la desintegración del orden social y la razón humana más oscuro y pesimista que sus predecesores.

La cosa (The Thing, Dir. John Carpenter, 1982) (01/10/2026) Un grupo de investigadores en la Antártida descubre una forma de vida extraterrestre capaz de imitar a la perfección a cualquier ser vivo. El terror a lo desconocido y la paranoia de no saber quién entre los tuyos ya no es humano. Considerada una de las mejores películas de terror y ciencia ficción de la historia.

Arrebato (Arrebato, Dir. Iván Zulueta, 1980) (01/10/2026) Un director de cine de serie B recibe una cinta de súper 8 de un viejo conocido, Pedro, un joven fascinado por la magia del cine hasta niveles perturbadores. La película de culto del cine español por excelencia: un viaje hipnótico hacia la adicción, el éxtasis y la autodestrucción a través del acto de filmar. Restaurada y reivindicada como obra capital del cine europeo.

Adolescencia, sexo y muerte en Campamento Miasma (Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, Dir. Jane Schoenbrun, 2026) (02/10/2026) Tras años de secuelas cutres y un fandom en declive, la franquicia slasher Camp Miasma es puesta en manos de Vera, una joven directora obsesiva y apasionada que creció viendo la película original en secreto. Cuando visita a la actriz de la película original —una estrella reclusa envuelta en rumores— lo que comienza como una investigación se transforma en una relación cargada de tensión e intimidad inquietante. La cineasta no binaria Jane Schoenbrun ( I Saw the TV Glow ) estrena esta comedia slasher en Cannes 2026. Con Gillian Anderson y Hannah Einbinder.

Belle (Belle / バケモノの子, Dir. Mamoru Hosoda, 2021) (09/10/2026) Suzu es una adolescente tímida que encuentra refugio en el universo virtual de U, donde se convierte en Belle, una cantante con millones de seguidores. Cuando conoce a una bestia perseguida y temida por todos, emprende una búsqueda que la llevará a descubrir la verdad detrás de esa figura. Una reinvención del cuento de La Bella y la Bestia que exploró los fenómenos de identidad digital, el bullying y la soledad adolescente. Candidata de Japón a los Óscar 2022.

Fausto (Faust, Dir. F.W. Murnau, 1926) (14/10/2026) ESTRENO ESTA SEMANA EN MUBI La cima del expresionismo alemán mudo. El viejo alquimista Fausto vende su alma al demonio Mefistófeles a cambio de la juventud eterna, desatando una cadena de tragedias. La película de Murnau es una de las obras visuales más impresionantes de la historia del cine, con efectos especiales pioneros y una fotografía que influyó en décadas de cine fantástico.

Principio y fin (Principio y fin, Dir. Arturo Ripstein, 1993) (16/10/2026) ESTRENO ESTA SEMANA EN MUBI Adaptación de la novela del Premio Nobel Naguib Mahfouz, trasladada a la Ciudad de México. Tras la muerte del padre, una madre decide sacrificar el bienestar de sus cuatro hijos para costearle la carrera universitaria al menor, el favorito. Un retrato devastador de la pobreza, el sacrificio y la destrucción de una familia. Ganó el Ariel a Mejor Película en México.

Colección de cortometrajes de Mark Jenkin (16/10/2026) ESTRENO ESTA SEMANA EN MUBI Una selección de cortometrajes del cineasta británico Mark Jenkin ( Bait , Enys Men , Rose of Nevada ), filmados en su totalidad en súper 8 y 16mm en las costas de Cornualles. Cada pieza es una exploración analógica de la memoria, la identidad y la relación entre las personas y los paisajes que habitan. Tomato (2017, 8 min.) — Retrato elegante de un artista; meditación lúdica sobre el paisaje, el color y el proceso colaborativo del cine. Vertical Shapes in a Horizontal Landscape (2018, 5 min.) — Una peregrinación a lo largo de la costa sur de Inglaterra hacia la casa de Derek Jarman en Dungeness. David Bowie is Dead (2018, 17 min.) — Un viaje de conciencia de flujo a través de Londres en el turbulento despertar de la muerte de David Bowie. I Saw the Face of God in the Jet Wash (2025, 17 min.) — Entre proyecciones alrededor del mundo, Jenkin reflexiona sobre influencias cinematográficas y la idea del hogar. Premio al Mejor Cortometraje Británico e Irlandés. Enough to Fill Up an Eggcup (2016, 36 min.) — Una parábola sobre el trabajo, la ecología y la humanidad, filmada en un pueblo pesquero de Cornualles. Cape Cornwall Calling / All the White Horses (2013, 6 min.) — Experimento según el manifiesto Silent Dancing Landscape Grain 13 de Jenkin.

Shot Reverse Shot (Shot Reverse Shot / Plan contraplan, Dir. Radu Jude y Adrian Cioflâncă, 2026) (23/10/2026) (Cortometraje, 22 min.) Entre 1985 y 1987, el periodista estadounidense Edward Serotta recorrió la Rumania comunista fotografiando la vida cotidiana bajo el régimen de Ceaușescu, en particular la comunidad judía. Lo que Serotta no sabía era que la Securitate, la policía secreta, lo seguía paso a paso y lo fotografiaba a él fotografiando. Cuarenta años después, Radu Jude y el historiador Adrian Cioflâncă reúnen los dos archivos en un plano-contraplano que revela la ironía cómica de la Historia. Presentado en la Berlinale 2026.

Toro salvaje (Raging Bull, Dir. Martin Scorsese, 1980) (23/10/2026) La vida del boxeador Jake LaMotta: su ascenso y caída dentro y fuera del ring, su brutalidad autodestructiva, sus celos enfermizos y su incapacidad para recibir el amor que su propia violencia aleja. Robert De Niro ganó el Óscar a Mejor Actor en uno de los papeles más físicos y perturbadores de la historia. Fotografiada en blanco y negro por Michael Chapman; considerada una de las grandes películas del cine americano.

El último vals (The Last Waltz, Dir. Martin Scorsese, 1978) (23/10/2026) Documental del concierto de despedida de The Band en el Winterland de San Francisco en 1976, con actuaciones de Bob Dylan, Neil Young, Van Morrison, Eric Clapton, Joni Mitchell, Muddy Waters y muchos más. Scorsese filmó con varios equipos de cine lo que se considera el mejor documental de rock de la historia.

Silencio (Silence, Dir. Martin Scorsese, 2016) (23/10/2026) Dos sacerdotes jesuitas portugueses del siglo XVII viajan a Japón para buscar a su mentor desaparecido, y se enfrentan a la brutal persecución de los cristianos por parte del gobierno Tokugawa. Una meditación profunda y austera sobre la fe, el martirio y el silencio de Dios. Con Andrew Garfield, Adam Driver y Liam Neeson.

The Chronology of Water (The Chronology of Water, Dir. Kristen Stewart, 2025) (30/10/2026) Debut en la dirección de la actriz Kristen Stewart, presentado en la sección Un Certain Regard del Festival de Cannes 2025. Adaptación de las memorias autobiográficas de Lidia Yuknavitch: una joven que crece en un entorno marcado por la violencia y el alcohol y encuentra en la natación y la escritura dos vías de escape. La película rechaza la narración cronológica y sumerge al espectador en una corriente de imágenes, frases, recuerdos y sensaciones. Producida por Ridley Scott y la propia Stewart. Con Imogen Poots, Thora Birch, Tom Sturridge y Jim Belushi.

Esta cercanía (This Closeness, Dir. Kit Zauhar, 2024) (30/10/2026) En Filadelfia, Tessa y Ben, una pareja en crisis, alquilan una habitación en el apartamento de Adam, un joven solitario y recluido que se convierte en testigo involuntario de los momentos más privados de su relación. El encierro en ese espacio diminuto desencadena una batalla íntima por el territorio, el afecto y los límites. Estrenada en SXSW 2023, con 91% en Rotten Tomatoes.

Tendaberry (Tendaberry, Dir. Haley Elizabeth Anderson, 2024) (30/10/2026) Dakota tiene 23 años y vive en el Brooklyn de inmigrantes de Coney Island y Brighton Beach. Cuando su novio regresa a Ucrania para cuidar a su padre enfermo, ella debe enfrentarse a la precariedad de aferrarse al pasado mientras forja su futuro en solitario. Estrenada en la sección Next del Festival de Sundance 2024.

Estrenos de series en Mubi (octubre 2026)

La noche que Logan despertó (La nuit où Laurier Gaudreault s’est réveillé / The Night Logan Woke Up) (15/10/2026) ESTRENO ESTA SEMANA EN MUBI Primera serie creada, escrita y dirigida por Xavier Dolan (Mamá, Matthias & Maxime), en la que también actúa. En octubre de 1991, un suceso terrible sacude a una familia de Lac Saint-Jean, Quebec: Logan viola a Mimi, de 14 años, en una noche que rompe para siempre la amistad entre dos familias. Treinta años después, Mimi —ahora tanatóloga de renombre— regresa al pueblo para velar el cuerpo de su madre y se reencuentra con todos. Los rencores y los secretos enterrados resurgen con una fuerza devastadora. Cinco episodios. Adaptación de la obra teatral de Michel Marc Bouchard, con Anne Dorval, Julie LeBreton y Patrick Hivon. Banda sonora de Hans Zimmer y David Fleming. Presentada en Sundance 2023.

Artículos

Estrenos Netflix – 12 al 18 de octubre 2026

Por: Staff Cine PREMIERE

¿Qué verás este mes?

Conoce aquí todos los estrenos de películas y también series nuevas que llegan a Netflix en octubre de 2026. Los estrenos de esta semana están destacados en amarillo. Cada mes, la plataforma de Netflix presenta nuevos títulos de películas, series y, por supuesto, de documentales y especiales. Así pues, conoce aquí los estrenos que hay de nuevas películas y también de series de Netflix.

¿Cuánto cuesta Netflix al mes?

Netflix ofrece varios planes para que elijas el más adecuado para ti. Consulta AQUÍ los beneficios y restricciones de cada uno.

Estándar con anuncios: $119 pesos al mes

Estándar: $249 pesos al mes (más posibilidad de agregar miembros extra por $69 pesos cada uno)

Premium: $329 pesos al mes (más posibilidad de agregar miembros extra por $69 pesos cada uno)

También te podría interesar los estrenos de:

Estrenos de series en Netflix (octubre 2026)

Al este del Edén (East of Eden) (01/10/2026)

Al este del Edén (East of Eden) (01/10/2026) Adaptación de la novela clásica de John Steinbeck, con Florence Pugh como la compleja antiheroína Cathy Ames. La miniserie de siete episodios explora la saga multigeneracional de la familia Trask, desde la California de principios del siglo XX, entrelazando los temas bíblicos de Caín y Abel con el libre albedrío y la ambición. Creada por Zoe Kazan, nieta del director Elia Kazan, quien filmó la versión de 1955 con James Dean.

El círculo (07/10/2026) Serie mexicana basada en la novela Los corruptores del periodista y escritor Jorge Zepeda Patterson. Cuando el asesinato de una famosa actriz desata una red de chantajes, cuatro amigos de toda la vida se ven atrapados en una espiral de secretos que amenaza con destruirlos. Dirigida por Alejandro Lozano (Matando Cabos) y protagonizada por Zuria Vega, Osvaldo Benavides, Raúl Briones y Michel Brown.

Bajo la superficie (Below) (08/10/2026) Cuando una misteriosa criatura marina aterroriza a un pueblo costero de Terranova, Canadá, un pescador recio y su familia luchan por proteger a su comunidad. Protagonizada por Josh Hartnett, Mackenzie Davis y Charlie Heaton. Creada y escrita por Jesse McKeown.

¿Es pastel? Halloween: Temporada 2 (Is It Cake? Halloween) (09/10/2026) Seis talentosos artistas pasteleros ponen a prueba sus habilidades al preparar dulces con temática de Halloween para engañar a los jueces y llevarse el premio mayor.

La chispa del amor (Take Charge of My Heart / 나를 충전해줘) (09/10/2026) Comedia romántica coreana. Un heredero de un poderoso conglomerado vive con un corazón artificial al borde de quedarse sin batería; una guionista con el don de generar electricidad en su cuerpo podría ser su única salvación. Entre ellos surge un trato que hará latir ese corazón en más de un sentido. Protagonizada por Kim Young Kwang y Chae Soo Bin.

El hotel embrujado: Temporada 2 (Haunted Hotel) (09/10/2026) Serie animada. Aun con todos los problemas sobrenaturales del Undervale, Katherine y su familia consiguen adaptarse. Pero ¿es posible construir un hogar en un hotel embrujado? Creada por Matt Roller (Rick and Morty), con las voces de Will Forte y Eliza Coupe.

100 días de engaño (100 Days of Deception / 100일의 거짓말) (10/10/2026) Drama de época coreano. En la Corea bajo ocupación japonesa de 1932, Lee Ga Kyeong, la mejor carterista de Gyeongseong, acepta una misión peligrosa: infiltrarse durante 100 días en el gobierno colonial japonés como espía del movimiento de independencia. Dirigida por Yoo In-shik (La asombrosa abogada Woo) y protagonizada por Kim You-jung y Park Jinyoung (GOT7).

Hollywood Arts (15/10/2026) ESTRENO EN NETFLIX ESTA SEMANA Spin-off de Victorious (Nickelodeon). La actriz frustrada Trina Vega (Daniella Monet) regresa a su antigua escuela de artes como maestra sustituta, donde sin quererlo inspira a una nueva generación de ambiciosos estudiantes. Creada por Jake Farrow y Samantha Martin.

La diplomática: Temporada 4 (The Diplomat) (15/10/2026) ESTRENO EN NETFLIX ESTA SEMANA Mientras Kate lucha por salvar su matrimonio, un ataque y un encubrimiento amenazan con destruir la alianza que forjó entre EE. UU. y el Reino Unido.

Las madres de los Pingüinos: Temporada 2 (Matki pingwinów) (21/10/2026) Serie polaca. Kama, Ula, Tatiana y Jerzy están decididos a dirigir su propia escuela, pero enfrentan dificultades para cuidar de sus hijos y de sí mismos. La primera temporada, dirigida por Klara Kochanska y Jagoda Szelc, fue elegida por el New York Times entre las mejores series extranjeras de 2024 y ganó el Águila a Mejor Serie de la Academia Polaca de Cine.

Nadie quiere esto: Temporada 3 (Nobody Wants This) (22/10/2026) Joanne y Noah dan un nuevo paso en su relación, pero deben enfrentar los conflictos y las intromisiones familiares, además de arriesgarse con un gran salto de fe.

Grande de España (Fading Grandeur) (23/10/2026) Comedia dramática española de seis episodios. El arruinado marqués Don Leandro intenta vender su decadente palacete madrileño a Sofía Carrington, una acaudalada empresaria con sus propios planes. Mientras el juego de seducción y negociación avanza, ambos descubren que el otro no es exactamente lo que parece. Creada por Álvaro Fernández-Armero y Juan Cavestany; protagonizada por Antonio de la Torre y Alexandra Jiménez.

Lupin: Parte 4 (23/10/2026) Tras pasar cuatro años en prisión, Assane quiere comenzar una nueva vida con su familia, pero cuando alguien decide imitar sus robos, Lupin vuelve a sus ardides geniales. Protagonizada por Omar Sy.

Estrenos de películas en Netflix (octubre 2026)

Contra el huracán (Dir. Jorge Michel Grau, 2026) (23/10/2026)

Las cartas de la vida (02/10/2026) Original de Netflix. A través de emotivas cartas, una madre soltera y un recluso forjan un vínculo que da paso a la redención, a la esperanza y a un amor improbable.

Animales (Animals, Dir. Ben Affleck, 2026) (09/10/2026) Un candidato a alcalde de Los Ángeles y su esposa se ven arrastrados a una red de engaños cuando secuestran a su hijo. Mientras se desesperan por reunir el rescate, las decisiones que toman amenazan con destruir su mundo. Affleck dirige, co-escribe y protagoniza junto a Kerry Washington y Gillian Anderson, luego de que Matt Damon abandonara el proyecto por su compromiso con The Odyssey de Christopher Nolan.

Lo dejamos acá (Dir. Hernán Goldfrid, 2026) (16/10/2026) ESTRENO EN NETFLIX ESTA SEMANA Comedia negra argentina. Un psicoanalista pragmático que ha perdido la fe en los métodos convencionales comienza a sobrepasar todos los límites éticos con sus pacientes. Protagonizada por Ricardo Darín y Diego Peretti.

Contra el huracán (Dir. Jorge Michel Grau, 2026) (23/10/2026) Thriller de supervivencia mexicano basado en hechos reales. En medio del mar, los hermanos Wirpul y Candi luchan por sobrevivir cuando una tormenta inesperada se transforma en el huracán Otis de categoría 5, frente a las costas de Acapulco. Con Benny Emmanuel y Kristyan Ferrer.

Colisión (Dir. Daniel Sánchez Arévalo, 2026) (30/10/2026) Primer thriller del director español conocido por AzulOscuroCasiNegro y Diecisiete. En plena crisis económica española, un grupo de atracadores irrumpe en un banco de Madrid y lo que parecía un robo más se convierte en una partida de engaños donde nadie es exactamente lo que aparenta. Con Laia Costa, Karra Elejalde, Luis Zahera y Álvaro Cervantes.

El regalo de cumpleaños (Felicidades, Dir. Álex de la Iglesia, 2026) (30/10/2026) Comedia argentina basada en la exitosa obra teatral de Mariano Pensotti. Un marido intenta revertir la crisis de pareja con una fiesta de cumpleaños perfecta para su mujer, pero la irrupción de un médium desata el caos y pone en evidencia los secretos de todos los invitados en una casa que parece tener vida propia. Primera colaboración del director español (El día de la bestia, La comunidad) con el cine argentino. Protagonizada por Adrián Suar, Griselda Siciliani y Diego Capusotto.

Schumacher 94: Nace una leyenda (02/10/2026) La primera victoria de Michael Schumacher en el Campeonato Mundial de Fórmula 1 cobra vida con entrevistas personales y material de archivo de la legendaria temporada 1994.

TYSON (13/10/2026) ESTRENO EN NETFLIX ESTA SEMANA Documental en cuatro partes que explora la explosiva vida de Mike Tyson, una de las figuras más temidas y fascinantes del mundo del deporte.

El de Matthew Perry (27/10/2026) Serie documental en la que familiares, amigos y compañeros de la estrella de Friends recuerdan su éxito, su largo y abierto combate contra las adicciones y la trágica muerte que conmocionó al mundo en 2023.

Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2 (20/10/2026) Night City. Un nuevo grupo de mercenarios. El mismo infierno. Una historia independiente contada en diez episodios del mundo de Cyberpunk 2077.

Entre series originales, capítulos nuevos, temporadas que hacen su debut y películas que podrás disfrutar desde tu casa, los estrenos de Amazon Prime Video este mes se perfilan para ofrecer mucho entretenimiento.

Encuentra los estreno de películas y series en Amazon Prime Video de esta semana destacados en amarillo.

¿Cuál es el costo de Prime Video?

Después del periodo de prueba de 30 días, Amazon Prime Video cuesta $99 pesos al mes en México , mientras que el plan anual tiene un costo de $899 pesos . Asimismo, disfrutas del resto de los beneficios de Amazon, como envíos gratis en 1 o 2 días a nivel nacional.

Ahora, que si lo que quieres es tener acceso al catálogo sin anuncios comerciales, tendrás que pagar $50 pesos adicionales. Conoce más detalles de Amazon Prime Video .

Asimismo, a través del catálogo de Amazon Prime Video también te puedes suscribir a las siguientes plataformas sin salir del servicio de Prime: HBO Max, Paramount Plus, ViX Premium, Crunchyroll, MGM Plus, MUBI, Looke, Adrenalina Pura, Sony One o Fox Sports, entre otros.

Películas de estreno en Amazon Prime Video, octubre 2026

Drive: The Pretenders (Dir. Sergej Moya, 2026) (28/10/2026) Comedia romántica alemana basada en la exitosa novela de Wattpad de Tamara Lush. Sarah Jenkins, una joven mecánica con sueños de convertirse en piloto, acuerda fingir un compromiso con Dante Annunziata, la estrella más escandalosa del automovilismo mundial, para salvar la reputación de él y abrirse paso en las carreras. Pero la mentira pronto amenaza con destruir sus planes y algo más. Con Lisa-Marie Koroll y Amin Baahmed.

Apocalipsis Z: Nuevo mundo (Dir. Carles Torrens, 2026) (30/10/2026) Secuela del fenómeno global Apocalipsis Z: El principio del fin (2024), la película original internacional más vista de Prime Video ese año. Las Islas Canarias se han convertido en el último refugio de Europa tras el brote del virus TSJ. Cuando una misión especial parte hacia la península en busca de suministros vitales, la operación se transforma en una carrera desesperada por la supervivencia entre hordas de infectados y lealtades divididas. Basada en las novelas de Manel Loureiro, con Carlos Alcaide, Julia Martínez y Berta Vázquez.

Series de estreno en Amazon Prime Video, octubre 2026

Carrie (07/10/2026)

Prefiero la muerte (02/10/2026) Serie mexicana de comedia y horror. Tras ser mordido por un zombie en una tienda local, Archie, el eterno perdedor de la preparatoria, une fuerzas con su mejor amiga gótica y su amor platónico para detener un plan maligno que amenaza con desatar el apocalipsis en Mendoza. Dirigida por Sebastián Sariñana, con Fernanda Castillo y Diego Bernal en los roles protagónicos.

Carrie (07/10/2026) Primera adaptación televisiva de la novela debut de Stephen King. Basada en el clásico de 1974, esta reinvención de ocho episodios traslada la historia de Carrie White al mundo de las redes sociales, donde el bullying adquiere nuevas dimensiones. El propio Stephen King, que calificó la serie de «brillante», participa como productor ejecutivo junto a su creador. Creada, escrita y producida por Mike Flanagan (La maldición de Hill House, Misa de medianoche). Protagonizada por Summer H. Howell como Carrie y Samantha Sloyan como su madre. Con Matthew Lillard y Amber Midthunder.

Masterplan (16/10/2026) ESTRENO EN AMAZON PRIME VIDEO ESTA SEMANA Comedia de acción franco-italiana. Un legendario ladrón (Stanley Tucci) reúne a dos jóvenes expertos para robar la Mona Lisa del Louvre: Chiara, una brillante hacker italiana (Simona Tabasco, The White Lotus), y Jay, un especialista francés en explosivos (Victor Belmondo). Antes de iniciar el atraco, les revela que son hermanos perdidos y que él es su padre. Dirigida por Thomas Vincent (Reacher, Bodyguard). Primera coproducción original en inglés entre Francia e Italia para Prime Video.

La lista terminal: Temporada 2 (True Believer) (21/10/2026) James Reece enfrenta una nueva conspiración global mientras emprende un violento viaje de redención. Basada en True Believer, la segunda novela de la saga de Jack Carr, esta temporada muestra cómo el ex Navy SEAL encuentra un nuevo propósito tras completar su lista. Protagonizada por Chris Pratt.

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter .", "links": [{"text": "Morning Links", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/morning-links/"}, {"text": "Breakfast with ARTnews", "url": "https://cloud.email.artnews.com/artnews-signup/"}]}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Good morning!"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Cindy Sherman is the cover star of the second volume of Chanel’s Arts & Culture magazine."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Austrian presidential candidate Gunther Fehlinger-Jahn says that if elected, he’ll return a 16th-century Aztec headdress to Mexico, currently located in Vienna’s Weltmuseum."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "A descendant of the 19th-century artist Jules-Eugène Lenepveu is taking legal action to demand the removal of Marc Chagall’s painting on the ceiling of the Palais Garnier opera house."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "The Headlines"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "SHERMAN IN CHANEL TWEED . On October 23, Chanel is dropping the second volume of Arts & Culture , its free 300-page magazine, graced with new photographs by Cindy Sherman , wearing — you might have guessed— Chanel. More like raw, unsewn Chanel, in the form of their archival fabrics that Sherman draped and wrapped around herself. As Vanity Fair reported, the brand sent Sherman rolls of vintage fabric to do with what she pleased. “I said, ‘Well, is it okay if I cut things up, cut holes into them and whatnot?’” Sherman told Vanity Fair . Yes, Chanel was very much ok with it, and just like that , the fashion brand had direct, exclusive access to Sherman’s latest series of photographs, titled “Fabric Matrons,” which will also be shown at Hauser & Wirth ’s Mayfair gallery during Frieze London . From the looks of a few photos published in Vanity Fair , it does seem like Sherman effectively played dress-up, cutting poncho-style holes in a whole lot of Chanel tweeds, and not to an unflattering or ridiculous effect. Sherman’s characters appear thoughtful, if solemn, as though weighed down by experience, draped in glamorous, bejeweled get-ups. “At one point I remember writing in my journal, ‘Who the fuck wants to look at pictures of old ladies anyway?’” Sherman said. I guess we’re about to find out. To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter .

Good morning!

Cindy Sherman is the cover star of the second volume of Chanel’s Arts & Culture magazine.

Austrian presidential candidate Gunther Fehlinger-Jahn says that if elected, he’ll return a 16th-century Aztec headdress to Mexico, currently located in Vienna’s Weltmuseum.

A descendant of the 19th-century artist Jules-Eugène Lenepveu is taking legal action to demand the removal of Marc Chagall’s painting on the ceiling of the Palais Garnier opera house.

The Headlines

SHERMAN IN CHANEL TWEED . On October 23, Chanel is dropping the second volume of Arts & Culture , its free 300-page magazine, graced with new photographs by Cindy Sherman , wearing — you might have guessed— Chanel. More like raw, unsewn Chanel, in the form of their archival fabrics that Sherman draped and wrapped around herself. As Vanity Fair reported, the brand sent Sherman rolls of vintage fabric to do with what she pleased. “I said, ‘Well, is it okay if I cut things up, cut holes into them and whatnot?’” Sherman told Vanity Fair . Yes, Chanel was very much ok with it, and just like that , the fashion brand had direct, exclusive access to Sherman’s latest series of photographs, titled “Fabric Matrons,” which will also be shown at Hauser & Wirth ’s Mayfair gallery during Frieze London . From the looks of a few photos published in Vanity Fair , it does seem like Sherman effectively played dress-up, cutting poncho-style holes in a whole lot of Chanel tweeds, and not to an unflattering or ridiculous effect. Sherman’s characters appear thoughtful, if solemn, as though weighed down by experience, draped in glamorous, bejeweled get-ups. “At one point I remember writing in my journal, ‘Who the fuck wants to look at pictures of old ladies anyway?’” Sherman said. I guess we’re about to find out. Related Articles Belinda Tate Departs Indianapolis Museum of Art, Glasgow's Arts Community Fights to Save CCA and Others, and More: Morning Links for October 9, 2026 Art Basel/UBS Report's Surprising Findings, Artists Say Tang Contemporary Owes Them Money and Artwork, and More: Morning Links for October 8, 2026

RUFFLED FEATHERS . Austrian presidential candidate Gunther Fehlinger-Jahn says that if elected, he’ll return a 16th-century feathered Aztec headdress to Mexico, currently in Vienna’s Weltmuseum , reports The Art Newspaper . For decades, the Mexican government has been requesting the return of the 4½ -foot-high and 5¾ -foot-wide, ornate Quetzal headdress, or quetzalapanecayotl , that once belonged to Aztec ruler Moctezuma, though it is believed he never wore it. It’s unclear how the artifact left Mexico in the first place. “Austria and Mexico should negotiate a bilateral solution based on friendship rather than confrontation,” Fehlinger-Jahn said. In 2020, Mexico requested to borrow the headdress for an exhibition, but Austrian officials refused to do so, citing the object’s fragility as the reason.

The Digest

A descendant of the 19th-century classical artist Jules-Eugène Lenepveu is taking legal action to demand the removal of Marc Chagall ’s iconic painting on the ceiling of the Palais Garnier opera house in Paris, because it covers an original oil on copper fresco by Lenepveu. [ The Guardian ]

In March 2027, French Galerie Christophe Gaillard is opening a new space in Bangkok, inside the Bangkok Kunsthalle . [ The Art Newspaper, France ]

A decade and a half after Amy Winehouse ’s death, her life is still being explored — even excavated — in a new exhibition full of simulacra of the singer’s personal items by artist Alex Margo Arden , titled “Nothing Personal,” on view through January 23. [ ARTnews ]

Two stolen Auguste Renoir paintings were recovered in “record time,” and are currently being examined for any damage by conservation experts, before their planned return to the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, according to France’s ministry of culture. [ press release ]

A Welsh medieval myth claiming that the Roman emperor Magnus Maximus set up a military camp near Frenni Fawr in Wales has just been backed by archeological evidence. [ The Guardian ]

The Kicker

A RADICAL WELCOME. Zoë Ryan , director of the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles, recently discussed how she plans to steer the museum into the next era and make it an anchoring focal point of the Westside Los Angeles arts district, reports the Los Angeles Times . For one, she is working to raise the profile of educational projects, including professional training for teachers who bring arts curricula to classrooms. Overlooked women artists are also a top priority, as shown with two major fall surveys of artists Huguette Caland and Mavis Pusey . Among other “bold projects,” Ryan wants to host a ground-floor room for artmaking, reading, and study, called the Nook, which she views as a “radical welcome.”

Yufan Lu: The Devil is in the Details

Artist Yufan Lu visited over thirty cosmetic surgery clinics in China with her self-portrait, asking consultants to assess her face. Her book Make Me Beautiful uses photography and text to document those encounters.

By Gaia Squarci. Photographs by Yufan Lu

You have a dividing line that splits your face into upper and lower halves,” one consultant tells Yufan Lu. “It brings bad luck to your career and wealth.” The artist turns cosmetic surgery consultations into a study of how beauty standards are sold.

The tone is always matter-of-fact, but no two verdicts are the same. A protruding mouth that needs bone surgery, body fat above the standard, a nose too wide, an asymmetrical chin. One consultant praises her eyes as among the few features that work; another begins by pointing them out as the problem. Celebrities are invoked as benchmarks, and it’s hard not to start scanning one’s own face for flaws.

The pressure is constant. “What do you need to think about? We’ve already analyzed all the pros and cons for you, there’s nothing much left to think about.” Lu’s images bring together her self-portrait, the pre-surgery portraits used by the clinics, and photographs of the clinics themselves, punctuated with classical depictions of beauty from art history and feminine symbols. Their calm, pastel-colored interiors are friendly spaces where self-confidence can be completely shattered.

The book Make Me Beautiful is published by Editorial RM and available at the price of 40 Euro.

content.article_text:
P rem Sahib turns the city inside out, twists it around and rips it apart. His show at the De La Warr Pavilion in Bexhill, a sort of mid-career survey for the 44-year-old English artist, is full of private spaces and urban nightmares that have been gutted and left on display. It’s minimal, claustrophobic, intense stuff.

A sodium street lamp hangs upside down from the ceiling, casting its sickly pale orange glow across the gallery. You feel like you’ve stumbled into some urban back alley where physics has been flipped, it has all the threat of an underpass, but surreal and inverted. Nearby, three puffer jackets have been squeezed between sheets of glass – are these the blokes who were waiting for you in the underpass? Or are they three strangers who you’ve caught mid-embrace?

That’s what Sahib does, over and over: he plays with the line between terror and pleasure, threat and intimacy, public and private.

So much here is geared towards an atmosphere of discomfort. There’s a deep bass throb echoing out of one space, its tone eventually rising to an ear-piercing squeal, before settling back into a chest-rattling sub. A table has been made out of a grossly overgrown flea’s body, a street sign has been left blank but its light is still on. Two space heaters constantly flick on and ramp up the temperature. It is liminal, weird, uncomfortable.

Queerness is central to Sahib’s work. The double doors you pass as you walk in were taken from a Mile End leather bar that closed in 2022, the water fountain encased in resin is from Chariots sauna in Shoreditch which closed in 2016. Private spaces, places of intimate pleasure, that have been erased from the city.

In one of his signature resin panels, clear droplets have accumulated on a sheet of black aluminium, like sweat gathering on a nightclub wall. You can almost smell it, almost feel hot, damp, writhing people coming together somewhere nearby. Hung up high, two acrylic discs nod to the visual results of rapid HIV tests. There’s intimacy here, but risk too.

Risk, and threat: an obsidian mirror hangs cracked on the wall, burbling out discordant sounds, a slowed down recording of a homophobic rant sent to Sahib on a gay chat room.

Is this all about architecture, as the wall text here insists? I don’t know. Architecture is already about architecture – I don’t need art to make me think deep thoughts about buildings. This feels way more intimate than that description coldly implies. It’s about bodies being pressed together, sweat dripping down a wall, and feeling like it’s all about to be torn away from you.

The whole way through, it’s as if Sahib is asking: what happens when the places that matter to me, where I express myself, are destroyed? What is left for me, for us? Who decides which spaces can survive, who decides what communities are worth preserving, who decides where bodies get to exist?

after newsletter promotion

I don’t think it all works. The recording of Suella Braverman hatefully talking about the migrant crisis that you listen to while looking out at the sea is a bit on the nose, and the little dotty images of the horizon that line one wall don’t really add a huge amount.

But for the most part, Sahib is brilliant, with an incredible knack for crushingly intense minimalist atmospherics. He’s been one of the most interesting artists working in this country for more than a decade now, and a big institutional show like this feels long overdue.

Prem Sahib: Chamber is at De La Warr Pavilion, Bexhill, from 10 October 2026 to 3 January 2027

content.article_text:
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the country’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of soldiers and officers interviewed in the investigative documentary NAZA and prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

The award-winning documentary, directed by the Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza. The film is in cinemas, including in the UK and the US, and will be shown in more than 50 countries.

In a letter addressed to the attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, the IDF chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, and the Shin Bet head, David Zini, the Israeli prime minister demanded they “act urgently to uncover the identity of all those who are involved or appear in the libel film”.

Netanyahu also called for “the opening of a criminal investigation and prosecution for serious information security offences, criminal defamation, and harming Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

NAZA premiered last month at the Venice international film festival, where it won the special jury prize after receiving the longest ovation in the event’s history. It takes its name from an acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicate how many civilians it expects to be killed in an airstrike .

The Israeli government has fiercely attacked Abraham and Szor, threatening to strip them of their citizenship and accusing them of treason. Government supporters have vowed to hound the film-makers on their return to Israel and picketed Szor’s parents’ home in Savyon, chanting: “Death sentence to traitors.”

Zamir denounced the film as an “attack on the state of Israel”, accusing it of spreading “lies and blood libels” . He had earlier ordered military and legal officials to identify the soldiers featured and examine possible legal action against them. However, the military advocate general, Itai Ofir, said criminal prosecution would require evidence of security violations or disclosure of classified material, although disciplinary measures remained possible.

The protection of journalistic sources is a cornerstone of press freedom under international human rights standards and disclosure orders are permitted only under stringent conditions.

Ricardo Gutiérrez, the general secretary of the European Federation of Journalists, representing over 320,000 journalists, said: “These threats constitute a blatant act of intimidation against journalists who have simply been doing their job, in strict accordance with ethical standards and in the public interest. I am not surprised by this outburst, which confirms that this regime is prepared to do anything to cover up its crimes against humanity and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.”

A Guardian spokesperson said: “After first threatening to strip NAZA’s directors of their Israeli citizenship, the Israeli government is now calling for an investigation into their journalistic sources. These moves are all attempts to distract from the urgent questions the film asks about the mass killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Journalists should be free to pursue public interest investigations without threats or harassment.”

NAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. Earlier this month, a Guardian spokesperson said the “process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film.”

In the past three years the team behind the film has “ interviewed more than 100 sources familiar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes”, the Guardian spokesperson added.

In recent days, the Israeli government has promoted an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA, in an attempt to challenge the real film’s findings. Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made NAZA: The Real Story, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians.

Film industry heavyweights across the globe, including the heads of the Locarno film festival, have expressed solidarity with Abraham and Szor , saying they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ rights to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal”.

Digger, the ambitious eco-fable starring Tom Cruise and directed by Alejandro G Iñárritu, is heading for an even worse financial outcome than previously thought , with reports suggesting it will lose around $245m (£185m), placing it among the biggest disasters in movie history.

According to a report in Variety , Digger’s estimated second weekend revenue in North America of $3.2m is a 60% drop on its opening weekend figure of $8m, meaning its current domestic gross is $14.4m, for a global total of $35.3m , with a projected final box office total of around $50m worldwide.

Though precise figures are not available, Variety estimates that Digger’s production costs are $160m-180m (well over the original budget of $125m), with another $100m spent on marketing the film. Another $15m was potentially on hand for awards-season marketing, but this is likely to be scaled back after the film’s failure. Given that cinemas keep around half the revenue of ticket sales, Variety estimates the film would need to make around $350m to cover costs. (A spokesperson for Digger’s producing studio Warner Bros, says that break-even point is $300m, suggesting a production spend of $150m.)

A $245m loss would put Digger on a par with such legendary turkeys as Cutthroat Island ($222m loss, adjusted for inflation), Mortal Engines ($224m adjusted) and The Marvels ($205-$250m adjusted).

Reaction to the film has likely played a key role in its underperformance, with critical opinion radically divided. In the Guardian, chief film critic Peter Bradshaw called it “an exasperatingly shallow, laborious, self-congratulatory satire” in a two-star review , while Guardian Australia’s deputy culture editor Sian Cain took the opposite position, describing it as “a masterpiece” . Warner Bros, whose last release this is before its takeover by David Ellison’s Skydance , tried to play into the controversy with a post-release advertising campaign quoting its negative notices , but it seems to have had little effect.

So far, 2026 has been a disappointing year for Warner Bros, as it prepares for new ownership, with poorly performing releases such as Supergirl and The Bride! and co-chairs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy due to leave ahead of the takeover. This contrasts with a successful 2025, in which releases such as A Minecraft Movie, Sinners and F1 propelled it to the second most successful studio, behind Disney.

Elsewhere, the Aaron Sorkin-directed The Social Reckoning also failed to live up to expectations on its first weekend, taking an estimated $5.5m at the North American box office and $9m globally . The sequel to The Social Network, which stars Jeremy Strong as Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg and Mikey Madison as whistleblower Frances Haugen, was comprehensively beaten by Jessica Chastain horror The Other Mommy, which led the North American box office with an estimated $27.5m, part of a global take of $45.2m.

content.article_text:
Reza Rahadian, Eva Celia and Christine Hakim Talk “The Sea Speaks His Name”, 1998, Political Memory and Finding Truth in Performance

Reza Rahadian, Eva Celia and Christine Hakim discuss “The Sea Speaks His Name”, Indonesia’s political past, acting and memory.

“The Sea Speaks His Name” brings together Reza Rahadian , Eva Celia and Christine Hakim in a story rooted in Indonesia’s political upheaval of the late 1990s, following young activists whose lives, relationships and families are changed by the violence surrounding the period. Based on the work of Leila S. Chudori, the film also marks another collaboration between Rahadian and director Yosep Anggi Noen , while giving Celia one of her first major acting roles after spending much of the previous decade concentrating on music.

The Sea Speaks His Name is screening at Busan International Film Festival

For Rahadian, the project actually began many years earlier. He had already played the character in a short film made around eight years ago for the launch of the book, giving him an early understanding of Laut and the world around him. Returning to the character for the feature therefore felt less like starting from zero than revisiting someone he had already encountered. As for playing a university student despite his current age, Rahadian joked that this was not particularly difficult since “most of the students” in the 1990s looked considerably older anyway.

Celia plays Rati Anjani, an art student involved in the movement and its organization. She meets Laut during a protest and the two gradually fall in love. Celia describes the relationship as one based strongly on intellectual intimacy and equality, with the pair sharing similar hopes for the future and a common understanding of the political work around them. Having known Rahadian for approximately 12 years, she felt that their existing familiarity also made the collaboration particularly natural.

Rahadian refers to a phrase associated with the period, “cinta bersemi setelah aksi” — love that grows after a demonstration. For him, this mixture of political commitment and romance is one of the most human aspects of the story. Two people can be participating in a movement driven by larger ideals while simultaneously discovering someone with whom they share those same convictions. He was also particularly pleased to work with Celia again, describing her as an actress he had wanted to collaborate with for some time.

His own memories of the 1998 period are fragmented but vivid. Rahadian was still in his final year of elementary school, but remembers his mother returning from work and telling him that she had travelled through the Sudirman area on a tank because roads and public transportation were blocked. He also remembers unrest reaching his own neighborhood and people taking goods from a store. At the time, he did not understand why any of it was happening. Only later, through books, news reports and his growing interest in politics, did he begin to understand the scale of what he had witnessed as a child.

Those memories helped him approach Laut, whose personality is more complicated than that of the stereotypically vocal activist. Rahadian describes him as contemplative and relatively quiet, carrying fear and courage at the same time. That contradiction became important because Laut is participating in a political struggle while not necessarily possessing the extroverted temperament people might associate with a movement leader. Even his attraction toward another senior figure within the organization remains restrained by hierarchy and his own reluctance to confront his feelings openly.

The character’s disappearance halfway through the film presented another challenge. Rahadian realized that his voice would have to continue carrying Laut’s presence after his physical absence from the screen. Narration consequently became essential, not simply as exposition but as another form of performance. He wanted the emotion behind the words to preserve the character’s presence and allow audiences to continue feeling him even after he was no longer visible.

For Celia, the emotional consequences of that disappearance become particularly demanding. Anjani initially refuses to accept that Laut has been kidnapped and begins interpreting signs and superstitions as evidence that he may still communicate with her. Celia describes this as a coping mechanism, a way for someone overwhelmed by loss and uncertainty to create an alternative explanation she can emotionally survive. Many of her scenes were therefore less physically difficult than psychologically exhausting.

Christine Hakim approaches the same absence from another direction, playing Laut’s mother, a photographer whose son leaves and simply does not return. For Hakim, the difficulty lies in portraying a parent forced to continue living without certainty. She sees the role as another example of the very different women she has been offered at this stage of her career, following characters including the woman she played in “Four Seasons in Java”. She expressed particular gratitude that younger directors continue trusting her with demanding parts and considers supporting younger filmmakers one of her responsibilities as an established figure in Indonesian cinema.

Hakim and Rahadian have already played mother and son several times, something that makes establishing their connection relatively easy even though the characters themselves are always different. Hakim considers him a “brilliant actor” and feels that their existing chemistry allows them to concentrate on adapting to the specific circumstances of each new story rather than having to manufacture familiarity from the beginning. She also points toward another upcoming project in which they again play mother and son, illustrating how differently the same pairing can function depending on the characters.

Aging has not made Hakim less interested in difficult roles. Quite the opposite: she says she now has to work five or even ten times harder than when she was younger. Physical preparation, diet, concentration and maintaining enough energy on set all require greater discipline. She rejects the idea of trying to remain permanently associated with the romantic roles of her youth, arguing simply that time cannot be stopped and an actor has to continue adapting along with life.

That adaptation also means participating actively in the construction of a character. Hakim speaks of performance through the combination of body, soul and mind. Costume, makeup and visual design may provide the physical exterior, but an actor must still discover how to give that exterior a soul. She is comfortable offering directors suggestions when they emerge from this process, citing her character in Four Seasons in Java, for whom she proposed having a chicken as a companion because it better reflected the woman’s isolated existence than a more conventional pet would have.

Rahadian and Celia describe Anggi Noen’s directing style as precise without being rigid. The director knows exactly what he needs from a scene, but creates enough space for the actors to explore how to reach it. Celia particularly appreciates that he establishes an environment and context rather than ordering an actor to produce a specific emotion. Rahadian summarizes the method even more directly: Anggi “never directs the feeling. He directs the motive.” Instead of asking someone to cry, he gives them the reason that might eventually produce tears.

The production could nevertheless be demanding. Rahadian remembers a major nighttime sequence in a cornfield as one of the most difficult, involving a large cast, rain, mud and filming into the early hours of the morning. The corn itself had been planted specifically for the production, requiring the filmmakers to wait around three months until the location was ready. Other scenes worked precisely because the production refused to artificially enlarge its spaces. A small family kitchen, for example, forced the actors to constantly move around and bump into one another, creating an intimacy and everyday busyness that Rahadian felt worked beautifully.

The political context inevitably led the conversation toward contemporary Indonesia. Rahadian believes civil space today is “a little bit shrinking”, although he emphasizes that conditions remain considerably better than in the 1990s. People can read, criticize the government and speak openly in ways that were previously far more dangerous, but new forms of intimidation have appeared, including anonymous cyberattacks and attempts to provoke conflict between citizens. The methods may have changed, but he feels some of the tensions explored in the film remain relevant.

At the same time, he is optimistic about Indonesian cinema itself. The range of Indonesian titles appearing internationally reflects what he sees as an increasingly diverse industry willing to engage with different social realities through very different genres and styles. Celia, meanwhile, is particularly grateful simply to have returned to acting. After her first feature around 12 years ago, she spent roughly a decade concentrating primarily on music before moving back toward cinema. “The Sea Speaks His Name” has now brought her to her first international film festival, something she describes with considerable gratitude.

Rahadian is also continuing to balance acting and directing. He is currently developing his second feature, “Casparina”, which he was pitching at the Asian Project Market. Based on his own family history, the film concerns the absence of a mother during the political upheaval surrounding 1965. His grandmother was exiled in Utrecht and returned to Indonesia 32 years later, after the fall of Suharto, attempting to reconnect with children who had grown up without her. Rahadian witnessed that homecoming himself as a teenager and now considers it the story he wants to tell next.

Hakim is expected to play the grandmother and has already begun turning down other projects so she can prepare properly for the role. Celia, meanwhile, is preparing for an action film whose details she cannot yet reveal. Their future projects may move in very different directions, but “The Sea Speaks His Name” brings all three together around a subject that continues to resonate: how personal lives absorb political history, and how love, memory and family persist even when someone is suddenly removed from them.

Excerpt: Reza Rahadian, Eva Celia and Christine Hakim discuss political memory, acting, loss and “The Sea Speaks His Name”.

content.article_text:
Galerie von Vertes is staging a major survey of Pop art, debuting in London before making its way to Zurich. The new exhibition, “ Pop-ism ,” brings together work from across more than six decades—from 1946 through 2008—and by some of the movement’s most recognized names, including Andy Warhol, Keith Haring, Robert Rauschenberg, Niki de Saint Phalle, Tom Wesselmann, Robert Indiana, and John Chamberlain.

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

London specifically is an apropos backdrop for “Pop-ism,” as Pop art first emerged in the English capital in the mid-1950s, pioneered by artists like Richard Hamilton and Eduardo Paolozzi. The exhibition premieres alongside PAD London, which runs October 13–18. Following that first week, it will travel to Zurich and continue through December 4. It is a coincidental boon for Pop art fans around the globe, as the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum is also running a Pop retrospective in New York, on view through January 2027.

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

Claes Oldenburg, Tea Bag (1966). Courtesy of Galerie von Vertes.

The title of the Galerie von Vertes show comes from Warhol himself, who used the term to describe the moment the long run of insular, theory-driven art movements gave way to something looser and more accessible. The show traces the shift toward approachability through a wide lens, presenting Chamberlain’s sculptures built from crushed automobile parts; Haring’s graphic, energetic cityscapes; Saint Phalle’s voluptuous Nana figures; Rauschenberg’s layered collages; and Wesselmann’s flattened, boldly colored compositions.

Complementing pieces from Pop icons are works by artists who paved the way for the then-burgeoning movement: The exhibition features Alexander Calder’s stabiles, Fernand Léger’s industrial still lifes, and Yayoi Kusama’s early soft sculptures, to name a few. Together, they illuminate a through line from Pop’s immediate predecessors to its heyday.

John Chamberlain, Potatopoultry (2008). Courtesy of Galerie von Vertes.

What Galerie von Vertes’s exhibition makes apparent is that Pop artists share more than a visual style; they share an instinct, an openness to abandoning the serious and rarefied materials, motifs, and techniques of generations prior in favor of accessible, mass imagery, commercial processes, and materials from everyday life. Instead of approaching art as something precious and exclusive, each artist approached art-making first and foremost as a conduit for ideas, borrowing the strategies and logic of advertising, embracing repetition, and finding new aesthetic potentials from within consumer and mass culture, rather than attempting to stand outside of it. In doing so, many of the artists took on the same attributes as celebrities or brands in their own right—a phenomenon that is treated within the exhibition as an indispensable facet of the work rather than an extraneous historical fact.

Tom Wesselmann, Daytime Still Life with Blonde and Goldfish (1999). Courtesy of Galerie von Vertes.

Galerie von Vertes also makes a case for Pop art’s long reach—both geographic and temporal—as it provided the fertile ground for successive movements, such as Neo-Pop, Minimalism, Conceptual art, and Political Pop. Accompanied by an exhibition catalog featuring a selection of important works by influential Pop artists and texts by art historian Dr. Quirine Verlinde, “Pop-ism” is a cogent exploration of what remains one of the most influential movements of the past century.

“ Pop-ism ” is on view at Galerie von Vertes through December 4, 2026.

content.article_text:
B ritish influencer/singer/content creator Chiara King stars as influencer/singer/content creator Chiara King, or some kind of parafictional version of herself, in this quease-inducing thriller exercise. The ick gets generated not necessarily by the eventual gore that erupts in the last reel, but by the tacky weirdness of the way the film apes the mannerisms of social media reels and streaming nonsense to both satirise the ugly side of the business but also exploit and profit off it at the same time. On one level, it’s an eerily clever exercise in bad faith, like a poor Michael Haneke film (think Funny Games) for gen-Z kicks; on another, maybe it’s just a crappy ripoff of online tropes that have been way overexposed already. Or both.

Anyway, here’s what happens: influencer Chiara gets invited to visit Copenhagen by a tourist organisation, a deal set up by her avaricious manager Alice (Jazmine Summer). Of course, this means practically every moment of her time awake in the city will be filmed, both by Chiara herself on her trusty smartphone, or a camera crew led by director Mike (played by Mike Nybroe, who is also director of The Influencer Project, ha ha); Mike is supported by sound man Daniel (Daniel Parmo) and cameraman Victor (Luca Storm). The early sections turn in all the influence-slop you would expect, with shopping trips to trendy merch vendors such as Baum und Pferdgarten, and meals at fancy local restaurants, and then a livestreamed visit to a “haunted house,” which is the big thing on Instagram and TikTok these days.

But the product placement is somewhat interrupted by moments of real fear (or “real fear”) when Chiara starts getting threatening direct messages (from someone calling themselves KingSlayer) who wants her to stop talking for reasons not clearly explained at first, otherwise he will kill and rape her, not necessarily in that order. This unsurprisingly creates a pall over Chiara’s trip, but if she just quits and goes home she’ll miss out on $100k in deals, so that’s not an option.

So are we supposed to despise Chiara for her greed or applaud her girl-boss fortitude in not being intimidated by a stalker? And what to make of the film’s claims that this was partly inspired by real incidents of stalking? Nybroe and co work the debate into the endless stream of comments we see scrolling alongside Chiara’s livestream – a river of chat that doesn’t let up even when the credits start to roll, ersatz dialectics for an age of digital proliferation.
