content.article_text:
The Artnet Bulletin is our daily digest of five items from around the art world that are worth knowing. A different writer takes over each morning.

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

A Papal Audience

Pope Leo XIV continues his campaign to champion and protect art. On Saturday, the pontiff welcomed the Bizot Group , the international network of directors from the world’s largest museums, to the Vatican for an audience. Speaking on the meeting’s theme of “materiality,” he described matter as a gift entrusted to human care, shaped by artists into expressions of transcendent meaning, and as a form of memory that museums carry across generations. He closed by praising the group, currently led by the Rijksmuseum ‘s director, Taco Dibbits , for safeguarding heritage that “belongs to all humanity,” according to a transcript of his remarks. The meeting came just days after the pontiff announced plans to bolster the church’s alliance with artists and cultural institutions, citing rising threats of censorship and homogenization posed by A.I.

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

Pope Leo XIV meets with directors of museums around the world during an audience at the Apostolic Palace on October 10, 2026 in Vatican City, Vatican. Photo: Simone Risoluti – Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/ Getty Images.

More Kennedy Center Developments

It’s impossible to guess what could happen next with the Trump-run Kennedy Center . The embattled arts complex, currently closed to the public, has appointed a new artistic director, according to NPR , Rick Canny has been serving as a consultant to the center since April 2025, through his talent-management firm Favor the Artist , during which time staff have lodged complaints about his business practices. His previous clients have included ZZ Top , Whitesnake , and Tommy Lee .

Meanwhile, the Financial Times reported that Gaurav Srivastava , a major donor to the center, was a secret FBI informant from 2019 to 2024. Unsealed court documents show that the bureau had flagged concerns about his “reliability and honesty.” The disclosure emerges from a lawsuit by sanctioned Dutch oil trader Niels Troost, who accuses Srivastava of defrauding him of more than $43 million, an allegation that Srivastava denies.

Brotherly Love

Tondo of the Two Brothers (Antinoopolis Tondo), second century. Courtesy of the Egyptian Museum.

Egypt unveiled a restored Tondo of the Two Brothers , a prized second-century Fayoum portrait. Specialists from Rome and conservators from the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir spent three weeks patching up the work, according to the Associated Press . Notable for its circular shape and double subject, the wax-based painting had suffered termite damage to its wooden support, and restorers recovered the features of the brother on the right. Egypt will lend a major part of the Fayoum collection to a Rome exhibition running from November 2026 to May 2027, marking the first time the work will travel abroad.

Backlash Over Smashed Porcelain

The British Museum is facing criticism after a Qing dynasty porcelain bowl and a ceramic box from the Sir Percival David Collection were smashed on October 4, provoking anger in Chinese national media and on social media. The bowl fell from its mount in a display cabinet in Room 95 and landed on the box below. Staff who reviewed CCTV can’t explain why: The mount was undamaged and the room was empty. A museum spokesperson told the South China Morning Post that the objects are already with the conservation team for repair.

Frieze Week Potpourri

Happy Frieze Week, London!

Among the countless gallery openings, one I wasn’t counting on: Harry Blain , formerly of Blain Southern , which shuttered abruptly in 2020 and allegedly left many of its artists financially in the lurch, is hosting a private view today at 23 Bruton Street for his new venture, Blain . The show, titled “The Best Way Out Is Always Through,” features works by Felix Gonzalez-Torres and Bruce Nauman. If you want to see Gagosian ’s blockbuster Magritte show , “This Is Still Not a Pipe,” leave extra time: When I went on Saturday, the line to get in snaked around the corner and down Mount Street. (I admit I used my press credentials to skip it.) It simply wouldn’t be Frieze without a big ol’ dino from David Aaron , which is bringing a remarkably complete 150-million-year-old Camarasaurus supremus skull to Frieze Masters. Priced at £1 million ($1.3 million), it has an Allosaurus tooth still embedded in its lower jaw, evidence of a Late Jurassic encounter. Plus, Wyclef Jean will headline the second annual British Museum Ball on October 17.

The wrap-around line to get into Gagosian’s “This Is Still Not a Pipe” show on October 10. Photo: Margaret Carrigan.

Tune in tomorrow when my colleague Ben Davis is in the driver’s seat.

content.article_text:
T he sound of mourning spills out into the streets. A single, endless wailing note echoes out of the basement of Ibraaz, a relatively new cultural centre in London’s Fitzrovia. This is Gabrielle Goliath’s heart-wrenching Elegy, each of its three films featuring a woman singing just one note until their lungs falter and another woman steps up to fill in for her. Just as a note is about to die, it is sustained. It’s a haunting, shocking act of mourning for murder, injustice and genocide.

And it almost never made it.

A panel of five leading South African cultural voices picked Goliath’s work to represent their nation at this summer’s Venice Biennale. Goliath has been working on the project for a decade, collecting voices, collecting stories. This was a work about femicide and the murder of LGBTQ+ people in South Africa, but it had expanded. The latest iteration dealt with the Ovaherero and Nama genocide in Namibia , and the death of a Palestinian poet in 2023. It was a step too far for Gayton McKenzie, South Africa’s sport, arts and culture minister.

McKenzie is the president of the far-right Patriotic Alliance party, and has been vocal in his support of Israel in recent years. He wrote a letter describing the work as “highly divisive”. He called for the work to be edited, for the offending passage about the Palestinian poet to be removed. Goliath refused, so McKenzie put a stop to the whole thing, cancelling her Venice pavilion. She fought it tooth and nail , taking her case to South Africa’s high court, but the case was dismissed. The South Africa pavilion at the biennale sat embarrassingly empty, a big, glaring visual metaphor for the global reach of the culture wars and a symbol of censorship in the face of violence.

Goliath instead found a home for the work in a nearby church , which is where I first saw it. It was devastating then, an almost overwhelmingly emotional piece of art in a beautiful setting. Ibraaz lacks the ornate, quiet atmosphere of that Venetian church, but has made up for it with absolute sombre darkness. The space is pitch black save for the screens. One film is in commemoration of Ipeleng Christine Moholane, a woman who was strangled and left for dead in a field near Johannesburg in 2015. Another is in honour of two women who died at the hands of German colonial oppressors during the genocide in Namibia between 1904 and 1908. The third is for the poet Hiba Abu Nada and the thousands of Palestinians who have died in Gaza since 2023.

This is not a soft, plaintive lament – the room is a discordant, uncomfortable place, filled with a wailing cacophony of clashing vibrato and just out of tune notes. It sounds angry, vicious, furious, because it is. It’s not just an act of commemoration, it’s a call to action, a demand for change and justice.

While it’s incredibly emotional and deeply moving, the main feeling you get is frustration and hopelessness, not sadness. What makes Elegy so powerful is the endless proliferation of horrifying images we have to deal with on a daily basis. If you want to see images of death and genocide, you just have to look at social media or the news. We have more access to shocking, real imagery of awful current events than ever before. But Goliath has stripped the imagery away and left you with only the emotion, so just the anger and heartache remains.

It’s an act of resistance against the image economy, against murder and femicide, against violence and genocide. It’s a feminist lament, a scream against it all.

But it’s also a significant modern artwork, a symbol of our times, of our wars and cultural frictions, and its sound lingers in your ears long after you’ve walked away.

Sur le papier, j’aurais dû résister. J’ai passé l’âge canonique, j’ai deux filles bientôt adolescentes et un esprit critique aiguisé par une mauvaise humeur chronique. Rien, rationnellement, ne devrait m’exciter dans une série comme The Shards . Et pourtant, je l’ai bingée avec la dévotion embarrassante d’une groupie d’un soir. La série de Ryan Murphy et Bret Easton Ellis coche toutes les cases du plaisir coupable : un tueur qui rôde autour d’un lycée ; des ados scandaleusement friqués et cocaïnés ; les mots d’Ellis, enveloppant comme la fumée d’une clope froide un lendemain de sexe débridé. Dès le premier épisode, tout m’emballe honteusement : les brushings, les piscines, la moquette même. Prendre la pilule bleue, replonger dans la matrice rassurante des nineties, redevenir celle qui découvrait Ellis dans sa chambre, sur du Kurt Cobain.

Sauf que la matrice était fucked up. Pour ma génération, l’entrée dans la sexualité et la terreur du sida allaient de pair. Désirer, c’était déjà côtoyer la mort. Ajoutez-y une culture qui érotisait l’abus, le prédateur en figure romantique, le danger en préliminaire, et vous obtenez un imaginaire bâti, malgré nous, sur une équation : sexe = péril = mort. Vingt ans à la déconstruire, mais le câblage, lui, tient toujours. C’est cette équation que The Shards remet sous tension. Le désir adolescent et le tueur qui rôde ne font qu’un. Ellis n’a jamais écrit autre chose, la prédation comme horizon du désir. Le coup de génie est dans le casting. Susan, c’est Kaia Gerber, affichant le visage de sa mère, Cindy Crawford. Robert Mallory, c’est Homer Gere, fils de Richard.

Le sourire de Kaia est une uncanny valley, « das Unheimliche » (« l’inquiétante étrangeté ») disait Freud : le refoulé qui fait retour. Nous ne regardons pas des acteurs mais nos idoles ressuscitées, et tout ce que leur époque avait implanté en nous. Le philosophe britannique Mark Fisher appelait cela la « lente annulation du futur » : une époque qui, ne sachant plus tracer son désir vers l’avant, en refait indéfiniment la boucle. Jusque derrière la caméra, où Max Winkler, fils du Fonzie de la série Happy Days, filme les héritiers d’un âge d’or qu’il a connu de l’intérieur. Voilà peut-être pourquoi je l’ai bingée sans oser l’avouer. Pas par nostalgie d’une esthétique, mais par fidélité honteuse à l’ado que j’étais, celle qui confondait l’excitation et le péril.

The Shards , disponible sur Disney+

content.article_text:
Hier comme aujourd’hui, la tentation est grande pour qui vit dans un régime autoritaire d’y faire face en se ménageant un espace privé, où l’on pourrait continuer à vivre sa vie comme si de rien n’était. Gleb, le protagoniste du brillant Minotaure d’Andreï Zviaguintsev , est un de ceux-là. Patron d’une entreprise de transport dans une ville moyenne russe, au quotidien partagé entre le travail et sa vie de famille avec sa femme, Galina, et son fils adolescent, Gleb ne parle jamais de politique ni ne mentionne l’invasion de l’Ukraine, survenue quelque mois plus tôt.

Pourtant, derrière ce quotidien de bon père de famille, aussi propre que le SUV neuf qu’il conduit dans une imagerie presque publicitaire, l’illusion vacille. Sa relation avec Galina se réduit à se faire servir son repas et à lui déléguer l’ensemble des tâches domestiques, tandis que la guerre s’infiltre partout en arrière-plan : un groupe de soldats en uniforme traverse la rue ; une de ses salariées regarde des vidéos de bombardements de villes ukrainiennes sur YouTube ; une affiche incite les jeunes hommes à s’engager pour défendre la mère patrie ; plusieurs de ses salariés émigrent pendant le week-end ; un train chargé de tanks estampillés d’un « Z » blanc roule devant lui à un passage à niveau. L’intrigue s’emballe lorsque le maire de sa ville lui ordonne d’établir une liste de salariés qui seront mobilisés et envoyés au front, et que sa femme décide de ne plus tolérer cette situation. Il est confronté à un choix.

Andreï Zviaguintsev : « L’enjeu principal, c’est celui du choix »

À l’inverse d’un de ses amis, qui abandonne tout vernis de moralité pour se complaire cyniquement dans une vie de plaisirs sans lendemain, Gleb ne veut pas voir ce dont son pays se rend coupable ni ce que son couple est devenu, et passe le reste du film à tenter de reconstruire l’illusion de sa vie d’avant. En fin de compte, Minotaure montre qu’il est impossible de dresser une frontière entre morale privée et morale publique. En cela, le film emprunte son argument à La République de Platon. À travers son analogie entre la psychologie de l’individu et l’organisation de la cité, Socrate y développe l’idée que justice individuelle et justice collective sont une seule et même chose, à deux échelles différentes, et que l’on peut difficilement avoir l’une sans l’autre. De fait, tous les efforts de Gleb pour restaurer son quotidien d’avant la guerre ne font que le pousser plus loin dans la compromission et l’immoralité. En cherchant à ignorer la corruption et la violence latente du régime, il en devient complice, et Zviaguintsev montre crûment les conséquences de ses actions. Le dernier plan, glaçant, résume l’avertissement que le réalisateur exilé adresse à ses spectateurs en Russie et au-delà : se préserver un espace de moralité dans une société injuste est voué à l’échec.

Despite the fuzzy archival recordings and now-outdated TV models, the video assemblages recall the fast-moving, addictive, and unstable logic of our current digital landscape."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://storage.ghost.io/c/16/43/16435400-f27e-4b41-b5f7-d0c24f5ce4de/content/images/2026/10/IMG_7815.JPG", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ArtAsiaPacific"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://storage.ghost.io/c/16/43/16435400-f27e-4b41-b5f7-d0c24f5ce4de/content/images/2026/10/IMG_7864-1.JPG", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ArtAsiaPacific"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Installation views of NAM JUNE PAIK ’s Time in Triangular , 1993, at “Nam June Paik: The 20th anniversary of his passing,” Watari Museum of Contemporary Art, Tokyo, 2026. Photos by ArtAsiaPacific ."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This conflux of nostalgia and contemporary resonance is pulled together by Time in Triangular and Forest of Cage / Revelation of the Forest (both 1993), created for Paik’s solo show at Watari-um that year. The former evokes both the museum’s own architecture and New York’s Flatiron Building; neon tubes illuminate its prow, while screens cover its walls, flashing clips from films and commercial TV distorted with a synthesizer. Forest of Cage , meanwhile, comprises 20-plus bulky TVs installed within a dense grove, each pulsing with kaleidoscopic imagery, forming a bizarre yet enchanting ecosystem in which nature and technology co-exist. Just as Cage prioritized chance and sonic hesitation, Paik treated the glitch as both creative expression and political intervention, unsettling the corporate authority of telecommunication systems. content.article_text:
Shows

Nam June Paik at the Watari Museum of Contemporary Art

NAM JUNE PAIK ’s

Forest of Cage / Revelation of the Forest , 1993, at “Nam June Paik: The 20th anniversary of his passing,” Watari Museum of Contemporary Art, Tokyo, 2026. Photo by

ArtAsiaPacific .

Nam June Paik: The 20th anniversary of his passing The Watari Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo Jul 19–Nov 23, 2026 In a 1974 essay, Nam June Paik observed with startling prescience: “The mass entertainment TV as we see it now will be divided into, or rather gain many branches and tails of, differentiated video cultures, Picture-Phone, tele-facsimile. . . . They all will form a new nuclear energy in information and society-building.” His prediction might no longer impress today’s jaded netizens but remains a relevant diagnosis of our hyperdigital age: Paik recognized that this device would not only upgrade our communication networks, but establish a novel infrastructure of perception.

The South Korean artist, widely known as the “father of video art” for his experiments with electronics, passed away in 2006 before witnessing the full-scale realization of his prophecy. Two decades later, what does it mean to look at his work from within the conditions he foresaw? At Tokyo’s Watari Museum of Contemporary Art (Watari-um), a compact yet immersive three-floor retrospective surveys Paik’s practice through mixed-media installations, works on paper, and personal documents from the institution’s collection.

Installation views “Nam June Paik: The 20th anniversary of his passing,” Watari Museum of Contemporary Art, Tokyo, 2026. Photos by ArtAsiaPacific .

On the first level, visitors enter a dimly lit den, where a low thrum surges through the body before one’s vision adjusts to the darkness. The room situates somewhere between a lush forest and an abandoned broadcasting studio: wood debris litters the floor; tropical foliage unfurls throughout; and retro TV sets appear to sprout from branches and undergrowth. Near the entrance, TV Egg (1982) nestles on a pile of mulch surrounded by ferns, a cathode-ray tube projecting abstract moving images onto its glass surface. The illusively organic form denotes both cosmogenesis and false representation, reflecting the allure of technology as well as its deceptive potential.

Further inside, the ambient buzz intensifies into an all-surround sound field of Zen Buddhist chanting, zither notes, audience laughter, and static. Some monitors glow with black-and-white footage of Paik’s zany Fluxus performances from the early 1960s, others present surreal visual mélanges of monks meditating before dawn, their figures dissolving into hypnotic bursts of color. Despite the fuzzy archival recordings and now-outdated TV models, the video assemblages recall the fast-moving, addictive, and unstable logic of our current digital landscape.

Installation views of NAM JUNE PAIK ’s Time in Triangular , 1993, at “Nam June Paik: The 20th anniversary of his passing,” Watari Museum of Contemporary Art, Tokyo, 2026. Photos by ArtAsiaPacific .

This conflux of nostalgia and contemporary resonance is pulled together by Time in Triangular and Forest of Cage / Revelation of the Forest (both 1993), created for Paik’s solo show at Watari-um that year. The former evokes both the museum’s own architecture and New York’s Flatiron Building; neon tubes illuminate its prow, while screens cover its walls, flashing clips from films and commercial TV distorted with a synthesizer. Forest of Cage , meanwhile, comprises 20-plus bulky TVs installed within a dense grove, each pulsing with kaleidoscopic imagery, forming a bizarre yet enchanting ecosystem in which nature and technology co-exist. A descendant of TV Garden (1974–77), the piece pays tribute to American composer John Cage (1912–1992), Paik’s friend and mentor. Just as Cage prioritized chance and sonic hesitation, Paik treated the glitch as both creative expression and political intervention, unsettling the corporate authority of telecommunication systems. He understood that the screen is not a neutral interface but a manipulable—indeed, “dictatorial”—medium whose subterfuge is concealed by its pervasiveness.

On the top floor, the exhibition turns to the afterlives of old appliances. Candle TV (1968) is a worn, hollowed-out Emerson TV sheltering a quietly burning candle. Conjuring the hush of a vigil, it mourns not only obsolete contraptions but the memories they contain. It also prompts a question: how does a world increasingly mediated by algorithms, cybernetic economies, and AI computing bear upon our collective psyche? Will human consciousness eventually succumb to the torrents of virtualization? Paik might not have lived these exact concerns, yet his work reminds us to stay attuned to the mechanisms of technology: to prod, tamper with, and disrupt the apparatus—if not to defeat it, then to at least preserve the human touch behind it.

Annette Meier is an assistant editor at ArtAsiaPacific.

content.article_text:
People

Shi Guowei: After the Festival

Shi Guowei sets down a box of cookies—a modest gift I had brought to Beijing from Hong Kong—and adds a platter of nuts and seeds, mugs for tea, bottles of Perrier. The spread is humble yet rich with quiet hospitality. I take a sip of water and prepare to record; beside me, an old harlequin cat, fur scruffy with age, climbs onto an empty chair and settles in for the conversation.

On the wall opposite hangs a large tableau, Drum (2026), from a new body of work soon to debut at Fotografiska Shenzhen this October. A constellation of red ceremonial drums sits on a nondescript floor, the base of an equally nondescript pillar visible in the composition’s upper register. The vantage is tilted downward, feeling accidental, except it isn’t—the instruments, scattered in derelict disorder, carry a disquieting, almost sentient charge.

“They were perhaps being played just moments ago,” says Shi, “then cast aside while people moved on to other festivities.” Shi’s method begins with a black-and-white photograph, which he paints over with water-based pigment in exacting, painstaking layers, in pursuit of what he calls an “authentic illusion.” Hand-coloring is a rigorous, largely obsolete technique, one that predates photography’s capacity for color. Trained as a photographer at Tsinghua University’s Academy of Arts & Design and later at the Fachhochschule Dortmund, Shi revives and redirects the age-old method—not toward verisimilitude, but toward displacing recorded fact for a particular emotional intensity, or what he terms “felt truth.” Here, the grooves in the grubby floor flare with scorched terracotta. The drums’ gilding has dulled with rust, their maroon lacquer worn and mottled by wear and stains. Yet their faces remain a stark, incongruous snow white, the characters 百年行 (“a hundred-year journey”) discernible atop.

Views of SHI GUOWEI ’s studio in Beijing. Courtesy the artist and Magician Space, Beijing.

“For some time I have found myself drawn to festivals,” Shi tells me, “but not their pageantry. What holds me is a quality I encounter around them, or after them.” His recent work marks a departure: after a decade spent rendering verdure, rock, and flora, he has turned his focus to the remnants of human celebration—its overflow, its sediment, its afterglow. In moments of isolation from crowds or in emptied corners of a carnival ground, Shi locates something resembling melancholy but stranger—subtler, yet somehow sharper. In Drum , it percolates most intensely in the barrels’ precisely calibrated plum-toned burgundy, faded through use yet all the more potent. That hue is echoed in a much smaller square study hung adjacent: a close-up of rock texture, the subject for which Shi is—for now, at least—best known. The stone, too, takes on a vital vermilion flush, its marbling rippling like sinew in raw flesh.

We walk over to another new work, Bridge (2026). Here the operant palette is green: a procession of round, scalloped cement forms appear to float on a pond, cast to resemble lotus leaves. The algae-filmed cement dons a jade cast while the water glimmers deep turquoise; upper left, brilliant chartreuse wavelets breach the serenity, lending the scene something at once magical and unsettling. The disturbance is produced by artificial light reflected from festivities nearby, just off-camera. “It was a tremendously crowded day,” Shi recounts. “I had to wait hours to capture this view without people.” The intrusion of yellow is deliberate: “On an ordinary day, the water would simply mirror a blue sky. But here there is something invasive. A quiet space has been forcibly entered. I wanted to convey that uneasy contrast.”

SHI GUOWEI , Drum , 2026, C-print and color ink, 126 x 135 cm (left); and Bridge , 2026, C-print and color ink, 145 x 126 cm (right). Courtesy the artist, Magician Space, Beijing, and Fotografiska Shenzhen.

Festivals divide time by returning. Each recurrence calls for celebration but measures all that passes in the interim—an illusion of progress and permanence undercut by an invisible accounting of absence and loss. A year, an anniversary, another gathering beneath lights—the shadows of which Shi inhabits. “Festivals are understood as collective occasions of happiness and hope,” he says. “But I am interested in what an individual experiences. Private feelings can diverge greatly from the noise and commotion. I want to ask what joy actually is.”

For years, Shi remained faithful to a vocabulary of motifs drawn from the natural world, accumulated largely during solitary walks in the mountains. I leaf through a catalog of earlier works: verdant shrubbery articulated in minute detail, severe faces of craggy cliffs, succulents alive and acerbic in saturated pastel tones. Their apparent stillness belies the peculiar temporality of their making. A photograph compresses an encounter into an instant; Shi reverses the process, re-inserting that isolated instant into the wayward currents of felt time. Over months, he revisits a single exposure through color and the repeated touch of his brush. There is something almost punitive in this sustained return, but also something relished: an obligation to look again, and feel again. The process amounts to a retrospective encounter, which chromatically loosens the image from the shutter’s grip; color stops being information and becomes qualitative, lived duration. Against an image culture organized around immediate edits and filters, Shi makes the almost foolish proposition that “some things require time.”

SHI GUOWEI , Fireworks II , 2025, C-print and color ink (left); and Garden II , 2024, C-print and color ink (right). Courtesy the artist, Magician Space, Beijing, and Fotografiska Shenzhen.

As I continue through the monograph, an instinctive recoil propels me past a page; catching myself, I double back. The image is an apparently innocuous close-up of a roadside thicket; beyond clusters of oleander in the foreground burns a scarlet horizon—muted yet feverish, almost malign. A brief silence passes, then the artist begins. “Some years ago, a puppy started appearing at my studio door every day,” he says. “I couldn’t afford to keep him, but I fed him and played with him. We went for walks. It was during Covid, and I was at a very low place. Watching him frolic in the fields became a kind of lifeline for me. His coat was entirely black, and when he sprinted into the distance, he blurred into a flash of black lightning.”

“Then one day he stopped coming,” Shi continues, his tone still stoic and even, but his countenance tightening. “At first I thought he would show up again, perhaps after a few days, but he never did. I searched the surrounding areas but never found him. It took me a long time to recover. It was a period when everything felt beyond my control, and there was nothing I could do.”

Eyes welling, I avert my gaze, fixing it back on the page. The lucent red behind the poisonous clouds of white oleander intensifies under scrutiny. It is a red before language, before thought or even consciousness. The same quality of red, in various shades and gradations, courses through Shi’s bushes, branches, and stones; beneath his pigments, their obdurate surfaces swell and soften—brittle as bone at times, tender and fragile as skin and vein at others. This slippage between mineral and animal matter goes beyond formal semblance into a Merleau-Pontian entanglement with the primordial flesh of the world. While traveling with itinerant herding communities in northeastern China, Shi once watched a rancher dissect a dead deer, its organs swiftly and surgically arranged and examined to determine the cause of death—disease, poison, or some other threat to human or flock. Shi was struck by the herdsman’s composure: here was a bond between man, animal, and land so profound yet so unsentimental—an intimacy forged by survival, capable of opening a body without ceremony.

Views of works-in-progress at SHI GUOWEI ’s studio in Beijing. Courtesy the artist and Magician Space, Beijing.

We rise again to examine two unfinished works. In one, a flamingo boat emerges half concealed by riverside shrubbery. The festive prop is at once ludicrous and regal—a majestic creature at rest, its curved neck maintaining its stately composure even while in repose. Its acidic pink bleeds into surrounding vegetation, folding boat, foliage, and beholder into a single sensory continuum; one imagines a child wandering from a picnic party, parting some leaves to come face to face with an enchanting creature. Nearby, another work-in-progress rests on an easel: visible through a curtain of trees is a couple on a canopied boat on the water. The perspective keeps us onshore, peering into an intimacy we cannot enter, and one which is already receding. The half-completed piece, part colored and part grayscale, recalls the Deleuzian crystal-image, in which the present co-exists with the virtual past it is already becoming. Shi’s camera records the first encounter; his colors enact the second; and the viewer arrives later still. Through perception, memory, and reception, the image continually accrues its distance.

Festivals promise that time will return, but no return is exact: the crowd changes, childhood ends, a beloved animal disappears. Shi’s color occupies that lapse between recurrence and loss: he does not paint the world as it is, but the interval between what once was and what passes beyond recovery.

Michele Chan is managing editor at ArtAsiaPacific.

content.article_text:
In 1962, the then French culture minister, André Malraux, reportedly bored by the ballet he was watching at Paris’s opera house, raised his eyes to the classical ceiling and decided it needed a makeover.

In his ennui, Malraux thought his friend and artist Marc Chagall , sitting next to him at the Palais Garnier at the time, was the man for the job and commissioned him to make a new ceiling.

Over the next two years, Chagall worked in secret and for free to produce 24 enormous and colourful wedge-shaped canvases, that were installed over the original 19th-century classical ceiling by the now forgotten artist Jules-Eugène Lenepveu.

Today, more than four decades after Chagall’s death, one of Lenepveu’s descendants is planning legal action to have the original ceiling uncovered and restored.

Arnaud Carayon says he has “asked nicely” for this to happen for three years, including writing two letters to France’s president, Emmanuel Macron. Now he has instructed a lawyer to take the fight to court.

“The Lenepveu ceiling is classified as a historic monument and yet it hasn’t been seen for 60 years and we have no idea what state it is in,” Carayon said.

“Today, everyone has forgotten Lenepveu. Unfortunately, he was swept away by the wave of impressionism, but in his time he was really a star. More importantly, he was specifically chosen to decorate the opera ceiling by Charles Garnier, who designed everything in the opera house right down to the last door knob.

“But on a whim, Malraux decided he did not agree with Garnier’s choice.”

Garnier’s opera house was commissioned by Napoleon III and opened in January 1875 in the presence of European royals and political figures including the then lord mayor of London, Sir William Cotton.

Lenepveu, who was Garnier’s friend and artistic collaborator, produced a classical and allegorical work painted in oil directly on the copper plates of the dome. The work, called The Muses and the Hours of Day and Night, and given historic listing in 1923, was considered perfectly in keeping with the ornate Second Empire style of Garnier’s palace.

Lenepveu, who went on to lead the French Academy in Rome, later produced a series of Joan of Arc frescoes in the Paris Panthéon, but his name is little known today.

Malraux is said to have wanted to give the fusty opera house a more modern, edgy feel. Chagall’s 24 cake-slice shaped canvases were spliced together around the central chandelier covering 220 sq metres (2,368 sq ft) of the dome. The work is divided into separate colours: red, blue, green, yellow and white; and features dancers, angels, musicians and the names of composers.

Even before Chagall’s work was installed, the row between traditionalists and modernists erupted and reached the other side of the Channel.

The Royal Institute of British Architects in London wrote to the culture minister asking him to abandon his plans to cover the original ceiling. “The unique character of this edifice [the opera house] is based on the fact that all its elements: architecture, paintings, sculptures and mosaics work together in harmony,” Riba wrote. Its plea was ignored.

The Palais Garnier will be closed for renovation between 2027-32, and Carayon, the president of the Friends of Lenepveu Society, said he had written to Macron to suggest alternating the Lenepveu and Chagall ceilings after it reopens, with each being shown for a decade. He said the Élysée Palace replied only that the president was “particularly attentive” to the subject.

“From the beginning, the Chagall ceiling was designed to be removable. It can be taken down without any damage. We thought the idea of alternating ceilings was very positive and promising, but it seems nobody has the guts to touch the Chagall ceiling,” Carayon said.

At a 2023-24 Chagall exhibition at the Pompidou Centre, the curator, Anne Montfort-Tanguy, said: “The ceiling [of the opera house] is Chagall: it’s his autobiography, his vision of Paris. All the artists he loved are represented as well as what he considered the most important Paris monuments like the Eiffel Tower … It’s a moving, fluid almost cinematic work. The ceiling is a complete work of art.

“It was Chagall’s gift to the country that welcomed him; an homage to France and to Paris,” Montfort-Tanguy added.

Alexander Neef, the director of the Paris Opera, told Le Monde : “The debate over the Chagall ceiling has gone on for more than 60 years. The Lenepveu ceiling has been listed as a historic monument since 1923 so its heritage value is recognised. That his [Lenepveu’s] descendants wish to defend his memory is legitimate.”

content.article_text:
H ome Alone meets Mad Max in this atmospheric seasonal chiller, named for Halloween and not a cheery greeting. A disease has wiped out most of humanity, leaving 16-year-old Pumpkin (Milly Shapiro) stranded alone in her rural family home in the middle of nowhere for the best part of four years. This classic American clapboard house has always been the perfect quaint yet unsettling place to celebrate Halloween, and she determines to uphold the family tradition and do just that, sending a radio broadcast to anyone listening to invite them to celebrate spooky season with her. Unfortunately, the message is picked up by some less than wholesome types, led by Thalia (Shannyn Sossamon), thus setting the stage for the proverbial to hit the fan.

It’s the first major screen role for Shapiro since her memorable debut as the little sister in Ari Aster’s Hereditary , and she is in almost every scene here, making for quite the showcase. It’s good casting: Pumpkin is an intriguing presence – at once young and old, presumably because she’s been fending for herself during such a key stage of her development. She’s not had any adult guidance since the age of 12 – arresting her development in some ways, while having to survive, be totally independent and grieve her entire family alone has simultaneously made her unusually tough in others.

This turns out to be invaluable in a horror film; it gives the script plenty of room to have her make naive decisions which are wholly justified, as well as to prove surprisingly resilient in ways that the character’s backstory supports. This gives a plausible, grounded core to the story’s more outlandish trappings, and the splendid production design – ranging from cosy cottagecore Halloween to a timeless Bates motel aesthetic – makes for an appealing storyworld. Hallowarrior is the feature debut of Ben Sottak, an experienced short film-maker, and on this evidence he’s likely to be worth keeping an eye out for.

content.article_text:
The Burkina Faso artist’s later work reveals the changing ethos and sociopolitical shifts in West African photography

When asked why The Photographers’ Gallery is displaying later colour works by the Burkinabe studio photographer Sanlé Sory – and why now – TPG curator Taous Dahmani’s answer is clear and direct: “Because I’m here now.”

“I had always wanted to think about the long tradition of West African studio photography as a global surface,” she adds. Fed up with dominant readings, Dahmani argues that these photographs require a relocation of function if they are to be understood in more generative, restorative ways. The job of photographer is political, artistic, often polemic and gestural; it is also, fundamentally, a job. It is labour. It is a means to get paid and a way to live one’s life, void of a punch card and with freedom to roam. Photography is a history of grafting, of making ends meet, of waking up and going to work. Dahmani looks away from the recent landscape of “revived” West African photographic exhibitions, literally blown up for the Western art powers that be, and instead sees them as they are: small and intimate. And that is enough.

Perhaps ‘fine art’ – whatever that means – is a poisoned chalice, a trapdoored pedestal, a gilded cage. Instead, Sory is here a master craftsman, but one looking to get paid rather than necessarily disrupt the canon. This curse of fine art, which fixes Sory’s oeuvre and character into something discovered, demanding recontextualisation, and subsequent elevation, in turn shuts a door into the modern world.

“[Sory’s later colour work] holds quite a significant shift in what we know about the history of West African practice” – Taous Dahmani, curator

Reductive readings often position this sort of photographer, and by extent photography, as a historical event over a living being. Dahmani says this limited reading “refuses entry into contemporality”, and perpetuates Western art narratives as “acceptable forms of nostalgia about this past of liberation, a call to the time ‘when we liberated poor Africans’”. On the two far sides of the Atlantic, and deep in the white cube, when we see West African studio portraits, it is always revolutionary times. Nothing ever changes, Africa is Africa, and the West is the West.

But Sory’s archive holds “thousands and thousands” of later colour negatives, many of which have never been printed beyond their original commission. Dahmani asks why and steers towards a relocation, a “re-anchoring” in her terms. Perhaps these colour works, a move on from the earlier black-and-white work of the 1960s and 70s, were deemed harder to digest for Western audiences, something less fixed than the story we know (or have been told). To Dahmani, Burkina Faso, and the wider African stage, is not a fixed event but a site to examine universal photographic systems, alongside the specificities of 20th-century African histories. “[Sory’s later colour work] holds quite a significant shift in what we know about the history of West African practice,” she says.

She reads the practice as both ubiquitous and unique; closer to the functional, political and social histories caught within the portraits, and understood as wholly commissioned artefacts. Yet by curating the show in London there is an awareness that home is not always a place one can return to, that there is perhaps no true contextual providence left. Instead there is a possibility to seek out new lands, ways of being and seeing, ones which bring the photographs to audiences new and old, but allow all those looking to see for themselves.

The Western art reading has a tendency to turn African nations into islands, dislocating them from neighbouring, concurrent histories. Dahmani refers to this as a “dictated, fetishised history”, one the market embraces with ease but which brings us no closer to understanding these images or people. “For me, colour became the starting point,” she says. “Can we think critically about this history through the lens of colour? Can we think of it as a form of politics? Most of the pictures we know are from the 1960s and 70s. Postcolonial moments of aspiration, of joy… at least that’s how it’s sold. Moments of ‘Finally, the freedom of the African people!’ But it stops there. No one wonders what happens after.”

Sory’s later portraits of street vendors, personable and direct, grew out of a slowing appetite for commissioned portraits. Cameraphones had arrived and times were changing. Dahmani also stresses the desires of the later sitters he was commissioned to record, commenting on their input into the images. “Sory printed in black-and-white, but when colour became more accessible, clients asked for it. It was more expensive, and he suddenly couldn’t work alone.” For Dahmani, both sitter and printer become producer and collaborator.

Dahmani traces stories of the sitters through historical relocations; every now and then you notice someone dressed fancifully for the camera, who is “wearing a suit slightly too small, their shoes maybe unvarnished”. Through these images Dahmani moves away from a fashion-first reading towards something more akin to socially informed style studies, an analysis of hand-me-downs and counterfeit designerwear. This becomes part of the re-anchoring, and perhaps a new type of non-hierarchical photographic kinship. It aids an understanding of universality, not exotic idiosyncrasy, though a story that is also deeply African.

Sory had to negotiate and barter with his subjects, as ultimately the images existed off their payments. He had to follow trends, keep up with the changing times. Suddenly people did not want his famed illustrated backdrops any longer. “They wanted to be part of a new technology, and a new capacity of being seen,” Dahmani explains. Sory, as with many West African portraitists, is rarely discussed within the contexts of an emerging contemporary. Entry into the modern world, with colour, Nike, Obama T-shirts, and iPhones, has not been curatorially permitted.

“I now don’t have to prove that photography is an art form,” Dahmani states. “But I do want to get back to the fact that actually, historically, there were things that we were too quick to put into one category, instead of allowing them to be a multiplicity of things. And I don’t think we often allow African artists to be a multiplicity of things.”

Sanlé Sory: Colour Years is at The Photographers’ Gallery , London, from 14 October 2026 to 21 February 2027. The accompanying book is published by GOST, priced £45 https://gostbooks.com/products/volta-colour

Isaac Huxtable is a Yorkshire-born, London-based writer and curator. He works across the photographic medium with a central focus on race and realism. Isaac is currently an Assistant Curator in Photography at the Victoria and Albert Museum. He studied at the Courtauld Institute of Art, followed by roles at the British Journal of Photography, the Photographers' Gallery, and the art agency Artiq. His words have featured in the British Journal of Photography, Elephant Magazine, Galerie Peter Sillem, The Photographers' Gallery, and The South London Gallery. He is particularly interested in documentary practices, gender, class, and the body.

Daily Newsletter

Raven Chacon’s Echoes on Park Avenue

The Pulitzer Prize-winning Diné artist on latest projects, art in NYC for Indigenous Peoples’ Day, and a Felix Gonzalez-Torres show misses the mark.

It’s a beautiful Monday to celebrate Indigenous Peoples’ Day, no matter what the federal government says. In a conversation with Associate Editor Phillip Pyle, Diné musician Raven Chacon discusses his recent improvised performances at the Park Avenue Armory, the “collision” at the heart of all music, and reclaiming the technologies of colonial violence through sound.

Read on for a guide to shows centering Native art around New York City — including Shelley Niro and Sarah Sense, two of my favorite artists — and a critique of a Felix Gonzalez-Torres exhibition that bizarrely glosses over the late artist’s AIDS advocacy and political spirit.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor

Raven Chacon Sounds the History of the Land

On Wednesday and Thursday night, sound mixers, synthesizers, pedals, speakers, whistles, a turkey call, and a ceramic horn sat on a table at the center of the Veterans Room in Manhattan’s Park Avenue Armory. Serving as the stage for Raven Chacon’s hour-long improvisation sessions for the Armory’s Artists Studio series, the table also offered audiences the rare opportunity to see the prolific artist at play. | Phillip Pyle

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://www.troiscouleurs.fr/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/LE-JOUR-DE-SON-RETOUR_Kim-Sunjin_Song-Sunmi-1024x576.jpg", "alt": "LE JOUR DE SON RETOUR Kim Sunjin Song Sunmi", "caption": "", "credit": "Trois Couleurs"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ce film-là n’est pas flou. Ici, l’image est en noir et blanc, nette, et le cadre tellement fixe dans un premier temps que l’on se demande s’il s’agit d’une nouvelle performance formelle. Presque. content.article_text:
Ce film-là n’est pas flou. On avait laissé Hong Sang-soo sur In Water (2024), où le point jamais fait à l’image donnait aux paysages des couleurs délavées, rappelant les œuvres de Mark Rothko ; et Ce que cette nature te dit (2025), qui jouait aussi d’une photographie nébuleuse. Ici, l’image est en noir et blanc, nette, et le cadre tellement fixe dans un premier temps que l’on se demande s’il s’agit d’une nouvelle performance formelle. Presque. Le réalisateur sud-coréen utilise ici la répétition : trois jeunes journalistes se succèdent pour interviewer Bae Jeongsu, une actrice sur le retour.

Elle vient de tourner dans un film d’auteur et répond différemment à chacun en fonction de microévénements de contexte – accepter une bière en plein milieu de l’après-midi peut tout changer. Plus tard, lors d’un cours de théâtre, l’actrice tente de rejouer ces entrevues pour mieux les revisiter… On pense à Hotel by the River (2018), à ce Hong Sang-soo qu’on aime, architecte de la parole qu’on a connu plus filou. Ce film aussi se tient bien, sans prétention dans sa réflexion sur la nature des échanges professionnels. Il y a bien quelques piques sur les journalistes, mais ce n’est pas un pamphlet satirique, et l’écriture ne rate pas le personnage de l’actrice non plus. Le film lui rend plutôt un hommage, et offre un dialogue réussi sur les choix et les chemins de vie.

Le Jour de son retour de Hong Sang-soo , Carlotta Films (1 h 24) sortie le 14 octobre

content.title_original: Dans « Low Expectations » d’Eivind Landsvik, girl in red trouve un premier rôle touchant
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://www.troiscouleurs.fr/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/496be15830c801e2260f290261bff31c-1024x510.webp", "alt": "496be15830c801e2260f290261bff31c", "caption": "", "credit": "Trois Couleurs"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sa dépression consume tout, alors autant ne pas le montrer. Élément secondaire de ce film norvégien qui exclut de sa mise en scène bien des gimmicks du drame psychologique, l’état psychique de Maja ponctuera plutôt ses élans de vie. La jeune femme est de retour chez sa mère avec un petit boulot de surveillante de lycée, après une carrière explosive dans la musique (sous le nom de Vongole, projet que l’on devine fun et hype) et un burn-out créatif – plus des excès de consommations diversement illicites."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Habile vertige, Maja est jouée par Marie Ulven Ringheim, que l’on connaît plutôt sous son nom de scène : girl in red. Mais le film a le bon goût de ne pas tout confondre et tient sa musique à distance – même si Low Expectations sonne déjà comme un morceau de l’intéressée : doux et puissant. L’ensemble est bien sûr à l’image de ce cinéma norvégien éthéré et mélancolique à la mode Dag Johan Haugerud (les tourbillonnants Rêves, Amour, Désir de 2025) ou Joachim Trier ( Low Expectations devient presque méta quand on voit la manière dont est filmé, vieilli, l’Anders Danielsen Lie d’ Oslo, 31 août ), mais reste plus terre à terre, dans l’air du temps. Glosant autour de cette question conventionnelle mais fondamentale : peut-on, à 29 ans, se demander si on a raté sa vie ?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Low Expectations d’Eivind Landsvik , UFO (1 h 45) , sortie le 14 octobre"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Retrouvez-nous sur"}]
content.article_text:
Sa dépression consume tout, alors autant ne pas le montrer. Élément secondaire de ce film norvégien qui exclut de sa mise en scène bien des gimmicks du drame psychologique, l’état psychique de Maja ponctuera plutôt ses élans de vie. La jeune femme est de retour chez sa mère avec un petit boulot de surveillante de lycée, après une carrière explosive dans la musique (sous le nom de Vongole, projet que l’on devine fun et hype) et un burn-out créatif – plus des excès de consommations diversement illicites.

Habile vertige, Maja est jouée par Marie Ulven Ringheim, que l’on connaît plutôt sous son nom de scène : girl in red. Mais le film a le bon goût de ne pas tout confondre et tient sa musique à distance – même si Low Expectations sonne déjà comme un morceau de l’intéressée : doux et puissant. L’ensemble est bien sûr à l’image de ce cinéma norvégien éthéré et mélancolique à la mode Dag Johan Haugerud (les tourbillonnants Rêves, Amour, Désir de 2025) ou Joachim Trier ( Low Expectations devient presque méta quand on voit la manière dont est filmé, vieilli, l’Anders Danielsen Lie d’ Oslo, 31 août ), mais reste plus terre à terre, dans l’air du temps. Glosant autour de cette question conventionnelle mais fondamentale : peut-on, à 29 ans, se demander si on a raté sa vie ?

Low Expectations d’Eivind Landsvik , UFO (1 h 45) , sortie le 14 octobre

content.excerpt_original: Ce drame, sur la dépression d’une jeune musicienne et vêtu des atours du cinéma norvégien moderne (réalisme et mélancolie pop), sonne juste. La musicienne girl in red y trouve un premier rôle cinématographique de choix.

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "In recent decades, Gustav Klimt has become one of the most sought-after artists on the international art market, with his paintings achieving record-breaking prices at auction. In this secluded setting, near members of the Flöge family—including his companion Emilie Flöge—the artist refined his mature approach to landscape painting. With oil on canvas, the artist transformed the humble building and surrounding vegetation into a richly patterned composition of vibrant foliage, vivid color, and mosaic-like brushwork. Unlike his meticulously prepared portraits, Klimt’s landscapes were executed with few preparatory studies, lending them a greater sense of immediacy and spontaneity. Created during the final phase of Klimt’s Attersee period, the work reflects his fascination with nature as a space of visual intensity. The first, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907), is now held by the Neue Galerie New York. The second, along with works such as Apple Tree I (see above), belonged to the Bloch-Bauer family collection that was looted by Nazi authorities after the annexation of Austria in 1938. After a prolonged legal battle, these paintings were returned in 2006 to Maria Altmann and the other heirs of Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer in a landmark restitution case. On November 8 of that year, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II was sold at Christie’s New York as part of an Impressionist and Modern Art Evening Sale. The painting achieved $87.9 million, setting a new auction record for Klimt at the time. It was during his summers in Litzlberg, on the shores of Lake Attersee, that the artist developed his profound connection with the natural world. The elegant silver trunks rise like “columns in a cathedral created by nature.” Their intricate patterns contrast with the deep green foliage, creating a richly textured surface. Landscape occupied a significant place in Klimt’s mature oeuvre, reflecting his search for harmony and visual rhythm. At Sotheby’s London in June 2023, Dame mit Fächer carried an estimate of more than £65 million ($80 million) and was backed by a third-party guarantee. content.article_text:
In recent decades, Gustav Klimt has become one of the most sought-after artists on the international art market, with his paintings achieving record-breaking prices at auction. From the gilded elegance of his celebrated portraits to the richly patterned views of Lake Attersee completed during his summer retreats, Klimt’s oeuvre embodies the decorative brilliance and artistic innovation that defined Viennese Modernism. The rarity and enduring appeal of these works among collectors have made them some of the most valuable examples of early 20th-century art ever offered for sale.

The market for Klimt reached new heights with landmark sales of such works as Lady with a Fan in 2023, Blooming Meadow in 2025, and Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer in 2025, each reaffirming the extraordinary demand for his masterpieces. Today, some rank among the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction, including the 10 paintings discussed below.

Landhaus am Attersee (Country House by the Attersee), 1914 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Landhaus am Attersee (Country House by the Attersee) depicts the forester’s house at the entrance to Austria’s Weißenbach Valley, where Gustav Klimt stayed during his summers on the southern shore of Lake Attersee. In this secluded setting, near members of the Flöge family—including his companion Emilie Flöge—the artist refined his mature approach to landscape painting. With oil on canvas, the artist transformed the humble building and surrounding vegetation into a richly patterned composition of vibrant foliage, vivid color, and mosaic-like brushwork. Unlike his meticulously prepared portraits, Klimt’s landscapes were executed with few preparatory studies, lending them a greater sense of immediacy and spontaneity. Created during the final phase of Klimt’s Attersee period, the work reflects his fascination with nature as a space of visual intensity. Offered at Sotheby’s New York on November 5, 2003, with an estimate of $18–25 million, the painting achieved $29.1 million. The result confirmed the growing appreciation of Klimt’s landscapes, now regarded as some of the artist’s most personal and innovative achievements.

Apple Tree I , 1912 Image Credit: Christie’s. Klimt’s Apple Tree I is a luminous example of his mature landscapes, depicting a single apple tree rising above a dense carpet of flowers and foliage. This oil on canvas is distinguished by its vibrant palette, shimmering brushwork, and richly decorative surface, reflecting Klimt’s interest in nature during his summers at Lake Attersee and the influence of Vincent van Gogh’s expressive approach to color and movement. First exhibited at the Große Kunstausstellung in Dresden in 1912, the work demonstrates Klimt’s ability to turn a simple natural motif into a striking decorative composition. Its provenance includes ownership by Adele and Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer and its restitution to their heirs in 2006. Offered at Christie’s New York with an estimate of $15–25 million, Apple Tree I sold for $33 million on November 9 of that same year. The sale underscored the enduring appeal of Klimt’s garden landscapes.

Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II , 1912 Image Credit: Christie’s. Klimt’s Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II is an oil on canvas depicting the eponymous Viennese socialite and salonnière , who was one of Klimt’s most important patrons and the only sitter to whom he devoted two paintings. The first, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907), is now held by the Neue Galerie New York. The second, along with works such as Apple Tree I (see above), belonged to the Bloch-Bauer family collection that was looted by Nazi authorities after the annexation of Austria in 1938. After a prolonged legal battle, these paintings were returned in 2006 to Maria Altmann and the other heirs of Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer in a landmark restitution case. On November 8 of that year, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II was sold at Christie’s New York as part of an Impressionist and Modern Art Evening Sale. The painting achieved $87.9 million, setting a new auction record for Klimt at the time. In 2016 the work was sold privately by its owner, Oprah Winfrey, who had purchased it at Christie’s, to an anonymous Chinese buyer for a reported $150 million, making it one of the most significant private art transactions of the decade.

Birch Forest , 1903 Image Credit: Christie’s. “I get up early in the morning, usually around 6 am, sometimes earlier, sometimes later. If I get up and the weather is fine, I go into the nearby forest. I am painting a small beech grove, mixed with a few conifers,” wrote Klimt in a letter to M. Zimmerman in August 1903. It was during his summers in Litzlberg, on the shores of Lake Attersee, that the artist developed his profound connection with the natural world. In Birch Forest (Buchenwald) , he captured a secluded grove with precision. The elegant silver trunks rise like “columns in a cathedral created by nature.” Their intricate patterns contrast with the deep green foliage, creating a richly textured surface. Landscape occupied a significant place in Klimt’s mature oeuvre, reflecting his search for harmony and visual rhythm. With each tree trunk bearing its own unique markings, the painting shows extreme attention to detail. Acquired by Adele and Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer and confiscated by Nazi forces, Birch Forest was returned to their heirs in 2006 before appearing at Christie’s New York on two occasions. In November 2006, the lot achieved $40.3 million against an estimate of $20−30 million. Returning to the auction house as part of the Paul G. Allen Collection in 2022, it realized $104.6 million, becoming the most expensive Klimt landscape ever sold at auction at the time.

Litzlberg am Attersee (Litzlberg on the Attersee), 1914 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Litzlberg am Attersee depicts the shoreline of Lake Attersee, with houses nestled beneath a densely wooded hillside and a narrow stretch of water in the foreground. Recent scholarship suggests the painting was executed in the second half of 1914. Its vibrant palette, flattened perspective, and densely layered brushwork exemplify Klimt’s decorative approach to landscape. The composition is believed to have drawn in part on a postcard photograph of the lake that the artist sent to his nephew in August 1914. Acquired directly from Klimt by Viennese patrons Viktor and Paula Zuckerkandl, the painting later entered the collection of Viktor’s sister, Amalie Redlich, a Jewish collector who was dispossessed following the Nazi annexation of Austria and deported to Łódź in 1941. After decades in the collection of the Museum der Moderne Salzburg, the work was restituted to Redlich’s heir in 2011. Later that year, it sold for $40.4 million at Sotheby’s New York, surpassing its $25–30 million estimate. A portion of the sale proceeds was donated to the Museum der Moderne Salzburg to support an extension named in Redlich’s honor.

Bauerngarten (Flower Garden), 1907 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Klimt’s Bauerngarten (Blumengarten) (Flower Garden), one of the artist’s most celebrated landscapes, presents an informal profusion of poppies, daisies, zinnias, and roses arranged into a riot of color and pattern. This oil on canvas gives a sense of Klimt’s summers at Lake Attersee and of his evolving approach to landscape, rooted in the symbolic ambitions of the Viennese avant-garde. Painted in the garden of the Mayr-Hof, his summer retreat in Litzlberg, the work shows how the natural and decorative worlds converged under his brush. First exhibited at the Kunstschau in Vienna in 1908, the painting attracted attention for its innovative composition and almost mystical treatment of nature. Offered at Sotheby’s London in 2017 with an estimate in excess of $45 million, Bauerngarten sold for approximately $59.3 million, becoming the most expensive Klimt landscape ever sold at auction at the time. The sale underscored the rarity of major Klimt landscapes appearing on the market, with many works of this caliber held in museum collections.

Portrait of Fräulein Lieser , 1918 Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons. A young woman clad in a flower-patterned cape sits in a frontal pose against a vivid red background. Her face is rendered with delicate, precise details that contrast with the looser, more expressive brushwork characteristic of Klimt’s late style. The identity of the sitter remains uncertain. Earlier catalogues identified her as Margarethe Constance Lieser (1899−1965), while more recent research has suggested that she may have been either Helene Lieser (1898−1962) or Annie Lieser (1901−1972), daughters of the Viennese patrons Henriette and Justus Lieser. Klimt began working on the portrait in 1917, with the model visiting his studio in Hietzing nine times during April and May of that year. The portrait was unfinished when he died of a stroke on February 6, 1918. The painting was known to scholars only through a black-and-white photograph, and its whereabouts remained uncertain for decades before it was discovered in Austrian private hands. On April 24, 2024, it was auctioned by Vienna’s im Kinsky, Austria’s second-largest auction house, recognized for its expertise in Klimt’s works and its experience handling restitution-related art sales. Portrait of Fräulein Lieser sold for approximately $41 million including fees, setting a record as the highest price ever achieved for an artwork at auction in Austria. The sale was conducted on behalf of the owners at the time and the legal successors of the Liester family, following an agreement based on the 1998 Washington Principles. The work was purchased by Patti Wong & Associates for an anonymous buyer.

Dame mit Fächer (Lady with a Fan), 1917−1918 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Dame mit Fächer is thought to be the last portrait Klimt worked on before his death in 1918; it was still on the easel in his Vienna studio at the time of his passing. The work represents the culmination of the artist’s late portraiture, combining the human presence of the unidentified sitter with the rich patterns and decorative experimentation that defined his last years. Returning to the square format he first employed in Portrait of Sonja Knips (1898), Klimt placed the figure at the center of the composition and surrounded her with motifs drawn from Asian art, including the phoenix and lotus blossoms. The sitter’s elaborate robe also evokes Klimt’s long-standing interest in textiles and fashion, an area closely connected to his companion Emilie Flöge, an influential Viennese fashion designer. At Sotheby’s London in June 2023, Dame mit Fächer carried an estimate of more than £65 million ($80 million) and was backed by a third-party guarantee. The painting was hammered in at $93.5 million, reaching $108.4 million with fees and establishing a new auction record for Klimt. The result surpassed the previous record of $104.6 million held by Birch Forest , highlighting the extraordinary demand for Klimt’s late masterpieces in the international market.

Blumenwiese (Blooming Meadow), 1908 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. In this painting of the meadows surrounding Lake Attersee, Klimt moves away from a traditional landscape format to offer a dazzling carpet of wildflowers—bellflowers buttercups, daisies, cornflowers, clover, and dandelions—that fills the canvas, Here, the horizonless view, square composition, and flattened pictorial space show the influence of late Claude Monet, Japanese art, and emerging Modernist photography. Executed likely in the summer of 1908, Blumenwiese represents a pivotal moment in Klimt’s landscape painting, when he pushed the genre toward greater abstraction. The radical composition was so unconventional that some contemporary critics dismissed Klimt’s style as the work of a “madman.” Its distinguished provenance, including ownership by Austro-Galician painter Broncia Koller-Pinell and her husband, Hugo Koller, further enhances its historical significance. The painting sold at Sotheby’s in 2025 for $86 million (including fees), becoming the second-most expensive Klimt landscape ever auctioned and reaffirming its rarity and enduring appeal among collectors.

Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer , 1914-1916 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914−16) exemplifies Klimt’s mature portrait style, where realism and decoration meet seamlessly. The subject emerges from an elaborate costume that blurs the boundary between figure and background. Completed after nearly three years of revisions, the painting demonstrates Klimt’s meticulous working process and extraordinary feeling for ornamentation. Commissioned by the Lederer family, among Klimt’s most important patrons, the painting is one of only two full-length portraits by the artist remaining in private hands. It survived Nazi confiscation during the Second World War and was restituted in 1948. Its provenance, later including a time in the collection of Leonard A. Lauder, makes it one of Klimt’s most significant surviving mature portraits. Estimated at $150 million, the painting was the centerpiece of Sotheby’s November 2025 sales. After a dramatic 20-minute contest between two telephone bidders, it realized $236.4 million (including fees), eclipsing Klimt’s previous record and becoming the second-most expensive work ever sold at auction, behind Leonardo da Vinci’s Salvator Mundi .

content.article_text:
Arthur Jafa is such a star these days that most art lovers know his story. It wasn’t always so.

Until about a decade ago, he was basically an artist’s artist, working between the cinema and art worlds. His reputation only exploded in 2016, when he was in his mid-50s, in the immediate aftermath of Donald J. Trump ’s shock defeat of Hillary Clinton .

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

His video Love Is the Message, The Message Is Death (2016) drew crowds to Gavin Brown’s Enterprise in Harlem in the days after the election, and emotional reactions from visitors and critics . Jafa has been treated as a sage ever since, receiving honor after honor. The New Museum ‘s recently opened retrospective of his work, curated by the museum’s director, Massimiliano Gioni , and its senior curator, Gary Carrion-Murayari , is only the latest.

The Gavin Brown tale has been so often recited that it’s almost not worth revisiting. I mention it to stress that the conversation around Jafa has been shaped by a very particular cultural moment: the post-2016 Reckoning and Resistance period, what writer Molly Fischer called “ Pop Culture’s Great Awokening .” Some now term it “Woke 1.0.”

Installation view of “Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony” at the New Museum. Photo by Ben Davis.

That phrase was popularized recently by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez . Disavowing some of her previous statements, the Democratic congresswoman alluded to a new common sense among progressive politicians: “Woke 1.0 was crazy.”

Is social justice washed? Or just moving on to something more practical? Is the culture trending post-woke, or anti-woke, or “dark woke,” or entering some kind of Woke 2.0 era? Anna Kornbluh ’s Immediacy , Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò’ s Elite Capture , Catherine Liu ’s Traumatized , and Anton Jäger ’s Hyperpolitics are all recent works of cultural theory, of varying degrees of acuity, that try to find a way to say that the liberal symbolic politics of the post-2016 period were reductive and destructive. (Big parts of my last book, Art in the After-Culture , were trying to work out some kind of non-reactionary critique of this era of culture as well.)

The museum world has so far shown only the most desultory interest in engaging that issue. Here, we can just ask how Arthur Jafa’s work lands now, in this new cultural climate—whatever we call it.

Installation view of “Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony” at the New Museum. Photo by Ben Davis.

The Message, Revisited

Love Is the Message, The Message Is Death began as a personal project, composed of clips that Jafa had on his computer that he strung together to screen for intimates. It’s a tough, hard-to-watch work, a harrowing montage of violence against Black people, alternating with joyous and stylish clips of Black celebrities.

Yet when I returned to it at the New Museum, what struck me about it now is that it is unusually direct for Jafa. Perhaps that is what its origin as a personal project let it be, actually: not unusually experimental, but abnormally blunt.

Arthur Jafa, Love is the Message, The Message is Death (2016). Photo by Ben Davis.

You get a moment with 16-year-old Hunger Games actress Amandla Stenberg , clipped from a viral 2015 video about cultural appropriation, “ Don’t Cash Crop My Cornrows. ” Stenberg gives the audience the one-line way to read the film’s upsetting juxtapositions: “What would America be like if we loved Black people as much as we love Black culture?”

And just like that, an artwork that was personal, shockingly violent, and full of tortured, unresolved feelings was distilled into something that could be read in a very simple way: as a teaching tool. Which is how it was used. In 2020, in the full flush of the George Floyd uprising, museums teamed up to show the work online, as if exposure to Jafa’s vision, somehow, would heal America’s soul.

A decade of cultural politics has shifted the meaning of the work’s imagery. Protests rose and fell. Corporate America responded by leaning on Black culture to insulate itself from those protests and to capture the cachet that only a righteous cause brings (including in mortifying ways: Kendall Jenner ’s “Black Lives Matter” Pepsi ad ; the Gushers brand tweeting solidarity with BLM; Jeff Bezos sending Amoako Boafo art into space to honor “Black joy”).

Arthur Jafa, Notebooks (1988–2007). Photo by Ben Davis.

Stenberg was elevated as high as you can go in pop culture: Disney made her the star of a Star Wars show. Critics praised The Acolyte for diverse casting and queer themes. But it was a turkey; Stenberg blamed its cancellation on racist online trolls.

Barack Obama ’s presence in Love Is the Message , singing “Amazing Grace,” was unifying and cathartic for the liberal audience at the time. A decade on, the millennial-and-younger left has defined itself against Obama’s brand of professorial centrism.

Kanye West ’s halting, lachrymose “Ultralight Beam” on the soundtrack granted Love Is the Message a lot of emotional punch. West spent the next decade becoming a more and more unnerving public figure (though Jafa still defends him ). He went on to stump for Trump and sell swastika merchandise .

All these developments trouble any use of Love Is the Message that turns on the simplest reading of that Stenberg line from 2015. But for Jafa himself, the shifting, complicated meanings of his subjects can be easily absorbed into his artistic project as a whole.

“My drive is to make things that are epic, and dense, and knotty, and Black—but at the same time completely refuse any sort of reductive idea of what Blackness is,” he has said . Jafa keeps saying things like that, and he keeps making works that are edgy, and uncomfortable, and hard to read; the audience keeps wanting to read him as offering clear-cut lessons.

Installation view of “Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony” featuring APEX (2013). Photo by Ben Davis.

Ultra-Violent Thoughts

You can see the wires of interpretation cross in the case of Jafa’s most recent major work, BEN GAZARRA (2024), more or less the grisly climax of the New Museum show.

It edits the final ultra-violent showdown of Martin Scorsese ’s Taxi Driver (1976) into multiple alternate versions, with subtle and not-so-subtle variations. But, always, you see a young, mohawked Robert De Niro storm a tenement to save a preteen Jodie Foster , who is in thrall to a pimp. We watch, over and over, fingers blown off, daggers gouging through hands, blown-out brains scattering across the wall. The twist is that Jafa has seamlessly reedited the film so that the pimp and his henchmen are Black.

The backstory is this: When he was in high school, Jafa saw Taxi Driver and had the idea that something was off, that these characters felt like they were meant to be Black. Later, he found out that Paul Schrader ‘s original Taxi Driver script had the pimp character as a Black man. According to film lore, Scorsese and the studio worried about charges of racism and changed the role. Harvey Keitel ended up playing the pimp.

Arthur Jafa, BEN GAZARRA (2024). Photo by Ben Davis.

In its accompanying explanation, the New Museum gently nudges the work back toward a moral reading, suggesting vaguely that it is “deconstructing the narrative faults of the scene,” and that the Jafa version holds up a mirror to contemporary racism by rendering De Niro’s avenging skinhead, Travis Bickle , in a way that reveals the film’s parallels to present-day white supremacist violence. This is the easiest hook for justifying such shocking imagery, and an almost automatic reflex of the discourse : “Black filmmaker corrects white filmmaker’s racism.”

Jafa has compared the Bickle character to Dylann Roof . But Roof slaughtered Black churchgoers, not child sex traffickers. The original film’s decision to cast the characters as white was meant to avoid staging stereotypes of Black thugs preying on innocent white girls that have always fueled white supremacist violence. Even critics who have long celebrated Jafa as a truth-teller scolded him for BEN GAZARRA , when the work debuted, finding its intention murky.

But if anything, Jafa seems drawn to the idea of the reedited Taxi Driver exactly because he doesn’t quite know what to do with the thought, because it is disturbing. (He told me that it “began as a joke,” like many of his works.) The many repeating versions of the Bickle killing spree read as Jafa trying to figure out what to do with a haunting, ugly idea, while always being pinned to the historical object.

Minor Works

Back in 2017, as the intensely moralizing period of #Resistance culture set in, art writer and now-dealer Chris Sharp penned an essay called “ Theory of the Minor. ”

Sharp was writing against the tendency—always active, but injected with steroids after 2016—of curators to favor art that flattened out into neat little homilies. This is what Sharp calls “major art,” art meant for public communication. (In recent history, I’d say Hank Willis Thomas is the epitome of “major art.”) Against it, Sharp defended art that is idiosyncratic, that comes from a distinctly personal place, that has no clear purpose or use. That’s what he called “minor art.”

Arthur Jafa, Picture Unit (Structures) II (2024). Photo by Ben Davis.

After seeing this New Museum show, my feeling is that if you can see Jafa’s work removed from the hyper-charged 2010s political and media moment that made his reputation, he looks very much like what he was before his 2016 breakout: an artist’s artist. This show is even organized more as a labyrinth than as a clear-cut career retrospective, as if to emphasize the fact of his difficulty.

Art historian Darby English has decried how the art industry tends to frame all Black contemporary artists alike, as communicators of moral truths about race and racism. Viewed clearly, outside these stock ideas, Jafa’s art is much more drawn to messiness than message; it starts from a place of personal psychodrama; and it is probably more for an art audience than a mass audience. It feels, in Sharp’s sense, minor.

Arthur Jafa, Townshend (2025). Photo by Ben Davis.

This means, also, that the work doesn’t always land. I do not personally believe that being hermetic is an end in itself. There’s a 2025 video in the show that is a wonky A.I.-animated image of the face of Pete Townshend , cofounder of the rock band the Who . The soundtrack is snippets of Who hits, punctuating silence. Whatever is going on here for Jafa doesn’t register, though I admire, sort of, how obdurate the work is.

The Texture of the Present

Then, on the other hand, there’s AGHDRA (2021). The heart of the show, for me.

Shown on a giant screen here, it is a digital video of a sun above a vast extraterrestrial ocean. The surface of this sea is some inexplicable form of black stone, like a mixture of tar and asphalt, seething up and down, somewhat crudely animated.

Fragments of distorted soul music come in and out of the soundtrack, as if we are picking up the last transmissions from Earth. Sometimes it is as if a storm picks up. The rolling berms of liquid rock become intense and threatening, filling the sky, blocking out the sun. Your head spins.

Arthur Jafa, AGHDRA (2021). Photo by Ben Davis.

Clearly, there is a symbolic association between this black ocean and Blackness. How striking that this work emerged in 2021, amid the Black Lives Matter protests that coursed through the culture, when the demands on Black artists—and on Jafa very specifically—to offer a righteous message were at their peak.

If Jafa’s mission is to make work that is “epic, and dense, and knotty, and Black,” but that “refuses any sort of reductive idea of what Blackness is,” AGHDRA takes that mission to its eerily abstract climax. It quite literally puts texture over meaning. It is sublime, and artificial, and bleak, personal and impersonal at once, and probably useless for teaching anyone anything.

It is an almost perfect work of contemporary art. And, incidentally, probably a good image for the unsettling period we are in right now, which no one seems to have the words to navigate.

“Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony” is on view at the New Museum, New York, through January 3, 2027.
content.excerpt_original: His New Museum retrospective offers a chance to make sense of a cultural shift.
