content.article_text:
With a world in crisis and an art market spinning out of control, ace art-world consultants Chen & Lampert deliver a quiz full of hard choices for Art in America readers from far and wide.

Fall is traditionally a time to reflect, so we hereby offer up this Hard Choices quiz as a chance for you to evaluate the advice we’ve been offering Art in America readers since 2019. Have we helped? How have we hurt? Are things better today than they were before you considered our counsel? Answer the following questions to let us know how we’re doing and where we can improve. Please send your responses to hardtruths@artinamericamag.com or share them with us on social media.

1. Reading Chen & Lampert makes me feel: a) Seen b) Peeped c) Stalked 2. The best description of Hard Truths is: a) Satirical but earnest advice column b) Ethical North Star c) Art world snitch sheet

3. My favorite part of taking the Hard Choices quiz is always: a) Tallying the score b) Learning new words c) Renewing my pledge to “never do this again” 4. Following Chen & Lampert’s advice has made me into: a) A stronger artist and all-around better person b) An incurable troll c) A GOD

5. Reading Chen & Lampert over the years has convinced me to: a) Pursue my master’s degree b) Finish my PhD c) Flee the art world to become a therapist who treats artists who become therapists 6. Chen & Lampert have proven to me that: a) Others wrestle with similar professional and personal dilemmas b) I am completely alone in this world c) Art problems are for coastal elites 7. The thing I like least about reading Chen & Lampert is: a) Their snide tone b) Their mercy for sinners c) The rest of the magazine 8. If Art in America stopped publishing Hard Choices and Hard Truths, I would: a) Immediately unsubscribe b) Initiate a boycott c) Finally be free of the mind goblins they gave me

9. Another Penske Media publication I would like to see Chen & Lampert write for is: a) Robb Report b) Women’s Wear Daily c) Vibe d) All the above—and they should also headline an event at SXSW

10. Chen & Lampert are people I could imagine: a) Hiring as consultants b) Having a beer with at my local bar c) Avoiding at public functions because of the shame they induce

SCORES

10–16: While doomscrolling Hyperallergic and fuming over Timothée Chalamet’s disdain for the slow arts, you inform social media that “art criticism is dead” because Chen & Lampert are besmirching the hallowed legacy of Art in America with hooliganism and puerile jokes.

17–23: Your love of Chen & Lampert is heroic. You are there for our merch drops and cannot wait to subscribe to our future Substack, which we’ll be forced to make if/when they fire us. But you won’t let that happen, and neither will the Pulitzer committee.

24–30: Deep down you’ve always known that Chen & Lampert’s uncomfortable sociological tour of the art world is actually a bighearted ploy to shape a society where artists and art will flourish and save humanity. You look forward to making their dream a reality.

content.article_text:
At the 61st Venice Biennale, Senegalese artist Caroline Gueye transforms Palazzo Navagero into an immersive exploration of perception, using gold to question how value is constructed and how our understanding of the world shifts depending on where we stand.

Gold has shaped economies, political power, and cultural histories for centuries, yet its value remains inseparable from the belief systems and perceptions through which we understand it. At the Senegal Pavilion of the 61st Venice Biennale, Caroline Gueye approaches this familiar material from an unexpected perspective. Her exhibition, WURUS , meaning ‘gold’ in Wolof, is less concerned with the precious metal itself than with the conditions that determine what we see, how we interpret it and what we consider valuable. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘Structural Field’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

Curated by Massamba Mbaye, WURUS transforms the historic building into an immersive environment where architecture and sculpture become inseparable. Darkness gives way to unexpected reflections, intricate brass-and-bronze polymer forms emerge from concealed spaces, and visitors navigate an installation in which their physical position continually alters what becomes visible. Drawing on her background in fundamental physics and astrophysics, Gueye approaches space as an active system of relationships rather than a neutral setting for objects. In conversation with ART AFRICA at the Senegal Pavilion, she reflects on representing her country, her unusual ability to visualise entire installations before they exist, and how movement, material, and perception can challenge established ideas of value.

ART AFRICA : Gold has long been associated with wealth, power and possession. What drew you to it as the starting point for WURUS, and how does the exhibition challenge our understanding of value?

Caroline Gueye: It is an honour to represent Senegal at the Venice Biennale, but it is also a big responsibility. For this exhibition, we chose the title WURUS , which means ‘gold’ in Wolof. Gold symbolises desire, power, wealth and history, but we wanted to approach it from a different perspective: the question of value.

Gold is a material whose value appears self-evident, yet that value is constructed through the meanings and systems we associate with it. In WURUS , we are not presenting gold itself. Instead, I wanted to create an experience that encourages visitors to question how they perceive something and how that perception influences the value they assign to it. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘After Collision’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

You have completely transformed the interior of Palazzo Navagero. How did you approach the architecture as an integral part of the artwork, rather than simply a space to exhibit sculptures?

We rebuilt the entire exhibition space, constructing walls and changing the room configuration because I wanted visitors to become part of the experience. Depending on where you stand and how you look at a work, your perception changes.

From the beginning, I conceived the transformation of the palazzo as an artwork in itself. The walls, passages, openings and viewpoints were not simply exhibition design but part of the artistic composition.

Working within a historic building required careful planning and collaboration with the local production team. We had to translate my vision into architectural drawings while respecting the building’s restrictions. For me, the exhibition is not a collection of separate artworks placed in a room. Everything is connected, and the space is as important as the sculptures themselves. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , Installation detail. Image © Alice Sartori.

Visitors encounter your sculptures through darkness, reflections and unexpected viewpoints. What interests you about disrupting the relationship between what we see and what we believe we are seeing?

When you enter the exhibition, you find yourself in a relatively dark space with very little light. Mirrors and reflective surfaces are everywhere, and sometimes you get a little lost. You see artworks reflected in different places, and you are not always certain whether you are looking at an object or its reflection.

I wanted to create this experience because perception depends on the conditions in which something becomes visible. Some sculptures appear immediately, while others are partially concealed or revealed only from particular positions.

Seeing something directly, from a distance or through a reflection produces different experiences. This connects to the question of value because how something appears influences how we perceive it. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , “Structural Field “Element’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

Movement is fundamental to the WURUS experience. How does the visitor’s physical position influence what becomes visible, and what does this reveal about the relationship between perception and value?

In French, we have the word parcours, which describes a path or journey. That is how I imagined this exhibition. You have to walk through it because you cannot understand the installation from a single position.

The visitor becomes an actor within the exhibition rather than simply an observer. A sculpture might be visible from one angle, disappear from another or reappear through a reflection. Movement changes the conditions in which the work is perceived.

We tend to think that what we see is fixed, but it depends on our position, distance and movement. I do not expect visitors to arrive at one particular interpretation. What matters is that they experience this shift and become aware that what they see depends on where they stand. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘Structural Field’Resonance’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

Your background in fundamental physics and astrophysics informs your understanding of space and the relationships between objects. How has this scientific training shaped your artistic thinking and the development of WURUS?

I think my background in fundamental physics and astrophysics shapes the way I work with three-dimensional forms and space. It may also explain why my sculptures are often quite intricate and complex.

My scientific background influences the questions I ask. With WURUS , for example, I became interested in where gold comes from. In astrophysics, gold is produced through extreme cosmic events, including neutron star collisions. I was also interested in its scientific and technological applications, where its electrical, thermal and optical properties are particularly valuable.

But science is not something I want to illustrate. It is a way of thinking, questioning and understanding relationships. For me, space is not simply an empty container but something active, shaped by the relationships between objects, bodies and positions. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘Structural Field’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

You have described an unusual creative process in which you can visualise an entire installation before producing drawings or models. How does this process unfold, and what challenges arise when translating these mental constructions into physical form?

My process is quite particular because I see everything in my head. It is so clear that I can walk through an entire exhibition in my imagination before it exists.

I discovered that this was perhaps unusual during the Dakar Biennale in 2022, where I received a prize for an immersive installation. People asked how I had created it, and I explained that I could see everything in my head. Through those conversations, I realised that not everybody works this way.

For WURUS , the process was the same. I could imagine the rooms, the sculptures, their positions and how visitors would move through the space. I do not necessarily need drawings to understand how something should look, although translating that vision into architectural plans and explaining it to the production team is another matter.

With individual sculptures, the process can require more experimentation, particularly when working with unfamiliar materials. Even a small change in scale or form can affect how a work is perceived. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , installation detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

Your sculptures are made from brass and bronze polymer, materials that resemble gold without possessing its material identity. How do these choices, together with light and reflective surfaces, contribute to your exploration of perceived value?

I like to have freedom when I create because the shapes I imagine are often intricate and technically difficult. I need materials that allow me to achieve those forms.

For WURUS , I used brass and bronze polymer, which can resemble gold without actually being gold. This distinction is important because the exhibition is about shifting perceptions of value. You look at something that appears to be gold, but it is not, which raises questions about how appearance influences what we think something is worth.

The mirrors, reflective surfaces and lighting are equally important. They are not simply atmospheric elements but part of the concept, influencing how the sculptures appear and how visitors experience them. Everything contributes to the uncertainty between what something is and what we perceive it to be. Caroline Gueye and Massamba Mbaye. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

At a time when economic, cultural, and symbolic values are increasingly contested, what broader questions does WURUS raise about how we construct meaning, assign value, and understand the world around us?

We are living in a moment when value is becoming increasingly abstract and detached from materiality. WURUS does not address this directly as a commentary, but it creates a situation in which people can experience how value is constructed.

The exhibition is about changing the conditions through which we perceive something. The objects themselves do not necessarily change, but the way we encounter them does. Their appearance depends on our position, movement, the light and the surrounding space.

I wanted visitors to become part of the installation because their presence contributes to what becomes visible. Something that appears obvious from one perspective may become quite different from another. I am not asking people to arrive at a particular conclusion, but to experience how changing their position can change their perception.

For a decade, the Art Basel and UBS Art Market Report has been one of the most widely cited surveys about the market. In this extended episode of Art Market Minute, host Margaret Carrigan sits down with Clare McAndrew , founder of Arts Economics and the economist behind the report.

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

McAndrew traces her path from studying cultural economics to measuring the global art market, and explains what 10 years of data have taught her about how it behaves under pressure. The episode also digs into her latest research on collectors, published in the Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting , which finds that Gen Z is spending the most on fine art, more collectors are using A.I. tools for art-buying advice, and buyers are playing it safe with their purchases.

content.article_text:
Après Faute d’amour (2017), qui sondait la déliquescence d’un couple à travers les yeux de son enfant, le cinéaste revient à ce modèle familial pour mieux le dévisager, le défigurer, le dé­construire. Parfaitement lisse, le trio formé par Gleb (Dmitri Mazourov), Galina (Iris Lebedeva) et leur fils unique adolescent apparaît déjà comme une utopie décharnée, isolée du monde et de ses vices.

Andreï Zviaguintsev : « L’enjeu principal, c’est celui du choix »

À ceci près que le couple se rend chaque jour en ville : Gleb pour se voir intimer d’envoyer ses salariés sur le front en Ukraine ; Galina pour rejoindre en secret l’homme qu’elle aime. Le cinéaste ne cherche pas à sauver moralement les apparences du masque social, autrement dit la vie de famille dans cette maison filmée comme un panoptique, où chacun des personnages se surveille et se contrôle. L’extérieur se lit alors comme l’envers du masque, le lieu d’une vérité inavouable à l’un et à l’autre et sans doute pour eux-mêmes.

À l’instar de Chabrol en son temps, Minotaure soulève une question glaçante : jusqu’où peut-on aller pour préserver le masque ? Jusqu’à quel degré d’aliénation ? Appliquée au contexte de la guerre en Ukraine, la réponse – tout aussi glaçante – n’en est que plus frontalement politique, car, enfin, Gleb fait partie des puissants de ce monde. Les pauvres, les chômeurs, les artistes, dont le « troisième homme » du récit en est une forme de synthèse, sont sacrifiés sur l’autel de l’indifférence. Un constat d’autant plus noir qu’il est filmé avec ce sens de la tragédie cher à Andreï Zviaguintsev, réduit à son essence muette : l’image d’un couple qui s’enlace dans l’obscurité, rien que l’obscurité.

Minotaure d’Andreï Zviaguintsev (Les Films du Losange, 2h15), sortie le 14 octobre

The mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, where Renoir lived out his final days, described the news as “a source of immense joy and a great relief.” He added that the paintings were “part of our city’s history, our cultural heritage.”

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

Two thieves broke into the artist’s former home, the city’s Renoir Museum , early on September 8. They attempted to take four paintings before dropping two in the garden as they rushed to escape. The value of the two stolen works, Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Young Woman at the Well (1886), was reported at a combined $10 million. Both belong to the Musée d’Orsay in Paris and were on loan.

The Marseille public prosecutor’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how the Renoir paintings were recovered. A press conference that would have given more details about the recovery was canceled so as not to interfere with the ongoing investigation.

France’s culture minister, Catherine Pégard , commended “the efficiency and determination” of the investigators in a post on social media. She also praised the “swift response” of local police, “from the moment the alarm was triggered,” as “remarkable.”

France has suffered a spate of museum heists in recent years. The highest-profile one occurred at the Louvre in Paris last October. Investigators uncovered various security failings that left the institution vulnerable to the shock $102 million theft, and the Louvre announced a $92 million master security plan .

Though Renoir continues to divide opinion , the Impressionist just broke box-office records at the National Gallery in London, with the museum selling over 22,000 tickets for its “Renoir and Love” exhibition, which is on view through January 31.

content.article_text:
I n Arabic, “fidai” means someone willing to sacrifice themselves for the greater good. Borrowing this word, which is at times used in a military context, for his collage film, Palestinian film-maker Kamal Aljafari stages a potent uprising of images against the tide of propaganda and historical erasure. Much of the film draws on archive materials once housed in the Palestine Research Centre in Beirut. In 1982, during the Lebanese civil war, Israeli forces raided the centre and seized the archive. Most of these documents on Palestinian history – books, newspapers, audiovisual artefacts – are believed to still be in the hands of the Israeli army.

Obtained through clandestine means, the footage that resurfaces in Aljafari’s film bears the physical traces of political suppression. The images are scratched, grainy and pixelated, yet through the power of montage they evoke startling visual parallels that point to the relentless violence endured by Palestinians through the decades. Black-and-white film taken during the British mandate show soldiers patrolling the streets and inflicting violence upon the Indigenous population; similar acts then committed by Israeli forces. In place of a chronological order, the editing builds a sense of continuity through recurring images. Time and time again, we see torn-down houses, terrorised children and the bodies of Palestinians murdered by occupation forces.

More than simply a work of compilation, the film also performs its own historical intervention. Many of the reels are imprinted with pejorative captions added by Israeli authorities, which Aljafari covers in streaks of red paint. In their place are excerpts from poems by Palestinian authors such as Ghassan Kanafani, whose words return a sense of humanity to these past images. Through these strategies of reclamation, Aljafari’s film brings liberation, if only momentarily, to a captive archive.

content.article_text:
F ilmed in Taiwan and set entirely inside a prestigious high school, Kiwi Chow’s gripping drama frames educational systems not merely as a preparation for the real world but as a microcosm of society at large. At this elite private institute, pupils studiously march in lines like obedient soldiers, their purple uniforms the only pop of colour in a grey building of glass and steel. The school’s operations have a touch of dystopian sci-fi: students check in with AI recognition panels, which also display their class standing and disciplinary scores. In this sterile environment where human worth is measured by standardised metrics, the breathing room for individuality is nil.

This panopticon atmosphere of surveillance and cut-throat competition is punctured by a shocking incident: an anonymous student drops a flurry of leaflets announcing their intent to take their own life on the day of the final exam, unless the school changes its authoritarian ways. The note sends tremors through both the administration and the students; intersecting narrative lines weave through a group of characters that include a model student, a dedicated but ambivalent teacher and a righteous slacker. Each carries a heavy secret that points to the moral rot beneath the facade of academic excellence.

Though grappling with heavy subjects such as self-harm, bullying and drug use, Chow treats these youthful foibles as evidence of a systemic malaise rather than individual failings. A staunch anti-authoritarian message is smuggled in the conventions of a whodunnit thriller; it parallels Chow’s previous films, including the 2021 documentary Revolution of Our Times , about the 2019-2020 Hong Kong protests . Like the rebellion in Deadline, that movement also began on campuses and was led by students. That both titles are banned in Hong Kong only underscores the urgency and importance of Chow’s film-making.

content.article_text:
T he image of the cowboy widely portrayed in westerns and popular culture has long been almost exclusively white. Yet Black cowboys hold an important place in the history of the American west. After the civil war and the abolition of slavery, many African Americans found work on ranches and on the great cattle drives westward. By the late 19th century, historians estimate about one in four cowboys were Black.

Among the Black figures who shaped this history was Bill Pickett . Born in Texas in 1870, he became one of the most celebrated Black cowboys and rodeo performers of his time, known in particular for popularising bulldogging, which would eventually give rise to modern steer wrestling.

After the national anthem, Josh, a member of the Outlaws Most Wanted, rides around the arena to a pounding hip-hop track as his teammates cheer him on at the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo in Conyers, near Atlanta , Georgia, on 2 August 2026

Members of the Outlaws Most Wanted joke and playfully challenge other riders, some of whom have travelled long distances to compete, backstage at the rodeo

His name was chosen by the promoter Lu Vason when he created the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. In 1977, Vason attended Cheyenne frontier days and was struck by the absence of Black cowboys in the arena. His research led him to the Black American West Museum in Denver, where he discovered the story of Pickett and the history of African Americans in the American west. In 1984, he created a rodeo designed to give Black cowboys and cowgirls a platform and bring greater visibility to this heritage.

More than 40 years later, that mission remains at the heart of the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. Part sporting competition, part spectacle and part space for passing on history and culture, its 2026 tour crosses the US from February to October, with stops including Memphis, Atlanta, Oakland and Los Angeles.

This year, I decided to join the tour in Atlanta.

A family on horseback waits to enter the arena at therodeo, reflecting the intergenerational nature of a cowboy culture passed down through families. 1 August 2026

While there, I met for the first time a contact I had been speaking with before my trip. He runs Diamondcut Ranch, where he works with and trains horses, and around which a wider community of riders has formed. It was there that I met the Outlaws Most Wanted, a team of “bronc riders” competing at the Bill Pickett.

The organisers allowed me behind the barriers on the condition that I stayed with them. I found myself in the space just behind the arena, where the riders wait for their turn and prepare their equipment.

Music is everywhere. The riders joke around, encourage one another and build each other up. The energy and adrenaline rise as their turn approaches, until each rider has to move away from that collective excitement and focus on the few seconds waiting for him in the arena.

Rachied Robins, AKA Django, a member of the Outlaws Most Wanted bronc-riding team, who became my main contact and a key voice in telling the group’s story during the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. 1/08/2026

One of them, Rachied Robins, AKA Django, describes the Outlaws Most Wanted as a group of Caribbean men, some of whom have come from difficult backgrounds, brought together by their love of horses. Some, he says, found “refuge in this horse world”. Over time, their bonds grew stronger: “We’re in a brotherhood now.”

Django grew up in Kissimmee, Florida, surrounded by rodeo culture. He started out in bull riding before changing disciplines after a bull stomped on his face. He now competes in ranch bronc riding and laughingly describes himself as an “adrenaline junkie”.

But behind the adrenaline, there is also fear. Before he gets on the horse, thoughts of the danger and all the “what ifs” run through his mind. Then he has to find a way to clear his head.

The Outlaws Most Wanted bronc-riding team at the Bill Pickett rodeo

“You just gotta clear your mind and leave it in God’s hands.”

He has to trust his technique and make it through eight seconds. And even once the ride is over, the danger is not: Django tells me that getting off the horse can be one of the most dangerous moments.

There is also a financial side to competing. Django tells me that the Bill Pickett is not among the rodeos offering the largest purses: at the April event he competed in, he says a rider could win up to about $1,500 (£1,135), compared with as much as $10,000 at some other rodeos. But money is only part of what is at stake.

“It’s not just the money, but also your name, the respect, ranking.”

What struck me most about the Bill Pickett, however, perhaps happens beyond the competition itself.

Riders wait to enter the arena in a solemn moment, hats held over their hearts, as The Star-Spangled Banner is sung a cappella at sunset before the start of the rodeo

Before the events begin, The Star-Spangled Banner is sung a cappella. Hats are placed over hearts, the riders stand still, and silence falls across the stands and the arena. I remember getting goosebumps and tears in my eyes.

Then, almost without transition, the atmosphere shifts completely and the adrenaline takes over.

All the riders enter the arena to a powerful hip-hop track. The volume rises, the horses come in, and the crowd shouts, applauds and dances. Within moments, the atmosphere moves from solemn stillness to an almost explosive energy.

That contrast captures much of what I felt at the Bill Pickett. History and memory are central to the event, but they are not frozen in the past. They coexist with hip-hop, fashion, competition and a deeply contemporary Black cowboy culture.

After his ride, a cowboy walks along the edge of the arena as the crowd cheers him on at the Bill Pickett

The audience is very much part of the spectacle. Western shirts, cowboy hats and boots fill the stands: people come to watch the rodeo, but also to gather, dance, show their style and celebrate a shared culture. Throughout the event, the announcers return again and again to the history of Black cowboys and the values the Bill Pickett seeks to pass on. That history is not confined to a few lines in a programme: it is an integral part of the event.

When I ask Django what the Bill Pickett means to him, he tells me that it is about more than just rodeo: “Bill Pickett means a lot to me personally. Not just because it’s a rodeo, but because it’s a platform for us minorities to come together.”

He talks about being able to show what they can do “as a group, as a unit”, but also about having a place where he can be himself and where he feels at home.

The Outlaws Most Wanted do not compete only at Black rodeos. Django tells me they compete wherever they have the opportunity and rejects the idea that these events are a form of separation. For him, they are above all about making a heritage visible: “We just want to bring out our heritage and bring out our history and show that we are part of this history, and this is part of our history.”

Members of the Outlaws Most Wanted bronc riding team gather behind the arena

It is also about passing something on. From trail rides to rodeos, horses create a space around which families, friendships and communities are formed. For some members of the Outlaws Most Wanted, this world has even become a refuge.

When I ask Django what he hopes the young people in the stands take away from watching him ride, he does not talk about becoming a cowboy or winning competitions. Above all, he hopes to show them that another path is possible: “Do something safe, do something legal, get out the streets, keep your mind right, don’t be another statistic.”

More than a century after Black cowboys helped shape the history of the American west while remaining largely absent from its popular image, the Bill Pickett offers a space where this heritage does not belong only to the past: it continues to be lived, passed on and reinvented.

Georgia

Horses

Photography

content.article_text:
From October 6, 2026, to January 6, 2027, the Cavaillon Media Library, in the Vaucluse region of southern France, will present 18 photographs by Dorothea Lange, on exceptional loan from the Musée Réattu in Arles. Among them is Migrant Mother , the American photographer’s iconic image, made in California in 1936.

This exhibition takes on particular resonance as the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art opens its doors in Los Angeles on September 22, 2026. Among the photographic works presented in its collections is Migrant Mother , now one of the most celebrated images in the history of photography.

Nearly 9,000 kilometers away, Lange’s photographs are leaving the collections of the Musée Réattu in Arles for an exceptional presentation in Cavaillon, where they will encounter a new audience. The exhibition is a rare event for the Cavaillon area. Migrant Mother is presented alongside 17 other photographs, offering a glimpse into Lange’s attentive gaze on the social and human realities of her time.

A photograph that has crossed the decades without losing its power: the face of a woman, a family and, through them, an entire era marked by the Great Depression.

The connection between Los Angeles and Cavaillon gives this presentation a particular resonance. Two institutions, two territories and two different contexts, yet sharing the same belief in photography’s ability to tell the truth of the world and the stories of human lives.

In Cavaillon, Dorothea Lange is the central figure of Le Regard en héritage , a year-long photography program taking place from September 2026 to September 2027 across the 16 municipalities of Luberon Monts de Vaucluse Agglomeration.

Supported by the French Ministry of Culture as part of the Bicentenary of Photography, the program brings together exhibitions, lectures, screenings, encounters and workshops. It creates a dialogue between documentary photography, contemporary practice, amateur photography and the transmission of photographic knowledge and skills.

Born in Oppède around the exhibition Le Verbe et l’Image , Le Regard en héritage has gradually expanded to include the municipalities and media libraries across the region. Bringing together the work of established photographers and participatory projects developed with local residents, the program explores different ways of looking: at landscapes, faces, memories, heritage and the transformations of a territory.

With Dorothea Lange as its point of departure, Le Regard en héritage places Luberon Monts de Vaucluse within the celebration of 200 years of photography, while making the photographic image a means of transmitting, questioning and renewing the way we see the world.

Dorothea Lange Exhibition From 6 October 2026 to 6 January 2027 Cavaillon Media Centre 60 rue Véran Rousset – 84300 Cavaillon Free admission Tuesday: 1 pm – 7 pm Wednesday: 10 am – 6 pm Thursday and Friday: 1 pm – 6 pm Saturday: 10 am – 6 pm Closed on Sundays and Mondays. www.mediathequeslmv.fr

content.article_text:
JOACHIM ROMAIN — LOOKING AT WHAT OTHERS NO LONGER SEE

Joachim Romain looks at images precisely where they generally cease to interest us. Torn posters, amputated letters, anonymous faces, faded urban signs, visual debris: His domain is not that of the spectacular image, but that of what remains after it. Since his early days in street photography, he has extracted fragments from the urban environment that the ordinary gaze has learned to overlook, removing them from their status as waste and giving them another existence. For Romain, to photograph is already to displace. This gesture lies at the heart of a practice that has never fully accepted the boundaries between photography, urban art, collage, and installation. He does not regard these mediums as separate territories, but as different states of the same gaze. Photography captures, appropriation isolates, collage recomposes, and installation displaces once again. What interests him, then, is less the image itself than what it becomes when its context changes when it loses its original function and acquires a new visual charge. An advertising poster is no longer simply a poster once it has been torn; a fragment of a letter is no longer merely a sign once it becomes material; a face torn from an image can suddenly become the portrait of an era. There is a form of contemporary archaeology at work here. But it is an archaeology without nostalgia. Romain does not seek to preserve the traces of the city; he puts them into tension. He is interested in the way images appear, disappear, overlap, and ultimately generate a memory of their own. His work reveals a city that is constantly producing and destroying its own representations. Through it, he also questions our relationship to images: their omnipresence, their speed of circulation, their obsolescence, and their strange ability, despite their proliferation, to become invisible. His gaze naturally belongs to a history of urban art in which Jacques Villeglé stands as one of its defining figures. Yet with Romain, the lineage is never simply a matter of quotation. Where Villeglé turned the wall into a space of revelation, collecting the anonymous tears of public posters as signs of a collective memory, Romain works within a landscape saturated with images, where the fragment no longer comes from the street alone. It also comes from the digital realm, commerce, advertising, screens, and a new visual economy in which everything is produced, consumed, and replaced almost instantaneously.

His participation in the exhibition devoted to Jacques Villeglé at the Musée Carnavalet takes on a particular resonance in this context. It places his work within a history that continually reinvents itself: that of artists who do not necessarily create their images from nothing but know how to recognize an image that is already there, buried beneath another, and give it a second life. For Romain, this act of revelation operates as much through photography as through material, gesture, and composition. It is precisely this logic of displacement that emerges in Défragmentation at Galerie Laurent Rigail. Alongside Jacques Villeglé, Quentin DMR, and the other artists brought together for the exhibition, Romain contributes to a reflection on the fragment as artistic material: a fragment of the city, of memory, of a poster, a photograph, or a sign. Yet the exhibition’s title could almost describe his own method. To defragment is not simply to break an image into pieces. It is to alter the relationships between those pieces in order to make something else appear. This idea runs throughout his work. Even when he photographs, Romain does not simply record. He selects. He frames. He excludes. Through the choice of what he decides to look at, he is already transforming reality. “Framing one part often makes you forget the rest,” he says in this questionnaire. The phrase could serve as a key to his entire practice. Because this is precisely where his art begins: in the awareness that looking is always an act of selection and that a fragment can sometimes say more than a complete image. His relationship to photography is therefore less documentary than critical. What matters is not only what the image shows, but what it leaves outside the frame, what it conceals, and what it suddenly allows us to see. Hence his recurring attention to detail, accident, and to that which is “not there for everyone else.” Romain searches for cracks in the surface of things. He finds stories there, tensions, sometimes simply an emotion. His visual practice extends this investigation without resolving it. He transforms visual waste into material but refuses to strip it of its disorder. He does not clean up the fragment; he allows it to retain the traces of its passage. Perhaps this is where the singularity of his gaze lies. In a world where images have become instantly available, retouched, and reproducible, Romain continues to search for those that have lived for images that still bear the marks of their own disappearance.

To look at the world with Joachim Romain is therefore to accept slowing down before what we have learned to pass without seeing. A worn letter. A half-erased face. A torn poster. A fragment of the city. Nothing, apparently. And yet, within that almost nothing, the possibility of an image.

Website : www.joachimromain.com Instagram : @joachimromain

Actu : Exhibitions : « Défragmentation » from oct 14th to nov. 14th 2026 Galerie Laurent Rigail 40, rue Volta 75003 Paris

Participation to the exhibition « Paris à l’arraché » dedicated to Jacques Villeglé at Musée Carnavalet.

What was your first photographic trigger? Joachim Romain: My father was a photographer. For my 15th birthday, he gave me a Nikon EM.

A photographic memory from your childhood? Joachim Romain: Me on the beach, photographed by my father.

The camera of your childhood? Joachim Romain: Polaroid, of course.

The one you use today? Joachim Romain: Canon 6D.

The man or woman of the image who inspired you? Joachim Romain: Brassaï.

The image you wish you had taken? Joachim Romain: The Woodstock album cover. I would have done two crazy things.

The one that moved you the most? Joachim Romain: Lee Friedlander.

And the one that made you angry? Joachim Romain: Marine mammals caught in fishing nets.

Which photograph changed the world? Joachim Romain: “Tank Man,” in Tiananmen Square.

And which photograph changed your world? Joachim Romain: A worn-out letter B and a face on a poster, photographed in Sarajevo in 2006. That image profoundly changed my photographic work and the subjects I research today.

What interests you most in an image? Joachim Romain: Its emotion.

What details do you look for in a face, a landscape, or an object? Joachim Romain: The one that isn’t there for everyone else.

Elliott Erwitt once said: “Color is descriptive. Black and white is interpretive.” Do you agree? Joachim Romain: To some extent, yes. But why choose?

Can technique sometimes take precedence over emotion in photography? Joachim Romain: For me, technique comes after the subject and the framing. But it remains a very important part, depending on the effect you want to achieve with your subject.

Is beauty in photography, for you, purely aesthetic? Joachim Romain: Absolutely not.

What can make silence visible in a photograph? Joachim Romain: A detail.

Does the uniqueness of a photograph come from the moment or from staging? Joachim Romain: The moment is unique and that’s everything.

Can a photograph be more truthful than reality? Joachim Romain: That’s where staging comes into play.

Can a photograph change our perception of an event? Joachim Romain: Clearly. Focusing on one part often makes you forget the rest.

Is photography a testimony or a form of manipulation? Joachim Romain: For me, a testimony above all.

What makes a good photograph? Joachim Romain: The emotion it gives you.

What quality is essential to being a good photographer? Joachim Romain: Going out to find your subject and waiting for the right moment.

How do you choose your projects? Joachim Romain: They are connected to my visual art practice, although originally it was the other way around: my street photography gradually gave birth to my visual art practice. Today, the two have become one body of work in which photography and visual art come together.

How would you describe your creative process? Joachim Romain: It depends on the work. With the photographic series Fast_Shop , for example, there is a whole research process beforehand, followed by a real exploration of movement and time.

An upcoming project that is particularly close to your heart? Joachim Romain: My project Made in Europe is about creating an exhibition that brings my street work, photography, and installation into dialogue.

The person you would like to photograph? Joachim Romain: my daughter, and I did it! But I’d happily do it again.

The person you would like to be photographed by? Joachim Romain: Mari Katayama or Zanele Muholi.

One essential photography book? Joachim Romain: Affichage_Libre 🙂 Otherwise, Chernobyl by Robert Polidori. And a book by Brassaï, Brassaï: Picasso and the Photographs , or Vivian Maier.

What is the last photograph you took? Joachim Romain: Portraits of artists in Turkey, in Izmir.

On social media, are you more Instagram, Facebook, or TikTok — and why? Joachim Romain: Instagram. There hasn’t been anything fun on Facebook for a while. And I’m not on TikTok at all.

What has changed in photography since the rise of social media? Joachim Romain: The quality, the framing… A bit like when digital photography arrived and everyone thought they were a photographer.

One Instagram account everyone should follow? Joachim Romain: Your friends’. The rest isn’t important.

What is your view on AI? Joachim Romain: A bit like when the first Adobe Illustrator came along: it’s a development that is difficult to avoid, but one we need to learn to master. The most important thing, in my view, is to remain the creative force, rather than simply following or letting AI do the creating for us. But, in reality, I think we won’t be in control of much for very long.

Color or black and white? Joachim Romain: Both, but with a preference for black and white.

Natural or artificial light? Joachim Romain: Natural.

Which city strikes you as the most photogenic? Joachim Romain: Marseille.

The city, country, or culture you dream of discovering? Joachim Romain: Africa.

The place you never get tired of? Joachim Romain: My bathroom 🙂 Seriously, though, definitely the Arles festival.

The image that, for you, represents the state of the world today? Joachim Romain: The photomontage of British Prime Minister Tony Blair taking a selfie against a backdrop of burning oil.

What do you think is missing from the world today? Joachim Romain: A strong movement toward nature and living together. It’s frightening right now.

If God existed, would you ask him to pose for you, or would you go for a selfie with him? Joachim Romain: That’s too disconnected from reality for me, so…

Your favorite drug? Joachim Romain: My studio.

Your best way to switch off? Joachim Romain: I haven’t found one. I dream of it.

Your latest act of madness? Joachim Romain: A Get 27–Ricard cocktail in Arles 🙂 I still have a headache.

The body of work you are particularly proud of? Joachim Romain: My Urban work, which consists of transforming what everyone considers visual waste into an art installation.

The job you would never have wanted to do? Joachim Romain: I respect people so much that saying “I wouldn’t want to do your job” feels a bit harsh 🙂

Which question throws you off the most? Joachim Romain: Who is your favorite artist?

The last thing you did for the first time? Joachim Romain: Rowing on the Olympic rowing basin in Montreal, with my family. It was great.

Your biggest regret? Joachim Romain: Not having gone to art school.

If you could start all over again? Joachim Romain: Maybe I would have taken school more seriously. But then again, I wouldn’t have had the path I’ve had, and I don’t regret it.

If I could organize your ideal dinner, who would be sitting around the table? Joachim Romain: Jim Morrison, Nina Kraviz, Jacques Villeglé, Anselm Kiefer. Music and art: everything I love.

What would you like people to say about you… afterwards? Joachim Romain: If they remember me at all, that’s already something 🙂

The one thing people absolutely need to know about you? Joachim Romain: Generous.

One last word? Joachim Romain: Together.

content.article_text:
中田友木の写真展「EMOTIONS, IN MY LIFE.」が、2026年10月20日から25日まで、大阪・南船場のギャラリー・ソラリスで開催される。自身の人生に残る怒りや悲しみといった感情の記憶を、「身体」の反応から捉え直した作品を発表する。

本展の出発点となったのは、感情と身体の関係だ。「怖いから逃げるのではない。逃げるから怖いのだ。悲しいから泣くのではない。泣くから悲しいのだ」と中田は記す。感情が先に存在し、それによって身体が反応するのではなく、身体に起こった変化を脳が察知することで感情が生じる——そうした考え方に着目し、自らの記憶を写真によって検証することを試みた。

中田が振り返るのは、これまでの人生で愚痴やぼやきとして記憶に刻まれてきた、激しい怒りや悲しみだ。それらも、もとをたどれば「ほんの些細な『身体』の反応だったかもしれない」と考え、過去の感情を生み出したであろう身体の動きを想像。カメラの前で中田自身がその動きを演じ、セルフポートレートとして写真に定着させた。それは出来事を事実として記録する一般的な自叙伝とは異なる、いわば「感情の記憶」による自画像だ。中田は「自叙伝やその記録の写真なんぞとても残す気になれない。でもこんな風な感情の記憶の写真なら残そうと思った」と語る。過去に何が起きたのかではなく、それによって身体に何が起き、どのような感情として残ったのか。身体を演じ直す行為を介して、自身の生を写真へと置き換えていく。

中田は京都府出身。2025年3月に京都芸術大学通信教育部美術科写真コースを卒業。同年4月、同大学通信制大学院の写真・映像領域へ進学し、現在は修士課程に在学している。

content.title_original: Hailun Ma Makes Ürümqi the New Brooklyn
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/hometown-2018-c-hailun-ma.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Hailun Ma Makes Ürümqi the New Brooklyn"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A leading light of China’s new photography, Hailun Ma, whose work slips between personal projects and fashion commissions, brings her first major solo exhibition abroad, “Hometown,” to Foam in Amsterdam, and carries us off to Xinjiang."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Hailun Ma ."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/hometown-2025-c-hailun-ma.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“The air always smells of dust,” Ma writes of her native land. Born in 1992 in Ürümqi, the capital of Xinjiang, on China’s far northwestern edge, and a member of the country’s Han majority, she grew up in a city where Uyghurs, Kazakhs, and many other peoples brush shoulders. In high school, she borrowed her parents’ digital camera to take her first pictures. The imagery of her homeland has fed her ever since, as these lines about summers spent with her father attest: “Poplar trees, narrow irrigation ditches, sheep under the apple trees. Donkey carts, livestock bazaars.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/dawazi-girls-2024-c-hailun-ma.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kashi-youth-c-hailun-ma.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In 2013, she left to study photography and fashion imagery at the School of Visual Arts in New York. Hailun Ma Makes Ürümqi the New Brooklyn

A leading light of China’s new photography, Hailun Ma, whose work slips between personal projects and fashion commissions, brings her first major solo exhibition abroad, “Hometown,” to Foam in Amsterdam, and carries us off to Xinjiang.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Hailun Ma .

“The air always smells of dust,” Ma writes of her native land. Born in 1992 in Ürümqi, the capital of Xinjiang, on China’s far northwestern edge, and a member of the country’s Han majority, she grew up in a city where Uyghurs, Kazakhs, and many other peoples brush shoulders. In high school, she borrowed her parents’ digital camera to take her first pictures. The imagery of her homeland has fed her ever since, as these lines about summers spent with her father attest: “Poplar trees, narrow irrigation ditches, sheep under the apple trees. Donkey carts, livestock bazaars.”

In 2013, she left to study photography and fashion imagery at the School of Visual Arts in New York. In Brooklyn, where everyone wears their roots with swagger, she began to see the city of her childhood in a new light. “I want to show the cool side of Xinjiang, a side I’m calling Uruklyn,” she said. The portmanteau, a contraction of Ürümqi and Brooklyn, gave rise to a project launched in 2021: residents of Ürümqi and Kashgar, an oasis city in the region’s southwest, strike poses on their rooftops and street corners, just as New York hipsters might. Kashgar is also the birthplace of the series “Kashi Youth,” in which a 2025 image shows a helmeted young woman in leopard print, pink tulle ruffles, and white sneakers, standing before a motorcycle draped in red lace like a fashion accessory.

Far from the images of surveillance and repression that dominate media coverage of Xinjiang, Ma turns her gaze to the everyday lives of its people. Through her lens, the young revive their parents’ traditions by running them through the filter of global urban culture. Within a single frame, an embroidered skullcap crowns a baseball cap, and sneakers tread on traditional rugs. Weaned on basketball and hip-hop, Ma’s generation saw Nike as a window onto the world, and the American brand is everywhere: “They’re not barefoot. They’re wearing the latest Dunks and Jordans,” the photographer notes.

Her eye lingers on details. Hometown (2018) isolates a smile that bares a gleaming set of braces. In Xinjiang Fashion Guide (2019), henna-stained fingers tuck banknotes beneath sheer tights, just above a hot-pink lace stocking. The frame also opens onto the Pamir Mountains, where Love in Tashkurgan (2025) shows women and children in embroidered pillbox hats, perched proudly in the bed of a pickup truck. The exhibition’s curator, Aya Musa, sums up what is at play in these images: “A color can hold a memory. A pose can hold a wish. A garment can hold a route between generations.”

Hailun Ma’s “Hometown” is on view through January 20, 2027, at Foam in Amsterdam, the Netherlands.

Artículos

Aaron Taylor-Johnson será Quicksilver en The Avengers: Age of Ultron

Julio Vélez

El protagonista de Kick-Ass ha confirmado su participación en Avengers 2 en el papel de Quicksilver. Evan Peters también lo interpretará en Days of Future Past.

The Wrap fue quien confirmó la noticia sobre que Aaron Taylor-Johnson participará en The Avengers: Age of Ultron , la nueva producción de Marvel Studios programada para el 2015, para interpretar a Quicksilver . Como recordarán, hace apenas algunos meses la misma fuente compartió que el protagonista de Kick-Ass encabezaba la lista de candidatos para el papel, pero que sus compromisos, producto de su contrato para la nueva versión de Godzilla , impedían que esto pudiera hacerse oficial. Sin embargo, ¡esto ha cambiado!

Mismo personaje, dos producciones

Esta noticia hace aún más curiosa la observación que les comentábamos antes: Taylor-Johnson será Pietro Maximoff en la segunda entrega de The Avengers de Marvel Studios, mientras que Evan Peters interpretará al mismo personaje en X-Men: Days of Future Past de Fox. ¿Ustedes recuerdan cuando ambos actores estuvieron juntos en Kick-Ass (2010)?. ¿Cuáles son sus opiniones para este giro?

Aaron Taylor Johnson se integra así a Elizabeth Olsen en el papel de Scarlet Witch y James Spader como el maligno Ultron . The Avengers: Age of Ultron se realizará bajo la dirección de Joss Whedon y el regreso de Chris Evans, Robert Downey Jr., Samuel L. Jackson, Scarlett Johansson , Chris Hemsworth y Mark Ruffalo.

Julio Vélez Colaborador en web y revista Cine PREMIERE desde 2006. Me especializo en anime/manga, comics, doblaje, tecnología y videojuegos. Mis sagas favoritas: Doctor Who, Star Trek, Dragon Ball y Star Wars. Batimaníaco, geek ochentero y hardcore gamer.

content.article_text:
On 21 March 1960, a crowd gathered outside a police station in a Transvaal township, part of a nationwide protest against apartheid pass laws used to control where black South Africans could live, work and travel. A young British photojournalist pushed his way to the front and took a few pictures of police across the fence who were standing atop their armoured personnel carriers. With nothing much happening, he turned back and headed for his car. Then – without warning – there was the sound of heavy gunfire.

The photographer, Ian Berry, who has died aged 92, captured images of the carnage, which soon became known around the world as the Sharpeville massacre . Dozens of demonstrators were killed, many shot in the back as they fled, and hundreds were injured in what turned out to be a turning point in the country’s history.

Berry and his colleague, the Drum reporter Humphrey Tyler, had ignored police warnings that they would be arrested, and were the only journalists there when the shooting started. It was the first time Berry had been shot at, or seen others killed, but it would not be the last in a career that took him to the Congo crisis following independence in 1960-65, the Vietnam war, the Aberfan disaster of 1966, in which coal waste engulfed a Glamorgan village, and the six-day war between Israel and its neighbours in June 1967.

He was tenacious, but his edge was his eye for human moments, capturing the people behind the headlines, often photographing scenes that were off-centre, and yet told a story better by focusing on individuals.

In 1968, when Magnum’s Paris bureau asked if he would go to Prague as Soviet tanks encroached, he took a plane to Munich, rented a car and drove to the Czech border, only to find that journalists were being turned away. With typical guile, Berry talked his way through, persuading a Russian officer that he was on his way to an architects’ conference, which he had read about on the flight. He captured memorable images of peaceful resistance during the first days of the invasion, then smuggled them out in the hubcaps and door panels of his rented Volkswagen Beetle for publication in Paris Match.

Born in Preston, Lancashire, Ian was the son of Walter, who owned garages, and Ethel (nee McKimmings), a housewife. He was a boarder at Rossall school, on the coast at Fleetwood, and from an early age had wanderlust. A postwar assisted emigration scheme took him to South Africa in 1952, when he was 17.

In Johannesburg he worked for a family acquaintance, Roger Madden, who had recently returned home from assisting the photographer Ansel Adams in the US. Madden taught Berry to use a large-format camera and to print in the darkroom, but he would find his own path using a diminutive Leica, the camera favoured by prominent visual journalists of the day.

Berry moved on to studio work and small-town editorial assignments, and worked for the Rand Daily Mail, covering the beginnings of the treason trial in 1956 that included Nelson Mandela as a defendant. After hearing that Tom Hopkinson, the former editor of Picture Post in London, was coming to edit Drum, a newly established South African weekly aimed at a black readership, Berry persuaded him to give him a job. A few months later, Hopkinson sent him to Sharpeville.

He was called to give evidence at the trial of the wounded, who had been charged with obstruction. The pictures also brought him to wider international attention, and through Hopkinson he became acquainted with Magnum Photos, the agency with whom he remained until his death.

When Berry moved to Paris in 1962, he met Henri Cartier-Bresson , one of Magnum’s co-founders, and became a full member five years later. By then, he had left Paris for London to become a contract photographer for the Observer, travelling abroad on reportage assignments while shooting members of the British arts scene for the paper’s weekend magazine.

He photographed actors, film people and artists, including John Gielgud , Dusty Springfield , Lindsay Anderson and Henry Moore , and gained a reputation for his observational portrait stories.

Berry’s magazine assignments were accompanied by projects pursued over years, and it is for these that he will be best remembered. In 1972, the Whitechapel Gallery in London commissioned him to photograph its East End neighbourhood, and two years later, an Arts Council bursary (said to be the first ever given to a photographer) led to the publication of The English (1978), a collection that observed class, ceremony and everyday leisure activities.

That seamless transition between commissioned journalism and self-directed work reflected the Magnum model, which allowed photographers to earn a living from magazines while retaining control of their pictures and developing subjects beyond an editor’s brief.

Travel assignments for Life, Paris Match, National Geographic, Geo and others took Berry across the world, and often fed into longer studies. His continuing engagement with apartheid South Africa resulted in Black and Whites: L’Afrique du Sud (1988) and Living Apart (1996), while other projects examined changing daily life in China and the former Soviet Union.

In later years, a commission to photograph Greenland’s retreating glaciers developed into Water, an examination of how water sustains life and how its scarcity, pollution and destructive force expose humanity’s impact on the planet. Drawing on 15 years of work, it was published in 2023, accompanied by an essay by his second wife, Kathie Webber, whom he had married in 1973.

Berry’s first wife was Shirley, a South African, with whom he had a daughter, and he had a son from another relationship; both children predeceased him. He is survived by Kathie.

content.article_text:
O n a sporting oval in a rural Australian town 15,000km from Knoxville, Tennessee, dozens of Dolly Partons saunter down the runway as a boisterous crowd cheers and swats away flies with their cowboy hats.

As the sun begins to set, Jim Beams are flowing and music is blaring. One lucky punter is about to be crowned this year’s best-dressed Dolly, complete with sash, trophy and bragging rights.

The Narromine Line Dancers chat before performing for the crowd

For one weekend a year, this is not the sleepy agricultural township of Narromine, 430km north-west of Sydney. This is Dollymine, home to the nation’s largest (and only) Dolly Parton festival.

Perfect pink shades

This is the fifth year the tribute festival has been running and the first to take place since the country music legend died in August. A record 1,600 tickets have been sold – equivalent to just under half of Narromine’s population.

Many in the crowd wear memorial tribute T-shirts, reading: “We will always love you, Dolly”, and “forever and always”.

Jen Ballhausen, a local resident, has volunteered on the festival’s committee since the beginning. She says the event was inspired by a desire to revitalise the community after a devastating drought from 2017 to 2019. Then Covid-19 hit and organisers had to wait until 2022 for it to run.

Juanita Kottek, who won best-dressed in 2025

“It was a fun group of people, mostly women, that had a common goal to provide something for the community, to support our community,” she says.

It was a super fan volunteer who suggested a Dolly homage, and the committee figured it was a no-brainer. “We needed a female icon,” Ballhausen says.

“The first year was overwhelming … the number of people that got dressed up, we were walking around going, ‘Holy moly, this is going to work.’

“We knew we’d set a bar, and this year has well and truly exceeded it. It just gets our town on the map … to not write off a little town. If we can at least highlight that small towns are great little communities, then we’ve won.”

Drag queen Timberlina

A town doused in rhinestones

It’s been a long day. The party starts at 9.30am in Narromine’s main street, which has undergone a metamorphosis to become a micro-Dollywood. Muted shopfronts have transformed into a sea of pink, rhinestones and butterflies. Parton’s beaming face is everywhere: plastered on to windows, on the top of cupcakes and merchandise.

There are line dancers, drag queens and children from the local primary school performing a stirring rendition of Baby I’m Burnin’, complete with pom poms.

Festivalgoers pose at a kissing booth

The temperature quickly climbs to 30C and those in Dolly-drag wipe makeup-laden sweat from their faces.

Narromine is 40km west of Dubbo and hundreds of kilometres inland – hot, flat country, and the shade awnings provide little reprieve. Some opt for tea towels to emulate Dolly’s cleavage in place of silicone to avoid overheating.

Wynonah Dove, a Dolly impersonator, grew up ‘dirt poor’ in Tennessee

Wynonah Dove, performing on Saturday evening as a Dolly impersonator, says Parton’s sudden death has made the event “especially poignant”.

“When Dolly passed, we had our first rehearsals the day after, and it was hard, I had trouble even singing the songs,” she says between tears.

“I just feel she’s here with us, any time there is love, light and inclusiveness being celebrated, she’s here in spirit.”

Dove grew up in Tennessee, from a working-class background similar to Parton’s. She recalled going a year without running water, “dirt poor”, and says that, thanks to Parton and her extensive work, the local economy exploded.

“She just wanted to make the world a better place,” she says. “None of us could afford to go on vacation, so we all went to Dollywood … Everyone felt like she was our best friend and we didn’t even know her.”

As the afternoon arrives, the crowd flocks to the local pub to re-energise with cold beers and live music. Many of the blow-ins are staying in its upstairs accommodation, which looks like a mini-tornado has passed through, leaving glitter, tasselled jackets and bottles of rosé in its wake.

Among them is Nikolaas Kostraby – AKA Dolly Delicious – who has travelled to the festival from Canberra for the past three years after a recommendation from a neighbour from Narromine. In 2023 he was crowned best-dressed Dolly. This year he’s on the committee and is a judge.

Nikolaas Kostraby as Dolly Delicious

“I was robbed the first year, however I came back the second year and cleaned up, and now every year I come back and dress up,” he says. “People are so kind out here, so respectful, there’s no judging.

“I was nervous the first time, like, I’m a man in a wig, in a regional area, but it’s been the complete opposite.”

Come 5pm, celebrations on the main stage kick off and a steady stream of people arrive at the oval armed with camping chairs and wigs. It doesn’t take long for a hoedown to occur. Couples, families and strangers link arms and twirl on the grass to the thrum of a banjo.

Lucas and his family custom-made T-shirts for the occasion, complete with their names and job titles for the “Dolly Department Company”.

Unique watches on while waiting for the best-dressed catwalk to start

His is “director of hair and volume”, while his partner, Scott, is “chief vibes officer”. The pair travelled from Sydney with Lucas’ sister and her two children.

“We decided literally a year ago to all come along together … but it’s even more special now after her passing to be able to come and celebrate,” Lucas says.

“I’m sure there’ll be many drinks and many sing-alongs tonight. It’s the soul behind her songs we love – just warming and inclusive .”

An eclectic cast of Dollys

Soon, darkness will descend, lipstick will smudge and cowboy hats may be lost. But first, a best-dressed winner must be crowned. And who better to lead the proceedings than the drag queen Timberlina, who grew up in regional New South Wales and has emceed the festival for the past five years.

Grace Wadley, 5, in costume for the best-dressed kids’ competition

In true Dolly fashion, she arrives in a vintage car and snatched rainbow dress, waving regally.

Children are judged first, then comes the best-dressed Kenny, a homage to Parton’s longtime collaborator Kenny Rogers. There are three finalists, including a man dressed as Woody from Toy Story.

Then the Dollys flock to the red carpet, as diverse and eclectic as the singer’s own career. One woman rides a blow-up horse. A small child somehow makes her way on to the stage. Fake breasts jut out of tight dresses like bowling balls waiting to be freed.

Dolly Delicious, sporting her victory sash from 2023, slowly walks among them, eventually landing on Colin Marshall – who is part of a tour group of 30 people who have travelled to Narromine from Brisbane. The tour is run by Fun Over 50 Holidays, and he isn’t the only man who has come in drag.

“It wasn’t just the look, it was the warmth, the attitude,” Dolly Delicious tells the crowd. Marshall booms: “Over 50s!”

Petina in the best-dressed competition

His wife, Leanne, crafted his outfit. He is wearing a hot pink tasselled dress, a blond wig, a cowboy hat, heels and large sunglasses, and accepts his sash as though it’s an inevitability.

For a full minute, Marshall sashays along the runway, swinging his arms with abandon. I ask him how it feels to win. “Good, great,” he replies.

“It’s hard work being a woman.”

content.article_text:
Born in London in 1975, Gareth Malone is a choirmaster and broadcaster. He began his career running youth and community choirs for the London Symphony Orchestra and first appeared on TV in 2006’s The Choir. He has since created choirs with Leicester schoolboys, Aylesbury prisoners, as well as the Military Wives, which produced the No 1 single, Wherever You Are. He lives in London with his wife and three children. His new live show, Sing-A-Long-A-Gareth: At the Movies, is on tour across the UK this autumn.

I was 15 and just coming into my own with my confidence , as you can tell by the double denim and the pose. The photo would have been taken at a party at my parents’ house in Bournemouth. When I wasn’t filling up guests’ drinks, I’d be playing some songs – it looks like I’m playing B flat major, so I suspect at this very moment it was Hey Jude.

For a few years prior to this, school had been difficult. We moved from a nice leafy part of Wimbledon to Bournemouth when I was 10, and until that point I had friends who were both girls and boys. Going to the all-boys grammar school in a new area was an aggressive gear shift and I struggled to make friends. There was no physical bullying, but it was a sustained period of ostracisation that went on for the first three years of secondary school and dribbled on into year 10. It wasn’t ever discussed. There was no “you’re being bullied. If you have a problem with any other boys, come and talk to us,” from the school. My parents probably knew because I wasn’t bringing any friends over. Instead I learned how to take care of my own problems, which was through music and theatre. My saving grace.

I feel so lucky that I had the music studio at school – a place to be expressive in a sea of business studies and maths. Playing the synthesisers started my lifelong passion for production and all-round music nerdery. We also had a piano at home and I used to sit at it and make sounds for what felt like hours.

Mum worked for Abbey Life Assurance and for the civil service. Dad worked for a bank. Neither of them were particularly career-minded – they enjoyed their life, their family and their house, hence friends often coming over. My grandparents were very important, too. Growing up as an only child made me very comfortable in my own company, but it did mean I wasn’t armed with some of the physical vocabulary that other boys had. I used to overreact when other kids were playing up. “Why are you speaking to me like that? No one speaks to me like that. Why are you behaving in this stupid way? No, I don’t want to play rough, or go and play football, because that’s what five-year-olds do.” I was far happier to sit and have a conversation. All of which is possibly why I gravitated towards the girls at school – they were a bit more sensible.

In my teens I got very into Led Zeppelin and Pink Floyd. I was singing a lot in bands – but I was also obsessed with Kenneth Branagh in Henry V, so I decided to study drama at University of East Anglia. I have fond memories of pretending to be a pig, and doing lots of clowning and mask work. Once that was over, I went on to study music at the Royal Academy of Music in London. It was a difficult transition for me – I went from that arrogant tweeny, liminal stage, as pictured, to realising that I was, actually, just fairly average compared with my peers.

After graduating, I went back to Bournemouth. I was selling ice-cream to make some money while sending out CVs. A friend got in touch and said they had seen an advert for some youth work in Poole, and thought I’d be good at it. They wanted someone young and musical to work with local children who lived on an estate with a high level of deprivation. They had a little music room with a couple of ropey instruments that I would try to teach them how to play. That’s where my passion for giving everyone opportunities – a safe space and music – came from.

I also realised that to get people to trust me, I had to be myself. I was from a totally different side of the tracks and I was wide-eyed, naive. The kids could smell the middle-classness on me, so any pretending to be cool and aloof wouldn’t work. I had to be rigorously myself.

My job is to give others confidence, but I’ve definitely gone on a journey with my own self-esteem, especially when it comes to being in front of the camera. I was working with the London Symphony Orchestra and running a choir when I first got the opportunity to be on TV. The producers of The Choir had seen that we had a high Google rating so they got in touch. The show was about starting a choir at Northolt high school in Middlesex, and throughout, I tried to apply the same method of authenticity on camera that I’d learned with the youth group. I had been given this amazing job that I’d never done before, but I was learning to do it on national television. I was being filmed constantly. The director said: “I want you when you’re angry, I want you when you’re upset, I want you when you’re happy. I won’t make you look like an idiot.” He stuck to his word, but I remember being nervous, trying to look in control, and dithering quite a lot.

after newsletter promotion

When you’re recognised it can be a great gift, but a burden when you’re, say, taking out your bins. When Military Wives got to No 1 , I was suddenly thrown into a new level of celebrity: I was meeting Simon Cowell, having tea with Gary Barlow and dinner with Andrew Lloyd Webber. My memories of that time was that it was intense – when you have a Christmas No 1, it’s like you’ve joined a weird club with people like Noddy from Slade and Shakin’ Stevens. None of the bells and whistles has ever distracted me from the reason I got into this industry in the first place 20 years ago, however. Focusing on my passion for music and the importance of art in people’s lives. There’s something so healing about music, and singing in a choir. When people come together, they are buoyed up by it. I lost a friend at the beginning of this year and before he died he said something deeply touching to me: “We never did go for that pint.” It was brutal. Such a simple thing that felt impossible as we were both absorbed in our careers. The telly, the degrees – all of those achievements are wonderful. It’s the foundation upon which a lot of my happiness is at rest. But it’s not the main thing. People and community are.

When I was 15 I had a clear vision of what I wanted with my adult life. It involved a music studio with lots of instruments in it. The teenage me would be overjoyed to know that at the end of my garden is a little den with a piano, drums, shakers, maracas, guitars, bongos, synthesisers, a computer and speakers – that there’s never a day when I’m not doing music, half of it tinkering alone, the rest making music with other people. He’d probably be confused about the amount of hot yoga I currently do. But glad to know I still like a denim shirt.

content.title_original: The Wrong Black Woman on the Fourth Plinth
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "In this critical reflection for ART AFRICA, Ayọ̀ Akínwándé examines Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue (2026), installed on Trafalgar Square’s Fourth Plinth, and questions the histories, stereotypes, and expectations carried by the monumental Black female body. Beginning with a conversation between Nicole Eisenman and curator Mark Godfrey, Akínwándé considers how authorship, artistic intention, and public space shape representation, and whether celebrating Black visibility has made its images harder to question. At its centre is a provocative proposition: can one Black woman ever be expected to represent the universal “everywoman”?"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Ayọ̀ Akínwándé"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "On 29 September 2026, I sat in the Royal Institution in London listening to Nicole Eisenman in conversation with curator Mark Godfrey. An artist carries a wine barrel. Above it sits a giant potato, then Eisenman’s cat, Edie. At the summit, the late British sculptor Phyllida Barlow balances a vase of flowers on her head. Courtesy of the artist and Hauser & Wirth. Photo: Ayọ̀ Akínwándé.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "During the conversation, Eisenman traced Stack to an earlier painting, Hindsight (2020), which appeared on the screen behind her. The architecture of accumulation was already there, but the figure occupying its upper reaches was different: a large, pale, naked figure, turned away from the viewer. During the question-and-answer session, a member of the audience asked whether the figure was intended to be Donald Trump. As I recall the exchange, Eisenman responded that it was not Trump, but simply a fat white man. I am paraphrasing the exchange from memory rather than quoting either speaker verbatim. Nicole Eisenman, Hindsight , 2020, Oil on canvas, 208.6 x 165.7 cm / 82 1/8 x 65 1/4 inches © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy of the artist and Hauser & Wirth.
