Entrevistas

O pioneirismo da fotógrafa sul-africana Ruth Seopedi Motau

Shebeen – Dobsonville 1997 , de Ruth Motau

Nascida em um dos vários bairros segregados (as townships ) de Soweto, a fotojornalista Ruth Seopedi Motau (1968) foi a primeira fotógrafa negra a trabalhar como editora de fotografia na grande imprensa sul-africana. Motau começou sua vida profissional no final dos anos 1980 e início dos anos 1990, período de viu a libertação de Nelson Mandela e o fim da política separatista do apartheid. Ela conta que naquele momento “a África do Sul estava no centro das atenções. Nesse período, muitos fotojornalistas vieram à África do Sul e David Goldblatt os convidou para o MPW. James Naftali veio e me lembro que também esteve aqui o Sebastião Salgado, que é o meu fotógrafo favorito.”

Em conversa com a pesquisadora e curadora Ana Paula Vitorio, Motau fala do início da sua carreira, do seu pioneirismo nas redações da grande imprensa como mulher fotógrafa negra e da importância de abrir este espaço dentro dos jornais: “Normalmente o que eu fazia era recrutar mulheres fotógrafas, mas mulheres negras ainda não havia muitas. Acho que um dos motivos era também a dificuldade da nossa cultura em reconhecer fotógrafos e artistas. Nossos pais diziam ‘o que você vai fazer da vida? Como vai colocar pão na mesa?’ Não havia muito suporte. Foi por isso que eu criei um programa de mentoria.”

Querida mãe, Meadowlands (1928-2023) , de Ruth Motau

Dra. Ruth, como começou a sua relação com a fotografia?

Ruth Motau: Eu nunca falo sobre isso, mas minha paixão era a música. Eu queria estudar música. Mas se naquele período [apartheid] você fosse negra e das townships era muito difícil. Então eu acabei na fotografia por acidente e me apaixonei por ela.

Como foi esse acidente?

RM: Eu visitei uma fundação com uma colega do ensino médio que me convidou para ir até lá. Ela disse que era um espaço de arte e que talvez eu pudesse encontrar algo que me interessasse lá. Mas quando você ainda está nessa busca, você nem sabe ao certo o que procura nem o que quer fazer. Um tempo depois e comecei a frequentar o Alexander Arts Centre , que era onde o Victor Matom dava aulas naquela época. Eu fiquei por lá por alguns meses, mas então ouvi falar sobre o que o David Goldblatt estava fazendo no Market Theatre . O Alexander ficava longe da minha casa. Para ir até lá eu precisava pegar dois taxis, mas para ir ao Market Theatre eu só precisaria de um – e às vezes eu não tinha dinheiro algum. Então eu comecei a fazer o Market Photo Workshop (MPW). Acabei ficando lá por três anos.

Naquela época eu não tinha certeza se eu teria um futuro como fotógrafa. Certa vez, no início dos anos 1990, um jornal abriu uma chamada para estágio. Meus colegas do MPW se candidataram e um deles foi contratado. Isso despertou meu interesse, uns anos depois eu comecei a ver as fotos dele no jornal e pensei “eu também quero estar lá”. Mas eu não tinha certeza se eu era capaz, sabe? Então me lembro que um dia eu estava no MPW e um outro colega que era branco contou que tinha se inscrito para preencher uma dessas vagas, mas que tinha sido recusado porque o jornal estava procurando por pessoas negras. Mesmo assim, eu não me candidatei. Então eu recebi uma ligação do Kevin Carter pedindo que eu levasse meu portfólio porque ele queria dar uma olhada. Eu fui até lá numa sexta ou sábado e no domingo ele me ligou dizendo “você começa na segunda”. Foi assim que aconteceu.

Dançarinos Gumbot , de Ruth Motau, Bapedi, Soweto, 1993

Esse foi o seu primeiro jornal? O Weekly Mail ?

RM: Sim, foi o início da minha carreira e foi quando eu comecei a entender o que é fotografia. Eu digo isso porque naquela época o Weekly Mail era publicado junto com o The Guardian , de Londres. Eu tinha acesso ao The Guardian e observava como eles publicavam as coisas. Eles faziam um excelente trabalho. O Weekly Mail publicava também notícias internacionais e isso para mim era muito emocionante.

A senhora pode me contar um pouco mais sobre como foi seu tempo aluna no Market Photo Workshop ?

RM: Naquela época David Goldblatt ainda estava dando aulas. Eu lembro de estar em algumas turmas em que ele foi professor. Era o começo nos anos 1990, a África do Sul estava no centro das atenções. Mandela tinha sido libertado, o apartheid estava chegando ao fim. As coisas estavam começando a tomar forma. Nesse período, muitos fotojornalistas vieram à África do Sul e David Goldblatt os convidou para o MPW. James Naftali veio e me lembro que também esteve aqui o Sebastião Salgado, que é o meu fotógrafo favorito. Todo mundo que nós admirávamos e que tinha trabalhos que nos inspiravam esteve aqui, deu aulas e palestras para nós. Eles nos motivaram. Essa foi a melhor época das nossas vidas.

Pensionistas no Ponto para pagamento de Mzimhlophe , de Ruth Motau

A senhora começou no jornal ainda na década de 1990. O que significava para uma mulher negra ser fotojornalista em um veículo sul-africano naquele período?

RM: No início, quando eu comecei no jornal, eu só queria ver como as coisas eram porque eu ainda não conhecia bem como tudo funcionava. Uma vez que você está contratada, eles te enviam para fazer uma história em Soweto sobre uma escola, por exemplo, você vai faz a história e volta. Na maioria das vezes, eles só iriam publicar uma fotografia e talvez nenhuma. Me incomodava muito o fato de as coberturas, especialmente quando se tratava de histórias sobre pessoas negras, não mostravam as coisas como elas realmente eram. Principalmente no que diz respeito às fotografias. Isso porque o jornal impresso é sobre espaço, venda de espaço, de publicidade para gerar lucro. Mas digamos que você vai fazer uma matéria sobre um programa de alimentação. Para mim, há a fotografia das pessoas que se beneficiam daquele programa, há a fotografia da comida sendo preparada na cozinha etc. É mais do que uma única imagem fotográfica. Tem a questão da origem desse alimento, a horta de onde ele vem, o preparo na cozinha, as crianças recebendo a comida e depois comendo. Mas muitas vezes eles [os editores] dizem que o que você tem que fazer é apenas uma fotografia, a da pessoa que oferece aquele programa de alimentação. Não é isso! As fotografias que realmente importam acabam ficando de lado. Foi aí que comecei a pensar: sei contar histórias melhor que isso. Então disse a mim mesma: preciso documentar nossas vidas, nossas histórias, porque se eu não contar as histórias da maneira que conheço, elas sempre serão distorcidas. Foi então que comecei a fazer esse tipo de trabalho, a tomar a iniciativa independente do que fosse. E isso durante aquela época de violência [apartheid]. Eu me lembro de contar ao Kevin, meu chefe, que eu era da township , que eu era diretamente afetada por toda aquela violência. Eu queria fazer algo diferente, criar histórias que nos fizessem sentir vivos, histórias que diriam que estávamos lá, que estivemos lá. Então comecei a criar histórias, reportagens especiais. Eu comecei a entender porque estava fazendo fotografia, era porque eu queria contar a minha própria história.

Mulher na porta , de Ruth Motau

O que a senhora costumava cobrir? Quais os principais temas e assuntos?

RM: Qualquer coisa. Eu cobria muitas igrejas porque havia muitas e diferentes igrejas. Era apenas o cotidiano das pessoas negras vivendo, entende? Às vezes, eu simplesmente carregava minha câmera e fotografava as pessoas ali onde elas estivessem. Eu passava por uma mulher sentada na porta ouvindo rádio e a fotografava. Eu gostava de simplesmente fotografar a vida cotidiana. Estava só tentando contar a nossa história. Porque não era tudo sempre sobre violência e morte. Havia pessoas, a vida acontecia. A mulher dessa foto estava lá sentada, vivendo e isso é lindo, entende? Eu tenho muitas fotografias como essa, sobre o que estava acontecendo nas nossas vidas. Porque a vida seguia, nós fazíamos coisas, estávamos vivos. Isso era o que eu documentava, a vida. Muitas vezes você olha o jornal, para a forma como eles nos representam e sabe que não é a verdade. E então eu disse a mim mesma: a única maneira de mostrar a verdade é lutando por ela, é fazendo o real trabalho que precisa ser feito.

Grupo de dança de Meadowlands , de Ruth Motau

A senhora se torna editora em um jornal logo após o fim institucional do apartheid. Como foi esse período e sua trajetória na edição de fotojornalismo?

RM: Eu nunca me vi como uma editora, eu me via como uma fotógrafa. Naquela época, eu costumava editar o trabalho de muitas pessoas, mas eu também saia às ruas e fotografava. Então eu não estava apenas lá na redação, tomando decisões lá de dentro. Eu também estava criando e trazendo trabalho. Apenas muitos anos depois de me aposentar foi que olhei para trás e entendi que o que eu fazia era de fato edição. Eu trabalhei com muitas pessoas de todo o país. Mas foi anos depois que me dei conta da enorme responsabilidade que eu tinha na luta por fazer com que a representação fotográfica no jornal fosse a melhor possível. Mas, às vezes, essa decisão não cabia apenas a mim. Eu tinha um chefe e às vezes ele dizia “eu quero isso e não aquilo”. A gente discutia, brigava. Às vezes eu ganhava, mas às vezes eu perdia. Só que há um momento em que você chega ao seu limite, quer fazer outras coisas. Depois de nove anos eu saí do jornal e comecei a atuar como freelancer. Eu comecei a fazer as coisas que amava novamente. Trabalhei com investimento social e viajava pelo país fazendo isso.

Um tempo depois eu fui recrutada para ser editora de fotografia no maior jornal diário das townships , o Sowetan . Eu cresci lendo o Sowetan , então eu cheguei lá e me deparei com todos aqueles nomes que eu havia lido por anos, foi muito excitante. Trabalhei lá por quatro anos e depois eu fui para o City Press , também como editora de fotografia. Lá eu fiquei por dois anos. Eu saí em um período em que as redes sociais estavam surgindo e a gente já podia sentir o impresso enfrentando problemas.

Shebeen – Dobsonville 1997 , de Ruth Motau

Na sua opinião, por que demorou tanto tempo para que jornais importantes contratassem mulheres negras como editoras?

Ruth: Não havia muitas mulheres negras nos jornais. Ainda hoje há poucas. Na minha época, o The Mailing Garden [formalmente, o Weekly Mail ] era o único. Quando eu saí de lá eu ainda era a única. Normalmente o que eu fazia era recrutar mulheres fotógrafas, mas mulheres negras ainda não havia muitas. Acho que um dos motivos era também a dificuldade da nossa cultura em reconhecer fotógrafos e artistas. Nossos pais diziam “o que você vai fazer da vida? Como vai colocar pão na mesa?” Não havia muito suporte. Foi por isso que eu criei um programa de mentoria. Eu comecei a atuar como mentora de mulheres negras das townships e das áreas rurais e dizia a elas, vocês podem fazer isso! Vocês podem publicar livros, trabalhar em jornais, fazer o que quiserem. Da mesma forma que os homens, vocês também podem fazer isso. Eu costumava ligar para jovens fotógrafas e as convidava para trabalhar comigo por três meses. Fiz isso por muitos anos em todos os jornais em que atuei. Lembro que eu contratei, por exemplo, Makgotso Gulube como fotógrafa no Sowetan . Eu poderia ter contratado homens brilhantes, mas a convidei. Para mim era sobre trazer mulheres negras para dentro.

Hoje a senhora tem um programa próprio de mentoria. Como ele funciona especificamente?

RM: Eu comecei durante a pandemia. No programa eu não ensino desde o básico, o que eu faço é ajudá-las a desenvolver as histórias que elas querem contar. Auxilio em como abordar essas histórias, como documentá-las. Às vezes as pessoas dizem: Ruth, eu quero desenvolver tal projeto, mas não sei como. Eu digo a elas: apenas continue fotografando. Não pare de fotografar e fotografar. Em algum momento você vai sentir no seu espirito: é isso, agora tenho fotografias o bastante. Pode ser que você consiga isso em um dia, mas pode ser que seja preciso mais tempo. Acho que é parecido com escrever ou com ouvir música. Às vezes a gente escuta uma música e ela simplesmente não faz sentido, pode ser que você sequer entenda a letra. Mas 20 anos depois, você escuta novamente e diz “ah então era sobre isso!”. Acho que é o mesmo com a arte.

Pensionistas no Ponto para pagamento de Mzimhlophe , de Ruth Motau

A senhora continua fotografando?

RM: Sim, mas não tanto. Hoje eu escolho o que fazer. Eu posso deixar a fotografia de lado, ficar entediada, fazer outras coisas por um tempo, mas eu sempre volto para a fotografia, ela é meu primeiro amor. É algo que eu posso fazer de olhos fechados, a qualquer hora e em qualquer lugar, então eu sempre volto para a fotografia.

E o que a senhora escolhe hoje?

RM: Estou trabalhando em um projeto chamado Black Beauty [Beleza Negra] que é sobre corpos negros. Eu não acredito que exista nada que seja feito. Tudo é belo por ser único. Mas nesse trabalho eu busco por figuras e posturas corporais específicas, é um projeto de retratos. O mundo nos fez acreditar que somos inferiores por causa da cor da nossa pele, do formato do nosso corpo. Mas somos lindas e na verdade eles querem ser como nós. Nós também queremos ser como eles por causa da mentira que nos contaram dizendo a nós que somos feias. Então esse projeto é sobre dizer às pessoas negras: seu corpo é lindo, você é linda. ///

Ana Paula Vitorio é pesquisadora. Doutora em Literatura, Cultura e Contemporaneidade pela PUC-Rio, atualmente é pós-doc no departamento de Linguística e Práticas da Linguagem da University of the Free State (África do Sul).

content.article_text:
De la mano de Rob Savage, con Jessica Chastain, Other Mommy arribó a los cines este 8 de octubre.

Other Mommy es una adaptación de la novela de Josh Malerman, Incidents Around the House . Cuando uno acude a la sala con la expectativa de que la producción estuvo a cargo de James Wan y Jason Blum, detrás de Atomic Monster y Blumhouse Productions, estima que la cinta estará a la altura: comienza a toda orquesta y se va desinflando con el paso de las escenas.

La historia sigue a Bela ( Arabella Olivia Clark ), una niña de siete años cuya vida se modifica cuando un ente sobrenatural llamado la “Otra Mamá” se manifiesta en su cuarto. La criatura “cobra vida” en la forma de su madre, Úrsula ( Jessica Chastain ), y al principio se presenta como una figura cercana y curiosa, aunque pronto revela su verdadera intención: obtener el corazón de Bela. La tercera pata de la familia es Russ ( Jay Duplass ), quien se muestra como un padre muy cercano a la niña, pero con poco desempeño para las tareas domésticas.

La premisa plantea un escenario con potencial para explorar el miedo infantil, la identidad materna y la fragilidad de la confianza, pero nunca desarrolla ese mismo potencial debido a que abusa de los jump scares y los movimientos repentinos con cambios de sonido. Rob Savage mantiene buenos planos, como en sus películas anteriores, pero no logra cautivar al espectador durante varias escenas, debido a que la intensidad brindada no condice con el desarrollo demostrado: nunca se llega a construir una verdadera atmósfera de tensión y terror.

El CGI, una deuda en la cinta

La visualización a través de los efectos especiales es poco convincente, por lo que no muestra lo que debería. A su vez, el espectador puede sumergirse por momentos en la historia, pero, en otros, verá que no hay demasiada cohesión en la historia.

A su vez, esta historia muestra la fragilidad de lo infantil y también de las relaciones intrafamiliares, pero ambas socavan siempre ante los intentos de sorprender al espectador con una nueva escena de persecución o aparición de la entidad, que deja todo a mitad de camino.

Te puede interesar

La aparición de “especialistas” de conjuros, de una abuela materna que da consejos y un final un poco absurdo terminan sepultando una cinta que tenía muchísimo más potencial del que terminó demostrando a través de 1 hora y media.

Calificación: 5/10.

AFRICA亲身经历了这种后果。我们专程来到威尼斯，报道非洲及全球非洲侨民国家馆，却没有收到海地、坦桑尼亚、乌干达、几内亚或新几内亚方面的任何联络：没有新闻稿，没有邀请，也没有人来接洽采访安排。随后，我们多次给威尼斯双年展官方新闻材料中列出的这些国家馆媒体联系人发送电子邮件，却没有收到回复；几个月后，我们仍未得到任何消息。古巴馆。图片由Brendon Bell-Roberts提供", AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们无从知道原因，这也不意味着这些国家馆没有在其他地方得到宣传。然而，如果主动寻求报道它们的专业媒体都无法通过所提供的官方渠道取得联系，它们又能多有效地触达那些原本并不知道其存在的观众？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，可见性只是问题的一部分。找到一个国家馆之后，另一个问题仍然存在：谁被选来代表这个国家，谁作出了这些选择，人们看到的又是这个国家的哪一种版本？塞拉利昂、几内亚、索马里和赤道几内亚都是首次参展，这些国家馆使上述问题格外突出。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "塞拉利昂首次参展，让这个问题尤其值得关注。由意大利人Sandro Orlandi Stagl和Willy Montini策展的《Mondi Presenti / Worlds of Today》汇集了16位艺术家：4位来自塞拉利昂，4位来自西非国家经济共同体（ECOWAS）的其他成员国——塞内加尔、多哥、贝宁和尼日利亚——7位来自意大利，1位来自墨西哥。策展陈述把该馆置于ECOWAS的语境中，同时提及非洲与意大利之间的交流史。因此，纳入来自西非邻国的艺术家，显然与这一框架有关。较难理解的是，为何7位意大利艺术家占据了塞拉利昂首次国家展示近一半的名额，墨西哥艺术家如何融入策展概念，以及归根结底，是谁决定哪一种塞拉利昂版本会进入双年展的官方记录。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "几内亚的首展《Le Son de l’Art: l’Écho de la Matière》由意大利策展人Carlo Stragapede策划，把问题进一步推向紧要处。展览汇集了约66位艺术家，其中包括相当数量的意大利人，而似乎只有很少一部分是几内亚人。问题不只是选了谁，更在于这些选择以什么为依据，以及这样一个大型国际展览如何在几内亚首次登上双年展国家平台时代表这个国家。以几内亚之名呈现的，究竟是谁对这个国家及其当代文化社群的理解？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "同样首次参展的赤道几内亚馆《The Forest The Undergrowth》由加泰罗尼亚策展人Joan Abelló策划，让这个问题变得更加直白。23名参展者包括来自意大利、西班牙、中国、罗马尼亚、芬兰、阿尔巴尼亚、喀麦隆、塞浦路斯、德国和以色列的艺术家，而可明确识别为赤道几内亚艺术家的只有Fernando Nguema Madja一人。国家馆还纳入了出生于加泰罗尼亚、曾在赤道几内亚生活和工作的Modest Gené Roig。在这里，代表性问题已经遭到该国文化社群内部的质疑。双年展开幕前，一群赤道几内亚文化工作者公开指出，该国当代声音大多缺席，并呼吁让本地艺术家和文化专业人士参与策展过程。绿园城堡。图片由Brendon Bell-Roberts提供", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_9907-1003x1030.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "绿园城堡。图片由Brendon Bell-Roberts提供", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "索马里首次国家参展，引发了一场更加直接的争论：谁有资格在威尼斯代表一个国家？《SADDEXLEEY》展出Ayan Farah、Asmaa Jama和Warsan Shire的作品，由常驻斯德哥尔摩的Mohamed Mire与意大利项目经理Fabio Scrivanti共同策展。索马里艺术基金会公开批评该馆，称其没有与常驻索马里的艺术家和艺术机构进行有实质意义的协商；索马里团体Warbixinta Cidda则要求撤换Scrivanti，并鉴于意大利在索马里的殖民史，质疑为何任命一名意大利人担任联合策展人。随后，一封公开信援引了两方声明，并表示若诉求得不到回应，将呼吁抵制该馆。这场争议为代表性问题增添了另一个维度：问题不只是选中了哪些艺术家，还包括咨询了谁，谁参与作出这些决定，以及最终以这个国家之名呈现的是谁对它的理解。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "综合来看，这四个首次设立的国家馆引出了一个更广泛的策展权威问题。问题不在于策展人的国籍，也不是说非洲国家馆必须由本国或本洲人士策展。关键在于谁有权代表一个国家，哪些知识和关系构成其选择的依据，该国艺术家与文化工作者如何参与这一过程，以及最终由谁决定什么会以这个国家的名义被人看见。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些问题并不新鲜。2013年的肯尼亚馆由两名意大利人策展，参展者包括8位中国艺术家、1位意大利艺术家和2位肯尼亚艺术家。2015年，人们再次对该国如何被代表提出类似忧虑，肯尼亚艺术家表示反对，政府随后撤回支持。2022年的首个纳米比亚馆《A Bridge to the Desert》也招致类似批评。展览由意大利人Marco Furio Ferrario策划，展出匿名艺术家RENN的作品；纳米比亚艺术界对该国如何被代表提出异议，纳米比亚政府随后撤回支持，但展览仍然举行。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些争议表明，官方参展与文化正当性之间存在差别。一个国家馆让人看见的不只是某个国家，也是对这个国家的一种特定呈现；因此，谁有权构建这种呈现，与这个国家究竟有没有被看见同样重要。巴哈马馆，装置现场。图片由Brendon Bell-Roberts提供。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_9169-1030x773.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "巴哈马馆，装置现场。图片由Brendon Bell-Roberts提供。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "可见性也受到汇聚于威尼斯的专业网络影响，开幕周尤其如此。博物馆馆长、策展人、收藏家、基金会、画廊和媒体会在几天紧凑的时间里停留于此；与艺术家、策展人或机构已有联系，可以帮助一个国家馆成为人们专程前往的目的地，而缺少这种关系的国家馆，则更依赖于在现有网络之外争取关注。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于记者而言，由于时间有限、威尼斯花费高昂，那几天往往是他们在当地采访艺术家和策展人的唯一机会。争夺注意力的活动如此之多——包括绿园城堡、军械库、100个国家参展项目、平行活动以及各种展览——更难找到的国家馆必须投入额外的时间和精力。此外，地理位置与专业网络还会相互作用：偏离主要路线的国家馆，必须付出更多努力，才能进入专业关注流动的渠道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，一个国家馆的观众并不限于走进展馆大门的人。媒体报道可以把展览带到威尼斯之外很远的地方，触达永远不会亲临双年展的读者和观众。评论、采访、照片、视频、播客、通讯和专业出版物，可以把艺术家及其作品介绍给全新的观众；一次采访也可能让某位从未在威尼斯看过展览的策展人注意到一位艺术家。这些报道还让国家馆在双年展的数月展期之外继续存在，形成一份即使展览结束很久后仍可流传的记录。从这个意义上说，国家馆之外发生的事，可能变得和馆内发生的事同样重要。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "国际媒体报道未必比全国性、地区性或专业报道更有价值；后几类报道能够提供综合性报道往往忽略的背景和语境。真正重要的是报道能传播多远，是否把艺术家及其作品介绍给原本不熟悉他们的人，以及这份关注能否在威尼斯之外产生任何结果。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "高度可见，并不一定意味着具有真正的影响。图片由Brendon Bell-Roberts提供", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_9219-2-773x1030.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "图片由Brendon Bell-Roberts提供", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在思考各国为何选择投资威尼斯时，这一点很重要，因为参展需要投入大量资金和机构资源，因此参观人数众多未必说明这笔投入物有所值。一个挤满观众的国家馆或许能获得一定曝光，却不一定取得任何实际成果；较少的互动反而可能促成展览、收藏、委托创作、出版，或建立长期的机构关系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "没有任何单一标准可以评判成功，因为本来就不该只有一个标准。然而，单凭参展也无法衡量成功。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如果国际曝光是参加双年展的一个理由，那么国家馆开幕后便会出现更具实质意义的问题。它是否让原本不熟悉这些艺术家及其各自艺术史的人注意到他们？是否有人在其他机构语境中撰文介绍、采访或展出他们的作品？艺术家是否获得了新机会？是否有任何关系在离开威尼斯后仍延续下来？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此，可见性的地理层面延伸到了威尼斯之外：它影响被发现的机会，引导专业关注，塑造与一个国家之名相联系的内容，并影响这种国家呈现此后能够延伸多远。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于非洲国家及全球非洲侨民而言，个中利害尤其重大。威尼斯双年展可以让那些长期被西方主导的叙事边缘化的艺术家与艺术史得到更广泛的关注，为他们打开通往原本可能遥不可及的观众、机构和对话的大门。然而，在双年展中拥有一个官方席位，并不能保证获得同等的被发现机会，也不一定会让艺术家和文化社群对于本国及本国历史如何被呈现拥有更大的决定权。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些差别早在大门开启之前便已出现，也可能在闭门很久之后继续存在。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此，到场只是开始。如果原本没有人在寻找你，威尼斯是否让他们开始寻找——而当他们真正看过来时，又是谁决定了他们会看见什么？", "translated": true}]

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Just because you are invited into the room does not mean you decide where you stand."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At La Biennale di Venezia, visibility has its own geography, and not every country enters it on equal terms. For African and global African diaspora pavilions, the question is not simply who is present, but who gets seen, how they are seen, and what determines the difference. The Senegalese Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_9214-773x1030.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "The Senegalese Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At La Biennale di Venezia, some countries have the privilege of being discovered; others have to persuade you to look for them. Walk through the Giardini and the Arsenale and national pavilions appear one after another, introducing visitors to artists and art histories they may never have intended to see. Beyond these venues, discovery becomes less assured. Some pavilions remain on routes visitors naturally take, while others require a conscious decision to find them. This creates a hierarchy of attention: some countries benefit from passing visitors, while others depend on visitors who already know enough to seek them out."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For countries whose artists and art histories have been marginalised by Western-dominated narratives of art history, this matters. Venice offers an opportunity to challenge that imbalance and bring their own histories to new audiences. But participation alone cannot guarantee that their pavilions will be encountered, that their artists will receive meaningful attention, or that greater visibility will continue beyond the Biennale."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Here, the geography of visibility begins."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In 2026, one hundred countries are taking part: twenty-nine at the Giardini, twenty-five at the Arsenale and forty-six elsewhere in Venice. Seven nations are exhibiting for the first time, four of them from Africa: Guinea, Equatorial Guinea, Sierra Leone and Somalia. Although these countries have the same official status, their situations regarding access, attention, and representation differ."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Egypt’s Silence Pavilion: Between the Tangible and the Intangible , by Armen Agop, and Brazil’s Comigo ninguém pode , by Rosana Paulino and Adriana Varejão, occupy permanent pavilions in the Giardini, while Morocco’s Asǝṭṭa , by Amina Agueznay, is located in the Arsenale. South Africa too has a long-term presence at the Arsenale, even though it did not take part this year. These locations sit within the routes where Biennale attention is already concentrated, allowing visitors to encounter the pavilions without deliberately seeking them out. Countries without permanent sites face a different challenge: they must establish their presence elsewhere in Venice and attract visitors to a location that may change with each participation. Permanent pavilions also acquire familiarity over time, becoming part of the geography returning visitors already know, while countries that move between venues must make themselves visible in a new place each time. Egyptian artist Armen Agop outside the Egyptian Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_9493-773x1030.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "Egyptian artist Armen Agop outside the Egyptian Pavilion.  Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A pavilion situated outside the Giardini or the Arsenale doesn’t necessarily mean it is peripheral. Senegal’s WURUS and Uganda’s Kampala are in adjacent locations right on the Riva degli Schiavoni. Cuba’s Hombres Libres / Free Men , which is on Via Garibaldi, is also in a similar position along the main pedestrian route leading to the Giardini and the Arsenale. The Democratic Republic of the Congo’s first pavilion, Simba Moto! Seize the Fire! Saisis le feu!, is also conveniently located on a busy square in Castello. These pavilions sit along paths Biennale visitors are likely to follow and can therefore see without having to look for them specifically."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Guinea’s first National Participation, Le Son de l’Art: l’Écho de la Matière , occupies a very different geography. Located on the island of San Servolo, it cannot be reached simply by turning down another Venetian street. Visitors have to decide to go there, allow time for the journey and pay for a vaporetto, turning a pavilion visit into a destination in itself."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mere proximity can also be misleading. The exhibitions Ethiopia’s Shapes of Silence , by Tegene Kunbi and curated by Abebaw Ayalew, and Zimbabwe’s Second Nature | Manyonga , curated by Fadzai Veronica Muchemwa, were both held at Castello, near the Giardini, Arsenale, Senegal, and Uganda. Yet finding them revealed how easily visibility can change within a few metres. Official Biennale signage on the Riva degli Schiavoni directed visitors down the alley towards both Ethiopia and Zimbabwe, but where the route divided, only Ethiopia was clearly signposted. We had deliberately set out to visit both and still struggled to find Zimbabwe. On a map, the difference was negligible; on foot, a missing sign made one pavilion considerably easier to find than the other."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Financial resources also shape visibility. Countries without permanent pavilions must secure temporary venues, often long before the Biennale opens, so budget size and timing can determine which spaces remain available. Funding can influence the kind of art that can be brought to Venice and exhibited, as well as the resources available for communications and for artists and curators to be present during the crucial opening days. The consequences are visible throughout: in where a pavilion is located, what audiences encounter when they arrive, who is there to speak about the work and how effectively the exhibition attracts attention beyond its doors."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ART AFRICA encountered the consequences firsthand. We were in Venice specifically to report on the African and global African diaspora pavilions, yet received no communication from Haiti, Tanzania, Uganda, Guinea, or New Guinea: no press releases, invitations, or approaches to arrange interviews. We then repeatedly emailed the media contacts listed for these pavilions in the official press material from La Biennale di Venezia, but received no response and, months later, still have not heard from them. The Cuban Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_9400-2-773x1030.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "The Cuban Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We cannot know why, nor does this mean that these pavilions received no publicity elsewhere. But if specialist media actively seeking to cover them could not make contact through the official channels provided, how effectively were they reaching audiences who did not already know they were there?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But visibility is only one part of the question. Once a pavilion has been found, another issue remains: who has been chosen to represent the country, who made those choices, and what version of the country is being made visible? Sierra Leone, Guinea, Somalia and Equatorial Guinea, all participating for the first time, bring these questions into sharp focus."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sierra Leone’s first participation makes this question particularly relevant. Mondi Presenti / Worlds of Today , curated by Italians Sandro Orlandi Stagl and Willy Montini, brings together sixteen artists: four from Sierra Leone, four from other ECOWAS countries (the Economic Community of West African States)—Senegal, Togo, Benin, and Nigeria—seven from Italy, and one from Mexico. The curatorial statement places the pavilion within the context of ECOWAS while also referring to a history of exchange between Africa and Italy. The inclusion of artists from neighbouring West African countries therefore clearly relates to that framework. Less clear is why seven Italian artists make up almost half of Sierra Leone’s first national presentation, how the Mexican artist fits within the curatorial concept, and ultimately who determines the version of Sierra Leone that enters the Biennale’s official record."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Guinea’s inaugural Le Son de l’Art: l’Écho de la Matière , curated by Italian curator Carlo Stragapede, raises the stakes further. The exhibition brings together roughly 66 artists, including a significant number of Italians, while only a small minority appear to be Guinean. The issue is not simply who was selected, but what informed those choices and how such a large international exhibition comes to represent Guinea on its first national platform at the Biennale. Whose understanding of the country and its contemporary cultural community is being presented in its name?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Also participating for the first time, Equatorial Guinea’s The Forest The Undergrowth , curated by Catalan curator Joan Abelló, makes the issue even more explicit. Its 23 exhibitors include artists from Italy, Spain, China, Romania, Finland, Albania, Cameroon, Cyprus, Germany and Israel, alongside only one clearly identified Equatoguinean artist, Fernando Nguema Madja. The pavilion also includes Catalan-born Modest Gené Roig, who lived and worked in Equatorial Guinea. Here the question of representation has already been challenged from within the country’s cultural community. Before the Biennale opened, a group of Equatoguinean cultural practitioners publicly argued that contemporary voices from the country were largely absent and called for local artists and cultural professionals to be included in the curatorial process. The Giardini. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_9907-1003x1030.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "The Giardini. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Somalia’s first National Participation has prompted an even more direct debate over who gets to represent a country in Venice. SADDEXLEEY , featuring Ayan Farah, Asmaa Jama and Warsan Shire, is curated by Stockholm-based Mohamed Mire and Italian project manager Fabio Scrivanti. The Somali Arts Foundation has publicly criticised the pavilion for what it describes as a lack of meaningful consultation with artists and arts organisations based in Somalia, while the Somali collective Warbixinta Cidda has called for Scrivanti’s removal, questioning the appointment of an Italian co-curator given Italy’s colonial history in Somalia. An open letter subsequently drew on both statements and called for a boycott if its demands were not addressed. The dispute adds another dimension to the question of representation: not simply which artists are selected, but who is consulted, who participates in making those decisions and whose understanding of the country is ultimately presented in its name."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Taken together, these four inaugural pavilions raise a broader question of curatorial authority. The issue is not the curator’s nationality, nor must an African national pavilion be curated by someone from that country or continent. What matters is who has the authority to represent a country, what knowledge and relationships inform their choices, how its artists and cultural practitioners participate in that process, and ultimately who determines what becomes visible in the country’s name."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These questions are nothing new; the Kenya pavilion of 2013, curated by two Italians, included eight Chinese artists, one Italian, and two Kenyans. content.article_text:
Just because you are invited into the room does not mean you decide where you stand.

At La Biennale di Venezia, visibility has its own geography, and not every country enters it on equal terms. For African and global African diaspora pavilions, the question is not simply who is present, but who gets seen, how they are seen, and what determines the difference. The Senegalese Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

At La Biennale di Venezia, some countries have the privilege of being discovered; others have to persuade you to look for them. Walk through the Giardini and the Arsenale and national pavilions appear one after another, introducing visitors to artists and art histories they may never have intended to see. Beyond these venues, discovery becomes less assured. Some pavilions remain on routes visitors naturally take, while others require a conscious decision to find them. This creates a hierarchy of attention: some countries benefit from passing visitors, while others depend on visitors who already know enough to seek them out.

For countries whose artists and art histories have been marginalised by Western-dominated narratives of art history, this matters. Venice offers an opportunity to challenge that imbalance and bring their own histories to new audiences. But participation alone cannot guarantee that their pavilions will be encountered, that their artists will receive meaningful attention, or that greater visibility will continue beyond the Biennale.

Here, the geography of visibility begins.

In 2026, one hundred countries are taking part: twenty-nine at the Giardini, twenty-five at the Arsenale and forty-six elsewhere in Venice. Seven nations are exhibiting for the first time, four of them from Africa: Guinea, Equatorial Guinea, Sierra Leone and Somalia. Although these countries have the same official status, their situations regarding access, attention, and representation differ.

Egypt’s Silence Pavilion: Between the Tangible and the Intangible , by Armen Agop, and Brazil’s Comigo ninguém pode , by Rosana Paulino and Adriana Varejão, occupy permanent pavilions in the Giardini, while Morocco’s Asǝṭṭa , by Amina Agueznay, is located in the Arsenale. South Africa too has a long-term presence at the Arsenale, even though it did not take part this year. These locations sit within the routes where Biennale attention is already concentrated, allowing visitors to encounter the pavilions without deliberately seeking them out. Countries without permanent sites face a different challenge: they must establish their presence elsewhere in Venice and attract visitors to a location that may change with each participation. Permanent pavilions also acquire familiarity over time, becoming part of the geography returning visitors already know, while countries that move between venues must make themselves visible in a new place each time. Egyptian artist Armen Agop outside the Egyptian Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

A pavilion situated outside the Giardini or the Arsenale doesn’t necessarily mean it is peripheral. Senegal’s WURUS and Uganda’s Kampala are in adjacent locations right on the Riva degli Schiavoni. Cuba’s Hombres Libres / Free Men , which is on Via Garibaldi, is also in a similar position along the main pedestrian route leading to the Giardini and the Arsenale. The Democratic Republic of the Congo’s first pavilion, Simba Moto! Seize the Fire! Saisis le feu!, is also conveniently located on a busy square in Castello. These pavilions sit along paths Biennale visitors are likely to follow and can therefore see without having to look for them specifically.

Guinea’s first National Participation, Le Son de l’Art: l’Écho de la Matière , occupies a very different geography. Located on the island of San Servolo, it cannot be reached simply by turning down another Venetian street. Visitors have to decide to go there, allow time for the journey and pay for a vaporetto, turning a pavilion visit into a destination in itself.

Mere proximity can also be misleading. The exhibitions Ethiopia’s Shapes of Silence , by Tegene Kunbi and curated by Abebaw Ayalew, and Zimbabwe’s Second Nature | Manyonga , curated by Fadzai Veronica Muchemwa, were both held at Castello, near the Giardini, Arsenale, Senegal, and Uganda. Yet finding them revealed how easily visibility can change within a few metres. Official Biennale signage on the Riva degli Schiavoni directed visitors down the alley towards both Ethiopia and Zimbabwe, but where the route divided, only Ethiopia was clearly signposted. We had deliberately set out to visit both and still struggled to find Zimbabwe. On a map, the difference was negligible; on foot, a missing sign made one pavilion considerably easier to find than the other.

Financial resources also shape visibility. Countries without permanent pavilions must secure temporary venues, often long before the Biennale opens, so budget size and timing can determine which spaces remain available. Funding can influence the kind of art that can be brought to Venice and exhibited, as well as the resources available for communications and for artists and curators to be present during the crucial opening days. The consequences are visible throughout: in where a pavilion is located, what audiences encounter when they arrive, who is there to speak about the work and how effectively the exhibition attracts attention beyond its doors.

ART AFRICA encountered the consequences firsthand. We were in Venice specifically to report on the African and global African diaspora pavilions, yet received no communication from Haiti, Tanzania, Uganda, Guinea, or New Guinea: no press releases, invitations, or approaches to arrange interviews. We then repeatedly emailed the media contacts listed for these pavilions in the official press material from La Biennale di Venezia, but received no response and, months later, still have not heard from them. The Cuban Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

We cannot know why, nor does this mean that these pavilions received no publicity elsewhere. But if specialist media actively seeking to cover them could not make contact through the official channels provided, how effectively were they reaching audiences who did not already know they were there?

But visibility is only one part of the question. Once a pavilion has been found, another issue remains: who has been chosen to represent the country, who made those choices, and what version of the country is being made visible? Sierra Leone, Guinea, Somalia and Equatorial Guinea, all participating for the first time, bring these questions into sharp focus.

Sierra Leone’s first participation makes this question particularly relevant. Mondi Presenti / Worlds of Today , curated by Italians Sandro Orlandi Stagl and Willy Montini, brings together sixteen artists: four from Sierra Leone, four from other ECOWAS countries (the Economic Community of West African States)—Senegal, Togo, Benin, and Nigeria—seven from Italy, and one from Mexico. The curatorial statement places the pavilion within the context of ECOWAS while also referring to a history of exchange between Africa and Italy. The inclusion of artists from neighbouring West African countries therefore clearly relates to that framework. Less clear is why seven Italian artists make up almost half of Sierra Leone’s first national presentation, how the Mexican artist fits within the curatorial concept, and ultimately who determines the version of Sierra Leone that enters the Biennale’s official record.

Guinea’s inaugural Le Son de l’Art: l’Écho de la Matière , curated by Italian curator Carlo Stragapede, raises the stakes further. The exhibition brings together roughly 66 artists, including a significant number of Italians, while only a small minority appear to be Guinean. The issue is not simply who was selected, but what informed those choices and how such a large international exhibition comes to represent Guinea on its first national platform at the Biennale. Whose understanding of the country and its contemporary cultural community is being presented in its name?

Also participating for the first time, Equatorial Guinea’s The Forest The Undergrowth , curated by Catalan curator Joan Abelló, makes the issue even more explicit. Its 23 exhibitors include artists from Italy, Spain, China, Romania, Finland, Albania, Cameroon, Cyprus, Germany and Israel, alongside only one clearly identified Equatoguinean artist, Fernando Nguema Madja. The pavilion also includes Catalan-born Modest Gené Roig, who lived and worked in Equatorial Guinea. Here the question of representation has already been challenged from within the country’s cultural community. Before the Biennale opened, a group of Equatoguinean cultural practitioners publicly argued that contemporary voices from the country were largely absent and called for local artists and cultural professionals to be included in the curatorial process. The Giardini. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

Somalia’s first National Participation has prompted an even more direct debate over who gets to represent a country in Venice. SADDEXLEEY , featuring Ayan Farah, Asmaa Jama and Warsan Shire, is curated by Stockholm-based Mohamed Mire and Italian project manager Fabio Scrivanti. The Somali Arts Foundation has publicly criticised the pavilion for what it describes as a lack of meaningful consultation with artists and arts organisations based in Somalia, while the Somali collective Warbixinta Cidda has called for Scrivanti’s removal, questioning the appointment of an Italian co-curator given Italy’s colonial history in Somalia. An open letter subsequently drew on both statements and called for a boycott if its demands were not addressed. The dispute adds another dimension to the question of representation: not simply which artists are selected, but who is consulted, who participates in making those decisions and whose understanding of the country is ultimately presented in its name.

Taken together, these four inaugural pavilions raise a broader question of curatorial authority. The issue is not the curator’s nationality, nor must an African national pavilion be curated by someone from that country or continent. What matters is who has the authority to represent a country, what knowledge and relationships inform their choices, how its artists and cultural practitioners participate in that process, and ultimately who determines what becomes visible in the country’s name.

These questions are nothing new; the Kenya pavilion of 2013, curated by two Italians, included eight Chinese artists, one Italian, and two Kenyans. When comparable concerns were raised about the country’s representation in 2015, Kenyan artists objected, and the government then withdrew its support. The first Namibian pavilion in 2022, A Bridge to the Desert , also attracted similar criticism. Curated by Italian Marco Furio Ferrario and featuring the anonymous artist RENN, this exhibition drew objections from Namibia’s arts community over the country’s representation; the Namibian government subsequently withdrew its support, although the exhibition took place.

The controversies showed the difference between official participation and cultural legitimacy; a national pavilion makes visible not only a country but a specific representation of it, so it matters as much who has the authority to construct that representation as it does that the country is seen at all. The Bahamas Pavilion, installation view. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts.

Visibility is also influenced by the professional networks that come together in Venice, particularly during the opening week, when museum directors, curators, collectors, foundations, galleries, and the press stay for a few intense days; having an established relationship with an artist, a curator, or an institution can help make a pavilion into a destination, while those who do not have such connections depend more on drawing attention outside of their current networks.

For journalists, those few days are often the only chance to interview artists and curators while in Venice, since time is limited and the city is expensive. So many events compete for attention—namely the Giardini, the Arsenale, the 100 National Participations, the collateral events, and the various exhibitions—that harder-to-find pavilions must put in extra time and effort. Moreover, geography and professional networks can interact: a pavilion off the main routes must work harder to enter the channels through which professional attention flows.

Yet a pavilion’s audience is not limited to the people who walk through its doors. Media coverage can take an exhibition far beyond Venice, reaching readers and viewers who will never attend the Biennale. Reviews, interviews, photographs, videos, podcasts, newsletters and specialist publications can introduce artists and their work to entirely new audiences, while an interview might bring an artist to the attention of a curator who never saw the exhibition in Venice. This coverage also gives the pavilion life beyond the months of the Biennale, creating a record that can circulate long after the exhibition has closed. In this sense, what happens beyond the pavilion can become as important as what happens inside it.

International media coverage is not necessarily more valuable than national, regional, or specialist coverage, which can offer the backgrounds and contexts that general reporting tends to ignore. What matters is how far the coverage reaches, whether it introduces the artists and their work to people who were not already familiar with them, and whether the attention results in anything beyond Venice.

Being highly visible doesn’t necessarily mean having a real impact. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

It is important when considering the reasons why countries choose to invest in Venice, since taking part requires a great deal of financial and institutional resources and therefore high numbers of visitors do not necessarily indicate that the investment has been worthwhile; a pavilion that is crowded may bring about some degree of exposure without achieving any real results, while fewer interactions could result in exhibitions, acquisitions, commissions, publications, or in the establishment of long-term institutional relationships.

No single criterion can judge success, since there shouldn’t be one. However, participation alone cannot measure success.

If international exposure is one reason for taking part in the Biennale, then more significant questions arise once the pavilion has opened. Has it brought the artists and their respective art histories to the attention of people who are not already familiar with them? Has anyone written about, interviewed, or exhibited their work in other institutional contexts? Have the artists obtained new opportunities? Have any relationships persisted after Venice?

The geographical aspect of visibility therefore extends beyond Venice; it affects the chances of discovery, directs professional interest, shapes the kind of content linked to a country’s name, and influences how far that representation will extend afterwards.

For African countries and the global African diaspora, the stakes are particularly high. La Biennale di Venezia can bring artists and art histories long marginalised by Western-dominated narratives to wider attention, opening doors to audiences, institutions and conversations that might otherwise remain out of reach. But an official place within the Biennale does not guarantee an equal chance of being discovered, nor does it necessarily give artists and cultural communities greater authority over how their countries and histories are presented.

The differences begin long before the doors open and can continue long after they close.

Presence, then, is only the beginning. If nobody was looking for you, did Venice make them look — and when they did, who decided what they would see?

来自意大利的七个,而来自墨西哥的一个。因此,来自邻近西非国家的艺术家的参与与这个框架有关,不清楚的是为什么七位意大利艺术家构成了塞拉利昂的第一届全国演示,墨西哥艺术家如何适应治疗概念,最终谁决定塞拉利昂的版本进入比内亚的官方记录。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "吉尼亚的开幕式《艺术之子:马蒂埃尔》由意大利教练卡洛·斯特拉加佩德(Carlo Stragapede)主持,进一步举起投注,展览会聚集了大约66名艺术家,其中包括大量的意大利人,而只有少数人似乎是吉尼亚人。以自己的名义呈现?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "加泰罗尼亚州的《森林之下》也首次出席,由加泰罗尼亚州长Joan Abelló主持,使问题更加明确,其23位展览者包括来自意大利、西班牙、中国、罗马尼亚、芬兰、阿尔巴尼亚、喀麦隆、塞浦路斯、德国和以色列的艺术家,以及仅有一位明确确定的加泰罗尼亚艺术家Fernando Nguema Madja。代表性已经受到国家文化社区的挑战。在展会开幕前,一群厄瓜多尔文化实践者公开声称,该国的当代声音大多缺乏,并呼吁当地艺术家和文化专业人士参与审查过程。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_9907-1003x1030.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "圖片來源:Brendon Bell-Roberts", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "索马里第一届国家参与引发了对谁在威尼斯代表一个国家的更直接的辩论。SADDEXLEEY,由位于斯德哥尔摩的Mohamed Mire和意大利项目经理Fabio Scrivanti陪同,索马里艺术基金会公开批评了该旗帜,因为它描述的是缺乏与索马里总部的艺术家和艺术组织有意义的咨询,而索马里集体Warbixinta Cidda则呼吁斯克里文蒂的撤销,质疑任命一个意大利联盟官员给了意大利在索马里殖民史的公开信随后引用了两份声明,并呼吁抵制,如果他的要求没有得到解决。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些四个开幕式的旗帜提出了一个更广泛的问题,审理权威,问题不是审理员的国籍,也不需要非洲国家旗帜由来自这个国家或大陆的任何人治疗,重要的是谁有权代表一个国家,什么知识和关系告知他们的选择,它的艺术家和文化实践者如何参与这个过程,最后谁决定什么在这个国家的名义上变得可见。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些问题不是什么新鲜事;肯尼亚国旗2013由两名意大利人治疗,其中包括八名中国艺术家,一名意大利人和两名肯尼亚人。2015,肯尼亚艺术家反对,政府随后撤回支持。2022由意大利马可·弗里奥·费拉里奥(Marco Furio Ferrario)和与匿名艺术家雷恩(RENN)相伴,该展览引发了纳米比亚的反对意见。艺术社区超越该国的代表性;纳米比亚政府随后撤回支持,尽管展览举行。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "争论表明了官方参与和文化合法性之间的区别;一个国家旗帜使一个国家的可见,而是一个具体的代表性,所以重要的是谁有权力构建这个代表性,因为它使这个国家完全被看到。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_9169-1030x773.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "巴哈马国旗,安装视图 布兰登·贝尔·罗伯特的图像礼貌。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "可见性也受到在威尼斯聚集的专业网络的影响,特别是在开幕周期间,当博物馆主管、校长、收藏家、基金会、画廊和新闻机构停留了几天;与艺术家、校长或机构建立关系可以帮助使旗帜成为目的地,而那些没有这样的联系的人则更依赖于吸引注意力在当前网络之外。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于记者来说,这些几天往往是唯一的机会采访艺术家和守护者,而在威尼斯,因为时间是有限的,城市是昂贵的。 如此多的活动争取注意力 - 即吉尔迪尼,阿森纳,100国家参与,附加活动和各种展览 - 更难找到的旗帜必须投入额外的时间和努力。流。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而,一座花园的观众并不局限于那些穿过门的人。 媒体覆盖可以展览远远超越威尼斯,到达读者和观众谁将永远不会参加博览会. 评论,采访,照片,视频,Podcast,新闻稿和专业出版物可以介绍艺术家和他们的作品到全新的观众,而一个面试可能会引导一个艺术家注意一个教练谁从未见过展览在威尼斯。博览会,创建一个记录,可以在展览结束后很长时间可以循环,在这个意义上,在旗帜之外发生的事情可以变得同样重要,就像里面发生的事情一样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "国际媒体覆盖不一定比国家、区域或专业覆盖更有价值,可以提供一般报道倾向于忽视的背景和背景,重要的是覆盖到底有多远,是否将艺术家和他们的作品介绍给那些已经不熟悉的人,以及是否注意力导致在威尼斯以外的任何东西。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "非常可见并不一定意味着有真正的影响。 布伦顿·贝尔·罗伯特(Brendon Bell-Roberts)", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_9219-2-773x1030.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "圖片來源:Brendon Bell-Roberts", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "考虑到国家选择在威尼斯投资的原因很重要,因为参与需要大量的财务和机构资源,因此,大量的访客并不一定表明投资是值得的;一个繁忙的旗帜可能会带来某种程度的曝光,而没有实现任何实际结果,而较少的互动可能会导致展览,收购,佣金,出版物,或建立长期的机构关系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "没有一个标准可以判断成功,因为不应该有一个;但是,参与不能单独衡量成功。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如果国际展览是参加博览会的一种原因,那么在博览会开幕后,会出现更重要的问题。 它是否引导艺术家和他们的艺术史到那些已经不熟悉的人的注意力? 有没有人在其他机构背景下写,采访或展出他们的作品? 艺术家获得了新的机会? 威尼斯之后有任何关系?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此,可见性的地理方面远远超越威尼斯,影响发现的机会,指导专业兴趣,形成与国家名称相关的内容类型,并影响该代表性随后将有多大。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于非洲国家和全球非洲大道,投注率特别高,美术馆可以让艺术家和艺术史长期被西方统治的讲话所边缘化,更广泛的关注,向观众、机构和对话开门,否则可能无法达到。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "差异在门开放前很长时间开始,在门关闭后很长时间可以继续。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如果没有人在寻找你,威尼斯会让他们看起来,当他们这样做时,谁决定他们会看到什么?", "translated": true}]
content.excerpt_original: Just because you are invited into the room does not mean you decide where you stand. Suzette Bell-Roberts 8 October 2026 At La Biennale di Venezia, visibility has its own geography, and not every country […]
content.translated_title_zh: 与在那里的距离与在维也纳博览会上看到的距离
content.translated_excerpt_zh: 只是因为你被邀请到房间并不意味着你决定你站在哪里。Suzette Bell-Roberts 2026年10月8日 在La Biennale di Venezia,可见性有自己的地理,而不是每一个国家的位置。

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Paris Photo and Aperture are pleased to announce the shortlist for the 2026 Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards—an annual celebration of the photobook’s enduring role within the narrative of photography. Now in its fourteenth year, the awards recognize excellence in three major categories of photobook publishing: First PhotoBook, PhotoBook of the Year, and Photography Catalog of the Year."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This year, Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards received a record number of books from fifty-six countries around the world, including standout entries from Armenia, Iran, Morocco, Venezuela, and more. On September 22–24, the 2026 shortlist jury met in New York for three concentrated days of review and deliberation by an international team: Alejandro Cartagena , artist; Alexandra Cunningham Cameron , director of design, Judd Foundation; Michael Famighetti , editor in chief, Aperture; Anna Planas , artistic director, Paris Photo; and Anshika Varma , curator and founder, Offset Projects."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Reviewing the many submissions from around the globe underscores how photography books are a quietly powerful medium with endless possibilities for design, storytelling, and reflection on human experience,” says Michael Famighetti. Anna Planas adds, “The jury brings together different perspectives on photography and publishing. Through the selection presented at Paris Photo, we aim to highlight the photobook as a space for experimentation and to celebrate its importance within photography today.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The shortlisted books will be exhibited at Paris Photo, open to the public from November 11 through November 15, followed by an international tour, including in Dublin at PhotoIreland, December 2026, New York at Printed Matter, January 2027, and other venues to be announced."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "On Thursday, November 12, a ﬁnal jury composed of ﬁve members will meet in Paris to select the winners for all three prizes, which will be revealed on Friday, November 13, at 3:00 p.m. (CET), at a ceremony at Paris Photo, and announced on Aperture.org and Parisphoto.com."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Below, see the thirty-five selected titles for the 2026 PhotoBook Awards shortlist."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "First PhotoBook"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/01_FIRST_Aperture2026-0102.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ivan Anisimov, Pants on Top of Shoes , Kult Books, Stockholm. content.article_text:
Paris Photo and Aperture are pleased to announce the shortlist for the 2026 Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards—an annual celebration of the photobook’s enduring role within the narrative of photography. Now in its fourteenth year, the awards recognize excellence in three major categories of photobook publishing: First PhotoBook, PhotoBook of the Year, and Photography Catalog of the Year.

This year, Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards received a record number of books from fifty-six countries around the world, including standout entries from Armenia, Iran, Morocco, Venezuela, and more. On September 22–24, the 2026 shortlist jury met in New York for three concentrated days of review and deliberation by an international team: Alejandro Cartagena , artist; Alexandra Cunningham Cameron , director of design, Judd Foundation; Michael Famighetti , editor in chief, Aperture; Anna Planas , artistic director, Paris Photo; and Anshika Varma , curator and founder, Offset Projects.

“Reviewing the many submissions from around the globe underscores how photography books are a quietly powerful medium with endless possibilities for design, storytelling, and reflection on human experience,” says Michael Famighetti. Anna Planas adds, “The jury brings together different perspectives on photography and publishing. Through the selection presented at Paris Photo, we aim to highlight the photobook as a space for experimentation and to celebrate its importance within photography today.”

The shortlisted books will be exhibited at Paris Photo, open to the public from November 11 through November 15, followed by an international tour, including in Dublin at PhotoIreland, December 2026, New York at Printed Matter, January 2027, and other venues to be announced.

On Thursday, November 12, a ﬁnal jury composed of ﬁve members will meet in Paris to select the winners for all three prizes, which will be revealed on Friday, November 13, at 3:00 p.m. (CET), at a ceremony at Paris Photo, and announced on Aperture.org and Parisphoto.com.

content.article_text:
Ce portrait a été initialement publié en 2024, lors de la sortie du folm,

Dans son salon, la lumière passe à travers des fenêtres en vitrail typiques de la Belle Époque. Derrière le canapé en velours sur lequel on discute, il y a un personnage de Disney (le vilain Jafar, dans Aladdin) en carton, fabriqué par son enfant, et, tout autour, des dessins, croquis, peintures ou photos, disposés dans une sorte de bazar ordonné. À mi-chemin entre un appartement et un atelier, l’intérieur de l’habitation de Louise Bourgoin, zen et chaleureuse, atteste d’une chose : ici, pas de hiérarchie entre l’art classique, les dessins de nus et les gribouillages enfantins. Dans Bis repetita d’Émilie Noblet, il y a une combinaison tout aussi grisante entre totems antiques et culture pop (on apprend les rudiments du latin en écoutant sur YouTube une version traduite en latin de « Pour que tu m’aimes encore » , le hit sentimental de Céline Dion).

L’actrice y campe avec une jubilation contagieuse Delphine, une prof démissionnaire d’un lycée d’Angers. Pas très à cheval sur la déontologie, celle-ci scrolle les offres de fringues sur des applications face à des élèves désintéressés au possible. Les deux parties ont passé un contrat : contre des 19 sur 20 dans les bulletins de notes pipés, les élèves laissent leur prof tranquille. Tout ce beau monde blasé doit remettre le pied à l’étrier quand la directrice (la géniale Noémie Lvovsky), les croyant surdoués, inscrit les élèves au championnat international de latin, à Naples.

Hasard du calendrier : en moins d’un an, Louise Bourgoin a campé deux profs au bout du rouleau, d’abord dans un registre plus grave chez Thomas Lilti, dans Un métier sérieux , et maintenant chez Émilie Noblet. Si elle interprète si bien ces enseignantes au bord de la crise de nerfs, c’est aussi parce qu’elle connaît par cœur et intimement ce milieu.

« Un métier sérieux » de Thomas Lilti : l’école au corps

AU PREMIER RANG

L’actrice, qui arbore une marinière (comme un subtil clin d’œil à ses origines bretonnes, elle qui est née à Rennes en 1981), avait tout pour être une enfant de la balle : sa mère était prof de lettres modernes ; son père, de philosophie. En grandissant, elle les a vus trimer : « Ils étaient régulièrement épuisés par leur travail. Et j’ai grandi dans les années 1990-2000, donc ce n’est pas un phénomène nouveau, même si on en parle plus aujourd’hui. C’est un métier extrêmement peu considéré en France, difficile, sous-payé. C’était une grande responsabilité de l’incarner à l’écran. »

Pas vraiment du genre dissipée à l’école ( « j’avais quand même la pression pour ne pas redoubler, ça aurait été horrible pour mes parents » ) ni dégoûtée par ce métier, la future actrice, attirée par les arts plastiques, cherche d’abord à marcher dans les pas de sa famille. Elle suit des études aux Beaux-Arts. Elle tente de rentrer dans le moule familial en s’inscrivant comme prof stagiaire à l’Institut universitaire de formation des maîtres, en vue de passer son CAPES. C’est après avoir échoué au concours qu’elle décide de passer des castings pour la télé et le cinéma.

Rétrospectivement, ce lancement dans le jeu sans filet ni formation a provoqué un complexe durable chez elle. « C’est un métier un peu magique parce que quelqu’un comme moi, qui n’a pas pris de cours, peut démarrer avec un premier rôle. Mais j’ai un sentiment d’illégitimité, je culpabilise de ne pas avoir fait le Conservatoire. » La première fois que le public la découvre, c’est sur le plateau du Grand Journal de Canal+, en 2006, où elle officie comme Miss météo.

Xavier Lacaille : « Quand je n’arrive pas à mettre mon masque social, ça me tord profondément »

Face caméra, elle lit des textes drôles, osés, malins et décalés, tout en entrant dans la peau d’une animatrice sexy, avec les limites et la stéréotypisation que ce rôle peut engendrer. Louise Bourgoin ne renie pas du tout cette expérience à la télévision – là encore, pas de hiérarchie, et peu de jugement. Il faut dire que ses performances télévisuelles ont eu le mérite de montrer que cette bonne élève, qui apprend ses textes longtemps avant le tournage et avec méthode (elle les recopie, puis mémorise les répliques en inversant les mots dans les phrases), excelle paradoxalement à incarner une forme d’irrévérence à l’écran.

STATUES VIVANTES « C’est une artiste qui m’a beaucoup marquée » , nous dit Louise Bourgoin quand on l’interroge sur son rapport à Louise Bourgeois, artiste française célèbre et provocante, dont elle s’est inspirée pour trouver son pseudonyme d’actrice. « Je l’ai découverte à mes 17 ans, puis j’ai regardé un documentaire dans lequel elle épluche une orange et parle de façon étonnante de son travail. Elle joue la naïve en disant que ses immenses phallus en albâtre sont des petites filles avec des cols roulés. Elle se moque des spectateurs et a une insolence dans son discours sur ses œuvres. »

Dans une scène de Bis repetita , les élèves et leur prof visitent les ruines napolitaines et bloquent sur des sculptures antiques de nus, avec un air mi-choqué, mi-amusé. Hors plateau, le nu passionne justement Louise Bourgoin. En 2012, elle a coécrit avec Edwart Minot Orsay mis à nu , livre dans lequel elle commente les plus belles œuvres déshabillées du musée d’Orsay. « J’ai toujours adoré dessiner des corps entremêlés, enlacés. Je n’aime pas dessiner des vêtements, parce que ça date une œuvre. Dans le livre, je me suis penchée sur des œuvres de la fin du xixe et du début du xxe siècle, avec peu de peintres femmes mais beaucoup plus de modèles féminins nus que masculins. »

Peinture et cinéma, même combat ? Longtemps cantonnée sur le grand écran à des rôles de muses (des personnages de séductrices ou d’amoureuses), l’actrice, qui aime jouer « des personnes pas très reluisantes, qui trichent, qui mentent » et qui a été chamboulée plus jeune par les films de Larry Clark ou Gregg Araki, semble enfin avoir droit à des rôles à la hauteur de son aura (voir la série Hippocrate de Thomas Lilti, dans laquelle elle incarne une interne en médecine brillante et ambitieuse) et de sa puissance comique (voir ses scènes alcoolisées dans Bis repetita , anthologiques).

Loin d’être en crise, la quadra atteint a contrario une forme de plénitude artistique – elle a osé exposer pour la première fois ses œuvres à la galerie Laura Pecheur, en 2022. Elle espère secrètement se lancer dans l’arène de films d’action (elle fait de la boxe française) : « J’aime beaucoup la violence féminine au cinéma, elle est encore trop rare. » À voir son visage anguleux et son regard féroce lorsqu’elle ne sourit pas, on se dit qu’elle pourrait tout pulvériser.

Bis repetita d’Émilie Noblet, Le Pacte (1h26), sortie le 20 mars.

Hello , I’m Cherry, I’m 14 and an aspiring film-maker. I love how your films capture what it feels like to be a young girl growing up. We hear so much about the famous men in your family, but how have the successful women in your family inspired and influenced you? Your films capture the experience of what it is to be a young girl in a way words often can’t. CherryEmma That’s nice to hear, thank you. I feel like I got a lot from my mom about being true to yourself, following what you’re interested in and seeing the beauty in your surroundings. My mom always noticed odd details in life, so a lot of my films are made up of those kinds of things.

Your films beautifully capture the isolation of hotel rooms – spaces completely detached from a character’s past or future. If you were forced into that stillness and could choose to preserve only one cherished memory while erasing another for ever, what would they be? Malpractice1 It’s hard to pick a memory, but recently we had a party in Versailles for the anniversary of Marie Antoinette and New Order played. When they started playing Ceremony [from the soundtrack] and the lights went on, I just know that in the future when I have to remember a happy memory, that’s going to be it. Even painful memories are part of making you who you are, and you learn from them, so I can’t think of anything I would erase.

I heard that some of Lost in Translation was filmed guerrilla-style due to a lack of permits. Which scene carried the biggest risk of getting you arrested? What if you had been kicked out of the country? catchytitled We had permission for most of it, but we had to grab the scenes with Scarlett [Johansson] on the subway with real people around. The same with the overhead shot of her at that famous Shibuya crossing – we just went into Starbucks because it had this incredible view, but we would have never got permission to film there. So we stole a few things in the spirit of guerrilla film-making. And I’m glad we didn’t get kicked out, yes.

What was the dynamic like between the five girls behind the scenes on The Virgin Suicides ? For instance, which girls were the closest, who was the loudest, who was the quietest, etc? Imogen067 Their personalities did kind of emerge. We did rehearsals where we all hung out together and had them interact as a family and they cooked together. They hung out off set and they started to bond. Chelse Swain was the most eccentric one.

The postmodern soundtrack in Marie Antoinette, all that post-punk and new romantic music, was so audacious that it took your film to a staggering level of artistry. What was the original idea behind bringing those two worlds together? Dmitry_S When I first started reading about Marie Antoinette in Antonia Fraser’s book, I was struck by how young she was. She was 14 when she came to Versailles and around 18 when she became queen. So I really wanted to convey that she and Louis were teenagers, and I thought back to the new romantic music I was listening to when I was a teenager. I was lucky that I had a big brother who exposed me to good music at a young age. I wanted to show it through that filter of Bow Wow Wow and Adam Ant. When the film came out, some people were offended because it just wasn’t usual to put contemporary music in a period film.

Your 2003 video for the White Stripes’ cover of I Just Don’t Know What to Do With Myself has been rated by Rolling Stone as one of the sexiest music videos ever . What other ideas were considered before you landed on Kate Moss pole dancing for three minutes? McScootikins Oh, wow, I didn’t know that. That’s so cool. I don’t know where it came from. It was just my idea, and I was glad that everyone was on board with it. I just asked Kate to do that, she said yes, and the band was into it.

Are you aware that you’re a girlblogger icon? sleepy_nym I don’t know that much about bloggers, but that’s nice to hear. I’ll have to ask my teenage daughters. I do appreciate that my work was made a while ago, so it’s great that it connects with young women of this generation.

What was it like working on Tim Burton’s 1984 short film Frankenweenie , before Tim Burton was “Tim Burton”? jasonaparkes That was such a fun experience. I was 12 or something. I think Tim Burton was right out of school. It was an early short film, so it was really fun to meet him and be on his set – he used to do drawings for me. I’d spent a lot of time on my dad’s film sets, so it was fun to be on someone else’s. I still like to visit film sets. I’m never jaded – I’m still impressed by movie magic.

Didn’t you mind having your mum filming behind the scenes for all those hours when you were making Marie Antoinette? Dr_J_A_Zoidberg My mom always had a grounding mom presence. It was a stressful shoot, so it was nice to have her there. She also appreciated all the beauty of the costumes and the details of the food and the flowers, so it was fun to show it to her, and she was really into filming all the details and how it was made. I forgot about the footage until recently and I didn’t realise how much there was. My mom had almost 80 hours of footage, so it was a real treat to have this home movie to revisit. I never thought we would do something with it.

You’re not going to answer this – but someone has to ask it anyway. What does Bob whisper to Charlotte at the end of Lost in Translation ? rolleyes I like what Bill [Murray] always says. He says, “It’s between them,” so I’ll leave it at that.

Sofia Coppola

content.article_text:
The artist shares how her flower-filled upbringing shapes her creative enquiry into colour and light through paint, in an attempt to connect to the divine.

Canvas: How has your painting practice come to be what it is today and how does the concept of legacy inform your work?

Shooq AlShawi: My parents were florists and so, growing up, we were surrounded by flowers. I would paint them over and over again without realising how meditative that was. I had a deep fear of death until I met the divine through my practice. That’s when faith became a lived experience and the depth of time really made sense. The more I sat with the flowers, seeing this cycle of life and death repeat over and over again, it became something really beautiful. That’s where all the colours come from, from this place where the eternal exists, where the soul is present. When I was pregnant with my daughter, I was in a meditation session, and the instructor kept asking what was coming up for me. The word ‘legacy’ kept coming through, without my fully understanding it at the time. Legacy has become my showing up for things, understanding something that’s beyond me and honouring this painting practice that existed before me and which I carry forward.

How is faith present in your paintings?

I’ve always been deeply inspired by divine movements, but it took time before that was fully apparent in my paintings. In my earlier works, it exists without fully letting you in. More recently, it’s just cracked open, and I don’t think it can be packed up again. This is another way I connect to this idea of legacy, which is the faith that exists within myself. I believe every artist has some form of faith within them. When you paint something, you have faith in this unknown that you’re trying to bring out onto a canvas.

How do your titles further connect you to this faith, such as Spiralling Into the Infinite (Diptych) (2025) or The Birds Are Praying (The Veil) (2026)?

The titles come to me and just make sense. The Birds Are Praying is from seeing birds across the bridge at sunset while cycling my kids home. I tell them that the birds are praying, and now they’ve started saying that. It’s about this faith in something that exists outside of ourselves in the everyday, not belief in one specific thing.

Are the colours in your work inspired by specific flowers or are they accidental?

I see everything through the lens of faith. Flowers appear along my path, whether they are collected, bought or gathered, they always deeply inform the work and act as silent witnesses to the process. I have towers of dead flowers in my studio that just stay there and become part of the story.

How do people initially react to your paintings?

I think you react to a work like a mirror into something deeper within. So everyone will naturally have a different reaction. The work is made to invite slow looking. There’s an ongoing questioning of how much space exists between the paint, the canvas and the viewer. To me, colour is an expansion of light and space, which can be used to tap in into further dimensions of the soul’s existence. I want it to speak initially for its depth, where you can feel like you’ve fallen into the work.

Your paintings are physically rather imposing. Is scale important to your practice?

The painting process is a physical outpouring of energy for me. I’ll use my body and just run at the canvas. I’m constantly covered in paint. In some works, you can see the fight with the canvas, and in others, where I had to let go and come at the canvas eyes closed. I’ve tried to trick myself into making smaller fragments of paintings, but it’s not the same.

Are your diptychs part of that exploration ?

The more recent ones started as an effort to control the scale. But then I’d start another painting in response to the first one, because if you put too much into one painting, it just becomes nothing. Then the two paintings would come together and become something bigger that you can’t separate, like an energy field. That just can’t happen on a small scale, where I feel like I’m restricted.

Where do you see your practice going from here ?

In my current residency programme at Turps in London, there has been a peeling back of colour. The tones have become more baroque, more mature. There was definitely a restraint in the amount of flowers I brought into the studio. Some colours are more present, like the red from these poppies in a field I would cycle by, or blue from the sky right outside the studio, where I would bring my canvases to paint. Some fundamental principles of Islamic art are coming through more overtly, such as the circling of the square. I’ve been repeating myself with this constant circular brushstroke, which has implanted itself without my even noticing. There’s also a lot of canvas left unpainted in these new works. Maybe this is my way of leaving this space for the divine. I’m allowing gesture to take centre stage along with a strong intention of stretching the paint and seeing what it does, in keeping with this idea of legacy.

This interview first appeared in Canvas 124: Prismatic
