content.article_text:
Get ready get set for Frieze week, as London opens the art fairs, new shows and Autumn seasons in the big institutions

The art world is gearing up for Frieze London and Frieze Masters fairs next week, which are open in Regent’s Park from 14-18 October. Photography, lens-based media and image-adjacent presentations figure large, with Frieze London featuring a curated programme including The Code Universe: Artists Interrogating a Post-Digital Age , selected by Carol Yinghua Lu, director of the Inside-Out Art Museum, Beijing, and co-curator of the 19th Istanbul Biennial (2027). Including work dating back to the late 1970s, it considers popular culture and the way it is produced, circulated and consumed, and includes Japanese artist Shinro Ohtake (presented by greengrassi and Take Ninagawa), who works across media to create collages and sculptural pieces. It also includes a new multi-channel video installation by Payne Zhu (Spurs Gallery), which explores the relationship between human perception and machine cognition.

Outside the curated section at Frieze London, PM8 / Francisco Salas will present historical colour photographs by Lithuanian artist Algirdas Šeškus, which were taken on the only official commission he received during Soviet times, but rejected as they did not fit the given standards of ‘official art’. Edel Assanti will present a ‘memory box’ booth designed by Polish artist Marcin Dudek after his childhood home, and show works by artists such as Vinca Petersen and Sheida Soleimani. Maureen Paley’s presentation will include Anne Hardy, Peter Hujar and Wolfgang Tillmans, while Soft Opening’s artists will include Ebun Sodipo, whose work includes mixed-media photographic collages.

Frieze Masters includes a trail titled Queering Modernism: Visual Languages of the 20 th Century , conceived of by German curator Anke Kempkes and featuring image-pioneers such as Claude Cahun (presented by Alberta Pane Gallery) and Ruth Bernhard (Galerie Albrecht). The spotlight section at Frieze Masters includes other artists neglected by the Western canon, including Chinese image-maker Lang JingShan (Each Modern) – a pioneer of composite photography in the 1930s and 40s, who combined multiple negatives with painting, inscription, and scratching. Frieze also returns to the Institute of Contemporary Arts with a new programme of artists’ film and moving-image works, screening on a continuous loop during Frieze Week and online at ica.art.

Beyond Frieze is a host of interesting shows in commercial galleries, plus new seasons opening across the big institutions. The Photographers’ Gallery puts the focus on colour this autumn, for example, with classic images by William Eggleston and colour portraits by Sanlé Sory, some of which are previously unseen. The National Portrait Gallery also embraces a rush of colour with an exhibition by Tim Walker, Fairyland , exploring queer identity, love and community. Tate Britain’s The 90s: Art and Fashion has just opened; the reviews have been mixed, it’s fair to say, but it features celebrated photographic projects by Juergen Teller, Eileen Perrier, and Nigel Shafran. Over at Tate Modern, Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography is a new show on Pictorialism which emphasises its international spread; a long-awaited exhibition, it looks set to revitalise interest in this long over-looked genre.

Graces Mews is presenting What Rose from the Cut , a new evolution of the hit feminist collage exhibition The Rose , put together by artist Justine Kurland, curator and collector Sarah Miller Meigs, the venue, plus Fiona Rogers, Parasol Foundation Curator of Women in Photography at the V&A and author of the recent book, Cut Out: A Feminist History of Photo Collage . Delving back into history with artists such as Claude Cahun, and right up to the present day with Keisha Scarville, it’s presenting an exciting take on an always-edgy form. Collage also features at Hauser and Wirth in a new presentation of Lorna Simpson’s work, which also features her paintings and sculpture; the exhibition is a double-hander and also features Cindy Sherman, including works from her new series Fabric Matrons.

Over at Phillida Reid, there’s a solo presentation by Joanna Piotrowska; Wyrwa is an installation of new works including images of the town in which the artist grew up, mounted in bespoke aluminium and hand-blown glass frameworks. The show also includes childhood drawings, folded and overturns, and close-cropped fragments from her father’s negatives, shown behind tinted-glass. Katherine Hubbard’s The Great Room at Studio Voltaire delves into the artist’s experience of caring for her mother, the medium of photography, and a very interesting-looking architectural installation; Phaidon is also celebrating work by women, launching a new book Great Women Photographers , which is edited by Charlotte Flint and includes image-makers such as Letizia Battaglia, Myriam Boulos and Rinko Kawauchi. The book is accompanied by an exhibition, hosted at Dorchester Collection’s 45 Park Lane.

Large Glass is giving Italian photographer Mario Cresci a second show, People I Care About , documenting people in the Southern Italian town Tricarico, between 1966 and 1967; also dating back to the 1960s is an exhibition by Daido Moriyama at Hamilton’s Gallery, picking out Japan’s abrupt shift into hypercapitalism, and Andy Warhol’s influence on the photographer’s work. Over at No.9 Cork Street, Frieze’s permanent gallery space in Mayfair, To Seek, To Find celebrates photographic commissions by the Mr & Mrs Smith hotel group, including classic commissions by Tina Barney and Martin Parr, and brand-new work by Kalpesh Lathigra.

And of course there’s much else to see beyond photography alone. Radical Living in the UK at William Morris Gallery is an interesting – even inspiring – survey show into alternative communities, dating back over the last 200 years but including Dial House, the self-sustaining anarcho-pacifist open house founded in 1967 by Penny Rimbaud and Gee Vaucher of punk band Crass. Es Devlin: Other Worlds at the Design Museum is a retrospective of the innovative artist and designer’s work with space, which has included installations, set design and kinetic sculptures. Cady Noland at Gagosian’s Davies Street gallery is the artist’s first UK exhibition in over 30 years; featuring new work conceived for the space, it explores the material and symbolic architecture of American identity, power structures, celebrity and racism. This Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte at Gagosian Gallery Grosvenor Hill is a reappraisal of the Surrealist painter which pairs his work with contemporary artists’, and emphasises his continuing relevance in our ever more image-saturated lives.

Frieze London and Frieze Masters are open from 14-18 October in Regent’s Park www.frieze.com/fairs/frieze-london

content.title_original: Can Ali G: Who Iz I? save character comedy cinema?
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "F or a man whose campaign slogan was once “Keep it real”, Ali G has his work cut out in the reality of 2026. The big dog of Da West Staines Massiv was the character with whom Sacha Baron Cohen carved out his own niche of gonzo-gotcha comedy in the late 1990s – and now he’s back with new film, Ali G: Who Iz I? But it’s unclear if his great creation has gone sufficiently fallow in the collective consciousness to still operate well in real-life situations, the kind of lethal idiot who once pitched Donald Trump anti-drip ice-cream gloves. And more critically, is the Ali G satirical project – which poked at 90s multicultural mores – still relevant and funny in far more rancorous times?", "links": [{"text": "Sacha Baron Cohen", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/culture/sacha-baron-cohen"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It’s not just Baron Cohen’s career as an undercover operative that’s on the line. It’s the future of character-led comedy as a going concern, now that he seems to be the last man standing in this once-noble tradition – in cinemas, at least. To be clear, character comedy isn’t merely comedy with characters; it’s comedy filtered through a central persona that overlaps with the comedian playing it and whose subversive sensibility colours the entire work."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/fd98d6ea50d262f3eb5839e0a8c30c8ade2030d4/0_42_1482_2077/master/1482.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Mike Myers’ swinging London exile … Myers and Heather Graham in Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me, 1999.", "caption": "Mike Myers’ swinging London exile … Myers and Heather Graham in Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me, 1999. Photograph: AJ Pics/Alamy", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mike Myers’ swinging London exile Austin Powers was the most commercially successful example – but the actor hasn’t made a film in that first-person style since his self-help spoof The Love Guru tanked in 2008. Will Ferrell , ruling the roost as fashion’s Dr Evil, Mugatu (in Zoolander), Buddy the Elf and Ron Burgundy, seemed the best successor. Mystifyingly, though, Ferrell has barely been able to get a film bankrolled in the last decade – and certainly not one putting him out front to that extent. Character comedy subsists on TV, from where it came, with the likes of Alan Partridge and Philomena Cunk. But unless the new Ali G can blaze a fresh hit of chronic satire into the genre’s bloodstream, it’s hard to see a future for it on the big screen.", "links": [{"text": "Will Ferrell", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/willferrell"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ali G was already controversial back in the day: the regular accusation was that while he was satirising the white appropriation of black culture, he in fact enabled straight lampooning of the latter. Now those criticisms are sharpened by the notion that, in 2026, he is past his sell-by date: both out of step with a more culturally mixed Britain and, overflowing with bifter gags and mad patois, dangerously adjacent to racist caricature that won’t pass these days. British standup comedian Dane Baptiste recently told Deadline : “After Black Lives Matter and the brief humanisation of black people and black creatives, it seems very dubious that we are now regressing back, not just five years, but 25 years, to bring back a character that was able to flourish because there were no accurate portrayals of black Britishness on screen.”", "links": [{"text": "recently told Deadline", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/09/ali-g-who-iz-i-writer-defends-amazon-sacha-baron-cohen-1237111031/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But it would be a shock if Baron Cohen wasn’t wise to the current sensitivities. In 2020’s Borat Subsequent Moviefilm , he mostly successfully updated the Kazakhstan reporter for the post-truth, Covid-era end times of Trump’s US. His choice of target interviewees in Who Iz I? remains to be seen, but it would be surprising if he didn’t pick a few where he can opportunistically needle both woke and anti-woke camps.", "links": [{"text": "Borat Subsequent Moviefilm", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2020/oct/21/borat-subsequent-moviefilm-review-sacha-baron-cohen-trump"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These debates are tricky ones, on cultural shifting sands, and Baron Cohen undeniably skirts close to reactionary goading at times (the fact that dumb Americans might actually believe Kazakhstan is that backward doesn’t escape the fact he’s propagating the idea it’s a potassium-, incest- and antisemitism-crazed shithole). But if the new Ali G film does fall foul of the post-Black Lives Matter climate, it’ll be hard not to also conclude that our splintered, fractious era lacks the unity – or at least consensus – that makes character comedy possible at all. To a large extent, audiences have to agree on the social phenomena these big satirical beasts feed off. In the late 90s, black street culture was sufficiently new and prominent a force in the UK mainstream to make this crip-sign-throwing buffoon a direct hit."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There’s no reason why character comedy can’t thrive off societal shifts, though – if the character is positioned carefully enough. In fact, this is how it originally manufactured tension, with the likes of Charlie Chaplin’s Tramp getting fed through the mangler of industrialised capitalism in Modern Times. Or Peter Sellers playing both old establishment nabob Sir John Kennaway and the trade union firebrand Fred Kite in 1959’s labour-relations satire I’m All Right Jack. With postwar Britain evolving rapidly, Tony Hancock picked up the baton in 1961’s The Rebel, both surfing and sending up boho nonconformism in his role as an accidentally successful avant garde artist. Alan Partridge’s long slide into local radio-bound insignificance has only attained glorious new parallels in the post-Brexit era."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/f6ea6d53a13132fc4fa6b9219faa5707f2e1b3a4/0_0_2400_1730/master/2400.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Peter Sellers, centre, in I’m All Right Jack, 1959.", "caption": "A massive influence … Peter Sellers, centre, in I’m All Right Jack, 1959. Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/Alamy", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Another reason why character comedy may have fallen from favour is its vaudevillian strut, a very human theatricality that seems old-fashioned in an age of frictionless CGI blockbusters. It revels in transformation and disguise (Baron Cohen now, of course, being so famous he has to layer on disguises on top of his original disguises – hence the new Rasta Ali G). The genre often compounds this ludic chaos by having its stars play multiple roles, as Sellers, Eddie Murphy and Mike Myers love to do.", "links": [{"text": "Eddie Murphy", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/eddiemurphy"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Somehow this protean fun allows the presiding comic genius’s essential quality to pierce through all the more clearly: in Sellers’ case, a kind of unnerving mildness that could transmute into mania, or Myers’ cheeky puerility. Mrs Doubtfire, from 1993, is one of the most revelatory uses of this ventriloquist effect. Another persona that the film’s divorced voiceover artist adopts in order to see his children more often, the Scottish nanny is really a conduit for the sentimental streak that underpinned much of Robin Williams’s work. And like the theatre, you can see the tactile human continuity between character comedy’s practitioners: Myers has often talked about his admiration for Sellers’ chameleonic powers. Dr Evil’s “one million dollars” faux pas is a lift of a similar gag near the end of Sellers’ 1959 geopolitics satire The Mouse That Roared."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6d2827ed178931f7aaa11421749080f77f699587/865_0_2218_1775/master/2218.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Robin Williams in Mrs Doubtfire, 1993.", "caption": "A sentimental streak … Robin Williams in Mrs Doubtfire, 1993. Photograph: Landmark Media/Alamy", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "By 2002, when Myers was doing silhouette gags about giving birth to Mini-Me in Austin Powers: Goldmember, this vaudevillian style was looking passe. With The Lord of the Rings and Harry Potter in full pomp, blockbuster film was firmly in the CGI era; comedy had moved on, too, to the edgier Frat Pack films and the realism of Judd Apatow."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But perhaps character comedy had also lost strong moorings by this point, with social comment largely absent from the genre since the 1980s. Instead, Austin Powers was an extended riff on 60s and 90s pop-cultural overlaps and discrepancies (Jean Dujardin did something similar in his later OSS-117 series), while Eddie Murphy’s multi-character outings The Nutty Professor and Norbit seemed largely there to prop up the fat-suit industry. Only Will Ferrell – via his blowhard news anchor Burgundy, but also in his general screen persona in ensemble work such as Wedding Crashers, Step Brothers and Talladega Nights – embodied a type that spoke clearly for the times: the arrested manchild."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That all changed the moment Borat and his wobbling producer Azamat Bagatov landed in New York in 2006. By injecting Borat with a raw hit of the reality format incubated on The 11 O’Clock Show and Da Ali G Show, Baron Cohen completely revitalised big-screen character comedy. Suddenly, it became thrillingly politicised as his sublimely ignorant aliases, Borat and in 2009 Brüno, flushed out American and Middle Eastern absurdities and prejudices. Not to mention the high-wire aspect of his escapades: Baron Cohen was somehow impervious to whatever peril he stirred up, whether that was desecrating the Star-Spangled Banner at a rodeo in Borat, or an interpretation of mano-a-mano quite different to what cage fighting audiences were expecting in Brüno. His gleeful brazenness was the signature quality that shone through.", "links": [{"text": "Borat", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/borat"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/136f087235a459501eaab7ab275a2e68baec8b56/303_0_2500_2000/master/2500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Will Ferrell in Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy, 2004.", "caption": "A type that spoke clearly for the times … Will Ferrell in Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy, 2004. Photograph: Dreamworks Skg/Allstar", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But Ali G has been dormant a long time. His last big-screen outing, 2002’s hit-and-miss Ali G Indahouse , was a very different, fully scripted endeavour. Beyond a gag about mistaking a pregnancy test for a vape, the trailer for Ali G: Who Iz I? doesn’t give much away about how sharply the character’s been updated; judging by the small-penis outro, some things are undying.", "links": [{"text": "Ali G Indahouse", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2002/mar/22/1"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Staines’s favourite son will need to pull more out of his XXXXXL puffa. content.article_text:
F or a man whose campaign slogan was once “Keep it real”, Ali G has his work cut out in the reality of 2026. The big dog of Da West Staines Massiv was the character with whom Sacha Baron Cohen carved out his own niche of gonzo-gotcha comedy in the late 1990s – and now he’s back with new film, Ali G: Who Iz I? But it’s unclear if his great creation has gone sufficiently fallow in the collective consciousness to still operate well in real-life situations, the kind of lethal idiot who once pitched Donald Trump anti-drip ice-cream gloves. And more critically, is the Ali G satirical project – which poked at 90s multicultural mores – still relevant and funny in far more rancorous times?

It’s not just Baron Cohen’s career as an undercover operative that’s on the line. It’s the future of character-led comedy as a going concern, now that he seems to be the last man standing in this once-noble tradition – in cinemas, at least. To be clear, character comedy isn’t merely comedy with characters; it’s comedy filtered through a central persona that overlaps with the comedian playing it and whose subversive sensibility colours the entire work.

Mike Myers’ swinging London exile Austin Powers was the most commercially successful example – but the actor hasn’t made a film in that first-person style since his self-help spoof The Love Guru tanked in 2008. Will Ferrell , ruling the roost as fashion’s Dr Evil, Mugatu (in Zoolander), Buddy the Elf and Ron Burgundy, seemed the best successor. Mystifyingly, though, Ferrell has barely been able to get a film bankrolled in the last decade – and certainly not one putting him out front to that extent. Character comedy subsists on TV, from where it came, with the likes of Alan Partridge and Philomena Cunk. But unless the new Ali G can blaze a fresh hit of chronic satire into the genre’s bloodstream, it’s hard to see a future for it on the big screen.

Ali G was already controversial back in the day: the regular accusation was that while he was satirising the white appropriation of black culture, he in fact enabled straight lampooning of the latter. Now those criticisms are sharpened by the notion that, in 2026, he is past his sell-by date: both out of step with a more culturally mixed Britain and, overflowing with bifter gags and mad patois, dangerously adjacent to racist caricature that won’t pass these days. British standup comedian Dane Baptiste recently told Deadline : “After Black Lives Matter and the brief humanisation of black people and black creatives, it seems very dubious that we are now regressing back, not just five years, but 25 years, to bring back a character that was able to flourish because there were no accurate portrayals of black Britishness on screen.”

But it would be a shock if Baron Cohen wasn’t wise to the current sensitivities. In 2020’s Borat Subsequent Moviefilm , he mostly successfully updated the Kazakhstan reporter for the post-truth, Covid-era end times of Trump’s US. His choice of target interviewees in Who Iz I? remains to be seen, but it would be surprising if he didn’t pick a few where he can opportunistically needle both woke and anti-woke camps.

These debates are tricky ones, on cultural shifting sands, and Baron Cohen undeniably skirts close to reactionary goading at times (the fact that dumb Americans might actually believe Kazakhstan is that backward doesn’t escape the fact he’s propagating the idea it’s a potassium-, incest- and antisemitism-crazed shithole). But if the new Ali G film does fall foul of the post-Black Lives Matter climate, it’ll be hard not to also conclude that our splintered, fractious era lacks the unity – or at least consensus – that makes character comedy possible at all. To a large extent, audiences have to agree on the social phenomena these big satirical beasts feed off. In the late 90s, black street culture was sufficiently new and prominent a force in the UK mainstream to make this crip-sign-throwing buffoon a direct hit.

There’s no reason why character comedy can’t thrive off societal shifts, though – if the character is positioned carefully enough. In fact, this is how it originally manufactured tension, with the likes of Charlie Chaplin’s Tramp getting fed through the mangler of industrialised capitalism in Modern Times. Or Peter Sellers playing both old establishment nabob Sir John Kennaway and the trade union firebrand Fred Kite in 1959’s labour-relations satire I’m All Right Jack. With postwar Britain evolving rapidly, Tony Hancock picked up the baton in 1961’s The Rebel, both surfing and sending up boho nonconformism in his role as an accidentally successful avant garde artist. Alan Partridge’s long slide into local radio-bound insignificance has only attained glorious new parallels in the post-Brexit era.

Another reason why character comedy may have fallen from favour is its vaudevillian strut, a very human theatricality that seems old-fashioned in an age of frictionless CGI blockbusters. It revels in transformation and disguise (Baron Cohen now, of course, being so famous he has to layer on disguises on top of his original disguises – hence the new Rasta Ali G). The genre often compounds this ludic chaos by having its stars play multiple roles, as Sellers, Eddie Murphy and Mike Myers love to do.

Somehow this protean fun allows the presiding comic genius’s essential quality to pierce through all the more clearly: in Sellers’ case, a kind of unnerving mildness that could transmute into mania, or Myers’ cheeky puerility. Mrs Doubtfire, from 1993, is one of the most revelatory uses of this ventriloquist effect. Another persona that the film’s divorced voiceover artist adopts in order to see his children more often, the Scottish nanny is really a conduit for the sentimental streak that underpinned much of Robin Williams’s work. And like the theatre, you can see the tactile human continuity between character comedy’s practitioners: Myers has often talked about his admiration for Sellers’ chameleonic powers. Dr Evil’s “one million dollars” faux pas is a lift of a similar gag near the end of Sellers’ 1959 geopolitics satire The Mouse That Roared.

By 2002, when Myers was doing silhouette gags about giving birth to Mini-Me in Austin Powers: Goldmember, this vaudevillian style was looking passe. With The Lord of the Rings and Harry Potter in full pomp, blockbuster film was firmly in the CGI era; comedy had moved on, too, to the edgier Frat Pack films and the realism of Judd Apatow.

But perhaps character comedy had also lost strong moorings by this point, with social comment largely absent from the genre since the 1980s. Instead, Austin Powers was an extended riff on 60s and 90s pop-cultural overlaps and discrepancies (Jean Dujardin did something similar in his later OSS-117 series), while Eddie Murphy’s multi-character outings The Nutty Professor and Norbit seemed largely there to prop up the fat-suit industry. Only Will Ferrell – via his blowhard news anchor Burgundy, but also in his general screen persona in ensemble work such as Wedding Crashers, Step Brothers and Talladega Nights – embodied a type that spoke clearly for the times: the arrested manchild.

That all changed the moment Borat and his wobbling producer Azamat Bagatov landed in New York in 2006. By injecting Borat with a raw hit of the reality format incubated on The 11 O’Clock Show and Da Ali G Show, Baron Cohen completely revitalised big-screen character comedy. Suddenly, it became thrillingly politicised as his sublimely ignorant aliases, Borat and in 2009 Brüno, flushed out American and Middle Eastern absurdities and prejudices. Not to mention the high-wire aspect of his escapades: Baron Cohen was somehow impervious to whatever peril he stirred up, whether that was desecrating the Star-Spangled Banner at a rodeo in Borat, or an interpretation of mano-a-mano quite different to what cage fighting audiences were expecting in Brüno. His gleeful brazenness was the signature quality that shone through.

But Ali G has been dormant a long time. His last big-screen outing, 2002’s hit-and-miss Ali G Indahouse , was a very different, fully scripted endeavour. Beyond a gag about mistaking a pregnancy test for a vape, the trailer for Ali G: Who Iz I? doesn’t give much away about how sharply the character’s been updated; judging by the small-penis outro, some things are undying.

Staines’s favourite son will need to pull more out of his XXXXXL puffa. Only the current culture wars – police violence, colonialism, cultural appropriation – can supply him with appropriately charged material that he can “booyakasha” his way through. Anything less, and the character’s age will show, and the once-cutting posturing and patois will seem less than ironic. Which would be a bad thing for character comedy – then the mask really will have slipped.

content.article_text:
The winner of the People’s Choice Award in this year’s Female in Focus talks through her work and how we can navigate a world where the physical and digital are increasingly intertwined

We have all experienced it: that heart-sinking moment when you look around the dinner table and realise that every person is glued to their device. “You’re together, but not together. And you’re all friends, so you’re probably all consuming the same content,” says Dutch photographer Jip Schalkx. She describes this as a “hybrid social reality” – a blended state of existence where our physical and digital worlds are increasingly intertwined.

The contradiction of this new reality, of creating an illusion of togetherness while actually promoting isolation, is what inspired the 28-year-old artist’s award-winning image, 4ever &ver &ver. In it Schalkx depicts six girls lying together peacefully, headphones on. The scene resonates instantly, offering a gentle critique on the impact of technology on our social and emotional worlds.

The image is a poignant commentary on one of the most defining issues of our times, and for that it has been awarded the People’s Choice Award in this year’s Female in Focus prize, curated around the theme ‘On the Cusp’. The annual prize for women photographers is organised by British Journal of Photography and sponsored by Nikon. “The photograph powerfully reflects how young people navigate a world where visibility and the pressures of social media increasingly shape everyday intimacy,” says Ruby Nicholson, senior communications manager for Nikon Northern Europe. “It beautifully captures the delicate balance between connection and isolation, making it a resonant and highly relevant image for our times.”

Shalkx reveals that the image belongs to a video piece, in which the girls sleep to a looping soundscape stitched out of audio grabs from social media. It includes clips from protests for Palestine, beauty influencers advocating for “vampire sleep” on TikTok, and Kylie Jenner’s viral “realising stuff” statement. It mimics the “forever loop” of scrolling, and the muddled lines between our physical and digital realities.

This video is part of a wider body of work investigating “how algorithmic modification influences how young people communicate in this capitalistic world”. For Shalkx, the questions began to emerge during an internship in Barcelona, after which she returned to the Netherlands and felt a jarring sense of alienation. “There’s this work-driven force,” she says, comparing the social codes of her home country to a city like Barcelona, which is noticeably laidback. She considers the Netherlands among the most capitalistic in the world, and “when I got back, I noticed it a lot more. I felt alienated, and I didn’t understand why”.

“The algorithm sees me. It knows what I want, before I even know myself” – Jip Schalkx

About How You Sell Yourself. Shalkx argues that in a world of hyper-capitalism and constant self-optimisation, the boundaries between our real personalities and our branded selves have collapsed. It is true, because the algorithm dictates who is seen and valued, and that requires us to sell ourselves in a very specific way. In drawing heavily on Guy Debord’s ideas of capitalism and image-consumption in The Society of the Spectacle, Shalkx argues that this has redefined how young adults in the Netherlands live their lives – what they choose to wear, how they talk to one another, what they eat, and how they behave.

Writing on this subject was all well and good, but translating these thoughts into images was a whole other challenge. Shalkx’s process combines deep research and constant observation – looking at people, but also Tumblr, Pinterest, books and magazines. It was through this process that the image at the centre of 4ever &ver &ver first appeared:“I saw it so vividly in my head, of the girls lying next to each other.” Her instinct, as a photography student, was to shoot a still image, until a friend suggested she film it instead. Filming, it turned out, gave the piece something a photograph could not: “That kind of friction, where it’s almost still, like they’re in ‘sleep mode’.”

Two more video pieces followed. The second features a dance sequence, choreographed by Ūla Naujokaitytė, and based on TikTok-style movements. “It’s about how language changes, and how social media has changed how we behave with our bodies,” Schalkx says. The idea came after seeing a group of teenagers communicating using TikTok-coded gestures. She staged the dance in front of a typical Dutch house, but with an ominous factory smoking behind it, deliberately slowing the choreography to subvert TikTok’s usual sharp, snappy energy and create a movement that is far from appealing “in the algorithmic sense”.

The third video takes a more satirical turn, and stars her friend Victor. “I’m part of something bigger here,” he says, professing his love for social media in a one-take monologue shot at a bus stop. “The algorithm sees me. It knows what I want, before I even know myself.” Shalkx wrote the script using AI, she says, prompting it with themes from her long-running conversations with Victor about social media. Alongside the three videos sits Cloud9 , a series of mirror portraits printed on glass. This work investigates the tension between the digital and physical self: who are we, Schalkx asks, the version of ourselves we perform online, or the version that exists in real life?

All of this is in part informed by Shalkx’s own conflicted relationship with the internet. She grew up mostly without a smartphone, and remembers social media’s arrival. “I come from the Tumblr era,” she says. “I loved that you could aestheticise things, like what you’d do with a magazine. Cutting things out and putting them on a mood board.” But the internet soon outgrew its innocence. “Back then there were no ads. It was just people posting stuff. Then it became more and more commercialised,” she says. “Enterprise culture became the norm.” It is a shift the writer Cory Doctorow has termed “enshittification”: the slow decay of once-useful platforms as they are optimised for profit.

These days, Schalkx’s own presence online is more guarded. “I love my images, but right now I’m taking a step back,” she says. Yet the same questions continue to occupy her practice, and her next body of work takes it a step further in a deeper exploration of self-branding and commodification.

“A lot of people are doing projects about the internet, and a lot of it adopts a very specific aesthetic,” Schalkx says, referring to glitchy collages, work that uses AI, or 3D rendered elements. “I never really resonated with this way of talking about it. It feels scary.” Rather than depicting the darkness literally, Shalkx wants to speak about the subject in a more human, recognisable way. “Making people scared – I don’t think that’s the only way we can communicate about it.”

Shalkx is right, because we have experienced these conversations too; long discussions about the ills of the internet that end with a collective sigh of doom. Schalkx’s work asks many questions, and while there is never an easy answer, the proposition of recognition rather than fear is a strong one. And maybe that recognition is the first step to finding a way back to each other.

Female in Focus is at International Centre for the Image until 25 October 2026

Female in Focus: On the Cusp has been created in partnership with Nikon

Marigold Warner worked as an editor at BJP between 2018 and 2023. She studied English Literature and History of Art at the University of Leeds, followed by an MA in Magazine Journalism from City, University of London. Her work has been published by titles including the Telegraph Magazine, Huck, Elephant, Gal-dem, The Face, Disegno, and the Architects Journal.

content.article_text:
Dans Blindfolded , Antoine De Winter s’intéresse à la disparition des glaciers des Alpes suisses en mêlant abstractions colorées et images documentaires en noir et blanc.

Des draps s’étendent à perte de vue sur le glacier du Rhône, au cœur des Alpes suisses. « Il s’agit de tissu géotextile, une sorte de feutrine épaisse et lourde qui recouvre le glacier chaque été afin d’en ralentir la fonte » , explique Antoine De Winter. Pendant quatre ans, l’artiste visuel (et médecin) belge a photographié ce paysage marqué par les effets du réchauffement climatique. « C’est comme mettre un pansement sur une hémorragie, poursuit-il. C’est mettre un bout de tissu sur quelque chose qui est déjà condamné. » Au fil de ses expéditions, Antoine De Winter a observé les transformations du glacier de ses propres yeux : celui-ci a reculé d’une centaine de mètres et certaines entrées des grottes de glace ont tout simplement disparu. « Il y a quelque chose d’un peu absurde dans l’idée de recouvrir ce glacier » , constate-t-il.

Prendre soin

Cependant, face à cette apparente absurdité, son geste photographique et plastique relève d’un véritable acte de soin. Une démarche qui donne naissance à Blindfolded , un projet décliné sous la forme d’un livre publié aux éditions Grani en 2024. Pour Antoine De Winter, il ne s’agit pas de documenter la disparition du glacier, mais d’entrer en relation avec lui. « Il y avait quelque chose de puissant dans ce lieu » , confie-t-il. De retour avec une soixantaine d’images, jugées trop documentaires à son goût, le photographe cherche une manière de faire dialoguer le glacier du Rhône avec la réalité de l’Anthropocène [concept géologique qui désigne la période durant laquelle l’activité humaine est devenue la force dominante de modification de la Terre, ndlr]. Habitué des procédés d’impression alternatifs, il imagine alors un dispositif permettant à ce site de devenir le témoin direct de son propre déclin. « J’ai récolté à la surface du glacier des pigments de carbone qui, comme toutes les matières noires, absorbent davantage d’énergie et accélèrent donc la fonte des glaces » , explique-t-il. Ce sont ces mêmes particules qui servent ensuite à révéler les images de Blindfolded . « L’idée, c’était vraiment de trouver un point de résonance physique où le lieu, dans sa matérialité, pouvait s’exprimer, pouvait lui-même devenir témoin autant que victime de ce phénomène. C’était davantage une manière de prendre soin que de montrer ou démontrer. »

La suite de cet article est à retrouver dans Fisheye #78 .

content.title_original: Why Arturo Béjar left Meta – and blew the whistle: ‘I don’t recall Mark ever being empathetic’
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "T he Social Reckoning hits cinemas this Friday, but the real world has already been working on a sequel – or rather, a threequel. Directed by Aaron Sorkin, the movie is a follow-up to The Social Network, detailing the further misadventures of Mark Zuckerberg and his social media empire, and in particular Frances Haugen , the employee who in 2021 leaked internal documents that appeared to show Facebook was aware of the harms its products had inflicted.", "links": [{"text": "Frances Haugen", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2021/oct/24/frances-haugen-i-never-wanted-to-be-a-whistleblower-but-lives-were-in-danger"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It’s no spoiler to reveal the film climaxes with Haugen’s testimony to the US Senate, on 5 October 2021. That very same day, Arturo Béjar, a consultant on the wellbeing team of Instagram (which is also owned by Facebook), hit send on a long-gestating email to Zuckerberg and other senior Facebook executives on a similar theme. “I wanted to bring to your attention what I believe is a critical gap in how we as a company approach harm, and how the people we serve experience it,” Béjar began, before laying out some shocking statistics from his team’s survey. For example: 24.4% of 13-15-year-olds on Instagram said they had received unwanted advances, and 21.8% said they had been the target of bullying on the platform in the past seven days . Furthermore, 51% of Instagram users said they had had a bad or harmful experience in the past seven days. Only 1% of them reported it, and of those, 2% had the content taken down – so just 0.02%. This was a far greater degree of harm than the company’s existing measurements suggested. Zuckerberg never replied.", "links": [{"text": "email to Zuckerberg", "url": "https://www.theripcurrent.com/p/memo-to-zuckerberg-what-if-policy"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "By that time, Béjar had worked at Facebook (which rebranded as Meta later that month) for a total of eight years. He had learned how to communicate with Zuckerberg. “You couldn’t talk to Mark about, ‘We have to do this thing to prevent suicide because it’s the right thing to do,’” he says. “You had to put everything in terms of metrics. That was his language. That’s how he related to things, which is also what’s behind all the grief in the world right now.”", "links": [{"text": "Facebook", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/technology/facebook"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5f77be0b14a2f3a0c3b168ce5bdcf5ed989dcc51/583_114_1699_1360/master/1699.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.", "caption": "Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning. Photograph: Everett Collection/Alamy", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Béjar has seen The Social Reckoning, and he recognises Jeremy Strong’s portrayal of Zuckerberg as a detached, awkward, humourless control freak all too well. “Oh, it’s accurate,” he says. “I don’t recall him ever being empathetic to the harm that somebody was experiencing and wanting to make that better … The only thing that really consistently came across in all my interactions with him was winning. He’s one of the most fiercely competitive people I know.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One time, Béjar recalls, he and Zuckerberg were walking together after a fraught meeting. “One of the things that I used to say when bad things were happening is, ‘Are we having fun yet?’ Just as a little kind of defusing humour thing,” says Béjar. “And he looked at me, very intense, and said, ‘I’m not here for fun – I’m here for impact.’ That was my experience of him, over and over and over again.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That 2021 email was the beginning of the end for Béjar. He was still hoping Zuckerberg would respond to his appeal to engineer a “culture shift” in the way Instagram dealt with protecting its young users. The next day, however, Zuckerberg issued a statement to Facebook employees about Haugen’s testimony and the leaked “ Facebook Files ” that were being reported by the Wall Street Journal and others. “At the heart of these accusations is this idea that we prioritise profit over safety and wellbeing. That’s just not true,” Zuckerberg wrote. But by then Béjar knew it was true.", "links": [{"text": "issued a statement", "url": "https://www.facebook.com/zuck/posts/10113961365418581"}, {"text": "Facebook Files", "url": "https://www.wsj.com/articles/the-facebook-files-11631713039?mod=article_inline"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "By 2023, Béjar was following in Haugen’s footsteps and testifying to the US senate himself. He has testified under oath against Meta at least seven times since, by his reckoning, in various trials and hearings. The most recent, and consequential, was the landmark trial in California in August, brought by the attorneys general of 29 US states, which alleged once again that Meta knowingly designed products that were addictive and harmful to minors. In his testimony , Béjar stated: “You just cannot trust Mark Zuckerberg with kids.”", "links": [{"text": "testifying to the US senate", "url": "https://www.c-span.org/program/public-affairs-event/former-meta-executive-testifies-on-social-media-and-youth-mental-health/634674"}, {"text": "landmark trial", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/aug/22/meta-trial-children-privacy"}, {"text": "his testimony", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/aug/19/meta-safety-trial-whistleblower-testimony"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d7292a23edb2e45f263edb6b3be6003b1b804a5a/969_291_3819_3055/master/3819.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "portrait of Haugen speaking at an event", "caption": "Frances Haugen, the former Facebook employee who testified against the company in court. Photograph: Mike Bowers/The Guardian", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In many respects Béjar is the perfect witness: sincere, calmly spoken, emotionally literate, able to express complex ideas in accessible ways, and possessing reams of inside knowledge. He’s seemingly the opposite of Zuckerberg. At times during our conversation, as we sit outside a cafe in north London, he has to pause mid-sentence, his eyes welling with tears. He apologises afterwards for getting emotional, but that seems to be exactly what these issues demand."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There’s another reason Béjar has been such a powerful spokesperson: he has a direct connection to the issues, via his teenage daughter. When she was in her early teens, in about 2018, she told him she regularly received sexist comments and unsolicited nude photos from men via her Instagram account. Her female friends experienced the same thing. There was no point reporting it, she told him, because it never resulted in any meaningful action. Commenters might get blocked – after which they would simply open a new account under a different name – or Instagram would judge that the behaviour didn’t violate their policies.", "links": [{"text": "Instagram", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/technology/instagram"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Until that point, like many early Facebook employees, Béjar believed he was making the world a better place. When he started in 2009, the company was booming and the idealism was infectious. “The promise was, we’ll create something that keeps you close to your friends. I think a lot of people back then believed in that. And that’s not what they built.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9181aa3fa52f5a7d797d82f35865205ed6555721/804_0_5741_4593/master/5741.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Arturo Bejar gestures, on a bench in a London square", "caption": "Powerful spokesperson … Béjar. Photograph: Ethan Parker/The Guardian", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Béjar, 55, was an early tech enthusiast. Born in Mexico City, the son of a doctor father and an artist mother, he taught himself to code and blagged his way into a job with IBM when he was 15. He came to Silicon Valley, after a spell in London, in 1993, and worked at Yahoo for 11 years before he joined Facebook."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As senior engineering and product leader at Facebook, Béjar was responsible for security but also for customer care: “developing tools that help people learn to be with each other online” – especially young people. For example, he developed a more nuanced way for young people to report content they didn’t like. If the button on Facebook said “report”, teens tended not to use it, but if it was changed to “I don’t want to see this”, three times as many teens would click on it. And if you could grade the intensity of that feeling, from “mildly annoying” to “really bad”, that made it easier to deal with problems."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Most people who behave aggressively online, if you give them private, respectful feedback, they’re like, ‘Oh sorry, I didn’t mean to,’” Béjar says. “And that’s how we work as a society, right?” He gestures to the pedestrian street around us; people are peacefully going about their business. “What makes this street nice is not that there’s police everywhere enforcing our behaviour, it’s that we have all these ways where we signal to each other what it’s like to be safe, even though you might have fundamentally different values.” He built more than a dozen Facebook products on that premise, he says, with extraordinary results. “Basically, half the people change behaviour the first time you go, like, ‘Yeah, we don’t do that here.’”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "He left the company, amicably, in 2015 because he was going through a divorce and wanted to spend more time with his young son and daughter. By the time he found out about his daughter’s Instagram experience, other young victims of social media were becoming known. In 2017, 14-year-old Molly Russell died from an act of self-harm in her London bedroom. The coroner’s report said her depression was exacerbated by her social media consumption, especially Instagram. Wider issues with Facebook were also beginning to emerge: its role in election manipulation, stoking ethnic violence, promoting inflammatory posts.", "links": [{"text": "14-year-old Molly Russell", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2022/sep/30/how-molly-russell-fell-into-a-vortex-of-despair-on-social-media"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/3357427cba7bfa97c45d6721db58d005f99784a5/167_0_1667_1334/master/1667.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "film still – A man jabs his fingers aggressively towards Mark Zuckerberg (played by Jeremy Strong)", "caption": "Under fire … The Social Reckoning’s vision of Meta. Photograph: Sony", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "After raising his concerns with the company, Béjar was invited to return in 2019, on a two-year contract as a consultant on Instagram’s “wellbeing” team. “I still believed that the reason the stuff that was happening to my daughter and all her friends, and every other kid I’ve talked to since, was because as companies get big, sometimes the general doesn’t know what the soldiers are doing. That was my thesis for almost all the time I was there: Mark doesn’t know … and if he knew, he would fix it.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Evidence to the contrary started piling up, though. “What I started finding when I came back is that they did know. They knew about addiction, they knew how bad it was. They knew about Molly Russell.” It later emerged that Facebook had internal research confirming Instagram’s negative effects on teenage mental health, but had kept it secret . The wellbeing team could not get anything done, Béjar says. “They could dream up a good product that would make things better, and they couldn’t get it out the door. You would put it through the review process and all the teams that would review it would just kill parts of it until there was nothing left.”", "links": [{"text": "kept it secret", "url": "https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/technology-58570353"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The ethos had changed, he says. For all the talk about connecting the world and bringing people together, the priority was simply growth, it seemed: attracting more users and keeping them on the platform for as long as possible. Video content was now set to autoplay; notifications were frequent, as were suggestions of other people to follow; “infinite scroll” algorithmically served up content tailored to users’ continuously tracked habits. All the customer care tools Béjar had previously developed – such as the “I don’t want to see this” button – had gone."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Béjar’s team developed a tool aimed at people with a history of posting comments that got reported and deleted – “the worst of the worst” – so that when they posted something inflammatory, they would get a community note telling them: “You might want to phrase this differently.” “We were in the process of getting that approved. And one of the people in the review meeting said, ‘What if 50 Cent gets this thing and makes fun of it? We can’t have that.’ That was the driver.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The anecdote chimes with Facebook’s secretive “cross-check” system , revealed in the Facebook Files, where posts by celebrities, politicians and other high-profile “business partners” were moderated more leniently, even if they violated the company’s stated policies.", "links": [{"text": "Facebook’s secretive “cross-check” system", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2022/dec/06/meta-protecting-business-partners"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Had he known what he knows now, Béjar would never have allowed his daughter on Instagram in the first place, he says. “Instagram is built on three pillars: addictive design, connecting you to strangers, and rewarding you for doing things that are exhibitionistic, performative or aggressive,” he says. None of these are safe or desirable for young people, most people would agree. He compares social media to the tobacco industry: “This is the equivalent of handing your kids a cigarette and being like, ‘Hey, you’ll be cooler if you smoke.’” On unwanted sexual advances, he says, “What Instagram is effectively doing is, while your kid is in the bedroom, it’s lining up strangers outside the window and inviting them in.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/96e9092fb60c60cefd23611454c5459924755a6b/1071_1387_3552_2842/master/3552.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Zuckerberg on stage wearing the glasses and a shirt that reads “building is my love language”", "caption": "Mark Zuckerberg showcasing Meta’s VR glasses last month. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Béjar believes that the tone is squarely set by Zuckerberg, as the longtime CEO, chair and controlling shareholder of Meta: “If Mark woke up tomorrow and was like, ‘I want to create something that’s genuinely good for kids,’ it would take the company six months to fundamentally shift all these things and drive all these harms down. They have the technology, they have the people, they have the expertise, they have the infrastructure. It’s his refusal to do that which creates a culture.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ultimately, Béjar faced the same dilemma Haugen did. Speaking out meant ending his career, as well as being ostracised from his colleagues and his community. But, he says, “You have to ask yourself: who am I protecting? Am I protecting the company or my way of life or my being? Or am I protecting other people? It took me years, to really walk away from the identity that I had developed when I was working there.” He was emboldened by Haugen’s courageous example and by the treatment she received afterwards: “Internally, they would call her ‘the leaker’. They wouldn’t say her name.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When approached for comment, a Meta spokesperson said: “We all share a common goal of providing safe, meaningful online experiences for young people. Our record shows that we’ve spent the past decade researching and developing numerous tools and resources to support teens and empower parents, including Teen Accounts, which place teens in protective settings by default. We’ll continue to make improvements and partner with parents and experts to keep teens safe.” Meta has repeatedly rejected implications that engagement stands in contrast to its commitment to teen safety."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Despite its best efforts to contrive a triumphant finale, The Social Reckoning ends on a bit of a sour note. There was no real reckoning for Meta. Donald Trump was re-elected; social media companies forgot about their commitment to fact-checking, Meta included. And Zuckerberg’s company continues to grow and profit from the digital economy – including the AI economy. Last month, still reeling from the reaction to Meta’s camera-enabled “ pervert glasses ”, Zuckerberg unveiled Muse, Meta’s cute and cuddly AI agent , which can perform personalised tasks such as shopping or sending emails. Even Haugen herself recently admitted : “We are worse off today than when I leaked the Facebook documents.”", "links": [{"text": "pervert glasses", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/aug/09/i-kept-catching-people-giving-me-dirty-looks-the-backlash-against-meta-smart-glasses"}, {"text": "Muse, Meta’s cute and cuddly AI agent", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/fashion/2026/sep/26/charming-and-disarming-how-metas-technology-packed-muse-harnesses-the-power-of-cuteness"}, {"text": "recently admitted", "url": "https://english.elpais.com/science-tech/2026-06-07/frances-haugen-we-are-worse-off-today-than-when-i-leaked-the-facebook-documents.html?outputType=amp"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Had they waited until this month, the film-makers might have been able to craft a happier ending. The landmark trial brought by multiple US states in August ended two days after Béjar’s testimony. Meta abandoned their challenge and settled the case (denying any wrongdoing). The company will have to pay out up to $18bn (£13.6bn); it’s a relatively small sum, considering that Meta’s revenue in 2025 was more than $200bn (£151.5bn). More significantly, for the first time, the company agreed to major changes to protect teens: two-hour daily time limits for under-18s across Instagram and Facebook; blocking notifications during school hours; blocking the apps at night; turning off autoplay; giving parents greater control; and other safety features.", "links": [{"text": "settled the case", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/aug/26/meta-social-media-addiction-trial-settlement"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6dd6b5a9144da9513ac95ca8ab44a4d57c40288d/91_0_2909_2000/master/2909.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Bejar outside the White House, with some people holding signs reading ‘protect kids online’ ", "caption": "Béjar speaking at a rally aiming to hold tech and social media companies accountable for taking steps to protect young people online. Photograph: Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Accountable Tech", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I think it’s an extraordinary accomplishment,” says Béjar. “Nobody else in the world has got them to agree that they will reduce the hours kids spend on the platform. Or that they’re going to be more transparent about how they assess age, or that it will reduce home notifications.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These measures won’t fix everything, but they’re progress. Meta lost another trial, brought by the US state of New Mexico in March, again over misleading the public about safety, and had to pay $942m (£713.7m) in fines and damages. There are dozens more cases in the pipeline. Governmental regulation is tightening around the world. Perhaps the tide is turning."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "If it is, it will be some relief to Béjar. He has spent much of the past three years campaigning, testifying, talking to governments, academics, regulators. He has other interests beyond the tech world. Even as he was quitting Meta, he was writing the libretto for a musical collaboration with the composer Philip Glass. content.article_text:
T he Social Reckoning hits cinemas this Friday, but the real world has already been working on a sequel – or rather, a threequel. Directed by Aaron Sorkin, the movie is a follow-up to The Social Network, detailing the further misadventures of Mark Zuckerberg and his social media empire, and in particular Frances Haugen , the employee who in 2021 leaked internal documents that appeared to show Facebook was aware of the harms its products had inflicted.

It’s no spoiler to reveal the film climaxes with Haugen’s testimony to the US Senate, on 5 October 2021. That very same day, Arturo Béjar, a consultant on the wellbeing team of Instagram (which is also owned by Facebook), hit send on a long-gestating email to Zuckerberg and other senior Facebook executives on a similar theme. “I wanted to bring to your attention what I believe is a critical gap in how we as a company approach harm, and how the people we serve experience it,” Béjar began, before laying out some shocking statistics from his team’s survey. For example: 24.4% of 13-15-year-olds on Instagram said they had received unwanted advances, and 21.8% said they had been the target of bullying on the platform in the past seven days . Furthermore, 51% of Instagram users said they had had a bad or harmful experience in the past seven days. Only 1% of them reported it, and of those, 2% had the content taken down – so just 0.02%. This was a far greater degree of harm than the company’s existing measurements suggested. Zuckerberg never replied.

By that time, Béjar had worked at Facebook (which rebranded as Meta later that month) for a total of eight years. He had learned how to communicate with Zuckerberg. “You couldn’t talk to Mark about, ‘We have to do this thing to prevent suicide because it’s the right thing to do,’” he says. “You had to put everything in terms of metrics. That was his language. That’s how he related to things, which is also what’s behind all the grief in the world right now.”

Béjar has seen The Social Reckoning, and he recognises Jeremy Strong’s portrayal of Zuckerberg as a detached, awkward, humourless control freak all too well. “Oh, it’s accurate,” he says. “I don’t recall him ever being empathetic to the harm that somebody was experiencing and wanting to make that better … The only thing that really consistently came across in all my interactions with him was winning. He’s one of the most fiercely competitive people I know.”

One time, Béjar recalls, he and Zuckerberg were walking together after a fraught meeting. “One of the things that I used to say when bad things were happening is, ‘Are we having fun yet?’ Just as a little kind of defusing humour thing,” says Béjar. “And he looked at me, very intense, and said, ‘I’m not here for fun – I’m here for impact.’ That was my experience of him, over and over and over again.”

That 2021 email was the beginning of the end for Béjar. He was still hoping Zuckerberg would respond to his appeal to engineer a “culture shift” in the way Instagram dealt with protecting its young users. The next day, however, Zuckerberg issued a statement to Facebook employees about Haugen’s testimony and the leaked “ Facebook Files ” that were being reported by the Wall Street Journal and others. “At the heart of these accusations is this idea that we prioritise profit over safety and wellbeing. That’s just not true,” Zuckerberg wrote. But by then Béjar knew it was true.

By 2023, Béjar was following in Haugen’s footsteps and testifying to the US senate himself. He has testified under oath against Meta at least seven times since, by his reckoning, in various trials and hearings. The most recent, and consequential, was the landmark trial in California in August, brought by the attorneys general of 29 US states, which alleged once again that Meta knowingly designed products that were addictive and harmful to minors. In his testimony , Béjar stated: “You just cannot trust Mark Zuckerberg with kids.”

In many respects Béjar is the perfect witness: sincere, calmly spoken, emotionally literate, able to express complex ideas in accessible ways, and possessing reams of inside knowledge. He’s seemingly the opposite of Zuckerberg. At times during our conversation, as we sit outside a cafe in north London, he has to pause mid-sentence, his eyes welling with tears. He apologises afterwards for getting emotional, but that seems to be exactly what these issues demand.

There’s another reason Béjar has been such a powerful spokesperson: he has a direct connection to the issues, via his teenage daughter. When she was in her early teens, in about 2018, she told him she regularly received sexist comments and unsolicited nude photos from men via her Instagram account. Her female friends experienced the same thing. There was no point reporting it, she told him, because it never resulted in any meaningful action. Commenters might get blocked – after which they would simply open a new account under a different name – or Instagram would judge that the behaviour didn’t violate their policies.

Until that point, like many early Facebook employees, Béjar believed he was making the world a better place. When he started in 2009, the company was booming and the idealism was infectious. “The promise was, we’ll create something that keeps you close to your friends. I think a lot of people back then believed in that. And that’s not what they built.”

Béjar, 55, was an early tech enthusiast. Born in Mexico City, the son of a doctor father and an artist mother, he taught himself to code and blagged his way into a job with IBM when he was 15. He came to Silicon Valley, after a spell in London, in 1993, and worked at Yahoo for 11 years before he joined Facebook.

As senior engineering and product leader at Facebook, Béjar was responsible for security but also for customer care: “developing tools that help people learn to be with each other online” – especially young people. For example, he developed a more nuanced way for young people to report content they didn’t like. If the button on Facebook said “report”, teens tended not to use it, but if it was changed to “I don’t want to see this”, three times as many teens would click on it. And if you could grade the intensity of that feeling, from “mildly annoying” to “really bad”, that made it easier to deal with problems.

“Most people who behave aggressively online, if you give them private, respectful feedback, they’re like, ‘Oh sorry, I didn’t mean to,’” Béjar says. “And that’s how we work as a society, right?” He gestures to the pedestrian street around us; people are peacefully going about their business. “What makes this street nice is not that there’s police everywhere enforcing our behaviour, it’s that we have all these ways where we signal to each other what it’s like to be safe, even though you might have fundamentally different values.” He built more than a dozen Facebook products on that premise, he says, with extraordinary results. “Basically, half the people change behaviour the first time you go, like, ‘Yeah, we don’t do that here.’”

He left the company, amicably, in 2015 because he was going through a divorce and wanted to spend more time with his young son and daughter. By the time he found out about his daughter’s Instagram experience, other young victims of social media were becoming known. In 2017, 14-year-old Molly Russell died from an act of self-harm in her London bedroom. The coroner’s report said her depression was exacerbated by her social media consumption, especially Instagram. Wider issues with Facebook were also beginning to emerge: its role in election manipulation, stoking ethnic violence, promoting inflammatory posts.

After raising his concerns with the company, Béjar was invited to return in 2019, on a two-year contract as a consultant on Instagram’s “wellbeing” team. “I still believed that the reason the stuff that was happening to my daughter and all her friends, and every other kid I’ve talked to since, was because as companies get big, sometimes the general doesn’t know what the soldiers are doing. That was my thesis for almost all the time I was there: Mark doesn’t know … and if he knew, he would fix it.”

Evidence to the contrary started piling up, though. “What I started finding when I came back is that they did know. They knew about addiction, they knew how bad it was. They knew about Molly Russell.” It later emerged that Facebook had internal research confirming Instagram’s negative effects on teenage mental health, but had kept it secret . The wellbeing team could not get anything done, Béjar says. “They could dream up a good product that would make things better, and they couldn’t get it out the door. You would put it through the review process and all the teams that would review it would just kill parts of it until there was nothing left.”

The ethos had changed, he says. For all the talk about connecting the world and bringing people together, the priority was simply growth, it seemed: attracting more users and keeping them on the platform for as long as possible. Video content was now set to autoplay; notifications were frequent, as were suggestions of other people to follow; “infinite scroll” algorithmically served up content tailored to users’ continuously tracked habits. All the customer care tools Béjar had previously developed – such as the “I don’t want to see this” button – had gone.

Béjar’s team developed a tool aimed at people with a history of posting comments that got reported and deleted – “the worst of the worst” – so that when they posted something inflammatory, they would get a community note telling them: “You might want to phrase this differently.” “We were in the process of getting that approved. And one of the people in the review meeting said, ‘What if 50 Cent gets this thing and makes fun of it? We can’t have that.’ That was the driver.”

The anecdote chimes with Facebook’s secretive “cross-check” system , revealed in the Facebook Files, where posts by celebrities, politicians and other high-profile “business partners” were moderated more leniently, even if they violated the company’s stated policies.

Had he known what he knows now, Béjar would never have allowed his daughter on Instagram in the first place, he says. “Instagram is built on three pillars: addictive design, connecting you to strangers, and rewarding you for doing things that are exhibitionistic, performative or aggressive,” he says. None of these are safe or desirable for young people, most people would agree. He compares social media to the tobacco industry: “This is the equivalent of handing your kids a cigarette and being like, ‘Hey, you’ll be cooler if you smoke.’” On unwanted sexual advances, he says, “What Instagram is effectively doing is, while your kid is in the bedroom, it’s lining up strangers outside the window and inviting them in.”

Béjar believes that the tone is squarely set by Zuckerberg, as the longtime CEO, chair and controlling shareholder of Meta: “If Mark woke up tomorrow and was like, ‘I want to create something that’s genuinely good for kids,’ it would take the company six months to fundamentally shift all these things and drive all these harms down. They have the technology, they have the people, they have the expertise, they have the infrastructure. It’s his refusal to do that which creates a culture.”

Ultimately, Béjar faced the same dilemma Haugen did. Speaking out meant ending his career, as well as being ostracised from his colleagues and his community. But, he says, “You have to ask yourself: who am I protecting? Am I protecting the company or my way of life or my being? Or am I protecting other people? It took me years, to really walk away from the identity that I had developed when I was working there.” He was emboldened by Haugen’s courageous example and by the treatment she received afterwards: “Internally, they would call her ‘the leaker’. They wouldn’t say her name.”

When approached for comment, a Meta spokesperson said: “We all share a common goal of providing safe, meaningful online experiences for young people. Our record shows that we’ve spent the past decade researching and developing numerous tools and resources to support teens and empower parents, including Teen Accounts, which place teens in protective settings by default. We’ll continue to make improvements and partner with parents and experts to keep teens safe.” Meta has repeatedly rejected implications that engagement stands in contrast to its commitment to teen safety.

Despite its best efforts to contrive a triumphant finale, The Social Reckoning ends on a bit of a sour note. There was no real reckoning for Meta. Donald Trump was re-elected; social media companies forgot about their commitment to fact-checking, Meta included. And Zuckerberg’s company continues to grow and profit from the digital economy – including the AI economy. Last month, still reeling from the reaction to Meta’s camera-enabled “ pervert glasses ”, Zuckerberg unveiled Muse, Meta’s cute and cuddly AI agent , which can perform personalised tasks such as shopping or sending emails. Even Haugen herself recently admitted : “We are worse off today than when I leaked the Facebook documents.”

Had they waited until this month, the film-makers might have been able to craft a happier ending. The landmark trial brought by multiple US states in August ended two days after Béjar’s testimony. Meta abandoned their challenge and settled the case (denying any wrongdoing). The company will have to pay out up to $18bn (£13.6bn); it’s a relatively small sum, considering that Meta’s revenue in 2025 was more than $200bn (£151.5bn). More significantly, for the first time, the company agreed to major changes to protect teens: two-hour daily time limits for under-18s across Instagram and Facebook; blocking notifications during school hours; blocking the apps at night; turning off autoplay; giving parents greater control; and other safety features.

“I think it’s an extraordinary accomplishment,” says Béjar. “Nobody else in the world has got them to agree that they will reduce the hours kids spend on the platform. Or that they’re going to be more transparent about how they assess age, or that it will reduce home notifications.”

These measures won’t fix everything, but they’re progress. Meta lost another trial, brought by the US state of New Mexico in March, again over misleading the public about safety, and had to pay $942m (£713.7m) in fines and damages. There are dozens more cases in the pipeline. Governmental regulation is tightening around the world. Perhaps the tide is turning.

If it is, it will be some relief to Béjar. He has spent much of the past three years campaigning, testifying, talking to governments, academics, regulators. He has other interests beyond the tech world. Even as he was quitting Meta, he was writing the libretto for a musical collaboration with the composer Philip Glass. He is writing an opera based on Charles Darwin’s theory of emotion in animals, with the British composer Jocelyn Pook. His daughter, by the way, now earns her living restoring classic sports cars.

There’s still work to be done. What’s really needed, Béjar argues, is independent assessment and comparison of the safety of social media sites – the same way we monitor, say, vehicle emissions. “ Every parent and every kid deserves to know: what is the likelihood that this bad thing is going to happen to you on any of these services? ” But at last it feels like things are headed in that direction, he says. “It’s still just the beginning, but I do feel hope.”

‘The weirdos were taking over!’ Tate Britain relives the 1990s – in pictures

A new exhibition curated by Edward Enniful looks back on the thrilling decade before smartphones, when art, music and fashion came together with a bang

Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.00 BST

Domenique, London, 29 September, 1998 by Juergen Teller

The 90s: Art and Fashion exhibition runs at Tate Britain, London, from 8 October 2026 to 14 February 2027 . Texts by Edward Enninful and Alex Farquharson

Pendragon at The Fridge, 1999, by David Swindells

Chopper Mark II, 2001, by Koto Bolofo

Northampton, 1997, by Elaine Constantine

Metalheadz, 1995-1996, by Eddie Otchere

Naomi Campbell, 1994, by Ellen von Unwerth

Susanne and Lutz, White Dress, Army Skirt, 1993, by Wolfgang Tillmans

Rosemary Ferguson, 1993, by Corinne Day

Vauxhall Bridge, from the series Pissing Women, 1995, by Sophy Rickett

Young Pink Kate, London, 1998, by Juergen Teller

Untitled, Afro Hair and Beauty Show, 1998, by Eileen Perrier

Alek Wek, 1996, by Mark Mattock

"text": ACCは、ニューヨークに本部を置く非営利団体で、1963年以来、ビジュアルアートとパフォーミング・アーツを中心に、アーティストや芸術分野の研究者などへの助成を通じて文化交流を継続して支援してきた。作品制作や展覧会・公演など、制作を直接の目的とする活動を支援するのではなく、現地での交流や実体験を通じて、新たな文化に深く関わり、視野や創造的な実践を発展させるとともに、国境を越えたネットワークを築くことで、国際的な対話、理解、尊重を促進することを目的としている。 写真家・七菜乃の個展「unlearn」が、2026年10月20日から11月1日まで東京・銀座のArt Gallery M84で開催される。森や室内を舞台に撮影した最新の集団ヌード作品約20点を通して、身体や裸に無意識のうちに結びつけられてきた意味や固定観念を問い直す。

長年にわたりヌードを撮影し、自らも被写体となってきた七菜乃。人間の裸は誰もが持つ自然な姿である一方、社会のなかでは現在も性的なものとして強く意味づけられていると考え、その見方が本当に「当たり前」なのかを写真によって問い続けてきた。近年、海外で撮影を重ねるなかで関心は裸だけにとどまらず、人や風景、物を問わず、光のなかで心を動かされたものへと広がっているという。

「unlearn」は、そんな七菜乃がしばらく離れていた集団ヌードに再び取り組んだシリーズだ。森を歩き、部屋に立ち、重なり、そして離れていく複数の身体。そこに作家が見いだしたのは、裸であることをことさらに強調するのではなく、「ただ人が共に在る」状態だった。展覧会タイトルの「unlearn＝学びほぐす」という言葉が示唆するように、裸を見ることを入り口として、見る側が自身のなかにある「当たり前」を捉え直すことを促す。

公開された作品では、柔らかくにじむような光のなか、森に集う身体や建築の内部と外部に点在する人々などが捉えられている。裸体そのものを強調するというより、身体が風景や光の一部へ溶け込んでいくようなイメージが印象的だ。

七菜乃は、身体と光の関係を通して、人の存在と共生の美を探ってきた写真家。国内外で作品を発表し、『LONG VACATION』『裸体というドレス』『My Aesthetic Feeling』などの写真集を刊行している。

Art Gallery M84（東京都中央区銀座4-11-3 ウインド銀座ビル5階）

content.article_text:
株式会社リクルートホールディングスが運営するBUGでは、2026年10月14日（水）より、藤岡亜弥個展「Forget Me Not」を開催します。1996年に自らの日常を写した「なみだ壺」で BUGの前身であるガーディアン・ガーデン主催の「写真[人間の街]プロジェクト」に参加。2005年に移民としてブラジルに渡った祖母にまつわる「離愁」で「第24回写真『ひとつぼ展』」に入選、2017年には個展「アヤ子、形而上学的研究」を開催するなどリクルートがデビュー当時からキャリアを応援してきたアーティストです。

本展は国内外で活躍する藤岡がBUGとのコミッションで新シリーズを展開。藤岡は9年前にオーストラリア・メルボルン在住の女性から、ある日本人女性の存在をめぐる一通のDM（ダイレクトメッセージ）を受け取ります。地元である広島・呉から遠く離れたオーストラリア、その二つの都市の戦後から現在までをつらぬく、まさしく「事実は小説よりも奇妙なり」というべき、めくればめくるほど謎が増してゆく制作がスタートしました。

サンパウロで祖母の軌跡を追う「離愁」、ヨーロッパを旅した「さよならを教えて」、5年過ごしたニューヨーク生活で生まれた「Life Studies」などこれまでのシリーズと違わず、今回も導かれるように世界を旅し、ファインダーから物語を編み出す藤岡の新機軸を打ち出す展覧会です。

新シリーズ、撮り下ろし、映像作品への初挑戦

本展の軸となるのは藤岡が初めて挑戦した映像作品を含んだ撮り下ろしによる新シリーズ《Forget Me Not》。 3年の構想・制作期間の本作で取り扱うのは、実際に自身の身に起きた未解決のできごとです。当事者として、自身もどのようになるか分からないできごとの現実が刻一刻と自分の選択とシャッターによって切り拓かれていくさまは、ドキュメンタリーでもルポルタージュでもなく、「①作者は作品の中に登場すべきではない／②選択によって作者の見解を示す／③創作的処理を必要とする」*というノンフィクション・ノヴェルの特色と重なります。 写真という決定的な事実に即したものを提示しながら、感情をかき立てるストーリーとしても提示するというアンビバレントな方法にて展覧会はつくられます。

呉とメルボルン、そしてサンパウロを結ぶ女たちの人生

藤岡の出身地である広島県は海外への移民送出の数が全国1位でした。藤岡の祖母も移民2世としてブラジルで生まれ、親が買った宝くじが偶然当たり、20歳のときに家族で再び日本に、広島・呉に戻ることになりました。その祖母、フジオカキミエと一文字違いのフジオカキミコを探すオーストラリア・メルボルン在住のとある女性から届いたメッセージから、祖母ではないその一文字違いの女性は誰か、 という謎解きをするために藤岡は呉とメルボルンに向かいます。 実在するかどうかも分からないキミコを探す旅は、さまざまな人々を巻き込み、彼女ら／彼らの勝手な憶測が飛び交い、笑いあり、涙ありの人間が持つおかしみに触れるものでした。 藤岡は呉とメルボルンをめぐる戦後の歴史とその中を生きた女性の人生、さらには、かつて軍港として、そして戦後は臨海工業地帯として発展を遂げながらも、衰退してゆく地方都市である呉の現在に目を向けます。 そのような偶然と必然に翻弄されながらも逞しく生きた女性たちが辿った人生と彼女らが暮らした街を藤岡の視線から捉えることが本展の大きなテーマです。

写真とはとりかえしのつかないもの

これまでスナップを自身の作品の撮影技法とすることが多かった藤岡亜弥は、小型カメラにて自分が見たものを瞬間的に捉えることで、自分が見ていなかったものまで捉えてしまう不可逆性のことを「とりかえしのつかないもの」だと述べてきました。 本展の制作において、藤岡はある家庭で保管されていた写真たちに出会い、いわばファウンドフォトと言えるそれらを通じた作品制作に取り組みます。ファウンドフォトもスナップと同様に被写体の匿名性が共通しているのにもかかわらず、それが誰かというミステリがスナップよりも色濃く宙空に吊るされます。 誰かも分からない遥か過去の写真を通じて、赤の他人が出会い、交流を重ねてゆき、謎を解決しようとすればするほど、それはヒントにならず謎そのものになってゆく。撮影するばかりであった写真が解き明かすものへと変わるとき、「とりかえしのつかない」写真の意味もまた大きく変化してゆきます。

*トルーマン・カポーティ、龍口直太郎訳『冷血』「解説」p.557（新潮社、1978年）

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Durante más de cinco décadas, Narcisa Hirsch (Berlín, 1928 – Bariloche, 2024) hizo películas, happenings, poemas y grafitis que circularon por espacios alternativos, encuentros informales y salas de cine experimental. Su trabajo eludió las categorías convencionales y siempre se movió en un intermezzo : entre el cine y las artes visuales, entre la acción pública y la exploración íntima. Ese lugar difícil de clasificar contribuyó también a mantener su obra durante largo tiempo en los márgenes de las narrativas dominantes del arte y del cine."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ella misma encontró una forma irónica de nombrar esa posición: una famosa cineasta desconocida . La expresión encierra una paradoja que hoy resuena distinto.
