That same year, Evans and his friend Leslie George Katz, publisher of Eakins Press, collaborated on an extensive interview. At this retrospective moment of his life, Evans wanted to record his thoughts on photography, his work, and the influences on him. He wanted to codify his legacy. In addition to the interview, Evans selected and commented on eight photographs that spanned the arc of his life’s work. While the interview and the photographs appeared at the time in Art in America , the project didn’t see book form until 1995, when Eakins Press published Walker Evans: Incognito . Charles Baudelaire, one of Evans’s greatest influences, wrote, “The observer is a prince enjoying his incognito wherever he goes.” This suggests that the observer, like a prince traveling in disguise, has a privileged position: They can move through the world anonymously, seeing everything while remaining unseen themselves."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The picture of a gutter was the most recent and least-known photograph in Evans’s selection. It is from 40 Studies of Street Debris, Manhole Covers, and Trash Bins, New York City (ca. 1968). Here is Evans’s accompanying text:"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While removed from nature, this picture of a gutter is in a sense very human. It is Baudelairean. I wish Baudelaire was alive to see it. The secret of photography is, the camera takes on the character and the personality of the handler. The mind works on the machine."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When Evans wrote “Baudelairean,” he was referring to this paragraph, describing a chiffonnier , a ragpicker, from Baudelaire’s essay “On Wine and Hashish”:"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Here is a man whose task it is to pick up all the rubbish produced on one day in the capital. All that the great city has thrown out, all that it has lost, all that it has disdained, all that it has broken, he catalogues and collects. He consults the archives of debauchery, works through the lumber-room of rubbish. He sorts things out and makes a selection, chooses astutely; like a miser, he collects the muck which, once more digested by the Gods of Commerce, will become objects of utility or pleasure."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/2026_Aperture264_1600x900_Fan_gray-copy.jpg", "alt": "Aperture Magazine Subscription", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Aperture Magazine Subscription"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Like the ragpicker, a photographer “catalogues and collects”—a photographer “sorts things out” and “chooses astutely.” Here, Evans looks at a city’s debris, a most common and lowly subject, and in the image he offers a taste of his mind. As Evans elaborated in the interview, “The mind works on the machine—through it, rather.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Writing now in my late seventies, I know that a time may come when a person reviews their past actions and experiences and recontextualizes them in the light of the perspective of a lifetime. In his interview with Katz, Evans looked back on the experience of his hot streak in the 1930s. He called the experience “a very exciting, heady thing,” adding that “it goes like magic” and “I use the word transcendent .” Evans is describing what I call a gift state. Many artists and writers have the feeling, for a period of time, of something taking over, of something working through them. Evans was now connecting the transcendence of his experience making the work with the transcendence conveyed by the images. They were imprinted with a quality of his mind."}, {"type": "quote", "text": "Focus is the nexus that connects the photograph, the world, and the mind. It is the door to the passage from the surface to the interior."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The only time I had the opportunity to hear Evans speak was at a lecture he gave at the Museum of Modern Art in the early 1970s. He showed Corrugated Tin Façade (1936)—a deadpan photograph of a dilapidated contractor’s office in Alabama, sunlight shimmering off the corrugation—and, by my recollection, called it a “transcendent document.” I knew that he had previously described “documentary style” as having the qualities of “severity, rigor, simplicity, clarity . . . without artistic pretension.” I was not expecting him to describe his work as transcendent. He was now indicating that below the surface of a “document” could lie an interior depth. He chose Matisse’s quote “L’exactitude n’est pas la vérité” (Exactitude is not truth) as the epigraph for his book Message from the Interior (1966). He is saying not to mistake the surface exactitude of documentary style for truth, but to look beneath the surface. Truth may be buried in its interior, the message from the interior. Truth can reside beneath the surface of the mundane, the quotidian. This recalls an Arab maxim, “The apparent is the bridge to the real.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "An Evans photograph in which I feel this depth, this undercurrent, an image that moves me most deeply, is Breakfast Room at Belle Grove Plantation , from March 1935. In an early act of urban exploration, Evans, accompanied by his future wife Jane Ninas and her friend Christine Fairchild, broke into the Belle Grove mansion. They shared a picnic breakfast in this space he would later call the “breakfast room.” Before making the photograph, Evans arranged the shutters in the center of the picture, allowing just a crack of light to seep through."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Belle Grove Plantation in White Castle, Louisiana, was built by the sugar planter John Andrews in 1857. The seventy-five-room Greek Revival mansion was one of the largest residential buildings in the American South during the antebellum period. Belle Grove exemplified the grand architectural ambitions of Louisiana’s sugar aristocracy and stood as a testament to the economic power generated by the brutal system of enslaved labor that perpetuated this culture. Without enslaved labor, the plantation could not be sustained. It changed hands several times after the Civil War and was eventually abandoned. By the early twentieth century, the mansion had fallen into serious disrepair."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/264MAG021_Notebook_Shore_HR.jpg", "alt": "Breakfast Room at Belle Grove Plantation, White Chapel, Louisiana. Walker Evans was given a major exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art in 1971. That same year, Evans and his friend Leslie George Katz, publisher of Eakins Press, collaborated on an extensive interview. At this retrospective moment of his life, Evans wanted to record his thoughts on photography, his work, and the influences on him. He wanted to codify his legacy. In addition to the interview, Evans selected and commented on eight photographs that spanned the arc of his life’s work. While the interview and the photographs appeared at the time in Art in America , the project didn’t see book form until 1995, when Eakins Press published Walker Evans: Incognito . Charles Baudelaire, one of Evans’s greatest influences, wrote, “The observer is a prince enjoying his incognito wherever he goes.” This suggests that the observer, like a prince traveling in disguise, has a privileged position: They can move through the world anonymously, seeing everything while remaining unseen themselves.

The picture of a gutter was the most recent and least-known photograph in Evans’s selection. It is from 40 Studies of Street Debris, Manhole Covers, and Trash Bins, New York City (ca. 1968). Here is Evans’s accompanying text:

While removed from nature, this picture of a gutter is in a sense very human. It is Baudelairean. I wish Baudelaire was alive to see it. The secret of photography is, the camera takes on the character and the personality of the handler. The mind works on the machine.

When Evans wrote “Baudelairean,” he was referring to this paragraph, describing a chiffonnier , a ragpicker, from Baudelaire’s essay “On Wine and Hashish”:

Here is a man whose task it is to pick up all the rubbish produced on one day in the capital. All that the great city has thrown out, all that it has lost, all that it has disdained, all that it has broken, he catalogues and collects. He consults the archives of debauchery, works through the lumber-room of rubbish. He sorts things out and makes a selection, chooses astutely; like a miser, he collects the muck which, once more digested by the Gods of Commerce, will become objects of utility or pleasure.

Aperture Magazine Subscription

Like the ragpicker, a photographer “catalogues and collects”—a photographer “sorts things out” and “chooses astutely.” Here, Evans looks at a city’s debris, a most common and lowly subject, and in the image he offers a taste of his mind. As Evans elaborated in the interview, “The mind works on the machine—through it, rather.”

Writing now in my late seventies, I know that a time may come when a person reviews their past actions and experiences and recontextualizes them in the light of the perspective of a lifetime. In his interview with Katz, Evans looked back on the experience of his hot streak in the 1930s. He called the experience “a very exciting, heady thing,” adding that “it goes like magic” and “I use the word transcendent .” Evans is describing what I call a gift state. Many artists and writers have the feeling, for a period of time, of something taking over, of something working through them. Evans was now connecting the transcendence of his experience making the work with the transcendence conveyed by the images. They were imprinted with a quality of his mind.

Focus is the nexus that connects the photograph, the world, and the mind. It is the door to the passage from the surface to the interior.

The only time I had the opportunity to hear Evans speak was at a lecture he gave at the Museum of Modern Art in the early 1970s. He showed Corrugated Tin Façade (1936)—a deadpan photograph of a dilapidated contractor’s office in Alabama, sunlight shimmering off the corrugation—and, by my recollection, called it a “transcendent document.” I knew that he had previously described “documentary style” as having the qualities of “severity, rigor, simplicity, clarity . . . without artistic pretension.” I was not expecting him to describe his work as transcendent. He was now indicating that below the surface of a “document” could lie an interior depth. He chose Matisse’s quote “L’exactitude n’est pas la vérité” (Exactitude is not truth) as the epigraph for his book Message from the Interior (1966). He is saying not to mistake the surface exactitude of documentary style for truth, but to look beneath the surface. Truth may be buried in its interior, the message from the interior. Truth can reside beneath the surface of the mundane, the quotidian. This recalls an Arab maxim, “The apparent is the bridge to the real.”

An Evans photograph in which I feel this depth, this undercurrent, an image that moves me most deeply, is Breakfast Room at Belle Grove Plantation , from March 1935. In an early act of urban exploration, Evans, accompanied by his future wife Jane Ninas and her friend Christine Fairchild, broke into the Belle Grove mansion. They shared a picnic breakfast in this space he would later call the “breakfast room.” Before making the photograph, Evans arranged the shutters in the center of the picture, allowing just a crack of light to seep through.

The Belle Grove Plantation in White Castle, Louisiana, was built by the sugar planter John Andrews in 1857. The seventy-five-room Greek Revival mansion was one of the largest residential buildings in the American South during the antebellum period. Belle Grove exemplified the grand architectural ambitions of Louisiana’s sugar aristocracy and stood as a testament to the economic power generated by the brutal system of enslaved labor that perpetuated this culture. Without enslaved labor, the plantation could not be sustained. It changed hands several times after the Civil War and was eventually abandoned. By the early twentieth century, the mansion had fallen into serious disrepair.

When I see the decaying Corinthian columns in the breakfast room, I think of Giulio Romano’s Sala dei Giganti (Hall of the Giants) in the Palazzo Te. Here the giants are trying in vain to hold up crumbling columns, massive columns tilting and breaking apart, the classical world disintegrating around them, as Zeus and the gods crush the giants for their hubris.

Look at the photograph Breakfast Room at Belle Grove Plantation . Slowly, deliberately, move your attention, your focus, along the side walls to the columns, then to the floor of the small vestibule, and then to the shutters. Notice the depth of space from the columns, across the vestibule, to the shutters. Do you have a sensation of your eyes changing focus? Do you sense Evans’s experience? Do you have a taste of Evans’s mind?

Focus is the nexus that connects the photograph, the world, and the mind. It is the door to the passage from the surface to the interior. It is a way of connecting with the mind that works through the machine.

Aseel AlYaqoub has been awarded the seventh Ithra Art Prize for Flora Incognita (2026), a speculative herbarium of hybrid plant forms that explores how botanical records have shaped perceptions of the Gulf. The King Abdulaziz Center for World Culture (Ithra) announced the winning project during a ceremony in Dhahran, where the prize was presented as part of the institution’s ongoing support for contemporary artistic practices in the region.

As part of the Ithra Art Prize, AlYaqoub received a USD 100,000 grant, with Flora Incognita also joining Ithra’s permanent collection. The work is currently on view at the Ithra Museum as part of an exhibition bringing together the five shortlisted projects . These include AlYaqoub’s Flora Incognita alongside Bady Dalloul’s miniature Matchboxes Drawings (2026), which examines imagery and collective memory; Heba Y Amin Elmahamly’s reworking of the historical Mahmal procession in The Last Carrier: Iteration I (2026); Ala Younis ’ Lifted Arches (2026), which brings Islamic architectural traditions into dialogue with modernism; and Jawad Al Malhi’s Ashes of Absence (2026) , which addresses disappearance and loss through a multimedia presentation.

The winning project was selected by a five-member international jury, including Farah Abushullaih , Tarek Abou El Fetouh, Dr Nada Shabout, Jérôme Sans and Nadia Kaabi-Linke .

Farah Abushullaih, the programmes manager at Ithra, noted:⁠‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​⁠ “The prize serves as a vital platform, bringing innovative ideas and artistic visions into dialogue and shaping the future of contemporary art in the region.⁠‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​⁠ By celebrating Aseel AlYaqoub, we are investing in a vision that disrupts conventional narratives and elevates the Saudi cultural landscape to new intellectual heights.”

The seventh edition also builds on the programme’s scope by supporting each of the five finalists with production funds, allowing them to create new projects responding to the region’s shifting histories and realities.

Shows

A Low Hum: The 16th Gwangju Biennale

JAMES T. HONG ’s

Apologies , 2012– , at “You must change your life,” the 16th Gwangju Biennale, 2026. Photo by Jeon Byung Cheol. Courtesy the Gwangju Biennale Foundation.

Each evening, the façade of the Gwangju Biennale Exhibition Hall lights up with James T. Hong’s Apologies (2012– ), an ever-expanding anthology of government officials and heads of state offering contrition. It is, in Hong’s words, “a timeline of political progress as unrepentant recidivism and contrite repetition.” The reel begins in 1937 with Japanese ambassador Hiroshi Saito regretting the sinking of the USS Panay, followed by German chancellor Willy Brandt falling to his knees before the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising monument, and closes in 2023 with the Dutch king apologizing for his nation’s role in slavery. In between, we see a procession of presidents, prime ministers, and a pope begging pardon for inherited legacies of discrimination, dispossession, and crimes. Delivered years, decades, sometimes centuries after the fact, these gestures accumulate into a tedious spectacle. What Hong’s work exposes, ultimately, is a paradox at the heart of any political change: the token of penitence stages transformation precisely in order to defer it. This monumental record of inertia is one of the few works in this year’s Gwangju Biennale that interrogates its title directive, “You Must Change Your Life,” showing how fast the imperative to transform can settle into ritual.

The directive itself is lifted from the closing line in Rainer Maria Rilke’s 1908 sonnet “Archaic Torso of Apollo.” Artistic director Ho Tzu Nyen has spoken of encountering the poem on an exhausted day and feeling an “expanded capacity.” The line carries urgency: it insists you change without explaining how or toward what. That openness allows Ho and his co-curators (Gahee Park, Brian Kuan Wood, and Che Kyongfa) to treat transformation as something layered across scales and rhythms, at times seismic, at times imperceptibly slow.

That split tempo is made tangible in the opening section, “Molecules and Me,” where Goldin+Senneby’s Resin Pond (2026) pools nearly two tons of pine resin across the floor into a luminous amber slick. Within the living tree, resin is at once a toxin that repels pests and fungi, and a sealant that closes wounds. It is also energy-dense, terpene-rich, harvestable for refinement into biodiesel and aviation fuel. Jakob Senneby, one half of the duo, lives with multiple sclerosis, a condition in which the body’s defenses chronically turn against its own nervous system. This experience with autoimmunity has reoriented the duo’s longstanding scrutiny of capital’s absurdities. Resin Pond proposes that the generative and the destructive are no longer separable—not in climate crisis, not in geopolitics, not in technology, and certainly not in the poison-cure logic of a market that carries within it both its own overcoming and its catastrophe: a perspective that regards change less as directional than conditional.

In the curatorial statement, Ho frames practices as techniques “repeated at regular intervals either to control or to conduct change,” and the tension between repetition and rupture runs through the exhibition. Scattered across the floors are clusters of volcanic rocks from Jeju, their contorted forms holding, within a single mass, radically unequal durations: the slow accrual of sediment, the violence of eruption, the long aftermath of cooling and weathering. Equally threaded through the space, and functioning as the exhibition’s connective tissue, are Sasaki Ken’s more than 60 small paintings of unremarkable things—a pair of Converse sneakers, workers’ boots, a light switch, a tennis ball. One of the canvases depicts an ominously overcast sky: Sasaki’s record of the Tokyo sky in the days after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake, when fears of radioactive drift from Fukushima hung in the air. Dispersed as they are, the rocks and the mundane paintings can feel opaque, even excessive. Yet their sheer persistence makes the argument that change moves at no single speed and takes no single form, and that it is often already underway, lodged in the textures of the everyday. Whether this constitutes a veiled hope for transformative force, or an oblique salute to Gwangju’s own insurgent heritage, the exhibition leaves deliberately open.

MAYA WATANABE ,

Liminal , 2019, still from video: 64 min. Produced by the Han Nefkens Foundation. Courtesy the artist.

“Molecules and Me” rewards sustained looking, and it repeatedly nudges the viewer toward the unfinished. Maya Watanabe’s Liminal (2019), a single-channel projection on a tilted, engulfing screen, offers extreme close-ups of human remains exhumed from mass graves of Peru’s internal armed conflict, which took place between 1980 and 2000. Decades later, roughly tens of thousands of the victims are still missing or nameless, and many crimes remain unacknowledged. Watanabe’s camera shifts constantly between focus and blur, refusing to let atrocity resolve into a fixed historical image. Even death, the work implies, withholds closure: mourning persists, identity stays suspended, and the past exerts its pressure from within a near-molecular anonymity.

Historical wounds and their seepage into daily life come to a point in the second section, “Bodies and Bonds,” where Mona Benyamin’s two videos furnish the exhibition’s most bracing case for art as a means of processing trauma. Her parents, who lived through the mass displacements of Palestinians during the Arab-Israeli conflicts, the Nakba (1948) and the Naksa (1967), are featured as performers cast into the formats of a sitcom and a newscast. In Trouble in Paradise (2018), they run through comic bits about the eradication of Palestinians, broaching the subject through gallows humor delivered with a Brechtian affect over a canned laugh track (“How do you make a Palestinian cry? You kill his family”). In Tomorrow, Again (2023), they reappear as anchors and bystanders: a newsreader who cannot stop weeping, an eyewitness to one disaster after another. Benyamin creates a condition of perpetual emergency and then asks, with a sardonic edge, how one is meant to change a life whose ground state is recurring ruin.

MONA BENYAMIN ,

Tomorrow, again , 2023, still from video, color, stereo sound: 11 min. Courtesy the artist.

SOHRAB HURA ,

Bittersweet , 2019, still from video: 13 min 48 sec. Courtesy the artist and Experimenter, Kolkata.

Time, kinship, and the slow labor of change take a more sensorial, elegiac turn in the pairing of Amanda Heng and Sohrab Hura. Heng’s Another Woman in Gwangju 1996, 2014, 2023 (2026) follows photographs of the artist and her mother across three decades, beginning with the mother’s request for a portrait and returning, in 2014 and again in 2023, to restage the original poses. As the two women age together, the roles of care and dependence visibly reverse, and the duration itself becomes legible. Nearby, Hura’s slideshow video Bittersweet (2019) and the black-and-white photographs, handwritten notes, and sketches of Life Is Elsewhere (2005–11) chronicle his life alongside a mother diagnosed with schizophrenia and her dog, Elsa. A letter penned by his mother details how the dog’s arrival remade her days: “As the years passed, I forgot all the reasons for not wanting her. She had become my dog and my friend a long time ago.” Change seldom arrives as a singular event, and neither do joy, grief, or hardship. It takes shape instead through fragments, the pieces by which a life is assembled.

From bodies and their bonds the exhibition widens to terrain and cosmos. Three works anchor “Cosmos and Change,” a darkened room of incantation and other-than-human vision: Bhenji Ra’s Biraddali Dancing on the Horizon (2024), drawn from the artist’s encounter with pangalay , a dance practiced by the Tausug of the Sulu Archipelago; Hura’s The Coast (2019), following devotees of the goddess Kali reveling in the roar of the surf on Tamil Nadu’s shores; and Saodat Ismailova’s enigmatic Melted into the Sun (2024), which trails an eighth-century mystic figure known as “The Veiled One” across the Amu Darya, the Chillpiq burial ground, and a Soviet-era solar furnace. The three soundtracks bleed into one another, wrapping the viewer in a field of moving images that is by turns harmonic and dissonant, and within which personal, familial, devotional, and national histories reveal themselves as continually rewritten by myth, ideology, and science.

JACQUELINE KIYOMI GORK ’s Not Exactly BPM (Variation Rrose), 2026. Commissioned by the 16th Gwangju Biennale, Supported by National Center for Art Research, Japan (NCAR), Tanoto Art Foundation (TAF), and Empty Gallery, Speaker equipment provided by Meyer Sound, Berkeley, CA. Courtesy Gwangju Biennale Foundation.

Jacqueline Kiyomi Gork’s Not Exactly BPM (Variation Rrose) (2026), presented in the final section, returns the focus to the body. It is a deconstructed nightclub built from centrifugal blowers, feedback, and transparent, sound-absorbing inflatables that swell into a sensory enclosure and then slowly exhale. A hypnotic score of kick drums and phase-shifting loops, built with the psychoacoustic artist Rrose, moves the room and its occupants alike. But instead of the euphoria of the dancefloor, the installation’s eerie self-awareness yields a low hum of anxiety and suspended anticipation, an artificial burnt-orange light filtering through vinyl walls.

Gork confronts the conceptually dense, politically freighted, and emotionally taxing works in the exhibition with a visceral reset, displacing intellectual reflection into corporeal attention: breath, pulse, the instability and the pleasure of an enclosed and rhythmic collective. If the biennale has spent its length imagining a “life elsewhere,” this last environment stages the pause before departure. It leaves the beholder with the question—how, having seen and felt all this, does one return to the world changed?

Louis Lu is an associate editor at ArtAsiaPacific.
content.excerpt_original: The biennale treats transformation as something layered across scales and rhythms, at times seismic, at times imperceptibly slow. Louis Lu

TOKAS Project Vol. 9「在ることの再演」 2026年10月3日（土）–11月8日（日） トーキョーアーツアンドスペース本郷 https://www.tokyoartsandspace.jp/ 開館時間：11:00–19:00（入場は閉館30分前まで） 休館日：月（ただし、10/12は開館）、10/13 展覧会URL： https://www.tokyoartsandspace.jp/archive/exhibition/2026/20261003-7578.html 出品作家：ウン・ジェピル、キム・ドヒ、ク・ドンヒ、パク・ミンハ、三野新

トーキョーアーツアンドスペース（TOKAS）では、国際的な交流を促進し、多文化的な視点で多様なテーマについて思考する展覧会プログラム「TOKAS Project」の9回目となる「在ることの再演」を開催する。TOKASは2006年よりソウルの4つの提携機関と協働し、相互にアーティストの派遣を行なってきた。その交流20周年を記念する本展では、過去にレジデンス・プログラムに参加した日韓のアーティストを中心に、自身の身体経験を軸に現実を紡ぎ直す5名を紹介する。 芸術の歴史において、人間は目の前に在る世界や生命の存在を時の流れから引き離し、絵画や彫刻、写真や映画／映像によって固定し、永遠の生としてつなぎとめようとしてきた。また演劇や舞踊、パフォーマンスといったライブ・アートは、パフォーマーの身体的な演技を通じて、現実世界における生をその場に現前化することを探求してきた。本展では、歴史、生命、人間、身体、社会といった多様な対象を「再演」の視点から捉え、アーティストたちがそれぞれ異なる視点から観察した生の姿を、フィクション、彫刻、デジタルメディア、身体表現などの実践をとおして展示空間に再び立ち上げる。単に現実を写しとり過去を再現するのではなく、その時の記憶や感情といった固有の身体経験を含めた現実を肉体化し、現在進行形のものとして捉えることで、今日における生の在り様を再考する。展示は、作家ごとに「歴史の再演」「生命のつながりの再演」「テクノロジーによる人間の再演」「女形の身体性の再演」「現代社会における身体感覚の再演」と題したテーマで構成される。

三野新 （福岡県生まれ）は、周縁化された場所やものに残る記憶や風景をつなぎ、「ここ」と「あそこ」の中間項を見つけ前景化させることをテーマに研究と実践を行ない、主に自身で撮影した写真や映像をもとに制作したフィクションを、自己と他者の身体やさまざまなメディアを用いて発表している。東京都と神奈川県を拠点に活動。2017年に東京藝術大学大学院美術研究科博士後期課程を修了。主な展覧会に「ぬけみち展 かわす・つくる・ともにいる―生きるための回路」（アーツ前橋、群馬、2026）、「山本卓卓＆三野新『ここに立ち、ここに立つ』」（サッポロ・パラレル・ミュージアム、北海道、2024）、「外が静かになるまで」（十和田市現代美術館 space、青森、2023）などがある。2025年度二都市間交流事業プログラムでSeMAナンジ・レジデンシーに滞在した。本展では、韓国の龍山米軍基地や戦後の占領期に関する歴史のリサーチ、戦争が現在の日常生活や身体に及ぼしている影響への考察をもとに書き下ろした戯曲「温室／オンシル」の舞台となる温室を展示空間に立ち上げる。「石」「鉄」「トラック」という三つのモノの会話によって紡がれる物語を、オブジェクト・シアターの手法によってインスタレーションとして「上演」し、日本と韓国の関係をめぐる歴史を、客観的な事実としてではなく、現在の自分自身の現実として捉え直すことを促す。 キム・ドヒ （1979年韓国・釜山生まれ）は、「物質としての身体」が生み出す摩擦や熱などの動的なエネルギーに関心を寄せ、それらが伝達される経路を探索し、そこに自身の身体を介入させることで、自己と他者、人工と自然、生と死の間の境界が曖昧になる儚い瞬間を捉えようとしてきた。即座の反応を引き出すことよりも、時間の経過に伴うエネルギーの堆積によって形成される感覚の層を明らかにすることに重きを置いている。ソウルを拠点に活動。2006年に弘益大学（美術学）を修了。主な展覧会に「Boundaries Resonate, Life Overflows」（Gimhae Museum of Art、金海、韓国、2026）、「Chanting the Hen’s Dream: Phantom Sensation」（Yangju Art Studio 777 Residence、楊州、韓国、2025）、「The Sound of Light Surface」（Seongbuk Young Art Space、ソウル、2024）などがある。2018年度二国間交流事業プログラムでTOKASレジデンシーに滞在した。2018年より、人間の生命の根源を象徴する「おへそ」に着目し、人々のおへそを型取るプロジェクト「Navel Mountain」を継続的に行ない、その過程で生まれるコミュニケーションをとおして、無数の人々との関係から成る生のつながりを体感する場を創出してきた。本展では、おへそのモチーフを拡張した鐘の彫刻作品《Navel Strike》を発表し、鐘を鳴らすという鑑賞者の身体的行為によって生じる音の振動を空間内に共鳴させる。

パク・ミンハ （1985年韓国・ソウル生まれ）は、実際の出来事や資料にもとづいた綿密なリサーチを下敷きに、SFとドキュメンタリーを融合し、映画や映像インスタレーション、出版物、音響作品など多角的な実践をとおして、人々の感覚世界を形作る枠組みを解読し、隠された物語を明らかにすることを探究している。とりわけ科学や歴史、メディア技術から派生した視聴覚的な副産物である光学の系譜に関心をもち、モノや場所、オンライン・アーカイブに現れる副産物をたどることで、そこに宿る亡霊のような見えざる者の声を発見し、物語をとおして可視化することを試みている。ソウルを拠点に活動。2013年にカリフォルニア芸術大学（美術）を修了。主な活動に、「CPH:DOX 2025 NEW VISION AWARD」（Kunsthal Charlottenborg、コペンハーゲン、2025）、「The Second Life」（アトリエ・エルメス、ソウル、2025）、「Foreverism: Endless Horizons」（イルミン美術館、ソウル、2024）などがある。2025年度二都市間交流事業プログラムでTOKASレジデンシーに滞在した。本展では、テクノロジー企業の効率性や精度への追求といった資本主義的な欲望によって、人間の労働がロボットやAIに代替され、テクノロジーの超生産性に人間が支配されていく現実を前に、デジタルに還元できない人間性とは何か、生命とは何かを映像作品をとおして問いかける。 ウン・ジェピル （1991年韓国・原州生まれ）は、移住の記憶という視点を通じて「帰属」や「故郷」の意味を探求し、簡単に翻訳できない個人的な感情や周辺的な歴史に焦点を当ててきた。伝統と現代性、そして西洋中心主義社会によってしばしば定義される男性的・女性的な概念の境界を解体することで、言葉による説明を超えた感覚的な体験をもたらす。韓国とオランダを拠点に活動。2017年に中央大学（ソウル）写真学科を卒業し、2021年にサンドベルグ・インスティチュートのアート・デザイン科を修了。主な活動に、パフォーマンス「Blue Night, Blue Shadows」（Seo-Seoul Museum of Art、ソウル、2026）、パフォーマンス／個展「Red Celebration」（Vleeshal Center for Contemporary Art、ミデルブルフ、オランダ、2025）などがある。2020年より、京劇の名女形・ 梅蘭芳 が考案した女形を表現する12のポージングと53の手の動きを収録した記録集との出合いをきっかけに女形の研究を行ない、現存する数少ない京劇の女形の師匠のもとで演技の技術を磨きながら、自身の身体をとおして梅蘭芳の身振りを演じ直すことで、生物学的な性別に囚われないクロスジェンダーな身体感覚を模索してきた。本展では、梅蘭芳の踊りを体現するパフォーマンスや銅版画作品によって、かつて存在した女形の姿を現代に蘇らせることを試みる。日本での作品発表は本展が初めてとなる。 ク・ドンヒ （1974年韓国・ソウル生まれ）は、日常の何気ない出来事や、テレビ、インターネット、都市生活といった身の回りの断片的な要素を素材に、それらをサンプリングしながら作品を再構成し、その中に不条理で奇妙な事象を介在させることで、人々の知覚を揺さぶり、当たり前の中に潜む違和感を浮かび上がらせる。制作過程において、あえて即興的なハプニングやゲームのようなルールを設けて緊張感を与え、予測不可能な展開を呼び寄せる。映像、写真、彫刻など異なるメディアを融合させたインスタレーションを特徴とし、特定の政治的・社会的な課題を直接的に示唆するのではなく、社会のシステムの限界をユーモラスかつアイロニカルにとりあげてきた。ソウルを拠点に活動。1998年に弘益大学彫刻学科を卒業し、2000年にイェール大学美術学部大学院（彫刻）を修了。主な展覧会に「Dear Alexa」（Art Archives Seoul Museum of Art、ソウル、2026）、「Tabula Rasa」（Audio Visual Pavilion Lab、ソウル、2023）、「Delivery」（Art Sonje Center、ソウル、2019）などがある。2007年度二国間交流事業プログラムでトーキョーワンダーサイト青山に滞在した。本展では、超情報化社会に従属する現代人の意識や感覚を探る映像作品をとおして、社会的な日常生活の中で形成された身体的な習性や固定化された規範を攪拌する。 会期中は、出品作家によるアーティスト・トークやウン・ジェピルによるパフォーマンスのほか、11月7日には三野新が作を手がけ、山本浩貴（いぬのせなか座）が演出する演劇パフォーマンスを上演する。また、美術批評家／インディペンデント・キュレーターの紺野優希をゲストに迎え、韓国の現代アートシーンをテーマとしたスペシャル・トークを駐日韓国文化院で開催する。

関連イベント アーティスト・トーク 2026年10月3日（土）15:00–17:00 登壇：ウン・ジェピル、キム・ドヒ、ク・ドンヒ、パク・ミンハ 会場：トーキョーアーツアンドスペース本郷 参加費：無料 ※日英逐次通訳あり ウン・ジェピル｜パフォーマンス 2026年10月3日（土）17:30–18:00 会場：トーキョーアーツアンドスペース本郷 スペースC（3F） 参加費：無料 三野新｜アーティスト・トーク 2026年10月10日（土）16:00–16:30 会場：トーキョーアーツアンドスペース本郷 スペースA（1F） 参加費：無料 ※日本手話通訳あり スペシャル・トーク「韓国の現代アートシーンについて」 2026年10月30日（金）17:00–18:00 登壇：紺野優希（美術批評家／インディペンデント・キュレーター） 会場：駐日韓国文化院5F ハンナレホール（東京都新宿区四谷4-4-10） 参加費：無料 ※展覧会の会場とは異なる。手話通訳を希望する場合は10/16までにメールで申込（詳細は TOKASウェブサイト を参照） 三野新｜演劇パフォーマンス 2026年11月7日（土）15:00–16:00 作：三野新 演出：山本浩貴（いぬのせなか座） 出演：石川朝日（Dr. Holiday Laboratory） 会場：トーキョーアーツアンドスペース本郷 スペースA（1F） 参加費：無料（要予約） ※10/11より TOKASウェブサイト にて予約開始

content.article_text:
Galerist marks 25 years with Labour of Love, as the Istanbul-based gallery looks back on quarter of a century of achievement in a changing social and economic landscape.

2001 was a watershed year for Türkiye. An overnight collapse in the stock market sparked the most severe financial crisis in the country’s history and the decimation of the lira. A USD 15 billion bailout from the International Monetary Fund led to major economic restructuring, and the first constitutional amendments for Türkiye’s since-stalled EU accession bid in the same year would in turn usher in comprehensive social and political reforms. In the trust vacuum following the crash and widespread voter disenfranchisement, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan established the AK Party. It would sweep the board in the 2002 elections, heralding what it would later rebrand as a ‘New Türkiye’.

2001 was also a defining moment for the Turkish art scene. While historically the state had been a great supporter of the arts, the IMF’s austerity measures saw cultural support slashed. Individual collectors and, later, the corporate conglomerates that now dominate Turkish arts funding, stepped in to fill this gap. This shift led to the 2001 opening of Istanbul’s first contemporary art museum, Proj 4L (now the Elgiz Museum), with others like Istanbul Modern, Arter and the Pera Museum soon following. In recent years, this boom in private museums – 23 opened last year alone – has expanded away from neoliberal-friendly Istanbul into the AKP stronghold of the Anatolian heartland.

Put another way, the Turkish art scene is unique globally in that it is overwhelmingly not only bankrolled by banks but its entire noncommercial infrastructure – from museums and biennales to cultural institutions like SALT – also relies on corporate philanthropy. Compared with the Gulf art scenes, which enjoy significant governmental support, the situation in Türkiye presents an alternative trajectory of development in terms of what happens to an ecosystem when the state logs off and it is forced to sustain itself?

While Türkiye’s earliest commercial galleries date back to the mid-1970s, it was this post-2001 recovery period that arguably birthed the contemporary art scene as we know it today. Blue chips like Galerist – which opened in 2001, with Dirimart following the next year – revolutionised the market, not just in the kinds of art they showed but also where they showed it. With a weak domestic market, they began to take Turkish artists to international art fairs, introducing them to the world stage. Whereas historically galleries had operated on a somewhat ad-hoc consignment model, Galerist pioneered an international-style representation and roster approach, signing artists for exclusive multi-year contracts and working to develop their careers.

Galerist’s 25th anniversary show marks this quarter-century, which saw it mounting nearly 200 shows and launching a publishing programme as well as the now independent Art Unlimited magazine. At the risk of rehearsing bromides about resilience, it is first and foremost a testament to a gallery’s ability to not just survive but also maintain the rigour of its programme in a period characterised by yodelling macroeconomic turbulence and an increasingly restrictive political climate. Fittingly entitled Labour of Love , the exhibition brings together 49 multi-generational, mostly Turkish artists: some current, some formerly represented, some who just passed by for a group show or two. We can understand it then, as a reunion: a ledger, above all, of long-term relationships, trust and the community that has been built.

So far, so celebration. But does it cohere? In the main, no. The works, which include 14 new commissions, are very loosely organised around the theme of self-portraiture, however abstract. Some of the most compelling pieces index a kind of pervasive​ collective anxiety. Hung on a maroon wall, Güçlü Öztekin’s Nameless 106 (2012) on wrinkled craft paper suggests a disassociating insomniac Humpty Dumpty. Next to it, Yeşim Akdeniz invokes the psychosocial barometric pressure of living in a volatile state with Walking on Eggshells (2025), with eggs balanced precariously on a pair of mailboxes, all painted black and stuffed with letters. Nearby, a 2025 video by Merve Morkoç, Humiliation has a number now , plays on a screen angled against a corridor wall, with a jacket insouciantly draped over one corner. Clad in a greige shorts suit, the artist lies on the floor, doomscrolling while balancing a tower of wine glasses on her raised legs. She visibly shakes with the tension of being reduced to digits and interpellated by unemployment statistics; of course, it all comes crashing down.

The show also includes iconic pieces which gesture at intergenerational kinship, including Nil Yalter’s video Skin Story (2003), an important touchpoint not just for artists like Morkoç but also Türkiye’s whole generation of radical feminist performance art. Personal artistic relationships are woven in, too: on view here are both a lucid dream of a painting from Haluk Akakçe and a figurative sculpture in burnished concrete from his former studio assistant, Ayça Telgeren.

As a whole, the show suggests some interesting questions. What does it mean for a Turkish artist to make a self-portrait at a time when Turkishness itself is so contingent, so loaded, so linked to a particular articulation of national allegiance? Does any kind of discernible supra-portrait emerge? How does a gallery structure and participate in its own mythmaking? These questions go unanswered or, more fairly, are perhaps illegible to someone lacking a solid grounding in Turkish art history. But listen – it is a reunion show that gets the gang together and celebrates a legacy hard-won, and sometimes that is enough.

Labour of Love runs until 7 November

content.article_text:
News

Christine Sun Kim Awarded 2026 MacArthur Fellowship

CHRISTINE SUN KIM . Courtesy the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation.

The MacArthur Foundation has named mixed-media artist Christine Sun Kim as one of its 2026 MacArthur Fellows. She is one of 20 recipients, among them the artists Rodney McMillian, Chip Thomas, and Vincent Valdez. Each fellow will be granted a sum of USD 800,000 over the course of five years to facilitate their research and practice.

Born in California in 1980 and based in Berlin, Kim has been Deaf since birth. Initially wanting to pursue graphic design but told that no university courses offered interpreters, she instead completed a BFA at the School of Visual Arts in New York in 2006, followed by an MFA in sound and music at Bard College in 2013. In her early career, she began to draw on her own experience as a Deaf person to explore how communication is navigated throughout cultures. In 2019 she participated in the Whitney Biennial with her Degrees of Deaf Rage series (2018–19), which comprises charcoal illustrations expressing her frustration at the hurdles she had faced in cultural institutions. In 2020, she received the Ford Foundation’s Disability Future Fellowship.

Her practice has since expanded into performance, music, and interactive installation, using dry humor to raise awareness of Deaf issues and to probe the societal, cultural, and bodily relationships to language and sound. Kim’s work has been exhibited internationally, including at the Museum of Modern Art, New York (2013); the Shanghai and Berlin Biennales (both 2016); the Museum für Moderne Kunst, Frankfurt (2021); the Secession in Vienna (2023); the Gwangju Biennale (2023); and the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, Seoul (2026).

The MacArthur Fellowship, informally known as the “genius grant,” has been awarded annually since 1981 to people in fields ranging from writing and the arts to science and teaching. Kristen Mack, vice president of communications for MacArthur Fellows and Partnerships, stated that past fellows have “defied boundaries by questioning conventions, crossing disciplines, and driving collective progress.” The foundation described Kim as an artist befitting of this legacy, citing her ability to explore “the political, cultural, and multisensory dimensions of sound, spoken language, and communication.”

Harison Butler is an editorial intern at ArtAsiaPacific.
content.excerpt_original: The artist is among 20 recipients of the coveted “genius grant.” Harison Butler

content.article_text:
News

Para Site Announces Departure from Quarry Bay Location

Hong Kong’s Para Site is departing its location in Quarry Bay, where it has been based for a decade. On the occasion of its 30th anniversary, the nonprofit will embark on what it describes as a “nomadic” program that will unfold across the city throughout 2027.

In June, Para Site began its experimental, collaborative program “Elsewhere in Me” across Hong Kong, which will continue to showcase new commissions by local and international figures such as Sydney-based artist Justin Talplacido Shoulder (Phasmahammer) in November and Hong Kong-based artist Yim Sui Fong in December. The initiative part will continue into the new year while Para Site furnishes its new venue, which is yet to be announced.

Para Site was founded in 1996 by Hong Kong artists Patrick Lee, Leung Chi-wo, Phoebe Man Ching-ying, Sara Wong Chi-hang, Leung Mee-ping, Tsang Tak-ping, and Lisa Cheung as an alternative platform for nurturing discourse on contemporary art and collaborations between curators and creatives. Originally based in Sheung Wan, Para Site relocated to Quarry Bay in 2015.

James Taylor-Foster, who joined the institution as its executive director in March, told South China Morning Post that the year-long program is an opportunity to “try things out”: new ideas, partnerships, and relationships. “All this will inform the kind of space that we end up moving into—a new anchor point for Para Site in Hong Kong.”

Harison Butler is an editorial intern at ArtAsiaPacific.
content.excerpt_original: The experimental, Hong Kong-based art space will organize a “nomadic program” across the city next year. Harison Butler

content.article_text:
武蔵野美術大学 造形構想専攻 映像・写真コースの菅沼比呂志ゼミによる展覧会「写真、その複数形 ～写真をめぐるいくつもの入口」が、武蔵野美術大学市ヶ谷キャンパス1/Mで開催されている。会期は2026年9月26日から10月4日まで。

本展には、学部4年生から大学院、博士課程まで計22人が参加。21歳から35歳までと年齢層も幅広く、そのうち15人を海外からの留学生が占める。大学で初めて写真を学んだ学生から、デザインなど別領域を経て写真へと進んだ学生、社会人経験後に大学院で学び直す学生まで、それぞれ異なる背景を持つ。

展覧会のタイトルにある「複数形」が示すように、焦点となるのは単一の写真観ではない。プリント、写真集、スクリーン、言葉などさまざまな形式を通して、写真を見るとは何か、写真を介して何を見るのかを22人それぞれの実践から問い直す。完成された答えを提示するのではなく、作品を「句点」「読点」「クエスチョンマーク」「イコール」「ダッシュ」にたとえながら、写真について考えるための複数の「入口」をつくり出すことが展覧会の試みだ。

そのアプローチも多岐にわたる。内藤翼の「FACTA」は、フェイクニュースと物理的に操作された写真を同一紙面上で交差させ、虚構から「現実らしさ」が生成される構造を検証。生成AIをはじめイメージの真正性が揺らぐ現在において、「現実とは何か、リアルとは何か」という問題を写真とメディアの双方から問いかける。

一方、寺井雅也の「注がれた景色」は、街の廃材だったやかんをピンホールカメラへと転換した作品。像が定着される以前の光学現象に着目し、やかんの内部へ反転して投影される風景そのものを鑑賞者が覗き込めるよう構成する。写真が「写真」になる以前の状態へと遡り、メディウムの原理そのものを体験へと変換する試みだ。

ほかにも、故郷や土地の歴史、記憶、都市、家族、身体、時間など、学生たちの関心は広範囲に及ぶ。中国東北部の土地と「満洲」という名称に刻まれた歴史を見つめる葛苡辰の「北満ノ森」や、日本で暮らすなかで自身と場所との距離を考察する郭暁頴の「ひとつにはならない」、幼少期の家族写真を思い出の場所へ投影し、過去と現在を一枚の写真上で交差させる陳泓毅の「記憶の面影」など、写真を「記録」に限定しない実践が並ぶ。

会期終盤にはゲストを迎えたトークイベントも実施。10月3日13時から批評家のきりとりめでる、10月4日13時から写真家の野口里佳が登壇し、学生たちの作品について講評する。

content.article_text:
HBO Max renueva su catálogo en octubre con nuevas series, películas, documentales, realities y una programación especial de terror por Halloween.

Octubre llega a HBO Max con una programación cargada de series, películas, documentales, realities y propuestas especiales para Halloween. Entre las principales novedades aparecen producciones originales, historias basadas en hechos reales y varios títulos de terror.

El mes también tendrá un estreno muy especial para la plataforma: Epitafios , la primera producción original de HBO realizada en América Latina, regresa en una versión remasterizada para celebrar los 35 años de HBO en la región.

Series

Guerra – 1 de octubre

Archie Renaux, Dominic West y Sienna Miller protagonizan este drama legal ambientado en el mundo de los grandes abogados de Londres. La historia enfrenta a dos prestigiosos estudios jurídicos mientras un joven abogado queda atrapado en una batalla marcada por la ambición, el poder y la traición.

Estado de Furia – Temporada 2 – 9 de octubre

La segunda temporada presenta nuevas historias protagonizadas por mujeres que quedan atrapadas en un sistema donde las situaciones extremas pueden transformarse en un espectáculo. Maribel Verdú, Carmen Maura, María León y Cecilia Suárez forman parte del elenco.

Epitafios – versión remasterizada – 15 de octubre

Para celebrar sus 35 años en América Latina, HBO recupera su primera producción original realizada en la región. Julio Chávez, Paola Krum, Antonio Birabent y Cecilia Roth protagonizan esta historia policial sobre una serie de asesinatos conectados con una antigua tragedia.

Te puede interesar

Qué ver este fin de semana: 4 películas y series que son tendencia en Netflix, HBO Max, Prime Video y Disney+

Recomendaciones de finde: 4 títulos para ver en streaming

El colombiano de Keko – 22 de octubre

Juan Cruz, Christian Tappan y Juan Pablo Raba protagonizan este drama basado en hechos reales. Andrés Ballesteros viaja a Tanzania en busca del amor, pero termina encarcelado injustamente por una acusación de narcotráfico y pasa ocho años intentando regresar a su hogar.

Documentales y true crime

Tragedia en el Estadio de La Corregidora – 15 de octubre

Este documental de HBO reconstruye los violentos acontecimientos ocurridos durante un partido entre Querétaro y Atlas en 2022. A través de testimonios inéditos y material nunca antes visto, la producción vuelve sobre las dudas y controversias que quedaron alrededor de aquella jornada.

Poeta Caníbal – octubre

El documental se mete en la historia de José Luis Calva Zepeda, conocido como “El Poeta Caníbal”, y reconstruye el caso a partir de testimonios exclusivos y una investigación sobre los crímenes que conmocionaron a México.

La Masacre de Flores – octubre

La serie documental reconstruye uno de los casos criminales más impactantes de Argentina a través de la historia de Matías Bagnato, único sobreviviente del incendio que terminó con la vida de sus padres, sus dos hermanos y un amigo en 1994.

Películas

Los domingos – 16 de octubre

Ainara tiene 17 años y, mientras su familia espera que decida qué carrera universitaria estudiar, la joven sorprende a todos al revelar que quiere convertirse en monja de clausura. La decisión pone a prueba los vínculos familiares. El elenco incluye a Blanca Soroa, Patricia López Arnaiz y Juan Minujín.

The Moment – 30 de octubre

Charli xcx protagoniza esta película sobre una estrella emergente del pop que debe enfrentarse a las presiones de la fama y de la industria musical mientras prepara su primera gira en grandes estadios. También participan Rosanna Arquette, Kate Berlant, Kylie Jenner y Rachel Sennott.

Realities

MasterChef: Profesionales Brasil – Temporada 6 – 9 de octubre

La versión brasileña del popular reality culinario vuelve con nuevos cocineros profesionales que deberán convencer a tres reconocidos chefs para quedarse con la victoria. El jurado está integrado por Erick Jacquin, Helena Rizzo y Henrique Fogaça.

Supervivencia al Desnudo: Brasil – Temporada 4 – 18 de octubre

Diez participantes intentarán sobrevivir en una región de Sudáfrica atravesada por una histórica sequía y poblada por animales peligrosos, entre ellos búfalos y mambas negras.

Comedia

Kate Berlant: Parmesano – 23 de octubre

La comediante Kate Berlant llega con un especial de HBO Original en el que aborda con humor y sarcasmo temas como la tecnología, la sexualidad y las contradicciones de la vida moderna.

Animación infantil

Hora de Aventura: Misiones Secundarias – 5 de octubre

Finn y Jake regresan a los primeros días de sus aventuras en una nueva serie de episodios autoconclusivos que recupera a varios personajes clásicos de la franquicia, incluido el Rey Helado.

Especial de Halloween

HBO Max también prepara una programación especial para octubre con varias propuestas de terror.

Evil Dead: En llamas – 9 de octubre

Una reunión familiar en una casa aislada se transforma en una pesadilla cuando sus integrantes comienzan a convertirse en Deadites . La película está dirigida por Sébastien Vaniček y cuenta con Souheila Yacoub y Hunter Doohan en su elenco.

Mother Mary – 23 de octubre

Anne Hathaway y Michaela Coel protagonizan esta película dirigida por David Lowery. La historia sigue a una icónica estrella del pop que se reencuentra con su antigua amiga y diseñadora de vestuario antes de regresar a los escenarios.

La herencia de Hope Hill – 23 de octubre

Una joven abogada viaja a Jamaica para investigar una disputa por una herencia, pero descubre que la propiedad involucrada está relacionada con las pesadillas que la persiguen y con un oscuro pasado familiar.

Devorador de almas – 23 de octubre

Un viaje de fin de semana a una mansión aislada en Irlanda se convierte en una pesadilla cuando una antigua criatura de la mitología irlandesa despierta y comienza a infectar a los protagonistas.

Además, durante octubre se suman otros títulos de terror como No te sueltes, Fear Factor: la casa del miedo, Junji Ito: Historias Extrañas para Noches de Insomnio, El Tormento, Noche Infernal, Cacería, Spree: Viaje Desenfrenado, Campeonato de Reposteros: Halloween, A Ciegas, El Carnicero y Los Cazamuertos .

Más estrenos de HBO Max en octubre

Series: La Favorita 1922 T2 (2/10), The Paper T2 (próximamente), Tip Toe (16/10, fecha por confirmar) y Georgie y Mandy – Su Primer Matrimonio T3 (22/10).

Películas: Un Pastel para el Presidente (2/10), Vieja Loca (2/10), Ninotchka (7/10), El Bazar de las Sorpresas (7/10), Maridos (7/10) y ¡Súper Agente Hitpig! (16/10).

Documentales y docuseries: Miller Night Football (3/10), Revista People investiga: sobreviviendo al asesino T2 (6/10), Mi relación con un asesino serial (7/10), Cuando Nadie me ve (9/10), Tierra de Crimen (12/10), Epic: Elvis Presley in Concert (16/10), Narco Hack (23/10), Sister Wives T14 (26/10) y Kordell: Slash & Burn (31/10), entre otros.

Animación: El Maravillosamente Extraño Mundo de Gumball T2 (9/10), Solo Necesitas Matar (9/10), Tom and Jerry Gokko Compilation-2 (23/10), Regular Show Presents: Terror Tales of the Park VII Halloween (4/10), Get Jiro (3/10), Gachiakuta (12/10) y Dragon Ball Beerus (16/10).

content.article_text:
20. Document of the Dead (1985)

Behind-the-scenes footage from Dawn of the Dead is the highlight of this aficionados-only affair, which follows the 1979 satirical zombie horror all the way through to distribution. Director George A Romero, makeup maestro Tom Savini and the occasional zombie actor shoot the breeze in the deserted shopping mall that provides the movie with its incongruous central location.

19. The Death of “Superman Lives”: What Happened? (2015)

Imagining what might have been if Tim Burton’s Superman Lives had got off the ground, documentary maker Jon Schnepp cosies up on screen with his interviewees and insinuates himself unforgivably into the story. The material is almost good enough to transcend his vanity: there is test footage of lead actor Nicolas Cage in his Man of Steel duds, plus interviews with Burton, original screenwriter Kevin Smith and producer Jon Peters, who was adamant that Superman should fight polar bears and a giant spider.

18. Becoming Bulletproof (2014)

A group of actors with disabilities form the bulk of the cast of the short western Bulletproof, shot in the California desert courtesy of the inclusive arts project Zeno Mountain Farm. Crucially, Bulletproof itself isn’t about disability, but rather an attempt to highlight the lack of on-screen representation – and plug the gap. This affectionate documentary tracks the film from preproduction to premiere.

17. They’ll Love Me When I’m Dead (2018)

Orson Welles spent five years shooting what became his final film, The Other Side of the Wind, with three years elapsing before its star – director and sometime actor John Huston – even stepped in front of the camera. After all that, the footage ended up impounded by the Iranian revolutionary government. A version eventually premiered in 2018 and is now on Netflix, along with this scattershot documentary, presented by Alan Cumming, which strings together archive footage, new interviews and typically Wellesian stories of on-set bluffs, tomfoolery and procrastination.

16. Filmmaker: A Diary by George Lucas (1968)

A half-hour snapshot by Lucas of his new buddy Francis Ford Coppola, who is hard at work on his fourth film, The Rain People, and not too shy to argue with his lead actor, Shirley Knight. Contains one choice detail: in preparation for driving across the country shooting this road movie, all the men on the crew, Coppola included, shave off their beards to look more presentable for any hippy-hating officials they might encounter along the way.

15. Boorman and the Devil (2025)

In declining The Exorcist but taking on Exorcist II: The Heretic, John Boorman perhaps displayed a preference for poisoned chalices over champagne flutes. He is candid and good-humoured, if still a little shell-shocked, as he recounts the experience of filming the sequel once derided as “the stupidest major movie ever made”, and the despair that led him to contemplate self-immolation on Hollywood Boulevard. Sand-related illness, a sozzled Richard Burton, locusts and tap-dancing: this has it all.

14. Doomed! The Untold Story of Roger Corman’s The Fantastic Four (2015)

Filmed in a rat-infested studio on sets recycled from the Jurassic Park rip-off Carnosaur, with special effects entrusted to a local outfit called Mr Film, this cheapo superhero adventure was made in a rush to prevent the rights to The Fantastic Four reverting from producer Bernd Eichinger to Marvel. (“That movie was never supposed to be shown to anybody,” said Stan Lee.) This heartening documentary, which shows the crestfallen cast refusing to let their film die, feels even more pertinent after Warner Bros recently shelved some movies as tax write-offs, including Batgirl and Coyote Vs Acme, the latter rescued only by the skin of its teeth.

13. Jodorowsky’s Dune (2013)

In trying to adapt Frank Herbert’s Dune in the mid-1970s, cinematic shaman Alejandro Jodorowsky (Santa Sangre, El Topo) bit off more than he could chew, just as David Lynch would when his version came to painful fruition in 1984. But Frank Pavich’s documentary proves that Jodorowsky’s intention to make “a film that gives LSD hallucinations without taking LSD” was not too fanciful. Among those in his corner were the artist HR Giger, who went on to design the monsters in Alien, and a cast including Salvador Dalí, Mick Jagger and Orson Welles, with the latter being bribed to take part with the promise of having his favourite chef on set.

12. Lost Soul: The Doomed Journey of Richard Stanley’s Island of Dr Moreau (2014)

When the studio New Line tried to ditch South African director Richard Stanley from his own HG Wells adaptation, he asked a warlock called Skip to pull some cosmic strings. That did the trick for a while, helping Stanley to charm the film’s star, Marlon Brando. But black magic was no match for cast member Val Kilmer, who demanded a 40% reduction in his own shooting days, then spent his time on set playing power games. There was nature to contend with, too, in the form of wild animals (a puma pisses on Stanley’s tailored suit) and a hurricane that ravages the location in Cairns, Queensland. Finally replaced by curmudgeonly veteran John Frankenheimer, Stanley refuses to leave Australia, which is when things go from mad to worse.

11. No Frank in Lumberton (1988) / Blue Velvet Revisited (2016)

Two behind-the-scenes Blue Velvet documentaries from one director. Peter Braatz was still a film student when David Lynch, with whom he had been corresponding for several years, invited him to Wilmington, North Carolina in 1985 to chart the making of what would become his twisted masterpiece. Braatz marshalled just under an hour of the resulting Super-8 material into his 1988 documentary, which straddled the line between orthodox and experimental. He then reshaped it into a full-on ambient head-trip for the 86-minute 2016 version, which mixes flickering footage and crisp black-and-white photographs with a woozy score and the voices of Lynch, Dennis Hopper and others to form an ethereal audiovisual collage.

10. The Sweatbox (2002)

Disney had high hopes for Kingdom of the Sun, a Prince and the Pauper-style animated musical drama set in the Inca empire. The studio sent Lion King co-director Roger Allers on a research trip to Peru and commissioned a suite of new songs by Sting. But it was back to the drawing board after a calamitous screening of an early rough cut; Allers and Sting were given the heave-ho, and the movie was retooled as the larky comedy The Emperor’s New Groove. Sting’s wife, Trudie Styler, charts every disastrous step in a documentary that Disney has done its darnedest to suppress .

9. From Darkness to Light (2024)

A 10-a-penny title for an account of a once-in-a-lifetime film-making folly: Jerry Lewis’s abandoned, incomplete 1972 Holocaust drama The Day The Clown Cried . Directing himself as a former clown who entertains children in a concentration camp, Lewis made a misguided bid to be taken seriously. “It was bad work,” he admits here. It wasn’t only the dubious material that defeated the former Nutty Professor: unbeknown to him, the option on the script had expired, rendering the entire project illegal. It was his decision, though, to hire a repentant former concentration camp guard as part of the crew. “He was a human being!” Lewis protests.

8. Poultry in Motion: Truth Is Stranger Than Chicken (2008)

Seventy-odd fans of horror exploitation studio Troma worked unpaid on Poultrygeist: Night of the Chicken Dead while living in a deserted church in a rundown corner of Buffalo, New York, with one cold shower between them. Meanwhile, the chicken-themed zombie flick was shot at a nearby abandoned McDonald’s. This documentary captures all the on-set horror, from the sexually disinhibited auditions to the hourly cast-and-crew bust-ups. Actors walk off, burst into tears and throw punches; a zombie extra accidentally sets himself on fire; and bilious co-director and Troma boss Lloyd Kaufman proves both lackadaisical and tyrannical.

7. Shirkers (2018)

When budding film-maker Sandi Tan met the enigmatic Georges Cardona, he cited Fitzcarraldo as his inspiration and claimed to know crew members from Apocalypse Now. Those pictures – famously troubled productions that spawned their own jaw-dropping documentaries – look like red flags considering what came next: Cardona directed Tan’s indie road movie Shirkers, swallowing up $10,000 of her savings when he ran out of money, then vanished with the resulting 70 reels of unprocessed film. She didn’t see the footage until decades later, when those reels were returned to her by Cardona’s widow. Tan’s sobering 2018 documentary attempts to make sense of the betrayal.

6. The Peddler (2010)

“Good film directors will notice many mistakes,” says prolific camcorder auteur and 67-year-old Santa Claus lookalike Daniel Burmeister. “But I like what I do: making hand-crafted films.” In exchange for a month’s food and accommodation, Burmeister sets up shop in a remote Argentinian village to bring the community together by shooting a movie from one of his own scripts. His budget may be nonexistent but his resourcefulness is boundless: in place of a dolly shot, for instance, he sits on a blanket, camera on his shoulder, while being dragged across the floor. This delightful, deeply humanistic portrait of grassroots DIY cinema has all the charm and idiosyncrasies of a Jared Hess comedy.

5. Lost in La Mancha (2002)

Terry Gilliam was happy to have documentary makers Keith Fulton and Louis Pepe on set for The Man Who Killed Don Quixote after being impressed by The Hamster Factor, their behind-the-scenes film on the making of his earlier 12 Monkeys. The anguished result shows exactly why Quixote was abandoned after six days’ shooting in Spain in September 2000. Takes were rendered unusable by the roar of F16s from a nearby Nato base; Jean Rochefort, co-lead opposite Johnny Depp, fell seriously ill; and the equipment was destroyed by a merciless storm. Gilliam’s on-set catchphrase sums it up: “We’re fucked!” (When Quixote was eventually made in 2018, Fulton and Pepe documented that shoot, too, in He Dreams of Giants .)

4. Henri-Georges Clouzot’s Inferno (2009)

The subgenre of documentaries about unfinished films stretches back to the BBC’s 1965 The Epic That Never Was, which investigated Josef von Sternberg’s planned version of I, Claudius starring Charles Laughton and Merle Oberon. But it reached its apotheosis with Henri-Georges Clouzot’s Inferno, Ruxandra Medrea and Serge Bromberg’s ravishing reflection on an early-1960s Proustian psychological drama from the director of Les Diaboliques. Lavishly funded by Columbia, Clouzot’s vision was impossibly ambitious, with three crews and a trippy array of complicated in-camera special effects. The director, who could not be dissuaded from shooting time-consuming test footage, suffered a heart attack three weeks into the 18-week shoot. The fragments of his vision, cherrypicked here from 15 hours of unseen footage, are intoxicating: where else can you see Romy Schneider covered in glitter, cellophane and olive oil?

3. Burden of Dreams (1982)

Deep in the rainforests of South America, Werner Herzog battles mud and misery, along with his leading man Klaus Kinski, to make Fitzcarraldo, about one man’s dream of building an opera house in the Amazon. Les Blank’s documentary, which is arguably more compelling than the movie it’s about, enables us to watch in disbelief as a film about a lunatic mission turns into one itself. Herzog’s initial footage has to be abandoned when the lead actor, Jason Robards, falls ill with amoebic dysentery and co-star Mick Jagger is needed on a world tour. Up and running again, the production is forced to relocate more than 1,000 miles away due to a border war, while Herzog’s plans to move a steamship up a hillside provide a textbook example of madness eclipsing method.

2. American Movie (1999)

Mark Borchardt, a Milwaukee junkyard poet with a mullet and plateglass specs, may be best suited to factory work or serial killing, according to his brother, but he positively glows with a passion for cinema. Lacking the funds to finish his feature debut, he instead tries to complete a short horror film, Coven, undaunted by his inability to pronounce the title. More Wiseau than Welles, he has optimism and indefatigability to burn. Not to mention a crew of colourful collaborators, including his mother, whom he enlists as an extra despite her protestations that she needs to go shopping; his bleary, poodle-haired pal and former acid-head Mike; and the gnarled, trailer-dwelling Uncle Bill, who needs 30 takes to deliver four lines. Director Chris Smith (who later made the priceless Fyre festival documentary ) rightly portrays Mark as one of cinema’s most inspiring heroes – even if he still hasn’t finished his first feature.

1. Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker’s Apocalypse (1991)

Megadoc, the forthcoming behind-the-scenes film about Francis Ford Coppola’s $120m passion project Megalopolis , is directed by Mike Figgis, though earlier Coppola-related documentaries tended to be family affairs. The director’s late wife, Eleanor, was responsible for Making Marie Antoinette, released later this month, about their daughter Sofia’s 2006 historical fantasia. And it was Eleanor, too, who co-directed the extraordinary Hearts of Darkness, which draws on her 60 hours of footage and 40 hours of audio recordings, as well as her own diaries, all from the turbulent 238-day shooting of Apocalypse Now. The film reveals her husband arguing on set with Dennis Hopper, frantically typing new scenes just moments before the cameras roll, and negotiating with Marlon Brando, who has piled on the pounds but neglected to learn his lines. “I’m thinking of shooting myself,” the director confides. “This is one crisis I can’t pull myself out of.”

content.article_text:
Some photographers light things up. Olivier Metzger looks for what light conceals, and finds it behind a hotel door, a sea-green curtain, the silhouette of Tilda Swinton in an olive suit. Take war as it comes, the French say, “à la guerre comme à la guerre.” Metzger answers in kind: he takes the night as it comes, amber, sodium-lit, haunted by cinema.

Born in Mulhouse in 1973, he first worked as a nurse. Caregiver, then director. At 28 he entered the École nationale supérieure de la photographie (ENSP) in Arles, graduated in 2004 and won the Prix Voies Off at the Rencontres the same year with his series “Data.” Then came Libération , Télérama , Le Monde , The New York Times (assignments, that genre where the subject sets the rules, and the hour too). Metzger slipped a dramaturgy into them, sculpting his images in “a delicate chiaroscuro, often tinged with melancholy.”

David Lynch surfaces quickly in critics’ pieces, and for good reason: in 2012, the filmmaker made the series “Smile (Forever)” his favorite at Paris Photo. A film? A dream? A hotel room? The doubt is maintained, and so is the fiction. Even a doe spotted by chance on a Nevada road ( Bambi, Nevada , 2010) enters it like a fairy tale. The world seems about to come apart, and Metzger lights it so that it holds a moment longer. Publisher Actes Sud introduces him as a “photographer of the strange.”

Then came the loss. On November 2, 2022, Olivier Metzger died in a road accident near Arles, his adopted city. In 2023, the Rencontres asked Éric Reinhardt for a tribute. The writer built his text from 49 songs drawn from the photographer’s Spotify library. 49 songs, 49 years. Three years later, the exhibition extends the echo, and the book, published in June 2026 (128 pages), takes the form of a two-voice dialogue fed by the music that accompanied Metzger. One can read it “as a farewell.” Reinhardt, the friend, wants us to feel an artist working “as if he were photographing his own destiny.” Even on assignment.

“Olivier Metzger, Somewhere and Somehow,” is on view at La Croisière , in Arles Arles, through October 4, 2026. The book Somewhere and Somehow is published by Actes Sud and available for €35.

Out of that chance session came a portrait that would help forge his status as a sex symbol: something carnal and animal emanates from it, a raw physical presence sharpened by the oblique, sovereign light of California."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Greg Gorman, trained in cinematography at the University of Southern California, and Matthew Rolston, discovered by the artist Andy Warhol while still a student at the ArtCenter College of Design in Pasadena, moved in the same creative circles as Herb Ritts, those of a Hollywood in full reinvention. Beyond that community, the three artists shared a singular gift: the ability to turn virtually any individual into an icon."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "To do this, they applied to photography codes as old as art history itself. Court painters relied on costume; religious painters, on light and scale. Herb Ritts photographed the Irish singer Sinead O’Connor with her head tipped back, her shaved skull offered to the light like a sacrament. The photographer liked to strip his subjects of every superfluous ornament to reveal the archetype beneath, treating light like a chisel."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Gorman, for his part, worked close to his subjects: his black-and-white images, tight, intimate, and shadowed, hunted for the spark particular to each gaze, as in his portrait of a young Leonardo DiCaprio. content.article_text:
In 1978, Herb Ritts photographed his friend Richard Gere, then an unknown actor, in a tank top, arms raised, muscles taut. Out of that chance session came a portrait that would help forge his status as a sex symbol: something carnal and animal emanates from it, a raw physical presence sharpened by the oblique, sovereign light of California.

Greg Gorman, trained in cinematography at the University of Southern California, and Matthew Rolston, discovered by the artist Andy Warhol while still a student at the ArtCenter College of Design in Pasadena, moved in the same creative circles as Herb Ritts, those of a Hollywood in full reinvention. Beyond that community, the three artists shared a singular gift: the ability to turn virtually any individual into an icon.

To do this, they applied to photography codes as old as art history itself. Court painters relied on costume; religious painters, on light and scale. Herb Ritts photographed the Irish singer Sinead O’Connor with her head tipped back, her shaved skull offered to the light like a sacrament. The photographer liked to strip his subjects of every superfluous ornament to reveal the archetype beneath, treating light like a chisel.

Gorman, for his part, worked close to his subjects: his black-and-white images, tight, intimate, and shadowed, hunted for the spark particular to each gaze, as in his portrait of a young Leonardo DiCaprio. Rolston, meanwhile, built sets, chose costumes with exacting care, and composed each image by invoking precise pictorial and cinematic references, elevating the portrait to the rank of a small theater, or a film dressing room. Under his lens, a fifteen-year-old Drew Barrymore, her hair cropped short and slicked back, dressed androgynously, recalls the features of a young Elvis Presley.

Vogue and Vanity Fair ‘s design director, Charles Churchward, named this constellation “The School of Los Angeles,” noting that their rise “marked a significant shift in the imaging of celebrity.” Matthew Rolston shares that intuition. As he told Print magazine: “I think glamour — and glamour photography — is a substitute for god and goddess worship. The altar is the photo studio. So the goddess comes to the dressing room like she would’ve come to the preparation chamber of a temple. She’s anointed with oils and potions — that would be the hair and makeup team. It is really the same thing.”

Andy Warhol, the founder of Interview magazine, played the role of go-between in this story. Upon discovering, within its pages, Matthew Rolston’s photo essay on a new generation of Hollywood actors, the inventor of Pop Art wrote in his diary: “Matthew is our best photographer now.” Greg Gorman, for his part, made one of the most striking portraits of Warhol himself: tightly framed, in opaque black sunglasses, his white hair haloed around his head, the New York artist appears as impenetrable there as the celebrities in his own silkscreens.

Magazine covers, album sleeves, music videos, films. The images of Herb Ritts, Greg Gorman, and Matthew Rolston coursed through the visual culture of an entire generation raised on MTV. Rolston traces that lineage himself: “Andy Warhol and Helmut Newton were the architects of the postmodern revival of Hollywood glamour.” Immortalized by Herb Ritts, Cindy Crawford, leaning over k.d. lang in a barber’s chair, her face lathered in shaving cream, moves in for a kiss.

This visual language, sensual and meticulously crafted, has long since outgrown California and the confines of photography itself, taken up the world over, even by reality television’s fleeting stars and influencers in the making. Models, after all, are never in short supply. Greg Gorman put it simply: “In my eyes, everybody is interesting; a celebrity, so to speak, in their own right.”

“The School of Los Angeles: Herb Ritts, Greg Gorman & Matthew Rolston” runs from October 1st through November 28, 2026, at the Fahey/Klein Gallery in Los Angeles. Opening reception: Thursday, October 1st, 2026, 7–9 p.m. Artist talk: Saturday, October 3rd, 2026, 2–4 p.m.

content.article_text:
Realising that the experiences of a whole generation of British-Bangladeshis will soon be lost – and motivated by celebrating the community in the midst of a rising far right – Seema Khalique built a multi-faceted piece of history now on show in London’s Bethnal Green

Seema Khalique’s father Abdul arrived in the UK from Bangladesh in 1956; her mother, Gulnehar, arrived in 1973, after the Bangladesh Liberation War. Abdul Khalique was in the restaurant business, and the family moved to Croydon in the 1970s after buying a restaurant there; later they moved to Eltham, once again following work. It’s a story that speaks of graft and determination, the sheer grit required to start a new life in a new country. But there are also gaps in the narrative. As Khalique’s father grew older, she realised she knew little about his early London years, or what it had been like to arrive in the UK. She realised that he and a whole generation of British Bangladeshis would soon pass away, and with them these experiences would be lost.

And so connecting with 12 individuals – many linked to her father – Khalique spent hours with each of them from 2021 on, listening to their stories, collaborating on their portraits, and looking through their archives. The result is Londoni Memoirs , a still on-going project supported by the National Lottery Heritage Fund, which gathers oral history, archive photos, ephemera, and new images to document Bangaldeshis who settled in Britain in the 1950s-70s. Some, like Khalique, are based in London, others are further afield, landing by luck and the work that was available when they migrated.

“Generally all the participants moved where there was work, so if that meant going to Birmingham, because of the factory trade there, they were in Birmingham,” says Khalique. “There was a massive community in the East End because of the factories there, and that created opportunities for women working from home – they could do sewing and tailoring, and be with the kids. Everyone had a sewing machine. Most people worked six days a week. One of the participants lived in St Albans and his general pattern, when he worked, was to work from four in the morning until four in the afternoon at a factory, then the evening shift at a restaurant.”

By working at this level people managed to set themselves up, says Khalique; many were also sending money to Bangladesh, particularly during the war [in 1971]. “Many people spoke about feeling that they had helped Bangladesh survive,” she says. “Family members didn’t starve because they were able to provide.”

Londoni Memoirs collects some heartbreaking stories, tales of people fleeing burning villages – the only ones to escape – and returning years later, not knowing who they would find alive. Few of the participants had spoken publicly about these experiences before, says Khalique, preferring to move on “though they still carry the trauma”. But Londoni Memoirs also records happier times, Khalique determined not to flatten a range of experiences into a monotone, or many testimonies into a single lumpen mass.

“One participant came from a very affluent family, he came to the UK to study law and his father basically funded him,” she points out. “He lived on the same road as The Beatles, and had these crazy stories about parties where the police would chase everyone away. Others spoke about squatting in London, as a solution to the housing crisis. It was interesting to hear about the parallel lives that were lived at that time, and to hear about not just the struggles that we associate with migration, but the enjoyment that comes from it. Experiencing cold weather, snowball fights, all of it.”

Khalique’s sensitivity shows in her portraits, which she made collaboratively. There’s a sweet photograph of her mother in her garden, wearing a green sari matching the foliage of a Bangladeshi Marrow Plant “which the Bangladeshi grow with pride in the summer months”. Some of the women preferred not to be shown looking straight at the camera though, wary of the sin of idolatry; Khalique has also collected other images, which present other images and do other things. There’s a formal studio portrait of Rajia Yaqub and family, for example, a snap of Makhlisur Rahman standing with his house and a smart car; often taken to send back home, these shots present carefully-constructed images of happiness and prosperity, not everyday trials or tribulations.

Khalique has also collected passport photos and official documentation, including an amazingly glamorous photograph of her mother in a passport due to expire in 1977, and a receipt from the Pakistan Relief Fund for £5, dated in pre-independence 1965 [when £5 was worth about £125 today]. Khalique’s exhibition at Four Corners includes 10-minute videos of the participants speaking; she’s also created transcripts of the videos, and published them in a newspaper. “I know not everyone will sit and watch all the videos,” she says. “So the newspaper was important, and then it can also travel.”

The location of the gallery is important too because, though Khalique still lives in South East London, she wanted to show the work somewhere close to the British-Bangladeshi community; Four Corners is in East London, near the long-standing Banglatown in Whitechapel and Brick Lane. Few of the participants could come to the opening night, as they’re now elderly and some in poor health, but ten were able to come for a special afternoon, and for Khalique that was deeply rewarding. They were wowed by seeing their portraits and archive photographs on the walls, she says, adding she had framed these images to ensure they felt properly honoured.

Khalique also arranged a family workshop in the gallery, allowing children to find out more about British, Bangladeshi, and British-Bangladeshi history, plus issues of representation; these issues have become more important to her, she says, because of hardening far right attitudes, and because she now has kids of her own. “I grew up in a very multicultural area, growing up I never felt racially different,” she says. “It’s only since becoming a mother I’ve realised that, and only in the last few years I’ve experienced it. And that pains me because, while I can fight for myself, my children can’t fight for themselves. So I felt I had to do it for them. I wanted to make work that would celebrate this community.”

Londoni Memoirs by Seema Khalique is on show at Four Corners until 10 October www.fourcornersfilm.co.uk www.seemakhalique.com
