content.title_original: ‘A saving gesture’: the art exhibition spotlighting US prisoners’ creations
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "W ith nearly 2 million people behind bars, America is the global leader in incarceration. When you look at it per capita, we have the highest rate of incarceration of any independent democracy and rank fourth overall in the world, just behind El Salvador, Cuba and Turkmenistan."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Despite these troubling numbers, mass imprisonment is largely invisible. “Our carceral system is something we as a society try to separate out from the everyday,” observes Terra Warren, an associate curator at Grand Rapids Art Museum, Michigan , who alongside curator Jennifer Wcisel brings audiences three solo shows from artists Julie Green, Gary Tyler and Ray Materson. They collectively aim to make us examine more closely just what prisons are doing to our society – and how art can prove transformative to those incarcerated.", "links": [{"text": "Grand Rapids Art Museum, Michigan", "url": "https://www.artmuseumgr.org/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In a major feat, Green’s show collects the artist’s work The Last Supper, rarely exhibited in full. This masterpiece took 22 years to complete and comprises nearly 1,000 plates, each depicting the final meal requested by an individual on death row before their execution. Poignantly, many of the plates are simply inscribed with the word “none”, indicating when an inmate opted not to eat a final meal. One imagines it would be hard to find an appetite under such conditions."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9699f7550d3d04e8fef2567819ed51e7e3ceb6f1/0_360_3600_2880/master/3600.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "White plate with the word “none” painted in the center", "caption": "Julie Green, The Last Supper [Texas 22 May 2002], 2021. Paint on found ceramic plates. Diameter: 6in. Photograph: Courtesy of Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, Bentonville, Arkansas. Gift of The Last Supper Irrevocable Trust", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In centering breaking bread, a practice that’s a cornerstone of our shared humanity, The Last Supper forces audiences to reckon with the contradictions of a system that at once gives the pleasure of consuming a fine meal, yet also dehumanizes and even puts to death those within its grasp. Additionally, the piece opens space for compassion and understanding by giving us a window into the lives of those who are rarely represented in any meaningful way at all."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“There’s one in particular where a prisoner opted to eat vending machine food with their family,” Warren says, recalling plates that particularly stood put in her memory. “There’s another whose mother was allowed to come in and cook their last meal.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Some of the plates also underscore the fact that the state will put to death individuals who are not even aware of what’s happening; one plate indicates that an inmate chose to save some of their last meal for later, not understanding that there would not be a chance to ever eat again. “One of the plates details that a person with an IQ of 61 was executed,” said Warren, indicating someone was put to death in spite of serious mental impairments."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "D eath row figures prominently in the life of Gary Tyler, an author and artist, who in 1974 was charged with the murder of a white teenager when Tyler was 16 years old. When he was convicted by an all-white jury and sentenced to death, he became the youngest person on death row in the United States. The case was marred by police misconduct, and Tyler is now widely considered to have been wrongfully imprisoned."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/1b071f0a91607e5d1e1ad3c9240e3a404aa7e9b8/38_0_1125_900/master/1125.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Quilting fabric embroidered with image of butterfly on open hand", "caption": "Gary Tyler, Fernanda’s Touch, 2025. Quilting fabric, thread and battling. 64in x 68.25in. Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Grand Rapids Art Museum", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Although Tyler was never formally exonerated, he was freed in 2016 following the supreme court ruling in the 2012 Miller v Alabama case, where the court held that it was unconstitutional to adjudicate mandatory sentences of life imprisonment for juvenile defendants.", "links": [{"text": "unconstitutional", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/law/2014/jun/24/minors-life-sentences-despite-us-supreme-court-ban"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While serving four decades in the infamous Angola state prison – known as the Alcatraz of the south and currently the largest maximum-security prison in the United States – Tyler began to make quilts to comfort inmates dying in the prison’s hospice. At first reluctant to work with textiles, he soon saw just how valued his creations were. “I saw that I could help the men in the hospice, so it was something that I warmed up to,” Tyler said. “I realized we were doing something that would last for generations in the family. When our patients passed, the quilt was passed into their family, and it was really moving for me.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/785d39dac35e6c3e893d2b4192fe3b01459f9624/167_0_1666_1333/master/1666.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Man with sewing machine", "caption": "Gary Tyler in his studio. Photograph: Dorian Hill, courtesy of the artist and Library Street Collective", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As Tyler continued making quilts for dying inmates, he developed a perspective that would later inform his transition to making textile art, and that would help him be able to tell his own story through the intricate quilts that he had made for years as an artist. “You realize that that could be you, and it will be you eventually, you’re just as human as the individual you’re taking care of,” he says. “Being a hospital volunteer was one of the greatest things in my life. I never would have thought that I had the creative gene in me.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tyler’s quilts tend to be backgrounded by static colors shot through with rich texture and repeating motifs – flowers in one, abstract tear shapes in another. The scenes they depict are vivid and powerful: a bull smacking over a red table, a man literally struggling under the weight of the world, a child in shackles with their back turned to us."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One work that stands out in Tyler’s mind depicts a moment from the trial, when he was being led away from the courthouse in handcuffs by an escort of police, while a crowd of supporters cheered for him. “I got this surge of energy,” he says. “I wanted to raise my hands in a fist, but I had handcuffs on, with deputies holding my arms, but I still managed to show defiance, that despite what happened I would continue to fight.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "T he Grand Rapids trio is rounded out by a comprehensive museum survey of Ray Materson, the outsider embroidery artist, who developed his signature technique of working with unraveled socks by necessity while serving seven years in prison due to drug addiction."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/0c6b5320fbf039a46f67fec27bb93869786f016a/16_0_614_767/master/614.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Embroidery of medieval scene", "caption": "Ray Materson. Lords and Ladies, 1989. Sock threads. 2.75in x 2in. Photograph: Courtesy of Bob Rennie", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While boxer shorts and bedsheets could supply Materson with plenty of white thread, socks were of special importance to him, as they gave him the colors that he required in order to create intricate scenes. He would spend hours and hours simply getting the dearly needed materials. “Ray said to me one time: ‘Your biggest enemy in prison is the clock,’” said Warren. “For him to be able to spend days and days in this meditative act was such a saving gesture.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Materson’s skills quickly became known to the other inmates, who soon began asking him to make embroidery of loved ones or items such as national flags with great symbolic meaning. content.article_text:
W ith nearly 2 million people behind bars, America is the global leader in incarceration. When you look at it per capita, we have the highest rate of incarceration of any independent democracy and rank fourth overall in the world, just behind El Salvador, Cuba and Turkmenistan.

Despite these troubling numbers, mass imprisonment is largely invisible. “Our carceral system is something we as a society try to separate out from the everyday,” observes Terra Warren, an associate curator at Grand Rapids Art Museum, Michigan , who alongside curator Jennifer Wcisel brings audiences three solo shows from artists Julie Green, Gary Tyler and Ray Materson. They collectively aim to make us examine more closely just what prisons are doing to our society – and how art can prove transformative to those incarcerated.

In a major feat, Green’s show collects the artist’s work The Last Supper, rarely exhibited in full. This masterpiece took 22 years to complete and comprises nearly 1,000 plates, each depicting the final meal requested by an individual on death row before their execution. Poignantly, many of the plates are simply inscribed with the word “none”, indicating when an inmate opted not to eat a final meal. One imagines it would be hard to find an appetite under such conditions.

In centering breaking bread, a practice that’s a cornerstone of our shared humanity, The Last Supper forces audiences to reckon with the contradictions of a system that at once gives the pleasure of consuming a fine meal, yet also dehumanizes and even puts to death those within its grasp. Additionally, the piece opens space for compassion and understanding by giving us a window into the lives of those who are rarely represented in any meaningful way at all.

“There’s one in particular where a prisoner opted to eat vending machine food with their family,” Warren says, recalling plates that particularly stood put in her memory. “There’s another whose mother was allowed to come in and cook their last meal.”

Some of the plates also underscore the fact that the state will put to death individuals who are not even aware of what’s happening; one plate indicates that an inmate chose to save some of their last meal for later, not understanding that there would not be a chance to ever eat again. “One of the plates details that a person with an IQ of 61 was executed,” said Warren, indicating someone was put to death in spite of serious mental impairments.

D eath row figures prominently in the life of Gary Tyler, an author and artist, who in 1974 was charged with the murder of a white teenager when Tyler was 16 years old. When he was convicted by an all-white jury and sentenced to death, he became the youngest person on death row in the United States. The case was marred by police misconduct, and Tyler is now widely considered to have been wrongfully imprisoned.

Although Tyler was never formally exonerated, he was freed in 2016 following the supreme court ruling in the 2012 Miller v Alabama case, where the court held that it was unconstitutional to adjudicate mandatory sentences of life imprisonment for juvenile defendants.

While serving four decades in the infamous Angola state prison – known as the Alcatraz of the south and currently the largest maximum-security prison in the United States – Tyler began to make quilts to comfort inmates dying in the prison’s hospice. At first reluctant to work with textiles, he soon saw just how valued his creations were. “I saw that I could help the men in the hospice, so it was something that I warmed up to,” Tyler said. “I realized we were doing something that would last for generations in the family. When our patients passed, the quilt was passed into their family, and it was really moving for me.”

As Tyler continued making quilts for dying inmates, he developed a perspective that would later inform his transition to making textile art, and that would help him be able to tell his own story through the intricate quilts that he had made for years as an artist. “You realize that that could be you, and it will be you eventually, you’re just as human as the individual you’re taking care of,” he says. “Being a hospital volunteer was one of the greatest things in my life. I never would have thought that I had the creative gene in me.”

Tyler’s quilts tend to be backgrounded by static colors shot through with rich texture and repeating motifs – flowers in one, abstract tear shapes in another. The scenes they depict are vivid and powerful: a bull smacking over a red table, a man literally struggling under the weight of the world, a child in shackles with their back turned to us.

One work that stands out in Tyler’s mind depicts a moment from the trial, when he was being led away from the courthouse in handcuffs by an escort of police, while a crowd of supporters cheered for him. “I got this surge of energy,” he says. “I wanted to raise my hands in a fist, but I had handcuffs on, with deputies holding my arms, but I still managed to show defiance, that despite what happened I would continue to fight.”

T he Grand Rapids trio is rounded out by a comprehensive museum survey of Ray Materson, the outsider embroidery artist, who developed his signature technique of working with unraveled socks by necessity while serving seven years in prison due to drug addiction.

While boxer shorts and bedsheets could supply Materson with plenty of white thread, socks were of special importance to him, as they gave him the colors that he required in order to create intricate scenes. He would spend hours and hours simply getting the dearly needed materials. “Ray said to me one time: ‘Your biggest enemy in prison is the clock,’” said Warren. “For him to be able to spend days and days in this meditative act was such a saving gesture.”

Materson’s skills quickly became known to the other inmates, who soon began asking him to make embroidery of loved ones or items such as national flags with great symbolic meaning. These pieces gave Materson a purpose and allowed the men he created for to experience a sense of identity and selfhood in a profoundly dehumanizing environment.

Life in prison has stuck with Materson, who to this day sources vintage socks like the ones he used while in jail in the 1980s. “Their nylon has the stretchability that he needs in order to work,” explained Warren. His work tends to depict intense scenes, often derived from the likes of Shakespeare, Ibsen and Chekhov, as well as royalty like Queen Victoria and Catherine the Great. While small, often measuring just 2in x 3in, the works are filled with pathos and are a wonder to behold.

“This show brings a lot of shock at the facts of what’s the reality for a lot of people, but they also bring a lot of hope,” said Warren, sharing her hopes that the art on display can both humanize and inspire, as well as show audiences that artistic creation can be transformative for them too. “Ray was on a track of death through his addiction, but because of art his life turned around into something defined by creativity and giving.”

Julie Green: The Last Supper; Gary Tyler: Rebirth and Ray Materson: Metamorphosis are all at Grand Rapids Art Museum from 3 October 2026 until 24 October 2027 (Green) and 3 January 2027 (Tyler, Materson)

ビックリするほど当たるためIMA御用達の占い師・マコが、12星座の今をタロット1枚で運気予報！フォトグラファー清水はるみによるファンタスティックな星座＆大アルカナのヴィジュアルと共に、明るい未来の指針を毎月前・後半でお届けします。

10月前半に思うこと

「床を拭いて運気を2トーン上げる魔法」

10月に入り、秋風が心地よく部屋を吹き抜ける季節になりました。今回のテーマは「お掃除で開運」です！

​我が家にも文明の利器「掃除ロボット」が鎮座しておりますが、秋の運気を一気にブーストさせたい時に私が絶対に譲れない儀式。それは「手作業の雑巾がけ」です。

​便利家電も最高ですが、自分の手で四つん 這いになって床を丁寧に拭き上げると、嘘みたいにその空間が途端に2トーン明るくなった気がするから不思議！​特に力が入るのが、全ての運気がなだれ込んでくる玄関です。

​ここで登場するのが、前回ご紹介したあの最強アイテム。そう、レモンとローズマリーを煮出した特製ハーブ液！そこに塩を勢いよくぶち込んで（ここ大事！）雑巾を絞り、一心不乱に玄関のたたきを拭き上げるのです。

​邪気を弾き飛ばすレモン、トラウマや停滞感を断ち切るローズマリー、そして強力な祓いパワーを持つ塩。この「開運・三種の神器」をしみ込ませた雑巾で磨き上げると、玄関に溜まった澱んだ気が一瞬で吹き飛び、空間の密度が変わるのを肌で感じます。

​仕上げのポイントはしっかり乾拭きすること！水分を残さないことで、ツヤと良い気がバチッと定着します。

​占いでも運は足元から入ると言いますが、床や玄関を磨くことは、自分自身の土台を整えることそのもの。

​秋の夜長、お気に入りのハーブ塩水で玄関を磨き上げて、明るくなったお家で最高にツイてる秋を迎えに行きませんか？

La actriz de Verity reveló una tierna anécdota familiar y explicó por qué Lionel Messi es “un puente hacia tantas cosas maravillosas”.

Lionel Messi volvió a aparecer en una historia inesperada que llega desde Hollywood. Esta vez, el protagonista indirecto fue el hijo de Anne Hathaway , quien encontró en el capitán argentino la clave para romper el hielo y comenzar una nueva amistad.

La actriz contó la divertida anécdota durante una entrevista realizada en el marco de la promoción de Verity , el thriller psicológico que protagoniza junto a Dakota Johnson y Josh Hartnett .

La pregunta sobre el astro que cambió todo

Hathaway explicó que su hijo estaba conociendo a otro niño, pero ninguno de los dos encontraba la manera de comenzar una conversación. “Los chicos pueden ser tímidos alrededor de otros. Son solo niños y no saben de qué hablar”, contó la actriz al recordar la situación.

Fue entonces cuando decidió intervenir con una pregunta que, inesperadamente, funcionó a la perfección: “¿Te gusta Messi?” . La respuesta fue afirmativa. El otro niño dijo que sí y el hijo de Hathaway rápidamente se sumó: “Me encanta Messi” .

A partir de ese momento, todo cambió. Según relató la actriz, los dos chicos encontraron un punto en común y terminaron convirtiéndose en grandes amigos. Para Hathaway, la historia demuestra el enorme poder que tiene la figura del futbolista argentino incluso entre los más chicos.

Te puede interesar

Lionel Messi y ¿su guiño? a Harry Potter en su despedida de la selección Argentina

¿Quién es quién en La Odisea de Christopher Nolan?

“ Es un puente hacia tantas cosas. Un puente para tantas cosas maravillosas ” , expresó la actriz al hablar del futbolista.

La actriz lo destacó como embajador

La anécdota surgió después de que Hathaway comenzara a hablar sobre su vínculo con la Argentina.

Durante la entrevista, la actriz recordó también su encuentro con Joaquín Furriel en Shanghái. Ambos coincidieron en 2024 durante un evento de Moncler, marca de lujo de la que son embajadores. En aquella oportunidad, Furriel había aprovechado para hablarle sobre la Argentina e incluso invitarla a conocer el país.

Cuando le preguntaron si el actor había hecho un buen trabajo promocionando nuestro país, Hathaway respondió que la Argentina tiene “tantos embajadores increíbles”. Entre ellos mencionó al polista Nacho Figueras y, naturalmente, al fútbol argentino. “Tienen a su equipo de fútbol entero. Tienen a Messi” , destacó la actriz.

La referencia al rosarino derivó entonces en la particular historia de su hijo, que terminó demostrando de una manera muy sencilla el alcance internacional de la figura del capitán argentino.

También habló de la Argentina

No es la primera vez que Hathaway tiene un acercamiento público con la cultura argentina y latinoamericana.

Durante la promoción de El diablo viste a la moda 2 , la actriz protagonizó junto a Meryl Streep un divertido momento en México al bailar Cómo te voy a olvidar , uno de los grandes clásicos de Los Ángeles Azules.

Ahora, con Verity como nuevo proyecto, volvió a referirse a la Argentina y a algunas de sus figuras más reconocidas. En la misma entrevista, Dakota Johnson también habló de Buenos Aires y contó que visitó la ciudad en varias oportunidades. Josh Hartnett , en cambio, reconoció que todavía no conoce el país, aunque manifestó sus ganas de hacerlo.

content.article_text:
Toiletpaper Comes Back for Seconds

The cult magazine by artist Maurizio Cattelan and photographer Pierpaolo Ferrari makes its return this autumn with Damiani Books, bringing a new issue of images as inventive as they are sharp, and an exhibition in Shenzhen, China.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Toiletpaper.

The 21st edition of Toiletpaper opens with a cover that conjures Martin Parr’s grotesque vision of summer leisure and the streak of bad taste that is the magazine’s hallmark. An elderly woman photographed from behind, blue swimsuit, pink plastic bag on her arm: her scarlet back reveals, in negative, a smiley face of unburned skin. Maurizio Cattelan, iconoclastic provocateur of the contemporary art world, and Pierpaolo Ferrari, art director whose practice blends fashion, advertising and surrealism, staged every inch of it.

The editorial venture was born of their first collaboration for W Magazine in 2009. “We had so much fun, we said, why don’t we do more of this?” Maurizio Cattelan told The New Yorker in 2011. Toiletpaper launched the following year: not a word, not an advertisement. Every image is built entirely in camera, meticulously staged tableaux vivants with saturated chromatism that subvert the codes of advertising, fashion and cinema.

“We keep homing in on what a Toiletpaper image is. Like distilling a perfume. It’s not about one particular style or time frame; what makes them Toiletpaper is a special twist. An uncanny ambiguity,” Maurizio Cattelan told The New Yorker in the same interview. In this edition, a monkey wrench locks itself around an ear, a fuchsia stiletto brims with a banana split in an equivocal nod to food porn, and a chef’s knife is held upside down, its bare blade turned toward the very hand that brandishes it: chic, precise and sovereignly unsettling.

Published three years after its predecessor, the issue is accompanied by an exhibition at the Fotografiska museum in Shenzhen, China, and a limited-edition 2027 calendar created with German photographer Ellen von Unwerth, high priestess of fashion and glamour photography.

Toiletpaper Magazine 21 , by Maurizio Cattelan and Pierpaolo Ferrari, is published by Damiani Books , 40 pages, softcover, $20. “ToiletFotoPaperGrafiska” , Toiletpaper’s first exhibition in China, runs from October 1st, 2026 to March 14, 2027 at Fotografiska Shenzhen .

content.title_original: As pessoas são lindas de costas
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ensaios", "links": [{"text": "Ensaios", "url": "https://revistazum.com.br/category/ensaios/"}]}, {"type": "heading", "text": "As pessoas são lindas de costas"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Pasta_PB_Orig_4_190719_1877.png?resize=1024%2C684&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Não conheci Carlos Moreira pessoalmente. Ele morreu em junho de 2020, e eu só chegaria ao seu arquivo no ano seguinte. Em setembro de 2026 Carlos faria noventa anos. Conhecê-lo, portanto, foi uma operação às avessas. Não pela pessoa, mas pelo vasto material acervado, pela caligrafia miúda nas jaquetas dos negativos, pelos desenhos delicados nas caixas, por aquilo que o olhar dele decidiu guardar ao longo da vida. É uma forma estranha de intimidade, construída de trás para frente."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Há coisas que só um arquivo conta. A pessoa viva ensaia a pose, escolhe o que mostrar. O arquivo guarda também o descuido, a repetição, a obsessão não confessada, aquilo que se fez tantas vezes que deixou de se perceber que fazia. Uma pessoa pode levar uma vida sem saber o que a move, mas seu arquivo sabe."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Fui convidado, com o historiador e conservador Rafael Sousa, para organizar, descrever e diagnosticar o conjunto de documentos e fotografias, batizado ali de Fundo Carlos Moreira, que os herdeiros Pedro Antunes e Regina Martins decidiram tratar como um todo indivisível. Era um trabalho técnico antes de ser qualquer outra coisa. Havia normas a seguir, uma planilha a alimentar campo a campo, uma massa documental a contar, medir e descrever. O Fundo Carlos Moreira era composto de seu arquivo pessoal tanto quanto de sua obra pública e conhecida. Um arquivo pessoal é a reunião natural do que uma pessoa acumula ao longo da vida, e descrevê-lo é fixar a identidade de cada documento a quem o gerou. Parte importante do trabalho era, então, garantir que Carlos permanecesse inteiro, reconhecível, pesquisável."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/capa-P9307097.png?resize=1024%2C683&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Os números dão a dimensão do que tínhamos diante de nós. Eram cerca de 230 mil fotogramas em filme 35mm, 500 folhas de contato em P&B, quase 3 mil ampliações feitas dos negativos P&B, dos anos 1960 ao fim da década de 1980, 25 cadernos de artista e um repositório digital que, descontadas as redundâncias, deveria guardar entre 520 e 600 mil imagens únicas. Mas seria enganoso imaginar esse material largado. Quando chegamos, boa parte do acervo já vinha recebendo cuidado havia tempo. Os cerca de 150 mil fotogramas coloridos das décadas seguintes já tinham sido acondicionados em caixas próprias e indexados num sistema; e os negativos em preto e branco, antes guardados em caixas de papel fotográfico reaproveitadas, haviam sido transferidos para folhas de printfile reunidas em fichários, com as respectivas folhas de contato. Era um trabalho de conservação feito por iniciativa de quem zelava pelo arquivo, muito antes de qualquer ideia de doação. E, na origem de tudo, havia um gesto do próprio Carlos, o detalhe que ainda me comove. Cada tira de cinco ou seis negativos ia num invólucro que ele mesmo recortava de papel de calculadora antiga, com a data e o lugar anotados à mão do lado de fora. Um arquivo reunido com esmero e, ainda assim, nunca revisitado por ele. “O dia em que eu me voltar para meu arquivo eu serei um fotógrafo morto”, dizia."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "O Carlos que conheci nesse mergulho era, antes de tudo, um homem de uma produtividade assombrosa. Rolos e rolos disparados numa única manhã, na caminhada até o centro, num almoço de família com o pai e a mãe, numa viagem ao litoral. Perto de um milhão de imagens, somando o analógico e o digital. E, porque fotografava assim, sem parar, era possível reconstituir passo a passo, rua a rua, o trajeto que ele fazia de sua casa, na Barra Funda, até o centro velho da cidade; ou cada parada e cada esquina de uma tarde na Paulista; ou os dias inteiros de uma viagem a Buenos Aires. O arquivo guardava percursos principalmente de São Paulo, uma cidade caminhada e recaminhada : o mesmo homem passando pelos mesmos lugares ao longo de décadas, deixando na película o rastro exato de seus pés. Além do caçador de instantes na rua, havia o trabalhador paciente da imagem, o artista plástico, o poeta visual. Ele editava, sequenciando fotografias em pequenos cadernos, ensaiando narrativas, testando o que uma imagem passa a dizer quando é colocada ao lado de outra. Alguns de seus cadernos de artista eram feitos de agendas comuns, onde ele colava impressões que fazia em casa e, aqui e ali, desenhava e adornava suas páginas."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Carlos foi preto e branco e foi cor. Analógico e digital. Foi fotógrafo de rua, e foi o fotógrafo afetivo, de família. Aliás, é preciso dizer com franqueza que conhecemos muito pouco do Carlos. Sua obra pública é, talvez, uma fração ínfima do que o acervo revela. Deixou ainda ao menos dois bonecos de livro prontos. Um, o mais recente, é uma desconstrução ruidosa de Buenos Aires, realizada em 2017, em sua última viagem à Argentina; o outro, um mergulho íntimo, quase tátil, feito de pequenos objetos dispostos entre porta-retratos e badulaques. Há também uma versão ampliada do Livro Branco, sua primeira publicação, de 1977. Mas nada disso é o Carlos que se conhece."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Havia, ainda, camadas que eu mal comecei a conhecer. A avó, Rosa Funchal, que estudou pintura na Itália em 1907, foi uma grande influência para Carlos. É em parte a ela que ele deve, ainda na infância, o gosto pelo desenho, pelos livros de capa de couro e pela arte. A bisavó, Nhá Laura, negra escravizada e depois alforriada. A herança negra que Carlos passou a vida buscando reconciliar, aproximando-se nos últimos anos do Candomblé e reconhecendo-se filho de Xangó."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Um homem inteiro cabe num arquivo, se soubermos onde procurar, ainda que nenhum campo de planilha, por mais bem preenchido, dê conta disso. A descrição fixa datas, suportes, estados de conservação, inclusive os negativos atacados pela síndrome do vinagre, que anunciam pelo cheiro o próprio adeus. Mas o afeto que atravessa um acervo escapa dos campos descritivos."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Foi ali, entre uma tira de filme e outra, que a figura apareceu."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Pasta_PB_Orig_6_190729_3110.png?resize=1024%2C680&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Um senhor. Sempre de costas. De terno, às vezes com um jornal debaixo do braço, meio fora do tempo, como se tivesse escapado das primeiras décadas do século XX e caminhasse, desavisado, pela metrópole. Ele reaparecia. Ora de chapéu, ora sem, sempre elegante. Não era, nunca, a mesma pessoa. Eram homens diferentes, flagrados em ruas diferentes, em anos diferentes. Ensaios

As pessoas são lindas de costas

Não conheci Carlos Moreira pessoalmente. Ele morreu em junho de 2020, e eu só chegaria ao seu arquivo no ano seguinte. Em setembro de 2026 Carlos faria noventa anos. Conhecê-lo, portanto, foi uma operação às avessas. Não pela pessoa, mas pelo vasto material acervado, pela caligrafia miúda nas jaquetas dos negativos, pelos desenhos delicados nas caixas, por aquilo que o olhar dele decidiu guardar ao longo da vida. É uma forma estranha de intimidade, construída de trás para frente.

Há coisas que só um arquivo conta. A pessoa viva ensaia a pose, escolhe o que mostrar. O arquivo guarda também o descuido, a repetição, a obsessão não confessada, aquilo que se fez tantas vezes que deixou de se perceber que fazia. Uma pessoa pode levar uma vida sem saber o que a move, mas seu arquivo sabe.

Fui convidado, com o historiador e conservador Rafael Sousa, para organizar, descrever e diagnosticar o conjunto de documentos e fotografias, batizado ali de Fundo Carlos Moreira, que os herdeiros Pedro Antunes e Regina Martins decidiram tratar como um todo indivisível. Era um trabalho técnico antes de ser qualquer outra coisa. Havia normas a seguir, uma planilha a alimentar campo a campo, uma massa documental a contar, medir e descrever. O Fundo Carlos Moreira era composto de seu arquivo pessoal tanto quanto de sua obra pública e conhecida. Um arquivo pessoal é a reunião natural do que uma pessoa acumula ao longo da vida, e descrevê-lo é fixar a identidade de cada documento a quem o gerou. Parte importante do trabalho era, então, garantir que Carlos permanecesse inteiro, reconhecível, pesquisável.

Os números dão a dimensão do que tínhamos diante de nós. Eram cerca de 230 mil fotogramas em filme 35mm, 500 folhas de contato em P&B, quase 3 mil ampliações feitas dos negativos P&B, dos anos 1960 ao fim da década de 1980, 25 cadernos de artista e um repositório digital que, descontadas as redundâncias, deveria guardar entre 520 e 600 mil imagens únicas. Mas seria enganoso imaginar esse material largado. Quando chegamos, boa parte do acervo já vinha recebendo cuidado havia tempo. Os cerca de 150 mil fotogramas coloridos das décadas seguintes já tinham sido acondicionados em caixas próprias e indexados num sistema; e os negativos em preto e branco, antes guardados em caixas de papel fotográfico reaproveitadas, haviam sido transferidos para folhas de printfile reunidas em fichários, com as respectivas folhas de contato. Era um trabalho de conservação feito por iniciativa de quem zelava pelo arquivo, muito antes de qualquer ideia de doação. E, na origem de tudo, havia um gesto do próprio Carlos, o detalhe que ainda me comove. Cada tira de cinco ou seis negativos ia num invólucro que ele mesmo recortava de papel de calculadora antiga, com a data e o lugar anotados à mão do lado de fora. Um arquivo reunido com esmero e, ainda assim, nunca revisitado por ele. “O dia em que eu me voltar para meu arquivo eu serei um fotógrafo morto”, dizia.

O Carlos que conheci nesse mergulho era, antes de tudo, um homem de uma produtividade assombrosa. Rolos e rolos disparados numa única manhã, na caminhada até o centro, num almoço de família com o pai e a mãe, numa viagem ao litoral. Perto de um milhão de imagens, somando o analógico e o digital. E, porque fotografava assim, sem parar, era possível reconstituir passo a passo, rua a rua, o trajeto que ele fazia de sua casa, na Barra Funda, até o centro velho da cidade; ou cada parada e cada esquina de uma tarde na Paulista; ou os dias inteiros de uma viagem a Buenos Aires. O arquivo guardava percursos principalmente de São Paulo, uma cidade caminhada e recaminhada : o mesmo homem passando pelos mesmos lugares ao longo de décadas, deixando na película o rastro exato de seus pés. Além do caçador de instantes na rua, havia o trabalhador paciente da imagem, o artista plástico, o poeta visual. Ele editava, sequenciando fotografias em pequenos cadernos, ensaiando narrativas, testando o que uma imagem passa a dizer quando é colocada ao lado de outra. Alguns de seus cadernos de artista eram feitos de agendas comuns, onde ele colava impressões que fazia em casa e, aqui e ali, desenhava e adornava suas páginas.

Carlos foi preto e branco e foi cor. Analógico e digital. Foi fotógrafo de rua, e foi o fotógrafo afetivo, de família. Aliás, é preciso dizer com franqueza que conhecemos muito pouco do Carlos. Sua obra pública é, talvez, uma fração ínfima do que o acervo revela. Deixou ainda ao menos dois bonecos de livro prontos. Um, o mais recente, é uma desconstrução ruidosa de Buenos Aires, realizada em 2017, em sua última viagem à Argentina; o outro, um mergulho íntimo, quase tátil, feito de pequenos objetos dispostos entre porta-retratos e badulaques. Há também uma versão ampliada do Livro Branco, sua primeira publicação, de 1977. Mas nada disso é o Carlos que se conhece.

Havia, ainda, camadas que eu mal comecei a conhecer. A avó, Rosa Funchal, que estudou pintura na Itália em 1907, foi uma grande influência para Carlos. É em parte a ela que ele deve, ainda na infância, o gosto pelo desenho, pelos livros de capa de couro e pela arte. A bisavó, Nhá Laura, negra escravizada e depois alforriada. A herança negra que Carlos passou a vida buscando reconciliar, aproximando-se nos últimos anos do Candomblé e reconhecendo-se filho de Xangó.

Um homem inteiro cabe num arquivo, se soubermos onde procurar, ainda que nenhum campo de planilha, por mais bem preenchido, dê conta disso. A descrição fixa datas, suportes, estados de conservação, inclusive os negativos atacados pela síndrome do vinagre, que anunciam pelo cheiro o próprio adeus. Um senhor. Sempre de costas. A figura de costas é uma imagem que aponta para fora de si para um destino que não veremos.

Ismail também escreveu sobre as paisagens de Carlos, da atenção quase religiosa que ele dedicava a um canto desgastado da cidade ou a uma figura humana imóvel. Mas acredito que a expressão vale para o arquivo inteiro. Para além da proeza do instante, o que resta na imagem de Carlos Moreira é a reconciliação. A cidade que ele tomava como sua; os personagens silenciosos (e aqueles senhores de costas) que fotografava, invisível no meio do movimento.

Houve, ainda, além da descrição, um outro gesto de guarda. Durante o trabalho, fiz três longas entrevistas, com Pedro Antunes e Regina Martins, os herdeiros, e com Rita Toledo Piza, a amiga que o empurrou para a fotografia e editou seu primeiro livro. São quase quatro horas de conversa, hoje também parte do fundo. Três retratos falados de um mesmo homem, por quem o acompanhou em campos distintos da vida. Somadas aos negativos, às caixas, aos cadernos, essas vozes ainda são apenas um começo.

Terminado o trabalho, o Fundo Carlos Moreira seguiu seu destino. Hoje está sob a guarda do Instituto Moreira Salles, instituição preparada para conservá-lo, catalogá-lo e fazê-lo circular, que é o que garante que uma obra permaneça viva. Cumpri, com Rafael e com os herdeiros, a parte que me cabia — a de organizar a partida, de deixar o conjunto arrumado e pesquisável para que outros continuem, agora, a catalogação até o último documento. É um trabalho que não acaba. Um arquivo dessa dimensão é sempre uma obra em aberto.

Carlos, afinal, recusou a última palavra sobre si. Não revia as próprias fotos, abria as gavetas, mas não se debruçava sobre elas. Nosso trabalho foi consciente dessa recusa. Não pretendíamos exaurir o Fundo Carlos Moreira, mas fazer dele um ponto de partida. Como um retrato tomado à distância adequada, que deixasse ver o conjunto da obra ainda que não todos os detalhes e – valendo-me de um clichê – ligeiramente fora de foco, mas no instante decisivo. Gosto de pensar que Carlos, com o humor que todos lhe atribuem, acharia graça em ser fotografado assim, de longe, por quem chegou tarde demais para lhe pedir que virasse de frente.

De tudo, levo comigo aquele senhor de costas. Sigo encontrando com ele quando ando pelo centro de São Paulo, pela Praça Ramos, pelo Viaduto do Chá, e vejo passar um homem apressado, de passo firme, que atravessa a rua sem olhar para ninguém. Por um instante ele é o pai de Carlos, no instante seguinte é o próprio Carlos, invisível na multidão. O homem de costas segue à nossa frente. E nós, enfim, começamos a segui-lo. ///

Felipe Garofalo é pesquisador, mestre e doutorando em História da Arte pela ECA/USP. Sua pesquisa investiga a fotografia brasileira e latino-americana e suas relações com memória e cidadania cultural. Atua também como curador e escreve regularmente sobre fotografia, aproximando a reflexão acadêmica da circulação pública das imagens. Recentemente, assinou a curadoria de Mkumba , de Gui Christ, para a edição de 2025 do Festival Foto em Pauta, em Tiradentes, e textos para o livro Parada , de Iatã Cannabrava, e para a exposição Suspensão , de Pedro Arieta. Seu trabalho se move entre a universidade, a crítica e a gestão cultural, sempre a partir da fotografia como campo de pensamento.

content.article_text:
Girls on the Edge of the American Dream

Belgian photographer Eva Verbeeck traveled across the United States to photograph, with a large format camera, more than four hundred girls between the ages of 8 and 18. America’s Girls, On the Edge of a Dream grew out of the encounter between the image she had as a young girl of the “girl next door” and the true face of America: plural, elusive, impossible to pin down.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Eva Verbeeck .

Eva Verbeeck grew up in Tessenderlo, a small town in northern Belgium where social life revolved around “a central square with a church, a Monday farmers’ market and a country fair held twice a year.” She found her escape dreaming of America through films, TV shows and comic books. The American girl played the lead role, whether cheerleader, goth, beauty queen or punk at heart.

The artist asked each young woman to bring whatever she is passionate about or finds inspiring. One poses with her horse, another with her electric guitar, a third performs CPR on a training dummy. Many arrive in sportswear.

The slowness of the large format process creates between them and the photographer “a space of conversation, vulnerability and trust.” Against the digital selfie, instantaneous and carefully curated, these portraits insist on analogue film and the gaze of an outsider looking in.

Uniforms and costumes only tell part of the story: behind the chosen outfits and accessories, the faces, often serious, slip free of any expected role. These moments of intimacy lead the images to “unintentionally describe something touching.” For if, online, photography has become for these girls “a language of projection and wish fulfillment,” the large format camera imposes a truth that escapes all staging.

In Ithaca, a fifteen-year-old swimmer shares with the photographer a personal essay on sexism and feminism. Something shifts: “we cared about the same things and had a responsibility to be heard.” America’s Girls , she adds, is “shaped by the courage and vulnerability of each girl who chose to be seen.” On the edge of the dream, they seem now to be waiting for America to keep its promises.

America’s Girls, On the Edge of a Dream by Eva Verbeeck is published by GOST Books (2026).

content.article_text:
田中久貴による写真展「大廈 The Buildings, Mansions.」が、2026年10月13日から18日まで大阪・心斎橋のギャラリー・ソラリスで開催される。

タイトルの「大廈」とは、中国語でビルや大きな建物を意味する言葉。本作で田中が向き合ったのは、2025年8月の香港だ。地下鉄やトラムを乗り継ぎ、高温多湿の街を歩きながら、建て増しと積層を繰り返す高層住宅や、その窓から突き出すエアコンの室外機、ベランダのない窓辺に干された洗濯物など、都市に刻まれた日常の光景を撮影した。かつて香港のイメージを形づくっていた無数のネオンサインは減少し、九龍寨城は公園となり、啓徳空港もすでに閉鎖されている。田中がカメラを向けるのは、そうした過去の香港へのノスタルジーというより、変貌を続ける都市の現在だ。隙間なく林立する巨大な集合住宅を見上げながら、そのスケールとは裏腹に感じられる「せせこましさ」や、建築の表面から漏れ出す生活の痕跡をモノクロームの画面へと取り込んでいく。

田中はステートメントで、大廈から「冷徹な眼で凝視」される感覚について記している。都市を一方的に観察するのではなく、自らもまた都市から見返される存在として身を置き、そこへ飛び込んでくる「日常としての香港」を受け入れる。その視線の往復から、建築物そのものだけでなく、そこに暮らす人々の存在や時間が浮かび上がる。

本作は2026年、文芸社「写真集大賞」で最優秀賞を受賞。同名写真集『大廈』として9月15日に刊行された。本展では写真集に収められた作品から16点を展示する。

In Dave Clarke’s photographs, on show until the end of September at Jardin21 in Paris, the compositions are raw, the monochromes contrasted, the grain powerful. Nicknamed “The Baron of Techno”, the DJ, producer and remixer has worked with Depeche Mode, The Chemical Brothers and Placebo. He first tried photography in his youth, borrowing his father’s old camera. “But film was expensive, and developing it even more so. How do scene photographers manage to impose their aesthetic, their own writing, when they capture the essence of an artist whose work already exists? Passionate about music, Jessica Attia and David Fitt have, like Dave Clarke, made the music scene their favorite space of expression. In the whirl of concerts and festivals, in the studio right beside the performers, or simply around a street corner, they turn composers and their fans into their preferred subjects. They capture an atmosphere, a sensibility, while preserving their singularity. It is a balancing act they have learned to master."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/img-6197-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/l12-2x3-f50-70-do01000388-copy-731x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/img-7940-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Forging Bonds"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I see my music and my photography as art forms that come together and symbolize my interpretation of the world, my need to try to understand it. The link between the two media seems obvious to him: “Eyes and ears are connected to the brain, so trying to separate their creative processes almost seems like an oxymoron,” he admits."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For Jessica Attia too, music is a binding thread, a necessary source of inspiration for her visual research. “It is constantly present in my mind and always finds a place in my images,” she confides. A devotee of Polaroid and analog film, the young photographer has already had the biggest names of the scene in front of her lens, among them Billie Eilish, Post Malone and DJ Snake. Their universes differ, yet she approaches every encounter the same way: fully immersed. “I think there is a part of truth, a part of themselves in their music, even if it isn’t the whole of who they are. That is why, as an artist, I have to listen to everything, feel their compositions, understand their creation,” she continues."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/3-ibrahim-mcginty-1024x679.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/4-jam-session-1024x679.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/1-billie-eilish-1024x684.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It was by “hanging around concerts all the time” that David Fitt made a place for himself in the rock and metal scene. “When I started getting interested in it, a photographer lent me his second camera body so I could experiment. I gave the images to the bands and, little by little, I became known,” he recalls. He often initiates the meetings with the artists he photographs, and considers himself lucky: “I work 90% of the time with people whose music I love,” he says. It is a starting point that allows him to build ties with those he admires. “I feel very privileged to be a collaborator, a fan and a friend to them all at once,” he admits. For him, such prior knowledge is essential: when you are already steeped in an artist’s compositions, it becomes easy to summon them through images."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Letting an Identity Emerge"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But how, as a photographer, do you resist the urge to disappear? content.article_text:
In the street, two silhouettes advance, wearing studded belts, sunglasses, leather biker jackets and torn tights. Further on, a couple kiss, their mohawks and tattoos matching. In Dave Clarke’s photographs, on show until the end of September at Jardin21 in Paris, the compositions are raw, the monochromes contrasted, the grain powerful. Nicknamed “The Baron of Techno”, the DJ, producer and remixer has worked with Depeche Mode, The Chemical Brothers and Placebo. He first tried photography in his youth, borrowing his father’s old camera. “But film was expensive, and developing it even more so. So I spent my pocket money on 45s and tapes instead, because you could always ‘develop’ those live, without waiting for a result, or record over them if you got it wrong,” he continues.

An emblematic figure of the techno scene, he draws inspiration from “gothic atmospheres, monochrome punk, soundscapes”, travels to many cities and gladly gets lost on foot. These experiences once again lead Clarke toward visual experimentation, a new way of translating the emotions he feels through sound. But how do the two media feed each other? How do scene photographers manage to impose their aesthetic, their own writing, when they capture the essence of an artist whose work already exists? Passionate about music, Jessica Attia and David Fitt have, like Dave Clarke, made the music scene their favorite space of expression. In the whirl of concerts and festivals, in the studio right beside the performers, or simply around a street corner, they turn composers and their fans into their preferred subjects. They capture an atmosphere, a sensibility, while preserving their singularity. It is a balancing act they have learned to master.

Forging Bonds

“I see my music and my photography as art forms that come together and symbolize my interpretation of the world, my need to try to understand it. I would say music makes me want to shoot, and shooting lets me empty my hyperactive mind. It’s a kind of zen,” Dave Clarke explains. The link between the two media seems obvious to him: “Eyes and ears are connected to the brain, so trying to separate their creative processes almost seems like an oxymoron,” he admits.

For Jessica Attia too, music is a binding thread, a necessary source of inspiration for her visual research. “It is constantly present in my mind and always finds a place in my images,” she confides. A devotee of Polaroid and analog film, the young photographer has already had the biggest names of the scene in front of her lens, among them Billie Eilish, Post Malone and DJ Snake. Their universes differ, yet she approaches every encounter the same way: fully immersed. “I think there is a part of truth, a part of themselves in their music, even if it isn’t the whole of who they are. That is why, as an artist, I have to listen to everything, feel their compositions, understand their creation,” she continues.

It was by “hanging around concerts all the time” that David Fitt made a place for himself in the rock and metal scene. “When I started getting interested in it, a photographer lent me his second camera body so I could experiment. I gave the images to the bands and, little by little, I became known,” he recalls. He often initiates the meetings with the artists he photographs, and considers himself lucky: “I work 90% of the time with people whose music I love,” he says. It is a starting point that allows him to build ties with those he admires. “I feel very privileged to be a collaborator, a fan and a friend to them all at once,” he admits. For him, such prior knowledge is essential: when you are already steeped in an artist’s compositions, it becomes easy to summon them through images.

Letting an Identity Emerge

But how, as a photographer, do you resist the urge to disappear? How do you reconcile two artistic representations? For Jessica Attia, everything comes down to connection: “I want to draw them somewhere they don’t expect to go. That’s where my own vision can take over. If I fully respect their identity, my emotional filter kicks in once we’re in the same room. It’s a kind of sharing: their world and their energy through my prism,” she explains.

David Fitt, for his part, does extensive research, looks at existing visuals, discovers who made them and asks questions to grasp what the band wants. “I also tell myself that if they come to me, it’s so that I make their universe my own,” he admits. He aims to combine the aesthetic of his subjects with his own language. In the end, the pictures fit together like pieces of a puzzle from which a global identity emerges. In Jessica Attia’s work, nearly all the details vanish into the penumbra, chiaroscuros turn abstract, and blurs summon an atmosphere, a mood, rather than a constructed narrative. In David Fitt’s portraits, colored halos set the scene, and enhance or conceal bodies and features. It is a dark, dreamlike universe from which the artists emerge as spectral, almost fantastical figures. “You have to be able to feel the atmosphere visually, or at least the image should show a facet that the music doesn’t give us,” he concludes. “Putting a face to a name makes a project more human, deeper, more compelling, all the more so at a time when AI is sweeping in.”

More information on Dave Clarke , David Fitt and Jessica Attia on their respective websites.

content.article_text:
27,846 photographs, 144 countries, and the top prize, worth 6,000 euros, went to a bathroom appliance: the hairdryer. Hairdryers, rather, held aloft at arm’s length by young women who fled Afghanistan. “The Cut” by Silvia Alessi was named Peace Image of the Year 2026 before a packed hall, in the Wappensaal of City Hall, where city councillor Alexandra Rezaei represented the mayor, Michael Ludwig.

A forbidden trade

In power since August 2021, the Taliban have also closed beauty salons to women. It was one of the last trades still open to them, and their hair, incidentally, disappears under the headscarf anyway. What their country refuses them, these young exiles now learn in Pakistan, in classrooms equipped with mirrors, hairdressing tools and mannequins.

Juror Peter-Matthias Gaede summed it up in his tribute: every hairdryer becomes a weapon for self-determination, visibility and the right to choose a profession. The word is strong, perhaps too strong for an image whose charm lies in its lightness. Sand, garnet and rust-coloured headscarves stand out against a grey wall, the cables hang like vines, and the half-masked faces look all the more directly at the camera. The symbolism is a little heavy-handed, but the insolence of the raised arms saves it from slogan. The photographer also received the prize for best single image, 1,000 euros provided by the Austrian Photographic Society (PHG).

In an earlier life, Silvia Alessi styled hair for a living. Born in Brescia in 1975, she worked as a hairdresser for over ten years before discovering photojournalism on a trip to Asia in 2004. She has since worked in Japan, India and Iraq, and been published across most major European countries as well as in Israel and the Philippines. Are there more decisive battlegrounds for women’s rights than the hairdressing salon, the school, the university, the doctor’s surgery? No doubt. But what she uncovered there is anything but trivial, she says: these women hold a tool of empowerment in their hands.

Making peace with the sea

Alongside the top prize, three series also received 1,000 euros each. Antonio Denti, born in Catania in 1972, studied anthropology in London before covering Kosovo, Afghanistan, Iraq, Israel and Gaza for Reuters, then the start of the Arab Spring in Tunisia, natural disasters, contemporary migration and the Pope’s travels. This time he followed, near Rome, African migrant women and their children born in Italy, encouraged to unlearn their fear of water. For them, the Mediterranean remains the memory of a crossing in a makeshift boat, a second desert after the one they had fled.

“I am an intruder into the lives of others,” he says, “and I must at least try, for a few moments, to sense what they themselves are feeling. Photography must be an expression of humanity.” Denti tracked down some of these women years after their crossing, and followed them from their homes to the beach and out into the water, capturing moments of relaxation and daring, but also faces where the fear had not quite lifted. Making peace with the sea is the project, and the series is called “Il Mare in Mezzo” (“The Sea In Between”).

Aleksandra Kossowska, 48, based in Warsaw and co-founder of the Poleczki.art centre, travelled to Sebeta, Ethiopia, to photograph blind and visually impaired children in black and white. They live in a spartan shelter, in cramped shared dormitories, far from their families, yet surrounded by care and driven by the desire to achieve independence in the world of the sighted. The photographer scattered clouds of stars over the portraits, then perforated the prints by hand so that the children could touch them too. “The world touches us when we touch it,” she says. Making blindness visible is impossible, she admits herself, and these stars are its translation. One may wonder whether they illuminate or embellish.

Wings among the ruins

A peace prize for a childhood in Gaza: the pairing is surprising at first. Yet Mahmoud Abu Hamda, 36, a former photography lecturer at the University of Gaza, shows children laughing, a boy playing the violin, swings set up amid the rubble. According to the prize organisers, the photographer was displaced, then injured when the Israeli Air Force bombed a high-rise building, and he documented hunger while starving himself. Perhaps he sought out these carefree moments, he told Magnum, because amid so much misery he too sometimes needed a place to rest. “To breathe.” Magnum has already published his work, which has been shown in Amsterdam, among other places, and won a Lucia Award in 2023.

For the Childrens Peace Image of the Year 2026, the prize went to Sesilia Shainidze, 11, from Batumi, Georgia. Her mother works as an insurance agent, her father as an offshore engineer, and her own camera is currently broken. For “My Family”, she staged a tableau at her grandmother’s house with her grandmother, uncle, aunt, cousins and dog, an idea entirely her own. She also enjoys painting and travelling, and mostly photographs animals, especially her dog, whom she raised herself. She took home 1,000 euros.

Last Thursday, in Vienna, actor Cornelius Obonya, honorary ambassador of UNICEF Austria, delivered the keynote and devoted his speech to the invasion of Ukraine. He closed with a wish: “May the message conveyed in and through your photographs lead to better news from the war-torn regions of this planet.”

One may regret that an awards list surrounded by so many speeches lets the cause speak louder than the writing. But the prize’s initiator, Lois Lammerhuber, had set the frame in his address: “peace is not the absence of war, but something I would describe as a ‘life well lived’.”

The 2026 winners and shortlist are presented on the Global Peace Photo Award website.

content.article_text:
Del 3 al 4 de octubre, Artishock participa en Feria Aparte con una selección de fotografía latinoamericana y obras de pequeño formato de artistas chilenos. Una nueva ocasión para llevar al espacio físico las conversaciones que, desde hace más de 15 años, desarrollamos principalmente desde nuestra plataforma digital.

Desde 2010, Artishock ha construido un lugar para el arte contemporáneo latino/ibero/americano desde Santiago de Chile. Durante todos estos años, gran parte de nuestros encuentros han ocurrido en nuestra plataforma online, a través de entrevistas, reseñas y ensayos que involucran a una amplia comunidad de artistas, curadores, directores de museos y proyectos independientes.

Pero la historia de Artishock también se cuenta desde algunos momentos fuera de la pantalla. Entre el 3 y el 4 de octubre volvemos a ese espacio presencial de la mano de Feria Aparte , con una propuesta que pone en relación dos conjuntos de obras que acercan prácticas y geografías que no siempre tienen la posibilidad de encontrarse físicamente.

El primero reúne fotografía latinoamericana , seleccionada a partir de una convocatoria abierta en la que participaron artistas de Chile, Venezuela, Colombia, México, Cuba, Argentina, Perú y Ecuador. Son trabajos que se acercan de distintas maneras al paisaje, el cuerpo y la vida cotidiana, y que permiten recorrer imaginarios diversos de la región sin reducirlos a una única mirada sobre lo latinoamericano.

Entre las obras seleccionadas se encuentran fotografías de Alexandra Busch, Carelyn Mejías, Diego Barriga, Edgar Martínez, Fernando Izaguirre, Frank Lahera, Gabriela de Echave, Joaquín Rodríguez, José Antonio Barrientos, Joseph Ladrón de Guevara, Lucía Pizzani, Misha Vallejo, Nicolás Rivas, Rafael Triana, Sebastián González y Valeria Arendar .

El segundo conjunto está compuesto por esculturas y objetos de pequeño formato realizados por artistas chilenos y chilenas . Cerámica, vidrio, cartón y otros materiales orgánicos e industriales configuran piezas que se mueven entre lo cotidiano y lo extraño.

Participan Borja Carbajal, Constanza Hermosilla, Daniela Pulido, Elizabeth Burmann Littin, Inés González, Isidora Kauak, Jessica Briceño, José Esteban Valdés, Las Honorarias, Martín Vásquez & Violeta Cereceda y Rocío Olivares .

En esta curaduría encontrarás obras de distintas escalas y rangos de precio, pensadas también como una manera de acercarse al coleccionismo de arte contemporáneo. Las obras estarán disponibles para la venta durante la feria y pueden consultarse tanto en nuestro catálogo online como en Artishop.

[Ver catálogo completo en PDF – Precios en pesos chilenos] [Ver obras disponibles en Artishop – Precios en dólares]

Del archivo digital al encuentro presencial

Participar en Feria Aparte significa para Artishock algo más que incorporar una dimensión comercial a nuestro trabajo. Después de más de quince años construyendo un archivo digital dedicado al arte contemporáneo de la región, estar frente a las obras, conversar con quienes las hacen y conocer nuevos públicos es también una manera de poner en práctica aquello que ha guiado nuestro trabajo desde el comienzo: conectar escenas y comunidades que están cultural y geográficamente cerca, pero que no siempre tienen oportunidades de encontrarse.

Por eso, esta participación también marca un pequeño cambio de escala para nosotros. Artishock nació en Santiago, pero su comunidad se ha extendido mucho más allá de esta ciudad y de Chile. Llevar a Feria Aparte una selección latinoamericana y, al mismo tiempo, compartir el trabajo de artistas que desarrollan sus prácticas en Chile, nos permite poner esas distintas escenas en relación dentro de un mismo espacio.

A esta participación se suma el Premio Artishock , que reconocerá a uno/a de los/as artistas participantes de Feria Aparte con un perfil dedicado a su trabajo en nuestra plataforma. La iniciativa busca que el encuentro no termine cuando cierre la feria: la obra y la práctica de ese/a artista continuarán circulando en el archivo digital de Artishock.

El arte es por acá

La quinta edición de Feria Aparte reunirá a 40 expositores para un total de más 200 artistas en la Ex Cervecería Ebner, edificio patrimonial ubicado en el Mall Barrio Independencia. La programación incluye conversatorios, talleres, música en vivo, recorridos y actividades de mediación, además de la exposición y venta de obras.

Para Artishock, estar aquí es también una manera de volver a casa: encontrarnos en la ciudad donde nació la plataforma, pero hacerlo ahora de otra forma, alrededor de obras, artistas y conversaciones compartidas.

¡ Los esperamos del 3 al 4 de octubre en Feria Aparte!

Ex Cervecería Ebner, Mall Barrio Independencia, Av. Independencia 565, Santiago 11 – 20 horas Entrada gratuita @feria.aparte

A news item by ArtThrob Editors on the 29th of September 2026. This should take you < 1 minute to read.

A new exhibition centers young people living around the Mau Forest to create rewilded visions for 2099.

‘Mau: A Forest Imaginarium’ , opening in Nairobi on 17th October 2026, presents a speculative world created during an eight-week Safari Studio by Kairos Futura in and around Masese, on the edge of Kenya’s Mau Forest.

Through drawing, printmaking, sculpture, wearable design, installation, and collective storytelling, participants have imagined the Mau of 2099, with an exhibition that presents a fragment of that imagined future.

The exhibition grows out of The Safari Studio, Kairos Futura’s travelling arts and futures programme. The project works with young people living around landscapes of major ecological importance, using art and speculative worldbuilding as tools for thinking beyond the immediate pressures of the present.

Ideas developed during the studio range from new relationships between people and elephants, rituals, forest technologies, forms of forest protection, healing spaces and new ways of living within a recovering ecosystem.

About Kairos Futura

Kairos Futura is an arts futurist organisation working across Kenya and internationally to explore how imagination can become a practical tool for ecological and social change.

Its programmes combine immersive storytelling, speculative design, visual art, making and field-based learning to create spaces where young people can investigate possible futures for the places they live. Through projects including The Safari Studio, Wild Future Lab, Jungle Room and other experimental arts and futures programmes, Kairos Futura works at the intersection of culture, ecology and future-making.

音楽家・渋谷慶一郎によるポートレート連載「Humanity」第2回。舞台は、渋谷が東京とともに拠点とするパリへ。街で出会い、時間をともにする人々をコンタックスT3で写し出す。モノクロームの柔らかなイメージの中に、パリに生きる人々の飾らない表情がこぼれ落ちる。

写真・文＝渋谷慶一郎

目次

Mae Mei Lapres（マエ・メイ・ラプレ、モデル／ヴィンテージ・コレクター）

Claude Gassian（クロード・ガシアン、写真家）

Justine Emard（ジュスティーヌ・エマール、ヴィジュアル・アーティスト）

Takami Nakamoto（タカミ・ナカモト、Nonotak共同ファウンダー／アーティスト／サウンド・アーティスト）

Noemi Schipfer（ノエミ・シプフェ、Nonotak共同ファウンダー／アーティスト）

Mae Mei Lapres（マエ・メイ・ラプレ、モデル／ヴィンテージ・コレクター）

グッチ時代のアレッサンドロ・ミケーレのミューズで、ルイ・ヴィトン、ミュウミュウなど多くのブランドのランウェイやキャンペーンを制覇しながらパリのクリニャンクールのテナントをDIYして、自分のヴィンテージショップ「MeiMei Vintage」を運営している。マイペースで自分を曲げない、わがままなところが僕と似ている。家で飼っている2羽のオウムにはすっかり懐かれている。

Claude Gassian（クロード・ガシアン、写真家）

この前パリで、今年11月にリリースするアルバム『Thereshold』のジャケットを撮影してもらった。今までにジミヘン、マドンナ、プリンス、パティ・スミスなど数多くのミュージシャンを撮影しているけど、特にミック・ジャガーとデヴィッド・ボウイはパリでは彼にしか撮らせなかったという伝説があるらしい。撮影の日はアシスタントも付けず自分でカメラと照明をイーストパックのキャリーで持ってきて、700枚撮影して颯爽と帰って行った76歳。日本のカメラマンも見習った方がいい。

Justine Emard（ジュスティーヌ・エマール、ヴィジュアル・アーティスト）

10年以上、僕と色んなコラボレーションをしてきたけど、僕が英語を話せるようになったのは彼女のおかげ。最近は大阪万博のフランス館のアーティスティック・ディレクターを務めたり、すっかり偉くなっていて嬉しい。ちなみにアンドロイド・オペラの映像もここ数年は彼女が担当している。フランス人離れした真面目さが面白い時がある。

Takami Nakamoto（タカミ・ナカモト、Nonotak共同ファウンダー／アーティスト／サウンド・アーティスト）

10年くらい前にパリで知り合ったけど、去年から僕の家が近所になったから特に仲良くなってよく家に遊びにくる。時間をかけて仲良くなったから、話しているとリラックス出来て非常に良い。Nonotakの作品が元々好きだからいつか一緒に仕事も出来たらと思う。とか書いているけど、普段は悪いことばかり話しているからここに書けることが少なくて困っている（笑）。

Noemi Schipfer（ノエミ・シプフェ、Nonotak共同ファウンダー／アーティスト）

Takamiと一緒にNonotakをやっていて、彼と同様に家にもよく遊びに来る。この前は「陰謀論とか言われていることは大概、人々の無知によるもので、そもそも世の中陰謀だらけ」ということで意気投合した。タトゥーのデザインもやっていて、それを見た時にNonotakのデザインのエッセンスを見た気がした。

渋谷慶一郎（しぶや・けいいちろう） 音楽家。1973年東京生まれ。東京藝術大学作曲科卒業。2002年に音楽レーベルATAK設立。先鋭的な電子音楽作品からピアノソロ、オペラ、映画音楽、サウンド・インスタレーションまで、幅広い領域で活動を行う。東京とパリを拠点に国内外で作品を発表し、人間とテクノロジー、生と死の境界領域を作品を通して問いかけている。 http://atak.jp/

People

Depot Reborn: Interview with Olivier Marty of Studio KO

KARL FOURNIER (left) and

OLIVIER MARTY (right). Copyright Nöel Manalili.

Olivier Marty, co-founder of the Paris-based architecture firm Studio KO, specializes in giving historic structures a considered second life. His latest project, the Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent (CCA Tashkent), does just that for the 1912 tram depot and diesel station in the heart of Uzbekistan’s capital, transforming it into the country’s first permanent institution dedicated to contemporary art.

Before Tashkent, Studio KO developed a distinctive approach to cultural buildings. The Yves Saint Laurent Museum in Marrakech (2017) is acclaimed for its restrained brick latticework and carefully controlled light, while the more recent Musée de la Mode et du Costume in Arles (2025) transformed an 18th-century townhouse into quietly elegant setting for one of France’s most extensive regional collections for textiles and costumes. Both projects reveal Studio KO’s preference for subtlety over spectacle, a design philosophy on full display in Uzbekistan.

Working with partner Karl Fournier, Marty chose to preserve, rather than overwrite, the building’s character. The main exhibition hall retains its original brick walls and vast proportions, a space they describe as “basilica-like.” A metal tunnel carries visitors into the galleries, while courtyards and subtle design elements nod to traditional Uzbek forms without turning decorative. The result is a contemplative environment flexible enough to house exhibitions, research, and public programs.

Ahead of CCA Tashkent’s public opening, Marty spoke with ArtAsiaPacific about the thinking behind the transformation, and what it means for contemporary art in Central Asia.

On the eve of the CCA Tashkent’s unveiling, how has working within a 1912 tram depot and diesel station—a layered site shaped by imperial Russian, Soviet, and Central Asian histories—shifted your understanding of adaptive reuse as something more than heritage preservation? What does it mean to give a structure a “new poetic life,” in a city still negotiating between its modernist and vernacular indigenous identities?

It takes time—the time to give attention and sincerity to each layer. First, we identified the recent additions to the building: elements that imitated the historic details of the original features without having their qualities. This was a time of choosing, selecting, and filtering. Then, what was kept had to be renovated using techniques that had disappeared from the country decades ago—brick and joint treatment, zinc cladding on horizontal elements, and so on. Then we made the choice of legibility when creating the contemporary flow, through excavation and the construction of new elements. The materiality of all these additions was, deliberately, in total contrast with the existing architectural fabric. They are dark, with the feel of poured concrete, as opposed to the modular brickwork typical of imperial architecture.

Exterior views of the Yves Saint Laurent Museum, Marrakech. Photos by Dan Glasser. Courtesy Studio KO.

Studio KO has long approached Morocco not as an exotic backdrop but as a laboratory of material intelligence, from the terracotta brickwork of the Yves Saint Laurent Museum in Marrakech to the earth and local craft traditions for private houses. How did these experiences of engaging climate, craft lineages, and cultural hybridity prepare you for the specific conditions of Tashkent?

We like to say that the Studio’s response is more an approach, an attitude, rather than a style. This is what we applied to this project: listen and observe a lot before making choices. The minerality of the country, the colors of the soil, the vernacular repetition of courtyards. In the end, there are similarities with our Moroccan projects, although the context is very different.

Installation views of TARIK KISWANSON ’s Nest , 2026 (left), and ALI CHERRI ’s A mouth, a wound , 2025 (right), at the Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent. Photos by Dan Glasser. Courtesy Studio KO.

In both Morocco and Uzbekistan, you have approached brick not merely as a building unit, but as a carrier of memory and technique. For the 2023 Uzbekistan Pavilion at the Venice Architecture Biennale, “Unbuild Together: Archaism vs. Modernity,” you worked with students and artisans around the mud-brick qalas, or Zoroastrian desert fortresses, of Karakalpakstan. How did that research into archaic brick cultures inform your treatment of Uzbekistan’s industrial brickwork and the new insertions at CCA Tashkent?

The discovery of the qalas was more about showing the chronological porosity between archaism and modernity. Having been built so long ago, their volume and layout have so much abstraction; accessible from below, like our tunnel leading to the diesel station, made of masses like many of our interventions—there was so much to learn from there. There were many experiences too with terracotta brick in part two of the workshop; we made many exercises with them, of both layouts and finishes, natural or glazed.

Rendering (left) and installation view (right) of the Uzbekistan Pavilion at the 18th Biennale Architettura, Venice, 2023. Photo by Gerda Studio. Courtesy the Uzbekistan Art & Culture Development Foundation, Tashkent.

The Venice pavilion was conceived as a collaborative laboratory involving Uzbek students, scholars, and artisans. How did that pedagogical and co-creative model inform the design process for CCA Tashkent? How do you see the architect’s role shifting when a project becomes the platform for transmitting knowledge rather than simply delivering a finished object?

It is hard to explain, because these workshops happened in the very middle of the global process of CCA Tashkent, when most of the drawings were already done. But the diesel station had almost the same dimensions as the Arsenale pavilion in Venice. Chance or destiny? Before the renovation works, we installed in the diesel station a crazy one-to-one model of the Venice labyrinth. There is an echo, both geographic and civilizational. Watching those kids discover, in Tashkent, the replica of what would be installed in Venice was very moving.

SHOKRUKH RAKHIMOV ’s

The Colour of Silence, In Search of Truth , 2026, in the courtyard of the Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent (CCA Tashkent). Courtesy Studio KO and CCA Tashkent.

The courtyard of CCA Tashkent is conceptualized as a contemporary version of a traditional mahalla , or residential community. How do you negotiate the tension between inventing a new communal spatial type and respecting the social and spatial logics of established Uzbek urban forms, particularly when designing a public cultural institution that aims to be both contemplative and open?

The enclosed space, big gate, perception of the surrounding construction and urban fabric—all of this is all the same, although the expression is different.

Your practice has always treated context as the starting point—from the desert light of Morocco, the maquis of Corsica, or the industrial fabric of Tashkent—rather than imposing a signature style from elsewhere. At a time when global cultural infrastructure often produces interchangeable “iconic” museums, how do you avoid homogenizing a place while working as architects across different continents?

I think it takes, on the one hand, a lot of modesty and respect for alterity, as well as a strong and confident vision on how to deal with it. Our years of practice have made this easier today, and clients come for this approach, which is very rewarding.

Interior views of the Musée de la Mode et du Costume, Arles. Photos by François Deladerrière. Courtesy Studio KO.

Having moved from designing private residences and the highly specific YSL museum to a major public cultural institution in a post-Soviet Central Asian capital, how has the scale and civic responsibility of CCA Tashkent changed your thinking about the relationship between architecture, cultural diplomacy, and the creation of new institutional “software” alongside physical form?

Scale-wise, even politically, there are many similarities, because the project serves a purpose combining altruism, power, and vision. But for the first time it is not dedicated to couture or textile like in Arles, but to artists. To watch them taking over the space you have designed for their installations is beautiful.

The main hall of the former diesel station has been described as a smaller version of the Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall. Rather than imposing a neutral white cube logic, you chose to honor the building’s industrial character while introducing a metal tunnel, courtyard, and other carefully calibrated interventions. What does it mean for a contemporary art institution in Central Asia to inhabit a space that still carries traces of its industrial and imperial past without erasing them?

It means that in this region there can be a path to modernity and development based on accepting the traces of the past, like existing buildings. It means a lot, both conceptually and practically. Uzbek authorities, at the highest level, now want to save a lot of buildings—it showed the way, maybe.

NADIA KAABI-LINKE ’s

Flying Carpets , 2011, at the Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent, 2026. Courtesy the Uzbekistan Art And Culture Development Foundation and Andrey Arakelykan.

Looking across the arc of your career leading to CCA Tashkent, how has your understanding of architecture’s afterlives—such as material sourcing, labor conditions, future reuse, environmental consequences—evolved? What specific afterlives do you hope this space will generate beyond its opening?

After a few super-intensive days leading up the opening, local users and teams have used every possible space and configuration! 5,650 visitors on the first day. Beyond photographs, honors, or prizes, this is the best afterlife we could dream of. Collective emotion.

Elaine W. Ng is editor and publisher of ArtAsiaPacific.
