The opening of the Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent marks the latest stop in Uzbekistan’s ongoing contemporary cultural journey.

Tashkent is a city of many incarnations. Once revered as a great medieval centre of learning and a prosperous hub on the fabled Silk Road, it was subsequently absorbed into the sprawling empire of the Russian Tsars, later expanding exponentially to become the fourth biggest city in the Soviet Union. Following a disastrous earthquake in 1966, which razed much of the historic fabric of the city to the ground, it was extensively rebuilt in Soviet Modernist style, later emerging from the collapse of the USSR in the early 1990s as the capital of the new sovereign state of Uzbekistan.

In a place where architecture holds centre stage, it is fitting that Tashkent’s latest cultural offering pays homage to the layered urban fabric of the city. In a nod to the value of preserving industrial heritage, the newly opened Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent (CCA Tashkent) is housed in a restored tram depot and diesel station dating from 1912, the first of its type in Central Asia and which has been thoughtfully restored and repurposed by the French architectural firm, Studio KO . The project is led by the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation, whose chairperson, Gayane Umerova , has long pioneered the adaptive reuse of historic buildings.

The new cultural landmark has been launched with the exhibition Hikmah , under the direction of the CCA Tashkent’s chief curator, Dr Sara Raza . It features new commissions and recent works by ten Uzbek and international artists, and seeks to explore the concept of hikmah (wisdom) in terms of its value and resonance across Uzbekistan’s wider landscape of multi-layered histories and recent rapid development. Works by Ali Cherri , Nadia Kaabi-Linke , Kimsooja, Tarik Kiswanson , Muhannad Shono , Nari Ward, Shokhrukh Rakhimov, Vladimir Pan, Bakhtiyar Saipov and Daribay Saipov are presented at the imaginatively recast former depot. The scale and configuration of the building calls for decidedly inventive staging and curation. “It’s certainly a non-conventional exhibition space,” says Raza, “but that is both the beauty and the opportunity.”

Participating artists have been invited to respond to the transformation of the structure in which their works are showcased. “It is a chance to think about the ideologies of architecture, but through the artist’s hand,” continues Raza. These words are encapsulated neatly by the installation presented in the Centre’s main exhibition hall, Flying Carpets (2011) by Nadia Kaabi-Linke. On loan from New York’s Solomon R Guggenheim Museum, the suspended steel sculpture was inspired by a visit made by the artist to the Venice Biennale in 2009. Noticing how illegal migrant street vendors – often from Africa or the Arab world – would display their counterfeit wares on simple rugs or sheets, ready to gather everything up and flee when approached by the police or other officials, Kaabi-Linke was moved to create a work that played with the ironic concept of a flying carpet offering boundless travel while also underlining the restrictions and lack of freedom endured by the vendors themselves.

The architectural quality of Flying Carpets – its proportions came directly from the vendors’ rugs – makes for a compelling presence in the gritty main space, but Tarik Kiswanson’s commissioned piece, Nest , speaks just as persuasively to its setting. Oriented around an interest in metamorphosis and renewal, it reflects both the character of its immediate context while also alluding to the wider artistic and cultural transformation underway outside the Centre’s century-old yellow brick walls.

With the CCA residency programme continuing in Tashkent, and soon to be extended to Samarkand, one of the most monumental participations in Hikmah is by a former resident. Developed during his residency, Muhannad Shono’s tubular – you can step inside – Tower for a Single Breath is made from black compressed composite tiles and draws on the Sufi traditions of Bukhara and Samarkand. The artistic and decorative traditions of Uzbekistan are further showcased within Hikmah by Shokhrukh Rakhimov’s The Colour of Silence, In Search of Truth , which spans contemporary expression and age-old craftsmanship in the shape of seven large-scale ceramic orbs, as well as through a selection of historical pieces and artefacts from the collection of the State Museum of Arts of Karakalpakstan.

The brokering of a conversation between the contemporary and the traditional is central to the ethos of CCA Tashkent and featured prominently in the approach to the restoration of the original building. “We wanted the contemporary interventions to be immediately legible against the historic fabric,” said Olivier Marty of Studio KO. “Our interventions were deliberately careful, adding only what is necessary and ensuring that every new element we introduce does not simply belong to any passing trend.” As CCA Tashkent moves forward as a venue for exhibitions, research, education and cultural production, the carefully calibrated approach to its creation and inaugural exhibition should serve as an exemplar elsewhere in Uzbekistan and across the wider region. “At its heart, the Centre is a space for dialogue,” concludes Raza. “Between artists and audiences, local histories and global ideas, [a place] where the past becomes a catalyst for future possibilities.”

Hikmah runs until 31 January 2027

This review first appeared in Canvas 124: Prismatic

News

National Gallery of Victoria Senior Executive Accused of $8 Million Theft

A former senior executive at Melbourne’s National Gallery of Victoria (NGV) has been accused of abusing his position and stealing approximately AUD 8 million (USD 5.6 million) from the institution over the course of six years. The individual allegedly siphoned the funds from a work account to purchase smartphones, which he then sold off at a profit, using his position to conceal his activity.

The alleged conduct is said to have continued from September 2019 until its detection in September 2025. NGV reported the matter to Victoria police and fired the staffer. The Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC), the state’s anticorruption watchdog, then conducted a year-long investigation before charging the man with eight offenses, including seven counts of theft and one count of misconduct in public office. He is scheduled to appear before Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on October 20.

Founded in 1861 and funded by the state, NGV is the country’s oldest gallery. Its AUD 4.8 billion (USD 3.3 billion) collection of over 80,000 artworks was reportedly not affected by this incident.

Harison Butler is an editorial intern at ArtAsiaPacific.

content.article_text:
写真家・藤澤一の写真展「A Light, A Live, A Life」が、2026年10月9日から18日まで、東京・神宮前のgallery&bar ニニニ・ニーで開催される。藤澤は1994年神戸市生まれ。コロナ禍をきっかけに写真を始め、人物撮影を中心に活動。これまで300人以上を撮影してきたという。本展では、同い年の俳優・大原海輝を約1年間にわたって撮影した作品を発表する。

2人が出会ったのは、藤澤が上京して間もない頃。初めての撮影で大原から掛けられた「人をちゃんと『人間』として撮れる写真家に久しぶりに出会った」という言葉が、今回の展覧会を構想するひとつの原点となった。

藤澤がテーマに掲げるのは、「人を写す」こと。ポートレートに写るのは、その人物の容姿だけなのか。同じ人物、場所、服という条件をそろえても、同じ写真は二度と生まれない。そこには撮影された日の感情や人生の断片、被写体の生き方、さらにはシャッターを切る写真家との関係までが入り込むと藤澤は考える。撮影は、朝5時の激しい雨が降る海から、気温マイナス20度の雪原、ベトナムの街角まで、さまざまな環境で行われた。藤澤は一連の作品について、「写り手と撮り手が剥き出しの命でぶつかり合った、生のエネルギーの記録」と表現する。

被写体となった大原は、俳優として映画、舞台、ドラマ、ミュージックビデオなどに出演する一方、プロデュースや脚本、演出にも活動領域を広げてきた。2025年からは今回の会場でもあるgallery&bar ニニニ・ニーのオーナー代表を務め、異なるカルチャーや表現をつなぐ活動にも取り組んでいる。写真家と俳優という「撮る側／撮られる側」の関係を1年間継続することで、その間に何が写真へ刻み込まれていったのか。「A Light, A Live, A Life」は、一人の人物のポートレートであると同時に、写真を介して向き合った2人の時間を提示する試みとなる。

会期中には藤澤と大原によるトークショーも開催予定。

Vida Útil es una publicación de artista que reúne 25 proyectos realizados por Camila Ramírez entre 2009 y 2024, articulando objetos, gráficas y acciones que reflexionan sobre arte, juego y trabajo. Concebida como un ensayo visual, la publicación organiza imágenes de archivo, anotaciones y obras en torno a tres conceptos y capítulos — Rojo, Juego, Caída — e incorpora textos críticos de investigadores y creadores nacionales, ampliando las lecturas poéticas, políticas y sociales de la obra. El proyecto busca trascender la monografía tradicional para ofrecer una visión integral de 15 años de trayectoria artística, con un enfoque en creación, archivo, escritura y difusión. Aborda temas de historia, política, memoria y percepción del futuro en Chile, combinando reflexiones filosóficas, experiencias personales y elementos visuales.

Nada más intenso que lo que jamás te ocurrió. Al menos 8 en la escala de Richter. Entonces es necesario hacer volver la intensidad, a los márgenes de lo cotidiano, por los detalles que pertenecen a la escena inicial: esos detalles, esa intensidad, es lo que constituyó como real al lugar del sujeto. Y al mismo tiempo la necesidad de reparar perdurará toda la vida. Y sobrevivir, o sucumbir, esa es la alternativa.

Anne Dufourmantelle

En el comienzo, un juego. Años después, una realización, una convicción y una serie de obras inspiradas en ello. Hoy, un libro, cuaderno y registro de obras que son, al mismo tiempo, juego y registro. Juego en cadena, juego en serio, juego en rojo, “el color con la mayor longitud de onda” (48), escribe la artista Camila Ramírez en rojo, al interior del libro Vida útil .

A comienzos del siglo XX, otro gran libro rojo había comenzado, también, como un juego-en-serio, deviniendo igualmente un registro de experiencias sentidas, imaginadas y simbolizadas (Jung). Lo mismo el pequeño cuaderno rojo que registra algunas increíbles anécdotas vividas por un escritor del absurdo existencialista y del misterio (Auster). Incluido el libro de Camila , en todos estos ejemplos “escribir es un caso de impersonation ” (Navarro, 2009, 20). Pero no en el sentido de suplantación de identidad, sino de necesaria distancia con el ser; distancia que materializa el acercamiento a la tan humana ocurrencia de buscar sincronías en la existencia, donde termina por encontrar-se lo real. La función para la cual parece haber sido creada.

Es en esa sincronía que la escritura exhibe un poco más claramente su carácter representacional. No es la experiencia, no es el sueño, no es el error, no es la falla. Es lo que ahí, en todo eso, logramos encontrar. “Si perdemos esta vez que sea otra cosa” (136). Un dibujo, quizás varios, algunos bocetos, fragmentos e ideas. Somos siempre todo lo que hacemos junto a lo que nunca hicimos, todo lo que (ya) no podemos hacer. Por eso, en el lugar donde la tradición ubica al texto, en estas páginas encontramos fotografías como cuerpos, cuerpos como letras, letras como texturas, texturas como imágenes, imágenes como planes, planes como medios. Medios para duelar. ¿Cómo se supone que se avanza en el duelo? ¿Se avanza? ¿Se queda?

En cualquier caso, duelar es un término coloquial. Y es precisamente en lo coloquial y en lo cotidiano donde se lleva a cabo esa adaptación que sigue a una pérdida; el duelo, “manifestación de dolor por la muerte de alguien”. O de algo. La etimología lo vincula antes al latín duellum , que significa “combate o pelea entre dos, a consecuencia de un reto o desafío”, “enfrentamiento entre dos personas o entre dos grupos”. Sabemos la historia del enfrentamiento que duró 17 años en Chile y queremos mantenernos calmas en la derrota. Vida útil es un libro de gestos para conectar con esta voluntad, y cada uno de ellos es al rojo como la utopía es al duelo. No se trata de encontrar una forma de conformarnos, sino variaciones y ensayos en que, de alguna manera, nos sea posible continuar.

La derrota es parte fundamental del duelo. En este caso un duelo que no se sostiene en el negro sino en su bandera. Es lo mismo: al final es una pérdida. Pero difiere al hallar en ello formas de honrar lo imperfecto, la espera de lo que no llegó más, la generación de una propuesta para sobrevenir a la pérdida. Imaginar y fabricar dispositivos a escala urbana; invitar a los lectores a armar palabras, completar crucigramas; archivar objetos cotidianos, lápices, libros, pelotas aplastadas; imaginar objetos y técnicas de otra manera. La página hecha objeto vale más por su simbolismo que por su significación. Imágenes, paisajes, bocetos, texturas, palabras, letras, los textos ilustran la imagen, están a cargo de un sentido otro. Ese que me permite recordar, ya no con desgarradora tristeza, sino con compasiva nostalgia, esas tardes esperando verla regresar a casa.

Al final, cuando “solo el que ama puede sentir con tanta agudeza el dolor de lo imperfecto” (38), no hay pensamiento comparable al hacer. Escribe Tununa Mercado que “ la que piensa es la escritura y después se verá si dice falso o verdadero”, que sería posible “aventurar[se] a sostener que no dirá otra verdad que la de su concatenación en el espacio” (2021) —de la página, que se ha hecho parte de la escritura. Así sucede en esta publicación, donde se lee sin texto, con texto, del otro lado, ya no importa si es texto, la esencia es siempre la misma: color, fondo, figura, obra. Esta lectura orienta nuestra capacidad de dar inicio, entonces, ahora, a otra etapa. Aquí la escritura, al atravesar la dictadura de la discursividad, atraviesa, igualmente, el problema. En ella se extiende y se eterniza, para la utopía, el tiempo estimado en que puede funcionar. Algo similar a la apórica vida útil de la caída.

Referencias

Dufourmantelle, Anne. “Mina Tauher”. En caso de amor: psicopatología de la vida amorosa , Nocturna, 2021, pp. 21-37.

Mercado, Tununa. “Arrebatos.” Veinte ensayos sobre literatura y vida en el siglo XXI , editado por Judith Podlubne y Julieta Yelin, 1.ª ed., CETyCLI / CELA / EMR, 2021. Libro electrónico.

Navarro, Justo. “El cazador de coincidencias.” El cuaderno rojo , de Paul Auster, Anagrama, 2009, pp. 7-24.

“Duelo”. Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, [4 junio 2026], https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duelo_(psicolog%C3%ADa). Consultado el 21 de febrero de 2026.

Vida útil fue financiado por el Fondo Nacional de Desarrollo Cultural y las Artes, ámbito regional de financiamiento, convocatoria 2025. La publicación cuenta con una primera edición de 200 ejemplares y fue impresa por Ograma en Santiago de Chile durante 2026. Con textos inéditos de Soledad García Saavedra, Vania Montgomery, Bernardita Croxatto, Hugo Palmarola y Diego Ramírez.

content.article_text:
Colin Dodgson, Saturation to Breaking Point

With Earthquake Weathe r, his debut monograph published by Loose Joints, the American photographer casts fragility, mortality and the everyday as allegories of a saturated world.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Colin Dodgson.

When he is not shooting campaigns for Dior, Gucci and Louis Vuitton in Vogue , W Magazine or The New York Times Style Magazine , Colin Dodgson pursues a photography entirely his own, printing his work by hand in the darkroom. In these images, his eye carries what his publisher calls “the dual inheritance of two formative disciplines”: “a surfer’s responsiveness to shifting conditions”.

Earthquake Weather dances along the faultlines between typology and sprawl: thumbed, dog-eared book pages worn soft by use; contemporary memento mori that turn to the flesh and its impermanence; plastic water bottles left on Japanese roadsides. So many figures of a precarious existence, gathered without hierarchy or imposed narrative, in burnished, copper tones.

Without warning, the sequence drifts towards a darker register. Fentanyl bottles appear, lined neatly in a row. Atmospheric CO2 readings insert themselves between the silhouettes and the worn books, alongside extracts from his collaborations with the World Land Trust — a British charity dedicated to protecting threatened natural habitats — across areas of ecological importance. The tenor of an uncertain age seeps in, uncommented upon, by simple contiguity.

What organizes Earthquake Weather is accumulation — not as rhetorical device, but as condition of the world. The book explores “the way we accumulate: in knowledge, within our bodies, through consumption, against entropy.” The images work as fugues, reacting across the page: beauty and ruin coexist.

Dodgson’s photography chases what “both hides and reveals itself within the same blink of an eye.” He has slipped into its pages photographs of volumes leafed through and annotated — and his own book might follow suit, becoming, through use, one of the photographs it contains.

Earthquake Weather by Colin Dodgson is published by Loose Joints , edited by Sarah Chaplin Espenon. 88 pages, 60 colour plates. €46.

content.article_text:
Bristol Photo Festival’s third edition creates a palimpsest of past, present and future, explains festival director Alejandro Acín

In Castle Park, central Bristol, there is a plaque paying tribute to men from the city who joined the fight against fascism in the Spanish Civil War. “It’s always been in my mind,” says Bristol Photo Festival director Alejandro Acín. This year marks 90 years since the Spanish Civil War but, with authoritarian governments and far-right activism rising across the globe, that moment now feels uncomfortably close.

It is a reminder that the past has a way of shapeshifting into the present, and this idea reverberates through the 2026 Bristol Photo Festival. Themed Time Machine , it includes a show taking place in a cave not far from the park featuring three artists exploring the contemporary resonance of the Spanish Civil War – Anna Jorné, Julián Barón and Natasha Christia. Their work is part of a city-wide programme of exhibitions in which photography is not simply a recording of the past, but an articulation of our non-linear experience of time. Memory of what has been and speculation about the future meet in the present day.

“Often the works that we bring explore historical events but from contemporary approaches, or vice versa, so there’s always this kind of entanglement of time that happens,” Acín notes, adding that Time Machine follows two previous editions focusing on movement (in 2024) and place (in 2021). “We can look at the three editions as almost a trilogy,” he explains.

“Culture this year is more political than ever. We are fighting to keep spaces that allow people to think, talk and look at the world differently” – Alejandro Acín

This year a show by Goa-based artist Akshay Mahajan responds to the British Empire and Commonwealth Collection held in Bristol, drawing on Indian folklore to consider how the ghosts of colonialism still haunt the border between India and Pakistan. Italian photojournalist Giulio Di Sturco’s Anthropocosmos invites viewers into constructed spaces designed by scientists and engineers, meanwhile, to test out space conditions. His images show how humans are preparing for a potential – as yet unrealised – future beyond Earth.

There is also an exhibition presented by Kegham Djeghalian, the son of the late Kegham Avedis Garabet Djeghalian – an Armenian-Palestinian photographer who set up Gaza’s first photographic studio. Djeghalian Senior’s images are a portal to a flourishing pre-Nakba Palestine, which stands in stark contrast to the horrifying images of destruction of recent years. Elsewhere Annie Wang’s Mother as a Creator charts the Taiwanese artist’s journey into pregnancy, through motherhood, and on to the shifting, overlapping terrain she now occupies between her maternal and creative roles.

This edition of Bristol Photo Festival is Acín’s second as director (after a stint as director of education and engagement for the first edition); alongside it he runs IC Visual Lab with co-director Ben GJ Thomas and designer/producer Safia Belhaj. ICVL is based in the middle of the city, in the one-time home of the South African Resource Centre and curator Christine Eyene is drawing on the building’s radical history for an exhibition there, featuring work by George Hallett. An award-winning South African photographer, Hallett was exiled to London in the 1970s and made portraits of anti-apartheid creatives, writers, artists and musicians.

The festival includes a busy opening week from 14 to 18 October, featuring parties, openings and a symposium; it will also include an ‘education weekend’ in its five-week run, featuring masterclasses led by photographers and industry insiders. “It’s about building relationships where participants can continue developing their work,” says Acín.

The 2024 festival was a resounding success. Amak Mahmoodian’s exhibition in it, One Hundred and Twenty Minutes , went on to earn a Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize nomination, while some 40 per cent of those who went to the Bristol Museum and Art Gallery during its run were visiting the institution for the first time. “We had visitors from every postcode in Bristol, so on a local level we had pretty good engagement,” says Acín.

However, since then much has changed in Bristol (and beyond), with arts organisations facing a tougher funding landscape than ever. Bristol Photo Festival consists of curated exhibitions – rather than depending on an open call – which provides an income for some; this puts more financial pressure on the festival, and more onus on partnership. The closure of the Royal Photographic Society’s gallery has also had an impact, as it was previously a key venue – although some new spaces have come on board.

The festival, along with the wider photography community, is also still mourning the loss of Martin Parr in December 2025, a long-term Bristol resident and keen advocate of the programme. “It was very sad,” says Acín. “Martin was part of the board and he was always helpful with contacts, interested and supportive of the festival.” The festival maintains close ties with the Martin Parr Foundation, whose group exhibition Dark Tales: British Documentary Photography and the Gothic will be on show during its run; the popular Books on Photography will also return to MPF on 17 and 18 October.

Acín is open about the difficulties, believing it is important for organisations to speak up about the impact of massive cuts to public arts in the UK, and the loss of access to EU funding post-Brexit. “It’s a reality that’s very palpable, very tangible,” he says. “Culture this year is more political than ever. We are fighting to keep spaces that allow people to think, talk and look at the world differently.”

Bristol Photo Festival takes place from 14 October–15 November 2026. BOP is the weekend of 17–18 October 2026.

Rachel Segal Hamilton is a freelance writer and editor, specialising in photography and visual culture, for art magazines, book publishers, national press, awards, agencies and brands. Since 2018, she’s been contributing editor for the Royal Photographic Society Journal, is a regular writer for Aesthetica and author of Unseen London, published by Hoxton Mini Press.

content.article_text:
Amadou Fall: Faces of Nouadhibou

Pattern is presented as the first book devoted to a Mauritanian studio photographer: Amadou Fall, who portrayed the people of Nouadhibou at his Studio Grand Fall from the 1960s onward.

By Gaia Squarci. Photographs by Amadou Fall

“Pushing open the door of Studio Grand Fall meant leaving the street behind. The dust stayed outside. The noise too,” writes photographer Adrien Tache. Amadou Fall’s son entrusted Tache with bringing the archive to life, after decades of leaving it untouched. Nomadic families, city dwellers, Spanish migrants, merchants and officials all sat in front of his lens. Together they form a collective portrait of an Atlantic port where North Africa, West Africa and Europe met.

The clothes in Fall’s portraits tell that same story. For a long time, Mauritanian dress favoured plain or indigo-dyed cottons. Then came wax prints: cottons whose bold, colourful patterns are created by using wax to resist the dye. Dutch and British factories first produced them in imitation of Indonesian batik, intending to sell them in Asia. It was in West Africa, however, that they found their public during the nineteenth century, as traders and their customers gave each motif a name of their own, linked to marriage, wealth, migration or independence.

Rather than replacing traditional garments, wax cloth was integrated into existing ways of dressing, and by the 1960s it had become a sign of modernity and aspiration. That same cloth now binds the book: each copy is covered in a different wax fabric printed in West Africa, echoing the patterns some of the sitters could have been wearing.

The book Pattern is published by Fraglich Publishing and available for 35 Euro.

But he photographed Gaza with luminous tenderness, his images capturing quiet gestures of affection, subtle exchanges of care, and the warm, amber lights of temporary shelters. Organising exhibitions of work by independent SWANA practitioners in a European institution is a change, even in an institution known for pushing the envelope; more than that, it is a linguistic, bureaucratic, and geopolitical battleground. A violent manifestation of this gatekeeping is the European Visa system, for example, which prevented Libyan artist Amera Elnaal from entering the Netherlands to attend her own exhibition."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Our Songs Came Through is an intervention in the contemporary photography landscape, gathering an eclectic group of somehow connected artists to move far beyond the tokenism that often plagues Western institutions’ attempts to showcase art from the SWANA region. Rather than grouping these artists under a banner of shared trauma, it highlights their shared commitment to visual sovereignty, formal experimentation, and archival repair. The artists gathered here demonstrate that, to restore a fractured archive, one cannot simply add more images. Rather, we must fundamentally reinvent the methodology of image-making."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Collectively, the SWANA artists exhibiting at BredaPhoto are dismantling the familiar, flat, media-driven narratives. They remind us that history is not merely written by the victors, even those who wield a camera; it is unobtrusively and persistently preserved in the songs that survive, the rituals that map, and the communities which refuse to be forgotten. The fractured archive is reimagined as a site of radical agency, resistance, and complexity, and it honours the nuances of daily human survival."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/This-AmeraAlNaal_TheSaltAteAwayHerEyes_47.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "My father is standing in our neighbourhood, after finishing his cigarette, enjoying the sunlight. From The Salt Ate Away Her Eyes © Amera Elnaal", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "BredaPhoto Festival 2026, Our Songs Came Through, is open until 25 October https://bredaphoto.nl", "links": [{"text": "https://bredaphoto.nl", "url": "https://bredaphoto.nl/bredaphotofestival/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/4dd523a61ee6976afe3bb6efd9c1c6e3274f1787d7b19548f69c4546373372cd?s=164&d=mm&r=g", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Farah-Silvana Kanaan is a Lebanese-Italian-Dutch writer, editor and creative consultant based between Amsterdam and Beirut. Her words have appeared in Kinfolk, Dazed, Rolling Stone, Discontent, Middle East Eye, and elsewhere."}]
content.article_text:
Held within the wider BredaPhoto Festival, a strand of exhibitions by artists from the SWANA region dismantles flat media-driven narratives to present richer, more nuanced perspectives

For decades, the visual vocabulary assigned to the Southwest Asia and North Africa (SWANA) region by the international world of photography has been an exercise in transactional observation. A hyper-visible taxonomy of ruin, anchored in flattened and anonymised rage and grief, manufactures a state of perpetual exception, flattening complex social topographies into spectacles that court Western pity while burying structural truth. Within global institutions, regional image-makers are mined for local authenticity but systematically stripped of political urgency; international editors sanitise symbols of local resistance to satisfy detached audiences, while treating practitioners’ lived experiences as barely compensated raw material.

Yet a slow but steady shift in lens-based practices is gaining momentum, even in traditional and so-called apolitical spaces. Rather than seeking to correct the distorted mirrors held up by so many foreign photographers, or bending to the restrictive mandates of international gatekeepers, an emerging generation of image-makers, researchers, and storytellers is choosing to bypass these institutions, or only engage with them on their own terms. They are constructing what can be termed a “counter-archive”, not as a nostalgic retreat into a static past, but as an intentional, self-authored historical record of perpetual survival towards ultimate liberation.

This critical reclamation underpins a strand of the exhibitions in the current BredaPhoto Festival, which is themed Our Songs Came Through . Co-curated by Mohamed Somji, Ileana L. Selejan, and Astrid Hulsmann, the biennial explores how individuals and communities find solace and comfort (or “troost” in Dutch) and how intimate imagery and memory can puncture institutional erasure. These questions are key in the SWANA context.

“ This kind of work gives us the tools to crack open a radical collective imagination.” Noor Abed

Somji’s curatorial approach is characterised by a rigorous push towards self-authored storytelling, honed through his experience programming at Gulf Photo Plus, including at its popular Slidefest evenings. There developing regional practitioners are given the space to express their grievances and interrogate their motivations, away from the Western gaze. Inherited hierarchies of recognition are consistently broken down. But manifesting this dialogue in an exhibition in a Western institution can be challenging.

“When we started talking about this theme toward the end of the last festival, I was skeptical about how easily it could become very kumbaya – a superficial ‘let’s all go into the mountains, cleanse our world, and come back’ approach, while mass killing and active displacement are unfolding in Palestine, Lebanon, Yemen, Sudan, Iran and elsewhere,” says Somji. “We went back and forth on the texts and the selections of artists, work, and more, to make sure the structural, political reality was firmly addressed.

“Through GPP, we’ve spent years building an infrastructure for self-authored stories, because we know the damage of institutional erasure,” he continues. “The artists featured here aren’t just capturing conflict, they are archiving the poetry, the domestic resistance, and the psychological architectures that endure when people insist on surviving on their own terms.”

Palestinian artist Noor Abed’s specially-commissioned video installation, we walk in our sleep , presents a poetic blueprint of Palestinian realities, for example, subverting the clinical approaches of mainstream media and military occupation. Outsiders’ depictions of Palestine have often relied on the iconography of the barrier – checkpoints, watchtowers, concrete walls, and actively-restricted freedom. This centres the occupier’s gaze, defining Palestinian life entirely by that which restricts it. Abed adamantly refuses this framework.

Working in close collaboration with her family and neighbours, she turns the lens inward to examine how land is claimed, remembered, and mythologised through collective, physical ritual. we walk in our sleep moves through a series of vignettes, showing people whose gestures hover between ancient agrarian labor and contemporary performance art. Synchronised figures moving across open hillsides, the subtle positions of their heads and hands invoke histories that predate violent colonial sketches. Projected in a completely darkened, small room with only a tiny bench to sit on, the film is difficult to categorise; it’s overwhelming, in a way that feels necessary.

Abed was initially inspired to make the film when she noticed people muttering to themselves on the streets of her hometown; after many sleepless nights of contemplation, she connected this phenomenon to something else she had already zoned in on, the sacred space between the living and the dead. Abed believes that the martyrs walk among us.

“For many, many years now, I’ve been contemplating the wide range of rituals around mourning and death, which is something we witness every day,” Abed explains. “In the last few years, it started to become physical. The dead are among us, I truly believe that. So for me, it’s almost like carving into this space, the air around me. It became an exercise of listening to and being close to the martyrs [those who have been unjustly killed].”

Abed’s work maps a psychological landscape that remains inaccessible to the colonial apparatus; a checkpoint can bisect a road, but it cannot erase the collective memory of a community that has walked, sung, and lived on that land for thousands of years. She refuses to use folklore as mere nostalgia, but positions it as a perpetual tool of survival, demonstrating its inherent political utility. Her lens is patient and meditative, a direct rejection of the high-velocity aesthetic of breaking news stories disseminated in a 24-hour cycle; instead it asserts an invisible, unbreakable network of spatial permanence.

“For me, it’s a work of deliberate digging, of continuous searching – instead of considering the past as framed and fixed,” she says. “Because this is very dangerous, particularly in the context of Palestine. Once the past is turned into mere symbols, there is a risk of not being able to breathe anymore. It becomes empty. And for me, the collective memory is all about the embodied practices, knowledge, our rituals and the visceral connection to our land – whether in joy or in loss, in a funeral for a martyr that turns into celebration.”

Abed insists on the preservation of memories, by transforming them and keeping them connected to the present. “To simply lean on the past in this utopian way, with distance, there is no resistance for that in me,” she says. “This kind of work gives us the tools to crack open a radical collective imagination, that gives us both the hope and the means to rehearse liberation. Because there is no future other than liberation.”

While Abed maps the deep roots of connection to the land, Fouad Hallak’s A Mind in the Past, Eyes on Tomorrow addresses the fractured geometries of exile and return. Born in Syria, Hallak fled the country on a migrant vessel to claim asylum in the Netherlands; his work shifts away from diasporic trauma towards an internalised psychogeography. His recent documentation tracks his return to his homeland, in transition following the fall of Assad, capturing the fragile space between historical devastation and actualised hope.

“After the fall of the Assad regime, I noticed that people often looked at what happened in two different ways – some stories were bright, and others were painful,” Hallak reflects. “But these feelings can exist at the same time. When I went back, I was not an outsider. I was part of the story. I see this in the photograph of Khaled, who protested and fought against the regime. He carries his history with him and still moves forward… Before, this possibility did not exist. Now it does. For me, that is hope.”

Fascinated by old studio portraiture, and saddened by its disappearance due to war, Hallak created a temporary mobile setup in the streets of Damascus. Inviting residents to have their portraits taken, he constructed a new archive of Syrian presence with his series, Studio Damascus.

“When survival becomes part of everyday life, the simple act of having a portrait taken becomes difficult,” he says. “I believe that having a portrait taken with your family can be a sign of stability. When I direct people in front of the camera, the connection creates a moment in which they can step away from their instability. Studio Damascus explores reunion, memory, belonging, and the human need for stability.” Hallak refuses to flatten the reality of a community navigating a shattered state. “After all these years, I still feel there is a desire to make these realities easier to understand,” he concludes. “I don’t think the problem is misunderstanding. This is what I search for in my practice – a language that comes from human feeling. Something emotional, intimate, and perhaps even spiritual.”

Meanwhile photographer and filmmaker Fatima Joumaa turns the counter-archive towards the structural realities of South Lebanon (Al-Janoub) and Beirut’s southern suburbs (Dahiyeh). In her intimate project From My Mother’s Novel: Returning to South Lebanon , she weaves images through her mother Layla’s old notes and sketches, creating a meditation on grief, memory, and women as keepers of history. Joumaa combines analogue photography, poetic video essays, and first-hand local testimonies to directly challenge the usual media representations of war.

Whenever life in Lebanon is ruptured – and there have been many compounding crises over the past seven years alone, long before Israel’s current genocidal assault and occupation of the South – global image-makers flood the streets, capturing the immediate violence and debris, the grief and rage, before equally swiftly departing. This high-velocity reportage leaves what Joumaa calls an “after-image” in its wake, a concept she has developed into a series for independent Lebanese magazine The Public Source .

Shifting her gaze toward the quiet, slow-burning aftermath and complex interiorities that unfold after the intrusive cameras leave, she fights the persistent clichés that reduce entire neighbourhoods and their inhabitants to passive sites of devastation. “I was always aware of how much the image is treated as an extractable resource, whether moving or still,” she says. “And often, when international media or institutions approach us, they want the image because it carries a kind of authenticity – but they want to decide what that authenticity is allowed to contain.

“I have been asked to remove flags, portraits of martyrs, political signs, or anything that might make the image appear too political to them, as if there’s anything that isn’t political,” she continues. “And I refuse to portray my people only as victims.”

Joumaa argues these signifiers are at the core of this landscape, not mere additions to it – and that removing them does not render the image more neutral. Quite the opposite. “It produces another complete image, one that is more comfortable for the institution,” she says. “To them, it simply checks a box of exclusivity [paying lip-service to local perspectives] rather than talking about what is fundamentally happening.”

For Joumaa, the Israeli assault on South Lebanon, and its systematic violent occupation and genocidal destruction of almost all of the land in the region, is an everyday reality. She could not return to her village in Janoub to bury her grandmother, as is the reality for many families in South Lebanon. But by integrating first-person local testimonies into her video essays, she ensures that the voices of the community dictate the narrative arc of the work; the record of survival is written in the smallest, most intimate – most often overlooked – pockets of human existence.

Centring the camera on home-bound networks of care, Joumaa suggests that sovereignty is maintained through everyday acts of defiance, not on a grand geopolitical stage. And her insistence on documenting the unseen, foundational rhythms of community forms a natural bridge to Kuwaiti photographer and researcher Huda Abdulmughni, whose work focuses on the ancestral landscape.

Where Joumaa’s lens operates as an almost forensic instrument within the targeted spaces of her land and people, Abdulmughni focuses on a different kind of survival – one grounded in ecological harmony and collective memory. Abdulmughni’s Nowruz Sayadeen documents the annual fisherman’s New Year on the Iranian island of Qeshm, for example, in which the village’s primary source of income is paused, out of respect for nature’s seasonal bounty. Using both analogue and digital media, Abdulmughni captures the highly-stylised, almost mythical cast of characters populating the shores, including the iconic shushis – figures adorned with white face paint and palm leaves.

But rather than presenting the figures as exotic subjects, performing in costume once a year, Abdulmughni captures a world that relies on ancestral knowledge of the seas. Depicting traditions passed down through the generations, outside the strict categories preferred by Western ethnography, Abdulmughni’s work demonstrates that regional sovereignty is preserved through seasonal rhythms and ancestral ecological care. But her work also shows that this is also a world increasingly impacted by climate change due to geopolitical conflict, in which the community’s harmony with the earth may be devastated.

The biennial takes a devastating turn to remind us of the stakes raised when gentle rhythms are severed by colonial violence, including a posthumous show by Majd Arandas, A Memorial in Fragments . Arandas’ work brings the viewer face-to-face with the realities of active elimination; born in Gaza in 1994, he was killed in an Israeli airstrike near his home in Deir al-Balah on 01 November 2023. Arandas had long ago been forced to sell his professional camera to survive the Israeli blockade, but continued to document with his mobile phone, and his archive has been retrieved and preserved by his brother.

Somji wanted to honour Arandas’ work and life, but also show the networks of solidarity that surrounded him, and now surround his archive. “Whether it’s a beautiful exchange between Majd and a friend about the plants in his beloved grandmother’s garden, or a photographer friend exchanging cat photos with him, it shows how communities find ways to bond together, and provide solace, despite everything that’s against them, despite the challenges of neoliberal worlds and neo-colonialist regimes,” Somji says.

Arandas’ surviving images testify to what it means to create an archive when your existence is being contested in real-time. But he photographed Gaza with luminous tenderness, his images capturing quiet gestures of affection, subtle exchanges of care, and the warm, amber lights of temporary shelters. His work refuses to let his people be remembered solely by their erasure, insisting instead on the profound beauty and unyielding right to exist that defined their daily survival.

These exhibitions help make Our Songs Came Through a significant biennale; they also surface the often behind-the-scenes negotiations required to present these images within a Western framework. Organising exhibitions of work by independent SWANA practitioners in a European institution is a change, even in an institution known for pushing the envelope; more than that, it is a linguistic, bureaucratic, and geopolitical battleground. A violent manifestation of this gatekeeping is the European Visa system, for example, which prevented Libyan artist Amera Elnaal from entering the Netherlands to attend her own exhibition.

Our Songs Came Through is an intervention in the contemporary photography landscape, gathering an eclectic group of somehow connected artists to move far beyond the tokenism that often plagues Western institutions’ attempts to showcase art from the SWANA region. Rather than grouping these artists under a banner of shared trauma, it highlights their shared commitment to visual sovereignty, formal experimentation, and archival repair. The artists gathered here demonstrate that, to restore a fractured archive, one cannot simply add more images. Rather, we must fundamentally reinvent the methodology of image-making.

Collectively, the SWANA artists exhibiting at BredaPhoto are dismantling the familiar, flat, media-driven narratives. They remind us that history is not merely written by the victors, even those who wield a camera; it is unobtrusively and persistently preserved in the songs that survive, the rituals that map, and the communities which refuse to be forgotten. The fractured archive is reimagined as a site of radical agency, resistance, and complexity, and it honours the nuances of daily human survival.

BredaPhoto Festival 2026, Our Songs Came Through, is open until 25 October https://bredaphoto.nl

Farah-Silvana Kanaan is a Lebanese-Italian-Dutch writer, editor and creative consultant based between Amsterdam and Beirut. Her words have appeared in Kinfolk, Dazed, Rolling Stone, Discontent, Middle East Eye, and elsewhere.

content.article_text:
Bvlgari ’s iconic designs are made with exemplary craftsmanship and vision, enhanced by its distinct approach to colour. Celebrating a revolutionary history, the Maison’s latest exhibition, Bvlgari Kaleidos: Colors, Cultures and Crafts , demonstrates there is much about colour yet to be explored.

Since its founding in Rome in 1884 by Greek silversmith Sotirio Bvlgari, the Maison has been known for exceptional refinement and artistic vision. However, in the 1940s, Bvlgari began exhibiting a distinct shift towards the unconventional. By moving away from the design standards of the time, which were oriented around platinum and diamond in geometric and Art Deco styles, Bvlgari quickly established a unique identity. “Its use of metals, gems and other unusual materials has allowed Bvlgari to create a truly chromatic language that is instantly recognisable,” says Gislain Aucremanne, Bvlgari Heritage Curator Director. Characterised by a bold foray into vibrancy, the embrace of colour would not only impact the trajectory of Bvlgari and forge the DNA for which it is now known but also reframe the understanding and use of colour in the industry.

“Throughout its history, three elements of innovation have marked the avant-garde of jewellery and distanced the Roman High Jeweller from the codes of traditional French fine jewellery,” explains Aucremmane. One was the incorporation of yellow gold – a metal that Bvlgari still favours. The 1950s then saw Bvlgari introduce striking combinations of precious and coloured gemstones. This inspiration came directly from its Roman roots – referencing art history and the landscape in its colour-blocking techniques and avant-garde chromatic mixes. The third was applying the cabochon cut to precious gems rather than just to lesser stones, as previously. An ancient technique dating back to antiquity, it was revived by Bvlgari in the mid-twentieth century as a way to enhance the depth of colour.

Revisiting and re-envisioning historical and cultural elements to fuel creative vision remains a core pillar of Bvlgari. Today, the Maison looks even further afield in pursuit of dynamic new inspirations to imbue its jewellery designs with deepened meaning, symbolism and aesthetic value, as well as to construct a further base of knowledge from which to draw. “Every exhibition is an opportunity for the Maison to look at itself from the outside,” notes Aucremanne. “When Bvlgari travels, it does not simply transport its heritage from one country to another. Each destination asks new questions of that heritage. These encounters expand Bvlgari’s creative vocabulary without altering its identity.”

Bvlgari – whether within its ateliers or through its art-focused Fondazione Bvlgari – embodies creativity, savoir-faire, inclusion, philanthropy, education and heritage preservation. It nurtures these values through international collaboration and cross-cultural exchange, which serve to generate dialogue, honour generational skills and shed light on fresh creative talent and craftsmanship, as well as explore new threads of research relevant both within and beyond the jewellery world. For example, courtesy of its iconic 1948 Serpenti design, Bvlgari has broadened the discourse around the iconography and magnetism of snakes through its jewellery, publications and multi-chapter Serpenti exhibitions across countries including India, South Korea and Italy.

The Maison’s history with colour has also taken a global journey. In 2021, Seoul’s Hangaram Design Museum displayed how Bvlgari harnesses the powerful creative energy of colour, while in 2025, the National Art Center in Tokyo hosted Bvlgari Kaleidos: Colors, Cultures and Crafts , marking both Bvlgari’s first exhibition in Japan in a decade, as well as its largest ever in the country. Now, Kaleidos opens a new chapter at mainland China’s first public contemporary art museum, Shanghai’s Power Station of Art.

Grounding the exhibition’s mission are two Greek terms, kalos (beautiful) and eidos (form), symbolising the evolving union of beauty and creativity. The immersive scenography across multiple spaces – created by architectural studios SANAA and Formafantasma – sees visitors enveloped by a powerful expression of the delicate relationship between architecture, light and materiality. Featuring more than 300 jewellery masterpieces from the Bvlgari High Jewellery collections, Bvlgari Heritage Collection and private Italian and Chinese collections, in addition to artworks by leading Chinese contemporary artists Liang Manqi and Zhang Ding , Kaleidos delves into how unexpectedly different the understandings, experiences and use of colour can be. The exhibition also investigates the difference between factual theories on colour – how it behaves and interacts – versus a more subjective take, in which an emotional context guides. “This is one of the fundamental questions,” says Aucremanne. “Colour is something we can study endlessly, yet ultimately it has to be experienced. This is why the exhibition moves progressively through science, symbolism and perception. The encounter becomes richer precisely because no perspective is sufficient on its own.”

Kaleidos presents Eastern and Western colour theory, touching on the more philosophical frameworks of the East and addressing the West’s more scientific approach before addressing more forward-facing queries. The exhibition unfolds across three chapters: The Science of Colors , Color Symbolism and The Power of Light . The first of these explains colour theory, touching on the core primary colours and the complexities of harmonies through the lens of German writer, poet and polymath Johann Wolfgang von Goethe – who argued that colour is the result of the interplay of light and dark, carries psychological value and that humans seek it in balance – and French chemist Michel-Eugène Chevreul, the first to propose relational perception or the law of simultaneous contrast, whereby colour is perceived in relation to its surrounding hues. In turn, Bvlgari displays its understanding of colour theory and fearless application through pieces such as a necklace crafted with cultured pearls, rubies, sapphires, emeralds and diamonds (Bvlgari Heritage Collection, 1991), as well as another necklace from 1960, which embodies bold colour harmony through its incorporation of gold and platinum alongside turquoise and diamond.

Next comes Color Symbolism , which investigates the philosophical and cultural values of colour, honing in on notions from the East and on how colour can function as a language by focusing on the Chinese Wu Xing (Five Elements system). A 2000-year-old philosophy, the five core elements or natural forces of wood, fire, earth, metal and water are attributed with a colour, symbolism, seasons and corporeal component. Here, wood is associated with green, represents spring, birth, growth and creativity, and relates to the liver, while metal is connected to the colour white, connoting autumn, harvest, structure and consolidation, and is related to the lungs. These values are continuous rather than static concepts and work in relation to each other. A central philosophy, Wu Xing has informed disciplines such as traditional Chinese medicine and feng shui. Bvlgari’s interpretation of a more reflective, symbolic approach is evident through its intentional gemstone choice, imbuing each piece with a backstory and deeper intrinsic value for the artisan as well as for the wearer or collector.

Kaleidos features a special, exclusive selection of jewellery creations, and in this chapter are pieces such as a 1993 gold necklace with rubies and diamonds, indicative of the vitality and prosperity expressed by the colour red in Chinese culture; convertible platinum pendant earring-brooches with natural pearls and diamonds from c.1952, which denote purity and refinement; and a c.1977 gold horse-head brooch adorned with onyx, ruby and diamonds in reference to 2026, the Chinese Zodiac’s Year of the Horse. The evolving dynamic between East and West has long been of keen interest to Bvlgari and informs much of its visual lexicon. This can be seen, for example, in the 1973 sautoir from the Bvlgari Heritage Collection, exhibited for the first time. Coral, onyx and diamonds in spherical form lead down towards an engraved jade medallion, as much in homage to Chinese tradition as to Roman frescoes. The display of the Monete Tubogas bangle in three-colour gold with Persian silver coin and diamonds from the 1970s is another example of the Maison’s ability to layer historical references while simultaneously demonstrating its pioneering use of metals.

A more technical, craftsmanship-oriented exploration is held in the third chapter, The Power of Light . Examining how light affects perception, Bvlgari appropriated this ability to turn gold, silver and gemstones into ‘living surfaces’. Here, a 1991 gold necklace with amethysts, citrines, pink tourmalines, sapphires, emeralds and diamonds evokes a luminous mosaic where the eye experiences shifting colour values and transparencies. Another highlight are pendant earrings (dating from 1993) crafted with gold, rubies, yellow, pink and blue sapphires, and diamonds that celebrate the vivacity of colour as a result of light interplay.

The final element, and the one through which Bvlgari looks to the future, are the two installations by contemporary artists. “An artist can make us perceive colour differently,” says Aucremanne. “This is particularly important when working across cultures. The artist can reveal something that a theoretical explanation cannot, such as a sensation, a memory, an atmosphere or a psychological response. In that sense, the artist is not simply illustrating the exhibition’s ideas. They are challenging them. They allow colour to escape the systems we construct around it and return to something more intuitive, emotional and personal. The artist becomes a mediator between the visitors and the core of the exhibition.”

Boundless Synesthesia by Liang Manqi – known for her interest in Chinese geometric abstraction – is an installation that occupies three-dimensional space. Across walls and the floor, therefore placing the viewer in the midst of the work rather than in front of it, colour is used as a tool to produce an environment inspired by the artist’s emotions as well as the rhythms of daily life and the natural world. Meanwhile, contemporary artist Zhang Ding presents The Form of Light , an immersive work comprising light panels that create a golden glow around transparent humanoid heads made of gemstone-like cut glass. The emphasis on the particular hue allows audiences to reflect on their relationship with light and on the ability of golden hues to evoke sensations of peace, purity and harmony.

Rather than being an exercise in comparing or contrasting individual pieces and works, or in establishing a hierarchy of systems, the most exciting part of the exhibition lies in its ability to generate resonance. Kaleidos invites viewers to consider each perspective as a physical phenomenon and cultural code, revealing the complex relationships between nature, science, society and artistry in singular and globalised contexts. The curation showcases the unique offerings of one epoch or culture and the expanded creativity which results when influences meet, as well as how a natural consequence of artistic output is the documentation and preservation of social and visual history. “Jewellery is an extraordinary form of historical memory because it carries knowledge materially,” explains Aucremanne. “A jewel can preserve a technique, a particular approach to colour or an aesthetic choice. It can also reveal the social and cultural context in which it was created. As sentimental gifts, pieces of jewellery bear the personal story of their former owners. They are a fragment of our human lives. This is why I believe heritage jewellery should not be understood simply as something beautiful from the past.” It is a means to read history, tastes and cultural exchange, not least – as Aucremanne adds – “because jewellery is made to be worn and carries something that many other forms of heritage do not. It was created to enter directly into human experience.”

By documenting the diversity of colour theory and expression through disparate cultures and exploring the nuanced zone of creative amalgamation and exchange, through Kaleidos Bvlgari is continuing its pursuit of opening new chapters for discussion. It is also widening the debate on the role in contemporary creation in advancing the discourse around colour. “Perhaps the greatest misconception is that colour is objective,” observes Aucremanne. “We tend to speak about colour as though red is simply red, but colour is profoundly unstable. It changes according to light, material, context, culture, memory and even the other colours surrounding it. A gemstone can reveal different personalities depending on the light in which it is seen. Two people can experience the same colour while having completely different emotional responses to it. That is perhaps the point at which Kaleidos ultimately arrives, highlighting how we need different perspectives to explain its complete potential. What remains fascinating is the space between colour as a physical phenomenon and colour as a human encounter.”

content.article_text:
The artist discusses his new commission, The Form of Light , for Bvlgari’s current exhibition in Shanghai.

Canvas: What can you tell us about your commissioned work for Bvlgari Kaleidos: Colors, Cultures and Crafts?

Zhang Ding: The Form of Light consists of an immersive light installation composed of two sets of golden light panels and glass humanoid heads with pixelated effects, all animated by light fluctuations.

What inspired the concept?

It was inspired by urban contemporary landscapes and new technology devices, and their inextricable presence in our society.

Why did you choose the title The Form of Light ?

A strong golden light emanates from the work, flickering and varying as if breathing. Here light becomes the essence of the work, immaterial yet immersive, infusing a spiritual dimension into the piece.

How does the gold light impact the perception of space?

The variations in light from dim to bright can sometimes be almost blinding to the eye, such as sunlight, while creating heat.

What is the significance of using the colour gold?

Gold – and its countless symbols – is a recurrent element in my practice. In this work specifically, it could be interpreted as a spiritual glow.

Are there any other colours that hold a special significance to you?

In my past works, I also repeatedly used phosphorescent green, for its ghostly luminescence.

What do the transparent glass humanoid heads suggest? How does the gemstone-like surface interact with the installation?

With their futuristic aesthetics, the glass humanoid heads are reminiscent of robotic heads. Simultaneously, their sharp shapes and translucency echo gemstones and the way they reflect light.

Do you see the light as spiritual, natural, technological or something else?

All of those. Light – as with gold – holds so many symbols and is intimately linked to human civilisation. The work plays on this dichotomy between natural and man-made.

Why did you choose to work with glass and light? What about these materials speaks to you?

Both elements represent a form of purity and resonate with the glow of gemstones.

How does this work expand on your current practice?

The work is part of a body of installations I have been working on these last few years, probing developments in new technology, their background and impact on our society.

What does Kaleidos mean to you? How does your work with Bvlgari expand on the exploration of colour and light?

The term Kaleidos brings to my mind multiple light, colours and geometrical structures, as well as the multifaceted perspectives of our reality.

This interview first appeared in Canvas 124: Prismatic

content.article_text:
News

National Gallery Singapore to Welcome Chng Hak-Peng as New CEO

CHNG HAK-PENG . Courtesy National Gallery Singapore.

The National Gallery of Singapore (NGS) and Singapore Art Museum (SAM) announced today that Chng Hak-Peng will succeed Dr Eugene Tan as chief executive officer of NGS, effective from January 1, 2027. Tan will step back from his NGS duties at the end of the year to concentrate on his role as SAM’s chief executive officer and director.

Chng brings over 30 years’ experience in Singapore’s arts and culture sector. From 2014 to 2022, he served first as deputy chair, then as chief executive officer, of the Singapore Symphony Group; under his leadership, the Singapore Symphony Orchestra was awarded third place in Gramophone magazine’s Orchestra of the Year 2021, the only Asian orchestra among the nominees. Prior, he spent a decade at the management consultancy Bain & Company. He currently serves on the boards of Library and Archives Solutions, a subsidiary of Singapore’s National Library Board, and Duke-NUS Medical School, and chairs the advisory council of Chua Chu Kang Secondary School. Chng is a PhD candidate in history at the National University of Singapore as well as a long-time volunteer docent for local institutions such as the Asian Civilizations Museum.

In a press release, Chng described the appointment as an opportunity to continue “making the arts accessible and meaningful to our communities . . . [and] to strengthen the role that the arts play in our society.” NGS chairman Peter Ho welcomed the appointment, stating that Chng’s “record of transforming the beloved ensembles of the Singapore Symphony Group speaks for itself,” and that they are “confident the Gallery is in good hands as it continues to grow its voice for Singapore and Southeast Asian art.”

Tan has held the role of NGS director since 2013 and took on the directorship of SAM in 2019. He was appointed CEO of both institutions in 2024. In stepping back from the NGS, Tan said he was “grateful to have had the privilege of leading both NGS and SAM,” and that this is “the right time for each to benefit from dedicated leadership.”

The joint statement framed the split as reflecting “the continued development of both institutions as they enter a new phase of growth,” while noting the two museums will remain “natural partners” that continue to work closely in promoting and showcasing art and culture from Singapore and beyond.

Harison Butler is an editorial intern at ArtAsiaPacific.
content.excerpt_original: Chng succeeds Eugene Tan, who will focus his leadership at the Singapore Art Museum. Harison Butler

The artist discusses her site-specific work and how colour and light convey the human condition in Bvlgari Kaleidos: Colors, Cultures and Crafts .

Canvas: How do you balance rigid geometric shapes with fluid human emotions in your colour palettes?

Liang Manqi: Everything has form, and everything is formless. Here, ‘form’ can be understood not only as pure geometric shapes but also as rules, boundaries and constraints within society. Living in the present, many of our real feelings are accomplished simultaneously within constraint and release. Balance and harmony do not need to be deliberately introduced – everyone is already dealing with them in their own way, every day.

How do colours communicate emotions that words cannot?

Colour is emotional and intuitive. I don’t overthink my use of colour – I just put it directly on the canvas. When too many colour blocks feel inharmonious, I cover and adjust. When the paint feels too thick and ‘blocked’, I wait for it to dry, then sand it down to make it thinner and ‘unblock’ it. Through the process of painting, I gradually get to know colour and have a dialogue with it.

How do your experiences of daily life and nature influence your colour palette?

In nature, colours change in different weather conditions and natural light spectrums. Under bright sun, colours are especially vivid and saturated whereas on cloudy days there is a natural grey filter – quiet and harmonious.

Is there a particular colour that holds special meaning for you?

The combination of orange and green – when paired at certain levels of brightness – feels very comfortable to me. This is just based on my own experience with colour mixing over more than a decade of painting, I wouldn’t say that it holds any special meaning.

What role do the concepts of spatial depth and overlapping layers play when you create a work or installation?

My understanding of spatial depth differs from the scientific understanding of perspective space. Different colours, the physical thickness of paint, and the layering and sequence of dots, lines and planes can also generate psychological spatial depth. On a two-dimensional canvas, this understanding and expression of space is very subtle. The process is more important than the final visual result.

Can you tell us more about your work, Boundless Synesthesia , for Bvlgari’s Kaleidos exhibition in Shanghai? What inspired the concept?

Boundless Synesthesia is a site-specific art experiment and an exchange of emotional experience. It combines my two-dimensional paintings with new colour-geometric acrylic installations. I chose acrylic because I wanted light to pass through it and refract unexpected surprises beyond the boundaries of the material itself. The hard-edged form instantly becomes formless, transforming in an instant into a flow of emotion.

Why did you choose the title Boundless Synesthesia and what does it signify?

The work is limitless, formless. What the eye can see is only a tiny fraction of the materiality of this world. Transforming and sensing it is what I want to convey the most.

How did you approach transforming painting from a two-dimensional medium into an immersive spatial environment?

I began experimenting with this as early as 2013, with my first project in Hangzhou. I was no longer satisfied with creating only on a two-dimensional canvas – and happened to have the opportunity to try working on a larger, three-dimensional ‘canvas’.

How does this work expand on your current practice?

The initial intention was very simple and direct – it was simply that energy overflowed. Over time, more galleries and museums began to invite me and I gained more opportunities to practice and advance my spatial painting installation.

What does Kaleidos mean to you? How does your work with Bvlgari expand on the exploration of colour?

Radiance, polyhedron, kaleidoscope. I had similar explorations of colour during 2015–18, so one could say it was a meeting of minds.

Do you see the viewer as an observer, a participant or a collaborator in this installation?

Collaborators – they must be collaborators. Without them, my site-specific painting would not come to life.

This interview first appeared in Canvas 124: Prismatic

content.article_text:
News

Fifth Thailand Biennale Announces Theme and Artistic Directors

JIRADEJ-PORNPILAI MEEMALAI: BAAN NOORG . Courtesy the artists.

Thailand’s Ministry of Culture has announced the artist duo jiradej-pornpilai meemalai: BAAN NOORG as the artistic directors for the fifth Thailand Biennale, scheduled to open in Rayong in December 2027. The edition will center on relationships and interconnection, framed within both local and global contexts.

Jiradej and Pornpilai Meemalai are mixed-media artists working across sculpture, video, photography, and installation. Their practice draws on the joys and hardships of their own marriage as a lens for examining the nature of human relationships more broadly, along with the way those bonds shape society and history. The duo has exhibited globally in solo and group shows spanning Taiwan, Germany, the US, and the UK, and has undertaken several international residencies including at the Headlands Center for the Arts (Sausalito, 2010), Lichtenberg Studios (Berlin, 2013), and the Civitella Ranieri Center (Umbria, 2013). They have previously participated in the 2019 Asian Art Biennial in Taichung, the 2021 Busan Sea Art Festival, and Documenta 15 in Kassel in 2022.

The duo will direct the biennale through Baan Noorg Collaborative Arts and Culture, the nonprofit artist collective they founded in 2011 in the Nongpo community of Ratchaburi province. Over the years the initiative has run residencies, workshops, exhibitions, and community programs, and has staged biennales of its own. Joining the Meemalais on the curatorial team for the Thailand Biennale are Emily Chin-Jie Lee, Gesyada Siregar, and Tyuki Imamura. Together they will present “Sin-Samudr, Turning Currents,” an exhibition exploring how art and place inform one another.

Inaugurated in 2018, each edition of the Thailand Biennale is held in a different province. Rayong sits on Thailand’s eastern seaboard and is known chiefly as a fishing and fish-sauce producing center, as well as a hub for chemical and automotive manufacturing. The location of the upcoming biennale reflects the government’s efforts to diversify and expand Thailand’s arts and cultural infrastructure beyond its major urban centers.

Harison Butler is an editorial intern at ArtAsiaPacific.
content.excerpt_original: The artist duo jiradej-pornpilai meemalai: BAAN NOORG will explore the theme of human relationships through local and international lenses. Harison Butler

写真家パスカル・グレコによるトークイベントが、渋谷の404 Not Foundにて開催される。グレコは、ビデオゲーム内の仮想空間を写真として捉える「インゲームフォトグラフィー」に取り組んできた写真家。建築や都市、風景を撮影してきたこれまでの視点をゲーム空間に持ち込み、仮想世界のイメージと現実の風景写真、記憶との関係を問い続けている。

本トークイベントは、9月25日から10月4日まで同会場で開催される写真・映像展「PHOTOGRAPHING THE VIRTUAL IN THE AGE OF ANIMA LUDENS」にあわせて企画されたもの。会期中の10月2日には、写真家の小林健太に、編集者、クリエイティブディレクター、アートプロデューサーの後藤繁雄を迎え、グレコを交えた三者によるトークを行う。デジタル環境のなかで「写真を撮る」とはどのような行為なのか。グレコの実践を写真史・現代写真の文脈から読み解き、現実と仮想空間を横断する今日の写真の可能性を考える機会となる。

なお本展では、グレコがビデオゲームの風景を撮影した写真シリーズ「Photography, Video Game, Landscape」に連なる作品と映像作品を紹介する。ぜひ会場に足をお運びいただきたい。

content.article_text:
写真家・早川勝夫による「pendulum Art Book & Fine Art Photo Exhibition」が、11月13日から18日まで、せんだいメディアテークで開催される。雪によって風景が消え、再び現れる現象を通して、写真が持つ「固定する力」と、絶えず変化する世界との関係を見つめるプロジェクトだ。

「雪に風景が消え、また現れる」。本作の起点にあるのは、雪がもたらす圧倒的な美しさと、視界を奪われる恐ろしさだ。降り積もる雪は風景の輪郭を覆い、距離や奥行きを曖昧にする。さらにホワイトアウトのなかでは、そこに存在しているはずのものさえ見えなくなり、「何を見ているのか」という知覚そのものが揺らぎ始める。

早川はこうした雪の性質と、一瞬を一枚の像として定着させる写真の性質を対置する。確かな輪郭を持っていた世界が白の中へ溶け、やがて再び姿を現す。その「見える／見えない」「存在する／消失する」という往還を、早川は「存在の還流」と呼ぶ。タイトルの「pendulum＝振り子」も、固定と揺らぎ、可視と不可視、存在と消失のあいだを行き来する運動に由来している。

本展の特徴は、展示とアートブックを一つの作品として構想していることにもある。アートブック『pendulum』は全270ページに62点を収録し、半透明のトレーシングペーパーを採用。ページをめくると、前の写真の気配を残しながら次の像が透過して現れ、重なり、そして消えていく。「見る」「触れる」「めくる」「待つ」という行為そのものによって、写真に内在する時間を体験させる仕掛けだ。

一方、会場では62点の作品から32点を選び、5つの章の流れを再構成するように大判プリントで展示。アルポリック板にマウントした作品をフローティングフレームに収め、壁面に固定されながらもわずかに「浮遊」するような状態を生み出す。ページをめくることで時間の中に現れるアートブックと、身体を移動させながら空間の中で像と向き合う展示。二つの異なる体験を往還することで、「pendulum」の世界を立ち上げる。

アートブック『pendulum』は2026年12月、Inunicより刊行予定。

Star Wars | Jon Watts, da trilogia Homem-Aranha do MCU, vai dirigir primeiro filme de nova trilogia

Escrito por Simon Kinberg, nova trilogia é especulada como o próximo capítulo na Saga Skywalker.

(Imagens: Getty Images, Lucasfilm)

Os Skywalker estão de volta. Segundo o THR , Jon Watts vai dirigir um novo filme de “ Star Wars “, que será o primeiro de uma nova trilogia.

O cineasta Simon Kinberg vem trabalhando na criação de uma nova trilogia para a Lucasfilm desde o final de 2024. Ao que tudo indica, o projeto deve servir como o próximo capítulo na chamada Saga Skywalker, que é composta pelos nove filmes entre “Star Wars: Episódio I — A Ameaça Fantasma” e “Star Wars: Episódio IX — A Ascensão Skywalker”. Rey Skywalker, a jovem Jedi interpretada por Daisy Ridley na trilogia lançada pela Disney entre 2015 e 2019, deve retornar na trilogia de Kinberg.

Para Watts, trata-se na verdade de seu segundo projeto da franquia. Em 2024, ele cocriou e dirigiu parte da série “Skeleton Crew”, que acompanha um grupo de crianças que se perde pela galáxia tão, tão distante em uma aventura à la “Os Goonies”. Watts é mais conhecido também por dirigir a trilogia principal de filmes do Homem-Aranha de Tom Holland para a Marvel, incluindo “Homem-Aranha: Sem Volta Para Casa”.

Segundo o relato, o projeto ainda está em desenvolvimento e não recebeu sinal verde da Disney, embora pareça ser o projeto mais avançado em produção pela Lucasfilm depois de “Star Wars: Starfighter”, estrelado por Ryan Gosling e dirigido por Shawn Levy. A princípio, também seguem em desenvolvimento os filmes de Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy, focado em Rey Skywalker, e o de James Mangold sobre a origem da Ordem Jedi.

“Star Wars: Starfighter” tem estreia prevista para 27 de maio de 2027, coincidindo com o aniversário de 50 anos da franquia.

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tiempo de lectura: 12 minutos"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "[lectura breve]"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Esta exposición en el Museo de Arte Miguel Urrutia (MAMU) quiere poner en evidencia un impulso universal y atemporal para hacer arte: la rabia como fuego creador de los individuos y de las colectividades, que no es vengativa ni destructiva y, además, permite la creación y la acción transformadora. A partir de obras y documentos pertenecientes a las colecciones patrimoniales del Banco de la República , esta muestra reivindica el sentimiento individual y el afecto colectivo como argumentos legítimos para la creación artística y poética cuando la rabia opera creativamente desde los sujetos hacia las realidades que considera hostiles, injustas y dolorosas. Esta exposición no es sobre esas realidades, ni mucho menos sobre las ideologías que han determinado los contextos adversos, sino que se propone abordar las posibles respuestas éticas y estéticas que plantean los artistas mediante sensaciones, gestos, acciones y símbolos y que dan fe de su malestar y disconformidad."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "No sentir rabia en el contexto actual equivaldría a sentir que no estamos vivos, que de alguna manera estamos muriendo de indiferencia. Por eso mismo, esta exposición resulta una oportunidad para confrontarnos con las formas de la rabia que atraviesan la existencia tanto íntima como socialmente. Con una selección de más de 200 obras [1] de las colecciones patrimoniales del Banco de la República , el relato curatorial pone en escena una emocionalidad que emerge de situaciones que han afectado cuerpos y espíritus llevados al límite, y cuya única posible reacción ha sido la furia. La rabia se nos revela visceral, pero también filosófica; se nos muestra en su estado más desgarrador, pero a su vez como potencia creativa y de disertación. Las obras nos revuelcan, pero nos conceden un espacio para comprender la necesidad urgente del estallido que es fulgor liberador.", "links": [{"text": "[1]", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/2026/09/26/digna-rabia/#_ftn1"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "El ejercicio de los poderes en el entramado de los acontecimientos históricos marca de forma contundente las posibilidades de los sujetos para constituir formas de vida y determina cuál es su lugar en ese acontecer, justo por las jerarquías que esos poderes establecen. Este hecho inevitable se hace visible en la apuesta curatorial de Digna Rabia , donde producciones estéticas de diversos periodos -en su mayoría de los siglos XX y XXI- presentan cuerpos individuales y colectivos resistiendo a las injusticias producto de poderes y discursividades que han sometido a otros a condiciones adversas a lo que sería una vida digna."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Digna-Rabia-2.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Vista de la exposición Digna Rabia en el Museo de Arte Miguel Urrutia (MAMU), Bogotá, 2026. Foto cortesía del MAMU", "credit": "Artishock"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "El estudio de la rabia como emoción enardecida toma como referente clave el libro de la filósofa colombiana Laura Quintana Rabia. Afectos, violencia, inmunidad (2021), donde la autora profundiza en los efectos individuales y sociales que tiene el ejercicio de poderes (sobre todo aquellos intangibles) sobre los cuerpos, y las formas en las que se reacciona ante la desigualdad y las violencias que ese ejercicio suscita: los cuestionamientos, los afectos, las reacciones físicas, las acciones de resistencia mínimas, los silencios, entre otras."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Enuncia Quintana en su libro: “En particular, me interesa indagar cómo tales afectos se anudan con la manifestación de una cierta impotencia, que se siente también de forma muy manifiesta en el mundo contemporáneo.
