content.article_text:
F rantically and even stroboscopically over-energised, this big new movie from DreamWorks about best friends for ever seems to me another example of exhausting AI-type content production in animation. You could make the same argument against plenty of live-action films of course, but it is in animation that this kind of soulless blitzkrieg tends to predominate. Forgotten Island is over-controlled and over-determined, a movie that never, or hardly ever, takes its pedal from the metal, never takes a breath or a moment to let its characters come to life. At times it seems to be aping the world of Japanese anime, but without its sense of character or capacity for calm.

The story, weirdly reminiscent of The Hangover of all things, is set in the Philippines in the pre-social media 90s. Jo, voiced by R&B star HER, is a lonely and super-imaginative teen always in trouble at school; like Moana she has a wise grandma who guides her to her ancestral destiny and has captivated Jo with stories of her culture and identity – stories of the forgotten island of Nakali. Jo makes friends with similarly lonely Raissa (Liza Soberano) who like Jo is smart but with a much more focused sense of academic discipline.

Their alliance is pledged and a friendship bracelet woven, but as the years go by, poor Jo winds up with a loser’s job in a fast food joint, whereas Raissa feels guilty about leaving Jo behind as she heads for college at Caltech in the glamorous world of America. (The moment when she tells Jo she is leaving – effectively breaking up with her – is a rare moment of silence in which real emotions emerge and something is recognisably at stake.) But it is now that Jo discovers a mystical portal into the magical forgotten island of Nakali and semi-accidentally makes Raissa tumble down through this portal with her; they awaken 12 hours later to discover they have already done things here of which they have no memory and need to find out what. They also need to discover the portal which will take them back.

This Hangover-style amnesia facilitates a quest narrative, in the course of which they meet a goofy pal in the form of a wacky shapeshifting dog called Raww (Dave Franco) and a scary batibat, or memory demon, resembling Jabba the Hutt called Batiba (Jenny Slate) to whom they may have to surrender precious memories in return for freedom. They also encounter the terrifying figure of Manang (Lea Salonga) who, like Batiba may have relatable vulnerabilities that we don’t yet appreciate. And so it continues, developing and resolving with algorithmic efficiency. It leaves you with a strange sense of emptiness.

content.article_text:
CREATIVE CLASS PHOTO EXHIBITION「CCPE」が、2026年9月25日から27日まで東京・杉並のstudio behind by sceneryで開催される。

「CCPE」は、デジタルクリエイティブ領域で活躍するクリエイターから直接フィードバックを受けられるオンラインスクール「CREATIVE CLASS supported by iDID」のフォトディレクションコースから生まれた初の合同写真展。同コースでは、写真家／ビジュアルディレクターのshuntaroがマスターを務めている。

今回参加するのは、アルファ／Alfa、Chiharu Kodama、Nenpa_、Syuheiinoue、木村洋達、トム・イシカワ、中村和貴、間宮真介の8名。会場となるのは、shuntaro率いるクリエイティブスタジオbird and insectの撮影スタジオ、studio behind by sceneryだ。

展覧会の中心となるのは、受講生それぞれが企画から装丁まで一貫して制作したオリジナル写真集。完成した写真を壁面に並べるだけでなく、一冊の本として写真を編集し、ストーリーを構築するところまでを作品として提示する。来場者は実際に写真集を手に取って閲覧できる。

さらに、それぞれの写真集が持つ世界観を会場空間へと展開。セレクトされた写真のパネル展示も行い、本という二次元のメディアと展示空間を往来しながら作品を体験できる構成となる。会場ではオリジナルグッズや写真集の販売も予定している。

CREATIVE CLASS PHOTO EXHIBITION「CCPE」

studio behind by scenery（東京都杉並区下高井戸4-1-20）

2026年9月25日（金）～27日（日）

9月25日（金）18:00～20:00（オープニングレセプション）、9月26日（土）・27日（日）11:00～17:00

content.article_text:
Two hundred years ago, Nicéphore Niépce set a tin plate before his Burgundian window and waited. Hours passed; light did its work. No brush, no chisel — only the chemical reaction of Judean bitumen under the sun, and the world inscribed itself, unaided, onto a sensitive surface. His contemporaries called it the “sun-drawing,” with the same wonder that would seize, seventy years later, the audiences of the Lumière brothers watching their first cinematic projection: a train pulling into the station at La Ciotat.

In the age of artificial intelligence, images can still be born without a camera. The “this-has-been” so dear to the philosopher of the image Roland Barthes, that certainty that some real thing had once stood before a lens, no longer holds. In 2026, faces, landscapes and hyperrealistic scenes are conjured from nothing. It is within this great technological trembling that the Cnap and the Hangar — a Brussels art centre dedicated to contemporary photography — commissioned twenty artists: fifteen French, five Belgian, selected through an open call. Neither nostalgia nor ritual celebration, but a shared experiment in what the medium might yet become.

The return to origins begins with matter. Brussels-based artist Julie Calbert recovers the chemical residues of analogue photography, reintroduces them into the laboratory and sets them back in motion. From the photosensitive surface emerge phenomena of formation, propagation and erosion that she calls “unstable cartographies.” The image arrives on its own, with an almost organic autonomy: photography reclaims its original condition — a chemical reaction left to itself — and the artist reclaims hers, as a witness who guides without commanding.

Others surrender to time. French photographer Marie Bovo shoots at night, on a large-format camera, with exposures lasting up to nine hours, lit by nothing but the moon and the stars. Her “Forêts d’Hypnos” series stretch from the mimosa groves of the Tanneron to the hills of Tipaza, in Algeria, where vegetation has overgrown ancient Muslim graves from the colonial era. The night sky is streaked by the luminous trails of satellites while the trees hold centuries of buried memory, “immobile condensations of movements perceptible only through duration.”

More radical still: the renunciation of the gesture itself. In a valley of the Haute Maurienne, in the Alps, photographer and documentary filmmaker Michel Slomka scatters a constellation of camera traps and surrenders the shutter to the forest, the wind, the seasons, the passage of wolves. These devices, he notes, are “less surveillance cameras than small, motionless witnesses.” He has simply “tried to reduce the human footprint to a minimum” so that the animal’s footprint leaves, in the end, a photographic one. The work poses the question: who, exactly, makes the photograph?

It remained to make the dead speak. French artist Stéphanie Solinas unearthed eighteen portraits of young women from the nineteenth century on the American West Coast, driven by a single question: “What do you have to say to me today?” Drawing on a chain of tools running from mediumship to artificial intelligence, the installation “Une sorte de bordel” (2026), on the second floor of the Hangar, conjures from these pioneers a contemporary and animated lineage. A table called “diseuse” — fortune-teller — fitted with a tactile silicone hand, invites the visitor somewhere between oracle and dating app. Algorithms have replaced the ouija board.

On the floor below, the spectacular installation by visual artist François Bellabas rises like a monolith: a body-scale screen pours out an abstract, sonorous matter from which an embryo of his double surfaces, sharpens, dissolves, is reborn. The artist fed an algorithm on his own images, then “cut the process” at the moment when forms are still abstract, before the machine could complete its invention. “Our images, turned into fuel for machines, are computed in alien times”: by intercepting that stream, he grants his digital double “a space in which to take form.” The longer the visitor lingers, the more the double solidifies. It is the viewer who ends up being watched.

The same tension — between the photographer and his machinic double — inhabits the work of Sébastien Van Malleghem. A seasoned photojournalist with fifteen years of social documentary practice in black and white across northern Europe, he pivots with “V”(2026) toward colour, toward the light of Madeira and the Azores, and toward the machine. His prints on baryta paper hang in dialogue with a film generated entirely by AI from his own photographs. “Where photography offers a space of calm and beauty, its animated double provokes a diffuse unease,” he notes. A way of anchoring the living in paper, and holding anxiety at arm’s length.

Laurent Millet, meanwhile, seeks weight in the places where photography resists. “I nearly gave up photography several times because of its thinness, which I could find unbearable,” he confides. His theatres of illusion and scale models, built from nineteenth-century techniques now accessible to all, set a sculptural density against the medium’s transparency. The more objective an image becomes, he argues, the more it operates as a window that erases itself: he demands that it be “something very present, concrete, that pushes back against the eye.”

“To speak of the Bicentenary,” says Delphine Dumont, director of the Hangar, “is necessarily to interrogate the time in which we find ourselves.” The time of history, of creation, of institutions? Perhaps above all, she suggests, “the time proper to art: a time that escapes calendars, but leaves traces.” The poet Théophile Gautier wrote as much in 1864, in a phrase the exhibition catalogue exhumes as its epigraph: “The sun is tireless and photographers will not succeed in exhausting its patience.” Two hundred years after the Point de vue du Gras , other suns are rising over Brussels.

“Reinventing Photography” is on view at the Hangar, Brussels , until 20 December 2026.

The Hangar publishes 200 Years Later: Photography Reinvented by Five Belgian Artists , a leporello devoted to the five Belgian artists in the exhibition — Hangar Edition (2026) . The CNAP and Éditions Poursuite (Arles) co-publish Réinventer la photographie , a book bringing together invited texts and an essay by Jean-Christophe Bailly on the fifteen French artists exhibited (2026) .

content.title_original: Punk, Anonymous and Feminist: the Anti-Selfie According to K8 Hardy
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kh-positions-7.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Punk, Anonymous and Feminist: the Anti-Selfie According to K8 Hardy"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "American artist K8 Hardy takes over MoMA with “Position Series”, featured in the group exhibition “Taking Back Our Space,” alongside the publication of Positions by MACK, which brings together the fifty photographs of the series for the first time."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "By Guénola Pellen. Photos by K8 Hardy ."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kh-positions-8.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Rooted in second-wave feminism’s claim that the female body is a site of political struggle, K8 Hardy transmutes that legacy into a deliberately unruly, genre-defying practice, playing with the codes of pop culture as much as she detonates them. A founding member of the queer feminist collective LTTR, she weaponizes “bad taste” to dissect systems of consumption. Long before Instagram, she was already staging herself to subvert the codes of capitalism and patriarchy. “I love to ruin something nice.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/kh-positions-3.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Position Series” (2007-2012) grows from that impulse. K8 Hardy mobilizes her sister, mannequins, and her own body — dressed in eccentric clothes, wigs, and makeup — to embody figures that spill beyond any normative categorization of identity and gender expression. Punk, Anonymous and Feminist: the Anti-Selfie According to K8 Hardy

American artist K8 Hardy takes over MoMA with “Position Series”, featured in the group exhibition “Taking Back Our Space,” alongside the publication of Positions by MACK, which brings together the fifty photographs of the series for the first time.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by K8 Hardy .

Rooted in second-wave feminism’s claim that the female body is a site of political struggle, K8 Hardy transmutes that legacy into a deliberately unruly, genre-defying practice, playing with the codes of pop culture as much as she detonates them. A founding member of the queer feminist collective LTTR, she weaponizes “bad taste” to dissect systems of consumption. Long before Instagram, she was already staging herself to subvert the codes of capitalism and patriarchy. “I love to ruin something nice.”

“Position Series” (2007-2012) grows from that impulse. K8 Hardy mobilizes her sister, mannequins, and her own body — dressed in eccentric clothes, wigs, and makeup — to embody figures that spill beyond any normative categorization of identity and gender expression. Each portrait is printed vertically, in magazine format, by mimicry as much as by subversive intent. MACK gathers the fifty photographs, expanded with unseen images, alongside a text by Brontez Purnell, a leading figure of the American queer literary scene and author of 100 Boyfriends .

In the darkroom, K8 Hardy methodically sabotages her own images: cutting negatives, taping them back together, layering them, deliberately choosing the failed shot. “The interventions become interference,” she says. Everything is aimed at unmasking photography as construction rather than fixed truth, at short-circuiting that moment of belief in an image. “It wasn’t about getting the shot, it was about making it.”

The series’ wardrobe follows the same logic of friction. “I see style as just another tool on my tool belt,” says K8 Hardy, drawing exclusively from thrift stores, never conceding an inch to luxury or designer labels. The looks generate a deliberate dissonance with their settings — a cafeteria, a chain-link fence, a floral armchair — captured across travels through Chile, Texas, Italy, and Argentina. The goal? “Stay common, but peculiar.”

In the lineage of surrealist trailblazer Claude Cahun, of Marianne Wex, who catalogued gendered body language, and of Coco Fusco, performer and critic of colonial representation, K8 Hardy constructs figures that are neither icons nor quite anonymous in their representation. Her model, she says with a laugh, is “a no one who is someone.” A concept our own era has since caught up with. “Now it’s impossible to look at this series outside the regime of the selfie,” she acknowledges.

The exhibition “Taking Back Our Space: Photographic Perspectives” runs at MoMA , New York, through May 2, 2027. Positions (2026) by K8 Hardy is published by MACK (128 pp., $85), in a limited edition of 1,000 signed copies.

content.article_text:
写真家YUTARO SAITOによる展覧会「72 CLUB TOUR」が、2026年9月18日から10月2日まで、東京・板橋のCOPY CENTER GALLERYで開催されている。

SAITOは2021年より、「NOT PLASTIC FASHION」をコンセプトに高齢者のファッションを撮影してきた。衣服がイメージとして大量に流通する現代において、彼がカメラを向けるのは、その背後にある身体と個人の時間だ。高齢者の装いを通して、「着る」という日常的な行為のなかに蓄積された記憶や習慣を掘り起こしている。

本展は、新たに刊行される写真集『72 CLUB CALENDAR』に合わせ、国内主要ブックフェアでの販売と全国各地での展示を行う巡回プロジェクト。同書は、これまでNOTEやFASHIONSNAPなどで発表してきた高齢男性へのファッションインタビューに、未発表作品を加えて再構成したものだ。

特徴的なのは、高齢者の装いが持つ「機能性」に着目していること。『72 CLUB CALENDAR』自体も、一般的な写真集にとどまらず、カレンダーであり、写真集であり、さらには展示物でもあるという複数の機能を併せ持つ。本展では同書とともに、高齢男性を写したポートレート作品や衣服、「NOT PLASTIC FASHION(2030)」シリーズからポスター作品を展示する。

流行や新しさが絶えず更新されるファッションの世界に対し、長い年月をかけて身体になじみ、生活の一部となった服は何を物語るのか。SAITOの写真は、装うことを表層的なスタイルとしてではなく、一人ひとりが生きてきた時間や身体の記録として捉え直している。

content.article_text:
O ne man and his dog have an amazing adventure in this survivalist drama starring Brad Pitt, from screenwriter Cameron Alexander and director David Ayer, for which the first and last words of the title have been carefully chosen to signal a mix of sentimentality and thrills. It’s an entertaining anthro-canine-mance, with man and dog relating to each other on a deep level … kind of like Owen Wilson in Marley & Me , only without Jennifer Aniston, or Bernie Winters and Schnorbitz, only without the devastating melancholy.

Pitt, who last worked with Ayer on the second world war action thriller Fury , plays a US military special forces veteran called Belmont, tough, self-reliant and laconically good-humoured in the classic Pitt manner, now spending his retirement roaming the breathtaking remote landscape of Alaska in his seaplane. He is accompanied by his beloved service dog Odin, or Odey (played by four different German shepherds), who saw action with Belmont in various fuzzily imagined flashback combat sequences. Odin took retirement with Belmont and is now his best and only pal. Whether or not Belmont ever had a human partner is never revealed.

Their lives together look heavenly, but a heartstoppingly dramatic event means that Belmont must make an extraordinary journey across rough and hostile terrain, on foot, during which he must look after Odin and Odin must look after him. And the dog is no mere passenger in this ordeal; at one stage Odin gets into a stare-out contest with a digital bear, and a mano-a-mano fight with some digital wolves. Visual effects work, however top-drawer it is, always slightly undermines the feeling of real jeopardy, which here is otherwise expertly maintained. Among the humans they encounter is a grizzled old former goldminer played by JK Simmons (channelling Walter Huston), and Anna Lambe as a young woman who fatefully enters the story at its very beginning.

The idea of a man and a dog having no one in this world but each other is an engagingly bittersweet idea; as well as calling up the hardihood of Jack London, it speaks of loneliness and companionship at the same time. Yet weirdly, Belmont is not unlike Pitt’s stuntman character Cliff Booth in Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, living in a trailer all on his own except for his loyal pitbull Brandy, a dog which can go into terrifying attack mode on a prearranged signal. (Belmont has the same setup with Odin.) Booth and Brandy are Mr Hyde to Belmont and Odin’s Dr Jekyll.

As for Pitt himself, his acting chops are tested when he has to sob and then laugh with joy when it looks wrongly as if Odin has been fatally wounded – but extravagant emoting is not why we love him. Heart of the Beast is a bit cheesy and the final moments will test your credulity, but Pitt is the right guy in the right film.

content.article_text:
Jordan Rossi has always walked a fine line. British with Italian and Irish roots, he shoots the London queer scene and luxury brand campaigns with equal conviction, never appearing to betray either. His gaze turns fashion photography — vivid, often irreverent — into a tool for intimate and social portraiture. With a single obsession: catching the moment his subjects drop the mask.

The title of your first exhibition, “Homecoming”, speaks of both return and belonging. What does that word mean to you?

Jordan Rossi : “Homecoming” felt like the only possible title. I grew up between two cultures, Italian and Irish, but I was born and raised in London — so I’ve always had a slightly complicated relationship with the idea of “home”. I don’t think I’ve ever felt entirely one thing or another.

Bringing this body of work to Italy feels like closing a circle. These photographs cover nearly a decade of my life, made in London, Los Angeles and elsewhere. Bringing them here, to a country that is part of my identity and my family, feels very personal. But with time, “home” has become less geographical for me. It’s the people you surround yourself with, the communities you find, and eventually the space you create for yourself. In that sense, “Homecoming” is as much about where I am now as it is about where I came from.

You have shot the queer community of East London just as much as campaigns for Rolls-Royce. Are these two worlds not in conflict, and how do you move between them?

Jordan Rossi : I’ve never really seen them as being in conflict. The scale, budgets and expectations might be completely different, but ultimately I’m still interested in the same things: people, character, and creating a world around them.

I also don’t think queer artists should have to exist solely within queer spaces. I can photograph someone in a club in East London and then direct a campaign for a global brand — both can still contain my point of view. If anything, moving between those worlds matters to me. The experiences and communities that shaped me inevitably find their way into the commercial work, and the resources of the commercial world feed back into my personal work. I don’t want either side of my career to exist in isolation from the other.

Your photography is generally described as queer, committed, rooted in fashion and portraiture. What would you add about your work and where it has taken you?

Jordan Rossi : I’d probably add that there’s a sense of performance running through a lot of it. I’m interested in the version of ourselves that we construct for the camera: fashion, sexuality, masculinity, femininity, celebrity, glamour. Portraiture can document somebody, but it can also give them permission to become something else for a moment.

Over the past decade that has taken me into very different rooms — from emerging performers and people within the queer community to actors, musicians, fashion houses and global brands. I’ve photographed people I admired long before I ever picked up a camera professionally, which still feels slightly surreal. But when I look across the work now, what interests me isn’t necessarily who is famous and who isn’t. It’s that the same curiosity runs through all of it. I’m drawn to people who have a strong sense of who they are — or who are in the process of discovering it.

You are a photographer, a filmmaker and a creative director all at once. Concretely, how do you hold those three roles together?

Jordan Rossi : What I’ve realised over time is that every time I’ve added another discipline, it has changed the way I approach everything else.

There are instincts and skills that move between them. Photography made me much more aware of the relationship you build with the person in front of your camera. It can be incredibly intimate — just two people trying to find something together. Learning how to create that trust changed the way I worked with performers when I returned to directing. In the same way, years of filmmaking and creative direction have made me think differently about still images. I’m rarely just thinking about whether something looks beautiful; I’m thinking about the world around it, the character, the emotion, and what the image is trying to say.

That’s ultimately how I hold all three together: they’ve become part of the same visual language. I’m constantly taking things I’ve learned in one area into another, often without consciously realizing it. I’m less interested now in whether something makes me a photographer, director or creative director — and more interested in finding the best way to tell the story in front of me.

In your work, you have chosen to show the joy of the LGBTQIA+ community rather than its trauma. Do you feel a particular responsibility towards that community — and if so, what does it look like?

Jordan Rossi : Absolutely — although I try not to let that responsibility turn into the idea that there is one correct way to represent a community as enormous and varied as ours.

For a long time, so many LGBTQIA+ stories were framed through tragedy, rejection or suffering. Those stories are real and important, but they aren’t the entirety of queer life. I became much more interested in photographing the other side of it: friendship, sex, humor, beauty, ridiculousness, confidence, intimacy and joy. Not as a denial of the difficult things, but because those things are also political in their own way. There is power in seeing queer people simply having a brilliant time, taking up space, being desired rather than apologising for being there.

My responsibility is really to the people in front of my camera. I want them to feel they have agency in how they’re represented, and I want the work to come from being part of a community rather than looking at it from the outside. I don’t think my job is to speak for LGBTQIA+ people. It’s to contribute my perspective to a much bigger, messier and more interesting story.

Jordan Rossi’s show “Homecoming” is on view at Galleria Rubin , Milan (Italy), from September 22 to October 3rd, 2026.

content.article_text:
A news item by ArtThrob Editors on the 22nd of September 2026. This should take you 2 minutes to read.

From November 26, 2026, to February 28, 2027, the Bienal de Yucatán will launch the first international contemporary art festival in Mexico. The first edition of the Bienal will bring together 76 national and international artists across four exhibitions within a circuit of 16 venues throughout the historic center of Mérida and the municipality of Maní, with free admission for all. The Bienal de Yucatán is a long-term project with three initial editions scheduled to take place in 2026, 2028, and 2030.

The first edition, titled VOCAL , is dedicated to a reflection on tongue, languages, and multiple forms of communication. The central exhibition of the same name, under the artistic direction of artist Abraham Cruzvillegas, will present 38 new commissions, 42 Mexican artists – including 18 from the region – and 34 international artists from 20 countries. The Bienal de Yucatán will offer a space for critical thinking, artistic experimentation, and contemporary cultural dialogue from the Mexican Southeast.

Yucatán: Cultural Territory Mérida offers an exceptional context as a territory where the richness of living Maya culture, tangible historical heritage, and a community with growing cultural infrastructure coexist – comprising museums, cultural centers, self-managed spaces, artist studios, forums, and universities, including the National University of the Arts of Yucatán (UNAY).

The name “Yucatán,” according to one of the most widespread interpretations, derives from a linguistic misunderstanding between Maya peoples and Spanish conquistadors: a first encounter marked by the complexity of translation. The Bienal takes up that narrative as a starting point to propose a space dedicated to building common languages – in the plural.

The Bienal de Yucatán is born from the conviction that Mérida and the Mexican Southeast harbor an extraordinary artistic energy that deserves an international platform to match. This is a project growing out of the territory, with the ambition of positioning Yucatán as a hub for critical and creative thought, in dialogue with the Caribbean and the world.

VOCAL VOCAL, under the artistic direction of artist Abraham Cruzvillegas, offers a reflection on tongue, languages, idioms, the written, the spoken, and what needs to be said. The showcase unfolds at the main venue, Casa de la Cultura del Mayab (a former 16th-century convent under SEDECULTA), and extends across different venues in Mérida’s historic center and the municipality of Maní.

Mayan culture developed an elaborate system of representing oral language, manifested in documents carved in stone that resisted destruction and looting since the colonial period. It has been the people who still speak Maya who have sustained the survival of their language, despite the efforts of a monolithic national will that attempted to erase cultural and linguistic diversity.

VOCAL brings together 76 artists and other participants–including linguists, filmmakers, poets, musicians, and dancers–who, as Cruzvillegas points out, offer us “words that affirm difference together, and that would together imagine other possible landscapes, and other ways of existing within them, collectively.”

“This international exhibition will focus primarily on tongue, languages, idioms, the written, the spoken, and what needs to be said. The works and individuals participating in this renewed version of the Bienal de Yucatán will make it one of inclusion and diversity, of languages and idioms that engage in dialogue and contradict one another.”

– Abraham Cruzvillegas , Artistic Director of the Bienal de Yucatán 2026

デザイナー・圷イサクによる新プロジェクト『shuku+ga（祝＋我）』の第一弾として、展示・受注販売会が代官山 ALにて開催される。

本プロジェクトのテーマは、「なんにもない日に、おめでとう。」自分と大切な誰かを祝うことを起点に、写真家・川島小鳥が、田辺あゆみ、TAEHEONら10名の飾らない姿と、その場に流れる時間を撮り下ろした。会場では、川島小鳥によるポートレートとともに、圷が手がけた3種のネックレス、松井正憲（METER）がデザインしたZINEとアートポスターを展示する。会期中は、これらを組み合わせたセットの受注販売も実施する予定だ。読む、部屋に飾る、身につける。それぞれの作品が、ひとつの空間のなかでつながる展示となっている。

初日の9月25日（金）17:00からはレセプションを開催予定。ぜひ足をお運びいただきたい。

Susan kae Grant: Sweet Dreams Are Made of This

American photographer Susan kae Grant has made dreams her material and her photographic territory. Night Journey , published by MW Editions, is the culmination of a life’s work: a sumptuous and haunting volume, in black and white, crafted with the precision of a haute couturière of the unconscious.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Susan kae Grant.

Susan kae Grant grew up in a small town in Wisconsin. A shy and silent child, she expressed herself by drawing, writing, and making collages. Alfred Hitchcock and Rod Serling, creator of the anthology series The Twilight Zone , served as her compass: “the way they created mystery came through tormented theatrical storytelling.”

Trained in photography at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, she went on to teach photography at Texas Woman’s University for thirty-six years. Her artistic lineage connects her to what critic A.D. Coleman called the “directorial mode” — a photography in which the scene is entirely constructed by the photographer, in the tradition of Duane Michals, master of narrative sequence, and Arthur Tress, explorer of childhood dreams and nightmares.

In the 1990s, Susan kae Grant agreed to have electrodes placed on her body and to be awakened during REM sleep to describe aloud what she had just seen. Listening back to the recordings, she discovered a voice she barely recognized, phrases spoken in an in-between state, neither fully asleep nor truly awake. “I realized that these recordings had been made in a different state of consciousness.” The words murmured in the dark — “She’s Afraid to Stop”, “Something Needs Constant Attention”, “We Act Like We Don’t Know One Another” — would become the titles of her photographs.

In her Dallas studio, Susan kae Grant works with a 4×5 camera fitted with a digital back. Rare in contemporary photography, she never photographs her subjects directly — only the shadows they cast. She layers models, props, and floral wire, repositioning directional lights dozens of times, sometimes over months, for a single image.

This shadow theater summons Murnau’s Nosferatu and German Expressionism as much as Plato’s allegory of the cave. “It’s like being inside a gigantic three-dimensional photogram that I can’t fully see until I’m behind the camera,” she explains. “I strive to design sets with a sense of mystery and ambiguity, to provoke a narrative that raises more questions than it answers.”

The silhouettes that populate her images have no faces. These anonymous bodies fall, embrace, reach toward something just out of frame. As essayist Deborah Willis writes in the book’s opening essay titled Mapping the Dream Terrain , these figures “function less as characters than as vessels for sensation and memory,” inviting the viewer to project their own nights onto the page. “The narratives are a representation of a representation, and they exist only in the imagination.”

Founder of The Black Rose Press since 1976, Susan kae Grant has produced twelve limited-edition artist books, held in the collections of the Getty Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum. Night Journey is their crowning achievement. With its gatefolds, triptychs, and an entire section printed on translucent paper where images layer like strata of memory, the book performs, down to its very design, the logic of the dream.

Night Journey by Susan kae Grant is published by MW Editions and available for $70.

content.article_text:
At the Martin Parr Foundation, the Gothic Next Door

The Martin Parr Foundation presents “Dark Tales: British Documentary and the Gothic,” an exhibition that reminds the viewer what makes an atmosphere distinctively British: a fondness for dark irony, layered emotional depth, and a passion for the absurd.

By Gaia Squarci. Cover Photo by Chris Shaw

Curator Isaac Blease drew the selection from over 5,000 prints in the Foundation’s collection, spanning more than 80 years, from the post-war years to the present. Together they build a haunted, playful narrative that shows photography’s power to visualise fear and fascination — proof, as Blease puts it, of the Gothic principle that horror lives closest to the familiar.

Rather than impose a single viewpoint, the show lets atmosphere serve as its thread, moving from historical documentation to domestic unease to class, into the rituals of appearance and respectability, where details of style are always an indicator of a deeper message. Fading industrial towns, claustrophobic interiors, and eerie nocturnal scenes recur throughout, in work by Bill Brandt, Anna Fox, Don McCullin, Lee Miller, Chris Shaw, and many others.

The exhibition “Dark Tales: British Documentary and the Gothic” is on view at the Martin Parr Foundation in Bristol, UK, until December 20.

content.article_text:
“Images don’t belong to us. Proust’s madeleine is the same for everyone.” Set as the epigraph of Clichés (in French, the word means both a stereotype and a photograph), Denis Boulze’s line has the candor of a confession slipped backstage, between two takes. The photographer knows the recipe, having served it for years in the pages of Vogue , Silhouette and Milk , for Hermès and JM Weston: a face, a hand, a shaft of light, and the reader’s memory does the rest. A proven recipe. On Roxane Moreau’s podcast Dans le bain , recorded on the evening of his first solo exhibition, Denis Boulze readily speaks of his “candy images.” Sweet, then, and a little guilty.

The taste goes back a long way. The son of a photographer, Denis Boulze started as an intern at 16 at Studio Rouchon in Paris, where he later assisted Sarah Moon, Jan Walter, Sofia and Mauro. A tough school, and a lucky draw. In the acknowledgments, he gives his father his due, the man who passed on to him “a taste for the image” and taught him “to see.” The rest reads like a travel journal, since this “beautiful profession,” he writes, “has always been a pretext for me to travel, meet new people and live experiences that have deeply enriched me.” A craftsman’s courtesy, which also salutes his agent, the formidable Florence Moll, and the printers David Dahan and Luis Escudero, thanks to whom color printing has, as the artist puts it, “today become an essential part of my work.”

So why a book? Weariness? Remorse? A big spring cleaning? On his professional profile, Denis Boulze once let out this cry from the heart: “Help, fashion! Seeing the same photographers, the same stylists, the same models over and over, I’m getting a little bored.” Clichés answers with the simplest gesture: opening the archive boxes, cutting, pasting, layering. The bags, the bottles, the logos evaporate. What remains are bodies, gestures, postures. Claire Luna, winner of the 2025 AICA-France Élisabeth Couturier Prize for art criticism, sees in it, in her opening text, “almost a visual coming out,” and extends the metaphor all the way to the closet: the curtain has risen, “but something still lies coiled.”

What you find inside: 16 faces striped with shadow, 16 hands raised as if to stop traffic, a white dove above a red and orange puddle, starfish clinging to an ear. A moodboard? Almost. Denis Boulze works in diptychs and strips, slipping a tab of red or khaki-green paper between two prints, the way one dog-ears a page in a cookbook. A woman’s profile answers an antique plaster head; two long-necked bottles bathe in a day-for-night blue, a Morandi gone to the movies; a transparent dress floats against black, a dry cleaner’s ghost. The painted lips, for their part, are doubled, like a rubber stamp pressed twice (Blumenfeld and Man Ray have been here before).

The strength of the whole lies in its softness. Everything here belongs to reminiscence, a tune hummed without knowing who wrote it, hence the title Claire Luna chose, “Comme une chanson populaire” (Like a Popular Song). Denis Boulze embraces this shared memory, which he also claims for his series “Portrait de famille” (Family Portrait), made every summer in a former chestnut-drying hut in the Cévennes: a series “very dear to me,” he wrote, “although it is unfinished and will probably remain so forever,” meant to preserve “this parenthesis of our lives which, in my opinion, resembles a gentle poetry.” Clichés shares this slow tempo, like a family album whose members happen to be strangers.

Designed by Line Célo and printed by LONGO in Bolzano, the book has the restraint of a portfolio laid on a table at a festival portfolio review. Generous white space, airy sequences, color used sparingly and all the more precious for it. Some plates read like a catalog of forms, plaster spheres and half-moons in a Bauhaus vein; others keep a touch of glamour that Denis Boulze owns without false modesty. One could see this as a limitation. One could also read it as a form of honesty: the photographer lays out his alphabet, worn letters included, and leaves readers to recognize their own words in it.

Which leaves the question of authorship. To whom does a hand resting on a cheek belong, an eye under makeup, a glass of milk on a dark table? To everyone, answers the epigraph. To whoever looks, the book corrects. Denis Boulze has known this since childhood, and closes his acknowledgments with his father, thanked for a lifelong lesson: “the importance of looking and cultivating my eye.”

Denis Boulze’s Clichés , with a text by Claire Luna, is self-published and available for €40. To buy the book, contact Denis Boulze directly via his Instagram account .

As Aperture moves to the Upper West Side, and puts a renewed focus on reaching out, executive director Sarah Meister reflects on its ‘tentacular’ past and future

Nothing says “killing it” like buying real estate in an outlandishly expensive culture-rich metropolitan hub. Aperture, the nonprofit publisher of sleek photobooks and the esteemed magazine, has done just that, purchasing and settling in a new permanent home that’s just opened to the public.

The 74-year-old organisation now occupies two floors of a New York City building dating back to 1886, refurbished by architecture practice Levenbetts (which was also behind the Queens Museum and five New York Public Libraries). “Because it was a residential building, it has an intimacy to it,” says Aperture’s executive director Sarah Meister, and the ground-floor entrance boasts street-level visibility to appeal more widely to passers-by, not just to photography devotees. (“Serious photographers will find you on the fourth floor of a side street in Chelsea,” Meister notes.)

Aperture’s new home is on the Upper West Side, which might seem unexpected given the centripetal force of New York’s downtown art scene. But “trendy arts neighbourhoods… move with fashion,” Meister reasons. By contrast, Aperture’s new neighbours are institutions such as the American Museum of Natural History and the New York Historical, and Central Park is just a stone’s throw away. They – and it – aren’t going anywhere.

Moreover, the singularity of the real estate gives it cachet. Meister points out that “it has 140-year-old load-bearing masonry, and it just has a great feel to it”, and Aperture was able to make the purchase through funding from private individuals such as Judy Glickman Lauder and Jon Stryker, as well as grants from New York State Council on the Arts and the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs.

“ It’s not a white box, and it never will be.” Sarah Meister

Inside the entrance – and past a Majestic Photobooth – the bookstore features Aperture’s output, which includes four issues of the magazine plus 12 books per year, and a backlist which unfurls as far back as the mid-1960s. It also features a pop-up collaboration with Dashwood Books, New York City’s de facto photobook purveyor; founder David Strettell will present a savvy selection of titles to sit alongside Aperture’s publications, and some of his knowledgeable staff will move uptown. “It’s just a smarter way of being,” Meister says, “rather than us trying to do what they do, because they do it so well.”

Aperture will host book launches in the shop, including for a new monograph by Elle Pérez, and for the Catherine Opie edition of The Photography Workshop Series; the Aperture PhotoBook Club will also create an opportunity for follow-up discussions. The shop features some lighthearted collaborations on merch too – there are Vik Muniz printed umbrellas, for example, and placemats printed with images from Stephen Shore’s American Surfaces . There are also baseball caps and tote bags, branded with the Aperture logo.

“There’ll be a handful of things in the store in collaboration with artists or people whose design sensibility we really respect,” Meister enthuses. “So we hope you come in for the books and the magazine, but there will be other fun things to buy too.”

The building’s two levels – one is half below street-level, and one is half above – give visitors views into key work areas, providing a behind-the-scenes peek into Aperture’s activities. The magazine team, the production team, and the book team are visibly present. “You can see in, and we’re happy about that. I think it’s going to give us a new understanding of our audience,” Meister says. Staff are encouraged to sit at a table in the bookstore, and listen and talk to people walking by.

The building also features a dedicated gallery space and the inaugural exhibition, which was curated by Meister, spotlights photographers who have been integral to depicting New York City, including Diane Arbus, Tina Barney, Dawoud Bey, Awol Erizku, Lee Friedlander, Nan Goldin, Deana Lawson, and Carrie Mae Weems. There’s a print loaned from the Robert Frank Foundation; some artists made new 8x10s.

Temporary exhibitions will generally be on view in the space for six to eight week stretches, though Meister says “we don’t want to become too rigid”. That ethos will run through the shows too, with most works leant on a picture rail on a shelf, rather than hung, leaving the original exposed brick undisturbed. “That lack of preciousness is very intentional,” Meister explains. “A little bit of informality feels like a nice thing. Our wall text is going to be printed on an 11×17 sheet with magnets on a beautiful little metal panel: very simple.”

In the longer term, Aperture is working with artists to develop different configurations for the space, allowing each individual to use it in their own way. “It’s not a white box, and it never will be,” Meister affirms, adding that Alex Webb, Dionne Lee, and Angélica Dass will be showing there in future.

Aperture will run public events in the gallery, with a series of conversations “between pairs of people who either know one another or one another’s work well”. Stephen Shore and Lucy Gallun, curator in the Department of Photography at the Museum of Modern Art , will speak together on 03 October, for example, then Gillian Laub and Jil Weinstock, director of Baxter St, on 14 October; Coreen Simpson and Rujeko Hockley, curator at the Whitney Museum of American Art , will be in conversation on 21 October. Aperture will also continue to organise large-scale touring exhibitions.

Aperture also offers an educational program, with online curricula offered free of charge to public school teachers and kids. As Meister says: “Somebody once described Aperture as tentacular, which I love – not just because it rhymes with spectacular! It captures the breadth of what we do.”

Aperture, 380 Columbus Avenue, New York, NY 10024 aperture.org

Sarah Moroz is a Franco-American journalist and translator based in Paris. Her words have been published in the International New York Times, the Guardian, Vogue, NYLON, and others.

Avant-garments: the wild world of wearable art – in pictures

Each year international designers gather in New Zealand for World of WearableArt – a festival in Wellington where art, design, fashion and theatre collide. It culminates in a competition where designers show off their creations, from gowns resembling birds, fish and telephones to surreal garments inspired by cultural heritage and the natural world.

New Zealand artist Kayla Christensen took out 2026 top prize – the Supreme Wow award – for Sacred Nightfall, an intricately stitched tapestry that summons a night goddess from the native forests of Aotearoa

写真家 若林満による写真展「Dérive（漂流）」がライカギャラリー京都にて開催される。

街を歩くなかで、ふと目に留まる風景。若林満は、そうした一瞬を写真に残してきた。そこにあるのは、特別な場所や劇的な瞬間を探し求めることではない。何気なく過ぎていく日常のなかで、ある風景に目が留まり、シャッターを切る。その小さな偶然の積み重ねが、若林の写真を形づくっている。

本展のタイトル「Dérive（デリヴ）」は、フランス語で「漂流」を意味する言葉。この概念は、移動というものを目的地へ向かう手段としてではなく、歩くことを通して環境や感覚を体験する実践として捉えたものだ。若林が「Dérive」という言葉に出会ったのは、自身がすでに長く続けてきた撮影のあり方を振り返るなかでのことだった。なぜその場所で足を止めたのか、そのときには自分でもわからない。けれども行く先を定めずに街を歩き、目の前に現れるものを受け入れていく感覚は、まさに「Dérive」という言葉によって捉え直すことができるものであった。

本展では、日々の歩みのなかで出会い、撮り続けてきた風景を通して、ひとりの写真家が「見る」という行為とどのように向き合ってきたのかを紹介していく。 若林の写真を通して、いつもの風景にもう一度目を向ける機会になれば幸いだ。

また、本展と同名の写真集『Dérive』を 2026年秋に刊行予定。詳細は公式サイトに更新されるので、是非ともチェックしていただきたい。 https://mitsuruwakabayashi.com/photo-book/

content.article_text:
Two Images Are Better Than One

In Frozen Features , American photographer and publisher Jason Fulford overlays his negatives at random. From each collision emerges a third image, forging its own syntax.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Jason Fulford.

A knife plunged into a white table, its shadow stretching long as an accusation, and around it, scattered like coins on a counter, watch faces stripped of their hands. Welcome to Frozen Features : a book where every image is already double, where meaning surfaces in the gap, sharp and immediate, before any explanation.

Jason Fulford holds ten thousand digitized negatives, thirty years of images kept in envelopes, boxed, stored in a cabinet. Last year, he began overlaying them at random, two negatives at a time, to see what their meeting might produce. From roughly a thousand pairs generated by chance, he kept a few hundred, then spent two days with Sarah Chaplin Espenon, editor at Loose Joints, whittling them down to fifty-four: purely intuitive work.

Only the combinations that “sing” survive. Charles Goslin, his graphic design professor, used to collect obituaries from The New York Times featuring people who had led double lives, two improbable existences fused into one. He asked his students to distill that duality into a single logo. Jason Fulford never stopped practicing that exercise.

For the photographer, two images placed side by side alter each other: from their encounter emerges an additional layer of meaning. Ferdinand de Saussure, the father of modern linguistics, put it this way: the value of a sign arises not from its own content, but from its difference from all the others.

A man seen from behind paints a madonna in watercolor against the New Mexico sky: without the straight road stretching beneath his brush, without the arid desert around him, the figure is nothing. With it, she becomes an apparition. Jason Fulford forges morphemes, minimal units whose meaning stays suspended, waiting for encounter.

Frozen Features opens with a line from American photographer Barbara Morgan, written in 1942: “Modern life is photomontage. In our thoughts and feelings, the images vital to us move together, skipping over the factual detail.” Jason Fulford takes her at her word, then goes further: he surrenders syntax to chance in order to surface the grammar buried beneath conscious thought.

TThese photographs each existed independently, made across thirty years of practice, yet were never intended to meet. In his address to the reader, Jason Fulford writes: “A metaphysical slot machine scoured my subconscious & fed it back to me, two memories at a time.” A fragmented face in a rearview mirror while a freight train barrels past in the background: two moments that never crossed paths now share the same second, and time ceases to be chronological. It becomes stratigraphic.

“The only way for them to last is for them to never fully be resolved,” says Jason Fulford — and one thinks of what American art historian Benjamin Buchloh wrote about Gerhard Richter’s paintings: vexations , puzzles that seem to promise a solution yet resist every attempt to reach one.

Roland Barthes, the French theorist of the image and founding father of modern semiology, called punctum that detail which pricks in a photograph and wounds, in the literal sense: a puncture, a breach in the gaze. Jason Fulford makes images with a double punctum : a toy dinosaur skeleton dissolving into the pink facade of a building at night, two simultaneous wounds contaminating each other. It is, as Loose Joints puts it, work that is “felt before it’s understood.”

Jason Fulford puts it plainly: “I always try to make work that the reader finishes.” And so Frozen Features is not a closed book: it is a half-written score, a sentence missing its verb. This is where the reader comes in. Two images are better than one, granted. But two images plus a gaze: that’s a complete sentence. Yours to make.

Frozen Features by Jason Fulford is published by Loose Joints , 104 pages, 54 color plates, $68.

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“There will be grain and seeds of gazes, music, strange processes, the LUX Tour and of course, the refreshment bar and local catering.” Monica Santos and Mat Jacob, the founders of Zone i, had announced it, and they kept their word. There was more: encounters, debate, swims in the river and live music."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As the first rehearsals of ABAL, a choir of Occitan polyphonic songs, ring out, a foghorn soon answers from the horizon. A rallying call goes out across the grounds: “Meet in the barn, the Photo Jam Session is about to start!” For the third year running, the Photo Jam Sessions invite photographers of all backgrounds and ages to present their work as a short projection. “The original idea was to evolve the portfolio review, where you find yourself face to face with maestros who assess your work,” explains Mat Jacob. The aim is to restore a form of horizontality with an audience, and to spark emulation, debate, advice and remarks. Mat Jacob sums it up simply: “It can be very enriching to be criticized with kindness.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/dsf0752-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/dsf0465-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While some projects are already far along, accomplished or even finished, most are still in progress or being shown to an audience for the first time. Practices intersect: documentary photography, experiments, video, editing or more singular technical processes. From Jean Puybaraud’s work on the genocide of the Yaghan people to Eve Campestrini’s series exploring the imaginary of a collective of farmers committed to the ecological transition, the subjects differ, but the social and environmental concerns echo each other."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Questioning the territory"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "From May to October, Zone i deploys a multidisciplinary program of exhibitions, talks, workshops, concerts and artistic projects around image, environment and education. The festival found refuge nearly ten years ago at the Moulin de la Fontaine, a former place of production and gatherings that is now a cultural laboratory dedicated to photography. Just as the miller once worked grain with the force of water, photographers now shape the grain of images there, capturing light, time and the stories of the living world. With “Graines et grain de regards” (Seeds and Grain of Gazes), five photographers from the area are invited to share one of their series as a carte blanche, in the Moulin de la Fontaine and along its banks."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In her series “Récit d’architecture ordinaire” (Tale of Ordinary Architecture), photographer Anne Piégu shows the traces of a rural world that is disappearing, along with the stories of those who lived in it. We meet Jacqueline, who married at 22 and joined her husband on the family farm. She was the one who milked the cows. And Colette, who arrived with her daughters 60 years ago. She was the first to have a house built in a small valley, facing the cellars of a village with a winemaking tradition."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/anne-piegu-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/eric-zeziola-683x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Through these stories, Anne recounts the transformation of the landscapes and ways of life that shaped her childhood. Her gaze goes beyond the rural world, because everywhere territories are changing, landscapes are shifting and certain ways of living are vanishing. What remains is photography, the only medium able to preserve the traces of what no longer exists. Beno Lelong bears witness to this with “Notes sur une ville qui n’existe plus” (Notes on a City That No Longer Exists). For several years, the artist roamed Nantes, living in squats and empty houses among other places. His images archive the remnants of an alternative city, the city of his memories, and also of a way of life that has since disappeared."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Between tribute and legacy"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sometimes photographs themselves become traces to be found. This year, some of the exhibitions bring back gazes that time had covered over. The first is Jean-Pierre’s, through the series “Jean-Pierre, Béquilles et Beautiful People” (Jean-Pierre, Crutches and Beautiful People), presented by Séba Lallemand. Jean-Pierre was homeless in Paris when Séba met him in the early 2000s, while working on a commission for an agency. They talked about photography, Jean-Pierre confessed his wish to try the medium, and Séba handed him his loaded Olympus MJU-II."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A curious trade followed. Séba developed the images, they arranged to meet “on a bench opposite the Fouquet’s on the Champs-Elysées, his headquarters,” and Séba showed him the prints. In the harsh light of the flash, Jean-Pierre captured the wealthy districts, the jet set and its share of pomp, luxury and glitter. He also captured the street, the pavement, the misery and those faces we pass every day without really looking at them. “People looked at him, the tramp, and he looked at people, the rich, the lost night owls, the poor.” Jean-Pierre got so caught up in the game that he bought himself small disposable Kodaks. “What was incredible is that he was as hooked on photography as he was on alcohol.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/seba-lalemand-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/beno-lelong-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/seba-lalemand-2-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The selection presented at Zone i is drawn from 47 rolls of film. There would be no 48th, as Jean-Pierre died before. Séba describes Jean-Pierre as having “the appearance of the celestial Parisian tramp, proud, drunk, with a smashed nose and greasy hair.” In the only image of him on show, he appears with eyes half closed, blinded by the sun, hair disheveled and cigarette hanging from his lips, a bling-bling chain (surely fake) around his neck. Of his identity, nothing is known: “he stayed very discreet about his past.” All that remains is his gaze, which transfigures the daily life of millions of people. A testimony free of judgment and a last thumbing of the nose at humanist street photography, with a Kodak snap."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "On the top floor of the mill, a second photographer is pulled from the dust of the attic. Forgotten after publishing 14 books, Christian Louis sees his work rediscovered after his death. It reveals a photography halfway between documentary and poetic narrative, one that seeks not the event but what happens beside it, in the interstices of reality. In chiaroscuro, he captures the jolts of a France in the midst of change, between industrial decline, urban expansion and new ways of life."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Out of frame"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A “clack” rings out in the middle of the field. It is the machine of Thomas Ozoux, the Photocotype: “an old photocopier to which I added a magnifying glass lens and that I covered with the panels of an old wardrobe.” It sits enthroned at the center of the Zone i labyrinth, a work made of around 100 old doors and recycled mirrors. Since childhood, Thomas has tortured his films and tinkered with his cameras. He continues to bend reality with his inventions. His long exposures recall those of the daguerreotype, while his “failures” and “monsters” reveal another side of reality. His photocotypes are also on show at the Moulin de la Fontaine."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the exit of the labyrinth, another “clack” rings out. This time it is an air rifle. After having your portrait taken, what better than to take a shot at a portrait? That is what Mat Jacob’s shooting stand offers, soberly titled “Innocentes photos de merde” (Innocent Crappy Photos). A tribute to the images that regularly appear before the court of public opinion and suffer, too, the violence of technology. content.article_text:
“There will be grain and seeds of gazes, music, strange processes, the LUX Tour and of course, the refreshment bar and local catering.” Monica Santos and Mat Jacob, the founders of Zone i, had announced it, and they kept their word. There was more: encounters, debate, swims in the river and live music.

As the first rehearsals of ABAL, a choir of Occitan polyphonic songs, ring out, a foghorn soon answers from the horizon. A rallying call goes out across the grounds: “Meet in the barn, the Photo Jam Session is about to start!” For the third year running, the Photo Jam Sessions invite photographers of all backgrounds and ages to present their work as a short projection. “The original idea was to evolve the portfolio review, where you find yourself face to face with maestros who assess your work,” explains Mat Jacob. The aim is to restore a form of horizontality with an audience, and to spark emulation, debate, advice and remarks. Mat Jacob sums it up simply: “It can be very enriching to be criticized with kindness.”

While some projects are already far along, accomplished or even finished, most are still in progress or being shown to an audience for the first time. Practices intersect: documentary photography, experiments, video, editing or more singular technical processes. From Jean Puybaraud’s work on the genocide of the Yaghan people to Eve Campestrini’s series exploring the imaginary of a collective of farmers committed to the ecological transition, the subjects differ, but the social and environmental concerns echo each other.

Questioning the territory

From May to October, Zone i deploys a multidisciplinary program of exhibitions, talks, workshops, concerts and artistic projects around image, environment and education. The festival found refuge nearly ten years ago at the Moulin de la Fontaine, a former place of production and gatherings that is now a cultural laboratory dedicated to photography. Just as the miller once worked grain with the force of water, photographers now shape the grain of images there, capturing light, time and the stories of the living world. With “Graines et grain de regards” (Seeds and Grain of Gazes), five photographers from the area are invited to share one of their series as a carte blanche, in the Moulin de la Fontaine and along its banks.

In her series “Récit d’architecture ordinaire” (Tale of Ordinary Architecture), photographer Anne Piégu shows the traces of a rural world that is disappearing, along with the stories of those who lived in it. We meet Jacqueline, who married at 22 and joined her husband on the family farm. She was the one who milked the cows. And Colette, who arrived with her daughters 60 years ago. She was the first to have a house built in a small valley, facing the cellars of a village with a winemaking tradition.

Through these stories, Anne recounts the transformation of the landscapes and ways of life that shaped her childhood. Her gaze goes beyond the rural world, because everywhere territories are changing, landscapes are shifting and certain ways of living are vanishing. What remains is photography, the only medium able to preserve the traces of what no longer exists. Beno Lelong bears witness to this with “Notes sur une ville qui n’existe plus” (Notes on a City That No Longer Exists). For several years, the artist roamed Nantes, living in squats and empty houses among other places. His images archive the remnants of an alternative city, the city of his memories, and also of a way of life that has since disappeared.

Between tribute and legacy

Sometimes photographs themselves become traces to be found. This year, some of the exhibitions bring back gazes that time had covered over. The first is Jean-Pierre’s, through the series “Jean-Pierre, Béquilles et Beautiful People” (Jean-Pierre, Crutches and Beautiful People), presented by Séba Lallemand. Jean-Pierre was homeless in Paris when Séba met him in the early 2000s, while working on a commission for an agency. They talked about photography, Jean-Pierre confessed his wish to try the medium, and Séba handed him his loaded Olympus MJU-II.

A curious trade followed. Séba developed the images, they arranged to meet “on a bench opposite the Fouquet’s on the Champs-Elysées, his headquarters,” and Séba showed him the prints. In the harsh light of the flash, Jean-Pierre captured the wealthy districts, the jet set and its share of pomp, luxury and glitter. He also captured the street, the pavement, the misery and those faces we pass every day without really looking at them. “People looked at him, the tramp, and he looked at people, the rich, the lost night owls, the poor.” Jean-Pierre got so caught up in the game that he bought himself small disposable Kodaks. “What was incredible is that he was as hooked on photography as he was on alcohol.”

The selection presented at Zone i is drawn from 47 rolls of film. There would be no 48th, as Jean-Pierre died before. Séba describes Jean-Pierre as having “the appearance of the celestial Parisian tramp, proud, drunk, with a smashed nose and greasy hair.” In the only image of him on show, he appears with eyes half closed, blinded by the sun, hair disheveled and cigarette hanging from his lips, a bling-bling chain (surely fake) around his neck. Of his identity, nothing is known: “he stayed very discreet about his past.” All that remains is his gaze, which transfigures the daily life of millions of people. A testimony free of judgment and a last thumbing of the nose at humanist street photography, with a Kodak snap.

On the top floor of the mill, a second photographer is pulled from the dust of the attic. Forgotten after publishing 14 books, Christian Louis sees his work rediscovered after his death. It reveals a photography halfway between documentary and poetic narrative, one that seeks not the event but what happens beside it, in the interstices of reality. In chiaroscuro, he captures the jolts of a France in the midst of change, between industrial decline, urban expansion and new ways of life.

Out of frame

A “clack” rings out in the middle of the field. It is the machine of Thomas Ozoux, the Photocotype: “an old photocopier to which I added a magnifying glass lens and that I covered with the panels of an old wardrobe.” It sits enthroned at the center of the Zone i labyrinth, a work made of around 100 old doors and recycled mirrors. Since childhood, Thomas has tortured his films and tinkered with his cameras. He continues to bend reality with his inventions. His long exposures recall those of the daguerreotype, while his “failures” and “monsters” reveal another side of reality. His photocotypes are also on show at the Moulin de la Fontaine.

At the exit of the labyrinth, another “clack” rings out. This time it is an air rifle. After having your portrait taken, what better than to take a shot at a portrait? That is what Mat Jacob’s shooting stand offers, soberly titled “Innocentes photos de merde” (Innocent Crappy Photos). A tribute to the images that regularly appear before the court of public opinion and suffer, too, the violence of technology. Fire!

And to restore some calm to all this, nothing beats soothing your heart by leaving with the photograph of one of your own pulses. The experience is made possible by the laboratory of the Trigone team, a member of the Lux network, which parks its caravan at Zone i for the bicentenary of photography. By bringing the electrical pulse of a heartbeat into dialogue with the movement of photons on a sensitive surface, the photographic process here transfigures one’s own heart into an image. These devices all remind us that Zone i remains above all a sensory experience, more than just a festival, and reflect the place’s determination, voiced by Mat Jacob: “to bring photography to life, whether it’s serious or not.”

content.article_text:
Zach Cregger traduz a tensão e o humor dos jogos em uma aventura que envolve o espectador pelas escolhas de câmera e pelas decisões desastrosas de seu protagonista.

A discussão sobre adaptações de jogos para o cinema costuma dedicar tanta atenção à fidelidade narrativa que uma exigência tão básica quanto “ser um bom filme” pode ficar em segundo plano. Reconhecer personagens e referências faz parte do prazer, mas pouco adianta quando a obra não encontra uma maneira própria de envolver o público. Felizmente, o diretor Zach Cregger compreende essa prioridade no novo “ Resident Evil ” e faz dela o caminho para adaptar a experiência dos games.

O longa acompanha Bryan (Austin Abrams), um sujeito completamente despreparado para a noite que terá pela frente. Sua jornada se resume a chegar a um lugar, descobrir como prosseguir e escapar do que aparecer pelo caminho. Essa simplicidade permite que Cregger concentre a narrativa no percurso e nas dificuldades que se apresentam. Objetivos aparentemente próximos por vezes exigem uma sequência de improvisos e decisões questionáveis que tornam o deslocamento até mais importante do que o que o espera no destino.

Essa estrutura oferece a base necessária para a adaptação trabalhar com liberdade. Os personagens reconhecíveis dos jogos estão ausentes, enquanto Umbrella e Raccoon City servem como breves referências para localizar os fãs, sem assumir qualquer responsabilidade de sustentar a história. O diretor utiliza o universo para construir uma aventura própria, sem gastar boa parte da duração preparando acontecimentos conhecidos ou explicando como cada elemento se encaixa na cronologia. O vínculo com o material original se estabelece pela experiência de atravessar aquele mundo.

Essa escolha reconhece uma diferença fundamental entre as duas mídias — há uma razão para o produto final se chamar “adaptação”, não “transcrição”. No jogo, avançar depende de quem está diante da tela, inclusive quando a vontade é apenas permanecer parado ou desligar a plataforma para evitar o próximo susto. No cinema, o percurso continua independentemente dessa disposição. Cregger busca recriar esse envolvimento exercitando constantemente a atenção do público durante a exploração dos ambientes, e as escolhas de câmera concretizam essa intenção.

Os enquadramentos mantêm vários pontos sob suspeita e estimulam a busca por ameaças. Há sempre alguma parte que ainda precisa ser vista, e a direção prolonga essa descoberta o suficiente para tornar a exploração desconfortável. Já as cenas em primeira pessoa restringem a visão, aproximando o olhar do espectador da perspectiva do protagonista. Cada movimento de câmera revela uma área e abandona outra, alimentando a tensão de que o perigo esteja justamente onde não dá para ver. Não é possível decidir por Bryan, claro, mas é possível avaliar (e julgar) seus caminhos, antecipar os riscos e sofrer (ou rir) quando ele faz exatamente o que parecia ser uma péssima ideia.

Embora sejam frequentes, os sustos repentinos se beneficiam dessa atmosfera que já deixou o público atento a qualquer mudança no quadro. Cregger sabe que a expectativa de uma aparição pode sustentar o desconforto por mais tempo do que a aparição em si. As criaturas rompem a espera com movimentos agressivos e violência suficientes para desestabilizar a percepção de como enfrentá-las. Mas essa experiência também comporta o absurdo, e é no acúmulo de problemas que o filme encontra sua característica mais divertida. O roteiro constrói uma espécie de progressão da desgraça na qual Bryan é incapaz de concluir uma dificuldade sem descobrir outra ainda pior. A mesma lógica que mantém a narrativa em movimento produz comédia.

É inegável o quanto Bryan contribui para piorar as próprias circunstâncias. Sua falta de preparo está longe de servir como ponto de partida para a descoberta de um heroísmo escondido. Ele faz besteira o tempo todo, e o filme tem plena consciência disso. Algumas decisões já parecem ruins antes mesmo de serem colocadas em prática (como as hilárias e irritantes sequências com os cadeados), enquanto outras só revelam a extensão do desastre quando já não há muito a fazer (como abraçar uma garotinha para lá de infectada). Cregger encontra humor tanto na antecipação do erro quanto na reação ao resultado.

Dessa forma, o bom trabalho de Austin Abrams é indispensável para equilibrar tudo. O ator se mostra capaz de retratar esse descompasso entre o ritmo frenético dos acontecimentos e a capacidade de Bryan compreendê-los, como se o personagem ainda estivesse tentando processar o problema anterior quando o seguinte já exige uma resposta. Seu espanto e a maneira de lidar com tudo rendem alguns dos melhores momentos, e a situação em que ele se coloca é tão absurda que é difícil não torcer para ele concluir sua missão — mesmo quando se comporta como um idiota.

É interessante observar que o humor participa ativamente da construção do protagonista e do ritmo da aventura. Uma reação pode aliviar a tensão por alguns segundos sem tornar o ambiente mais seguro, assim como uma escolha engraçada pode produzir consequências violentas logo depois. Essa simbiose impede que o filme se acomode num revezamento previsível entre a hora do susto e a hora da piada porque, muitas vezes, os dois efeitos pertencem à mesma situação. O espectador ri do tamanho do problema enquanto continua preocupado com a possibilidade de Bryan não conseguir sair dele.

Com 1h35 de duração, o longa mantém essa dinâmica sem precisar expandir a história para justificar a importância da propriedade intelectual que está adaptando. A progressão quase em tempo real favorece bastante a sensação de que os acontecimentos não são etapas de uma explicação maior sobre aquele universo, e sim dificuldades que precisam ser resolvidas agora.

Essa concentração também expõe algumas limitações. No ato final, esse mecanismo de acumular obstáculos para o protagonista já está bem evidente, e a sucessão de desafios acaba perdendo parte do impacto. Além disso, a tentativa de desenvolver uma trajetória dramática para Bryan acrescentando uma preocupação com a paternidade recebe bem pouco espaço para amadurecer. Essa camada acaba parecendo dispensável, afinal, o vínculo com o personagem já era convincente por outros meios, sobretudo pela atuação e pela convivência com sua sucessão de calamidades.

“Resident Evil” reconhece que a passagem de uma mídia para outra exige reconstruir o envolvimento do público. Para isso, Cregger aposta nas ferramentas do cinema (principalmente o uso da câmera) para recriar o sentimento de jogar um terror de sobrevivência. O resultado é tenso e muito divertido, sendo capaz de preservar a aflição e o prazer inexplicável de atravessar um lugar hostil, mesmo sem oferecer qualquer controle sobre o percurso. Bryan se encarrega de tornar essa jornada o mais desastrosa possível.

content.article_text:
写真家・伊丹豪の個展「a plan for all things」が、2026年10月3日から27日まで、東京・神楽坂のCAVE-AYUMI GALLERYで開催される。本展では、すべて自身の自宅で撮影した新作を発表。会場デザインを建築家の板坂留五が手がける。

伊丹はこれまで、画面内のすべてにピントを合わせる「全焦点」の写真を通して、写真を「見ること」と「撮ること」の関係を考察してきた。被写体の一つだけを際立たせるのではなく、画面に存在するものを等しく鮮明に写すことで、鑑賞者の視線に無意識のうちに生まれるヒエラルキーを揺さぶる。一方、その写真は鮮やかな色彩や大胆な構図にも特徴があり、鑑賞者は視覚的な面白さに引き込まれながら、次第に「何が意図され、何が偶然なのか」という問いへと導かれていく。

今回、伊丹が被写体とするのは、自宅にある家具や日用品など、ごく身近なものだ。それらを選び、動かし、配置することで画面を構成していく。その背景には、過去に見てきた写真や絵画、美術の構造を、生活空間に存在する物の配置へと置き換える行為がある。撮影を終えれば配置は解体され、実際の空間から消えてしまう。写真の中にだけ、そこに存在した物と、すでに存在しない一時的な関係性が残される。

展覧会タイトルの「a plan for all things」には、「plan＝計画」と「plane＝平面」という二つの意味が重ねられている。物を選び、配置して撮影するという「計画」と、それらすべてが同じ密度で定着される写真という「平面」。美術からの引用も日用品も、作為も偶然も、一枚の表面では等価な存在として並ぶ。

「写真は目の前を複製することしか出来ない」と伊丹は語る。だからこそ、何を写し、どのように配置し、どの技術によって複製するのか。その選択の積み重ねに、写真を撮る行為の誠実さを見いだしている。作品の中で何が重要なのか、何が偶然なのかという答えはあえて明示されない。判断は見る側へと委ねられ、「何を見るか」という行為そのものが、私たち自身の価値判断を浮かび上がらせていく。

さらに本展では、これまでも建築家やデザイナーらとの協働を行ってきた伊丹の姿勢を引き継ぎ、板坂留五が展示空間を設計する。板坂は新たな造形を加えるのではなく、「しんとした空気の部屋」をつくり、鑑賞者が写真へゆっくりと近づいていける空間を構想。ギャラリーにもともと存在する壁や床、躯体の凹凸と伊丹の写真を組み合わせることで、写真に表れる独特の物の捉え方を空間へと拡張する。

伊丹豪「a plan for all things」

CAVE-AYUMI GALLERY（東京都新宿区矢来町114 高橋ビルB2）

12:00〜19:00

content.article_text:
Aperture Opens at 380 Columbus Avenue

The new home for photography, now open to the public as of September 18

Aperture Ribbon Cutting, New York, September 2026. Photo by Lloyd McCullough

Aperture News - September 18, 2026

To mark the momentous opening of Aperture’s permanent home in New York’s Upper West Side, supporters, artists, and neighbors gathered for a ceremonial ribbon cutting on the morning of September 18, following festive celebrations the evening before. The opening events toasted Aperture’s new chapter at 380 Columbus Avenue—a dedicated space for “serious photographers and creative people everywhere,” as its founders envisioned seventy-four years ago.

Honoring Aperture’s past and future, more than thirty artists gathered to take a group photograph, marking the significance of the occasion. Other artists in attendance included Emmet Gowin, Richard Renaldi, Sable Elyse Smith, Naima Green, Philip Montgomery, Edward Burtynsky, and Carlos Jaramillo.

Cathy Kaplan, Chair of Aperture’s Board of Trustees, welcomed guests and recognized the many funders and organizations whose steadfast support made the new home possible. Public officials, including New York City Council Member Gale A. Brewer; Erika Mallin, Executive Director of the New York State Council on the Arts; Diya Vij, Commissioner of the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs; Miesha Smith, Deputy Borough President for Manhattan; and Erik Bottcher, New York State Senator, joined to celebrate Aperture’s contributions to New York’s arts and culture landscape.

Just before the ribbon-cutting moment, Aperture Executive Director Sarah Meister expressed deep appreciation and emphasized the significance of 380 Columbus Avenue as a welcoming forum to gather, share ideas, and engage with photography. “Just like each brick in the beautiful arches of this load-bearing masonry building needs its neighbor to serve its function, each of us has played an essential role in making this historic moment possible,” said Meister, in thanks to the supporters, staff, and community.

At the celebrations, guests previewed the bookstore, stocked with new and classic Aperture publications along with titles in collaboration with Dashwood Books, New York, and Offset Projects, New Delhi, and visited the gallery space featuring the inaugural installation Aperture Loves New York , which showcases artists anchored in Aperture’s publishing history with photographs and corresponding Aperture books that have advanced the medium of photography and captured the complex spirit of New York itself. Guests also stopped by the new photo booth, which will remain available for visitors. Now open to the public, Aperture hosts a full season of artist talks, panel discussions, and book celebrations.

Aperture thanks and Zabar’s for their generous support of the opening celebrations, with champagne provided by Ruinart and wine provided by Massican. Promotional support for Aperture Loves New York is provided in part by the New York City Tourism Foundation.

Aperture’s capital campaign to date includes transformative gifts from Judy Glickman Lauder, Melissa and James O’Shaughnessy, Vasant Nayak, Thomas R. Schiff, and Jon Stryker and Slobodan Randjelović, as well as from Michael Hoeh and the Thompson Family Foundation. Aperture received significant grants from New York State Council on the Arts; and City of New York, including the Manhattan Borough President, New York City Council, and New York City Department of Cultural Affairs. Support for the campaign reflects the full participation of Aperture’s Board of Trustees, along with generous contributions from other individuals and foundations. The acquisition of the new space was led by Cathy M. Kaplan, Chair of Aperture’s Board; Helen Nitkin, Chair of the Board’s Real Estate Committee; and Sarah Meister, Executive Director. Financing has been provided by LISC NY, a nonprofit community development institution.
