content.article_text:
Armed with his film Leica, Alexis Duclos roams the city in search of the unexpected. Where his first exhibition, “En Ville” (“In the City”), captured the poetry of Parisian streets, “Downtown” extends his gaze to other horizons. He builds a monochrome series with a vibrant grain, in which black and white contrasts make light the guiding thread of this urban wandering. The sun rises and floods a Parisian facade, blazes over a Tokyo boulevard at its zenith, then its last rays timidly caress a New York building: across 20 photographs, the exhibition itself becomes a wandering that mirrors the photographer’s own.

We move from one metropolis to another without transition, carried by the same invisible thread linking streets across the world. In the end, it hardly matters where an image was taken, since the city rocks us with the same refrain, as if all cities shared a common language that only the eye could reveal.

Larger than life

From the cover image on, Alexis Duclos shows us that the monumental city and ordinary bodies share the same sky. A knee bent like an arch, a hand wrapped around it. Below, a row of curved backs, bare shoulders, legs dangling at the water’s edge, and far in the background, tiny, almost shy, the iron lady watching over Paris. In this oversized foreground, where flesh becomes landscape, we are plunged into the almost indecent intimacy of the framing.

The photographer plays with dimensions, shifting scales, inviting us to look differently. The fairground is transformed into a Hollywood spectacle, where a papier-mâché King Kong, turned silent guardian of a carousel, looms above the crowd, jaws open on a silent roar, reaching an arm toward the sky as if to pluck the silhouettes spinning at the end of their metal cables.

Nothing is ever quite what it seems, and facades sometimes turn into backstage. That is the case with this image, titled Ascension, where the giant shadow of a service staircase unfolds across a metal fence. We see only the staircase’s reflection, a ghostly, projected version, theatrically lit. As if the building were watching itself, and the cast shadow were the only stage where the real spectacle could finally play out. A set worthy of theater or cinema, it is impossible not to think of The Truman Show. One almost expects to see the character, mid-ascent, reach the top, turn to the audience, take one last bow, and deliver a final line: “Good morning, good afternoon, and good night.”

Film photography, a return to the source

For more than twenty years, Alexis Duclos worked at the heart of current events. Starting in 1985, after a stint at Associated Press, he joined the Gamma agency, where he covered conflicts, political news, sports, and major international events. A photographer honored with several awards, he developed a practice marked by the diversity of terrain he explored. In 2005, as photojournalism underwent major upheaval, he decided to leave Gamma to devote himself to independent projects, moving between documentary photography and audiovisual production. Then, over the years, he gradually turned away from reportage to rediscover the simple pleasure of a photography freed from economic and editorial constraints.

Like a flâneur, Alexis Duclos lets himself be guided by chance. He moves forward with no apparent itinerary, attentive to what escapes hurried eyes. For him, photographing means learning to see, frame, and release the shutter at the right moment. His photographic style is distinctive, built on a rigorous composition in which every element finds its place and contributes to the image’s meaning. “I compose with light and framing to express a moment that, I hope, provokes emotions. That’s when a photograph can speak to me, can speak to us. Or not. It’s simple and complex at once.”

The only constraint the photographer imposes on himself is his choice of focal length: a 50mm lens, the one whose rendering comes closest to human eye perception. Alexis Duclos works exclusively on film: “I love black and white film for its grain, its texture, its material quality, and its aesthetic.” In his view, unlike digital photography and artificial intelligence, where images can be recomposed or artificially generated, film embodies a return to a photographic practice grounded in the materiality of the negative, an indisputable sign that a moment truly existed.

Here, implicitly, we find Roland Barthes’s intuition about photography’s indexical power: the image as trace, as proof that something truly was there, in front of the lens, in a light and an instant that will never occur again.

“Downtown,” by Alexis Duclos, is on view at La Caverne D’Art & Miss gallery in Paris, from September 24 to October 24, 2026.

content.article_text:
グローバル・ラグジュアリー・グループのケリングが、2026年10月27日、第39回東京国際映画祭 提携企画として「ウーマン・イン・モーション」トークを開催する。プログラム創設から11年目、日本での開催は9年目を迎える。現在9月30日まで観覧者を募集中だ。

今年は、映画監督・是枝裕和によるオープニング・スピーチに続き、アカデミー・ミュージアム・オブ・モーション・ピクチャーズ館長兼プレジデントで、アカデミー・コレクション統括責任者のエイミー・ホンマ、歌手・俳優の二宮和也、映画『国宝』（2025）の企画・プロデュースを手がけた映画プロデューサーの村田千恵子が登壇。

世界の映画文化を俯瞰するホンマ、日本映画を世界へ届けてきた村田、国内外の映画制作現場を経験してきた二宮。それぞれ「映画文化を継承・発信する立場」「作品を生み出す立場」「作品を体現する立場」から、日本映画の魅力や可能性、世界から見た現在地、次世代へ向けた映画文化のあり方について議論する。さらに、ジェンダー、多様性、アライシップの観点から、創造性を育む環境についても考える。

ホンマは2024年、アカデミー賞を主催する映画芸術科学アカデミーがロサンゼルスに設立したアカデミー・ミュージアムの館長兼プレジデントに就任。現在は同館の展覧会や上映、教育プログラムなどに加え、5200万点を超えるアカデミー・コレクションを統括している。

二宮はクリント・イーストウッド監督『硫黄島からの手紙』（2006）への出演をはじめ、第78回カンヌ国際映画祭でワールドプレミアされた『8番出口』（2025）に主演するなど、国内外で俳優として活動。村田は『キングダム』（2019）などの製作を経て、2025年公開の『国宝』を企画・プロデュースした。同作はカンヌ国際映画祭「監督週間」でワールドプレミアされ、第98回アカデミー賞メイクアップ＆ヘアスタイリング部門にノミネートされた。

トーク終了後には、ホンマが自身に影響を与えた画期的なアメリカ実写映画のひとつとして選んだ、ルル・ワン監督『フェアウェル』（2019）を特別上映。中国系アメリカ人監督であるワン自身の体験をもとに、アジア系移民のアイデンティティと家族を描いた作品だ。

ケリング「ウーマン・イン・モーション」は2015年、カンヌ国際映画祭とのパートナーシップのもと、映画界でカメラの前後を問わず活躍する女性の創造性と功績に光を当てるプログラムとしてスタート。現在ではジェンダーだけでなく、文化的背景や人種などを含む多様な声へと視点を広げ、よりインクルーシブな文化環境を目指す国際的な取り組みへ発展している。

Toyo Field 45CF, Daisuke Yokota

横田大輔、濵本奏、宇田川直寛、古田直人、草野庸子、渡邊聖子の6名の写真家によるグループ展「soft room」が、2026年9月17日から27日まで、東京・代田橋のflotsam booksで開催される。2023年にSprout Curationで開催された「幽霊の道具」展以来、3年ぶりとなる展覧会だ。

本展が着目するのは、完成した写真作品だけではなく、それを生み出す「カメラの側」。一般的なカメラ紹介と作例紹介という形式をあえて用いながら、作品や展覧会という完成形からはこぼれ落ちてしまう機材、撮影プロセス、物質、行為へと視線を向ける。そこから、通常は記述されることのない文化や存在、現象が複雑に絡み合う場を「部屋」として捉え直す。

写真を見るとき、鑑賞者の意識は往々にして「何が写っているか」や「写真家が何を表現したのか」に向けられる。しかし写真は、カメラやレンズ、フィルム、デジタル機器といった道具、さらには撮影や現像、プリントなど複数のプロセスを経て生み出されるメディアでもある。「soft room」はそうした写真を成立させる周縁的な要素を表舞台へと引き出し、作品と制作環境の関係を考える試みとなる。

展示に合わせ、6名それぞれの作品を構成するカメラや機材、撮影プロセスの詳細を収録したアンソロジー冊子『soft room』も刊行。展示作品だけでは見えてこない各写真家の「部屋」を、制作の方法論や道具から読み解くことができる。価格は2,000円。

また会期中には、参加作家6名による写真集やZineなどを販売するブックフェア「FancyshopDrivein」を実施。9月19日と26日には、30歳以下の表現者を対象としたポートフォリオレビュー「Standin」も開催される。一般的な講評会ではなく、ポートフォリオと、可能であれば実際に使用しているカメラを持ち寄り、参加作家との対話から、まだ形になっていない作品を言語化・具体化するための手がかりを探る。

content.title_original: Resident Evil review – Zach Cregger’s rebooted action horror is a wild rollercoaster ride
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "T ypically horror fans react to blatant on-screen stupidity with vocal derision. Don’t go in there! Girl, get out of the house! Guys, ignore that distress signal! But genre aficionados may find themselves falling a little bit in love with Bryan (Austin Abrams), the hapless de facto hero of the new horror film Resident Evil . It’s not that Bryan is traditionally hunky, or even a caricatured version of a square-jawed warrior, like Bruce Campbell in his later Evil Dead outings. But Abrams is in possession of a Campbell-ish charm, even in the face of his character’s repeated blundering, as well as an everyman relatability that makes this wild carnival-ride movie play a little closer to the ground.", "links": [{"text": "Resident Evil", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/games/resident-evil"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Bryan is a courier – a glorified Postmates driver, in his own estimation – who postpones the end of his shift to take one last night-time run, driving an important item from one hospital to another in a snowstorm without the proper tires or four-wheel drive. After all, the distance and urgency means double pay. When he hits a mysterious woman who emerges suddenly on to a slick road, he’s drawn into a hellish outbreak that will look familiar to fans of the Resident Evil video game series (or maybe the previous six-movie Milla Jovovich franchise, which apparently drifted afield from the games’ storylines)."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The key to Abrams’s winning performance as a perpetual loser is in how the actor and cowriter-director Zach Cregger take care to show Bryan stumbling his way through sloppy versions of doing the right thing. When he hits the clearly zonked woman, Bryan attempts to take her along on his hospital run. When he’s quickly pulled over by a cop, he makes little attempt to weasel out of his situation, attempting to prioritize his medical task. The man tries, even if some of his efforts in certain areas are lamentably weak (supporting his unseen girlfriend in a non-outbreak-related couple crisis) or understandably incompetent (wielding a firearm against undead creatures). His oscillations between overconfidence and panic make him a particularly fresh point-of-view character for a zombie/monster movie."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In short, he’s not unlike a guy who’s been dropped into a video game before learning the proper controls – in keeping with Cregger’s reported desire to replicate the experience of the game without adapting any of its stories directly. Abrams manages to humanize this unspoken and potentially arch conceit of an avatar learning the rules as he goes. It’s tempting to compare his many scenes without other human characters to silent comedy – only he’s not quiet enough to qualify, unleashing a hilarious symphony of profane and frustrated muttering. At one point, well after his life has been endangered multiple times, he can be heard complaining about his wet socks."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Good as Abrams is, alone and when playing opposite skeleton-crew supporting cast, he’s not exactly a one-man show, either; the guy behind the camera is his constant scene partner. Cregger, who has become a horror brand name on the strength of the similarly inventive Barbarian and Weapons, orchestrates the mayhem with expert command of pacing, comic-horrific timing, and even that old standby, the lowly jumpscare. (There’s at least one genuinely masterful version here.) The movie’s comic side isn’t quite Sam Raimi broad (or bold), but Cregger’s sketch-comedy roots are just as delightfully visible here as they were in Barbarian, without the aid of that movie’s clever shifts in timeline or perspective."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Indeed, Resident Evil has a streamlined single-mindedness, and as it barrels through its gamified plot, the tension and entertainment value never flag. Cregger only falters in the tail end, and it’s more a sin of omission than a big misstep. Resident Evil flirts with becoming a full-on monster movie where its cinematic predecessors tended to keep circling back to zombie action (at least in terms of their horror elements; let’s not discount Jovovich’s action bona fides). content.article_text:
T ypically horror fans react to blatant on-screen stupidity with vocal derision. Don’t go in there! Girl, get out of the house! Guys, ignore that distress signal! But genre aficionados may find themselves falling a little bit in love with Bryan (Austin Abrams), the hapless de facto hero of the new horror film Resident Evil . It’s not that Bryan is traditionally hunky, or even a caricatured version of a square-jawed warrior, like Bruce Campbell in his later Evil Dead outings. But Abrams is in possession of a Campbell-ish charm, even in the face of his character’s repeated blundering, as well as an everyman relatability that makes this wild carnival-ride movie play a little closer to the ground.

Bryan is a courier – a glorified Postmates driver, in his own estimation – who postpones the end of his shift to take one last night-time run, driving an important item from one hospital to another in a snowstorm without the proper tires or four-wheel drive. After all, the distance and urgency means double pay. When he hits a mysterious woman who emerges suddenly on to a slick road, he’s drawn into a hellish outbreak that will look familiar to fans of the Resident Evil video game series (or maybe the previous six-movie Milla Jovovich franchise, which apparently drifted afield from the games’ storylines).

The key to Abrams’s winning performance as a perpetual loser is in how the actor and cowriter-director Zach Cregger take care to show Bryan stumbling his way through sloppy versions of doing the right thing. When he hits the clearly zonked woman, Bryan attempts to take her along on his hospital run. When he’s quickly pulled over by a cop, he makes little attempt to weasel out of his situation, attempting to prioritize his medical task. The man tries, even if some of his efforts in certain areas are lamentably weak (supporting his unseen girlfriend in a non-outbreak-related couple crisis) or understandably incompetent (wielding a firearm against undead creatures). His oscillations between overconfidence and panic make him a particularly fresh point-of-view character for a zombie/monster movie.

In short, he’s not unlike a guy who’s been dropped into a video game before learning the proper controls – in keeping with Cregger’s reported desire to replicate the experience of the game without adapting any of its stories directly. Abrams manages to humanize this unspoken and potentially arch conceit of an avatar learning the rules as he goes. It’s tempting to compare his many scenes without other human characters to silent comedy – only he’s not quiet enough to qualify, unleashing a hilarious symphony of profane and frustrated muttering. At one point, well after his life has been endangered multiple times, he can be heard complaining about his wet socks.

Good as Abrams is, alone and when playing opposite skeleton-crew supporting cast, he’s not exactly a one-man show, either; the guy behind the camera is his constant scene partner. Cregger, who has become a horror brand name on the strength of the similarly inventive Barbarian and Weapons, orchestrates the mayhem with expert command of pacing, comic-horrific timing, and even that old standby, the lowly jumpscare. (There’s at least one genuinely masterful version here.) The movie’s comic side isn’t quite Sam Raimi broad (or bold), but Cregger’s sketch-comedy roots are just as delightfully visible here as they were in Barbarian, without the aid of that movie’s clever shifts in timeline or perspective.

Indeed, Resident Evil has a streamlined single-mindedness, and as it barrels through its gamified plot, the tension and entertainment value never flag. Cregger only falters in the tail end, and it’s more a sin of omission than a big misstep. Resident Evil flirts with becoming a full-on monster movie where its cinematic predecessors tended to keep circling back to zombie action (at least in terms of their horror elements; let’s not discount Jovovich’s action bona fides). Cregger’s monster-mashier shift is a welcome one, and presumably closer in spirit to the games. But he doesn’t bring the movie close enough to whatever line separates monstrousness and the humanity that might be lurking underneath.

It could be that there’s not supposed to be any – in which case the movie more or less just screeches to a halt before it gets too thorny. Weapons had a creepy, evocative aversion to simple metaphorical reads that ultimately increased its effectiveness; the same isn’t quite true here. Resident Evil foregrounds one obvious bit of character change for Bryan, but after doing a great job making us care about him for more than 90 minutes, Cregger seems to abandon him a few steps shy of completing any real journey. Is he awaiting a level up that never arrives? Hard to say. But maybe bringing a video game sensibility to the big screen while keeping any gamer cheesiness on the margins is journey enough.

Resident Evil is in cinemas on 18 September

content.article_text:
Before the South, there was New York. And before the portraits, the vast emptiness of its architectural structures. Born in 1951, Baldwin Lee grew up in Manhattan’s Chinatown. He first studied under Minor White, a presiding figure of contemplative photography, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, before going on to Yale, where Walker Evans’s teaching — Evans being the undisputed reference of American documentary photography — completed the formation of his eye. “I would tell my students that my photography teachers, White and Evans, were the equivalent of having studied with Matisse and Cézanne,” he recalls in an interview with Jessica Bell Brown published in Baldwin Lee (Hunters Point Press, 2022).

After graduating in 1975, he returned again and again to the city of his childhood, a 4×5 view camera on a tripod over his shoulder, moving through Manhattan at dawn, often in winter, when the sidewalks emptied of their inhabitants. “My trips to New York City from New England were an exploration of buildings as organic forms,” the artist confides. “Rather than approaching the work as architectural photography, I saw it as a way of capturing a landscape. It was my first time using a large-format camera. Early in the morning, with no one around, I felt an overwhelming intimacy — as if I were walking through my own private garden.”

His subjects include Wall Street at dawn, Times Square, and the streets and vacant lots of Lower Manhattan where the World Trade Center looms in the distance. Baldwin Lee records a city suspended between neglect and ambition, where remnants of the past remain visible alongside the structures of the new. Worn brick facades, Cadillac Eldorados parked along the curb, the twin towers still new: these images carry the trace of a human presence temporarily absent but not gone. “If the buildings were people it would be acceptable if they did not speak,” he tells Blind. “The silence can be a metaphor for spaces, once occupied, now vacant. The lack of people points to an unfulfilled potential.”

Baldwin Lee went on to teach at Yale, then at the Massachusetts College of Art. In 1982, he moved to Knoxville, Tennessee, where he founded the photography program at the university, which he would lead for more than thirty years. The following year, he embarked on an extensive series of journeys through the American South. Between 1983 and 1989, he made nearly ten thousand photographs, principally of Black communities — a body of work celebrated as a major social testament to rural Black America. “The photographs I made in the South would never have come about without adequate education and awareness: North/South, Black/white, male/female, private/public, poor/rich, powerful/subjugated,” he tells Jessica Bell Brown.

The New York photographs reveal a different but related aspect of Baldwin Lee’s practice. Their careful organization of architectural space and sustained attention to the character of place helped establish the distinctive visual language he would carry into his later work. They demonstrate a sensitivity to form and order, but also to the humanity inscribed in the built environment. His vision of New York is a record of what people made, inhabited, altered, and left behind.

The prints selected for the exhibition present his images at a scale he has never seen before. “No, I have not seen them printed at that scale,” he confides to Blind. “At this large scale the photographs and the viewer have a different relationship. A dialog between the photograph is possible and encouraged. The viewer is now capable of entering the space of the photo making for a more intimate experience.”

The twin towers that dominate several of his images have since vanished from the New York sky. The city Baldwin Lee once photographed as his own private garden no longer exists.

“Baldwin Lee: New York (1975–1979)” is on show at the Howard Greenberg Gallery from September 18, 2026 to October 31, 2026.

A reception with the artist will be held at the Howard Greenberg Gallery on Thursday, September 17, 2026 from 5:00 to 7:00 p.m.

Baldwin Lee is published by Hunters Point Press (2022).

content.article_text:
ビックリするほど当たるためIMA御用達の占い師・マコが、12星座の今をタロット1枚で運気予報！フォトグラファー清水はるみによるファンタスティックな星座＆大アルカナのヴィジュアルと共に、明るい未来の指針を毎月前・後半でお届けします。

9月後半に思うこと

「瀬戸内グリーンレモンに恋した理由」

それは、滋賀の日吉大社、奈良の橿原神宮、そして天河大弁財天社を巡る聖地巡礼の旅から始まった。神聖な空気に触れ、心身が大きく震えた直後、私はなぜか「塩レモン」に強烈に取り憑かれることになったのだ。

気になって仕方がなくなり取り寄せたのは、今しか手に入らない瀬戸内のグリーンレモン「璃の香」。形はいびつで傷もある「訳ありレモン」だ。しかし、見栄えの良いエリートよりも、野生の生命力が詰まったその姿に愛おしさが爆発。さらにレモンの輪切りにローズマリーとバニラエッセンスを合わせて火にかけ、じっくりと煮出してみる。部屋中に広がるすっきりと鋭いハーブの香りと、すべてを包み込むような甘い香り。その贅沢な香りを胸いっぱいに吸い込んでいる時間が何より心地良かった。

実はこの衝動、単なる料理ブームではない。私は今、人間関係を軽くし、過去の恐怖を克服して、新しいことに挑戦したい！という人生の転換期に立っている。この時、私が出合えた3つの素材は、私の決意を支えるスピリチュアルメッセージが隠されていた。青々と香る「ローズマリー」は古来より「記憶」と「トラウマの解消」を司る聖なるハーブだ、過去の恐怖を整理しメンタルを強く保つための戦士のような強さを授けてくれる。鋭い光を放つ「レモン」は澱んだエネルギーを強烈に弾き飛ばす」邪気払い」の象徴。特に今回選んだ「グリーンレモン」はハートチャクラを癒やし、未熟な状態からステップアップする「リスタート」のサイン。最後に、甘く漂う「バニラ」は、過去の恐怖で傷つき、固くなっていた内なる子供の心（インナーチャイルド）を「もう大丈夫だよ」と優しく抱きしめる「絶対的な安心感と自愛」をもたらす。

過去の恐怖を克服しようとする時、心は大きなエネルギーを消費する。ローズマリーで過去を断ち切り、レモンで道を拓き、バニラで自分を最大に愛するという「魔法の調合」なのだ。そこに祓いの代表「塩」が加わり私は最強になれるのです！

自分で仕込んだ塩レモンを、玉ねぎセロリ麹、ニンニクと合わせて豚しゃぶでいただく夜。レモンが瓶の中でじっくりと発酵していくように私の新しい人生もまた、ここから力強く豊かに熟成を始めていく。ハズ……。

content.article_text:
Joel Crawford e Januel Mercado articulam experimentação visual e intimidade em uma animação sobre preservar lembranças e continuar na vida de alguém.

É emocionante ver Jo e Raissa prometerem permanecer juntas para sempre antes de terem ideia do que isso significaria. Ao terminarem o ensino médio, a mudança de Raissa para os Estados Unidos coloca essa certeza em dúvida. A amizade continua, mas a rotina próxima e intensa que permitiu construí-la está prestes a acabar. “ A Ilha Esquecida ” se encontra nesse intervalo, representando bem esse medo de deixar de fazer parte do cotidiano de alguém e isso se tornar o começo do desaparecerimento da vida dessa pessoa.

Ambientado nas Filipinas dos anos 1990, o longa acompanha a última noite das amigas antes da mudança. A despedida toma outro rumo quando um portal transporta ambas para Nakali, uma ilha habitada pelas criaturas das histórias que ouviam durante a infância. Quando descobrem que voltar para casa pode custar a memória da própria amizade, a aventura reforça ainda mais a urgência que já estava estabelecida pela iminente separação da dupla.

Os diretores Joel Crawford e Januel Mercado, de “Gato de Botas 2: O Último Pedido” , desenvolvem a relação das protagonistas com bastante carinho e atenção aos detalhes — antes de colocá-la em perigo. A sequência que acompanha Jo e Raissa desde o primeiro encontro até o presente aproveita uma linguagem típica dos animes, e a formação da amizade se torna uma epopeia frenética. A montagem atravessa os anos com poucos diálogos, construindo a intimidade nas pequenas expressões e na maneira como as duas compartilham as situações. Quando a ilha começa a ameaçar essa história, já nos importamos o suficiente para temer o que está para ser perdido.

Esse compromisso de colocar a imagem a serviço da narrativa orienta a concepção visual de todo o filme. Ainda na cidade natal das protagonistas, proporções exageradas e cores vivas estabelecem um mundo que responde à energia das duas. A chegada a Nakali extrapola essa liberdade, com criaturas e paisagens que alteram constantemente a percepção de escala. Uma galinha pode ocupar o espaço com a imponência de um monstro, enquanto a aparição de um Cãobizomem parece perfeitamente aceitável. A opção da direção de arte é claramente recusar que o extraordinário possibilitado pelo gênero se comporte de maneira discreta.

Essa liberdade visual se aproxima daquela que “Aranhaverso” , “A Família Mitchell” , “As Tartarugas Ninja” e o próprio “Gato de Botas 2” ajudaram a consolidar na animação comercial. Crawford e Mercado exploram essa possibilidade para construir uma linguagem bastante adequada à história. O trabalho em 3D convive com passagens em 2D, sobretudo nos relatos sobre o passado, cujos estilos variam conforme o personagem da vez. Isso faz com que as lembranças também sejam novas formas de contar histórias, cada uma com uma aparência particular, em vez de receber um tratamento padrão apenas para indicar que se trata de um flashback. Em um filme sobre aquilo que as pessoas carregam consigo, essa escolha dá às memórias uma identidade que vai além de sua utilidade para explicar a trama.

A própria organização da aventura também se beneficia disso. Parte do percurso envolve reconstituir os acontecimentos que levaram as protagonistas àquela situação, no melhor estilo “Se Beber, Não Case!” . O recurso alimenta o humor e permite que novas revelações e informações incertas reorganizem o sentido de momentos anteriores, além de colocar o ato de lembrar no centro da ação. Jo e Raissa precisam recuperar o passado para decidir o próximo passo, enquanto tentam proteger uma história compartilhada que corre o risco de deixar de existir.

Nem sempre, porém, o filme administra bem a quantidade de coisas que coloca no caminho. O segundo ato acumula encontros com personagens cuja função inicial parece se limitar a apresentar uma nova excentricidade e render algumas piadas. Vários deles são divertidos, mas o tempo dedicado às apresentações enfraquece momentaneamente a urgência da fuga. É curioso que uma animação tão movimentada e frenética consiga parecer parada em certos momentos, enquanto o conflito das protagonistas espera sua vez de avançar.

A expressividade dos personagens e o contraste entre suas reações e o absurdo das situações produzem excelentes sequências, mas algumas gags insistem além do necessário, acrescentando exageros a cenas que já funcionavam. Ter um estilo com muitos estímulos não é, por si só, um problema. É que, por vezes, essa escolha acaba interrompendo uma aproximação emocional ou prolongando um encontro sem acrescentar muito ao que já havia sido estabelecido.

Essa distribuição desigual de atenção também prejudica a vilã. Sua presença salpicada pela história mantém a sensação de perigo, mas seu desenvolvimento não corresponde ao destaque que recebe na vida das protagonistas no primeiro ato, das referências em um trabalho escolar à fantasia usada pelas duas amigas. O filme não hesita em encontrar tempo para desvios cômicos e figuras passageiras, enquanto sua principal antagonista merecia um pouco mais de espaço para tornar seu conflito mais envolvente.

Quando os elementos apresentados ao longo da jornada finalmente se encontram, “A Ilha Esquecida” dá um peso emocional ainda maior à promessa que abre o filme. Perder as lembranças uma da outra significa também perder uma parte de si próprias. Apesar dos desvios, a aventura consegue transformar o medo da separação em algo igualmente íntimo e fantástico. Algumas amizades continuam fazendo parte de quem somos, mesmo quando já não fazem parte dos nossos dias.

content.article_text:
In America, fortune is often written in the plural of houses. Will Vogt owns three, which have also served as his hunting grounds as a photographer: a home in Corpus Christi, on the Texas Gulf coast; the family ranch, also in Texas; and, in Watch Hill, Rhode Island, the summer house where his family has gathered — and let themselves be photographed — for generations.

The boy he once was grew up elsewhere, in Haverford, Pennsylvania. More drawn to books than to sport, he discovered F. Scott Fitzgerald at boarding school, fell for his hero, Gatsby, and received his first camera not long after. From then on, it was his own world he turned the lens toward.

More than 70,000 images later, Will Vogt is far more than a chronicler of American wealth. His debut, These Americans , published in 2023, sold out. Three years later, Behind the Hedges returns to the same rituals — epic hunts, grand weddings, private society rallies — but the snapshot has given way to something more composed, and the urgency of youth to something more restrained. Interview.

Your previous book, These Americans , caught the moment. Behind the Hedges , your new book, composes it into tableaux. In practical terms, what changed in the way you shoot and sequence images between the two books?

Will Vogt: I’m not sure that the way I shoot changed as much as my material has. The advent of digital photography has also allowed me to capture more detail, which in turn makes larger tableau images possible.

These Americans drew heavily from photographs I took in the 1980s when I was younger and life around me was moving pretty fast. Behind the Hedges returns to many of the same people, places and traditions thirty years later. I’m older as are many of my subjects and as a result the pictures have slowed down a little too.

What did change enormously was my understanding of editing and sequencing. Before working with Jennifer Garza-Cuen on These Americans , I really had no idea how a photography book was put together. I learned that it isn’t a collection of your best photographs. In a book, the individual images have to work together, create a rhythm and tell a story.

In Behind the Hedges , your frame often leans on the natural or built architecture of a setting: a leading line draws the eye toward the façade of Lainston House, table and chairs arranged in the foreground; elsewhere, a swimming pool fills the foreground of the image. What place does aesthetic hold in your work?

Will Vogt: A very important one. I may be documenting something but I still want to make great photographs. I’ve always been conscious of composition, light and the relationship between people and the places they inhabit.

The surroundings are also part of the story. A house, a swimming pool, a shooting field or a dining room tells you something about the people in the photograph before you know anything about them. Sometimes the setting is every bit as important as the people.

In the essay he wrote to accompany These Americans , novelist Jay McInerney, author of Bright Lights, Big City , says “there’s no pane of glass” between you and your subjects. Doesn’t that closeness encroach on the distance a photographer sometimes needs from his subject?

Will Vogt: Familiarity gives me great access, but more than that it allows people to be comfortable around me and the camera. That is a tremendous advantage.

I think that is where the photographer has to create his own distance. You’re part of the scene but you’re also removed enough to document it. I’ve been doing that for most of my adult life, so I don’t think about it very consciously anymore.

One photograph in Behind the Hedges shows nothing but the filthy window of a Range Rover, finger-written with the line: “I wish my wife was as dirty as this.” The gap between a message that crude and a world that buttoned-up seems to delight you, as though you were forever hunting for the grain of sand that might jam the machine…

Will Vogt: I do like that photograph and particularly the contradiction and the humor. I don’t think I’m hunting for something to jam the machine. I’m looking for things that make the picture more complicated and thought-provoking than what you might expect.

There are plenty of preconceived ideas about this world and photographs like that one upset those expectations a little. People are rarely as buttoned-up as they appear. That’s what makes them interesting to photograph.

Behind the Hedges opens on a quote from F. Scott Fitzgerald, as an epigraph, before the first photograph. What place does literature hold in your eye as a photographer?

Will Vogt: I’ve always read a lot and I’m certainly attracted to writers who are good observers of people and social worlds. I fell in love with the writing of F. Scott Fitzgerald as a boy, about the same time I started taking pictures. He understood that wealth and privilege could be both seductive and complicated. I think I have documented some of that in my own work.

When I’m taking a photograph, I’m not thinking about Fitzgerald or trying to make an image look literary. Those connections tend to emerge later. A photograph can contain a whole story without explaining it. In that sense, I suppose photography and literature have quite a lot in common.

Behind the Hedges returns again and again to scenes of killing: a pit of zebra carcasses, partridges hung in neat rows, hares laid out on moss. What do these scenes of slaughter reveal, in your view, about this supposedly well-mannered society?

Will Vogt: I probably wouldn’t use the word slaughter. Hunting has been a large part of my life and of the world I photograph. Those images are part of the reality of it. I don’t see a reason to sanitize that reality by showing the shooting party and leaving out the dead game.

There is also a long tradition surrounding hunting, particularly in England and South Texas. The game, the land, the dogs, the people and the rituals surrounding all of it are connected. I photograph what is there and leave it to the viewer to decide what he or she thinks about it.

The English photographer Martin Parr, who died in December 2025, spent his life photographing the British middle and working classes and their mass leisure — but as an observer, from outside that world, with an eye that was affectionate and often satirical. You do the opposite: you’ve always photographed the American elite you were born into, from the inside. Do you feel any kinship with him nonetheless?

Will Vogt: Absolutely. I have always admired Martin Parr’s work. We came at our subjects from slightly different angles but I think we shared an interest in the small details that tell you something larger about people and the way they live.

Parr was brilliant at noticing things that other people walked right past. His photographs could be funny without simply making fun of people. I hope there is some of that observational quality in my work.

Jennifer Garza-Cuen, the editor of Behind the Hedges , places your work alongside Larry Sultan, Stephen Shore and Tod Papageorge. What did you take from each of them, and what shows up from those influences in your own eye?

Will Vogt: Those three photographers are masters of their craft and I am honored that anyone would mention me in the same sentence with them. Robert Frank was obviously the earliest and most important influence on my work. I have collected photographs and photography books for many years and inevitably some of what I’ve absorbed has become part of the way I see and photograph the world.

If someone opened Behind the Hedges knowing nothing about you and decided it was satire, what would you tell them?

Will Vogt: I’d tell them they are entitled to see it that way. Once you put photographs into the world, you lose control over how people interpret them.

But satire isn’t my intention. I’m not trying to celebrate these people and I’m not trying to ridicule them. I’m recording a world I know and have been part of for my entire life. There is humor in the photographs because there is humor in life. There are also contradictions and occasionally absurdity. I don’t think you have to manufacture any of that. You just have to notice it.

As a teenager, you saw Jimi Hendrix live — a world at the opposite end of the one you’ve been photographing ever since. You also cite the Beatles and Bob Dylan among your influences. Doesn’t that irreverent spirit find its extension in the way you photograph high society — as a bit of a troublemaker yourself?

Will Vogt: I like the idea of being a troublemaker, although I’m not sure I’ve earned the title.

Music was a huge influence on me when I was young and still is. Hendrix, Dylan and the Beatles all arrived at a time when a lot of accepted ideas about how you were supposed to live were being challenged. I was certainly affected by that.

Maybe some of that does show up in the photographs. I’ve never felt any obligation to make this world look the way it might like to see itself. If something is funny, strange, awkward or a little outrageous, I’m probably going to take the picture. Maybe that is my small contribution to troublemaking.

“Will Vogt: These Americans” runs through December 6, 2026 at the Art Museum of South Texas .

Behind the Hedges (2026), photographs by Will Vogt, edited and with text by Jennifer Garza-Cuen, is published by Schilt Publishing . These Americans (2023) by Will Vogt is published by Schilt Publishing .

“I don’t believe in ending stories. I just don’t do it.” Stacy Kranitz drops the line by Lake Geneva, on the afternoon of the Images Vevey Book Award ceremony, between two questions about swimming. Seventeen years she has been working in Appalachia, the mountain range that runs more than 3,000 kilometers from Canada down to Alabama. Or twenty, she hesitates. The book takes its title from a gospel song by Brother Claude Ely, a Pentecostal preacher from those mountains. The jury chaired by Rineke Dijkstra crowned it; Éditions Images Vevey and the American publisher Terrible Baby brought it out in June. One idea governs the whole: every image manufactures a little of the reputation it claims to describe.

At the Musée Jenisch, the installation applies that principle to the letter. Stacy Kranitz’s color photographs, made in a West Virginia hollow, face the images produced about the region by outsiders since 1850. Missionaries raising funds, photographers on the payroll of the coal companies, envoys of the Farm Security Administration, reporters covering the War on Poverty: each wave arrived with its commission in hand and its framing already written. And a documentary film directed by the photographer holds the center of the display. “There’s no visual literacy in America,” she says. “Nobody knows, understands, or processes how images circulate in the world, the different kinds of apparatuses that are at play. Nobody thinks about this stuff.”

It all starts on a Friday night in 2013, in West Columbia, West Virginia. Stacy Kranitz is invited for a beer at the home of a man who, within the hour, gets into three fistfights, throws chairs and punches his friend Dozer in the face. On the back of his neck, a tattoo: “Honkey.” The lawyer Harry Caudill would have filed Pat Greene among what he called the “dullards” of the back hollows. The photographer, for her part, keeps coming back for a decade, then another. “To me, he really identifies as a mountaineer,” she says of her host. “He really embodies the idea of living mountain life.”

One late summer, on a strip mine reclaimed as an ATV trail, Stacy Kranitz climbs on behind Dozer, camera on her back, after a dozen beers for him. The caption of one picture in the book says the rest: “Stacy and Dozer on his four-wheeler, the moment before it flipped.” Dozer, 95 kilos, lands on her; the quad, 340 kilos, lands on Dozer. One bruised elbow. Back at Pat’s, someone hands her a crushed Lortab to snort for the pain. Participant as much as observer, she photographs from inside the circle, with the risks that implies and the standing it earns.

Then comes the long history, the one the book unfolds through documents. Families left Europe to escape a class system, found themselves indentured, climbed into the mountains and lived a century outside capitalism. Then coal climbed up after them. “They literally stole the land,” Stacy Kranitz says. “They didn’t know they needed to have deeds. Nobody told them they need to have deeds. So who decides that they need to have deeds? The coal companies.” On April 24, 1964, Lyndon Johnson sat on the porch of Tom Fletcher, an unemployed miner in Inez, Kentucky, who had earned about 400 dollars the previous year. The picture became the emblem of the War on Poverty. Fletcher died poor in 2004, worn out by the reporters who came back every ten years to ask whether he still was. At the end of the volume, a “lexicon of dispossession” lines up the words coined to keep these people outside the human contract, from waste people to trailer trash . Four centuries of vocabulary, a single function.

Then there is Harry Caudill, the dark heart of the affair and the subject of the film. His essay “The Rape of the Appalachians,” published in The Atlantic in 1962, and Night Comes to the Cumberlands a year later, turned America’s attention to a region bled dry by coal. Twenty years on, the same man explained poverty by genetics, invited the eugenicist William Shockley to his Kentucky home and floated cash bounties for sterilization. Stacy Kranitz unearthed the footage in which he makes that claim on camera. On November 29, 1990, facing Pine Mountain, Caudill shot himself; his farewell letter is reproduced in the book. One detail from the same archive amuses his Swiss publishers. “He mentions the Swiss. He says, we want to do it like the Swiss,” the photographer reports. The film, for its part, turns back on its own author and asks the question that holds for the entire project: what does an image of poverty do, once it is loose in the world?

Next comes J. D. Vance, whose Hillbilly Elegy (2016) recounts an Appalachian childhood and hands his own people the blame for their decline. Stacy Kranitz places the two men in the same frame and notes the coincidence: Pat’s daughter was taken by child protective services just as Vance was named running mate. “It’s my form of politics,” she says of that montage. “I don’t know why we’re not talking about eugenics more. We are still lurking in that conversation in every direction.” A Nieman Fellow, she is spending the year at Harvard, where she studies eugenics and pronatalism.

The book saves its most troubling object for last. In 2016, a photograph of Pat shirtless in his yard became a meme: “Poor southern conservatives have been voting Republican for generations. And they’re still poor.” Pat, with a criminal record, cannot vote. The essayist Whitney Phillips devotes one of the book’s texts to it. Stacy Kranitz has known the mechanism since 2012, when CNN ran her images of a Pentecostal snake handler and a Ku Klux Klan gathering under the headline “Everyday life in Appalachia.” It took a week on the phone to get the headline changed. “Photography has done a lot of harm to that region,” she says. “That doesn’t mean that you can’t or shouldn’t.” She describes the model that governs the news: “A flood, an earthquake, some disaster, we descend on the region, everyone’s there at the same time, and then we abandon ship.” Her work does the opposite, slowly. “Art allowed me to slow down and tell the story over a much longer period of time. You can’t really do it in journalism.”

So she stays. Stacy Kranitz went through every caption with Pat Greene, recorder on the table. “I really needed him to see what I wrote,” she says, “to make sure that he agreed with the context, with the way that it was being used in the book.” The last pictures date from March 2026. As the book went to press, Pat was in jail, with no one to post bail. “We love to put poor people in jail for no good reason,” she says. Five weeks of silence, then a rehab center, where she was able to visit him. “I’ve never seen him more contemplative,” says the photographer, who has always known him in survival mode. The book ends in the dark; life has turned since. Such is the advantage of stories that keep going. “I will probably be there for a long time, and I will not be leaving.”

Ain’t No Grave Gonna Hold My Body Down by Stacy Kranitz is published by Terrible Baby / Éditions Images Vevey and available for $70. The exhibition at the Musée Jenisch, part of the Images Vevey Biennial , runs through September 27, 2026.

content.article_text:
写真家・蓮井元彦と倉島水生による二人展「故郷」が、2026年9月16日から10月5日まで、東京・御徒町の229GALLERYで開催される。二人がそれぞれ自身の故郷を撮影し、土地と記憶、家族、そして時間の経過によって変化していく「故郷」のあり方を見つめる。

本展の原点となったのは、約2年前に二人が制作したZINE「故郷」。今回の展覧会に向け、蓮井の故郷である東京・国分寺と、倉島の故郷である岐阜・飛騨高山を、二人と229GALLERYのメンバーがともに訪れた。普段は一人で撮影することの多い二人が、他者とともに故郷を歩き、かつて過ごした場所やそこにまつわる記憶を語る。その経験は、2年前とは異なる距離から故郷を捉え直す機会にもなったという。

蓮井にとって国分寺は、家族も実家もなくなったことで「少し閉じかけていた」場所だった。今回、仲間とともに小学校や図書館、神社、中学校、昔住んでいた家の周辺などを歩き、35年間通うラーメン店で食事をする。その翌日には偶然、中学時代の同窓会への誘いが届き、28年ぶりに同級生たちと再会した。過去の記憶によって成立していた故郷に、新しい人間関係と記憶が書き加えられる。蓮井はその変化を「僕の故郷は第二章へと進んだのかな」と綴っている。

一方、倉島は2年前のZINEで、「故郷とは家や土地であり、それは人間が完全に所有できるものではなく、本当のところは故郷なんてないのかもしれない」と記した。その言葉をきっかけに、高山で暮らす母親から届いたのが、自身にとって現在の住まいこそ、子どもたちとの喜怒哀楽の記憶が息づく「HOME」なのだという言葉だった。

その後の5年間で家族の形は変化し、近づいたり離れたり、ときには血縁者さえ他人のように感じたりするなかで、倉島自身の「故郷」や「家族」に対する考え方も変わり続けてきた。血がつながっているからといって、すべてを理解し合えるわけではない。それでも母や姉たちが健やかに日々を送っていること自体を幸福だと感じる。故郷を特定の土地や家に固定するのではなく、人との関係や記憶の変化から捉え直している。

二人の写真から浮かび上がるのは、「帰る場所」として固定された故郷ではない。そこから離れ、時間が経ち、人間関係や自分自身が変化することで、その意味もまた書き換えられていく。かつての記憶を記録するだけではなく、現在から過去を見返し、さらに新しい記憶を重ねていくこと。蓮井と倉島、それぞれ異なる二つの「故郷」を通して、鑑賞者自身が自らの帰る場所や、そこから現在まで続く時間について考える展覧会となる。

content.article_text:
アクネ ストゥディオズが、ブランド創立30周年を記念したキャンペーンを発表した。撮影を手がけたのは、アメリカを代表する写真家ナン・ゴールディン。ブランドの原点である「デニム」をテーマに、これまでアクネ ストゥディオズと関係を築いてきたクリエイターたちをポートレートに収めている。

アクネ ストゥディオズの歴史は1996年、ストックホルムで制作された100本のローデニムジーンズから始まった。「Ambition to Create Novel Expressions（新しい表現を創造する野望）」の頭文字を取った「Acne」として活動を開始し、ジーンズを地元のアーティストやクリエイター、友人たちへ贈ったことがブランドの出発点だった。2006年に現在の名称へ変更し、ファッション、アート、カルチャーを横断するブランドへと発展してきた。

30周年を迎え、共同創設者兼クリエイティブ・ディレクターのジョニー・ヨハンソンが改めて目を向けたのが、その原点であるデニム。ブランドにとって初のコラボレーションとなるゴールディンは、過去30年間を象徴するデニムの現行モデルやアーカイブ、復刻モデルをまとった人々を、親密かつダイレクトなポートレートとして撮影した。

被写体となったのは、ミュージシャンのエリー・ロウゼル、モデル兼写真家のグィネヴィア・ヴァン・シーナス、アーティストのジョナサン・リンドン・チェイス、写真家ジョーダン・ヘミングウェイ、俳優兼ミュージシャンのジュリエット・ルイス、アーティストのピーター・シュレシンジャー、俳優兼モデルのラヤ・マルティニー、俳優の福島リラ、アーティストのサンドラ・ポールソンら。いずれも過去のコラボレーションや対話を通して、ブランドの現在を形づくってきた人物たちだ。

「モデルとしてではなく、友人として出演してもらいたかった」とヨハンソンが語るように、今回のキャンペーンはスターを並べることよりも、ブランドと人との関係性に焦点を当てている。長年、友人や恋人、アーティストたちの私生活を親密な距離から撮り続けてきたゴールディンの写真と、コミュニティとの対話を重視してきたアクネ ストゥディオズ。その両者の姿勢が重なり合うプロジェクトとなった。

content.article_text:
Vic Bakin: Fading

In Materia , his second book following the monograph Epitome , Kyiv-based photographer Vic Bakin sets images against the decay of their own physical support.

By Gaia Squarci. Photographs by Vic Bakin

This work began with two portraits of the same man, made ten years apart. Bakin printed these and other portraits, together with interiors and details hinting at lingering moments, on discontinued photographic paper from the 1960s to the 2000s. Each batch aged differently: faded, spotted with mold or marked by fingerprints.

The paper’s decay seems to mirror the vulnerability of the skin. Fragility, desire, and the relentless pull of time all surface from the same image. As Bakin puts it: “For me, thinking happens through making. I rarely begin with a clear concept. Instead, I make pictures first and then spend months trying to understand what they are telling me.”

The book Materia is published by VOID and available for 60 Euro.

content.article_text:
The photography of Chardchakaj Waikawee, born in Bangkok in 1980, resists easy classification. It belongs neither to social documentary, with its cool rigor, nor to art portraiture, with its aestheticizing restraint. It is something else, something harder to name, and therefore more precious. His work has traveled internationally for more than fifteen years. “Youth”, the exhibition devoted to him by London’s Graces Mews, brings together a body of analog photographs taken between 2008 and 2020.

The title borrows the Thai phrase wai run , a term that reaches far beyond its literal translation to describe an inner disposition, an energy of being that neither age nor poverty can extinguish. Waikawee’s subjects include motorcycle-taxi drivers, street vendors, and more broadly the young people who survive on the margins of Bangkok’s economy. “Bangkok is chaos,” he says. “Heaven and hell exist on the same street.”

One enters the exhibition through a filmed portrait of the photographer, his voice continuing to murmur through the galleries like an undertow. This sonic device anchors the images in a meditation on memory, time and value: sober words for photographs that are anything but. For Waikawee’s eye plays as much as it bears witness. One need only look at the boy sipping Coca-Cola from a plastic bag, staring straight into the lens with quiet defiance, to be convinced of it. Or the punk whose extravagant pink mohawk bursts through the open sunroof of a champagne-colored Mercedes.

What strikes one, technically, is the deliberate insolence of the process. Waikawee works with expired film, repaired cameras, hand-printing techniques. Cross-processing produces unpredictable chromatic shifts — lemon yellow, scorched orange, acid magenta — which the photographer treats as so many traces of time’s passage upon the material itself. The scratches, the dust, the chemical marks are not accidents but the visible memory of the making, a reminder that every image is also a physical object.

Full of life, these portraits are anything but miserabilist. “Each image reflects a relationship before it becomes a photograph,” Waikawee notes. He foregrounds the personality, the friendship, the singular sense of style of his subjects, who wear their appearance as armor against the social and economic invisibility the city imposes upon them.

Take the laborers crammed into the back of a truck, riding home at night in a tableau at once baroque and entirely ordinary. Or the boy whose back, tattooed with sacred Sak Yant script, is covered in inscriptions down to the waistband of his jeans. One will long remember, too, the doll-like face of the young woman, her eyes lined in black, holding the camera’s gaze without flinching. So many ways, for this sidelined but defiant youth, to compose, with whatever means are to hand, a presence in the world.

“Youth” , by Chardchakaj Waikawee, runs until 19 September 2026 at Graces Mews , London.
content.excerpt_original: In the portraits of Chardchakaj Waikawee, Thailand's marginalized youth astonish with sheer presence. L’article The Brazenness of Bangkok’s Street Youth est apparu en premier sur Blind Magazine .

content.article_text:
There’s a jump scare about 30 minutes into the glossy romantic drama Love of Your Life that’s about as effective as anything you’ll see in a horror movie this year.

The film is focused on the life and loves of Maya (Margaret Qualley), a twentysomething Boston nurse who meet-cutes with the nerdy and idiosyncratic Charlie (Gabriel Basso) during the purchase of a nightstand. We follow the initial giddy rush of their courting as they progress all the way to an impromptu wedding over the course of a few years, marked by Maya’s change in age announced in text. But just as we’re about to process the unsettling introduction of Charlie using Chekhov’s inhaler, a news report interrupts the sunny tone. Spoiler: it’s March 2020.

Rather like the ending of the otherwise anodyne romance Remember Me which shows Robert Pattinson’s character looking out of the World Trade Center on 9/11 (!), it’s revealed that we are in fact watching a Covid movie, at least for the first act, which ends, unsurprisingly, with the death of Charlie. This then propels Maya on to an international odyssey from Portugal to England to Japan as she tries to figure out who she is without the man she thought she would grow old with (it involves what’s described as “solitary hedonism” AKA one-night stands with guys who have tattoos and croissants in the bath). That journey pushes her away from her best friend, played by Patrick Schwarzenegger, and mother-in-law, played by Catherine Keener, and toward Aaron Pierre’s charming single father.

It’s Eat, Grieve, Love which is by no means a bad thing given how few mainstream films attempt to zero in on the vast lives of women both in and out of relationships (I remain a staunch defender of Ryan Murphy’s prettified yet emotionally resonant adaptation of a book I am otherwise unbothered by). There’s also a bit of How to Be Single (minus the bawdy humour), another film I’m often defending or at least drawing attention to and there’s something admirably ambitious about settling in with a female protagonist for such a long period of time to see how they live and learn after a loss many of us couldn’t imagine surviving.

The script was the subject of a heated auction back in 2024, sparking interest from studios like Paramount and unlikely names such as Taylor Sheridan, who usually prefers his female characters blond and hypersexual. It sold for $2m, a virtually unheard of amount for a spec script in this climate, recalling the mostly long-gone glory days of someone like Shane Black or Paul Verhoeven. It sold to Ryan Gosling, as producer, and Amazon and comes from the Nyad writer Julia Cox although it often feels like it was adapted from an elevated beach read.

It’s a sumptuous trip around the world and through the grieving process that’s mostly smooth sailing, steered by a director who knows how to fully transport us. Cinematographer turned film-maker Rachel Morrison went from capturing the small (Fruitvale Station) to the epic (Black Panther) and she’s brought both to her work as director. I was disappointed her excellent boxing drama The Fire Inside didn’t reach a wider audience and while I understand the unwillingness to bet on a genre more commonly suited to streaming, it’s a shame Amazon isn’t giving this one a wider big-screen rollout especially given how lush so much of it looks (it’ll have a token week in cinemas before it’s next to your shampoo order).

There’s perhaps not quite as much depth or texture as one might hope, especially as a rambling third act scrambles for something close to profundity, and the finished product, together with its weirdly muted rollout, might not quite justify the intensity, or the high price, involved with the auction. But it is refreshing to see a battle over a grounded drama rather than heightened genre for once (I’m assuming the Covid angle is what launched it into the marketplace).

It also gives Qualley one of her most grounded roles too, a challenge for the actor to play a real, relatable person after mainly doing the opposite in films like The Substance, Poor Things, Honey, Don’t and Blue Moon. It’s an easy fit for her, more so than her last attempt, Maid, and we buy her grand gamut of grief (devastation, frustration, horniness) without the need for her to histrionically overplay the life-changing horror of it, also helped by Basso’s believably specific performance, someone who is admittedly hard to forget.

If Schwarzenegger feels entirely miscast as her bestie and their lived-in long-term dynamic hard to buy then a more neatly suited Pierre more than makes up for it. He’s another actor who has mostly been limited to something else – action, an American accent – but he’s an incredibly charismatic romantic lead here and it’s not hard to buy how he might find a way to break down the walls of Maya, that have been understandably built up so very high.

Their electric chemistry helps to power the film as it plods into a final third that feels considerably more aimless than it should. The journey we take with Maya has been in many ways such an epic one, in both literal and emotional scope, and it feels like after all of that, we should be taken somewhere more meaningful and left with insights more incisive than what we end up with. For a film so set on exploring the monumental sweep of both love and life, the end result soothes rather than soars.

Love of Your Life is premiering at the Toronto film festival; it will be on limited release in cinemas on 7 October and on Prime Video on 14 October

content.article_text:
東京・銀座のArt Gallery M84でベッティナ・ランスの写真展「密室」No.12が2026年10月5日から17日まで開催される。同ギャラリーでは12回目となるランスの個展で、代表作「Chambre Close（シャンブル・クローズ／密室）」を中心に約30点を展示する。

1952年パリ生まれのランスは、1970年代後半から写真家として活動。ストリッパーやダンサー、娼婦などを被写体としたポートレートやヌードで頭角を現し、1980年代には『VOGUE』『Figaro』などの雑誌や広告へと活動の場を広げた。女性を主要な被写体としながら、華やかさや儚さ、美しさと苦悩、憂いといった相反する感情を写真に捉えてきた。

本展の核となる「Chambre Close」は、作家・セルジュ・ブラムリーとのコラボレーションによって1990年から92年にかけて制作されたシリーズだ。パリの女性たちを親密な距離から撮影したヌード作品は、その大胆なポーズと濃密な色彩で注目を集め、同名写真集はヨーロッパのみならずアメリカ、日本、韓国、オーストラリアなど各国で広く知られることとなった。

「Chambre Close」は、ランスにとって初めて本格的にカラー写真に取り組んだシリーズでもある。室内の鮮やかな壁や家具、衣服といった背景を積極的に画面へ取り込みながら、モデルの身体や視線を演出。代表作「Chambre Close Octobre I, Paris.」でも、赤を基調とした室内と女性の肌、黒い衣服が強いコントラストを生み、私的な空間を覗き込むような親密さと緊張感が共存している。

ランスはその後も、ジェンダーやセクシュアリティ、身体をめぐる表現を展開。1995年にはフランス大統領の公式カメラマンを務め、1998年にはイエスの生涯を現代に置き換えて撮影した「I.N.R.I.」を発表するなど、ファッションとアートの領域を横断して活動してきた。

今回の展示では、ランスが女性の身体とその内面をどのように写真へと変換してきたのかを約30点からたどる。モデルの視線や身振り、室内の色彩、写真家と被写体の距離。閉ざされた「密室」のなかで交わされる視線を通して、1990年代を代表するランスの写真表現を改めて検証する機会となる。

content.article_text:
L atif, the solemn hitman played soulfully by Mahershala Ali , carries diapers in his kill kit. I can’t tell if that’s because they come in handy when soaking up pools of blood on the fly; or because at a moment’s notice the hitman has to switch over from his brutal occupation to daddy duties. Or perhaps it’s both for this contract killer who comes armed with a blade and baby wipes, who takes lives and nurtures them, whose life is composed of jarring and poetic contradictions, much like the movie he’s in.

Those contradictions are on full striking display in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’s opening moments, an explosive close-quarters brawl in a restroom, after which Latif uses the baby wipes to clean up the mess he made with that blade. It’s a lovely image, in a film filled with so many, cutting right through the tension within this character. It also feels like a wink to the audience from Ali and writer/director Bassam Tariq, a way for them to acknowledge right off the top the distracting mess made by that other Blade.

Tariq and Ali were collaborating on Marvel’s Blade reboot . Ali was announced to star as the vampire-slayer formerly played by Wesley Snipes all the way back in 2019. Tariq signed on to write and direct in 2021 but departed a year later. Ali recently revealed that, after being strung along for seven years in development, the reboot was not happening. It’s easy to assume that some of the ideas Tariq and Ali had for Blade made their way into this new collaboration, in which Ali gets to finally wield a blade and John Cho, of Harold and Kumar fame, stuns as a vampiric foe. The echoes and parallels are there but minimal, perhaps even coincidental.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is its own beautiful singular thing, partly a stylish and pulpy neo-western thriller about a father racked with guilt, navigating violence that comes heavy and uneasy, but first and foremost a drama about a family reconciling their Muslim faith with their actions, their environments and their grief.

Both Tariq and Ali are Muslims. The former’s debut, Mogul Mowgli, and his directing work on the Prime Video series Bait, both starring Riz Ahmed, were about young British-Pakistani men who internalize hostility towards their faith. In Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, Tariq builds an even more nuanced portrait of faith around Ali, who seizes the rare opportunity to explore his religion onscreen.

Ali’s Latif, who once taught kids at prayer school, fashions himself as a righteous killer with a code, meting out justice to those who offend Islam. Getting paid for it is beside the point, he argues, when a supportive but critical Imam played by Giancarlo Esposito takes Latif to task.

As the film opens, when Latif is bashing that victim’s head against a bathroom sink and unceremoniously tying up his corpse, his own wife (Shakirah DeMesier) lies there dying, her body delicately cared for by their community in Houston (the movie was shot in Atlanta). That leaves Latif a widower who, alongside his eldest, Fatiha (Adia, quietly mesmerizing), cares for a curious young son (Jahleel Kamara) and infant daughter who won’t take formula.

So much of Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is propelled by Latif’s frantic search for breast milk, inspired by the writer and director’s own ordeal when his wife fell ill. Ali is especially breathtaking in these moments, with Latif looking weathered and exasperated, but fighting to maintain his wits and composure, as he’s turned away from a milk bank that requires a prescription and accosted by a doctor in the family (Tramell Tillman) when seeking help. Latif finally has to square the assistance he gets from a breastfeeding sex worker (Tiffany Boone) with his at times rigid and hypocritical moral and religious code.

Those negotiations are constant and granular. At every turn, Latif and Fatiha figure out how to make their Islamic faith work for who they are and the situations they’re in. How important is fasting when your frantic ordeals make you forget to eat altogether? How do we grapple with scriptures that limit growth and empathy, but not ignore the profound lessons also found in those texts? In the grand scheme of things, does it matter that your adolescent daughter is using the Mormon neighbour’s wifi to watch Furry porn, which must be all kinds of Haram? These are the questions that make Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother so grounded, compassionate, and, dare I say, divine.

That spiritual journey is also the bridge between the intimate family story and the thriller plot. Latif finds himself caught in a beef between his employer’s son, a producer of “Habibi porn” (Abubakr Ali) who tests what the former stands for, and Cho’s Pastor Hwan Yoon. The latter, captivating in a gold grill, cowboy hat and southern drawl, is an Iraq war veteran who turned evangelical after he supposedly rose back from the dead on the battlefield. His heel turn towards religious fanaticism means surrounding himself with tooled-up mercenaries and preaching about Christ at gunpoint.

Tariq deftly navigates the divide between Latif and Pastor Hwan, setting up binaries and conflicts that could easily give in to Muslim versus Christian sensationalism. But his approach is soulful and considered, allowing everyone their convictions and bandwidth for the mercy and grace the movie ultimately preaches about.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother isn’t just interrogating faith. It’s embracing and appreciating those jarring and poetic contradictions that come with the territory.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is premiering at the Toronto film festival and opens in select theaters in New York City and Los Angeles on 25 September, following a wider release on 2 October and 9 October. It is released in the UK on 20 November

シャネル・ネクサス・ホールにて、「Icons and Image Makers ナショナルポートレートギャラリー展」が開催される。

本展ではロンドンのナショナルポートレートギャラリーが所蔵する世界屈指の写真コレクションから、 英国のファッション、音楽、映画界を象徴するアイコンたちのポートレートを厳選して紹介。国際的に高い評価を受ける写真家たちの作品を通して、英国カルチャーを彩った人物像と、時代を映し出すポートレート写真の魅力に迫る。

ポートレートの中には、私たちの視覚文化に深く刻まれ、時代を象徴するイメージとなったものがある。その一方で、公のイメージの背後にある、一人の人間としての姿が捉えられたこともあった。こうした魅力的な肖像は、ナショナルポートレートギャラリーのコレクションの核心にある問いを投げかける。——イメージとアイデンティティはどこで交差するのか？——本展は、英国文化を牽引してきた アイコンたち、そして彼らの姿を形づくってきた写真家たちのクリエイティビティを称える展覧会である。

また会期初日には、ナショナルポートレートギャラリーのアシスタントキュレーターによるガイドイベントが開催されるなど、関連イベントも実施予定。この機会にぜひ足をお運びいただきたい。

content.article_text:
ジル サンダーが2026年秋冬キャンペーンを発表した。シモーネ・ベロッティによるクリエイティブ・ディレクションのもと、フォトグラファー／ディレクターのモニ・ホーワースが撮影。モデルにはエディ・キャンベルとウエダ ダイスケを起用している。

舞台となるのは、自家用飛行場の滑走路。そこにはラテックスで覆われたテーブルやアルミ箔に包まれたソファなど、本来は室内にあるはずの家具が野外に配置されている。明確な間取りも壁もなく、「住まい」という概念だけが断片的に残された空間。離陸と着陸の両方を受け入れる滑走路を、何かが始まる場所として描き出した。

ベロッティが追求したのは、ジル サンダーの根幹にある研ぎ澄まされた抑制美と「力強いシンプルさ」に、わずかな違和感を差し込むことだ。「余剰」が不可欠なものへと変わり、「加える」行為が「取り除く」行為と呼応する。相反する要素を共存させることで、断片的かつ緊張感に満ちた視覚的な物語を構築している。

物語には明確な筋書きが用意されていない。ヒッチコックやライナー・ヴェルナー・ファスビンダーを思わせる気配を漂わせながら、見る者がその空白を自由に補完できるよう意図的に抽象性を残した。キャンベルとウエダは、滑走路で暮らしているのか。これから旅立つのか、それとも到着したばかりなのか。その判然としない状況そのものが、キャンペーンのサスペンスを生み出している。

ビジュアルは、ホーワースが手がけたショートムービーから切り出されたスチールで構成。ざらついたテクスチャーと色褪せたVHSを思わせる色調によって、緊張や高揚、自己の内面と向き合う瞬間を捉えている。さらにSpace Afrika feat. Deuénによる「If This Is Hell」が、映像の断片性と不穏な空気を増幅させる。

「最小限の手法で、緊張感と驚きを表現したかった」とベロッティ。ジル サンダーらしい「少ない要素でより多くを表現する」という美学を保ちながら、今回はそこから一歩踏み込み、影と官能性を帯びた世界を構築した。エレガンスと不穏さ、抑制と官能。完全には解読できない相反する感覚のあいだに、ベロッティ率いる新たなジル サンダーのイメージが浮かび上がる。

content.article_text:
Eileen Perrier, Untitled, Afro Hair and Beauty Show , 1998 © the artist

Featured - September 11, 2026

The Editors

Hometown , 2018

Courtesy the artist

Hailun Ma — Amsterdam

It was only after moving to New York to study fashion photography that Hailun Ma began to recognize the artistic potential of her native Xinjiang—China’s westernmost region, home to twenty-five million people and more than forty ethnic groups, many of them Muslim majority. “If you search for images of Xinjiang online, you get these very National Geographic images,” she once told Vogue . “I wanted to present a younger perspective of what is happening.” Her first major solo show outside of China gathers photographs that delight in the everyday traditions and style of Uyghur teenagers, Kazakh cowboys, and other communities sidelined in mainstream depictions of the country.

Hailun Ma at Foam, Amsterdam, September 18, 2026–January 20, 2027

Let’s Take Back Our Space: “Female” and “Male” Body

Language as a Result of Patriarchal Structures , 1977

© 2026 Marianne Wex Estate and courtesy The Museum of Modern Art, New York, Committee on Photography Fund, and The Modern Women’s Fund

Taking Back Our Space — New York

From 1972 to 1977, Marianne Wex collected thousands of images tracing the connection between gesture and gender. The result, Let’s Take Back Our Space , juxtaposes Wex’s own snapshots of body language from the streets of Hamburg with sources reaching back to antiquity—showing, say, how the pose of a manspreader on a park bench descends from the uninhibited contrapposto of Doryphoros . In this exhibition, Wex’s opus, arrayed across systematized panels à la Aby Warburg, is paired with work by contemporary artists such as Nona Faustine, K8 Hardy, and Wendy Red Star, who extend observation of everyday public space into defiant acts of reclamation.

Taking Back Our Space: Photographic Perspectives at the Museum of Modern Art, New York, September 20, 2026–May 2, 2027

There’s no start or finish (detail), 2026

Courtesy the artist

Taryn Simon — New York

For over two decades, Taryn Simon has mined the hidden systems of power and influence that covertly order our lives. Father Country I Do Love You will be the largest debut of a new work ever at the Guggenheim, and the first single-artist exhibition by a photographer in the rotunda. Across forty-two works of photographs, text, video, and sculpture, Simon traces the life of a real, unnamed federal agent, examining how his individual decisions reverberated across lives and nations in ways he never knew. It’s Simon’s most personal project yet, as the work lives in the shadow her own father, who traveled the globe for the US government before transitioning into a career selling arcade games. “America is the best story on earth,” he once told her, “if you could find someone to tell it.”

Taryn Simon: Father Country I Do Love You at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York, September 18, 2026–March 14, 2027

Couple dancing , 1956

© The Estate of Roy DeCarava

Roy DeCarava — Los Angeles

Listening, for Roy DeCarava, was far from a passive act. For his series the sound i saw , he tuned his camera to the rhythms of midcentury New York’s jazz world, immortalizing titans—Trane, Count, Duke, Lady—in his signature palette of charcoal and smoke. He also captured peripheral scenes: tender embraces, dancehall silhouettes, quiet moments of downtime. The result is a deeply personal exploration of how American life, as Ralph Ellison once wrote, “comes to focus” through jazz. Curated by Ebony L. Haynes, this exhibition brings together 130 photographs from the series, accompanied by a listening room inspired by the records DeCarava cherished most.

Roy DeCarava: the sound i saw at David Zwirner, Los Angeles, September 19–October 31, 2026

Young Pink Kate London 1998

© the artist

The 90s: Art and Fashion — London

Hoist the Union Jack: The 90s: Art and Fashion looks back at a decade when Britain’s irreverent cultural renaissance ruled the runways, airwaves, museums, and magazines. Curated by Edward Enninful, The 90s will bring together fashion by Vivienne Westwood, John Galliano, and Alexander McQueen; works by the (formerly) Young British Artists; and, of course, photographs by the likes of Corinne Day, David Sims, and Juergen Teller, who chronicled a new era of Swinging London in the pages of i-D and The Face .

The 90s: Art and Fashion at Tate Britain, London, October 8, 2026–February 14, 2027

Edge Control_edv c, 2023–

© the artist

Deana Lawson — New York

Diane Arbus has always been a north star for Deana Lawson, the artist renowned for her regal photographs of Black people she meets in various scenarios, often pictured in domestic settings and bestowed with a transcendent, otherworldly, yet sometimes strangely specific presence. Like Arbus, Lawson can astonish and unnerve. For her first solo exhibition with Gagosian since signing with the gallery in 2022, Lawson presents recent portraits that gesture to vernacular photography and Old Master painting, together with a new series called Edge Control , about the phenomenon of surveillance in beauty supply shops, where shoplifters are tracked on cameras and their likenesses posted to store windows to deter theft. Beauty—and scrutiny—is in the eye of the beholder.

Deana Lawson at Gagosian, New York, September 10–October 24, 2026

KEYHOLE 12-3 (IMPROVED CRYSTAL)

Optical Reconnaissance Satellite Near Scorpio (USA 129), 2007

Courtesy the artist and Fellowship, Jessica Silverman Gallery, San Francisco, and Pace Gallery, New York

FotoFocus — Cincinnati

FotoFocus returns with its eighth edition, The Long View , offering seventy-four exhibitions in sixty-five venues throughout Greater Cincinnati, Dayton, Columbus, and Northern Kentucky. The “long view” of the title refers, in part, to the quarter-millennium of the United States, inviting artists and viewers to contend with the nation’s past, present, and possible futures. Standouts include exhibitions by Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Nancy Rexroth, and Trevor Paglen, whose work—spanning facial recognition technologies, alternate-reality games, and AI rabbit holes—probes the dark infrastructures of surveillance and power that govern how we see the world, and how it sees us.

FotoFocus Biennial 2026: The Long View , Cincinnati, Ohio, October 1–31, 2026

Le Coup de Fil Sportif (The athletic phone call) , 1998

© the artist and Tezeta and courtesy David Hill Gallery

Sanlé Sory — London

Sanlé Sory cut his teeth photographing car crashes for newspapers. When he acquired his own equipment, in 1960, he opened the Volta Photo studio and turned to a more celebratory subject: the vibrant youth culture of newly independent Upper Volta (now Burkina Faso). Like his better-known peers Malick Sidibé and Seydou Keïta, Sory redefined the photography of West Africa by portraying its people on their own terms. This show focuses on his rarely exhibited color portraits—images of irrepressible panache made during the restive 1980s and ’90s, when his country sought a new identity focused on anti-imperialism and self-reliance.

Sanlé Sory: Colour Years at the Photographers’ Gallery, London, October 14, 2026–February 21, 2027

Untitled (Teenagers at soda fountain) , c. 1950

© President and Fellows of Harvard College and courtesy Harvard Art Museums

Barbara Norfleet — Cambridge, MA

In the 1970s, the sociologist and curator Barbara P. Norfleet began assembling a vast archive of images from the 1930s to 1960s taken by photographers working on commission across the United States. Consisting of over twenty-thousand photographs depicting social rituals from weddings to corporate gatherings, the archive formed what Norfleet called a “unique and valuable record of American life.” This fall, the Harvard Art Museum stages the exhibition The Way We Never Were , drawn from Norfleet’s archive. Thematic sections ranging from the rise of suburbia and cultural conformity to growing struggles for equal rights centers the role of the professional photographer and commissioned image in shaping how midcentury America came to define itself.

The Way We Never Were: The American Professional Photographers Collection at Harvard Art Museum, Cambridge, Massachusetts, through May 9, 2027.

Hostage Situation , 1979

© the artist

Flashback — Baltimore

In Paula Gillen’s Hostage Situation (1979), a young, masked child yanks a woman’s leg—clad in fishnets and yellow peep-toe heels—protruding through an unfinished ceiling. It’s one of countless gems in Flashback , an unprecedented survey of Baltimore photography spanning almost two hundred years, from daguerreotypes of Frederick Douglass, to A. Aubrey Bodine’s deadline-driven pictorialism, to the zany world of John Waters (that dangling leg belongs to Susan Lowe, a regular in Waters’s films), to younger talents such as Devin Allen and Gioncarlo Valentine who are shaping the city’s photographic landscape today.

Flashback: Two Centuries of Baltimore Photography at the Baltimore Museum of Art, October 4, 2026–February 7, 2027

23 Wall Street , 1977

© the artist and courtesy Howard Greenberg Gallery and Hunters Point Press

Baldwin Lee — New York

Raised in New York’s Chinatown, Baldwin Lee studied with Walker Evans at Yale in the early 1970s. He would return to New York in the following years to photograph the city’s empty, early-morning streets with a 4-by-5 camera. These images, which resonate with German photographer Thomas Struth’s similarly unpeopled streetscapes from the same era, were printed in 2025 for this exhibition at Howard Greenberg Gallery, which previously presented Lee’s now-celebrated large-format portraits made in the 1980s on road trips through the American South. Lee’s portrayal of New York shows how both the skyline and the sidewalk have changed, as in his image of seemingly abandoned Financial Center lofts beneath the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center—a monument to a bygone era.

Baldwin Lee: New York at Howard Greenberg Gallery, New York, September 18–October 31, 2026

Pledge of Allegiance, 1899 , 2017

Courtesy the artist and Gladstone

Arthur Jafa — New York

Named for the pioneering jazz drummer Tony Williams, Arthur Jafa’s exhibition I Am Tony presents video installations, paintings, photographs, and sculptures across two floors of the recently expanded New Museum. Renowned for his trenchant explorations of race and American culture, the artist will premiere new works alongside searing video montages including Love Is the Message, The Message Is Death (2016) and The White Album (2019), as well as early works such as the photograph Monster (1988), an unflinching self-portrait of the artist as a young man.

Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony at the New Museum, New York, September 24, 2026–January 3, 2027

Untitled , 2004, from the series

the eyes the ears

Courtesy the artist

Japanese Women Photographers — New York

A much-needed counterpoint to the male-centric canon of Japanese photography, I’m So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now reframes the history of the medium through the work of twenty-eight intergenerational artists. Presented in partnership with Aperture in conjunction with the 2024 monograph , this exhibition is curated by the book’s editors, Pauline Vermare, Lesley A. Martin, and Takeuchi Mariko. I’m So Happy spans the medium from installations to photobooks, providing an indispensable introduction to the contributions of Japanese women to photography by showcasing intimate observations of everyday life, critical perspectives on history, and radical experiments with form.

I’m So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now at International Center of Photography, New York, October 15, 2026–January 11, 2027.

Crosby Street and Grand Street, New York, New York ,

February 24, 1974 , from

Uncommon Places (Aperture, 1982)

© the artist and courtesy 303 Gallery, New York

Aperture Loves New York — New York

Aperture Loves New York pays tribute to photographers who have shaped—and been shaped by—the city. Showcasing artists long championed by Aperture and anchored in our publishing history, the presentation brings together important and memorable photographs with corresponding Aperture books that have advanced the medium of photography and captured the complex spirit of New York City. Organized by Aperture’s executive director, Sarah Meister, the installation features photographs by more than twenty artists ranging from past to present—including Diane Arbus, Deana Lawson, Stephen Shore, Awol Erizku, and more.

Aperture Loves New York at Aperture, New York, September 18–November 1, 2026.

content.article_text:
Jurandir Filho , Rogério Montanare , Thiago Siqueira e Fernanda Bermoltz batem um papo nostálgico sobre o ano de 1996 nos cinemas!! Esse podcast é mais uma edição da série We Have to Go Back , onde voltamos no tempo e revisitamos os grandes filmes de um ano específico. Além disso, é um programa nostálgico, pois relembramos os acontecimentos desse ano, as músicas, as evoluções tecnológicas, os jogos de videogames, as curiosidades, os costumes e muito mais!!

Falamos sobre “Um Drink no Inferno”, “Twister”, “O Corcunda de Notre Dame”, “Missão-Impossível”, “Matilda”, “Independence Day”, “Pânico”, “A Rocha”, “Jerry Maguire”, “101 Dálmatas”, “Space Jam”, “Trainspotting”, “Romeu + Julieta” e muito mais.

At the Musée de la Confrérie des Vignerons, guardian of a festival held every 25 years, “once a generation”, Rineke Dijkstra, a fixture of the world’s great museums, agreed to be shown “in pocket format”, as Stefano Stoll puts it. It all starts from an absence: his uncle, who died of AIDS, erased from the family albums by shame. “Growing up, I only had one Polaroid of my uncle”, Pacifico Silano told BOMB magazine in 2024. The installation also honors his mother, devoted to her own. The family album gets its torn-out pages back. Same museum, another lineage of men: Abdulhamid Kircher, a Grand Prix laureate, studies Turkish oil wrestlers, a tradition dating to the 14th century and practiced within his father’s family, caught between virility and tenderness.
