content.article_text:
H ere is a disquieting documentary about what Israel’s military chiefs in Gaza reputedly call “Naza”, meaning civilian collateral damage – itself a queasy euphemism. The calculated “Naza” number is the amount of projected civilian deaths from each military strike, and perhaps it will come to have the same connotations as the US military term “body count” during Vietnam. The directors are Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, two of the film-makers behind No Other Land , which was about attacks by the Israel Defense Forces on Palestinian West Bank villages. NAZA is executive produced by Jonathan Glazer and James Wilson and appears under the production auspices of the Guardian, in which some of the stories have already appeared.

There are flaws: interviews were conducted on the condition of anonymity, but if no-one can be persuaded to put their name and face to their words (and of course it is terribly dangerous) then the impact of this as testimony is lessened. But even so, the film is casting a chilling light on what is happening now in Gaza .

Their faces in shadow, appearances and voices digitally altered, disillusioned Israeli intelligence officers and personnel speak to the directors about the war in Gaza. They do this semi-furtively on the dark night-time rooftops of Tel Aviv, the home of Israeli intelligence, supposedly for journalistic secrecy purposes – but it also provides a dramatic backdrop, as well as ambient footage of the city in all its eerie heedlessness and heartlessness. Periodically, the camera’s eye will drift across the gleaming apartment buildings, zooming in on glimpses of prosperous lives just 60km from Gaza.

The interviewees reject the whole concept of “human shields”. They allege that it is not a question of Hamas operatives hiding behind civilians; rather, Israel’s intelligence services have subcontracted their attack recon to AI. A computer program reportedly analyses the call pattern on phones belonging to known Hamas terrorists and finds which of the other tens of thousands of phones they have under surveillance exhibit the same tendencies – and then attack the owner, invariably at night, in the apartments whose whereabouts are already minutely documented by the state. A 15% permitted “error” rate for this is mentioned at one stage, and another respondent talks about an expected “Naza” rate of 20 for each action – but clearly this is elastic to say the least. Gaza’s civilians are considered to be all tacitly complicit in the grotesque antisemitic pogrom of 7 October, and whole buildings and vast numbers of people can be wiped out in one computer-generated assault.

Elsewhere, the officials talk about the logistics involved in “cleansing” northern Gaza and in sniper attacks on Gazan civilians who, desperate for food, don’t know they have crossed some invisible line into a militarised zone. Another part of the film talks about an intelligence unit unofficially loyal to prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu personally, engaging in dirty tricks undermining international human rights bodies who might be antipathetic to Israel’s political leadership.

The ahistorical comparison to nazism is inevitably and glibly invoked by one speaker. But Gaza, however horrendous, is not the same as the Holocaust. This specious parallel is all too readily available; the bombing of Dresden is the more obvious comparison. At all events, the anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus.

代官山ヒルサイドテラス・ヒルサイドフォーラムで2026年9月23日から10月4日まで、写真展「『いつでもいま ― ガラスに映す光』柿本ケンサク写真展」が開催される。映画やドラマ、広告映像を手がける一方、国内外で写真・現代美術作品を発表してきた柿本が、ガラス作家・三嶋りつ惠の透明なガラスを通した光を、新作「Hikari」シリーズとして提示する。

柿本にとってヒルサイドテラスは、写真家としての活動における重要な場所でもある。2016年に同会場で「TRANSLATOR」を開催し、2021年の「TRANSFORMATION」では時間と記憶をめぐる実験を展開。2026年、三度同じ場所に戻り、今回は写真を「光の記憶」として捉え直す。

本展の核となるのは、「写真は光を固定する。ガラスは光を揺らす」という二つのメディアの性質だ。柿本は三嶋による10点のガラス作品を、いわば光を描くためのレンズとして使用。ガラスの位置を数ミリずつ動かし、角度を変えながら、そこを通過する光を撮影した。目の前の風景を忠実に写すのではなく、偶然に生まれる光の屈折や揺らぎと対話しながらシャッターを切ることで、時間の流れや季節の空気、身体の動き、ガラスそれぞれの個体差までを写真の中に定着させている。

写真とガラスという異なるメディアが交差することで立ち上がるのは、「固定」と「流動」、「定着」と「融解」、「点」と「線」のあいだにある緊張関係だ。点として固定された光が時間のなかで線へとほどけ、曖昧になった記憶が見る者のなかでもう一度像を結ぶ。作品は、光を記録する写真というメディアそのものの性質を改めて問い直す。

資料に掲載された「Hikari」シリーズでは、花や水辺、都市風景などがガラス越しの光によってにじみ、歪み、時に抽象的な色面へと変化している。被写体の輪郭を明確に示すというより、光によって世界が別の像へと移り変わる瞬間そのものが写し出されている。

三嶋は1962年京都生まれ。ヴェネツィアと京都を拠点に、ムラーノ島の職人との協働によって無色透明のガラス作品を制作してきた。周囲の光や空気を取り込み、空間のなかに光の輪郭を生み出す作品で知られる。本展では、三嶋のガラスが単なる被写体ではなく、光と風景を変容させる装置として柿本の写真表現に組み込まれている。

会期中の10月3日16時には、柿本と三嶋によるトークイベントも開催（1000円、1ドリンク付き）。それぞれが写真とガラスを通して向き合ってきた「光」と「時間」をテーマに語り合う。また、南青山のLUMIX BASE TOKYOでは、本展と連動し、LUMIX L10で撮影した別作品群による写真展「いつでもいま」も同時開催される。

Digger | Tom Cruise é um bilionário excêntrico que precisa salvar o mundo no trailer do novo filme de Alejandro Iñárritu

Filme chega aos cinemas nacionals em 1 de outubro.

(Imagens: Warner Bros.)

Foi divulgado o trailer final de “ Digger “, novo filme de Tom Cruise dirigido por Alejandro González Iñárritu . Assista acima à versão legendada e abaixo à dublada.

Foi divulgado também o novo cartaz nacional do filme, abaixo.

No filme, Cruise interpreta Digger Rockwell, um barão do petróleo que desencadeia um enorme desastre ecológico global graças aos anos de exploração. Ele é o único capaz de resolver o que parece ser uma crise de derretimento acelerado de icebergs, e recebe ordens do atual presidente dos EUA para agir e evitar o fim do mundo.

Além de Cruise, compõem o elenco Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg e Jesse Plemons.

“Digger” chega aos cinemas brasileiros em 1 de outubro.

Saiba Mais: Alejandro G. Iñárritu , Digger , Tom Cruise

content.article_text:
H ollywood loves giving young actors their own historical epic as much as audiences seem to dislike watching them. Timothée Chalamet and Chris Pine’s least remembered roles are in the medieval set films The King and Outlaw King (no relation), Ridley Scott’s The Last Duel made back only a third of its $100m budget and earlier this year, the Saudi-backed seventh-century drama Desert Warrior starring Anthony Mackie and Ben Kingsley quietly became one of the biggest flops of all time. Last week, it was reported that Scott blamed the failure of Gladiator II on Paul Mescal not being “masculine enough” in a logical leap which only makes sense if your barometer for masculinity is a man who throws hotel phones and yells at producers in storage closets.

On paper, The Uprising should be different: it’s a historical epic from a blue-chip director (the Bourne trilogy’s Paul Greengrass ), a nuanced, introspective leading man ( Andrew Garfield ) and a milieu that uncomfortably chimes with the western world’s backslide into repressive authoritarianism (The Peasants’ Revolt of 1381). In reality, it is a disjointed slog through the mud with the emotional depth of a History Channel rerun.

Through Greengrass’s lens, late 14th-century England seems like an utterly wretched place, not only because of the sludge-grey sky, scratchy brown sacks that everyone wears and the fact that no one seems to have had a wash in weeks, but because a despotic king treats the country’s people like scum, gouging them out of what little they have with hefty taxes to advance his own vainglorious agenda. Garfield’s character, who identifies only as Ploughman (“I am what I do,” he grunts), is mourning the loss of his wife and two children after they died from the plague, and will not stand for it any more. When asked for proof of his family’s death, one day he swipes clean the table of the taxman. “We’ve given you enough,” he cries, as the townspeople’s collective rage boils over into a riot.

He’s an unconvincing hero, this gruff Ploughman. The character seems to have been constructed as an everyman figure who unites the common people of England, but without any particular magnetism or spice, he often feels like he could be any man. His troupe soon meets two people who actually were in the Peasants’ Revolt: the priest John Ball and rebel leader Wat Tyler ( Jamie Bell and Cosmo Jarvis : both great and, unlike Garfield, both look like they actually could be from the late middle ages). “Join us, Ploughman,” beckons Tyler, as Garfield’s character, his band of brothers and a tomboy named Alyce, Thomasin McKenzie , unite to march on London with an aim to confront the king and restore England to the egalitarian principles of the Domesday Book.

Thus follows a rather hectic-feeling race from one greige setting to the next as the rebels have their run of modern-day Kent, assembling in Maidstone before storming Canterbury cathedral, and then traveling to meet the king and his men in Blackheath. Greengrass’s camerawork can occasionally swoon, with stunning aerial shots of a flotilla on the Thames, but his signature handheld style is a trick that has gone stale: the only uprising I felt during the seasick fight scenes was my breakfast threatening to return on me.

High points briefly come from Katherine Waterston’s satisfyingly icy turn as the king’s mother as well as Tom Hollander and Stephen Dillane as members of the slimy royal counsel, and there is one wickedly gruesome moment in the third act that feels genuinely envelope-pushing. But there are far too many scenes revolving around the Ploughman ominously polishing his scythe or extended debates at Windsor Castle.

Garfield does the best he can with the material, but by the time Ploughman has a righteous and rageful awakening, it is far too late. And the failure of the film to nail the uneasy parallels to today’s political life feels like looking a gift horse in the mouth. There’s certainly a lot of points of identification for a modern audience with downtrodden people who don’t feel heard by the powers that be, but Greengrass barely lets the audience pause for breath, let alone trust them to join those dots.

A couple of weeks before release, the US distributor Focus Features briefly changed the film’s title to The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood, suggesting that it would show events “that helped inspire the legend of Robin Hood”, even though the Peasants’ Revolt took place nearly 200 years after the time of the folkloric outlaw and his merry men. Meanwhile, The Uprising makes no mention of Robin Hood: almost as if it was all a last-ditch attempt to drum up buzz for a movie that is about as fun as trench foot.

The Uprising is out in the US on 11 September, the UK on 9 October and Australia on 22 October

content.article_text:
If a thing of beauty is a joy forever, as English poet John Keats would have us believe, then what is to be made of a show that highlights decrepitude? Is its job to remind us of the ephemeral nature of life and everything in it? That the value of the grotesque and the repulsive is in its mere existence, as it allows pretty perfection to stand out further? Or, alternatively, does the unpleasantness itself hold value as a much-needed contrast to whitewashed ideals? These are some of the questions that come to mind upon browsing through ‘Party is Elsewhere’, a multi-artist showcase which took place in February this year as an India Art Fair Parallel offering.

Zarina Hashmi, Untitled, Image Courtesy: The Radial

More interesting than its content, though certainly that deserves praise as well, was the location chosen for this temporary, standalone exhibition put together from private collections, including that of the Devi Art Foundation. It was housed in an abandoned nightclub in Block F of the iconic Connaught Place outer circle, the shape of which inspired the interesting name: The Radial. It sat in a state of grave decay for years, and when curators Reha Sodhi and Amit Kumar Jain, came across it while out for another task nearby, the space became the inspiration for the show.

Its mouldy walls, falling beams, broken toilets, stained tiles, ill-lit staircases and gloomy remnants of giddy epithets like ‘OMG’ dating back to the nightclub’s heyday, took the space beyond backdrop and made it a work of art itself. The party in this experimental space was certainly over, sparking comparison with the state of the art world, and perhaps the world in general. Upon visualising the project, the curators recalled a quite literal artistic reference i.e., Sudarshan Shetty’s 2005 kinetic sculpture titled Party is Elsewhere , which was first shown in Mumbai at a gallery which later burned down. In it, the brightly lit visage of a neon sign declared the art work’s name, as two large mechanical arms periodically beat down on a table filled with old wine glasses. Its shock value was both literal and conceptual, as the loud bang resonated far beyond the first viewing, making one think of the cost of over-construction in cities. The piece then fittingly became the showstopper and namesake of the show.

Vivan Sundaram, Great Indian Bazaar, Image Courtesy: The Radial

The rest of the South Asian and international artists whose paintings, sculptures and installations adorned the grungy walls, floors and nooks of the Radial, were chosen for their pieces to converse with each other in a meaningful way, while also sparking queries and conversations from viewers. In furtherance of the complete eschewing of the white cube gallery format, the art works were presented without any tags, boards or explanations. With only a brief explanatory note at the entrance speaking about the vision of the show, visitors witnessed the art without preconceived notions, and engaged with it differently than they would have knowing artist names, histories and market prices. They could also assign their own meaning to what they saw, or no meaning at all.

Were one to keenly notice a thread running through the display of art, however, they would see a focus on questions of temporality and the fleeting nature of existence. As announced in the curatorial note: “Like a musical composition orchestrated by pauses and subtle resonances the exhibition’s tones swell and recede, each artwork pulsing within a shared rhythm. Moving between reflections, flux and transformation, the exhibition invites us into a contemplative ether where memories hover like half-remembered dreams and the boundaries of here and elsewhere softly erode.”

When one delves into the selection of the artists whose work was on display at Party is Elsewhere, one discovers a variety of practices, geographies, and material choices. On display is subtle abstraction and literal figuration, traditional modes and methodologies as well as experimental conceptual inquiries. Some works that stood out include Alwar Balasubramaniam’s pair of Untitled sculptures made in 2004, which face each other in their demarcated glass boxes. One made of sand looks perfect, while its neighbour, made from camphor, is in a permanent state of decay, on its way to completely disappearing in a few years.

Sheba Chhachhi, Mermaid Mirror, Image Courtesy: The Radial

A heap on the floor is far from the disorderly mess it seems at first sight. On close inspection, each small rectangular piece shows vintage photographs encased within bright phone covers. Great Indian Bazaar by Vivan Sundaram is an ode to the exuberant disorderliness of Indian markets. It is offset by a bright painting of Bharti Kher’s The Walls Have Ears (The Private Softness of Skin), whose signature whorls and bindis form the backdrop to a massive insect inching towards a comfortable looking bed and its intended victims.

Atul Dodiya’s 26/11 is a large shutter that bears a Munsch-esque Screaming figure on the outside as a comment on the heinous violence of the Mumbai attacks of 26/11. In Mermaid Mirror, a series of doll-like TV sets by Sheba Chhachhi, are set in a circular pattern and show videos of Bollywood actress Meena Kumari. Susanta Mandal’s It Doesn’t Bite makes a big impact through a simple sculptural mechanism. His machine makes bubbles at one end and destroys them with a sharp pincer at the other. Conundrums , a projection of thousands of ants on the floor of a toilet by Mithu Sen, makes one recoil. It’s a deliberately orchestrated reaction so one can think about the implications of consumerist excess.

Other noteworthy artists include Ayesha Sultana, Himmat Shah, Hiroshi Sugimoto, Jitish Kallat, Jyoti Bhatt, Krishna Reddy, Mithu Sen, Monika Correa, Mrinalini Mukherjee, Nalini Malani, Nasreen Mohamedi, Rana Begum, Raqs Media Collective, Sakshi Gupta, Sankho Chaudhuri, Shilpa Gupta, Shovan Gandhi, Subodh Gupta, T Venkanna,Vipeksha Gupta, Vivan Sundaram, and Zarina Hashmi among others.

Through Party is Elsewhere , Sodhi and Jain sought to do away with the intimidation usually associated with viewing high-end, beautiful art. Through a careful curation of works that fit their vision, and the removal of any reference to perceived meanings and understandings, they were able to achieve this goal. The revelry is long gone, what remains now is its aftermath, both in art and in life.

Party is Elsewhere, January 31- 28 February 2026, The Radial.

content.article_text:
ONE DOES NOT have to look too far to find the defining images of today’s India. They stare back at us in public, like the arresting, belligerent face of a saffron Hanuman, popularised in 2018 and pasted on the windscreens of cars. Or they crawl their way into our social media feeds, like the suited-up, sunglass-sporting, victorious insect in the logo of the newly emerged Cockroach Janata Party.

Archana Hande. The Narmada Fish. The Last Rust. Chemould Prescott Road, Mumbai. 2023

In her solo show The Last Rust , Archana Hande turns her attention to older, more revered images. Drawing from Émile Durkheim’s conception of totemism, she revisits symbols in the context of the Indian nation-state: institutionalised ‘totems’ like the national bird and animal, sans nostalgia. To this end, she constructs sculptures from scrap—blades and scissors, for example: scavenged from Gujari (flea) markets organised on Sundays. Fittingly, sickles and a long machchu or iron bill hook are woven together to form the torso and limbs of The Royal Bengal Tiger . The same menacing machchu blade, combined with farming and horticultural tools, assumes a more graceful form in The Indian Peninsula Peacock , which seems to evoke both the subcontinent’s unique geography, and the Ashoka Chakra.

On display, first and foremost, is Hande’s ability to transform what is deemed detritus into something entirely new, while holding onto past meanings, resulting in multilayered installations. For example, in Historical Amnesia , housed within light boxes, she sketches on carbon paper collected from a typist near Mumbai’s Bombay Sessions Court. If the viewer peers closely, they will see remnants of the carbon papers’ past lives. “These monuments subvert symbolic expectations by evoking skeletons, corpses, and carapaces—decomposing and mutating. Each object within the assembly carries its own class, gender, and caste history, embedded within the lives of those existing on the margins of society,” architect and filmmaker Rohan Shivkumar observes in his text accompanying the exhibition.

Archana Hande. The Indian Peninsula Peacock. The Last Rust. Chemould Prescott Road, Mumbai. 2025-26

On her visits to scrap markets like Bengaluru’s Shivajinagar Market and Mumbai’s Chor Bazaar, Hande does not typically walk in with pre-imagined frameworks; instead she takes away objects that speak to her, and revisits them at her studio. Many of these objects are the tools of highly skilled workers, thus making the works in The Last Rust a juxtaposition of totemic power and the labour of highly skilled workers across community kitchens, garment weaving, construction and agriculture. The subversion inspires interpretation, provoking the viewer to wonder about the greatness of India and how central workers in formal and informal sectors, invisibilised, unlike entrepreneurs and scientists, have been to it. Beyond interpretations of a more simpler nature, one wonders if and how these national symbols speak to the workers’ realities.

The formation of ‘rust’ over institutions and symbols is an inevitability in a changing society; every few years, a new India forms, like a tree’s growth rings or layers of earth building upon each other. A scratching of the surface, the artist says, reveals what came before. To Hande, who initially conceptualised these works for the 2022 Kochi-Muziris Biennale, rust is a metaphor for the corrosion of democratic and secular values that India once espoused. At a time when the names of stadiums, bridges and even cities are changed to sever connections to history: colonial or otherwise, and controversial deletions in school textbooks have been normalised, rust is a powerful vehicle to convey how outward signs of societal decay point to an inward hollowing.

Archana Hande. Historical Amnesia. The Last Rust. Chemould Prescott Road, Mumbai. 2022

In combination with its metaphorical value, the use of rust, at once brittle and abrasive, is compelling. Intrinsic to the state in which the objects were found, rather than an effect artificially engineered in the artist’s studio, it seems to be material and medium, melding together disparate objects from entirely different contexts, enabling them to take on a new, shared meaning. It is to Hande’s credit that something as heavy and weatherbeaten as horseshoes can be imbued with a sense of lightness and delicateness in a work like The Cloud .

By virtue of being sourced at scrap markets, the objects are now living out their second or third lives. In present times, India’s repair economies, from the art of rafoogari (expert darning) to low-cost appliance repair, are slowly losing out on past relevance thanks to a use-and-throw culture taking hold. (Hande is no stranger to this culture, as a documentarian of “rejected gods” in a series of photographs from 2011, where she captures how even pictures and idols of gods are abandoned and dumped in public because of defects.) The Last Rust opens up a conversation about hope-giving repairwork of the social kind, “where a new future can be assembled out of discarded scraps as a defense against despair,” as Shivkumar articulates in his note.

Archana Hande. The Royal Bengal Tiger. The Last Rust. Chemould Prescott Road, Mumbai. 2025-26

It seems to reflect in Hande’s own practice: Weaving Light , a tessellating installation whose surface is made of jacquard punched cards once used in textile looms, shapeshifts across exhibitions and biennales, without ego or rigidity. Or as gallerist Shireen Gandhy recalls of a video taken after the 2022 Kochi-Muziris Biennale: the artist recorded the demolition of her works, only to rebuild them for the 2026 show.

Archana Hande, The Last Rust , 7 March 2026-30 April 2026, Chemould Prescott Road.

content.title_original: On Unequal Burdens: Waste and Toxicity in Navjot Altaf’s New Works
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Humans have always generated waste but there is a distinct quality to the kind of waste we have generated since the invention of plastic: waste that does not return to life, waste that fills the land and floods the oceans. It can break down to the point of invisibility but it still lingers at micro and nano scales. The ubiquity of plastic is such that it has been traced in placentas and breastmilk. That is to say that capitalism and its extractive technologies, which rely on oil and its by-products, have reshaped not only our landscapes but also altered the constitution of our bodies."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://takeonartmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/8-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "TAKE on Art"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Navjot Altaf, Karvy, Strobilanthes Callosa; Waste Archives as Landscape , 2025, Courtesy the artist and Volte Gallery"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The disturbing experience of encountering a mound full of electronic waste amidst a forest, next to a watering hole visited by a herd of elephants, led artist Navjot Altaf to conduct field visits to larger landfills on the outskirts of cities like Mumbai and Ahmedabad. This new direction in her practice has its roots in her work around mining and loss of land and life in Chhattisgarh, which she has documented since the 1990s. Shifting focus over the last two years, Altaf produced paintings, a video, and an installation to highlight the unequal burden of toxic waste in the marginalised areas and communities. These works were exhibited in Mumbai in Waste Archives as Landscape ."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The exhibition takes its title from a series of gouache paintings, which assemble fragments of images of various landfills located in India and elsewhere. From a distance, some of the paintings show a wide view of garbage-filled areas on the fringes of settlements but most of them depict undistinguished heaps: an emphasis on their gradations of colour rather than objecthood. In this latter set, a few parts of machines or pieces of structures emerge when the eye leans in but there is otherwise an overload of detail making us hover over the surface, darting here and there, unable to anchor ourselves. Parts of the route of Khian Sea, a ship filled with 14,000 tons of ash from Philadelphia, are traced on the paintings in the form of abstract lines. Altaf’s interest in Khian Sea’s journey – wandering for two years between 1986 and 1988 before dumping near Haiti, and in the waters between Singapore and Sri Lanka – comes from the illegal transfer of waste to less powerful countries, which continues to take place and is increasingly legally sanctioned."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://takeonartmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/7-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "TAKE on Art"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Navjot Altaf, Waste Archives as Landscape , 2024-25, Courtesy the artist & Volte Gallery"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The collective title of the paintings, Waste Archive as Landscape , suggests they are meant to be archives. If so, they are archives that are out of reach, whose contents cannot be discerned. Perhaps this effect is a reference to the impact of the limitless cycles of production of products that humans cannot entirely grasp or catalogue. On the contrary, those who live on the edges of landfills, both humans and nonhuman living beings, suffer the consequences viscerally. The reality is not distant and the horrors are inescapable. The sensing of such an atmosphere of horror comes through in the short video Instinct , 2024–2025, in which a dog ambles over a landfill. Since it is a scene reconstructed through animation there is an aura of nightmare hovering over it. Smoke rises in the distance. content.article_text:
Humans have always generated waste but there is a distinct quality to the kind of waste we have generated since the invention of plastic: waste that does not return to life, waste that fills the land and floods the oceans. It can break down to the point of invisibility but it still lingers at micro and nano scales. The ubiquity of plastic is such that it has been traced in placentas and breastmilk. That is to say that capitalism and its extractive technologies, which rely on oil and its by-products, have reshaped not only our landscapes but also altered the constitution of our bodies.

Navjot Altaf, Karvy, Strobilanthes Callosa; Waste Archives as Landscape , 2025, Courtesy the artist and Volte Gallery

The disturbing experience of encountering a mound full of electronic waste amidst a forest, next to a watering hole visited by a herd of elephants, led artist Navjot Altaf to conduct field visits to larger landfills on the outskirts of cities like Mumbai and Ahmedabad. This new direction in her practice has its roots in her work around mining and loss of land and life in Chhattisgarh, which she has documented since the 1990s. Shifting focus over the last two years, Altaf produced paintings, a video, and an installation to highlight the unequal burden of toxic waste in the marginalised areas and communities. These works were exhibited in Mumbai in Waste Archives as Landscape .

The exhibition takes its title from a series of gouache paintings, which assemble fragments of images of various landfills located in India and elsewhere. From a distance, some of the paintings show a wide view of garbage-filled areas on the fringes of settlements but most of them depict undistinguished heaps: an emphasis on their gradations of colour rather than objecthood. In this latter set, a few parts of machines or pieces of structures emerge when the eye leans in but there is otherwise an overload of detail making us hover over the surface, darting here and there, unable to anchor ourselves. Parts of the route of Khian Sea, a ship filled with 14,000 tons of ash from Philadelphia, are traced on the paintings in the form of abstract lines. Altaf’s interest in Khian Sea’s journey – wandering for two years between 1986 and 1988 before dumping near Haiti, and in the waters between Singapore and Sri Lanka – comes from the illegal transfer of waste to less powerful countries, which continues to take place and is increasingly legally sanctioned.

Navjot Altaf, Waste Archives as Landscape , 2024-25, Courtesy the artist & Volte Gallery

The collective title of the paintings, Waste Archive as Landscape , suggests they are meant to be archives. If so, they are archives that are out of reach, whose contents cannot be discerned. Perhaps this effect is a reference to the impact of the limitless cycles of production of products that humans cannot entirely grasp or catalogue. On the contrary, those who live on the edges of landfills, both humans and nonhuman living beings, suffer the consequences viscerally. The reality is not distant and the horrors are inescapable. The sensing of such an atmosphere of horror comes through in the short video Instinct , 2024–2025, in which a dog ambles over a landfill. Since it is a scene reconstructed through animation there is an aura of nightmare hovering over it. Smoke rises in the distance. The dog walks from one end of the frame to another, without much force or intention, stops to vomit towards the end of the trajectory before disappearing. Although we cannot distinguish the waste the dog is surrounded by, we can gather that it is toxic, that it has undone something in the animal’s being, and that it has altered its fate. As we watch this scene unfold over a few minutes, the dog comes to be demarcated as a victim of its circumstances despite having played no role in the generation of the waste that has poisoned its body.

Navjot Altaf, Waste Archives as Landscape, 2024-25, Courtesy the artist & Volte Gallery

Elsewhere, footage of thriving plants and lush waterfalls forms the backdrop to a discussion on the caste-based politics of land theft in Chhalbal , 2024-25. In this 35-minute video, four actors from Ahmedabad-based Budhan Theatre present a Dalit perspective on the myth of Durga. Through a didactic discussion, they question the supposed feminist agency of the Hindu goddess, whose act of slaying Mahishasura reinforced Brahmanical supremacy. Much of the argument is based on the book Mahishasur: Ek Jannayak , edited by Pramod Ranjan, but the video extends the context to the present with a reference to the clashes among students at the Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi over a commemoration gathering for Mahishasura. The video notes how indigenous or adivasi world views, which advocate harmony and balance between land and living beings, stand in opposition to patriarchal and capitalist ownership models which place the extractive human at the centre of their ideologies. With its instructive dialogues, the video functions like an essential accompanying text to outline the conditions of injustice emerging from supposed progress and development in India. Perhaps, a direct evocation of local or national infrastructures of waste and their relationship to global networks of capital would have enriched the discourse presented in the work.

Navjot Altaf, Waste Archives as Landscape , 2024-25, Courtesy the artist & Volte Gallery

These ideas are explored through metaphor in the site-specific installation Take-Make-Waste , 2026 in which a network of PVC pipes fixed to the ceiling spews out chips used in electronic machines whenever a visitor walks by. In the background, sounds of planes and meditation bowls mount a contrast between their individual use of metals. Although meant to illustrate the manner in which waste fills up and pollutes the earth, there is a playful aspect to the installation that turns it into a game for the visitor. Complicity does not feel concerning because the parts that emerge from the pipes appear new with a shine, no less enticing than LEGO bricks. There is a sense of possibility to them as functional objects, arrested here in the form of an installation, which may be quite different from the qualities of e-waste when it begins to disintegrate and release toxic chemicals into the environment. As the proportion of dumped e-waste grows faster than any other solid waste stream in the world, the necessity to grasp this fact and its consequences is important even if its dimensions grow larger than the human capacity to imagine. Perhaps, art can provide expressions to these concerns in concrete form. But the installation leaves us wondering: how can the subject of e-waste be tackled in art in a way that captures the environment it creates, the impact it has, and the unequal burden of its creation and disposal?

Navjot Altaf, Waste Archives as Landscape , Curated by Puja Vaish, 12 March – 10 June 2026, Jehangir Nicholson Art Foundation.

content.article_text:
Ghulam Ali Khan, Two Men Wrestling, Tashrih-al-Aqvam, Gouache on Paper. 1825 AD.

The first thing one notices about an akhara is the earth. Carefully maintained—turned over, watered and sometimes scented—it forms the centre of the wrestling pit. Early in the morning, before the heat settles in, wrestlers step onto it barefoot. Some touch the ground before entering; others rub earth onto their arms and chest. The smell is distinctive: mustard oil, ghee, sweat and soil. Earth and bodies mingle in a way that feels almost consecrated. This is where wrestlers train, compete, exchange stories and spend long hours together. Outsiders rarely find their way inside. Akharas are not public spaces in the conventional sense but tightly knit communities held together by routines, hierarchies and a shared devotion to wrestling.

When we encounter wrestlers in Indian miniature painting, a different set of questions emerges. Who is looking at these bodies? What drew the artist’s eye? What did audiences see? Strength? Skill? Masculinity? Or something else entirely?

Looking at a nineteenth-century miniature depicting two wrestlers in practice, I am struck by something unexpected. The scene is deceptively simple. Two men are locked in a grappling hold while jori clubs and weights lie scattered about. These men clearly embody strength and physical discipline, yet there is remarkably little emphasis on muscle itself. What stands out is not the muscularity of the wrestlers but its relative absence.

Seen alongside other depictions of wrestling from the Mughal and colonial periods, the image points toward a broader visual tradition in which bodily strength was understood differently from how it often is today. Whether wrestlers appear grappling before Emperor Shah Jahan, entertaining courtly audiences, or training amidst clubs, weights and fellow practitioners, the emphasis rarely falls on the detailed rendering of muscular anatomy. The men are undoubtedly powerful, yet painters seem more interested in wrestling itself and the social worlds surrounding it. Wrestling appears simultaneously as discipline, spectacle, performance and patronage.

Mir Kalan Khan, Painting of the Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan Watching a Wrestling Match, Delhi or Lucknow. Gouache on Paper. 1750 AD.

Today fitness culture encourages us to associate strength with visible muscularity. Whether scrolling through Instagram, watching fitness influencers on YouTube or passing advertisements for gyms, we encounter bodies designed to be admired. Defined abdominals, broad shoulders and pronounced biceps have become visual shorthand for health and physical power. The wrestlers in these miniatures suggest a different ideal. Their bodies appear compact and functional rather than sculpted for display. What matters is not appearance but action. The emphasis falls on movement, leverage, balance and technique. Strength resides in what the body can do rather than how it looks.

Historically, Indian wrestling cultivated a distinctive understanding of bodily development. Wrestlers trained intensely and followed demanding routines of exercise, diet and discipline. They sought endurance, resilience and stamina alongside strength. The goal was not simply to build a body but to cultivate a particular way of life. The training equipment depicted in miniature painting points toward this broader world. Indian clubs, or mugdars, have long been associated with wrestling traditions. During the nineteenth century they travelled far beyond South Asia, becoming popular exercise tools in Europe and North America before largely disappearing and then recently returning through contemporary fitness culture. What appears innovative is often a reworking of much older practices.

Yet the relationship between wrestling and bodybuilding is far from straightforward. Wrestling has undoubtedly shaped broader ideas about masculinity, discipline and physical strength in India. Throughout the twentieth century wrestlers became symbols of masculine achievement and national pride, while physical culture movements drew inspiration from wrestling traditions alongside influences from Europe and North America. At the same time, wrestling and bodybuilding do not produce identical bodies.

The wrestler’s physique emerges through grappling, swinging clubs, performing dands and baithaks, and training with opponents. Fitness and bodybuilding place far greater emphasis on the visual presentation of the body. It would be a mistake, however, to imagine that kushti wrestling has remained unchanged. Nowhere is this transformation more visible than on social media. Many younger wrestlers maintain active Instagram and YouTube accounts where they document training sessions, share dietary advice and post carefully composed photographs of their physiques. The body has become something to be viewed as much as something to be used. Visibility now matters in ways that would have been unfamiliar to the wrestlers depicted in older paintings. As a result, the physiques displayed by many contemporary wrestlers increasingly resemble those associated with bodybuilding.

Looking back at these paintings reveals not only how wrestling has changed but also how our ways of seeing bodies have changed. In one image wrestlers perform before a royal audience; in another British soldiers and Indian spectators observe demonstrations of physical training and martial exercise. Together these scenes remind us that wrestling was never simply about individual bodies. It connected rulers and subjects, teachers and pupils, spectators and performers. Strength derived meaning from these relationships rather than from the isolated display of muscle.

The wrestlers in traditional miniature paintings are presented differently from the bodies that dominate contemporary fitness culture. Their physiques matter, but they are rarely the central subject. Attention is directed instead toward movement, technique, ritual and the communities gathered around these practices. What emerges is a vision of strength that is fundamentally relational rather than individual. The muscular body was certainly present, but it had not yet become the primary object of attention that it would later become in the worlds of bodybuilding, fitness culture and social media.

Bibliography

Alter, Joseph S. 1993. “The Body of One Color: Indian Wrestling, the Indian State, and Utopian Somatics.” Cultural Anthropology 8(1): 49–72.

Alter, Joseph S. 2000. “Subaltern Bodies and Nationalist Physiques: Gama the Great and the Heroics of Indian Wrestling.” Body & Society 6(3–4): 45–72.

Baas, Michiel. 2020. Muscular India: Masculinity, Mobility and the New Middle Class . New Delhi: Context/Westland.

Baas, Michiel. 2024. “The Muscular Body in Public Space: Masculinity, Middle-Classness and the ‘Urban Villagers’ of Delhi, India.” Boyhood Studies 17(2): 65–85.

Gupta, Abhijit. 2012. “Cultures of the Body in Colonial Bengal: The Career of Gobor Guha.” The International Journal of the History of Sport 29(12): 1687–1700.

content.article_text:
Gargi Chandola, Puge, Gouache on Wasli.

She is her Self.

She is memory, and body.

She is also the landscape and forest.

She is soft and strong, loud and quiet, beautiful and grotesque…

She evolves with the consciousness of a thousand women before her, and will pass it on to ten thousand after. She is a mountain of love, concealing and revealing mythologies.

To describe the work “God Empress of Dune” by Gargi Chandola without employing poetic responses would be doing it an injustice. It is a timeless contemporary visualisation that embodies the spirit of countless beings and generations; representing experiences, memories, power and vulnerability, and the identities of women across time and space. For me, it also embodies the lens through which this essay explores the work of three women – Vinita Sharma, Mainaz Bano, and Gargi Chandola – who are working within the visual legacy of miniature painting, sharing a common contemporary. Each of them highlights an innate capacity to poetically bring forth what is personal and private, even while engaging with and shaping collective thought and expression. Through their work, we encounter what they witness, how they understand, define and express, where their lives’ experience is leading them. We are introduced to their visions of their past and present, their dreams for the future. Significantly, we understand how they derive from, and yet break-away and redefine the rules of miniature painting.

The Storyteller

Vinita Sharma has been painting for around three decades. With a natural affinity to art and aesthetics, she was guided by her husband, prominent miniature painter Ajay Kumar Sharma, in the intricacies of miniature painting. While their repertoire includes Pahari, Kangra and other Indian styles, the larger focus is on the Mughal tradition. After her training, as their children grew older, Vinita had more time to spend on painting, and moved between creating experimental compositions, and more traditional ones that were commissioned and in demand.

An early self-portrait titled “Wandering Thoughts” demonstrates her fluid use of the medium, and her comfort with the rules of miniature painting, that she dissolves in order to express something deeply personal. The composition, in soft blues and browns, depicts the protagonist seemingly in a day-dream while her imagination is fed by the many manuscripts and books that are perhaps her learning blocks as an evolving artist.

Vinit Sharma, Untitled, Waterbased colour on Indian Wasli Handmade

When questioned about her favourite element in miniature painting, she replies with great joy that it lies in the rich detailing – she loves the minute and painstakingly developed patterns – on a sword, a dress or carpet; the delicacy of line and the luminosity of colour that complement each other to make a vibrant whole. She explains how intrinsic the natural pigments and time intensive techniques are to the results, and the manner in which she and Ajay Sharma strive to continue the long-standing practices, even when organic materials (like Khadia or alabaster clay) have become scarce and harder to come by. With their expertise, together they teach workshops on miniature painting, invited to universities and museums both in India and abroad.

Geometric design is another fascination for Vinita. Having spent extended time hosting workshops in West Asian nations, she has used her inspiration from Islamic architectural elements and combined it with her knowledge of distinctive Mughal patterns in order to construct compositions that are as playful as they are compositionally balanced. In a current series of paintings on Kabir, she includes the celebration of the festival of Holi, utilising the structures offered by the geometric designs to create intuitive figurative scenarios.

Exploring the sensitive subject of physical distance and longing, another very popular series of works by her picturises the emotional status of every would-be grandparent awaiting the arrival of a grandchild in a far-away land. Expanding into a wider narrative of domestic spaces, she has painted naughty children, disobedient pets, and preoccupied mothers in these tableaus of love, imbuing the portraiture with a distinctive sweetness and producing interesting detailing such as trees filled with patterned motifs rather than leaf forms.

In her work, factual experience finds form in imaginary storytelling and vice versa, and her image-making process moves freely between varied vocabularies of the miniature, uniting the regional and global, and bringing the past and present together in seamless rhythm.

The Chronicler

Resonating with a methodology and visual practice similar to that of Vinita Sharma, Mainaz Bano has developed a unique style that positions her work within the city of Lucknow, where she is based. Surrounded by Indo-Islamic architecture, and the once renowned ‘ganga-jamuni tehzeeb’ a syncretic culture that speaks of the confluence of the rivers as well as people, their language, beliefs and practices – Mainaz has continually absorbed and chronicled elements from this experience. The worlds she paints are inhabited by characters that traverse historical and contemporary narratives, building bridges between personal observations, popular culture and socio-political realities. For her, the past is what makes the present possible and relevant, and therefore research forms a strong part of her process.

In love with painting and drawing from her childhood, Mainaz was drawn to the aesthetics of miniature painting in her school years, at first diligently making copies and later going on to pursue it while earning a Masters degree in creative landscape painting. Though she trained in the use of traditional pigments, she turned to the use of acrylic on canvas as she began to make larger works. Her compositions make lyrical use of space, colour and line, juxtaposing areas of intricate detail with vacant or minimally handled sections within which objects, flora-fauna and figures emerge; she compares this visual arrangement to the pace of life, that needs pauses amidst the chaos in order to understand oneself and move forward in a balanced way.

Gargi Chandola, Treasure Hunt, Gouache on Wasli.

An unusual and ambitious painting in her repertoire is ‘Evolution 2’, wherein she includes her self-portrait, seated at a table with the (in)famous Begum Samru, a catholic convert who started her life as a nautch girl but navigated her circumstances to become a powerful mercenary ruler in the region of Sardhana, in the early nineteenth century. Deeply intrigued by stories of women such as her, Mainaz presents a translated version of an earlier court miniature ‘ Begum Samru and her household’ (circa 1820, Delhi, Chester Beatty Library). The ninety-five animated figures represent historical characters as well as her friends and several others known in Lucknow society. The environment opens out into the distinctive Mughal Charbagh, with the University Library as the backdrop and a modern street in the foreground. Deeply philosophical about the human condition, she employs linear forms as a device to comment on life’s transitions and its incompleteness; she also infuses her scenes with elements of humour, invoking the absurd alongside the solemn.

The Critic or the Learner

Humour and satire also form an essential visual and conceptual layer in Gargi Chandola’s versatile practice. Significant in her recent body of work is a series of miniatures that include the presence of Rhesus Macaques, a species of monkey indigenous to the forested areas of the Aravali mountain range where the artist resides. Sometimes relegated to the richly pigmented borders, and at others paired with the Nayika within a lush landscape, these creatures embody behaviours that offer parallels to human nature, demonstrating greed and desire, aggression and dominance, and the will to survive, among other things.

As seen in works like ‘Treasure Hunt’ and ‘Purge’, the Nayikas appear fully in control of their wants and nonchalantly take charge of their surroundings. While a certain sexual symbolism carries forward the commentary on gender hierarchies and power play, the Nayika’s themselves transcend objectification, representing instead the wisdom and playfulness, the resilience and righteousness of the Woman in plurality. Here is a being who embraces and envelopes the multilayered quality of feminine existence, that Gargi says comes from her own deep relationships with all the women in her extended family.

While being connected to creative making from her childhood, Gargi found her calling as an artist after having trained in the guru-shishya parampara to learn the techniques of Basohli, Pahari and Kangra schools of painting. Deeply interested in the pursuit of traditional art forms, she recently took time to teach herself the challenging technique of Turkish ebru-marbling on paper, a process that she is now experimenting with to represent the rugged rock formations that are so much part of her home environment.

Miniature painting, which may have experienced a low period a decade or two ago, is riding on a good wave now. As Vinita Sharma shares, a lot of artists from the younger generations are investing time and energy in learning these old and trusted techniques, often reframing them to fit within personal contemporary explorations.

Vinita Sharma, Mainaz Bano and Gargi Chandola may have never met, but their works connect and share common space, bringing varied perspectives, thoughts and ideas to this dialogue. Womanhood is never singular or fixed, nor is the expression of it. Every sketch, every composition holds multiple stories, mythologies and lived experiences. The individual voice carries the resonance of multiples.

She is the mother, the nautch girl, the matriarch

The black sheep and the white, the found and the lost,

She encompasses all

She belongs. She is.

content.article_text:
写真家・久井唯花の作品展「QUALIA」が、2026年9月4日から17日まで、東京・銀座のソニーイメージングギャリーで開催されている。色感覚を伴う共感覚の経験を背景に、視覚と非視覚的な感覚が結びついた記憶を写真によって記録してきた久井。2025年に刊行した同名写真集にもつながる作品世界を紹介する。

久井が制作の主題としているのは、人それぞれに異なる「知覚」のあり方だ。大阪芸術大学大学院で写真を学び、自身の共感覚の経験を起点に、目に見えるものだけでは捉えきれない感覚や記憶を写真へと置き換えてきた。2025年には、10年にわたって撮影した記録を写真集『QUALIA』としてまとめている。

タイトルの「QUALIA（クオリア）」は、あるものを見たり、聞いたり、感じたりした際に生じる、個人に固有の感覚的な質を指す言葉。本展に寄せたステートメントで久井は、「わたしの祈りは叶わないまま輝いている」と記している。過ぎ去った時間や、他者とは共有することのできない感覚。それらがどのようなかたちで写真として定着したとしても、その「輝きは、失われることはない」と語る。

展示作品にも、そうした知覚の揺らぎを思わせる像が現れる。資料に掲載された作品では、光に溶け込むような人物や水面、魚、海へ伸ばされた手などが、鮮明な記録というよりも記憶の中の光景のように写し出されている。色彩のにじみやブレ、強い光によって被写体の輪郭が曖昧になり、見る者自身の感覚や記憶を呼び起こしていく。

写真は世界を客観的に記録する装置である一方、撮影者が何をどのように「見た」のかを残す、極めて主観的なメディアでもある。「QUALIA」はその性質を手がかりに、同じものを見ても同じようには感じることのできない、人間の知覚の個別性へと目を向ける展覧会だ。

久井唯花 作品展「QUALIA」

content.article_text:
Godzilla Minus Zero | Sequência do filme vencedor do Oscar ganha primeiro trailer oficial — assista

Filme estreia em 5 de novembro no Brasil.

(Imagens: Toho)

O Rei dos Monstros está de volta. “ Godzilla Minus Zero ” ganhou seu primeiro trailer internacional completo, continuando a história iniciada com o filme vencedor do Oscar, “Godzilla Minus One”, de Takashi Yamazaki . Assista acima (legendado em inglês).

Foi divulgado também o novo cartaz nacional do filme, abaixo.

Ainda não há confirmação sobre o enredo de “Minus Zero”, apenas que se trata de uma nova ameaça para o povo do Japão após os eventos do primeiro filme. O trailer, no entanto, mostra raios amarelos sendo disparados contra a população, contrastando com o tradicional azul de Godzilla. Com isso, fãs especulam que pode se tratar de King Ghidorah, um dos maiores inimigos do Rei dos Monstros.

O novo filme ainda traz em sua campanha de marketing os dizeres: “Assim que a humanidade conseguiu se agarrar a uma paz duramente conquistada, uma nova ameaça surge, destruindo a esperança num instante. Não haverá uma terceira vez. Tudo termina aqui.” Ou seja, este pode ser o fim desse capítulo de Godzilla nas telonas.

“Minus One” foi um marco para a franquia do Rei dos Monstros. Produzido com um orçamento estimado em apenas US$ 15 milhões, o filme desafiou expectativas e arrecadou mais de US$ 113 milhões em todo o mundo. O longa também se tornou o primeiro na história de 70 anos da franquia Godzilla a ganhar um Oscar, levando para casa a estatueta de Melhores Efeitos Visuais em uma categoria repleta de grandes produções de Hollywood com orçamentos muito maiores. Também se tornou o filme japonês live-action de maior bilheteria de todos os tempos na América do Norte.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” será o 31º longa-metragem japonês da famosa franquia de kaiju (sem incluir as coproduções americanas feitas com a Legendary Entertainment). No Brasil, o filme estreia em 5 de novembro e tem distribuição da Sato Company.

content.article_text:
Agente 86 | John Mulaney pode estrelar nova adaptação para a Warner

Série original foi criada por Mel Brooks e Buck Henry.

(Imagens: Getty Images, Everett Collection)

Um dos agentes secretos mais queridos da televisão está voltando. Uma nova adaptação de “ Agente 86 ” está em desenvolvimento pela Warner, com o comediante John Mulaney cotado para interpretar o protagonista Maxwell Smart (via Deadline ).

A série original de “Agente 86” foi criada por Mel Brooks e Buck Henry e exibida nos EUA entre 1965 e 1970. Funcionando como uma paródia de “James Bond”, a trama acompanha os agentes Maxwell Smart (Agente 86) e a Agente 99 trabalhando para a agência Control, que trava uma batalha constante contra a organização maligna Kaos. Durante os episódios, Smart frequentemente leva a melhor sobre a Kaos graças a cacarecos como o icônico sapatofone, apesar de sua aparente incompetência.

Em 1980, “Agente 86” ganhou um filme com o retorno do elenco original, com outro longa para televisão sendo lançado em 1989. Em 1995, um revival da série original rendeu apenas sete episódios. Em 2008, a Warner lançou uma adaptação para o cinema estrelada por Steve Carell, Anne Hathaway, Alan Arkin e Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson.

O desenvolvimento da nova adaptação ainda está em estágios iniciais, com Seth Grahame-Smith, de “Truque de Mestre 3”, escrevendo o roteiro. Chuck Roven e Andrew Lazar, que produziram o longa de 2008, também produzem o novo filme.

Ainda não há previsão de estreia para o novo “Agente 86”.

Artificial | Andrew Garfield é Sam Altman, criador do ChatGPT, no trailer do novo filme de Luca Guadagnino

Filme tem estreia prevista para o dia de Natal nos EUA.

(Imagens: divulgação/NEON)

A NEON divulgou o novo trailer de “ Artificial “, filme de Luca Guadagnino em que Andrew Garfield interpreta Sam Altman, fundador da empresa OpenAI e criador do ChatGPT. Assista acima (sem legendas).

O filme narra os dias que antecederam a demissão repentina e a recondução de Altman ao cargo de CEO da OpenAI, num momento em que o destino do controle da tecnologia — peça central de uma corrida armamentista de IA — estava em jogo.

Além de Garfield, o elenco conta com Mark Rylance, Andrew Garfield, Yura Borisov, Monica Barbaro, Billie Lourd, Jason Schwartzman, Cooper Koch, Cooper Hoffman e Ike Barinholtz. Guardagnino dirige a partir do roteiro de Simon Rich.

“Artificial” tem estreia prevista para o dia de Natal nos EUA, ainda sem data brasileira.

content.article_text:
M uch has changed in the universe, cosmic and otherwise, since the Owens witches last graced the big screen with their practical magic of sleeping draughts, midnight margaritas and generational love curses. For one, movies like the 1998 cult-ish classic Practical Magic – a compellingly bizarre mashup of genres, aspirational 90s fashion and sisterly affection starring Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman in their movie-star primes as lovelorn sorceresses in Puritan-lite Massachusetts – largely stopped reaching theaters. For another, nostalgia cycles only intensified and tightened, our algorithms clogged with unsolicited sequels and dupes for Bullock’s impeccable vintage 90s Levi’s.

Which makes Practical Magic 2, reuniting both Kidman and Bullock, and Stockard Channing and Dianne Wiest as their lovingly eccentric aunts, somewhat of an anomaly, at once a seeming inevitability and, as a matrilineal romance comedy (though decidedly not a romcom) starring two 60-year-old women , an oddity . There’s no circumventing nostalgia bait, but Practical Magic remains so idiosyncratic in tone and, well, kookiness, that a sequel somewhat appeals.

The new film, directed by Susanne Bier from a script by original co-screenwriter Akiva Goldsman alongside Georgia Pritchett and Kelly Marcel (and again based on a book by Alice Hoffman ), doubles down on the distillable ingredients of the original – hairpin tonal turns; strange CGI flourishes; needle drops by Stevie Nicks, that patron saint of witchy white women – though perhaps to a fault. Once again, Bullock’s Sally, the older and more neurotic/sensible of the central sisters, has given up practicing magic, much to the chagrin of Kidman’s looser, airier Gilly. Though she ended the first film believing that she broke the centuries-long curse that every man an Owens woman loved was doomed to die, life offered no such happy endings; her second husband, played in the original by Aidan Quinn, lasted only a few years, prompting her to supernaturally erase any memories of magic from her daughters’ minds, lest they too knowingly love a man to death.

This requires a little magical fudging of the timeline: though the original took place in March 1998– so says Quinn’s investigator Gary Hallet when interviewing Sally for the suspected murder of Gilly’s serial killer ex (it’s kooky!) – new headstones place the events in early 2000s. That’s all the better for Kidman and Bullock, both older now than Channing and Wiest were in the original but with fewer laugh lines, to hover somewhere in the uncanny valley of Hollywood middle age and keep Kylie (Joey King) and Antonia ( Maisie Williams ), who should be in their mid-30s, in the young 20s heyday of first real love. (Sorry to the recast Evan Rachel Wood and Alexandra Artrip.)

This will prove irksome if you, like me, are timeline-sensitive, but the original’s playful sense of tone, logic and rules in general was admittedly central to its appeal. I find it endearing that the magic in the Practical Magic franchise allows for generational curses, purgatorial spirits and the automatic stirring of coffee cups but not, say, levitating suitcases upstairs, forcing poor Kidman to lug oversized bags through three separate scenes.

So it goes – though Gilly obliquely warns Kylie that “love is our undoing” with “ heartbreak feels good in a place like this ” camp sincerity (complimentary), Kylie goes on loving anyway. And when her doting college boyfriend Gideon (Xolo Maridueña) ends up cursed in a coma, she, like her mother before her, tearfully rages against the powers that be and, guided by a recently unearthed Book of the Raven, flees to the Owens’ ancestral homeland of England. Sally and Gilly, whose old-pro sparring could sustain a lesser sequel, chase after her, leaving poor Williams and Channing – by far the film’s most luminous screen presence – stranded at the hospital in Boston. A shame, as I would love Aunt Fran’s take on the men they meet abroad, a fascinating dichotomy of masculinity in the hetero-pessimist age: one, an occult professor played by 6ft 5in internet boyfriend Lee Pace, openly pines for Sally, encouraging her to feel her feelings and embrace her power while covered in tattoos; the other, a brooding warlock with a mask of affability (Solly McLeod), craves Kylie’s power, seething with a resonant, almost too pointed sense of aggrieved entitlement.

The plot beats, guiding all the women through said men back to both magic and each other, are characteristically odd and mostly beside the point; if you’re watching the Practical Magic sequel, it is probably to see Kidman and Bullock channel their unique movie-star sorcery – beguiling eccentricity and earthy exasperation, both singularly endearing in their primes – and they conjure it with muscle memory that is fascinating in its own right.

Still, there is some comfort in the Owens’ narrative circularity; in the occult realm, as in the real one, we never truly escape our inheritances nor ourselves, even as times (and men, and hair) change. The overarching, if occasionally overwritten (“no magic is stronger than sisterhood”), theme of feminine solidarity through cyclical adversity is winning enough. The midnight margarita redux may feel obligatory, but there’s just enough magic here to still, despite everything, cast a peculiar spell.

Practical Magic 2 is out in US and Australian cinemas on 10 September and in the UK on 11 September

content.article_text:
写真家・三浦憲治の個展「三浦憲治写真展 2026 ミウラヒロシマ Vol.13」が、2026年9月8日から14日まで、東京・恵比寿のALで開催される。2014年から故郷・広島をテーマに毎年発表を続けてきた「ミウラヒロシマ」シリーズの第13回となる。

1949年広島市生まれの三浦は、東京写真短期大学在学中に写真家・長濱治に師事。雑誌『MCシスター』でキャリアをスタートさせる一方、ピンク・フロイドやレッド・ツェッペリンなど、来日した海外ミュージシャンのライブを撮影するようになる。その後も松任谷由実、矢沢永吉、YMO、井上陽水、奥田民生など、日本の音楽シーンを代表するアーティストたちを数十年にわたって撮影。ステージ上の決定的な瞬間からアーティストの素顔まで、音楽と並走するように数多くの写真を残してきた。

そんな三浦が2014年から継続しているもうひとつの重要な仕事が、自身の出身地を見つめる「ミウラヒロシマ」だ。長年にわたりミュージシャンや音楽の現場にカメラを向けてきた写真家が、毎年故郷へと立ち返り、その時々の広島を撮影し、発表を重ねてきた。

13回目を迎える今回も、一度きりの撮影によって土地を記録するのではなく、同じ場所へ繰り返し足を運び、時間の蓄積とともに変化する広島を見つめるシリーズの現在地を紹介する。

content.article_text:
You Can See Everything | Documentário sobre Elizabeth Holmes da A24 ganha primeiro trailer

Filme tem direção de Nathan Fielder e Lance Oppenheim.

(Imagens: divulgação/A24)

A 24 divulgou o primeiro teaser de “ You Can See Everything “, documentário de Nathan Fielder e Lance Oppenheim sobre Elizabeth Holmes. Assista acima (sem legendas).

Foi divulgado também o primeiro cartaz internacional do filme, abaixo.

Diz a sinopse:

“Trinta e quatro dias antes de ser enviada para a prisão, a notória fundadora do Vale do Silício, Elizabeth Holmes, convida uma equipe de filmagem cética para documentar cada um de seus passos. O que começa como um retrato íntimo de uma condenada enigmática transforma-se em uma jornada alucinante de três anos rumo ao abismo.”

Holmes ficou conhecida ao fundar a startup de biotecnologia Theranos e inventar um suposto dispositivo milagroso de triagem sanguínea, sendo condenada por fraude pouco depois. Trata-se de um dos casos mais emblemáticos da justiça estadunidense, sendo tema de diversos documentários, dramatizações e reportagens investigativas.

“You Can See Everything” tem direção de Nathan Fielder, conhecido pelas séries “Nathan For You” e “O Ensaio”, e Lance Oppenheim. A dupla produziu a obra em segredo ao longo dos últimos quatro anos, utilizando imagens de Holmes e de seu parceiro; o casal os convidou para morar em sua casa e registrar o cotidiano de ambos nos 34 dias que antecederam a prisão dela.

“You Can See Everything” estreia nos EUA em 16 de outubro, ainda sem data brasileira.

content.article_text:
L ance Oppenheim is the acclaimed documentary-maker who has made his feature debut with a strangely overwrought and heavy-footed drama-thriller, which for all its elaborate neon-lit atmosphere of noir danger isn’t at all sure what it wants to say about media or morality, or anything else.

The subject is the controversial top-rated US TV reality show To Catch a Predator which ran from 2004 to 2008; that title was evidently taken from the Hitchcock movie To Catch a Thief, which in turn was inspired by the phrase “Set a thief to catch a thief”. In search of prey, the show’s researchers baited paedophiles in online chatrooms posing as children, lured them to “sting houses” where actors played underage teens on the front porch to get the abusers inside, where they can be clearly filmed expressing criminal intentions. But before anything could happen, sonorous host Chris Hansen appeared from nowhere and confronted these cringing abusers – which made for fantastic television. After this the cops made an arrest, and they and the state prosecutor did the heavy lifting of overseeing due process and presumably debating the merits of entrapment in court, although this obvious issue is not raised in the movie.

Robert Pattinson certainly looks and sounds good in the role of the preening, pompous Hansen, gleefully overexcited when his show is promoted to a primetime slot, solemnly congratulating himself on cleaning up America and relishing the bizarrely melodramatic moment each week when he gets in the astonished abuser’s face, sauntering down the stairs with the insouciance of a talk show host. “Big night planned?” Merritt Wever plays Andie Bender, a hardbitten (fictional-composite) female executive in charge of Hansen’s live-ammo theatrics – Bender’s persona inherited from Faye Dunaway in Network – and Skyler Gisondo plays a needy, baby-faced wannabe actor Dan Plumb (another fictional-composite) who is the jailbait decoy that gets to lure the paedo indoors. He is persuaded to take the job by Hansen flatteringly taking him out for a drink, a scene slyly placed before us as a quasi-grooming episode.

Plumb worries that this will not help his acting career long term and of course effectively invites the audience to worry that this is all just playacting anyway, all bread-and-circuses exploitation. The tension ratchets up when everyone realises they have to do something extra to maintain ratings; Hansen becomes obsessed with the rumour that there is a “whale” to be brought to justice in a righteous Texan small town – a high-ranking public figure, not just another sweaty nobody.

But the movie’s own actual drama appears to reside in the backstairs office politics and gossip. Hansen is trying and failing to break off an extra-marital affair and Bender is being headhunted by a rival network prepared to offer huge bucks so she will produce a copycat version of Hansen’s show and crush it and him in the ratings. For a while, some intriguing conspiratorial possibilities present themselves. But none of that leads anywhere. Really we are just heading to the gruesome denouement which surely had to happen if paedophiles were hunted and shamed for sport; the film coasts up to a crisis, after which the drama is deemed to be at an end, although how or if Hansen has changed or conceded or learned anything is a mystery. It’s a disappointment.

content.article_text:
花代 「よのなかばかなのよ Are we not drawn onward, we few, drawn onward to new era?」 © Hanayo & Reiji Saito

花代 「よのなかばかなのよ Are we not drawn onward, we few, drawn onward to new era?」 © Hanayo

タカ・イシイギャラリー京都は、花代による個展「Hanayo V – よのなかばかなのよ Are we not drawn onward, we few, drawn onward to new era?」を2026年9月6日から27日まで開催する。1996年の同ギャラリーでの初個展から30年という節目にあたる5回目の個展となる。

本展では、ギャラリーが位置する京都市下京区矢田町に伝わる祇園祭の山鉾「伯牙山」の故事を主題とした新作映像を中心に、彫刻、書、舞踊、そして近年継続して制作している「箱」の中で展開される写真彫刻作品を発表する。

着想の源となったのは、中国の琴の名手・伯牙と、その音楽を深く理解した友人・鍾子期の物語だ。鍾子期の死後、伯牙は自ら琴を壊し二度と演奏しなかったという逸話は、「知音」という言葉の由来としても知られている。花代はこの物語を、自身が長年使い続けてきたカメラとフィルムの未来に重ね合わせた。

作家はステートメントの中で、フィルム写真文化の衰退に対する複雑な感情を語る。日常を写すための道具として親しんできた写真機とフィルムが失われつつある現実のなかで、「理解する人がいなくなったら写真機を壊すのか」という問いを投げかける。映像作品では、その思索が伯牙の物語と交差し、時空を超えた寓話として展開される。

会場では、花代の創作の根幹にある「続けること」への意志も浮かび上がる。舞踊や花柳界での経験、写真表現への長年の取り組み、そして変化し続ける社会への不安と祈り。フィルム文化の終焉を見つめながらも制作を続ける姿勢が、映像や写真彫刻、身体表現を横断しながら立ち現れる。

花代は1970年東京生まれ。芸妓、ミュージシャン、モデル、写真家として国内外で活動し、自身の日常を幻想的な色彩で切り取る写真やコラージュ、インスタレーションで知られる。近年は東京とベルリンを拠点に活動を続けている。

会期初日の9月6日15時には、『Frieze Magazine』編集長のアンドリュー・ダービンとの対談企画も開催。また会期最終日の9月27日には、アーティスト・木村友紀とのトークイベントも予定されている。

A diretora Susana Garcia sabe que o principal atrativo de suas protagonistas é essa ligação construída pela dupla fora das telas e explora essa relação como elemento central da narrativa."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As atrizes interpretam Clara (Ingrid) e Júlia (Mônica), duas mulheres na faixa dos 50 anos atravessando momentos diferentes. As duas decidem viajar juntas para Portugal, aproveitando o percurso para visitar as filhas e repensar escolhas deixadas em segundo plano ao longo dos anos."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Quando explora a relação entre suas protagonistas, o filme funciona melhor. Ingrid e Mônica possuem uma química evidente, e os momentos mais divertidos surgem da naturalidade com que elas dividem a tela. A sensação é de acompanhar duas amigas reais conversando, provocando uma à outra e reagindo a situações inesperadas. content.article_text:
Ingrid Guimarães e Mônica Martelli se divertem em uma comédia sobre maturidade e amizade, mas a conexão entre as atrizes revela também os limites da narrativa.

A história de “ Minha Melhor Amiga ” envolve amizade e desafios da maturidade, mas o longa parece construído mesmo para homenagear a parceria entre as atrizes Ingrid Guimarães e Mônica Martelli. A diretora Susana Garcia sabe que o principal atrativo de suas protagonistas é essa ligação construída pela dupla fora das telas e explora essa relação como elemento central da narrativa.

As atrizes interpretam Clara (Ingrid) e Júlia (Mônica), duas mulheres na faixa dos 50 anos atravessando momentos diferentes. A primeira tenta reorganizar a vida após perceber que o casamento perdeu sentido, enquanto a segunda resiste à possibilidade de abrir espaço para um novo relacionamento. As duas decidem viajar juntas para Portugal, aproveitando o percurso para visitar as filhas e repensar escolhas deixadas em segundo plano ao longo dos anos.

Quando explora a relação entre suas protagonistas, o filme funciona melhor. Ingrid e Mônica possuem uma química evidente, e os momentos mais divertidos surgem da naturalidade com que elas dividem a tela. A sensação é de acompanhar duas amigas reais conversando, provocando uma à outra e reagindo a situações inesperadas. Algumas situações envolvendo encontros amorosos, diferenças culturais e dificuldades da viagem conseguem extrair graça puramente da espontaneidade e do carisma da dupla.

O problema é que essa conexão fora das telas também expõe a principal limitação da produção. Clara e Júlia não passam a sensação de serem personagens construídas para o filme, mas extensões da imagem pública das próprias atrizes. A narrativa se apoia no conhecimento prévio dos espectadores sobre a dupla (ou na simples capacidade de relevar um desenvolvimento mínimo), além de apelar totalmente para a familiaridade de Ingrid e Mônica para preencher as lacunas dramáticas.

As questões levantadas pelo roteiro são interessantes, envolvendo envelhecimento, amor, maternidade e autonomia feminina, mas nenhuma delas recebe atenção o bastante. Os conflitos aparecem e logo se tornam conversas longas e expositivas que diminuem o espaço para interpretações e tornam alguns momentos emocionais previsíveis e muito didáticos, quase como lições de auto-ajuda. Em vez de deixá-las descobrirem seus caminhos por meio das experiências, o filme prefere conduzir o público até conclusões já estabelecidas pelo próprio roteiro.

Essa tendência torna a história artificial, e os eventos vão surgindo sem muita progressão narrativa, como um amontoado de lembranças de uma viagem ditos sem grande precisão e apenas organizados em ordem cronológica. Algumas situações se tornam engraçadas por conta da reação das atrizes, que visivelmente estão improvisando e se divertindo como se as câmeras nem estivessem presentes. A intenção de preservar essa espontaneidade é tanta que alguns desses cacos são mantidos no corte final, incluindo momentos que normalmente seriam retirados, como quando Ingrid e Mônica respiram fundo após crises de riso e retornam ao texto.

Algumas sequências juntam narração em off e cenas de paisagem, em mais um indício de que não parecia haver uma estrutura clara para seguir, dando a impressão de que foram necessários remendos para ligar ou finalizar certas cenas. O restante do elenco também é prejudicado pelo pouco desenvolvimento, a exemplo das filhas das protagonistas, que estão presentes nas discussões relevantes, mas suas histórias existem principalmente para provocar mudanças nas mães. Até participações de forte valor afetivo, como a homenagem a Paulo Gustavo, estão muito mais ligadas à memória das atrizes e do público do que ao próprio longa.

Também existe uma limitação na perspectiva escolhida pelo filme ao acompanhar mulheres com recursos e liberdade para reorganizar suas vidas. É evidente que isso não invalida sua proposta, já que a intenção nunca foi construir um retrato social amplo. Mas essa escolha acaba se concentrando em uma experiência confortável de maturidade, evitando conflitos mais complexos sobre as dificuldades concretas que atravessam diferentes realidades.

Ainda assim, Ingrid Guimarães e Mônica Martelli carregam o filme. O timing cômico e a energia das atrizes criam uma dinâmica agradável na qual diálogos simplistas ainda garantem momentos de identificação. Em suma, “Minha Melhor Amiga” é uma celebração de uma amizade conhecida do público que busca a todo momento homenagear essa conexão, mas não consegue construir uma história que exista além dela.

content.article_text:
写真家・遠藤文香の作品展示が、東京・虎ノ門ヒルズ ステーションタワー4階の「虎ノ門 楽㐂（らっき）」で開催されている。写真集『Ayaka Endo: Kanoko』（7920円）の刊行を記念した企画「食べる、見る、読む。」として、2026年9月1日から10月31日まで、写真と文学、料理を横断する展示を展開する。

『Ayaka Endo: Kanoko』は、日本文学と現代写真を一冊の中で対峙させるシリーズの第6作。今回取り上げられたのは、歌人・小説家であり岡本太郎の母としても知られる岡本かの子の短編小説『鮨』だ。小説が写真の説明にならず、写真もまた小説の挿絵にならない。それぞれが独立した表現として向き合うことで、文学作品を新たな角度から読み直す試みとなっている。

遠藤は1994年生まれ。2021年に東京藝術大学大学院を修了し、現在はロンドンを拠点に活動する。動物や自然を主な被写体としながら、人間と自然のあいだに古くから存在する秩序や感覚に関心を寄せて制作を続けてきた。今回、店内では『Kanoko』の世界と呼応する写真作品を、食事を楽しみながら鑑賞することができる。

会場となる虎ノ門 楽㐂は、「NEXT JAPAN」をテーマに、江戸前寿司や旬の食材を用いた料理を提供する和食店。虎ノ門ヒルズ駅に直結する店舗で、通常のギャラリーとは異なり、食事と作品鑑賞が同じ空間で交差する。

さらに会期中は、岡本かの子の『鮨』と遠藤の写真世界から着想したスペシャルディナーコースも用意。前菜、刺身、焼物、揚物、握りなどで構成し、『Ayaka Endo: Kanoko』1冊が付属する。作品を「見る」、小説を「読む」、そして料理を「食べる」という3つの行為を重ねることで、一冊の写真集を視覚だけではなく味覚や身体感覚へと拡張する。価格は15000円。

ギャラリーや美術館を離れ、日常的に人々が食事をする場所へ写真を持ち込む今回の試み。岡本かの子が「鮨」という食を通して描いた文学世界に、遠藤の写真と現代の料理が重なることで、写真を見るという行為そのものを別の角度から捉え直す機会となりそうだ。

遠藤文香「食べる、見る、読む。」

9月上旬、ロンドン在住のフェイイ・ウェンによる初写真集 『butterflies are quicker than rock』 （torch press）が刊行される。本書の刊行を記念し9月12日〜20日、渋谷・(PLACE) by methodで刊行記念展覧会が開催される。会期中は作家が来日し、トークイベントやサイン会なども開催される予定だ。

写真集『butterflies are quicker than rock』でウェンは、東洋思想を手がかりに、生態系の脆さと時間の儚さを見つめている。タイトルは移ろうものと永続するもののあいだの緊張を表し、危ういバランスにある今の生態系を象徴している。大英図書館でレファレンス司書として働くかたわら、自然や風景を主題に自身の撮影したイメージと、ときにはファウンドフォトのイメージを使いながら作品を作り出している。ウェンの作品の特徴はその制作方法にあり、伝統的なプリント技法や新しい現像技法を組み合わせ、スキャンや加工、再撮影、プリントを重ねることで、色褪せた風合いや複雑なレイヤーを生み出し、風景の質感を映し出している。それらを組み合わせて構成することで、写真は固定された記録から、記憶やアーカイブが物語を紡ぎ直す流動的な対話へと変わっていく――自然のモチーフや風景は、伝統的な中国の山水画のようでありながら、幾層ものレイヤーが加えられることで、新しい風景として立ち現れていく。そして、風景を見ることとはどういうことかを、私たちに問いかける。

9月12日には、ウェンと河内タカによるトークイベントも行われるので、予定を合わせてぜひ足を運びたい。

濱田祐史が渋谷 MINAで始まるMINA WORLD COLLEGEにて、全10回のラーニングプログラム「見ることのプラクティス／Practices of Seeing」を開催する。申込締め切りは9月13日まで。

本ワークショップでは濱田祐史と約1年をかけて、「見る」という行為によって、どのように世界を認識しているのかを学び、考察する。写真の歴史を学び、身の周りのものからピンホールカメラを制作し、写真を自ら編集し、太陽光で像を定着させるサイアノタイプを体験する。それらの実践を振り返りながら、最終的には空間展示という形で成果発表を行うという。またゲストには山西もも、若山満大（東京ステーションギャラリー学芸員）、鈴木理策、小林孝行（flotsambooks）、伊藤貴弘（東京都写真美術館学芸員）などが登場する。ラーニングプログラムの記録集をグラフィックデザイナーの星加陸が手掛けるなど、様々なゲストで彩られワークショップは進行していく予定だ。

「Practice of Seeing｜見ることのプラクティス」は、「見ること」を起点に、「まだ見えていないもの」に気づき、世界を楽しむ選択肢を広げていくための実践講座。ぜひ体験してみたい。

content.article_text:
Ridley Scott encontra belas imagens entre as ruínas, mas não personagens ou ideias capazes de dar profundidade ao cenário pós-apocalíptico.

O mundo inteiro de “ Ponto Sem Retorno ” está destruído diante da câmera de Ridley Scott, mas pouco dele parece existir além do enquadramento do diretor. Jacob Elordi interpreta Hig, um sobrevivente que atravessa esse cenário acompanhado de seu cachorro. A possibilidade de encontrar outras pessoas o retira de uma espiral depressiva e dá início a uma jornada que reúne elementos típicos do gênero, como comunidades isoladas, recursos escassos, grupos violentos e alianças instáveis. Contudo, a obra não encontra qualquer perspectiva particular nessas convenções.

Scott inicia de forma bastante contemplativa com a intenção de dimensionar a solidão do protagonista e comunicar a extensão do colapso. Só que o filme demora a fazer com que todo esse espaço vire uma história de fato. Não existe qualquer curiosidade sobre como os sobreviventes reorganizaram suas vidas ou sobre as consequências práticas de anos vivendo depois da queda da sociedade. Todas as ruínas acabam compondo uma emulação limitada do imaginário pós-apocalíptico já visto em tantas outras produções do gênero.

Toda essa superficialidade é um limitador também para os personagens. Elordi funciona nos momentos de silêncio e estabelece uma relação afetiva com o cachorro, mas seu protagonista é definido unicamente pela melancolia, sem que isso seja utilizado para aprofundar qualquer outra característica ou sentimento. Até sua aparência excessivamente preservada enfraquece a sensação de desgaste que deveria acompanhar aquela existência. Josh Brolin tem presença como o sobrevivente experiente e protetor, embora o roteiro pouco faça para afastá-lo desse arquétipo. Margaret Qualley, Guy Pearce, Benedict Wong e Allison Janney são grandes nomes que se dedicam, mas recebem menos espaço do que suas presenças poderiam sugerir.

Apesar de ter menos de duas horas, o filme aparenta durar ainda mais. Muitas sequências, principalmente as tomadas aéreas, são bonitas de se ver, mas parecem existir apenas para reforçar o ofício de piloto de Hig. O longa mostra resquícios de energia quando Scott rompe a inércia inicial, organiza o espaço em torno das ameaças e finalmente se aproxima da ação. Acontece que o cineasta não consegue aproveitar nem mesmo uma ambientação interessante, encerrando o conflito sem riscos e antes de explorar plenamente suas possibilidades.

Também é problemática a maneira como os grupos hostis são representados pelo diretor. Não vemos diferentes formas de organização que poderiam surgir após o colapso, desperdiçando uma oportunidade de tornar o universo socialmente mais complexo. O filme os reduz a hordas agressivas, definidas por gritos e pinturas corporais — quase uma releitura de uma iconografia antiquada de “selvageria” comumente associada a nativos americanos. Enquanto os protagonistas mantêm comportamentos e roupas reconhecíveis, seus adversários são desumanizados para que a divisão moral permaneça imediata.

À medida que o longa se encaminha para o desfecho, uma desarmonia narrativa fica bastante exposta. Os personagens principais chegam a um aeroporto convertido em uma comunidade, em mais uma oportunidade de mostrar como a sociedade poderia estar tentando se reconstruir. Mas a sequência introduz um registro de tom tão satírico que parece pertencer a outro filme. Allison Janney abraça a excentricidade e parece se divertir com o papel, porém toda essa atuação expansiva, junto com a organização retrô do lugar e o humor repentino, entra em choque com a sobriedade anterior, apenas evidenciando a falta de unidade.

Essa distância entre dimensão e conteúdo define “Ponto Sem Retorno”. No trecho final, a jornada começa a perder propósito justamente quando deveria encontrar sua recompensa, prolongando uma história que já revelou praticamente tudo o que tinha a oferecer — e não era muito. Sobram imagens amplas e genéricas de um mundo devastado; faltam pessoas e ideias capazes de fazer esse mundo parecer perdido de verdade.
